These bills simply say if a guardian is going to move an individual out of their home and into a facility that the court must find that this is in the best interest of that individual. Friends, I want to talk about a hard truth that Washington and Lansing Democrats do not want to admit or understand because it exposes one of the biggest scams ever sold to the American people, the so-called Green New Deal energy agenda. We were told about innovation, about the future, about saving our planet while creating good-paying jobs. But what it really became was a political narrative chasing applause lines instead of economic reality. And American workers are the ones paying the price. Look at this Michigan real-world example. Ford Motor Company is writing down $19.5 billion in losses because of their strategy of going to EVs. Now let me remind you, less than 15 years ago, two of the big three went bankrupt and Ford didn't. Why? Because they put the whole company in hock and borrowed about $23 billion to come up with a new plan. They're here today because of that. But writing down $19.5 billion is not a strategy change. It's not innovation. This is the cost of chasing a political narrative instead of a business model. Ford bet billions of dollars that Americans would pay a premium price for electric versions of their trucks and cars. They assumed government subsidies would last forever. They assumed glowing headlines would replace consumer demand. They assumed political pressure would force people to buy what they were selling. And they were wrong. The electric F-150 was never a profitable machine. It was a press release on wheels. And that's the fundamental problem with the Green New Deal mindset. It treats press conferences as profits, subsidies as sustainability, and mandates as a market. Now let's be clear. This isn't about being anti-technology. It's about being pro-reality. Ford tried to graft EVs onto a system built for gasoline, built around unions, dealerships, regulatory approval, incentives, and decades of sunken cost. The math never worked, and it wasn't going to. Now even Ford's CEO is saying quietly, large electric vehicles do not make money. That's the polite, PR-friendly way of saying that Tesla is eating their lunch. In this role, Donald was able to continue serving the farming community and advocating for sustainable practices and policies. He served in this role until 2010. And whereas the legacy Donald left behind will be remembered fondly by those who knew him. By his colleagues, Donald will be remembered as a tireless advocate for the Upper Peninsula and agricultural community, as well as someone who treated everyone with dignity and respect. By his family, he will be remembered as a loving and devoted husband, father, and grandfather. His family includes his wife of 55 years, Pamela, his four children, Adam, Matthew, Timothy, and Catherine, his four grandchildren, Jacob, Connor, Nolan, and Emma, as well as his faithful furry companions, Daisy and May. And whereas upon Donald Koivisto's passing, we offer our condolences to his loved ones. His contributions to these chambers and the state of Michigan will be remembered. Now, therefore, be it resolved that we offer this expression of our highest tribute to honor the memory of Donald Koivisto, a member of Michigan's House of Representatives from 1981 to 1986, and the Michigan Senate from 1990 to 2002. And be it further resolved that copies of this resolution be transmitted to the Koivisto family as evidence of our lasting esteem for his memory. Mr. President, the rules have been suspended to allow for immediate consideration of the resolution and there are no amendments pending to the adoption of Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 10. The question before the Senate is on the adoption of Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 10 and for discussion. The President recognizes the Majority Leader, Senator Brinks. Thank you, Mr. President, and I ask that my remarks be printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. Colleagues, I rise today to honor the memory of one of our own, former Senator Donald Koivisto. Senator Koivisto began his legislative career in the Michigan House of Representatives in 1980, and he later went on to win a special election to represent the 38th District in the Michigan Senate, holding this seat for over a decade. A proud, born and raised Yuper, Senator Koivisto was a staunch advocate for Michigan's farming communities throughout his tenure. In fact, one of his most notable accomplishments was the crafting of the state's Right to Farm Act, which helped bolster our agricultural industry. Known for his spirit of bipartisanship, his humble nature, and his responsible leadership, Senator Koivisto was not only a practical, pragmatic lawmaker, he was also a dignified pillar of his community and his family, serving in the roles of teacher, high school coach, juvenile officer, school board president, director of the Michigan Department of Agriculture, loving grandfather and father, and reverent husband of 55 years. Senator Koivisto will be remembered for his exceptional leadership, his valuable mentorship of future leaders, his loyalty to his Upper Peninsula community, and his unwavering devotion to his loved ones. So, colleagues, let us express our deepest gratitude for Senator Koivisto's many contributions to this chamber and for his exemplary service to the people of Michigan. We offer our sincerest condolences to his family. May Senator Koivisto rest in peace. Thank you. For further discussion, the President recognizes Senator McBroom. Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like my remarks printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. Mr. President, to you and to my colleagues, it's a real honor for me to get to be here and offer some remarks to memorialize Senator Don Koivisto. When I was in seventh grade, which was sometime mid-'90s, Don was our senator, and I don't exactly remember how I knew that, but I was a real nerd, which probably doesn't surprise any of you, and we used to play a game in seventh grade social studies class every week on Friday called Current Events. And Mr. Kasselis asked our team the question, who's our UP senator? And somehow, I don't even remember how, but I remember very distinctively just like pulling the name out of, it seemed like out of the thin air. It's like, oh yeah, it's Don Koivisto. And he was a real important person in the Upper Peninsula. He was our first senator after the long tenure of Senator Joe Mack had begun his service while Dominic Jacobetti was still there and continued on past that, carrying on a lot of that continuity that the Upper Peninsula values. I reached out to surviving UP legislators who served with Don. One of them has joined me here today. Many of you know our famous House Clerk, Rich Brown, but before this gig, he served as state representative in the Gogebic area, same as Don had. I think the last two Gogebic representatives, perhaps. And all the other members that I talked to send their greetings to the family and to all of you. There just aren't very many of us. There's only four people from the UP at any given time, and Don was larger than life, having served in the House, served in the Senate for 12 years, then served on the Department of Ag. A few years ago, when I was at a meeting on the west end of the UP in a little township of Matchwood, a farmer there hobbled into the meeting named Pat Kitzman. He was ski pole in one hand, wood walking stick in the other one, walks in, and he wants to talk to me about federal PILT dollars and how since the late 70s, early 80s, those federal PILT dollars have been stolen from where they used to go to the townships, the schools, and local services, and now they go to the counties. And this has been Pat's issue for 50 years. And he wanted me to run some legislation on it. He said, Don Koivisto did this for me. So I called up Senator Koivisto, found his number, and I told him what I'm working on right away. He's like, is this about Pat Kitzman? Right away, he knew exactly what I was talking about. He's like, how's Pat doing? Hadn't seen him in years, but he knew what I was talking about. Like Senator Brinks mentioned, he was a very humble man, but he cared about his district. He cared about the people that he served. One thing that's left out of his tribute that perhaps Don was also very, very proud of and so many of my other former representatives and UP senators mentioned when I brought him up is that he was a very proud Finlander. He was always proud to stand as a Finnish man. He loved hanging out with the guys like Prussi and Adamini and mentioning their Finnish heritage. And that's such an important part of the Upper Peninsula, particularly on the West End. His work for farming, too, cannot be overstated how important that was, the right to farm act. But even as director, his stayed defense for farmers in this state against the ever-encroaching push and the crush from bureaucrats on environmental issues. And Don at some times was the lone defender that Michigan agriculture had. Perhaps one of the strangest ties that Don and I experienced and we talked about, too, was how we both ended up serving on a committee set up to review the qualifications of our colleagues to serve. And interestingly, Don, having also been a co-chair in the situation here in the Senate, was the lone no vote in the whole Senate on expulsion of a member. He was not afraid to stand alone. He was not afraid to speak his mind and to stand on the convictions of his own conscience, even when it put him all alone and outside of the rest of the group. It's a tremendous thing to serve in this chamber, and especially for one person from the Upper Peninsula to have this privilege. Don was just a great template of what we look for in a statesman and in a senator from the UP, and I'm very proud to be following in his footsteps and proud to stand here today with my friend Rich Brown and offer our condolences and remarks to his family and to share some memories of him. Mr. President, I move the rules be suspended and allow for the immediate consideration of House Concurrent Resolution No. 4. Without objection, so ordered. Mr. President, the House has transmitted to the Senate House Concurrent Resolution No. 4, Concurrent Resolution providing for the final adjournment of the Legislature. The House has adopted the concurrent resolution. There are no amendments pending to the adoption of House Concurrent Resolution No. 4. The question is on the adoption of House Concurrent Resolution 4. Is there any discussion? Seeing no discussion, all those in favor will say aye. Those opposed will say no. All those opposed will say no. The ayes have it. The resolution is adopted. President recognizes Majority Floor Leader Singh. Thank you very much, Mr. President. Mr. President, I move the Senate proceed to the order of statements. Without objection, the Senate will proceed to the order of statements. President recognizes Senator Camilleri. Thank you, Mr. President. Colleagues, last week, House Republicans reminded us once again of their values and priorities. House Republicans used a legislative maneuver to try and eliminate $645 million in ongoing work projects throughout the state, unilaterally, with no transparency, no discussion, and no debate. We're talking about programs that support health care costs for pregnant women and newborns, programs that help supply wigs for kids undergoing cancer treatments, public safety projects all over the state, educator preparation programs, and so much more. And on the list are countless community projects that are absolutely critical for our residents, which we already approved during the last session. In Downriver and Western Wayne County, Republicans are attempting to cut millions of dollars from the Downriver Community Conference for a public safety and economic development project that is literally under construction as we speak. They are also trying to cut $1 million from Romulus for a public safety building, $5 million from Taylor for lead line replacement, $2 million from Wyandotte for an art center, $1.5 million from Brownstown for an aging township building, $2.5 million from Wayne Metro, and the list goes on and on and on. In what world would these appropriations be considered wasteful? The only waste that I see here is in the form of half-completed projects and wasted goodwill. This decision by Speaker Hall and House Republicans undermines the entire budget process that our state relies on to operate and sets a dangerous precedent going forward. The accountability that work projects provide is clear. The state is able to verify and keep projects on track through the documents that they provide to us. Money is released when recipients and contracts are submitted. That's a good thing for the taxpayer. The House Republicans' decision is only harmful to the people we represent. You know, for months, for months, all we heard from the Speaker in his rambling press conferences was how happy he was with how he negotiated the budget. He's obviously one of those Lansing insiders who loves to hear himself talk. But let's be clear, single-handedly slashing $645 million through a loophole is not a sign of strength. It is actually a sign of major weakness. He lost the budget negotiations this last year so badly that he had to enact a corrupt plan and cheat Michigan residents out of their local investments, all so he could feel better about himself. Because he doesn't care about his members or their districts or the state of Michigan. He even has Republicans publicly opposing him since this happened. Good. I hope all of you House Republicans who are saying things out loud continue to do so. That is the only way that we're going to get through this toxic environment that he is trying to create for all of us. Senate Democrats are ready to fight to keep these funds where they belong, in our communities. Because we gave our word and we intend to keep it. Thank you, Mr. President. Senator, would you like your statement printed in the journal? Without objection, so ordered. President recognizes Senator Runstad. Thank you, Mr. President. T'was Lansing at Christmas where Dana Nessel held court

which charges for Republicans filled briskly in sport. An Attorney General who serves as a corrupt Master of Ceremonies, orchestrating cover-ups to protect her spouse and political cronies. Yet for a lawyer from the transition team, the story is quite stark. $50,000 walked off from an elderly client gone dark. A judge she will be, deemed Whitmer the Grinch. Not a problem at all, said Nessel without flinch. Firewalls be damned, she said, close the investigation, close it down now. What kind of justice is this? Is this how you keep your sacred vow? But a pattern is what it is, yes, the corruption is rife. Charges against Republicans, but none for my wife. For some snowball indictments, for others just cheer. Merry Christmas, Michigan, enforcement's far from impartial this year. Senator, would you like your remarks printed in the journal? Without objection, so ordered. The President recognizes Senator Chang. Thank you very much, Mr. President. I'd like my statement printed in the Senate Journal. Without objection, so ordered. I would like to think that public safety and improving health outcomes are priorities that cut across partisan lines in both chambers. But after last week's action by Michigan House Republicans, I can't say that's true. Michigan has a shortage of nurses. We all know that. Michigan hospitals alone have almost 5,000 unfilled nursing positions, and Michigan is on track to have a 15% nursing shortage 10 years from now. Wayne State University's College of Nursing, together with a coalition of health systems, federally qualified health centers, and behavioral health sites, are ready to create a new center for nursing workforce. This center will create alternative models of clinical education and health professions to increase the number of nurses in Michigan. They're set to develop more nurse clinician educators. They are set to support the pipeline of APRNs in partnership with health centers. And they secured $4 million in a previous DHHS budget for this badly needed nurse workforce program. But last week, Michigan House Republicans... Members, there's a senator addressing the body. Thank you. Last week, Michigan House Republicans cut their funding. In Detroit and the Jefferson Chalmers neighborhood, residents face river flooding every time there is a major storm. We secured $1 million in a previous budget to support flood mitigation, but half has been cut. So the next time it storms, what will be the message from House Republicans to people when their homes and their streets flood yet again? Wayne Metropolitan Community Action Agency is set to revitalize and modernize the Cortland Center, which is a former elementary school in Highland Park. The funding was set to create an accessible community gathering space where children and families could find hope and opportunities. The work on the building will help Wayne Metro run its Head Start programs, home weatherization programs, housing and homelessness services, and workforce development. They were actually set to break ground in early 2026 on this very important project for Wayne County residents. But after last Wednesday's action by Michigan House Republicans, will those residents still have the chance to see the Cortland Center? Meet more of the needs of the communities, especially during this time when more and more are struggling to keep their homes and pay their bills? In Hamtramck, the fire chief and several of their firefighters have explained to me just how badly they need replacement of their fire trucks. One of the trucks has actually broken down on scene at an incident. That is just dangerous. From the time a municipality signs a purchase agreement to the time a fire truck can be built and ready to deliver, it can be 26 months. That's 26 months, folks. Hamtramck has a signed purchase agreement for a new fire truck due to the $800,000 that we secured in the budget. And they signed that purchase agreement because they trusted that we as a state would follow through on what we passed, that we would honor the contract. But last week, Michigan House Republicans said to Hamtramck residents and businesses, they don't care about keeping you safe from fires. They don't care if the fire truck doesn't make it to your home or your place of work. So much for valuing first responders and public safety. So now we're in the holiday season, a time for family, a time for giving back to those in need, and a time for hope. Despite last week's action by Michigan House Republicans, I still do have hope. And I have that hope because people across the state are speaking out. Michiganders are rising up to say communities, not cuts. And this week in the Michigan Senate, we took action to make things right by restoring the cuts. The House should do the same. Thank you, Mr. President. President recognizes Senator Moss. Thank you, Mr. President. I ask for my remarks to be printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. Thank you. I woke up Sunday morning to a flurry of text messages about the horrific mass shooting at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Australia, a deadly anti-Semitic attack on Jews observing the first night of Hanukkah, evoking a feeling of terror in Jewish households across the globe. Fifteen people were murdered, including a 10-year-old girl and a great-grandfather who had survived the Holocaust, just for being Jewish publicly. Worse than the feeling of terror, I think, is the feeling of unsurprised, that this has become too familiar. Jews around the world have been signaling a five-alarm fire about the global rise in anti-Semitic conspiracies, vandalism, and violence. It has hit us here, too, in Michigan. Even right now, the East Lansing Police Department is investigating a horrific case of vandalism on the Chabad Jewish Center. We have been compelling allies to listen to Jewish voices in peril, to speak out, and to act. It will take all of us to snuff out this untenable hatred. And here in the legislature, we've begun that important work to act. In the 2024-2025 budget, a majority in this legislature approved an immediate solution to the short-term problem, to provide a grant to the Jewish Federation to shore up the security in our institutions, like our synagogues, schools, and social service agencies. We've also focused on the long term, ensuring that the Holocaust Center in Farmington Hills can continue to educate future generations about the consequence of unchecked anti-Semitism. This is funding that we provided to fulfill a state requirement on age-appropriate Holocaust education in Michigan. Matt Hall and Ann Bolin and the House Republicans have called these efforts to combat anti-Semitism waste, fraud, and abuse. And without debate or deliberation, voted unilaterally to cut that approved funding. The Republican leader here has called it Democrat fun money. And I know the speaker's been having these press conferences all week to justify cutting these funds. On this specifically, really the appropriate forum would be to go on Nick Fuentes' podcast and cheerlead that move there. It would be very well received. I was on the board of my synagogue during Charlottesville and Tree of Life synagogue shooting, and we had to make tough decisions on how to remain a welcoming and open space while ensuring the safety of our community from a shooting. Every synagogue has grappled with the same. I really, I do not know about the protocols of how others in this chamber, how the ease of how you enter into your church. But on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, just about every synagogue in Oakland County has a municipal police car out front, armed security at the front door, or plainclothes security inside. It is not fun to enter into a fortress to safely practice your First Amendment right. Ultimately, over the last several years, I think the existential question facing all of us is can you live your life without the plight of Jews impacting you? Can you live in a world in which Jews are unsafe? I cannot. Matt Hall and Ann Bolin and the Republicans on the Appropriations Committee have signaled that they can. We are a small community in this state, in this country, and in this world, and we depend on others to stand up and say Jewish security is our priority too. What does your caucus say? Tiny flags on your desks simply do not cut it. This past week here has been truly shameful, and the actions from House Republicans have reverberated throughout my community and many, many others throughout Michigan. We have demonstrated as Senate Democrats that we will lead the way to stand up for the people that Republicans have cast aside.

President recognizes Senator McBroom. Thank you Mr. President. Mr. President, I find myself as an old man in this chamber, a few others who have served as long, and I grow weary of the tit-for-tat and the excusing of the tit-for-tat for justification. There's a lot to be angry about right now. There's a lot to be angry about for either side. There's a lot to stomp around and very righteously declare to be unjust. I think that I understand where people come from and why they're angry about things and angry about the injustices they see to their communities. But one wrong compounded by another wrong doesn't make things right. And this especially comes home to roost for me today with the decision that was made after months and months of hard work and especially over the last three weeks seeing my constituents sacrifice days and weeks of their time to be here, time away from their families, investing their personal time and treasure away from kids' Christmas programs and many other events they'd rather be at because they're here defending their jobs. They're here defending a way of life, a very small community of only 300,000 people. And I spent the last hour or so debating how to express my anger and my frustration. But it's Christmas. And as is traditional for me on the final day of session before Christmas, I want to wish my colleagues a Merry Christmas and express goodwill. The Bible tells us that when Christ was born, the angels came to the shepherds who were in their fields and said, Glory to God in the highest and on earth peace, goodwill towards men. I have goodwill for all of you. Merry Christmas. Senator, would you like your remarks printed in the journal? Without objection, so ordered. President recognizes Senator Bellino. Thank you, Mr. President. And I request that my remarks be printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. Friends, I want to talk about a hard truth that Washington and Lansing Democrats do not want to admit or understand because it exposes one of the biggest scams ever sold to the American people, the so-called Green New Deal energy agenda. We were told about innovation, about the future, about saving our planet while creating good-paying jobs. But what it really became was a political narrative chasing applause lines instead of economic reality. And American workers are the ones paying the price. Look at this Michigan real-world example. Ford Motor Company is writing down $19.5 billion in losses because of their strategy of going to EVs. Now let me remind you, less than 15 years ago, two of the big three went bankrupt and Ford didn't. Why? Because they put the whole company in hock and borrowed about $23 billion to come up with a new plan. They're here today because of that. But writing down $19.5 billion is not a strategy change. It's not innovation. This is the cost of chasing a political narrative instead of a business model. Ford bet billions of dollars that Americans would pay a premium price for electric versions of their trucks and cars. They assumed government subsidies would last forever. They assumed glowing headlines would replace consumer demand. They assumed political pressure would force people to buy what they were selling. And they were wrong. The electric F-150 was never a profitable machine. It was a press release on wheels. And that's the fundamental problem with the Green New Deal mindset. It treats press conferences as profits, subsidies as sustainability, and mandates as a market. Now let's be clear. This isn't about being anti-technology. It's about being pro-reality. Ford tried to graft EVs onto a system built for gasoline, built around unions, dealerships, regulatory approval, incentives, and decades of sunken cost. The math never worked and it wasn't going to. Now even Ford's CEO is saying quietly, large electric vehicles do not make money. That's the polite PR-friendly way of saying that Tesla is eating their lunch. And this is what happens when government tries to pick winners and losers. When politicians write industrial policy based on liberal climate space ideology instead of economics. When energy policy is driven by activists instead of engineers and the real numbers. And let's not forget who ultimately pays for these mistakes. It's not politicians. It's not us who made the promises. It's the workers facing layoffs. Families watching plants close. Consumers paying higher prices. And taxpayers underrating billions and billions in losses. The real energy future is about competition, innovation, consumer choice, not mandates, subsidies, and green slogans. America doesn't need energy scam dressed up as progress. We need policies that respect markets, reflect efficiency, and we need to let innovation succeed on its own merits. That's how you build a strong economy. That's how you protect workers. That's how you secure America's energy future without bankrupting industries in the process. Thank you Mr. President. God bless you. Merry Christmas. Happy Hanukkah. And Happy New Year. President recognizes Senator Shink. Thank you Mr. President and I would like my remarks printed in the journal. Without objection so ordered. A little over a week ago, House Republicans cut almost $650 million away from the people of Michigan. Without consulting any of the people affected. Without consulting Senate Democrats. Without really thinking ahead about the consequences that would ensue. They took money away from unborn babies and their mamas. From veterans. From people with mental illness. In my district, District 14, they yanked $4.5 million from the Hayes Hotel. A beautiful building but one that has sat empty for 20 years. From a downtown that has been working hard to revitalize and needs the over 80 units of housing and retail space. Work started two weeks ago. The roof is leaking. Water will be coming in all day and then it's going to freeze tomorrow and it's going to cause more damage. They've had to stop work. They've had to break their contracts. They took money away from emergency shelter for unhoused people in Jackson. Jackson has an incredible level of poverty compared to many communities in our state. And that housing is vital to save lives. They took money from a park development in my little township. A park that would revitalize Whitmore Lake. Again, another downtown that has struggled to revitalize itself after disinvestment. That park is where people come together. We, the Senate, passed a supplemental to bring that money back to the people of Michigan. And today, the House could have passed that supplemental. They could have fixed the problem they solved. And they chose not to do it. That money belongs to the state of Michigan. It belongs to our communities and we want it back. Thank you. Thank you.

I recognize the Senator Plankey. Thank you, Mr. President. I rise today because I'm sickened. I'm sickened by the 16 Michigan House Republicans who voted last week to take back funding from organizations like Wigs for Kids with Cancer, Kids Talk for Kids Who've Been Sexually Abused, and Rx Kids for Mothers and Infants in Low-Income Communities and Dozens of Other Worthy Projects. Mr. President, my Republican colleagues never seem to miss an opportunity to lecture women on how they should handle their pregnancies. But when the opportunity arises to help kids and their parents, they rip the help away. Every Republican who voted for this and every Republican who supports this questionably legal tactic should hang their heads in shame. Thankfully, yesterday, five Senate Republicans joined all Senate Democrats in passing a bill that reinstates this funding. In passing this bill, we're giving the Michigan House Republicans another chance to fix their mistake, to redeem themselves, to outrage Michiganders, and more importantly, to do the right thing. The ball's in your court, House Republicans. Thank you, Mr. President. I ask that my remarks be printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. The President recognizes Majority Leader Brinks. Thank you, Mr. President. As you might expect, I have a lot to say about this year. But right now, all I'm going to do is wish you a very Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. Thank you, Mr. President. Would you like your remarks printed in the journal? Without objection, so ordered. President recognizes Majority Floor Leader Singh. Mr. President, I move the Senate do now adjourn. Senator Singh moves that the Senate do now adjourn. Without objection, the motion prevails. The Senate shall adjourn and stand adjourned until Tuesday, December 23rd at 11 a.m. President recognizes Majority Floor Leader Singh. Mr. President, I move the Senate do now adjourn.

title: Government Operations — Thursday, December 18, 2025
transcript:
The House Government Operations will come to order. First of all, welcome to everybody. Today we're going to be hearing testimony on the Senate Bill 304 sponsored by Senator DeMoss. Senator DeMoss, welcome. This bill would amend Local Act 437 of 1899 to grant the City of Mackinac Island the authority to regulate all aspects of ferry service to and from the city, including the ancillary fees and charges to the consumers. I know there's a lot of people who want to speak today and we're going to be limited on time so we're going to restrict everybody to about three minutes or so. Mr. Clerk, would you please take attendance? Chair Begold? Here. Representative Harris? Here. VanderWaal? Present. Fitzgerald? Here. McFaul? Here. Mr. Chair, you have five members present, a quorum. Thank you. Representative VanderWaal moves to excuse any absent members here and moves to approve the minutes of the December 10th meeting. Without objection, so ordered. Okay, Mr. Senator DeMoss, if you want to... Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and I respect your time limit. I may ask for a little indulgence because I really want to explain this. There's a lot of complexity to this. And I thank you, first of all, for agreeing to hear this testimony today on Senate Bill 304. It is a bill to allow the City of Mackinac Island the opportunity to update their charter. Yes, despite what many of us have heard, that is all that this bill does. The City of Mackinac Island, for whatever reason, was established long ago as the only city in the entire state of Michigan that does not have what is called home rule. If we were talking about any other city in the entire state, the state legislature would not need to be involved in this matter at all. We wouldn't even be talking about it. The city council could just, in those places, could just propose changes to their charter, put up a vote to its residents, and it would either pass or fail. I also want to point out this bill only applies to Mackinac Island because of this issue related to home rule. What this bill does is take the language the city would like to change in their charter, and if we can get a two-thirds vote, it only allows them to put it on their own ballot for a vote by their own residents. That's all this bill does. Before I explain why the city wants to take this action, let me clarify another aspect of this bill that seems to have generated a fair amount of confusion. Make no mistake, this bill does not in any way give any unit of government the ability to regulate any private business. The bill does not give any governmental unit, local or state, the ability to regulate any prices. The bill does not give the city of Mackinac Island the ability to regulate any ferry company. They already have that ability, and they've had it in statute since 1899. That's not up for question. That right has been challenged and affirmed all the way up to the Michigan Supreme Court and to the United States Supreme Court. Every decision has reaffirmed the legitimacy of their rights in this public-private partnership. So what is the city of Mackinac Island hoping to put on their own ballot for their own people to vote on? Throughout history, the difficulty of getting to the island and the reliance on private corporations to access these public lands, and 80 percent of the island is public land, led to the creation of laws to protect that access and keep it affordable for visitors. Since there is no actual road to the island, the ferries basically are the road. It has been a mutually beneficial relationship where the island benefits from the safe and efficient transportation and the ferry companies benefit by being able to make money transporting people to a location that the state, private industry, and people have invested so much to make so desirable. To be sure, ferry companies are entitled to fair compensations for their services, but the arrangement has always been the product of a public-private cooperation whereby their services are provided under strict oversight and regulation to ensure affordable public access to this important part of the state. A few years ago, there were three ferry companies. Then Starline bought Arnold, and there were two. Then in 2022, Shepler's Ferry was acquired by the Hoffman family of companies, a private equity firm headquartered in Naples, Florida, that according to their materials has acquired

Standard Plus brands and properties in 400 locations in 30 countries around the world. Then in 2024, that same company purchased Starline and the takeover was complete. One private company now owns all of the ferries and even more importantly, all of the ferry docks on Mackinac Island. They now completely control virtually all access to Mackinac Island, including, as I said, that state park that occupies more than 80% of the island. Because the private equity firm has purchased all of the docks on Mackinac Island, there is now no place for a competitor to even land on the island, making legitimate competition impossible. I'm sure that the company which owns all the ferries and docks is a perfectly fine company, and I know many of the people who work for them. They're terrific. This isn't about that. But we have all seen what can naturally happen without competition and without oversight. And keep in mind, we are partially to blame as a state for the fact that there is no competition or can be no competition, because we've made the barriers to entry insurmountable. And many of them are set in stone by Michigan law. Nobody can just go and open a new dock. It would take years to even get to a study to get to a permit to build a new pier. There are strict controls from EGLE, DNR, EPA, and others over the construction of any new commercial dock, even if there was a space for it. So the only check that we have in the whole system are the laws that were designed with this exact situation in mind and started in 1899. Let me tell you what's happened since last year, when the final competitor was basically absorbed. Last year, in 2024, there was no fee for parking. Earlier this year, a minimum $10 fee was added if you parked in the remote lots, which are the cheapest ones. Since then, that minimum parking fee was raised to $15. Last year, when there was still competition, the entire ticket for a trip to the island was $34. That's what showed up on your credit card bill. This year, it went from $34 to $36 to $38 plus a $3 convenience fee, and day parking, which was free, went to $10 at the cheapest rate, and that went to $15. So with none of the extras like the new line cutting feature added, at a minimum, the cost for a single person going to the island for a single day went from $34 to $55, a whopping 62% increase since competition was eliminated just a year ago. What this bill is allowing the island to do, and this is an important thing, is to get back to common sense. The language has always been clear to people who were thinking with common sense. Whatever it cost a person to get to the island on a ferry was subject to the regulation from the island. But we no longer live in such a clear-thinking day. Nowadays, people parse words to the point where, with clever wording, a person or a company could get around this existing law by recategorizing fees in a creative manner. And that's exactly what happened this time. When this company went to Mackinac Island to ask for a rate hike, as happens from time to time throughout history, this time Mackinac Island said no. And the response was basically thumbing their nose at the statute that's been in place since 1899. No fare increase? Fine. We could just raise the fees for bikes or bags or, in this case, we'll jack up parking fees. I'm all for the free market, but there's a reason that the state and federal governments have always gone out of their way to protect competition, especially in the face of an uncompetitive environment that has such dramatic implications for access to an important public part of our state. Ideally, we'd live in a world where people could still read the 1899 law for what it is and what it has always been understood to mean for 125 years. But unfortunately, we need a little more clarity in our modern litigious society, where too often we have to wonder what the definition of is is. This bill allows the city of Mackinac Island to put some language that spells out what ferry costs mean. That's it. And I ask for your support on it. I'm open to questions, but I know there's a lot of experts who are ready to testify, too. So it's up to you. Okay, I don't see any questions, so thank you for your testimony. Thank you. Okay, next we're going to hear from Mike Cavanaugh and Dennis Clothorn. I am Dennis Clothorn, an uncompensated volunteer for the city of Mackinac Island. Sir, there's a red button in front of you. If you could just put the... There we go. Thank you. I am Dennis Clothorn, an uncompensated volunteer for the city of Mackinac Island. I'm a registered voter there and have been since I left the legislature many years ago. And for over 20 years, I was a member and chairman of the Mackinac Island State Park Commission by appointment of both Governors Engler and Granholm. There are a number of misapprehensions and impressions about SB 304. I will say that the senator did a good job on correcting many of those misimpressions, but I would like to reinforce and expand on them. Mackinac Island is the only city in the state of Michigan that is not a home rule city. We are a special act city and received our charter from the legislature in 1899. This means that if the city wants to amend its own charter, it must come to the legislature, yet it's okay to put these changes on the ballot so that the city's voters can then determine whether or not they want to amend their own charter. That's all this bill does, is to allow the voters of the city of Mackinac Island to decide whether or not they want to amend their charter. So this is the ultimate in local control. With SB 304, we are asking you to give us the opportunity to amend our own charter to clarify and strengthen provisions of our existing charter. That's all this bill does. Now, and I want to emphasize also that no other city is affected by this legislation. Now, why do we want to amend our charter? For many years, Mackinac Island was served by two and sometimes three ferry companies. The city and the locally owned ferry companies worked closely together. Prices were fair and services were satisfactory. All that changed in 2024. One company based in Naples, Florida bought up all the stock of the three ferry companies. That company, of course, is the Hoffman Company. And by the way, the head of that company has self-proclaimed himself as being one of the 400 richest people in the world. That company, as you heard earlier, has 200 businesses that it owns at 400 locations in 30 countries. That's the company who bought our ferry boats. What has been the result of that monopoly? Ticket prices were jacked way up, mainland parking charges soared, and other additional charges were imposed and proposed. Believe me, when you legislators come to Mackinac Island this next spring for the Detroit Chamber, you will see that these charges will hit you like a ton of bricks. You'll see that what I've been saying is not just rhetoric. The city of Mackinac Island is not trying to fix ferry ticket charges. We don't care what they are so long as there is competition. Only competition will keep prices reasonable. Right now, only one party is fixing those ferry charges, and that's a Florida company that is ripping off Michigan tourists and doing so because it is as a monopoly they can do so. The charter amendments the city would like to adopt by local vote are designed to give the city at least some chance of controlling the monopoly's excesses. Please give us a chance to defend ourselves and thousands of Michigan tourists, including your constituents. By voting yes on this bill, you are giving us a chance to amend our own city charter. I very much hope and trust that you will stand with your constituents and us in opposition to the Florida multi-billionaire monopolist. Thank you. Thank you, sir. Mr. Kavanaugh? Good morning. Thank you for the opportunity to speak. My name is Mike Kavanaugh. I'm a Lansing lawyer, but I've represented the city as outside counsel for about 50 years, often on ferry boat issues. And as been pointed out already, ever since 1899, the law in Michigan has been that the city of Mackinac Island has the right to license, regulate ferries, and regulate their fees and charges. In the past, there's always been competition, and in the distant past, very vigorous competition. In the early 1970s, there were five companies providing ferry boat services to the city of Mackinac Island. Then one dropped off. In 1975, the city realized it was necessary to...

to have a more formal structure for regulating ferries, and at that time the city adopted what's known as the Ferry Boat Ordinance. The ferry boat companies that were in existence at that time immediately sued. The circuit court upheld the city's power to regulate and license ferries. The Court of Appeals affirmed that, and in 1980 the Court of Appeals issued its decision affirming the city's rights. It was appealed to the Michigan Supreme Court that again affirmed the lower decisions, and then the ferry companies took it to the U.S. Supreme Court, and the U.S. Supreme Court dismissed the appeal for want of a substantial federal question. In other words, the city's regulation of ferries did not violate federal law. But at that time the city still had vigorous competition in the ferry boat industry. There were, as I said, five companies, then down to four. By 2010 the city was down to three companies providing ferry boat service. Then in 2016, Starline purchased Arnold, and we were down to two companies. In 2022, Hoffman Family of Companies, as has been explained, purchased Shepler's, and then in 2024, Hoffman purchased the last competitive ferry company, which was then called Mackin Island Ferry Company. So at this point the city is faced with an absolute monopoly. There is no competition. The city to deal with that amended its ferry boat code to provide a system to review the prices of ferry tickets to make sure they are fair and reasonable. Ferry service to Mackin Island is a utility. It's a privately owned public utility, and it needs to be regulated, much as Consumers Energy is regulated or Detroit Energy or any other company that provides a necessary service. And the essence of regulating utilities is to provide a fair and reasonable charge to the public while also giving the provider of the utility the opportunity to receive a fair return on its investment. And that's exactly what the City of Mackin Island's ferry boat ordinance does. We're here before you today because after Hoffman bought all the boats and all the docks and all the parking, they did raise prices, and they came to the city and at first said, we would like permission to increase the ticket price. And the city declined to approve it at that time because Hoffman would not provide any information to justify it. What are the costs of operations? What is the revenue that's being received? Why is this a reasonable charge? And so the city declined to approve it at that time. And so the response was to go out and jack up the ticket prices. And I think all of us understand that the cost to get to Mackin Island includes tickets, parking, and any of the other ancillary charges that they add on, such as a baggage charge, a priority boarding charge, a convenience fee, all of those things. The Hoffman Marine is absolutely refusing to submit to any regulation of that. And in the past, it's been clear that ticket prices could be regulated, but now we need to make it absolutely clear that that language in the 1899 charter includes all costs associated with the ferry service. And so that's why we're here before you today, and the city desperately needs some help, some clarification of the charter. Thank you. Okay. And it looks like we have a question from Representative Fitzgerald. Thank you, gentlemen. I appreciate you being here, and thank you for your testimony. One question I had is that there's mention of the dock. We obviously have the ferry services as well. In recent years, we've also seen an uptick in Great Lakes cruise liners frequenting the island. Those who do dock at the island, also those who more in the straits or other places around the island. Does this at all impact the ability to price or regulate the dock fee or the fees that would take the dinghy vessels, you know, the shuttle ships, if you will, from a cruise liner to the dock? The proposed amendment of the charter does not deal with that at all. Okay. Thank you. Representative Harris. Thank you, Mr. Chair. And again, thank you both for being here. And I'm going to pose this question to you because I think you guys probably have some experience down this road. So is there a current contract right now between the island and the ferry company or companies? The city issues a franchise, and there is currently a franchise that expires in June of 2027, I think, is the expiration. It's a little less than two years to run. I'd like to make two points. Sometimes people have said, well, isn't the amendment of the charter an impairment of the contract? And the answer is no, because the city already on the charter has the ability to regulate fees and charges, but we just want that clarified to indicate that that includes all the ancillary charges. The second part is once this charter is amended, it's effective even past the expiration of the franchise. So this legislation is important going forward so that when the franchise is reissued, it's clear what is being covered. Thank you. And, Mr. Chair, if I can have a quick follow-up or a second question. So there's currently litigation on this issue, correct? That's correct. And I read, and I didn't bring it with me, and I apologize, but there was something where the courts addressed the monopoly piece, didn't they? Can you refresh my memories to what they said? I can. Hoffman Marine sued the city, and not only is the city getting strangled with the ticket prices, but it's getting strangled with litigation costs. So Hoffman Marine has sued the city. They contend that their franchise, the existing franchise that's in place for the next two years, does not permit the city to regulate all these other charges. That is currently being litigated, and also the city filed a counterclaim alleging violation of the antitrust laws. The court said that the city's complaint alleging a violation of the antitrust laws did not contain enough facts, and so it dismissed the complaint, allowed the city to amend. The city has amended, and there's another motion now pending to dismiss. So that's still being litigated, and that will play out in the courts. The court entered an injunction saying the city could not enforce its ordinance to regulate rates until the court decides whether or not there is competition. That decision is on appeal to the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Sixth Circuit has granted expedited consideration, and they will hold oral argument on June 29. So all that's playing out in the courts, but over and apart from that, the city needs to have clarity through the amendment of the charter so that everybody knows going forward what the rules are. And interesting, as I was preparing to come over today, I came across a transcript from the Michael Patrick Shield Show where Chris Shepler appeared on the show in August of 2026 and stated that people did not need to be worried about price gouging because the city would regulate rates. Michael Patrick Shields asked this question, I know supply and demand, you could gouge everybody and bump up the price now if you wanted to, right? Chris Shepler responded, no. People are saying that, but that's not true. The Mackin Island City Council has the right to regulate fares and schedules. So we fall under whatever they tell us to do, basically, so there's no bumping up of rates. There's no gouging. None of that. It's regulated by the city of Mackin Island, so we work very closely. And for instance, when we added to shut down the Mackin Island Ferry Company. So they knew. They knew they had a monopoly. They knew the city had the right to regulate them. And now they're out there doing just the opposite, claiming the city can't regulate these charges, and they're out there gouging the public. Does Bill address anything to do with those cities regulating or imposing taxes, zoning, or whatnot that could cost the ferry companies money to operate in there, but yet they wouldn't be able to adjust their pricing unless approved by the island in another city? Yeah, let me point to some specific language for you that would give rise to concern. I think the language is on page 4, line 12. So it authorizes, under existing city charter, the city of Mackinac Island to license and regulate, under current law, its ferries. Now it's all aspects of ferry service. That's a pretty broad term, right? So what activities relating to the ferry are now within the scope of the city charter, presuming the legislature has the constitutional authority to enact this bill? And then the – I guess it's a five-word phrase that always results in lawyers giving some language some increased scrutiny. Included but not limited to, right? So essentially, the city of Mackinac Island can regulate all aspects of ferry service, not just in the city but under this bill on the mainland, right? Not limited to the city of St. Ignace or the village of Mackinac City. Presumably, this could lead to regulation of, let's say, billboards advertising ferry service throughout the state of Michigan. By use of the included but not limited to language, it's not a limitation. It's a broad grant of authority to the city of Mackinac Island to license and regulate all aspects of ferry service, not just on Mackinac Island but throughout the mainland of the state of Michigan. I guess it's actually two mainlands, right? The Upper Peninsula is a mainland and the Lower Peninsula is a mainland. And so I think that's the concern that I would have as a lawyer with regard to the overbreadth of the language in the bill before you today. Okay. Thank you. Thank you for your testimony. Great. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair and members. Appreciate your time today. Okay. Next we'll hear from Sonny Cook from Americans for Prosperity Michigan. Okay. I'm being advised that's a Zoom meeting, do we? No? Here we are. Thank you, Mr. Chair. You're welcome. I appreciate it. And members of the committee, I appreciate the time. I'll be brief because I know there's a lot of people that want to testify. I'm Sonny Cook, legislative director with Americans for Prosperity Michigan. We find Senate Bill 304 to be very, very concerning to us, and that is why we're here in our opposition of the bill. I think the previous speaker really kind of took away a lot of my testimony, so I'm not going to repeat it, but we agree with page four, his concerns on page four. So if anybody has any questions, happy to take them. But since there's a lot of people that want to speak, I want to give them the opportunity to speak as well. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Okay. Next we'll hear from the Mackinac Center, Mr. Ted Bolma, if I'm pronouncing that right. Yes, that's correct. Yeah. Good job. Yes. Dutch name from the west side of the state. I live in Holland. So thank you for the chance to speak to the committee, Mr. Chairman. I'm a senior fellow with the Mackinac Center for Public Policy. I retired a couple years ago as a university professor of economics and joined the Mackinac Center at their invitation. I just have an interest in this matter because I do go to Mackinac Island. I enjoy the island, look forward to taking the ferries more in the future. Last July I wrote a piece for the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, which I understand the center has submitted to the committee. So I'll do two things. I'll talk kind of briefly about what's in that piece, and then I'll make a comment on something else that's been said already today. But anyway, the title of the piece is Mackinac Island Ferry Regulation is Bad Policy. So I think you see where I'm coming from on this. In the piece I said, you know, this is kind of like a regulatory whack-a-mole, trying to knock down all the areas where the ferry operator might be charging more. And this reminded me a lot of what happened with transportation regulation nationally, where we started out with rate regulation of railroad rates. We don't have them anymore, but at one time railroad rates were regulated by the Interstate Commerce Commission. But then, you know, railroads were competing with trucks, and there was some intermodal transportation going on, and that led to truck regulation, even though you'd think trucking would be one of the more competitive industries out there. We actually had truck regulation for about 40 years, and the result by the 1970s was that, you know, railroads were all declaring bankruptcy. The whole system wasn't working, and, you know, trucks weren't doing well either, and finally Congress just gave up on the whole thing. And in a series of bills in the 1970s just wiped out all of that regulation, and now we don't have any of that rate regulation. We have safety regulation and things like that, but we don't have the rate regulation. So, I mean, this kind of seems to be going down the same sort of path that didn't work well at all in that particular area. I've also heard some comparisons to ferries being like public utilities, like electricity, and I'm not sure I quite agree with that, that it doesn't seem like a ferry should be a natural monopoly the way we treat electricity. But even setting that aside, you know, rate regulation historically is not the best way to keep prices down. And, you know, that seems to be the focus of all this. How do we hold prices down? Well, you know, maybe in the short run that works, but, you know, rate regulation is normally a cost-plus sort of regulatory system where companies that are subject to rate regulation just don't have the incentive to hold costs down, and there are all the underlying cost factors that have their own economics underneath it all that in order to keep companies in business, even under rate regulation, you have to allow them to at least recover their costs. So, yeah, just look at your electricity bill. They've been going up pretty fast lately. I think faster than the fares for Mackinac Island ferries. But, you know, it's just not a particularly effective way to go. I agree with some of the first speakers that said what we really need is competition. Are there ways that Mackinac Island and the legislature can be making getting into this market more attractive for other companies? I took a cruise a couple years ago on American Cruise Lines, and now I'm getting mailers from them this year that they're coming to Mackinac Island next summer. So it seems like there is some ability to get into this market. So, you know, I agree with the speakers that said what we really need is competition in the market. But this bill doesn't do that. This is a rate regulation bill. It's not a promote competition bill. And so, you know, that's my concern about the bill. Happy to take any questions if you have any. I don't see any questions, so thank you very much for your testimony. Okay, next we'll hear from Landon. It's a little bit hard to see. Is it Chulski? Come on up, Mr. Chulski. I just want to start by saying thank you to the chair and to the committee for giving us all time to speak today. I really appreciate the accommodation. My name is Landon Chulski. I'm an Eagle Scout. I was part of the honor guard that actually helps maintain the fort on Mackinac Island, so I have a lot of experience up there and travel up there. You know, I'm obviously a little older now. I'm a husband. I'm a father. And I bring my family to Mackinac City and the island every summer I can. And when I bring my family, one of the last things I honestly think about is the price for a ticket to get on the island. Usually I'm thinking about the budget for lodging, food, and the fudge budget. And, you know, today I'm here to oppose this bill. I think that this bill expands the authority of the island to implement fees and regulations on the aspects of the ferry service to and from the island, including ferry tickets, baggage, and parking of vehicles by persons accessing the ferry service, which includes the city of St. Ignace and Mackinac City. This bill is not a small change to the 1899 charter that has been previously referred to. It would allow Mackinac Island the authority to handle fees and revenue in two different municipalities, one being in two different counties than itself, which I might also add is why the local governments of Mackinac City and St. Ignace have both publicly opposed this bill. They would literally face taxation without representation as we're coming up on the 250th anniversary of our nation's founding,

responding on the principles of only being taxed with representation. I would also say that this bill sets a dangerous precedent moving forward that would allow the state to grant authority of any municipality to have certain controls over other municipalities through future bills. They would cite this bill as a reason for doing so. Representative Fitzgerald, I actually have lived in your district for most of my life. I remember when you ran for city council and I could imagine that while on city council you would be frustrated if the city of Grand Rapids were granted by the state the ability to regulate the price of parking in our city of Wyoming. It doesn't really make sense to me. I also might add that a court has ruled that the ferry companies are not a monopoly as defined by Mackinac Island. The ferry companies have also spent, and this is just a quick Google, $4 million in repairs on existing ferries, projects building new ferries and promises for repairs on the docks. This is also, the city also has a franchise with the ferry companies and I think it's great if they want to negotiate that when this franchise expires in the next two years. I don't understand why they would need to come to Lansing and ask the state government to break the franchise two years before it expires. And that is what I have to say. I would also note earlier it was asked, is there competition in parking? I know that there is public parking in both St. Ignace at the marina and in Mackinac City. Whenever I personally go up there, I always use the public parking and I just walk the extra minute or two minutes to the dock. It's never been a big deal for me personally. Okay, thank you very much. Representative Fitzgerald. Mr. Schultzke, I just want to say thank you so much for coming and being engaged. It's always great to see constituents coming to be involved in the process that we have here in Lansing. So thank you for making the trip from Wyoming to do that. You mentioned, I just want to ask one thing, is that you mentioned that it's not a consideration of the cost of the ticket, right? The fudge budget. If you didn't know this, the tourists on Mackinac Island are affectionately known as fudgies. That's right. That is an affectionate term used up there. The idea here is there are always people who do not have to consider cost. There are always those who are very fortunate to not have to consider those costs. Obviously, good budgeting is also a West Michigan value. We have that here, I think. But there are families who I think are concerned by that initial step off, right? The minute you step out of your car that there is that charge. And I think that there would be families that, depending on the continued use of fees, would find it unnecessary to have a stroller fee, to have a bag fee, to have a second fee, you know, continue to be charged for the utilization of that service. And so I just want to say I think that your point here today is that is it out of control now for the majority of families? I don't know. I'd love to consider that data. But I think that the concern is that it would get to that point where every aspect of that transportation be abnormally priced or exorbitantly priced to thus prevent people from enjoying the island. So I'm glad that you – and thank you for your service as an honor guard up there as well. They helped that fort run day in and day out during the summer months. So thank you. Do I have a second to respond to that? I'm sorry. In the best interest of time, we've got a couple other people who'd like to speak. Thank you, Mr. Chelsea. Absolutely. Okay, next we'll hear from Catherine Buzzard. Good morning. Thank you, Mr. Chair and committee members for the opportunity to speak today. I am presenting – I turned in prepared comments to the clerk written by myself and Professor William Wagner, constitutional attorney and professor of law. And in my own experience, I currently serve as the executive director, COO of Salt and Lake Global. I've also held office at the local level for a little over a decade, serving as the mayor of my city, serving for many years on city council as a DDA director in economic development. And Professor Wagner and I looking at this bill had many concerns along the lines of what the gentleman representing Shepler's Race and beyond even our state constitutional concerns. There are some very genuine concerns with the legality of this bill, even as you start looking at the federal constitution and just basic principles of good governance. And I'll try to be brief. I'm not going to go through my whole prepared testimony. It's there if anyone would like to read it. But I'll try to highlight just a few things momentarily. And when you think about good governance, there's a couple of basic tests that anything adopted by a body such as yourselves should pass before being adopted. The first is whether or not the body really has the authority to take the proposed action. And the second is whether or not that action would potentially interfere on the civil rights of anyone that that body is responsible for protecting. And I feel like this policy in its current form really does fail both those tests. I love Mackinac Island. I understand many of the good reasons that the representatives from the island and Senator DeMoose have brought forward. There's good reasons to be having the conversations we're having. But in its current form, there are serious flaws with this bill. And if I go back to that language on page four and page nine, the broad new term that all aspects of ferry service, whether within the city or on the mainland, will now be able to be established, authorized, licensed, or regulated exclusively by the city of Mackinac Island. That premise alone is very concerning. When you look at our constitution federally, Article 4, Section 4, Clause 2 contains the guarantee clause that says that the United States shall guarantee a republican form of government, and that means a representative form of government. The city of Mackinac Island does not represent the citizens of the city of Mackinac or the city of St. Ignace. And those cities are still protected by that constitutional clause. They deserve representation. And when it comes to things like that city's planning and zoning, their master plan, their waterfront, their shoreline, their business development strategies, allowing premium shorefront to be regulated by the city of Mackinac Island without really any clause for input for those other municipalities whose jurisdiction that land actually is, raises a real serious constitutional concern. Where do those citizens have a place to voice their opinions, to talk to their representatives when the city of Mackinac Island doesn't represent them at all and has exclusive authority? The policy here suggesting that all aspects of ferry service will be regulated in the future by the city of Mackinac Island, including things on the city or mainland, is so broad. And if you stop and think about that, you know, this law has been around since 1899 for 126 years. The intent today may not be to affect the shoreline or management. I'm sorry, I'm going to have to ask you to make your final statement here. It may not be to affect the shoreline or management of those areas, but that focus could shift in the future. And there's so much more I'd like to say about pricing. I just want to say the current ticket price, even if you adjusted up a little bit, it accounts for a point, 0.0818 of 100 percent of the average Michigander's income. The cost of making this affordable at the expense of the representative voice of other municipalities, at the risk of continued costly litigation wasting public tax dollars, is simply not worth it. Thank you. Thank you. Okay, we'll have time for just one more. Lance Griffin, if you could just keep your comments brief, please. I'm not known for that, Mr. Chair, but I will. Very good. As a concerned citizen, a business owner, a frequent visitor of Mackinac Island, I oppose Senate Bill 304. I'm also from the Grand Rapids area. Representative Fitzgerald, Representative Skaggs is my state representative, and I'm glad to be here today and appreciate the opportunity. Despite what you heard earlier from the bill's sponsor, indeed, this bill does seek to grant the city of Mackinac Island sweeping new regulatory powers over private ferry services. While the bill is framed as a means to enhance local control, it fundamentally violates a core principle of limited government. The state should not be in the business of breaking or interfering with private contracts. This legislation represents an unnecessary expansion of government authority that could disrupt established agreements between private entities, ultimately harming consumers, businesses, and the free market. The broad mandate goes far beyond basic safety or operational oversight. It allows the government to insert itself directly into the pricing and operational decisions of private ferry operators. These companies have long operated under private contracts with customers, vendors, partners, agreements that set terms for services, fees, and business practices without undue interference. Consider the real world

implications. A private ferry company might have multi-year contracts with tourism partners for bundled pricing on tickets and parking or agreements with customers or season passes or fixed rates. Under Senate Bill 304, the city could unilaterally impose new fees or rate structures effectively nullifying or altering these contracts midstream. This is worse than regulation. It's more like coercion. State governments exist to enforce contracts, not rewrite them to suit local whims. The granting the city such unchecked power, the bill risks creating a precedent where municipal governments can override private arrangements wherever they see fit, eroding trust in the marketplace and deterring investment in Michigan's tourism economy. We heard earlier about parsing words. That's what proponents are doing to promote this tyranny. It's shocking to hear this from a limited government Republican. No level of government, local or otherwise... I'm sorry. We've run out of time. If you want to submit the rest of your testimony to the clerk here, you can. We'll make sure it's on the record. Thank you. You're welcome. I do have a couple cards to read in here, and that goes, it looks like we just had one other person that wanted to speak, Cindy Todel. I'm sorry. Okay, so if you'd like to submit your statement to the clerk, you could. And then we have not wanting to speak in support of Bill Frank Foster of the Grand Hotel, not wanting to speak in support of Bill Scott Ellis of Michigan Licensed Beverage Association, not wanting to speak in support of the bill is Kelly Saunders of the Small Business Association of Michigan, and not wanting to speak in support of the bill is John McNamara of the Michigan Restaurant Lodging Association. So, not seeing any further business before the committee, we will stand adjourned. Thank you.

I rise to speak in support of House Bill 4774, a bill I sponsored to update Michigan's request for proposal process for soliciting work by engineers and architects in the design of state facilities. Currently, Michigan law requires the state to favor the lowest bidder, a practice that 40-some other states and the federal government have abandoned, as it denies the state the opportunity to select design architects and engineers who would seem best suited to execute the project in favor of those that offer the lowest bid. With qualifications-based selection, or QBS, professional services are procured based on a firm's demonstrated competence, qualifications, and experience rather than simply on the lowest cost. QBS procurement is mandated for federal projects under the Brooks Act and requires that firms be evaluated on the criteria, technical ability, and project understanding, with the fees being negotiated only after the most qualified firm is identified. QBS is intended to ensure the successful outcome of complex projects by prioritizing expertise and value, leading to high-quality project documents, better long-term value and outcomes.
