title: Economic Competitiveness — Thursday, December 18, 2025
transcript:
The House Committee on Economic Competitiveness will come to order. Would the clerk please take attendance? Chair Holdley? Here. Representatives Bonack? Here. Altman? Here. Harris? Begole? DeBoer? St. Germain? I'm here. Grant? Here. Brixie? Here. Tate? Here. Kofiya? Mr. Chair, you have seven members present. You do have a quorum. Great. Representative Bonack, or excuse me, Majority Vice Chair Bonack, makes a motion to approve our previous committee minutes from December 11th. Seeing no objections, the minutes are approved by unanimous consent. So first on our agenda today is Senate Bill 27, introduced by Senator Kleinfeld. Her bill is very straightforward. Therefore, the plan today is to take testimony and have a member of Senator Kleinfeld's staff before us today, and we will likely vote that out after. So if you would, please come up and we'll take testimony. Thank you, Colin. Start when you're ready. Good morning, Chair Holdley and members of the committee. My name is Colin Fowler. I'm the Legislative Director for Senator Veronica Kleinfeld, who is the sponsor of this bill. She can't be here today, unfortunately, but I am grateful for the opportunity to speak to you today about Senate Bill 27 on the senator's behalf. The bill is, as the chair says, is very simple. It's a technical update in statute to change procurement technical assistance center to APEX accelerator, a name change that became effective in fiscal year 2023. This is a reintroduction of Senate Bill 481 from 2023, and both the 2023 and 2025 bills passed the Senate unanimously. I'm happy to take any questions. Obviously pretty thorough, Colin. There are no questions. We do, however, have a substitute offered by Representative Brixie. If you'd like, Representative, would you like to speak to your substitute? I would. Thank you so much for the opportunity, Chair Holdley. This substitute tiebars House Bill 4576 to Senate Bill 27 and makes no substantive changes to Senate Bill 27. So the point of House Bill 4576 is to restore much of the cuts made earlier last week to the vulnerable Michiganders who were promised and counting on funds from work projects totaling $634 million. If approved, this restoration would be a bipartisan effort to support our families in need all over Michigan just before the holiday season. I'm sorry, Representative. I'm sorry, Representative. You're speaking to the bill that you offered, the tiebar, but your substitute is simply the tiebar, this bill. So keep it brief, please. I was just finished. So moved. Representative, would you like to make a motion? Do make a motion to... I move my substitute. Very great. Representative Brixie makes a motion to adopt her substitute. Madam Clerk, would you please take roll? On the motion to adopt the H-1 substitute to Senate Bill 27, Chair Holdley? No. Representatives Bonak? Nay. Altman? No. Harris? No. Fegol? No. DeBoer? St. Germain? No. Grant? Yes. Brixie? Yes. Tate? Yes. Kofiya? Mr. Chair, you have three yeas, six nays, zero pass. The motion does not prevail. The motion does not prevail. All right. So moving on, we will now vote out Senate Bill 27. Representative DeBoer makes a motion to report SB 27 with recommendation. Would the clerk please take roll? On the motion to report, Chair Holdley? Yes. Representatives Bonak? Yes. Altman? Yes. Harris? Yes. Fegol? Yes. DeBoer? Yes. St. Germain? Yes. Grant? Yes. Brixie? Yes. Tate? Yes. Kofiya? Mr. Chair, you have ten yeas, zero nays, zero pass. The motion prevails. Senate Bill 27 is reported with recommendation. Moving on, we're switching gears here. We're going to take testimonies from Representative Meerman and Snyder on House Bills 5168 and 5169. Representatives, when you are ready, would you please come up and begin when you are ready? You know the SOP, so hit the red button when you're ready. Thank you, members of the committee, for the opportunity to speak on House Bills 5168, 5169, by the bipartisan legislation that will support the state's robust agriculture economy. I want to thank Representative Snyder for his partnership with this important proposal. Good morning, Chair Holdley, committee members, and thank you for taking up this package of bills this morning. House Bills 5168 and 5169 are basically the same in substance but modify different acts. My bill would modify the Use Tax Act, while Rep Meerman's modifies the Sales Tax Act. These bills exempt large agricultural processing development from both taxes in the following circumstances. First, investment or development in a project must exceed $100 million. However, I do believe a substitute is being drafted that would reduce that threshold to a lower number, to $50 million. Secondly, the project or development must meet the criteria for the following three uses, construction or expansion of an agricultural processing facility, infrastructure improvements for an agricultural processing facility, or retooling of an agricultural processing facility. This large amount for the investment cost is a reasonable level to offer some support for what are truly transformational projects in our local communities across the state. The estimated impact would be 6% of the total cost, so that's a tax savings of approximately $6 million per $100 million of investment. It makes this a much more targeted

Much more scalpel approach rather than chainsaw-like instrument compared to economic development programs of the past like SOAR. West Michigan and our entire state are a bit of a cornucopia of farm products. Michigan has enjoyed the second most agricultural economy in the entire country. It's an underestimated industry here in the state, but we are a national leader in cherries, blueberries, apples, asparagus, pickles. And much of that is in western Michigan where Rep. Meerman and myself call home. Food processing is consequently a very valuable industry to invest in our state. It's a major value-add step that helps turn commodities like milk into valuable products. There has been a lot of talk about making it in Michigan. Well, we clearly grow things in Michigan, and our bills would work to keep things in Michigan. We are creating a healthy ecosystem for suppliers, small family farmers across the state to have their goods purchased and kept here in the state of Michigan. What projects over the last few years would be ones that might qualify? I've highlighted two here. Niagara Bottling recently completed an approximately $100 million project in Shelby Township. Roskam Foods, an $80 million investment in Grand Rapids in 2019. Or the over $555 million investment at the state-of-the-art St. John's Dairy Center in St. John's. So I just believe that these bills are making smart, strategic investments in products and sectors that we already excel in that will power growth of good-paying jobs and importantly impact both our rural and urban areas while supporting Michigan farmers. I think it is important to highlight that these bills do not pick winners and losers in the economic development space, but give equal opportunity for large-scale food processing investments across the state. And I'll just add a few things from my own personal perspective as some people would call a recovering dairy farmer. I always like that term because I'll always consider myself a dairy farmer, and it's just kind of in my heart and blood, and it just always sticks with you. But in the agriculture world, and I think probably in a lot of other industry worlds as well, further processing is just incredibly important. And it does two things. Number one, it keeps you from paying transport to go to the processing. So the closer the processing is to your farm, the less transport you have to pay. The second thing I think is more important is it drives demand. So, you know, for instance, if St. John's milk plant making cheese there, if they expand or double or any other place, Fairlife, now all of a sudden they need milk to provide to that plant, and so your price as a farmer goes up because you're closer and they're asking for more product. I think this is the kind of economic incentive things that we want to do because we're telling the prospective businesses, you build it, and then we'll waive the sales and use tax. So that's all I have to say, and I'd love to take questions. Thank you both for your testimony. We do have some questions. Minority Vice Chair Grant, go ahead. Thank you, Mr. Chair. My question is, and you've kind of answered this, but do you all see this more as a tool that will help with retention and expansion, or do you also think it will help with attraction of businesses to the state, as you mentioned, those larger projects that we've seen recently? I think it will be both, personally. I know that we recently lost a Chobani to an out-of-state offer somewhere else, I believe New York, and they were looking at Michigan. This is creating a tool in the toolbox for an industry that we excel in, and I think it would be both. And I think putting this out there would create a tool that could exist, and maybe the Chobani experience could have been different, the outcome. Go right ahead. And then my second question, just to be on, have you guys on record for this, these are dollars, we're not losing dollars necessarily. It's an investment. They're not taking dollars that the state already had. When they make an investment, then the state is basically being a partner because of that investment. Yeah, they're taking the risk. They're putting the money in the ground. They're building it. They're planning that this is going to work. We're just saying sales and use tax doesn't need to be paid. Correct, because those funds don't currently exist. Thank you. Moving on, Representative Brixey. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Mr. Meerman, how would this help a small dairy farmer like you used to be or one of the myriad of other small farmers across the state? That's a great question, Rep. Yeah, my two brothers are still milking cows. Actually, I'm going to milk cows next week. They're going on vacation. So I still get my hands dirty sometimes. I think sort of in my opening remark, I'll just kind of go back to that, that as a small dairy farm, when you have a demand of need of product in a processing plant, it's going to drive up demand and drive up prices. And these prices go for everybody. This isn't just certain people get to go to these processing facilities. It rises all boats. So do you have any kind of estimates from Treasury on what the fiscal impact would be? Rep. Snyder maybe can answer this too, but this is potential looking forward, so we don't know who might take advantage of this. Yeah, I would say we do not have anything from Treasury. It's hard to quantify an undetermined amount looking into the future, but these are dollars that the state currently does not take in on a future investment. So on the dairy side, I wouldn't say at this time because we're looking at future growth as well. You know, other commodities there might be. And as I look at that, you know, you're talking about the local food price. I hope it doesn't go lower for the farmers. I want to keep that local food price as high as we can. But the other part of it is all the input sides, you know. We'd love to have you come out to Agra Expo and take a look at what some of the costs are of some of these tractors and equipment that keep on rising year after year that's been through either inflation or tariffs and that. You know, building materials, you know, veterinary service as well. You know, we have not a lot of veterinary service graduates coming out working on large animals. So there's a lot of different factors out there besides that price as well. But I want to keep that price as high as I can at the farm gate level for those farmers and those farm families. Right. I would think in a perfect world you'd have, you know, the supply exactly meet the demand number in a perfect world. And I know it's hard to have the crystal ball on that. But, you know, again, going back to, you know, it's either higher profit margin or higher volume that really dictates costs. So I just wanted to get kind of a feel on, you know, what that looks like in a world of overproduction or, you know, an inflated per unit price that, again, is passed along to the consumer. An example I had of before that St. John's facility was built, the overproduction and how much of that was an economic deterrence to dairy farmers. You know, our farmer owners benefited that invested in it, but the other dairy farmers in the state also benefited from it that might not have been a direct investor. Absolutely. So, I mean, bottom line is we want to be able to reduce the cost of production, right? And that includes the production of the production is what this bill addresses. So I do appreciate that. We do have one more question from Representative Brixey. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thanks for your testimony and helping us understand all of the pressures that farmers are under, price pressures. So you talked about the desire to, you said something along the lines of hopefully there will be more exporting to Canada. And is that realistic given the tariffs and the current situation with the tariffs that are happening with our biggest trading partner? I'd love to have more dairy exported in Canada. But I know we have a lot of other ag commodities that are there. It's just been a longstanding many decades fight on that dairy portion going into Canada. And maybe we'll make some headway there soon, I hope. When I go fishing there, I export as much dairy as I can when we go to our fishing camp, but it's not enough. But, yeah, we'd love to do more there because it's a large market as well. Great. Thank you for your testimony. Very insightful. Appreciate it. That does conclude our agenda this morning. Representative DeBoer moves to excuse all absent members. There being no objection, absent members are excused. There being no further business before the committee, the committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Health Policy — Wednesday, December 17, 2025
transcript:
The House Health Policy Committee will come to order. Would the clerk please take attendance? Chair VanderWaal? Present. Representatives Thompson? Yes. Meerman? Here. Tisdell? Here. Beerlines? Let's do this. DeBoer? Here. Preston? Here. Schmaltz? Here. Saint Germain? Here. Bonick? Here. Frisbee? Witzit? Carter? Here. Whitwer? Here. Neely? Hoskins? Foreman? Mr. Chair, you have 11 members present. You do have a quorum. Thank you, Madam Clerk. Representative Thompson moves to adopt the minutes of the December 10 meeting. There being no objection, the motion passes. Today we are hearing testimony on a few bills and voting out a few others. We're going to start with Senate Bill 413, introduced by Senator Voino. We have Bill Drake from the Senator's office and a few other guests. If you guys would like to move forward to the testimony table, I believe we have, is it Teresa? Yes. All right, Teresa. Thank you for being here. Teresa's from MPA Master's Committee and she will be, when you guys are ready, the floor is yours. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Good morning, members of the House Health Policy Committee. Thank you very much for taking up Senator Voino's Senate Bill 413. Unfortunately, the Senator cannot be with us this morning, but sends his best wishes. Senate Bill 413 amends Public Act 368 of 1978 to change the criteria for the practice of a limited licensed psychology here in Michigan. This bipartisan legislation passed the Senate on September 18th earlier this year with a vote of 33 to 0. As we are all well aware, the need for qualified and dedicated mental health professionals here in Michigan is critically important. And the major change that this legislation addresses is the supervision requirement here in the state of Michigan. Currently, an individual with a limited license in psychology must be supervised by a holder of a doctoral license for their entire career. In this legislation, an individual could practice psychology after the appropriate education, training, and experience requirement, which includes at least two years of supervised postgraduate experience totaling at least 4,000 hours. Additionally, the bill would alter the makeup of the current Board of Psychology by replacing the three seats currently held by public members with one doctoral licensed psychologist and two limited licensed psychologists. This bill is important because it would bring thousands of limited licensed psychologists across the state in line with other master's level health practitioners and provide much needed care to thousands of Michiganders. In addition, the bill is a reintroduction of House Bill 5785 from last session, which passed the House with strong bipartisan support and unfortunately did not get a vote in the Senate. Once again, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, thank you for considering these bills, taking them up. We have Teresa Gosicki here with me now to give a few remarks. Good morning. Thank you so much for having me. My name is Teresa Gosicki and I'm a limited licensed psychologist practicing here in Michigan. I earned my master's degree in 2014 and I've been working in the mental health field for close to 10 years now. I chose this field because of the depth of training I knew I would receive in psychological assessment and evidence-based treatment and because I wanted to do clinical work with people in my community. What I didn't fully understand when I entered the field was how the restrictions of the LLP license would shape my career long-term. Despite being trained to assess, diagnose, and treat mental health conditions, LLPs are subject to a career-long supervision requirement that no other master's level mental health professional faces. This requirement creates barriers with insurance participation, attainment of additional certifications, and employment. I have seen many capable colleagues leave the field altogether because of these limitations. At one point, I seriously considered doing the same. Michigan currently has roughly 4,000 LLPs. Our education and training are comparable to other master's level mental health professionals in Michigan. However, our ability to practice is significantly more restricted. This difference affects how and whether we are able to continue providing care over the course of our careers. Allowing LLPs to practice independently within the current scope of our education, training, and competencies will help expand access to care, to retain well-trained clinicians, and allow more providers to fully serve Michigan residents without compromising quality or safety. I thank you all for the opportunity to share my experience. And while there may be perhaps one opposition to this bill, I will say that we have the support of over 1,000 individuals and organizations backing us up. So thank you for taking the time to consider this crucial change that has the potential to improve the lives of so many. Thank you, Bill and Teresa. Committee, any questions for our guests today? The one question I had, you mentioned there was 4,000. Do you know how many people have left the field because of our restrictions right now? I don't know that exact number. I can tell you that it is a lot. I know that there are many, many individuals that have faced hardship and have decided to seek alternative careers. Very good. Seeing no other questions, I want to say thank you. Oh, one, we do. Representative Bonick. Thanks for your testimony. I just wanted to ask, so at least reading this, it seems to me that you can't call yourself a psychologist? We could call ourselves a limited licensed psychologist, but that stipulation needs to be in there. And that is not anything that we are trying to change. We recognize that that's a protected term, and we are not arguing to be able to call ourselves that. Okay. Thank you. Very good. Thank you both for being here and give our regards to Senator Voino for us, please. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, members of the committee. On Zoom, we have Mary Clark, a limited licensed psychologist. Yes. Thank you, sir. She just came on, and I was going to introduce her. Mary?

Welcome, and the testimony floor is yours whenever you're ready. Okay. I've got... I'm sorry, I've got us... Okay, can you see me? We sure can. All right, good. There we go. First of all, thank you for allowing me to do the virtual presentation. I'm 78 years old and I'm struggling right now with sciatica. And the drive up there would have been rather painful. So, thank you. I appreciate your accommodation today. My name is Mary Clark. I have a doctorate in counseling psychology and I have practiced as a limited licensed psychologist for over 40 years. And this is my story. Until the spring of 1979... Notice the date. Until the spring of 1979, a person could qualify for a full licensed psychologist with a PhD in psychology or equivalent education. Spring 1979, the Board of Psychology changed the qualification to only allow the PhD in psychology for the full license and not allow the equivalent education. Those not qualifying for the LP, for the licensed psychologist, were offered the LLP license with the requirement that they be supervised forever. In December of 1979, about eight months later, I graduated with the equivalent education. I no longer qualified for the full license, the LP. My only option was to obtain an LLP in order to practice. Because I was licensed as an LLP, over the past 40 years, I've been required to have supervision every month. Over the past 40 years, I have had to turn patient referrals away because their insurance will only pay independent providers. Over the past 40 years, I wanted to devote part of my practice to low-income people, but Medicaid only pays independent providers. If you have any constituents in your areas who have Medicaid, you must know how difficult it is for them to get appointments for mental health services. SB 413 will help them. Over the past 40 years, some patients who eventually qualified for Medicare couldn't be seen by me anymore because Medicare only pays independent providers. They had to start over with someone else. Granting LLP's independent practice will not compete with other providers. There is certainly enough need for many unfulfilled jobs. SB 413 will help solve a massive mental health access problem. I've been involved in efforts to gain independent practice since 1990, and I am grateful for your help today, and I look forward to see it finally happening. Thank you. Thank you, Mary. We appreciate any questions from the committee. Yes, we have Representative DeBoer. Yes, so Mary, if you had not pursued the education and strictly gone by your doctorate in psychology, you would have been fully licensed for these 40 years and not have to go through all this stuff? Or not? Yes. Yes. If I had had my five years of education plus my dissertation, if it had been a PhD in psychology strictly, I would have had a full license for 40 years. But I had what they called the equivalent education, which was acceptable at that time. I had what's called the equivalent education because they changed it six months before I graduated. I was not able to have the full license. Now, I had a friend that took my very same program a year ahead of me, and she has a full license. Wow. The power of licensing and what we do to people's lives. Thank you for all the help that you have given people through all these slings and arrows of outrageous fortune. We appreciate your care for them. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Mary. I see no other questions. I appreciate your time today. Thank you for being here. Next up, wishing to speak is Joshua Tershawn, PhD. Welcome. Thank you for being here. And he's speaking on behalf of himself and opposes the bill. Thank you. And have you pushed the little red button at the base? The testimony table is yours. Great. Thank you. Can you hear me? Yes, we can. Thank you all for your time today. My name is Joshua Tershawn, and I'm a practicing doctoral-level psychologist in the state of Michigan. I would like to start my testimony today by saying that I do support the master's-level practice of psychology. My testimony is a request that Senate Bill 413 be amended to meet the recommendations and guidance of the American Psychological Association to differentiate the master's from the doctoral level of practice and help aid the public in clearly distinguishing the two professions. I hold a terminal master's in clinical psychology and then returned to school and completed a PhD in counseling psychology. I can speak from my experience as both a terminal master's and doctoral-level psychologist. Additionally, I'm a training director at a large clinical training program consisting of both pre-degree and post-degree master's and doctoral-level psychology students. Today I stand before you to ask that you amend Senate Bill 413 because it will have consequences for the practice of psychology and protection of the public that are not being taken into consideration. Currently in Michigan, master's-level psychology practitioners are called master's-level or limited-licensed psychologists, and the doctoral-level psychology practitioners are called licensed psychologists. In Michigan, there's virtually no scope of practice difference between the two. The one distinguishing factor between them is that master's-level practitioners require ongoing clinical supervision. Senate Bill 413 aims to remove that requirement. My master's-level colleagues have fought hard for this bill, and I agree that lifetime supervision for psychotherapy is likely an undue burden. But if Senate Bill 413 is passed without amendment, there will be virtually no distinguishing the practice of psychology at the master's from the doctoral level, despite the significant differences in training and education between the two. For example, master's degrees commonly take between one and two years. Doctoral degrees take between five and seven years. There are currently no national accreditation standards for master's-level psychology, although APA is currently in the process of developing them. Doctoral-level psychologists are required to complete an APA-accredited doctoral program or its equivalent. Master's-level psychology requires a 500 pre-degree clinical practicum with no direct service hour requirement, while doctoral-level psychologists typically have three years of practicum and have to have a 2,000-hour APIC or APA internship with a minimum clinical requirement. Senate Bill 413 is suggesting that master's-level psychology should have 4,000 hours post-degree supervised practice, while doctoral psychologists still have to have another 2,000 hours after their degree of supervised practice. Master's-level psychology practitioners need a passing score on the EPPP of 350, while doctoral-level providers need a passing score of 500. As you can see, there are significant differences in training and education, but SB 413 will create a functional equivalency for the scope of practice.

So the American Psychological Association, the leading accrediting scientific and professional organization for psychology, has continuously asserted that the terminal degree to practice psychology and the title of psychologist is at the doctoral level. Without amending Senate Bill 413, the state of Michigan is functionally creating the master's degree as the terminal degree for practice of psychology in the state of Michigan. Master's level practitioners will be called limited license, but there will virtually be no limit to their practice. Recently, the APA has decided to make the practice of psychology a multi-tiered profession. This includes new guidelines for the training and accreditation of the master's level. In August of 2025, APA approved operational principles for master's level psychology to guide current and future development of licensure for master's level. Some of the recommendations are as follows. Master's level practitioners in psychology should have an appropriate title that does not include psychologist, but establishes its base in psychology. So, for example, consider how there are not master's level physicians. There are physician assistants and physicians. Both practice medicine, but there's a clear distinction in name. Other states have addressed this by calling master's level psychology practitioners psychological assistants or psychological associates. The APA has gone on to say that master's level practitioners should be able to provide some services independently, including psychotherapy and diagnostic intake. But they've gone on to say that the practice of doctoral level psychologists is distinct from that of master's psychology and that doctoral level psychologists should provide a broader range of services as well as conduct complex and comprehensive testing and assessment relative to their master's counterpart. So, in summary, I'm asking that this committee follow the recommendations of APA. Before you consider passing the bill, please amend Senate Bill 413 so that the title and scope of practice for master's psychology is distinct from the doctoral level psychologist, which would include, one, a title change that does not include the word psychologist, and two, limiting psychological testing and assessment to the doctoral level or continuing that the supervision requirement for testing and assessment by master's level psychology. If you cannot amend this bill, I ask you to vote no. Thank you for your time. Thank you. Questions from the committee? Representative Meerman. With the acute need of psychologists out there, what is your idea of how we get more psychologists on the front lines? Yeah, so again, I'm asking for an amendment. I do believe that psychotherapeutic practice should be unrestricted and unsupervised. I think lifetime supervision for psychotherapy is inappropriate. I'm just asking that there – I don't think that this bill takes into account that there is a distinguishing factor. There's a difference between master's level and doctoral level. And doctoral level psychologist is the terminal degree to practice, but this bill essentially creates a functional equivalency. So I ended up going back to school and going $100,000 in debt so I could practice the terminal level of psychology. So I'm not – again, I'm sorry to meander a little bit, but I'm not suggesting that we should keep it the way it is. I just think that this bill should be amended so that there's a distinguishment between the two. Thank you. Thank you. Seeing no other questions, I want to say thank you for being here today. We appreciate your testimony, and we look forward to working with you on this bill. Thank you. A couple cards to read in. Not wishing to speak in support of the bill, Gabe Basso, Blue Cross. Not wishing to speak in support, Stephanie Seismas, Mosaic Counseling. Not wishing to speak in support, Dr. Kristen Votruba, Michigan Psychology Association. Thank you. Next up, we will be taking up House Bill 5150, introduced by our very own Vice Chair, Representative Thompson, pertaining to licensing of respiratory therapists. And I believe we have Stephen coming up. Stephen Hammock, Michigan Society. And I believe we also have Nicholas Pruszcz, Michigan Society. Welcome to all of you. The testimony table is yours, and we look forward to hearing from you. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Good morning, Chair VanderWaal and members of this committee. Thank you for taking the time today to hear this very important legislation from myself and from several respiratory therapists here in the state of Michigan regarding House Bill 5150. Respiratory therapists, to many of us in this room, may be an unknown profession. But as we look at policies in health care, we really need to be making sure that we are looking at policies that affect the entire health care team. And I don't want to stress that enough. We have many members of our health care team that are integral to making sure that patient safety is implemented and that good patient outcomes are addressed. Respiratory therapists are a specialty. Professionals that are specialized in the heart and lungs. They work on improving lung function in patients in addition to providing treatments such as oxygen therapy, trach care, and mechanical ventilation. These are highly skilled professionals. They're working alongside the nurse and the doctor. As a nurse myself, I have had the pleasure of serving alongside many of these respiratory therapists. And I appreciate their unique expertise. House Bill 5150 accomplishes three very important changes. First, it adds a requirement for continuing education. Currently, respiratory therapists in the state of Michigan are not required to complete any continuing education upon renewal of their license. This bill changes this to require that these therapists complete at least 15 hours of continuing education courses per their license renewal, which actually mirrors our sister states, Indiana, which requires 15 CEUs, and the state of Ohio, which requires 20. For example, as a nurse, I am required to complete 25 hours of continuing education upon renewal of my license every two years. Secondly, this bill adds a limited license for respiratory therapist students. I cannot stress how important that is to allow them to practice what they have learned when they are in hospitals training to complete their licensure. A limited license provides clarity on what a student can do in a medical setting during hospital employment and as a respiratory care assistant. Finally, this bill aligns the definition of respiratory care services with the correct practice of respiratory therapists. This includes specifying that a respiratory therapist can evaluate cardiopulmonary function and assess the effectiveness of the treatment. House Bill 5150 strengthens the field of respiratory care. Continuing education promotes staying up to date on latest treatments. Limited license provides clarity and uniformity for our early professionals in this field. And this bill makes clear that respiratory care services actually include, and I wanted to talk about that because if you look at the opposition to this, I think it's really important that when we look at our policy analysis, the opposition is this likely is not needed because there are not a lot of limited licensure respiratory therapists here in the state of Michigan. But what we really need to be addressing is that this actually changes it so that there are a limited license for our respiratory therapists. So we're changing it. Currently it states it's temporary. This in legislation will change it to a limited. And this actually would put us in line with Michigan and Ohio. And I think when we look at access to health care, lower cost to health care, bringing more people into the field, we have to be looking at our sister states here in the Midwest. And that makes it very clear. So what I want to do right now is pass it over to the professionals, to our respiratory therapists that came all the way here to Lansing to say why they support this legislation. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Very good. Thank you. And we'll turn the table over to you, too. Well, thank you very much. Oh, I'm sorry. Thank you very much for having us here today. As Representative Thompson stated, we are highly specialized, licensed health care professionals throughout the United States. We're trained in critical care in college, and we care for patients, as Representative Thompson said, with cardiopulmonary diseases. We work very, very closely with physicians and nurses to develop the care plans for our patients. We work in hospitals. We are part of the ER trauma team. We work in physician offices, particularly pulmonary offices. We work

life flight. We work in sleep labs. We work in home care and we work in other settings. So as Representative Thompson previously stated, under direction of physicians, we provide a multitude of respiratory therapies from home oxygen all the way up until critical care. The ICU is we manage the ventilators, mechanical ventilators. We're also trained in managing emergencies such as cardiac arrest and respiratory failure. And we assist in resuscitation and provide life-saving interventions. CPR, we're part of the CPR team as well. So we're kind of a small profession. A lot of people didn't know who we were until COVID came around. And we have to build all these ventilators. Well, there's got to be an RT behind those ventilators to run them. What we're seeking for in particular is the limited license for student practitioners. Those are students that moonlight in the hospitals. And they work as respiratory care assistants or respiratory care interns, depending on what the term is that the hospital uses, the job position. And they work under the license of a respiratory therapist. Why we're seeking licensure like Ohio, I mean limited license for them, like Ohio, Indiana, West Virginia, Kentucky, is we received in the last 10 years, we received two calls from two RTs that worked up north who are very concerned that there were these students that were working in the hospital without a licensed RT on campus. And they were in the ICUs running mechanical ventilators. That scares all of us because they're not licensed to do so, but that's just kind of how it was. So what the limited license would do is would restrict their scope of care, what they could provide, basically basic therapies, oxygen, delivering medications, breathing treatments. It would really limit their scope, and that's defined in the bill. And so we won't have any more of these incidences of getting these calls. One of the other things that we're seeking is the RRT as the minimum entry credential for licensure, and I'll turn that over to Nick. Thank you, Chair. Thank you, everyone, for allowing me to speak today. My name is Nicholas Prush. I'm a PhD, but by trade I'm a respiratory therapist, and I currently serve as the administrative director at Michigan Medicine in Ann Arbor, as well as I'm on faculty there to teach in the Bachelor of Science in Respiratory Therapy program, where I serve as the program director there. And I think to touch on the point of the limited license, and you think about our sister state, when we try to hire individuals who are practicing, so they're students, they come and perform their rotation with us, and we attempt to want to hire them or bring them on as a student, a temporary technician, they've already got a job in the state of Ohio because Ohio has a limited license and can bring them in, and they start to hire them fresh while they're still in school. In Michigan, we don't have that, so we're losing a lot of our really good therapists early on to go to the sister states. On top of that, the RRT as the minimum, so we have two exams to get our licensure, essentially, or what we're hoping to get out of this bill is that right now in the state of Michigan, we have, across the nation, there's two exams to get licensure. The first one is a multiple-choice exam. Once you pass that exam nationwide, you get to be a CRT or what's called a certified respiratory therapist. Here in the state of Michigan, once I pass that first exam, I can apply and obtain my license, and you can practice as a licensed respiratory therapist by only passing one exam. In the nation, what happens for those that carry on to get the RRT or the registered respiratory therapy exam, once you pass that multiple-choice exam, you then go on and you're eligible to sit and take the clinical simulation exam. Once you pass those two, you then obtain the RRT credential. Our House Bill 5150 is looking for us as a profession that these individuals to obtain licensure pass both of those exams to then become licensed in the state of Michigan, and that will pull our profession up and not allow those that don't want to take the clinical sim exam to be then licensed in the state of Michigan. Thank you. Very good. A few questions for you. Representative Meerman. Thank you, Chair. Who's currently doing the work in the state of Michigan? Which work? What do you mean? Let's say we have the license. Let's say this bill passes and we have this licensure, but today somebody's doing the work that these licensed therapists would do. Who's doing it today in Michigan? So we have the licensed practitioners, the registered respiratory therapists in-house. What we're looking to do is for the up-and-coming ones that are currently in programs, things of that nature, that number one, we can have a limited license for those to then practice while they're still in school in a limited scope. And then the next piece is to get those that are graduating to take both exams before they can obtain licensure, not just a singular exam. And are we seeing negative results for the system we have today? As far as? Outcomes, I guess, for patients? I would say not negative outcomes on patients. However, the amount of, I wouldn't say the amount, but the level at which the therapist works at, the CRT therapist versus the RRT therapist, is two different and distinct individuals. One that has gone on to finish and complete the clinical simulation exam works at a higher level and knows and has that knowledge base at that higher level than that of the CRT. Thank you. I would also add that a lot of times there's different stages of these licensures. So the first, the certified is just kind of like a stepping stone. And what they're able to accomplish in a work setting is not the same as what someone who is registered as a respiratory therapist are allowed to do. And then when you look at students that are going into the profession and they're still not fully finished, hospitals really need to know what the boundaries are, what they're allowed to do, because sometimes hospitals or certain medical settings will allow them to do certain things but won't allow them to do other things. And their training is allowing them to do that, but we're restricting them to be able to get the on-site use of their skills while they're being supervised by a physician. And that's what the important thing is, to make sure that across the board we know and it's in statute what they are allowed to do and not allowed to do. And I think that would actually allow them to do things that they're training to do while they're practicing, opposed to having them graduate and then throwing them to the wolves. But when we break the population by their gender and race, the highest weight gain was found in African-American males. And in African-American females and Caucasian males, their weight gain is about two pounds. But African-American males is three pounds. While for Caucasian females, the weight gain is minimal. So there are race and gender disparities in how much weight we gain after sleep restriction. And on top of that, the hormones, like ghrelin, leptin, those are hunger hormone and satiety hormone, they change after sleep restriction. So more hunger hormones and less leptin satiety hormones telling our body, our brain, we have enough food, we stop to eat. And the insulin sensitivity also drops. So decreased insulin sensitivity is actually a pre-diabetic sign. So those are the studies support the link between sleep deprivation, obesity, and metabolic syndrome. Very good. Thank you. We've got time for a couple more questions. We'll go to Representative Foreman. Thank you for this information. I just want to share with our committee and you all that I worked as an educator before I got to the legislature. And in one of my last years of educating, we switched our school start time from 7.15 to 9.15. And we did see an increase. At first it was an adjustment. It was an adjustment for everyone. I am a person who likes to go to bed early and get up early. I'm like you're 8.30 in the bed and 4.30 up. If the sun is down, I need to be sleep. That's the end of the story. But we did, after that, we began to see an increase in test scores. We began to see an increase in attendance. So I think it was really important. While it was a big adjustment, especially when the time changed and the kids were getting home when it was dark, that was a huge adjustment for the district. But it was really beneficial for them. And that was middle school. So that was 6th, 7th, and 8th graders. And they were able to adjust and build their schedules and their lives around a different time frame. And it really did work out. So as we've said, we all know about sleep deprivation up here. But I think that I really appreciate the data and your presentation today and just wanted to highlight that. I do have experience with that and have seen the change that can happen when we do adjust some of these start times, especially for kiddos. You're welcome. Thank you, Representative Bonick. Thank you for your presentation. It seems to me that there are exceptions to the 8-hour rule. Anecdotally, President Trump supposedly is 4 to 5 hours. I read where Obama was something like 5 hours of sleep. And Margaret Thatcher in Great Britain, they even coined a term, the Thatcher gene. And I think they've even tried to isolate that gene. Maybe you could speak to that, that there are exceptions to that 8-hour rule. Absolutely, there are. And a lot of this is determined by your genetics, too. So, yes, there are genes. We call them clock genes. And they determine what is my natural sleep time is going to be. But the long, large population-based studies that look at not just one individual, they're looking at millions of Americans. And that's where this data is coming from that, okay, this is about the number of. So, you know, one number that I remember is 7 hours and 50 minutes. That's, you know, sometimes we. But this is for adults. This is not for teenagers. Teenagers, their total sleep time has to be much longer. And then middle schoolers, elementary even longer. So as my brain is developing and I'm getting older, my total sleep time is going to shift. And it'll shift even as an adult, too. So if I'm an adult in my 30s and 40s versus when I'm in my 70s or late 60s, 80s, my total sleep time is going to be very different. So it's not even same for that same individual throughout the course of their life. So you're absolutely right. So the sleep needs has individual differences. And one of my current research projects is actually on this condition called familial short sleep. And those individuals, it's running family, as you mentioned. Those individuals only need four or five hours of sleep. And they are upbeat. They are energetic. They don't suffer any health consequence associated with sleep deprivation. But as Dr. Sani mentioned, it relates to their very specific genetic makeup. So there is a variant in their clock gene underlying their really amazing traits. I'm actually currently collaborating with psychiatrists in University of Michigan. We're trying to find out what's the neuro mechanism, what makes them so resilient to sleep deprivation. But that's very rare traits. Not everyone has that. The vast majority still need eight or more hours of sleep to have our brain function, to keep our body healthy. Very good. And finishing up the last question, we've only got a couple minutes left, is Representative Schmaltz. Thank you, Chair. And thank you for the presentation. It was very informative. So we know it's a big problem, especially for our young people. And starting school later is one way to help this. But what are some other solutions that we can look toward to try and tell them how important it is to get enough sleep? So there are lots of different things we can do. Number one, I think, educating the constituents, educating parents about the need for sleep in their children. I think it's important we look into screen time. Educate. We're not going to get rid of the screens. But I think when I do outreach events, people – so white light is all kinds of wavelengths of light, and blue light in the evening is – like it impairs your sleep. So education of the parents, of the children, you know, getting them off the screens so when their body can actually sleep, that they're ready to sleep. So those are like educational approaches we can take. I will say that research has shown when the children go to school with well-rested, they learn more during the school day. They have less homework to do because they get it done during the school day. And the homework they need to do, they do it faster. So actually allowing children to sleep frees up time for them to do extracurricular and social activities after school simply because they don't have to relearn again and again what they did have to learn. So, yeah, education about the value of getting enough sleep, allowing children to sleep. We still do not have a magic drug to actually advance the biological sleep of teenagers, and we don't know why they delay. So we don't know if there's a reason they delay. We just don't know. So I would also not give them sleep medicine to sleep earlier because it's their biology, and there might be a reason that happens. So all we ask for the committee members is to sleep more. We need you guys to live longer. So thank you so much. We appreciate your presentation today. As you can tell, everybody was very interested. So I want to say thank you for taking some time

and visiting with us today here in the Health Policy. So, wished you guys a great day and make sure you get your sleep. All right, moving on. Representative Preston moves to excuse absent members. There being no objection, the motion prevails. There being no further business before the committee, the committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Oversight - Homeland Security and Foreign Influence — Wednesday, December 17, 2025
transcript:
Test one, two, mic check. Test one, two, mic check. All right, the House Committee on Homeland Security and Foreign Influence will come to order. Will clerks please take the roll? Chair Brook? Present. Representative Meerman? Here. Shriver? Present. Menser? Here. Conlon? Here. Mr. Chair, you have a quorum? All righty. Minority Vice Chair Menser moves to approve the minutes of November 12th. Hearing no objections, they are approved. All right, well I hope you guys have had a wonderful week. Always trials and tribulations every week and every day, but we try not to let them keep us down. But as we get closer to the end of the year, this will be our last committee meeting of the year, 2025. So I just want to say thank you to all my committee members. In case I forget at the end, because I know my mind and my memory, so I just want to say thank you for all the effort and the involvement that each one of you have put in this committee all year. So I appreciate it. I'm thankful for you and I hope you have a wonderful New Year and holiday Christmas. And that way I don't forget at the end. But moving on to the business today, we have a couple experts to present. Mr. Jim Riker, president of the Michigan Research Institute. And not the original George Patton, but Mr. George Patton, who just happens to be a military subject matter expert. I met Jim up at Operation Northern Strike earlier this year. And, you know, I offered for him to come down to committee and he accepted. So that's awesome. It's an honor to have you both here today. Just please, just for the committee members, just introduce yourself and press the red button, the mic button, and then introduce yourself and then proceed with your presentation. Thank you for being here today. So Mr. Chair, Chief, I'm retired Army Lieutenant Colonel George Patton. I'm the managing partner of PM Partners located in Oakland, Michigan, doing a lot of work for the military, especially the Michigan National Guard, through my company called PM Partners. So last few years we've been doing a lot of contest logistics on behalf of the Michigan National Guard. And so that's my role. I apologize. We have one. Luke? I'm sorry. Your name is amazing. He's one of my favorite generals. You know, I've read so many books on him. So anyway, it's kind of cool you have the same name and you're here to talk to us about this stuff. So sorry, Mr. Chair, but it just really struck me. I'm like, holy cow. I was an armor officer. Yeah. What's even more amazing, if you ask the question, is General Patton and his father, he would say yes. It's not the same General Patton. So your father was a general. Right. Not the General Patton, but another General Patton. He was a general in the Pennsylvania National Guard. He was a retired Army colonel and a brigadier general in the Pennsylvania National Guard. The plot thickens here. You know, I think there's... Patton is a classic if you have three and a half hours. Yes, it was a great, great movie. Oh, sorry. No, it's okay to go on tangents here. But no, we appreciate your family's military service too. But yes, General Patton, I've read

some books, but Representative Merriman is definitely the history expert on this panel here. But all right, well, I didn't mean to interject too much. Hopefully it didn't get you off your game. But being a military officer that you were trained to respond, I mean, being a light colonel, like maybe your response would be yelling at us, but you can't yell at us in this environment. But no, we appreciate your service. So please continue, sir. I'll add one thing for George. He fielded the V3. I'm 182. The M182 tank out of the Detroit Arsenal. So I'm Jim Richter. I'm the president of the Michigan Research Institute. Just a real thumbnail and a quick background on that. Before I do that, Mr. Chairman, about how long would you like us to take during this briefing? You have a good half hour. Okay. 20, 25, 30 minutes or so. We're going to have questions most certainly. So we want to leave time for questions, but I want you to be able to fully demonstrate what you have. I appreciate that. And if you have any questions anyway, just yell out. We'll answer them when we come. So a little background, Michigan Research Institute. We're a not-for-profit 501c3. We've been around 25 years. We're located in Ann Arbor, Michigan. We actually, on the side as a community service, operate a 35,000 square foot wet lab incubator for startup biotech companies. And we kind of did that way back then because there really wasn't much in the incubator space in Michigan. And as some of you are aware, it's the highest cost space to develop and it's the riskiest customers. So doing it as a not-for-profit was the way to go on it. But during that time, we've done a lot of work both mainly with the federal government as well as with the state in certain instances. Our economic development purpose is basically to take advanced technology that resides in our universities, federal labs, or even in commercial companies and either further develop or repurpose it to solve a national problem. And so as a result, we pull together projects that span from technology development all the way through to prototyping and insertion into whatever platform that may be. If it's in the military, it might be on a tank, on an F-35 jet. If it's, we do medical technology. So we do pharmaceuticals, we do medical devices, we do manufacturing technology, anything that looks like it's a critical, it solves a critical problem out there. And we do projects one-off. So we bring all the people together to solve that problem from whatever area they come from, subject matter experts. They come together for that project, we complete it, those people disseminate, and we move on to the next project. So that's kind of what our business model is. What we're going to describe to you today is a thing we've been working on for the last probably seven, eight years. And it's how do we bring additional missions to the Michigan National Guard that nobody's thinking about right now? As you know, what we are doing currently at Selfridge, we're competing with all the other states out there for F-35 or the current fighter wing that we're getting now. The Detroit Arsenal has come under fire basically and moving it to Huntsville, Alabama. And so how do you do things that enhance what we have in the state here and either maintain that mission or grow that mission? And so those are the kind of things that we kind of think about, but we think about it through advanced technology. We think about what do we have that's unique here that we can utilize to either preserve that mission or bring additional missions here. What we're going to show you today is the whole area of contested logistics. And it's not well defined because the Pentagon hasn't even defined it yet. All I can say is that if you look at the next slide, last month they came out with their list of critical technologies and contested logistics is on there. We've been working on it for five years. If you ask them what it is, they don't have a formal structure to address it right now. It's all hodgepodge. It's rapidly evolving. And so the jump that we've had on this in helping to define this area and actually develop technologies and insert them actually into the field has given us a leading edge on this. So we look at this for the Michigan National Guard as an opportunity to see where the future is going and get there before anybody else or any of our competitor states try to fill that role. And we have some things here that uniquely qualify us for that role as well. So we've got a lot to build on already as a state. For the non-military, you're going to wonder what the term contested logistics means. So logistics is basically what Amazon does for you every day. And they fly it in, drive it in, ship it in. So we use this cute little phrase called contested logistics because in war or near war, like war, there are people that are trying to disrupt Amazon from getting those logistics to you. They are contesting our ability to get fuel, food, ammo, vehicles, weapons to the front. And that's what we call contested logistics. So I don't want you to be thrown by this phrase. You go, what the heck is that? Well, that's what it is. So there's the fight to get logistics to the front crosses all domains, includes cyber, electronic. It's not just people and bullets. There's a lot of things that happen to intercede those logistics getting to the front. And so since that really underpins what we're talking about, I wanted to make sure that you all knew what the heck that funny little phrase was, contested logistics. There you go. So with respect to training our forces on that, there does not exist anywhere in the country or the world a facility that trains logisticians on how to become better at that job. And it's an area that all of a sudden has emerged. As a matter of fact, if you think back to when the Ukraine war started, you know, everybody thought they were going to roll into Kiev and in three days they were going to take it over. Well, it didn't happen. Well, one of the reasons why it didn't happen is because instead of just shooting at the forward maneuver units, the tanks and so forth, they also shot at the supply lines. And if you stop the supply lines, you stop the forward movement. That's contested logistics. So how you deliver with somebody shooting at you. So as George said, Amazon with UPS and the post office shooting at them as they're trying to deliver it to your house. Okay, that's contested logistics. We've got some phenomenal capabilities here in the state that already give us an advantage to training that to a group in the military that normally doesn't train by themselves. Okay, they don't get the focus. The focus is on the maneuver units, the guys that shoot stuff and the logisticians kind of come along with them to train, but they're basically just supplying them. But nobody really trains those logisticians. And there's a ton of them in the military as well as in foreign militaries. We've got a great opportunity because Camp Grayling is already set up for Northern Strike. And one of the reasons is it has landmass. It has access to sea and air capabilities. You have great military operating areas for the Air Force to train in in Michigan, the same thing on the waterways. So we can train in all three spaces at once here that some other states can't. Number two, we can train all weather. Okay, you can't train all weather down south. You can't get into snow. You can't get into freezing conditions. All those things affect training. So we have some unique capabilities here that are already here. And the fact that we've got that we have Camp Grayling, we have the air combat, Alpena Combat Readiness Center, as well as Selfridge. So we've got some great attributes here as well that support that. Okay. From an economic development standpoint, if we start drawing these things in and start training at Grayling, not just for Northern Strike a couple times a year, but now we start training many times a year and as well as for Alpena and Selfridge, that just multiplies the amount of troops, both foreign and domestic here that are utilizing those facilities and as well as all the people that come with them. So it's a great economic development activity as well as for the military. We've basically put together a three-phase program that we've been executing now. So this is not us coming to you and say, hey, this is something we'd like to do. We've been doing this for a while. One of our big supporters, or two of them I should say, have been Congressman Jack Bergman and Congressman John Moolenaar. They've supported us with the funds in the military that have been developing some of these technologies that we began inserting into Northern Strike 25 this last August. So phase one is already funded under contract and we are doing that and we are doing it in conjunction with the Ground Vehicle System Center out of the Detroit Arsenal. So we're tying together the R&D groups in the military all the way to the people that are training in the Guard. The second piece, which is what we are asking the state for right now,

One time only contribution to this is $15 million that accomplishes two things. And we're going to go through them in detail. But broadly, one of them is to add the infrastructure to Grayling and Alpena that allows us to train contested logistics. The second piece is to insert a mobile medical technology capability that will reside out of all three places but mainly be housed at Selfridge that can deliver emergency mobile medical care as close to the front as we do right now with canvas tents, basically. And that has some other components to it that affect emergency preparedness in the states as well, both Michigan and the other states. And so I'll go into that more detail. And then the third phase is, and by the way, the state funding is important because it's for infrastructure. It's not for research and development or things of that nature. And so that's a very important piece to us because for us to get that federally, it's about a seven-year timing schedule to get that out of the Milcom budget. So we just don't have the time to wait for that. Phase three is already in process, and this is more R&D funding from the federal government. And Congressman Bergman's put that in for us again. We're in the 26th federal budget in the House appropriations bill being a conference right now with the Senate. So that's the broad plan here. The objectives, as shown on the screen here, is to set up the first modern contested logistics training facility that's just basically dedicated to a joint and allied partner nation sustainment formations. That's what we're all about here. And in parallel, have the capability to experiment, evaluate, and test all new sustainment technologies that are coming out of GVSC or elsewhere within the military at our facilities. George, I'm going to let you take over here in terms of what our goals are here that are in our campaign plan for Grayling. So the A-tag for initiatives, General Scott Myers, we've worked very closely with him for a number of years now. He's the guy that drafted the campaign plan, the National Logistics Training Center campaign plan that Jim provided to the committee. We are working with him to, as you can see, develop a shopping list. There are a series of capabilities that we need to be able to install at Camp Grayling, and that's so these goals are directed at creating, you know, getting that gear and then creating that environment to be able to do the kinds of things that Jim was just talking about. So we have Major General Rogers is obviously a very big supporter of this. Part of the reason is what Jim said, that currently there is no other state that does this. We don't have to compete with anybody. We compete with everybody on everything, and frequently we lose. Most of the time we lose. This is one we can win because nobody's in the hunt yet, number one. Number two, Camp Grayling is the largest landmass in the United States military complex within the National Guard system. There's no other place that can do what Camp Grayling can do. That is what makes it ideal and really what got General Rogers, General Myers, General Wogg behind this, is that really there's no other place to do this. You've got to do it in bits and pieces. So for the first time, Michigan is super competitive for a mission that is emerging. It's still not defined yet, and so we've established these goals that get at that, and I mean get at it quickly so that nobody can keep up with us. We will be out front. Logistics, Mr. Chair, as you well know from your military experience, it's the last thing people spend any time on, and yet it's the first thing people need to focus on. So we're always worried about the shooters. That's understandable in a way, but if the shooters don't have stuff and there's not a way to get them that stuff, we've got a problem. And we see the technologies, you'll see this, that bumper sticker at the bottom. Everything that we're doing here is near-term and very achievable. There is nothing risky here. All of this is known, and we can do it. So with a little bit of funding, we basically have a no-risk, no-threat capability that Michigan will have for an enduring mission. To Jim's point about the economic development, we will bring in joint, which means all the services, multinational, which means our allied partners. There will need to be more hotels, restaurants, and so on all around the Grayling area and the rest of NADWIC, the National Domain Warfighting Center, like Alpena and Custer and Selfridge. So now to get to those goals, we have a series of tasks. These are pretty straightforward. So what we're here to talk to you about is basically the ask that we made from the state for the investment to help achieve those goals is to go complete these tasks, which number one is acquire a bunch of stuff, and that's where all this money is going to. If we buy this, and that is a lot of equipment for $15 million, that's a lot. And part of it is that we know exactly who to go to. These are guys that are the experts in the business, and we've been doing this kind of thing, experimenting with them for seven years. We know exactly what to do. So these tasks that you see here are basically the next step. In August of 25, so this most recent Northern Strike, we started knocking out those tasks. So we installed this software called Jedi and LogFast at Camp Grayling permanently. It's there. We're training their people. Done. We have that capability now. So we need to get the rest of this. Now as we go forward, there's an array of other tasks, and we've laid out for the TAG and any of the House members that we've talked to what we think would be the timeline that we can do these things if we get funding in the timeframes that you see on the right. We can achieve these tasks. At the completion of these tasks, we will have, whether anybody declares it yet or not, the National Logistics Training Center in Michigan for the Department of Defense. So there's a lot of words there and some of these acronyms, QRTF, like a quick reaction task force. That's military speak. I'm sorry. We should have spelled that out. But a lot of it you do know, AR, VR, MR, so the augmented reality, virtual reality, mixed reality. We are bringing technology so that we not only train in today's fight, we train for tomorrow's fight. So this is going to be a powerful capability at Camp Grayling, center to Camp Grayling, but it will involve the whole NADWIC if we're able to do this. So unless there's any questions on that. So the question marks you see on the funding, okay, once again, I'll make this very clear, the only state funding is for 26 this year. All those are just out years on federal funding. Federal. Okay. Any questions on these tasks for either the near term or the near future? Representative Conlon. Well, this is very exciting, and I'm from the Ann Arbor area and know certainly the Michigan Research Institute, so thank you for that. And I also had the chance to go on a tour at the engineering school at U of M to their automotive research lab where I got to be on one of the simulators, and they have digital engineers making these autonomous vehicles, have these intelligence systems. And I kept saying, do you take them up to Camp Grayling? And I think they do. But I guess one, obviously I hope you're speaking to the Appropriations Committee on this, because this sounds like a lot of bang for your money, the $15 million, if we can get all of this. I did not get to Northern Strike this year, but I did go the year before and saw the tents that they're doing their medical training and everything. And so I guess I just want to, it feels like so much that you're getting for the $15 million. You really feel that that's a number that is big enough to do all of this? And also I like the ideas of hotels and things, and would that be for the people who are coming and participating in the training, or is there any element that's for just Michiganders interested in, you know, because I know you can stay at Camp Grayling now even if you're not in the National Guard. So that's my question. Yeah, we'll need, there will be more permanent staff there as well as all the visiting units. So the hotels are for the visiting units, but there will have to be more apartments and grocery stores because there will have to be more people living there because the people, if you've ever been to the National Training Center, it takes thousands of people to run that. So this would grow the opportunity set for Michiganders working there as well as the transient, the units coming in. Have you done any, like, estimation of what kind of, you know, revenue stream could maybe come in just from doing this in the Grayling area or no? We really haven't because we just know it's large. And the other thing besides the economic development is...

This will be a revenue generator for the Michigan National Guard. And so being able to expand their capability there, but there can be more troops coming over paying to train there, especially when we started including the Indo-Paycom countries who are not participating right now. And that's an area that we're actively working with, with Indo-Paycom to start getting those countries connected to Camp Grayling for Northern Strike as well as for this. We do have some numbers that we're not responsible for. So we talked to Terry Sabo in General Rogers' Legislative Affairs Office. They know what the number is in terms of the economic value to Northern Strike. And so they multiplied that. So they have an estimate. We shouldn't be sharing that. That really is for them to do. But they have estimated what that economic value is. And it's several multiples of what we currently get with Northern Strike, partly because we'll be all year round. On that slide, I did want to, to your point about the $15 million, and I don't want to be conscious of the time, but in the middle of that slide it said Maven. And Maven is a software program offered by Palantir. Palantir's most recent contract award, most recent, was for $250 million for software, half of which is vaporware. We're going to do all of this, and we know it because the software has already been exhibited, demonstrated at Camp Grayling. So that's why I say there's nothing for us to guess about, whereas those guys, and you can go into the reasons why they're getting these awards, but whatever. You're exactly right. There is no bigger bang for that $15 million than I'm aware anywhere around the military. To give you an example, right now, up until now, load technicians, they work a lot with spreadsheets, okay, unfortunately. And when you get into an environment like UCOM and you're working with NATO, every country has its own system. They don't talk to each other, okay? So when we're fighting in a multinational force, the commanders don't have the ability to say, hey, Germany, you know, what kind of ammo do you have? Where is it at, okay? How much do you got? You know, hey, France, what do you got? You know, how much fuel do you got, okay? The technology that we've just inserted at Grayling in Northern Strike 25 is what we call a translator. It's an inexpensive piece of technology, and Chairman, you saw it when you were up there, where it takes and it translates between all the databases of all the countries and now can tell you to tell somebody on a screen, on a computer, who's got what, where it's located at, and the best way to move it from point A to point B, because in Europe, you're going to use trucks, you're going to use rail, you're going to use boat. You have to go across multiple country lines, so you need all the permitting. It takes all of that and displays it on a single screen. And one of the ways we accomplish that is we put transponders on everything. So we put them on tanks, we put them on Jeeps, we put them on pallets of ammunition, we put them on fuel. And so now we can tell where that is in the fight immediately for a planner. That hasn't existed up until now. And so that's a great first technology that we've put in that we can start building on now. And we touched on the future part because what we in the military will say that the next war will be won if you can get from the fort to the port and then the port to the front. Because it's going to be contested every step of the way. This is no longer just, you know, you roll your army through Europe. You've got to get from home station to the port and get your stuff to the front. And so what Jim's just talking about, we now have a way to track it all the way from the fort. That's never been done before so that we know how much stuff is actually going to get to the front so we know what we have to fight with. So this is a very cool thing. So I didn't want to bash the Maven thing too much, but Maven does operations and intelligence and weather. Nothing about logistics. That's the vaporware part that I was talking about. We are filling that gap. That's what we do. Nobody else is doing that right now. And so you'll hear out of the DMVA, fort to port, port to front, and that's the game that we're in right now. It's going to be an important one. Okay. Well, I do appreciate that. And I know you have the task. I'm waiting for the conditions and standards coming forward, you know, just to keep with the military vernacular. But we do have a couple questions. We'll probably do a couple questions and then get into the next portion. But as you were speaking, because it's kind of important, this contested logistics. So there's always been contested logistics, whether, you know, World War II, there were subs, German subs in the Atlantic that, you know, it was contested, but it was a singular contest. You know, even I'd go to Iraq or Afghanistan. There was contested logistics, but, you know, it was kind of a singular contest, you know, whether they could hit the trucks on the road, you know, whether they could, you know, with IEDs or whether ambushes or some other mechanism contest things getting to the fobs. And sometimes it was difficult depending on where you were in the country, whether you got your water shipment that week or had to wait a week, et cetera. You know, but we could fly things in and there wasn't a lot of contested logistics when it came to the flights, which is, I believe, you know, as we morphed in Iraq, a lot of logistics were flight at certain points. But at some point you have to get boots on the ground and wheels on the road. So when you're talking contested logistics with cyber and AI and all the electronics that are now, it's not just a diesel engine on wheels that they're trying to stop or, you know, you've got to stop the wheels or the engine or the man or woman inside.
