So whether it's through the shield package in the area of drones, we want to be the lead in the nation on innovation, on homeland security, and certainly this would fall into that category where we're looking at that mobility logistics being the center, the lead in the nation, being the center and the lead in the nation on whether it's medical equipment, medical capability that's quick, easy to deploy, and easy to redeploy, which is usually the problem, you know, when you're deploying a hospital. And I was an engineering warrant, so I know I helped set up hospitals. You know, that was one of the 120 Alpha jobs was getting a hospital up and running and getting it electrified, getting that power, enough power to power cat machines, et cetera. That's a lot that's needed. One last kind of question and let you guys finish up, do your closing statements because we have, well, less than five minutes. So we do need to get out of here. But in the area of drones, because that's very important, what we're working with, various legislations, do you see drones being utilized within this contested logistics arena that you're talking about? And how will drones be used in the future when it comes to logistics in the military? And is that part of your plans and on your platforms? On the near-term shopping list, there are drones, right? So first of all, there are already shootable drones. So we can train. We can shoot them down at Grayling today. We're going to buy some non-shootable drones that, you know, they're investments. And then those drones are going to get bigger. And we're going to do things right up through medical where we'll do the airdrops. So we'll be training how to do that. So there'll be little drones, medium size, and large drones. So some of them are already at Grayling, and more are coming. And then to add to that, you're going to see drones being used more in, you know, like the Amazon delivery method, okay? And especially when it comes to, so once again, kind of go into the overall concept that we're going to be fighting in places where it's going to be contested and we don't want to put soldiers in harm's way if we don't have to. So when we look at strategies like for Indo-PACOM, we're looking at drones that will deliver fuel from a ship onshore to an island without a person being present on it, okay? So that if somebody tries to interdict that, they're not taking out a soldier. The same thing with delivering parts. If you've got a tank that is broken down, forward moving, okay, you could drive a part out to it to fix it, okay? Or now we've got drones that can carry a couple hundred pounds that can deliver a part right to that platform without exposing an individual soldier. So you're going to see drones integrated in a lot of different ways, but a lot of it's going to be with the new environment we're going to fight in, which is trying to keep soldiers out of harm's way. Well, we truly appreciate you, Jim and George, for being here today and your presentation. And certainly there'll be some conversations moving forward, and hopefully this is a good platform as well for your requests and asks as related to homeland security. And so we're glad that you were here today and appreciate your willingness and your testimony and all the work that you guys are doing where people don't even know. Civilians or military, they're not seeing what you're doing. So we appreciate you making this public and certainly everything we said and the slides, et cetera, will be on our public website as well moving forward. So thank you. Thank you and really appreciate the time and the questions. And by the way, you're all invited to Northern Strike next year in August if you want to come up and we'll give you some demos on technology and so forth. And also George is really good at integrating VIPs into the broader thing up there so he can also coordinate with Terry Sable and people like that if that's of help to you. As long as I get another ride, should I? I will vote on the Black Hawk, okay? Or the little birds. If you can get little birds.

All righty, we better end here. Seeing there's no excuse members and being no further business before this committee, we stand adjourned.

of this year, Haider Al-Fadawi of Dearborn, Michigan was badly beaten. He filed a police report on Friday the 22nd identifying the suspect. Well, the desk person says, I don't know, we don't want to give you your guns back, so you got to wait. So they didn't give him his guns back. So about 2 p.m. that afternoon, a member of the MSU Police Department who'd never met my client, never been on the scene, swears out an IRPO affidavit, which is immediately granted. So when we talk about most of these are granted, yeah, the process is loose, right? And so we're based on hearsay based on hearsay, actually, that application for an IRPO because the person, the sergeant who signed it, had no personal knowledge whatsoever. And she's reading police reports that it turns out we got a hold of later were wildly exaggerated. At no time, and we've got body cam video and audio, at no time during that interrogation did my client ever indicate that he was thinking of hurting himself or anyone else. What he did say under a lot of questioning at 3 a.m. by two armed police officers crowding up against him in the hallway is they said, have you ever thought about suicide? And he was dead honest. He said, well, yeah, hasn't everybody? Kind of something like that. So that was enough. And, of course, he thinks about suicide. He's been through all this military training on suicide, right? He's not going to lie. So that was enough for this red flag order to be issued, this ex parte order to be issued. So now he's got to come back to Michigan. He's got to hire an attorney because it's civil. He doesn't have a right to counsel, right? So his family gets together some money to hire me. I'm not a cheap service. And I start looking into it. I get a hold of the prosecutor and show the prosecutor that the MSU Police Department knew that he had been cleared by mental health before they ever signed the order. She says, well, that's some BS. I'll agree to dismiss it, right? So now we go to court. I'm standing next to the prosecutor, and we do what we try to do on the record, a stipulation to dismiss. But the judge, who's a well-meaning judge with a great reputation, says, well, these are kind of confusing. We're going to have to figure this process out together because she's got a bench book about an inch thick from Supreme Court Administrative Office. It's only the third one in the county, by the way, at that point. So she says, I don't think I can dismiss it. This isn't criminal. This is civil. I think I have to have your client come back for another hearing. Sir, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but you literally have like one minute. All right, I'll wrap it. We have to adjourn. Ultimately, we got my client's guns back, but he had to come back for two hearings from out of state and pay me and pay for all that travel in order to get his guns back for something that never should have happened, right? And now he's subjected to an investigation by his chain of command in the Marines because he has a potential mental health problem. Happy ending. Now, a year and a half later, he's doing well. He's been brought on full time in the Marines, and he's a full time active duty Marine now. But he went through hell, essentially, because of this law and how loose the procedures are. Thank you. Thank you, sir. And thank you to everybody that came today and participated. Like I said, we have numerous cards and emails that will go on the record. The clerk will record them on the record. I'm sorry we couldn't get to you today. Seeing no further business before the committee, we will adjourn. Thank you.

The Speaker, on behalf of the entire membership of the House of Representatives, offers House Resolution number 230, a resolution of tribute offered as a memorial for Martin Griffin, former member of the House of Representatives. Whereas it was with great sorrow that the members of the House of Representatives learned about the passing of Martin Marty Griffin. He will be remembered as a dedicated public servant by his constituents in Jackson County and the people of the state of Michigan. And whereas, born and raised in Jackson, Marty Griffin graduated from Lumen Christi High School and received a degree in communications from the University of Michigan. Marty's career in public service started during college as an intern for U.S. Representative Carl Purcell, who Marty continued working for after his graduation. And whereas Marty first began working in the Michigan legislature as a communications analyst before returning to Jackson to serve as a member of the city's planning commission and as mayor from 1995 to 2006. As mayor, Marty championed Jackson's economic redevelopment and served as a mentor to many of the future leaders of Jackson. And whereas Marty followed in his father's footsteps by serving the people of Jackson in the House of Representatives. Marty was elected twice, serving from 2007 to 2010. While in the legislature, he served on several committees, including the committees of agriculture, commerce, Great Lakes and environment, health policy, and new economy and quality of life, and was vice chair of the transportation committee and chair of both the Michigan Capitol committee and the committee on oversight and investigations. Marty was a capable legislator, sponsoring and co-sponsoring the adoption of many laws related to Michiganders' health, taxes, and public safety during his terms. Marty will be remembered by this chamber for his respect, humility, and love for the community he represented. And whereas Marty's commitment to public service did not end after his terms in the House of Representatives. He again served as mayor of Jackson from 2011 to 2013, making him the longest serving mayor in Jackson history. His commitment to Jackson continued after his mayorship, leading local volunteer organizations, working as a real estate professional within his beloved community, and serving as the Jackson City treasurer until his passing. And whereas Marty's legacy as an exemplary public service will live on and continue to touch those in the Jackson community and across the state of Michigan. Honoring his years of service to Jackson, the city has since renamed a park in tribute to him, his father, and his brother. And whereas upon Marty Griffin's passing, we offer our condolences to the bereaved as they mourn his loss. His contributions to this chamber and to the state of Michigan will be remembered. Now, therefore, be it resolved by the House of Representatives that we offer this expression of our highest tribute to honor the memory of Martin Marty Griffin, a member of the House of Representatives from 2007 to 2010. And be it further resolved that copies of this resolution be transmitted to the Griffin family as evidence of our lasting esteem for his memory. Speaker recognizes Representative Schmaltz. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. We come together today to remember and honor Martin Griffin, known to his family, friends, and everyone in Jackson as Marty. Marty spent his life in public service, the longest serving mayor in Jackson, holding office for 13 years, 1995 to 2006, and again from 2011 to 2013. He focused on urban revitalization and economic development, and he was successful in both of those areas. Marty was elected twice to represent Jackson in the legislature, 2007 to 2010. His father, Mike Griffin, served for 26 years as a Democratic representative. Marty was very proud of that. Mike, or Mick, as he was known, passed away last year. title: Education and Workforce — Wednesday, December 17, 2025
transcript:
The House Education and Workforce Committee will come to order. Would the clerk please call the roll? Representative Lenting? Representative Lenting? Here. Fox? Koons? Here. St. Germain? Here. Pablo? Here. Wilson? Here. Coulter? Here. Weiss? Here. Burns? Here. Madam Chair, we have 10 members present. You do have a quorum. Thank you. Vice Chair Lenting moves to adopt the minutes of the December 10th meeting. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. Thank you, Madam Clerk. The committee will begin today by taking further testimony on House Bill 5044, sponsored by Representative Wenzel. First, we are joined by Michelle Eddy, an attorney with the Thruon Law Firm here in Michigan. I understand her practice focuses primarily on special education, student issues, Title IX, and general school law matters. She is testifying in opposition. Please make your way to the table. We're happy to hear. Thank you, Chairwoman DeBoer. I appreciate the opportunity to speak to this committee in opposition to House Bill 5044. My name is Michelle Eddy. I'm an attorney with the Thruon Law Firm, and I am here on behalf of the over 1,000 members of the Michigan Association of Administrators for Special Education, or MASE. That includes special education administrators from local intermediate school districts as well as public school academies. As a way of background, the Thruon Law Firm is an education law firm. We have represented school districts in this state for over 75 years. We represent over 525 school districts here in the state of Michigan, and so our practice takes us throughout the state, including the UP. And so for me and for the last 30 years of my legal practice, I have focused specifically on special education issues as well as some other general school law matters, and it's with that lens that I come to speak with you today. As you know, a number of students with autism and other disabilities have been receiving outside ABA services or other therapies or medically necessary therapies, and there's been an increase of that over the years. And we have seen schools really struggle with how to properly address requests and demands from outside providers for things such as giving them space in the building during the school day to work with the student or to have the provider accompany the student throughout the school day, even though maybe that student already has a paraprofessional. While school officials value and recognize the importance of collaborating with these outside partners, they are struggling to balance the important role that they serve in educating students with the efforts and the responsibilities of those outside providers. I think it's important to note that school districts have legal obligations to our students with disabilities under both federal and state law. Specifically, they have an obligation to provide those students educational programs and services at no cost to their parents or guardians that will allow the student to receive meaningful educational benefit while they're in school, or what we refer to as FAPE, a free appropriate public education. That is what the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act requires of schools to provide all eligible students with a disability, as that term is defined under the IDEA, a free appropriate public education. And part of providing a free appropriate public education requires that we ensure maximum access to the school district's general curriculum and providing curriculum and programming that offers our students with disabilities an opportunity to earn a regular high school diploma consistent with the Michigan Merit Curriculum. Additionally, schools have an obligation to educate those students in the least restrictive environment to the extent appropriate for the student, which means time with their non-disabled peers is essential and required in students' IEPs for those who can participate in general education offerings. So it's with those obligations that schools struggle with House Bill 5044. Unfortunately, the bill interferes with the school's ability to comply with these key laws and important mandates and could result in students not receiving all of their required IEP services, having access to non-disabled peers, or the required access to the general ed curriculum as schools attempt to try to juggle coordinating these outside services with mandated educational services provided for under the IDEA and other laws. Some key points to consider. ABA therapy has been consistently defined in case law as either special education or a related service by the courts. IEP teams, that's going to be the team that knows the student best, who designs

student's educational plan. They are legally required to determine if or when and under what circumstances a student requires ABA services in order to receive a free appropriate public education. So IEP teams should already be looking at whether or not ABA services are educationally necessary for providing that student a free appropriate public education. And in fact, many schools do indeed incorporate ABA therapy into students' IEP goals or in terms of related services or supplemental aids and supports. It's already in many students' IEPs. Additionally, the U.S. Department of Education Office of Special Education Programs, as well as state and federal courts, have concluded that there is no per se entitlement to ABA services during the school day or even on school property, even if those services have been determined medically necessary by a student's physician or other health provider. Instead, schools are required to ensure that their decisions regarding the student's needs, and that the student's IEP reflects the student's unique needs. And if that means that a student can only receive meaningful educational benefit from their education through ABA services, the school is required to provide those services themselves as part of providing the student a free appropriate public education. It's been argued by proponents of this bill that ABA services or medically necessary treatment in the schools is required under the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act as a required accommodation. That position is not supported by the text of Section 504 or the ADA or the case law interpreting those statutes. As most of you are aware, the primary purpose of the ADA and Section 504, two federal disability discrimination statutes, is to provide individuals with disabilities equal access to an entity's programs, activities, and services. Part of that process is to engage in an interactive process with the individual with a disability to determine what accommodations may be needed. It's not an automatic. And so, therefore, that is the falsehood in that argument. There isn't an automatic entitlement to ABA services in the school as a reasonable accommodation. Reasonable accommodations are determined on an individual review of a particular individual with disabilities' circumstances, what their needs are, and taking a look at whether or not the accommodation results in an undue burden or a fundamental alteration of the school's programs and services. Now, proponents have said that ABA services would essentially in the school would help maximize the student's potential and allow them to grow and be successful in all settings. But that goal is a far cry from equal access required under Section 504 and the ADA. Equal access is not the same as maximizing an individual's potential. And that's the crux of both Section 504 and the ADA. Finally, I want to note that I believe there were some questions from the committee about how insurance might play a factor in here. And I'll be the first to say I'm not a Medicaid or insurance guru, okay? That's not my thing. But I do think it's important to note a 1999 case here in Michigan that involved a Michigan public school. They had a young man who was involved in a very tragic bike-car accident and became severely disabled because of that. And as a result of that accident, the student required round-the-clock nursing services, which his insurance company paid for. When the student was well enough to return to school, the nursing services continued because he required that level of care. Fast forward a few years later, the insurance company sued the school district, seeking a declaratory ruling as well as reimbursement for the funds that they had expended in providing nursing services to the student during the school day. Because the insurance company's argument was that these medically necessary services were needed during the educational day, and therefore the school district was required to provide that as a component of a free appropriate public education. So the insurance company essentially made a subrogation, advanced a subrogation theory, and they prevailed. And the school district was required to reimburse the insurance company for those services during the school day. So I think that that case alone causes me a bit of a pause about this bill and how insurance companies may approach this if services are being provided in the school, during the school day in the school. And how do you essentially balance that with who's responsible? Because once you say that we need to provide those services during the school day, does that indeed become the school district's responsibility under their obligation in the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act? So what's the answer for all of this? I will tell you, I think it is the guidance, the recently issued guidance from the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services and the Michigan Department of Education. This is the first time that schools have received some guidance on these issues. And clients that I've talked to, schools that I have talked to, were excited to learn that there was some guidance there to help them navigate these tough questions that they are dealing and trying to balance these issues and the requests from parents and outside providers to provide services within the school setting. I think the most important part of this guidance is the fact that it clearly reminds school officials that they must first consider whether or not they as a school under their obligations under the IDEA must provide these services to the student in order for the student to receive meaningful educational benefit from their IEPs. And what I like about the guidance is that it also goes further. It gives a good first step, but it also talks about considerations such as liability and other concerns which schools rightfully have when you're talking about outside individuals coming into the school, working with students, being around other students, and largely not being supervised by anybody in the school. There are certainly liability concerns. And this guidance talks about those considerations and helps schools, giving them a framework to help guide some of the decision-making in this regard. I know you are going to be hearing from the Michigan Department of Education next about this guidance, but I was excited to see this issued in May. And when I have shared it with my school clients, they've been excited to see it and they were like, thank you, some guidance. Because they want to do what's right.

Schools want to do what's right, but they also want to ensure that the students receive all of their IEP-required services, that they get true access to the general ed curriculum, and that they get to maximize those opportunities with their non-disabled peers. And the question is, how do we do all of that in a school day when we are also looking at mandating outside services in the school setting? Thank you. Thank you, ma'am. Any questions? Representative Koontz. Thank you, Madam Chair. Counselor, I apologize. I try and ask very direct questions. So in advance, I apologize. The guidelines are not binding. Wouldn't it be better to put this in statute? I don't know. Obviously, we're all here. We're trying to do the right thing. So again, forgive my vagueness on the question. But the guidelines are not binding. So when we get people in, they say, well, that's just a guideline. We don't need to do that. So here's where I'm struggling is, wouldn't it be better to quantify this? I think that's a great question. And you're right. We are always very quick to say, well, that's guidance. That's not the law. So we don't have to follow it. But guidance is important because this is guidance from an administrative agency. And courts will give deference to that guidance in court cases, even though it's not, quote, binding law. They look to the administrative agencies as being experts in this area. So they will give deference to that guidance. Two, I think it is important with this guidance just being rolled out to kind of see whether or not it has the desired effect before perhaps taking those next steps of going the route. When did the guidance come out? In May. OK. Yes. And Madam Chair, if I may follow up with a question. You had referenced some conflicts that this proposed legislation, 5044, conflicts with federal law. Could you expand on that? Did I misunderstand that? Well, school districts have an obligation to ensure that students with disabilities receive a free appropriate public education. I won't use acronyms, FAPE. And part of that is providing students programs and services that are going to allow the student to access the general ed curriculum and to provide them a meaningful educational benefit. And so that for some students could involve some specially designed instruction or special ed with a special teacher during certain times of the school day. They may be pulled out to be working with a speech therapist or an occupational therapist during the school day. So all of those things are legally required by the student's IEP. Failure to provide those services can result in liability to the school for failing or what we refer to as a denial of FAPE for the student. So that is one thing. Compliance, the IEP is essentially a written contract. It's a commitment by the district that they're going to ensure to provide those services. Additionally, schools are required to measure the student's progress towards those goals. And if the student isn't making progress for whatever reason, including that they're not having enough time to receive those services because they're being pulled out or directed to outside ABA services, then districts are required to review and revise that IEP to try to ensure that the student is able to make progress to goals and objectives. So the concern is that the provision of outside services during the school day may interrupt the regular programming and services that students are required to receive, not only under their IEP, but a lot of the students are also in general ed classes for reading, writing, math, social studies, science. When do you look to pull a student, if that's what is being proposed, out of what class? If we look to say, hey, we'll pull a student out of recess or a special or elective class, those times are oftentimes the only time that a student might have opportunities to be interacting with their non-disabled peers. So they won't be able to take advantage of those inclusion opportunities. So that's the concern. Thank you. Thank you, Counselor. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you. Representative Weiss. Thank you. Thank you for your testimony today. I did want to follow up on a concern that you brought up around insurance. And it has been something that we haven't really discussed that much in committee around this issue. As written, as the bill is currently written, is there any clarity in terms of who would be responsible for paying for these ABA services if they were offered during the school day? And also, could there be additional concerns around liability perhaps as well? And is there anything in the bill to address either of those issues? And could there potentially be? Okay. Sorry, that was a lot. A question and one question. So in terms of insurance, my read of the bill is that issue is not currently addressed. So that, again, sort of raises concerns for me. Liability is also not specifically addressed in the bill. I guess perhaps it is contemplated that that could be part of policy that is required by the bill. But that is certainly a concern. And I will be blunt. That is, as a lawyer, when I'm talking with clients and they are talking about the risk of having an outside ABI or any other service provider in, that's one of the primary issues that I do discuss with my clients. Because, again, these individuals, they're not employees of the district. We would not know if there have been background checks, you know, fingerprinting done. They're not employees, so they're not subject to the revised school code requirements that there be a comprehensive background check. If they're working individually with a student who's providing supervision and oversight, that person is not a school employee. So that's not the principal. It's not the teacher. And so even those small issues like that cause me concern and certainly make me pause when we talk about having anyone outside coming in. And I'm not sure that simply doing a quick background check or filling out sort of a volunteer form would satisfy those potential liability concerns. And that is not addressed in the bill as currently written. Okay. Thank you. Any other questions? No. Oh, yes. Representative Paquette. Thank you, Madam Chair. So do you, kind of back to Representative Coons' points, do you suspect then, like, with the guidelines being implemented, that this will remedy some of the problems of facilitating outside services coming in and then wait and see? That would be my hope. What timeline would you say would be a good time then to return to this down the road? That's a very good question. And I think right now it was rolled out in May, but quite frankly, I have to laugh. One of my clients brought it to my attention. So there wasn't a lot of fanfare to it. I mean, I usually kind of try to stay abreast of things, and the client said, well, I've gotten this, and I said, what are you talking about? And so I first learned of that guidance probably in June of this year. So I don't think that there's been an adequate rollout of the guidance. My understanding is that is going to occur, and I'm going to defer to MDE to kind of talk about that. Why wasn't it adequate, the rollout? Why wasn't it adequate? From the standpoint, I'm not sure that every school district or public school academy in the state is aware that that guidance is out there. I know that certainly my office has we do newsletters and things of that nature, and we're trying to get that information out to our clients, but I'm not sure it's been publicly disseminated. Maybe it did occur in May, but I'm still talking to

schools that were not aware that that guidance was out there. So that's why I'm saying I think there needs to be either a bigger rollout or some other type of announcement to make sure that people are aware that it is out there. Gotcha. And so kind of back to that timeline question is when do you think would be an appropriate time to return to this to be like, oh, were the guidelines effective or not? I would say that we would I think it would make sense to at least once there's been an appropriate rollout or announcement of that, maybe revisiting this anywhere from a year, year and a half down the road to get feedback on whether or not we're seeing any changes. Thank you. Thank you. Okay, thank you so much. We appreciate you coming in. Thank you very much again for having me here. Thank you. So in continuing with the testimony on House Bill 5044, we have testimony from the Michigan Department of Education on the guidelines for the provision of the applied behavior analysis, ABA, in public schools. This recent document was mentioned during previous testimony, but not in any detail. So please introduce yourselves and begin when you are ready. Good morning, members. Can everyone hear me okay? All right. My name is Olivia Ponti, and I am the legislative liaison for the Michigan Department of Education. So thank you so much for the invitation to come in and talk about the guidelines for the provision of ABA in schools this morning. Yeah, like you said, there were a few questions from some of the previous committee hearings about what's in the guidelines, when did they come out, as was just discussed, they're pretty hot off the presses. So I have Rebecca and Amy here with me to discuss what is in the guidelines. And with that, I'm going to turn it over to them. All right. All right. Thank you, Madam Chair, for allowing us the opportunity to come in and the rest of the committee as well. I am Rebecca McIntyre. I'm the assistant director in the Office of Special Education at Michigan Department of Education. I bring with me experience as a special education teacher in a local school district and special education administration at an intermediate school district before joining the team at Michigan Department of Education. As well, I served on the Michigan Autism Council while I was both at the intermediate school district and Michigan Department of Education when I moved here. So bring that lens as well. Good morning, everyone. I am Amy Matthews, and I'm going to kind of talk about a few different hats that I wear. I am faculty at Grand Valley State University in the psychology department, have been there for about 27 years. And I am also the director of the Statewide Autism Resources and Training Project START, funded by the Michigan Department of Ed Office of Special Education. And I'm the chair of the Autism Council, but I am not here representing the Autism Council today. I'm a licensed psychologist, board-certified behavior analyst, but I've been working in public schools for the past 25 years and worked in private programs before that. Okay, so before we get started, we're here today to provide you some information about the guidelines for the provision of applied behavior analysis, ABA, in schools. So Amy's going to provide you with some historical perspective, and I'm going to talk about the development of those guidelines before we get into the meat of the guidelines. But I do want to start by saying that these guidelines center on the obligation of school districts that they have and the roles and responsibilities of the private providers, the ABA providers, and the behavior analysts and how those can be provided in school. Okay, so we have, we're going to walk through these. We are going to be using acronyms, so I like to set the stage here because it will speed this up just a little bit. So we will be talking about autism spectrum disorder, so ASD, free appropriate public education will be FAPE, LRE, least restrictive environment, the IDEA, Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. So these are things that you're going to see school districts having an obligation for. So IEP, individualized education program. We'll also have IEP teams that we'll talk about. We'll also talk about multi-tiered systems of supports and positive behavior interventions and supports. Those are provided within school districts as well. Then we'll also talk about ABA and what is it, and board-certified behavior analysts and assistant behavior analysts and registered behavior technicians. Those are the roles that we are seeing within schools to provide ABA services. All right, so I'm going to provide just a little bit of historical perspective, like how did we get to this place where we would even need these guidelines? So I had mentioned I've been doing this for a long time. I've been working in the field of autism, behavior analysis, education for about 35 years. So I saw where we were in the past and kind of where we are now, and despite the fact that there are some tensions, I think we're in a much better place as far as offering services to students. But we know a lot of autistic students need more intensive services in order to meet their needs in the areas of communication, social interaction, learning, regulation, adaptive care skills, and we want them to be able to be successful across environments, school, home, and community. Historically, services were primarily provided to students in the school environment. That's where I was, you know, early on. So the reason I worked in private schools early on is there just weren't a lot of ABA services in any other settings. There wasn't insurance-based services. Insurance did not reimburse for applied behavior analysis for individuals with autism. So in 2012, legislation was passed in Michigan so that ABA services would be covered under both public and private insurance, and that was happening across the country. So for the first time, ABA would be a covered service. Before that, families paid out of pocket for ABA services. And board-certified behavior analysts are the folks who provide those insurance-based services. So why is this important? Well, this becomes important because now we have schools providing services to students as they have for as long as students with disabilities have been given services within schools. But we also have board-certified behavior analysts providing ABA services in a clinical setting. So we suddenly need opportunities for them to be able to coordinate and collaborate around those services. So this is fairly new. Within the past 13 years, we've really had to kind of look at coordinating these services in a way that we didn't have to in the past. So the Michigan guidelines were our effort to look at how we can create these opportunities for better collaboration and coordination between schools and providers. Because we were hearing that there were some tensions around coordinating these services. So I know one of the questions was, like, how long will this take in order to see some kind of outcome? And what we know from research is three to five years for complete systems change. I think it should be monitored every year to see if we're making progress, but I don't anticipate that full changes are going to happen immediately. So I think the guidelines do need a little bit of time and intentional effort to see some real progress. Okay, so in 2019, and this was when I was serving on the Autism Council as well, the Medicaid expansion, the Caring for Students expansion applied to all students, general education and special education, and it included a very specific opportunity for reimbursements for BCBAs and BCABAs in schools. And so really the intent of that was to allow for BCBAs and BCABAs to work in the schools supporting multi-tiered systems of supports through PBIS, through any behavioral supports, whether it be whole school, classroom, individual students, but working to support behaviors. It wasn't until 2022 there was a recommendation through the Autism Council because there were conversations going on about legislation and introducing legislation that would require, I believe the legislation was similar to the state of Colorado's, and bringing that here into Michigan. And the patent is what really makes us special and sets us apart is because, as Roy was saying, we host, grow, and distribute beneficial bacteria right in the body of water. And that's what's so exciting about our technology is that it makes us exponentially more powerful. But when we put the system in the water, we're actually becoming part of the aquatic system so that when you grow microbes in the body of the water the way that we are, you actually become part of the aquatic system and you're growing what's successful because it's survival of the fittest in nature. I know it's a little bit different than, say, a typical... Algaecide is a healthier aspect of a pesticide or an herbicide or those type of things, right? There will be lakes that maybe DNR manages. situations like in my local town when I was on a lake improvement board it was actually a river that opened up into a lake and then of course it drained out into Lake Michigan. So Michigan has one of the highest application fees among the states, and this would cut it from $10,000 to $5,000, which could result in more captive applications. And also it aligns Michigan with other domestic domiciles. And then lastly, it also streamlines the exemptions and waivers and allows DIFs to, we can more easily grant a lot of these exemption waivers that we currently do so. And removing this requirement would decrease the cost of regulation and allow captives an accommodation that traditional insurance companies already are entitled to. Overall, these bills serve as a great opportunity to make some important modernizations. And currently in Michigan, Michigan companies that have a captive, they choose to domicile in another state. So, and a lot of times that is due to, at least in part, our regulatory framework being restrictive and outdated. DIFs conducted a thorough review, compared ourselves to other states, engaged with companies and put this proposal together. And these reforms are a simple way to update our law and make Michigan more competitive. So thanks for the opportunity to kind of go over these bills and happy to answer any questions. And if I may, Mr. Gregory

Orkowski practices law specifically in the captive insurance arena. Thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. I appreciate the opportunity to talk today. My name is Greg Nowakowski, as mentioned. I work for a law firm called Honigman that does a lot of different captive insurance work, whether it's in Michigan or many other states. And so that's been my practice for the last, not to have old jokes attached to me, for the last 15 years. But at least I'm glad that Representative Tisdale took the hard work in laboring on trying to describe to you what a captive insurance company is, because I struggle with that. You know, when you do your elevator speech, meeting new people, what do you do? I represent captive insurance companies. Well, what is that? And then you're sitting there trying to figure out how to explain that. So you did a nice job of laying that forward for the committee. We are in support of these bills to modernize and enhance Michigan as a captive domicile. If you look at some of our competitor states, Vermont, biggest domicile in the world, had something like 683 or so different captives and has similar language to what DIFTS is proposing in terms of the captive enhancements that are proposed by the bills. Then you come into a couple of foreign jurisdictions that are second and third, and you get to states like Utah and North Carolina, Delaware, and Arizona that are in the 200, 300 captive insurance companies ranges. And, of course, there's probably two different ways to think about measuring captives, and one is what Jenny had mentioned in terms of premium dollars. And then there's number of captives. Obviously, statistics can count all kinds of different funny ways about how many captives there are. But the point is Michigan with 27 is not in the hundreds yet, and we want to make sure we try to enhance that, particularly for Michigan companies. It's important for them to consider Michigan. But when we say consider Michigan and then you run into the speed bumps that the current statute has from 2008 when it was first enacted, it becomes an impediment to bringing more and more captive business to the state of Michigan, which is really what we're trying to do. I won't repeat any of the other marks I had because they've already been covered. You have some written testimony to enhance your midnight reading when you have nothing else to do. But I will make one other comment to one of the bills that talks about clarifying what a captive insurance company can and cannot write under its limited certificate of authority in the workers' comp compensation coverage arena. And obviously there are two regulatory regimes, at least two regulatory regimes here we're thinking about. One is the workers' compensation authority, not what we're talking about here. That's a different arena. Here we're talking about insurance and what that limited certificate of authority can be used for in terms of workers' comp. And there's some language in there that is designed to say, listen, if there's a commercial workers' compensation carrier involved, but let's say there's a $100,000 deductible on that commercial insurance policy, can you put the $100,000 deductible in a captive insurance company? And the way the statute was originally written, there's an argument to say, no, you can't. I think DIFTS, and you can speak to this, I suppose, I think DIFTS is traditionally regulated and Dave Piner's office is regulated in the sense that the statute is unclear and you can put that in a captive insurance company. So one of the bills is designed to clarify that language, and we've suggested some language as well for the committee's consideration in the written memo that further clarifies that if we're talking about a deductible piece, if we're talking about excess over and above what the workers' compensation statute requires to be written by a commercial authorized carrier, or if we're talking about reinsuring some of that workers' compensation risk in a captive, that a captive could do that vis-a-vis the limited certificate of authority that DIFTS issues to a captive. So that's sort of the ending, concluding part of our memo to you. Fantastic. Thank you. Well, thank you all for being here. If you don't mind sticking around for a minute in case we have questions, and I'll just start off. So you had mentioned, I'm just going to pick on you specifically, since I already beat up on my vice chair. You can pick on me now. So you mentioned Vermont and maybe a couple other states that this is a really attractive thing in those states. What makes them more attractive? The distinguishing factor is I think the statute is a little more flexible, and so that's a large part what the proposed amendments are designed to do. You've already mentioned this, but I'll give you an example. Company comes, they have a fiscal year that's 6-30 instead of calendar year, but the statute says you have to make a filing with the insurance department based on a calendar year cadence. The information isn't available, so you have to do a bunch of extra work to make up management, financial accounts, or something to give to meet your obligations of the statute, but then you're struggling to make your fiscal year mirror what's going on in Michigan. So it's a much more flexible regime. It provides more regulatory authority to Dave Piner's office and the captive group, who's done a fantastic job, of course, with what they have, but we need more flexibility to them to say, listen, make sure we monitor your filings. We need to make sure your captive insurance company doesn't go bankrupt. That's important. We want to make sure the coverage that we write to Michigan residents has some real force and effect behind it, but do it in a way that the department can have flexibility and regulation and say, listen, your timeline is your timeline. That's fine. File within three months of your fiscal year. Give us the same information, just make it work for you. And so I think that's largely a part of it. I think in Vermont, they were earlier in the process. Captives originally started really related, for the most part, to the medical malpractice crisis. Oh, 50 years ago now makes some old comments. Some of us were around, some of us weren't. But back in those days, I feel like I'm going to get the hook. So when hospitals couldn't find malpractice insurance to put those coverages forward, in Vermont, the Cayman Islands, and Bermuda were sort of the leading domiciles. So they've been around. Vermont's been around for a lot longer than Michigan, Michigan being in 2008, so it hasn't had enough time to sort of develop. So that's another reason that's just a fact. It's not really related to the legislation, just the background information for you. Great. Thank you. Any other questions from the committee? Rep Fitzgerald. Thank you all. Appreciate the information. Yes, we did see this last term. You know, one question that I do have is obviously we do have other states and domiciled locations that I guess have had the open sign out for quite a bit longer, right? Vermont and others. We are wanting to make sure that we attract new captives here. How are we putting out that open sign to when we have established networks in North Carolina, Vermont, Delaware, and others? How do we compete against that as Michigan now? Are we doing enough with just this legislation to say we're open for business? We want to see this come here. Or are there, you know, I guess I'm in a competitive world, like you have experienced, you know, representing some of these captives. Are we prepared to compete? A couple comments there. One is Michigan, if we have a Michigan-based company, Michigan has to be on the list of considerations for potential domicile. It always is. We'll always do that. That's from my personal perspective. That's only a small piece of it, admittedly. From a larger perspective, there are a number of different avenues to get the word out, and I believe Dave and his group goes to conferences, the Vermont Captive Insurance Conference, the South Carolina. Every domicile usually has some sort of conference where the group gets out and gets the word out saying, hey, we've amended and enhanced our captive statute. You should consider Michigan as a domicile, as a marketing matter, and to try to get to those clients and prospective clients, prospective captive owners to form in the state of Michigan. You can maybe speak to some of that. I don't know. Dave goes to all those different conferences in your group. Yeah, I'm happy to add to that. And, you know, just to take it back a little bit. So to 2008 when Michigan first implemented our captive statue, I think there was some level of skepticism on the part of the department at the time of is this a good path we want to go down? We've had a lot of time since then to see what's been impactful in the industry, and it's a good alternative option for some businesses to consider. So since that time, I would say six, eight years ago or something like that, we started to really dive in deeper on what some other states did better. How are they incentivizing captives to domicile there? As mentioned, Dave Piner goes to these conferences, has those conversations, and has overwhelmingly heard these are the things that we need to change in Michigan statute to incentivize captives to try to domicile here. It is painful when we have a large manufacturer in the state that decides they want to domicile their captive elsewhere, and we want to do everything we can within our power to try to incentivize them as an economic development thing, as a fairness thing to locate in Michigan and have their captive in our state of Michigan as the primary regulator. Can you remind me, is it a requirement that the board of the captive meet in the domiciled location annually? Is it required that they meet in that physical location? I can't recall. The current statute, I believe, requires one meeting, at least one meeting per year in the

We're willing to do it if someone has to. If you don't mind, I just would like to point out that the bill eliminates the requirement for the in-state board meeting each year to provide that flexibility. Thank you. All right, any other questions? No? Well, thank you all for being here, and thank you guys for presenting this. With that, we need a motion to excuse absent members. Rep. Fitzgerald makes that motion. Oh my gosh, I can't talk today. Absent members are excused, and with no further business before the committee, the committee is adjourned. Thank you.
