title: Appropriations 25-12-16
transcript:
I am not the one who is going to be able to do it.

Okay, good afternoon. Oh, I guess good morning. The Senate Committee on Appropriations is called to order. Mr. Clerk, will you please call the roll? Chair Anthony. Here. Senator McCann. Here. Senator Cherry. Here. Senator Bear. Here. Senator Santana. Here. Senator Shink. Here. Senator Irwin. Here. Senator Hertel. Here. Senator Kavanaugh. Here. Senator Kleinfeld. Here. Senator McMorrow. Here. Senator Camilieri. Here. Senator Bumstead. Here. Senator Albert. Here. Senator DeMoose. Senator Heisinga. Here. Senator Altman. And Senator Tice. Madam Chair, you have 18 members present. You have a quorum. Thank you. I move to adopt the minutes from the December 9th, 2025 hearing, supported by Senator Bumstead. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. Colleagues, many of you know that years ago I was a legislative staffer in the House, and it taught me a lot about this place. And I remember watching the former chair of the House Appropriations Committee, George Cushenberry. He provided what was called chairman's remarks. And this is something that I have not employed since I've been in this role, but this moment I believe requires and demands it. Last week, the House Appropriations Committee employed a rarely used provision in the Management and Budget Act that allows either the House or the Senate Appropriations Committee to disapprove any work projects. Now, like so many actions taken by the committee across the hall over the course of this year, House Republicans made decisions behind closed doors, without debate, without deliberation or public discussion, without the ability of impacted communities to discuss the merits of their grant funds. Mind you, they didn't reject all the work projects in an effort to find waste, fraud, and abuse. No, they made decisions. In a back room, they decided to approve funding for large corporations, but cut funding for lead-poisoned children or mental health services for sexually assaulted children here in the mid-Michigan area. By clawing back funding, RX Kids, the popular program that helps new and expected parents with the ever-increasing costs, are now in jeopardy. And local units of government like Hamtramck must now wait on delivery of a fire truck that might save both lives and property. Mind you, the same chamber that for the entire year has preached the gospel of transparency and accountability, only to show themselves as obedient to hypocrisy, cruelty, and partisan politics. Keep in mind, this was an exercise in political gamesmanship that has not only impacted Democratic constituents or Republican constituents, all of our constituents have been impacted across the state. Now, mind you, and some of us come from local government, when someone's house is on fire, they don't ask if a Democrat or a Republican fought for the funding for the fire truck. They ask, did you bring enough water? Local governments, hospitals, nonprofits, workforce partners made hiring decisions, signed contracts with the state based on the reasonable expectation that these funds would be there, that they could trust our word, that the state budget that was duly negotiated by the House and the Senate, approved and voted on by Democrats and Republicans and signed by the governor, would provide some assurances that their funds would be available to serve Michiganders without delay. They changed the rules midstream. It's a bad fiscal policy and terrible governance. What does this say about our reputation as a state? Let me be absolutely clear. As the chair of this committee, I will fight and use every tool available, legislation, negotiations, the budget process, to work with my colleagues and the governor to restore these funds and protect the integrity of our budget process.

It's all we have in this room is our word. No one person, no one chamber has the authority to undermine the budget negotiations, previous or future. Gutting these important programs using a unilateral process needlessly and without forewarning poses the very real risk of causing harm and endangering lives. And the results have the potential to be catastrophic for the families that these grantees serve. On to the purpose of the hearing today. I want them to have the opportunity that they didn't have in the chamber across the hall. I want them to be heard. I want you all to hear directly about the impact of the sloppy, politically irresponsible, and dare I say corrupt action of the House Republicans. Members, this is our charge for today. I want you to listen to the collective voices of our constituents and ask yourself these questions. Are the supports for new moms and babies, is that waste? Do you consider infrastructure projects for school districts, fraud? Funding for public safety, is that abuse? And ultimately, do the knee-jerk, secretive actions of the House Republicans warrant the chaos and confusion inflicted upon our local partners? Spoiler alert, I don't think it warrants it. We will start out by having testimony virtually, out of respect for time. We will start with Maggie Varney with Wigs for Kids. Could you please just again restate your name and in maybe three to five minutes just talk a little bit about the work project that was rejected and any additional commentary for the committee. Hi, my name is Maggie Varney and I'm the founder and CEO of Maggie's Wigs for Kids of Michigan. What we do is provide wigs and support services for children all throughout the state of Michigan, even up into the Upper. And we have serviced over 6,000 children since we started this organization 23 years ago. Due to the Michigan state law, commercial health insurance does not cover wigs for children under the age of 18. And because of their treatment, due to their treatment, they lose their hair. Therefore, we fill the void for the children in the state at no cost to them and their family. We are fortunate to have been included in the budget, the 24-25 budget, and receive approval for $125,000 in funding to help us provide wigs and support services for these children and their families. We work hand in hand with representatives from Michigan Department of Health and Human Services throughout the entirety of the project. And we're told repeatedly that the funding we were granted was secured and could continue to be used until the end of, and not only the end of September, but the end of the year. It takes approximately three months of time when we order a wig because each one is custom made for the children. So they don't charge us until we take receipt of the wig. And these orders were filled in confidence that the funds would be there and cover the cost of the wigs. Unfortunately, with the actions taken last week by the House of Representatives, we have lost $56,500. Now we are a small grassroots nonprofit. That is a lot of money to us for sure. And that would be available for us to pay for the wigs that we had ordered. Because we explained to them that when we order them, we can't pay for them until we receive them. And they told us, of course, the money would be there. We feel caught in the middle and blindsided by the decision to recapture funds. We have done this work for 23 years and will continue to do our very best to serve the children and their families at no cost. I want to thank you for your time and attention this morning. And thank you for being the voice for these children who obviously can't speak up for themselves. Thank you, Maggie. Members, are there any questions? Senator Hertel. Thank you, Madam Chair. And Maggie, thank you for being with us here virtually today. I go back to about a decade ago when I first toured Wigs for Kids with Maggie. My wife was with me. We left there in tears seeing the services that they provide to kids not only in St. Clair Shores, where they're located, not only in Macomb County, not only in Southeast Michigan, across the entire state. Kids that are going through cancer treatment, through other diseases, and the confidence that they receive from the services that Maggie and her team provide are without a doubt life-changing for them. And knowing Maggie and her team and working with them for over a decade, there is not a dollar that goes into this organization that doesn't go to service a child. In fact, I remember years ago, Maggie, when we were talking when you were going through a lawsuit from an organization in, I believe, Ohio that was challenging your name. And you told me that you would never take a dollar to spend on legal fees because that money should go to the kids that need help. And so when I found out last week about this grant being pulled back, I was infuriated. There is no reason politically or any other reason that this should be happening right now. And the reality is, it's as simple as this, as you stated, Maggie. There is a bill coming for $56,000 to your organization that you believe you had money from. You worked with the department to ensure those dollars would be there. The wigs are coming for those children. The bill is coming to your organization, and now you will not have that $56,000 to pay that bill, which means those resources then have to come from somewhere else. It's not any more complicated than that right there. Did anybody from the House Appropriations Committee, any representative from the committee, reach out to you and ask you any questions about this funding before the decision was made last week? No, I had no idea that this was going to happen. And you can imagine these wigs, like you said, are already ordered and need to be paid for. And that's a lot of money to a small organization. So we really appreciate you, Kevin Hertel, Senator Hertel, I'm sorry, stepping up not only now, but for the last 10 years and always being there in our corner and helping us to get the word out so we can reach more children and service more children. We work with all nine hospitals all throughout Michigan that service pediatric oncology. And that is our focus, and over 50% of our kids do have cancer. But these kids need these wigs for other reasons. They need them when they have a dog bite or a hydrocephalus or blood disorders. And there's so many different reasons why children need these wigs. And they get bullied at school. And this allows them to just be a kid and go back out into society and feel and look like their peers and fit in and have a sense of belonging. Well, Maggie, I thank you for all the work that you do. It's been an honor to work with you on all of it. You have my commitment that I will do everything that I can to make sure we work in a bipartisan way to get these resources put back so that your organization gets the money that it's due through this grant. And I apologize that, you know, this is a perfect example of how dysfunctional this place has become when we have to have these conversations about dollars that were rightfully appropriated by this legislature and now have been clawed back for no other reason than somebody is looking for a negotiation tactic or playing petty political games. There's no place for it here, and I'm sorry that your organization has been impacted. We will do everything we can to fix it. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Senator Hertel. Thank you, Maggie. We appreciate it. Thank you, Senator. Thank you. Also on Zoom, I believe we have someone from Seriously Dexter. Is Chrissy Kimser? Yes. Hi, I'm Chrissy Kimser, and I'm here representing Seriously Dexter. I'm not sure if it's possible for me to share my screen. I did put together some slides just to help guide the work that we do. So I'll try to do that now. But hi, I am the coalition director of Seriously Dexter. We are a local nonprofit community coalition that works in Dexter, Michigan to prevent youth substance use prevention or to prevent youth substance use.

support youth mental health. We were also impacted by the decision made by House Republicans. Our coalition has been around since 2012. We've formally been supported by federal grants, but those grants are only 10 years long, and so we were able to work with local legislators to get our labor and economic opportunity grant of $125,000 that would have provided us funding through October 2026. The bulk of that funding is to pay for staff time because we do a lot of work in our community, and then a lot of that funding also will go to projects that are led by students. We, just like Maggie, were completely blindsided, did not know that grant funds that had been signed into contract could be taken away, and we are entirely scrambling to make sure that our work can continue in our community so that we can keep impacting and helping youth who need help. Just a very quick overview. We, like I said, work to support youth mental health, decrease substance use, strengthen positive connections between youth and their community, their schools, et cetera. We do that through hosting and leading and organizing programs and events that decrease environmental risk factors for youth and help increase and support protective factors for youth, which you can see listed there, hopefully, if you're able to see my screen. But our work is data-driven. We use research best practices for prevention work that is directly from the CDC, the National Institute of Drug Abuse, and from SAMHSA as well. So how is this going to affect us? Like I said, the majority of our staffing is supported by this LEAH grant, so it is honestly unclear at this point if our coalition and all the work that we do can continue. So that means that over 300 students, and next are going to get emotional because I really care about these kids, will no longer get to participate in our youth-led programs and clubs, and we work across three different school buildings. We've provided 200 direct service hours to youth and families and schools over just the past year, and we have tons of points of contacts throughout the community where we're providing resources, education, training, leadership skills to youth and families. In FY24 alone, we are able to have those touch points with 2,500 people. I'm sure many of you know that prevention works. Cuts to prevention programs is going to harm Michiganders across the whole, specifically in Dexter. With our cut to our programming, you can see there that data is supporting the work that we do. We do see decreases in substance use among youth in our community, and those decreases are more so than what we see nationally, which means that our programming is making an impact. And of course, there's a return on investment from prevention programs as well that will now no longer be in existence. It's hard to quantify the work that we do. I tried in the last slide, but I just wanted to show some very quick pictures of some of the youth that we help, and they help their community too because they are leaders in these programs. Thank you so much for your time and for letting us speak on this issue. Thank you, Chrissy. Members, are there any questions? Senator Schink? Thank you for testifying. The reason that I ended up supporting this program is because when I was a county commissioner, there were a number of suicides in our community, and seriously, Dexter has become more active since that time, and the number of suicides among young people in our community have gone down. I can't say that it's just seriously Dexter, but when I go into the high school in Dexter and I hear the kids talk about it, I believe that it is because seriously Dexter works with young people who reach other young people where they are and in a way that's really supportive and inclusive of them developing healthy habits. We don't know how many lives are saved by seriously Dexter. I hope to God that we do not find out how many are lost because of this lost funding. Thank you, Senator. Senator McMorrow? Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you for being here. I have a very simple yes or no question. Did anybody from the House Republican Caucus contact you to inquire about how your funding was spent or any of the program details before making this cut? Thank you. Thank you. Senator DeMoss? Yes, Madam Chair. It's a brief question. I don't know if this is the right person to ask or if it's you or if it's a future, somebody else who's testifying here, but I'd like at some point today this to be addressed that I'd like to know the impact this has on future budgets going forward now knowing that this is a possibility. For instance, when I hear this and recognize that the only funds that were cut were those that weren't dispersed until, that weren't dispersed by September 30th, it feels like it creates almost a perverse incentive to blow all the dollars you get immediately. I don't know who to ask that to, but what does knowing this as a possibility, what does this do to people who receive future grants? So please be conscious of that. Maybe we can bring that out. Thank you. And we can talk more about it a little bit later, but you're right. We've received this question multiple times from stakeholders, from your colleagues. How does this impact the integrity not only of the process, but for grantees, how this looks, right? We're still looking for guidance both from the department as well as the administration, but this is one of the biggest questions that when you do something as unprecedented as what was done in the House Appropriations Committee, ultimately we're all left scrambling. So appreciate the question. Senator Kleinfeld. Thank you. I did want to respond very quickly, Senator DeMoss. When I heard about this, when I negotiated the 2024 budget, I included my Republican counterparts on the committee. They will vouch for that. You know that I did that. This was such a betrayal to me that I don't know how to negotiate next year. How do we sit down and negotiate and come to an agreement if I have no trust as to what happens after that? So that's where we are right now. Thank you. Thank you. Senator Albert. Thank you, Madam Chair. And to Senator DeMoss to address your question, there is, it's quite common. In a budget, in many instances, you will put works project authorization for an additional three years right in the original bill that's voted on at the time. What we're seeing here is there's an alternate way to approve work projects funding, and that's if it's not written in the original bill, the budget office can put out, these are what we're going to work project, and either chamber can opt out. So what I practically, going forward, what I think is going to happen is you're going to see work authorization is going to be more expressly written throughout the original budget document. And that will be akin to, in the 2019 budget, when the governor put the transfers of like over $600 million. So ever since that's happened, what you've seen become practical throughout all the budgets is there's boilerplate language added in every budget, giving more weight to the legislature to prevent those types of budget transfers that weren't part of the negotiation. So to answer your question, practically speaking, how is this going to change and how is this going to add trust? Well, I think the work project is going to have to be negotiated up front, I think practically speaking, for what that's worth. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you. And thank you, Chrissy, for your time today. We appreciate it. Next, we have Wayne State College of Nursing, Dr. Ramona Benkirk. Are you with us via Zoom? Yes, I am. Welcome. Well, thank you. Good morning, Chairwoman Anthony and members of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Yes, I'm Ramona Benkirk. I'm the Dean of the College of Nursing at Wayne State, and I'm here to express my disappointment with the recent House Appropriations Committee's elimination of several vital projects, but I'm going to focus mostly on my own that were already approved, as you've already said. The projects for Wayne State were designed to support the state's health and competitiveness, particularly small businesses, expectant mothers, and health care workforce needs, which, interestingly, the two previous speakers, nurses are key to connecting these individuals and communities to those particular resources. So I think one of the key points I want to make is that this was elimination of our $4 million project that was to create the Center for Nursing Workforce. Because as all of you know in this room, and I think you've all received our letter,

Like most of the nation, Michigan has a continuous and persistent overall nursing shortage. And those shortages are virtually in every health care setting, from hospitals to smaller clinics. And it's really due to a very complex array of factors that I outlined in the letter that you received. So I'm not going to go through all of those. But I want to say it's a very complex set of factors that contribute to this. And so to build on the work that the legislature has already addressed, attempted to address health care workforce, we pursued state appropriations to create a more innovative and new approach to tackle these complex problems. The intent of the $4 million over several years, of course, was a statewide project spearheaded by the college in collaboration with the Division of Health Affairs, the Michigan Area Health Education Center, a coalition of multiple health systems, community health organizations, which was intended to tackle the supply and demand of the nursing workforce from multi-pronged approaches. So specifically, our new center was developed to address these factors that are creating the shortage by designing and testing scalable approaches to clinical education to try to relieve these existing barriers in our pipeline. While the project has a strong emphasis on Southeast Michigan, it's really designed to be scalable and testable for across the state and possibly nationwide because we are working with systems that aren't just solely located in Southeastern Michigan. So what we're doing is we developed and are evaluating alternative clinical models so that we can possibly train more nurses to get them out into the field. Longitudinal clinical placements so that they are in one space for a great extended period of time, more than just one semester. Increasing the placements and also working with health systems on their nurse residency programs because one of the other challenges, which is workforce burnout and stress, is that nurses, while they work in the hospital, may leave within 18 to 24 months. And so we're working with the systems to enhance and improve upon their residency programs. We're developing new training approaches to improve patient care throughout the state. The other piece that was critical to this project was expanding the number of nurse clinician educators. So for all the schools of nursing, including our own, we use actively practicing nurses as nurse clinician educators to offer the clinical training within the hospitals. But many of them may not have had a nurse education experience. So we are offering the graduate certificate nursing education to these nurses so that they have the skills and abilities, even if they only have a bachelor's degree, they will be able to get the certificate. And we were planning on including several of our clinical educators in the winter of semester of 2026. So as you can see, there's lots of pieces to this. So it's a residency program. It's longitudinal clinical relationships and clinical placements. It's training bachelor's prepared nurses to improve their teaching and educational skills within the system. And so that's why it was a multi-year project. It's not a one fiscal year approach as we've been working with our systems. So I just want you to know we really were so disappointed when this happened. We had already hired staff. We had already completed MOUs with the health systems and the organizations that were working with us. And so I just wanted to thank all of you for listening, for allowing me this opportunity to speak and to really hear it here out and also thank you for your support. And really, Senator Anthony, for bringing this forward as a topic that needs to be heard by actually all of Michiganders, but particularly our leadership in the Senate. So thank you again. I'm happy to answer any questions that you might have. Thank you. Colleagues, are there any questions? Thank you again for your time today. Thank you. Next in person, we have Superintendent Ben Schulter. He is the superintendent for Lansing Schools. I'm the superintendent, the very proud superintendent of the Lansing Public School System for the next six weeks. And it is really the last five years that I want to speak about. In the last five years, the Lansing School District has raised its graduation rate by 26 percentage points, has raised its attendance rate by 15 percentage points, has raised its AP pass rate by over 630 percentage points. We're doing some really great work with our children, thanks to our community, our educators, our children. But I also want to say thanks to you. The funding that the school districts have gotten throughout the state have been really quite wonderful over the last five years of my time here. You know, more at risk money, more bilingual ed money, more general money. It's been terrific. And I really don't get to say this very often to all of you. Thank you. It really means a lot. And that money has been terrific for us. However, if you've ever been around Lansing, you know that some of our capital, our buildings, tend to be a little bit old. We have passed some wonderful bonds, and thanks to the great people of Lansing, we are building brand new schools. We just opened up Mount Hope. We're about to open up a new school, Willow, and a new school, Sheridan Road, and a new school, Luton. But we do have needs when it comes to our physical structures. That's why we were thrilled when we saw in the state budget that we were going to get $2.5 million to rebuild a track at Everett. Amazing. That track, a bit old. Maybe it had enough cracks that when you were running through it, you might trip. And so we were thrilled that we could get some money to help rebuild the track. And I have the little document here. I don't have cute pictures like other people do, but I had a document, and it says, This agreement will commence on October 1st, 2022, and continue through September 30th, 2026. So as a superintendent, I see that. I go, Amazing. We're thrilled. And then we start to build. We go out for RFPs. We go out and get contracts. We have relationships with builders, with architects. And over those two years, we have a plan. If anybody knows building, there's an old adage, you can do something cheap, you can do it fast, or you can do it good, but you can't do all three at the same time. So, of course, we want to be good stewards of taxpayer money. We want to do it well. We also want to make sure that it's high quality. We want to make sure that it's done well. We had two years. So the way most construction projects work is you take those two years. Currently, we've redone the track. We've paved it. We've put up some fencing. We've done half of it. Now, as many of you know, it's quite cold outside. There's ice. There's snow. And so we've made sure that we've been able to wait until it thaws, and then we're going to build the next section. But then, if the money is pulled, what are we supposed to do? We have contracts. We have relationships. We have a plan. We're building it based on the timeline we were given, and it's now going to put the school district in a really difficult position because we're half done. We don't have the shot put. We don't have the other part. We don't have the concession stands. We don't have the bathrooms. Those were all part of the plan because we were told you had $2.5 million. 2026 is the end date. And it's going to put school districts and educators in a really, really difficult position because we want to believe that what you've given us is true. We want to believe that the numbers make sense because then we go to our building partners and then we go to our architects and we go to our community and say, look, this is it. This is not fraud. As Jan has been stated, we're in the same building as they are and the construction is about 80% completed. One of the big ones is the escape stairwell that leads between the third floor and the basement. That's not done. Until that's done, this building cannot open. And that's a significant cost that we have not been able to get paid for. Also part of that is we have to have a 24-hour backup generator to run the PSAP. And there's $300,000 outstanding on that when that generator gets commissioned. That's due to be commissioned this Saturday. But those funds are not going to be available for us, so we're not going to be able to go forward with this commissioning unless we find to take some way to bring that money from another portion and what would deplete the needs that we have to run the dispatch center. So we also have some infrastructure needs that we're waiting to get done. As we do these, we do RFPs on all this. We want to be good stewards of the public's money. And as those RFPs are being done, an evaluation of the projects that's awarded takes some time. It doesn't get done in a week. It sometimes takes up to three months to do this. We've been diligent about that. And now that we've seen these signed contracts, we don't know that we're going to have the money to pay these and we're not going to be able to open. So we need to have these funds that were promised to us by the state of Michigan through this grant. And to pull those funds as of last week, we don't know when we're going to open. And without opening, that puts the safety of the public of the downriver area at some jeopardy. Thank you. Thank you both so much for your testimony. Senator Camilleri. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you both for being here. You know, when we first won this grant in 24, it was with great joy that we came back to the downriver community, all of our communities, the hundreds of thousands of residents that we serve with the ability to talk about this large public safety program, but also the workforce development, small business grants, veteran services that the DCC all provides. And it was one of those things where, honestly, one of my proudest moments in the legislature to bring back this funding because I know that this amazing nonpartisan entity that is led by a board of directors of all of our local municipalities felt like they were heard out of the Capitol. For the first time in who knows how long, our region received specific funding for a project that they've been advocating for for a really long time. And to have that trust broken was heartbreaking this past week. And to be in a situation where we're now, again, trying to just fight for a project that keeps people safe and gives people jobs and gives access to services for veterans is really unconscionable that we're at this point. And so I'm very sorry, even though it wasn't us who did it here in the Senate, but just know like my colleagues, we're going to fight every day to make sure that we restore these funds and make sure this project goes on without a hitch because the safety of our residents is really who we should all be thinking about. And this funding is really important for that. My question and then I'm happy if anybody else has something to add, but really just focuses on that piece. What did this mean for Downriver that we got this type of funding to support a large project for our region? I'll start off. This really, as I said, is unprecedented. And it really gave our Downriver residents and our organization a home that we were wanting to showcase that the Downriver residents deserved. The facility that we're in currently, pipes are bursting. We're on top of each other. There's not enough space for the actual number of residents that we're wanting to serve on a regular basis. The technology was completely outdated. So this is a secure, new, improved building that we felt that Downriver could be proud to come and get the services that they needed. So it's more than just a building. And we wanted it to be a welcoming, safe place that people can come when they are in need and feel that they can get the help that they deserve, really. But the aspects of having a state-of-the-art, top-of-the-line public safety facility, we built this in a way and designed it in a way that would be accessible for future disasters as well. We wanted it to be future-proof. We wanted it to have space in order that it could become an emergency operations center should a disaster, God forbid, ever happen in our region. We built it with space and technology and capabilities that would service the whole county or an even larger region if it would be needed. So we were doing this in a very thoughtful and strategic way that was mindful of our dollars being able to meet current and future needs. Yes, and the police and fire chiefs, which were stakeholders, as we designed and built this public safety answering position, as we said, we're 80% built. They have come. They have visited. The police and fire chiefs are excited. They want this done. They understand the need. They understand what it takes to have a dispatcher that can answer all the questions they have while they're out in the field so they can concentrate on what's going on. The fire chiefs can concentrate on the building fire. The police can concentrate on that. And they know that they're going to have people in-house that are going to be able to relay this information and get any resources they need. So they're all excited to get this going. And to put this on the back burner now and wait for funding is going to be very disheartening to those chiefs. Thank you. Any additional questions? Senator McGuire. Thank you. Very simple yes or no question. Mr. Matthews, did anybody contact you from the House Appropriations Committee to inquire about your project before making these cuts? No. Ms. Danzy, did anybody from the House Appropriations Committee contact you to inquire about your project before making these cuts? Not at all. Thank you. Thank you so much for your time. We appreciate you. Next we have Canton Township Supervisor Ann Marie Graham-Hudak, as well as Senator Polhenke will be joining her. Good morning. Good morning. Thank you for letting me testify with Senator Polhenke. Thank you very much, Chairwoman Anthony. I'm here to speak on behalf of the Township of Canton in western Wayne County and the region. And more importantly, on behalf of the children and families who would be directly harmed if this community project was defended under the label of waste, fraud, and abuse. I want to be very clear. There is no waste, fraud, or abuse here. What this is is a project that simply has not had enough time to be completed. One of two projects that were pulled from Canton, though I'm talking here about Kids Talk. This project is at risk. It's a renovation of Canton's historic Sheldon Road School to create a Kids Talk Children's Advocacy Center serving western Wayne County and the region. Kids Talk serves children who have experienced sexual abuse, physical abuse, and neglect. Some of the most traumatic experiences a child can endure. These are not abstract cases. These are real children, real families, and moments that will shape the rest of their lives. Kids Talk provides a safe, welcoming place where children can tell their story once in a way that does not re-traumatize them. Instead of sitting in a police station or a courtroom, a child sits in a child-friendly space with trained professionals who know how to listen with care and compassion. Law enforcement, child protective services, medical professionals, and advocates work together so that the child does not have to relive their trauma over and over again. Our police department brought this program to us because they have seen the difference it makes. They have seen children treated with dignity instead of fear and families supported instead of overwhelmed. Expansion of this program into this facility in Canton helps to reduce the already long waiting list of kids and families waiting to be seen. This Canton location would change that. Today, families in western Wayne must travel long distances to access these services. This Canton location would mean less travel, less stress, and faster access to care at the moment families

need it most. About a year and a half ago, Canton Township broke up a pedophile ring. It was a horrific pedophile ring, and it reached way beyond Canton. It was in a very wealthy neighborhood. It reached beyond Canton. It reached beyond Wayne County. It reached beyond the state of Michigan. A program like this helps families cope after something like that happens. It helps families. It helps the children who are traumatized by this event get through this. Melanie Richards of Kids Talk, she's the executive director. She's here if you want to ask certain questions about that. But I do want to state, our contract did not start until the end of March of 2025. Even though you read the contract, it starts in January of 2025, we did not have signature until 2025, and it ends September 2029. As an engineer myself who worked on construction projects, supervised construction projects, and have many completed as supervisor, you can't complete construction projects in five months. You have to engineer them. You have to put them up or quote. You have to do the construction. There is no way that this money could have been spent that way. We've already entered into contracts. We've spent funds on design and planning. The state has already reimbursed some of those costs. This project is real, active, and moving forward, and stopping it now would leave a critical gap in services for abused children in our region. In closing, before Senator Hankey speaks, this project is a responsible and contracted investment in child protection community infrastructure. It is well within contractual timelines, incurred legitimate obligations and critical regional needs. So not only does it serve Canton, but it serves all of Wayne County. So thank you for your time, but defunding this project would not save money. It would break commitments and halt active work right now. We've already signed these contracts. And most importantly, it would harm people, children who have been abused. So please, I respectfully ask for you to look beyond that label. Thank you for your time, compassion, and your consideration. Thank you, Supervisor. Thank you, Madam Chair. Madam Chair, I am sickened by the 16 Michigan House Republicans who voted late last week to harm hundreds of children by cutting the funding for Kids Talk, which Canton was so excited about, and which was legally appropriated by this body in 2024. Every Republican who voted for this and supports this questionably legal political tactic should hang their head in shame today. Thank you. Thank you. Senator Cherry. Thank you, Chair, and thank you for the testimony. And yourself and a number of other folks who testified have pointed out what you're doing is not waste, fraud, and abuse. I just wanted to take a moment to say I think what we've hopefully discovered over the past year is that the House Republicans do a lot of projecting. Because you're right, these projects aren't waste, fraud, and abuse. What is wasteful is when you cancel an IT project halfway through the bill because you pulled the funding. That's wasteful. What's fraudulent is when the state doesn't honor its contracts with the people that they signed the contract with. That's fraudulent. And what's abusive is when you cut funding that's supporting survivors of sexual abuse. That's abusive. So I wish all of the folks coming to testify didn't feel the need to defend their projects as not waste, fraud, and abuse because it's completely the opposite. What's waste, fraud, and abuse are the actions of the House Republicans last week. Thank you, Senator. And thank you for your time. We appreciate you. Next, we have the Hamtramck Fire Department. Chief Matt, I ask that you give me grace and say your name for me as well as Senator Chang. Good afternoon, Madam Chair. It's Matthew Weichelski. You're not the first person to stumble a little bit on that. First, I'd like to thank you for letting me come speak to you to this body today. It's a very important subject to us. The Hamtramck Fire Department is an old organization. We're a smaller organization. And the money that was allocated through this body to purchase a fire engine represents a large investment for our department. It's been a number of years. I've been chief since June of 2022. I've been with the department since 1998. I've been preaching to our city council on the need for updating and modernizing our fire equipment. Senator Chang and I met somewhere in the process here and she took up our cause. She brought it to your body and made this appropriation, which was a very welcome relief for myself as fire chief because this is a large, this is a very significant investment for our department. And not only is this an investment for our department, it's an investment for our entire area. In 2014, the city of Hamtramck, along with the cities of Detroit and Highland Park, entered into an auto aid agreement. What this does is blurs the borders. It allows us to respond to the person in need with the closest appropriate emergency vehicle. As the chair said in her opening, we don't ask if you're a Republican or a Democrat when we respond. We respond, we mitigate the situation, make sure everything's safe, and we go back home. Our job is to keep not only our citizens safe, but our firefighters safe. This investment is huge for us. Our current fleet, I have three pumpers. Two of them are approaching 15 years old. 15 years old is the time you're supposed to put them into reserve service and use them as needed sparingly. My reserve piece that I have to rely on is a 1996 pumper, which was purchased before I was hired nearly 30 years ago. This was going to allow me to retire that piece of apparatus, modernize my fleet, and make it more safe for the community. When we received news of this on Friday, it was kind of a punch in the gut for us. We found it in Cranes Magazine. Nobody bothered to notify us. Maybe they just weren't going to respond when we asked for the check for the fire engine. But buying a fire engine is not like going to the lot and buying a car. They take a long time to build. There's an entire process. So once we received notice that this funding was coming to us in October of last year, we immediately began the process, produced the RFP, went out to bid, selected everything, and we were ready to go by January. And we actually signed the agreement. We met with Spartan Fire Apparatus Manufacturers right here in Charlotte, Michigan, to begin the build process. Now, we have signed a contract that has us, you know, we are now on the hook for over a $900,000 piece of apparatus that, frankly, my controller and I are trying to figure out how we're going to pay for now. Okay, at this point, I feel a little gut-punched. You know, through the years, Hamtramck has gone through some rough patches. We've stepped up. We've done what's been asked of us by the states, either through the financial manager or what was dictated to us. We have gone into the regionalization. We work very closely with our neighbors in Detroit and Highland Park. And when this opportunity arose, it was like a rainbow opened up over the city for once. And it was a godsend, and we're very happy for it. Now, hopefully the rainbow will come back. I have faith that this body will do the right thing. And sitting here today, I feel a lot of outrage at what has happened here by this body. And it's restored a little faith in me. And hopefully, I wish you all the best in your fight and restoring these projects for everyone. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Chair. And thank you, Chief. Those Polish last names are a bit hard. There's a lot of continents in that one. I just want to echo a couple of things. I did not know when I was first approached by a couple of your guys as well as yourself about the need for a new fire truck that it took 26 months to actually get a fire truck. And so that's an extraordinarily long time. Of course, we want to make sure that the fire trucks that are being delivered are built properly. And so let's make sure that we're following that process. However, clearly, this is not waste, fraud, and abuse. This is simply the process by which a municipality acquires a fire truck. And I would just like to remind the entire committee that over the course of time in this legislature, we have over and over again reiterated our support for first responders and reiterated our support for public safety. And so I would hope that after the actions of the Michigan House Republicans last week that we can all remind ourselves yet again that first responders deserve our respect, they deserve modern equipment that allows them to do their job. And I hope that these cuts can be restored. The last thing I will note is that I have heard stories of times when this particular fire truck has actually broken down on scene. We cannot have that happen. It is dangerous. And I hope that we are able to remedy this situation for the residents of Hamtramck

and beyond. Thank you. Thank you. Senator McMorrow. Thank you, Madam Chair. Chief, I have a very simple yes or no question. Were you contacted by anybody from the House Appropriations Committee before they made this cut? No. Thank you. Senator Baumstad. Thank you, Chief, for coming in today and testifying. Being an old hose puller for over 20 years myself, and I served on a fire command board, I think members need to know every nut and bolt that was in a special ordered fire truck doesn't come from the hardware. They're all special items that are very, very expensive, and it takes up to two years from when you think about when you need a truck to when it actually gets delivered. It takes a long time, sometimes over three years, so just wanted to let folks know that. Thank you, Senator. Senator Kleinfeld. First of all, thank you for coming in. I appreciate it. There actually was a public safety line item that didn't get clawed back, and I suspect it's because House members were trying to avoid exactly what we're seeing in front of us. Unfortunately, they didn't take a closer look at some of the other line items had public safety things in them. I just want to point out to everybody, we're just getting a tiny, tiny snapshot today of the money that was taken and the different organizations affected. And so we really got to look at this as trying to restore the whole because we're talking about hundreds and hundreds of entities. It'd be very difficult to have all of them in and hear them out and fight for them individually. That's not directed at you, though. That was a statement because we're towards the end of the meeting. Thank you. Thank you, Chair. Thank you both for being here. Thank you. Next, we have Brandi Johnson with the Michigan Community College Association. As a reminder, we've heard from many local voices, but there's also statewide organizations that have been impacted, and we want to give a small snapshot there. So thank you, Brandi, for being here. Thank you, Madam Chair, and I'll be brief. Members of the committee, Merry Christmas, Happy Holidays, and thank you for the opportunity to testify today. I'm Brandi Johnson, President of the Michigan Community College Association. Frequently, the Michigan Community College Association is asked by the legislature and state agencies to manage statewide projects that directly support student success. The association is a widely respected organization with a strong track record of delivering real results in a way that is cost-effective, transparent, and always in compliance with state and federal law. Two notable examples include the redesign of the Michigan Transfer Network and the development of 10 statewide transfer pathways from 2017 to 2020, as well as the Academic Catch-Up Program, a $10 million initiative that supported summer bridge programs to address COVID-related learning loss. In 2024, MCCA was again approached by legislative leaders to help address another issue impacting students, the lack of strong intentional pathways into specific high-need careers that help Michigan communities. Named in legislation, Local Heroes was designed in direct response to that request. Local Heroes is a grow-your-own workforce initiative intended to strengthen pipelines from high school to community college into careers in three areas, teacher education, allied health, including radiography, respiratory therapy, surgical technology, and others, and public safety, including police, fire, EMS, and corrections. We began work right away. We're already seeing progress in the teacher education component of this work. For example, MidMichigan College has developed new coursework to prepare students for the alternative route to certification program offered through Schoolcraft College. To date, 15 community colleges are actively participating in the allied health portion of the Local Heroes initiative, demonstrating strong statewide engagement in these high-demand fields. One of the primary barriers to expanding the healthcare workforce is the limited availability of clinical sites. MCCA is working diligently with the Michigan Health and Hospital Association and the Michigan Health Council to identify incentives to expand clinical placement capacity while colleges continue preparing programs so that they are ready to scale when sites become available. The public safety component was to be focused on helping community colleges partner with local K-12 districts to align career and technical education and dual enrollment coursework with post-secondary pathways into police and fire academies. For example, a high school student in Ludington with a goal of becoming an EMT could begin that pathway in high school through CTE or dual enrollment, seamlessly aligned with the EMT program at West Shore Community College. Or a student in Traverse City with a goal of becoming a law enforcement officer could begin that pathway through dual enrollment and enroll at Northwestern Michigan College's police academy. Or near and dear to my heart is the daughter and sister of firefighters. A kid right here in Lansing could begin their coursework in high school to get a head start at LCC's rigorous fire science program. The work plan for this initiative was developed through September 2027, consistent with the scope and complexity of building statewide systems-level pathways and aligned with how similar work projects have been implemented in the past. That plan assumed the availability of funding through the standard work project process, including established reporting deadlines for narrative updates and expenditures that support fiscal responsibility, transparency, and strong stewardship of taxpayer dollars. However, the statute did not specify whether the FY25 funding would be available beyond the initial fiscal year absent a work project not rejected by an appropriations committee. That lack of clarity created a misalignment between the project timeline and the funding structure. As a result of the House reduction, we are now forced to abandon the public safety portion of the work, despite the fact that public safety workforce shortages remain among the most urgent facing Michigan communities. I want to emphasize that this is a clearly defined, scoped workforce development effort with specific deliverables and timelines tied to student pathways and high-need fields. The work has proceeded as outlined in the approved plan and has remained focused on implementation rather than expansion. MCCA approaches all state-funded work with a strong commitment to accountability, transparency, and oversight. We regularly collaborate with state agencies, institutions, and partners, and we welcome questions, data requests, and opportunities to provide updates on progress. In this instance, we were not contacted to provide information or context about the project prior to the funding reduction. Had we been asked, we would have been more than willing to share details about the scope of work, progress to date, and remaining deliverables. This experience underscores the importance of clear expectations, defined timelines, and open communication when implementing legislatively directed multi-year initiatives. Those conversations help ensure that all parties share the same understanding and that projects remained aligned with legislative intent. However, the rules of the game shouldn't have been changed midstream or applied retroactively. We often hear legislators emphasize that employers and businesses operating in Michigan need stable, predictable policies and transparent processes that reduce uncertainty to be a business-friendly climate. The same consistency is important for all organizations doing business with the state and for partners working to carry out its priorities. Maintaining that predictability also supports Michigan's reputation as a reliable place to invest, both for employers considering locating or expanding here and institutions and partners already committed to serving our communities, as the Local Heroes Project has demonstrated. We respectfully urge the legislature to restore full funding for the Local Heroes Program so that community colleges complete the work as originally envisioned and continue building pathways that support student success and meet Michigan's workforce needs. Before closing, I also wanted to briefly note the impact of the cancellation of the Department of Labor and Economic Opportunities Talent and Growth Work Project funds. The announcements of these cuts came just as several community colleges had finalized and signed agreements related to the Michigan College Credit for Apprenticeship Program that was recently announced. This program is a joint effort amongst LEO, MILEEP, the Michigan Workforce Development Board, MCCA, our colleges, and 14 skilled trades partners to award consistent and sizable college credit for the on-the-job training that occurs in registered apprenticeship programs. This initiative was more than a year in the making with Talent and Growth funds supporting third-party evaluation of apprenticeship curricula to determine how much college credit an apprentice would earn upon completion. In most cases, apprentices would just be five courses away from earning an associate degree, creating a clear win for workers, employers, and Michigan's talent pipeline. Thank you for your time and consideration. Thank you. Senator McCann. Thank you very much for your testimony, and I believe I heard in there the answer to Senator McMorrow's question that's been asked multiple times today, so thank you for clearing that up as well. I wonder if you could just speak a little more to the impact of the Reconnect Navigators that you just closed on particular institutions that have had this rug pulled out from under them, this ability, as you said, to stably plan and know what the future holds and implement a multi-year program and to have that completely pulled out from under their feet is unconscionable in my view, and for the House Republicans on the Appropriations Committee and their colleagues to do that I think is very irresponsible, but talk a little bit more about institutions across the state of Michigan, community colleges that are going to have a specific impact.

Thank you, Senator McCann and Madam Chair. In addition to the projects I mentioned, another line was eliminated in the community college budget or clawed back, and these were the Reconnect Community Action Grants. We are obviously still trying to fully understand the impact of those programs, but it is our understanding that specifically two grants to Northwestern Michigan College in Traverse City and Oakland Community College will be impacted. At NMC, this project was in partnership with Michigan Works, and it was working to create the Northern Michigan Attainment Collaborative, uniting over 20 organizations across 10 counties to support adult learners through wraparound services and a step-by-step credentialing path to maximize the impact of the Michigan Reconnect Program, a bipartisan initiative. And at Oakland Community College, there was a grant to expand the highly successful Oakland 80 Navigator Services to strengthen outreach and workforce alignment. So in addition to the projects impacted by the Community College Association, there are several projects that were committed to individual colleges that were impacted as well. Any additional questions? Thank you, Brandi, and thanks for being a great partner to the state. Finally, we have Abby Clark. She is with the Natural Resources Defense Council here to talk about some of the additional impacts from an environmental perspective. Thank you for being here. Thank you so much, Chair Anthony and members of the committee. My name is Abby Clark, and I'm with the Natural Resources Defense Council. We work to ensure the rights of all people to clean air, clean water, and healthy communities. But many people may not realize that our top priorities here in Michigan are very focused on making sure that Michiganders are able to afford the water and energy they need every day. Clean air and water can feel like luxuries when people are struggling to pay their bills, so much of what we do is focused on affordability. Obviously, I'm here today to share our deep concern about the actions of the House Appropriation Committees last week. There is so much uncertainty about this maneuver that some of the programs I mentioned may not be as negatively impacted as we fear, and I really hope I'm mistaken. We would be very relieved to hear that some of these programs remain intact. But regardless, this situation is chaotic and uncertain and causing people real anxiety right before the holidays. And tragically, some of the people who stand to be most impacted are some of the same people who just suffered through the pause in SNAP benefits and other interruptions caused by the federal government shutdown. So as I said, much of our work is focused on making sure Michiganders can live in healthy homes and afford their utility bills. One of the many reasons people in our state are stuck paying high bills is old, inefficient housing stock. Drafty houses are expensive to heat, and those bills can drive people into poverty. This is why we were so alarmed to see cuts to a number of programs focused on affordable housing, like the Ingham County Housing Trust, but also programs all over the state, in Portage, in Grand Rapids, in Sterling Heights, and also programs to develop the workforce to build and upgrade housing to be safe, healthy, and affordable, like the Michigan Energy Academy, a program intended to build Michigan's clean energy workforce, and AmeriCorps programs that focus on energy efficiency efforts, and the Clean Michigan Initiative, a major source of state support for environmental cleanup, land reuse, and redevelopment. Any reasoning for cutting affordable housing, energy efficiency, brownfield redevelopment, and job creation programs is very difficult to understand, given the consensus on our state's core economic challenges right now. We are also deeply concerned about cuts to water assistance funding, which was already at a level well below the actual need. It is impossible to live in dignity without running water. And we're already falling short when it comes to setting up funding structures to ensure no Michigander ever has to try to figure out how to survive without running water at home. Until we pass Senator Chang's water affordability bill package to fix these problems once and for all, our water assistance programs need state dollars to keep people's water on. And now, even more families are in danger of trying to cope with the nightmare of having their water shut off right before Christmas. This is like something out of a Charles Dickens novel. And it's frankly embarrassing for our state. Very concerningly, some of these cuts appear targeted at specific communities, like Flint and Lansing. This is not at all what we expect from state government. We deserve leaders who want every child born in this state to succeed, regardless of their zip code or racial or ethnic or economic background. My colleagues at NRDC have advocated for and represented the people of Flint in court for many years, seeking justice for the people there, most of all the children. The idea of taking resources from children and babies in Flint or anywhere in the state who have done absolutely nothing to deserve their circumstances is incomprehensible. There are so many other programs impacted by these cuts that touch our work, like the work we do on safe, affordable infrastructure and transportation. Tens of millions of dollars are threatened for community enhancement grants used for sidewalks, bike lanes, trails and parks. And we were frankly shocked to see cuts to programs to ensure Michigan children get to school safely and to keep construction workers safe while repairing our roads. I could go on, but I will close by saying that government matters. The people of Michigan, just like all Americans, deserve a government that stands up for their interests, understands their needs, protects them from risks and dangers in their environment, and makes their lives more safe and secure. Chaotic surprise budget maneuvers are needless and exhausting. They are not fair to any of us, and they're certainly not what we need to attract new people and businesses to our state. I want to thank the chair again for this opportunity and for her tireless work on the budget and for the people, especially the children of our state. And I am very grateful to all the leaders here who keep our kids' future as their focus. Thank you. Thank you, Abby. Members, are there any questions? Thank you. Thank you for your work throughout the state and for your testimony today. Senator Bumstead, did you have remarks? Yes, Chair Anthony, thank you. I kind of have to relate everything I'm going to speak about kind of in my past life. A lot of you might know I was a building contractor for 35 years. So I worked a lot in the contracting. I would sign contracts with subcontractors, painters, plumbers, electricians. Then I would get their contracts and go to the homeowner, and they would either accept the contract and sign a contract with me or say no. And when you break a contract, that never happened to me in the construction business. All the 35 years I was building houses, I never once was ever sued as a building contractor, and I never had to sue anybody to get paid. And I take pride in that. And I stayed busy because of that. That means we probably did a pretty good product, and people trusted us, and they trusted me. I remember one time there's a young couple. They wanted to let me wander for a minute. They were young, in their early 20s, maybe mid-20s, and they just wanted a price on roughing in a very small house, 1,000-square-foot house. It came to like $12,000. There's going to be four of us there three weeks, something like that. And I never looked at the bid I gave them, and I messed up. The dot was in the wrong spot. It said $1,200, and I never caught it. And I gave them a bill for $12,000. They came to me crying. I said, what's wrong? They said, we thought it was $1,200. Well, it was in my contract. They got a $1,200 house. That's what you do. You stick to your contract. And when I sit there at the end of the table and sign a contract, I'm representing Senate Republicans, Senate leadership. I'm sitting there in Senator Santana's chair, and I'm signing that contract. It's a contract between the Senate Republicans and the Senate Democrats. And to me, a person is only as good as their word, and we can't lose that. We can't lose people's trust. So that's all I wanted to say. Thank you. Thank you, Senator. You only heard a snapshot, as Senator Kleinfeldt mentioned, of the voices of individuals, organizations, local government partners throughout the state of Michigan that have been impacted by the reckless

behavior of last week. This fight is just beginning. As you heard, we are called upon to stand in the gap for men, women, and children in this state. And as Senator Bumpstead just mentioned, all we have in this world, all we have in this building is our word. And so we will continue to have discussions and as I mentioned at the beginning, use every tool that we have to make these communities whole. So with Senator McCann moving that we adjourn and Senator Kleinfeld supporting, the Senate Committee on Appropriations stands adjourned. Thank you.

title: Senate Session p1 25-12-16
transcript:
Too much of me. Good morning, Jeremy. The Senate will come to order. Mr. President, Senators Brinks and Nesbitt offer Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 10, a concurrent resolution of tribute offered as a memorial for Donald Coyvisto, former member of the Michigan Senate and Michigan House of Representatives. Whereas it was with great sorrow that members of the legislature learned about the passing of Donald Coyvisto, he will be remembered as a dedicated public servant by his constituents in the Upper Peninsula and the people of our great state. And whereas, born in Bessemer, Michigan in 1949, Donald Coyvisto was a born and raised Yuper. He graduated from Luther L. Wright High School in 1967, and he later earned a bachelor's degree in political science from Central Michigan University in 1971. And whereas, prior to joining the legislature, Donald served his community working as a teacher and a football and basketball coach at Morris High School. From 1974 to 1980, Donald worked as a juvenile officer in Ontonagon County. He started his career in elective office when he won a position on the Ontonagon School Board of Education, where he served as president in 1976. And whereas, in 1980, Donald was elected to represent the 110th District in the Michigan House of Representatives, which covered the Western Upper Peninsula. During his time in the House, he served as the chair of the Agriculture and Forestry Committee, as well as a member of the House Committees on Agriculture, Colleges and Universities, Conservation, Energy, Environment and Recreation, Consumers, Economic Development and Energy, Military and Veterans Affairs, Public Utilities and Tourism and Recreation. And whereas, while serving in the House, Donald was a fierce advocate for the farming community. And as a co-sponsor, he helped craft Michigan's Right to Farm Act. Donald sponsored the public act that established the Forest Products Industry Development Council. During this time, he also worked to address other concerns of the Upper Peninsula, which included employment, education and tourism. And whereas, after serving in the House, Donald left public office to spend more time with his family. During this time, he stayed engaged as a political consultant to Representative Louis Dodak, former Speaker of the House of Representatives, and Representative Michael Griffin, former chair of the Joint Committee on Administrative Rules. And whereas, in 1990, Donald returned to public office when he won a competitive special election to represent the 38th District in the Michigan Senate. He would hold this seat for 12 years until 2002. While in the Senate, Donald served as the Minority Vice Chair of the Senate Committees on Agriculture, Forestry and Wildlife, Gaming and Casino Oversight, Hunting, Fishing and Forestry, and Natural Resources and Environmental Affairs. He was also a member of the Health Policy and Appropriations Committees, as well as the Senate Appropriations Subcommittees on Agriculture

capital outlay, higher education, and natural resources and environmental quality. Donald also served as a member of the Joint Committee on Administrative Rules. And whereas during his time in the Senate, Donald continued advocating for the farming community. This was particularly important to him as he and his wife were operating her family's centennial farm where they raised corn, soybeans, and hay. This gave Donald firsthand insight into the challenges and needs of the farming community. His support for the Upper Peninsula also extended to other areas, including casino oversight. Donald wanted to protect the interests of all of his constituents, which included tribal communities. He also sponsored Public Act 443 of 2002, which addressed the taxation of iron ore in order to keep the mines open and retain jobs. And whereas Donald also understood the value of bipartisan relationships, and he was committed to working with everyone who shared his concerns. His closest friendships spanned the state from Detroit to Battle Creek to northern Michigan. However, Donald was never one to shy away from controversy or be afraid of being the lone voice. This included him serving on the Senate Ethics Committee, which dealt with senator discipline. And whereas during his tenure, Donald was known for his independent voice, loyalty to the needs of the Upper Peninsula, and mentoring of many future leaders, including former Representative and House Clerk Rich Brown. Serving rural communities was important to Donald, and he displayed many of the characteristics that are important to these communities, consistent standards, responsive leadership, and practical support. While he was humble and quiet, his legacy was one of promoting good public policy for the state. And whereas upon leaving the legislature, Donald continued to serve the state of Michigan. He worked as a lobbyist for the iron mining industry with Cleveland Cliffs, promoting the same policies he supported as an elected official. In 2007, it was announced that the Michigan Commission on Agriculture had named him as the new director of the Michigan Department of Agriculture. In this role, Donald was able to continue serving the farming community and advocating for sustainable practices and policies. He served in this role until 2010. And whereas the legacy Donald left behind will be remembered fondly by those who knew him. By his colleagues, Donald will be remembered as a tireless advocate for the Upper Peninsula and agricultural community, as well as someone who treated everyone with dignity and respect. By his family, he will be remembered as a loving and devoted husband, father, and grandfather. His family includes his wife of 55 years, Pamela, his four children, Adam, Matthew, Timothy, and Catherine, his four grandchildren, Jacob, Connor, Nolan, and Emma, as well as his faithful furry companions, Daisy and May. And whereas upon Donald Coivisto's passing, we offer our condolences to his loved ones. His contributions to these chambers and the state of Michigan will be remembered. Now, therefore, be it resolved that we offer this expression of our highest tribute to honor the memory of Donald Coivisto, a member of Michigan's House of Representatives from 1981 to 1986, and the Michigan Senate from 1990 to 2002, and be it further resolved that copies of this resolution be transmitted to the Coivisto family as evidence of our lasting esteem for his memory. All right, we're going to start it. Good morning, everyone. The Michigan Department on Health and Human Services Subcommittee on Appropriations will come to order. Will the clerk take the roll? Chair Santana. Here. Senator Cherry. Here. Senator Kavanaugh. Here. Senator Bayer. Here. Senator Kleinfeld. Here. Senator Outman. Here. Did I miss Senator Irwin? I'm here. Sorry about that. Senator Huizinga. Here. Senator Houck. Here. Senator Tice. Madam Chair, you have a quorum. Thank you. I need a motion from Senator Cherry to adopt the meeting minutes from June 24 for 2025. Supported by Senator Bayer. Without objection, it is so ordered. The minutes are adopted. Good morning, everyone. Thank you all for being here this morning. I know it's been a while since we've met for our subcommittee. But there's a lot that has happened here across the state and across the country as far as our Health and Human Services Department and budget. And one of the biggest things that we have discussed over the course of the last year is reduction in our error rate for SNAP benefits. And today we will be hearing from the department's chief operating officer, David Konyzik, to discuss some of the modifications and newer changes to the error rate requirements in order to make sure that things are running swiftly as they should in the state and that we're reducing the error rate. We appropriated dollars to help support that effort. And so this committee hearing is designed to actually hear from the department and see how things are moving forward and answer any questions from committee members. I know that the House actually had a hearing in oversight to discuss the same matter, but we want to hear from the department as well to make sure that we're getting the comprehensive information necessary. So without that further ado, we will hear from our chief operating officer, David Konyzik. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Chair, and good morning to you. Good morning to our majority vice chair, Senator Cherry, and our minority vice chair, Senator Outman, and all the members of the Appropriations Subcommittee on Health and Human Services. I'd be remiss also if I didn't wish a belated happy birthday to Senator Outman. And in case any of you were wondering, it is definitely more fun sitting on that side of the table than it is this one. But hope to have a good conversation with you all today about the department's work around SNAP and the payment error rates and the work that we're doing, partially supported by appropriations that came in from the legislature in the FY26 budget. So I don't have control of the slides, if I'm able to just ask that we advance. We'll jump into the presentation. Pardon me. Oh, I do have control of the slides. Pardon me. What was that, Senator? See, it's more fun on that side. All right, one second. So just briefly walking through the mission of the department, of course, we provide services and administer programs to improve the health, safety, and prosperity of the residents of the state of Michigan. It's something we take very seriously. It's something that our staff is wholly committed to on a day-to-day basis and on a 24-7 operation. I'm

failing to advance the slides. Off to a good start. All right, we're back into it. So first, it's a very brief overview of the SNAP program in general. There are 42 million Americans that maintain eligibility for SNAP benefits across the country. 16 million of them are children. 8 million seniors. They rely on SNAP to buy groceries and help put healthy food on the table. Here in the state of Michigan, we have 1.4 million people who rely on SNAP to support their families and their budgets. We at the department talk about the importance of accuracy and timeliness as it relates to the processing of those SNAP benefit applications, as well as accountability. We want to make sure that we're doing everything right, that we're in compliance with the law, and if and when mistakes are made, that we take the necessary steps to remediate those issues. I think I can skip past this slide. I just talked about it relatively quickly. A snapshot of what things look like here in the state of Michigan. 43% of SNAP households have children. 51% of SNAP households have a person with a disability in the home. 36% of those households have older adults. And 78% of those households include someone with earned income. That last point is always important to me because I know there's a lot of narratives out there that frankly don't align with the reality around who is receiving SNAP benefits. The overwhelming majority, as you can see, are going to individuals that do work, that do have an income that they're pulling in, and just need a little help bridging the gap between what they're earning and what they need in order to put food on the table for their families. We also talk about SNAP as an economic generator. And so we wanted to talk a little bit here on this slide about what that economic impact looks like in the state of Michigan. Locally, we have over 9,700 retailers who accept SNAP benefits. And those retailers redeemed $3.2 billion in SNAP dollars for fiscal year 24. Fiscal year 24, you'll hear me talk a lot about today. There's generally a lag between the end of a given fiscal year and when the SNAP dollars are finalized and fully accounted for by the federal government. That always happens in June of the subsequent year. So we won't have FY25 numbers until June of FY26. So you'll hear me talk a lot today about FY24, the most recent year that we have complete data for. In terms of the amount of benefits that people are receiving, again, I think it's important to highlight the average benefit that an individual receives in Michigan is $173 per month. Again, I think important as we're talking about different narratives that we see in the press around SNAP beneficiaries, $173 per person, or it breaks down to roughly $5.68 a day. We know that every $1 in SNAP benefits leads to $1.54 in economic impact. Those were data points provided to us by the USDA in terms of their assessment of economic impact from SNAP benefits. The benefits are not conditional on your participation with the quality control process. The benefits are purely conditional upon whether you meet the eligibility criteria, the income requirements, et cetera, for those benefits. And before you said it, I was going to say with regard to my questions, long story short is my preference. Yes, ma'am. Okay. I'm interested in the recouping of money. How far back can the individual get where they owe money? The second piece in terms of how far we can look back, Senator, I would have to follow up with you on that.
