And so you as an individual might not have that review done on you once every couple years because it's a purely random sample. We don't say here's the 650,000 homes. We're going to move through them one at a time. It's purely random. You could be randomly selected in September and then you could get randomly selected in March a couple months later, right? But in terms of the recoupment process, I'll use a round number. If you're supposed to get, if you were getting paid $150 in benefits every month and we went through that quality control process and we determined this person is only supposed to get $100 a month. So we overpaid you $50. Once that was identified for your next monthly payment, you would receive a $50 payment, $50 less than what you're supposed to be getting because we paid you $50 more. And that would continue in perpetuity until we recouped all those dollars. And there's a scale to it depending on the dollar value, depending on the size, all the way up to and including referrals to the federal government and tax captures and things of that nature. But if you want a build out of what that entire process is and the options for recoupment, I'm happy to get that to you. Okay. Because that could be problematic if individuals spend the money, you know, we're looking at that with other individuals recently, if they spend it and then they have to, it's just cut off of their next one, they don't have food for their kids. So thank you. Yes, ma'am. All right, I'm going to try to fly through. How much time do I have, Senator? Lord have mercy. I'm going to be fast. I don't know. I don't know if I can do it. I'll give you one error example. Let me find a good one for you. This is earned income. If you want, Deputy, I think one of the big questions I have is regarding just the immediate initiatives to reduce SNAP. Sure. Obviously, what my question is, is around the return on investment of all of those different areas, eight areas in which the reduction in the error rate will apply. So if you can probably, you know, talk about that, that would be good to see how the dollars that we invest would help to support that effort. So in order to make sure that we were good stewards of the dollars, so this is a $15 million general fund appropriation that came out of the FY26 budget, as I spoke of earlier, 50-50 match currently on those dollars. So we're hoping to pull down that full $30 million. Before we even started spending the money, we went through a five-week diagnostic to confirm the specific type of errors so that we were going to start attacking the right problems and not taking a scattershot approach to things, and then generated a targeted list of root causes around those errors. I flew through or flew past it in a previous slide, but in terms of the root cause data, overwhelmingly related to earned income and reported changes to your earned income, different deductions that an individual might have in their application process, the number of household members that they have within their group size, and then unearned income that they have coming in from other various sources. And so we went through, we identified and prioritized eight different initiatives across 35 different work streams to try and tackle that work. One of the things that we jump into on the next slide is we talk about, again, those quantitative values around what is driving the error rates. We went through and broke it down to the error type, what counties, characteristics of the individuals and the clients that are creating those errors, and then the immediate initiatives, the eight that I spoke of, we talk about right here. The first one being on that client information submission process, making sure that we are improving their understanding of the requirements, doing those, like I said earlier, you can't do the hard stop, but we're calling them nudges. If you're filling out information, you go click next to the next slide, the nudge pops up. Did you really mean this? Here's what we're looking for. Go back and take a second look at it to make sure that we're getting what we need. The second initiative around our client interview support, making sure that all of our specialists have information at their fingertips to try and support that process. Again, this was an initiative that we started before HR1, going through, reading the policies, redoing the policies, making them more digestible and accessible for our staff so that they're asking the questions that we need them to ask and getting the information that we need them to use. Our staff deployment strategy, Michigan is what's called a universal caseload state, and so we have the ability for individuals all across the state to access and support and process benefits from anywhere else in the state. UCL is a task-based work stream, and so we've built out new tasks that incentivize and prioritize other upstream individuals catching potential errors that were made by staff before them and rewarding those benefits or those catches along the way. Multiple Bridges system updates, this is something that we are very excited about. Folks will talk all the time about the amount of money that are spent on these very large IT systems. I always equate it to the building that we're sitting in now. It costs money to build the building, it costs money to maintain the building, it costs money to make enhancements to that building. The same is the case with our Bridges application system. And so when I talk about those nudges and all the other changes that we're making within our Bridges system right now, we've identified 30 IT and tech updates that we want to make to our Bridges system, 10 of them that we think are critical to mission success related to these dollars. And so those are the priorities that we're focusing on now. And then finally, any sort of oversight mechanisms that we can engage with or support with the federal government around waivers and around additional support that we can use to support these processes. So in addition to the technical changes that you're going to see within Bridges, within our forms, within our client review process, and with our supports for our staff, you are also going to see a statewide ad campaign around this effort as well. We find a lot of times, particularly when we were looking at the redetermination process coming out of COVID, it's not always that folks don't want to participate. Sometimes it's helpful just to remind them of the fact that they need to and should participate. And so the same type of ad campaigns that we've seen in the past, you should expect to see those same campaigns statewide this year as well. I know that I saw the slide deck late last week around what that campaign will look like and where it's going to be. So I'm happy to jump into some more specifics, but I want to be sensitive to the time and any questions that folks have. And of course, I'm happy to come back in again and chat if you need to, Senator. Well, thank you, and thank you for your presentation, although cut short, definitely we would love to have

you as well as Director Hertel back to discuss more of the investment and the changes to the structure of the system for the stamp benefits and the error rates as well. I had thousands of questions, but yes, we can have another meeting. But let's see here. I will move to excuse any absent members and we will adjourn the committee. I will entertain a motion to excuse absent members, so supported by Senator Kleinfeld. Also second by Senator Kavanaugh without objection. Absent members are excused. And being no further business, I move to adjourn the Senate Subcommittee on DHHS, supported by Senator Cherry. Without objection, the subcommittee is adjourned. Thank you. Thank you.

I rise in support of Senate Bill 611 and 612. I want to start by thanking the Chairwoman for her bipartisan work with me on this important issue to protect women and other victims of domestic violence and stalking in our state. Michigan is an outlier, and not in a good way. At least 43 other states' personal protection orders, or PPOs, are automatically and promptly served by law enforcement at no charge to the victims. But not in Michigan. In fact, federal law requires that PPOs be served at no charge to the victims. But for the past 30 years, Michigan has gotten around this provision by telling victims that the order can be served by a friend or family member. Sending somebody's mom or dad or brother or sister or a friend to serve the abuser with a PPO is not a good, safe alternative. Every single minute, on average, 20 people are abused by an intimate partner in the United States. We must do better to protect these individuals. $1 million has already been approved in the current budget to support this effort. And we've addressed the vast majority of stakeholder concerns and will continue to work with stakeholders as this legislation moves forward. But as I stated previously on this floor, while it's worthwhile discussion to have about statutory maximum fees for process service, this is well beyond the scope of these bills. I urge you to step up today and to protect the men and women in our state who are in much danger for the personal safety that a court has granted them a personal protection order. Do not make them jump through hoops and do not make them have a family member confront a violent aggressor in order for this order to be served. I urge my colleagues to support these bills and request that my remarks be printed in the journal. Thank you. Without objection, so ordered. Further discussion, the president recognizes Senator Chang. Thank you very much, Mr. President. I request to speak to both bills and that my remarks be printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. In August, Latricia Brown was stalked and murdered in her workplace by her estranged ex-husband, Mario Green, at Henry Ford Health's main hospital in Detroit. She had been stalked for a long time and was fearful of what might happen next. She had actually been granted a personal protection order, but that order had not yet been served. In her July 20th petition for a PPO, she said, I have tried being cordial because I feel that the system has now let me down each time that I have tried to make reports on this man. My father was murdered and now with this situation, I am now in mental distress and scared, not knowing what to do, where I have PTSD of this whole situation. I have to constantly look over my shoulder to make sure this man is not following me to hurt me like he has done in the past with physical abuse. I am asking for help before this goes too far and things are too late. Patricia's PPO was never served on her ex-husband. And so on August 22nd, he entered the basement of the hospital, pulled out a handgun and shot Latricia several times, and she is no longer with us. Michigan, as we have heard, is an outlier in the United States, where 43 states, the District of Columbia and two territories require that PPO service take place free of charge. In Michigan, the cost to serve a PPO can include not just a service fee, but mileage traveled, which could easily amount to $100 or more. Costs vary from county to county, so a PPO survivor in one county might have to pay twice as much in another county to ensure their safety. Some counties, like Chippewa, Mackinac and Midland, have already eliminated the fee requirement, recognizing that this is just good policy. And others, like Antrim, Genesee and Delta, have a free or low-cost sliding scale in place. The law currently allows a victim to identify a friend or family member to serve the PPO, but that can clearly lead to a dangerous situation. So Senate Bills 611 to 612 will require that a PPO be served as soon as practicable within 72 hours at no cost to the victim by a law enforcement agency as designated by a judge. And this requirement was changed specifically due to the suggestions from the Michigan Sheriffs Association. The designated law enforcement agency would be reimbursed for the cost of service from the PPO service fund, which we were pleased to secure an initial $1 million, which is likely enough to cover service statewide this year. Future legislatures, though, must make sure that the PPO service fund is funded adequately. The Violence Against Women Act ensures that a PPO granted in one state must be enforced equally in any state. But victims in Michigan are currently being left behind if they are unable to pay to serve their PPO. I know that it takes a lot of courage for someone who is experiencing domestic violence to ask for help, to share details of what one has gone through. But to put it on paper and file a petition for a PPO for a judge to consider is a truly brave and extraordinary step. So when someone is reaching out for help and trying to protect themselves, we should not put up a financial barrier to their safety. Quite simply, it is time that we remove this unnecessary and dangerous barrier for those experiencing domestic violence, stalking, harassment, or assault. And the impact of this legislation will be felt not just by victims, but also their families and innocent witnesses, like Latricia Brown's coworkers. Thank you especially to the Senator from the 24th District for your partnership on this legislation, along with Wayne County Prosecutor Worthy, the Michigan Coalition to End Domestic and Sexual Violence, and the Michigan Domestic and Sexual Violence Prevention and Treatment Board. Colleagues, I urge your support for this bipartisan bill package to improve public safety in our communities and support survivors. Thank you. A board of roughly some 130 people overall coming up with recommendations for a 10-year economic development plan. This isn't China or Cuba. Seeing no further discussion, the question before the Senate is on the adoption of Albert Amendment No. 1. All those in favor will vote aye. All those opposed will vote no. The Senate will proceed to vote. The Secretary will close the board and announce the vote. Mr. President, on Senator Albert's Amendment No. 1, there are four aye votes. An insufficient number of senators having voted, therefore the amendment is not adopted. Mr. President, Senator McMorrow is offering a floor substitute to the bill. It is available on SessionWeb and identified as Amendment No. 2. Senator McBroom is offering an amendment to the McMorrow substitute. It is available on SessionWeb and identified as Amendment 2A. The question before the Senate is on the adoption of the McBroom amendment to the McMorrow substitute to Senate Bill 213. Is there any discussion? The President recognizes Senator McBroom. Thank you, Mr. President. My amendment simply asks that the legislature be involved in the process of approving these plans. I recommend a yes vote. Thank you. I'd like my remarks printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. Further discussion, the President recognizes Senator McMorrow. Thank you, Mr. President. I appreciate the spirit of this amendment. To be very clear, the plan does not require the legislature to take any action. It merely makes informed suggestions from experts from all around the state for us to use as a guide. And the legislature may make decisions on whether or not to enact or introduce any legislation appropriately. So while I appreciate the spirit of the amendment, I request a no vote. Seeing no further discussion, the question before the Senate is on the adoption of the McBroom amendment to the McMorrow substitute. All those in favor will vote aye. All those opposed will vote no. The Senate will proceed to vote. The Secretary will close the board and announce the vote. Mr. President, on Senator McBroom's amendment 1A, there are two aye votes. An insufficient number of senators having voted, therefore the amendment is not adopted. Mr. President, there are no further amendments pending to the McMorrow substitute amendment number 1. The question before the Senate is on the adoption of the McMorrow substitute. Is there any discussion? Seeing none, the question is on the adoption of the McMorrow substitute. All those in favor will vote aye. All those opposed will vote no. The Senate will proceed to vote. The Secretary will close the board and announce the vote. Mr. President, on Senator McMorrow's substitute number 1, there are 19 aye votes. Majority of the members elected and serving having voted, therefore the substitute is adopted. Mr. President, there are no further amendments pending to the final passage of Senate Bill 214. The question before the Senate is on the final passage of Senate Bill 214. Is there any discussion? Seeing none, the question before the Senate is on the final passage of Senate Bill 214. All those in favor will vote aye. All those opposed will vote no. The Senate will proceed to vote. Seeing no members present having voted, without objection, the Secretary will close the board and announce the vote. Mr. President, on the final passage of Senate Bill 214, there are 20 aye votes, 13 no votes and 4 excused. Majority of the members elected and serving having voted, therefore the bill is passed. The President recognizes Majority Floor Leader Singh. Mr. President, will the Senate proceed with the order of resolutions? Without objection, so ordered. Mr. President, Senator Albert is offering Senate Resolution No. 8A, a resolution calling on Governor Whitmer to opt in to the new federal tax credit scholarship program for K-12 education. The resolution will be referred to the Committee on Government Operations. The President recognizes Majority Floor Leader Singh.

Mr. President, I move the Senate proceed to the order of statements. Without objection, so ordered. Statements. The president recognizes Minority Floor Leader Lauer. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I just want to make a brief comment about the need for us to take action on unemployment agency today. Over the years, in fact, twice now, we've had committee hearings where the director was before us, and we were asking questions in earnest about issues that were going on. This predates COVID. And we were told everything is under control, there's nothing to worry about, nothing to see here. Twice since I've been serving, we've had independent companies come to us and say, listen, you know, we know we're really not supposed to have access to all this information, but we do, and we could make this whole system run far more effectively, far more efficiently, and actually we wouldn't even charge you to do it. Twice we've had those offers in two separate committee hearings, both times rejected flatly. I only point this out to say it's too bad we even have to go through this, and it's too bad we've put our constituents through this. When we have good people who are willing to step up and voluntarily help us fix these systems, but as a state and a bureaucracy, our bureaucracy says, no thank you, we've got it under control. Clearly we do not have it under control, and I really wish we would be willing to accept that kind of help when it comes our way. Thank you. Would you like your remarks printed in the journal? Without objections, so ordered. The president recognizes Senator McBroom. Thank you, Mr. President. With a couple of bills that we passed today regarding economic commissions or boards that would reach out to other countries, I'm thinking perhaps I need to introduce some legislation that we have a special economic commission set up so this state can understand the Upper Peninsula. May we need an Upper Peninsula Economic Commission. And I know I can say that somewhat lightheartedly, but I know a lot of you are being spoken to and approached regarding the situation and the looming crisis for the Upper Peninsula when it comes to the loss of our natural gas-fired units and electrical generation. And I just want to encourage my colleagues to come and speak to me about it if you have any doubts of the serious nature. I want to express my appreciation to the leader and to the floor leader who are working very hard on this issue with me, but we're running out of time and it's getting desperate and I need your help for the place that I love. So thank you. I'd like my remarks printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. The president recognizes Majority Floor Leader Singh. Mr. President, I move the Senate do now adjourn. Floor Leader Singh moves that the Senate do now adjourn. Without objection, the Senate will adjourn and stand adjourned until Wednesday, December the 10th at 10 a.m. The Senate is now adjourned.

title: Families and Veterans — Tuesday, December 16, 2025
transcript:

Something's wrong. Something was in the rocks. The House Families and Veterans Committee will come to order. Would the clerk please take attendance? Thank you, Mr. Clerk. Rep. Fox moves to adopt the minutes of the December 9th meeting without objection. So ordered. So our first order of business today is to hear testimony on House Bills 4696 and 4697 from Representatives Meerman and Representative Young. Anytime you're ready, you can start. All right. Well, thank you so much, Madam Chair and to the committee here on Families and Veterans. So honored to be before you all to talk about this important legislation regarding the Guardianship Assistance Program. One of the things that I'm really excited about is to be sitting here with my good colleague, Representative Luke Meerman, who has such a heart for all things child welfare and wanting to do things right and to be certain that our children are being looked after. I'm also excited to have with us today Demetra Starling, the Senior Deputy Director of the Children's Services Administration with MDHHS. He'll be joining us to provide testimony as well. Now, this bill ensures that relatives and licensed foster care parents who have already been caring for a child can access guardianship assistance in a clear and concise way, all while keeping the safety and overall well-being of children in care as our top priority. And I'll repeat that as our top priority. When caregivers receive the support, they're more easily able to care for these children and the children are able to remain in a consistent family-based environment, which is so very important. Oh, my goodness. Forgive me, you guys. I'm glasses on. Y'all know I turned 60. I like telling people I turned 60 and I have to wear my glasses. It is important for children and youth in foster care to have a permanent, safe, and stable home in which to live and to grow with nurturing caregivers. The Guardianship Assistance Program provides financial help to support permanency for children who may otherwise remain in foster care or even actually have to go into foster care. Federal requirements around relative caregivers or kinship caregivers changed, allowing states to create a streamlined approval process for family members who stepped up to care for one of their own who's now in need. Michigan adopted this new process which ensures children's safety but reduces some of the barriers that kinship caregivers face when welcoming a child that is part of their family. However, the state's statute that sets eligibility for gap payments for these relative caregivers excludes anyone approved with this new process because it specifies licensed caregivers only. And that's the thing that we're trying to address. And so myself, Representative Meerman, our bills 4696 and 4697 look to update the statute to include relatives who are approved by the streamlined process, fixing a problem that excludes many relatives from receiving critical financial help while they care for a child or at times children in their own families. This is common sense bipartisan legislation that supports both kinship caregivers across the state and the vulnerable children in their care. The bills will also make the path to becoming a kinship caregiver more accessible to family members who want to help but might not be financially suited to do just that. And so with that, I'd like to pass it over to my good colleague, Representative Meerman. Thank you, Madam Chair. Appreciate this opportunity, committee, to come before you and talk about these bills. I too appreciate my colleague here sitting with me and our efforts over years of working for foster kids in particular, standing and speaking for them. The bills before us today deal with foster children and adults responsible for their care. When a child enters foster care, circumstance forces their placement to keep them safe. This is a tumultuous moment in a child's life, which is why such strong efforts are made to place children in care of a relative or individual whom they have a personal connection. No one can predict circumstances when a child enters foster care. There are people in that child's life who would rise to the occasion for caring for the child. Currently, such an individual would be unable to qualify for guardianship assistance to help cover costs of caring for a child unless they are licensed foster parents. So even if a child's relative wishes to care for a child, they are ineligible for assistance until they become licensed. These bills offer a solution to that constraint. They allow a relative or individual with strong ties to the child to become eligible for guardianship assistance if they care for a child for, at a minimum, six months before applying for assistance. To become eligible, an individual will still have to be approved for foster care placement by the department, and they must complete all background and central registry check requirements. Permanency outcomes for children are best when they can maintain connections with their families. We must consider solutions such as this to encourage family to take their relatives into their home to keep them out of the foster care system. Thank you, Madam Chair, for the opportunity to speak to this this morning. Thank you, Representatives. We have some more people to testify, but we can take a few questions. I think this is an important bill, so thank you for bringing them to our committee. It's really important, as you said, to make sure if we can keep the kids with relatives, that's important. And I think what you said was a relative approved. So can you talk a little bit about that again? Yeah, I know that Representative Meerman just talked about the background checks. So all those things will still be in place because, as I mentioned in my testimony, the well-being of the child is our utmost priority. And so none of those things will be lax, but the difference between licensed and approved, you can be approved and still have all of those checks and balances in place, and that's what we're looking to do with this legislation. Okay, let's go to a few questions. Rep. Burns. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you both for your testimony on this legislation today. So I know you mentioned that the goal is to streamline the process for families looking to care for a child, which I appreciate. Can you tell me what would you estimate in terms of time saved for family members if they were to be able to go through the approval process with the department as opposed to the licensure process? How much time do you think that would save families roughly? I'm not exactly sure. I know that Director Starling can address that. But we do know when we look at a licensure in context to an approval, it's going to be streamlined, and that's really important. We talk about kinship care. Representative Meerman mentioned there are people who have close ties to family who should be eligible to be approved to take care of these kids, so that's what we're looking to do. Thank you so much. To add to that, I think the important thing to remember is timeliness overall. So I'm not answering your question directly, but any way that we can make the process

more appealing, smoother, straightforward for adults around those kids, appropriate adults around those kids to step forward and do the care. You know, just the idea that, you know, hey, you've got to go through this foster care process might make a very appropriate adult say, I don't have time for that. Maybe I'm nervous of that. And we just need to make sure the outcomes for these kids are so much better when they have some connection to the adults that are raising them. I mean, it's just night and day, even if it's a second cousin. Like, you know, I still know Grandma. I still know so-and-so. It's huge for these kids. Yes, it's always a stressful situation in foster care, as we know. And somebody they know, if they're able to stay with them, we know that's very important. Rep Thompson? Thank you, Madam Chair. I have a question and then a statement, if that's okay. Sure. My question is, this guardianship assistance act, is that income-based for the families? So no, I did a little research on that, and no, it's not. It's to provide additional support. You're bringing in additional mouth to feed into the household. You already have your budget probably set, but because you have the heart and the ability to care for these young people, we want to provide some assistance financially, and so no. To my understanding, it is not income-based. And then I want to thank you both for bringing forward this legislation. I know you too know, and I know many of my colleagues know that I am the guardian of my three grandchildren. And having to navigate this system that I do get emotional still talking about it because it's only been four years, I chose to be guardians, and I didn't go the foster care route. I think I felt it was my duty as their grandmother and my daughter's mom to raise her children and to be their mom because she's no longer with us. But what we had to do in order even to get guardianship, we had rearranged our home because we were almost empty nesters. So we had taken out walls, so now we needed to put up new walls so that there would be three bedrooms for each child just to get guardianship. And I think what you're doing is really important, and I urge everyone to talk to the grandparents and other family members that are raising children that are not their biological children but that are within their kinship. I do know also that sometimes when these children come, there's four or five of them, and a lot of the elderly, late retired aged folks that they're living on a fixed income, and they would gladly take these children into their home, but they don't know how they would afford to do so. And like I said, there are structural needs. There are beds that need to be purchased. There are dressers. There are clothes. There's a lot that comes along with it, and I never would have thought to. I did not want to personally apply to be a foster parent because in my mind that took away my grandchildren as being mine. They came from my daughter. I never looked into that, and I was told by a lot of people to check that out, that I would have been given a lot of other resources if I would have chose to go the foster care route, and I personally didn't. So I just want to thank you guys and know that you have somebody in the legislature that this legislation impacts, and I understand what families are going through with that. So thank you very much. Thank you, Rep. Thompson. And, again, it's always important, too, if possible, to keep siblings together. We always read about that, and that makes such a big difference with these kids if it's possible to keep siblings together. So we always look at that. Yes, ma'am, Madam Chair. To Rep. Thompson's point, just over the Thanksgiving holiday, I went to visit one of the seniors in my community. She had hip replacement, and I hadn't checked on her, and I took her, I think, some Welch's bubbly. That's the strongest I drink these days. And while I was there, her three grandchildren were there. She's raising her grandkids. And just to your point, and she doesn't get any assistance either. She's like, they're my kids, right? But I know that just being there with her that short period of time, that something like this would be a benefit. The girls were talking about getting their hair braided. It costs $200, some of these styles that these kids want. I'm pretty sure that this would benefit her and so many others. So I just wanted to share that quick little testimony as well, Madam Chair. Thank you. Rep. Wozniak. Thank you, Madam Chair. Nice bill. My question is when the assistance actually kicks in, is this going to be retroactive to when the child goes into the home? It could be a year before approval, but the minimum of six months. We're going to let the department speak to that. Yeah, I don't want to guess. I don't think it is, but I'm going to let the department speak to that. I can get back to you on that. Yes. Thank you. Good question. Yes, we do have additional testimony on this, so thank you, representatives. Okay, all right. Thank you, Madam Chair and committee. The additional testimony on House Bills 4696 and 4697 will be given by Demetrius Starling, Senior Deputy Director of the Children's Service Administration, and also Rachel Wineland. Just push the red button and you can start any time. Right. Good afternoon, Madam Chair Smarts and members of the House Families and Veterans Committee. Once and foremost, thank you all for the opportunity to be here today. Again, my name is Demetrius Starling. I'm the Senior Deputy Director for Children's Services with the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services. And with me today I have Rachel Wineland, who is my State Administrative Manager over legislation, policy, and transformation. I also would like to express my deepest gratitude for Representatives Meerman and Young and the many co-sponsors of House Bills 4696 and 4697 and for their leadership in advancing this important legislation. These bills propose a vital amendment to the Guardianship Assistance Act, allowing relatives who have been approved rather than licensed to qualify for guardianship assistance programs. These changes aligns Michigan's law with federal standards and supports timely, safe, stable placements for children with family. So the question may arise, what does this legislation do for our families? This legislation amends the Guardianship Assistance Act to modify eligibility for guardianship assistance payments. Specifically, it expands assistance to relatives that are providing kinship care, have met the requirements for approval, but are not licensed foster care providers. Federal law now already permits states to claim Title IV-E guardianship assistance for children placed with approved relative caregivers. In Michigan's current statute, however, limits that gap eligibility to licensure, creating an unnecessary barrier for kinship families and delaying permanency for children who are already safely placed with relatives. This legislation also aligns Michigan statute with federal requirements by allowing relative approval to meet those gap eligibility standards. The approval process maintains child safety without requiring full foster care licensure, reducing the unnecessary burdens for relatives caring for children within their own family structure. This also allows for relative approval to start the six-month gap eligibility clock, which would significantly shorten time to permanency for our children and our families. In fiscal year 2025, relatives were approved an average of 48 days from placement compared to 208 days from enrollment for families pursuing licensure. So I believe that answers your question that you posed earlier. Beginning eligibility at approval rather than licensure allows children in relative care to achieve permanency sooner and exit our foster care programs more quickly. This change also has a direct and meaningful impact on children and families by supporting earlier access to guardianship assistance, faster legal permanency, and creating a greater stability for youth who are living with families. It also reflects the reality of kinship care. And as folks know, Michigan is a kin-first state where relatives often step in to be that supportive stance for our families immediately during a crisis without the prior licensure, and they should not be penalized for choosing more most timely and appropriate paths to care. Overall, this legislation change strengthens our kin-first practice, removal of the structural barriers for relatives, and creates, again, that permanency within the outcomes for our families while keeping children safely connected to their communities, their caregivers, and also allowing our families to have that financial support needed for long-term stability. So in Michigan, there are two ways that caregivers can be approved to care for children in foster care. One is licensure, and one is approval. Licensure is for non-relatives, and it really follows really strict state laws and rules. Approval is for relatives, and it's a simpler process based on our departmental policy. The approval process allows children to be safely placed with family without requiring, again, that full licensure process. To be approved, again, families must pass all background checks, including fingerprints, and to have a safe and stable home for our children, and also participate in a suitability assessment focused on the ability

meet the child's needs. If a relative wants to care for a child that is not related by definition within our Michigan State statute, then they must then go through the full licensure process. The Guardianship Assistance Act currently only allows for guardianship assistance payments to be made when an individual is licensed only, and it does not allow for the approval process, unfortunately. This legislation, if passed, will amend statute to allow for relatives who have been fully approved when meeting all federal eligibility requirements and to be able to receive full federal funding through our Guardianship Assistance Programs. So what are the guardianship assistance payments? GAP, or Guardianship Assistance Payments, is a federally funded optional program under the Social Security Act. It provides financial support to relatives who become legal guardians of children in foster care become under juvenile guardianship as a means of permanency. The federal requirements for funding of guardianship assistance include that a child must do one of the following things. Have lived in an approved or licensed relative foster home for at least six consecutive months beginning after the caregiver's relative approval or licensure. Two, have reunification or adoption ruled out as a permanency option. Three, have a strong attachment to the prospective guardian. And lastly, have a guardian who is committed to permanent care. So why are guardianship assistance payments important for our families? Guardianship is sometimes the best resolution for a child in foster care because it offers stability and permanency while preserving family and cultural connections, which is so important for our families. In a guardianship, the parental rights are not terminated, which can be in the child's best interest as deemed by the court in order to allow for the child to maintain a safe connection to their birth parents. It also offers the child a safe, stable, and permanent living arrangement with cultural and familial-like connections in case the biological parents are unable to care for that child long-term. Providing relative guardians with guardianship assistance payments is important because it recognizes the importance of family and the familial-like connections. It reduces the child welfare system and the strain by allowing the child to be in a safe, supportive, and permanent living situation and, as Rep. Young and Rep. Merriman know, that's been something that's extremely paramount for our department, finding different ways to narrow that front door of CPS intervention and open up a larger door to prevention and giving the power back to families and community. It also reduces financial strain for guardians. It provides flexibility for states and tribes. It preserves parental rights. It allows children to benefit emotionally by staying with the people that know and trust their experience by less future disruption. It allows for improved outcomes in education, mental health, and social development. In closing, House Bills 4696 and 4697 really offer a practical and compassionate solution to obtaining safety and permanency for children in our child welfare system. By recognizing relative approval as a valid pathway to guardianship assistance, we honor the role of family in providing safe and stable and permanent homes for our children. This legislation also will help children exit our foster care systems even more quickly by, again, reducing the unnecessary burden on our kinship caregivers. I really and truly urge your support for these bills and, again, thank the sponsors, Rep. Young and Rep. Merriman, for their support, their leadership, and moving this policy forward. And, again, thank you, Madam Chair Smarts and the members of the committee for your time and thoughtful consideration. So I welcome any questions that you may have at this time. Thank you very much for your testimony. I appreciate you explaining all that. That was wonderful. Would you like to talk first, Rachel? I'm good. He said everything that represents the benefits of the legislation, so thank you for that opportunity. But I think it was already included. Okay, great. We do have a few questions, so let's go to Rep. Johnson. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you for your concern in this area. We all share it, really. Can you give me an example, give us an example of not the objective qualifiers to become a guardian? Let's say they checked all the boxes and a suitability assessment passes. Is there a time where subjectively the approval process results in saying, no, we cannot approve you? I mean, are there other parts to this that would cause an individual or a couple to not be approved that's more subjective? No, I think that as long as there's a good and adequate feasibility study, the background checks come back clean, the fingerprints come back clean, we do our home assessments and everything is in order, there's nothing that from a policy or even a department perspective that would be subjective for these families to be prohibited from being the caregivers. Rep. Bosniak. Thank you, Madam Chair. I had previously asked a question about how the assistance is dated, so to speak, and my inquiry is whether or not since we had that six-month requirement before approval and then we've got another 48 days before approval is granted, would it make sense because we do have the requirement to make it retroactive to that six-month date? So we have a federal compliance division and in similar situations, we have the ability, the capacity to go back and do a six-month review and do retroactive payments. I'm almost certain we can do that also, Rep, but let me make sure before I give you a solid and firm response to that one, but I'm almost positive that we can go back and do a six-month retroactive payment. That'd be great if we could. Okay. Thank you. Rep. Thompson. Thank you, Madam Chair. So with the adoption aspect, so if they have guardianship of their grandchildren, their kins, if they have the guardianship for a long period of time and they got to a point that they decided and then they were approved for this and they were getting the stipend and then they decided that they wanted to adopt and make it more permanent, then they would lose this because they've adopted? They could then be eligible for adoption assistance under adoption assistance. So there's the different categories, but there is potential that they still could receive some assistance through that adoption assistance. So it sounds like we've been giving this money to the foster care facilities or people that we're paying them to help us raise children, which they need that income to make sure that the children have clothing, beds, and food, but they could potentially be living with family members who can't afford to do that, so they're not doing it. So the money is going to be given to somebody to care for the kids. So putting it with loved ones and people in their family is the goal for this, right? That's correct. So you said facilities. We wouldn't have given money. No, it's private, so it would be private. Oh, I did have one other question about the fingerprinting. So everything you said about the background checks and coming up on a central registry and everything. So when my husband and I got guardianship of our grandchildren, we went through all of that, but they did not do fingerprinting. So this would be an added component with the fingerprinting? I'm curious if you were in an epic guardianship, so that was one of the older guardianship cases that came through. It happened in 2021. So epic guardianship does not involve the child welfare system. So the child doesn't come into foster care. It's more through where a person petitions probate court in order to obtain guardianship. And in those instances, this would not apply because it's not from foster care. So they would have had to have originated in foster care and then have been looking. So because my grandchildren never went into foster care, they immediately came to live with me. That's why there was no fingerprinting. So you did a petition for? Correct. So that was an epic guardianship. That's called an epic guardianship. Thank you for that information. Correct. Rep. Bosniak, are you done, Rep. Thompson? Another question for Demetrius. So doing the math, I'm doing a retroactive 180 days, say $23 is a little over $4,100. And then the 48-day waiting for the approval would be another $1,100. So $5,244. Would that seem feasible within your system? I think with that question. So before they're in the guardianship or before they're receiving guardianship assistance payments, they are foster care children. And they would be placed with the relative that they would be entering the guardianship with. So that relative, through the relative approval process, would already be receiving foster care maintenance payments, which are the same as the guardianship assistance payments. So there really would not be any retroactive

because they're already getting paid that payment, but it falls under foster care, and then when they receive the, when they obtain the guardianship, then they would receive the guardianship assistance payments. Do most foster parents apply for those payments? Yes, most relative providers receive the foster care assistance payments. Thank you. Seeing no further questions, thank you both for your testimony. Appreciate you being here. Thank you, appreciate it. We have one more person who would like to talk in support of these bills, Joy Inglesman. So whenever you want, come up and just push the red button. Good afternoon. Thank you for the opportunity to testify, Madam Chair. My name is Joy Inglesman, and I work as a licensing and adoption program manager at D.A. Blodgett St. John's, which is in Grand Rapids, Michigan. D.A. Blodgett has been around since 1887. We have three divisions, a child welfare division, which includes foster care, adoption, and licensing. We have campus support, which includes residential and independent living, and a family preservation department, which includes counseling and case management services. I have worked in child welfare at D.A. Blodgett St. John's since 1998. Do the math, it's a long time. Our agency is a member of Michigan Federation for Children and Families, and I've been the Michigan Federation co-chair of the Adoption Member Interest Network for the last several years. When I first started my career in child welfare, children were removed from homes due to abuse or neglect were most often placed with strangers in licensed foster homes. When it is determined that it's not in the children's best interest to return home, the majority of the children either lingered in foster care and aged out of the system, or they were adopted by their foster parents. Over time, the shift has been a positive one towards prioritizing placement with relatives. This benefits the children because kinship care minimizes separation from family and community. It preserves important bonds, which are linked to better outcomes for children in foster care. Relatives are no longer required to become licensed foster parents, and the state created a separate assessment and approval process, which previous testifiers have talked about, to ensure that the children are safe with their relatives. Relatives also now get paid the same rate that licensed foster parents receive when foster children are placed with them. Recently, the state also expanded their definition of relatives to include kin, people who are not related but have a significant relationship with the child. In 2023, the federal government updated Title IV-E policy to reflect this same shift. Federal rules now allow us to use Title IV-E funds for approved relatives, not just licensed foster parents. And this flexibility also applies to approved relative guardians. However, Michigan law has not been updated to reflect this change and still requires relatives to be licensed in order to receive guardianship assistance. A majority of my time in child welfare has been working in adoption. Michigan does not require adoptive parents to become licensed foster parents. Those who adopt from the foster care system are able to apply for adoption assistance. Adoption assistance is financial support, most of the time equivalent to the rate the caregivers receive when the child is in foster care, which is paid to the adoptive parents until the children they adopt become adults. A few years ago, when I began working in foster home licensing, I learned that there are times when judges rule out the goals of reunification and adoption, and the goal becomes permanent juvenile guardianship. I learned that there is guardianship assistance, just like adoption assistance, instead paid to guardianship parents versus adoptive parents. But in order for relatives to qualify for this, they had to become licensed foster parents. If they don't, they do not qualify. The requirement for families to become licensed is a large barrier, as most of them either don't want to become licensed because they are providing only care for their relatives, or some cannot become licensed due to the licensing rules and requirements. Requiring relatives to become licensed foster parents after they have already been assessed, deemed appropriate, and have cared for their relatives most often for years, delays permanency for children, and they typically end up remaining in foster care for at least an additional year while this process takes place. This requirement uses agency and state resources, requiring families to jump through additional hoops that are unnecessary and keeps staff from licensing other homes that don't have the appropriate relatives. D.A. Blodgett St. John's currently has a 17-year-old who's been in foster care for four years. He has been placed with his aunt the entire time. The aunt previously raised his two siblings under a power of attorney with no assistance. She is single, has two children, she's working two jobs, she's going to school full-time to get her nursing degree. The goal of her nephew is guardianship, so she has to become, under the current law, a licensed foster parent to get assistance. She was required to attend numerous hours of training, complete a physical, participate in hours of interviews, and meet all of the state licensing rules. This child could have been out of foster care years ago if the aunt was not required to become licensed. So I started questioning, how could adoptive parents qualify for assistance without becoming licensed, but guardianship parents could not? Then I found out that it was the language in the law that was the barrier, and I began advocating for it to change. I'm very thankful for Representative Meerman and Young for sponsoring and introducing these bills. These bills would alleviate the current barrier requiring licensure to get assistance and would allow children to exit out of foster care quicker. So I'm asking that you support these bills. Thank you very much for your testimony. Do we have any questions? Thank you for being here. Thank you. We have some cards to read in. In support of the bill, Danielle Siriani, Michigan County Social Services Association, Elizabeth Henderson, Michigan Federation for Children and Families, also in support, Bianca Miles, Michigan's Children, also in support, and Dr. Heather Bumstadt, Michigan's Children, also in support of the bill. Representative Young moves to excuse absent members without objection, so ordered. There being no further business before the committee, the committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.
