And it is important that states take ownership of this and protect their citizens and prevent these illegal chambers from being imported into your state and endangering your first responders, avoiding your health care licensing laws and health care regulatory process. Thank you. Are there any other questions? Rep. McDonnell. Thank you all for your testimony. I do think it's a little bit complicated and sometimes a little plain speak is very helpful. In that vein, could you say why you think there are more incidents today than there have been? Why the last 24 months have been bad? Just trying to speak plain. I'm sorry, you were asking why 24 months? The last 24 months, why have there been a huge uptick in incidents? Well, I think mostly because of the awareness. So the past 24 months, the number of chambers have been, the number of imports have increased. And so we have been tracking, Mr. Workman mentioned this 400 page report. That report at one point, I want to say it was a couple hundred pages. But just in a short period of time, we've added a couple of hundred extra pages reporting on either non-code compliant chambers, facilities, these wellness facilities that are popping up in communities across the country and around the world. And so what we're hearing is because the UHMS is the quasi governing body for all of hyperbaric medicine across the world. We are the oldest with the exception of Japan. We are the oldest medical society related to undersea and hyperbaric medicine. And so we are in communication with our peers across the world and our peers societies, medical societies. And they are reporting similar incidents. And so this past 24 months, I think it is because the popularity of the treatment driven by influencers. If you, you know, Justin Bieber, you look at, you know, a couple of years ago, there was, you know, one or two celebrities that would be, you know, hawking these devices. And, you know, but now it's, you know, you've got celebrities, you know, that are representing these companies and they're showing off their wares. And we do know that sports organizations have engaged in some of these, but now these organizations have now turned to formal hyperbaric medicine providers. And so these are sports teams. You know, you have a hundred million dollar baseball player. You really want them getting in a chamber like this and having an incident. No, you would want to pay the money, have a formal code compliant chamber with somebody who's trained, you know, to observe and supervise that chamber. But I believe that and we've seen incidents rise in the past 24 months. So that is the reason for my reference of 24 months. OK, another question. I know the FDA, how many conditions are hyperbaric chambers approved for and do those can those conditions also be treated by the non-medical hyperbaric chambers like the soft sided ones that are not delivering as much oxygen? Thank you so much. I would like to defer to my physician team, either Dr. O'Neill or Dr. Wainwright to talk about the medicine, the difference in protocols and et cetera. Thank you. OK, hi. So thank you for that question. So one thing that the UHMS does not do is we do not tell people what they can treat and what they can't treat. OK, there are people doing research. There are people who are presenting some publications which may show some legitimacy in treating certain conditions which are considered off label and off label, meaning not one of the 15 or 16 conditions that the UHMS has approved for treatment. And what we do want to definitely get the point across is that we're looking at safety. We're looking at whether the physicians are properly trained, whether the physicians are on site during the treatments, whether the nurses have been certified, trained and certified, and the technologists have been trained and certified by the National Board of Diving and Hyperbaric Medical Technology and also the Baromedical Nurses Association. As Tana explained, we want to make sure they're using equipment that has been stamped by the American Society of Mechanical Engineers and pressure vessels for human occupancy. And the one way we can sum all of that up is that if a center has UHMS accreditation, they have met all that criteria.

So once they're accredited, we're not necessarily looking at what they're treating. We're looking at how they're treating it to make sure, such as the athletes, that they're being treated for an off-label condition in a safe environment. That's being conducted by the appropriate individuals that are properly trained and on site. And I'll yield to Sandra if she wants to add to that. So in my area, I practice in the state of Connecticut, part of the Yale system and a larger New York City metropolitan area. There are some, we call them office-based hyperbaric practices that are run by physicians using good equipment, and they will treat the off-label indications as Dr. O'Neill had mentioned. And about 30% of their patient population will be the insurance paying indications approved by the UHMS. So they do a hybrid of some things. So I've seen that in some of the better office-based centers. Okay, and if I can just add to that, I mean, my knowledge is that FDA-approved conditions being treated is generally covered by, say, Medicare and Medicaid, where off-label are not necessarily covered or maybe are never covered or rarely covered. And that I'll just say myself without having you say it, that one of the problems is that in some of these cases, such as the Oxford Center, they claimed that it could treat 125 conditions. And I understand we are also in this for safety. I think it's known that I'm working on some legislation about regulating this industry. And we're just, we're not going to try to stop off-label use, but we're very concerned that people understand what has been proven in research and what has not. So thank you for your presentations. Thank you. Thank you. So just a question about hyperbaric chambers. And correct me if I'm wrong, because I don't have personal knowledge of them, but I was told that there's like different types of them and that some of them can be dangerous if the correct safety protocols are not used, but that there's other types that really just can't be dangerous and result in injury, even if you are kind of an inexperienced user. Can you elaborate on whether that's somewhat accurate or not accurate at all? I'm happy to clarify. I think all hyperbaric chambers are dangerous. In my own facility, we do regular safety drills. We collaborate with the local fire department. We do monthly safety meetings. Every patient goes through a safety check prior to every hyperbaric treatment. And when I consult on the patients, I inform them fully of the risks and the benefits. And so I think you're asking a very good question because there's so many subtleties and nuances in this field, and you're doing the best that you can to try to make it as safe as possible for your citizens. But basically the guidelines that Mr. Workman had discussed, where you have FDA, ASME, and PVHO, those are the engineering codes for proper vessels. And then having trained personnel from a legitimate training organization and some form of accreditation are basically the guide rails that you need to have a safe facility, but you can't guarantee that there won't be a risk of injury to the patient 100% of the time. The patient can have a seizure. They could have a new medical development as their disease progresses that could make now what was a safe hyperbaric environment for them. Maybe they developed a big tumor in the lung and you keep treating them with hyperbaric, and then you could cause an injury even in a facility like mine. I hope I answered your question. Yes, thank you. Thank you all for your testimony. Appreciate your time today. We're going to give the last 15 minutes to Corwell Health today. I'd like to welcome Dr. Drew Orwig and Robert Van Slyke. Go ahead and push the button and start whenever you're ready. Sorry about the time constraints. Good morning, committee members. Thank you for having us. I won't belabor too many of the points that have already been discussed because I know we're a bit short on time. I think maybe what most pertinent would be just to discuss an example of a chamber that operates according to the UHMS standards here in Michigan. So I'll just kind of review my background and training and what we do to make sure that the providers are working and operating safely. So just my background, I'm an emergency medicine physician, board certified in emergency medicine. And then I also did a fellowship in hyperbaric at Hennepin County Medical Center in Minneapolis. And I'm also board certified in hyperbaric medicine. Since 2017, I've sat as the section chief for wound and hyperbaric at Corwell Health West. And when I took over, we did a lot to improve the standardization of our workflows. So we created guidelines that we all follow for all the providers according to UHMS indications manual, making sure that we're all doing similar consultations, discussing risks and benefits, getting a written consent, kind of all following the same playbook, if you will. So I kind of have the, you know, that's kind of the highest tier of education that you can get for hyperbaric from as a physician level. But there are some, I mean, I would say if you, you know, there are some providers that are on staff that have done a 40 hour hyperbaric course, which is also considered adequate to supervise hyperbaric. And so there's a number of providers both within our system and within our state that have that as a bare minimum and UHMS does approve that as kind of the minimum standards. Additionally, because we're the only center in the state that does 24-7 emergency care as well as critical care, most of our providers that take call also go on to do kind of an abbreviated fellowship. It's called a path course, it's a six month kind of self-directed learning. So you're getting not a full fellowship, you can't sit for the boards, but you have another kind of tier of education to be able to care for those emergent patients. So then in addition to that rudimentary knowledge, we also do a practiorship when the providers come on, where I supervise their initial consultations, all of their initial supervision of hyperbaric is reviewed by me as well as retrospective case reviews, making sure they are following our guidelines and treating appropriately. And then we also continue to have, it's a requirement of UHMS that we do 12 hours of continuing medical education every year. We actually offer our providers and staff a monthly CME hour. So if you come every month, you get your 12 hours, but we talk about various safety topics and clinical topics just to make sure that everybody's getting appropriate ongoing education. We do simulations and drills that practice our policies and procedures that we both, Rob and myself have created and revamped over the years as new information has come out. But we practice fire drills and any kind of simulation as far as what patients may encounter in the chamber. We go through those, we go through all of our clinical care equipment, at least biannually with all the providers. So then after that, we typically, again, I know I don't wanna belabor too much about the accreditation, but we are accredited with distinction. That's kind of the highest level of accreditation you can get. We're one of 48 centers in the world that have that level of distinction. And I've sat through two of those accreditations, but that just, again, as they've already mentioned, rigorous review of our practices and policies, making sure we're adhering to the highest level of standard that they've already mentioned. So that's kind of how we operate. I don't know if you have any questions specifically for me, or I can have Rob talk about the safety perspectives. Rep. McDonald. Thank you. So why did Corwell decide to go through the accreditation route, including with UHMS? Well, I can't speak, I wasn't there for the first one. They were accredited when I took over. But again, it's having trained and sat for board certification, that is considered the appropriate thing to do. Again, because of the rigorous review that they do, I think it speaks highly about the care that we provide, and we're able to show that we review all that with our regulatory body and are able to pass those standards. And you talked about the kind of training that you get, and it seems like you guys really go above and beyond what's required. Today, under Michigan law, in a standalone

What kind of training is required by the state of Michigan? I don't believe there's any training required. Thank you. We'll go ahead and move on and then we'll see if we have questions for everybody. Good afternoon. Robert Vanslyke. I'm the safety coordinator currently at CoreWell Health West. Licensed as an EMT in the state of Michigan. Certified through the national board as a hyperbaric technologist. And I also hold an additional certification through the hyperbaric certification commission, specifically in hyperbaric safety. Our colleagues at the UHMS, they really provided a lot of the information and the background on the safety and development of hyperbarics. So we won't touch on too much of that. The big thing I'd like to emphasize from that concepts that they provided is really hyperbaric safety is based on risk management. That risk management starts with the equipment. The approval of FDA equipment is really the basis of a solid program. When we get into these off-market types of equipment and machinery, that's really where you start to go astray on your safety protocols already. So the big part of this is just overall risk management. We start with good equipment. We do proper training throughout the processes. Then we have processes already listed out for us that show us what we need to do as a standard. If we look at the NFPA guidelines for safe operations of hyperbarics, that really gives us all the information we need to operate safely. That tells us the types of grounding we need, the types of trainings to run, what our equipment is going to do, how to monitor that equipment. And really, if we find those guidelines, we follow those. We keep a solid safety program. We add that with training of our staff in our particular organization. We require a minimum of all staff that's going to operate a chamber to be the minimum of the 40-hour course. That then lines them up for national board certification as a hyperbaric technologist. And that's really our minimum standard of training. We encourage all of our staff to go on and get that certification. However, that certification itself is not required. Now, with the NFPA guidelines, it's really in the state of Michigan currently, it's more of a presumed positive intent type situation. There is no monitoring that any individual entities are complying with those NFPA regulations at this time outside of accreditation. And really, that's the big positive of the accreditation program. Accreditation provides that monitoring, provides the recognition and overall insight as to how these chambers are being operated. The extensive process you go through with the accreditation is really what gives you that backbone of safety. As you're working through this process for accreditation, it can take somewhere in the neighborhood of three to six months if you lay the whole process out between preparation on the side of your agency all the way through the final verdict from the accreditation body. That really shows that strength and safety. They review all aspects, and they'll go through everything that we do, just like Dr. Orr said previously, all of our trainings, our simulations, all of our maintenance systems, and that's really the strongest way we can currently monitor the safety of a program is through the actions of the program and then confirmed via an accreditation process. So I think it can't be overemphasized how important that accreditation really is. The other thing to look at, I think, currently is there's several other organizations that have developed accreditation programs, and I would suggest while looking at legislative actions, if we look at UHMS being the known body within the accreditation space, I think your best option is to start with a known body and perhaps expand after that when there's more information available on some of the other accrediting bodies. That's not to say there's anything wrong with those. That's just a suggestion based off a long-term process. That's all I have for you right now. Any questions? Thank you. What kind of patients typically do you see through hyperbaric chamber? Who gets referred to you? So as Dr. Wainwright mentioned, there's 15 approved UHMS indications, so that's the most common things we treat. So I would say that the vast majority would be delayed radiation injuries. So patients that have had radiation for cancer, the radiation then does damage to the healthy tissues, sometimes bleeding, wounds that don't heal. Hyperbaric actually helps to reverse those processes. And then probably the next most common is diabetics that get non-healing wounds, so they typically have a lot of problems with their small blood vessels. So that just helps to perfuse the area a little bit better with the high oxygen concentrations. And there was a comment about off-label use. I will say we do occasionally get referrals. I would say we tend to take it on a case-by-case basis. There is some evolving research on things like frostbite and strokes of the eye and where the research is suggesting that there's a positive benefit, but it's not sound enough that it's fully approved and FDA approved. I think we base it off of the situation. I mean, if it's a significant risk for the patient, we might entertain trying to do hyperbaric as a last-ditch effort for those patients, but not something we do routinely. Do you ever get referrals for patients who had maybe previously had hyperbaric procedures through a non-accredited location? Occasionally, yes. Do you get to talk about their experience with them at all and how that goes? Any feedback that you'd like to share? Yeah, I mean, I think that we have one locally in our area. I think that they are allowed to take cell phones into the chamber. This particular place does have chambers that are one of those 510K or what appear to be on the outside. I haven't seen them in person. But the oxygen concentrators on the outside, I'm not sure the concentration of oxygen that they're getting. They wear a nasal cannula, so I think that they're compressed with air, and then they breathe oxygen through a nasal cannula, so you don't really know how much oxygen you're getting, and then you're allowed to take electronics into the chamber as well. And it's supervised by a chiropractor, and typically the state of Michigan requires someone in a medical degree, so podiatrists, chiropractors, things like that, they're not allowed to supervise hyperbaric. Do we have any other questions? Okay, seeing none, thank you for your time. I appreciate you coming in today. I want to apologize to Senator Hill and Dr. Tettlebeck who did not have a chance to testify. We just ran out of time. We do have a hard stop, so I appreciate everybody today, and I'll make sure to get in contact with those individuals shortly. Representative McDonald moves to excuse absent members. There being no objection, the motion prevails by unanimous consent. And there being no further business before the committee, the committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Oversight — Tuesday, December 16, 2025
transcript:
The House Committee on Oversight will come to order. Mr. Clerk, would you take attendance? Chair DeBoer. Here. Representatives Bierlein. Here. Bierman. Here. McCat. Here. Makara. Here. Brub. Present. Green. Rebus. Here. Schreiber. Wolford. Present. Miller. Here. Hutzke. Here. Conlon. Here. McDonald. Here. Spencer. Here. Cerny. Here. Bogella. Here. Mr. Chair, you have a quorum. Thank you, Mr. Clerk. Seeing that Rep. Green is absent and Rep. St. Germain is present, I would elevate alternate committee member Representative St. Germain.

Representative Menser moves to approve the minutes of the November 4th meeting. Hearing no objections, they are approved. Our first order of business is the adoption for the authorization of a subpoena for the testimony of a whistleblower who was a former employee at the Michigan Department of Corrections Women's Huron Valley Correctional Facility. At this time, I would open to Representative Pahutski to give us some background. Thank you, Mr. Chair. So just for a little bit of context, we have heard testimony before the committee about issues at Women's Huron Valley, and I know a number of us have also received outreach about particular issues around mold and inmate health. The chair and I and I think some other members may have received information about one particular inmate, including some of her medical records that indicate that she has mold now growing in her ears and in her lungs. And as part of all of that, there's been outreach from a number of advocates and as the chair alluded to, former employees. And there's one particular employee, former employee, Larisha Thornton, who is willing to testify should we subpoena her. And that is the matter before us. So thank you, Mr. Chair, for your work on this with me. Thank you, Representative Pahutski. Chair would recognize Representative Regas. Good morning. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Members of this committee have been investigating several issues involving the Michigan Department of Corrections. The House Oversight Committee and more broadly, the House of Representatives has a clear legislative purpose in examining the conditions of the MDOC facilities. Depending on the findings of such an investigation, members of the House may desire to sponsor legislation to address the treatment of individuals at MDOC custody. Ms. Thornton is a former employee of the MDOC and she has agreed to testify before this committee. However, she has asked to be subpoenaed by this body. The party to be subpoenaed is Mrs. Larisha Thornton to appear and testify before the House Oversight Committee. Mr. Chair, I move to authorize the witness subpoena. Thank you, Representative. Will the clerk please take the roll? On the motion to authorize the subpoena to Larisha Thornton. Chair DeBoer? Yes. Representatives Beerline? Yes. Meerman? Yes. Paquette? Yes. Kara? No. Brooke? No. Green? Regas? Yes. Shriver? Wolford? St. Germain? Miller? Yes. Pahutski? Yes. Conlon? Yes. McDonald? Yes. Mensur? Yes. Cernaglu? Yes. Waguela? Yes. Mr. Chair, you have 16 yeas, 0 nays, and 0 pass. The motion prevails. Thank you, Mr. Clerk. Next, we're going to hear some testimony from members of the House Legal Counsel presenting on two cases that this committee subpoenaed the Attorney General's Office back on July 22nd. We're going to hear a report from the General Counsel, as I mentioned, Catherine Edwards, House Legal Counsel's Omar Shahra and Casey Markarian. The report they will give focuses on two document requests that were made via legislative subpoena by this committee. Those documents were for two cases at the Attorney General's Office, one regarding Tracy Kornack and another regarding the Bipartisan Solutions Fair and Equal Michigan ballot initiative. Our attorneys have worked hard to limit information provided to this committee to be purely factual in nature, so while we will allow time for questions, please try to avoid asking for opinions or conclusions from our staff as they will not answer those or provide any opinion or conclusion today. Instead, the focus of this hearing should be the unethical breaches of isolation walls in both of these files. You will hear how Tracy Kornack was connected personally with Attorney General Dana Nessel. You will hear about the investigation the Attorney General's made into allegations of embezzlement from a vulnerable adult named Rosalind Bird, Rose Bird, by Tracy Kornack. You will see an isolation wall that was put up a couple months into the investigation by the Attorney General's Office. That should have walled the Attorney General Nessel from even seeing these files. Citing a personal relationship to Attorney General Nessel and being a part of Nessel's transition team, you will hear how 13 days after Dana Nessel sent an email asking for the case file after being contacted by Ms. Kornack, the case was closed in the AG's office. The reasons why this may have happened are up to you as members of this committee, but you will hear that Tracy Kornack was seeking a judicial appointment in Kent County at the time these allegations were public. And you will see three separate entities that come to a different conclusion or have taken much more substantial actions than the Attorney General's Office. The Kent County Sheriff's Department, Ms. Bird herself, and the Allegan County Probate Court. Then evidence will be presented on the alleged Michigan campaign finance violation regarding the bipartisan solutions fair and equal Michigan ballot initiative. You will hear that Attorney General Nessel's spouse was a co-chair of fair and equal Michigan. You will hear that an isolation wall was put in place for that exact reason by the Attorney General's Office prior to any alleged violations. You will hear that the Michigan Campaign Finance Act provides investigative authority to the Secretary of State on violations like this. And despite that, the Attorney General did their own investigations prior to making a decision on enforcement of the penalties the Secretary of State sustained. You will hear that the Attorney General's investigation included a wrong address was used. They tried to send it back to the Secretary of State for this reason. And the Secretary of State legal counsel pushed back on the idea that there was even legal authority that would allow for this. Finally, you will hear that after this pushback and despite an isolation wall, Attorney General Nessel then picked up the phone directly to call Secretary of State Benson, who then agreed to take the case back over her legal counsel's objections. That is just a summary of evidence, not the entirety of either document dump we received from the Attorney General via our subpoenas. You all have binders in front of you and you will be able to follow along while our attorneys present. But before that, I just want to touch on communications with Attorney General's team prior to this hearing. First, you'll see redacted portions on several of the exhibits used today. This is not for a lack of trying on our end. We specifically requested unredacted documents after we received the initial dump of several hundred pages. The Attorney General's office declined to provide any of the documents you will see unredacted. I find this response especially interesting considering the interview Attorney General Nessel did over the weekend complaining about redactions of documents for Detroit Edison, a private company who, generally speaking, has more ground to stand on for redacting documents pursuant to a government request than an executive branch agency would have when a request is made via legislative subpoena. Second, according to the Attorney General's office, both of these files have since been closed. The letter attached with the document dump indicates that both of these files are now in a closed status and no enforcement of the criminal penalties occurred on either file, as far as we know. Third, for additional context, and to jog everybody's memory, back on July 22, 2025, this committee voted 15-0 to authorize a subpoena to the Department of Attorney General for documents regarding bipartisan solutions case. Also on July 22, this committee voted 17-0 to authorize a document subpoena to the Department of Attorney General for documents regarding the Tracy Cornack case. These two subpoenas required the production of documents by August 5, 2025. However, the department failed to produce the subpoena documents. Due to the department's failure, on August 26, this committee voted 17-0 to authorize the issuance of a subpoena to have Attorney General Dana Nessel appear and testify before this committee on September 16. Attorney General Nessel stated publicly that she would comply with the subpoena and appear before the committee on the aforementioned date. Then on September 11, 2025, the Attorney General's office complied with our previous subpoenas and provided us with requested documents. Unfortunately, due to a scheduling conflict, the committee hearing for September 16 had to be postponed. Fourth and finally, we invited Attorney Jessel to attend this hearing so she could provide her side of the story and answer any questions members may have about the evidence we are presenting. We first invited her for last Tuesday, December 9.

And we're told that she would be at the National Attorney General's Conference and unavailable to attend. The Attorney General's Office also stated that they would provide a list of dates Attorney General Nessel could attend only after we provided a list of questions first. We informed them that all questions would be about these two cases, and the Attorney General's Office then stated Attorney General Nessel would not attend any hearing on these two cases due to the isolation wall, an Attorney General having no knowledge of the files. We also offered today, December 16th, as an alternative date for the hearing, and the Attorney General's Office offered their Assistant Attorney General, who worked on the files instead. So rather than taking her up on that offer, since the focus of our hearing today is the Attorney General Nessel's unethical conduct and failed campaign promises about how she would protect one of the most vulnerable sets of our population, our seniors, we instead decided to take her own words and show them to you. Would you play slide two, please? Out of our desire to combine the resources of the state of Michigan and more than 55 statewide advocacy organizations who share our goal of protecting Michigan's senior population from abuse, neglect, and economic exploitation. You'll also get recommendations from an attorney on how to avoid guardianships and conservatorships. I'm going to open the floor to our House Oversight Committee General Counsel now to give us the facts of this case based on the information that has been provided to us. Counsel Edwards, feel free to begin. Thank you and good morning, Chair DeBoer and members of the House Oversight Committee. Just to clarify, I'm the Deputy General Counsel, not the General Counsel. My name is Catherine Edwards. With me today are my colleagues, Casey Markarian and Omar Shahra. We are three of the House Central Staff attorneys assigned to advise the House Oversight Committee and its subcommittees. Today we are here to provide a report to the committee regarding a matter involving the Michigan Attorney General. You will recall that on July 22, this committee authorized two document subpoenas to the Michigan Attorney General's Office. The first subpoena involved a criminal investigation by the Attorney General's Office into allegations that Michigan Attorney Tracy Cornick committed embezzlement from a vulnerable adult. The second subpoena involved a criminal referral from the Michigan Secretary of State to the Attorney General's Office for prosecution of an entity called Bipartisan Solutions for alleged violations of the Michigan Campaign Finance Act. Today we will provide you with a report regarding the documents received from the Attorney General's Office in response to this committee's subpoenas. I do want to take a moment to stress that staff is here today to provide you with the facts, documents, emails, and timelines. We are not here to offer our own opinions or conclusions. It will be up to each representative on this committee to decide their own opinions and conclusions that flow from the documents we will be sharing with you today. So at a later point in the presentation, if you ask us a question that calls for a conclusion, please forgive us when we say that we are just here to present the facts and that the conclusions are up to you. In both cases that we will describe today, the Michigan Attorney General's Office established a conflict wall or isolation wall. We may use those terms interchangeably. We will explain in detail what that is and how the Attorney General's staff is required to act when one of those isolation walls is in place. We will also share with you the documents from the Attorney General's own files, which establish that Dana Nessel breached the conflict wall in both cases as she intervened on behalf of her personal friend in the one case and on behalf of her family member in the other case. It is Attorney General Dana Nessel's conduct when there was a conflict wall in place that is the subject of this presentation. To some extent, however, we do have to explain the underlying matters being investigated so that you have context for the actions of the Attorney General and her staff. Hopefully we won't get too lost in the details of the two cases the Attorney General's Office was supposed to handle, but we do need to give you some context for what these two cases were about. At this point, I will turn over the presentation to Mr. Shahzad to explain to you what a conflict wall or isolation wall is and how the Attorney General and her staff members are required to act when there is a conflict wall in place. Thank you, Ms. Edwards. Now, isolation walls are used in situations where there is a conflict of interest or a potential for one in a particular case or investigation. Isolation walls are implemented for the purpose of preventing any appearance of impropriety or a bias and to keep intact the integrity of an investigation. Now, the Attorney General's Office has its own internal manual that provides the framework for creating an isolation wall. This framework ensures that an individual with a potential conflict in a case is completely shielded from any communication, correspondences, or documents related to that matter. The decision to put up an isolation wall is made by senior leadership within that agency to include an ethics officer who drafts the isolation wall language. It's important to note that a conflict exists at the time a conflict exists and disclosure of its existence is necessary without exception. Later in this presentation, Mr. Markarian will show an exhibit of this exact isolation wall document as provided by the Attorney General's Office. In addition, the Michigan Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.7 to 1.9, govern conflicts of interest for all attorneys and prosecutors. Every attorney in the state swears an oath to uphold these rules, which further ensures when conflicts arise that they are managed appropriately and investigations are handled fairly and without issue. There is also the Michigan Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 3.8, the special duties of a prosecutor. This rule exists for one fundamental reason. Prosecutors are entrusted with extraordinary power. They hold the pen that can alter lives and their decisions can directly shape the outcome of a case. Because they serve not merely as advocates but as ministers of justice, their authority carries a weight unlike any other in the legal system. With that power must come an equally high standard of accountability. The integrity of our justice system depends on ensuring that prosecutors exercise their authority with impartiality, restraint, and unwavering commitment to fairness. As we begin today's presentation, I want to center the committee on the governing standard for attorney conduct in the state of Michigan. Rule 8.4 of the Michigan Rules of Professional Conduct defines what constitutes professional misconduct. I ask that you pay particular attention to subsection C, which provides that an attorney engages in misconduct with the engaging conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice. This principle is critical to our work today. As you listen to the testimony and examine the facts surrounding the alleged breaches of the isolation wall, I urge you to evaluate whether these actions individually or collectively may have compromised, undermined, or otherwise interfered with the fair administration of justice. Now, in this particular case, the Attorney General's Office triggers a firewall in an individual by the name of Tracy Cornick due to a relationship established with the Attorney General. Now, it's important to note that this was an internal decision that was made by senior leadership in the AG's office who deemed it necessary at the time. Tracy Cornick is a licensed attorney in the state of Michigan. At the time of this investigation, she had a personal relationship with Attorney General Dana Nessel, served on the Attorney General's transition team, and was under consideration by the Governor's Office for a potential judicial appointment. She also previously held a leadership position as treasurer of the Michigan Democratic Party. I think the one big hurdle right now is the lack of funding. We're not able to maintain the project at the time it needs to be maintained. Once you roll past a year or two beyond that, Lance has showed many, many slides where you see performance curve. They'd start to go like that, and then they drop down very drastically. So that's, I think, where we're falling short. It's not having the money to fix it when it's time to fix it. And then I guess I'll ask one more, and I'll turn it over to other members for questions. But if we could just hone in on bonding requirements and accessibility, you'd mentioned repeatedly throughout your testimony the concern about small contractors and would bonding requirements under design-build-maintain make it harder for smaller firms to compete? Is that a fair assessment of your guys' concerns? Yeah, I think in terms of small contractors, I don't think it's just the bonding capacity that they would be limited in. It's the legal. We've come up with a few scenarios already in the questions from the committee on this legislation to talk about some of the legal battles that I foresee coming. And I just don't think small contractors have the capacity to defend themselves in court. And if they get a bad ruling in court, are they going to be out of business because they are noncompliant in the contract and aren't going to get the last five years? And then what happens to their bonding capacity after that? And so I don't think it's just the bonding capacity that small contractors are going to have a problem with. I think it's just the overall sophistication of understanding how to manage a project like this, understanding what the risk is for 10 years or longer on a project like this, understanding when the capital preventive maintenance needs to be met because they're not experts at that stuff. They're experts on how they build a road. And so preventing further abuse to that road or maintaining that road is not something that they're familiar with. So I just think that there's a lot of variables that are out there that the general contracting community in Michigan aren't really experts at, that this would require them to be at immediately in the procurement process. They'd have to assume that they're experts already and then put in that risk in their bids. Sure. And so in your opinion, it's beyond bonding. It's a liability that is attached to it as well with this method. And I could see how that would be concerning. Obviously, we want more competition, not less. And so that would be certainly something to keep in mind moving forward. I guess I'll turn it over to other members for questions. We'll start with Representative Coons. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Mr. Beaumina, you had mentioned you thought there was a place for this. There were specific applications. I believe you referenced it also. Can you elaborate on that? Where is this a good fit? Yeah, so I know Representative Carr mentioned the I-75 project, and that isn't perfect. It wasn't 100% successful. But I will say when I first started at MIDA, there were Detroit News articles left and right suggesting that this would take 20 years to fix that road. We were able to put in a design-build-maintain finance through probably the only contractor in the state that can do that and was able to get that project done in three years rather than 20. And I think everyone in Metro Detroit is probably happy about that. So I do believe that there are situations in which this can, for very complex projects, and there are examples across the country where private-public partnerships have already been utilized, which this is very similar to. Again, requiring this on everything we don't think is appropriate. Anything to add on that? Okay, very specific. Okay, thank you. Representative Carr. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you, gentlemen, for coming in to testify today and, Lance, for all the conversations we've had over the past five, six years on this legislation. In terms of cost savings and whether or not you guys think there'd be cost savings, we have seen our budget grow, whether it was too low to start with or not, it had grown 10% or 15% each of the past five, six years, and then there was a proposal to have a 50% increase in funding for the roads, and then we settled at closer to a 30% increase after those recent 10% to 15% increases in the past five years. And to me it just seems like a market process where government gives money, says to do a certain project, have warranties that are difficult to enforce, and then just do that on repeat but have more cash flowing would be very financially lucrative and to not have that accountability on yourselves. To me that's a business model, that's a dream for companies who don't get that opportunity of taxpayer funding for your model. So my question for you is do you believe that you in the private sector are better at making market decisions than government, or do you think we should trust government to make market economic decisions? You know, in every, I don't think that's a blanket yes or no, quite honestly. I think in this regard when you're talking about a public asset and managing that public asset, I think the collaboration between private industry and that owner of that public asset are probably the best way to manage that. As a contracting community, that's not our asset, and so while we have some liability to make market decisions, what if we're wrong and now we're drug into the legal process when we've made a market decision but someone else decided that the preventative maintenance should have happened at year 8 or year 12, and we did it at year 15. I just think those variables, the collaboration between public and private are good in that situation.

You know, who ultimately holds that responsibility if there is a failure? While the liability in the contract is for the contractor, but it's still the public asset. It's still the public road. Another question to Representative Wartz's conversation about the heavy vehicles. Wouldn't it be possible to have an insurance policy for a contracting company that says, hey, this is the limitation for the road. It was at this weight. Things changed in the contract that we had with, we'll say, MDOT. It said that this was the number for this 10 years. If something is to change and a big project were to go in, then we would recalibrate and dynamics would change. And they could have an insurance policy if there are too heavy of vehicles that were not supposed to be on the road. So I feel like the idea of insuring is something that would be productive for the companies to consider. Do you have any thoughts on that? Yeah, certainly. Just like bonding, that's going to be a limitation on how much we can insure. And it will cost money. So it will just increase the cost of the project. And when those things happen, when we don't have design, build, maintain, those are costs that the state of Michigan or local road agencies absorb when things like that happen anyway. So I kind of feel like it's a little bit unrelated to the conversation at hand. But thank you. And I guess just one last question for me. If we could stick on the liability portion of the issue here. And maybe you guys touched on this, so I apologize if this is a little redundant. But my question is, as contractors, how would you assess that liability risk when you're responsible not only for building the road, but for maintaining it for a decade? Yeah, certainly. And going back a little bit to Representative Carr's comment. Yes, it is accurate that we are insuring those costs when there is a failure. But if now you're going to insure against failures for every project, you've increased it across the board rather than the one or two times when you've had a failure. I also believe that to Brett's point earlier, you aren't seeing media outlets that are suggesting or even national watchdogs suggesting that our pavements are failing in Michigan. We've had examples. We can certainly point to a few. And there's been a few that have been warrantied and the contractors had to go in and replace whatever they warrantied and that has failed prematurely. But I certainly don't think, and the fact that Michigan contractors are also operating in other states, the pavement failures just aren't there. But I do believe assessing that liability and that risk, Mr. Chairman, actually will increase costs for every project across the board. Sure. And I mean, naturally I would think it would. But I guess to your point, with so many different variables, how do you even assess that risk? I mean, it just seems pretty complicated. Won't be cheap. Sure. I guess that's all I have for you guys. Members, do we have any other questions for the folks testifying? I guess one final question. What's better, asphalt or concrete? No, I'm just kidding. Thank you. Thank you all for your testimony. I appreciate it. I do have one additional – oh, no. We have one person wanting to testify, Ed Noyola from County Road Association. Ed, do you still want to testify? Sure. I appreciate – excuse me. Ed Noyola, County Road Association. I am the chief deputy legislative director. Just a quick comment. You guys have touched on pretty much everything that I needed to talk about, especially when it comes to liability and cost for the agencies. These are not going to be inexpensive type projects for sure. We're not generally geared up for those excessive costs, especially when it comes to doing the preliminary engineering analysis and looking at the bids themselves. Only a few of our road agencies have the capability of looking at what does a 10-year warranty look like, how much would it add to the cost, et cetera, et cetera. We also have to look at some of the implementation processes, the appeal resolution process, if there's a disagreement in the type of preventative maintenance or routine maintenance that's being done out there. And lastly, that leads me into the topic that you all haven't talked about is the maintenance part of it. These are not inexpensive pieces of equipment. If you've been on the road or you've passed a plow truck or a maintenance truck, they are very expensive pieces of equipment and not common to the private sector. The road agencies are the ones that do all the maintenance for their roads. They're the ones that have that very detailed, specific piece of equipment for that purpose, to plow snow, to fill potholes, to maintain the roadbed, the road surface itself. So that's a thing that I don't know how many contractors have or could purchase that piece of equipment. Right now it's a two- to three-year waiting list to get a truck replacement, and that's just a chassis. We're putting on all the other bits and pieces in order to make that a true maintenance vehicle. So that's kind of a tricky little area that I don't know how the contractors would really actually do that. It seems like a really expensive capital investment for 10 years, if it goes that long. The other thing that they touched on was traffic volumes. Traffic volumes could increase. Traffic weights could increase. The use of the type of use on the roadway could increase. How do you deal with those sort of circumstances? And I appreciate the previous speakers talking about that a little bit. And here's my last comment. Sixty-three of the 83 counties do MDOT's maintenance. So are we going to have sort of a hodgepodge of who's maintaining the roadway when it comes to these warranty contracts on the maintenance end of the agreement? If we're going to do that, then maybe we should just turn it all back over to the department to do the maintenance. But that is going to be a very significant problem for us to try to work. Do we stop to pick up our blades and move on for 10 miles and then we drop our blades? Or do we do a workaround? How is this supposed to work? I think that's not a very effective way to do routine maintenance on our infrastructure or the state's infrastructure. Those are all great points that you raised there. I guess I have just a brief series of questions for you. So given MDOT's failure to provide corrective action and timelines for warranties, and this is not coming from me. This is coming from the Auditor General's reports in the past. Do you believe that additional accountability and oversight is needed in the current process? I think that is being addressed through the inspection, the testing, the departments on hands-on oversight. We have the same type of criteria. We generally use what the department uses for these type of designs, and we will continue to do that. We will continue to do the testing and the monitoring and the oversight. That's just part of how we operate. That's how the road agencies have been operating, and I think they've been successful at it. I can't hear you. Sorry about that. Do you think there are some loopholes with pavement and performance warranties currently? Not that I'm aware of. But I'm not an engineer either. I play one on TV, though. Very good one. That's all the questions that I have for you, Ed. Do we have any additional? Oh, Rep. Cara. Yeah, thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you, Ed, for being here. I just want to clarify, county roads' official position, is it neutral still? No, we have not taken this through our normal internal process. It's officially nothing. Officially, I would recommend to our board that we oppose. You would recommend a, that what you did two terms ago? Because we have the May language in there for the road agency. And I appreciate that. Thank you. I should have recognized that, that you did do that, and I do appreciate that. But by the same token, we are still concerned about how we're going to do the maintenance with the state. Sure, well, and I appreciate you giving the number on the 63 out of 83 counties do the maintenance for MDOT. I had not heard that number before, so thanks for sharing that today. I think it's very safe to say, correct me if I'm wrong, but through this bill, the contract could have it to where you subcontract with the local road agency to do those maintenance efforts. It's not like they have to go out and buy a snowplow. That contract can be built in a way that the road agency is the ones doing the maintenance in that circumstance. Is that correct? They could, but does that mean that's an extra cost to the department rather than going directly to us to do their maintenance? They're going to have their maintenance costs on their contract, and they're going to pass it on. Are they going to use our dollar rate? If there's a contract between MDOT and a company to build a road, and then the road subcontracts with their local road agency to do the maintenance, to me that's a very productive way to have some private sector involvement in this process instead of just trusting government at the state level to work with government at the local level and make wise and prudent decisions.
