title: Finance — Tuesday, December 16, 2025
transcript:
Let's call this meeting to order. Good morning and welcome to the regularly scheduled December 16th, 2025 meeting of the House Committee on Finance. Clerk, please take attendance. Chair Tisdell? Here. Representatives Frisbee? Here. VanderWaal? Here. Leitner? Here. Martin? Here. Posthumus? Here. Alexander? Here. Aragona? Schuette? Here. Hoskins? Here. Carter? Neely? Breen? Young? Ties? Present. Mr. Chair, you have 11 members present. You do have a quorum. Very good. Nick McLaren moves to adopt the meeting. I need a representative to motion. He's been bugging me to get his name in the record. So, all right. Well, there you go. Merry Christmas. We'll make it Vice Chair Frisbee then. Moves to adopt the minutes for December 9th. No objections. That's unanimous consent. House Bill 5318. Representative Frisbee, let's take testimony, please. I tried. I tried, man. Begin. Introduce your guest, please. This is Tim Poxon, who's the legislative chair of the American Legion here in the state of Michigan. So, he'll be speaking in just a second. Thank you, Chair and members of the committee, for the opportunity to testify in support of House Bill 5318. House Bill 5318 makes practical, targeted updates to Michigan's General Sales Tax Act to ensure that charitable organizations, schools, churches, hospitals, and veteran service organizations can continue to serve their communities effectively in the face of rising cost. The current sales tax exemption for charitable fundraising and vehicle purchases were last adjusted in 2018. Since that time, inflation has dramatically increased the cost of vehicles, equipment, and goods commonly used for fundraising events. What may have been reasonable thresholds just a few years ago no longer reflect the market realities. As a result, many organizations are finding it increasingly difficult to raise funds or acquire reliable vehicles needed to deliver essential services. 5318 addresses the challenge in a responsible way. First, it increases the sales tax exemption for fundraising events to $75,000 in aggregate sales per event for schools, churches, hospitals, parent cooperative preschools, and nonprofit organizations

provided the sales are for charitable purpose. This allows the organizations to run effective fundraisings without being penalized by outdated limits. Second, the bill updates the fundraising exemption for veteran service organizations by raising the cap for a single event from $25,000 to $75,000. Fundraising to provide transportation, emergency assistance, and community support to those who have served our country. This change reflects both the respect for their mission and recognition of today's cost. Third, 5318 modernizes the exemption for sales tax-free purchases of personal property and vehicles used to raise funds or obtain resources. The bill raises the exemption limits to $60,000 for personal property and $75,000 for vehicles, levels that better reflect the actual cost of safe, reliable equipment and transportation in today's market. 5318 also ties these thresholds to the consumer price index, ensuring the law remains current over time. While the bill may result in a modest reduction in sales tax revenue, the fiscal impact is limited and targeted. In return, the state enables non-profits and veterans organizations to operate more efficiently, raise funds more effectively, and deliver services that otherwise might fall to the government. I respectfully urge the committee to support House Bill 5318, and I'm going to turn it over to Tim Paxson. Thank you, Chair and members of the committee. It's an honor to be here. The American Legion Department of Michigan does support House Bill 5318. Michigan House Bill 5318 of 2025 seeks to offset years of inflation by bringing provisions of the General Sales Tax Act as they relate to 501c19 veteran group organizations back to an impact level where they were afforded back in 2018. This bill provides identical treatment of 501c3 charities and 501c4 social welfare organizations related to fundraising events and purchases of vehicles and other tangible personal property used for their charitable purposes. The background on this is when enacted, Public Act 530 provided sales tax relief to veterans organizations up to the amount of $25,000 for each qualified individual purchase, such as the purchase of vehicles, while leaving the purchase threshold a mere $5,000 for charities and social welfare organizations. There was no provision in the act that allowed per fundraising event exemption amount to charities and social welfare organizations. The emphasis behind this bill is to return the buying power of the tax-exempt organizations back to the level they were afforded back in 2018. And just in a review on page two, which you all, by the way, should have a copy of, this legislation will increase the sales tax exemptions for schools, churches, hospitals, and nonprofits for the purpose of charitable fundraising. Under the General Sales Tax Act, the first 10,000 of sales by above groups has been aggregated sales of 25,000 were exempt from the sales tax. And currently, these charitable tax organizations purchase of vehicles with a sales price of less than $5,000 or $25,000 for veteran groups receive a sales tax exemption. Within the past 10 years, inflation has dramatically raised and this legislation needs to be updated in accordance with the times. This bill would exempt $75,000 in aggregate sales of personal property for each fundraising event by the above listed organizations as long as the sales were for charitable fundraising. The $25,000 veterans organizations would be increased to $75,000 and would increase the sales tax exemption for personal property or vehicles raised, obtained, and resources from 5K, 25K to 60K for personal property and $75,000 for vehicles. Again, it's an honor to be before this committee and I appreciate your time today and hope you'll support. If you have any questions, I'd be free to take them. I'll just add one example. The local VFW that wanted us to help, the American Legion wanted us to help in the market to try to buy a new pickup to haul one plow, two haul trailers. And if you've bought a four-wheel drive pickup and a heavy-duty pickup, you know what those cost these days. They're up into the $70,000 easily, even for a very non-decorated or equipped model. So this will allow them to be able to operate in the marketplace and fulfill those needs. Okay. Representative Martin. Thank you, Mr. Chair. So I think we ought to add also the whole scope of what veteran service organizations do for veterans and technically then for the state because the state's not supplying that activity for the veteran. The veterans are doing it for the veterans. We report every month the number of hours that we've – actually, it's an annual thing, but we report it every month – how many hours we spend doing the volunteer work. You know, at the cost of the Federal Labor Department, the number of hours we take to do the Great Lakes Cemetery in our case, in my case, the value returned to the community is much greater than any tax – sales tax thing you're going to see here that we're going to lose, quote-unquote, to the state. So whether it's giving – helping handicap equipment or rehabilitation equipment, transportation for people to get to medical appointments and so forth, things that necessarily don't go reported because it's volunteer work, it's extremely beneficial to the entire state, much higher cost than what the sales tax loss is going to be. Well stated. Thank you. Any other questions? That's it. Thank you very much, gentlemen. Thank you. Now we're going to move to voting on House Bill 5256, which is my bill. We have a substitute presented by Representative Young. Representative Young, would you like to speak to your substitute? Thank you so much, Mr. Chair. And again, thank you for bringing the legislation forward. We heard good testimony when we were here last regarding your legislation, and I just wanted to uplift that. We know that good health doesn't start and stop with the health center or with the country club fitness center, but good health is also being able to afford fresh, healthy groceries. That's a part of good health, particularly when we're looking at the skyrocketing cost of groceries for everyday Michiganders. We know that good health also includes being able to afford prescription drugs. One of the things that I've really been dealing with lately is I have a good friend who is experiencing a serious illness. She doesn't have insurance. And this is what she said to me the other day. She said, sickness won't take us to the grave, but poverty will. Sickness won't take us to the grave, but poverty will. And so when we look at these opportunities to provide a relief for Michiganders around health and fitness, I want to be certain to include along with the fitness centers, groceries, as well as prescription drugs. So with that, I offer my substitute. Thank you for the time this morning, Mr. Chair. You're welcome. And would you like to motion to take that and be a... Yes, I would like to motion that we bring this before the committee for a vote. Representative Young so moves to adopt the substitute. Clerk Campbell Crawley, please take the roll. On the motion to adopt the H3 substitute, Chair Tisdale? No. Representative Frisbee? Pass. VanderWaal? No. Leitner? No. Martin? No. Postumus? No. Alexander? No. Aragona? No. Schutte? No. Hoskins? Yes. Carter? Neely? Bream? Young? Yes. Pies? Yes. Mr. Chair, you have three yay, eight nay, one pass. The motion does not prevail. All right. Thank you very much. I've got one card to read in. This is wishing not to speak and opposing the bill, Sean Sorensen Abbott from the Michigan Department of Treasury. And I just can't help myself, but if everybody got a look at the House fiscal analysis, and the claim is that this deduction would cost somewhere between $50 and $70 million on an annual basis. Well, as I testified last week, at $1,500, the maximum credit would be $63.75. To get to $50 million, you would need 784,000 Michiganders to itemize their taxes

and take the maximum deduction. To get to $70 million, you'd need 1.1 million Michiganders to itemize their deductions and take the maximum amount. We have one problem with that. There are only 440,000 Michiganders that itemize. And on average, only 25% of Michiganders have a club membership. So that brings it to about 110,000. So if 110,000 that itemize and have a club membership took the maximum deduction, that would be about $7 million. So the House fiscal analysis or this estimate was only off by 7 to 10 times. And then if you want to know, well, the $7 million, what does that mean to the school aid fund? Well, 23.8% of income tax revenue goes to the school aid fund. 23.8% would equal 0.008% of the school aid fund. So Representative Aragona moves to adopt this or move it forward. Take the roll, please. The motion to report, Chair Tisdale. Yes. Representative Frisbee. Yes. VanderWaal. Yes. Leitner. Yes. Martin. Yes. Pashimus. Yes. Alexander. Yes. Aragona. Yes. Schoody. Yes. Hoskins. Pass. Carter. Pass. Neely. Breen. Young. Pies. No. Mr. Chair, you have nine yay, one nay, three pass. The motion does prevail. Thank you very much. And that will be reported with recommendation. Vice Chair Hoskins moves to excuse absent members. No further business in front of this committee. The committee stands adjourned. Thank you.

title: Senate Session 25-12-11
transcript: The Senate will come to order. Pursuant to Senate Rule 1.101, the Secretary of the Senate shall preside. Pursuant to Senate Rule 3.104, the Senate may handle routine business, motions, and communications. Mr. President, there are informational communications available on Session Web. For the Secretary for the Record, the President recognizes Senator Cherry. Thank you, Mr. Secretary. Just wanted to take a moment to remark upon some of the actions that occurred yesterday afternoon in the House. There were a series of decisions made. Actually, I suppose it was one decision, but with multiple consequences in the House Appropriations Committee. One of the things that occurred as a result of that decision is the House Appropriations Committee defunded services for lead-poisoned kids in Flint. As I was looking through the document that the House took action on, I noticed that they decided to continue to fund grants to businesses through the Michigan Strategic Fund. They decided to continue to send $45 million to businesses through the Going Pro Fund. But for some reason, those are okay and not waste, fraud, and abuse, but providing services to lead-poisoned kids is. You know, I don't tend to begrudge my colleagues when things happen to support issues in their district. I mean, I see that one of the things that was not removed was a bridge replacement in Hillsdale County. I never drive through Hillsdale County personally. This does not affect me or my constituents really one way or other, but I don't begrudge the fact that there's a bridge in Hillsdale County that needs to be replaced. But for some reason, it seems some of my legislative colleagues in the House feel that they need to deny help to kids facing lead poisoning in Genesee County while it's okay to fund bridge replacements in their own county. Yesterday, I voted in committee to advance an issue that doesn't affect my constituents, but helps the constituents of a representative from West Michigan dealing with a trespass issue. Don't mind it. Glad to be able to support resolving an issue that affects his constituents, although it has no effect on mine. Because generally, it makes sense to help people when it doesn't hurt your own constituents. But apparently, that same representative feels that services should be denied to lead-poisoned kids in Flint. I find that extremely disappointing. And I have to ask my colleagues over there who vote this way, is that the way that you think government should be run? Where you're here to actively attack constituents of other legislators? That's not the way that I've operated in the years I've been in the legislature, actively attacking the constituents of other legislators. But apparently, that's the way that the House believes government should function. I do not believe that. But we've got to figure out how to work in an environment in which apparently the majority of the members in another chamber do believe that the purpose of government is to actively attack the constituents of others. Extremely disappointed by the action yesterday in the House. I've also been a little bit surprised that we have heard nothing from the governor of our state. No comment. Well, I would ask the governor if she believes that the House action to deny services to lead-poisoned kids in Flint is something that she agrees with or not. Thank you, Mr. Secretary. In absence of a quorum, pursuant to Senate Rule 3.104 and Joint Rule 15, the Senate will adjourn and stand adjourned until Tuesday, December 16th at 10 a.m. in the morning. The Senate is now adjourned. Thank you.

title: Appropriations 25-12-09
transcript:
Well, good morning. We'd like to call the Senate Committee on Appropriations to order. We will have members coming in later due to our awful Michigan weather. But Mr. Clerk, will you please call the roll? Chair Anthony. Here. Senator McCann. Senator Cherry. Senator Baer. Senator Santana. Senator Schenk. Senator Irwin. Senator Hertel. Senator Kavanaugh. Senator Kleinfeld. Senator McMorrow. Senator Camilleri. Senator Bumstead. Senator Albert. Senator DeMoose. Senator Heisinga. Senator Outman. And Senator Tice. Madam Chair, you have 12 members present. You have a quorum. Thank you. First, we will begin with Senate Bill 729 related to capital outlay. Senator McCann, would you like to summarize your bill for the committee? Thank you so much, Chair Anthony and my colleagues on the committee for the opportunity to briefly discuss Senate Bill 729. This bill provides an exception to adjust the limit of outstanding obligations of the State Building Authority in light of federal changes that altered the State Building Authority's future bonding capacity. My bill would address this issue by ensuring that the previously excluded portion from the advanced refunded 2015 Series 1 is no longer applied toward the bond capacity. This would apply towards this series only and would free up approximately $421 million in bond capacity. This, in turn, will make more funds available for potential capital outlay projects for higher education institutions as well as potentially state buildings so that they can continue to better serve our constituents, students, and their communities. And for more details, since this is an interesting and technical topic, I'd like to invite Josh Sefton from Senate Fiscal Agency up to provide a little more background on the issue regarding Senate Bill 729. And here you are, sir. Nice to see you. Good morning. Thank you for joining us, Josh. Thank you, Madam Chair, members of the committee. As Senator McCann mentioned, I'm Josh Sefton with Senate Fiscal. Just a little bit more background on this bill and kind of where that $421 million number came from. Taking a step back, though, the SBA, as Senator McCann alluded to, it provides financing for state buildings, facilities at universities and community colleges, and it funds those projects through bonding. And as Senator McCann mentioned, there's a bond cap set in statute at $2.7 billion. The bill, the only thing the bill does, it exempts that Series 1 from 2025 from counting towards the bond cap. There's a phrase in that bill used called advanced refunding. So there's two types of refunding with bonds. There's advanced refunding, which is refunding a bond, so basically refinancing like you might do with your mortgage, but with a bond instead before the call date. So the call date is the date when a bond issuer can refund the bond at no penalty. Before the call date, they can't necessarily do that, so they have to do a tactic called advanced refunding. We'll get more into that in just a second. Currently there are 13 outstanding capital outlay project planning authorizations that were authorized both in 2023 and 2024. The state share of both of all 13 of those projects from both of those bills is just under $260 million. So with or without this bill, so either with the increased bond cap or without the increased bond cap, there's likely to be enough room under the bond cap to fund those. It kind of depends on timing and when those projects are actually completed. Everybody should have a handout on their desk. It's on white paper. It looks like this. There's two tables on it. The top table shows what bonding capacity will look like going forward under current law. So that's the status quo, and then the bottom one would be under Senate Bill 729. You can see out in really when you're talking about doing new capital outlay projects, these liabilities don't hit the bond cap until several years after they're approved. So really if you're looking at new capital outlay planning authorizations going forward from today, you probably would be putting those liabilities in like the 2029-2030 column. Typically with appropriations we think, okay, it's this year's issue or next year's issue. This is a few years down the road. So a little bit on the $421 million figure. As I mentioned before, when there are favorable interest rates, sometimes bond issuers want to refinance their bonds or refund their bonds. And before the call date, if a bond issuer wants to do that, they have to do what's called advanced refunding. So mechanically what they would do is the bond issuer would go back to the bond market. Let's say they're three years out from their call date and they have a $500 million bond. They would bond for another $500 million at today's interest rates. They would put that money in escrow and usually invest it in money market accounts or some very low-risk investment vehicle, wait until the call date of the bond, and then use the proceeds from that new bond to pay off the old bond. Back in 2017, effective January 1, 2018, the federal government changed, some laws changed, and that tactic is no longer something that tax-exempt bond issuers can do. So that would be states, local units of government, nobody can do advanced refunding on tax-exempt bonds. Taxable bonds, that's still acceptable and allowable under federal law, but tax-exempt bonds, you can't do that. So the issue where that comes in with the state building authority, so regardless of what this body and your colleagues in the House do, the federal law is not going to change here. But the way that federal law is treated under the SBA statute, which has a special exemption for advanced refundings in counting toward the bond cap, that's really what this $421 million issue is addressing. So under current law, advanced refundings aren't counted toward the bond cap. Back in June of 2025, SBA did about a $750 million total issue of that. $421 million had previously been advanced refunded and not counted toward the bond cap. So earlier this year, we got a memo that said that basically when we refinanced this, we didn't realize we hadn't counted that $421 million, and so that took $421 million off of the bond cap or the space allowable for new projects going forward. I think that's about all I have in my notes. Again, the tables show you what future bonding scenarios look like under both scenarios. I don't know that I could give you a number of like, hey, how much can we do? But those numbers in the table should give you an idea of where those limits might be going forward. With that, I'd be happy to take any questions. Thank you, Josh. Senator Albert? Thank you, Madam Chair. I apologize, Mr. Sefton. Maybe I'm just not understanding it properly. So I get what you're saying up to the point of when they do the advanced refinancing. It's to get lower interest rates. That makes sense. I'm struggling to figure out what the issue is after that point. So is it that the debt would get double counted, so you would count the original bond plus the refinancing, and they didn't – is the issue that the SBA wasn't counting that $400 million plus by accident or an error? What's the issue? So it gets into – really, there's a larger policy discussion that I won't weigh in on given my role, but the advanced refunding versus current refunding. I think there's – and I don't know the history of how that exemption got written into the SBA statute. It's been in there for quite a while as far as I'm aware. There would be that interplay. So let's say you have – let's say we bonded back in 2020, call dates 2030, and interest rates next year just fall through the floor, and it makes sense to refund this particular issue. Well, okay, if we're in 2027, we've still got three years until 2030, and so for those three years, your liabilities are going to be doubled, right, because you have two bonds for the same amount of money. From a balance sheet perspective, like assets and liabilities, your net liability is the same because even though you've doubled your amount of debt, you've also got an equal amount of cash in the bank to equal one of those two bonds, so your net liability is still the same. So for counting that – that double counting for those three years, I think that's probably where that advanced refunding exemption came out in the statute. But practically speaking, that not counting of the advanced refunding, it persists after that – after the old bond is still paid off. You know, we've hit the call date, the cash that was sitting in escrow is now used to repay the old bond. The SBA statute as it's currently written continues to exempt that advanced refunded portion, and so that expectation is kind of where this $420 million surprise came from when that memo was sent out. So SBA hadn't been counting that $421 million toward the bond cap because it was previously exempted, and then now they can't advance refunded again, like they couldn't have done that in 2025 because the law was changed in 2018 to preclude that.

It's not a very clear issue. I apologize if that's not clear. So just to make sure that $427 million, that's real money that still needs to be paid back despite the fact that it was the advance? Correct. Okay, thank you. Thank you, Senator. Any additional questions for Josh? Okay, thank you. So we've talked a little bit about the numbers. There are a few institutions that wanted to provide a little bit of local context to this issue. We wanted to bring up Dr. Paul R. Watson II, who's the president of Kellogg Community College, just to speak briefly about capital outlay on his campus. Welcome. Good morning, everyone. It's great to be among friends and to see several familiar faces. Chairwoman Sarah Anthony, Senator Sarah Anthony, and members of the Appropriation Committee, thank you for the opportunity to speak today in strong support of SB 729 and the urgent need to move forward with community college capital outlay authorizations. At Kellogg Community College, our capital projects are not simply about improving facilities. They are about expanding Michigan's workforce in the fields where our state needs talent the most. Allowing colleges to proceed with planning and construction is urgently necessary. Every year we delay, construction and equipment costs rise dramatically, and community colleges who operate leanly and responsibly are disproportionately impacted. These delays reduce the number of students we can train and the number of health care and technical professionals available to serve our region. This urgency is especially true in our health, energy, skilled trades, and manufacturing programs, fields that require modern, high-tech, capital-intensive learning environments. These buildings are not just classrooms. They house simulation labs, radiography equipment, dental operations, modern nursing labs, skilled trade shops, and real-world clinical training environments. They are truly the engines that power Michigan's workforce pipeline. At KCC specifically, our health care facilities are at capacity right now. While the Michigan Board of Nursing has approved the college to admit up to 280 nursing students each year, we can only admit 208. We cannot reach that number of 280 because our existing labs, simulation spaces, and the classrooms simply cannot support the volume. As a result, space, not demand, is the limiting factor in producing more nurses from our institution for the great state of Michigan. Our workforce outcomes, we are able to produce, already demonstrate the impact of our programs. We are unique as a community college in that we offer a full-time program, a part-time program, and a cohort of nights and weekends program, which we have opened up a second cohort because we have students who are traveling up to two hours to our location to actually participate in that. Right now, our first cohort is going to graduate this December. And as of this moment, when I asked our director of nursing, 96% of their students, four weeks before graduation, already have a job lined up post-graduation. This is a clear indicator of both need and employment demand. This demand extends far beyond nursing. Programs such as radiography, dental hygiene, physical therapist assistant, medical assistant, and EMS are all facing applicant pools that far exceed the number of students we can currently serve because our facilities have not kept pace with workforce needs. This is why the role-building renovation, and I provided a handout if you're curious to see that for you, is so important and critical. This project addresses aging infrastructure, expands instructional space, and modernized simulation and training labs essential for contemporary health care education. Supported by Representative Steve Frisbee, who serves in the Michigan's 44th State House District, this renovation will allow KCC to increase nursing enrollment, as I shared, from 208 to 280, and simultaneously expand our other high-demand programs, an impact that directly aligns with Michigan's workforce priorities. Health care careers offer strong labor market outcomes, family-sustaining wages, and immediate community benefit. Our local hospitals, our clinics, our dental practices, our EMS agencies, and long-term care providers are always asking us for more graduates. We are ready to meet that need, but we cannot do it without the modern spaces required to properly train them. SB 729 provides the essential step forward. Capital outlay projects at community colleges are workforce projects. They are talent development projects, and they are economic vitality projects for the state of Michigan. On behalf of Kellogg Community College, my fellow 27 community colleges within the Michigan Community College Association, and the communities we serve across Calhoun, Berry, and Branch County as our institution, I respectfully ask for your support of SB 729 and for timely authorization of these urgently needed capital investments. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Members, are there any questions? No, we're somewhat pressed on time. Thank you again for your testimony. We appreciate it. We also have visiting with us virtually Steve Mackey, the Senior Vice President of Finance at Oakland University. So I think that you are with us virtually. You can just unmute yourself, and we just ask that you kindly keep your remarks to about two to three minutes because we have some testimony for the next bill before us. Yes, thank you for having me this morning. Thank you, Chair Anthony, committee members, for the opportunity to testify. Oakland University deeply appreciates your continued support of capital outlay funding. Oakland is a vital asset to the state. We generate over $1.9 billion in annual economic impact. We are the definition of a brain-gain university. 95% of our graduates stay in Michigan, immediately bolstering our workforce with an average starting salary exceeding $65,000. When you invest in OU, you are investing in keeping talent and prosperity right here in Michigan. I'm here today to advocate for construction authorization of this much-needed project. It is not a project about expansion. It is about modernizing the core of our STEM education. The Science Complex project is absolutely critical because it creates immediate economic impact. This project will support over 180 construction jobs. It impacts every student. Every one of our 13,000 undergrad students make at least one class, take at least one class in this complex during their time at OU. And it drives research. Approximately 60% of our university's funded research runs through Dodge Hall, which currently houses both of our engineering and biology departments. Simply put, maintaining the competitiveness of OU's STEM programs means modernizing Dodge Hall. The capital outlay program is a vital funding source for regional universities like Oakland. While we maintain a strong balance sheet and robust reserves, OU is not large enough nor do we have the debt capacity to just self-fund a critical project of this magnitude on our own. This project is ready to move forward. Having completed the rigorous state approval process, the timeline of our Dodge Hall Science Complex project began in October of 2021 when the university board of trustees unanimously approved it as a priority request to DTMV. Our submission was reviewed, scored, and ranked by the Department of Technology Management and Budget, and it received planning authorization from the Michigan legislature and approval from the governor in December of 2023. The $10 million university match was used to cover the costs associated with this phase of the process. However, since the initial planning phase in 2020, we have already had to make significant and regrettable scope reductions, scaling the project from a two-building complex down to a single building just to manage the escalating costs. As this committee knows well, time is cost in construction. Every delay in authorization and legislative action translates into increased project costs, threatening further scope reduction that will ultimately degrade the quality of education we can offer to Michigan students. Chair Anthony and members of the committee, we are requesting your immediate approval to move forward with the Dodge Hall Science Complex. This investment yields high returns, retaining Michigan talent, supporting STEM education and research, creating high-quality construction jobs. We ask you to take legislative action as soon as possible to approve this critical project, locking in the current scope and preventing further cost escalation. Thank you, and I welcome any questions you have. Thank you so much. Members, are there any questions? Okay. We do have quite—thank you so much for your testimony. We appreciate you. We do have cards to read in. Mr. Clerk, will you please read the cards? Organizations supporting Senate Bill 729. Ferris State University, Delta College, Michigan State University, Macomb Community College, WCCD, Washtenaw Community College, Central Michigan University, Western Michigan University, Northern Michigan University, Eastern Michigan University, Michigan Community College Association, Michigan Association of State Universities, University of Michigan.

Michigan Dearborn, St. Clair County Community College, Traverse Connect, Northern Michigan Chamber Alliance, Oakland Community College, Lake Michigan College, Saginaw Valley State University, and Northwestern Michigan College, and Jackson College. Thank you so much. All right, I need a motion to report Senate Bill 729 to the floor with recommendation that it pass. Moved by Senator McCann, supported by Senator McMorrow. Mr. Clerk, will you please call the question? Chair Anthony. Yes. Senator McCann. Yes. Senator Cherry. Yes. Senator Baird. Senator Santana. Yes. Senator Schink. Yes. Senator Irwin. Senator Hertel. Senator Kavanaugh. Senator Kleinfeld. Senator McMorrow. Senator Camilleri. Senator Bumstead. Senator Albert. Senator Moose. Senator Heisinger. Senator Altman. And Senator Dice. And I appreciate our colleagues for understanding the speed of getting this before our committee. This is something that we wanted to ensure was a part of the ongoing conversations around economic development and making sure that we have multiple tools for our communities to utilize to revitalize every corner of our state. So I'm excited to hear from the local communities and we'll actually listen to their testimony first if we can, Mr. Zinn, and then we'll bring you back up for some clarification. So we wanted to start out from the folks who made the trek up here and bring up some of our local voices. We'll start off with our deputy county executive from Macomb County, J.P. Rhea, if you are here to come and speak to the Transformational Brownfields Program. There's a button. There you go. Sorry, I'm just from the east side. This is all a little bit out of sorts for me. Thank you, Madam Chair. Really appreciate it and distinguished members of the committee. It's always wonderful to be in Lansing. And as you alluded to, the weather is absolutely exceptional today. It is a wonderful, wonderful opportunity to be here with so many friends across the entire state of Michigan. And with all of our friends and colleagues here today, we're here in partnership to express our support for this Transformational Brownfield Bill that is under consideration this morning. I want to preface my comments this morning that I am not an environmental remediation expert, nor am I a project financing expert. And this is work that we love to do every single day with the 27 communities that make up Macomb County and all of our partners around the region in southeast Michigan. Having the opportunity to work with so many communities, my role as an economic developer has given me the opportunity to really scope and scale major projects that have helped transform Macomb County's economy over the past 15 years from a $33 billion economy to a $56 billion economy. And this isn't done with one project. This isn't done with one incentive. This isn't done with one industry. It's done by a collection of individuals and we're empowered not only by the state legislature, economic development agencies, regulatory agencies to tackle hard projects that the creativity of our local communities, like our friends in Sterling Heights that are here with us today. What this bill and this package of bills does for us is it gives us the ability to not only scope these projects, but most importantly, it gives us the ability to be collectively accountable. Using the structure of what the state empowers us with, we can work with our local communities and really focus on one of the key elements when we look at any incentive that the state considers is eligibility. So thanks for being here. Good morning. Good morning very much. Madam Chair, excuse me, Senator Anthony, thank you so much for your leadership and your friendship to our community. You're amazing. And thank you to the bipartisan nature of the committee and supporting economic development. My name is Bob Tresize. I'm president and CEO of Lansing Economic Area Partnership, LEAP. We represent Ingham, Eaton, and Clinton County. I also am representing the Economic Development Leaders for Michigan this morning. That's the top 10 CEOs from regional economic development agencies across the state. We represent 90% of the state's population and collectively have hundreds of years of experience, including several in our group who have worked in other states. Economic Development Leaders for Michigan is unanimously supportive of this bill today, and thank you for your continued work to build Michigan into a competitive and more competitive, better place across the nation. If you're an environmentalist, I think you're for this bill. If you're for increasing the tax base so we can support quality services for people in our neighborhoods, I think you should be for this bill. I also think that economic development often is profoundly a psychological game. They want to see if buildings are being rehabbed. They want to see if our skyline are being changed. They want to make sure that buildings on the corners that they drive by are not dilapidated. And so I think from that perspective, too, this bill has a profound impact. Here in the city of Lansing, Mayor Shore, the Lansing EDC, City Council have put together with the MEDC an amazing project, which is called New Vision Lansing. It absolutely would not happen without the additional gap financing, if you want to look at it that way, provided through the brownfield transformational bill. So it's changing our skyline. And we want to congratulate Paul Genovosi, who is taking enormous risk to take on these series of projects. Finally, right at this moment, I'm not sure if I'm right, whether the geographical representation has been taken out or has been put back in.

Honestly, I don't quite know at this moment, but the EDLM group, we think that's important to have geographical equitability to make sure that all projects can find a home. So if we can provide any assistance on what that formula continues to look like, you know, we're here to help as well. So I really thank the bipartisan support. I think this is one of the profound ways to change the state of Michigan and make it a more prosperous future for especially younger generations and to make sure that all communities have access to this excellent progressive tool. Thank you. Are there any questions for Bob? Senator Altman. Not as much a question as a response to the geographical requirement. As I see it right now, it looks like that is out. And, you know, those of us who are from the smaller, more rural areas, that's something that's significant for us. And not sure why it was pulled, whether it was they couldn't get enough buy in or they couldn't get enough projects to make it worth having. I mean, I don't know what the rationale was, but I'm a little disgruntled that it's out of there and would certainly like to see that put back in, too. So thank you for bringing that up. Thank you, Senator. Any additional questions for Mr. Tresice? OK, thank you for being here. Thank you, Madam Chair. OK, we'll now turn over to Hassan Bedeun, who is the group executive economic development director or point person for the city of Detroit. I believe he's joining us virtually. Yes, good morning, Madam Chair and committee members. My name is Hassan Bedeun. I'm the group executive of economic development for the city of Detroit. I'm here today to testify in strong support of Senate Bill 723, which would expand the state's transformational brownfield program by lifting the program caps to allow for more projects to utilize the program. This legislation reflects a welcome return of one of the most trusted and proven tools in our state's economic development toolbox, the TBP program. It's an absolutely critical program because without it, there would be no hope in developing the most challenging brownfield sites across Michigan. These are sites that have huge potential to transform their surrounding areas, but would otherwise sit vacant for decades because prior uses make their redevelopment financially impossible. And the TBP program is great policy, not just because it allows for the creation of vibrant places that drive long term growth, but because it's fiscally responsible. It relies only on performance based incentives and bucks the trend of providing upfront cash to incentivize development. That means if the project isn't completed, it doesn't get the benefit of the incentives, period. And the incentive is entirely needs based, meaning that it only provides reimbursement to the extent necessary to close the financial gap and make a project economically viable. And those incentives don't negatively impact the existing budget at all. And while this legislation is crucial to the revitalization of Detroit's riverfront, it's important to recognize that it's critical to all areas of the state. In short, every area of the state would either directly or indirectly benefit off expanding the TPP program. And I think thank both the bill sponsor and our counterparts in the House and colleagues here in this committee for hopefully advancing this important legislation to that end. Thank you, Hassan. Members, are there any questions? Senator Schink. Thank you. I was reading the Brownfield report last night that the state of Michigan put out. And third, there is the Henry Ford slash Detroit Pistons Future of Health redevelopment that was most recently approved last year, I believe. Thank you. Thank you. Any additional questions for Hassan? Thank you so much for joining us. Yes, ma'am. Thank you. Thank you. All right. We also have Mark Vanderpool, who's the city manager of Sterling Heights. Come on up. We appreciate you being here today. Thank you, Madam Chair and honorable committee members. Let me skip through these and get to what the current situation is. I don't think anyone would disagree that this really falls under a brownfield category. This mall is vacant now. It is closed. Aside from the Maytag repairman, there is no one there in the mall. This is where we want to be with this program that has been validated as a success not only in the city of Detroit, but in Muskegon and other areas. There's little question that this would be absolutely transformational, not only for the city of Sterling Heights, for the region, and for the state of Michigan. So here's what's happened over the last 20 years. You can see the taxable value nosedive. It hasn't bottomed out yet, but it's getting really, really close. And that's the problem for the state, too, when you think income tax and sales tax loss opportunity because of the decline of this, what has become a brownfield. And then with the new project, you can see the projected taxable value increase as we go on with the full development. So it's all about revitalization. It's all about returning to the vibrant area that this once was. And we can't do it without the transformational brownfield program. The city has gone as far as it can. The developer has gone as far as it can. The last hurdle in this project is the transformational brownfield program. It's worked in other areas. It can work in this case. And the expansion, lifting the cap, will undoubtedly cause many other projects across the state, as you know and as you've heard, to proceed as well. So it's part of the prosperity agenda in Michigan. These projects are vitally important. They're not only important for income from the state, local tax dollars for the locals, but the economic impact by way of jobs, which is hundreds of millions of dollars over time. So with all that in mind, we respectfully request in Sterling Heights on behalf of the city of Detroit

and all the other cities that will benefit from this, that you approve this Bill 723. And I'm happy to address any questions. Thank you. Thank you. Members, are there any questions? We appreciate your... Oh, Senator Schink. Thank you. I spent many enjoyable hours at Lakeside when I was a youngster. I also remember how Lakeside helped empty out my town of Port Huron, which was also facilitated by other people who invested in land just outside the town and then built malls there. So I have mixed feelings. But I guess what I'm wondering from you is, are you blocked if we don't raise the cap? Is it impossible to do this if we don't raise the cap? Thank you, Senator. I would say the short answer to your question is I would say yes. The project would not move forward in its current form. Would it move forward in some other fashion? Nothing against Amazon warehouses, nothing against a traditional neighborhood, but could we get something like that that's permitted under the current zoning? Sure. But is that transformational? Are we making a difference in the region and the state with a sort of run-of-the-mill project? We're looking at transformational projects that generate prosperity. I understand what you're saying for the city of Port Huron. But Port Huron is potentially a beneficiary of this project program down the road as well. And Port Huron is thriving under various economic development programs also. So we recognize the competing forces, but doing nothing in this case and not taking advantage of these programs that have proven to be highly successful means that there's a race to the bottom. Let me give you just an analogy of this situation. Remember when the manufacturing facilities were closing? There's countless examples across Michigan. There was an example in Sterling Heights. The assembly plant was scheduled to close through bankruptcy. When those plants close, they suck the life out of an area. And you see it. I don't need to elaborate on it. We've experienced it in the state of Michigan. You can see that this 100-acre vacant brownfield site will suck the life out of the area. Not just Sterling Heights, but the region. And will that impact Port Huron eventually too? Sure. So this is all about rising tide lifts all boats, and we hope you'll approve it. Thank you. Any additional questions? Okay. Would you mind reading the cards of support? Organizations supporting Senate Bill 723. The Business Leaders for Michigan. Luna? Oh, Ayuna. Ayuna. The Detroit Regional Chamber. The Grand Rapids Chamber. The Michigan Downtown Association. Networks Northwest. Suburban Collection Showplace. Bedrock. The Justin Fisher, the Mayor of Novi. And then opposing Senate Bill 723 is the Mackinac Center for Public Policy. Thank you, Mr. Clark. So members, we do have another committee that is beginning in a few moments. So this committee will go at ease and then reconvene a bit later. Thank you. All right. We will now resume our Senate Committee on Appropriations. I think we left off talking about transformational brownfields. And we again appreciate the individuals who came in person as well as testified virtually. We have been having conversations both today and in the last few days around this particular plan. And we wanted to lift up an S1 sub in order for our members to consider. I want to give a few highlights of what that S1 sub would look like. And then we will invite David Zen up to come up and answer questions both related to the bill before us as well as the S1 sub. As talking to members, and we wanted to make sure to lift up several of our committee members who have been particularly helpful in leading in economic development ideas and strategies, particularly Senator Cavanaugh, Senator McMorrow, Senator Bayer, who have helped us reimagine what some of our tools will look like. Here are a few highlights of what we'll see in today's substitute. We will be increasing the post-construction incentive cap by $1.9 billion. The existing $200 million construction phase cap would not increase. It institutes a new state tax capture for statewide priorities related to small business support, housing, and child care. It would work like this. So each time a new transformational brownfield project is approved, MEDC would capture an additional 25% of the taxes on top of each tax capture approved for the project. 25% of the tax captured would be allocated as follows. 5% going to small business support. In many of our communities, small businesses, the corridors that we shop at are really important to members. So 5% going to small business programming and placemaking, 10% going to child care investments, and 10% going to the state's housing fund. The annual cap in the substitute would essentially raise the annual cap by $80 million. However, the increase would only be dedicated to new projects yet to be approved. The bill also makes several programmatic changes to protect taxpayers and encourage best practices. Here are a few of those examples. Requiring any tax exemptions, not just tax captures, to count towards the incentive cap. Requiring projects to complete construction no later than 10 years. Prohibits tax captures for simply relocating existing programs into new transformational brownfield locations. Requiring that all of the transformational projects with housing to include an affordable or workforce development housing component. The bill would also incentivize transformational brownfield projects to relocate businesses from high demand industries from out of state. And it would allow MEDC to take action to reduce a project's incentives if their capital investment requirements are not met. Now in addition, similar to the work that we've done all year, particularly in this committee, we wanted to make sure that transparency and accountability were front and center with these captures. So we've done the following in the substitute. Approving MEDC reporting requirements by developing a comprehensive database of all brownfield projects in the state. Requiring a dedicated website with all MEDC documents related to transformational brownfield projects, including a requirement that the MSF board meetings are live streamed. Anytime a transformational brownfield project is on the agenda. Requires all brownfield projects to have a clear annual milestone posted online and tracked the progress. This is something that our friends in the media have been looking forward to and this is something that was important to committee members. Requiring that the webpage have a fiscal dashboard that includes information on the status of each project, including levels of investment and of the amount of incentives received. The bill also requires a projection of incentive costs annually to provide a greater level of certainty to the budget. Which by the way, the substitute also makes sure that we are mining our balance sheet by increasing predictability and tracking for us as appropriation members. And first, I wanted to open it up for members who earlier flagged that they may have some technical questions related to the program. Senator McMorrow. Thank you, Madam Chair. title: Government Operations — Thursday, December 11, 2025
transcript:
The House Committee on Government Operations will come to order. Just a reminder, anybody wishing to speak on the bills that we're going to have on the agenda today, please fill out a white card on the testimony table and turn it into our clerk here. Representative VanderWaal moves to approve the minutes of November 13th without objection. Mr. Clerk, would you please take attendance? Chair Bregold. Here. Representatives Harris. Here. VanderWaal. Present. Fitzgerald. Here. McFaul. Here. Mr. Chair, you have five members present, a quorum. Thank you. Okay, now Representative VanderWaal moves to approve the minutes of the November 13th meeting without objection. So ordered. Okay, we're delighted to have Senator Chang here today. Senator Chang has a bill that she'd like to speak to us in regards to. So this would remove the sunset on two property tax delinquency programs. Senator Chang. Good morning. Good morning, Mr. Chair, and thank you so much for the opportunity to talk about Senate Bill 423. I also wanted to invite Representative Myers-Phillips to join me as she is also very familiar with the bill and has sponsored the equivalent House bill. But I'm really honored to testify about a cause that would help keep struggling families stable and housed, reduce tax foreclosures, and help local governments remain more efficient in collecting property taxes. In this time of rising costs on just about everything, from food, health care, getting to work and child care, we must continue to do everything that we can as a state to help families to be able to stay in their homes and prevent homelessness. About a decade ago, you may remember there was a large crisis across many of our communities' tax foreclosure. In 2015, almost 25,000 properties in Detroit alone were foreclosed on. And it was devastating for people across our entire state to lose their homes because they were behind on property taxes. In more recent years, the legislature created the Delinquent Property Tax Payment Reduction Program and the Tax Foreclosure Avoidance Agreements, also known in my neck of the woods as Pay As You Stay and the Interest Rate Stipulated Payment Agreement. So the PAYS program was started in 2020, passed by a Republican legislature almost unanimously, 36 to 0 in the Senate, 105 to 2 in the House, and was sponsored by Representative Wendell Bird. So the PAYS program allows foreclosing governmental units to significantly reduce delinquent property taxes owed by homeowners who qualify for poverty exemptions. And the program is three parts. Once enrolled, all interest, penalties, and fees would be eliminated. To reduce an undue burden on homeowners, the balance due would be limited to back taxes only or 10% of a home's taxable value. And the remaining balance would be paid back over three years at 0% interest. Homeowners who qualify for a full or partial property tax exemption and enroll in future years would be eligible for the program. The tax foreclosure avoidance agreement program allows county treasurers to enter in foreclosure avoidance agreements with owners of properties for terms of up to five years and reduce the amount required to redeem a tax foreclosed home. So in Wayne County, the URSPA program reduces the interest rate to 6% from 18%. And that makes a tremendous impact for our residents. This program also received broad support in a Republican-controlled legislature, receiving unanimous support in both chambers. While these authorizations originated in the aftermath of the Great Recession, they have still proven useful year after year and should be allowed to continue. So I want to give you a sense of the numbers. In Wayne County, over 3,000 taxpayers are on the URSPA plan. And the total redemption amount reduced by this program was over $4.4 million. But this program is set to sunset on June 30, 2026, as currently written in Michigan law. As far as the PAYS program, there are over 2,000 taxpayers on the plan in Wayne County. And over 12,000 have benefited over time and received a zero balance since the program's inception. And this program actually unfortunately sunsetted already this past July. So year after year, we have seen the benefits for families and communities under these policies, and it would be unwise to leave them to expire in the times that we are currently living in. So my bill, Senate Bill 423, which was passed in the Senate almost unanimously

Ms. Lee, 34 to 1, would amend the General Property Tax Act to remove the sunset on both programs. These programs have been working in the counties that have them and will continuously allow treasurers the option to create these programs to help families stay under their roofs and contribute by continuing to pay their taxes, which is a win for everyone. This bill, if enacted, will help more homeowners stay in their homes, prevent blight, and provide more tax revenue for local governments than if they were to expire. So I ask for your support, and I'll hand it over to Rep. Myers-Phillips. Thank you so much, Senator Chang, and good morning, colleagues. Tanya Myers-Phillips, State Rep, House District 7. Thank you for the opportunity to speak in support of SB 423 this morning. I can't stress how important this legislation is. I agree with everything Senator Chang has shared and other people with sharing testimony today. I'll just share a bit more from my personal experience living through the foreclosure crisis. I'm a Detroit resident, lifelong Detroit resident, and I recall while we were going through this, neighbors, homes, people that I fellowshiped with, had company with, vibrant neighborhoods just began to disappear. Families that once held houses that once held families and vibrancy became vacant, became blighted. And you could just point down the street and say, so-and-so used to live there, so-and-so used to live there, gone. Because of a very difficult systemic issue of property taxes and being able to arrange, have the tools in place to be able to pay your bill and stay in your home. I remember working as an advocate at Michigan Legal Services, often 10, 12 hours a day, just counseling people through this process and advocating for the ERSPA legislation when it first came to the Statehouse. And coming on the other side of that, like so many of us here, we've seen the benefit of these tools. We see these tools working and people being able to stay in their homes. I mentioned before, and I stand behind it, I believe that these tools are perhaps some of the most successful pieces of bipartisan legislation that this state has passed in recent history. Because they don't cost the state much, not really. And they keep people in their homes. You're just allowing people to have the tools to stay in their homes, to raise their family, to build their lives, to build their communities with dignity. So they work. I wholeheartedly support them and ask you to support them and pass them as well so we can keep building up our cities, building up our counties, and building up Michigan. We want families to stay. And Senator Chang's legislation does exactly that. Thank you so much. I'm happy to answer any questions. Representative Fitzgerald. Yeah, thank you, Senator and Representative for bringing this forward. And, Senator, I think that the bill really does, I think, fit a really, while it may be a look back, I think it really fits a need going forward as well. Ensuring that communities are stable, that we have a compassionate taxing system that allows families to stabilize their lives, to make sure that this isn't something that continues to disrupt communities, neighborhoods, that neighborhood impact, you know, street by street in Detroit and communities across the state. I'm sure we have seen that, you know, everyone probably has a story from their home community of where that has occurred. I think the work of local treasurers is important to be made aware of these programs. And I think that by eliminating these sunsets, it may increase that investment and the use of this program to ensure that it is something that can help to, again, stabilize those municipalities. So I really appreciate this. I just kind of wanted to underscore that I think this will increase that utilization and have that local impact, eventually saving both local municipalities and the state money. Thank you for the comments. And I know that you'll hear next from the Ingham County Treasurer about the fact that there are county treasurers across the state who are actually really interested in starting these programs, but obviously they can't if the law expires. And so I'm really hopeful that not only will we be able to continue to help residents in my own community, but really that residents in your own communities across the state will be able to benefit, but that only will be able to happen if we remove those sunsets. So just really grateful for the opportunity to testify about the bill today. Thank you for your comment. Okay, not seeing any further comments, I want to thank you both for your work on the bills. Nobody wants to see somebody lose their home, and these are good programs that at least help prevent that. So thank you both for coming in today. Good to see you. Okay, we got some cards we need to read in. Wishing to speak in support of the bill is Alan Fox, Ingham County Treasurer, representing the Michigan Association of County Treasurers. Mr. Fox, welcome. Come on up, and the floor is yours. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. As I said, my name is Alan Fox. I'm the Treasurer of Ingham County. I also have the honor of serving as Legislative Co-Chair for the Michigan Association of County Treasurers, alongside former Senator McGregor from Kent County. And I do want to stress the bipartisan nature of this proposal. The vast majority of county treasurers across the state are not Democrats. They don't represent urban areas such as Wayne and Ingham County. And as Senator Chang suggested, many of them are interested in this program. It takes a little bit of work to set one up, and so the sunsets have been a deterrent to doing that. Since long before I became treasurer, Ingham County has prioritized property tax foreclosure prevention. In Ingham, we contract with our community action agency to provide services to property owners who are at risk of foreclosure, and we've worked to expand our contacts with these property owners so that we can catch problems earlier in the cycle and help people find the resources they need to stay in their homes. When the state provided the much-needed resources through the Michigan Homeowners Assistance Fund, my office worked with various nonprofit partners to extend those resources to eligible homeowners. People could apply for that online, but we discovered that the people who most needed it couldn't do that. And so we brought housing counselors from several agencies, as well as the computer equipment, printers, and scanners that homeowners needed to apply for those funds to libraries, community centers, churches, and other locations across the county to help people enroll. My half, of course, expired. The federal money that funded it ran out, and we started to look for other ways to continue to provide resources to our homeowners. In 2024, Ingham became the second county after Wayne to offer the two programs that are the subject of this hearing. They're the only methods that we have to reduce interest and other delinquency charges that can very quickly begin to add up to as much as the base tax that we're charged by law with trying to collect. In 2024, we began offering tax foreclosure avoidance agreements under MCL 2178Q, and we also introduced the poverty exemption reduction initiative under 2178G. Our programs have some slight differences from Wayne County's, but they function in essentially the same ways, and they let us move struggling homeowners from treading water to actually getting out of the swamp and onto some solid footing as they deal with all of the other financial circumstances they face. Nobody we talk with has delinquent taxes as their only financial or other problem. They've got other issues, and we're committed to not squeezing at those other problems by demanding the taxes or their home as a choice. So that's one of the reasons we work with our community action agency so that we can provide other resources to people. So after a little over a year here in Ingham County, we have 64 families under tax foreclosure avoidance agreements. We have 18 families that have already successfully used the program to pay off their delinquent taxes. Another nine are receiving poverty exemption reduction initiative assistance, and by law, we have not been able to enroll additional households into that program because that one expired on July 1st. And these programs have, of course, been of great benefit to these families. They are not in danger of foreclosure. They are dealing with other issues. But I should also note that they've brought $140,000 in delinquent tax payments to the county, and they've ended the possibility that those delinquent taxes will at some point have to be charged back to the local governments and schools. Many county treasurers, as I said, were reluctant to initiate these programs because they were perceived as difficult to manage. I think our experience in Ingham County is one that I've talked with other treasurers about, and they're now ready to take up. Ottawa County, I know, is preparing to use these sections of the law pending passage of this bill. And I hear from other county treasurers that they'd look at it as well, but that the sunsets really are a deterrent to setting up a program, setting up the processes, and then getting in a situation where they can't continue to do that. The programs do require some administration. They require one-on-one

contact with the people who are benefiting from them and it's a grave disincentive to start up a program like that and then have to give up on it after a short time. I also want to add, I'm also co-chair of the legislative committee of the Michigan Land Bank Association which also supports Senate Bill 423. Land banks handle property after it's been subject to tax foreclosure and the Land Bank Association recognizes that the better way to preserve households, neighborhoods, and communities is to keep people's homes out of foreclosure and keep them from falling through to the point where a land bank has to take them over. So members of the committee, I urge you to send Senate Bill 423 to the full House for action. All county treasurers do everything we can to keep homeowners out of tax foreclosure. Not all will use these two tools, but more will if we know that we can do it going forward. I haven't said as much about the Wayne County program as Senator Chang has and I know there's another speaker from the Wayne County Treasurer's Office who can give you some further information about that. But we're really looking to be able to expand these tools throughout the state of Michigan. Thank you. Thank you. I just got a quick question. How do you get the word out that these programs exist? You said sometimes there has to be like a one-on-one between your office and maybe somebody that's fallen into foreclosure. Do you send something in the mail or do you actually call them? We will call some people. All county treasurers are required to do a hearing, a show cause hearing, where people can come in and we're often able to rescue people at that point. That's very late in the process. That's a month or two months before foreclosure. We keep trying to move things like that earlier in the cycle. In Ingham County, we invented something. It's called the pre-publication hearing. December of each month, every county treasurer has to publish the parcels that are at risk of foreclosure. If any of you happen to pick up the City Pulse, not the current one, but next week and the week after that, you'll see the entire list of Ingham County foreclosures. We invented something that we called the pre-publication hearing. Sent notices out to people, got 50 people in to talk about how to get out of danger and fed them into the programs that way. We do things like that all the time. In Ingham County, we, thank goodness, do not have tens of thousands or thousands of problem properties or people at risk. I have a foreclosure prevention staff of four people. By the time we get homeowners who are a year or more into the cycle, we're reaching them by phone, reaching them by mail, reaching them any way we can to encourage them to come in. Sometimes that doesn't happen until late. We do the best we can with it. I know other counties do that as well. Some of the counties that have much less of an issue than Lansing does, the treasurer will knock on people's doors and will find people that way. That's a very critical piece of what we do. Thank you. That's great to hear. I hate to see a program like this in place and then somebody fall through the crack not knowing about it. Thanks for coming in today. Thank you. Next, we'll hear from Mr. James Barry, Wayne County Treasurer, who would like to speak in support of the bill. Good morning. I'm here to support Senate Bill 423 on behalf of the Wayne County Treasurer. My name is James Barry. I am the acting deputy treasurer for Wayne County. I've been in this position for five years. Just to give you some background, I was the attorney for the treasurer going back to 2008. I've been involved in the foreclosure process since its really inception when the bubble burst, which was in 2008 really. We immediately had thousands of people that would line up for the show cause and judicial foreclosure hearings because they were facing foreclosure. We didn't have any tools at the beginning. We eventually developed the stipulated payment agreement, which was just an installment payment agreement, did not do anything to affect the interest. In fact, the interest continues to accrue, but it would give additional time for taxpayers to pay. That was very helpful. We had people, I don't know if you're familiar with the City County Building in Detroit, but we would have a line from the courtroom going from the court side of the building all the way around the corner, all the way down the hall of the city portion of the building. Literally thousands of people were showing up and we would have to vet them in the halls. It was quite a production. I can tell you the two tools that are in this bill have been incredibly successful and incredibly important to the treasurer in helping taxpayers avoid foreclosure. In particular, these two programs, unlike the original stipulated payment agreement, which was offered to all taxpayers, these single out families. These are owner-occupied programs. Families, of course, are the most important thing, I think, that we have to keep in mind in trying to keep families together, keep families intact. These two programs help that. It's very important that we don't allow the number of properties that we've seen, particularly in the Wayne County area, to go into foreclosure, to have to go through public auction and to be sold because inevitably we would find hundreds, if not thousands of properties that wouldn't be sold. They would end up stranded. If they're abandoned for any short period of time in the city of Detroit in particular, they would be stripped. What you have are properties that are abandoned blights on the city. They're not productive, right? And the general property tax act, what is the mission of the general property tax act? To keep property in productive use. These two programs do just that. They keep properties in productive use. They don't go into the abandoned situation. They don't become blight. They stay productive. And both of these programs accomplish that. In Wayne County, as was mentioned, we have the interest reduction stipulated payment agreement. And there's also the PAYS program, the Pay As You Stay, that has also been very effective. Unfortunately, we lost that this year and we have not been able to advertise that program. The question was asked, how do you get the word out? In Wayne County, because we're dealing with initially in the petition of foreclosure, tens of thousands of properties, the Wayne County Treasurer has instituted a monthly program called Ask the Treasurer. And so every month we'll get on and we'll do a Zoom call with the community and you'd be shocked. We'll get from 100 to 300 taxpayers that will get online with questions. And inevitably it comes down to the ERSPA and the PAYS program because those are the two most effective programs for taxpayers. And so we have been very able to help so many people, thousands, thousands of families stay in their homes. So I would again like to echo and build on the comments and support of the senator and the representative, also the Ingham County Treasurer's comments. I would adopt those. This is very important that we get this. And if we can get PAYS enacted, if you can get this bill enacted, we can still offer PAYS before the March 31st deadline coming up in 2026. It'll help thousands of people, literally. So we would encourage you to send this bill forward for full House approval. And we certainly thank you for your support up to this point. And I would be happy to take any questions that you might have. Representative Fitzgerald has a question for you. Thank you. And thank you very much for being here today. I appreciate your comments about what has been successful in your communities. And I would like to maybe, you mentioned kind of the quantitative data side of this, right? How many families have really been impacted by this? And do you or your office have information about how many foreclosures or avoidance of foreclosures have occurred because of programs like this? Committee on Agriculture will come to order. Clerk, would you please take the roll? Chair Nygaard. Here. Representative Lorts. Here. Leitner. Alexander. Here. Fox. Present. Coombs. Present. Pavlo. We've got a lot to get through today and other members that will have to get to other committees to testify, so we'll try and make this as expedient as possible. We'll start out with Senate Bill 93. This is a companion bill for Greg Alexander's 4122 CODGE bills. Clerk, would you please take the roll? Oh, sorry. Greg Alexander moves Senate Bill 93 be reported with recommendations to the House floor. Clerk, would you please take the roll? Chair Nygaard. Yes. Representative Works. Yes. Leitner. Alexander. Yes.
