Senate Bill 93 is reported with recommendations. With that, we're going to move on to Senate Bills 385 through 390 and, or excuse me, Senate Bill 685 through 690 and 693-99. These are very important that we get this done today and I would ask Michaela from MDARD to come forward and give us some clarity on what's happening here. Thank you, Chair and members of the committee for allowing us to speak on this package and for bringing it up as well. As the Chair said, this is a time sensitive package that we are happy to support. With me, I have Jamie's Metco Summers, the Director of MDARD's Agriculture Development Bureau, and I'm actually going to turn it over to her for a little bit of background on the program. Okay, great. Good morning. The Farmland and Open Space Program is housed within the Agriculture Development Bureau within the Michigan Department of Ag and Rural Development. The one portion is also known as PA-116 commonly and is used and intended to preserve farmland by protecting it from being developed for non-agricultural uses. That program allows for landowners to then apply for and receive tax credits if they are eligible. Within the program, we also have a variety of other tools that we are able to use to preserve farmland and open space, including farmland development rights agreements, conservation easement donations. We have our agricultural preservation fund that provides grants to local groups to protect farmland, local open space easement, designated open space easements, and also the purchase of development rights, which the department at this point is not running a purchase of development rights program.

is leaving that to all of the local groups to do that work. A little bit of a background on PA-116, the landowner voluntarily enters into these temporary farmland development rights agreements with the department agreeing to keep the land in agricultural use. We currently have over 43,000 agreements that are in place and that our team works with each year that covers approximately 3.1 million acres of farmland across the state. These agreements can run anywhere from 10 to 90 years and that is determined by the landowner when they are signing up or renewing their agreement with us. The landowner is then eligible to claim a tax credit through their state income tax and are exempt from certain special assessments. And that is something that we work in very close partnership with the Department of Treasury on to provide them that information on who is eligible so as they are processing tax applications they can reference that to ensure those landowners are enrolled in the program. So a little bit on what spurred this bill package. As part of a routine review of credit eligibility by the Department of Treasury, tax credits ended up being withheld for a few dozen landowners who were claiming PA-116 tax credits. Essentially what happened was these landowners had entered into a permanent easement where the state of Michigan was not a co-owner. To support the protection of farmland through these PDRs, the program utilized consent agreements which were filed with the registers of deeds and waived the state's interest in the name of supporting permanent protection. That allowed landowners to continue to be considered enrolled in the PA-116 program. However, because those consent agreements resulted in the state providing tax credits for a lease rate that we had no enforcements to, it was ultimately deemed to be in violation of the statutory language. So to simplify the situation, same parcel of land was enrolled in more than one option and it violated the statute and it created confusion over the ownership of development rights on that specific parcel. Once MDARD became aware of the extent of the problem for the impacted landowners, we worked together with Treasury to get the majority of the returns released. At this point in time, we are aware of no more returns that are being held. That routine review by Treasury, though, then spurred an MDARD review of the existing consent agreements. So we notified impacted taxpayers and kept them updated as we engaged in open dialogue, searching for a solution, trying to figure out how we can sort this out. We spoke to impacted groups, including NRCS, to sort out a solution. We proposed that the landowners and conservancies amend the easements to include MDARD as a co-holder in order to remain eligible to receive that tax credit. However, some conservancies were concerned that the solution would end up putting their nonprofit status and accreditation at risk. Given these concerns, we were happy to engage in discussions with bill sponsors, landowners, and conservancies to develop a legislative fix, which is what you all have before you now. I won't go into detail on what the bills do, but I do want to flag two considerations. First, as written, these bills do go beyond what is needed to rectify the situation. This is what we see as an expansion of tax credit eligibility. The fiscal impact of that is not currently quantifiable. So that is just something that you need to be aware of. The changes in the bills also result in increased administrative burden to the department. In addition to the expanding eligibility, MDARD staff are required to establish new processes and procedures. With that, we are advocating for an increase in the statutory cap, which you'll find in Senate Bill 699, just to allow us to utilize the funds that have already been allocated. So these are not issues. They are just things that we need to be aware of and accommodate. We are supportive of this bill package, very happily so, and are very pleased to have seen it come up. I do want to flag also that we have previously advocated for an increase in the statutory administrative cap in past sessions. There were concerns about the inclusion of a consumer price index. This iteration of the bill does not include the CPI adjustment. The other common concern that we hear is that raising the administrative cap will reduce available funding for ag preservation grants. First, unfortunately, those concerns do not account for the staff time needed to administer grants and conduct outreach to eligible grantees. An increase in the administrative cap will provide the PA-116 program with access to the funds, again, already allocated, that are needed to develop the outreach and educational materials and allow for an expansion of the program to cover more acreage. Further, we have been a strong advocate for the increase in the allocated funding for these grants, which has held steady at $1.9 million for multiple years now. I will wrap up there, take questions at the discretion of the chair. I do want to point out that you have a handout on both the methods by which land could be preserved under the program, as well as a memo kind of further detailing the need for the increase to the administrative cap. I'll take the lead on a couple of questions first. The funding that keeps this program going, could you maybe explain how that comes off the last seven years, and so that way it isn't a drain on the general fund? It's a self-funded program, correct? Correct. This comes from restricted funding, not from general fund. But that money is derived from when a person that decides not to renew their contract, that last seven years is paid back into the fund, and that's what's providing the funding for operations and also for grants, correct? A portion, yes. Yes, okay. All right. And any other questions? Representative Pice. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Two questions. One, I'm wondering, since this is 90 years for a contract, are new owners then grandfathered in to this? So it's already there when they buy the land, or does this apply only to something that stays in the family? And my second question is I'm wondering if these allocations are affected at all by yesterday's appropriations cuts. So as to the first question, these agreements are valid for up to 90 years. They do move with the land if the land is sold. That does mean that any new owner of the land will continue to receive the tax credits. There is paperwork that you'd have to fill out if there is a transfer of ownership. But, yes, it does move with the program. This program is not impacted by anything that occurred yesterday with work projects. Representative Fox. Yeah, so I've been having some of my constituents ask about PA-116 in particular. And I'm trying to figure out did some changes take place in PA-116 during the last couple of years that also impact solar land usage being you're no longer able to get PA-116 if you have solar on your property? That's the question I've been getting. And if that's the case, explain how that works. I won't go into full detail. It gets very technical. But you can still receive PA-116 tax credits on land that does have solar on it so long as you meet specific requirements and fill out specific paperwork. So then my bottom line question is, and this is still my constituent talking, is that double dipping? I actually don't know the answer to that one. I'll be completely honest. That is something that we can take a look at and come back to, though. Okay. Thank you very much. Representative Wartz. Thank you. Thanks for being here today. One thing you mentioned, you said this legislation would expand the scope. Can you give any more detail on that to what extent you see as expansion? Yes. So the inclusion of additional MCLs under the Zoning Act and a few other specifics within the bills, we look at as not something being explicitly allowed under the PA-116 program previously. So we are anticipating additional applicants and additional folks enrolling in order to receive those tax credits based on the land that they have enrolled in these other agreements. Do you have anything specific, like an example you could give of what that might be like, forestry land, or do you have something specific maybe you could expound on? As of right now, we do not have specifics. Part of the issue that we've run into with trying to calculate the fiscal impact of this and why it's not currently quantifiable is that there is no state agency currently tracking all of these types of consent agreements. So we are kind of waiting to see what the impact will be, and unfortunately we're not going to be able to give specifics or quantify anything until we see that impact. What I can tell you is that...

On average, our website on PA 116, or our website overall receives, I believe, 30,000 hits annually. After these bills came up in the Senate, we saw an increase up to 80,000 specific individual hits to the PA 116 webpage itself alone. So we are anticipating a lot more folks being interested in this program, being aware of this program, and hopefully enrolling. And with that, we really need to be aware that this might see not only an increase in enrollment, but an increase in the types of folks who are enrolling. Sure. Well, I just want to say I think that's excellent and great and an excellent way to support agriculture and protect our land. As a former conservation district manager, as you know, I signed off on these and submitted them to you guys at MDARD. And it was really shocking to me when I was in that role how few people utilized the program. So I think the fact that you're expanding, I mean, well done to the department. I think you need to own that. That's what you're here for, is to promote and support rural agriculture and protect and preserve our farm ground. So well done, and we need to figure out how to fund this. So thank you. Absolutely. Thank you. And that is why Senate Bill 699 is so important. What we don't want to see happen is we don't want to see a whole bunch of folks enroll, and then we can't actually turn out the responses that they need and make sure that we – so we need to be able to support the program and have that outreach to the folks that are enrolling. We love this program. I've never heard anybody say a bad word about this program and its goals. Representative Fox, if you could please. Yeah, sorry to bother you again, but I guess I'm feeling a lot like this is one of those things where we'll figure out what's going to happen, and then you pass it, and then we'll figure out what's going to happen. So I'll lay that worry that I have rattling around in my head. Is your worry specific to the fiscal impact or specific to the expansion? It's kind of everything. The first time I saw this was on my desk today. Oh. Yeah, so. Well, as far as the fiscal impact, 699 increases the statutory administrative cap to $1.7 million from $1.4. We've been allocated for several years now $1.68 million. We have not been able to access anything over $1.4 because of that statutory cap. So there's the fiscal aspect. We're not asking for more than we've already been given. A little bit more, but just to make sure that we keep at that cap. It would have been a little silly to put into the bill $1.6813, but we would have done it if we needed to. As far as the expansion, we want to see this program grow. We want to see more people enroll, and we want to see more people be aware of this. But until we have a grasp on how many that can cover, we truly cannot tell how big this program will grow. But that's not a bad thing. Okay, thank you. I'm still thinking. All right. Okay, with that, thank you, Michaela, and thank you for your time laying this out for us. With that, we have a few people that would like to speak. If Steve and Barry could make their way forward there. If you would please state your name and then proceed, please. Good morning. I'm a county for 34 years and currently the president of Tremor Ecology and Land Services Consulting Firm, which consists of me. It staffs five township programs that are funded by dedicated millages. In the last 25 years, collectively through the City of Ann Arbor Greenbelt Program, the Washtenaw County Natural Area Preservation Program, the Legacy and Southeast Michigan Land Conservancies. If you haven't already, could you hit the red button there and they'll turn on your mic. Should I start over? No, you're good. Okay, thank you. So in the last 25 years, the programs that I cited a moment ago collectively conserved 25,000 acres in Washtenaw County alone, which is most of which is farmland that are protected with permanent deed restrictions that we call conservation easements. The impacts of these programs have been a couple. One of them is stabilizing the land base for agriculture. Farmers now see a future for agriculture and are less likely to sell for non-agricultural use. They also use the proceeds from the conservation easement sales to buy land and invest in their businesses, which then multiplies the impact in the community. The second major impact is the transfer of land to a younger generation who are able to afford land at $4,000 an acre. We have 20 conserved farms now that are producing fruit, vegetables, and animals for local markets. For the last 25 years, conservation easements have worked in concert with state farmland development rights agreements. I have at least a dozen in my five townships. What we're seeking to do through the package of six bills is to align statute with the practice of the last 25 years. The conservation community strongly believes that farmland owners who have made the ultimate commitment to forever protect their land should be eligible for state tax credits. We should be incentivizing permanent land conservation. And so we support the passage of all six of the bills. One of the folks who has a conservation easement on his property and a state farmland development rights agreement is to my left here. Thanks for hearing me today. My name is Steve Drake. So thank you for allowing us to be here today. And I support all four of these bills, I guess six of them, six bills there to get this straightened out so that we can continue farming. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you for taking the time to come down here today. With that, any other questions from the committee? Okay. All right. With that, thank you, gentlemen. If Mike and Chris as well, could you please step forward? Good morning. Thanks to everybody here at the committee for allowing me to speak today. My name is Mike Ackma. I'm the manager of easement stewardship at the Grand Traverse Regional Land Conservancy. We're a 35-year-old organization that does private land conservation in northern Michigan. I've been with the organization for about 20 years. In general, the fact that Michigan has these two amazing tools, being PA 116 and perpetual conservation easements, is a testament to the state's commitment to land protection and food security. It's obvious that these two different but similar tools share the same underlying purpose, that they're here to ensure that the most significant resources of our state aren't lost to development and to foster economic security. We feel that voting yes on this bill package will allow PA 116 and conservation easements to work in tandem to provide the maximum protection and maximum economic support to the farmers in our region and in the state at a time when they need it the most. title: Appropriations - Corrections and Judiciary — Thursday, December 11, 2025
transcript:
Thank you, everybody, for being here this morning for this meeting of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Corrections and Judiciary. We're going to call the meeting to order. And let's see, Clerk, I would ask that you would take the roll for us. Chair Slaw. Present. Representatives Markanen. Here. Beeson. Cabot. Here. O'Neill. Mr. Chair, you have three members present. And we have a quorum, right? Yes. Yes, okay. I didn't hear you say anything. Rep. Cabot moves to approve the minutes from the subcommittee meeting held on September 9. There being no objections, the minutes are approved. And we're going to start with Brad Warner from the Humanity for Prisoners organization. Brad, I've got three minutes for you. Hopefully you can do that in a three-minute time frame, and we can then move on to other stuff. Please, come on down. Let's see, it's a game show thing, right? And we're going to need to push the – there should be a button there for you to push to get started on the microphone. Excellent. Thank you. And you are on. Well, good morning, Chair Slaw, members of the committee. Brad Warner, Humanity for Prisoners. I've submitted my full testimony to the clerk, but just to summarize, drawing on 30 years of lived experience inside the MDOC, I can tell you that while the drug epidemic is real, this legal mail policy will not have a significant impact. The uncomfortable truth is that the vast majority of contraband walks right through the front gate carried by staff. When the state stripped away competitive wages and gutted pensions, it devalued the badge. You lost the professionals and replaced them with a workforce that is overworked, underpaid, and unfortunately, in many instances, comparatively to how it used to be, susceptible to corruption. To put it bluntly, you get exactly what you pay for. Shredding legal mail is just – it's a cheap way to look busy without writing the check for what actually works. If you want law and order, you have to fund the order. Use the budget to restore professional wages and pensions so the MDOC finally has leverage to hire the best and the fortitude to purge the corrupt staff who are actually bringing the drugs in. Shredding the Constitution is free. Real safety costs money, and I urge you to choose safety. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Warner. I appreciate that testimony. With that, Kyle, I believe you're on deck, so come on forward, and let's see what you got for us today. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. I do have a presentation, and I will move through it without delay, but I do think I have to pause here and, if allowed, just make a brief statement here that I'm disappointed by the previous testifier and really the unfounded accusation that they have cast on thousands of dedicated state employees working for the Department of Corrections. We recognize as an agency that drugs can come into our facilities through a number of different means, and we have strategies aimed at addressing all of those. We're here today to talk about an avenue for introducing drugs that is very real, and you can speak to any of our employees that work at a facility, and they will tell you that special handling mail has become a significant problem.

a known source of drugs over the last few years. But the fact that we're addressing this does not mean that we are taking our foot off of other efforts to prevent drugs from entering our facilities from any potential source. So I just want to make that clear. But with that, I'll move on to talking about our special handling mail process. So the challenge, U.S. mail is a known source of contraband introduction in jails and prisons. This is not unique to Michigan. This happens all over the country. And because of that, in 2020, the MDOC actually took the step of adopting a new general mail policy for mail that comes in that is not subject to special handling, where all of that mail is photocopied prior to delivery to the recipient. When we did that, we immediately saw a reduction in the amount of drugs that were being introduced through normal mail. But very shortly after that, we started to see an increase in the amount of drugs that were being intercepted coming in through special handling mail. And so that is the concern. I'll have a couple photos in the slide deck here. Some I'll talk about, some maybe not. But just to kind of cover the photos here, you see essentially a plain-looking manila envelope. The history on this, and I've blurred out the person's name, the history on this is that under our current process, we contact attorneys and others who are sending special handling mail and confirm that they're actually the sender. In this case, when we first called the attorney, they said, yes, I have sent mail to my client. But then the attorney actually called us back and said, actually, you called me about this recently, didn't you? And we said, well, no, this is a new envelope that we received from you. And the attorney said, no, I did not send a new envelope. Would it be possible to show me a photo of the envelope that it's purported I sent to my client? And when we did, the attorney reported back that those are not the labels he uses, and this was somebody else masking mail as if it was coming from his office when in fact it was not. We opened that envelope, and I believe there were 51 pages of loose leaf paper in it with various things printed on it. And pages 23 and 24 were saturated with drugs. So that was obviously an attempt by somebody else to hide those drugs within that bundle of paper using a fake envelope from somebody who had a legitimate client, legal attorney-client relationship but had not sent that. The document in white, you can kind of see it on the screen about a third of the way down the page. There's kind of this weird clear or lighter white. That is where the page has been saturated with drugs. So that is legal mail that was intercepted at a facility. It's being held up to a light board so that you can see it more clearly. But that's what we're talking about here when we're talking about adulterated mail. It is very hard to discern and discover, but that is the problem we're dealing with at every facility around the state. And then finally, in the upper right, that's a little test. So that is a piece of legal mail that we have tested and has come up positive for THC. Again, so it's not as if somebody put THC as you might imagine it, marijuana or a marijuana product in there. It's actually saturated into the paper, but we had reason to believe that that paper was saturated and when we tested it, it did come up positive. So what is special handling mail and kind of how does it differ from normal mail? So certain groups and individuals do have a right to send confidential mail to incarcerated individuals. That's true in Michigan. Again, that's true everywhere else as well. The most common form of this is legal mail where attorneys are sending legal mail to their clients. There are also certain legal services organizations that have special handling privileges as well as certain government offices. Again, the purpose of special handling ultimately is to maintain the confidentiality of the content of the mail. But because of that, it has created challenges for us as an agency to ensure that it's not bringing in contraband. One of the things we had to adopt over the last couple years is actually having to manually confirm the sender of all special handling mail. So if you go back kind of pre-COVID times, for the most part, special handling mail was not a consistent source of drugs. And so while we might confirm periodically that the sender was actually the sender, we didn't have to do it in every single case. Now our mail rooms have to call or email for every special handling document they receive to confirm that the person is the sender and ask a couple other key questions. And part of what this policy change will do is greatly simplify that for our mail room staff and allow for essentially instantaneous validation of the sender. So how is special handling abused? There's probably more sort of categories, but I think there's three big categories that I wanted to walk the subcommittee through because these are the things that we're seeing at our level within the MDOC. The first is when the person who has legitimate special handling privileges is intentionally misusing them to introduce contraband. So they are part of a criminal enterprise. They know what they're doing in the sense that they are intentionally trying to introduce those drugs into our facilities. We will seek prosecution in every single one of those cases. We've had some prosecutions in cases such as this in the past. And so this is a very legitimate concern that some folks, not all folks, but some folks, there's a small portion of the folks who have this special handling privilege that are utilizing this. Another scenario, which we know happens, is that it's a person with legitimate special handling privileges, but they are unknowingly introducing contraband into the facilities. And how this is generally done is they might receive a letter that appears to be coming from a correctional facility that says, hey, I'd really like for you to look at this grievance document, or I'd really like for you to look at this misconduct report, and would you potentially represent me in a case against the MDOC, et cetera? And if you can't, can you do me the favor of sending this report back to me because it's my only copy and I really need it to talk to another attorney if you're not going to take my case? Well-meaning folks might see that and say, you know what, this is not my area where I practice law. I don't have interest in this case, but I don't want to be the person who deprives them of the possibility of finding another attorney, so I'll just repackage that letter that they sent me and send it back into the facility. What that sender doesn't realize is that the letter did not come from the facility. The letter actually went from the facility to somebody in the community who adulterated it with drugs and then sent it on to the attorney using an envelope to make it seem as if it had come directly from the prison. And again, so that person is unknowingly forwarding that letter back into the facility, but it's already been adulterated by the time they get it. Because of that, one of the questions we ask, our mailroom staff ask every time we deal with special handling mail now is, did you create all of the documents in this envelope? And even though we've done a pretty robust educational campaign through the State Bar Association and others, we still oftentimes will hear back where people say, well, no, I received some of those documents from an outside source. And again, that is a susceptibility from the current process that we will be addressing with the new process. Finally, it's sort of that scenario I laid out with that Manella envelope on the front. Folks who do not have special handling privileges but who are masking themselves as people who do. So they are doctoring up an envelope, doctoring up documents, et cetera, to make it seem as if it's coming from the law office of so-and-so or the clerk's office from such and such county. But in fact, it's not coming from those folks. And that's why it's really important that we have a way to authenticate our senders because what we find oftentimes, or certainly sometimes when mailroom staff contact some of these senders and say, hey, we've received this letter that you're purported to have sent to your client. Did you send this? And the answer is, I have no idea who that person is. And I've never sent them mail before in my life. And so that's a significant concern that we need to address through authentication. So just to share a couple real-world examples of mail that we find. So this is two pages of special handling mail. This was actually from earlier this month. This is actually the day I started to put the PowerPoint together, this email came through. So I thought this was pretty timely. You can kind of see on the left-hand photo, it's a little harder to see on the PowerPoint, but there's a couple areas of discoloration at the bottom of the page. On the right-hand photo, it's a little easier to see that discoloration. That is some form of drug that has been adulterated into the paper. And that will be, had it made it into the facility, had it not been intercepted by our staff, certainly would have been sold and then used within the facility. This is from September of this year. So this is several pages that came in. They looked pretty standard, looked like some forms, maybe some court documents. When we received this one, we contacted the sender. This is a case where the sender said, I did not send anything to that person. So we knew that it was not real special handling mail. And with that, we tested it and it tested positive for THC that had been saturated into the paper. This one is from August. This one, again, it's a little hard to see on the screen, but there's discoloration at the bottom of the page where there's been some saturation. This one actually came

and then the original is destroyed. Because of the rules around special handling that we will be changing, but up until now, because of the rules, the special handling mail, the actual paper was delivered to the recipient. And so when paper was saturated, it would make it into the facility if it was not first intercepted by staff. One of the challenges, and I'll talk a little more about this, is because of the confidential nature of this type of mail, staff cannot scrutinize it in the same way that they can scrutinize other things coming into the facilities. So if we're receiving a book order or we're receiving normal mail, we can scrutinize that very, very closely because there's no confidentiality. In this case, though, we can open it in the presence of the prisoner and we can look for obvious contraband. But once we've done that, we cannot read or skim it. We cannot spend extra time with that document. We have to hand it over to the recipient. So if staff can feel it right away, if they can see it, if they can smell it, there's not an opportunity to intercept that and potentially not have that mail delivered. But like I said at the beginning, when you have a 51-page stack of loose-leaf paper and two of the pages in the middle are adulterated, it is very difficult for staff to do that on a consistent basis. So as I said, it's sort of the soaking or adulteration of the paper that's the main thing. I mean, there are still scenarios where we find actual clear drugs like suboxone strips, et cetera. But really, I think the enterprise here, the criminal enterprise, has moved forward into this soaked paper because it's so much harder to track. When we test it, THC comes up quite often. There's obviously synthetics out there, not all the synthetics. They're always kind of one step ahead of the testing even. Fentanyl is a concern. We've also found sort of non-narcotic things, embalming fluid, wasp spray, et cetera. The concern here is these are very dangerous things. They're dangerous for our staff to have to handle. They're dangerous for the people who may ultimately seek to ingest them. Imagine, and in no way am I condoning the behavior, but imagine you're purchasing a scrap of paper believing that it's somehow going to get you high, and what you're actually ingesting is embalming fluid. That's a real danger to everybody. Everybody should agree that we should take action to make sure that situations like that can't happen. Then imagine your staff. You're searching a cell, and you're going through a stack of paper, and you're potentially coming into contact with these substances unknowingly. It's not like they're labeled. No one's writing this is embalming fluid or this is wasp spray or this is fentanyl on the sheet of paper. It's just a sheet of paper as far as you can tell. And so that's why it's so dangerous, and that's why we need to make such a significant change in this area. So how are we going to make that change? Effective January 5th, we will be adopting some new policies, processes, and procedures for special handling mail. These changes are the result of one of our EPIC teams, which we've talked about in the past. Those are the multidisciplinary teams that exist within the MDOC. So this one was a mix of facility staff that work directly on these issues, legal, others, leadership staff, et cetera, who developed kind of a comprehensive strategy of how we're going to address these issues with special handling mail. Also, I should mention, I showed you some slides of special handling mail. I said one was from December. I think one was from September. One was from August. This is happening every week at the facilities. I get emails every week telling me multiple times a week about special handling. So any claim that this is not a problem is not rooted at all in the reality of what we're dealing with at our facilities around the state. To be clear, these changes do not impact normal mail that friends and families send, that other non-legal organizations send, et cetera. Those have been subject to photocopying since 2020, and that will continue to be the case. So to kind of quickly walk you through the side by side, the current process for special handling mail is it arrives at the facility. We then have to email or call the sender to confirm that they are the sender, confirm that they essentially are responsible for every document that's within that envelope. Once we have that confirmation, we would call the prisoner out. The prisoner would be with staff. Staff would open the envelope in the presence of the prisoner. They can look for obvious contraband, but they cannot read or skim the contents. At that point, the recipient would be provided with the original documents under the current policy. They would take them back to their housing unit, et cetera. And at that point, the MDOC has no control over those objects or that paper. Under the new process, special handling mail will still arrive directly at the individual facility, but at this point, the sender will be confirmed and authenticated through our text behind sender authentication system, and I'll talk a little more about that on the next slide. That will eliminate the need for the back and forth with phone calls and emails to confirm the sender because the envelope will arrive with a unique QR code on it that we will know indicates that it came from somebody who actually has the authority to send that mail and have that mail handled as confidential mail. Once again, the prisoner will be called out. They will be in the presence of staff. Staff will open the mail in their presence, and we will immediately photocopy the mail using a photocopier that does not keep any kind of file or any kind of record. So it's just a copy. The copy will be presented to the prisoner, will then be able to look at the copy and attest to the fact that it appears complete, like all the pages are there, all the pages are legible. And at that point, the original will be shredded still in the presence of the prisoner. So the prisoner will know that the only other original has been shredded in their presence to maintain confidentiality. At that point, the prisoner, the recipient, will be able to go back to their housing unit with the copy, which is done on clean paper provided by the MDOC. Again, there are three steps here that have to be done in the presence of the recipient, opening the envelope, copying the contents, and shredding the original. That maintains the confidentiality through this process, and we are confident in that approach. I think some questions may have been raised by some outside groups, well, what about somebody who's in a specialized housing unit, segregation, etc.? Does not matter. They still have to be present. They will be brought up as part of the facility's operation to the control center or another appropriate area with staff, and they will go through that exact same process of the envelope being opened, the contents being copied, and the original being shredded in their presence. That will be the case for every special handling envelope. We will also document all of this. We document it currently, but we'll continue to document when we receive special handling so that we're sure that that's being abided by. So the sender authentication system, I want to talk just briefly about this. The MDOC has contracted for this service. This service will be paid for by the MDOC. It will be at no cost to the people who use it. We, as part of this process, what will happen is individuals who are eligible for special handling will go to a website, and they will register. They will provide proof that they're eligible for special handling. So like the most common form of this would be an attorney. They'll provide a copy of their ID and their, you know, P card number so we know that they're an attorney, and they will be verified. Then when they would like to send special handling mail to the facility, they'll go into this platform, and they will select their recipient or recipients, and they will essentially say, yep, this is who I'm sending it to, or there's an option if they want to send it to a group of individuals. This is the group I want to send it to, and they will be given a unique QR code for that mail. They can print it on the envelope. They can print it on a label and stick it on the envelope. It's kind of up to them how they do it, but they will put that on the outside of the envelope. They'll drop that in the U.S. mail. When that arrives at our facility, it will be scanned by our staff, and we will be able to know this is sent by somebody who has the authority to send special handling mail and that it's actually reaching the intended recipient. It's not just being sent to another facility. If it's sent by an attorney and it lacks a QR code or the QR code is not right, we will just send it back unopened because that would be legal mail. If it's sent by another organization that doesn't have legal mail status, we would copy it and still provide it to the prisoner, but it would not be subject to special handling at that point. But, again, if we don't have the right QR code for the folks who have legal mail handling privileges, it will just go back to them unopened so that they can correct their error and hopefully resend it. Again, this will eliminate the need for our mailroom staff to call and email on every single envelope that they receive for special handling. That will be a significant improvement in all of their eyes. It will also expedite the handling of special handling mail because right now we're oftentimes waiting for a response back to our phone call or our email, and we just have to hold that mail during that time. We can't deliver it. Now we'll know as soon as it arrives at the facility, is this valid special handling? If so, we can immediately

people masking themselves as having special handling privileges when they don't. So only those that are really eligible for this will be able to send the mail in the future. Two, it ensures the prompt delivery of the legitimate special handling mail because now we'll know instantaneously when it arrives at the facility by scanning that QR code who the sender and who the recipient are and will know that it's valid, will know that it's not somebody trying to sneak something through using that process. Three, and importantly, maintains the confidentiality of special handling throughout the process. Again, and I'm going to beat this drum because it's so important, opened in the presence of the recipient, copied in the presence of the recipient, original destroyed in the presence of the recipient. The standard remains the same. Staff in policy cannot read or skim the actual content of the mail. Their job is simply to make sure that the copies are made, no record of the copies are kept, the recipient agrees that the copies are complete, and then get the original destroyed in the recipient's presence. Ultimately, obviously, kind of checkmark number four here, taken in totality, will help ensure that we're not seeing contraband introduced by special handling mail. Again, we're not suggesting this is the only way that drugs enter or can enter prison, but this is a known way in which they are entering prison today, and we need to address this as a state, and that's why the agency is taking this step forward. And then finally, you know, why we're doing this ultimately is to protect those that live and work within our prisons. We have dangerous substances coming in in a form and format that is very hard to detect, but is potentially very dangerous. And so we need to find ways to reduce that, and this process taken in totality aims to do that, and we think it will be effective. So with that, I'm happy to take any questions. Have we heard that person making statements that make us think they could be involved in this, or are there reasons to believe they're not involved in this? Thank you.

I'm here today to express concern regarding the state of Michigan's new Lara Business Portal that went live in June of 2025. Under the previous system, anyone could conduct a state of Michigan business entity search and view basic information and public filings for a Michigan business entity. However, to conduct actual business with Lara, such as filing forms or making changes to business records, each business was required to set up a unique username and password, and only authorized individuals within that business could access and modify their account. This important safeguard is no longer in place. In the new Lara Business Registry Portal, a business still logs in with its username and password and can submit forms and file reports online. The issue is that once a user is logged into their own account, they can access other registered Michigan companies. On your logged in account page, there is a search button that lets you find any registered Michigan business. When you click on a business's name, it then allows you to view that business's information and past filings. Then in the lower right corner of the screen, there is a request access button that asks you to answer two simple questions about that business. And the answers to the questions that they ask have already been provided by Lara on the screen when you did the business entity search. Once granted access to another company with the information that Lara provided, you can file forms and make changes to someone else's business information without any verification that you are authorized to do so. When this occurs, the impacted business's registered email receives an access granted notification indicating the username, name, and email address of the person who accessed your account. However, the notification does not state whether any changes were made to your account nor what those changes might be if they were made. The notice also includes the following corporation's division disclaimer. There's two disclaimers they put up. It says the corporation's division cannot revoke user access to a portal and the corporation's division does not determine or verify ownership rights to business entities. At the time when cybercrime is increasing and many government agencies and private sector organizations are strengthening security through two-factor authentication and other measures, this level of access and lack of verification is deeply troubling. It exposes Michigan businesses to potential fraud, unauthorized filings, and reputational or financial harm. To protect Michigan businesses across our state, we respectfully and urgently request that Lara remove the access button from the portal, eliminating the ability for users to access and modify other businesses' records when they are not authorized to do so. Implement an appropriate authentication and authorization steps to ensure that only verified, authorized individuals can access and make changes to a specific business entity. Michigan businesses rely on secure, transparent, and trustworthy systems to operate and comply with state requirements. We urge you to address these security concerns promptly and strengthen safeguards within the Lara Business Registry Portal. Thank you. title: Finance, Insurance, and Consumer Protection 25-12-10
transcript:
The Committee on Finance, Insurance, and Consumer Protection is called to order. Would the clerk please call the roll? Chairwoman Kavanaugh. Here. Senator Irwin. Here. Senator McCann. Senator Bayer. Here. Senator Camilleri. Senator Heisinga. Here. Senator Tice. Senator Daly. Madam Chair, you have five members present. There is a quorum. I will entertain a motion to adopt the meeting minutes from December 3rd. So moved by Senator Irwin. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. I make a motion to excuse absent members, and without objection, the motion carries. So today we will be hearing testimony. It seems very appropriate in the weather, and I'm glad everyone made it here very safe. Today we'll be discussing Senate Bill 245, brought to us by Vice Chair Irwin. Senator, can you please explain the legislation to the committee? Thank you for being here today. Absolutely. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you, members of committee for the opportunity to hear Senate Bill 245. Again, this is legislation that we've been talking about in this committee for some time, and the reason we've been talking about this legislation for some time is because right now we have a lot of residents who are not being treated fairly by their insurance company, and this bill, Senate Bill 245, seeks to protect consumers against insurance companies that unfairly deny their claims. And I just want to take a little step aside to say that if a resident, if a policyholder can go into court and prove against an insurance company with all their lawyers and all their money that that insurance company should have known that this was covered and that what they did was unfair, that really says that that person has a good claim, because it's pretty hard to fight against these insurance companies. They have a lot of resources. And so once again, when these insurance companies are engaging in a strategy of deny, delay, defend, and just trying to wait out people with valid claims and make their lives more difficult for them to get their claims paid, I think that we have an obligation as a legislature to make sure that the insurance code provides some accountability for that and provides some guardrails and some protections for our residents, for people who are paying the premiums. So currently, if someone can go into court and prove that they were wronged by their insurance company and they've had to wait months or years to get their claim paid, the insurance companies really don't have to do much more than pay what was owed and a very, very small amount of interest. Now, if we pass this legislation, that will allow residents who've been wronged in this way and who have proven that their insurance company treated them unfairly, it would allow them to not just get what was initially owed in the first place, but would also allow them to sue for damages caused by the delay. It would also increase the penalty interest, and it would also create an opportunity for them to recover their legal costs. The final thing that this really does is it says that if an individual can show that an insurance company willfully and recklessly denied their claim even though they knew that the claim was valid, then it allows them to seek punitive damages. I think all of that's appropriate because I think that is the way, that is the only way that we can really hold insurance companies accountable because our regulators really aren't doing it. They don't have the tools, and there isn't the law for them to actually be able to penalize people who act in ways that are verifiably unfair to their customers. So I mentioned at the very, very beginning that we were hearing this again. This bill has come before the chamber before, but I do want to mention that this is not exactly the same proposal as I brought forward last time. In fact, we have changed this proposal to address some of the concerns that the industry raised. First off, they said that they didn't want a whole new act. They thought this should be in the unfair trade practices portion of the insurance code, and that's where we're seeking to put this. They pushed back against the penalties that we had in the previous bill and said that they were too large and not appropriately focused on the worst cases. So that's why we did that. And they also complained that we had included a policyholder's bill of rights in the previous package. That is also gone now. So this is a more streamlined package really meant to just provide an opportunity for people who've been wronged by their insurance company to get accountability and to get justice in the courts. This is about protecting consumers, and this is about making sure that the insurers who are operating in our state do so faithfully and lawfully. And when they don't, there's some accountability for it. Thank you. Thank you, Senator. Any questions from committee members? Senator Heisinga. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you, Senator, for your presentation today. One of the things that I consistently hear from my constituents is increasing fees and rates, whether it's gas, rent, groceries, you name it. And I'm concerned that this bill will increase costs for people overall for their insurance. Someone has to pay for that. And although I do support what you're saying, like insurance companies need to do what they need to do, but it does seem to me that that should be governed under DIFs. And if this doesn't do that, well, then we should provide more tools and resources. And obviously we've heard many times of stories about the attorney general needing policy that would augment what their ability to do in that department as well. So I just want you to know that although I support taking care of our constituents and taking care of people that are wronged, we have to make sure that we do it in the right way that doesn't cause a significant increase in fees for them. I totally agree with you that the affordability of insurance is a big problem. If you look at some of the bills I've introduced, you'll see a couple that I think are really all about addressing the affordability problem with respect to insurance. So I will agree with you with that. But my only element of sort of pushback on behalf of this bill, which I will acknowledge your point, but my pushback is that if you're paying insurance every month and you're chipping in and you're chipping in and you're chipping in, and then when you need that insurance and it's not there for you, those folks who experience that have been ripped off so tremendously that I just don't think it's just. And insurance, no matter how affordable it is, if it doesn't actually cover you when you have an accident, it's not worth anything. Thank you. I do have a question. Do you know what other states might have done similar legislation and what kind of benefits might have come from that? I don't have on the top of my head exact states. My understanding is that there are many states who have policies very similar to this, but I'll leave it to future experts who might be able to do that comparative analysis that I can't. Great. Senator Tice. Thank you, Madam Chairwoman. Actually, there are quite a few states that started this and ended up backtracking because of the additional cost that it implied. Because when an attorney sues an insurance company and receives 33% plus whatever the other folks get, the attorney is getting paid where DIFs doesn't get paid. The attorney is getting paid and that money has to come from somewhere. And we require under law that insurance take enough premium that they can pay those claims out. So when they start paying, they have to take more premium if they're going to be paying more. Now, I agree with you 100% that if the contract says that's something they're supposed to pay for and they don't, that there ought to be a penalty associated. And I believe that already exists. I haven't heard from DIFs yet that it hasn't, but they can even take away their ability to do business in Michigan. They can take their licensure away. So if, in fact, this is a common problem, something that a particular organization continues to do, then it seems like that would appropriately be within DIFs. But I have a few questions for you about the way the bill is written. On page five, it talks about if the loss exceeds the limits of the insurance coverage available, the insurer, regardless of the limits of the insurance coverage, is liable for the full amount of the loss. Now, how are they supposed to assess the risk in order to determine the appropriate premium? Yeah, let me respond to your question but also respond to your observation. The accountability that's in the law now is incredibly weak. And it is so weak that it is financially advantageous for insurance companies to delay and deny claims because even if they're proven to be wrong in the end, the penalties they pay are so minuscule. It's less than even what it costs to carry that money. And so they're making money just on holding that money while they're not paying the person, making more than they're paying in interest and penalties. I think that's outrageous. I'll also say that DIFs is a toothless tiger. DIFs does not have the backing in the law to really enforce anything against these insurance companies. And in my experience watching insurance regulators in Michigan, they are not aggressive on behalf of citizens. I think they're a toothless tiger, and one fact that I think backs it up is that when DIFs was here and they talked about how they have the power to revoke someone's license, I asked them, in the history of DIFs, have you ever revoked a license? And the answer I think I heard was no, they've never done it. Now, your more specific question about the legislation, I just want to point out that that provision is only triggered if the policyholder can prove in a state court that the insurance company didn't just erroneously deny their claim, but they willfully and recklessly denied that claim. That's an incredibly high standard to move into that zone, and I think that it's very similar to, like, gross negligence. And I think of an insurance

to the courts. If you're standing outside a car spraying it to car wash it and you slip and fall, that's not an auto insurance injury. But sure enough, that's what the courts deemed. So on page 13, there's a sentence that says that the insurance company shouldn't be construing ambiguous provisions in an insurance contract or policy in favor of the insurer. Could you explain to me what that would look like? Well, I don't have an example off the top of my head, but I think the idea is that if something's written in the contract and folks are looking at it afterwards and saying, oh, it's sort of ambiguous. It could be interpreted to benefit the insurance company. It could be interpreted to benefit the client. I think in those cases, it should be interpreted to benefit the client. If that's language that you'd like to work on with me, I'd be happy to have that discussion. But that's the idea, is to solve these ambiguous clauses in favor of the person who has less power and information in the contractual relationship. I trust people to be able to understand contracts. I agree with you, though, that they are complicated. But this language itself is extraordinarily ambiguous. Thank you, Senator. I'd love to continue to work. Go ahead. Yeah, I'll just say one final thing, which is that I think you and I could probably both come up with a number of anecdotes from cases in Michigan that might make one policy or another seem too generous or not generous enough. I would rather sort of look at the aggregate and say, what's fair? And to me, if an individual who's been paying their premiums gets denied coverage and then can prove in a court that really that should have been covered, there has to be some penalty there, or else the people in the industry are going to abuse consumers to their own benefit. It's too beneficial to these insurance companies the way we've set up the law for them to abuse our residents. And so therefore, the rules should be set up so that they're encouraged to not do so, because if it's proven that they've willfully and recklessly denied someone's claim, they could be on the hook for more financial payments. If DIF's the regulator is toothless, then I suggest we should give them some teeth. But I haven't seen that yet. I'm eager to co-sponsor your bill. Thank you, Senators. And as we discussed, I do think there's a delicate balance between affordability and accountability as we discuss a lot of these issues. And I do think there's avenues for both. One thing can't solve both. So I appreciate you bringing this. And I appreciate the conversation as this is testimony, and we're going to continue to work on this bill as a sponsor sounds very open. Appreciate it. Next, I'd like to welcome up Peg, Skip, and Sean Whedon, along with attorney Nick Andrews, current president of the Michigan Association for Justice. Welcome to committee. Thank you. Thank you. In great Red Wings jacket. There's a button at the base of the microphone, and then you can give your testimony. Thank you. Thank you for being here. Thank you, all of you, for being here. Thank you. We lived through the process 27 years ago. My son Sean was in a car accident, TBI. So some of the words dysphagia, some of the other words spasticity may not function for you people. But trust me, we learned all those. You know, I've been the biggest problem I'd have to say was the insurance company. You know, I hate to blame, but, you know, I worked with them. I worked with DIFs, worked with them for a whole year and explained all the things that the insurance company would. And I won't mention any names. I'm not here to do that. But it didn't work out, and we were not happy. But at the end of the year, I was working with DIFs. They said, well, we realize you have some issues, but find an attorney. So we went and found an attorney, and a fantastic gentleman has really helped us and alleviated a lot of the pain. I mean, they play around with financial things. They send us to doctors that didn't know Sean, and they'd make some future that Sean would never have. I mean, they told me he was going to die or he'd be dead in three years anyway, you know. No, we're at our 27th year, and it's been a blessing. And so that's my Sean, and that's my Peg and Skip Whelan here. I'll let Peg tell you more, but not to alarm you, but this is what we found, and trust me, you can learn a lot by seeing your son this way. And I was down in the library after bugging the doctor a lot. What can you do? What can I do? The rest of the people were up there in the hospital with Sean saying, oh, I wish he was going to be all right. I wish this didn't happen. But I said, my way is we're going to help this guy as long as he can live. And he volunteers. You know, he's feeding America, and so he's paying back the society for all the love that people have given throughout the years. So I want to thank you all, and I hope that you will consider what we've done as the truth because it is. And I'll have my wife talk. She's a little bit better than me, and I love her, and we couldn't have done it without her. Trust me. And Sean has been fantastic. He gives 200% every time. Thanks, man. So, yeah, it's hard to put into words 27 years of struggling, and, you know, one minute your son is a teenager going to high school playing hockey for Kenawa Hills Hockey, and the next minute he's in the hospital and you don't know if he's going to live. And now we have a new Sean. We don't have the Sean that we used to have. He's a different person. He's been reborn, and we love him dearly the way he is. He requires 24-hour care. He has a script for 24-hour care, but when the auto no-fault laws changed in 2021, we lost our 24-hour care, and the insurance company said that all we can give you is eight hours a day. Well, who's supposed to take care of him for the other hours a day when we have a 24-hour script? So we fought tooth and nail with this back and forth with them, and we tried to work with them, and they finally got it up to 16 hours a day, and then they stopped paying us altogether. So we worked with DIFs, as my husband said, and then they said get an attorney, so we got an attorney, and then they stopped paying us altogether. They didn't pay us for over a year. And so some people would say, well, you got what you wanted. You went through the battles, and that shows that that works, but why do we have to go through this when in 1997 we paid a contract with the insurance company for lifetime care for my son. So we thought, okay, we're done in 2023. They should pay what they should pay based on what the jury decided. Well, they ignored it, and I think for even a few months they didn't pay anything. I'm happy to take any questions and I really appreciate the opportunity for the Wheelans and for myself to be here with you today. No, and I appreciate you guys being here. State, I'm sorry. All right, thank you. So, yeah, so she would say that they had to find out more information from the other side. Back in 2022 of December, T-minus four days till Christmas, my family experienced a devastating house fire. I had at the time a very small three-year-old son and a five-year-old daughter, and my husband and I watched our house burn from the driveway of our home. As we sat in the car, I could not help but feel thankful and blessed that we were all okay and we were at home to be able to leave for safety. And I was very thankful that we were insured. I remember kind of feeling like, all right, this is something that we can get through. I purchased my home when I was 20 years old. I thought that was a great accomplishment. It is located right across the street from Claussen's beloved little neighborhood park. I imagined one day having our family, my future husband and children there. We did not get to enjoy that park for about three years because of a very straightforward claim and loss of a home. When I filed the claim, I remember just waiting in the driveway for the emergency services to leave for my parents to pick up our terrified children and for me to just sit there in that driveway and make the phone call to put the claim in. After three days of just waiting, I realized at that point that it would probably be just easier for me to hire an attorney and a public adjuster to take the stress off of dealing with the insurance and also knowing the backtracking of insurance companies liking to hold out, we had professional help right away. We started the 2023 school year in a hotel. From the fourth floor, we came down every morning and got to school. Our accommodations had to move again at the end of that month just to find a home for our family. That was also done by ourselves. Their temporary accommodations wanted to move us completely away from where I do work and where our kids go to school. So we moved back into a home. At the time also, it was a struggle to find a home to rent for less than a year because that's what our insurance guaranteed us, that this would not take that long for the type of loss that we experienced. So at one point, we agreed to a certain number in our rent for 12 months and we ended up having to pay even more of an increase to stay in that home because we didn't know when this was going to end. And the people that we were renting with to avoid having to move again really wanted a year lease, two-year lease. We had no answers. We had no commitment from our insurance. We had all of our belongings inventoried and on the desk of our insurance company by the beginning of March, so two months after the date of the fire. And it took them until the summer to give us back what they would agree to, which was about 25% of our policy max. Even though we had multiple quotes from different contractors, they then put it into a third-party neutral appraisal that also added on extra time. In September of 2023, they could no longer wait or deny the fact that the claim was larger than what they originally committed to. So we ended up finally getting money. Our house sat in just carcinogenic ash with all of our belongings in it for months on end. It was very kind of shocking to see that you can just leave contaminated items in a home for that long. And once we finally got the first payment and we could deconstruct the home, then we again had to wait to put the home back together. At this time, we blew through $100,000 of loss of use, which was actually insane to think about how much money they could have kept of that to just not delay that process that went to our rental furniture. We were running out of money.

Return our rental furniture and then end up buying more furniture for the rental house, paying movers to then move that furniture. Our children really wanted bunk beds because they wanted to sleep in the same bedroom. So we just like had forts on the floor and slept on mattresses for about six months just because it was like we don't know when this is going to end. This deliberate delay obviously had kind of crushing circumstances. First financially, double the utilities for that duration of time. Seventeen thousand dollars out of our pocket for rent after we went through one hundred thousand dollars based on delays. Two thousand dollars for movers. You know, hiring a lawyer and a public adjuster just to help you navigate through the system as a person that pays a premium. I would just assume that it would come with, you know, directions. I have the intellectual capability to read through a contract and to be able to, you know, hold somebody to that. But we also had diffs involved twice. They sent us a packet of our claim about this thick and closed the claim before the claim was even closed. Then we had to re-invite them back into our case like throughout that process as well. And that really did not help us actually at all. I don't really know. That was just another step that we had to do to kind of put a little bit of pressure on. And then plus another additional twenty thousand for code updates. Our roof was actually on fire. They did not want to cover that. So there were so many steps of things like at one point you're just like during the savings and let's go home. And that's pretty much where we ended up. The real damage obviously is the fact that we missed out on so much time with our kids being small just with the location. Three Christmases. This is our first Christmas home after 2022. So we're looking forward to that. And then just having your family's finances in limbo. I've been financially stable and out of my house since I was 18 years old, like always took pride in that. I've never had the stress of finances. That was huge, especially when, you know, children are relying on you to keep you floating around. I am very thankful that we had the family help, the professional support and guidance and a savings account to get us through this. But today I'm here to, you know, kind of advocate for the people that aren't as lucky as some of us. So for this, I urge you to support this legislation that holds insurance companies responsible for acting in bad faith. Without a real penalty, there's really, you know, I mean, a simple timeline, a 30 day response. Like these are all basic business principles that you have to do in any other job. And I don't really think that people have like that kind of dependency on my job. But just out of good faith, you would just respond in a timely fashion to save the money that you're getting. So I really I thank you for your time and thank you for having me here. And I welcome any questions. Thank you for your testimony. Thank you for being here.
