title: Education 25-12-10
transcript:
Committee on Education is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairwoman Polanky? Here. Senator Geis? Present. Senator Chang? Here. Senator Campbellary? Here. Senator Irwin? Here. Senator DeMoose? Here. Senator Johnson? Madam Chair, you have five members present. There is a quorum. I will entertain a motion to adopt the meeting minutes from October 28th. So moved by Vice Chair Geis. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. Make a motion to excuse absent members. Without objection, the motion carries. We'll begin today with Senate Bill 433, which I introduced. We adopted an S-1 substitute to the bill in our previous meeting. And just as a reminder, this bill requires schools to annually provide parents with information about the dangers of tobacco products, vapor products, alternative nicotine products, THC cannabis products, and synthetic intoxicating hemp. I will entertain a motion to report SB 433 as substituted to the floor with a recommendation the bill pass. So moved by Vice Chair Geis. Will the clerk please call the question? Chairwoman Polanky? Yes. Senator Geis? Yes. Senator Chang? Yes. Senator Campbellary? Senator Irwin? Yes. Senator DeMoose? Yes. Senator Johnson? Madam Chair, there are five yeas and zero nays. The bill is reported. Next, we'll move to Senate Bills 470 and 471, brought to us by Vice Chair DeMoose and Senator Singh. And I'm very thrilled to give these bills a hearing. There's probably not much that's more important than school safety. Last year, we passed legislation requiring the behavioral threat assessment management teams. And this bill extends on that to create some coordination. So I'm very much looking forward to passing this legislation. And with that, Senators, take it away. Thank you very much, Madam Chair and members of the committee. I want to thank you for taking up these bills. Senator DeMoose came to me last session with this idea. He had obviously been taking a look at other states and what other states were doing around behavioral health assessments. We were having that whole conversation in the legislature at that time. And one of the things that I found very exciting about the legislation that he brought forward was this idea that we could create a comprehensive statewide system that could be worked through with our friends at MSP. And that, to me, is the next step. We were able to pass legislation requiring behavioral health assessments, but right now it's being done on a school-by-school basis, I mean ISD basis or a school district basis. But we need to be doing something more comprehensive, and I think the state can be very helpful in that. And so I'll turn it over to Senator DeMoose since this is legislation he's been leading and working on and that he can kind of walk you through more of the details. Thank you, Senator Singh. Thank you, Madam Chair. And I know that this, having served with you for several years here, that this is one of your top priorities and a real passion for you, school safety. And I mean, at the end of the day, school safety is something that every one of us inherently supports. As a parent, I can't imagine the horror of something happening to my child. And we've had people in this very room who have survived or are surviving that unspeakable tragedy. And to be honest, I don't know how they even have the strength to get through every day. I can't relate to that type of strength. At times, we may have different ideas, which we've seen in this committee, as to what's appropriate in trying to keep our kids safe and our teachers and staff and school employees safe in our school. But we are all one when it comes to understanding that this is one of the most important things that we must do as elected officials entrusted with leading this great state. The bills that we are presenting to you today, Senate Bills 470 and 471, are a continuation of the efforts that were approved in Public Act 272 last year of 2024 related to behavioral threat assessment and management. More importantly, they're a continuation of the state's response to the horrific shooting that occurred just over four years ago right now at Oxford High School. The ensuing investigations revealed that there were more than enough warning signs before that shooting, and it's critical that we now put into play systems that would allow us to take action on those warning signs. Bills passed last year mandated teams be developed to assess and manage and monitor potential and real threats on our school campuses before a targeted act of violence occurs. The goal was to get ahead of the violence and not merely respond once a terrible act has occurred. Our work in this regard is not done. The next step is to provide the tangible tools necessary to initiate these teams to effectively and accurately make those assessments and intervene when necessary. Senate Bill 470 creates a centralized web-based secure platform as part of Michigan's comprehensive school safety plan. Senate Bill 471 provides a two-year work project appropriation to a revolving fund for initial implementation. The legislation requires the state police to create and implement the program based on minimum technological standards outlined within the bills. The behavioral threat assessment and management platform will be a proactive, evidence-based tool that will help identify individuals who may pose a risk to themselves or to others. It also facilitates intervention, which is really important, with those troubled individuals and refers them to appropriate support services before any harm is done. All of these activities and referrals are maintained and monitored for follow-up as necessary. One important challenge we must address is the lack of access to a statewide case management system that enables those teams to share relevant information safely and efficiently across systems when necessary. We just dealt with a similar plan related to kids being withdrawn from school, and we see what happens when there isn't proper communication from one school to the next, particularly if you're removing a troubled child because of this type of behavior, and the next school doesn't know what they're getting. This information sharing, while respecting privacy rights, which is an important issue, no question, ensures that individuals who are identified as potential risks receive timely coordinated support and cannot move undetected to another school without appropriate follow-up. This type of system is best managed at the state level while being utilized consistently across all schools to maximize its impact. If we do not take this step, we're forcing school administrators to independently acquire non-uniform, non-centralized tools for their threat assessment teams. This results in an incomplete plan with a possible disastrous outcome. The language in these bills reflect the safety and security actions that were recommended by the Marjory Stoneman Douglas Public Safety Commission in its final report in January 2019. That commission was formed following the 2018 Parkland School tragedy in Florida, and this legislation is very much based on similar legislation that's proven very effective in both Florida and Ohio. Florida has, in fact, implemented a statewide behavioral threat assessment to enhance school safety by utilizing a very similar standardized instrument for behavioral threat assessments. Michigan students, school personnel, and others on our school campuses deserve a safe environment, and we're hoping we can take action now before another tragedy occurs. We're open for any questions, but there's other people who are going to testify with more details, so I believe via Zoom. Senator Singh, I think your bill funds this, so that's important, no unfunded mandates. I think the Michigan State Police have indicated support in concept and just want to work out the details with you guys. We're perfectly fine. The goal is not to create a burdensome problem here. The goal is to utilize their expertise in this, and we want to work with them. So I spoke with a State Police representative before this meeting and said we'll make whatever changes are necessary. Any questions? Vice Chair Geis. Yeah, thank you, and thank you, colleagues, for bringing this forward and to us. Is this for school districts that utilize security staffing, whether it's in conjunction with, whether it's a private company or whether it's in conjunction with the local PD or both combined? Is this information that would also be accessible to the first responders at the school, for want of a better term, not just faculty and staff and administration? I believe that's the intent of this, for sure. I mean, we're trying to solve the problem here. They would be an important player in that. Okay, and in a way that it would be proactive as opposed to, like, surveillance-style. We'll have to look at how it's written. I believe it does that, but if we need to enhance that part of it, we're more than willing to do that. Okay. I think that this is definitely something that's necessary. As some of you might recall, I had to leave quite unexpectedly when my son was still in high school and to send a very troubling message to my husband and I saying, like, if I don't make it, I love you. This was during our first term. And so I think, like, being able to identify

those folks who could pose that type of threat and get them the help they need. It's scary out there right now. We have an 11-year-old, and he was telling me the other day about being on lockdown, and the most alarming part of it to me was how casual he was about lockdowns, because he's had four of them so far this year. This is a terrible environment out there, and so I respect the other things that you've done. I respect even the ones I couldn't get behind. I do respect the intent behind it, and that's sort of what we're trying to accomplish here. It's sad that kids are, that the society has to live like this. Yeah, we can definitely work with the school community. I know as they've reviewed these bills and they're going to provide additional feedback, I think we want to balance the privacy aspect for students, but at the same time, the safety piece of that, and I know they're thinking through a number of those pieces as they're creating their own tools and systems right now, and if there's additional language we need to put in here to provide for that, I think we're very open to doing so. Thank you, Senators. Thank you. So my goal is to, there's almost every senator on this panel has Senator Irwin's committee at noon, so we're going to get everyone out of here at 11.50, 5.00. We do have one testifier about this set of bills, then we can adjourn. On Zoom is Tom Miller, Vice President of Government Affairs and Strategic Engagement at Versaterm Public Safety. Madam Chair, thank you. I appreciate the opportunity. Hopefully you guys can hear me okay. I want to first recognize Senator DeMoose and Senator Singh for their support and their action on this issue, and I do want to recognize the legislature for their efforts last year in passing House Bill 5549, which really was the enabling act that set up the behavioral threat assessment teams. There's about 11 states in the country now that require behavioral threat assessment teams, and this legislation that's before you is really about providing tools in a toolbox for those team members. The nice thing, I heard some questions regarding access to the platforms and how information is being shared. All of that is completely controlled by the end users, by the school districts, either at the district level, the school level, or even at the state level. There's a lot of flexibility in the platform to allow role-based access, all of the standards-based recommendations coming out of the Department of Homeland Security are really developed and implemented within the software platforms. As I mentioned, or as was mentioned by Senator DeMoose, there's a lot of states that are really tackling this now. So this legislation really does provide those important tools to be able to do their job every day and to control it, control access to it. And really, it's not about punishment. It's really about intervention. The software platform really gives the teams the opportunity to identify a problem before it becomes a problem, get a student the help they need, and to be able to track it. It's not something written on a notepad in a file cabinet or in some disparate records management system. It's getting access to the information to the people that need to have it to provide the students with the services that they need. The state took steps not too long ago to standardize, and being a former law enforcement person, retired from the Michigan State Police as a deputy director, I really recognize the importance of traffic safety. And the state standardized the traffic safety initiative years ago when they went to a standardized UD-10 form and did information sharing between agencies relative to traffic crashes and to be able to gather and accumulate data on those. If an issue like traffic safety is important, I think the issue of school safety is equally as important. So the ability to standardize and give these teams tools is critically important. We've seen that in other states that I've been working with. The state of Georgia is going to introduce legislation very similar to what's before you today to be able to provide their teams with the tools they need to do the job every day. So if there's any questions that the committee has, Madam Chair, I'd be happy to answer those. But I do appreciate the opportunity, and I want to recognize the efforts of the whole legislature to address this important school safety issue. Thank you. Are there any questions for Mr. Miller? Thank you, Mr. Miller. Mr. Clerk, can you please read in the cards for the record? Les Tankwicz, Michigan Catholic Conference supports both bills. Brian Broderick, Michigan Association of Nonpublic Schools, also supports both bills. There being no further business, the Senate Committee on Education is now adjourned.

title: Civil Rights, Judiciary, and Public Safety 25-12-10
transcript:
The Senate Committee on Civil Rights, Judiciary and Public Safety is called to order. Will the clerk please call and announce the roll? Chair Chang. Here. Senator Schenk. Here. Senator Voino. Here. Senator Irwin. Here. Senator Santana. Here. Senator Runsted. Here. Senator Johnson. Madam Chair, you have three members present. There is not a quorum. All right. We'll adopt some minutes later, and when we reach quorum, if we do, we will take care of some other stuff. But first, we're going to hear about House Bill 4045 from Representative Hope. Representative Hope, we're eager to hear your testimony. Thank you, Madam Chair. I'm here to share my testimony. Good morning, everyone. Glad you made it here safely. I'm here to talk about SLAPP lawsuits, which many people have heard of, but some haven't. Those are retaliatory lawsuits intended to silence, intimidate, or punish an individual who speaks out on an issue of public interest. House Bill 4045 would allow a court to dismiss these lawsuits early on in the process before a lot of discovery has taken place and a lot of money has been expended by the defendant. Bad actors, oftentimes wealthy corporations or individuals, file these suits knowing that the defendant does not have the resources to actually fight the case. In other words, these cases are not seeking to right a wrong. They're intended to harass, intimidate a person into silence. This legislation would allow the target of a lawsuit 60 days to ask a court to dismiss the case on the grounds that it's designed to silence or intimidate someone from speaking out. Plaintiffs that can back up their claims that do have maybe a more substantiated case would be allowed to move forward with their cases. So this doesn't prevent anyone from bringing a legitimate, for lack of a better word, a legitimate case into the court. And I'll offer a couple examples. These pop up in many different areas, including in the scientific world, journalists, sex abuse survivors, all of these groups and many others have been the subject of slap suits. Last term, I had a slap suit victim from southeast Michigan get in touch with me. She's a retiree who's taken a new interest in local government, and she was sued for defamation by a developer after she had posted on social media her concerns about her local government's dealings with a private entity. She was sued by the private entity. Even though there wasn't sufficient evidence to support the case, it was a defamation case, the lawsuit could have cost her up to $50,000 to defend. I've also had a slap suit victim contact me from southwest Michigan. This is litigation that's ongoing. The Saugatuck Dunes Coastal Alliance, which is a nonprofit, opposed the development of a marina and high-end housing at the mouth of the Kalamazoo River. They were sued. I will have a more detailed account of this case because it's pretty interesting and it's ongoing to send to you after the hearing, and I apologize that I don't have it now. So Michigan is one of only 12 states that doesn't have an anti-slap law. This is the third time I've introduced legislation, and last term the bill almost made it across the finish line. It was a victim of lame duck and didn't quite make it. Don't fault anyone for that, but it did manage to pass the House of Representatives earlier this year back in October unanimously. That happens so rarely now in the House. I think it's worth pointing out because it reflects the really nonpartisan nature of this bill and the inherent fairness that people from both sides of the aisle want to see in our judicial system. And kind of in keeping with that, the bill has broad support from a bipartisan group of stakeholders, nonpartisan group of stakeholders. You'll see written testimony from the ACLU of Michigan, and then Americans for Prosperity Michigan, Sierra Club, and the Michigan Coalition to End Domestic and Sexual Violence to name a few. More specifically in a state level, retaliatory tariffs cost Michigan farmers more than $277 million in export revenue. Now, that's the tangible picture we have from the first administration. In looking at the latest data from USDA, this helps paint the picture of where Michigan ag exports are since the beginning of the year. Specific crops have seen reductions in export levels. Now, there's natural variability to these figures and we're not explicitly able to attribute reductions in exports to any one source. The destination for Michigan apples, for instance, has a lot to do with the Pacific Northwest crop. But anecdotally from stakeholders, we're hearing Michigan companies are having challenges remaining competitive in the global marketplace right now. And to me, that's the concerning long-lasting impact of the current federal approach to trade policy. The United States is increasingly being seen as an unreliable, unpredictable trading partner. I hear firsthand from exporters, the buyers in other countries are prioritizing traditionally inferior products from other countries, but those are products with stable supply chains. We're seeing this play out in the soybean market. Brazil has overtaken the US as the world's leading soybean producer. China has invested in that production capacity and is now predominantly sourcing soybeans from South America instead of the United States. Other countries are displacing US agricultural products in many of our longstanding markets. We're right to prioritize domestic food and value-strengthened American supply chains that create jobs, but US ag is dependent on exports. We have 40 years of farm policy that's built around shipping premium value American crops around the world. The financial stress that we're seeing on farms today and the uncertainty about planning for tomorrow is in large part due to those abrupt changes in trade policy. So we'll continue to track the impacts of federal tariff policy and what this means for Michigan producers and consumers. While we can't necessarily control the current uncertainty, we can listen and we can respond to stakeholder needs and create opportunities at a local level. At MDARD, and thanks to ongoing bipartisanship and support from all of you and your colleagues, we're running full steam ahead to strengthen resiliency in our regional food supply chains through one of Governor Whitmer's innovative programs, Farm to Family. This year, we've invested $730,000 in 15 food hubs and farm stops. And these are middle of the supply chain operations, food hubs providing essential aggregation and distribution roles, farm stops serving as an important new market outlet for crops, and they're filling gaps in communities. In the first three months of this work, starting in July, these investments have helped move 64,000 pounds of local produce, 20,000 pounds of local meat, and all of this progress has contributed to food access for nearly 1,400 Michigan families and nine Michigan school districts. It equates to around $340,000 in economic value back to Michigan farms and counties up and down and side to side across the lower peninsula. And we're excited about continuing to make progress, including into the upper peninsula in 2026. MDARD's launching a project called the Good Food for Michigan program. We're excited about this new initiative that focuses on engaging institutions and helping community colleges, childhood education, K-12, health systems, to help develop plans to take action steps towards purchasing Michigan food from Michigan farmers. The project will be led by the nationally renowned Center for Good Food Purchasing in partnerships with our colleagues at Michigan State University Regional Food Systems, who you'll hear from shortly. Continuing to be responsive to what we hear from stakeholders across the state, we're soon to launch a last mile food delivery grant, which will include investing in refrigerated vehicles across Michigan to facilitate delivery of locally produced and procured food for distribution and customer outlets. We'll be exploring on-farm processing support in the coming months for small livestock producers, particularly those engaged in regenerative ag practices where livestock are present as well. Much more coming as we build out these programs and in response to what we continue to hear. We've built these programs out with a lot of intention to address the needs of small and medium sized farmers, producers, businesses, and we're creating more ways for Michiganders to have access to locally grown healthy food. So it's a win-win for our industry and neighbors across the state. So there are certainly concerning issues in the broad agricultural economy today and we're taking purposeful steps in Michigan here to capitalize on our state's unique ability to grow and make things and create pathways for opportunities for Michigan farms and communities. Thanks for having me here today. Thank you. Colleagues, do you have any questions? I have some. If the tariffs continue, how do you think this will impact Michigan's agricultural export industry? Do you think it'll adapt or do you think it might suppress exports even more? Well, I certainly would never underestimate the ability of Michigan farmers and producers to adapt to situations. And a lot of the strength of our export markets today are our businesses and our farmers responding to opportunities here. So, you know, the unpredictability continues to be perhaps one of the

The more concerning aspects of this of how do you make investments today for returns tomorrow when we're not certain about what the economic conditions are going to be tomorrow. So, you know, it speaks to the need to continue to add resiliency and diversity into our systems. But there's a tremendous capacity of Michigan production here to be continuing to build greater opportunities and economic impact in rural areas. Thank you. Senator Cherry has a question. Thank you, Chair. And thank you, Director Boeing, for the presentation. On the presentation, you kind of had that graph where we have production costs going up, revenues from sales going down. And you talked a little bit about work that you're doing in terms of developing markets, presumably to help, you know, change that sales figure. Can you talk a little bit about things the department may or may not be doing to maybe reduce the cost curve? There's a lot of pieces to this, too, right? So it's going to be tough to summarize all the work that we're doing across this within a brief presentation. The market development piece is a big piece of it, certainly. But continuing to work with farmers on how you can control costs and limit the need or maybe turn to alternatives besides current high input prices, right? A lot of our regenerative ag work is certainly focused on getting greater environmental returns for how we implement conservation of the practices. But there's a strong component of this, too, of enabling farmers to have the tools to be improving soil health, to manage soil biology in a more holistic way. An ancillary aspect to that, then, is being able to potentially be in a position where we're not so dependent on agricultural inputs. So reduced fertilizer dependency shifts in a way from pesticide usage in quite the same way. Those aren't whole scale changes that necessarily promise to turn farmer balance sheets around for next year, but they're meaningful aspects here about how farmers can go about producing things in a different way that can have, over time, a pretty meaningful impact on what bottom lines look like and seek to address some of those cost control measures. Thank you. Any other questions? All right. Thank you very much. Thank you. Joining us next from the MSU Center for Regional Food Systems are Dr. Jahi Chappell, Director, and Lindsey Scalera. Oh, I'm sorry. It's going to be a rough day. Joining us next for a presentation, then we're going to have Dr. David Ortega, Professor, and Noel W. Stuckman, Chair in Food Economics and Policy with MSU Department of Agriculture, Food, and Resource Economics come up to talk for a bit. Thank you so much. Good morning. Chairperson Schink and members of the committee, thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today. I'm David Ortega, and I'm a professor in the Noel Stuckman Chair in Food Economics and Policy at Michigan State University. My research focuses on food supply chains, agricultural trade, decision making, and food price inflation. I've advised policymakers at the state and federal levels on this very topic and frequently work with the national media to provide analysis on tariff impacts and the forces affecting food prices. I appreciate the opportunity to share with you how tariffs and trade policy are affecting Michigan farmers, agribusinesses, and local communities. Simply put, tariffs function like a hidden tax. They don't appear in a line item on a receipt, but they show up in the form of higher prices. They can influence how our food supply chain operates, how it invests, and how it grows. Michigan's food system is deeply connected to national and global markets. This means that trade policy decisions can translate quickly into real economic consequences here in Michigan. Let me briefly ground my remarks in three key points. First, tariffs are raising food prices for Michigan families by increasing costs throughout the supply chain and compounding other inflationary factors. They affect everyday foods that people rely on, and they fall most heavily on low-income households. Second, Michigan's agri-food system is extremely diverse and highly reliant on trade. That makes us particularly vulnerable to tariff shocks. Third, uncertainty around tariffs discourages investments. That can weaken supply chains and keep costs elevated. One stated goal of tariffs is to support domestic production, but for many food and agricultural products, that is not a switch that can be flipped very easily. We import roughly 15 to 17 percent of the food that we consume, with specially heavy reliance on fruits, vegetables, and other horticultural products to support year-round consumption. Some foods we are simply not able to grow here domestically. Foods produced here in Michigan also rely on imported inputs. Packaging materials like tin steel for canned goods, so when tariffs raise the cost of these intermediate goods, the price of the final product can increase as well. This is what Michigan families have been seeing at the grocery store, and remember, it takes time for these costs to make their way down the supply chain, so their effects are only just being seen on retail prices. If we take something as simple as coffee, for example, that is almost entirely imported. Retail prices are up nearly 19 percent over the year. Now, this has been primarily driven by supply issues, but for months we've seen coffee from Brazil, our largest supplier, facing tariffs as high as 50 percent. And those additional costs are moving directly to store shelves. Bananas, which are found in nearly all homes here in Michigan, are entirely imported. Those prices are up nearly 7 percent. Canned foods illustrate another channel. Tariffs on imported steel have raised packaging costs, which has translated directly into higher prices for these products. Now, we've seen some recent tariffs rollbacks, but that won't lead to sudden food price decreases. Food prices are what we call downward sticky. They rise quickly, but come down slowly if they do at all. Since the turn of the century, price decreases have occurred only twice and very briefly. Tariffs raise the price level or baseline, creating a ratchet effect. Once they click up, they rarely move back down. But consumers are not the only one feeling these cost pressures. Our farmers and producers rely on imported machinery, fertilizer, animal feed, and other critical inputs from abroad. When tariffs raise the cost of those items, it becomes more expensive to produce food here in Michigan. We also export a lot of what our farmers grow. This exposes Michigan producers to potential retaliation. We've seen this recently with our soybean farmers, who face narrowing export channels at the same time that their input costs remain elevated. When those two things happen together, farmers face shrinking margins and a great deal of uncertainty when making planting, harvest, and investment decisions. Another critical way that tariffs are affecting Michigan's food system is through a very high level of uncertainty. Businesses aren't just struggling with the ever-changing tariff landscape. They depend on stability and predictability to plan, to invest, and to grow. This is what motivated my colleagues and me to develop a framework to analyze how firms navigate this tariff shock. Our work, which is published in the Journal of Supply Chain Management, identifies the current tariff environment as one of the most disruptive events to global supply chains since the COVID-19 pandemic, surpassing the 2018-2019 trade war in magnitude and unpredictability by a wide margin. Our research and emerging data point to the same pattern. Input costs are rising, new orders are slowing, and capital investments are falling. For Michigan, this could mean delayed upgrades on farms, slower expansion of agri-food production and processing facilities, and potentially weakened export capacity. These are the investments that make a food system more efficient and better able to withstand shocks. When they don't happen, the system becomes more fragile and expensive. I want to bring this back where these policies ultimately land, around kitchen tables all across Michigan. For Michigan households, tariffs can contribute to higher grocery bills, tighter budgets, and tougher choices. Tariffs and the uncertainty surrounding our trade policy are shaping what families can afford to put on the table and can also affect the strength of our agricultural economy in the years ahead. Before I close, I want to briefly highlight two developments that will be important to watch in the coming months because of their potential impact on trade policy and Michigan's agri-food economy. First, the Supreme Court is expected to rule on the legality of the IIPA-based reciprocal tariffs. Either way that the court decides, the ruling will shape the scope of future tariff authority and will have significant impacts on the agri-food system. Second, there is an upcoming joint review of the USMCA, arguably our most significant trade agreement, which will influence market access and competitiveness for Michigan agriculture. These decisions will shape the conditions under which Michigan's farmers, agribusinesses, and families will navigate the food system in the years ahead. Thank you for the opportunity to share this testimony. I look forward to your questions and remain available after the hearing if I can be of further assistance.

Thank you very much. Members, do you have any questions? I have a question. I guess you talked a bit about the effects on consumers. So I have two questions. One is, do you see any concrete benefits to the economy or consumers from these federal tariffs? So when we're looking at the tariffs, the tariffs are a duty on imported products into the U.S., on the value of the product. By definition, they raise revenue, but that is revenue from taxpayer dollars and also from businesses. As far as we can see from the data on the agricultural and food sector, we haven't seen any materialized benefits from the tariffs because they're creating a great deal of uncertainty at the moment that are affecting our businesses, our farmers, as well as our consumers. Thank you. That's what I'm hearing, too, that there's all costs and no benefits. Are you concerned with – do you have any maybe illustrations you could give us about what's happening to families that are struggling at the same time that our social safety net is being eroded by the same administration that is imposing the tariffs? So what I can say on that topic is that food prices and the cost of food has been top of mind for many consumers over a number of years. Over the past five years, we've seen a significant rise in the cost of food, roughly more than 25 percent increase over the past five years. Now, the recent uptick in food price inflation – and when we talk about inflation, inflation is the rate of increase. And so we've seen that rate of increase come down over the past couple of years, but it's starting to tick up, and that is very consistent with the evidence that we would expect from the tariffs. And so when we look at this current uptick, it's coming at a time when consumers are strained. And we've also seen, when it comes to the safety net that you've mentioned, Chairperson, there are cuts to programs like SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 1.5 million Michiganders depend on SNAP. And so that just adds significant more stress to some of these families. And it's important to keep in mind that when we talk about food price increases, it really affects low-income consumers and low-income households the most because they spend a significantly higher share of their disposable income on food. Thank you. So it makes it harder for hardworking families to support their kids. It comes at a very tough time for many families. Thank you. Do you think that it's possible also – I've talked to my Canadian colleagues who have been really upset and worried about the tariffs and have said that they're hurting their economy. But do you think that Michigan is maybe more susceptible to tariff stress because of our close connection with Canada? So we have – and historically we've had a very good trade relationship with our closest foreign neighbor, Michigan. There is a lot of trade that happens, cross-border trade. Our agricultural sector is well integrated with Canada. And so when we see disruptions to that relationship because of federal trade policy, it does impact our ability to engage with our partners. So there are some consequences to some of those federal-level policies that we're seeing. Thank you very much, Dr. Ortega. Any other questions? Okay. Thank you. Now we will have from the MSU Center for Regional Food System, Dr. Jahi Chappell – I hope I said your name right, and if I didn't, please correct me – who is the director, and Lindsay Scalera, Director of Policy and Leadership Education. When you're ready, please go ahead with your presentation. We appreciate you being here today. Good morning. Thank you, Chairperson Schink and members of the committee. So I'm Dr. M. Jahi Johnson-Chappell. I'm the Kellogg Foundation Endowed Chair for Food, Society, and Sustainability and the Director of the Michigan State University Center for Regional Food Systems. But for today's testimony, I'm going to be turning it over to Lindsay Scalera, who's the center's assistant director for policy and director of policy leadership education. Thank you, Dr. Chappell, and thank you, Chair and members of the committee, for having us today. As our director said, my name is Lindsay Scalera, and for over 20 years, the Center for Regional Food Systems has been working with people, organizations, and institutions to develop what we call regionally integrated food systems, so that local and regional food systems. Much of that work has been supporting institutional food procurement, regional food distribution, and supply chain development throughout the state. So today, I want to talk about how tariffs are disrupting institutional food procurement. I'm really sorry. We had a problem with the agenda, and we have Senator Polhenke back. We need to quick take a vote. I don't have to leave. I know, but Senator Singh does. So we need to interrupt you for a quick moment. You can stay right there. We are going to vote on a bill that is about trespassing on people's land. And so we'll just do that real quick, and then we'll keep going. I appreciate your patience. You guys are awesome. I will entertain a motion to report House Bill 4013 to the floor with a recommendation that the bill pass. So moved by Senator Singh. Will the clerk please call the question? Chair Schenk? Yes. Senator Cherry? Yes. Senator Singh? Yes. Senator Polhenke? Yes. Senator Daly? Senator Victory? Senator Hoinga? Madam Chair, there are four yeas, zero nays. The bill is reported. Thank you. Okay, we'll go back. Thank you so much. So today I want to talk about how tariffs are disrupting institutional food procurement, making local and regional food procurement a little bit more difficult for those who are committed to supporting our local food economy. But I'll also highlight a few ways that Michigan is poised to address those challenges thanks to some of the longstanding partnerships and key investments, especially that Dr. Boring talked about earlier. So before we get started, I do want to – we kind of talk about this in terms of a regional food value chain, so I do want to just define that for a moment. So the USDA AMS kind of describes this as these trusting alliances between or among supply chain partners, and they recognize the importance of our interdependence and collaboration as we work to provide food to our communities. So kind of in that vein, every day I get to work with folks across the state who are advancing this concept of good food. Our shared vision is captured in the Michigan Good Food Charter, which was updated in 2022, and that is a roadmap of strategies developed by contributions from over 150 organizations and about 500 people that we could count across the state to build a food system that ensures food is accessible to everyone, promoting healthy communities, using fair and sustainable production methods, and supports a diverse and equitable society. In practice, and I'll kind of leave it on here, this looks like robust food, regional food production and distribution through food hubs, produce and meat processors, and partnerships with family farms of all sizes. It looks like community voices encouraging positive changes at the local, state, and national levels through organizations like food policy councils and other similar efforts. It looks like strong supports in place to help develop those farm and food businesses. Our state is uniquely positioned to grow as a specialty crop state with such diverse agriculture. And it also looks like institutions like hospitals and universities and schools who are anchors in their communities committing to using their spending power to keep dollars in the state and region and improve health. So rising tariffs, as we've heard, kind of cause a cascade effect throughout the food system. So we're seeing increases in the cost of ingredients, packaging, equipment, and logistics. And all of those kind of undermine the affordability for families, farmers, food processors, and institutions alike. So it's very similar what others are seeing at the institutional level. And they are feeling this on the ground. So to paint a picture of what that looks like, so hospitals are navigating providing quality nutrition for vulnerable folks while they're also committed to improving public health in their communities. K-12 and early childhood food service are operating on razor-thin margins while serving meals that meet strict nutritional standards. And I will point out that the School Nutrition Association, through a national survey of meal program directors, found that virtually all of those folks are citing challenges with food costs, labor, and equipment as increased pressure. And the federal reimbursement programs do help, but they are broadly considered to be insufficient to meet rising costs, those reimbursement rates. So with already tight budgets, price hikes coming from tariffs in these especially staple goods can result in trade-offs such as offering fewer fresh options and cutting staff. And we in Michigan have done a lot of work to build up those fresh offerings, offering fresh, healthy, local food through our institutions. Another kind of impact of this, kind of the other side of this, so rising costs can drive institutions to be looking more for domestic and local alternatives.

which is great, and there's been a lot of work to try to move our food system to be able to meet that demand. But a couple challenges that are important to note is that domestic food producers are not exempt from these rising input costs. And as was mentioned earlier, shifting these strategies to accommodate both on the producer side and the purchaser side, there's a lot that goes into sourcing food, especially in institutional food purchasing. That costs time and money to make those changes. And especially for some of the smaller agri-food businesses, we worry about them being able to keep up. And then in Michigan, our local and regional food distribution and transportation is still a really big challenge. And there's lots of folks working on that and working on place-based and systemic solutions, but definitely more support is needed and working to understand that challenge better. So all of that said, I do want to point out some of these key investments and partnerships that have been improving our local and regional food value chains in Michigan and kind of points out the opportunity. So we hear from other states all the time that folks look to us in Michigan as an inspiration. And so we've been kind of over the past 10 years or so, at least from my view, as long as I've been working in it, are kind of proving that local and regional food systems can work. And the way I explain that to folks when they ask, how are you doing it, is that there's kind of a puzzle piece effect. We've got critical state agency support. So MDARD, Department of Education, Health and Human Services, and even EGLE kind of making these targeted investments and providing different technical assistance and supports aligned with this ecosystem of partnerships and organizations throughout the state at local and statewide levels, all kind of linking through that Michigan Good Food Charter. It's led to, in the case of farms institution, more institutions working to increase the value of agriculture, of local and regional agriculture through that purchasing power. So more commitments to purchasing local. And a few examples, and although funding for some of these programs has fluctuated recently, these efforts have been proving to be bridges between institutions and growers. So 10 Cents a Meal has been providing matching grants to help schools and early childhood sites purchase more local food. The unfortunately now terminated local food for schools program had about 500 farmers, mid-scale and small farmers geared up to start or increase their purchasing relationships with schools. We do still have the Healthiest School Meals for All program, and one of the visions and promise of that program is when that's paired with some of these local purchasing incentives and commitments, that we can keep more local food dollars in our state and our farm economy. And then as was mentioned earlier, the Farm to Family program, where that's really aiming to strengthen these market opportunities for local and regional agri-food businesses. So just in conclusion, the tariffs are kind of squeezing us from both sides of the plate. Institutions need to be able to afford the food, but farmers also need to be able to make a profit and rely on distribution and processing capacity that we are still growing at the local and regional level. And I think, just to kind of close it out, this Farm to Institution value chain that we've been building over the past more than 10 years, really, it kind of opens our doors for growers and communities to provide avenues for healthy eating and really contributes to that local and regional food economy in Michigan. So I think that's it. And if you have any questions for me, I'll open the door. Thank you, colleagues. Any questions? I know when I've visited some of the local food banks, they are saying that they aren't able to provide as much meat, and they are suffering from cuts in their budgets because of federal cuts. And I'm wondering, is the cost of meat rising? Is that part of the tariffs too? I wouldn't be able to speak super clearly about that, but I have heard that. And I do think we could get back to you with some data about that. I know that we meet processing capacity in Michigan is something that is of interest. Yeah, that's definitely something I've been working on too. Okay, thank you very much for taking the time and also for being patient with us going back and forth a little bit. We also have a lot of committees going on today, so it makes it a little bit that way. I understand. Thank you so much. Appreciate it. All right, thank you. Thank you, everybody, for making the trek in, and there being no further business, the Senate Committee on Natural Resources and Agriculture is now adjourned. Thank you.

And then we have our emerging aviation section that has been doing a lot of work on how the integration of right-on-time deliveries with drones and the new vertical takeoff and landing aircraft that you've been hearing a lot about, which are still crude aircraft, but that we have a small group of people that are working on the integration of that into our airspace system, which is one of the hardest things to do. And at this time, we'll take questions. Thank you for your fast testimony. Just real quick, how many employees are in MDOT for that division? So we have 48 full-time employees that have been appropriated within the budget. We have a couple vacancies, but our total number is 48. And it's similar to our roads where you, registration, fuel tax, and parking for funding. Thank you. Rep Slaw, you have a question? I do. Thank you, Madam Chair. So what's a tall structure review? And you said 6,000 to 7,000, I think. So tell me, how do we get that? Are we letting trees grow up that fast, or what's the deal? So there's what's called the Michigan Tall Structures Act. And how I explain it real quickly is FAA controls how pilots fly and airports operate. And then the states have control of what touches the ground so that FAA doesn't have authority over a tall structure that might impede airspace. So the Michigan Tall Structures Act was enacted in 1959. And then any structure in proximity to an airport that might prohibit that or prevent that aircraft from coming in safely or departing safely gets reviewed. And there's set criteria for it. And there's 6,000 to 7,000. I think last year we did 7,200 applications. Includes buildings, cell phone towers. And then any structure over 200 foot, irregardless of proximity. So that'll drive the number up. So anything over 200 foot in height will have to come through and get what's called a Michigan Tall Structure Permit. And is that 250 feet from the ground, or is it 250 feet from the lowest spot in the neighborhood? So 200 foot above ground on that. So any structure 200 foot above ground, irregardless of proximity to an airport, does need a review. And the quick answer to that, too, if you're driving down the road and you see a light on a tower, I'm going to give you a 99% chance it's over 200 foot. So we're going to put a condition that that tower can be built, and that's proper use of airspace, but we're going to need an obstruction marking light on it. And then I have an additional question. You mentioned that we're one of 10 states that take the federal grant in as a whole and then distribute it. Why are we one of 10? Because that always brings questions to me. And what is the value of that versus having it obviously distributed by the FAA? Really, really good question, and I'm glad I'm sitting here to answer it because it's very near and dear to my heart. So the biggest advantage to be in a block grant state is that you get all of the funding as once. And so there's state apportionment funds that can be distributed to those airports, non-primary airports, but to those general aviation airports. So we can look at the state-specific needs through our system planning efforts and know which the best use cases for those. So we have goals as a state, as outlined, and I think in Brian's last presentation, he provided the Michigan Aviation System Plan. So what the goals as a state were. So that is the largest advantage that I can think of to be a block grant state. Just to finish that up, do you know what the other nine states are? No, I don't. Can you get that for me? Yeah, I can. Absolutely. Thank you. Absolutely. Thank you, Lynn. I really appreciate your testimony and coming here today and waiting. I'm sorry to make you wait, so it's not my intention. So with that, I'm going to have you step aside because I have five more minutes, and I'm going to have our next presentation from Matt Slowak, Vice President of the Kinswater, Dowling & Associates, and the Kalamazoo Battle Creek International Airport Director, Craig Williams. And I welcome you both. And like I said, I'm sorry to keep you waiting. And whenever you're ready. Four minutes or less. Four minutes. All right. I do all the talking. All right. Let's see here. We'll skip through pretty quick here. Well, thank you for the opportunity to speak to this committee. It's always important for the airport community to have our voice heard there. I would be remiss if I didn't share that the good work and the partnership we have with MDOT Aeronautics. Lynn, I've had the pleasure of working with and Brian for a long time. Who are we? Who are the Michigan Association of Airport Executives? We operate and maintain the airports, the 220 airports that you've heard about across the state. We support Michigan's public safety and sustain tens of thousands of jobs. We are unique because we must meet extensive federal safety and regulatory requirements while relying on a funding system that blends federal and state and local resources. I'll go into a little detail on each of those as we move forward. Mentioned there's 220 licensed public use airports. 18 of these provide airline service. Now, you've heard 14 commercial service airports, 15 in the state, but 18 of those provide service. And it's just a difference in designation of how the FAA classifies that. You will have primary commercial service airports. Those are airports that have more than 10,000 in plane passengers, people getting on airplanes. But there are four airports in the state who have less than 10,000, but they still have airline service. Communities like Iron Mountain, Muskegon, Manistee, those are the communities that are airline service but not necessarily commercial service primary. Aviation is a major economic engine in Michigan. Airports support over 183,000 jobs in our communities and generate $7 billion in direct labor income, contributing to a total economic impact of more than $22 billion annually. We handle 39 million passengers in 2024 and roughly 601 million pounds of cargo and U.S. mail. At our airport in Kalamazoo, we support both commercial service and general aviation. Flight training is being a bulk of our 50,000 annual operations. We have 645 on-airport jobs and support another 405 jobs across the region. This equates to a total local economic impact of $240 million, including $56 million in labor income and about $6 million contributed in state taxes annually. So I mentioned the commercial service airports. Those are the ones that have at least 10,000 passengers, and they're served by 17 different airlines.

of Delta and American as they serve Kalamazoo, but you've got others that are Southwest. Denver Air Connection, which is a connection for airports in Ironwood and Muskegon and Manistee. You've got Avello, you've got Frontier, Allegiant, which has a big presence in Traverse City, Flint, and Grand Rapids. They serve airports all across the state. General aviation airports are equally important. Commercial service airports get a bulk of the attention, but general aviation airports are all over and commercial service airports also serve general aviation needs. I like to call them the hidden job incubators. Many provide the same services as commercial service airports, but they are critical connections in rural communities. They allow medical teams to reach patients quickly or allow patients to be quickly transported to critical care units around the state in short order. Also, general aviation airports connect the community with the world, allowing companies the ability to visit their operations that they may not be able to quickly access using airline services. Excuse me. Funding is critical. You've heard that from our last two presenters. Airports come in different shapes and sizes, and as the slogan goes, if you've seen one airport, you've seen one airport. Yet we all of us have one thing in common, and that's maintaining our infrastructure through capital investment. It's critical. According to the Airports Council International North America, Michigan airports face $2.9 billion in infrastructure needs from 2025 to 2029. That's a survey of airports across the country of which I've also participated. These cover runways, taxiways, navigation aids, safety improvements, and critical support equipment like fire and snow removal. FAA funding is expected to cover about 50% of that. State funding will be about another 10% of that, and airports are responsible for the remainder 40%. We'll do that through revenues we collect, millages, and also bonds as well. I hate to interrupt you, but they're calling me back to session, so I might have to have you come back if that's okay, or if you have one final closing. I'll have one last slide here. I apologize in advance. The airports need to be a part of the state's strategic approach to transportation. We need a fuel tax revenue paid by users of airports directed to support, and we need the continued support of that metro parking tax extended when it's scheduled to end in 2030. Also, it needs to be said that investment in air service development programs, like has been done for the last couple years, needs to continue. The state's contribution of $50,000 is not enough. I'm being asked by airlines for minimum revenue guarantees of $2 million, $3 million, so $50,000 doesn't go very far, and that's hard to compete when you have a state like Ohio that has $6 million annually funded to support that. We have 18 commercial service airports vying for air service. In Ohio and Indiana combined, there's only nine, so you can see the competition for it in Michigan. I do have written comments you can have, and if there's any questions, I'm happy to come back anytime. Thank you. And we will defer to questions later and reach out to you if necessary in the future. So I really appreciate you gentlemen coming in and waiting. You're worthwhile listening to because I have had you in the office, and I appreciate what you have to offer so we have a better understanding of our aviation. So with that, Representative Bort moves to adopt the minutes of our October 22nd meeting. No objections. The motion prevails. We would like to excuse Rep Morgan, and we need to adopt that or that. You already did that. I'm sorry, and to correct the October 29th meeting minutes. So all those in favor, we don't have to say that. And then with no further business at hand, the meeting is adjourned.
