title: Education and Workforce — Wednesday, December 10, 2025
transcript:
The House Education and Workforce Committee will come to order. Would the clerk please call the roll? Chair DeBoer? Here. Representatives Linting? Here. Kett? I'm here. Fox? Hoon? Present. St. Germain? Pavlov? Pass. Here. Wilson? Pulzar? Here. Weiss? Burns? Here. Madam Chair, you have seven members present. You have a forum. Thank you. Vice Chair Linting moves to adopt the minutes of the November 12 meeting. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. And thank you, Madam Clerk. The committee will begin today by taking testimony on House Bill 5154, sponsored by Speaker Pro Tem Smith. Welcome to the House Education and Workforce Committee. Please begin when you are ready. Well, thank you. Good morning, Chair DeBoer and members of the committee. Thanks for letting me come before you today and speak on behalf of the legislation that I have here, which is very simple, straightforward. It would require public schools to accept cash as a payment for admission to middle and high school sporting events. My intent with this legislation is to ensure ticket payments remain accessible and inclusive for all who wish to attend. Not everybody has credit cards or smartphones for digital pay, yet there is an increase for schools only allowing these methods of payments. I have particularly had this, several constituents reach out to me and express this frustration. Grandparents that don't have a smartphone, they don't want to have a smartphone, and it's becoming a real problem that we're seeing actually not just in my district but across the state. So, though it is a minority of people that don't have smartphones or credit card payments methods, it's still important to make sure that these Michiganders can watch their family and friends play at games, which is why I hope that this committee will join me in supporting this very straightforward, logical piece of legislation. With that, I will open up to any members if anyone has any questions. Yes, thank you. Any questions? Yes, Representative Fox. Thank you for your testimony, Rep. Smith, and I did experience this myself, and the question I had when I experienced it because I went there with cash in hand, and then they said, well, where's your credit card? The thing I experienced was they said, well, it's an MHSAA rule, okay? And did you investigate that at all in your process? It seemed like it's MHSAA that was driving it, not just simply the local school. This was a district game, okay? That is true when it applies to district and regional games. You have to purchase them through the MHSAA website or payment portal, however that works, because they are in charge of all that. This is for just basic, regular season, middle and high school sports for, like, the local school districts. So this would only pertain to that, not, like, district, regional playoff games. Well, now I'm going to put on my tinfoil hat. Is this with the MHSAA, is it a drive toward a cashless society, you know, and is that the game that's being played here? Well, I can't really answer that question other than, I mean, I think they want convenience, and we have seen the shift moving into cashless society, but I can't answer that question as to whether... If you'd grant me, and Madam Chair, if I may, as an official for the MHSAA, they collect all of the money for playoff games. So they want it to be cashless because they get the money, and that's what pays for it. That's what pays for the rentals. That's what pays for all the officials. So the host school in a playoff game gets the concession stand. But that's why MHSAA wants it in an electronic form because it's easier for them to collect. So thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you. Thank you, Representative Polzar. Thank you, Madam Chair. And actually, I was kind of thinking that, too, that the playoffs, I know, have a different rule than regular season. I guess my question, because anecdotally, I went to a game earlier this year, a local football game, where they did take cash. So I guess my question, because I agree with you, there should be a cash option. Do we have any idea of how widespread this is now that they're saying card only? I'm just curious, like, how many are doing this? I don't have the specific numbers as far as school districts that are not allowing cash method of payment, but I do know that it's a problem because I have seen it in, like I said, many schools within my district as well as hearing it from colleagues that said, yeah, I mean, I was actually couldn't get into a regular season through the school to get in because they did – I mean, they got in, but they couldn't use cash, excuse me. So I just – it should be an allowable method of payment. Anyone else? Representative Smith. Representative Smith, what is the penalty if they don't? I don't believe there is a penalty in this bill. Okay, that would mean. Anyone else? No? We're good? Okay. Thank you, Representative Smith. We appreciate your testimony. Thank you. Thank you. Okay, we didn't have any cards on that. Okay, we had a card from David Randles from Oakland Schools. He did not wish to speak, and he opposes the bill. Okay, next the committee will be taking up House Bill – do we have – okay, great. House Bill 4836, sponsored by Representative Paquette, and Senate Bill 349, sponsored by Senator Paul Henke. Before we begin taking testimony today, we do have substitutes on both these bills, which will push back the implementation date one year. So Representative Paquette moves to adopt the H1 substitute to House Bill 4836. Would the clerk please call the roll on that H1 substitute? Chair DeBoer? Yes. Representative Linzing? Yes. Paquette? Yes. Fox? Yep. Coons? Aye. St. Germain? Yes. Pavlo? Yes. Wilson? Yes. Polzar? Yes. Weiss? Burns? Yes. Madam Chair, you have 10 yeas, 0 nays, 0 pass. The motion prevails. Thank you. Representative Paquette moves to adopt the H1 substitute to Senate Bill 349. Would the clerk please call the roll on the H1 substitute? Chair DeBoer? Yes. Representative Linzing? Yes. Paquette? Yes. Fox? Yep. Coons? Aye. St. Germain? Yes. Pavlo? Yes. Wilson? Yes. Polzar? Yes. Weiss? Burns? Yes. Madam Chair, you have 10 yeas, 0 nays, 0 pass. The motion prevails. Thank you, Madam Clerk. And welcome to the House Education and Workforce Committee, Senator. And please begin testimony when you're ready. Thank you, Madam Chair. Great to be here. I want to kick it off by saying it was cool to hear, I think, a reference from Coons and Colazar to these bills and talking about ACT work keys when we talked about your guys' bills and the writing assessment and SAT. I'll be very brief. You said, Minister, this test will proctor it when I taught juniors. And, you know, some students came up to me and they said, Paquette, why do we have to take this test? Is it possible to opt out? Things like that. And, you know, over the last seven years, we've been taking cracks at this to no avail. But here we are today to allow for the option to opt out of this test for kids that don't see like it's necessary.

Yield that over to Senator Polhanke, who I'm very grateful to be able to work with. Thank you, Rep. Kett. Thank you, Chairwoman DeBoer. Ditto. I also taught 11th grade students, and boy, did I try to prepare them for this work keys test, and there was always the why, because they're 17. They want to know why, and I never had a great reason for them. Thank you for the opportunity to testify on these bills today. They're designed to give Michigan students and families more flexibility in their educational journey by allowing an opt-out for the WIN work readiness exam, formerly the ACT work keys exam, in the 11th grade without jeopardizing school funding. The good intentions with which the MME work skills assessment initiative was enacted in 2024 have not come to fruition. Today, aside from some skilled trades groups who you'll hear from today that use the work skills scores as their entrance test into apprenticeship programs, it appears that few businesses or manufacturers use the test scores as originally intended. As a state, I think we need to do an even better job to promote the skilled trades as a viable career option for students who are not college-bound. By still requiring the state to offer and pay for this test for kids who may want to go into the skilled trades, it demonstrates we're serious about helping kids in the skilled trades if they so choose. What this bill does is preserve that option for kids who may want to pursue the skilled trades, but it removes the requirement to take the test for kids who are not interested in the skilled trades. For schools and students, my bill would mean reducing the number of hours all kids are required to engage in standardized testing by about three hours. That was based on the work keys assessment, which is a laborious three-hour test. And depending on how many juniors opt out of the test, it could also mean that an entire half day may not be needed to reserve the gym, alter transportation schedules, silence the bells, announcements, pull juniors out of class for a half day. Once again, my bill is an opt-out bill, meaning all Michigan juniors would have to take this work readiness test unless the parents and the kids themselves choose to opt out with the full knowledge of what they're opting out of. And to that end, we would be providing parents with a first-ever letter describing what the test can be used for. So if the parents opt out and the kid chooses to opt out, they know what they're opting out of. And this bill directs the Michigan Department of Education to create a waiver letter in consultation with representatives from the skilled trades, business, manufacturing, and the waiver would be distributed to school districts and made available to students and their families. The parent or guardian would have to sign off on it, ensuring that the decision to opt out is thoughtful and informed. Should this bill become law, it would take effect for the 26-27 school year. I'd love to do it for this school year, but the creation of the letter would have to take place by December 31st, and it's literally impossible to get that done before this September. And the sub reflects that date change. Thank you for your attention, and I respectfully ask for your support on these bills. Thank you so much. We appreciate your testimony. We have questions from any committee members. Representative Colzar. Thank you both for introducing these bills. I've always said when it comes to testing, I have no problem with it if it's relevant to the students that are taking it. And I think by you creating this opt-out method, you are making sure that those who want to take this, that want to go in the trades, have that avenue. My question to you would be more of, do you anticipate, how long do you anticipate this, you know, I think it's been around for a long time. I'm curious how long you think it'll take before students start realizing if they don't wish to take this test, they don't have to, or how long do you think it'll get for word to get out, so to speak? I'm curious if you've had conversations in your districts or how you think that's going to go. Well, we know how letters home to students don't always make it home to students. So the first year might be dicey. Some kids might be taking it because they didn't read the letter, the parents didn't read the letter. They don't want to take it, but they're going to take it. So it might take a year or two for the word to get around if the kids want to opt out because this pathway is not for them that they can do that. Maybe you have. Obviously speculative, I think it'll be pretty immediate. But for people like me, I love taking tests. I love to see where I line up on anything. I'm kind of weird like that. But I think the word will get around pretty quick. Representative Burns. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you both for your testimony today. Just a quick clarifying question leading off of Rep. Colazar's question. I know we're talking about a letter. Is this a physical letter only? Is it something that can and will be emailed to parents? Because obviously that's just a quick, easy method of communication. It can be physical or email. Okay, wonderful. Perfect. I think that'll help close that gap. I do too. Appreciate it. Any other questions? Okay, seeing none, we do have some people that would like to speak and support the bill. Grace Roberts from the Operating Engineers 324. Would you like to come to the table and begin when you are ready? Chair members of the committee, thank you for your opportunity for me to speak today. My name is Grace Roberts. I am a first year apprentice at the Operating Engineers Local 324. I'm also a proud graduate of the class of 2022 from Okemos High School. And I'm here to voice my strong support for the House Bill of 4836. The bill matters because it helps make sure students like me understand and can access the incredible opportunities that exist in the Michigan skilled trades. The House Bill 4836 ensures that a standardized test that can be used for entry into the registered apprenticeship programs remains available for our high schools. And that parents and guardians are informed that the test measures and why it is so important. My own experience shows why maintaining the test and informing families is very important. When I graduated high schools, I had grown around the trades. I'd grown up with family in the trades for years. I was always very involved and loved watching equipment and being hands on. But like many students, I was told over the years that college was only my real option. I never had any other options. So I followed that path and I went to college and I studied nursing for two years. Although it took me a while to realize nursing was a great profession, it was not my profession. And I decided that I was going to take the next step that I wanted to build and operate equipment and be a part of Michigan's infrastructure. But even with that realization, I didn't know if I could get there or how I could start. What made the difference was having taken the work keys in high school. I didn't understand its purpose. No one had explained the score or what it was going to be used for and that it could help me qualify for a registered apprenticeship program. Had my family and I been given that information, my path would have been more direct. When I was ready to pursue the trades, that score allowed me to enter the Workforce Development Institute's Women in Skilled Trades program. It is a pre-apprenticeship program and there I was able to explore the trades hands on. I took applied math, I earned my OSHA 30 certification, and I learned directly from skilled tradeswomen. The program helped and informed me of what my opportunities could be and it helped me prepare for what I needed to do next. Using that same score, I applied for the apprenticeship at the Operating Engineers in January. After my evaluation, I entered into the program and I worked for Hoffman Brothers in Marshall. There I operated front end loaders, marukas, dozers, rollers, and I had finally realized that I had chosen the right path. I began my classroom instruction in January of 2026 and I am excited to continue building my career. The reason the testing matters is simple. When measures the essential real world skills, applied math, workplace documents, and graphic literacy, the tradespeople use in jobs every single day. It is also the tool that the U.S. Department of Labor relies on and ensures the registered apprenticeship programs meet federal standards. Without a validated and standardized assessment like WIN, entry into the programs like mine become harder for students to gain access to. This is why House Bill 4836 is so important. It keeps a valuable test in schools and ensures parents understand its purpose and helps future kids recognize that apprenticeships are high skill, high wage, and high demand careers. It's not a fallback, but it is a first choice. If I had known in high school that the work keys was measuring and how it connected to a career in the trades, I might have found this path sooner. But I am grateful that the test was available and brought me to WIST and the operating engineers. And on behalf of myself and on behalf of the future students who deserve to know more about the House Bill, I urge you to support House Bill 4836. Thank you for your opportunity. Thank you so much. And in a state with, we might have some questions for you. Yeah, and we are the state of Rosie the Riveter. We better keep testing for that, right? Absolutely. That's our heritage. Thank you so much. Any questions? Oh, Representative Coons. Grace, thank you for your testimony. What is a maruka?

A maruka is a machine where it does have a bed on the back and it can go up and we put like small pea stone in it and when we dig our trenches we put pipe in it and then we fill the trenches with the pea stone and later on put sand over it. Thank you. Any other questions? You're taking us all to school. Thank you so much Grace. Really appreciate your testimony. Thank you. So we also have Brad Pierce who would wish to speak and supports the bill from the Iron Workers Local 25 Labor Management. Would you make your way to the table? Oh, he wants to speak. He's just not here. Okay. Well, if there's a sighting of Brad, let me know. So we're going on then to Robert Mead. Is he here? Okay, great. He would like to speak. He supports the bill and he's from UA Local 85 Plumbers, Steamfitters and HVACR. Thank you, sir. Begin when you're ready. Well, good morning. I want to take the opportunity to speak today. I want to talk to you a little bit about something that directly impacts the strength of the apprenticeship programs in St. Michigan and the quality of our workforce and also the future of the construction industry for that matter. House Bill 4836 and the role of workforce readiness testing. In the construction trades, we guys, us guys and gals, know better than anybody that a good foundation in terms of the strength of a structure, right? So in the start of the solid footings, everything that builds on top of that stands strong. The same is true in our workforce. The House Bill 4836 and the workforce readiness testing it supports helps to build that strong foundation. Is your mic on, sir? Thank you. I apologize. Let's start with the core idea behind the bill. Ensuring that individuals entering into the skilled trades have the essential competencies needed to succeed, right? Not advanced skill, not specialty knowledge, just a baseline reading, math, and problem-solving skills. Something that every apprentice needs today and every day. This is exactly what this bill and those tests measure. It isn't about school-based academics or trick questions. It focuses on real workplace skills, right? So mathematics, the kind of mathematics that we're going to utilize to calculate fall and pipe and what the length of pipe is, estimating materials, verifying measurements, using math on a job site just isn't an inconvenience. It's our day-to-day. And if you screw it up, it costs money, time, and labor, right? Reading and information, okay? The ability to understand safety documents, code language, installation instructions, that's a big one, right? Job site directives. If somebody can't read or interpret critical information, they're a liability. Not because they aren't smart, but because the nature of the industry demands precision. And location information and graphic literacy. These skills are tied directly into reading blueprints, isometrics, schematics, and technical drawings. And modern construction worker must understand visual information as well as written information. So these are the core competencies that determine whether someone can thrive in an apprenticeship program or struggle in the first few months. House Bill 4836 recognizes this reality and provides structure, standards, and accountability. It says, let's not guess. Let's not hope. Let's measure, identify gaps, and prepare people for success before they even set foot onto a job site. For training centers like I manage, this means better placement, better apprentice retention, and better apprentice outcomes. For contractors, it means a qualified skilled workforce that is prepared, productive, and less likely to have costly mistakes. For students and applicants, it means a clear, fair, and objective way to show their readiness regardless of their background or prior education. So let's be honest. In our industry, it's changing fast. When I started, it's a completely different world from 20-some years ago, right? Technology is advancing. Building codes are evolving. Blueprints are digital. We have tablets now. We don't have paper on the job sites anymore, right? Safety expectations and regulations are higher than they've ever been, right? The testing that is given gives us a way to ensure that these new apprentices are ready for these modern demands, not just physically, but mentally and academically. House Bill 4836 also matters because it promotes equity and opportunity. When using consistent assessments, we level the playing field. We're not judging someone by where they went to school, who their family is, or what they've done before. We're judging them on their actual physical skills. This opens the door for many more people, including those who didn't have the best academic support growing up, right, to enter the trades and succeed. At the time when our state and our country are facing a massive skilled trades shortage, we can't afford to bring in unprepared workers. We can't afford to turn away people who can thrive with the right support. Testing helps us solve both problems. So in short, House Bill 4836 and the testing it provides and helps gives us a stronger pipeline to skilled apprentices, safer job sites, more effective training programs, reduces dropout and failure rates, and a fair, objective way to measure one's readiness for this program. This isn't about barriers. It's about preparation. It's about setting up someone for long-term success, not just getting them into the program, but helping them finish it, build a career, and contribute to the future of the trades. We owe it to our industry and to the next generation of tradespeople to make decisions that support safety, quality, and opportunity, and I feel that House Bill 4836 will do exactly that. I'd like to thank you for your time and your consideration. Thank you. So are there students that come to you that had no idea they had these skills? What I see the most of, ma'am, is I will see the students when they come in. We have our interview process, ranks their scores for part of interview, and it's all weighted, right? So they don't take it serious, right? So we require a four or better, and it only goes to seven. You have to have a four to at least apply, so you have to have at least 12 points to apply. And I see a lot of folks come in with at least just 12, and I'm like, I'm going to tell you what right now, out of the applicants we took last year, out of 400, we took 22. And I promise you not one of them had a 12, right? We use that very extensively. It lets us know that they're ready to go into a classroom setting. So yes. So you think that these tests may not be as respected as they should be when the students take them? Absolutely. So they really are not informed about what the work keys tests can open up. And they need to be informed. Yes, exactly. Yeah, 100%. Yeah, that is the last thing we want to communicate to the workers of our state at this juncture especially. Agree. I appreciate all your articulate reasons that don't often get said. And we do have to do a much better job communicating with the parents and the students of the amazing opportunities that are out there and that they are individually gifted to achieve for the best of our state. When I was an apprentice and left high school, no one told me about this avenue. I went to college. If my grandparents, if my grandfather wouldn't have worked at General Motors, I never would have been able to go to school. My mom and dad couldn't afford it, right? And they made just enough for me not to get FAFSA, right? So my grandfather was able to help me. I do have a welding engineering degree, and I'm still a construction worker because I see the value in it and I love what I do, to be honest with you. But no one told me. So yes. Yeah, we like to shorten that journey for people to find it as soon as quick as possible. Absolutely. Representative St. Germain. Thank you, Madam Chair. I don't have a question, more of a story. I have a 22-year-old son in the trades, HVAC, and through high school he really struggled with math. It was such a journey with him. But then after he graduated, he started with his career and quickly decided he was then a mathematician. When he was able to use the math skills in the field, everything changed for him. So here he is today, 22 years old. Now he's in the union and in the program. And kind of a funny story, he started the program and the first week of school, it was a Monday, he was in school all day at the union hall, and he came home and he's like, are you going to ask me how my day went? And I was like, okay, how was your day? And he was like, I was in a classroom all day. And so, of course, I had to explain to him, you realize how fortunate you are to be getting this education and starting this journey. And honestly, he makes more money than I do. So kudos to the trades. Thank you very much. Thank you. Any other questions? So, sir, you would say you're very familiar with the work keys test yourself? The contents of it, not particularly. The scoring of it, yes.

Okay, so I'd be interested in your feedback on how well you think that test measures what you need in your profession. So I can't answer that because I can see a direct correlation from when they come into the program to when we start our mathematics and our science and all that stuff. So the students that scored higher in some of those tests do tend to, I would say statistically, they tend to track a little higher in class. Is it across the board? Maybe not because math isn't always for everybody. Reading blueprints isn't always the easiest thing. But I think I do notice a tick up when they score high on the work keys that they are a little more apt to be a little better in the schoolwork itself. Okay, thank you. Appreciate your testimony. Thank you for coming. Thank you. Also, I saw one gentleman come in. I'm not sure if he is Brad Pierce. Is Brad Pierce here? No, okay. Well, I'm sure he had a lot of good things to say, but we'll maybe catch him later. We have some other cards from people not wishing to speak. Mike Johnson from MMA does not wish to speak. He supports the bill. We have Don Crandall from the Home Builders Association. She does not wish to speak, supports the bill. Randy Gross from the Michigan Chamber does not wish to speak, supports the bill. Eli Issa Gil from the Michigan Regional Council of Carpenters and Millwrights. I hope I didn't hurt your name. He does not wish to speak and supports the bill. We have William Miller from the Oakland County Board of Commissioners. He does not wish to speak and supports the bill. We have Ryan Fewens from the Michigan College Access Network. Does not wish to speak, supports the bill. David Michelson from the Michigan Education Association does not wish to speak and supports the bill. Jeremy Garza from the Michigan Pipe Trades Association does not wish to speak and supports the bill. And Tim Hicks, the UA Local 333. He does not wish to speak and supports the bill. Thank you all so much. I love the way that this committee is the wedding of education and workforce. I mean, that is what we're here for. We want students to learn what they're good at and help that fit with what the world needs. And kids don't always know what they're good at. And so the world of education, I believe, is here to walk alongside a student and help them discern their own gifts and abilities and inspire them to develop those gifts and then show them a track with which they can use those gifts to help the world. And we have just gone a little too far in the college only method. And there are way more opportunities available in the world today. And we really need to help students find those other paths if it fits them. And they will feel fulfilled and productive and the whole community succeeds because of going back to the student and finding what they're best gifted with. So I just so respect all of you and the work that you do, especially in the world of the challenges for skilled trades. We have just need to respect the skilled trades so deeply in our state and do whatever we can to encourage students. This is not a lower path. This is exactly the right path for you. And we need you in the workforce. If this fits you, we so need you today. And we want to communicate that message at this committee and wherever we are across the state. So thank you so much for being here. So we want to then go to Representative Paquette moves to report House Bill 4836 as Substitute H1 with recommendation. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chair DeBoer? Yes. Representative Lenting? Yes. Paquette? Yes. Fox? Yep. Coons? Aye. St. Germain? Yes. Pavlov? Yes. Wilson? Yes. Colzar? Yes. Weiss? Yes. Ernst? Yes. Manchuria of 11 yeas, 0 nays, 0 pass. The motion prevails. Thank you. And I hope that we can communicate with these parents in a very articulate way about what these tests do and what the possible future for their students can be through taking these tests. And that's our job. So thank you so much. There being no further business before the committee, the House Education and Workforce will stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Insurance — Wednesday, December 10, 2025
transcript:
Gary, can you please report to the front of the room, please? Thank you. The House Insurance Committee will come to order. Mr. Clerk, will you please take attendance? Chair Harris. Here. Representative Sistel. Here. Leitner. Here. Postumus. Aragon. Here. Nyer. Here. Schutte. Here. Carter. Here. Tate. Here. Fitzgerald. Here. Witzette. Mr. Chair, you have nine members present, a quorum. Thank you. And can I have a motion to approve the minutes of the October 29th meeting? And Minority Vice Chair Carter makes that motion. Seeing no objection, the minutes are approved. All right. On the agenda today is testimony on House Bill 5298 and 5299, introduced by myself and Representative Jason Morgan. I'm going to read in a couple cards today and then give you a brief overview. And then we have some guests that are going to come up and speak as well. Let's see. Not wishing to speak and opposes the bill, Mitch Albers from the Michigan Association for Justice. Not wishing to speak, supports the bill, is Craig Puckett from the Big Eye of Michigan. All right. With that, a quick overview of the bill, both bills. Rep Morgan wasn't able to be here today, so we'll cover his as well. Members of the bills before us would remove language in the insurance code that requires passengers of limousines to claim benefits through the insurance policy of the business if they are injured in an accident. Currently, the code, which you'll hear more about in a minute, allows a carve-out for different types of public and private transportation. However, limos were not included in this back during the insurance reform. Going forward, under this bill, limo passengers would claim benefits through their own auto policy or the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan, just as some of these other groups like Uber and whatnot are able to do. We will have a sub that we're working on finalizing some language for next committee, and we appreciate all the stakeholders that have weighed in on this and provided some feedback and kind of steered us towards those changes. So with that, I'm going to turn it over to Sean Duvall and Chad Cushman, who are operators in the industry. Gentlemen, if you want to come up, you can start whenever you're ready. Thank you. Excuse me. Thank you, Chair Harrison. Thank you, members of the committee. We're very grateful to be allowed to speak here today. Many of us are small, family-owned businesses that support tourism, hospitality, workforce transportation, senior care, and airport access across the state. The issue today isn't really whether or not we should have or carry insurance because we do. The issue is when and why that insurance is forced to pay. Under Michigan's current no-fault structure, certain passenger transportation providers are placed at or near the front of the PIP order of priority. In real terms, that means our commercial policies are required to pay medical benefits even when we're not at fault, even when another driver caused the crash, and even when the injured passenger has their own auto insurance. I'm going to give you an example from my own company. One of our vehicles at 2 o'clock in the morning, taking someone home on a paratransit trip, stopped at a stoplight in a turn lane and out of nowhere, because of how the priorities rules work today, we had a rear-end collision. We didn't do anything wrong. We were just sitting there. Because of the way the priority rules work today, that collision on a $30 trip cost me and my $50,000 deductible $17,000 to repair my vehicle and almost $25,000 in medical benefits for the person in the backseat of the car. Well, that doesn't make any sense at all for a $30 trip out-of-pocket to cost an operator that kind of money. We have that $50,000 deductible because that's what we had to have in order to get insurance in a normal market, not going through the assigned risk. The scenario is not unusual. For Golden Limousine International, we could suffer that loss, and it's painful, but we got through it.

This is going to bankrupt a lot of companies. You can imagine a $50,000, $45,000 to $50,000 claim bankrupting a company. The result of these kinds of scenarios is that insurance companies stop writing premiums or stop writing policies for companies in our industry. They don't know what the risk is. Every soul on board, $250,000 per person, regardless of whether we're at fault or not. Our liability takes over when we're at fault, and that makes all the sense in the world. Our liability coverage is there for when we do something wrong. But from a medical standpoint or a medical coverage or PIP coverage, when we're not at fault and we're getting these claims, it is a business killer. The insurance companies have basically not taken themselves out of the state from being registered in the state to insure. They just don't write the policy. They don't give you a quote. And because they don't give you a quote, you get one, maybe two quotes on your policy. They're at the highest end, and then the other opportunity you have is with assigned risk, which is just terrible for anybody in our. So when we're at fault, like I said, we accept full responsibility, and our liability kicks in. We have $5 million, sometimes $10 million of coverage. On the limousine side, you have $1 million of coverage. You don't have that on the PIP coverage. It's just we're responsible for medical coverage first in the order of priority, and that is what we're trying to fix today. We appreciate the opportunity, and for those of you that don't know me, I'm Chad Cushman. I'm the president of Indian Trails Michigan Flyer, a 115-year-old family-owned company based right here in Michigan, third generation. I would say we're probably one of the largest motorcoach companies in Michigan. We have a lot of the familiar contracts that people know about. Hopefully you've either in the last few years rode Michigan Flyer. For those of you that are in southeast Michigan, D2A2, the commuter service, DAX. We are a 50-year contractor of the Michigan Department of Transportation. We operate all of the inner-city bus service under contract with MDOT throughout the entire northern part of Michigan, the UP. I want to give you some perspective on how this is impacting our company and how critical this is. In the last five years, our loss ratios have averaged about 20%, which is excellent in our industry. In that same five-year period, our premiums have gone up 112%. Four years ago, when we introduced the first version of that House bill, we spoke before the committee on what we had experienced the previous three, four, five years before that. From about 2015 to 2020, our premiums had gone up 75%. Now keep in mind, this is a company with excellent loss ratios, with excellent business, a 115-year-old financially stable company. Part of the reason we cannot get competitive rates is because when insurance companies are requested to provide quotes for us, and we typically will go out and ask about 15 to 20 different companies to quote, and they're all registered to quote in Michigan, the last three renewals, we've only gotten quotes from two different companies, one that was on the fence. And when we asked them, why is it that you won't quote us? We have excellent loss ratios. We have excellent history. We're a reputable company. We're financially stable. We have an excellent safety record. It has nothing to do with any of that. The number one response we get from those insurance companies is venue. And when I say venue, it's not just the city of Detroit, because we do a lot of services in the city of Detroit. When they say venue, they're referring to the state of Michigan. We cannot continue to absorb 20%, 30% rate increases. We just had a board meeting with our owners a few weeks ago, and we've talked about this insurance issue. And we're doing, Sean and I both, doing everything we can to figure out how we can stay in business next year and the year after. We're not giving our people the type of raises they deserve because we have to absorb more insurance premiums. We're not able to give the bonuses that we'd like to give because we have to continue to absorb these premiums. If you're not familiar with our industry, we are an extremely low-margin industry. If we make 10% profit in any given year, that's great. Our owners, and this is how critical this is, 115-year-old company, our owners are starting to ask me, what should we do about possibly transitioning out of this business? Our company is worth more if we simply liquidate the assets and just move on because we're not going to continue to absorb these premium increases. And here's what's going to happen. When you have companies like ours that leave or just exit the industry, and I'll give you some statistics. In 2020, before COVID, there were 230 registered private sector transportation companies here in Michigan. Today, we're down to about 150. Now, a lot of those companies exited because of COVID, but I would say probably half of them because they either couldn't get an insurance quote, despite their experience, or they couldn't afford the premiums. And that's how critical this is. And if you don't have Michigan-based companies operating the type of services we're doing, you're going to have companies that are, and it's already happening whether you see it or not. If you're driving down the highway and you see these buses rolling down the road that you've never seen before, it's because they're coming from out of state to operate service here in Michigan with out-of-state employees that don't pay income taxes in this state. They don't pay business taxes. They're taking our business because we don't have enough companies to operate the business that's here. Our face, the type of business we operate, yes, we're a big scheduled service operator. We operate Michigan Flyer, but we do a lot of charter work. We do a lot of convention work. I'll give a couple examples. Back in 2004, Sean and I worked together to handle the entire European contingent of Ryder Cup. Huge contract. For our two companies combined, it was about half a million dollars in revenue in one week. One week. A lot of other hodgepodge companies. There was a broker called the Convention Store that handled the entire U.S. contingent, and the service was deplorable. Michigan-based companies got the contract with the European contingent. We handled it. We did Super Bowl together in 2006. We did the NCAA Final Four in 2007 or 2008. Any of these big convention groups that come in, when they need transportation, they're depending on companies like us to do it. And if we're not here, there will be companies coming in from out of state that are going to take it over. And we won't come back. And part of the reason our owners are looking to liquidate right now, I'm not saying they're going to, but this is how serious the discussion is. New motor coaches since 2020 have gone up in cost about 60%, 70%. So all of our used equipment, because people aren't buying new coaches anymore, if you've ridden on the Michigan Flyer Indian Trails, those new motor coaches now cost about $750,000. Now all of a sudden our used assets are worth so much that it becomes kind of an attractive thing, option, to look at possibly liquidating your business. Selling to other companies isn't necessarily an attractive option because our profit margins are shrunk so much that we don't have the type of EBITDA or cash flow that's attractive to them. So I am asking today for you to not just seriously consider this, but let's get this bill through because if companies like us fail when we are probably arguably one of the best operating in Michigan, then I know others are going to follow. And this whole insurance thing, it's not just a Michigan issue. I can tell you our industry across the country, it is the number one item and it is putting other companies out of business in other parts of the country. But statistically, Michigan is seeing more companies going out of business in the last five years as proportionately than most other states. And it's because of this insurance law. If we can get this fixed, we can then, when I go out to bid for my fleet liability renewal, if I can get 15 companies to now provide quotes because now it's attractive to write policies here in Michigan, prices will come down. That's what brings the prices down. The companies that are left that are willing to write policies in Michigan, they're jacking prices up because they know they don't have competition. And we're forced to pay it because if we're going to run

ola bust on the road, we're federally required to have this insurance in place. So I appreciate the opportunity. I appreciate you accepting my passion and talking about this, but this is how critical it is. And I again would argue we're one of the most financially stable companies in the industry. If this is what we're looking at right now, if we don't fix this, what's going to happen to the others? Thank you. And I can just say, you know, to reiterate some of it, part of what gave me interest in this is the fact that my district, we're close to a lot of entertainment venues. We're close to an airport. We had numerous limousine companies and whatnot that operated within our district. And my neighbor also had a lot. We have seen the industry just decimated. We've seen all these businesses close. I think we have one limo company left and they struggle. But all the other ones that typically ran these things every day, we don't see anymore. And you're right, in southeast Michigan especially, we see a lot of out-of-state companies coming in and providing coverage, which is a shame. Yeah. And like the D2A2 and DAX contract, when that RFP was issued by the RTA of southeast Michigan, 38 different companies downloaded the RFP. Almost every company was an out-of-state company. We got the contract. We just got it renewed in September 2025, one more year for two one-year renewals. If we didn't operate that service, a Michigan-based company with Michigan-based employees paying taxes in Michigan, it will be an out-of-state company that would take it over. Not just that, but the MDOT contracts, all of that stuff. And I want to make sure I let everyone else get a chance to ask a question too, but can you cover, I mean, my intention is not to give you guys some special treatment, right? And I know some of your colleagues have heard me say parity over and over again. Can you talk about how this addresses kind of a parity in the insurance code? Yeah, the challenge is that you have limousine services that are specifically first in the order of priority. That means in an event of an accident, the limousine company's insurance is what, the limousine company's PIP insurance is what pays the medical benefits for anybody that's injured in the vehicle. Workers' comp obviously pays for the driver, but the passengers, and if it's one person, then it's one person up to $250,000. If it's eight people, it's eight people up to $250,000 each. Very challenging on an underwriter at an insurance company to try and manage that risk. First in the order of priority is a position where the limousine industry is unique. Taxis, transit, Uber and Lyft, one other one, are all third in the order of priority. So instead of the limousine industry, which is just, it could be a car service taking you to the airport or a taxi taking you to an airport, the car service pays first in the order of priority, the taxi pays third in the order of priority. So we're not asking not to pay insurance, we're not asking to reduce coverage for anybody, we're just asking for parity with all of the rest of the passenger carrying industry. If you're on a transit vehicle, if you're in a taxi, those all, Uber and Lyft, those all are third in the order of priority. That's where the limousine industry should sit as well. Any questions from other members? Rep Fitzgerald. Thank you, Chair, and thank you both for being here today. You're right, the insurance market is incredibly challenging for large auto risks such as yourselves, and that has been the case for probably the better part of a decade, if not a little bit longer as well, predating actually the reform, I bet. Because auto has a very high frequency of loss, and with what you mentioned there, a new motor coach having 60 or 70 percent additional cost, a lot of that is technological, a lot of that is parts costs. And so I talk about this sometimes in this committee with personal autos, is that a side mirror, I changed my wife's side mirror 15 years ago for $30 on a Saturn vehicle. Today it has cameras, it has sensors, it has all sorts of things. So that same $30 fix from 15 years ago is now $2,500 in some cases when a side mirror is gone. Exactly right, and there's a huge lead time on those same costs. And so if the vehicle is non-drivable, there's extended costs to the insurer as well, it's a problem and it's a challenge. With all of this to be said, is that that's all regarding property damage, the physical damage to the property that we have, which I don't disagree is a problem that we have within the marketplace that you are seeking to have that risk. But the two issues between physical damage and medical liability are really two different issues that are, I think, being conflated into one driver for the marketplace. I wonder if you can tell me a little bit more about, you mentioned that the standard market and then the assigned risk pool are really the only two options. But alternative risk solutions such as captive insurance, especially for people who have great loss ratios, 20% would be, I would venture to guess, is industry leading. Yeah. Yeah, and I can address that too, and Sean and I were talking about that a little bit before we came up here. So when I'll clarify too, for 2025, our renewal, 30% with 10% loss ratio in 2025. And by the way, that was with $100,000 deductible on the liability claims and $50,000 deductible on the physical damage claims. So for all intents and purposes, we were self-insured because we paid all but one claim because they were all under the deductible. So to address that, and this is a good example, there are captive options available. We both pursued the same captive option on our renewals this year. He was able to get into the captive option. We weren't, even though we have excellent loss ratios. And it was through a company called Captive Resources who handles the majority of the captives. And when they got back to me and said, we will be declining to quote you, I said, why? Their number one reason wasn't venue this time, but their number one reason was with a company like us, we are a public transportation provider. We operate all of the Indian Trail scheduled services. We operate Michigan Flyer. We operate D2 DAX. We have a higher percentage of passengers that don't own cars, that don't have car insurance, they don't have medical insurance. And in every instance, we will be the ones responsible for their medical bills. So it's beyond, for us now, the venue, it's because of the customers that you serve. And the thing that makes me so irate is the service that we provide under contract with MDOT, which is all of the 53-11F rule route services. These are the most underserved people in our community, in our state. Average household income of an inner-city bus rider in Michigan, based on the last survey, about $22,000, $23,000 a year. They don't own cars. So the insurance companies are telling us, we don't want to quote you because of the people that you're serving. And I can't do anything about it, but you all can help us do something about it because it's not right. Representative Fitzgerald, the issue really isn't about whether or not we can repair our vehicles. This is truly 100% about the PIP coverage. So the PIP coverage that we're first in the order of priority for at $250,000 per person, if you have a 50-passenger coach, that is an unimaginable number for the underwriter to try and manage, especially when you're not at fault. So that's really, it's not about repairing the vehicle, the cost of the equipment, the cost of the bus. This is strictly about the medical coverage for the passengers on the vehicle and where their car insurance, their household insurance, and then MACPA should come into play. Instead of that, our industry is first in the order of priority. And if I could add one other thing, the majority of our premiums combined between liability and physical damage are a result of the liability coverage. Liability coverage is the big part of it. We have no concerns with the physical damage quotes that we're getting provided. But when an insurance company won't provide you with a quote period, not only do you not have physical damage, you don't have the liability portion. So they won't quote one without the other. And I think just to bring another factor into this, because this is really, I think, maybe demonstrating to the committee as well as anyone who may be interested in this, kind of the complexities of the underwriting that comes into a commercial risk, especially those with, again, auto is a high risk environment because these are, again, it's property that is mobile,

does have that liability that you're talking about, and some of this is also driven by court decisions about awards, and especially those when we talk about the 18-wheelers and we talk about the large vehicles that are on the road, including large buses, the awards are increasing that. We call that social inflation, right? And we see that the million-dollar claim from eight years ago is now an $8 million, $10 million award based on today's market. And so I can understand that the liability is pushing that forward because of the risk that you do have, the risk profile that you do have. We are certainly understanding that the liability is, again, a federal requirement. It's on us, and we accept that. The PIP coverage is what's different. The medical coverage is what's different. I don't want anybody to think that we're here arguing about paying for liability insurance when we do something wrong. 100% we accept that responsibility. What we are struggling with is being first in the order of priority, not the same as any other passenger-carrying entity, whether it's transit, taxis, Uber, and Lyft. Just put the limousine industry at the same level as everyone else for medical coverage. And everybody has statutory requirements for liability. You can do whatever you want in terms of your lender will allow you to do in terms of caring for your vehicle, in terms of your physical damage. Liability will take responsibility for PIP is something that we just want parity for. Thank you. Minority Vice Chair Carter. Thank you, Mr. Chair. And thank you for your testimony. I'm familiar with what you're talking about. I just want to get you to explain to me if these bills are introduced as is, how would that risk be distributed when it's taken off of you? And I understand the need to have it taken off. The example of the 250 per 50 passenger bus was frightening. But tell me, who will absorb the risk if you're no longer responsible? So I'll say two things about that. First, the same way that a taxi, the transit agencies, Uber, and Lyft, there's still a mechanism. First, it's your car insurance. Then it's your household insurance. So if someone in your household has insurance, that medical coverage would fall to their insurance. After that, then it goes to MACPA. In your particular situation, Uber, Lyft, taxis, they're third in the order of priority. So your car insurance, household, taxis, that level, and then MACPA. In this situation, we're first. So it doesn't get to your car insurance. It just comes to us, and they'll exhaust those resources from us. Okay, thank you. I understand that part. I guess where I'm headed with this is that one of the things you mentioned was the large population of uninsured and underinsured that utilizes your services. Would the assumption that they're uninsured or underinsured and not able to absorb this risk, where would it go from there, assigned claims or what? So we do fall into the order of priority. So we're third in the order of priority. So we would have some risk assigned to us. But I would just say that what Chad said is real. If his business goes away, all of those folks are going to be on the road. They're going to drive without insurance, and that's going to end up in MACPA as well. So people are a little concerned that MACPA is going to be overwhelmed because the limousine industry and our 140 carriers go away. But if those people start driving, that's still going to go to MACPA. One more thing, Mr. Chair. I want to thank you about mentioning a word called captives, okay? I want Mr. Chair to hear that word, C-A-P-T-I-V-E-S. Thank you so very much. If I could add, too, really quick what Sean was saying. Keep in mind the goal of this is to get insurance companies to come back to the state to provide quotes. The problem will take care of itself in the long run if we can simply get these insurance companies to come back. And it's not going to happen overnight either. It's going to take some time, but this is where it starts. Understood. Thank you for that. And, you know, I think, Minority Vice Chair Carter, along with the captives, I'll let you spell it again. You know, I think, again, the thing that I think brought me to the table on this was that you guys were excluded versus everybody else. And for life of me, I'm not sure why. That was obviously before my time. But I'm sure that's something that you can hit on. I can tell you why. So when you think about all the other modes of transportation in Michigan, from public transit to who are represented by MPTA, Amtrak, they have huge budget. We are small, privately owned companies. We don't have the budgets to be able to hire people to advocate and lobby for us. We were simply left off the table when all that work was done in the no-fault auto reform, which shouldn't have been. And as we were meeting with senators and representatives, the kind of response was, oh, we left them out of this? Oh, that wasn't the intent. It wasn't the intent to leave us out. It was just it was an afterthought. It was an oversight. Thank you. I suppose, Minority Vice Chair Carter, I'll allow you one more question because I like you. What it is is you're on this paper. No. So just for clarity, this is limousine services only. No? No, this would represent – keep in mind, Sean's company, Golden Limousine, but he doesn't just operate limousines. He operates mini buses. He operates motor coaches. That's what I wanted to clarify. Companies like ours, you see the big 45-foot Prevot MCI motor coaches, but we also operate shuttle buses, like campus shuttles here in East Lansing. We do the lodges shuttles. And this whole package was excluded, correct? Yes. That's the clarity I needed. Thank you. Any other questions? No? Okay. Thank you both for being here. We appreciate it. All right. With that, can I have a motion to excuse absent members? Rep. Schutte will handle that for us. I appreciate it. And without objection, absent members are excused.
