title: Natural Resources and Tourism — Wednesday, December 10, 2025
transcript:
House Committee on Natural Resources and Tourism will come to order. Will the clerk please take the attendance? Chair Martin? Here. Representative St. Germain? Here. VanderWaal? Present. Altman? Here. Codeley? Here. Johnson? Present. Preston? Bonak? Here. Fairbairn? Here. Wurtz? Here. McFaul? Here. Scott? Here. Weiss? Here. Arbit? Forman? Myers-Phillips? Wooden? Mr. Chair, you do have a quorum. Thank you. Representative Altman makes a motion to approve the minutes for our previous meeting. The minutes are approved by unanimous consent. We're now going to take up House Bill 4445, sponsored by Representative Wurtz. Representative, please come forward and present your legislation. Well, good afternoon. Thank you, Chair, and thank you, committee, for taking the time to hear my testimony. This is legislation that I actually introduced at the very beginning of my term here, and it was recommended to me by a former sheriff in Hillsdale County that I fix the deer baiting issue in Michigan, which I began to do some research on and would just like to share with you some of the statistics and the challenges that we face, particularly in my district, with a huge overpopulation of deer. In southern Michigan, over the last 40 years, the deer population has increased by about five times, from 200,000 to a million deer. Near my home this time of year, it's not uncommon to drive by a 40-acre farm field and see 20 or more deer. In fact, last Christmas, I looked out the window in our kitchen into the field just to the north of us. There was at least 20, if not 30 to 40, all in a herd, and I opened the door to go take a picture, and then they all proceeded to run across a road, which is a pretty heavily trafficked road. It's the main thoroughway in and out of Quincy, south and northbound. So to say that that adds other issues, I'll get into later with also auto accidents in our community. Michigan has the second highest deer population of any state in the country, only behind Texas, and I'd like to point the significance of that out. Texas and land is three times the size of the state of Michigan. So we have two million, where Texas has a deer population of 5.3 million, but their state is three times larger in landmass than it is to Michigan. According to the DNR, about 35 to 40 percent of the herd must be harvested annually to maintain a stable deer population. In 2023, approximately 17

20% of the estimated population in Michigan was harvested by hunters. So about half of the harvest size that's needed. And that's continued to be an issue as we've moved forward in recent years as well. Michigan license sales have dropped from $871,865 in 1995 to about $594,348 in 2023, representing a decrease of over 30%. Hunters reported taking 2,870,664 deer in 2024 hunting season, which was a slight increase, 5% more from 2023, but then there was a decrease in 2020. So it kind of washes out the increase. Since 1995, the number of registered hunters in the state has decreased by approximately 32% from 800,000 to 600,000. Thanks to new hunts and extended seasons, Michigan's 2024 deer harvest increased 5% from the previous year, but more action continues to be needed. And I'll just tell you, we've filed crop damage permits for the first time this last year, which was helpful. We took six deer on our property. But when you have a crop damage permit, you have to do that during the hottest season of the year, which is August, September. It also happened to be during our fair season or our fair week, which is also for rural farm families, usually tends to be the most busiest time of the summer for you. And so with very limited time out in the field, we were still able to take five or six deer. But on opening day, my son shot four deer. And a few weeks later, my mother-in-law called and said, why don't you come back? There's eight more deer out here in the yard. But at that point, hunting season was over. So the opportunity is still great in our community for the need for more deer to be harvested. Last thing I'd like to highlight is auto accidents. American Automobile Association said Michigan had almost 59,000 deer-related crashes in 2023. 2024 report estimates 55,000 deer vehicle collisions per year in the state. We were driving home on election night of 2020 from my parents. It was my dad's birthday. And a deer ran into the side of our vehicle, totaling it entirely. All the airbags deployed, made it undriveable, and the damage obviously led to totaling it. Hillsdale County in my district, roughly one-third of accidents, that's where that deer auto accident happened that I mentioned, one-third of accidents in 2024 were vehicle-deer collisions. And while we were waiting for the officer to come, she said, you're my third car-deer accident of the night. Unfortunately, deer accidents don't just affect people in that vehicle, but it drives all of our auto insurance costs up because we're a no-fault insurance state. Crop damage. I had an individual that was planning to attend today but due to illness was unable to make it. But the amount of crop damage that is happening in our community is rampant, and the cost to farmers is very great. Crop damage causes millions of dollars every year in Michigan, making deer the most expensive farm pest in the state. Patrick and Mark Kyes in Hillsdale County have a 3,000-acre cash crop farm in Allen, just 11 miles from the Indiana-Michigan border. They apply hinder on 160 acres of soybeans. The deer deterrent costs them $41 per gallon to cover the soybean field. It costs the Kyeses roughly $21 per acre in application. At one of their 24-acre soybean fields, they've watched helplessly as their 70-bushel yields of soybeans dropped to 15 to 20 bushels an acre, costing them thousands of dollars in revenue that they simply cannot afford to lose. Lastly, I'd like to highlight that DNR chose not to attend today. I wish they would have been here to present their side of the case to the committee. As you can see, they did send written testimony. They claim that this bill would undermine the authority of NRC to regulate baiting. This is not true. My bill does nothing to stop the NRC from regulating baiting based on sound scientific practices. It only prohibits them from banning it altogether. My bill actually allows for baiting during deer season, is what it states in the bill. The law has many requirements that Natural Resource Commission has to abide by. The NRC can't raise the cost of a deer tank, for example. DNR supported Senate Bill 276 just a few months ago, which would have invalidated current NRC orders banning deer and elk baiting. If they'd like to come to the table and work towards a compromise and a solution, my door is always open. Thank you, Chair. Thank you. First of all, I have to ask, you said you had a main thoroughfare through Quincy? Yes. There's a traffic jam in Quincy every morning school is in session. Just checking. So, does your bill, purely for baiting, doesn't address feeding? Is there a difference? It legalizes deer baiting. In my humble opinion, as far as science goes, we could increase the number of hunters, it's just my belief, there's no data because it's not there, that if we had baiting and somebody could go out on a weekend and harvest a deer on a weekend and have a good chance of being successful, we'd probably have more hunters again, especially if we allowed them to do that without bothering them too much in the field. Also, if we increase the number of deer taken and baiting helps that, if the science is that the deer are congregating too much and spreading disease, then the solution is to decrease the amount of deer so they don't congregate and have the disease spread. So, we have to do something to take more deer. And anything we can do to that. The Deer Management Initiative, the one group we had in here gave testimony, is doing the same thing in farmers' fields because there's some farm fields, the cost to put the combine in the field is too costly for the amount of harvest they're going to get out of that field. So, these things have to be addressed. I agree with you that just saying that you can't ban it completely. I'm all for, for example, the USDA controls the area up in Mount Morenci, Alpena area that has tuberculosis with farm animals. And as long as we can control that, because it's maintained between 1% and 2% transmission anyway, so whether we have baiting or not, it's still been, before baiting there was a 1% to 2% transmission, and then today there's still a 1% to 2% transmission, even with a baiting ban. So, I'm not going to address, you know, we can protect that area because the USDA has to control it, but it still shows that the transmission rates really haven't changed that much just because of baiting alone. So, we do have to harvest more deer. Representative Altman. Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Representative Wurz, for testifying in your bill. The chair touched on my question a little bit, but did you have conversations with the DNR when you were working through this process? We did. We had a meeting in the office with them and talked through some things and some of their concerns. I actually thought they would be here today. So, I'm kind of surprised. Okay. I was just curious in your conversations that you had with the Department of Natural Resources, and I know they don't set the baiting ban. That is set by the NRC, you know, per Prop G back in the 90s, but they support the ban in place. And I guess my question is, and you touched on this as well, in terms of crop damage and when deer are, you know, destroying our crops, they are nose to nose. They're grazing over the same areas that other deer have grazed. And so, what is the DNR's rationale between, you know, the bait piles versus what occurs in, you know, their natural, you know, naturally, what occurs naturally in nature, I guess is what I'm trying to get at. Well, thank you for that question. I think one of the concerns is a cost factor. Is there going to be a, you know, some sort of a license that we could put on baiting? That's not included in my bill. I wasn't interested in doing that at this point in time. To add to your point, I've sent many pictures to the chair on this issue all summer long, our sun-raised pumpkins this year and last year. And you can walk out and they're all congregated together. They go down and drink.

from the lake or the stream. Together, they are a herd-type animal. They exist together. So to think that if we ban baiting, that's going to fix a disease, is like saying a five-year-old going to kindergarten isn't going to get a cold. It's impossible. They are creatures of habit and creatures that exist together. It's just that's the way that God designed them. And so it's not reduced. I've got someone that will be testifying a little bit from Michigan State University. And as you can see, there was written testimony submitted by Farm Bureau as well, Michigan Farm Bureau. And it's not really reduced any disease. All it's done is increase crop damage because they're going to find the easiest source of food somewhere and consume it. Right, and I would agree with that. I guess my question is do they acknowledge that or do they totally dispute that? I mean, what is their rationale when you had that discussion with them? Vague. That would be their rationale. We might get some information on overpopulation here in a minute with other testimony. Yeah, the baiting and nose-to-nose transmission is different than the hemorrhagic, the CWD, anything that could be in the soil. So the overpopulation spreads it more over the soil. It's not necessarily that they get it from the food itself. So we do have to look at just the density of the population more than looking at the contraction of the disease per se. Because if we can decrease the density, then the soils won't be as contaminated. Because I was wondering how Genesee County ended up with the first CWD when the joining counties don't have it. And some other animal, some other process could have brought it into the soil, and then that deer picked it up. So there's things we have to do for the density, not just the nose-to-nose type thing that we keep talking about with baiting. So that's why it comes up. Why is baiting a problem when we could harvest more deer and make it more successful to hunters on the weekends that don't have as much time when inflation and so forth? They're out there trying to make a buck to pay for the groceries, and going out deer hunting has become a luxury. And if we can make it enjoyable and successful, maybe we can take more deer. Can I add one more thought to answer your question, Rep. Altman? I find it strikingly odd that they submitted this letter when, again, they supported Senate Bill 276, which is pretty much the same thing as my legislation here. So I'm not really sure. I'm also perplexed as to, other than what they stated in the letter, what their concerns are. And I should also comment, just for the record's sake, that NRC will take up their new hunting rules in the spring. Vice Chair McFaul. Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Representative. My question actually might be for the next person, because I just wanted to understand more of the science behind it, because to me, whether they're congregating at bait or at your kid's pumpkins, of course, I'm also not an animal scientist, so I don't understand. So I'd just like to have a better understanding of the science behind their decision as to being against it, I guess. So I kind of wish they were here as well. But I can just wait, I guess, until the next person comes up. Yeah, I think the testimony from the doctor at MSU might give you a little more clarification on some of those. Okay, thank you. Yeah, it should also be noted that anywhere in the state you can plant a food plot and hunt over the food plot, but you can't bait. Of course, it takes a little more effort. And the one thing I mentioned about feeding is I don't want to attract a tract of land where somebody focuses on attracting deer and takes them away from their neighbors. I want their neighbors to have the same enjoyment of potential of deer hunting as anybody else. So I don't want feeding definition to interfere with attracting from others to enjoy the sport and surrounding properties. Well, I think what I was thinking is more than the transmission. Yeah, that's what I was thinking about is the science. Well, like she said, even in Genesee County, I'll drive between sandhill cranes and deer. You probably can see the field and geese. The field is covered with animals. Representative Weiss. Thank you. Mr. Chair, and thank you for your testimony. You touched on this, and I just want to make sure it was just a clarification question. You were talking about conversations with the DNR. Did you also have conversations with members of the NRC as well? I did not talk to the NRC directly. Okay. Because my main concern here is that I do think that it is a legitimate concern that this is currently under their purview in terms of making this decision. And I have concerns about superseding their authority. And I wonder, too, like where they specifically would be at if they are, as the chair suggested, going to be potentially revising their rules in the spring, if they're already potentially looking at doing this or what their thoughts are. I would like to hear more directly from members from the NRC about that as well. And then I did have one other follow-up question that might sound a little off the wall, but I know that in the past, before my time here in the legislature, there was debate around a program at the time. I believe that the city of Ann Arbor had applied to the DNR for a waiver to be able to trap and spay and neuter their deer. And this became very controversial. And at the time, the legislature passed a law to prohibit their ability to get a permit to do that. And I just flagged that. I know your bill is specifically around baiting and hunting, but particularly in areas like mine where I live that are extremely densely populated, where we do not want people hunting deer, but where there are deer that could potentially cause accidents and fatalities, it seems like a good potential solution to be able to help manage the population. I just wondered if you had come across any of that in researching your bill and if you had any thoughts on that. I have actually heard of that idea, and I didn't know, I guess, I thought actually that the city of Ann Arbor was doing some work in that. I'll double check. My understanding is that they had in the past, but that the legislature kind of preempted their ability to do that by legislation, and I might be wrong on that, but that's my understanding. I know there's a definite cost factor there, and I believe Representative Markinen had a solution for that too. Representative VanderWaal. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you, Representative, for bringing this forward. A couple things. First off, I'm going to address Representative Weiss. I actually chaired that committee that put the ban in for Ann Arbor because of the expense, and there was no proof that we, because one buck will travel seven miles to impregnate a doe if she's in heat, and to neuter doe or to sterilize a buck was very expensive, and there was no science that proved that it actually slowed the population. So we did ban that, and I served as chair on that committee. But also in 2019, we worked very, very tirelessly on a package that came out of the House at that time by Representative Hottinga, which is the same one I believe that's on Senate Bill 276. I was in the Senate at the time, and we worked with scientists, the DNR, and actually inside that bill placed some pretty stiff stipulations on how many gallons of bait could be used and what it needed to be spread so that it wasn't just put in one mass pile. It had to be spread over 400 square feet. It couldn't be any more than five gallons of bait at a given time. I'm curious on your thoughts of looking at some of the bait restriction lines of how much could be dumped at one time and in one location. As everybody on this committee knows, I'm a huge and avid outdoor person, and actually now to get around baiting on my property, I'm fortunate enough that I go in and till up a section of land and put in food plots, which aren't considered baiting, and they're large food plots. And I will tell you, deer do congregate in one side. They're a social animal, and they're with each other. So

I fully support what you are. I do believe that we need to look at some option on some square footage and amount that can be dumped at any given time and would love to hear your opinion on that. Yeah, thank you for that background information too. I'm open to suggestions and that was one thing we did discuss with DNR and I'm willing to, you know, if there's an amendment that we need to put forth with some guide rails around that. Obviously, like I said, when I introduced this, it was the beginning of the term and I'm kind of a free market economist that believe in individual rights so that you should be able to assess on your own whatever is best and good for your area. But, you know, if there is some credible, I guess, reasoning or explanation for why we should do a poundage per food plot, I'm agreeable and open to that consideration as well. One quick follow-up, if I may. I appreciate that and I do think that we all need to be cognizant here on this committee as we work forward to come into an agreement with the NRC and the Department of Natural Resources. Our farmers are taking a beating right now. We have a huge reduction right now in the lines of licenses and deer take in the state of Michigan. My friend that is a farmer, you know, everything is science now inside that combine and he can actually tell you on the outside rows per acre what he loses because of deer eating his crop and he's looking for any option of what we can do to pull those deer away from his fields. So, fully support what you're doing here, excited that our chair would bring this up and we'll do everything in our power to help you move forward so that we can come to some agreement here in the state to bring this back statewide. Thank you. Thank you. Well, I would just add too, it's not even just sometimes the eating of the crops, but I had a constituent message, sent me a text, I think it was July 1st to August in the midst of wheat harvest and he said, I've never had so much damage. It's not that they were eating the wheat, but they're bedding because it's a prime area. And then unfortunately, before you can even sometimes see, you end up running over the fawns and so he lost more acreage to that, to the bedding this year and the risks that that can impose as well in a food source has become a concern as well. Representative Bonick. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you, Representative. It's interesting where I live, we have just the opposite problem. We have no deer and it's because of predators, but I'd like to ask you, and maybe you've already touched on this, has the DNR come up with any constructive solutions that you could apply? Well, I suggested we do a roundup like they do out West, a cattle roundup, and we do a deer roundup and then we haul the deer up to your area and you can have them. I think all it would provide is a temporary feeding for our predators. Well, that's actually, I think that our professor, we were just discussing that before, that would, yes, be a feasting ground for the wolves, but at least they would stop eating corn and soybeans in our community. So, yeah, they kind of laughed at me like you all did, but I mean, honestly, like we think with science we have all the answers and we've lost good common sense and the common sense reality is we have way too many deer in southern Michigan and you don't have enough deer in northern Michigan. It seems pretty simple to me. Let's load them up and move them out. How do you think the moose get to the UP and to Isle Royale? Representative Preston. Thank you, Chair. Thanks, Rep, for bringing this up today. First off, there's been a lot of questions about the DNR. I just find it completely inexcusable the fact that they're not here today. You know, when we were talking about license fee increases, there were a whole bunch of deals that were supposedly floated around regarding baiting and the openness to baiting and now all of a sudden it's a closed subject that they can't talk about or even show up to a committee hearing for and basically ignore this committee, the validity of this committee, and not show up to talk about something that's real. You know, when you're talking about food plots, baiting, it's all relative. Preon diseases are a cervid disease. CWD is a preon disease. They're exclusive pretty much to the cervid population. Nobody can really figure out yet how it's spread. One commonality that we have found is overpopulation is what really triggers it. And I just think it's Mother Nature's way of taking it out. But I don't know that I necessarily have a question here. It's just striking that the DNR, again, is not here in front of a committee that they should be in front of answering questions that many on this committee have. I just really wanted that to be on the record because in my mind it's inexcusable. Thank you. And if I could just add maybe one thought on why they may be opposed to this bill. I was texting, and I apologize for doing that, but I wanted my staffer to confirm this. But a ticket for baiting can be up to $500. So they can fine someone up to $500 for baiting. So it's, again, the financial piece, I believe, is one of the reasons that they are opposed to this legislation. And they don't need a warrant to go find that baiting. No, and as we know from one of our own colleagues who was ticketed for baiting and he was simply feeding deer. And if they were here, they should simply tell us what their motivation is. Feeding birds. Sorry, feeding birds, not feeding deer. They thought he was feeding deer. He just was feeding the birds. Thank you, Representative. Anybody else have anything further? Thanks again, Representative. Yeah, thank you. We're not going to hear, well, before I go to the next testimony, the DNR did turn in a card in opposition and submitted the written testimony. It's on the committee's website. I think you may have a copy. They're concerned with the NRC's authority in which Representative Wirt's approach by saying that it just doesn't say when and how to ban. It's just that they can't just totally ban. So now we have Dr. Jerry Blunt from MSU, a presentation on overpopulation of our deer herd. Thank you, sir. Yeah, red button there. Thank you, sir. That works much better. Thank you. Hey, I just want to first thank Chairperson Martin and members of the committee for allowing me the opportunity to speak to you this afternoon. And so as Chairperson Martin mentioned, I'm just going to provide some remarks relative to deer abundance, overabundance, if you will, and some of the issues that are surrounding that. And so first I want to just mention that it's important to understand the term overabundance. And what we want to realize is that it's not a scientific term, but rather it's a value-based term. And in the context of these remarks, we can consider it when a wildlife population exceeds some human-derived threshold of tolerance. And so specifically the white-tailed deer, it could be the amount of crop damage a producer is experiencing. It could even be the number of deer or number of times deer are observed in a crop field, the number of deer vehicle collisions, or the impact of deer herbivory on native plant communities. So consequently, because it's a value-based qualitative term, it'll vary across people what it actually means. And even within the same person, it can vary over time because it's based on numerous factors beyond the actual species abundance, in this case white-tailed deer. Now, as Representative Wurtz mentioned, there's considerable evidence that white-tailed deer populations in the lower peninsula of Michigan have increased over the last several decades. But I want to make clear that there aren't any recent scientifically credible estimates of deer abundance in Michigan across large spatial extents. We simply don't have that information. However, for many species of wildlife that are managed for sustainable use, such as hunting, specific estimates of abundance or density, they're not necessarily required. Rather, using indices or trends based on harvest or the impacts of wildlife, in this case deer,

year on an environment or society often can be used to effectively manage these species and identify where additional management is warranted. Now, there's been an overall decline, as you're all aware, in the percentage of the U.S. population that participates in hunting. Specific to deer in Michigan, the number of deer hunters has decreased in recent decades from 758,000 in 2000 to just over 530,000 hunters in 2024. And this decline in deer hunters has corresponded with a decrease in the estimated deer harvests. In fact, in 2000, the year 2000, over 540,000 deer were killed, whereas only 373,000 deer were killed in the 2024 seasons. And so while removing antlerless deer from the population is considered the most effective harvest strategy for population management of deer, particularly if the goal is to reduce abundance, most hunters in Michigan, in fact, about two-thirds in 2024, did not purchase specifically an antlerless deer license. An antlerless harvest comprised only 44% of the total harvest in 2024. Hunters in Michigan also, on average, only take 1.2 to 1.3 deer per hunter. And so overall, the hunter success rate is about 53% in the southern lower peninsula as of last year. And I also mentioned that of these hunters, only 7.2% of hunters in 2024 took more than two deer. So success rate was 53%, but very few people take more than two deer. And obviously, as Representative Worts mentioned, there are exceptions, but as a rule, not many. So we don't know the relative contributions of declining harvest and land use patterns on deer abundance. However, they've undoubtedly had an impact, particularly in the southern lower peninsula. And these increased abundance estimates have resulted in a number of interactions. And one big one, as Representative Worts mentioned, was agriculture damage. And so I'll start by saying that present, like deer abundance, there's no rigorous large-scale estimates of the economic losses to agriculture caused by white-tailed deer in Michigan. However, there's clearly losses, and these losses can be substantial, as we've heard, particularly to individual producers. But again, the overall magnitude of these losses, we just don't know. So the most relevant data I could come up with in Michigan associated with the extent of crop damage are the deer damage control permits issued by the Michigan Department of Natural Resources. And the number of tags issued under the DDCPs, or deer damage crop permits, in the lower peninsula has increased 331% over the last decade, from about 5,100 in 2015 to over 23,000 in 2024. During 2024, or last year, 10,754 deer were reported taken under these permits across the lower peninsula with an average harvest per county of 158. But that ranged up to 1,118 deer in a single county. The permits and associated harvest have increased at a greater rate throughout the lower peninsula since 2019. So they've been increasing overall, but in the last six years, five years, they've increased even more rapidly, especially in the southern lower. And most of these permits are issued in the east central counties like Sanilac, Tuscola, and Saginaw counties, likely in part because of the amount of agriculture in these counties. But the percentage of deer harvested under these permits has remained relatively constant. So in 2015, 49% of the tags issued were filled, and in 2024, 46%. So the number of permits have increased, and the number of deer taken into these permits have increased, but the actual percent or proportion of the permits tags issued each year has remained about the same. So one might assume the increase in deer harvested under these permits reflects a corresponding increase in deer abundance. You know, an increase in the extent of the problem and amount of damage over these years certainly could have occurred and very likely has. However, a greater awareness of the program, shifting tolerances toward deer markets and other factors could also influence permit allocation. So what I'm meaning by this is it's not to say that the issue has not increased, but there's also other factors that have, and so we can't use the deer damage control permits as a direct measure of increased severity of crops, is my point there. When thinking about deer abundance and societal impacts, it's also important to consider deer vehicle collisions. In recent years, Michigan's ranked in the top five states nationally in number of deer vehicle collisions and was ranked third by State Farm Insurance in 2024. Michigan averaged 62,000 deer vehicle collisions annually from 2012 to 2023, as reported by the Michigan Office of Highway Safety Planning. And this is a big deal. These collisions have resulted in over 15,000 human injuries, 135 deaths, and more than $3 billion in damages, which represents more than $300 million in damages annually, if we assume $5,000 per deer vehicle collision per the Michigan Department of Insurance and Financial Services. In a recent study we conducted in the lower peninsula from 2012 to 2023, we identified relationships of percent agriculture, specifically cultivated cropland, and deer harvest at the county level with deer vehicle collisions. And what we found is that once the percentage of cultivated crops at the county level exceeded 11%, deer vehicle collisions also increased. We also found that once harvests reached 12 to 15 deer per square mile, deer vehicle collision rates stabilized. title: Oversight - Corporate Subsidies and State Investments — Wednesday, December 10, 2025
transcript:
The House Oversight Subcommittee on Corporate Subsidies and State Investments will come to order. Will the clerk please take attendance? Chair Cara? Here. Representatives Green, Bierlein, Lagella, Pawhowski? Here. Mr. Chair, you have four members present. You do have a quorum. Representative Lagella moves to approve the minutes of the November 5th meeting without objection. So ordered. Today we will be hearing testimony on NAYA Enhancement Grants. Welcome Kristen Armstrong from the MEDC. Looking forward to your testimony. Thank you for being here today. Good morning. Here just today, as you note, to discuss the legislative enhancement grants to the National Association of Yemeni Americans. There were two grant agreements administered by the MEDC that were approved as part of the state budget in FY22 and FY23. These grants are no longer active, both having expired by their terms. One on 9-30 of 2022, the other on 9-30 of 2023. While the MEDC is the entity charged with administering these grants, these are pass-through grants. They're made in accordance with legislative appropriation. These are not grants that we generally advocate for, advise on, and often don't have visibility into prior to any appropriations bills being introduced or passed. With that said, our team strives to administer these grants in a way that follows the clear legislative intent and ensures proper stewardship of tax dollars. In the course of FY22 and FY23, we received nearly 350 legislatively directed spending grants here, each of them unique in purpose and intent and all subject to the requirements set forth in the boilerplate. There is no administrative funding to administer these grants. We absorb this work into our normal operations. We're going to talk about the process by which these grants had been administered over the years, but as you are no doubt aware, the legislature recognized that this process to award these direct grants is extremely problematic. You took action to adopt transparency guidelines and processes related to legislatively directed spending items, and we commend that action and wholeheartedly welcome those changes. It's important that we're all aligned on the fact pattern here as it relates to the legislatively directed grants generally and as to these two specific grants. So I'm going to walk very quickly through what the process looks like after the appropriations bill is passed. We cannot speak to what happens in the rooms with you all in the legislature on passing the budget bills. We get this information, and so you see, starting at appropriations bill signed, there's a packet of information distributed from the state budget office to the legislative offices. Those legislative offices complete letters and work with the grantees to submit materials to us. That information is then taken and is the basis really of the grant agreement. We do, for ease of administration, have a grant template that's been developed based on the budget boilerplate, but the application packet from the legislative offices plus the boilerplate are the information that we use to compile these grants. We get those signed by the parties, and we are into then administration of the grant. I'll speak through those a little bit here, but according to the boilerplate, these grants are dispersed 50% up front. I do want to just note one particular step in this process is that the legislative offices have a role in securing the information. It is our expectation and understanding that the legislative offices sponsoring these grants have done some level of due diligence on the awardees in connection with sponsoring the funding. I'm going to flip now to the next two slides here. We're going to go one by one. This shows the specific budget boilerplate for both FY22 and FY23 grants to the Naya organization. As I just mentioned, this language plus the materials we receive from the legislative offices lay out the parameters for these grants. As I also mentioned already, for ease of administration, and particularly given the high volume of these legislatively directed grants in FY22 and FY23, again, nearly 350, the MEDC developed a grant template. We did that in consultation with state department partners, up to and including the Attorney General's Office. The grant templates include a description of the grant activities and a project budget, also lays out the reporting obligations, and includes some other standard contractual provisions that are included in most state grant contracts. Consistent with the plain language of the budget boilerplate, 50% of the funding is dispersed upon execution of the agreement. This is in the law. This is directed by the legislature in these legislatively directed grants. I want to be abundantly clear on that point. Additional disbursements are made after the grantee demonstrates that the previously disbursed funds have been used in accordance with the grant agreement. Our team confirms that these expenditures have been properly incurred through a variety of supporting documentation, which may include general ledger reports, personnel payroll records, copies of receipts and invoices. As I mentioned previously, these are all unique grants, each one with very specific uses. So the types of materials we're going to get on each of those is going to be very specific to those grants. Expenses in that process may be deemed ineligible, unreasonable, or we may determine that the documentation is insufficient to support expenditure. We receive a lot of supporting documentation. Some of it includes information that is not pertinent to that grant but has a specific expenditure line item that is eligible on that grant. So you may see in reporting and others a litany of information. Not all of that is counted. We track in our own internal processes what is eligible, what is not. In addition to these two, the verification of the expenditures, grantees are required to submit quarterly reports.

that provide a narrative of the grant activities completed and include an expense reporting. They are reviewed and if anything on that report seems off or problematic, then we ask questions and seek additional information or documentation as needed. I'm going to quickly just point to these two boilerplates you're going to see, and I believe this is part of the packet, Brie, but you have the grant agreements, I believe you have the applications for each of these grants that we received from the legislative offices, and I believe the boilerplate here, and if not, we would be happy to provide you with the legislative boilerplates so you know exactly what we're looking at and what we're working with. And with that, we'll answer any questions. Thank you for your testimony. And I guess my first question I have before I'll open it up to others is those quarterly reports, was Naya current on all of their quarterly reports? Yes, Naya submitted all of their quarterly reports. Okay, but in the record, Chair, there are the two last quarters. We didn't give you all quarters because there was a whole lot of paperwork trying to save some trees, but we can provide those at any time. Could you say that again, please? Those only include the last two quarters. If you want all of them, we can provide that information. Yeah, thank you. All right, my next question for you is I understand these decisions are made by the legislature. You guys simply administer them in this situation. It wasn't your decision. It was decisions made by people, my colleagues. And in that process, at what point did the MEDC become aware that the IRS filings were not current for Naya? During the term of our agreements, we believe they were current with their IRS. The two agreements administered by the MSF were FY21, FY22. During that term, we believe and understand to be compliant with their IRS requirements. And then were they administered by LEO or DHHS for the more recent years? I believe the most recent years were LEO and DHHS. Could you know which one was what? No, you'd have to consult those departments. Okay, thank you. And let's see. Has the MEDC ever recommended pausing or suspending disbursement of funds if you've recognized that a nonprofit is not current on their filings? I think the challenge on these, and you all rightfully noticed when you enacted some new legislation, is 50% goes out the door. That's a problem, right? And that's not how we structure grants through the MSF or MEDC typically. So we are going to have to reconcile payments. And then to the extent we find any issues in that first batch of funding, yes, we would have the ability to spend future disbursements. And potentially claw back if we found something that triggered a claw back under the agreement. And those grant agreements too, you'll see there's an event of default section in there that lists out the triggers for what might suspend obligations to disperse or even trigger a claw back. Okay. And I guess my... Oh, are you ready? You had a question. I'll turn it over to Representative Beerline for a question, it looks like. Thank you, Mr. Chair. So during this process when you're going through funds, do you do on-site inspections or do you verify that they're spending funds the appropriate way? Is there any follow-up outside of the reporting that they provide to you, that they're spending funds in the way that the grant says that they should be? So does MEDC do any of that follow-up? Yeah. We're not, I would say on most of these, these are, as I said earlier, 350 in these two fiscal years alone. We did not get admin support to be able to ramp up any staffing support on these. We had to absorb this. So we aren't doing site visits on these to answer that question. We are verifying their expenditures. So there's really, like I would say, two components of compliance to this. One, you get your disbursement. We are confirming that you have expended that as outlined in the grant agreement. And that occurs at the disbursement request, which may or may not coincide with a quarterly report. So we're going to confirm your expenditures. You are also submitting quarterly reports. And it's a very interactive process where we are asking questions. And if we're not getting documentation or there's insufficient documentation, we would ask for additional work. And if there is an issue, then we do not disburse additional funding. That much is clear in the boilerplate. If you have not disbursed 50% on eligible expenses, then we're not able to disburse that second half. So I guess just like looking through the boilerplate that you provided, and it's dedicated to empowering communities, individuals, families, groups, and businesses to achieve their maximum goals through direct service. How do you verify that that – how do you quantify that you're empowering the community? It's a great question. I think what you're seeing on these grants to provide services, I think, in particular services that are not in our wheelhouse. These are community services that are not economic development activities. But that those grants tend to support operational costs of these grantees because you need human beings to provide the services on the other end. So salaries, office space, IT, those types of things are then what we would be verifying on an operational service. And if you're looking, those agreements will have a budget that identify how much should be spent on personnel costs, on leasing, rent, and to the extent there are any very specific activities they need to fund against that. And then we're getting narrative reports as well explaining all the activities they've done. I just want to add also, as you point out, there are no metrics associated with the requirements. So we would be artificially putting those in absent of the legislature. So we have to follow what's in the boilerplate. And maybe you can't answer this. Can anybody – what is the service they're providing? I mean, if it's operational costs, like it's people, what is the service that's being provided? Is it a homeless shelter? Is it food banks? Is it all of the above? I just – I don't know. And I don't think I see it as part of the language. And we're going to give money so they can do this because I don't know what it is that they're doing. Yeah, I mean, in there, right, the boilerplate is slim. It doesn't really specify what that is. And we're sort of hamstrung by some of that. And then we get what we get from the legislative office. I think what I would suggest, and if you don't have the last two, maybe we need to – we've got to probably follow up and give you the full detail. But they're going to explain what they did. Like mental health services to community members are some examples of what they're doing. They're providing some support to bilingual – folks who maybe English isn't their first language and they need somebody to help make some translations, things of that nature. So I think it's really just a wraparound service for anybody who might need it from them. But as I'm looking, they've reported on supporting – providing support on immigration issues, civil rights, job training for new arrivals, culture and religious barriers that face some of the – or that can cause some communication barriers, and really supporting a community that needs support. That's what we understand was the intent of this grant. Thank you. Yeah. Do we know the salaries of the director or the president or employees of Naya? Yeah, it would be included – the amount that they reported for salaries would be included in those reports. Let me see if I can find that at the top of my pile here. But yeah, they were – when we looked at them, you know, they were reasonable for what we thought a nonprofit organization would be paying. Let me see if I have that here. If not, we'll follow up with you on the specifics. Yeah, let's – can we report back to you on what that total amount was spent on? We should be able to say, and I think if you look at the budget, you can see the maximum amount they could have spent on all salaries and kind of benefit offerings. But we'll follow up with the actual itemized line item. Thank you. Next question from Minority Vice Chair Wiggela. Some of the description, by the way, is in the grant application. My colleagues are interested. But my question was – I think like one of the concerns is like nothing in the boilerplate requires a 990 to be submitted, if I'm not mistaken, which I think probably we should have our nonprofits be submitting their tax filings to the state to make sure that they're in compliance. So my question was kind of two things. What recommendations would you have for the legislature to put into the boilerplate to make sure that things are as above board as possible with these nonprofits? And then secondary, how has the boilerplate changed over time? It looks like the one you provided us was the 2022 budget. Have you seen changes throughout your time here in Lansing, and what have those changes been? Yeah, I mean I can take maybe the first pass, and you can talk about the changes. So your first question, what are some recommendations? I think a lot of what you already adopted into the new guidelines around legislatively directed enhancement grants are great. I think you should require that they need to be in good standing with the state of Michigan. They should be in good standing with their tax filings, with the IRS. I think you have to recognize there's a cost to doing that business for the state of Michigan employees, so you've got to make sure there's resources for people to be able to effectively do that. But yeah, certain compliance requirements, you've got to be properly registered. You've got to be up to current with your tax

sponsors are saying. So I think yeah, what are those things that you know should be met and should be a condition to maintaining an award? So just quick follow-up to that. Is there anything besides what we've passed into law over the last year here that you would recommend us taking it even a step further? We have lots of recommendations. We'd love to continue the conversation. These grants have evolved significantly over the time in which that they have come to be. I think the recognition by the legislature to remedy the issues that I think are being brought forth in this oversight committee. You guys laid out a beautiful piece of statute with PA 33 that was just enacted, excuse me, signed on November 18th. So we're going to take and run with these, but we have additional, we'd love to have side conversations and develop them. Yeah, defining what do you think is eligible for these things or even if you were going to do infrastructure grants, for example, that's a wholly separate piece of work than a service. And so it's a lot easier to identify hard costs, right? And so I think defining or putting some parameters around what an eligible expense, what do you think the taxpayer dollars should be used to support and maybe some reasonableness standards too, right? That authorize us to have some reasonableness. We're making some of those judgment calls on our own, but we're right on the line of whether we're able to, right, under the boilerplate. So to the extent that they should be filing their 990 forms with the federal government, that's something that is on the nonprofit to do regardless of what action we take as legislators.
