Everybody has their project they want to sponsor in their community to help provide services and to bring things together. Boy, we have done a really bad job at this from the legislative level to continue giving monies away. You know, I mean, I'm reading through the news article that kind of spawned a lot of this. And to be providing funds to an organization that is leasing office space back to legislators seems not above board at all. And I think as the chairman just said, that wasn't on you. That's on us. We need to do a much better job in this. I'm glad that it seems we're heading in that direction. You mentioned recommendations for how this could get better. Would you be willing to put together a report that would kind of outline some of those recommendations and present them to us? We'd be happy to do that. I don't want to volunteer work for the other departments, but to your point, Rep, we are not experts in human services. So having others within those unique skill sets advising on those, I think is really key imperatives too. The way that these were administered previously, they were thrown into whatever department I think worked, quote unquote. But having that be a component of the decision making could be really important as well. Thank you. You mentioned earlier your support for the recent public act that has transparency around these legislative directed spending items. Prior to that decision we made this term, would you say that the evolution of legislatively directed spending items was getting worse or better from your experience? You know, I can only speak to my time within two different departments. I think that each year certain components got clearer, better with everybody working towards it. I think evolution of things, the nature of oversight in general is to identify places that can be made better and provide remedies. And it just so happens that you all provided a remedy even ahead of us coming into this committee. Yeah, I will say too, you know, over the last probably 2018 I think is when we really started to see an uptick in these types of grants. And through that process, we definitely provided feedback to either the state budget office or legislators. And I will say there were improvements in terms of documentation. Obviously a lot more work needed to be done and we're glad to see that you all took that action. But even just having a form from the legislative offices that could help us understand like who do you actually mean for one, right? And what are services? Like that was an evolution that we provided feedback and we're happy to see was scaled across the state government. Now there was a huge gap still that I think you are filling with this new legislation to get even better and tighten up some of those requirements. So it's gotten better but also worse. I don't want to say. So maybe we're on the upswing now with some actual statutory requirements around this. Yeah. Okay. Thank you. The Detroit News put out an article a month or two ago regarding the legislative directed spending items that and who the sponsors were for Naya in the past five years. And the state budget office apparently had that information. Are you guys aware of how we came to know without having as much transparency as we have now? How did we know who the sponsors were for Naya in the past few years? Absent, you know, the budget process, I don't know that there was a publicly facing document or documentation for that. I just don't know how it became clear to the state budget office of who those individuals were because we have our deliberations, we work with people in leadership, decisions are made, these earmarks are put into the budget, and that's just kind of all done behind closed doors. So how the state budget office becomes aware is still a little bit fuzzy to me. These two, I can tell you, Chair, these two grants as in your packet did have legislative sponsors attached to them. So previous to that, I can't speak to what that process was, but starting for the FY 22 and 23, they did have to have identified legislative sponsors. They did have to? Yes. With the state budget office? Yes, those are the forms that are in the packet. Okay, and then so we would get that information from the state budget office if people wanted to find that online or something, would they maybe not be able to unless they FOIAed that information, or what's that process? Can't really speak to it. You'd have to direct that towards the SBO. We can only speak to our portion of it. Fortunately now, though, with the new public act, as you mentioned earlier, there's more transparency around these things and a step in the right direction. Is that fair to say? Yeah, 100% yes. Okay, good. Thank you. Looks like we have another question from Minority Vice Chair Wigella. So I'm just looking at the legislative grant boilerplate, and it says necessary identifying information and tax identification information. I'd imagine the federal government doesn't publish what identification numbers are out of compliance. So

I guess the only way to, I mean, maybe I don't understand that part of tax law federally, but I would imagine like for privacy reasons they're not just saying what, they don't have like a standing list of nonprofits that are out of compliance and a list that are. So are you suggesting like, because when I read that I think of like, okay, well, I would have thought that the MEDC would be checking in to make sure before giving money that these were in compliance, but are you suggesting that that actually is on the legislature individuals to essentially request a 990, receive it, verify it? It's just, I think it's interesting. I think we should definitely write that in there, but I guess I wouldn't have necessarily realized that prior to some of this being revealed. I don't know if my colleagues would have realized that. Yeah, I mean, the reason we get, as you're taking the identifying information in the tax ID, so we know who you mean, right? Who is the grant actually supposed to go to? And so it's not to make us do any other due diligence. Again, you guys have already decided by the time it gets to us that this entity is getting the money. And so absent some other directive or authority to deny that, we have nothing to go in. So we would be building in, and again, you remember there's 350 grants between these two fiscal years, all different types of organizations. You had municipalities, you had nonprofits, you had for-profits, I think, in some of these, like all manner of awardee that puts a pretty huge, again, I would have, my expectation is if you're going to sponsor an award, you probably want to know who you're sponsoring and are they a good, you know. No, I agree. I guess, I mean, I don't know for the folks who requested these particular grants if they, you know, I mean, like you can have a nonprofit in a community that's doing a lot of work, but I don't know if people are asking generally, and maybe my colleagues have asked people, but like to submit to their tax filings to them. So I just kind of figured that would be part of the verification process as a legislature. So I think it certainly should happen, and we definitely need to, as a legislature, make sure if tax money is going to nonprofits that we are holding these nonprofits accountable and that they are in compliance. It's just kind of an amazing situation. Yeah, and we do, I mean, we'll check against like the state databases to confirm like who is the legal entity, are they in good standing with the state of Michigan, and you know, that's kind of the level of these. If we're talking some of our other programmings, we would dive a lot deeper, but these are handed to us, and so we have limited discretion there. But excellent news, Rep. There is a specific line in the new legislation that says you've got to do that. So well done. What are your thoughts on state legislators having office space inside of a building that is getting taxpayer-funded grants? Is that something that's appropriate from your perspective? I don't think that's something we can or should offer an opinion on. I think that's probably a legislative ethics question. Okay, so that'd be up to us to decide whether or not that's prudent and legitimate. Okay. All right. Well, I don't – oh, I do see a question from Representative Bhataski. Thank you. Just a clarifying question. When you said that you verify at the state level to make sure that the nonprofit is in good standing there, are you looking for similar information as to what was not dealt with properly at the federal level with this particular nonprofit? Or like what's the different type of information at the state level versus federal? Yeah, yeah, that filing – or that's a search of the LARA, right, Licensing and Regulatory Affairs database. So we can look in there and determine that they're in good – in standing with the state of Michigan, that they're properly registered, that they're authorized to transact business in Michigan, and that the state has considers them still in good standing. Now, I think if their nonprofit status had fallen away, they wouldn't be able to make that filing with the state of Michigan, right? Like I think there's sort of a trail you would get there because they have to make annual reports to the state to keep themselves in good standing. And if that changes, I assume there would be a change in there. Now, I'm not an expert by any stretch on the LARA filing requirements, but that that sort of shift would probably necessitate some filing updates. Thank you. Another question from Minority Vice Chair Bagala. I was reading in the Detroit News article that the organization had essentially talked about bringing in an independent audit. Have you seen the results of that, or has there been any update on that? We don't have a live grant with this organization right now, so they have no reason to provide us any updates on that. I don't know, again, if LEO or DHHS has an active contract with them, but ours have been expired for almost three years. Okay. All right. Well, thank you for coming in as always and testifying. I'm seeing no further questions. Representative Bierlein moves to excuse absent members. And there being no objection, the motion prevails by unanimous consent. And there being no further business before the committee, the committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Appropriations - Human Services — Tuesday, December 9, 2025
transcript:
House Oversight Subcommittee on Child Welfare will come to order. Would the clerk please take attendance? Chair Meerman. Here. Representative Regas. Here. Pappet. Here. Conlon. Here. McDonald. Here. Mr. Chair, you have five members present. You do have a quorum. Representative Regas moves to approve the minutes of the November 4 meeting without objections. So ordered. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The House Oversight Subcommittee... House... Wrong one. The House Appropriation Committee on Human Services will come to order. Clerk, will you please take the roll? Chair Roth. Here. Representative Kelly. Here. Mueller. Beeson. Here. DeSanto. Here. Edwards. Here. Longjohn. Here. Mr. Chair, you have a quorum. Thank you very much. And Representative Kelly is going to approve the minutes of September 9th's meeting. And being no objections, the minutes are approved. It's with great pleasure that the Oversight Subcommittee on Child Welfare is today joined by the Appropriations Subcommittee on Human Services. This morning, we'll hear from testimony about Michigan's children's caring institution, the population of youth they serve, and the staff responsible for their care. On May 13th of this year, the Child Welfare Oversight Subcommittee received testimony on this subject where we learned that Michigan's bed capacity for residential treatment programs is decreasing with no sign of reprieve. This drop in capacity is not because the children don't require care, but because of an overall reduction in programs. I would like to invite Kevin Roach from MCHS, Family of Services in Redford to testify. Kevin is Chief Executive Officer of MCHS. Please begin when you're ready. There's a red button there in the middle. Good morning, Chair Meerman and Chair Roth. Thank you once again for the invitation to sit here and testify and certainly answer any questions for the group here. My name is Kevin Roach. I'm the President and CEO of MCHS Family of Services. We've been around since 1917 and for over 100 years have provided residential treatment under that child caring institution licensing rule on the sin. We've evolved since then to include a number of other services related to child welfare, housing, education, and behavioral health services, but still the residential treatment care that we continue to provide to this day remains of utmost priority for us in the work that we do. In my role as the President and CEO of MCHS Family of Services, we certainly look to continue to partner with the State of Michigan and with the Department of Health and Human Services to truly meet the needs of those young people and those families in care. I also am honored to sit on the board for the Michigan Federation for Children and Families, which is a six-member plus association serving children and families throughout the State of Michigan, as well as serving on the Executive Board for the Association for Child Residential Community Services. I'm blanking on the name and I should remember it if I'm on the board. And I've been serving in that capacity for some time. In this current role, I've been here for 10 years, but certainly have been involved in the broader systems of care for about 20 years here in the State of Michigan. And I'm excited to certainly be here to share my thoughts and observations about truly what is going on. I'll open up with at least the notion that certainly we are facing some challenging times, to say the least. And certainly that testimony that was provided by a number of my colleagues on May 13th, those have continued to persist on this end. The one thing that I will mention is that certainly we're seeing a diminished capacity

a bed available for those who need it the most. And I'm hopeful that this committee continues to ask questions and identify solutions that certainly can help us move towards a place where every young person in the state of Michigan truly gets their individual needs met, regardless of what that looks like. We know that crucial to these conversations is having a fully funded continuum of care, where residential treatment is certainly one of those many options that are provided on this end. But we know that for those young people who do need a residential treatment services, there are a number of providers here in the state of Michigan who are ready to step up, who continue to provide those services, but certainly are looking for more solutions to better support the workforce that's in play to meet the high acuity of those young people who are in care, and certainly to engage those families that are dependent on all of us here today to make the right decisions for their children in care. With that being said, I'll certainly entertain any additional questions that this group might have, but certainly wanted to at least lead off with at least some of those initial comments. Thank you, Chair Meerman. I do have a question, Kevin. Thank you for being here today. We really appreciate it. This is probably the most important thing I think we do as a state with our children and making sure we have good care here and we cover all the spectrums that we need to. How is employee retention? Have you lost employees to different injuries? I mean, how is the employee situation at your facilities? Yeah, I think that's a great question, Chair Roth, in terms of when we take a look at the workforce and how do we develop and engage that workforce. Certainly they are encountering a different population than we have normally or typically have seen. I heard this from a policy fellow in Washington, D.C., where he said something along the lines of we are dealing with children with 21st century problems and applying 20th century solutions to. And I think about that with our workforce in particular and that they are looking for tools. We are asking for generally people who are committed, who are passionate, who are dedicated to doing this work. In the words of one of my staff members, essentially being thrown into the lion's den, knowing that the youth that they're encountering today is a lot different than the youth that they were encountering just a few years ago. And so as a result, we as an agency and certainly knowing many of my colleagues as well have really looked at different ways from a professional development standpoint, mitigating those risks and certainly doing better coaching, training and implementing a better operating system for our workforce. But we still know that those issues are exasperated, right, when that acuity of care is to a point that we can't safely manage the behaviors or meet those behavior health needs of those young people. And so we have certainly seen an increase in the turnover rate, which once again flies in the face of trauma-informed care where these young people who are in the system need continuity, need stability, need more structure in place. And so we constantly feel that tension at our agency. But certainly in the last couple of years, we have seen that turnover rate almost double for us. And for an agency that historically has been a leader in having lower turnover rates, it's definitely a bigger shock to our system. Along that line, Kevin, do you see it more as mental health issues? Is there more violent mental health issues? What in particular? Can you give me any kind of what you're seeing that could be the most important part why we're having issues with staff being injured? Absolutely, Chairman Roth. What I had sent to at least members of the department and certainly many of you here have seen this document where we did talk about certainly a surge in safety incidences that are across the board. And whether that is assault on staff, peer-to-peer assault, or certainly property damage, one of the things that we certainly track amongst all these statistics is certainly, for instance, that peer-on-peer assault, right, and seeing those numbers almost triple in just a short amount of time, right? And for our young people, I mean, for our young people in care, right, they know they deserve to feel safe in a setting and an environment that is conducive to their treatment and upbringing. When they are afraid of being assaulted by one of their peers, we certainly know that that exasperates the very trauma that we're here to take care of and address on this end. With that being said, we also know that that workforce that's in place with the amount of de-escalation training that we do provide, with the amount of trauma-informed family engagement, active listening, you name it in terms of the whole swath of training and inventions that we do provide at our agency, we know that we can only do so much on this end and that what is taught in a classroom or what is taught in the field in terms of the training simulations that we do provide certainly only begins to touch on the increased security that we're seeing, and that does go into not only that physical aggression and verbal aggression, but certainly the property damage as well as what we would say other criminogenic-type behaviors on this end that we know lead to certainly a more poor outcome for these young people. And just expand a little bit on the actual facility damage. What kind of things are you seeing? When we look at that facility damage, right, we know that we have made it explicit that through the rules that have been defined by the department, which includes the elimination of restraints and seclusions, that when a young person is engaging in some level of property destruction, restraints is always a last resort, but certainly it seems like it should not be used as an intervention when we are looking at property damage of that kind. And so this is something that we have started looking into even more and can say that just in the past year, even though we are serving half of the capacity of youth that we were previously serving, as we're under 20 at this point, and that's been our choice, we know that property damage has actually doubled. And this year, as we wind down the last few weeks of this year, MCHS will have paid approximately a half a million dollars to cover those costs, and that ranges from broken windows. As I tell our window company guy in Bradford, I'm putting his kids through college on that end because of the amount of destruction that we've seen, but certainly damage to vehicles, whether that's our agency vehicles or staff vehicles, as well as the wear and tear that these buildings are going through, whether it's outdoors or our walls. But it's that constant level of destruction that we continue to see. That's once again in light of the fact that we will not physically restrain a young person, no matter the amount of damage that they're doing. We will engage in a lot of other interventions, but we know that at some point, once we have called the police, which we will do if that destruction gets so severe that there seems to be no way to stop it, we know that in those instances, there's very little that an agency like ours could do. Thank you. I'll open it up for questions on my side. Representative Kelly. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you for coming here today. I think you kind of answered the first part of my question. One of these things was what enforceable behavior boundaries have been diminished, and it sounds to me like it's the seclusion or restraint that has been the biggest – is that the biggest behavioral boundary that's been diminished? What I would say, Rep Kelly, to that end is that certainly I think myself as well as many of my colleagues in this field understand that the role that restraints and seclusions do provide in the treatment and addressing and meeting the needs of our young people and keeping them safe and generally meeting their treatment needs, that restraint and seclusion is not the first option. And I want that to be clear that for us as an organization, where maybe 20 years ago this would have been more of a regular intervention approach, that no longer is the case. I think the extensive efforts that we've taken to minimize those restraints and seclusions is certainly a testimony to the endurance and resilience of our employees. At the same time, we do know that there might be a time and place when that is needed because this is not a one-size-fits-all and that when mental health manifests and surfaces, we know that that can look and feel in so many different ways. And knowing that that could be an

available to our young people in an effort to keep that young person safe or others safe around them is certainly something that needs to have a lot more conversation around. Yes, to that point, I'd love to see some sort of economic study on the cost of removing seclusion and restraint. Obviously, it's costing you $500,000 a year in damage. I think there's other further things that could be gone, whether it's in K-12 classrooms or anywhere else. I think this policy that we started about eight years ago with the elimination of seclusion and restraint has been a great disaster and one that I think we're trying to act like this is all good and we've had nothing but bigger problems since that we've gone down this. And I think we're trying to be people's friends more than we need to do the necessary job of getting these people in line. With these people, when you're doing the kind of actions that are described in some of these, these people should be bounced immediately from these facilities. Not any coddling, not any trying at second, third, fourth chances, but bounced. So anyway, I think we've created a lot of our own problems with some of the policies that we've developed in the last few years. Representative Vice Chair Edwards. Thank you. Good morning. I kind of agree with some things Rep Kelly has said. But I'm wondering what are the guardrails for children who are doing the violent and breaking the windows? If we can't restrain them, what are you doing to protect them from harming themselves or harming the staffers? I think that's where residential treatment has a critical role in the reduction of trauma symptoms and the advancement of their life skills and understanding and navigating the tremendous challenges that go with being a teenager, becoming a young adult on this end. And I say that residential treatment facilities have a critical role because for far too long, we've been misunderstood. It's just a roof over the head, three meals a day, a warm bed and clothing on the back. When we say residential treatment, that treatment piece generally becomes secondary to the larger conversation of what a good operating residential treatment facility looks like. One that does tap into the mental health needs of these young people, understanding the trauma that they have endured that got them to this place, understanding the trauma that may have been exasperated by other systems of care, such as juvenile justice or the child welfare system, and that this can be a safe harbor for them to overcome not only those trauma, but really start to develop the life and social skills that they need to become independent, self-sustainable adults on this end, self-sufficient adults on that end. So we do everything from individual therapy to group therapy to family therapy, and that's all under the designation that residential treatments have called QRTPs, Qualified Residential Treatment Providers, where we are mandated to include evidence-based practices and approaches to engaging those families, to treating those young people, and certainly in keeping the health and safety and permanency of these young people all around. And so when a young adult is active in a crisis episode, where they may be engaged in property destruction or engaging in peer-on-peer assault, we know that there is a wide range of interventions that we will be utilizing at that point, short of restraint and seclusion, with the ultimate goal that if and when we did have to go through that process, we would have exasperated everything else up to that point. I'm sorry, that's really cute, but I'm wondering, you still didn't really answer my question. So if they're in the middle of the act, what do you do to help that child from harming themselves? You explained you give them therapy, you did all that, but in the middle of the act, you're not going to give them therapy in the middle of the act. So what do you do to protect the child from harming themselves? In terms of in the moment that they're having a crisis episode and would need to be physically restrained on this end, I'd say that that would be one of those options that we would have to certainly explore is physically restraining that young person. But I would contest in saying that we're not doing therapy in that moment. We're relying on our relationship skills. We're talking them down. We're utilizing any other intervention approach, whether it is de-escalation and deflection. I mean, we have such a wide array of those interventions that it's not just we're going to resort to physically restraining the child. We're going to tap into a wide range of other things to distract, to minimize, to engage in active listening, to utilize emotional first aid, to see what the power struggle is that might be taking place. You name it. We're utilizing a lot of those different interventions short of coming to that point where we would have to physically restrain on this end. Thank you. Thank you. I wonder if you want to make reference to a letter or document sent to the department signed by, I think, six of your residential facilities and just maybe broadly talk about what that represents for how many beds in the state and then maybe some of the main topics that these residential facilities were seeing as issues. And I mean, I would say this is a pretty drastic action to take to put this letter together and get it to the department. Feeling like I think these six facilities are really pressured and things aren't going well. I think that the letter that you're referencing, Chair Meerman, was certainly a policy brief that we had authored called The CCI System is Broken. Here's How We Can Fix It on this end. And outlined in that letter certainly was looking at some of those key challenges that we as a residential treatment industry, community sector was facing on this end. And certainly to the heart of that is all of us who provide residential treatment care have the sole laser North Star focus on improving the health, safety and permanency of those young people. And when we feel like the partnership that we have with the department, that we need to be able to advance that and improve that to the point that we know that any young person who would need a residential treatment facility certainly would have that opportunity on this end. When we look at some of those challenges that we faced, right, we also wanted to identify some of those solutions as well, Rep Meerman. And looking at we're looking at a number of child care institutions that either are reducing their capacity or closing the doors, but essentially eliminating another option that would be available to a young person anywhere in the state of Michigan. We certainly wanted to be proactive in saying we recognize that this is a growing issue. We know that staff are getting more and more injured. We know that there are other escalating costs to doing this type of work that once again, we are not a facility nor most of my counterparts where we're just a roof over the head and a warm bed and three meals a day. But we're really involved in that clinical intervention, that crisis de-escalation, those long term outcomes, the development of those life skills, everything that is certainly required to have stable, independent, self-sufficient young adult. All of us know if any of us are parents in this room, we know that parenting is tough as it is. As the father of three, I could certainly attest to that. When we now are looking at a child in the system who's had that level of disruption, we know that their trauma symptoms certainly require a heck of a lot more intervention and approach. And so we talked about certainly how the current system of care that we have in the child care and institution certainly is making that more challenging or more difficult on this end. One of those pieces we did talk about, Chair Meerman, was certainly on the contracting side and how we can develop a contract that is more mutually collaborative and really looking at what are those outcomes that we want to have under the lens of the best trauma-informed care possible on this end. And then we also talked about the various solutions that we thought were certainly imperative to improving this level of system of care, of getting more beds online, of ensuring that a young person in Michigan that needs a place can stay in Michigan, that they're not going elsewhere out of the state or relying on other states to provide care for a Michigan child on this end. And so some of that was really taking a look at how do we modernize the regulatory process and include due process, how do we ensure that there is that clinical autonomy and a full understanding of the trauma and the symptoms and the stories of these young people, how do we ensure that there is a more fair and transparent contracting process, and most importantly, I think, on our end is investing in a full continuum of care where once again we

We see residential treatment as one of many options. But when it is treated on a linear continuum of care and seen as a placement of last resort, we oftentimes will see a young person who has gone through 10, 15, 20, 30 different types of placements. And in some cases, that trauma is so far gone that they're going to need something much more intensive to keep themselves safe as well as certainly those around them safe on this end. Thank you. I would just point out, I think everyone has in front of them the report itself. It's there and just at least breeze through the black bullet points numbered and then read the conclusion at the back. Representative Collin has a question. Thank you, Chair Merriman. Thank you, Mr. Roach, for being here. And thank you for the work you do because this is so challenging. And sitting on the subcommittee, we've heard a lot of the challenges you face and issues that we have. I'm wondering, because I know you originally, or not originally, but back in 2020, you know, were very much against or wanted a ban on restraints after the death of, I think, Cornelius Frederick. But it does sound now like you don't want it to be the first option, certainly. But it sounds like maybe you do want us to look again at this ban on restraint and seclusion and maybe think again about how this could be administered. I know we had somebody who mentioned a 10-year-old on top of a roof and they couldn't restrain that child. And obviously that is not a safe situation. So it does feel like maybe we need exceptions. But I just wanted your thoughts on that, how we might improve that part of the system. Yeah, thank you, Rep Conlon. I think that when we think about having a more thoughtful and meaningful conversation about the appropriate use of restraints and seclusions, that would certainly involve the various stakeholders whose lives are impacted when a child is restrained. That not only includes the department and that specific private provider, but certainly other individuals in that young person's orbit, whether it is their parent or whether it is a guardian or a relative in this case. When we think about that use of restraints and seclusions, we certainly once again know that this cannot be the first option, nor could it be the second or the third option. But that completely eliminating it deserves to have a more thoughtful conversation about what are some of those unintended consequences that could result from a total ban on this end. Five years ago when I offered an op-ed saying that, calling for more attention to the restraints, it's amazing how much our child welfare system has even evolved in those last five years from when that op-ed appeared in I think May of 2020 to certainly where we are at many years later on this end. At that time, right, when we take a look at the child care and institution landscape back then to where it is now, I think most of us could agree that probably restraints was not being used as a last resort and probably used a lot more frequently than it needed to be on this end. And when you take a look at what that restraint process looks like, everything from what happens before, all the antecedents, to certainly the consequences, the aftermath of what takes place, the debriefing, the safety plans that are put in place to prevent future incidences, how that treatment plan is adjusted and adapted to once again de-escalate and prevent anybody, much less that young person, from getting into that situation. I don't know if those conversations were being had at such an in-depth level or that tension was there. It almost seemed like it was just kind of an accepted part of that system of care. Now we know, right, and now we better understand, and this isn't just in Michigan but certainly throughout the country, that we know that when we are looking at the use of a restraint and seclusion, it really has to be done under the high scrutiny, right, where it's not the individual possibly making that decision, where there is a much more expansive debrief, where there is a clinician potentially involved, where there is medical staff available and ready if, once again, there is injury sustained from that. When we think about all the ways to then safely create conditions and respond to a young person in care, we know that the conversations, more conversations are needed in those areas before any of us try to make a decision as to whether there's a total ban or not. Thank you, Representative Longjohn. And thank you for being here as well, Mr. Roach. I appreciate that my colleague brought up your editorial from 2020. I represent the 40th House District where Lakeside Academy resides, where Cornelius Frederick died, and I appreciate your thoughts on this over time. Science changes. We get new information. And I hear you saying that the data that you have now been looking at is kind of leading you to question where we're headed next. To my colleague's point to my left, Rep. Edwards, it sounds like you might have more thoughts about what criteria are used in terms of restraint, or maybe you could just kind of add some thoughts about that. What would be the criteria that staff would use in a moment of conflict? What criteria would we evaluate over time to know that whatever shifts are made in policy are in fact contributing back to evidence?
