One of the worst egregious that I heard from a facility was in the treatment plan for a specific child was restraining food, locking the fridge, because they were eating themselves to death. And the department said, that's restraint. You can't do it. I couldn't be more frustrated, Representative Rigas. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you, Dan, for being here again. So I have like a two-part question. So you've previously spent discussed the efforts or the effects of the inability to restrain or stop the destructive, dangerous behavior on employees. And like Chair Merriman just mentioned as well, the impact on the children as well, the other patients in the facilities. Can you touch briefly, I know we're short on time, can you touch briefly on the effects of the progress that some of the other patients have decreased their progress in their treatment? And also the second part of that was, so the department put a no reject, no eject policy in place without collaborating with agencies. How has that affected the amount of beds in the state? Thank you, Representative Rigas. I really appreciate the question on the contagion effect, if you will, on when you have a higher concentration of youth that are stabilizing, are unstable, and what that does. We have seen, and I don't have the numbers on the...

on the top of my head right now, but we have seen that there is a contagion. When you have more than one or two individuals within a milieu, within a home that is unstable and stabilizing, we see the behaviors of other clients in that program who may have gone through their own trauma and are stabilized themselves revert back. That is common and so forth. So that's our conversations with the state and there is no policy on this. And it touches on the policy that it was impacted in October 2024 about admissions policy that we put the limit on no more than one or two individuals in a milieu that are stabilizing. Even if we might have an open bed, we have to honor the commitment there. So every one of our home has acuity score based on behaviors, based on a whole bunch of factors. Every home is evaluated based on, is it a healthy place for children and adolescents to engage with their trauma and move forward? So yes, it's a big issue and I'll be glad to get you some numbers later on. And back to Rep. Meerman's point about the staff. When any part, staff or client feel unsafe, nobody is safe and you're not able to move forward. It has to be paramount. Can you imagine a green on an industry where you know that two times a week somebody's going to get injured? Who would accept that? That's no way to build a solid business, especially when individuals, youth, and these aren't bad youth, they've had bad things, awful things happen to them, okay? Put them in that environment. We have to and we can do better in that regard. The touch on the admissions policy in October, and I would just say that's where we can come together with this provider advisory council. That's the intent, is that we can get the providers and the funders and policymakers together to see exactly how this works out and what is working out in real time. Because I believe people are reasonable and I believe we have the best interests of the youth in mind. But what happens sometimes is smart people who really want to do the right thing have two different ways to come up with the same solution. That's fine, but we need to work those differences out through this positive friction and come together with something we can agree on and say let's move forward this direction. I think that's what we need more of. And I've talked with Demetrius even this morning, Demetrius, Director of CSA, and his heart is there. And I think we need to come together, providers and agencies, to work this out together. And I think we can. But I would just ask, I think we need legislature with that third hand on that bowl of Jell-O, providers and agency and legislators to really make this happen and move together with some accountability. Thank you, Dan. One more question, and then we're going to move on to one of the former workers. Representative McDonald, if this fits for him, I know you've been waiting a long time. Actually, it's all so complicated that it's hard to pinpoint a question. But I do agree with you. Reform is needed. And I hope to work with you on that very soon because it's obviously needed very soon. I've also been struggling, though, to come up with a few things like trying to root cause this. I think there's a difference between finger pointing and trying to figure out why these things are happening because, like Rep. Longjohn was talking about, you know, how do we prevent this from happening in the first place instead of always having to fix it after it's a disaster. But it sounds like things are kind of cycling, not just that there's a simple root cause and, like, it's not just that kids today are more aggressive and therefore maybe foster parents don't want to take in kids because they're getting more aggressive. But, you know, what's your best attempt at root causing what's happening? Is it just the lack of facilities that are appropriate for the kids? Yeah, what is it, the cart or the horse or the cart or the egg? The chicken. I think it is a confluence of several different factors. And we started seeing the mental health of youth decline before COVID, okay? Smartphones, forward-facing cameras, compare and despair, and so forth and so on. Then COVID happened, and we disconnected, and then it broke. At the same time, you had the collapse. You had 200% turnover on frontline staff during the height of COVID. Tenure dropped. These are trained, highly professional individuals, and the great retirement happened and so forth. So I think that also added to that, the drop in beds and availability and the higher concentration as well as some policies. I think you have a complex problem, and we're not going to get out of this any type soon. I think we need to both work on policy and rulemaking and interpretation of those rules together. We also need to look at how do we rebuild capacity. I believe it needs to be up 650 beds in residential, and that will relieve some as we go forward. So how do we build capacity out? We had a 30-day program when I started at Wedgwood. Now it's six months. I really think it needs to be a two-year program for entry level to really hone those skills that's needed to meet these kids where they're at with what they need when they need it. So I would say it's complex. You're right. We need to find a way to force us to come together, work together, and take a long-term approach on this, not just a knee-jerk response. There's no silver bullet here. And I'm sorry. I know it's so close to the end of the meeting, but no one has mentioned funding at all. Has funding come down? Has that been a problem as well? We did not receive a funding increase over this last year, even though wages and so forth are going up 2.8% or more. I think we need to look at funding relative to where these needs are and maybe, and yes, we need to figure out what that is. I believe we need to pay our frontline staff above market, our YTSs, and we need to invest in their training long-term. I think it's a really, really good investment. We do that at the crux. I think we'll meet kids, stabilize, and help them move through the system, not age out of the system. But funding is always a need and always a question. I would like to take it. Where should the investment be? Thank you. Thank you both. Appreciate it. Appreciate it, Rep. McDonald. Good questions. Now we're going to hear from Duncan Benson, a former CPS worker and former staffer in one of the Michigan child care institutions. Duncan, you can begin when you're ready. I just want to alert my fellow members, at least in my committee, if you have a noon, you're very welcome to leave. We understand. And, Duncan, I'm just going to apologize to you for having you at the end and not having a lot of time for you. I really appreciate your time and your effort to come here. It means a lot to us. Chair Representative Luke Meerman and members of Child Welfare Subcommittee, thank you for the opportunity to speak today. My name is Danika Benson. I am here to share my experience as a former Michigan Department of Health and Human Services employee as well as a director of a residential facility. And I'd like to speak about how the practices within DHS have resulted in a lifetime sanction that I was never informed of and has profoundly affected my career, my stability, and my life. I began my work with the state of Michigan in April of 2011 as a foster care worker. I worked for two years and I relocated out of the state and returned in 2015. I served families with pride, purpose, and a deep sense of calling. As someone who experienced abuse and neglect as a child, I knew firsthand what it felt like to fall through the cracks. My personal mission was to ensure no child that I served would ever be able to say, as I once did, that the system failed them. My dedication was not just professional, it was personal. And it helped, it shaped every decision I made. As a foster care specialist, I thrived. I had a strong record, strong outcomes, and no disciplinary history. I never received a write-up in more than a decade of service, never called off working consistently with above what was required because I believed the work mattered. After two more years, I was promoted, not into foster care supervision where I had excelled, but into CPS supervision, where it became clear that some expected me to fail. Instead, I excelled again. I sought out all the training that was never provided but nonetheless expected. I committed myself to the safety of the children and the integrity of the process. But along with the promotion came a shift, sudden, sharp, and damaging. I faced consistent bullying for asking questions or challenging practices that I believed compromised children and families. I was

placed under a supervisor who instead of developing and guiding her team, seemed intent on belittling, isolating, and undermining me. For the first time in my career, I was placed under multiple internal investigations, none of which alleged anything I had done directly. Instead, they focused on actions of staff members and were used to build a narrative that I was failing as a supervisor. The situation became so severe, I began experiencing intense stress responses to the point where receiving a call from the office triggered physical symptoms. My therapist diagnosed me with severe PTSD resulting directly from my work environment. She pulled me from work and provided DHS with documentation after each session. Despite this, I was told that I could not request a reassignment. The environment that had once given me purpose now left me feeling destroyed. Ultimately, I resigned. I left the career I had poured my heart into because it had become a threat to my health, my stability, my family, and my life. And even after leaving, I never fully recovered from what that period stole from me. Years later, after rebuilding my education and experience, earning another master's degree and working across several agencies, I was offered a position serving individuals connected with the Michigan Department of Corrections. My background cleared, but I was unexpectedly contacted and informed that the state of Michigan had issued a lifetime sanction against me. I was told that I was ineligible to work for the state or any of its contractors or affiliates. This was the first I had heard of such a sanction. I never received a letter. I never received a notice. I never had the opportunity to respond, appeal, or even understand what the basis was. Yet the sanction effectively blacklisted me from an entire sector of work, a sector I served for most of my life. Despite this, I continued to rebuild. I accepted a position as director of Wolverine Human Services, a private agency with previous challenges in its relationship with the state. I made it my mission and priority to repair that relationship. I rewrote programs, updated policies, strengthened oversight, and invited state leaders to observe the progress. I received praise, including from Mr. Starling, who noted significant improvements in the reduction of physical incidents and complimented my leadership. Local emergency personnel echoed the same. But accountability brings pushback. Staff who were being held accountable and being held to new standards were under investigation themselves, retaliated against me by filing false CPS complaints. In August of 2025, I became the subject of an allegation of verbal abuse allegations investigated by two individuals. I knew the reputation from my time with the state, Carrie Roop and Venus Decker. From the start, the investigation lacked transparency and integrity. I was never informed that I was the subject of the allegations until the end. My staff later reported that during their own interviews, they felt intimidated, doors were slammed, voices were raised, and pressure applied to change their answers to fit a predetermined narrative. When I was finally interviewed, I answered every question truthfully. I was then told that every staff member said the opposite of what I said. Based on my knowledge of the staff involved, including the one that was under investigation at the time, and another recently returned from suspension, I questioned whether that was accurate. When the final report was released, my concerns were confirmed. The report prepared by Ms. Roop contained false statements, omissions, and personal opinions unsupported by testimony. She added allegations no staff member ever made, including claiming I called a youth worthless and, excuse my language, a fuck-up. Statements that no witness reported and that I have never made. She omitted critical context, including the youth's history of over 200 incident reports for severe behavior challenges and ignored testimony regarding the conduct of staff involved. Fortunately, I had recorded my interview and those recordings proved the certain statements attributed to me or to staff never occurred. My attorney submitted formal requests for an amendment in these reports. Those requests were ignored. My request for review, I was ignored. And because the report was allowed to stand, my professional credibility and my ability to continue serving vulnerable populations was put in jeopardy once again. I have now taken steps to pursue legal action, not because I seek revenge, but because my career, my credibility, and my reputation have been permanently harmed by false allegations and an investigation process that lacked transparency, fairness, integrity, and accountability. This is the second time that DHS has taken something from me. First my career, then my ability to work in the field at all. I will not allow this to be swept under a rug because I know I am not the only one. When systems operate without oversight, without due process, and without accountability, good professionals are pushed out and vulnerable children are the ones who suffer. My story is not about bitterness. It is about accountability. It is about ensuring that no worker is ever sanctioned for life without notice, without explanation, and without a chance to respond. It is about ensuring that investigations are conducted fairly, transparently, and without intimidation. And most importantly, it is about ensuring that the child welfare system in Michigan protects not only children, but the integrity of the professionals who serve them. Thank you. Wow. Thank you for your testimony. That's very alarming to hear that you could be sanctioned for life from a state employee job without any kind of notice. I mean, that's not acceptable. But thank you for having the courage to come and testify today. Any of my members have any questions? No. Yeah, again, thank you for your time coming in here. At this point, do you know if you're on the CPS list? I am not on central registry, no. My colleague and I, Rep Legrand, worked hard at reforming CPS, so there was notification given to people that went on that list. And I remember specifically pushback from the department because they wanted to have the ability to put people on the list they decided they wanted to put on there without this notification stuff. Now, this is a little bit different story because you're not on that list currently. But I'm just bringing it up because to me it points out further that the idea that the department has decided they know everything and they're going to decide who can be around kids and who can't be even without any sort of due process. And this is the department that we're asking, we're relying on to be there for the kids when they want them. But it seems like in your case they've got a vendetta out there against you personally. I don't know if you want to share any more about, I guess, why you think they went down this road. I actually have no idea. I accepted the fact that I was not going to work in child services. I really felt like I could never go back there just from the history of working there, which is why I moved to the private sector. I'm not placed on central registry, but they have prevented me from working with children. And I would not fight this so hard if it was true. But I fought my entire life to advocate for children that are abused, not because it's just something that I want to do, but because I really did feel like I fell through the cracks growing up in the abuse and neglect system. This was noted. This was explained. And although I'm not placed on central registry, they treat me as if I am. If I apply for a job that has to do with central registry check, they have to give me permission to work. And they have not. So I, who went back to school for social work for the sole purpose of working with children, have been prevented from doing what I absolutely love, something that I was once praised for, I am now unable to do because I called out unfair practices. I was a CPS supervisor. I would not have ever permitted an investigation to take place like this. And it just so happened under Ms. Roop's investigation, they called in a separate investigation on me, but they were not the ones that did the investigation. There was another investigator. Same allegations, same company, same everything, but a totally different outcome. No findings at all. And I am aware that Wolverine has a volatile history with the state of Michigan. That's why I accepted the job. I wanted to change how everyone viewed Wolverine Human Services. I worked there

out of undergrad and I came back as an older adult knowing juvenile justice, knowing foster care, knowing CPS. I paid for personal training so that I could be everything that I needed to be for the children. And now it's as if it was all done in vain because of a personal vendetta against Wolverine. I was informed by Mr. Starling when I asked him personally and I told him I would like to know what can I do to repair the state of Michigan's relationship. And Mr. Starling told me that as long as our vice president at the time was working for Wolverine, that would be very difficult to do. So they could not go after the vice president. And although the state of Michigan shut down Wolverine's human services programs, I want to say three, their secure treatment center and two more camps. They shut them down and I knew that their history was volatile. I wanted to repair that. I wanted them to see that under leadership and under people that actually benefited having these children involved could help. I was ripped away from the children that I served every day. I served as their director and their therapist. And they deemed me unfit to work with children. And in her determination, she put that I had caused threatened harm. A determination that is supposed to be done by a licensed mental health professional. Again, more holes in her report and it was never amended. I wouldn't be here today if they had just amended their report. But they have shown and proven that they hold power that no one is willing to fight. And I cannot sit back and allow my career and my credibility to be at risk because of personal vendettas and personal relationships within the department. Thank you for that. And I will point the committee to testimony that we had in the full oversight hearing from the prosecutor from Marquette County. There was testimony there read by the prosecutor from frontline workers indicating some of the things that you've suffered as well. I don't believe this is isolated. I'm going to stop there and turn it over to Chair Roth. Just want the committee to know, I want the Michiganders to know my frustration is beyond a level I've known before. I'm just, you know, we're failing the kids. We're absolutely failing these kids. And if you're a parent and you're trying to get help for the kids, you can't get help. And if you're a foster parent, you're left dealing with these kids that don't belong in a foster home. They belong in a residential facility. And, you know, we've got a prosecutor up in Marquette being asked to charge these kids so they can get help in the juvenile justice system. I mean, to me, it's just an absolutely system that's collapsing in front of our eyes in the last year. And I better stop there because I'm getting pretty frustrated. But Chair Roth. Thank you, Chairman Meerman. We appreciate this. Thank you for coming forward for the testimony. We have to do better. We want to do better. I think we all want to work together here in our committees to do a better job for our children and workers. We can't forget the workers that are involved out there and make sure we're protecting them. But everybody in the system should be safe, and we need to do better. Thank you for your testimony. No absent members. Thank you, committee, for all being here. No, no, we were good. There being no further business before the committee, the Appropriations Subcommittee on Human Services will stand adjourned. No further business for Subcommittee on Oversight on Children's Welfare. We will stand adjourned.

title: Finance — Tuesday, December 9, 2025
transcript:
Good morning and welcome to the December 9, 2025 regularly scheduled meeting of the House Committee on Finance. Call the meeting to order. Clerk, please take the roll. Chair Tisdale? Here. Representative Frisbee? Here. VanderWaal? Present. Leitner? Here. Martin? Here. Poshimitsu? Alexander? Here. Aragona? Shooty? Here. Hoskins? Here. Carter? Neely? Breen? Young? Here. Mr. Chair, you have nine members present. You do have a quorum. All right, thank you. And they all gave prior notice of their inability to get here. Representative Hoskins moves to adopt the minutes from the November 4th meeting. There being no objections, that passes unanimously. We'll start with testimony. House Bill 4682. Representative Wolford, come on up. And your guests. Guests. If you would please introduce your guests, that would be great. Absolutely. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Chair and committee members. With me today, I have Ramon Baca, Director of Livingston County Veterans Services, and Kelly Johnson, Senior Veterans Service Officer, who are available to answer any questions. And I'll be testifying, and then they both will as well, and then answer questions. So, again, Mr. Chair and committee members, thank you so much. House Bill 4682 is a bill about honoring service and protecting surviving spouses and ensuring our disabled veterans and their families are not punished by red tape. Right now, Michigan's 100% disabled veterans and surviving spouses of those who died from a service-connected injury must file paperwork every single year to keep their hard-earned property tax exemption. Rules vary by township. Forms get missed during illness or grief, and families who still qualify can suddenly lose this benefit through the fault of not their own. This is especially heartbreaking for widows and widowers receiving federal dependency and addendum compensation, DIC, the federal government's clear acknowledgment that their spouse died because of military service. Yet even with that federal recognition, a missed form or an inconsistent local process can strip them of this tax exemption promised by Michigan. I've seen it time and time again. I've seen the weaponization in our own community by one of the townships, a person who is upset that there are people getting this property tax exemption and doing everything that she could to derail. So House Bill 4682 fixes this. It makes the exemption permanent for those who already qualified, particularly surviving spouses on the DIC program. This will be so that they never lose those benefits. They'll never lose it because of paperwork or bureaucracy, as talked about previously. It creates no new exemptions and costs local government absolutely nothing extra. It simply stops eligible families from being removed by accident or bureaucracy. Mr. Chair, when Michigan makes a promise to the men and women who serve this country and to the families who stood beside them through war and its aftermath, we must keep that. This bill delivers stability, dignity, and certainly to those who have already sacrificed everything, even when they're gone. Joining me today, as mentioned, are Ramon Baca, Director of Livingston County Veterans Services, and Kelly Johnson, Senior Veterans Service Officer, who are available to answer any questions. I respectfully urge the committee to support this bill. Thank you for your time and your consideration and look forward to answering any questions that you have. And before I turn it over to Ramon, I will just say a majority of these folks, these veterans and their families, much like the bill that is going to be passed, the bridge renaming bill for Lance Corporal Hanks, he's gone. He's buried. Hopefully he's in the presence of God. But behind that loss is a family that has been through and continues to go through chaos for as long as they're on this planet. And that story is repeated time and time again. One of those stories are just like this.

first sergeant who served our country, and I'm sure he'll talk about that, but we cannot forget about these family members and make sure that we support them. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Just to make sure I understand this completely, so we're talking about a spousal benefit for those entitled to dependency and indemnity compensation. A spouse whose husband or wife veteran passes away from an affliction incurred during active duty would be due indemnity compensation, and that's a part of this definition. Absolutely, and the simpleness of it is just making sure that they don't get lost in having to file paperwork every year or those trying to change unlawfully what they need to submit. This would fix that going forward. Okay. Ramon, go ahead. Yes, sir. Good morning, everyone. Thanks for having me. Let me move over a little bit. So under existing law, a surviving spouse may qualify for the Disabled Veteran Property Tax Exemption only if the veteran held a 100% permanent total disability rating or equivalent through the individually unemployability during their lifetime. This framework excludes surviving spouses whose veterans died as a direct result of a service-connected condition but who were not rated at the time of death at 100%. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs grants dependency and indemnity compensation to surviving spouses under the following conditions. The veteran's death resulted from a service-connected disability or the veteran was rated at 100%, including individually unemployable, for at least 10 years prior to the death or since release from active duty and for at least five years prior to death or at least one year prior to death if a former POW. To receive DIC, the veteran's death must be a result of a service-connected injury or disease. Currently, surviving spouses receiving DIC are excluded from Michigan's property tax exemption unless the veteran met the state's disability rating criteria while alive, as I previously discussed. This creates a discrepancy between federal recognition of service-connected death and state recognition for property tax relief. Local impacted data for at least Livingston County. Approximately 200 DIC awards have been processed through our office since 2019. We estimate an additional 100 surviving spouses may become eligible in the next five years as aging veterans pass away due to their service-connected disabilities. Due to the advanced age of most of our DIC recipients, the overall number is expected to remain relatively stable, as new recipients will generally replace those who pass away. So the point is, if we're currently at a steady state of approximately 200, we'll always remain around that number. In some cases, veterans pass away from service-connected disabilities that are clearly severe enough to be fatal, even though they were not rated at 100% during their lifetime. This group of surviving spouses whose loss has been officially recognized by the VA as service-connected should also receive property tax exemption for their homestead to obtain meaningful relief. Their household income drastically decreases upon the veteran's passing as the VA disability compensation ceases, regardless of the rating, and they continue to bear the ongoing obligation of property taxes. We respectfully request legislative consideration to extend property tax exemption eligibility to surviving spouses receiving the DIC due to the service-connected death. Aligning state with federal determinations and ensure greater consistency and fairness in benefits provided to surviving spouses. Thank you for your attention in this matter. Open to any questions, and of course, I do have Kelly here to speak. Hi. Kelly? There you go. Good morning. My only thought process on this is surviving spouses receiving DIC deserve property tax exemptions because they have endured the ultimate sacrifice by losing their loved one who succumbed to a condition that resulted from their service. The financial and emotional burden that follows is profound. When a veteran passes, there are instances when the veteran's disability rating at the time of death is not an adequate reflection of severity of service-connected conditions. A property tax exemption is a fair, compassionate, consistent way to honor the veteran's sacrifice and protect the spouses from who now face life without them. Basically, with this, if you don't know much about the DIC program, as Ramon kind of summed up for you, a veteran has to be service-connected at 100% to get the property tax exemption. Now, with that being the case, it might not be a connection that is severe that's going to take their life, but it's an exemption that they get, where if you have a veteran who passes of an illness that ultimately took their life but didn't get them the 100%, I don't see that being fair to them that they're not eligible for that particular exemption. So I would ask that you take that into consideration. Thank you. Representative? Also, Mr. Chair, I want to give this to Ramon to talk about, but getting to 100% is not an easy thing. And I don't mean this disrespectful to the Department of Veterans Affairs, but you have people who 100% are and should be 100% disabled and fight sometimes their entire life up until their death to get the benefits that they rate. And so with that, would you just speak to that? So as an example, I actually served in combat myself, Afghanistan, Iraq. I have a soldier who is a triple amputee from Afghanistan. For example, an amputation doesn't consider you 100% right off the bat. It's a limited percentage. A lot of the times when folks are rated at such high, at the high percentage of 100, it's because multiple things attributed to it and they were stacked. And VA math is a very difficult thing to understand. I've been in this job for around four years, and it's not one plus one equals two. As you start reaching the 60%, 70%, 80% thresholds, another contention of like a 10%. If you're at 80, plus a 10% is like 81% or 82%, and then they round down. So the point is that it's not all that easy to get to 100%. And so therefore, it's almost rare, for lack of a better term, that people are 100% and even far more rare that widows will get DIC, if that makes sense. Yeah, I mean, in the disability insurance world, there are all sorts of formulas as to what constitutes total disability or can you go out and get some kind of employment. So there's a need for that. On the other hand, there are people that have genuinely incurred significant life-altering injuries or diseases. And the price to be paid for that goes on. You indicated that there might be what kind of incremental extension or numbers, maybe 100? Yeah, currently in Livingston County, we estimate approximately, since 2019, approximately 200 have been granted the DIC. And so the way I estimate is that relative number will remain the same. Because my point is that a lot of these widows are older themselves. And so unfortunately, as they pass, a new claim may come in to replace that. So I feel like we would remain at that stable number going forward. Yeah, and that's for Livingston County. Yes, sir. Granted, that's for Livingston. That's one county. It's a tricky thing when you see a need, you want to reward service on a national basis, recognized by the state, but asking us to give away somebody else's money, the locals' money. So, I mean, we need to take all those things into consideration. But obviously there is a price being paid here, and an ongoing price. And I personally understand the desire for some recognition of that. Questions? Representative Frisbee. Vice Chair Frisbee, may I add? Thank you, Chair Tisdale. The DIC is the trigger that you're requesting that it remains and it stays flowing. What ends it? And are there penalties to be considered if somebody tries to take advantage of that? And I'll give you a for instance. If someone puts a family member who's not eligible, like a son or a daughter, into a title or a deed, and that doesn't get reported, what's the reporting mechanism besides a death certificate? And you have to remember, in some counties, the deed and the clerk's office are separate, some are together. So what triggers this event to make that go away? Okay, if I'm understanding the question correctly, I think to avoid other parties to become part of the deed and become exempted, is that, okay. So as it stands right now, the veteran, or if the veteran's 100% or if the

and passes, the widow is extended that as well, so long as they remain on the deed itself. And I think the question is how do we prevent someone like a son or a daughter becoming part of that deed and inherit that, and then continuing to get the exemption. I think that would just be an audit of sort that as the person passes away, say the widow passes away, that the assessors need to ensure who's now currently owning the home, and then they are excluded, because at that point it needs to run out, whether it's the veteran and then the spouse, and then it needs to end at that point. But in that assessor role, they only look at who's on the deed, the current deed. So I think we have to have some sense that there's an ability at the local level to say the spouse has passed on, now that exemption is gone. So we can prevent anybody trying to take advantage of that. Correct, they need that ability to ensure that doesn't get in. So I don't know how that would look at the township or county level, but I think we need to think about that a little bit. That's what we pay them to figure out, assessors and auditors. Well, assessors are only going to look at the current deed. Representative Leitner. Thank you, Mr. Chair. My question is along those lines also. Obviously it expires upon death, but also there's a trigger in there for if the surviving spouse remarries. And I was just curious, along the same lines as Rep. Frisbee, is there room for some sort of audit of those circumstances? Because right now is it just merit-based? Like my township, we just all got our township bills, right? Not too long ago. But anyways, like say my father-in-law or somebody was a surviving spouse and got remarried, and now they're not eligible, right? But what's the reporting for that? So with the federal VA side, you're eligible for DIC, and you can remarry after the age of 55. If you remarry prior to that, then that DIC ends. So then, but this makes it permanent that they don't have to reapply every year to the township, right? So if we eliminate that oversight, how do we know? You get what I'm saying? I'm not arguing about them being eligible for the benefits, just like in general. But what if these happen, there's no mechanism in there to oversee that. The way I understand the new state tax commission and the way they do is not earlier than three years may the townships make you reapply. But they can, every third year, audit. So I think in the same sense, I think they could audit and ensure that in this case the widow didn't remarry or what have you and they have to reapply every three years. Some townships have elected, as I understand throughout ours, I think we have 20 total in our county, some have elected just to forever be done with it, while others will exercise what the state tax commission has told them and do every three years or so. So this is a formula of what the township wants to do. But I think it's fair to say they get audited. There's a process in place. And I think the township should be able to audit and ensure that to the point of a son or daughter doesn't get put on the deed or the spouse doesn't get remarried and they must provide the ample documentation to prove such. Okay. And then real quick, Representative, do you know statewide about how many people this would affect? I mean, I had your Livingston numbers just statewide about rough number. I mean, if we say 200 and we times it by how many counties we have, you know, yeah. Thank you. It's a very small amount considering the nearly 10 million people that are in this state and those that have paid the ultimate price for us. Representative Martin. Thank you, Mr. Chair. So surviving spouses can also purchase a new homestead qualified property. Correct. I want to make sure that they're not burdened by having to do so many business things in a sense where they're now a widow, a widower. They're buying a new property and they go to closing. If they don't bring the closing document property tax to the city, township office, there's two ways to appropriate or proportion the prorate the taxes. I don't know why. We'd have to look into that. There should be just whatever time frame we're at this house, what the property tax is, it should be done. But there's two ways to do it. I have a constituent right now that is hit by $4,000. They expected more when they bought this new property, but there's two ways to do the proportionment. So it needs to be looked at. I want to make sure they're held harmless. I don't know if that could be included in this bill or if we have to take it up in some other way to make sure that in a difficult situation, the loss of a spouse and so forth, and they still qualify purchasing a new place and all the paperwork that goes along with that, that they're held harmless. And we're honoring that service by making it easier on them. And I want to add one other caveat. All this stuff we talk about for 100% permanent disabled, I would like to make sure the state holds the municipalities, townships, cities harmless in that because we're patting ourselves on the back how great we're helping our veterans, but we are using somebody else's money to do that, and we should consider that. Okay. Thank you very much. Let me read in some cards. There are no other questions. Let me read in some cards here. Wishing not to speak but in support, Brad Ward, Michigan Realtors. Not speaking in support, Joanne Misaraka, Michigan Mortgage Lenders. Not speaking opposed, Judy Allen, Michigan Township Association. Thank you very much for coming in today. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you, Committee. We're going to go at ease, and I would ask Mr. Reif and Ms. Tushman to come forward, please, to the testimony table. I'll turn this over to Vice Chair Frisbee. The committee will come back to order. We're ready to go. 5256 is a relatively simple and straightforward bill. I have Alyssa and Brian here with me this morning. As I've said from this testimony table before and from day one, you get more of what you subsidize and less of what you tax. Many commercial insurance, health insurance policies, and certainly Medicare through their Silver Sneakers program, recognizes the value of exercise. And so what we want to do is translate that into a state tax recognition by making a gym membership or a fitness club membership up to $1,500 a year tax deductible. At the maximum, it would be about a $63 benefit a year. But it's simply a recognition that this is something we would want to endorse and that we would like people to get more involved with. About 20% of the entire national economy now is driven by health care. And if we can help restrain that growth a little bit by encouraging people to exercise, that would be great. So I'll turn it over. So the most important thing to us, of course, is the health and well-being of our members. And we often see a lot of people who leave because they've been injured or they're sick. I think that the physical therapists do a great job when somebody's injured, but when people are ready to be discharged, they often don't know what to do from there. They don't have any access to care that's careful and they'll re-injure. So physical therapists, of course, are compensated and covered, and so we would just like to also be able to care for our members with some incentives as well. There's, of course, all of the science behind. There's a lot behind cancer. If you're exercising and also diabetes, heart disease, it goes on and on. So we would like to see people energized and coming in to move more. Sitting is the new smoking.

My name is Brian Reif. I'm the president of the Michigan Fitness Association. I'm also a Planet Fitness franchisee, and I'm serving my second term on the governor's council on physical fitness, sports, and exercise. I think along the lines of what Alyssa suggested, we're looking to encourage much better behavior and taking better care of ourselves. And we've been involved with the Michigan Fitness Association since the pandemic. We are, I think, light years ahead of where we were four years ago, but we still have a lot of work to do. And I think that the emphasis that we would like to highlight here is we're not necessarily going in the right direction. If you look at CDC statistics, in Michigan alone, about a third of the population, the adult population, is obese. And then another about a third of those are diagnosed today with type 2 diabetes. Obesity is the leading cause of noncommunicable chronic disease. And it's a scenario that is solvable with exercise and diet. And what Representative Tisdale has put together is a step in the right direction in terms of encouraging people to take better care of themselves and focusing more on lifestyle as opposed to treatment. And it's a small step in the right direction. We would certainly like to see more progress as it relates to encouraging those behaviors. But putting something like this as a simple incentive for people to join a gym is absolutely something that we would encourage and support. Just one thing. We are actually one of, I think, only two or three state associations still left from the pandemic. We're pretty proud of that. And I think with that, Michigan has a great opportunity to lead the charge on something like this and to getting our population more healthy. I think we could be pioneers here and do something really outstanding. And just one other thing, Brian and I actually were just discussing that GLP-1s are great. And what a great step they're taking to fight disease. But without eating properly and building muscle, there come some serious disadvantages with that. And muscle loss, you can fall. I mean, there are just some serious side effects if you don't take care of your body. And again, this is not some huge giveaway. You know, for Brian, for Planet Fitness now is what, $15 a month. So, you know, a year's worth of a benefit would be about a $7 tax credit. So it's a recognition that this is something that the state values and just want to communicate that to the taxpayers. All right, we have some questions. Representative VanderWaal. Thank you, Mr. Chair. And thank you for being here. Just a couple quick questions. One, how many people do we have record of how many people in the state of Michigan are involved in fitness centers? Do we have an estimated number? Yes, we do. And if you look at national statistics, today it's about 20% of the adult population that has an active gym membership. And I think that's replicated pretty close in terms of the statistics that we track here statewide. Right. So specifically, I mean, there's a lot of different memberships out there that could be qualified as a fitness membership, I'm assuming, correct? I mean, being a member of a country club potentially could be that way too. Is there some pretty stiff verbiage inside? It's specifically defined in the legislation. And again, there's a cap of $1,500 annually. And like we indicated with Planet Fitness, for example, many club memberships, fitness club memberships are much lower than that $1,500. Correct. Yeah. And I guess I just want to make sure that it's specified. I understand that it's up to $1,500. If it costs more than that, you're not going to get your credit towards that. I guess I just, as always, I think we do want to encourage people to get out and exercise. It alarms me on, you know, we have a tendency as Americans to take the easy way out right now. And just because there's some new medications out there to help us reduce weight doesn't mean that's really technically making us healthier. So I appreciate it and look forward to working with you on this bill. Thank you. Thank you. Representative Martin. Thank you, Mr. Vice Chair. So questions I have, one, Representative Tisdale just answered as far as actually on the $1,500 credit, it equates to about $7 of an actual. That would be about $63 at the $1,500. But for example, for Planet Fitness, it would be about $7 a year. And that would be for people that actually itemize. Correct. For those that itemize and not certainly, I think that's less than half now. I'm looking at the total amount of money the state would have to, you know, lose for revenue. That's not going to be a huge amount. The one-third of people with diabetes that are obese and the one-third of the population are obese. How many of them itemize? I mean, how many of them are of a low-level income? Because that goes hand-in-hand. The type of food and diets go hand-in-hand with their income level. So I don't think we're losing a lot for the state as far as an income level by having this deduction. It would be just a small step forward. Which was my point, and this is symbolic encouragement. And we don't want to give away the store. On the other hand, even for those that do itemize, it's not a huge gift. That's another question. Thanks. Minority Vice Chair Hoskins. Thank you, Mr. Chair. And thank you for bringing us this legislation. I think I had a similar thinking as Representative VanderWaal, which is the types of facilities that would be covered under this too. I too was thinking about country clubs and, you know, someone taking advantage of this in whatever facility. But, like, you know, I think there's an idea of, like, getting a tax credit or a tax deduction to go to, you know, some posh country club, even if there is a cap on it. But that's one concern. But another question too is just I like this legislation and I like the overall goal too. And I'm just curious, was there any more thought to other ways to kind of incentivize a healthier lifestyle? Even when we're talking about, this is just for facilities and I don't want to necessarily muddy the waters and make this even bigger than it has to be. But there's a lot of ways that I think we can really incentivize people to be healthier. And, you know, if it's wearables, if it's, you know, you talked about the GLP-1s, for example. If there are other things, I'm just curious, was there a conversation around that too? How much time do we have? Yeah, but one thing I can tell you with the cancer, sorry, with the cancer research, I'm pretty loud. With the cancer research is that supervised exercise is a definite deterrent of that biology. So, I mean, there are a million things to your point. But, yes, there are a lot of things. And with a lot of our fitness centers come, you know, diet. For instance, if you work with one of our personal trainers, I'm sorry, I only have one little location in Clawson, Michigan. Just, you know, Brian's a giant contributing to your state, to our state. But we ask that you track your water, your sleep, your diet, send pictures. I mean, there's a lot that goes into it. But, again, even with the physical therapy when people are hurt, I think it seems like a necessity. Because as you know, when you get older and if you take a bad fall, that's it. I mean, we're just trying to encourage all these good behaviors and muscle. Muscle protects a lot. So in that instance, how does one track all that information? There are a lot of apps, great technology, excellent technology. Yeah, and I think the higher level answer to your question, we are working behind the scenes and collaborating with hospital systems, with insurance companies. You get into some really complex issues. And it's easier said than done to say, you know, well, insurance should cover a gym membership. We understand that. But we are working systematically and collaborating. We've got some very world-class researchers here in the state of Michigan that we're fortunate enough to work with behind the scenes. But, again, I think that so there is a lot that we are working on. This to us seemed like it was certainly a simple step in the right direction. And I think

It really does set the foundation for future types of suggestions that we have in terms of encouraging physical activity. Is that your aura ring you're wearing? That is my aura ring. So yeah, there are a lot of apps you can download. I mean, your cell phone measures your steps that you're taking every day and can create averages and if you're above and below and all that kind of stuff. But you're right. I don't know. I'm game for anything. But like I say, this is recognition that the state sees this as a benefit and we want more people to participate. Representative Young. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you, Mr. Chair, for bringing this before us. Of course, being healthy and taking care of our bodies, the only body we get. So we know that. So I think that's all amazing thinking out of the box. But I can't help but be concerned about, and many of y'all know I'm a minister, so I use terminology like the least of these that you find in scripture. Because obesity and poor health is tied to poverty. It just is. And so people that are dealing with those types of circumstances, though they should want a gym membership and probably do, they just can't afford it. They just can't. And so I'm concerned about this potentially being like have and have nots type of legislation. And I know that's not your intent. I know that. But then what do we do? I appreciate Planet Fitness and that you make it like affordable, 15 bucks. But even with that, some folks can't afford that. And then there's a whole education component of why it's so important. Or even have the transportation to get there. Yeah, all of those things, all of those things. So I just wanted to lift that up. I know we're really trying to do a good thing, you know, thinking out the box. I don't know what Medicaid offers along those lines. I know that Medicare through its silver sneakers program has some benefits for that. Many commercial insurance carriers do offer benefits for that as well. But that would not impact the lower socioeconomic. But I don't know what Medicaid offers or if there's something that the state could introduce. Right. Well, we'll have to look at that, too. Thank you. So even with breast cancer survivor. So even with breast cancer, right, there are communities that are underserved. They don't have the right access. And so in certain communities, you see the numbers for not just diagnosis, but survival go way down. And it's horrible. So one thing I've noticed as a trend is that there are wonderful people in communities that maybe you would look into rewarding who do work to get people to move, who start charities to fund people who can't afford proper treatment. I think on a community level, people are doing wonderful things and it's heartening to see. Yeah. You have one question. I'm just curious. And we'll just use COVID as a baseline. Have you seen your numbers start to improve in terms of memberships? Where are they pre-COVID and post-COVID in terms of your paid memberships? Sure. I mean, he has a lot more gyms, so I'd rather Brian answer. For us, not going in the right direction in terms of what I thought coming out of the pandemic we would have seen. We're seeing year over year joins are down for us and may or may not have to do with the GOP ones. I think that old habits die hard. And despite going through what was a horrible pandemic, it's in the rearview mirror now. And so the numbers statistically for us, the numbers are joins this year year over year are probably down about 8%, which that's discouraging. And I think to your point, everybody's expenses have skyrocketed with 30 to 40%. And so even with Planet Fitness, it's just less affordable. And so any incentive we see is a great idea to get people to move and to join to be healthier. Thank you. Any other questions from the committee? I have one. First of all, the movement is a key to staving off many things, including memory issues on dementia. And I heard you say a fall and a broken hip is a devastating – as a paramedic, I always said that could be the beginning of the end, and it is for many. So movement is a key. One question, does this bill define if you have out-of-pocket expenses is when you're eligible? So silver sneakers, for instance, and it's going to pay for a partial or a full gym membership, are they allowed to take this deduction or not? Well, I think a deduction has to be an actual expense. So if it's paid for, you're not going to be able to show anything as an actual expense. Good point. Any other questions? All right. We'll go at ease. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, sir. Okay, we'll call the meeting back to order. We have 5305 and 5306, Representatives Van Workum and Bagul. And our intent here is to hear testimony and to vote this along for timing purposes. This is the expansion or extension, rather, of a sunset. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you, distinguished members of the committee. It's good to be back before what was known as the tax committee, but now is the finance committee. Chair Tisdell, my bill, House Bill 5305, would simply extend the sunset on the Commercial Redevelopment Act that is set to expire at the end of this year. This act allows local governments to establish a commercial redevelopment district, which would consist of commercial property that is either obsolete, blighted, or vacant. Approved projects within these districts would then qualify for tax relief for up to 12 years. While this act is administered by Treasury, it is entirely up to our locals to utilize it in a way that makes sense for their communities. The Commercial Redevelopment Act and the Commercial Rehabilitation Act have been vital tools for our local communities and have helped breathe new life into our aging commercial corridors. Since 2008, this act has been used for 82 different properties. And combined, these two acts have supported nearly 500 total projects across the state. Helping our locals invest in projects like health care expansion in Marquette, creating space for small businesses in Wyandotte, or opening hotels and new housing projects in Detroit and Muskegon. Unfortunately, due to the sunset of this bill, there were many projects that had to be tabled this year. I hope we can move quickly to preserve this tool for our locals. And thank you for your time, and I'll give it to Representative Gohl. Thank you, Mr. Chair, members of the committee. As my colleague had pointed out, this is a very valuable program, been utilized by a number of municipalities and different places to clear up a lot of blight. So they'd like to continue this, and our bill would extend the sunset until December of 2030. Okay. Any questions? Vice Chair Hoskins. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Just a quick question. Do you guys know kind of the history of why we keep doing these sunset extensions? I mean, my community has very much taken advantage of these, and it's been fantastic for my community, my district. But I know since I've worked in Lansing, I've now worked on this twice. This is the third time this has come before me, and so we keep extending it for what I think is a very good program that's been helping a lot of communities, as you both pointed out. So I'm just curious if there's been thoughts of just not doing a sunset at all and just making it permanent, making the sunset longer. Right. There certainly has been discussions of making the sunset longer, and we would certainly be open to those conversations. I think any time you're talking about the sunsets, it's the legislative review process to make sure that the projects are working, the bill is working as intended to do. So this one, both of our bills, has proven to be effective, so it gets maybe a lighter review than maybe some others, but there's always a different governor or different legislature that wants to review economic development and how you do economic development. So I think that's kind of the general concept of the sunsets, but I think this one has proven very well and could certainly look at maybe a 10 year if the committee or the legislature was interested in that. All right. Well, I would be interested in that, but it's up to you.

the powers that be. And that's certainly something we could address with a sub on the floor or an amendment on the floor, and that's been raised by some of the stakeholders as well. This particular go-through to end, my understanding is to end the sunset would have involved multiple bills as opposed to just the extension. So for expediency, we're just doing the extension right now, but I'd be more than happy to see it go 10 years. We've renewed this maybe half a dozen times now. So Representative Young. Ditto to my last year. I'm good. Okay, very good. Representative Breen. Thank you, Mr. Chair. I want to be a yes, but I want to clarify that there's no impact to school funding. Is that correct? Each of our bills are different on part of that. Mine, you certainly have issues that you are setting the value of the property right now. So you would get that continued dollars. It's now that you are redeveloping that property. So for up to 12 years, based on how long the local extends, you're not losing the money, but they're not gaining those dollars from that redevelopment because you are holding that property the same. So there's no cut to it's whether that project goes, whether then after a certain amount of time, based on how the locals do it, then you would capture those dollars. Now, in specific to my bill, there is the state education tax, which is set to be set, but the treasurer can make a decision of whether to cut that by 50%. But the state would only have 25 opportunities a year to do that. So as far as any decrease to school funding, what you're saying is it's not going to happen because it wouldn't have happened without this otherwise. Correct. Okay, now what about the fiscal impact to local units of government? Well, the beauty of this legislation is the local governments are making this decision. They are the ones that are going to decide whether they want to do it and then base that on how many years that they're willing to do it. So it is their decision. Thank you for verifying that. I should have just cut you off when you said you wanted to be a yes. Representative Martin. I think I'm just revisiting sunset real quickly. Some projects didn't start because we didn't address this review early enough. Is there a way to put in there a time when we have to review something so the sunset doesn't affect a planning decision if a program is going to be there when they need it? A year out, for example, like you mentioned, because you wait until December, when it expires in December, then nobody's done anything with it and they're trying to do the next fiscal year. I just want to know when we actually review these for the sunsets. Yeah, I mean a lot of that's the local control. I was aware of a project in Detroit where they've been trying to get on the docket for several months, but because of the time constraint that they had that they couldn't get on the docket in time, and now they're running into the deadline. So I don't know of forcing locals to make a decision by certain date. Not the locals. I'm talking about our responsibility. So the locals know that it's been extended and the sunset has been extended. If we wait until the last month of a bill before we extend it and review it, that doesn't help the locals at all with their planning process. It's incumbent on us to give them the time they need. Do we have a process in place to review our sunsets in a timely manner for locals to make those decisions? I don't think we can address that statutorily. I think that is an internal discussion. It may be something to address statutorily that will apply to all sunsets. That's something you'd like to work on. A sunset to the sunset. That's right. No more questions. I've got some cards to read in. Not speaking in support, Patricia Herndon, Michigan Bankers. Not speaking in support, Randy Gross, Michigan Chamber. Not speaking in support, Judy Allen, Michigan Townships. Not speaking in support, Jen Rigterink. I think I even got that right, Michigan Municipal League. Not speaking in support, Peyton Hines, President and CEO of Northern Lakes Economic Alliance. Not speaking in support, Sean Sorenson Abbott, Michigan Department of Treasury. Not speaking in support, Brian Schoff, Detroit Regional Chamber. Not speaking in support, Katie Fuller. Thank you, gentlemen. And at this point, we'll take a motion to move this forward. Anyone? Vice Chair Hoskins makes a motion to report 5305. Please take the vote. On the motion to report, Chair Tisbo. Yes. Representatives Frisbee. Yes. VanderWaal. Yes. Leitner. Yes. Martin. Yes. Posthumous. Alexander. Yes. Aragona. Yes. Schuette. Yes. Hoskins. Yes. Carter. Neely. Yes. Breen. Aye. Young. Yes. Pies. Yes. Mr. Chair, you have 13 yeas, zero nays, zero pass. The motion prevails. And that will be reported with recommendation. Motion for 5306. Vice Chair Frisbee, take the vote, please. On the motion to report, Chair Tisbo. Yes. Representatives Frisbee. Yes. VanderWaal. Yes. Leitner. Yes. Martin. Yes. Posthumous. Alexander. Yes. Aragona. Yes. Schuette. Yes. Hoskins. Yes. Carter. Neely. Yes. Breen. Aye. Young. Yes. Pies. Yes. Mr. Chair, you have 13 yeas, zero nays, zero pass. The motion prevails. And that will be moved forward, reported with recommendation. Vice Chair Hoskins moves to excuse absent members with no objections. That motion prevails. No further business in front of this committee. We stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Families and Veterans — Tuesday, December 9, 2025
transcript:

Pablo? Here. Wolford? Young? Burns? Here. Grindon? Here. Song? Madam Chair, you have eight members present. A quorum. Thank you, Mr. Clerk. Thompson moves to adopt the minutes of the November 4th meeting without objection. So moved. Our first order of business is to hear further testimony on House Bills 4530 and 5220 from Representative Hudson. Good morning, Madam Chair, members of the committee. Thank you so much for having me back. I'll be brief. There's nothing huge that has changed with these bills, but there are substitutes before you. The most substantive changes are in, well, it's a new bill, so it's a pretty substantive change, I would guess. House Bill 5220, that is Representative Regas' bill. It still does all of the same things, just makes sure that mandatory reporters take ongoing education, giving them information about child abuse and neglect. It's in a different section of law, though, which I mentioned was likely to happen the last time I was here. And one other change clarified a concern that I believe a committee member brought up. It does explicitly state that if you have to take ongoing education already as part of your job, and you take something that covers child abuse and neglect, that's fine. That will meet this requirement. You won't have to take an additional second continuing education course. And because that ended up in a new bill to deal with drafting guidelines, the only change to my bill is we broke the tie bar. So it's not tie bar to a bill that we're not moving anymore. But I'm happy to take any questions that anyone has. Does anyone have any questions? Well, thank you for the further testimony. We appreciate it. Thank you. And thanks again. We have a couple cards to read in in support of the bill. H Bill 5220 and Conan, Michigan League for Public Policies in support, Rebecca Mastie, Michigan Catholic Conference in support, Elizabeth Henderson, Michigan Federation for Children and Families in support of the bill. So our next order of business is to hear a presentation from Ryan North, co-founder of One Big Happy Home and Joe Benedict. Rev. Johnson will formally introduce her guests. Thank you, fellow committee members and Chairwoman Schmaltz. I'm bringing this before you today for testimony and for review. Excuse me, because we all know that we need to assist and try to improve everything we can for our children in the state and to partner with DHHS in every way possible to make things better for foster care in this case. One of my constituents, Joe Benedict and his wife, Brittany, brought it to my attention that they had found a really good foster care training out of Texas. Go Lions. We just beat Dallas. That's the reference. I'm sure you get it. Just salt in the wound a little bit. But they found this really good training and it improved their ability to foster children so much better. They had been fostering for years in addition to their own children. And so they introduced me to Ryan North of One Big Happy Home. He and his wife have developed over years this foster care training that many groups are using around the country, finding great success and a great rate of being able to keep the children in the foster care home because the parents are much more equipped. And that's why I bring this to you today. Hopefully we can convince DHHS to make this an option for training to really give parents a better chance to be able to keep the kids in the home and be able to continue fostering as they desire. So without further waiting, I introduce to you Joe Benedict of Nashville, Michigan, and who's giving testimony of his experience with One Big Happy Home and Ryan North from Dallas, Texas with One Big Happy Home. Thank you. Thank you. Good morning. It's great to be with your committee and I've heard a lot about your committee and not only preparing for this, but knowing Representative Johnson was on it. So I'm really excited, humbled, and privileged to just be able to speak with you all today to consider what's best for families in Michigan and what I believe is a fantastic partnership that Michigan could have with One Big Happy Home. We may just find that we are on the same page. And let me repeat it again, when it comes to intentions, oftentimes we share the same intentions of love, concern, and care for what is best, safe, and helpful for families within Michigan. And somehow we get clouded with decisions, so many decisions that the lines become blurred as to what's truly best for families and what we personally think is best. And I want to tell you a story about my family. My family is dear to my heart. The world of parenting, fostering, adoption has truly changed my life forever. Because of how grateful I am for all that I've learned, I can only hope that what I have to say today will, in my greatest and most earnest hope, enhance Michigan's approach to foster care and families in a way that will leave a truly recognizable improvement for the better for individuals in care who truly matter in this state. My wife and I actually struggled with infertility from the very beginning of our marriage. And we were told by a specialist that we would most likely never have biological children. After two very heartbreaking miscarriages, we considered this our plight and we thought, what next? Adoption, foster care, becoming house parents? We didn't know what we wanted to do, but we knew we wanted to serve children and to serve them the best we could, to raise them with love, structure, encouragement, and see them thrive. But that dream is not realized without children. And so, in order to speed up the time frame here, I will share with you we were blessed in 2013 with a biological son, Jonah, then also Claire, and Myrie, and then Preston in 2017. Four children in a short time span due to our fertility specialist's recommendation. Just following this answer to our heart's longing being gifted with four kids, four and under, I was diagnosed with cancer when my youngest child was only six months old. We had the kids at this point, and we were quite happy raising four biological children. But what would we do about the possibility of not surviving to raise them as their dad? And questions that would only be answered in time. So as we dealt with this cancer, we were faced with the brevity of life. Life goes way too fast.
