Fox, Altman, Alexander, Hoadley, Pablo, Wooden, Polzar, Song, Crescent. Madam Chair, do you have a quorum? Representative Hoadley moves to adopt the minutes from November 4th. There being no objection, the motion prevails by unanimous consent. Well, good morning. Today we will be taking up House Resolution, House Bill 5091. We will hear testimony from Representative Steele testifying in support of her bill. Good morning, Rep. Steele. Good morning. Come forward and you may begin when you are ready. Thank you. Thank you for allowing me to testify today. So the bill is 5091 and it requires county executives and commissioners from certain counties to file personal financial disclosures. So as you may recall, in 2022, Proposal 1 was passed by the Michigan voters with more than 66% in favor, which altered legislative term limits and added new personal financial disclosures. This does the same thing, but it does for county commissioners and county executives. So what it does is amends the Public Officers Financial Disclosure Act, PA 281, to expand and clarify financial reporting requirements for certain elected officials in Michigan. And so what we do is we add public officer, which like what I said is county commissioners and executives for counties with a population of greater than 150 residents. And so these individuals would be required to file an annual report similar to what we file covering the previous calendar year. So the report would include earned income, salaries, wages, tips, bonuses, and commissions, unearned income, dividends, annuities, pensions, and retirement income. And the exclusions would be inheritance and gifts from immediate family members and the liabilities for mortgages, other debts, including revolving debt, unearned, certain unearned, I'm sorry, unsecured debt and debts owed by business entities. So gifts, any gifts that must be reported by lobbyists or lobbyist agents under Michigan law. So the Secretary of State is tasked with creating and publishing the standardized disclosure form to ensure consistent reporting across all covered officials. This effort will give the public meaningful insight to potential conflicts of interest and strengthen the trust in local government decision-making. So the counties in which it would, the 150 threshold, 150 residents threshold is 16. So Wayne, Oakland, and I'm from Oakland County, Wayne, Oakland, Macomb, Kent, Genesee, Washtenaw, Ottawa, Ingham, Kalamazoo, Livingston, Saginaw, Muskegon, St. Clair, Jackson, Monroe, and Berrien. So it was brought to my attention by former city attorney from Royal Oak, and he can further speak to this bill. And he is Mr. Charles Semchenna, and he is via Zoom today. So. All right. Well, thank you very much, Rep Steele, for being here before the committee. And I believe we will just turn it right over on here, testimony from Mr. Charles Semchenna, former attorney for the city of Royal Oak, testifying in support of House Bill 5091. And we will take questions after we hear testimony from Mr. Semchenna. Good morning, Mr. Semchenna. Please begin when you are ready. Yeah, I'm ready, if you can hear me. I'm pleased to have the opportunity to speak to you. And I'd certainly appear today to express my very strong support for the bill amending the public act regarding the public officers financial disclosure requirements that extends the financial disclosure obligations to public officials in the larger counties. And I have to be very blunt based on my recent experience here that this legislation is long overdue, and it's necessary not only as a matter of good government, but as a matter of restoring public trust at a time when that trust has been badly damaged. In Royal Oak and in Oakland County, our community has recently endured a series of investigative reports by the Free Press, Detroit News, Cranes, Detroit Business, Oakland Press, Daily Tribune, Channel 7, 4, 2, and others documenting a wide ranging political corruption scandal in Oakland County. These reports are jaw dropping, and the public correctly views these reports as being very credible. And what's most disturbing about the reporting and the facts that have been disclosed is that the wrongdoing comes to light not because of any statutory financial disclosure obligation, but because journalists did the work our laws currently did not require public officials to do. The public has reacted and has been shocked, angered, and vocal in demanding safeguards that prevent these abuses from reoccurring. The proposed amendment directly addresses the current absence of a meaningful, enforceable financial disclosure system for public officials in larger counties. This gap in the law has produced exactly what everyone should expect, unreported conflicts of interest, unseen ethical violations, elected officials using public positions for private gain. But the public has only discovered these issues through investigative journalism, not through any required transparency from Oakland County itself. The county's response so far, suggesting voluntary disclosure, offers nothing more than an appearance of transparency without any accountability. Voluntary compliance is not oversight. Voluntary disclosure is not a safeguard. Voluntary ethics rules never protect the public from corruption. This bill provides mandatory enforceable transparency that the current system utterly lacks. And let us be clear, the amendment does not impose anything radical. It merely holds county officials to the same disclosure standards already required of other public officials in Michigan. In other words, it simply requires them to tell the full truth, nothing more. There's no legitimate reason for any ethical public official to oppose that. Michigan law already has a statute requiring conflicts of interest. It's the standards for public officers and employees. It's Public Act 196 of 1973. And it's a long statute, but I put in my written testimony a couple segments. But basically, a public officer cannot solicit money, accept a gift, or anything of value or benefit for a private organization that tends to influence another public official or employee. And that's what's happened in Oakland County with the county commissioners and one in particular influencing other public officials at city and township levels. But these laws already exist, but the problem is they cannot be enforced if the public has no access to the information necessary to detect a violation. The law even provides a right for a private legal action, but without disclosure, citizens cannot know a violation occurred within the statute's timelines. This makes this very good law effectively unenforceable. But the new amendment helps fix that. The need for this legislation is not theoretical. It's been publicly reported that an Oakland County commissioner may have violated state ethics laws by representing sheets before multiple local government bodies and by influencing other public officials to approve a private client's project. According to reporting, the commissioner has acknowledged being paid for these efforts. Residents, hundreds of them in Royal Oak, objected to these approvals by the local officials. They raised serious concerns about public safety at what's been described as one of the most dangerous and traffic congested intersections in the city. Yet the public

had no access to required financial disclosures that might have alerted them earlier to these potential conflicts of interest. They discovered the problem only because journalists investigated, not because the law required transparency. This is exactly why this amendment is indispensable. When financial disclosure is optional, conflicts can be hidden, public trust erodes, officials inclined toward misconduct face no real deterrent, and the public is left defenseless unless the media happens to uncover the wrongdoing. This is not how a constitutional republic is supposed to function. Mandatory disclosure is not punitive, it's protective. It protects residents, it protects the honest politicians and officials, it protects the integrity of county government. This amendment is not merely good policy, it's a necessary safeguard for public trust and a vital companion of Michigan's existing conflict of interest statute. Our residents deserve more transparency, they deserve accountability, and they certainly deserve to know that their elected officials are serving them, not private clients or hidden financial interests. I urge this committee to adopt the amendment without dilution, without delay, and without deferral. And I thank you for your attention. I can answer questions based upon my recent experience here in Royal Oak and my experience representing the city of Royal Oak as their city attorney and as an elected official in Royal Oak. And I work for the county as an assistant county prosecutor. I understand the relationship between elected officials at the county level and the city level. Oakland County is a 900-pound gorilla, and if an elected official from Oakland County chooses to influence an elected official in a city, smaller cities, it's easy for them to be intimidated. At least if the public officials at the county level are conducting county business and interacting with the cities, and that's my experience as a city attorney. I negotiated transactions, real estate transactions with the county. It was fine. But when the county officials representing a private entity for personal gain, that influence can still be there, and it shouldn't be there. The conflict of interest laws that protect us need to be effective. They need to have disclosure. Bringing this into the light of day, the information that should be disclosed is the best cure for an existing problem. Thank you, Mr. Sanchez. We will move forward with some questions that we have from the committee, if you are open to that, Representative Steele. So, Representative Kolasar. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you for your testimony, both of you. Thank you for this bill. Transparency is good. We want that. My concern, though, has to do with our voters in rural areas. And I'm curious, well, really, it's a two-part question. One, why is there a population threshold? And two, would you be open to an amendment to eliminate that population threshold? Yes. Yes. And so I think that what it was is that you have counties that probably only represent, I don't know, 200 or 300 people in the whole county, you know, like in the UP north of the knuckles. And some of those positions are more like voluntary positions. And I think that there has been a rash of people not running for those positions because they're, you know, sometimes more trouble than they're worth. Whereas, like, Oakland County, they actually get paid for their services, like at a part-time level. And I just thought that you would lose some of the county commissioners in some of those smaller counties because they have an onus to disclose something that is nonexistent. So that's what made me think of just picking the bigger counties. And I'm not sure if the ones that we picked at 150 or more were all paid positions, but if it was anything like Oakland County, I just assumed that it was. And that was the reasoning behind it. Thank you. We have Representative Altman. Thank you, Madam Chair. And thank you, Representative Steele, for being here to testify on your legislation. I appreciate your efforts and what issues you're trying to solve here. And obviously, it's a tale as old as time, right? Elected officials using their position for personal gain. And we want to, you know, prevent that. And as Representative Kulizar said, we want as much transparency in our government as possible. I just have a couple of quick technical questions. Actually, Representative Kulizar asked one of them, and that was the population threshold. But the other one is, you know, I'm from a very rural part of Michigan, and we obviously don't have county executives. I guess my question is, what role do they play in the county commission, those county executives? It looks like we have three of them in Michigan. Could you just touch on that briefly? If I could just, like, put it into, like, a perspective. You know, we have 110 representatives, and then we elect a Speaker of the House, and they run almost the day-to-day of the business of the House with the business offices and stuff. And the county executives work in the same manner. It is an elected position in Oakland County. However, they have the commissioners that make the rules and the laws, and the county executive executes what has been voted on. So, like, a city manager, a supervisor, Speaker of the House, it's in that same capacity that they do. And the previous executive, which was Al Brooks Patterson, was like a strong executive. And it was like he ran the county, but this has been the opposite direction that the commissioners allow. You have the executive of the—not the executive, but the chair of the commissioners more so in charge of running the county. So it's kind of like a switch of power, but that's basically how it's ran. Representative Song. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you, Rep. Steele and Mr. Sanchez for your testimony. I also want to thank you for introducing this legislation. I think it is extremely important, and I think we've seen that investigative journalism is a great way to keep us as elected accountable, so I'm glad to see that that is working. My question is there are other countywide electeds, including treasurer, clerk, prosecutor, sheriff, and as you may recall, in Macomb County, we had a prosecutor who was prosecuted for wrongly using his campaign finance, or violating campaign finance laws. So why doesn't this legislation include those other countywide? I would think that a treasurer, especially handling millions of dollars of county tax dollars, should also be subjected to this type of disclosure. And would you be open to doing an amendment of that sort to include those countywide electeds too? Good point. Yes, maybe I would agree with that. Yes, I could see why you would bring that forward. Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Chair. Representative Alexander. Thank you very much. You well know as a county elected official since 2008, I had to file up to three or four campaign finance. Every elected official all the way down to the township level, unless they sign a waiver for $1,000 or less, that gives them a waiver, but they all, treasurer, everybody, the sheriff, everybody fills out the campaign finance act anyway. It's important to recognize that this is something additional above and beyond. This is a fifth report that we all have to fill out that's been added. I've been filling out three and four of these campaign finance act forms as a county elected official since 2008. But unless we look at those campaign finance act numbers and stuff, I mean, it's already there. And my secondary question is why are you stopping at the $150,000 threshold? There is corruption under $150,000, which you can find most often in the campaign finance act that they fill out at the county level. It just doesn't report to the state. It reports to the county clerk. Can I respond? It talks about your campaign finance, but it doesn't talk about your LLCs, your spouse's LLCs, different businesses that you might be a part of, the campaign finance, to my knowledge, doesn't address those. And the nefarious activity is happening with these separate companies of going back from campaign finance back to these companies, back to lobby work, back to private

Businesses that are paying you as lobbyist to then pay you on the front end as a lobbyist, but then on the back end as campaign contributions. So you see one side of it, but you don't see the other side of it. And this allows you to see both sides of how that circle completely comes to a full circle. May I have one more question? Yes. Then we've since created this additional report. Should we maybe consider amending the Campaign Finance Act in itself so it does include that stuff? Wouldn't that be a simpler way of doing it? I don't necessarily think so because, I mean, literally all you're taking is the law that already exists and adding two names to it. And at the same time, it gives the teeth because it pulls in that you can't get these contributions from lobbyists. That already exists in this law. And then you just are naming the people that have to file the paperwork that touches that law to say that you can't do that. So that already exists and all you're doing is adding positions to something that already exists that was written, I think, in the 70s. Yeah. And my biggest concern comes back to what Rep. Solomon and Kolisar and Pat said, you know, why do it for some and not for everybody? I think it should be a blanket for everybody. And if you're open to that amendment, that's great. Our final question we have is from Representative Fox. Okay, thank you very much. And it's good to see that investigative journalism has been doing something. I hope that they will broaden that to the federal level where people come in very poor and leave very rich and our federal officials too. But secondly, and I'm a little bit editorial here, I need to remind us all that our Constitution was made only for a moral and religious people. It's wholly inadequate, the government of any other, John Adams. And I think that it would pay for us all as elected officials to remember that very well and to even wrestle with what it means to be a religious person. There's a lot behind that one word. And we finally ended up getting sent a PDF that we had to fill out by hand and then submit to the Secretary of State. I mean, we can't play that type of game if we're going to go down this path. I mean, we need to be professional. And if we're spending, from what I heard, a lot of money to get that form set up, we need to have our ducks in a row. Our customers pay the true cost of their service that they receive. This also means that we are regulated at the local level, either by a utility board or a city council. And while we do fall under some state regulation, and Dave is going to get into more of those details, we have been accountable to and regulated by our local communities now for over 100 years. And I hope that most of you are familiar with this little tune, but when I say, where everybody knows your name, that's us. That really is. You can't go into a grocery store in most of our towns without seeing somebody from your electric utility. We're your neighbors. You go to church together, kids' baseball teams. We know each other's names. Lastly, I want to touch on this. We believe that as a direct result of that public power model, you see significant savings in Michigan public power communities. And we're really proud of this. You should all have the full report in front of you. But this is one of the key takeaways. Public power, and this was just in 2023. So in one year, Michigan's public power customers saw an annual savings of over $400 million in one year. And you can see the other point here too at the bottom is that if you live in a public power community, like a Holland, for the course of your lifetime, which in this study was 75 years, you can save over $120,000, which today is significant savings. People would love to use that money on other things besides their electric bill. So I would encourage you to take a look at this report. We partnered with Utility Financial Services to do this report, which is a very reputable firm. They work with municipalities and co-ops across the country to do financial reports, rate studies and designs. And so we partnered with them. I mean, our members have always known how great they are, that they have the lowest residential rates, the best reliability. But MMA was really excited to have the opportunity to create a comprehensive report to tell that story to all of you across the entire state and public power and the impact that we have. Lastly here, I want to touch on mutual aid. So mutual aid is what we call storm response. I will say that in 2020, as Dave knows, it became a little bit more of a pandemic response. And it was something that we used as all utilities across the state came together and we were actually helping each other get PPE. But generally speaking, it is what happens when there is a storm and utilities need assistance to restore the power. So here in Michigan, you never know what the weather is going to bring, as you noted this morning, Chairwoman. But we need to be prepared. So this picture right here is actually from the ice storm that struck northern Michigan, did impact our communities up there in March of this year. And I'm going to go through some very shortly after that ice storm, actually, we had some tornadoes that were down in southern Michigan. And as I'm going through these pictures here, I do want you to note the utility trucks. We have our logos on those. You also see here poles and wires are down. And I often get asked questions, do you guys actually own your own infrastructure? We do. We do. We have the same kind of infrastructure and equipment as some of our larger counterparts across the state. We are utilities. Our customers get bills from these utilities with these same logos. So I just wanted to call your attention to that. And you can see we have mutual aid coordinators strategically placed throughout the state, and they will reach out to other utilities and say, hey, do you need assistance? Or if others do, what do you have available to provide aid? And we also do provide assistance to utilities down south. It's usually down south. When a hurricane strikes, we have pictures from Florida. And also we've gone to the Carolinas. But our crews are very eager to go and assist others. And it's certainly something that we take a lot of pride in is being able to help each other in times of need. And this is from Hurricane Milton that was in Florida. And you can see the turnout there that we were able to provide. So with that, I'm going to now turn it over to Dave. All right. Thank you, Katie. And thank you, Chair Wenzel and the committee. Thank you for your time this morning. I want to spend a little bit of time highlighting a specific situation with one of our members here of MMA, which is the Holland Board of Public Works. Talk a little bit about community engagement and what that did in terms of leading to what's been a very successful project in Holland with Holland Energy Park and the energy work that we've been doing in our community. And then also spend a little bit of time talking about some of the impacts that we're seeing from the recent legislation that was enacted late in 2023. So again, I'm very blessed to be able to work alongside about 200 team members in Holland. I've been with Holland for about 34 years now. We operate four different utilities in Holland, the electric, water, wastewater, and broadband now. We're growing our broadband, offering a fiber to the home solution throughout our entire community now in Holland. And we are overseen by an independent board that ultimately is responsible to our city council. So we have that local representation and voice at every level of that governance in our community with very major initiatives going on in each of our utility areas. Our mission in Holland is to provide competitive, reliable, and innovative public utility solutions to the greater Holland area in a sustainable manner, looking at that triple bottom line of social, environmentally, and financial responsibility. And our vision really is to try to improve quality of life and economic development for our community. We are the lifeblood really in those utilities or what helps make our community grow and go. And as Katie talked about the value study that is in front of you, there really are three factors that kind of go into that. Affordability among municipals, we are not-for-profit entities. Every dollar that you spend on your service goes back into the service that we're providing. And so we tend to be lower cost providers among our membership. And Holland is no exception to that. Our reliability also, we tend to outperform as it relates to reliability. And you see that here with Holland BPW, the network of mutual aid that we have, and among our members generally we have very outstanding reliability across our entire membership. And then this local voice that I mentioned, that community connection is sort of a priceless aspect. I'm going to highlight how that comes into play with regard to the work that we've done in Holland a little bit. But if we were to quantify that for the Holland BPW, it's a little over $38 million in local economic benefit just to the Holland BPW. And that comes by way of, again, that reliability is about a $15 million benefit on an annual basis. On the residential rate savings, this is about $500 per residential customer really within the Holland BPW service territory that stays in their pocket on an annual basis from that rate differential. So that's about a $14 million improvement and savings to our community. And then we support our general fund as well. We have a dividend payment, and municipals really across the state support their general fund to help keep taxes low in their community and service level high. And last year we brought in about $8.5 million to the city of Holland's general fund to support that. And as I mentioned there, the local control and decision-making is priceless. We think it's something that really has a great benefit to our community that's hard to really quantify in dollars. One example of that here with our utility in Holland, we have about 32,000 customers, and you're seeing the picture here of the Holland Energy Park. It's been a really tremendous project for us and really stakeholder-driven, as I'm going to spend a little bit of time detailing. That project was completed in 2017, and we've already been able to pay the debt off completely, which is going to save our customers over $45 million in interest costs that they would have seen if that would have continued throughout the life of the bond. We've also been able to improve the environmental performance of our utilities tremendously by moving away from our coal generation in Holland and building Holland Energy Park and incorporating renewable technology into our portfolio as well. We've been already able to cut our carbon intensity of our portfolio in half since

actually 2010, and the projections are that we're approaching a 70% reduction over that number by 2030. So continuing to make great progress in that. A unique fact, I think, for municipalities as well as the customer concentration that you see in commercial and industrial. Holland is no different here. 84% of our power actually goes to businesses in our community. And we have a thriving business climate there across a number of different sectors, and we support them in that work. So while by number they might be small in terms of the customers, by the amount of power demand they have, they're very large in each of our communities. So as I mentioned, we have the Holland Energy Park is really the result of almost a decade of work in close consultation with our community. When we were looking at what to do, instead of just moving forward as a utility, we decided first to back up and bring stakeholders into this process. And so this is really a story of stakeholder engagement all along the way that I want to highlight here. And the first part of that was education, helping our customers understand just what goes into a power supply decision-making process, having speakers come in to talk about that, and then bringing together a group from business and government and special interests all around the table to really solve the problem of power supply, to look at it more holistically than just the financial, but what are the non-financial costs and benefits that accrue from that decision-making process as well. So again, that group came in, and we put all the different costs and benefits that might come in. If you think about it, on a local level, for example, we have a snowmelt system in Holland. Maybe if you have taken that in or seen that around the wintertime, probably would enjoy that today along 196 or, you know, frankly, it's probably too big of an infrastructure to snowmelt all of it. But in Holland, we have about 800,000 square feet of area, about five miles of walkable area, and that was served from our power generation's waste heat. So it's BTUs that were already being sent back to the environment that we're capturing and putting to good use. And so we wanted to make sure that what we looked at from a power generation standpoint took that into consideration. What if we didn't build anything new in Holland? How would that be met? We had cargo ships that were bringing in coal, and so we were getting our harbor dredged. So what would happen if we lost that? So all those different costs and benefits went into this analysis, and what it really brought the community together was that it gave very clear visibility around all the societal impacts that come from this decision. And what it yielded was a decision for us to move away from our coal generation in Holland, let that retire, redevelop our waterfront for other uses, and then build a very efficient natural gas combined cycle plant that could serve our snowmelt system and also allow it to grow in Holland, while we also would add to our portfolio in renewables along the way. And that really brought our community together in a very positive way. We enjoyed that process so much as a stakeholder process that we said, well, let's do it again. Let's actually think about where the plant is going to be developed. What is it going to look like? What's it going to be to our community? And so we brought together a blue ribbon panel in our community made up of neighbors of the area that we were going to be looking at, our township representatives that were kind of in the same jurisdiction, frankly, as the plant was being built, and a number of different people to sit around the table. And before we even drew what the plant would look like at all, we said, let's think about the outcomes of the big words that we really want to make sure that this plant represents. And those are first and foremost resource, a world-class energy resource for our community. Two, it's an opportunity to be a destination for people as a community-owned resource. We've had tour groups come through our facilities for years, but can we actually purposefully design this in? And it's our eastern gateway to the community. So what we do here has to represent something that's visually attractive and still a good transition to our downtown. So we had all those things in mind when we developed Holland Energy Park, and we've, I think, achieved all of that. And when we went through the process of actually building the plant, we also wanted to be very intentional all along the way of making the best use of the property that we could. The area that we acquired, 26 acres, had 61 individual properties that we had to acquire and clean up in a lot of cases. And so along the way, we took care to recycle all the different things that we could in there. We pulled fixtures out of homes that were being bought and repurposed, and those fixtures went into a local not-for-profit, Julie Ministries, for reuse in other homes. You see the recycling that happened here with a lot of concrete on site. We saved trees that were going to be part of the park setting afterward as well. As homes were, again, going to be repurposed, instead of just bringing them down, we brought law enforcement in to do exercises, SWAT exercises, rooftop fire exercises, just to make sure that we could not miss an opportunity there as well. We had at-risk youth in the community work with our general contractor, Barton Mallow, who was a Michigan company building the plant, and they were working on the trail systems around the plant as well. Again, just to do what we could to make sure that this project was leaning into every need in the community possible. We developed a microsite on our webpage so that people could track the large equipment coming in from different areas. These are the heat recovery steam generators that look like the boilers on the plant. When they came to Holland and they landed on the dock at Verplank Dock and went on a travel through the town, Tulip Time is the largest parade in Holland, and we're not going to rival that, but it was a close second because people were lining up, putting out lawn chairs, and they were following this along the parade route into our site where it landed on the crane, and then we received an applause after that. This is the site where it was built. We built an observation platform so that people in the community, whether it's grandparents with kids coming in checking out that, or maybe somebody formally from the construction industry wanted to follow what was going on site, they could do that, and it was a very popular site for people throughout the construction process. In the end, what we have is we have this park-like setting with a power plant in it, and it's a beautiful facility, and if you have a chance to come out, we certainly encourage you to come check it out. It has this beautiful outside area where we're demonstrating best practices on stormwater management. Along there, we've built certain features into the design of the plant, such as the windows to invite people in as they're driving through town to kind of wonder about what's happening inside and be inspired by that. We built a visitor center on the inside, and so we're telling the story here about great energy decisions that have happened in our community throughout its existence, and those are through the decisions that you make in the home, in our community, and in the technology that's used in the plant. Just this last year, we had 2,800 kids from school groups from schools around the area that came through and were able to tour our plant, and we have curriculum developed at every age level to complement the state's learning objectives, and so we have dedicated staff to helping with that as well, and so it's just a great asset for our community as well, and so we have achieved resource destination and gateway. And for that work, where a lot of other communities are having some challenges in terms of bringing people together here, I think you see the newspaper articles that really resulted from it really gelled our community and brought a lot of sense of pride in what we were able to do. And we also, from our Economic Development Corporation, received an innovation award for the work that we did in preparing for the growth in our economic sector in Holland as well by building this plant. And finally, the plant received an Envision rating, and if you don't know what Envision is, it's basically like LEED for infrastructure buildings. No other power plant had been rated by Envision yet, the Institute for Sustainable Infrastructure, but we were the first one to receive it, and I'm pleased to say we received the highest rating possible, which is platinum, and it really has to do with our work across the different categories there of quality of life, leadership, resource allocation, the natural world, and our climate risk. Anything that we did to try to address those categories, we're into that scoring rubric. So with that backdrop and the freshness of that plan and what it's meaning to our community, I did want to spend a little bit of time talking about the energy bills that are out there and also what we're seeing in our community as a, or the energy law rather, and what we're seeing in our community as it relates to the ability to comply with that and maybe some unique aspects of municipals that really kind of are challenged based upon the energy legislation. And my focus really is going to be on the renewable and clean energy standards out of the three bills that were part of the November 2023 package. It's the renewable energy mandates that I really want to spend a little bit of time with. And in those, I think you all know pretty well, but just a reminder here that right now we're under a 15% requirement and that moves up to 50% in 2030 and then 60% in 2035. And clean energy mandates kick in at that point with an 80%. And everything that's renewable counts as clean, and then there are other

talked about as well. Through 2034, we can actually source credits that are not tied to energy and capacity but just are independent credits anywhere throughout the regional grid operator's area. After 2035, though, that changes. And that's really what I want to spend a lot of time with is that after 2035, it has to be paired with energy and capacity in order for it to be able to be counted for the compliance. And then we also have a provision in the bill associated with large loads because as you can imagine, a municipality the size of Holland BPW or Daggett or some of these other smaller members, some of us have very large customers that represent a significant part of our demand base. And if something were to happen to that customer, that also poses unique risks from stranded cost perspective to our communities. So I want to spend a little bit of time with that. But there is a provision that if a customer represents more than 25% of your peak load, then you can use the credits that that customer obtains. But as I'm going to talk about with Holland specifically, that's a very tenuous situation. And again, just a reminder here, again, this compliance occurs with credits. I'm not to belabor it, but again, through 2034, we have this flexibility to get credits that are sourced independently. After that, they have to be paired with the energy and capacity. Now, why is that important? For Holland, we've had this period of tremendous growth. And one of the companies that you see here, LG Energy Solution, came to Holland in 2012 to build lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles. And they have an objective, and you can see the facility here is actually represented growth. By 2022, they actually added their second phase facility, and they are poised to still sometime in the future add a third phase to that. If they build all of it, it could bring LG Energy Solution to close to 40% to 50% of Holland's energy supply on an annual basis. Right now, the way they've added on their second phase, and they pivoted on their second phase from EV batteries to battery energy storage, same stuff that we're looking at for our distribution system, they're building that in Holland right now. But right now, they represent just over 20% of our energy demand. So they're not quite at that 25% level. To address risk in our community, one of the things that we did is similar to what I'm going to point out with the other members, is sometimes we don't want to be in a situation where if we make very long-term power supply commitments for one customer, they represent a very significant part of our demand, and then something happens to them, the rest of our customers then, because essentially that has to be passed on to others, that becomes a very significant risk. Just to give you an example of why municipalities are unique here in that regard, this chart shows that 15 of our members, and there's 40 of us across the state, 22 within the Michigan Public Power Agency organization, those 15 members each have a customer that represents more than 10% of their demand in one customer. It's as big as in Sebeween with Michigan Sugar that represents close to 73% of their demand. But Zeeland has Gentex, and Eaton Rapids has very large automotive Tier 1 supplier as well, and so there's very significant customer concentration among our membership. So overall, though, what's interesting is if you look at these customers on a statewide level, they only represent 1% of the state's energy demand, right? So it's still a fairly small piece of the overall energy demand on the state, very, very impactful for our communities. What we've done to address this in Holland is we've said to LG, we want you to grow. We want you to be here, and we're delivering the power to you, but we built the infrastructure under very good criteria in terms of their obligation to pay for that either up front or through a repayment on the delivery infrastructure if their load doesn't materialize. On the actual power supply, however, we've said once you get above 10%, you now have too much of a risk in terms of us having to build another power plant or going out and making very long-term commitments on power supply. So our approach with LG is simply to say we're going to pass through the wholesale market to you, allow you to go out and actually construct the portfolio that makes the most sense for you and to take on that decision about risk for you. This is not dissimilar throughout the country. This is happening really in a lot of places. If you look at throughout the country and some of the major entities of Google, Amazon, Walmart, there are companies out there that are doing virtual purchase power agreements or themselves investing in power supply. We want to encourage that. Frankly, we think that's a good solution to help mitigate risk for Holland, but still letting that economic development to occur. Now remember, though, that after 2035, the law requires us to pair energy and capacity with the credit. So that actually takes away the solution that we had for dealing with risk in Holland and putting it back on us to say, no, you can't qualify under the energy law for the accreditation unless you've actually made that commitment because a solar developer out there isn't going to say, oh, you can have it next year, but the next year after that, I know if you don't want it, that's fine. They want a 20- or 30-year commitment for us to be able to receive the power from those type of facilities. And so that really is the rub that's here. So what have we done in Holland? We've been looking at this very closely. A lot of utilities throughout the state on a periodic basis do what's called an integrated resource plan. An integrated resource plan is

title: Civil Rights, Judiciary, and Public Safety 25-12-03

The Senate Committee on Civil Rights, Judiciary, and Public Safety is called to order. Will the clerk please call and announce the roll? Chair Chang. Here. Senator Schink. Here. Senator Voino. Here. Senator Irwin. Here. Senator Santana. Here. Senator Runstad. Senator Johnson. Madam Chair, you have six members present. There is a quorum. I'll entertain a motion to adopt the committee minutes from the November 13, 2025 meeting. A motion made by Senator Schink. Without objection, the minutes are adapted. Good to see everyone here. We have four different topics that we're going to cover today. And we are going to start with the Stop the Bleed bills. They are a set of both House bills and Senate bills. House Bill 4105, 4847, and Senate Bills 590 and 591. So I will invite up Representative Frisbee as well as Cameron from Representative Preston's office and Senator Altman to join us at the table. Thank you for this bipartisan collaboration. And whenever you're ready, go ahead. Thank you, Madam Speaker and esteemed members of the committee for allowing me to testify in support of this Stop the Bleed legislation. This legislation sponsored by Representative Preston and I here in the House and the Senators Chang and Altman in the Senate empowers ordinary citizens to act in those critical first minutes after a traumatic injury before first responders arrive. Uncontrolled bleeding remains one of the leading causes of preventable death after an accident or violence. By ensuring legal protection for good Samaritans, we give our communities a real chance to save lives. This is not just about preparedness. It's about recognizing our shared responsibility to protect each other. I urge you to support this legislation because when every second counts, we want every citizen ready to act. I taught EMTs and paramedics and first aid to the public for years. Often one of the questions they asked at the end of the training, am I going to get in trouble? Can I be sued? Over simple things. We've made CPR, defibrillation and other things in first aid part of the Good Samaritan Act. Stopping bleeding is a great way to save lives and a citizen should never think twice about the legality of doing that and their protection within the Good Samaritan law. Thank you and I'll turn it over to Mr. Bruno from Representative Preston's office to elaborate further. Thank you Chair, members of the committee. I think that Representative Frisbee has really hit all the important points. So I think, well let me just start by apologizing. Representative Preston would have liked to have appeared but he has office hours today and we tried to figure out if he would be able to testify virtually but on his route today we weren't sure that he'd be in a good place with cell reception in order to stop and join you all today. So he sends his apologies that he's not able to be here. But like I said, Representative Frisbee really hit all the points. I'll just reiterate that the importance of regular people being able to feel empowered to intervene to save a life, especially when it comes to severe and traumatic bleeding, really seconds count. You know, minutes is often an extended period in these sorts of circumstances. So this law has been amended to add other protections. CPR was added in 1986, AEDs in 1999 and the opioid antagonists were added as recently as 2016. So this is a law that has been continued to be amended to reflect our understanding of life-saving techniques over time and adding tourniquets and bleeding control to the Good Samaritan law has been consistent with what the legislature has done over the last several decades. So with that, I'll turn it over to the Senator. Thank you Madam Chair and members of this esteemed committee and Senator Boynau. And I want to thank Senator Chang for allowing me to be part of this package and of course Representative Preston and Representative Frisbee. This is just a continuation of some of the things that we've done to you know, it is something that you have to be concerned about. I'm sure in the middle of what's going on, if you come upon an accident, you aren't thinking about the legalities of it. You know, a typical person is just rushing in to help. But you do need to think of those things or hopefully have those bases covered when it's all said and done. And you certainly don't want to deter anybody from being anxious about stepping in to help. And that's what this package is all about. And so I'm just happy to be part of this and thank you. Thank you all so much. I will just add that my bills are just companion and identical to Representative Frisbee's. And I know that you all have also received a good number of letters in support as well as written testimony from folks who have actually saved other people's lives using Stop the Bleed kits and recognize how important it is that we're providing this opportunity for more folks to feel that sense of comfort and ability to step in and save lives. So are there any questions from committee members? All right. Thank you all so much. Thank you. And we are going to hear from Laura Walker who is joining us on Zoom. She is with the Michigan Trauma Coalition. Hi, thanks for having me. Can you hear me okay? Yep, we can hear you. All right, thank you. My name is Laura Walker. I started out in EMS at the age of 17 in a rural community. I continued my education to become a nurse and have been a nurse for over 30 years. A large part of my job right now and as being a member of Michigan Trauma Coalition is going out into the communities and trying to stop some traumatic events from happening. And if we can't stop them, we need to learn how to put measures in place to minimize the repercussions of a traumatic injury. And that's where Stop the Bleed comes in. It's a national initiative to teach bystanders what to do in those first couple of minutes after an accident happens at your home, at your church, on your way home from work, or anywhere out in your community. It teaches bystanders how to help somebody else in those first couple of minutes with the potential of saving their lives. We teach this class out in the community, in schools, and find that it's important that everybody knows these three simple things as of putting a tourniquet on, holding pressure, or packing a wound. These three simple measures can make a huge difference in saving someone's life and will make our state safer. As we promote and teach this class out in the community, people are engaged. They want to learn. But when they hear that it's not covered under the Good Samaritan law, you see that little bit of an awkward pause. So we need to add a layer of protection for those people. You see them pause and not maybe think twice about whether they've helped save someone. Unfortunately, I just taught this class at a large business in our area, and everyone was on board. They bought the kits, but when the corporation found out that they would not be covered under the Good Samaritan law if a bystander did those three simple things of holding a pressure, packing a wound, or putting a tourniquet on, they decided to pull the kits from their area of business. Maybe overkill, but it shows you that people are concerned. So I would urge you to think about this and help support changes in the Good Samaritan law that would protect our bystanders as well as encourage students to learn the skill of stop the bleed in the classroom just like they learn CPR before they graduate, because we have the potential of saving a lot of lives and making our states safer. In the end, the only thing more tragic than a death is a death that could be prevented, and we all have the power to do that by learning stop the bleed and protecting those people with the Good Samaritan law. Thank you for your time. I'd take any questions if you have them. Thank you so much, Ms. Walker. Are there any questions from committee members? Okay. Madam Clerk, could you read in the testimony cards? Certainly. Regarding House Bill 4108, not wishing to speak in support, Sade Burton representing MDHHS. Regarding House Bill 4108, 4847, 590, and 591, Mitch Elbers representing the Michigan Association for Justice, opposed. Regarding House Bills 4108, 4847, 595, 91, Matt Saxton representing Michigan Sheriffs Association, supports. Regarding Senate Bills 590, 591, House Bill 4108, and House Bill 4847, Elizabeth Cutter representing Michigan Health and Hospital Association, support. And the last card regarding House Bill 4108, 4847, 595, 91, in support Michigan Trauma Coalition, and that is all of the cards, Madam Chair. Thank you very much. I will entertain a motion to report House Bill 4108 to the floor with recommended

that it pass. Motion made by Senator Schink. Will the clerk please call the question. Chair Chang. Yes. Senator Schink. Yes. Senator Voino. Yes. Senator Irwin. Nope. Senator Santana. Yes. I'll entertain a motion to report House Bill 4847 to the floor with a recommendation that it pass. Motion made by Senator Voino. Will the clerk please call the question. Chair Chang. Yes. Senator Schink. Yes. Senator Voino. Yes. Senator Irwin. Senator Santana. Yes. Senator Runstead. Senator Johnson. Yes. Madam Chair on the motion to report House Bill 4847. There are five yeas, zero nays. The bill is reported. All right. I'll entertain a motion to report Senate Bill 590 to the floor with a recommendation that it pass. Motion made by Senator Johnson. Will the clerk please call the question. Chair Chang. Yes. Senator Schink. Yes. Senator Voino. Yes. Senator Irwin. Senator Santana. Yes. Senator Runstead. Senator Johnson. Yes. Senator Schink. Yes. Senator Voino. Yes. Senator Irwin. Senator Santana. Yes. Senator Runstead. Senator Johnson. Yes. Madam Chair on the motion to report Senate Bill 591. There are six yeas, zero nays. The bill is reported. Thank you very much. Up next we are going to hear from Senator Santana about Senate Bill 592. Senator Santana, we're eager to hear your testimony. We will make sure the minutes accurately reflect a... On Senate Bill 591, Senator Irwin... Senator Irwin passed. Right. Senate Bill 591. Senator Santana. Thank you, colleagues. And it's an honor to be here today to talk about Senate Bill 592 of 2025. Over 11,000 prisoners are released annually from Michigan Department of Corrections. This includes individuals released after serving their sentences and those released on parole. For example, one source reports that over 11,440 prisoners were released from Michigan prisons in 2019. Releases on parole or discharge are more than 10,000 prisoners are released on parole or discharged from Michigan prisons each year, according to the Michigan state data. Reentry services are also critical, a part of that as well, because it impacts the facility's successful integration into the community as well as reducing recidivism and promoting public safety. This service provides essential supports to job training, housing, assistance, counseling, as well as access to health care and helping individuals overcome any barriers to rebuilding their lives as they reenter back into our society. By investing in comprehensive reentry programs, Michigan also can create and develop safer neighborhoods, lower incarceration rates, as well as give justice-involved individuals the opportunity to become more productive citizens of society. We as a state have also taken some initiatives as well as I just want to highlight a few of the articles that have been supportive of this legislation as well as making sure that we're doing it right here in our state. Michigan Works, for example, talks about reform, resolve, and restart. They describe how formerly incarcerated people in Michigan face big obstacles to stable employment and housing and argue for stronger safety levels of reform including housing access, reentry supports, and also records expunged to support them as well. The Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity recently awarded grants to expand housing access for justice-involved individuals. So I just wanted to highlight a couple of those things that we are doing as a state to help to provide those resources for individuals. And as we continue to see that reduction in incarceration, hopefully, in our state, it's imperative that we continue to make sure that people have their IDs, to make sure that they do have that component for rehabilitation as they do integrate back into our communities. So I'm going to digress from there, but we have several individuals who will be coming up to also support this piece of legislation, and I encourage all my colleagues to support it as well. Thank you. Thank you, Senator Santana, for your leadership on this issue. Any questions from committee members? All right. Thank you so much. We are going to next hear from Priscilla Bordeo. She is with Crime Survivors for Safety and Justice. There we go. All right. Hi, my name is Priscilla Bordeo. I am the manager of partnerships for Crime Survivors for Safety and Justice, and I'm also a victim of childhood sexual assault. What I want most is for what happened to me to never happen to anyone else. I also want what happened to the victims that I work with to never happen again. Senate Bill 592 is a short bill with a deep impact. This bill changes the statute to address the possibility that a person may be immediately discharged from custody after resentencing and allows the department to provide vital documents, including a state-issued ID, a birth certificate, reentry housing, and transitional housing to those persons subject to resentencing. Why is this bill important? Because safety is paramount to victims of violent crimes like me. We appreciate MDOC, prisoners' families, and community reentry organizations that help prepare people leaving prison with the tools and support they need to succeed. Current law does not provide MDOC with the authority to help juvenile lifers transition from prison to the community, like it does for all other people leaving MDOC. This bill changes that. These individuals may have gone to prison at the age of 17 or younger, and today they are full-grown adults. Senate Bill 592 will allow the Department of Corrections to begin the transition process sooner and play a critical role in making the transition from prison to the community safer, by connecting the prisoner access support for housing, necessary medical care, and other supports. The type of support proposed in this bill is a commonplace for everyone else leaving Michigan's prisons. This kind of help could make the difference for someone leaving prison, even helping prevent an individual from losing hope and committing a crime. As a citizen, a voter, and a victim of a violent crime, my only request of lawmakers is that you vote to give the department the tools it needs so that these newly released individuals have the opportunity for success. On behalf of crime victims in Michigan, I thank you for including our voices in this process and in this bill. I ask that you stand with us in support of the Senate Bill 592. Thank you. Thank you very much, and I'm always inspired by you using your voice and your experience to help advocate for justice and for safety. So thank you for your ongoing leadership. We have great partners around the state who work with them without state payment to try to help them. But we really, as a state, need to take on that group and help them through their transition as well. We're probably looking at less than 100 cases that we're talking about here. So the department is not seeking any additional funding to make this happen. We'll utilize our existing reentry resources and funding to get this done. But for those people that this impacts, it will be significant. It may very well be the difference between having a roof over their head and not having a roof over their head as they leave prison. Because again, of that immediate discharge in these cases. So the department fully supports the legislation. We thank the sponsor for working on it and are happy to take any questions.

Thank you very much and appreciate all the work that you're doing to help people acclimate back into the community. I guess I did have one question regarding the shorter time period that you just alluded to earlier in your testimony for folks who are being resentenced as juvenile lifers. So I think operationally these cases present a challenge no matter what, but we have done enough of these cases that we have a pretty clear sense of how we would handle them. That being said, we are a system that likes a certain amount of order, as you might imagine. What's happening is criminals are stealing large quantities of inactive gift cards from retailers. There are numerous other methods of fraud being employed as well. Our bills amend the Organized Retail Crime to broaden and expand the scope of penalties for violating the act. Acquiring possession of gift card or gift card redemption information, altering or tampering with gift card redemption information, obtaining money, goods, services, or any other thing of value from a gift card or gift card information acquired in violation of this legislation. In response to the rising gift card fraud and its associated risks, the Department of Homeland Security launched Project Red Hook to raise awareness, identified strategies of preventing tampering and scams, and hold fraudsters accountable for the crimes. Project Red Hook has led to the arrest of over 150 fraudsters engaging in gift card tampering since its launch of January in 2024 under the Biden administration. Under the state level, our Attorney General Nestle has fortunately been working hard on this, both from a prosecuting perspective as well as an educational campaign. Back in 2012, when Michigan first passed our Organized Retail Crime Act, this type of fraud was not anticipated, and especially with this level of sophistication we're seeing. By passing these two bills, we will, without question, be making Michigan better and safer. We'll ensure stronger protections for Michigan consumers, especially seniors and families, who are disproportionately targeted. We'll reduce losses to retailers, translating into fewer costs passed on to its consumers. Empower our law enforcement, giving prosecutors clear statues to chase organized fraud rings. I hope you will join me in supporting these bipartisan bills, and if you have any questions, please feel free to reach out. This is for those big organized retail organizations that are coming into play. When they launched Project Red Hook, a lot of this had to do with the Chinese government coming in in massive amounts. I think anyone who's served on one of her senior town halls or been to one of them, she has mentioned this. I appreciate the intent, but I'm interested in what's going to happen five years or ten years down the line when prosecutors and police get this law and use it to apply huge penalties to people who may have done something relatively minor. I completely understand where that question is coming from, and your concern.
