That's where the original language came from. When we first did the Organized Retail Crime Act in 2012, there's a lot of missing pieces that we've continued to move forward. I believe it was 2021 or 2022, we introduced the INFORM Act. So that was to target marketplace crimes. So as we move forward, we're probably going to have to continue to add things to this act as technology has become way more sophisticated. I tend to agree with Senator Chang that I think the language needs to be tightened up as to the specifics, like just the amounts, and then aligning that with any type of fees or whatever the potential penalty might be. Absolutely. I'll have a chat. We can talk more offline. I can work on some language for you. We've done this before in this committee, especially when we had some of our increased penalties for transit workers and things like that. So able to work with the committee and make sure that that language is tight enough. Thank you. Yeah, absolutely. Senator Johnson. Are you familiar with the theory of Q-Day? No. Okay, so I'm glad you said to keep up with what's going on technologically. There's a theory that hackers will break all of our computers with quantum computers, and it will be in the next five years. Already, our computers are attacked every single day here at the state, and we do have sensitive information, and it will impact what you're doing too, I think. So I think we all better gear up just in case there is Q-Day because it's getting worse every month with people that are trying to steal things that have the technology. Thanks for trying to protect everyone. I appreciate it. Thank you, Senator. Any other questions? Okay. Thank you very much. Thank you. Up next, we're going to hear from Drew Beardsley from the Michigan Retailers Association. Thank you, Madam Chair, members of the committee, and thank you to our sponsor for her presence and for her dedication to this issue today. She really said it all, so I don't want to belabor the point, but I'm available for any questions, especially as we talk about specificity and ways to target that. I want to make it very clear that, to your question, Senator, this is about going after, yes, individuals are going to be charged, but only in the context of putting things under the umbrella of organized retail crime. It's already illegal under the Michigan Penal Code to steal a gift card, and you could be prosecuted for that, but the prosecutors in the force team at the Attorney General's Office are focused on those individuals that are also committing the other crimes that fall under the umbrella of organized retail crime. So there'd be no incentive for going after one person that stole one grocery store gift card to buy food, whatever, as organized retail crime. But it's when we have these groups, sometimes from out of state or out of country, that are coming in and stealing mass amounts and then using that to buy products, selling those on a secondary market and falling under this category of we're seeing all these other crimes that are going with that. So it's not just the gift card fraud by itself. We want to recognize that that will also fall under this umbrella sometimes. Thank you. I appreciate that explanation. I guess if you could maybe help us, as given a couple of us are interested in seeing how we can refine the language a little bit more, do you have any thoughts on, I guess maybe a different way to ask the question is, I guess looking at gift card fraud in Michigan, what kind of range of total number of cards or dollar amounts are we looking at here in terms of what does that look like? Yeah, I mean, I think as far as dollar amounts go, it's like we said, it's in the hundreds of millions or billions. And certainly we can talk about what it would look like to have it be based on a number of cards. Typically when we see these higher profile cases, it's not just one or two cards here and there. It's like boxes full of cards. So yeah, we can have that conversation about what additional language we want to have in there to make sure that we're targeting the people that we know are committing these kinds of crimes. Much appreciated. Thank you. Senator Irwin. I wonder if you could shed some additional light on exactly what it is we're talking about here. When the representative testified, she mentioned inactive cards. Could you run through sort of how the theft is orchestrated in most of these cases? Yeah, so what you have is you would have the criminal actors going into a retail store or otherwise acquiring large quantities of cards that have not been activated yet. These are on the rack at the retail store. Steal them off the rack. You acquire the 16 digits on the back and the pin and then either re-adhere the cards or they have in some cases scanners that can get that information without having to peel off the little sticker. They hang it back on the rack, wait for somebody to go and buy it. And as soon as that person buys it and activates it, then they can digitally redeem it. And so what they're doing is they're constantly monitoring the websites where you can check your gift card balance to see what's on there. And so they're sort of spamming that over and over again to learn exactly when that card has been activated, loaded, and then they can clear it. And so what happens then on the back end for the consumer? The consumer goes in, they try to redeem their gift card, it's been emptied. What then do the retailers often do or is there not a uniform way it's dealt with? What can you share with us about that? Yeah, I would say there's not necessarily a uniform way to deal with it. I think part of the reason that this has been so pervasive is that a lot of folks that are victims of it don't know they've been the victim of organized retail crime. They think, oh, my grandma bought me a card and must not have loaded it right or we got a dud. There was some error in the process and it wasn't an assumption that, oh, man, somebody definitely stole this. And so it might vary retailer by retailer when you go back in if it was something that they can be made whole right then or grab a new card, whatever that looks like. Any other questions? Okay. Thank you very much. Thank you so much. And let's continue talking about refinements. Madam Clerk, could you read in the cards? Certainly. Regarding House Bill 4598 and 4599, not wishing to speak in support, Ashley Steffen, representing the Michigan Department of Attorney General. Also not wishing to speak in support of both bills, Matt Saxton, representing the Michigan Sheriffs Association. Again, in support, not wishing to speak, supporting both bills, Rachel Carl, representing Walmart. Not wishing to speak in support of both bills, Katie Fuller, representing Michigan Downtown Association. Not wishing to speak in support of both bills, Eric Douglas, representing the Home Depot. Not wishing to speak in support of both bills, Emily Egiscani, representing ICSC. And the last card, not wishing to speak in support of both bills, Casey Thierfelder, representing AARP. That is all the cards, Madam Chair. Senator Santana, did you have a question? Can you come back up, please? My question just dawned on me. Because this is a situation where corporations potentially are writing off the loss under taxes, I'm just wondering from a recourse standpoint, because essentially if it's a loss, right, essentially the corporation might be writing that off as a loss to business. What does that look like as far as potentially putting in some type of consumer protections for those individuals who may have been a victim of this situation? Because to me, essentially it's double dipping in some respects. So I'm just wondering. Yeah, no, I appreciate that. I think, again, we get back to the retailer might not know that this happened. Okay. You know, I mean, if it's at the checkout, somebody buys a gift card, it's activated, and that person leaves. If that doesn't get reported, the retailer doesn't know that that happened. So they can't write it off as loss if they don't know that it happened. So it's, I mean, there are multiple victims of that crime, right, from the customer that is out the money.

to the retailer that's out the money or to the gift card manufacturer. There's all the way down the line. Because essentially the victim is the consumer, correct? Yes. So then my other question for you is, has there been any conversations with the manufacturers of the gift cards to see if there's any type of other safety mechanisms that can be put in place in order to counter the technology advances of the offenses that are being taking place? Yes, absolutely. The gift card companies have been involved in that Project Red Hook that Representative Steckler spoke about. And they are advanced. I mean, there's additional improvements you can make to the gift card packaging or making it more tamper-proof. They're trying to keep up with that as well. Okay, and then my other burning thought is, I know that we have retail fraud bills too as well for just these larger situations where people are stealing things from retail stores like Home Depot and putting them online through Amazon and things of that nature. Have we taken up any legislation around those issues as well? Just like retail fraud in general? That's not for you. That's for the chair. Sure. I can't remember, so we'll have to look. I know that was a big issue for just overall. So I think if we're going to take up legislation such as this, we should probably be looking at the fraud overall. Always appreciate your insights. Thank you. Thank you. Thanks so much. Thanks again. Okay, last but not least, we are going to hear about Senate Bill 613, which is a bill that I sponsored, and I will talk about the bill from here. So this is Senate Bill 613, which creates a violent crime clearance rate grant program. And I worked on this legislation with my House counterpart, Chairwoman Sarah Leitner, and the Niskanen Center, who you'll hear from on this bill. And Senate Bill 613 is identical to House Bill 5097. And I believe you have a copy of a joint op-ed that we wrote about the bill. Across the country, even as violent crime rates are dropping, the rate at which these crimes are going unsolved is unfortunately increasing. In the 1960s, police solved roughly 90% of murders. Today, according to crime analyst Jeff Asher, about 60% of murders are solved nationwide. And non-fatal shootings fare even worse. Across the country, even as violent crime rates are dropping, the rate at which these crimes are going unsolved is unfortunately increasing. In the 1960s, police solved roughly 90% of murders. Today, according to crime analyst Jeff Asher, about 60% of murders are solved nationwide. And non-fatal shootings fare even worse. Many departments solve fewer than one in five. In Michigan, clearance rates are worse than the national average. According to state data, just over half of murders in Michigan were cleared in 2024, and just 38% of non-fatal shootings were solved that year. Michigan's clearance rates for other violent crimes are often even lower. This is not a phenomenon happening in just one city or one region, but we know that both urban and rural communities around our state are affected. According to data compiled by CSG, in Detroit, only about four out of every 10 violent crimes were solved last year. In Calhoun County, the overall violent crime clearance rate was about 56% in 2024. In Muskegon County, they cleared less than half of its violent crimes. And we have to remember that behind every unsolved case is a victim and their family who hasn't received the closure that they deserve or expect from our justice system. And someone who has committed a crime may potentially hurt more people in our communities. So Senate Bill 613 will create the Michigan Violent Crime Clearance Improvement Grant Program. And the program will help law enforcement agencies across the state get targeted resources they need to solve more violent crimes. It's a common sense, practical investment in justice and safer communities, because when violent crimes go unsolved, the result may be more violence. And we know that that deterrence, one of the main goals of our justice system, works best not necessarily because of longer, more severe sentences, but actually instead when punishment is certain, swift, and fair. In other words, if we solve more crimes and increase the feeling that a crime will be solved and the person will be caught, we might deter more crime from happening in the first place. What decades of data and failed deterrent methods have shown us is that improving clearance rates is one of the most cost-effective, evidence-based strategies to reduce violent crime. Research shows that when the likelihood of being caught goes up, crime goes down. If would-be shooters think that the police won't catch them, they're more likely to pull the trigger, no matter how severe the potential punishment is. So the Michigan Violent Crime Clearance Improvement Grant Program would provide resources in the form of grants directly to local law enforcement agencies to help them strengthen investigative capacity. Currently, law enforcement must often race against the degradation of evidence and the absence of nearby forensic expertise. So with the passage of this bill, law enforcement agencies could use the funds to hire or retain more detectives or acquire and upgrade evidence processing technology, hire crime analysts, and support witnesses to improve cooperation. We build in accountability and transparency into this legislation. And to get a grant, a law enforcement agency would submit plans for how they would use the resources to catch more violent offenders. And the Michigan State Police would track results and report annually on outcomes so we can actually have a better, clearer picture of clearance rates and see what's working and improve accountability for taxpayer dollars. And the department may contract with a third party to conduct an evaluation. We also built in language so that not more than 20% of the allocated funds could be given to any one agency and smaller agencies could join together to apply where it makes sense to share equipment or personnel. By investing in the capacity of law enforcement to solve violent crimes, we're not only taking violent offenders off the street, we'll prevent some violent crimes from happening in the first place. Polling by Arnold Ventures this fall indicates that Michiganders overwhelmingly support this proposal. 82% of voters support this proposal and support is high among Democrats, Republicans, and Independents. The same poll also showed that 75% of voters in Michigan believe the best way to prevent crime is to ensure that crimes are solved and hold people accountable through proportionate sentences, not just increasing prison sentences. So that is it for me, but happy to entertain questions. Senator Irwin. Yeah, just two questions. One, I think a really straightforward one, which is that it looks like the bill authorizes MSP to take 15% off the top for administrative costs. I'm just interested in how that number was determined. Seems higher than what is normal for a program like this, so I'm curious about that. And then also sort of more of an atmospheric question. The state of Michigan and our local governments have been investing billions and billions more over the recent decades in law enforcement. At the same time, clearance rates for violent crimes have been going down. So why would we suppose that even more investment into the same approach that we've been using and failing with is going to somehow produce the opposite result it's been producing for the last decades? Thanks very much for the questions. On the first question, the 15%, I can't exactly remember where it came from, but I know that in other bills that I've worked on where we've created grant programs, 15% has been about the average, but I'm happy to look at decreasing it. And actually, I know that one of the stakeholders we're working with actually does propose decreasing that 15% down. So I'm open to that suggestion, obviously, pending conversations with the state police about what is required to administer the grant program. As far as the second part of your question, I think that one of the reasons why I decided that I wanted to sponsor this bill is because, like you, I want to make sure that we're spending our taxpayers wisely. I want to see more accountability and transparency and best practices used by our law enforcement. And where this bill, I think, is different from other proposals that have been out there, that I have had some level of concern about, is that this is very, very targeted and is specifically looking at things that are listed in the bill, like detectives, like technology, like things that law enforcement agencies do need in order to solve more crimes. So I definitely appreciate the sentiment and where the concern is coming from. But I think that this bill is really trying to get at sort of the core things that law enforcement agencies need in order to solve more crimes. Are there other questions from committee members? Okay, thank you so much. Up next, we are going to hear from Helen Weston. She is the advocacy and research associates at the Niskanen Institute. Chairman Chang and members of the committee, thank you so much for having me and for the opportunity to speak in support of the Violent Crime Clearance Act and why improving clearance rates in Michigan helps all Michiganders. My name is Helen Weston and I'm here representing the Niskanen Center, a nonpartisan think tank based in Washington, D.C. The Niskanen Center advances an evidence-based criminal justice policy agenda to reduce the costs of crime and punishment. Our priority is to deter crime and reduce violence and thereby reduce levels of incarceration. We seek to accomplish this by building effective systems that deliver proportional punishment swiftly and

effectively and by ensuring law enforcement has the capacity to keep our neighborhoods safe. I couldn't say any better than the chairwoman. Nationally, violence crime clearance rates falls right around 50 percent, meaning if I go out and commit a violent crime, there's a 50 percent chance that I get caught. Should I be the victim of that crime, there's a 50 percent chance I receive the justice that I deserve. Low clearance rates reduce the cost of choosing to commit a violent crime in Michigan. The most important variable in crime deterrence is the perceived probability of punishment among would-be offenders. Those who believe they'll be caught don't commit crimes. Those who think they'll get away with it do. Allowing violent crimes to go unsolved sends a signal to criminals that they have a good chance of getting away with it. The result is more violence. By contrast, solving more crimes sends the opposite message. Commit a violent crime in Michigan at your own risk. The result is safer streets across the Great Lakes State. It's important to note that low clearance rates do not reflect poorly on law enforcement, who do everything in their power to bring violent criminals to justice. However, police departments, both urban and rural, are today faced with numerous challenges that have strained their capacity across the board, including the ability to investigate and solve crimes. Despite these challenges, law enforcement continues to work tirelessly to clear every offense committed in their communities. Like the chairwoman suggested, for improvements to be sustainable, especially if crime rates rise in the future, we must ensure that the resources available to law enforcement match the importance and the urgency of their work. Evidence suggests that resources are critical in solving cases, particularly those that would otherwise go unsolved. In particular, the evidence suggests investments aimed at hiring, training, and retaining homicide detectives, violent crime investigators, and non-sworn crime analysts, acquiring and upgrading forensic and investigative technology and equipment, and supporting victims, their families, and witnesses with things like funeral services, crime scene cleanup, relocation expenses, lost wage assistance, etc., to encourage cooperation with law enforcement during the investigation. The Violent Crime Clearance Act will provide law enforcement agencies in Michigan with additional resources to help them improve their ability to solve violent crimes. These resources will go to police departments of all sizes and both urban and rural jurisdictions throughout the state. The bill will also support more robust data collection and reporting on clearance rates. Finally, it requires an evaluation of policies and procedures to identify best practices that can be replicated and scaled across Michigan. Today, when a violent individual victimizes someone in Michigan, they have a decent chance of getting away with it. The answer lies in improving law enforcement's ability to identify, apprehend, and prosecute violent criminals, which will require a robust and sustained commitment to ensure that investigations are adequately resourced. Solving violent crimes is not just about accountability. It's the best way to fight violent crime. The Violent Crime Clearance Act reflects an evidence-based approach to crime reduction and will help make Michigan safer. The Niskanen Center looks forward to continuing to work with all of you and Chairwoman Chang to get this important piece of legislation on the governor's desk. Thank you. Thank you for your testimony and for all of the work they do across the country, really, to help advance criminal justice policies. Are there any questions? Senator Irwin. Thank you. I'm personally very concerned about the way that this money could be spent. I'm worried about some agencies deciding to use this new money in some new and inventive ways and whether there are any limitations on the requirements for MSP in determining who would get the money. I'm not seeing them in there, but I'm wondering if you know of any limitations in this bill that I'm not seeing or elsewhere in the country. So, for instance, it seems to me that this bill would provide source of funding that MSP could allow a community to invest in, like, surveillance technology, like a shot spotter, or like that Vision Zero thing that some people want to put in the schools that's the Palantir product, right? This would allow that, it seems to me. Would you agree? I don't know the answer to that question completely. I would like to defer to the chairwoman if she has comment. Okay, it seems to me that this would allow funding for shot spotter and other surveillance methods as long as the community said that they thought it would help them solve violent crimes, and MSP said, yeah, it might, go for it, right? That seems to be the only requirements in the law. I'm also worried about other sort of discredited methods of investigation that our state still spends a lot of money on, things like fiber analysis, bite marks, some of the fire analysis that the taxpayers spend a lot of money on, and then you later find out that, oh, that is disreputable, not good science, and now we have to go back and wrongful conviction suits and all that kind of nonsense. So I'm worried about this being a vector for creative spending on discredited methods or on methods that may be like public surveillance, that there may be some reasonable concerns that members might have. So it doesn't sound like you see anything in here that would restrict that or that would limit MSP's authority. So I'll just jump in if I can. So in the bill, we do say one of the allowable expenses would be acquiring, upgrading, or replacing technology or equipment used for evidence collection or processing or for forensic testing. In my mind, that doesn't necessarily apply to what you're talking about, but if it's helpful to explicitly prohibit the use of certain things, and the examples that you listed are things that I have concerns about as well, I'm happy to entertain adding some language around the prohibition of the use of those funds for that. Thank you, Senator. Any other questions? Okay. Thank you very much. Wonderful. Thank you. Madam Clerk, could you read in the cards? In Senate Bill 613, not wishing to speak in support, Michael Sager, representing the Michigan Fraternal Order of Police, and written testimony was provided. Again, not wishing to speak in support, Julian Snyder, representing our Street Institute, and written testimony was provided. Not wishing to speak in support of Senate Bill 613, Oakland County Sheriff Michael Bouchard, written testimony was provided. Not wishing to speak opposed to Senate Bill 613, Matt Saxton, representing the Michigan Sheriffs Association. And the last card, not wishing to speak in support of Senate Bill 613, Elliot Alessandri, representing the Prison Fellowship. That is all the cards, Madam Chair. Thank you very much. I will move to excuse the absent member. Without objection, the motion carries. Being no further business, the Senate Committee on Civil Rights, Judiciary, and Public Safety is now adjourned. Thank you.

title: Health Policy 25-12-03
transcript:
The Senate Health Policy Committee is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairman Hertel. Here. Senator Santana. Here. Senator Voigt. Here. Senator Cherry. Here. Senator Kleinfeld. Here. Senator Geis. Here. Senator Weber. Here. Senator Houck. Here. Senator Heisinga. Here. Senator Runstead. Mr. Chairman, you have six members present. There is a quorum. Thank you, Madam Clerk. I will entertain a motion to adopt the November 12, 2025 committee meeting minutes. So moved by Vice Chair Santana. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. I will also take a motion from Senator Weber to excuse absent members at this time. Without objection, absent members are excused. Today we're going to take testimony on Senate Bill 447, which is sponsored by myself. It's a bill to require insurance coverage for children with PANS Pandas. I will be that brief on the explanation of the bill because I think it is that simple and I know we have a lot of individuals who want to testify today. Given other committee meetings that are meeting today and schedules, we wanted to make sure we could get this meeting in, but we do have a hard stop at 2 o'clock. I know we have a lot of individuals who want to testify and I want to do our best to get to everybody that we can get to today. And so I would ask that people be as brief and concise as possible while making your point. And the testimony we will hear today is extremely important. So I don't want to take away from that, but I want to make sure we get to as many people as we can. So with that, I will call up Bruce Goodman to testify. And we will work our way through the list of folks that are here as well as on Zoom today. Thank you, Chairman Hertel and members of the committee. I'm Bruce Goodman from Grand Rapids, Michigan, one of the people who is heading up the Michigan PANS Pandas Alliance. I appreciate the opportunity to speak with you today. My job is to introduce the problem that Senate Bill 447 is designed to solve, a problem that many of you have already discussed with me directly or in some cases with your staff. Today you will hear from Michigan parents whose lives were turned completely upside down, sometimes literally overnight, by a medical condition known as PANS or Pandas. You will also hear from a physician who has treated hundreds of these children and has seen firsthand both the devastation of the illness and the remarkable recoveries that are possible with proper medical care. I've put before you a binder that will have a lot of the backup information that I'm going to refer to today. And I'll refer you to tabs as I go along. PANS Pandas basically is a form of sudden onset brain inflammation that occurs in children. And it's better defined at tab 1. It occurs when an infection or environmental trigger causes the child's immune system to mistakenly attack healthy brain tissue. The results can be dramatic and terrifying. Severe OCD, tics, eating refusals, emotional regression, debilitating anxiety and cognitive decline that appear almost out of nowhere. I saw this happen to my sweet 5-year-old granddaughter, Una. She went to bed as a regular happy 5-year-old. She woke up in the morning with severe OCD. She couldn't stand having her blankets be wrinkled. She started wringing her hands over and over again. Over the course of a few days, she would go outside and pick up every single stick that she saw on the ground, every single leaf. We had to carry her into stores with her eyes closed. Then it got to the point where she wouldn't eat her food unless we photographed it. She said, I want to remember that piece of chicken. And she insisted that we photograph six sides of the chicken. Well, of course, we couldn't do that. We told her that it was being done. She never asked about it. But it's just very strange, strange, strange behavior. And you'll hear from other people, different symptoms. In the extreme, the kids stop eating. When Arkansas passed a law similar to this law, it was because there was a suicide. Children do get to that point. In Colorado, before they passed the law, a pans child jumped off a parking structure and committed suicide. The parents struggle because the child that they had has been kidnapped by this particular condition. It's just heartbreaking. For years, many believed the condition affected roughly 1 in 200 children. That's the number that's been thrown around. However, newer, more rigorous studies estimate the prevalence to be closer to 1 in 11,000. And the explanation for that computation is at tab 28 of your binders. SB 447 would require Michigan health insurers to fully cover the evidence-based treatments for pans pandas. Today, insurers routinely cover antibiotics and steroids for this condition. But when the treating physician determines that a child's case is severe enough to require IVIG treatments, insurers deny or delay coverage. Now, I won't go into all the details on IVIG. It's a therapy used for the most severe and extreme cases of pans. And that's about roughly 5 to 10 percent of children. It's not the first line of treatment. I know Senator Heising and I have talked about this two or three times. It's not the first line of treatment. Antibiotics, steroids are. Tab 4 shows the extensive process by which a child is treated with antibiotics, then on to steroids and then on to IVIG. You will likely hear strong lobbying from the insurance industry against the mandate of 447. In the binder, I've attempted to respond to every argument they are likely to raise. Please use the binder when you meet with the insurance industry. What you're likely to hear from them is first, IVIG is off-label and therefore not FDA approved for this condition. That's a misleading and irrelevant argument. Off-label use of medications are commonly used for medically appropriate conditions. Tab 27 has four or five pages on this particular issue. Sometimes the insurance companies approve one IVIG treatment, but then are denying the necessary follow-up treatments, thus delaying the child's recovery. Insurance industry also makes the bogus statement that IVIG is experimental. Tab 26 shows the 11 most recent studies showing that IVIG works. Delays and denials virtually guarantee that children worsen, suffer additional brain inflammation, and ultimately require more long-term care at higher costs to insurers, school systems, and societies. 16 other states have faced this issue and adopted legislation similar to SB 447, often near unanimous votes, bipartisan efforts. Georgia, I think, voted 168 to 2 in the House in favor of this type of legislation. Louisiana voted 99 to 0 in the Senate on this bill. Tab 2 will show you the 16 states and will also show you the votes that have taken place in 2025. Those states recognize that the cost of providing appropriate medical care is minimal compared to the human and financial cost of failing to treat these children. In fact, the most recent actuarial review conducted in Virginia estimated that the cost to the insured population would be half a cent per month in additional premium costs. Actually, it was 0.46 cents in additional costs. So costs shouldn't be any part of the argument, although the insurance industry may argue that. As you hear the testimony today or as you read through the various testimonies that are in the binder,

I ask you to pay attention to the recurring theme, the extreme emotional and financial anxiety created by insurance denials and delays, and the cruelty, and there is no other word for it, of refusing a treatment that quite literally can give a child back their life. Circling back to Una, she got an IVIG treatment because she had insurance out of Maryland, and she recovered. She's a normal kid now. None of that OCD. Occasionally she'll get a cold, she'll flare, but she is cured. Again, if you read the testimonies, you'll see the parents talking about how their child has recovered. Thank you again for your time and your thoughtful consideration of SB 447, and we'll move on to our next witness. Thank you. Thank you, Bruce. I appreciate it. I appreciate the work we've been able to do together and the conversations we've had on this policy as well. Next, I will invite up Susan Youngs. I would ask, just given the time frame that we do have, if we can keep the testimony to as close to two minutes as possible for each individual. Thank you. I'm Dr. Susan Youngs. I'm a triple-boarded, certified physician. I'm the medical director of a major neurodevelopmental center in Michigan. I've served there 27 years, and I've taken care of over 300 patients with pandas and pans, and I consider myself one of the state's experts on this disorder. I've been treating kids with pandas for over 15 years, and this testimony really isn't about pandas itself. It's about what my experience has been with Michigan health insurance companies who have been systematically and increasingly blocking access to IVIG for pandas and pans patients. Let me be clear. Insurance companies are interfering with patient care, and at many times this is serious and oftentimes very dangerous to children. They are doing this despite a world of evidence that IVIG works for kids. There have been 11 studies, as Bruce referenced, and there are published guidelines in the literature, and the National Institute of Mental Health, the Pandas Physician Network, Stanford, Harvard, Mass General, Centers of Excellence, all endorse IVIG for children with pandas and pans who have moderate to severe illness, and yet the denials in Michigan have gone up. I had a really great experience when I first started treating kids with pandas and pans. For the first eight years of my career, I worked alongside Dr. Constantino at Henry Ford Hospital, and almost universally when we submitted for insurance approvals for kids with pandas and pans, we were able to get approvals. And so I felt like I was the luckiest physician in the whole world because I got to see firsthand the benefits of IVIG in my patients, and it was life-changing for them. They went from catastrophically affected children to kids who were better. So then it worked. We followed the data. We documented the outcomes. But in recent years, this has changed dramatically. Probably in the last five to six years, almost universally IVIG has been denied to our children. And if it's not denied, it's delayed for so long that the kids are having catastrophic neurologic outcomes from it. Insurers in Michigan now claim that IVIG should be only approved for one narrow form of autoimmune encephalitis. That's called anti-NMDA autoimmune encephalitis. They're really short-sighted. Their focus is very small. They don't even understand pans. They don't understand what it is. They don't understand the treatments. So in July of 2024, I personally met with the people at Blue Cross Blue Shield. These were medical directors and policy decision makers. They gave me a meeting. So we went through it. I brought evidence. I offered collaboration. I proposed solutions. I submitted all the relevant IVIG studies, none of which they read. And I explained the harm that was being done to children and to families across the state. And what was the result? No policy change, no formal response, more denials, not fewer. And even when I, a skilled physician, brought evidence to the table and said, let's collaborate on this, basically the follow-up was left, quote, open-ended. And they never followed up. So let's be clear. There's not a difference in opinion between doctors on this issue. Skilled, knowledgeable doctors who actually treat pans patients all agree that IVIG is life-changing for this disease. The leading experts on this disorder meet at a conference once a year called the Inflammatory Brain Disorders Conference. I went this year and have gone in the past. And when they present cases of pans and pans kids, it's an automatic. They just talk about, and then the kid got IVIG, and then the kid was better. In Michigan, we are way behind the times. When asked to name an FDA-approved treatment for PANS and PANDAS, they couldn't. There is no approved treatment. The denial has nothing to do with medicine and everything to do with avoiding costs. Families should not have to choose between financial ruin and watching their child lose their childhood. Sixteen other states have passed this legislation to stop these bad-faith denials, and Michigan must do the same. Please help ensure children like Madison receive the treatment their doctors prescribe, not the cheaper one insurance companies prefer. Thank you. Thank you. coverage by insurance companies. Senate Bill 584 is, I think, just a simple cleanup of our laws to reduce paperwork and unnecessary work. So this requirement on pension administrators to do this withholding was originally adopted back in 2012 on the heels of the retirement tax that Governor Snyder signed back in 2012. Well, now that that retirement tax has been repealed, this requirement is really no longer needed. And that's why we're getting rid of it. Why require our pension administrators to go through this process every year for every single person, even if it's not necessary? It was originally meant to try to get compliance with a new tax. Now that tax has been removed and the implementation of that removal is now fully integrated into our tax system. We really don't need this anymore. So it's just a simple paperwork reduction bill. Thank you, Senator. Any questions from committee members? All right. Next, we'll invite the Department of Treasury, Sean Sorenson Abbott, Legislative Liaison, David Foose, Director, Direct Taxes Division, and Jesse Kirchener, Director of Law Specialist, Indirect Tax Division. Welcome. I'm short. All right. Good afternoon, Chair Kavanaugh, members of the committee. Thank you for allowing Treasury to come speak in support of Senate Bills 583 and 584 today. I think most of you are familiar with me, but I'm Sean Sorenson Abbott, Legislative Liaison with Treasury. With me today is two of my colleagues from Treasury's Bureau of Tax Policy, David Foose, Administrator of Treasury's Direct Taxes Division, and Jesse Kirchener, Administrative Law Specialist with our Indirect Taxes Division. Senate Bill 583 and 584 before you here today are two statute modernization bills that our department has been working on this session. They're pretty simple, so this may sound a little repetitive, but just want to make sure we get our point across. I'll start with Senate Bill 583, which would give Treasury the ability to offer an electronic notice option to taxpayers who prefer to receive notices via email. As currently written, the Revenue Act requires Treasury to provide notices required by law to taxpayers via certified mail or personal delivery, that is, directly handing it to the taxpayer and hasn't been used for some time. You may have noticed that the statute does not forbid the department to provide notice electronically. However, we would still be required to provide notice via certified mail or personal delivery in addition to the electronic notice right now. I want to underscore that this would be entirely optional and would require taxpayers to proactively opt into electronic notice and provide an email address. If they wish to change the email address to receive notice, they would just be able to update that email address with Treasury, much like the current process with physical addresses. The idea for this legislation was brought forward by Treasury's Business Tax Advisory Group, which includes a wide variety of industry advocacy groups. We believe that the business community in particular may benefit from this notice email over snail mail, as mail delivery is no longer seen as the most reliable or effective method of communication. I want to also point out that this could produce meaningful savings for the state over time as well. Notice by certified mail, let alone personal delivery, is expensive. The number of official notices Treasury sends per year will fluctuate, but certified mail itself costs upwards of $9 per notice to print, insert, and mail to a taxpayer. So we really see it as a win-win for everyone. Moving on to Senate Bill 584, this proposal would remove an outdated requirement on administrators of pension and retirement systems to verify that taxpayers have satisfied the withholding tax requirements. This verification requirement was placed on retirement account administrators to help capture that expanded retirement tax passed in 2012 so that newly taxable benefits would have income tax withholding. Since then, there have been many changes to how retirement income is taxed that make this provision unnecessary. The raised subtraction limits and lowered age for subtraction makes this section no longer required for future tax years. Therefore, Senate Bill 584 effectively would make this requirement for retirement account administrators optional, effectively turning a shall into a may. This would provide some relief to those administrators who are still required to verify, despite it being extremely rare that a tax would be due. Treasury staff would also see some relief, as the department must still publish forms and instructions for a tax that generally will no longer apply to retirees. With that, thank you again for allowing me to testify, and we hope you will support these two modernization efforts.

Jesse are available as the experts if you have any technical questions. Thank you for your testimony. I know this is a very technical and kind of common sense legislation. I've been referring it Treasury Modernization Initiative or even TMI, a little too much information for how much this will change. Any questions from committee members? Senator Tice. Thank you, Madam Chair. My question just has to do with the email communication. Lots of people don't get the emails that we send them, and I understand that we have the same problem with snail mail. But once somebody has opted in and then they forget that that's what they're dealing with and they change their email, how do we know that they've received notice? Is it entirely on them? Do they end up, like what does that end up looking like? Hi, thank you for your question. So the way the statute is written, if the email has been transmitted from Treasury, then it's presumed that Treasury has done what it's required to do under the statute. So there's no confirmation of receipt on the other end for documentation that they might absolutely need with respect to their taxes. I think in effect Treasury staff, if they saw a bounce back, would address that. But this is also something that we see really commonly with physical addresses as well. People move all the time and you have to go in and change that address with Treasury. It doesn't always happen that way and we get mail sent back as well that way. But maybe moving this to a more online process, they'd have that account open and they could then change it. If they had already given us an email address, presumably they can find a way to update that as well. I think that's a lot of presumption that will end up costing people on the other end significantly if they're unaware that they're not following through in the same way that they are. I'm not saying that this isn't the way to go. I believe email is significantly better. But I have concerns that somebody, that it went to their junk folder and they didn't see it. Because you sent it out, you have an assumption that they received it and now it's entirely on them to figure out that they received an email from Treasury that they had no idea was coming. And they're supposed to search their junk box in order to ensure that it is. And then there's penalties associated with their lack of response to things that your department is sending out. So I would like us to have more safety features involved than just we assume they received it if we emailed it. Yeah, I'm happy to talk about that more. Absolutely. Thank you. And just for clarity, if someone opts out, can they opt back into the mail service? Yes, this would be absolutely an opt-in, opt-out. They'd be able to have that option. Great. And I'd love to have continued conversation of maybe a streamline of if it does bounce back, a qualification of the department instead of up to. But further conversation I'd love to. Senator Heisinger. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thanks for your testimony. Similar to Senator Kavanaugh's comments, what would exactly the process be in the event that that email did bounce back? Would you then revert and try to find them or would you move to a mail process? I don't totally know because we can't do this right now. So this is something that we'd have to develop a policy for internally. So that would be something we would have to discuss or address in the legislation. Or maybe in a substitute language. Thank you. Ongoing conversation. Thank you. Senator Irwin. Yeah, also hopefully to inform that ongoing conversation and to follow up on the question that Senator Tice asked. If you send certified mail to my address tomorrow, what's the verification that you have that I have received that? Does that have like delivery confirmation? Do I have to sign for that? Or is it just confirmation from the USPS that it's been delivered? I'm not 100% certain on that. I'd have to get back to you on that. Thank you. A lot of follow-up questions and ongoing conversations. No further questions from committee members. Thank you for your testimony. Mr. Clerk, can you please read the cards in for the record? Randy Gross, Michigan Chamber, supportive of 583. Bob Doyle, Michigan CPA Association, supportive of 583. Thank you. Being no further business, the Committee on Finance, Insurance, and Consumer Protection is now adjourned. Thank you.

title: Veterans and Emergency Services 25-12-03
transcript:
We'll call this Veterans and Emergency Services Committee to order. Clerk, could you please call the roll? Chair Kleinfeld. Here. Senator Hertel. Here. Senator Polhanky. Senator Outman. Here. Senator Lindsay. Here. Madam Chair, you have four members present. There is a quorum. And Senator Polhanky will be replacing Senator Santana on this committee. She'll be starting at the next meeting. I'll entertain a motion to adopt the committee minutes from June 11, 2025. Moved by Senator Hertel. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. Okay, so the first order of business is House Bill 4189, Representative Wolford Highways Memorial Bridge over Highway I-96 designating as Lance Corporal Michael W. Hanks Memorial Bridge. I believe we have these individuals on Zoom. We have Rep Wolford and Melissa Hanks-Ketchel to testify. Is Rep Wolford here? Yes, I am. Okay, why don't we let you go ahead and open up and then we'll let her speak. Okay, thank you. Good morning, Chair and members of the committee. Thank you for allowing me to speak on this important bill, this bridge bill, bridge naming bill. This bill, as mentioned, designates a portion of the bridge in Fowlerville that goes over 96 and Grand River to be called the Lance Corporal Michael W. Hanks Memorial Bridge. This is near and dear to my heart for multiple reasons. One, as a citizen, a patriot, and a United States Marine, as well as my wife who served in the Marine Corps and my daughter currently serving in the Marine Corps. So this has a lot of meanings to me and to our community. But Lance Corporal Hanks was a Gregory native in Michigan, a proud Michigander, a Marine, a Marine who left a lasting impact on those who served alongside of him. And I know that his sister will speak to some of those heroic events that took place and eventually took his life. He was obviously a Marine of Marines. His awards included the Silver Star, the Purple Heart, and those awards obviously speak for themselves. So today is about making sure that Michiganders never forget people, especially like Lance Corporal Hanks, who paid the ultimate price in giving his life that all of us, including us today in this meeting, have the abilities and the freedoms to sit here. And so I'm so thankful, and so I respectfully ask for your support so that we can permanently honor this United States Marine. Thank you. Thank you. Ms. Ketchel, who's the sister of Lance Corporal Hanks. Good morning. Good morning. Thank you for the opportunity to speak. It's a little early in California. I am a Michigan native and a Gold Star sister, also the president of the Michael W. Hanks Legacy Foundation and the founder of Mission Hanks, which is a national registry built to ensure families of the fallen are connected with service members and their loved ones. But most importantly today, I am the sister of Lance Corporal Michael Hanks, United States Marine Corps. I want to begin by explaining why this bridge matters. It is more than an overpass in the town of Fowlerville. That overpass is the marker of home. While we lived in Gregory, he attended Fowlerville High School, Fowlerville Elementary School, Fowlerville Middle School. Every football game he played, every baseball practice, every day of school, he went under that bridge. As an adult, when Michael flew home from California on leave, that was the exit sign that told him he was almost home. For 13 years, I've had to try to have this bridge named in his honor. My request was dismissed, delayed, or set aside over and over again. I was told it was sitting on someone's desk to wait for one person and another. And at one point, we were told that everyone thinks highway namings are an emergency, as if taking the time to honor a Marine killed in combat is an inconvenience. I've spent 13 years trying to make this happen, so I would appreciate your vote today. But let me tell you a little bit about Michael. He earned this bridge by how he lived and how he served. If you've never walked through the Battle of Fallujah with a man who survived it, it's hard to understand what they carried. Fallujah, Iraq, day 10 of the battle. The city was torn apart and still refused to fall. Every surface was pockmarked with bullets and shrapnel. The air held a heavy mix of metal and diesel and pulverized concrete. Patrick O'Donnell wrote in the book, We Were One, that the Marines were young, dirty, fearless, and old before their time. If you served with Michael, you knew that was true. He had already lived a lifetime in combat. He pulled wounded Marines out of open fire, killed insurgents prepping ambushes at close range, and he cleared enemy positions so his squad could survive. His Silver Star citation describes his actions, but citations do not capture the whole story. Sergeant James Connor told what happened in the courtyard that day. Between him and Michael was one Marine and two Iraqi National Guard partners who were fighting alongside our Marines, all alive but unable to move. There was no time to think. Out of the corner of Connor's eye, he saw Michael stand, the unspoken signal to start laying down fire. Mike, wearing nearly 100 pounds of gear, ran straight into enemy fire, scooped up the wounded Marine without stopping, and carried him over his shoulder back into the street they had come from. He kicked open a door mid-stride and delivered him to safety. That one act restored the confidence in the Iraqi National Guard who were rattled by the fight, and they set up security and held their ground. Mike came running back, dropped behind a tree just long enough to take two breaths, then he was up again. As Connor fired toward the enemy, Mike repeated the run, scoop, and shoulder move with one of the ING. After dropping him off, he did it again. Three times he exposed himself to intense enemy fire to rescue not only a fellow Marine, but two of his Iraqi partners. On November 17th, he did what he always did. He moved toward danger and ran where the firefight was thickest. He was mortally wounded in that assault. Michael Hanks died protecting Marines beside him. The men who fought with him remember the details that never make it into citations. They remember how he fought, how he never hesitated, and how he seemed untouchable until the moment he wasn't. He walked through the worst days this country has asked of its sons, and he carried people out of hell on his back. 21 years later, the men that were there still talk about him, not because he died, but because of how he lived. That is why his name belongs on that bridge. The overpass is not a random location. It is a sign that meant home to him. It was the point where he relaxed a little, knowing he was almost back into the town that raised him, the town he never made it back to, and the bridge he'd never crossed again. I'm asking you to vote yes on this bill to be part of something meaningful. Naming a bridge after someone exceptional is not a small gesture. After everything my family has been told for more than a decade, I'm asking you to finally let his name stand in the place that shaped him. Michael Hanks was here, and having his name set on that bridge allows us as a community to honor him in the place that raised him instead of leaving his memory to fade. I also want to take the time to thank Representative Woodford for carrying this bill forward and keeping the commitment he has made to my family. Thank you all for your time. Thank you. I want you to know any delay this year specifically had absolutely nothing to do with your brother not having the right to be honored in this way. We've been inundated with road-naming bills, and so we wanted to create a set of criteria of which your brother absolutely fits into to kind of weed out individuals that didn't die in service. I mean, I even got a request for a business owner. It's just so I apologize for any delay this year. Prior to that, I hadn't seen yours, but I'm really sorry for your loss coming from a military family. I'm very lucky given the amount of people in my family that have served in the military that I haven't had the same loss. I'm really sorry for yours, and I am more than happy to honor him. Does anybody else have any questions? Okay, I have one for Representative Wolford. I have a favor to ask of you. Sure. This committee over the last couple of years has continued to pass through road-naming bills that have come from Republicans in the House and the Senate. We've had one request from a Democrat on our side of the aisle for a road-naming bill for a soldier who died in Afghanistan that is sitting in the House and isn't moving because the House isn't moving Senate Democratic bills. I'm asking you to talk to Matt Hall and say this is not a partisan issue. The Senate continues to pass bills of individuals that are deserving of it without any regard to party, and I think that's the way it should be. And I just want you to know that I have concern that there's hesitation to continue doing that from some of my colleagues when the family of that particular individual

It has to sit and see that happening. So what I'd really like is I'd like to see both these bills move and I'm asking you to work on that and I will work on this one on my end. Absolutely, thank you so much. Thank you. Okay. We have one card to read in. Courtney Payne representing the Hanks family, not wishing to speak in support of House Bill 4189 and that is all the cards, Madam Chair. Thank you. And I will entertain a motion to report House Bill 4189 to the floor with recommendation that the bill pass. Moved by Senator Altman. Clerk, please call the question. Chair Kleinefelt. Yes. Senator Hertel. Yes. Senator Polhenke. Senator Altman. Yes. Senator Lindsey. Yes. Madam Chair, on the motion to report House Bill 4189, there are four yeas, zero nays. The bill is reported. And thank you, Ms. Ketchell, for taking the time to tell us your story. I think it's really important that we're reminded of them. Thank you, Rep. Wilford, for bringing this forward. Thank you so much. Okay, so now we will invite Rep. McFaul and Trent Atkins of Mutual Aid Box Alarm Systems to summarize the bills along with Chad Whitehead. I'm assuming is with Mavis? Yes. Okay, and this is on McFaul's 4302 Bill Vehicles, Emergency Vehicles, Exception to Commercial Driver's License for Authorized Emergency Vehicles of Mutual Aid Box Alarm Systems. And I want you to know I had to do a little research because yesterday I thought we're designating a specific vehicle, so I wanted to know what that vehicle was. So I've done my research, and I understand the situation. But let's go ahead and start with Rep. McFaul. Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Committee. Thank you for taking the time this morning to listen to my testimony today on HB 4301 and 4302. This bipartisan two-bill package modifies the Michigan Vehicle Code to assist the Michigan Mutual Aid Box Alarm System, also known as Mavis, with equipping and operation of their emergency vehicles. What is Mavis? The mission of Mavis is to coordinate the effective and efficient interstate and interstate mobilization and deployment of fire, emergency medical services, and special operations mutual aid resources during natural and man-made emergencies and disasters. Simply put, Mavis is a statewide mutual aid agreement that covers liability and authority to receive and provide mutual aid to other fire departments that have signed the Mavis agreement. These department resources then come from across the state or in the neighboring community. With approximately 800 members statewide, it's entirely likely that one of your communities is a member of Mavis. Through mutual aid, Michigan Mavis has the capability to provide emergency response locally or statewide when lives, property, or the environment is threatened by man-made, technological, or natural disasters or emergencies. By deploying fire resources, emergency medical services, technical rescue teams, hazardous materials teams, and other special rescue operations needed and requested by the host or stricken community. In the last few years, Michigan Mavis has been involved with the Gaylord Tornado, Midland, the Flood and Dam Failure, Hemlock, Grain Fire, Menominee, Paper Mill, Factory Fire, and most recently, the MSU Active Shooter Event. HB 5341, sorry, typo, 501, sponsored by Rep. McGoal, amends the Michigan Motor Vehicle Code to allow Michigan Mavis vehicles to operate with red, white, yellow, and green oscillating lights on the way to an emergency and on site at the emergency. My bill, HB 5302, amends the Michigan Vehicle Code and allows a Michigan Mavis employee or member to operate authorized emergency vehicles without a CDL if they have met the driving standards published under the Firefighters Training Council Act. To answer questions as to why these changes are needed to the Michigan Vehicle Code, I would like to turn the testimony over to Trent Atkins. He is the former Executive Director of Mavis and the current Emergency Management Coordinator for Shiawassee County. We cannot speak more highly enough of Trent after retiring from the Lansing Fire Department and a few other positions. He came to work for Rep. McGoal when he was sheriff and currently serves as their Emergency Management Coordinator. Rep. McGoal could not be here today. He sends his apologies, but thank you for taking the time. Okay, thank you. And before I call on you, I just want to apologize for that. I missed 4301 was Rep. McGoals and 4302 was Rep. McFalls and I missed that at the beginning. Thank you. Thank you. Go ahead. Yes, thank you for the opportunity to be here and speak to all of you. Representative McFall did a great job of describing what Mavis does. One of the things that I'd like to add to that besides being the statewide fire and emergency services mutual aid agreement and coordinating organization, we also sponsor Michigan Task Force One. Michigan Task Force One is the only Type 3 urban search and rescue team in the state of Michigan. They have responded even more recently than MSU. They supported the ice storm that took place in lower northern Michigan this spring. They bring a lot of assets from logistics to boots on the ground when they're able to support these disasters. Michigan Task Force One has also responded at the governor's request to other states throughout the country, especially during hurricanes that we've seen over the last few years and major rainstorms that have caused mass flooding and have required not only search and rescue, but river rescue as well. A couple of pieces of background on this. Currently, Mavis, specifically the vehicles that are run by Michigan Task Force One, are not recognized as emergency vehicles because we are under the Urban Cooperation Act, but we're not one specific fire department or agency that owns it. It's owned by many. And so 4301 would allow the recognition of those vehicles to be considered emergency vehicles and be allowed to have lights and sirens put on them, not necessarily because we respond around the state with lights and sirens during disasters, but because it is a safety issue when we're on the scene and being able to be identified as an emergency vehicle when we arrive is always important. And then, of course, 4302, currently, firefighters, state certified firefighters that have been through the state requirements to drive big fire trucks every day because they now step into a vehicle that is like a fire truck but not the same color of a fire truck, they now have to go through CDL training, which is really a duplication of what they're required in their current fire training to be drivers of fire trucks. The Senate Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chair Geist. Present. Senator Kleinfeld. Here. Senator Voigt. Here. Senator Hertel. So we added a section

There can't be a change at least for 10 years. Hopefully, it'll be much longer than that, but we wanted to at least have that assurance for folks. So that's really the gist of the changes. And through my own experience in other positions that I've held, I have seen government buildings named after individuals who then, unfortunately, ended up in prison for the very job that they got named after. So it's always good that the person is no longer living and you don't have to worry about that. So anyway, that's the gist of these bills is just to put some parameters. There never have been any. Members, do we have any questions? Roger, could your highways have to wait? I do believe that Senator Voino has a question. Thank you, Madam Chair. Just a quick question. Highways that presently have a name that would not meet this criteria, does the clock start 10 years for that name, and could that name be replaced 10 years from now? That name could probably be replaced 10 years from now. What we have now is it could be replaced tomorrow. But these bills won't affect it with regard to restrictions if there are roads that these restrictions didn't apply to. They were put in place before the restrictions and we're not looking backwards. Thank you, Senator. And Senate Bill 709, as Senator Kleinfeld, S2 of Senate Bill 709, as Senator Kleinfeld alluded to, sets those parameters for who is eligible for having, who or what, I should say, is eligible for having a highway or bridge or other state-controlled road named after them. As many of you know, especially those of us who were on this committee last term, my predecessor did make this attempt as well. There have been situations where, and I will admit we almost missed last year, a very key event, a historical event in the state of Michigan that is still being awaited, final passage in the other chamber. So making sure that we are also giving space for such events, whether it's a historical event or group or individual, is also necessary that it's not just people in uniform. Do we have any questions from members? Seeing no questions from members, do we have any public testimony? We do not. We do not have any testimony cards. And we have no cards.
