There being no further business before the committee, without objection, the Senate Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure is adjourned. Thank you.

title: Regulatory Affairs 25-12-02
transcript:
Didn't break this time. I am calling the Senate Committee on Regulatory Affairs to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chair Moss. Here. Senator Polanki. Senator McCann. Present. Senator Bueno. Yes. Senator Santana. Here. Senator Hertel. Here. Senator Singh. Present. Senator Houck. Here. Senator Weber. Here. Senator Lowers. Here. Senator Bolino. Go. Mr. Chair, there are 10 members present. There is a quorum. Senator Polanki, we are going to move to excuse her. I'll take the motion by Senator McCann. Without objection, Senator Polanki is excused from today's meeting. And I'll take a motion from Vice Chair Houck to adopt our committee minutes from our November 13, 2025 meeting. Without objection, committee minutes are adopted. All right, we have one vote and then testimony on four bills. So we'll go first into the vote on the bill that we heard at our last hearing. It's Senate Bill 198, sponsored by Senator Singh. Are there any further questions? I see Kurt Barron blinking in the crowd there. Anything for Kurt or for Senator Singh? Sparkling. Sparkling, blinking. Seeing none, I'll take a motion from Senator Singh to report the S-1 version of Senate Bill 198 to the floor with a recommendation that the bill pass. Will the clerk please call the question? Chair Moss. Yes. Senator Polanki. Senator McCann. Yes. Senator Bueno. Yes. Senator Santana. Yes. Senator Hertel. Yes. Senator Singh. Yes. Senator Houck. Yes. Senator Weber. Yes. Senator Lowers. Yes. Senator Bolino. Yes. Mr. Chair, there are 10 yeas, 0 nays. The bill is reported. All right, a good unanimous consumer protection bill that will move along. All right, we will then queue up our presentation from Senator Singh on Senate Bills 472 and 473 for testimony only. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair, members of the committee, for giving me the opportunity to talk about the More Jobs for Michigan package. We dropped these bills in June of this year. These are payroll tax withholding credit bills. I think many of us might be familiar with a similar type of mechanism that was developed when many of us were in the House called the Good Jobs for Michigan package. That as well was a payroll tax capture and I thought was a fairly effective tool that was created. During that period of time, we put a two-year sunset on that. We wanted to sort of give it a shot to see how it worked and then give the next governor or the next legislature an opportunity to make some modifications to the program. Unfortunately, the legislature decided not to take up the sunset bills, to change the sunset or extend the sunset on the Good Jobs for Michigan and decided they wanted to create a new tool. That tool we called SOAR. I think we've had now an opportunity to take a look at that tool over the last few years and I don't know if I've found anybody in either party or either chamber that is very excited about that program. That program has sort of lived its life and it's time for us to find different types of tools. What I wanted to do and I want to acknowledge my colleague Senator Mary Kavanaugh who worked on a similar package last year in last session on this, that we had the opportunity to take a look at revamping what was the Good Jobs for Michigan tool and make it even stronger. Today I'm going to go briefly through a PowerPoint presentation about the bills as they were introduced. I want to acknowledge that I am having conversations with the Speaker as well as the Speaker's staff on the bills that they have introduced in the House. What will eventually I think come out of those conversations will be something that is similar but probably different than what I'm presenting today. But I wanted to at least give everyone a baseline of where we're at and then as things change I'll come back to the committee and let you know what those changes are. The first thing I want to say is that this isn't just a Good Jobs for Michigan 2.0. It is different. It has different provisions. Some of the provisions, and I'll walk through these in a little bit more detail as we go through the PowerPoint, is we wanted to ensure clawback provisions on things that were inappropriate. We wanted to ensure that there were environmental protections, workforce development, MIOSHA protections. We wanted to ensure that there was a timeline for performance so just somebody didn't get a credit and then they just kept those credits and they kept them for a long period of time, never got the jobs. We want to make sure that those are moving. We want to ensure that there's ongoing compliance and then something that I thought was very important because I think some of the issues that we saw with SOAR was that we also want local feedback on the front end. We want the local community to say, yes, we want this project in our community or we want these businesses in our community. We wanted to have that local control aspect. It's not really a control, but it's an acknowledgement from the locals that this is something that is positive for the community. So what we did last session, including in this session, is that we looked at jobs and we started off initially at 50 jobs last session. But with conversations that I had with, at that time, Senator Weber as well as Senator Victory, they had asked us to take a look at smaller companies and smaller job amounts. And so we did change that to 25 new job instead of 50, that you would have to be at 175% of the prosperity of your annual salary in your prosperity region. In a slide from here, you'll see all the regions and sort of where they're at, but you'll see at least here on this slide, the Detroit metro area as well as northeastern Michigan, northern Michigan type of amount. So you get a sense. We said for larger job creations, for 250 new jobs or more, that they could have a smaller amount for the median wage, and that's at 150%. And then for projects of 1,000 new jobs or more, they would require a billion dollar investment by a company, and then there could be a higher capture time period and then take a look at 150% of the prosperity median wage. As this was thought about originally, the 1,000 job piece, there were a lot of programs at the federal level that were looking at large production opportunities. A lot of those have sort of gone to the wayside under the new administration. So I think there'll be some openness to discussion about whether that stays here in the same type of format or not, just because some of those larger opportunities might not be viable for the short term. As I mentioned, you have this in front of you, but these are sort of the prosperity regions, the median hourly wage, and you can see sort of what we're trying to do. The key here is to ensure that the jobs that are being created, the jobs that are being incentivized, are higher paying jobs than the median wage of the area. Also, because of some of my conversations with our colleagues in the Senate Republican side, I was asked to consider that maybe some of our smaller counties might never get to 150%, let alone 175% of median income. And so we created a piece here for rural areas at 135% of the median wage. Again, this is for the smaller projects, 25 new jobs, and we specifically geared that to counties of 50,000 and below. So I want to just acknowledge that those were obviously conversations I had with our Republican colleagues last session on these. We've kind of kept those here based on those conversations. As I mentioned before, there is local control. It allows for the governing body of the municipality to have to indicate support for the project, the expansion, or if there's a new location coming up, they should be able to do that. The other key here is I just want to walk through some of the compliance and clawback issues. What I always thought stronger about a payroll tax capture versus a program like SOAR is that there's no upfront money leaving the state going to the company. The company only gets to keep the payroll taxes that they would be normally sending to the state once those jobs are created. So they keep the money that they would have sent to the state instead of us

giving them money upfront. And I think a lot of the concerns that we had about other programs in the last couple of years, this piece, I think, addresses some of the concerns that I've heard from both Democrat and Republicans about no upfront money through this program. If the company fails to create the minimum number of jobs, they will never collect any of the revenue. Those jobs will have to be certified by Treasury. You have a Social Security number. They tell you who they are. These are new jobs. They can verify that. And if you don't hit your minimum requirements, you'll never be able to keep those payroll taxes. We also know in the ebb and flow of a company, sometimes you have to make cuts in a given year. If something like that happens, we look at the base employment and the new jobs. And if they don't get to maintain at least those minimum new job standards, or they have to cut some of the existing jobs, they will forfeit the tax for that year. So for those who are concerned about some of those ebbs and flows that we see in the business community, that is put here. And then, you know, I often get the question, if there's no upfront money, why do you have to claw something back? There's always a possibility of somebody maybe misrepresented something in their application, or we found out something that, hey, they said they were going to go for X and we found out they could never achieve those numbers. We want to be able to claw back any of the dollars that they did keep. And we also want to penalize them for that. And you'll see that in this legislation. Again, these are, I think, some key provisions that are different than what was in the previous good jobs piece. One of the things that my colleague, Senator Kavanaugh, was very concerned about was that some of these projects could take multiple years to sort of, they'll sign up for the credit, they don't get the credit because they have to build out perhaps a new facility, or they take a long time to hire. And so she wanted to put some really key provisions in here. And so some of these are still in here. So if you're building a new location or you're sort of building out of an existing location, we give you an opportunity to break ground within three years. The first hire has to happen within two years of the breaking of the ground, and then your minimum requirements have to be there within three years of the first hire for you to be able to keep those payroll taxes. We do think in this unique environment, especially with the tariff situation happening at the federal level, that you will see some level of consolidation from perhaps companies that have overseas facilities that they might want to bring back to Michigan, or they might want to consolidate different portions of their work. They might want to take perhaps, you know, engineers and research that perhaps in Europe, they might want to bring them to the state and kind of consolidate in an existing facility. This would allow for that. Obviously, if there's no construction requirements, there's a set of requirements there. In the legislation that was passed last session, we created some provisions to ensure that a company did not receive tax incentives if they were considerably out of compliance on environmental or by OSHA standards. That information is still included here. And then we also wanted to ensure that there was workforce requirements that are in there. So you'll see here, we want to ensure that as people are hiring new employees, especially on the new employee side, that there's a workforce development plan. We also give them credit for working with our local Michigan Works agencies, as well as other local coordinating bodies to ensure that more workers have access to these jobs. And then one of the things that is sort of newer to the conversation, but has come up from a lot of my colleagues in the conversations that we've been having has been around childcare and long-term economic development planning. And so if somebody is providing childcare or wants to use some of the investment dollars that are required for childcare, we want to be able to incentivize that. So that is an overview of sort of the new job component. There is, as I said, a retaining job portion of this. It's also a tax capture. This is not what was in any of the bills from last session. So this is new to the conversations. We wanted to take a look at, because of the opportunity for consolidation, because of the tariffs, there is more opportunity for things to sort of move back to Michigan. And we wanted to ensure that if somebody wanted to sort of protect current jobs as well as bring in other jobs back, that they could. And so what we have here are a number of items. So the company would have to maintain 50 or more full-time jobs that might be at risk to going to another state or elimination. It requires a base employment level for those protected jobs. But the key here is that there have to be making a financial investment, which is a hard financial investment. You don't just get to say, hey, we're going to potentially lose some employees and we want to protect them. You know, you have to be investing in your plant, you have to be investing in your research, and it requires a new investment in Michigan of at least $100,000 per protected employees. And we give them a five-year window for that. Then they also have to meet some of the requirements that this has to. They either have to have their North American or global headquarters here in Michigan. At least 30% of their business operations in Michigan are non-manufacturing or their principal business operations are in Michigan. So they have to meet one or more of those factors here. We heard loud and clear that, hey, this is not just about bringing new companies to Michigan. We want to protect companies that are here as well. And so we do that. So, you know, what is the benefit to the state by having this? You know, we want to ensure that, you know, we're not losing impactful jobs. We want to ensure that these new investments are going to be impactful, that they're going to be creating opportunity for employment and strengthening the economy. And then for each project, they are going to be required similar to what we do in some other tools is to do an economic model for some cost benefit to say, hey, if we did lose these jobs, what would we lose and what would it make sense? So there would have to be an ROI for this level of investment. The last slide here is that, you know, we want to ensure that the base employment and those protected jobs, we will give the, there's a duration of the agreement. We give some flexibility for how many years these tax capture dollars would be the same kind of mechanism that is located here. The business must demonstrate that they paid all their federal, state and local taxes. And then we're asking them as well as the people who will be reviewing this at the MEDC to ensure that these jobs align with our strategic plan as a state, make sure these are jobs that are in geographically disadvantaged areas. Those that will be a benefit as well. And then, you know, what is the impact of these jobs on the supply chain and what other opportunities are there for a positive return on investment, as I mentioned before. So let me just say a couple of things based on some of the conversations I've been having with our colleagues in the House. You know, I do think we've been asked both by, I think our colleagues here in the chamber, and I want to thank all of you who've talked to me about this, but also in the House of, can we look even to a smaller number? So not necessarily 25 jobs, could we get down perhaps to 10 jobs? And I think we're open to doing that. I think there's been some discussion. What do we do for the small micro business? You know, somebody that might be 10 employees or less. And we're having some conversations about how you create a separate program specifically for those businesses that's not similar to this, but could still be using a tax capture or tax credit opportunity. And so I just wanted to acknowledge a couple of those pieces that have come from our conversations, both here from senators of both sides of the aisle in the Senate, but also with our conversations with our colleagues in the House. I'm going to stop there, open for questions. We do have staff from the MEDC if there's some more technical questions that they could answer. But I wanted to spend a little bit more time. So thank you for that opportunity, Mr. Chair, members of the committee, to give you a broader overview of what we're trying to do with economic development through these tax capture bills. Thank you, Senator Singh. And as you mentioned, we do have Josh Hunt and Bree Anderson from MEDC here available for questions. I'll just lead off an incredibly thoughtful, taking in all concerns from all sides and all parties, very comprehensive presentation. I think you very much dotted the I's and crossed the T's and really kind of found a precise way to go after economic redevelopment and development in our state. I will mention this too, you know, as we've seen over several years, all this can be for nothing if there's no local buy-in. And so when it was good jobs when we were in the House or when it was SOAR my first term in the Senate, I fought for that local component. And I'm very appreciative that I didn't have to fight for it this time, that it's baked in, that this has to have local buy-in from the local community. The community is going to hold a public hearing, take a look

Although have some sort of conversation at the local level to see if the program, if the policy, if the proposal is congruent with the local community. So I don't know if you want to shed more light on that, but I think that is a key piece here that this state program really starts at the grassroots. Yeah, that's one of the things we've heard, you know, in a number of opportunities from my kind of listening sessions with our colleagues in the Senate that, hey, local control is a component of this. Some of the larger projects that were looked at, there was concern in the local communities about the projects. We didn't want to have some of that. And so, you know, we can always create stronger language if there is a desire, but we wanted to allow the local community the ability to sort of create what the right mechanism is for themselves. But we wanted to ensure that that local piece was there. You know, one thing I did want to acknowledge is I think Chris, my staff, Young, has also given you a document that we've got from MEDC that talks about other states' programs that look at payroll tax capture. So you also have that hopefully in front of you that will allow you to take a look at what's being done in Ohio and Indiana, Tennessee, New Jersey, and a couple of other states. So you can see how we're sort of building off of some programs that states that we're competing with as well. Great. Senator Lauer. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thank you, Senator Singh. I know this is something you're working hard on, and so I want my comments to be taken as constructively as they can as an employer. But so many times when we see these programs, to me I label them as steal my employees. Because in the end what it does is it takes taxpayer money and gives a, unless I'm the one qualifying for the project, it gives my competitor an advantage. And it seems a little unrealistic even how it operates because if I've got to pay somebody 150 or 175 percent of the median income wage rate, those are my employees. Even if I'm the qualifier, those are my employees. So now I've got to go hire people that are going to pay 50 to 75 percent more than you're getting if you're one of my employees, right, to qualify for this thing. So that has its challenges. You know, I don't, if these programs took people that were not working and put them to work, I would be right behind it. I would think that's great. But I have lived through enough of these programs to know what happens when a new employer comes to town and they pay a premium over the going rate, it's not the people who aren't working that go to work for this new company. It's the people that are already working for me and my other colleagues that go to work for them. And now I'm stuck with going out and trying to recruit new employees. And as an employer, if you don't know that it takes four years to make money on an employee, you've never worked with people. Because the first year you work with someone, you lose money. The second year you work with them, if they're really good, they don't lose any money. They break even. The third year you work with them, they make back the money they lost you the first year, you hope. The fourth year you work with them, they make you money. That's kind of the reality of the situation when you're hiring someone without job experience and exactly what you're paying them for. Now, these jobs probably would hire people with experience, right? And you're going to pay them premium for it. So you're not going to pay a premium of 50 to 75 percent for someone that isn't currently working in that industry. So I still struggle with how we're going to find an economic development program that doesn't pit one employer against another, that raises the whole boats, if you will, raises the tide. I would like us to find something to do. I have some other comments here that I don't want to make quote of the day, so I'm not going to share them. But I really think I agree that you have to have something in your bag, right? People go around and shop jobs. We all know that. Companies go around and shop jobs. But when we – I mean, this program actually, one of the provisions directly targets our 100-plus-old-year companies. Because we say, you know, if you're in manufacturing or I think of our sugar companies, I think of our flour mills. You know, these are businesses I'm very close to. They're over 100 years old. They've been in the state forever. They hardly ever ask for anything, but they're directly excluded. Yeah, if I could say, Senator, I appreciate that and be pleased to work with you if there's ideas that you have. One of the reasons why we have these workforce development components is to try to see how we expand the workforce. These are not just for new companies coming into Michigan. So if somebody wanted to expand their plant, let's say the sugar company wanted to expand by another 25 employees, they could make the case here. And so existing companies, we wanted to ensure that this was as useful of a tool to existing companies who want to expand. And so there's no restrictions for any Michigan-based company who wants to do that. So I do think there are a number of provisions here. I think you're absolutely right in the sense of needing a tool because we are competing in a global environment, you know, with other states, other countries. And so having a tool like this, like other states have, I think is there. I think the key, though, is these questions that have to be answered. What is the return on investment? Is this type of incentive needed to bring this company here? You know, I know I've heard some of my colleagues maybe in the other chambers say, hey, let's give a tax credit to anybody who's hiring. That's not what this is. This is like but for this incentive, we would not be coming to the state or we would not be able to expand and so forth. And that's sort of what the intent of that is. But I understand your point of view. That's why we try to create some of the provisions in here that would protect from some of that. Thank you. I don't know the feeling of not wanting to make quote of the day. I'll bring them over to you, Mr. Chairman. All right. Any other questions from committee members? We have a whole lineup of folks who are here to testify. All right. Thank you, Senator Singh. We'll call. Oh, Senator Santana. I'm sorry about that. Senator Singh off the hook that easy. That's right. Thank you for your presentation. I think one of the things that, you know, I believe that some of the things that we need to do as a state is really try to prioritize making sure that we are putting individuals who are returning citizens back to work as well because I feel that that is a missing component to our economic opportunities when it comes to employing those who have been through our administering and Department of Corrections and as far as rehabilitation of those individuals back into our society. And so one of the things that I'm looking for is just how does this jobs package help to incentivize employers across the state of Michigan to not only consider those who are returning citizens but also prioritize it as a culture for Michigan to be able to succeed because oftentimes those individuals have developed skills within the Department of Corrections that unfortunately when they're out of that system do not transfer over into job opportunities so that they can move forward in their lives. So that's one of the things that's more of a comment but also more of a criticism and also an opportunity for Michigan to be able to do things a little differently. So I'm hoping that, you know, as this package moves forward that we do see some opportunities for employers who are being incentivized through tax credits to also transition those tax dollars that we're spending locking people up into actually putting them back into society for job opportunities and growth. I appreciate that and if there's things that we can do within the existing workforce language or additional workforce language that's in these bills, I'm open to that conversation. And to your credit, we've done a lot of that work too here in the legislature and have had many packages to accelerate folks who are leaving incarceration and reducing state barriers to employment and we got more work to do. So I appreciate you highlighting that. Anything else from committee members? All right, we'll call Tim Souten, VP of Public Policy and Research, Business Leaders for Michigan. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, committee members. I greatly appreciate the opportunity to be here today to testify on this very important legislation. My name is Tim Souten and I'm here on behalf of Business Leaders for Michigan, our organization, if you're not familiar with us, is made up of the chief executives of the state's largest employers. And together, our members employ hundreds of thousands of people across the state and represent a major share of the state's economy. Our mission is straightforward. We want to make Michigan a top 10 state for jobs, education, and broadly shared prosperity. I want to begin my testimony with a very simple point, and that is that to compete effectively, Michigan needs sound fundamentals, competitive tools, and long-term consistency. The payroll tax credit created by the bills before you will work best when companies in this state can build, hire, and grow with predictability. Clear rules, reliable processes, stable policies make every incentive dollar go further. Other states have recognized this and strengthened all three areas.

and Michigan must do the same, not just for whatever the next project is, but for the next decade. Now with that perspective, there are several principles we believe should guide deliberations on this legislation. First, the program should reward high-wage job creation with flexible qualification paths that work statewide. A significant project in Alpena may look very different than one in Kalamazoo, which may look very different than one in Detroit. A well-designed tool must reflect that while maintaining strong standards. Second, eligibility should remain broad and as inclusive as possible as long as wage thresholds are met. High-wage jobs should have a consistent path to qualify with exclusions used sparingly and only when clearly justified. Third, employers need predictable, stable value with minimal proration or midstream changes. Businesses plan years ahead and sudden shifts or reductions can undermine confidence. Fourth, when employers meet their commitments, the state should honor its agreements. Reliability builds more trust, more trust attracts further investment. Fifth, the program should be simple and workable for employers of all sizes. Clear instructions, timely decisions, and straightforward administration make the tool accessible to more people across the state. But the main message and what I really want to leave you with is this key theme of the importance of consistency and sustainability. Two of our longest-term competitors and closest neighbors, Indiana and Ohio, demonstrate this very well. Their major job creation tools, the EDGE credit in Indiana and the Ohio Job Creation Tax Credit, have been in place for more than 30 years with minimal structural changes, broad political support, and predictable formula-driven rules. That stability sends a very clear and powerful message to employers that these are reliable places to invest in for the long term. Indiana and Ohio have also approached this question of retention in a very disciplined and responsible way. Retention incentives in both states are used sparingly and only when a major employer faces a credible threat of leaving and the economic risk to the region or state is substantial. This prevents overuse while ensuring that the state can act when the stakes are genuinely high. Now, any payroll credit is only one part of a broader environment that companies consider. And so, you know, other tools that this body has deliberated over the years, brownfield redevelopment, statewide site readiness, support for innovation and entrepreneurship, talent, all those things matter as well. And when Michigan strengthens these complementary tools, it increases the effectiveness of a payroll tax credit and reinforces the state's long-term competitiveness. So in the end, we support this legislation. We believe that we can quibble about some of the tinker with some of the things around the edges, but this is directionally the right thing to do. Make it flexible, make it inclusive, make it predictable, disciplined and accountable, and supported by strong overall fundamentals, and we can win more high-wage jobs, protect our existing base, and secure our long-term growth. Thank you, Mr. Chairman and Committee. I'd be happy to take any questions. Are there any questions from committee members? All right. Thank you very much, Tim. We'll call up, we have Maureen Kraus on Zoom, President and CEO, Detroit Regional Chamber, Detroit Regional Partnership, and we are setting up that Zoom screen. Just one second. Maureen, are you there? I am here. Can you hear and see me? We can hear and see you, so have at it. Perfect. Thank you so much, Mr. Chair and members of the committee. I really appreciate being with all of you today. I'm Maureen Donohue Kraus, President and CEO of the Detroit Regional Partnership. We represent the city of Detroit and the 11-county surrounding region, about 5.5 million Michigan residents. I was going to be with my partner, Randy Thalen, from The Right Place in Grand Rapids. He had to punt for a meeting, so he has gifted me with his comments as well, and I'm going to try to consolidate them in a way that makes sense for all of you. Randy and I are members of a group called Economic Development Leaders for Michigan. We are about six years old, and we represent close to over 90% of the state with our membership, the 10 largest regional economic development programs in Michigan. We are your boots-on-the-ground resource because we talk to companies, whether they are existing companies that are looking to expand or new companies coming into our state every day. And I think the one thing also to keep in mind is we're all on Team Michigan. We do not really compete against each other. I don't compete in the Detroit area with Marty Fotante in the Upper Peninsula. I rarely compete with Randy. We're all Team Michigan, and so we have been working really for the past few years looking at good jobs for Michigan, which we do believe was a very successful program. I think the only problem with it was it only lasted two years, but we have been looking for a better, more modernized income tax capture tool to encourage growth in Michigan. I will say that I appreciated what we've heard from Senator Singh. It really, you know, this is, I will say from my observation deck here, I'm grateful for the approach. I know that both sides of the aisle, both, you know, the House and the Senate, Republicans and Democrats are having these conversations on how can Michigan win more, how can we keep our companies and our talent here, as well as attracting new. It's never an either-or conversation. It's an and conversation. And so working on more jobs for Michigan is a great step in the right direction. I know it has, you know, addressed a lot of the issues. We learn every time we have a new tool, and how does it work in the real world. You know, one of the things we do is always do that benchmarking against other states. And I will say of the 10 members of Economic Development Leaders for Michigan, five of us have worked in competitor states. I spent three years in Indiana, so I'm very familiar with the EDGE program in Indiana. And what our competitors do, I always say I had a three-year internship just a few years ago in our number one competitor. Indiana and Ohio, for the purpose of this conversation, we did a comparison, which I think you've been provided a chart that sort of analyzes the differences between proposed bills here in Michigan and what Indiana and Ohio do. We know that we've fallen behind in the past few years as our tools have changed as well as just expired. But we also know that the companies we're talking to are making long-term investments and long-term decisions. And so we need to have that same approach to tools. Frequently, a project we will work on can take us 18 to 24 months from start to finish, and they don't always coincide with a legislative session. And, in fact, you know, we can't talk about a tool that expires midway through a conversation with a company. So we are always looking for, and I think you're going to hear this consistently. I know Tim addressed it. Randy certainly would have. Consistency, long-term nature, so we can work as business works. So we've looked at what, you know, Indiana and Ohio have done in particular. They have a, you know, a much clearer, better funded effort that companies can use to predict their plans. And, once again, we get asked, will you do what Indiana does, will you do what Ohio does or Tennessee? We want to be able to be in the game to win jobs. Once again, not just for attraction, but, you know, companies who are expanding also look at these other states. We know that Indiana and Ohio are up here in Michigan every week talking to our companies about a possible relocation. So just a couple of points I'd like to make in, you know, to be sensitive to the time that we have here. We would love, as regional economic developers, and we really appreciate having that local voice. We don't do a deal in a community unless we ask the community first if they're interested in it. The regional organizations can really help that process along because we work with our local communities every day. We have 348 in my region, cities, villages, and townships. We would like to be at the table to help make those decisions clearer. We also would hope

that while we have 10 prosperity regions, that the program not be capped. But if it is, we have the ability to look towards the end of the year, if we sort of allocate it by prosperity region. If someone hasn't used up their allocation, we want to get projects done throughout the state. So we'd be able to sort of reassess where the money is going and move it to where project activity is happening. The other criteria that we haven't heard, and maybe it's in there, we didn't see it in the bill, we would like this to really be net new jobs to Michigan commitment. We do not want this tool to be used to move companies from one part of the state to another. No one really wins in that. So I think it's very important that we look at net new jobs to Michigan. Once again, we're happy to continue to work with you as this is evolving and little pieces of it are debated and tweeted, happy to give our tweets, happy to give our impression of that. We are just really happy that these conversations are happening, that you have sought plenty of feedback, including from ours, and that it's being incorporated into tools that once again will help Michigan win. You'll be getting a letter from us where we sort of outlined our top 10 priorities, what was important to us. In addition to this, extending SmartZone program is important, removing the caps and continuing the transformational Brownfield program is important to maintain a competitive advantage or just to be consistent, doubling the R&D tax credit, and replacing the site readiness program with something, a tool that will work for all because that's also a very important part of what Michigan needs base level to compete, to keep our talent here, our kids here, our talent here, our companies here, and encourage growth with most innovative companies and jobs of the future. Thank you very much, and if there are any questions, I know you have other speakers, but happy to answer. Any questions for Maureen? Thank you very much, and we did have a card in from Randy Phelan, president and CEO of The Right Place that Maureen folded into her testimony, so we'll stay on Zoom. We'll go to Daniel Witt, head of state and local public policy for Lucid Motors. Can everyone hear me? Yep, we can hear and see you. Great, thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today. My name is Daniel Witt, and I lead state and local public policy efforts at Lucid Motors. Lucid is a rapidly growing electric vehicle manufacturer, and we recently opened and are quickly growing a business and engineering hub in Southfield in Oakland County. We are in the process of considering a substantial expansion of our existing footprint and investment in Michigan, an opportunity that would bring hundreds of new high-paying knowledge economy jobs to the state. These are six-figure careers with full benefits, exactly the type of and the kind of long-term talent that Michigan is seeking to attract and retain. Attracting and retaining these types of business investments starts with creating the kinds of jobs which strengthen local communities, generate tax revenue, and support Michigan's communities. Tools like an income tax capture mechanism make it possible for companies to grow here, ensuring that Michigan remains a magnet for business attraction and innovation. Lucid is actually a very recent example to this in Michigan. To give you a sense of our trajectory, in November of 2024, Lucid had fewer than 30 full-time employees in the state. Today, just 13 months later, that number has surged to nearly 300 at a facility integral to both the development of our upcoming midsize vehicles, which are designed for a much broader audience, and our autonomous technology research efforts, which will help to bring mobility to even more individuals. This growth underscores the potential for even greater hiring and investment if the right tools are in place, but candidly, the landscape is competitive, as some of the other folks have discussed, and for us as a company, we are in the position of having to consider multiple options for our future. As you evaluate some of the details of the incentive structure, we want to be on record as supporting the approach that's outlined in Senator Singh's legislation. I have personally evaluated a myriad of economic development tools and policies and state strategies, and I've been on record in meetings with many of these committee members and others in this legislature that this approach is one I deeply appreciate due to the payments being tied directly to job creation and performance. Lucid is one company that we feel very confident that we can meet the requirements set forth in this bill, and I really appreciate that we will be held accountable to deliver on the promises that we make to the state. Importantly, the program's flexibility encourages growth. Allowing a payment of up to 100% of the withholding tax capture for up to 10 years would be meaningful for us and provide that meaningful support during this crucial capital-intensive phase as we are hiring and scaling our operations in the state. By contrast, non-refundable tax credits often fail to support innovative pre-profit companies, exactly the type of businesses we think that Michigan wants to attract. These credits only have value if a company is profitable and paying significant taxes already, which typically occurs years after the initial investment in job creation. For companies in high-growth capital-intensive sectors like mobility, support is critical during the early scaling phase when hiring and investment are happening at an accelerated pace. We have experienced this in California, where Lucid hasn't been able to access an $18 million non-refundable tax credit that was awarded over five years ago, despite having achieved all the metrics in the agreement. Refundable or capture-based incentives bridge that gap and make Michigan competitive today, not years down the road. In closing, a modern performance-based incentive structure like the one contemplated in Senator Singh's legislation will help ensure Michigan continues to lead in mobility innovation, driving job creation, wage growth, and long-term economic prosperity for communities across the state. Lucid is committed to being a partner in this process, and we'd be happy to serve as a resource on implementation details or share additional insights from our experience as an innovative employer navigating competitive site selection decisions. Thank you for your time and consideration. All right, thank you. Are there questions from committee members? All right, thank you very much. We appreciate your testimony. And in person, Mike Johnston, Executive Vice President, Government Affairs and Workforce Development, Michigan Manufacturers Association. Mr. Chair and committee members, thank you for the opportunity to be here today. Senator Singh, thank you for your leadership and continued efforts to keep Michigan in the game for economic development. In the ongoing free market competition between states, Michigan must stay in the game if we want to have a chance to attract and retain large-scale investment and jobs. It's a lot like the new NIL market for college athletes. Some schools are doing very well in that market. Others who aren't playing aren't doing very well at all. Our true guiding principles in economic development include, first, Michigan must be in the game for economic development to have any chance to win new jobs and investment. And secondly, the state's investment proposals to potential investors must be competitive with the offerings of other states to have any chance to win. Mr. Chair, we have had many conversations with Senator Singh over the years on his bills. We truly appreciate his efforts, but we disagree on some of the details. In the interest of being productive, I'll lay out some ways that bills could be improved to meet the competitive standard with other states. First, we believe the 150% of the median wage requirement is too high to be competitive with other states. Even with 135% in some places and 175% with just 25 jobs, the median wage multiplier is too high. Ultimately, to grow the economy, it's not about how much people make relative to the median wage. It's about the number of jobs and the capital investment attracted and retained. We believe the high wage requirement relative to other states dissuades companies from making investments here. So the high wage approach will bring fewer jobs here. The median income is the right level if you set a level at all. Moreover, manufacturers tend to set the median wage in their areas, so setting wage standards higher than the median wage forces companies to compete against themselves for wages and benefits. It does not encourage more investment in Michigan-based companies. As we have discussed, the problem is acute in Region 10 as we have suggested averaging Region 9

intend to shave that uncompetitive peak. We are concerned about the provisions that block potential investors that have five or more notices of violation. This provision disadvantages Michigan companies as out-of-state companies that operate under less regulations are given an advantage over Michigan-based companies. In addition, bigger companies have more operations and are likely to have received more notices creating a disadvantage for them. We suggest striking this provision from Michigan companies to operate on a more level playing field. As a final point, let me be complimentary. We appreciate this bill incentivizes protected jobs. Job growth first requires retaining existing jobs. If Michigan companies grow elsewhere, they will likely take the existing jobs with them with the new growth. So incentivizing protection of existing jobs is critical to any job growth strategy. In conclusion, thank you for the opportunity to share our views today and our constructive suggestions. We appreciate Senator Singh's efforts to compete in the free market between states because if we don't play, we can't win. Thank you very much. Thank you. Are there questions from committee members? Senator Lauer. Mr. Chairman, do we have other witnesses coming forward today? Yes. Yeah, just a few more. Okay, I'll hold off then. Yep. All right. Thank you very much. And with that, we'll call up James Holman from the Mackinac Center wishing to speak opposing the bill. I think we have a document too from Mackinac Center on our desks. Yep. Again, I'm James Holman. I'm the director of fiscal policy at the Mackinac Center. And economic development programs should be judged based on whether they develop the economy more so than alternative uses of taxpayer cash. And this should be directly accountable to the state's economic outcomes. And I don't think this program is going to meet that standard, but I wanted to raise a couple of other issues about the bill that have been brought up already, one of which is about retention credits or retention tax withholding payments being part of this program. This reminds me a lot of the Michigan Economic Growth Authority because the retention credits, going from a job creation program to a job retention program is what changed MEGA from being a program that handed out tens of millions of dollars a year to a program that handed out hundreds of millions of dollars a year. It can add an incredible expense through doing retention efforts. And in part, this is because job creation deals rarely happen as expected. So we talked about the good jobs for Michigan program already. The deals in that program pledged to create 9,000 jobs. Only 500 jobs have been created under that program. Now that tells you something about the effectiveness of our job creation programs, but because payments were tied to actual job creations, it also meant we didn't spend as much on this program as expected. But if you look at the MEGA retention credits, a lot of companies met those expectations. It was far easier for companies to pledge not to eliminate jobs than for companies to actually create jobs. And so that will magnify the cost of these programs. Now, yes, the bill does require companies to assert that these jobs wouldn't happen without credits or jobs would be lost without these tax withholding certificates. However, unless the program randomly decides to deny applications for some of the applicants, that assertion can neither be tested nor trusted. And again, going back to the MEGA program, we saw that there were companies who had already made their decisions about locating to the state of Michigan before they were authorized MEGA credits despite the assertions being required. And we also saw in the rare cases where applicants were denied credits, those applicants who were ready to pledge that they wouldn't have located within the state of Michigan without special assistance located in the state of Michigan without special assistance. And so with that, with these retention credits being an issue, with this assumption that these deals are absolutely necessary for these companies to proceed, it also matters to the cost-benefit assessments that are required under this program. So unless you are modeling against accurate assumptions about what would happen in lieu of these credits, you're not going to get accurate results. In fact, these cost-benefit assessments are always going to be positive unless you model against alternative uses of taxpayer dollars and if you discount based on the idea that these might not always be determinative of the actual economic results. Now, I do think that the overall standard for judging an economic development program ought to be whether economic development programs develop the economy. It's up to you guys to determine that standard. I hope you look at this and adjust those cost-benefit assessments that are part of this bill. Thank you. Thank you. Any questions? All right, thank you very much. Some cards to read in. Brian Schoaf, Detroit Regional Chamber, not wishing to speak, supporting the bills. Beth Schoen, Michigan Forward Network, not wishing to speak, opposing the bills. Paul Jordan, representing himself, not wishing to speak, opposing the bills. And Jeff Stoutenberg from Dow Chemical, not wishing to speak, supporting the bills with amendments. Those are all of our cards. I don't know, Senator Lauer, if you have any additional comment. I just want to mention to you, Mr. Chairman, and to our sponsors, Senator Singh, that I thought what Ms. Kraus said about net new jobs is an important principle, and I wanted to acknowledge that because things so highly of my colleague, Sam Singh, and wanted to make sure that he knows that I'm looking for a way. Yeah, and I kind of gravitated to that remark, too, and I think you alluded to that in your comments as well. I think that's the goal here. Chair, it is the goal. I think we can make language that's stronger to make that solid within the bill. I agree. Two more bills quickly on our agenda that I've sponsored, Senate Bills 721 and 722. I'll call up Peter Moorman now from Treasury to help explain these bills a little bit. These both extend the sunset for the Commercial Rehabilitation Act and the Commercial Redevelopment Act. I will tell you, the very first bill I ever introduced as a House member was to eliminate the sunset for the Commercial Rehabilitation Act, and if that had passed, we wouldn't even be here right now. But instead, we extended it. It was a Senator Horn bill in 2015 that extended it for five years. It was a Senator Stamas bill in 2020 that extended it for another five years, and here we are, and this program is still successful and it still works, and how it's set up is at the local level, a local community can either identify a Commercial Rehabilitation District or Commercial Redevelopment District, and the properties within that district, they can partner with the developers. On the Commercial Rehabilitation Act, it's old and vacant properties. On the Commercial Redevelopment Act, it's replacement facilities, restored facilities, and new facilities, and work with the developer. The local government has the tools to decide how long and at what level to alleviate property taxes up to 10 years, so long as that investment is put right back into the property, and then if it's a 10-year agreement, on year 11, the property taxes pick right back up where they should be. So it's been a successful tool. I can speak to it at the local level. When I served at the local city council level, we used this numerous times to bring blighted, vacant properties back online and give the developer, alleviate some of the upfront costs while they were putting that investment into the property. In 2024 alone, 43 projects statewide were approved under the Commercial Rehab Act. Many would not have been financially viable without this tool. A few tweaks in addition to extending the sunset for another 10 years, so I won't even be here. So 10 years down the line, some other legislature will deal with this, but it will also allow for the time credit of the tax agreement to go from 10 years maximum to 12 years maximum. The reason we're doing that is it brings it in line with other tools such as the Obsolete Property Act and the Industrial Facilities Exemption provided under PA 198. So that's kind of a brief overview of an act that I made use of at the local level. I've been championing here literally for 10 years, kind of a bookend moment for me to head into the last year here still championing this, and I'll kick it over to Treasury with additional remarks. Thank you, Chair Moss, members of the committee. Also thanks to Senator Kavanaugh for being one of the sponsors and leaders in this package. I'm Peter Moorman, Director of

of the Department of Treasury. With me is Larry Steckleberg. He's the director of our Bureau of Local Government and School Services. Boy, you've covered much of what I was going to cover. But Senate Bill 721, 722, extend the sunsets to two key economic development programs, encouraging rehabilitation and redevelopment of commercial property. These are locally developed programs, a local opt-in to abate taxes generated from new investment for a specified period. Specifically, the abatements are on buildings and structures, not the underlying land. So Senate Bill 721 is the Commercial Redevelopment Act, 722, the Commercial Rehabilitation Act. You know, generally speaking, these are older, possibly vacant properties, otherwise in poor condition or would be considered obsolete. These properties are more costly to develop than, say, new construction in a greenfield parcel, therefore providing temporary property tax relief to help overcome those costs, boost the value of property, and eventually restore the redeveloped property back into local tax roll at the normal ad valorem rate. We're not the experts in economic development at Treasury, but through the State Tax Commission, we have an oversight and guidance role in administering these programs. Locally approved abatements are filed with the State Tax Commission, or in the case of the Commercial Rehabilitation Act, actually approved by the commission. So in addition to the sunset extensions, the bills do contain provisions that we've asked for to clean up some of the administrative issues that have arisen over the years, trying to streamline the processes, provide some more consistency between these statutes as well as among other similar programs. You mentioned the one provision that might be considered more substantive, which is in Senate Bill 721, extending the maximum abatement period from 10 years to 12 years. So that statute was created, I believe, in 2005. Not sure why 10 years was picked at the time, but the other ones have a maximum period of 12 years. So we just thought consistency made some sense there. Larry and I are happy to try to answer any questions you might have. And it doesn't have to be 12 years. I think the average in my local government was six years, just because that's just how each agreement worked out differently. So again, talking about the last bill, local control all the way, local decision making, but the state has the role to kind of approve these, and it's been a successful program. Any questions from committee members? Yeah, Senator Lauer. One quick one, just to distinguish on that, Mr. Chairman, are we talking about the sunset renewal is separate from the local controls, local bodies agreement? Yep, yep. And Peter can correct me if I'm wrong. You know, this program expires entirely this year, but if a local unit offered something this year and it was a 10 year agreement, that would still extend beyond the life of the expiration of the statute. Yes, so there are probably a lot of active, including 43 from 2024 alone, that are active redeveloping these properties, but there could not be a new one starting next year unless we move these bills. Correct. Yep. All right. So time's a ticking on this one. So let's see future action. I hope on this soon. One card to read in, Jen Hayes, Invest Detroit, not wishing to speak, supporting the bills. All right, that's all for our agenda today. And no further business before our committee, the Committee on Regulatory Affairs is now adjourned. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like my remarks recorded in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. Thank you, Mr. President. To you and to my fellow colleagues and to other folks here today, I'd like to call to attention the passing of a good friend of mine and somebody I owe a lot to, and that's the passing of Sandra Gunderman. She is a longtime reporter here at the Capitol, dating back into the 90s at least, maybe further back than that. Primarily, she supplied her reports to radio stations around the state of Michigan, particularly to many Christian radio networks. As somebody who grew up listening to Christian radio constantly, it was on in our barn, on in our tractors, in our house, I heard Sandra's voice and her interviewing many people over the years, including Senator Cherry's father. I remember her interviewing him, John Sr., and Tom Casper when he first started. My first exposures to Rick Jones were on Sandra Gunderman reports and so many others over the years. When I first came to Lansing after getting elected in 2010, I was out at a reception at what used to be Tropo, and I was just up there at this reception with hundreds of people packed in the place, new members, outgoing members, and I was just in a corner, people watching. And somebody asked, isn't there anybody you want to meet? I'm like, I don't know any of these people and who knows how many of them are real versus fake and superficial. And I said, you know, there's one person that I've heard from Lansing, one name I know that I've heard many times, and that was Alan Cropsey, because he was interviewed by Sandra Gunderman. And so I said, you know, I guess I'd like to meet Alan Cropsey if he's around, because I didn't know any other names. Just a guy from the UP. I didn't come down here during the campaign. I stayed up in my district. And so I said, well, Alan Cropsey's here, so they brought him over.

We were able to have a conversation because I had listened to him for so many years being interviewed by Sandra Gunderman. And he asked me if he could help me, and I said, well, I have 50-some people who have applied to work in my office. I have no idea how to choose a good staff person from who's a bad staff person. He said, come to my office tomorrow, I'll introduce you to someone. And he introduced me to Paul Burns, who's been with me since then. And, you know, Sandra just—Sandra is the reason why that happened. And then when Paul came to work for me, I said, you know, we have to meet Sandra Gunderman. And so she found out Paul worked for me, and then she never stopped calling. Never stopped calling. There were weeks where she called me every single day of the week while she'd be working on a story. And I know she called you, Mr. President. Sometimes I told her to call you because I knew you were the guy who knew what was going on with a particular story. She could find the most obscure stories and be like a dog with a bone after it. And if you had a chance to read her obituary, you see just an amazing life that she had. She's from Escanaba, grew up in a huge family. I think she had 12 siblings, became—she went to become a theater major and worked on many off-Broadway productions, dated James Earl Jones, worked with Jane Fonda in theater productions. Just an amazing life. And then got married, moved back to Michigan to the Lansing area, and after her kids were older, decided to become a reporter. And that was her career. And I talked to Curtis Hertel, and he was telling me about how his dad would interview with Sandra. And she knew where all the outlets were in the building because she worked with a tape recorder. Any of you who interviewed with her know she still used the tape recorder to do those interviews. So she was a great-hearted woman, cared about our state, cared about all of us and what was going on. And she loved bringing the news to the public, and I just wanted to offer this memorial for her. She was a very special lady. And, Mr. President, if you would do a moment of silence for her, I'd appreciate it. Thank you. Absolutely. Very memorable person, an intrepid reporter with that tape recorder. Would all members and staff please rise for a moment of silence for Sandra Gunderman? President recognizes the Senate Minority Leader, Senator Nesbitt. Thank you, Mr. President. I ask my remarks be printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. Mr. President, for years, Governor Whitmer and her allies have told us they just want common-sense gun safety plans. They've told us they respect the rights of gun owners. Well, Mr. President, last week we learned the truth. We learned the truth of what she really wants, and none of us should be shocked by this. It's the same pattern we've seen for years. This governor says the right thing on one hand and does the wrong thing on the other hand. Last week, the governor's hand-picked task force of unelected bureaucrats officially demanded what we knew they wanted all along, a total ban on certain semi-automatic firearms with certain cosmetic features. All of them banned in the state of Michigan. What exactly are these firearms? Nobody really knows. They didn't even describe them. Another shocker, they didn't say. But, Mr. President, let's call this what it is. It's not a safety plan. What this is is a stunt. Again, the governor seems more focused on scoring partisan political points for her left-wing base in order to audition for whatever her next ambition is. And as she has done time and time again, she's more than willing to trade people's rights to pad her own political resume. If Governor Whitmer thinks she can bypass the Constitution with a wish list from a radical committee, if she thinks she can criminalize the most popular sporting rifle in America and turn lawful Michiganders into felons overnight, she has another thing coming to her. Hell no, not on my watch. The Second Amendment is not a feel-good nod just to go hunting. It is about a promise of our God-given rights for self-defense. And the security of a free state. We will not give you another inch. We will not apologize defending our freedoms here at home and our country we love. We will not let this administration disarm law-abiding citizens. The President recognizes Majority Floor Leader Singh. Mr. President, I move the Senate do now adjourn. Floor Leader Singh moves that the Senate do now adjourn. Without objection, the Senate will adjourn and stand adjourned until Wednesday, December 3rd at 10 a.m. The Senate is now adjourned.
