And their profits are diminishing because the big box influences are devastating them. And the big box businesses are not good for Michigan. They're good in general, but these are people that come and invest in Michigan at a few locations. And then when they get their money, they take their money out of the state. Whereas these retailers that are Michigan people, Michigan taxpayers, Michigan citizens, they come in, they put their sweat and tears into these businesses, and then they use that money to educate their children, buy investment properties in Michigan. And we need to support these people just for the simple reason is that the efficiency of the money that they reinvest in their own cities and states and townships is important. We can't let these people go. And if you have any other questions, I'm here to answer other questions if you have them. The question's from committee members. All right. Thank you very much. We appreciate your testimony. I'm going to read in some cards. We have Jerry Griffin here again from the Midwest Independent Retailers Association wishing to speak in support of the bill. Thank you again, Mr. Chairman, Stranger, getting back up here. And we're going to have to change the M in there. Everyone keeps saying Michigan and it's Midwest. But I thank you for that. I want to come up and echo the comments made by my colleagues with the chamber. First of all, I want to thank Representative Steckloff and Representative Aragona for proposing this bill and moving it along so quickly out of the House committee. As you have heard, it was passed with significant majority of votes last session. It was even more than that. And I just want to give you something to think about as it relates to this bill. Yes, we are talking about increasing the discount that retailers would receive when purchasing liquor wholesale through the MLCC. Our members and our affiliates with the authorized distribution agents, I mean, we're all partners with MLCC to make this system work. The state of Michigan makes a handsome profit from the sale of distilled spirits. Last year it was over $400 million. We are simply asking that a modest sharing in that profit come back to our members. Our members, as it was stated, I mean, we're all family-owned businesses. I mean, they bought the buildings or leased the buildings in the communities in which they operate. They own homes there. They pay local property taxes. And as it was stated, the margins that many of our members operate on, as Senator Bellino well knows, are very small. And to compete with large big box operators, particularly in the liquor business, it is very difficult for our members to sell liquor at the state minimum price and keep their doors open. I do acknowledge that this increase in the discount would go to all licensed holders, including big box retailers. But if they're already operating and selling at the state minimum, this allows us to be a little bit more competitive with those folks as well. And it is a great point that Representative Steckloff brought up about the credit cards. That is another big hit on local businesses. Credit card usage is much higher nowadays, and the credit card fees that we pay in this country are certainly much higher than in most countries. And we are hoping that that is addressed at the federal level as well. But that is a really good point, that that really eats into whatever pennies that these small businessmen and women are making, comes off of these credit card fees. So we would certainly hope that you can move this legislation along and pass it and get along to the Senate floor very quickly. And one other thing I do want to make a point on. The increase in this discount will not cause prices to go up for consumers. This is simply the amount that when the state does their 65% markup when they purchase the liquor, this is just the discount that they're giving us for buying it from them. This is not going to result in higher prices for consumers. So I just wanted to make sure that everybody understands that point as well, and I'd be happy to answer any questions anyone has. Thank you. Are there questions? Vice Chair Houck. So you make 17% on what you sell a bottle. Is that what you're talking about? Mark it up. So what ends if you mark it up? Because you can mark it up to whatever you want to, right? Well, the 17% relates to the discount that we get from the state. The state gets a bottle for $10. They mark it up 65%. They then sell it to us at a rate 17% below that. But I mean, right now you can buy a bottle of vodka and say the state minimum is $10. You can sell it for $20, right? You can sell it for $20, but you won't be open for very long. Yeah, but there's a lot of stores that, I mean, there's very few party stores that I've been in that sell it for the state minimum. Well, and again, that's part of it. I understand that's up to them, but yeah. Okay, I was just wondering. Yeah. Okay, thank you. All right, Senator Bellino. Yes, thank you, Mr. Chair. And thank you, Senator, for telling us that people are selling above state minimum because many do if you're in a rural area and you don't sell as much liquor. But a lot of us, we sold our fifths, half gallons at the state minimum to match Meijer, but I sold my half pints and pints at more than state minimum so I could make a few more pennies. But living on a 17% markup is kind of tough. Thank you. Anything else from committee members? Vice Chair Paul Henke. When was the last time that this discount was increased? Decades? 80s, is that what was said? Yeah, 1980s. That's a long time. Thanks. All right, anything else? All right, thank you very much. Thank you. I have some cards to read in from folks who do not wish to testify. We have Dave Marvin from the Michigan Liquor Control Commission opposing the bill. We have Scott Ellis, Michigan Licensed Beverage Association supporting the bill. John McNamara, Michigan Restaurant Lodging Association supporting the bill. Matt Sowash representing Distilled Spirits Council of the U.S. Discus neutral on the bill. And Tony Mitchell, Michigan Spirits Association neutral on the bill. All right, thank you very much for the testimony on that. We will move on to Senate Bill 198 for testimony only as well, sponsored by Senator Singh and I'm sure Kurt Berryman. Why don't we call you up from the Michigan Auto Dealers Association. Thank you.

All right, thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, for listening to Senate Bill 198. This bill was something we started working on last session, and it basically does a few things. As we know, data privacy is a significant issue for all of us here in the legislature. It doesn't matter what industry you're in. As our cars have become more sophisticated, as the computers that are in our cars become more sophisticated, we want to ensure that we are protecting the data of our dealers, but also the data of our end consumers. And this bill basically creates a framework for that, which will be now the new Motor Vehicle Dealer Data Collection Act. It will take a look at a variety of things. It will ensure, for example, that manufacturers get written consent to access dealers' data systems. It establishes regulations on contracts between dealers and third parties, and it poses obligations on entities that provide dealer data systems. And so it kind of creates a comprehensive system. A number of states have recently made modifications to their system, and we were pleased to sort of work with Kurt and his association to bring this legislation forward. I want to thank Kurt and his team for working with the manufacturers to bring forward this substitute. I know that Mr. Berryman can answer any of the specific questions that might come from the committee, but I want to thank you for the opportunity to bring this in front of the chamber. Ready for you. Are you ready? Are you ready? You may proceed. All right. Yes. I don't know if I'm uneasy or very comfortable being wedged in between tobacco, liquor, and pot bills. Welcome to the Committee on Regulatory Affairs. I guess I feel right at home. Thank you, Mr. Chair. I want to thank Senator Singh for taking the lead on this important issue. As he mentioned, data is so important. I mean, how many times has this legislature, this Senate, dealt with data privacy, data breach legislation? And today, the Magnificent Seven and the New York Stock Exchange, those are all data companies. I mean, data is the money. Data is the money, and dealers have the good data. We have very good data. And rather than go into a lot of detail here, the why of the bill. Why do dealers need this bill? Probably unlike any other industry, you can probably think of one, but we are intertwined with our manufacturer partners on an auto sale, so the data, when we sell a car, the data that we gather is automatically connected to the manufacturer. So the dealers and the manufacturers share the data. What does that mean? Well, for warranty work, for recalls, for notices, for updates, for anything to do with a vehicle, we kind of share data. Now, we still have the ultimate responsibility, legally, morally, it's just important to us to protect our consumer data. So we're in a system where we're sharing data with a manufacturer. It is our customer, so we have a responsibility and a liability to protect that data. So as Senator Singh said, this legislation tries to set up, and I think it does a good job, setting up some guardrails and a program where there's definitions involved, there's allowed uses of protected data, there's allowed uses of shareable data, and I think we did a good job. I would like to thank, as Senator Singh said, worked with the Automotive Alliance and coming up with an agreement. They represent most of the manufacturers, all the main manufacturers in the nation and in the state of Michigan. They had some suggestions on allowable uses. We tried to work very hard if there is a reason that a manufacturer needs data, again, for a warranty, for recall, for notification, to really distinguish the types of data and when the uses are and when prior consent is needed from a dealer to release it. So with that, I'd be happy to answer any questions. Vice Chair Polanki. Thank you, Mr. Chair. So if this bill does not pass, what are some potential bad things that could happen or have happened with this data? Like what's the bad scenario that we want to avoid? I'm not going to out any manufacturer or OEM, but there was a very public case of data being used not properly and a fine being levied. Okay. You know, Senator, I think it's the danger with any breach that takes place. You're talking financial, you're talking all of the information involved with a car sale. For the dealers, for us, getting down to the weeds a little bit on protected data, is within our computer system, you're talking operations of the dealership, time cards, social security numbers. I mean, really getting deep, and that's why it's important that we believe that dealers are a little bit different in their relationship with the manufacturers and why this data needs to be protected and a system set up. I see. Thank you. I would just add, you know, our dealers have a lot of third-party relationships where they have vendors that they work with and so forth. And because of the very close relationship between a manufacturer and a dealer, perhaps you could see a manufacturer want to put pressure on, you know, which third-party vendor do you use or not use and so forth. And not suggesting that that has happened, but those are also levels of protection that we want to have in this legislation that sort of protects some of those relationships. Vice Chair Houck. So basically what you're saying is right now there's very – there's not really much of a limit on what a manufacturer can request from an auto dealer as far as information. Is that what you're trying to stop? You know, I would say, Senator Houck, that they have – they try to enter into shared data agreements right now. And I think that's important. What this legislation does is that, you know, there's 600 dealers, 13 manufacturers. As Senator Singh said, third-party providers that provide this information on behalf of the manufacturer. So in between the dealer and the manufacturer collecting the data. Yeah, I – Yeah, you need like a framework or some kind of a bill that says this is how it needs to process or how we need to do it. Yes. Okay. All right. Any other questions from committee members? What you have testified to is on the sub that we want to adopt. I'll just put a note that we have a card from Karen Johnson from Toyota, not wishing to speak, but supportive of the bill with the sub. So now that we have as many members as we have here, I think we can take a vote just to adopt the sub if there are any questions. It's what was reflected in the testimony. So I'll take a motion from Senator Singh to adopt the S-1 version of Senate Bill 198. Will the clerk please call the question? Chair Moss? Yes. Senator Polanky? Yes. Senator McCann? Senator Vorno? Senator Santana? Senator Hertel? Senator Singh? Senator Houck? Senator Weber? Senator Lauer? Senator Bellino? Yes. Mr. Chair, there are six yeas, zero nays. The substitute is adopted. All right, that is all the business on our agenda today. I appreciate everyone's patience, and now the Senate Committee on Regulatory Affairs is adjourned. Thank you.

title: Transportation and Infrastructure 25-11-13
transcript:
Good afternoon. The Senate Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairwoman Geis. Present. Senator Kleinfeld. Here. Senator Boehner. Here. Senator Hertel. Here. Senator Chang. Here. Senator McCann. Present. Senator Bolino. Senator McBroom. Senator Victory. Here. Senator Bumstead. Here. Madam Chairwoman, you have eight members present. There is a quorum. Thank you. I will entertain a motion to adopt the October 28th, 2025 committee meeting minutes. Motion made by Senator Bumstead. I saw his hand first. Sorry. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. I also will make a motion to excuse the absent members. And being no objection, absent members are excused. I want to thank everyone for being here and being patient with us, particularly as we are not meeting on our normal date and time. Today we are going to take up two bills and vote them out. We already heard testimony on them. We're taking up Senate Bill 507, which we heard testimony on during our October 28th meeting. Senate Bill 507 is the next of kin plate sponsored by Senator Lowers. And it would create a new plate for the family, the next of kin of a person who died serving in the armed forces. Senator Hertel is offering an amendment to the bill. Senator, would you please explain your amendment? Thank you, Madam Chair. In discussions with the department, I believe agreed to by Senator Lowers as well. This just changed the effective date to 180 days from 90 so the department has enough time to implement. Thank you. Do members have any questions about the bill? Do we have any, and we have no one scheduled to speak. Do we have any cards in support or, okay, thank you. So I need a motion to adopt, to entertain a motion to adopt the Hertel amendment to Senate Bill 507. Motion made by Senator Hertel. Will the clerk please call the question? Chairwoman Geis. Yes. Senator Kleinfeld. Yes. Senator Voino. Yes. Senator Hertel. Yes. Senator Chang. Yes. Senator McCann. Yes. Senator Bellino. Senator McBroom. Senator Victory. Yes. Senator Bumstead. Yes. Madam Chairwoman, you have eight yeas and zero nays. The amendment is adopted. Thank you, Madam Clerk. We're going to go at ease for a moment so that we can have Vice Chair, our Vice Chair up here so that he doesn't miss a vote. So we will be at ease at call of the chair. The Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure shall return to order. Now that we have adopted the SWAN of Senate Bill 507, I will now entertain a motion to report Senate Bill 507 as amended as a clean substitute to the floor with a recommendation the bill then pass. Motion made by Senator Victory. Will the clerk please call the question? Chairwoman Geis. Yes. Senator Kleinfeld. Yes. Senator Voino. Yes. Senator Hertel. Yes. Senator Chang. Yes. Senator McCann. Yes. Senator Bellino. Yes. Senator McBroom. Senator Victory. Yes. Senator Bumstead. Yes. Madam Chairwoman, you have eight yeas and zero nays. The bill is reported. Thank you, Madam Clerk. Our next bill that we will be voting out is Senate Bill 532, which we also heard testimony on during our last meeting. This bill, sponsored by Senator John Cherry, amends the Michigan Vehicle Code to allow active duty members of the U.S. Armed Forces to be issued special registration plates from the Secretary of State. Do we have any questions from committee members on this bill? Do we have any cards to read in? All right. Seeing no cards and no further testimony, I will entertain a motion to report Senate Bill 532 to the floor with a recommendation that the bill then pass. Motion made by Senator Kleinfeld. Will the clerk please call the question? Chairwoman Geis. Yes. Senator Kleinfeld. Yes. Senator Voino. Yes. Senator Hertel. Yes. Senator Chang. Yes. Senator McCann. Yes. Senator Bellino. Yes. Senator McBroom. Senator Victory. Yes. Senator Bumstead. Yes. Madam Chairwoman, you have nine yeas and zero nays. The bill is reported. Thank you, Madam Clerk. And I do want to acknowledge that we do have members who are also on reg affairs, which is meeting simultaneously, and they are also having votes today. So members who do need to leave for committee, please do so when you need to. Thank you. Okay. Our next part of today's committee hearing. We have a presentation regarding, we just lost a lot of members, so I apologize for that. We were not expecting today to be so unusual. We have a presentation regarding the federal government shutdown that was recently ended and the impact it has had on air travel. At this time, I would like to invite up Captain Justin Berg and First Officer Logan Woods, who are pilots with the Airline Pilots Association. Gentlemen. And there is a, at the base of the microphone to the right of it, there's a little button that you can press and that will turn the mic on. And thank you both for being here. And you may begin when you are ready.

Good afternoon Chair Geis and members of the committee. My name is Logan Woods from Grand Rapids and I'm a first officer for Delta Airlines based in Detroit. Joining me is Captain Justin Berg from Brighton who is also a Detroit-based Delta pilot. We'd like to thank you for the opportunity to provide you with the perspective of the Airline Pilots Association and our 80,000 commercial airline pilot members. ALPA is the world's largest pilots union as well as the world's largest non-governmental aviation safety organization. ALPA is a trusted voice at the national and international level regarding aviation safety. Whether we're ensuring that all commercial aircraft maintain at least two well-rested and well-trained pilots on the flight deck or continuing our decades-long push to install secondary barriers on commercial aircraft to help decrease the likelihood of another 9-11-style attack, safety is our top priority. During the entirety of this government shutdown, ALPA pilots stood in solidarity with our brothers and sisters at the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, with transportation security officers, and with all the federal workers who are continuing to work without a paycheck to keep our aviation system safe and secure. As ALPA President Captain Jason Ambrosi stated nearly a month ago, quote, the job of keeping aviation safe and secure is tough on an easy day, but forcing them to do it without pay undermines the safety and security of our entire system. We are at a critical moment in aviation safety and we need our leaders to be focused on the necessary infrastructure and staffing improvements, end quote. At the federal level with the shutdown ended, that means removing air traffic controllers from the discretionary budget so that their jobs and the training pipeline of future controllers are not harmed by future shutdowns. It took too long, but we are pleased that the shutdown is finally over and we have long said that FAA operations, including the workforce, should be outside of the congressional appropriations process. This level of unpredictability is unacceptable for the people who we trust to keep our skies safe. I'd like to tell you about my experience flying passengers during the shutdown. First and foremost, I can confirm that my air traffic control partners performed professionally and with the expertise that I rely on every time I operate my aircraft. The TSA employees also continued to screen passengers and crew efficiently, both in Detroit and at airports across the country. They have worked tirelessly and we have the utmost confidence in them. For nearly two months, air traffic controllers and other federal aviation workers have needlessly suffered as a result of the gridlock in Washington. The stressors on those workers have introduced risk into the system. Last night, the Federal Aviation Administration announced the cancellation and replacement of an emergency order on limitations on the use of navigable airspace. Originally, on November 5th, the FAA announced capacity cuts on airlines operating to and from the highest used airports, including Detroit Metro Airport. The new order from last night freezes in place the current capacity restraints on flights at a 6% reduction relative to the original federal order. This means that the original plans to phase in increases will end, but the FAA will lock in the current capacity cuts for affected airports, including Detroit. They will then determine when it is safe to ramp back up. For Detroit and nationwide, the shortage of controllers and the FAA order caused delays and cancellations. This led to missed connections and unnecessary risk. For example, I was flying on Sunday morning during the first measurable snow, and early in the morning there was one single ground controller in Detroit managing traffic on the ground during the first major de-icing event of the season. This ground controller had to guide planes into the de-icing queues during reduced visibility while contending with runway closures to clear the snow, as well as managing the timing delays for planes going to various airports with staffing limits. The exasperation in his voice was palpable. Elsewhere, I have seen numerous delays and cancellations due to the shutdown. Just recently, I have seen extended take-off wait times in Las Vegas due to limited staff available to control departures, and I have seen entire departure corridors closed out of the New York airports, meaning all departures in those directions were held on the ground until they had staffing available on their route. But perhaps the best example comes from Atlanta, the busiest airport in the world, where Saturday saw a weather event that was made unmanageable due to staffing that dropped the arrival rate to just 30 airplanes per hour. With five runways, Atlanta is capable of executing triple simultaneous landings and at its peak is capable of well over 200 operations per hour, which includes take-offs and landings. As expected, this slowdown led to holding, diversions, problems with flight crew duty limits, and cancellations that reverberated for days in a scenario where normal staffing would allow relatively quick resumption of operations after the weather event ended. I'd also like to note that what we call normal staffing is still understaffed, as the FAA's own numbers show a shortage of nearly 3,000 controllers, and that was before the shutdown. As pilots, I can assure you that we don't like delays more than anyone else, but we are trained to deal with ATC slowing traffic, and it is a regular occurrence. The flying public should be reassured that for each and every pilot, their safety is our number one priority, and we operate to that standard on every flight at every airport, capacity constraints or not. ALPA appreciates the opportunity to share our perspective, and as a Michigan-based pilot, I would also like to thank you for working with ALPA and the Michigan AFL-CIO to ensure that flight crew can use the recently passed Michigan paid sick time law like other Michigan workers. Thank you for your time. Thank you. And Mr. Burke? No. Yeah, you are Mr. Burke, sorry. You may begin. I came here simply to support First Officer Woods, and he speaks for all 80,000 members of the Airline Pilots Association. I have nothing to add. Thank you both for being here. It has been noted that the shutdown did end late last night. Can you talk about a little more what the lag time will be for getting things back up and running and back to normal, or I guess normal-ish, with how many people short that for staffing levels, that's not ideal. So if you could talk about what your members can expect, what the public can expect as things, even at that 6% reduced capacity, which is not ideal, but as things get more normal, what people should be expecting and how that's impacting your members. Yeah, so the 6% number is essentially the clearest indication that we have so far. It's a good thing that we're not getting up to the 10% number that is kind of where things were headed, I guess. Really, though, the FAA is going to kind of run point on when things go back fully to normal. We kind of defer to them. They were the ones running and seeing the exact numbers as far as staffing in each individual facility, but those things can also change day by day. I mean, there was a time in Orlando during the shutdown where they didn't have any controllers available for a certain period, but a lot of that change is just based on absences for the day. So all that we're really starting to see is hopefully things are approaching normal before the holiday. I know that's kind of the big, busy travel season that I can speak for myself. I'm going to be working straight through it. So I certainly hope that's the case. But yeah, I would expect just kind of a gradual wind down of the 6%. Okay, thank you. Do we have any other questions from members? Just thank you for coming. So with the 6%, do you anticipate flight cancellations or is 6% going to be manageable to – I know we have to get caught up, but with respect to existing flights, are you still anticipating flight cancellations for the next few days? Yeah, I mean, yeah, 6% is a reduction, so I would anticipate cancellations. Yes. Okay. That's right, because it's 6% of flights. Duh. I was thinking something else on the percentage. Yeah, it'd be nice if there weren't, but yeah. Yeah. Okay. There's a lot of us flying a little nervous about it. Thank you. And if I can ask one of the things I think people don't necessarily know is that – is this correct that for you and for the flight crews, the flight attendants, the folks that passengers are seeing, that you guys aren't on the clock until those doors close and you're moving to the tarmac and that it's only that time between doors closed and landing and doors opening again that you guys – so the longer you're not actually moving people – and I would have also – this probably is also true for cargo flights as well – that it's also impacting your personal bottom lines for your households and your families. And if we're cutting 6%, if we're only having 6%, those are people who might have been relying on those hours and that pay who aren't getting it. Is that a good assessment? Essentially, yeah. Every – that one's a little bit harder to speak on because within those 80,000 airline pilots that we represent, we have a lot of different pilot groups within that. So every airline is going to have their own contracts that are going to govern that in a different way. So what happens to the Delta pilots in the scenario of a delay or a cancellation, it might be different than what specifically the United

track looks like, but you are correct about getting paid from the time the door closes to the time that it opens, yes. If I might, you know, we referenced the 6% reduction now, and that's simply where the reduction stopped. And the Department of Transportation's job now is to analyze when they can allow the airlines to begin moving back towards a normal operation, and that will entirely be based on the FAA's ability to staff air traffic control centers and towers and restore the infrastructure back to something that will allow the normal staffing. And something to note is that this was so impactful personally to so many of the air traffic controllers that their retirement rate spiked tremendously during the shutdown. It's something I would like to note that this is something ALPA has been working on for several years now is to change the way that air traffic controllers are paid during a shutdown so that in the event of a future shutdown, it doesn't reduce safety, and that federal legislation is called the Aviation Funding Stability Act. It doesn't change where the money is coming from. It just changes the fact that during a shutdown, it wouldn't reduce the safety services and the safety impact of the infrastructure that we rely on for safe air travel. Thank you. And so a lot of people chose to retire. Then what does that pipeline look like? Because I understand that it is a long and arduous process, a lot of education for air traffic controllers, also for pilots. What is that lag time between filling, losing that talent and that expertise and filling those spots or even coming close to filling those spots? Well, I can say that at the beginning of last year, the FAA reported that they were over 3,000 controllers short nationwide. At this point, I don't believe even I don't have an exact number, but I don't believe they're any closer to that to filling that gap, even though there has been a significant effort to hire controllers. You are correct. The lag time is significant. And it's because even after you're hired as a controller, there's a long period of training for the specific sector that you go and work on. And that's something that the Department of Transportation is working on, the FAA is working on, but I don't think I'm the best person to answer any more specifics. I just don't have them in front of me. I'm sorry. No, thank you. I appreciate that. By sector, do you mean like sector within the industry or region? Each controller operates a sector of airspace. And so that's what I mean. All right. Clearly, I'm not going to be an air traffic controller anytime soon. That's OK. I'll see you there. I'm learning all sorts of new things. How has... Oh, I already asked that question. I'm taking my notes here and writing at the same time. Do we have any other questions from members? No? All righty. Well, I want to thank you both so much for coming. I'm like, I think many of us are probably all of us, very happy that the shutdown has come to a conclusion and that we'll get some more certainty, hopefully for our residents and the people that we all serve. And so thank you for your time. Thank you. Thank you for having us. Next, I would like to invite up Amber Hunt, who is the CFO for the Wayne County Airport Authority. Thank you so much for being here. At the bottom of your mic, at the base on the right side, there's a little black button. And you are now wired for sound. Thank you for being here. And you may begin when you're ready. All right. Thank you so much. Again, my name is Amber Hunt. I'm the Chief Financial Officer for Detroit Metro Airport. And, you know, I just like probably everybody in the room, I'm also excited and relieved that the government seems to be moving toward opening back up. You know, I echo everything that the gentleman said. As pilots, well-spoken, I'm sure that there's so much more that they could say. This has taken a significant toll on the traveling public, on the corporations, and on us at the airport as well. So with that, I would say that from an airport standpoint, you know, it's kind of hard to understand the kind of sync between the traveling public and the airlines as we are, you know, we oversee the infrastructure, all the funding for that infrastructure, try to make sure that everyone is kind of moving in the same path and making sure that the traveling public also feels safe moving through our facilities. For us, very specifically, when it comes to this reduction, just to put in perspective, the gentleman spoke about Atlanta. We have over 800 operations a day. So when you're talking about a 6% cut, that's about 50 planes coming or going, but 25 each way, that aren't going to be getting off the ground. And so, you know, that causes concerns, obviously, from a regional level, but it also creates, I'm going to say, exponential concerns about travel in general. For us at the airport, that relates to dollars. So every time a person walks through our doors, we get federal funding that's tied to that for the call passenger facility charges. When you buy a ticket, next time you look at your ticket, if you really want to dig into it, there's all the fees and taxes. It's a $4.50 fee. It's used for infrastructure completely. And so every person that doesn't get on a plane properly or gets worried about buying their tickets, it's a dollar for dollar impact to us. And that funding just doesn't exist anymore. So, you know, it's going to take, this is going to take an exponential toll, even if the, you know, as the skies are opening up, let's just say it that way, you know, people are going to skip going places during the holiday season and that you don't get to make that up. It's like, oh, well, I'm going to, you know, not go this week, but I'll go next week. That's not exactly how it works around the holidays for us. So we're going to be missing substantial funding. You know, we have about 30 million people. So just multiply that times $4 is a simple math. So, you know, that's, it's, there's going to be a long-term impact on this because it takes a little while for people to regain that trust and making sure they get from place to place. And then the second thing is we get a secondary amount of funding through AIP and that is based on our overarching numbers. So as we continue to, or as we have lost passengers, this is just pure numbers at this point, we're going to see a reduction in overarching funding again for infrastructure. And so, you know, I think that that's important for, you know, from our standpoint, along with everything that the pilots have said, there's so much complexity and I don't really want to speak on behalf of the airlines, even though I probably know more than I should about, you know, their operations. This has caused just havoc inside of the airlines. I think that all the CEOs have spoken about it. But once you put restraints on this, as, you know, seemingly needed to do, there's going to be long-term impacts to this. And so I think that that's where I think if we can, you know, anything I can do to work with anybody that wants to work through this, I am more than willing to help try to figure out how to move our essential workers, the air traffic controllers, TSA agents, you know, if they're, which they do have to go to work, people have to travel from place to place. That's just how it is. And there should never be any reason why these people don't get paid. It's not OK. You know, so I think that anything we can do to change that legislation is imperative.

Whereas it is with great admiration for her lifelong dedication to public service that we pause to mark the passing of Irma Clark Coleman. The members of the Michigan Legislature were shocked and deeply saddened by the loss of such a dedicated, driven individual who represented the people of Detroit at the state and local levels for decades. She will be remembered for her vibrant spirit and her steadfast belief in the power of public servants to make the world a better place. And whereas Irma Clark Coleman was born in rural Georgia but moved to Michigan at a young age, attending Pershing High School in Detroit and earning a bachelor's and master's degree in communications from Wayne State University. She was the first person in her family to graduate from college. In 1967, she began her career in Wayne County government, starting as an entry-level stenographer and rising to become the director of human relations. She also served as assistant director of public information for the road commission, media relations manager for former Wayne County executive William Lucas, and press secretary to county executive Edward H. McNamara. In 1991, she was appointed to the Detroit Board of Education, where she served as president from 1996 to 1998. And whereas after three decades of service at the local level, Irma Clark Coleman turned her attention to state government, being elected to represent the Detroiters of the 11th District in the House of Representatives in 1998. Her experience on the Detroit Board of Education was immediately recognized with her appointment to the Committee on Education. During her two terms in the House, she also served on the Committee on Great Lakes and Tourism and the Committee on Insurance and Financial Services. And whereas in 2002, Irma Clark Coleman sought election to the Senate, and she went on to represent the 3rd District, which included Dearborn, River Rouge, and parts of Detroit, for eight years. During her first term in the Senate, she served as minority vice chair of the Committee on Education and the Committee on Senior Citizens and Veterans Affairs. And she was a member of the Committee on Banking and Financial Institutions and the Committee on Families and Human Services. In her second term, Irma Clark Coleman was appointed to the Committee on Appropriations. She continued to lead on education issues, serving as minority vice chair of the Subcommittee on Community Colleges, as well as the Subcommittee on History, Arts, and Libraries. In addition, she served as a member of the Capital Outlay Subcommittee, the Federal Stimulus Oversight Subcommittee, the K-12 School Aid Education Subcommittee, and the Committee on Energy Policy and Public Utilities. During her tenure in the Senate, Irma Clark Coleman was appointed by Governor Jennifer Granholm to the National Education Commission of the States and the Sherry Commission on Higher Education. And whereas in her 12 years in the Michigan Legislature, Irma Clark Coleman was an advocate for children and families with a particular focus on educational reform. She repeatedly sponsored legislation to reduce class sizes in kindergarten through third grade and to require school districts to adopt specific standards for the promotion of students to the next grade. In 2004, a package of legislation, including one of Clark Coleman's bills, was enacted to permit students studying theology, divinity, or religion at certain institutions to receive state scholarships and grants. She also successfully shepherded legislation to clarify grandparenting time and to provide assistance to family members acting as guardians for abused or neglected children. And whereas Irma Clark Coleman embraced the spirit of bipartisanship and in her farewell speech mentioned many shared memories, happy and sad, with colleagues from both sides of the aisle. Perhaps the most memorable moment from her time in the legislature is when she brought the four tops, two of whom were her high school classmates, to the Senate floor to celebrate their 50th year together. Clearly, Irma Clark Coleman created strong connections with her fellow senators. And whereas following her service in the legislature, Irma Clark Coleman returned to Wayne County government. She was elected to the Wayne County Board of Commissioners in 2010, a position she held until her passing. As of 2025, she was serving as chair of the commission's Committee on Public Safety, Judiciary, and Homeland Security and the Wayne County Community Corrections Advisory Board. And whereas throughout her lifetime, Irma Clark Coleman was involved in numerous organizations and received a multitude of awards for her service to the people of Michigan. She was a life member of the NAACP, served on the Board of Directors for the Travelers Aid Society, and was co-chair of the Detroit Goodfellows Drive. She was also a member of Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, an organization she honored with a resolution on their centennial anniversary. While she volunteered with too many organizations to list, these also include the United Way, the National Association of Black County Officials, the National Alliance of Black School Educators, the Civic Center Optimist Club, and the Detroit Works Partnership. Irma Clark Coleman received the Spirit of Detroit Award from the City of Detroit, a Distinguished Service Award from the Wayne County Clerk, and

the 2005 Legislator of the Year Award from the Michigan Association of School Social Workers. And whereas we offer our sincere condolences to Irma Clark Coleman's family as they mourn her passing, Wayne County and the state of Michigan have lost an exemplary leader and public servant, but Irma Clark Coleman's legacy will live on for years to come. Colleagues, the stench emanating from the top of the Michigan State Police just keeps getting worse and more putrid every single day. This week, we learned that the agency quietly awarded a public relations contract worth more than $400,000, stretching through 2027, to none other than the former chief of staff of the current campaign advisor to gubernatorial candidate Governor Mayor Mike Duggan. $400,000 taxpayer dollars for crisis management. title: Health Policy 25-11-12
transcript:
The Senate Committee on Health Policy is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairman Hartell? Here. Senator Santana? Here. Senator Voino? Here. Senator Cherry? Here. Senator Kleinfeld? Here. Senator Geis? Senator Weber? Here. Senator Houck? Senator Heisenga? Here. Senator Runstad? Mr. Chairman, you have eight members present. There is a quorum. Thank you, Madam Clerk. I will now entertain a motion to adopt the November 5th, 2025 committee meeting minutes. So moved by Vice Chair Santana and without objection, the minutes are adopted. And I will accept a motion from Vice Chair Weber to excuse absent members at this time and seeing no objection from committee members, absent members are excused. I do want to acknowledge we have three medical students from Wayne State University with us today. Please help me welcome them here to the Health Policy Committee. Thank you very much for being with us today. We are going to now take testimony on House Bill 4309. I see Representative Preston in the audience. If you'd like to come up and testify. Please begin when you are ready. Thank you, Chair Hartell, members of the committee. I'm a little out of breath because I came running over. I just got out of my own committee meeting. I appreciate the opportunity today to talk about House Bill 4309 that would amend the Public Health Code to enter Michigan into the Physician Assistant Licensure Compact. The PA Licensure Compact is designed to remove bureaucratic barriers, streamline the process for licensed PAs looking to work across state lines or to move across state lines. The compact also, the compact works by simply giving compact privileges to PAs with out-of-state licenses. If a PA is licensed in another state and is practicing under the compact, they must follow our laws and rules or face consequences outlined in the compact and in their home state where their license resides. Under the compact, the home license state has the sole power to impose adverse action against the license. However, the other compact states can't take action against a PA's compact privilege if they are found to be violating that state's laws and or rules. Michigan would appoint a delegate who must be a PA or a member of the licensing board to the PA Licensure Compact Commission that oversees the compact nationally. The compact includes our neighbors, Wisconsin, Ohio. When we introduce other states that included Arkansas, Colorado, Kansas, Montana, Maine, Nebraska, Minnesota, Oklahoma, Washington, Utah, Virginia, West Virginia, and since introduced, we have also added Connecticut, Delaware, Iowa, North Carolina, and Tennessee. The compact is good for many reasons. It will help address health care shortages like the one our state is facing, especially underserved communities where I live, like in the UP. It will also help in communities where physician assistants struggle with dual licensure across state lines. For example, Marshfield-Dickinson Hospital, located in Iron Mountain in the Upper Peninsula, struggles with this dual licensure problem when they get short-staffed because most of their medical system is Wisconsin-based. The PAs who might otherwise be able to help don't have a Michigan license, and without the compact, they're not able to freely cross state lines. The compact will also promote continuity of care, which will help protect patients from unnecessary patient handoffs, which can sometimes lead to adverse patient outcomes. In underserved regions, this compact is going to strengthen our health care system in an exponential way. Allowing PAs to practice across state lines will help bring more providers to the state, both physically and via telehealth. Patients who travel or live near border states will especially see their outcomes improve in a big way. With that, I'm happy to answer any questions. Thank you, Representative. Any questions from committee members? Seeing none, we're going to let you off easy. Thank you very much. Next, I will invite via Zoom Jody McCollum, who is the Trauma Program Manager for UP Health System in Marquette. Jody, are you with us? I am. Hello. Can you guys hear me okay? Please begin when you're ready. We are on somewhat of a tight time frame today, and we have a lot of votes to get through before members go to other committees. So I would ask those providing testimony on the rest of this bill to please be as concise as possible. Thank you. Thank you, Chairman Hartel. Thank you for allowing me to be here on Zoom today. Again, my name is Jody McCollum. I'm the Director of Trauma Services at UP Health System Marquette. I've been a physician assistant for 23 years in the Upper Peninsula. I feel passionate about the Interstate Compact for Physician Assistants in Michigan. It's going to be very helpful for our friends, families, and neighbors in the Upper Peninsula as well as other rural areas in Michigan. Recent studies show that there are 256 health professional shortage areas in Michigan alone. Less than half of Michiganders' primary care needs are being met. Border states Wisconsin and Ohio are already part of this Interstate Compact for PAs, and we feel it's time for Michigan to join this as well. Rural areas like where I live lack access to primary care, mental health, and subspecialty services. PAs provide much-needed coverage in many of these areas, but we're limited by the state line. This bill allows PAs to provide faster, more cohesive care to Michigan families and friends. Distance, weather, and a shortage of health care providers is often a lethal triad for our families and loved ones up here in the Upper Peninsula. If you're in the rural Upper Peninsula and your primary care provider is a physician assistant, say you have a chronic illness that sometimes causes things like low blood counts, you travel to Wisconsin for vacation or taking care of an elderly loved one and need to be in Wisconsin for an extended period of time, you start to feel run down, tired, lack of energy, you're concerned about your health, you call your primary care physician assistant who's in Michigan, and generally if you were in Michigan, I would send you in a lab slip, I would check your labs, maybe order you a prescription, but because you're in Wisconsin, I can't do that. Another example is the lack of subspecialty services that are provided throughout our rural areas, things like rheumatology, certain cancer surgeries, endocrinology are just some examples of subspecialties that we do not have access to across the Upper Peninsula. So to get the expert care, you have to travel three to five hours, and if you're elderly and you have debilitating rheumatoid arthritis, this distance, this travel is just not feasible and not possible. That's how I diagnosed my first saddle PE, which is a life-threatening blood clot that is notoriously hard to detect. The ER doctor called me on that one and said, how in the world did you know? I know you is why I sent a 35-year-old healthy female for cardiac testing when she just had neck pain.
