title: Judiciary — Thursday, November 13, 2025
transcript:
The House Judiciary Committee will come to order. Clerk, please call the roll for attendance. Chair Leitner. Here. Representatives Bagold, Wozniak, Harris, DeBoer, Johnson, Schuette, Carter, Hope, Breed, Scott, Madam Chair, we do not have a quorum. The Senate Committee on Civil Rights, Judiciary, and Public Safety will come to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chair Chang. Here. Senator Schink. Here. Senator Boyer. Here. Senator Irwin. Here. Senator Santana. Here. Senator Rothstein. Here. Senator Johnson. Madam Chair, you have a four-member present. There is a quorum. Thank you very much. Senator Schink moves to approve the minutes of our November 6 meeting. There being no objection, the minutes are approved. Thank you. I'm just going to make a brief announcement. For those individuals today wishing to make public comment during this meeting, please fill out a card and give it to the clerk up here so we can have your information if we have time to call on you. If any members of the public do speak after the presentation, please remember that public comment is an opportunity to address the legislators, not interrogate others. In addition, public comment is not a question and answer session. It's simply a chance for people to speak to the legislative body. We have limited time today due to the Senate meeting and the House having additional meetings and committees, so we will be adjourning by 9.55. If we run out of time, given the length of the presentation by our invited guests, public comments are still welcome to be submitted in writing to the committee clerk, and they will be included for the record. With that, we have Tom Boyd from the State Court Administrative Offices and Mike Bosanic from Monroe. He's a Monroe County Administrator to give a presentation today on the alternative funding for trial courts. It's been a long process. I know you're no stranger to me either. This started way back in the day when I served as a county commissioner as well, so I'm looking forward to seeing what you have here and then having robust conversations in the future. Thank you very much. We'll begin by just saying thank you for inviting us. I'm Tom Boyd. It's my honor to serve as administrator for the Michigan Supreme Court. Maybe I'll try this microphone, and good morning, everyone. I'm Michael Bosanic. I'm the Monroe County Administrator and Chief Financial Officer. I've served on the Trial Court Funding Commission, appointed by Governor Snyder as a representative of the Michigan Association of Counties, and I've continued in this role trying to get to a solution to trial court funding, and great to be with you this morning. We would like especially to thank the committee for taking this matter up so promptly, for taking this matter up together, and for taking this matter up in a substantive law committee. It would be fairly easy to say, wow, this sounds like an appropriations issue, and we want to note and respect your decision to treat this as a substantive law issue. We really believe that the relationship between the courts, law enforcement, and the community can be corrupted by the way that we handle our finances. In fact, if you read the Detroit News this past weekend, you saw the article entitled Interactions Between Cops and Citizens are Becoming More Dangerous in Michigan. One of our premises is we can end profit-motivated policing and profit-motivated courts by changing the way the money flows, not giving anybody a free ride, not even changing some of the competitive philosophical issues that the committee will eventually face, trying to chart a middle path through what might be disagreement to a way that we can fund the courts without agitating the conflict between the courts and the community. We're going to start with just looking at our overall project goals and then talking about the brief history, and then we'll get into the recommendations on implementation from the Judicial Council, which is what we're here to talk about today. Starting with the Trial Court Funding Commission, and we're going to dive into the history a little more, we're looking at what we're trying to address. The problems here are a potential serious or, sorry, real or perceived conflict of interest between the judge's responsibility to collect taxes and responsibility to administer justice. We have a system that is inadequately funded across the board because of an over-reliance on local funding, and it ends up with an unequal access to justice for those most vulnerable. As a result, the recommendations from the Trial Court Funding Commission, echoed in Public Act 47, echoed by the recommendations of the Judicial Council today, call for redistribution, a centralized collection with a redistribution of this money to meet the court's operational needs, balancing the funding responsibility a little differently between the state and the local governments, while maintaining accountability, but taxing people based on their actual costs and only if there aren't indigent. So this recent history, there's a long history, right? Michigan's first constitution in 1835 says all penal fines go to the libraries. It's pretty well recognized that that's for two purposes. One is people in the beginning of the state believed that people who are educated were less likely to commit crimes, that the key to avoiding recidivism is public education. In an 18th

35, that meant the public libraries. The second goal was to keep money away from judges. And that's not new. That comes from our ancestors, no matter where you come from in the world. Ruth Bader Ginsburg, in a brilliant United States Supreme Court decision from about six or seven years ago called People v. Timms. Sorry, it's Timms v. Indiana. The prosecution was People v. Timms. Timms v. Indiana. The question is really what to do with the asset forfeiture. Timms was arrested. His very expensive SUV was forfeited to the government. And the question to the Supreme Court was, does the Eighth Amendment's provision on excessive fines apply to the state through the Fourteenth Amendment? Very esoteric legal issue. However, Justice Bader Ginsburg walks through the history of trying to keep money away from judges. She goes back to the Magna Carta and talks about the corrupting influence that money can have on the justice system. Michigan's first constitution and every constitution since accepts that premise. Bless you. Unfortunately, we have not, in our Constitution of 63, done the things we need to do with finance to protect that. So if we look at the current history, in the spring of 2014, the Michigan Supreme Court decided People v. Cunningham. Cunningham essentially said that the courts do not have authority to assess costs of the court because the legislature never gave it to them. The legislature, in return, created that authority. Amending the statutes to add MCL 769.1K1B3. 1B3 allows a court to assess to a defendant any costs reasonably related to the actual costs incurred by the court itself. That's new in Michigan law in 2014. Now, I can tell you, I was appointed to the bench in 2005, and the first thing they trained me on was how to assess court costs. So I've already told you, every constitution in Michigan since 1835 has had this provision. In 1962, at the Constitutional Convention, the conveners tried to, again, push money out of the judicial system. They abolished the justice of the peace system. If you read the campaign literature from 1963, you can see they did this to get money out of the court system. They said instead, within five years, the legislature should create courts of limited jurisdiction. Today we call those the district courts, where I served for about 14 years. The district courts were created by the legislature in 67 and 68. They came online in 69 and 70. Already by 1982, there's a court of appeals case where the library of Saginaw sued the district court judges. And the library said, where did our fines go? They told the court of appeals, these judges have made up something called court costs, and they're stealing all our fines. The court of appeals in 1982 said, well, they couldn't have done that. There's no such thing as court costs. But there were always court costs. And they were shot down in 2014 in Cunningham. The legislative response to create court costs. However, there was not, and I might respectfully suggest may still not be, common agreement on whether this is a good idea. So while creating 769.1k1b3 costs of operating the court to a criminal defendant, there was not majority support in the legislature to do that permanently. The three-year sunset was added so conversations could continue. At the end of the period of time, the legislature, oh, I'm sorry, I want to talk about one other thing. So think about 2014. So I've already said that in the spring, we have people versus Cunningham. And in the fall, we have the passage of 769.1k1b3, sponsored by John Walsh, the majority floor leader at the time. So this was a leadership position that could not get enough majority support to be permanent. That summer in Ferguson, Missouri, with the death of Michael Brown, civil unrest ensued. The civil unrest was mostly aimed at the police. Those of us sitting in Michigan watching it on TV sure looked like a riot against the police. The following summer in 2015, the following spring in 2015, the Department of Justice did an after-action report, and they told us in their report that the focus of the civil unrest was not only the police, it was the courts. That the focus on revenue generation had compromised the local court. They concluded that the court primarily used its judicial authority as a means to compel payment of fines and costs to advance the city's financial interests, and that the result violated the 14th Amendment's provisions of due process and equal protection for the people coming before the court. So those legislators, your predecessors who were looking at this problem in 2014, saw Ferguson happen. And I guess one of the things we're here to tell you today is that Michigan's court finance system today looks a lot like Missouri's did in the summer of 2014. So the legislature, again, at the three-year sunset, revisited the issue. This time, however, with the leadership sponsorship of Representative Rob Verhulen from Kent County, the legislature also created the Trial Court Funding Commission. The sunset is extended. The Trial Court Funding Commission is asked to do the deep dive that was sought three years earlier in 2014. The Trial Court Funding Commission was created by the legislature, appointed by the governor, and met in 2017-18, concluding with a final report in 2019. The Trial Court Funding Commission found that there's a real or perceived conflict of interest between the judge's duty to impartiality and her responsibility or obligation to use court-generated revenue for operating the court. That there was inadequate funds from all sources due to an excessive reliance on local funding, and that it resulted in unequal access to justice for the people most vulnerable. These are the same principles we talked about at the beginning of the presentation. So I really think this is a pretty good example of how the three branches of government in Lansing wrestle with a very complicated problem. The Supreme Court called it out, passed the ball to the legislative branch, who put in a temporary fix, then passed the ball to the executive branch, creating the Trial Court Funding Commission within the Department of Treasury, appointed by the governor. This is when Mr. Bassanek and I first met and started working together. The Trial Court Funding Commission issued its report and sent back to the legislative and judicial branches. We still don't have consensus yet, so we had the pandemic, of course. So when the sun sets in 2020, there's an extension. Many of you were here by that time. When the sun set again in 2022, there's an extension. And this is simply because those of you who are wrestling with this problem, we just didn't have the answer. We didn't have a way to move forward. At the same period of time, the judicial branch, under the leadership of Chief Justice Bridget Mary McCormick, created the Judicial Council. The Judicial Council met and began planning. The first strategic agenda for the Judicial Council prioritized strategic goal number one to be court funding and technology infrastructure. Technology infrastructure is a topic for a whole other day. Happy to talk with any of you about it at any time. But for today, we're here talking about the first of these court funding. The first work group created by the Judicial Council finished its work in 2023, delivered a report to the legislature, and you then, many of you here, created the Trial Court Funding Act in 2024, which we call PA 47, and that's how we'll refer to it today, at the same time as extending the sunset. So what we see is a continual back and forth about what is it we need to do and how do we advance the work in this complicated environment. Remember, the Trial Court Funding Commission had five recommendations. Four of them were substantive, and the fifth was procedural. The fifth recommendation was we should follow an iterative path to solve a little bit of this at a time moving forward, which is the path we eventually are on. I'm going to turn this over to Mike, to Mr. Bassanich, to talk about the work of the reconstituted Trial Court Funding Commission after Public Act 47. Well, thank you, Tom, and again, good morning. So Public Act 47 of 2024 authorized the State Court Administrative Office under the Michigan Supreme Court to develop a full plan and create a legislative proposal to improve trial court funding system here in Michigan. The report that was created and provided to you is that finished product from the work group. The implementation plan also importantly aligns with the goals that were outlined in the Trial Court Funding Commission's report of 2019. The Alternative Funding Work Group created the organizational structure that you see. It's on the screen there. There were four teams that were created, each with a core responsibility, and then underneath that, the bottom line of boxes that you see, you see TCF-C and then you see MJC. It ties into the Judicial Council's work and then Public Act 47. The teams were responsible for addressing those particular sections of Public Act 47. Our deadline to complete this work was May 1 of 2026. We've delivered it six months ahead of schedule. And I think that really speaks to the importance of the issue and providing the legislature an opportunity well in advance of the sunset of December 31 of 2026 to begin the conversation

to begin the engagement of how we move forward to maybe finally solve the issues that are in front of us and that have been outlined in the report that has been provided to you. Over 70 individuals participated in this work product, individuals with expertise in operating Michigan courts, in public safety, local government finance, and other expertise. They were supported in their work by experts in public finance, by Manor Costarison, a public accounting firm here in Michigan, and the Pew Charitable Trust with their expertise to help staff these teams to make sure that they could complete the work that was in front of them. Importantly, the structure that we created also helped define for the teams as we brought new members in that we didn't have what we call mission creep, that look, we had a defined set of objectives that we needed to complete. We needed to complete it efficiently and stay on task, and I think that was an important part of that organizational structure that was there. I think also important to know is that throughout our process, as we made progress on developing these recommendations, we spread out across the state. We made presentations to various stakeholder groups to keep them informed, but also to get feedback from them along the way. And I think that's an important aspect of the overall recommendations, include that feedback and that kind of consensus, not just within the work group, not just within the teams, but the stakeholders who we've been engaging with along the way. In September, the recommendations and report were submitted to the Michigan Judicial Council. The Council reviewed those and they accepted that, and the report from the Council was then finalized. As Tom laid out the history of trial court funding, you saw the work that's been undertaken since 2017. I will tell you, in my experience, it's been a deliberate path with over a decade of research, analysis, brainstorming by stakeholders, and ultimately consensus building that created the implementation recommendations that are before you. I think we also have to recognize that change will create challenge from some stakeholder groups. We understand that. However, the recommendations should be viewed in totality as together they represent a transformation in the way Michigan trial courts are funded and in part how they operate. So let's talk about our recommendations, and we're going to give them to you at a high level, a lot of work that's bubbled up to the point that I'm going to talk to you about the team recommendations. So the first one is the team, the operational cost funding model team. They had two goals. Essentially each team had two goals other than the collections system. They actually had three goals, and so it's easy to kind of keep track of them that way. So the first goal of this team was to develop the financial plan for the courts under the new funding model. And so the new financial plan meets the goal outlined under the trial court funding commission's recommendation in creating a stable court funding model. We believe the model will be the tool to invest and improve justice and performance outcomes for our state. And so that's important. This isn't just for the court systems, not just for local units of government and other stakeholders. It's for our citizens. And the financial plan rebalances future financial obligations between local units of government and the state. This is essential to ensuring stability in this model. And the second goal of this team was to develop a plan on how to finance court facility capital improvements going forward. And so let's talk about the financial plan and how we created it. There are four funding sources in the new model. They're actually the same funding sources that are in the current model, but there are key differences in the new approach. First, local units of government were the funding units, and there are 135 primary funding units across the state, will continue funding what they currently pay to support their local courts. The plan does not ask them to pay any more than what they're currently paying. Currently, 58% or $704 million of the total $1.22 billion that it takes to operate the trial courts in Michigan each year are financed by local units of government. We think that that's a pretty hefty price tag in terms of sharing that financial burden. What the funding units are already paying would be memorialized in a maintenance of effort, an MOE or a MO, for short. The MO would be adjusted annually, though, by the change in the taxable value of the funding unit. This is unique in our funding plan than maybe you see in other ones. There's a CPI cost escalator. CPI is just a cost escalator, doesn't talk about anybody's ability to pay. When I talk about anybody, those are local funding units. And so as the local funding unit's taxable value changes, that indicates, you know, in terms of how they generate revenue for their general funds, it's primarily the property tax. And taxable value then is assessed, it's created, and then they apply a millage rate. So that talks about a local unit's ability to pay. So it would be changed by that increase in the taxable value, but capped at 3%. We think that that is reasonable. The second source of revenue would be the existing court-generated revenues. They would be used to continue to help pay the operational costs of the Michigan trial courts. However, our plan is different in this approach. Court revenues would be deposited into the new trial court fund within Michigan Treasury. No longer would money be assessed locally and retained locally. All money would be deposited into the new trial court fund in Treasury. Currently, this represents 20% of the overall cost to operate the trial courts, or about $242 million. The other aspect of this approach with this plan is that it is more transparent. It's clear. The current model that we have is very complex. There's six different funds where money flows in and flows out. Not very transparent in that approach, and it's also inefficient to administer. The third source of funds is from state and federal funding. Now, I'm going to talk briefly about funding from the federal government. It's about $101 million, or 8% of the total. But this is used primarily for child support services and funding in our local friend of the court operations, and that's Title IV-D funds. And then Title IV-E funds are child care fund monies that go in for foster care and child support programs in our youth centers, and those are administered under the probate courts here in Michigan. The fourth leg of our funding model stool is where the plan is most different. Under the current model, the state is funding about 14%, or $177 million. But that's a little deceiving. And it's deceiving because local courts transfer money to the state. The state captures that money, and then they redistribute that money back. Not all of it, but a fair amount of that. It's very complicated to track the money, but I will just simply tell you at a high level, it's less than the 14%. So in terms of the state's general fund obligation to the trial courts, it's not that much. And again, the ideal of this new funding model going forward is that there has to be more of a balanced funding approach between all the funding partners. And the two primary ones would be the state of Michigan and local units of government. When we look at the maintenance of effort, even the $704 million that is being contributed right now, even with a 3% increase in that, it's $21 million of additional money from local units of government. And so when we look at this model, we see that there's going to be a continued effort from local units of government. They're not walking away from it. We're just simply saying going forward, we'd like this arrangement to change a little bit where the state becomes more of a balanced funding partner with us. In the next slide, as we determine the operational costs of the trial courts, one of the things that's underway right now is a court operations resource report. That's really a workload analysis based upon the workload of each one of the trial courts across Michigan. It's been done before. The judicial resource report looks at the number of judges based upon case weighting and case loads. It's never been done for all of the other positions in the court. That is underway right now. That's going to inform in terms of the total operational costs. So total operational costs are staffing, supplies, other expenses, those kinds of things that go into operating any kind of an organization, same thing here. We're going to be informed by this to help us understand what the staffing looks like. It also is going to help us inform about uniform staffing so that courts across the state have kind of a uniform approach, an equal number of staff to manage their workloads. This looks at case weighting in the sense that if you're mostly traffic tickets, traffic tickets are 15, 20 minutes apiece to process. That's a low case weighting. But if you have criminal cases going on with defendants coming in, judges involved, many staff, that's a much heavier case weighting. So it looks at that so that there's a true balancing in that overall arrangement. And then finally, the operational cost funding team looked at how do we finance facility costs going forward. There are many different court facilities across the state where operations take place. One of these ideals that we believe is important is that whoever you are, when you appear in a court

in the state of Michigan, you ought to be assured a basic level of safety and security whether you're a witness, whether you're a litigant, whether you're a victim. And the ideal here is that the state court administrator's office would create guidelines for state or county court facilities to be able to meet those. They would apply for funding to a grant program which would have $17.4 million. Local units of government in the courts would match that. And in fact, they would exceed that because they have the first 1% of any project upfront, 1% of their general fund that would go into that. So in our county, our general fund is called $60 million. We would have the first $600,000 of any capital project. Beyond that then, the courts with the local funding unit would jointly apply for program funding out of this grant program and then we would share the cost 50% after that. So that's very high level. That's the recommendation from that team. The second team was the funding distribution team. There are two primary goals. Create a plan establishing the trial court fund that I had previously talked about that would centralize all revenue generated from the trial courts. And second, develop a process for distributing the money from the trial courts back to the local courts. These distributed amounts would be based upon that local court's total operational cost or their budget essentially. So within the new trial court fund that would be established, with limited exception, all court generated revenue would be deposited in this trial court fund. Three points with this model. Number one, no longer would money assessed locally be kept at the local court. Instead, it would all be deposited in Michigan Treasury into the trial court fund. On this point, this is really important. Mr. Boyd talked about the three challenges that the trial court funding commission identified. This model achieves the goal of removing any real or perceived conflict in the generation of court revenue by any court personnel that could directly benefit the court from assessing and then collecting that same money. And I think this is really important. Yes, it's a financial plan. Yes, it's a model. But it achieves what one of the challenges were to eliminate this conflict. And then all money in the trial court fund would only be used for judicial branch functions. Currently, court generated revenues are being transferred out. I talked about various transfers. They're being transferred out and used for executive and legislative functions. So on this point, we call for these transfers to end. But we want to be clear. We are not saying that these are not important functions. They are. They're really important. We're just simply saying the judicial branch should not be funding executive or legislative functions. The court generated revenue should only be used for the judicial branch functions with the caveat that only under this new model where the generated revenues go into the separate trial court fund. The other point is by moving to this model, we can enhance the clarity and transparency in the current model to make one that is simpler, that's more efficient in administering and make it clear from where the funds are coming from and where they're going back out to. If you look at the current model, it's kind of a spaghetti mess of complex transfers from general tax revenues, court generated revenues. And I said going into, there's six different funds that make up the funding plan currently for the Michigan trial courts. And then finally, the team developed a framework for dispersing the money from the trial court fund back to local units of government. Again, to pay for the local trial courts in those communities. The funds would be allocated based upon these approved budgets. Local units of governments would have to designate or set up a designated fund to receive all those monies and essentially manage the trial court funds in these separate funds within their existing financial accounting systems. And then any residual funding in these funds that is not spent by the court, it would reside there as an incentive to be fiscally responsible with the funds that are distributed. And then we've created a process for local court budgets to be developed. You know, we're not taking any responsibility away from local units of government. Under Public Act 2, which is a uniform budgeting and accounting act, local units of government are still responsible for the financial reporting, still responsible for developing the budgets. It's just we're going to be introducing the state court administrator's office to help develop these budgets. And again, as the court operations resource report is laid in, and we understand what the staffing needs are based upon a proven methodology, then we're informed about what are the real needs of the trial courts on a uniform basis across the entire state of Michigan. And the process that we have, it goes through, you know, we're lining up several different budget sequences and the other things that take place, both at the local level, with the courts, and the states, and we roll all this up into this model so it makes sense. And if you look on page 27 of our report, on page 13, we've defined this so that we understand there are some timing issues, but we think in the model that we've created, we can get there. The next team addresses the uniform assessment and determinations of indigency. Tom's going to walk through the goals of this team, and I think it's important that even in this recommendation from this team, or the two recommendations from this team, they provide the same ideals that are carried through on all of these teams, clarity, transparency, and just a better way that we address the funding needs of our trial courts in more of a balanced relationship with all of the funding partners. Tom? Thank you. So you can see the goals for team two, to develop a uniform way of assessing costs and to determine the standard for indigency. I want to talk just a little bit about the problem. So today, if one of us gets a speeding ticket on the way home, according to the statute, the financial consequence is a fine, and each offense has a range that the judicial officer can set that fine at, and a cost, not a court cost, not 769.1b3, but the cost of bringing the matter before the court. This is a calculation of how much it costs to have a law enforcement officer on the road to then electronically file this ticket that we're going to go online and pay tonight. The problem is courts don't know this. Law enforcement does. Law enforcement, every chief, every sheriff knows how much it costs to have a human being on the road. But we do not follow this law. So we start with the recommendation that we should follow the current law rather than make up what we think the cost is. To make that point, when Representative Walsh passed the bill to add 769.1b3, he then brought in Representative Verhulen and said, I'm leaving the legislature termed out. Rob is going to help you. Please feel free to ask Representative Verhulen. He was an incredible partner in the creation of the Trial Court Funding Commission. But his first instinct was we don't need a body to do this. The legislature can fix whatever problems exist. I brought to him a list of the financial consequences for impeding traffic at the district courts in Kent County where he lived and at the district courts in Ingham County where I presided over a district court. And in each case, there were two consequences for impeding traffic. Impeding traffic means literally your car was in the way of the flow of traffic. The first fine is if you were impeding traffic. It's rarely cited. People are rarely cited for impeding traffic. However, people often have their charge for speeding or some other infraction that comes with points at the Secretary of State's office reduced to impeding traffic because it doesn't have points. So each court had two charts. One is if you were really impeding traffic and the other is if you were getting a break and not getting points. And that was just higher. Basically the courts determined, well you're getting a break, you're not getting points, you're going to pay more for that privilege. There's no statutory authority for this. Every single court. One of the courts just had a blank line for the second kind of impeding because they were going to look you up and down and see what they thought you could pay. Quite literally they're going to see what kind of a bag you're carrying, if your iPhone is newer than the judge or the magistrate. That's a really nice suit and they're going to determine what you can pay and that's what you're going to pay that day. So the first recommendation is we should really follow the current law. But the key to that is we have to remove the profit incentive for the judge because these problems are tied together. The second is a uniform way of determining what the cost is to the court. So today there's some guidance out there about how to establish what your court costs are. But we need the recommendation from the workgroup, from the judicial council, is that we have a standard way of doing that. In fact, we go further and say it would be great if the legislature just set a cost. It would be different in different regions of the state. We're not suggesting that it costs the same to run a court in southern Oakland County as it does at the tip of the mitt. What we're saying is we know the difference. And now with the deep dive from Maynard Casterson, we actually can tell you how much it costs to run the court in Birmingham, the 48th District, and how much it costs to run the 96 in Newbury because we now have those numbers. So the idea here is to use that data that we now have. And again, we sent you a report that's 45, 50 pages of writing and 60 pages of data. We also provided to the chairs like 300 pages of draft legislation.

The point is that the detail here is deep, but this is the deepest dive we've ever done into court financing. And we now know, as Mike said, $1.22 billion is how much it costs to run the court system. And he gave you the numbers about how that breaks out. So the goal here is to be able to look at that data and figure out what is the appropriate share to each person coming before the court. Not giving anybody a break, having them pay their fair share. Second is a uniform... I'm going to go talk about this. Our goal in trying to end the real or perceived conflict is to separate the business function of the court from its function related to public safety and the administration of justice. If we take away the fact that the judge keeps what he or she kills, separating the assessing from the spending equation, we can separate the business function of the court, how do we pay our bills, from the administration of justice. This work group, the implementation team, in order to get to these results, separated the work into two buckets. They have an accountability bucket, and the accountability bucket is the fine that we talked about, and any restitution. Significantly, today, in a criminal case, if someone is convicted and ordered to pay restitution, when they pay a dollar to the court, only 50% goes to the victim. Because the profit motive on the court is so strong, they keep 50% of every dollar until the restitution is paid off. Judicial Council recommends that we give $1, 100% of each dollar to the victim until he or she is made whole. We have to end the fact that the court has to compete with the victim for scarce resources. The accountability bucket also includes the state system for compensating victims who are not fully compensated, the Crime Victims Rights Act. That assessment today goes to compensate victims who are not fully compensated, but also goes to pay for executive branch employees, both at the state level and at the local government level. The recommendation is that we keep that money for victims, as it was originally intended. The second bucket is the tax bucket. Now, we can call them fees, we can call them costs, as the statutes do, but both the Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court have called these taxes, and they treat them like taxes. So we have two separate things, accountability and tax. As it relates to accountability, the recommendations of the workgroup is that they continue to be assessed as now, the judge's discretion. That the judge retains the discretion to determine if the individual who's assessed a fee, a fine, cannot pay, or if they are exercising due diligence to pay. As Mike said, as it relates to the local unit of government, we want to move forward with their ability to pay. All we're recommending is we do the same thing to the defendants, the same thing to the people with the speeding ticket. We look at their ability to pay, not the accountability portion, but the tax portion. The accountability portion does not go through an indigency screen. It's totally up to the judicial decision maker. The tax bucket goes through the indigency screen to determine if they're able to pay. The second bullet on this slide is Mike's point about transparency. Today we send money to something called the state minimum costs, and then you see the spiderweb of where that money goes next. The idea is to go to transparency, the money goes from the court to either the victim or to the trial court fund. All right, I'm going to talk about the termination of indigency. The legislature has, in a very similar context, the need for a public defender, described what indigency is. It's Public Act 93 of 2013, where it's asserted that someone who is indigent should, consistent with the United States and Michigan constitutions, receive counsel without charge. But it goes on and says, what does it mean to be indigent? And then authorizes the Indigent Defense Commission to further elaborate. So the legislature has, in the very similar context, the beginning of a criminal case said, what's indigency? In a related context, the Supreme Court's done the same thing. If you want to sue your neighbor, there's a filing fee. However, in the court rule, there's a way to determine that you're indigent and don't have to pay that tax, that filing fee. So what the recommendation is, we take those two provisions, Public Act 93 of 2013, the court rule on filing fee waiver, and set a determination of what is indigent, a legislative determination of how that tax should be applied. The fourth implementation team is talking about collections. Their goals are, how does this work? What are the logistics of centralized collection? What does it do to the local courts and the users? And then to determine an implementation process. So the Trial Court Funding Commission brought in expertise from around the country. We had people flown in from Minnesota and Arizona and Ohio to present on different models of court funding. What we learned through that process is states that went from court-based collections to state-based collections, Department of Revenue-based collections, increased their revenue and decreased their costs. So that was a recommendation from the Trial Court Funding Commission, echoed by the first workgroup of the Judicial Council, and echoed by Public Act 47. So here's what we're talking about in terms of how to get that done. The Judicial Council report recommends that the Department of Treasury knows what they're doing. They already have the infrastructure in place to successfully collect money owed to the state. The recommendation is in creating a centralized system for receipts, collections, and dispersals under Teams 1 and 2, that we can create a more efficient and effective way of collecting these court assessments. Finally, the idea is that the courts would partner with the Department of Treasury so that if someone's assessed a $100 payment, they walk out of the courtroom and they give $100 cash to the counter, the court's computers lets the Treasury's computer know right away that that $100 was paid. If they would go home at night and they pay online at the Department of Treasury, Treasury's computers let the court's computers know the payment was made. So it's this integration between these two systems which leads to one payment system run by Treasury. Going forward, the courts will order assessments, hearing requests for waiver of the assessments on the accountability bucket that I described earlier, receive restitution either directly from the defendant or indirectly through Treasury if that payment was made to Treasury through an electronic funds transfer, pay it immediately over to the victim. What this system does is we no longer impose bench warrants for failure to pay, failure to pay a court debt, no more probation revocations and jail for failing to pay a financial obligation, and no more driver's license suspensions for failure to pay to the court. These things that interrupt the life of an individual, their family, and their employer are not effective. I'm going to come back to that point in a second. What Treasury will do is receive the assessment and then do what Treasury does. They'll impose late fees as they think appropriate. They'll use their own practices and policies regarding the debt. They'll decide when debt is collectible, when it should be written off, except for restitution, of course. Constitution is protected and never written off, always collected, continued collected. They'll use their existing tools to do this. The Department of Treasury knows how to collect debt. This is it. Tom's rolling through and doing a great job. The one thing that really stood out for a lot of the members of the teams is that even treatment. So there's courts across the state of Michigan all doing this collection effort. They're not probably doing it all in the same way, maybe in the same level of efficiency. If Treasury is doing this, think about the equal treatment. If somebody owes debt to the government, whether it's the court or anybody else, the treatment is equal from Treasury. Everybody's treated the same. Right now, we don't believe that it is, and we also believe that this is a much more efficient model. So, you know, I'm a finance guy from that standpoint, and, you know, efficiency has kind of rung a couple of bells for me. So in this model and these recommendations, we think that there's a lot of benefits in terms of adopting this model and this approach. Sorry, Tom. It's all right. So the current model is court debt is collected by law enforcement. A judge sits down and issues a bench warrant. Johnny didn't pay. Bench warrant. The cost then shifts to the executive branch and falls into a black hole. You know, I know from my experience in Ingham County that it costs a law enforcement officer to make a drunk driving arrest about $200 to $225. I know that because I wouldn't compensate the law enforcement unless they gave me a bill, and they did regularly. So $200, $250. That's a routine arrest. Take someone off the side of the road, bring them to the jail. It doesn't cost their overnight stay in the jail, just their arrest. So I'm going to focus on this chart, which is in the report, and look at 2019, seven years of collections ago, and focus on the fact that look at the sixth year of collections and every year since 2005. Only once did we collect more than 1%. So police chiefs have told me that they are tired of arresting Johnny and bringing him, holding him overnight and bringing him to court the next day because he owes $100 just to have the judge say, boy, you really need to try harder to pay that $100. The collection system we're doing is ineffective. So let's look at how this works. So if you look at the data from 2019, so far we've collected 79% of those assessments. But 71% or 89% of the total happened in the first two years. Maybe the pandemic affected our collections. Let's go back to 2013, seven years before the pandemic. You can see

collections. The point is we are bad at this. This is ineffective. Anyone who tells you differently is mistaken. And I say that because people will tell you differently. I've heard it from law enforcement. I've heard it from county clerks. We need to be able to collect this debt. A judge from the 48th District Court told me when you created Clean Slate and wiped away certain misdemeanors that she was upset and she was going to sue because that was her money. The point is we are very ineffective. Yes, yes, Senator. Thank you very much. If you can do 30 more seconds and wrap up and then we'll get to some questions. Yes, Senator. The point is that if you look at this chart, every year in the first year we're between 55 and 60 percent of collections. Every year in the second year we're between 15 and 20 percent and it drops off precipitously after that. What we're doing does not work. And I'll just as we answer questions reiterate the points we made at the beginning. Senator. Thank you very much. I appreciate both of your presentations and recognize the tremendous amount of work by not just you two but your whole team as well as many different stakeholders on this report and we're all excited to continue digging into it. Before I go to Senator Johnson for her question, if you could share some information with each of our offices about the other states that you mentioned and the cost savings and increased revenue generation from those states just so we have that background, that will be helpful. Senator Johnson. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Chair. I have two quick questions. I know a lot of hard work went into this and there's many good things. I was wondering if it would somehow have any impact. I see one county has six quasi-judicial staff per the Michigan Judicial Workload Assessment Report, six more than what they're supposed to have. Would this address when there's too many staff? So we don't actually have the Court Operations Resources Report completed, so there isn't a recommendation yet about any particular county. However, the question is the same and that is would it address if there's too many staff? The idea is that the court would say how many staff you need. There's a number there. And then local control would determine how that's allocated. So a county might have more quasi-judicial officers or more clerks. They might have more probation officers. I used to pride myself on the fact that in Mason I had three and a half probation officers per judge, way higher than anybody else. The idea is that local control will still run the court. We're just going to tell you how many people you need. So there is a possibility that a court or two has more people than they need. We're going to be surprised to see that and we'll know that soon. Okay, last question. You had a slide that showed the task force members who participated. With feedback, we have a letter from MML, MTA, SEMCOG, the sheriffs, and the police opposed to the recommendations. Another letter from Michigan Association of Counties voiced concerns. It doesn't seem like most of the task force agrees with the recommendations. So are you ready to go ahead with these with that kind of input from these organizations? Senator, we are. The point is that when you read the letters, and obviously those are not new to us, the point is that there's lots of things we can do here to move forward. There's objections to the consternation of shifting away from guaranteed court revenue to possible appropriations. The question is, and we've heard this from libraries and courts and law enforcement, is there the level of comfort with the annual appropriations process that they have with just waiting for the people in black robes to bring the cash in? There isn't that level of comfort. We all live in this environment. We all watch the annual appropriations process. Many of us are involved in it. We trust that process. The question becomes, is it comfortable? No. As Mike said, there's going to be concern because we're moving from a steady stream of revenue coming from the judicial branch to back to the legislative branch to say it's your responsibility and your authority that's being exercised on an annual basis. There will be concern about that. Thank you. As you know, I have a history of looking into this trial court funding issue. Pre-COVID, I tried working on some of this according to the first set of recommendations back in 2019. But I know that a lot of conversation has happened within your guys' world right now. Looking at it from not only a policy lens but also an appropriations lens, I do have concerns in regards to some of this movement, but this is a good first step and we'll have robust conversations in the future. But what I'm kind of wondering is it was potentially a three-year phase-in. Is that correct? Real quick, this will lead into more. Three-year phase-in? I think that if you were to look at all the recommendations, it'll take way more than three. But the initial trial court fund that you're talking about and then phasing out assessments and all of those, that initial part in Department of Treasury, I mean, basically what I'm getting at is the legislature is still going to have to extend the sunset. The sunset is December of 2026. As you know, I've done the last two or three. And I think there's going to be more robust conversation on the function of some of these because, as you know, some of these things that you mentioned, assessments and stuff like that, don't even fall under the judiciary budget. It's under Department of Corrections or General Government or whatever it may be, Attorney General. And I'm just curious what the plan is to kind of backfill some of the assessments because it does end up being a lot of money, especially when you talk about in the trial court fund that no monies will ever lapse. I'm like, well, if it has additional money in there, then they're really, you know, the state appropriation in my mind would go down because you already set your MOE for locals at a fixed amount. So, you know, functionally as far as appropriations go in the different funds and the assessments, you know, I just want to make sure we have robust conversations because, you know, if you ask me in regards to some of these, you know, you talk about legislative and executive branch functions, you know, I look at the child advocacy centers. Well, since, you know, we've moved into the technology age, a lot of our kids, it's easier for them to testify on a screen. You know this. And our child advocacy centers have that set up for the courts to help with the court function, a piece of the function. So, you know, I think there's just going to be a lot more robust, so I guess this is more of a request of more information, a continued, you know, relationship back and forth to talk through some of these policies and functioning and appropriations and, you know, all of that because we're looking at this. It's a big, huge lift, as you know, and it's been years and years and years, and I picked on Mike Bassanik. I was like, you're probably never going to be able to retire because it's going to take this long. But, you know, now also with term limits being basically extended in one, you can serve all your years in one chamber, now you can't just wait us out too long. We actually have to do stuff. So I think I'm looking forward to continued conversations. You know, I have a desire to make this work. I think a lot of us here do. And, you know, thanks for at least being here and being available for us. We are out of time. I know that we've got a couple of folks who had questions. I would just encourage members to reach out to SCALE to have these conversations. Let's keep talking about this. This is a really important topic. We do have a couple cards to read in. Go ahead. Okay. I am sorry. It is 9.56. We are out of time. I know some people did submit testimony, and I just want to read the cards for the record that we did have West Nakagiri here who wanted to speak, is neutral right now on the presentation, but did submit written testimony as well. We have Jody White here that wanted to speak, opposes the funding. Cynthia Mifsud, wishing to speak, didn't have a position. And Tom Howe, wishing to speak and opposes this function. But you guys can submit your testimony, like we said, to the clerk as well. So thank you with that. This side is adjourned. And I'm going to move to excuse the absent member, there being no objection, that is ordered. And there being no further business before the committee, the Senate Committee on Civil Rights, Judiciary, and Public Safety is adjourned. Thank you.

Illegitimacy.

To the Speaker of the House of Representatives, dear sir, I herewith transmit to the House Senate Concurrent Resolution Number 8, a concurrent resolution of tribute offered as a memorial for Irma Clark Coleman, former member of the House of Representatives and the Senate. The Speaker recognizes Representative Scott. Thank you, Madam Speaker. Today I rise in strong support of this memorial resolution, honoring the life and legacy of Irma Clark Coleman, a former member of the Michigan House of Representatives and the Michigan Senate. Irma Clark Coleman's story is not just one of public titles and elected offices. It is a story of a woman who believed deeply in the transformative power of public service, a belief she lived out in every role she held, from county offices to the state capitol to the neighborhoods of Detroit that she loves so dearly. Those of us who had the privilege of knowing her know that Irma never lost sight of the people behind the policies. She was quick to return a constituent's call as she was to debate an appropriations bill. She saw service as a measure of trust, not a transaction. And that sense of duty earned her the respect of colleagues across the aisle and across generations. Irma's leadership was rooted in her lived experience. A child of the South, she came to Detroit and built a life defined by perseverance and purpose. She knew what it meant to work hard, to rise through the ranks, and to open doors for those who would follow. She was definitely a mentor of mine, and she did that for me. Whether she was advocating for children in our classrooms, for fairness in our courts, or for the opportunity in our communities, she did so with an unwavering belief that government could and should be a force for good. Beyond her policy achievements, Irma brought warmth and grace to this chamber. Her vibrant energy reminds us that this work, though serious, can still be done with joy. As we pay tribute to Irma today, we are not only remembering her service, we are challenged to emulate it, to carry forward her example of mentorship, compassion, and courage, to lead as she did with both heart and conviction. So I urge my colleagues to join me in supporting this resolution. Let it stand not only as a memorial to an extraordinary public servant, but as a reminder of what each of us can aspire to, a legacy measured not by the offices we hold, but by the lives we touch and the positive change we make. House Resolution Number 218, introduced by Representative McDonnell, a resolution to declare November 2025 as Adoption Month in the State of Michigan. Speaker recognizes Representative McDonnell.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in support of my resolution to recognize November as Adoption Month in Michigan. Recently, while driving down Larch Street in Lansing, I passed a billboard with a photo of a mother and child and the words, Who Adopted Who? I smiled in wholehearted agreement. My husband and I are the proud parents of two wonderful daughters whom we just happened to adopt. We were older when we did, having spent years focused on our careers and traveling the world, and by the time I turned 30, I wondered if I'd waited too long to start a family. When I finally met the man I wanted to spend my life with, we were ready to begin that chapter, but for three painful years, it didn't happen. Many of us know that heartbreak, the monthly disappointment, the sense of failure, the quiet grief as others around you grow their families. Eventually, we turned to adoption. A doctor had suggested further expensive treatments, but I'd had enough of medical letdowns. Adoption wasn't easy either. There were costs, stacks of paperwork, and even FBI fingerprinting. But at least we knew that each step brought us closer to becoming parents. Two years later, we adopted our first daughter, and two years after that, her little sister. Both were born in China. They arrived without much history, a little malnourished, and deeply in need of love and family. We've done our best to give them everything they need, and in return, they've given us more than we could have imagined. Some people hesitate to adopt, understandably worried about bonding, about differences, or about unknowns in a child's background. I would argue that if people truly understood how hard all parenting is, biological or not, the human race would have fizzled out long ago. Of course, there have been challenges, awkward questions, moments of sadness, reminders of what may have been, but nothing insurmountable. Because ultimately, we gained the blessing of adoption and the blessing of family. Over the past 23 years, we've shared everything, birthday parties, scraped knees, teenage dramas, tears, dance classes, messy rooms, health scares, hugs, laughter, and all the chaos that comes with raising children. Our daughters, who began their lives in very uncertain circumstances, are now thriving, loved, and full of promise. People sometimes tell us we're special because we adopted, but I always disagree. The truth is that our daughters adopted us. They gave us the family we longed for, the love we dreamed of, and the life we cherish. That's why I hope you'll all join me in recognizing November as Adoption Month in Michigan, celebrating not just the parents who open their homes, but the children who open their hearts. Because in the end, family isn't defined by our blood ties, it's created by love. Thank you. The question before the House is on the adoption of House Resolution 218. It's a reminder to stand with the Michigan businesses that have always stood with us and to recognize Michiganders for who they are, strong people who create great things. Specialist David Anthony Wilkie Jr. was born in Norway, Michigan, and raised in the heart of our beloved Upper Peninsula. He was a true UPER, through and through, an avid outdoorsman who cherished hunting, fishing, and the natural beauty of our region. His classmates and neighbors remember him as a young man of exceptional character, compassion, always quick to help others, deeply rooted in his tight-knit community. At the age of just 22, David answered the call to serve. He deployed to Iraq with 1st Infantry Division based out of Fort Riley, Kansas. He left behind a young family, his wife, a one-year-old son, a stepson, and an unborn child that he would never hold. Tragically, on June 18, 2007, Specialist Wilkie made the ultimate sacrifice when an IED detonated near his unit in Baghdad. title: Oversight - State and Local Public Assistance Programs — Thursday, November 13, 2025
transcript:
Thank you. Oversight Committee on State and Local Public Assistance Programs will come to order. Will the clerk please call the roll for today's attendance? Chair Wolbert. Here. Representatives Bruck. Present. Kara. Here. Sernavlew. Here. Menser. Here. Chair Wolbert, you have five members present. You do have a quorum. Thank you. Representative Kara moves to adopt the minutes from October 30, 2025 meeting. Hearing no objection, the minutes are adopted. Well, before we get started today, I want to take a moment and first say thank you to David Kanizik. Learning that you're a United States Marine and a sniper, that's pretty motivating. So I look forward to hearing from you today. We know that you're the chief operating officer at the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services. David, thank you for taking the time to be here voluntarily to have a discussion with us today. As many of you know, the recent federal findings around Michigan SNAP program have raised serious and quite honestly alarming concerns. The state's error rate has climbed well above the national average for the second year in a row. And that kind of trend doesn't just signal a few mistakes. It points to a systemic problem that can allow waste, abuse, and even fraud to slip through the cracks. You know, we know that this is a $3.2-ish billion business. And, you know, when we look at nearly a 10% potential error rate in the for-profit world or normal company that would send a business into two to three years of bankruptcy. And so I know this is something that we'll be working on and you'll be working on and looking forward to hearing that. And so this committee obviously takes this very serious. SNAP is meant to be a lifeline for families who truly need help putting food on the table. But when oversight breaks down and when the verification steps aren't being followed and when the federal auditors start questioning our state's management, that hurts both our integrity and our program.

and the trust that taxpayers place in it. So our goal today is not to throw stones. It's to truly understand what's being done and what still needs to happen and how the legislature can help ensure that every SNAP dollar is being spent properly. We want to make sure that Michigan gets this corrected and gets it corrected quickly and that it will restore compliance with federal standards and rebuild confidence in the system and also for the taxpayers that are funding these programs. So David, again, thank you. I almost called you Devil Dog, but that's all right. David, again, thank you for being here and for your leadership throughout what I know has obviously been a challenging situation. We look forward to hearing from you today on your perspective from your department and what the next steps are and how we can truly work together to make sure that this program serves the people of Michigan in the way that it was designed to do. So with that said, carry on. Thank you, sir. Good morning, first and foremost, to the chair, Representative Wolford, to our majority vice chair, Representative Bruck, and our minority vice chair, Representative Cernoglu, and all the members of the committee. I really appreciate the opportunity to be here and then, of course, we were remiss if I didn't wish you a happy 250th birthday to a fellow Marine. There you go. My name is David Kniezik. Opposition. Oh, is she on Zoom? She's on Zoom. Good morning, Mr. Chair, members of the House Regulatory Reform Committee. Can you hear me OK? Yes, I believe we can. OK, great. My name is Megan Stokes. I'm the state policy director at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, testifying in respectful opposition to House Bill 4388. We share the goal of the sponsor and the legislature in protecting children online, and we want to work with the Michigan legislature to achieve this goal. I'm here in opposition of HB 4388 as it presents serious concerns. Courts have consistently prohibited similar laws requiring age verification and parental consent, finding that they violate the First Amendment. These laws burden lawful speech, reduce access to critical resources, and introduce vague compliance standards that can lead to arbitrary enforcement. Moreover, age verification technologies are not only unreliable, they raise significant privacy risks, especially when they require collection of sensitive data like biometrics or government IDs. These mandates could deter users, threaten small business viability, and ironically expose individuals to greater privacy harms. If passed, House Bill 4388 may unintentionally encourage platforms to block all minors rather than risk legal consequences, denying teens access to educational and supportive communities online. CCIA firmly believes that children are entitled to a higher level of security and privacy in their online experiences. Our members are already addressing these concerns through parental controls, time limits, enhanced privacy settings. We urge the committee to support efforts like digital citizenship education and to work with businesses to refine their existing tools rather than imposing what amounts to a blanket ban that infringes on individual rights. Thank you. I'm available for any questions you might have. Thank you. Any questions for this representative Thompson? Thank you, Mr. Chair. My concern again goes back to that minors cannot consent. And we look at anything else that a minor cannot consent to. So if a minor is caught drinking alcohol at 14 years old in a bar, does that bar get sued? Does that bar get a fine? Yes, the simple answer is yes. Yes, I'm not familiar with Michigan law, but where I'm from, yes. You're not with Michigan law then? I thought you were speaking. I'm not familiar with Michigan law. I'm with the Computer Communications Industry Association. I just want to make sure I'm not going to get tripped up by something that might be specific to the state of Michigan. Yeah. I think just overall, some of the things that you stated about First Amendment rights and a right to speech, I think those are all fine and good. But I think that we need to, you know, actually taking the time to come and oppose this is a little bit more frustrating than the fact that we have so many parents that are trying their hardest to protect their children from things. And if social media, and maybe this is a greater question, if they can't be sued for your child getting online without your permission and your knowledge, I don't understand how other businesses can be sued for a child or a minor doing something wrong. Because parents are still accountable to their child. And this seems to be like a greater issue of parental right and control. And I will say that, you know, many of the committee have spoke openly about things with their children. We have an 11-year-old grandson that we're raising that he does not have a cell phone. And he will not have a cell phone because he has no reason to have a cell phone because of these things that kids are doing without our knowledge that are putting them at greater risk. So thank you for coming and testifying. But I strongly disagree with you. Any further questions? Seeing none. Thank you, Megan. We're going to move on to Kayden Rosenbaum also testifying in opposition. Thank you, Mr. Chair, members of this committee. My name is Kayden Rosenbaum, and I'm the managing director of tech policy at the Reason Foundation, nonprofit, nonpartisan organization provides pro bono consulting to public officials and stakeholders to help them design and implement technology policy reforms around AI, data privacy, child online safety, and free speech. I'm testifying today in respectful opposition of HB 4388, not because I disagree with the intention behind the bill, but because HB 4388 runs the risk of violating the First Amendment, is fraught with privacy concerns, and is nearly identical to bills that were passed in other states that wound up being blocked in the courts at no small expense to taxpayers. Contracts and smartphones are really only a minor point in this bill, and there are other bills in other states that are far more specific to contracts for minors. The reason for that is that this bill before you today was thrown out in favor of different, more refined bills. This bill 4388 is give or take a few words. It's very similar to the first one that was passed in Utah in 2023. I publicly opposed that bill to no avail and watched nearly the same thing pass in Louisiana, Georgia, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Arkansas. But as of now, not even Utah, the pioneer of this model, follows that approach to child online safety. In fact, Utah scrapped that bill and started over the very next year with an entirely different approach that's unlike that described to you today in HB 4388, much more specific to contracts. To be clear, many of these bills that I'm referring to as being blocked by the courts are currently on appeal, and they're bound to make their way through federal circuit. Hopefully, they'll be resolved. But Michigan has nothing to gain by throwing its hat in the ring, other than bearing the costs of hefty attorney's fees to defend a bill that has been abandoned even by advocates in Utah, the state that pioneered this bill. The bill before you today places a burden on people's First Amendment right to speak by requiring them to identify themselves with privacy-invasive age verification requirements. That would mean showing an ID or forking over biometric information just to prove that they're adults to speak their mind, to disclose the truth, or even just learn what others have to say. And that's regardless of whether they're adults or minors. For all these reasons, I do urge the committee to reject this bill and seek alternative methods for protecting children online and empowering parents. And I want to thank the committee again for the opportunity to testify. And I hope I have the opportunity to work with some of you on a more specific bill, more narrow bill that does achieve the same result. Thank you. Representative Rigas. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you for your comments. So I'm not, and forgive me, I'm not an attorney. But the Supreme Court has upheld laws that restrict the distribution of sexually explicit material to minors. Although these laws must be narrowly tailored to avoid infringing on the rights of adults, when we're talking about, you mentioned, you know, freedom of speech and the rights that minors do, minors do have the right to free speech. However, we do have a right as a state to seek and protect minors from harms on social media by requiring age verification and parental consent for online activities. Critics of these laws argue that they infringed on a minor's First Amendment by restricting their ability to speak and access online information. However, as parents, we do have the rights to restrict our child's access to certain materials. There are obscenity laws in place to protect our children. So why not, why would you be against a bill that would empower parents to keep obscene materials out of the hands of our children, is my question to you. Thank you, Representative. First, I want to be clear that there are other bills that I would be much more willing to support. But to that case, to Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, what the court said in that case was that there are very specific situations where a bill isn't subject to scrutiny when it burdens the First Amendment, because it is one of the greatest burdens. The only cases that they mentioned that have ever happened are the terrorism content. And now the second is obscenity content. Obscenity is a really narrow definition. It is very specific. It's very hard to have obscene content. It's even different from explicit content. The First Amendment is very robust protection for all of us. When it comes to speech online, it's not obscenity. It's anything else, right? It's not just that very narrow definition of obscenity that I won't bore you with. But as the Supreme Court noted, any bill that goes beyond obscenity, that attaches to anything else, is subject to strict scrutiny. And that's where states have gotten in trouble with a bill like this, because with strict scrutiny, that's the highest standard of, that's the highest burden. And you have to prove that the bill justifies the means, and oftentimes it doesn't in a very facial case. And so as to why I wouldn't want to empower parents, I do want to empower parents. And I do have model bills that I'm looking at, that we're tweaking, that we're working through with other states and other state legislators. This bill is just an outdated version. It's one of the earlier forms of age verification mechanisms that have been struck down by the courts, but was a good start. And I do believe in the intention behind the bill, to be clear. And if I can add one more thing, please. So the Supreme Court has affirmed that students, although they do not lose their rights at the schoolhouse gate, but schools can restrict speech that is disruptive, disorderly, or violates the rights of others. So I feel like we're empowering schools to limit our children's right to free speech, but we're not empowering parents. And as you know, there is a big fight across

country to empower parents and limit schools, because we ultimately control that. Sure. I think that's a really important point to make. Parents, the First Amendment right for kids flows through their parents. It's not a First Amendment right for you as a kid until you're 18. It flows through your parents who have the burden of being responsible for what you say. And when you turn your kid over to school, school stands as a locus parentis, I think is the right term. I might be botching that. But in other words, they are now responsible for what you say, you know, the things that your kid does in school, they're in charge of taking care of all the kids in school. When it comes to empowering parents on social media, that's more about, you know, having conversations with kids and making sure there's an opportunity for it. When it comes to contracts like this bill, like the bill sponsors mentioning, there are more specific ways to do that that are not this model. Representative Dievendorf. Just a statement. Thank you for being here today. And I want to thank the sponsor for the intent of this bill, certainly understand it and the concerns. I used to teach at a college and we taught social media responsibility, but also the psychological impact of it. We do have ways for parents to be empowered, and that's for parents to decide how a kid is raised and what they're exposed to, as we just discussed. And I do really appreciate that as well. And I believe our good representative over there who denies their child a cell phone at a young age is a great example of that. So I would encourage us to, sure, continue to try to keep up with social media and technology, but look at other ways. And last, I think we can all agree that Al Gore is responsible for all of this. Okay. Any further questions? Seeing none, thank you very much, Caden. And one last person to testify, Amy Boss from NetChoice testifying virtually in opposition. Yes, thank you, Mr. Chairman, members of the committee. My name is Amy Boss. I'm the Vice President of Government Affairs at NetChoice. NetChoice is a trade association working to make the internet safe for free enterprise and free expression. We share the goal of protecting young people online. Our members have taken teen safety seriously and have rolled out numerous new parental tools, safety features, and protections to empower families. But I'm here to respectfully urge you to oppose HB 4388 because an unconstitutional law protects no one. It just guarantees litigation while kids remain no safer. Federal courts have repeatedly struck down age verification laws similar to HB 4388. Earlier this year, a federal judge in Arkansas permanently blocked a nearly identical law, stating that Arkansas takes a hatchet to adults and minors' protected speech alike, though the Constitution demands it use a scalpel. Similar laws in Ohio, Utah, and California, which the other witness mentioned, are also enjoined. Beyond the constitutional problems, this bill creates a privacy nightmare. To verify age, platforms must collect personal information, such as government IDs, biometric data, or other documentation, not just for minors, but from every Michigan user. This creates a honeypot of personal data vulnerable to breaches. Bad actors would love nothing more than a database linking real identities to social media accounts. And additionally, perhaps most troubling, this bill substitutes legislative judgment for parental judgment. Michigan parents already have access to built-in parental controls, screen time limits, and content filters. HB 4388 tells parents that Lansing knows better than they do when their children should be online and what platforms they can use. We shouldn't be empowering parents, not overriding their decisions. Instead of mandating this approach, we encourage Michigan to adopt the existing parental tools and digital literacy education programs that many states have implemented. Parents need better information about these controls, not a law that will ultimately be challenged in court. I urge you again to reject HB 4388. And we are always happy to work with you on constitutional alternatives that truly empower parents. Thank you again for the opportunity to testify. Great. Thank you, Amy. And we are running out of time here, so I am going to read in a couple of cards. Mary Wodkowski has not sent in a card of opposition. I don't see an organization that she's with, so I think it's just her personally. Kyle Zawicki from the ACLU does not wish to speak, opposes the bill. And Paul Stankiewicz with the Michigan Catholic Conference does not wish to speak, supports the bill. Representative Liberati moves to excuse absent members without objection so ordered. And seeing no further business before the committee, we are adjourned. Thank you. Thank you.

title: Agriculture — Thursday, November 13, 2025
transcript:
can you come to order. Clerk, if you could please take the roll. Chair Nygaard. Here. Representative Ward. Here. Leitner. Here. Alexander. Here. Fox. Present. Coons. Present. Tableau. Pies. Present. Evendorf. Here. Reingans. Here. Skaggs. Here. Mr. Chair, you have 10 members present. You have a quorum. Thank you. Representative Alexander moves to adopt the meetings from the previous session with no objections. Minutes are adopted. First on the agenda, we'll take up a vote on House Bill 4917. Rep. Leitner moves to report out House Bill 4917 with recommendations. Clerk, could you call the roll? Chair Nygaard. Yes. Representative Ward. Yes. Leitner. Yes. Alexander. Yes. Fox. Yay. Coons. Aye. Tableau. Pies. Stephen Dorf. Pass. Reingans. No. Skaggs. No. Mr. Chair, you have six yeas, two nays, two pass. The motion prevails. All right. Thank you. 4917 is reported out with recommendations. With that, I would like to introduce and have come forward our folks from the, let me get the correct title, please, from our Michigan Apples. Diane, would you please come forward and proceed, please? There we go. Hello. Thank you so much for having me here today. I'm just going to give some background and some issues that are facing the Michigan Apple industry, bring you up to date. Let me see. So who are we? We're the Michigan Apple Committee. We actually started as a state apple commission back in 1939, but when Public Act 232 was enacted, we became part of that and became the Michigan Apple Committee. We represent the growers in the state, and our main job is to do marketing, communications, education, and research. Our mission is to enhance the reputation of Michigan apples in everything that we do and aid in the profitability and sustainability of the industry. So pretty big job. We have 850 family-owned farms in the state. So a lot of farms.
