We produce in 2024 1.28 billion pounds of apples, and that's on at least 17.6 million trees, and we are the second largest producer in the U.S., behind Washington State. But if you put all of our other states together, we don't equal Washington State. So we are going to always be number two. Apples account for 71% of the cash income that's generated from fruit grown here in Michigan. So we are the largest and most valuable fruit crop in the state. And we produce apples in 80 of the 83 counties. So pretty much everywhere you can find some Michigan apples being grown. Big business. I'm preaching to the choir here when I talk about agriculture's big business for the state. Michigan apple industry, obviously we play into the economy with the trickle-down effect with allied industries and jobs that come into the state for harvest but also are here year-round. So we constantly are at the forefront of everything, especially the economy in a lot of rural communities. But besides labor being our number one issue, we have another really big issue, which is apple consumption. We are down 10% over the last decade. Only 12% of U.S. adults meet their daily fruit intake recommendations. And, you know, apples' consumption being down is really not – I mean, there's a good explanation for it. As we all know, when we were growing up, there weren't fruits available year-round like they are now. We have a lot more competition in the produce department. So that plays into it. When you look at even bananas are down in consumption rates. So those mainstays obviously do take a little bit of a hit when you can get access to a lot of different fruits year-round. So, you know, that is probably the number one issue behind labor is the consumption issue. Our industry has done quite a bit in terms of researching that, seeing what we could do different. We do understand that there are a lot of varieties of apples, and that can be a little confusing for some consumers. When you go into the grocery store, you see a whole shelf of a bunch of different names of apples, and they're all red, and you wonder, well, which one do I want? So that is something as an industry that we probably really should address a little bit more aggressively than we do, but, you know, everybody has their favorites. And so, yeah. And then conversely, you know, 56% of total expenses for a grower are labor. So we have some pretty big numbers that are hitting. I'm going to get into the labor thing in a little more detail here. But first, I'm sure all of you have heard of AWER. It is the wage rate that's set by the Department of Labor for our workers that come into the state under the H-2A program. We do have to pay all workers this, though. It doesn't matter if they're H-2A or not. It's the set, you know, rate. Right now we're at $18.15 an hour for harvest. And so there have been some updates, and it is in the registry for comment right now on the federal side. And starting with work orders starting October 1, so it's not taking effect for what we harvested this year, but there are going to be some lowering of the dollar amounts, and they're going to be basing it on two different skill levels of workers. Most likely, apples is probably going to be in the top tier because it is a skilled labor that we need. But we do have an adjustment of housing costs, which is something that we've never had before. So that alone would bring down the, you know, hourly rate because housing is required and provided for our workers. So getting into that cost

the production. I mentioned that 56% of the per acre cost is labor. You know, looking at USDA numbers, the cost of labor for fruit and tree nut farms is at 40% nationwide. And if you put all farms together, it's 12%. So as you can see, apples, we rely on a lot of labor and it requires a lot of money. So other expenses that are large for our growers are, of course, overhead and taxes. We expect that. Bin and storage. Irrigation is at only 1%, but also crop protection. Crop protection is obviously at 10% and a big expense also for our growers. Now let's look at grower returns. We broke this down to a three-pound bag of apples. You can go in the grocery store, everybody can see a three-pound bag of apples. Let's say it costs $2.99. The retailer is going to make about $1.06 on that. The grower is going to make $0.19. So they're making 6% of what the sale of that bag of apples is going. There's another $1.74 that is going to the sale, the storage, the packing, the shipping of that apple to get to the retail. So when you look at only getting $0.19, it's pretty grim at times, especially when your labor costs and everything keep rising year after year. Another area that's really important to our industry is trade and exports. We're down in 2024 by about 31%. I would attribute a lot of that to crop size and pricing, market availability. Did tariffs play a part at the beginning of this year? It may have a little bit in terms of not tariffs on apples, but tariffs discussions with countries that maybe we didn't get some sales, like say in Mexico, because our numbers are down in Mexico, and that is a market that we've been aggressively trying to get. But I think mainly what we can attribute that 31% down is to pricing and the opportunity for sales in the marketplace in those markets. Central America is our number one market, and it is down as well. And again, same reason. I would say that if you look at the two years before that, though, we were averaging a 400% increase in exports, and those were really like record crop years. So it just kind of makes sense that when we came back on a smaller crop year, there wasn't as much availability. Trade, obviously, is very important. Michigan Apples is part of a group of all the apple-producing states except for Washington. We have an organization that our U.S. Apple Export Council that we utilize MAP dollars through the federal government, and we have representatives in different regions of the world helping us sell the apples in those regions. One thing that we really need, though, for healthy trade and exports is Washington needs to export 30% of their crop, or it's bad news for all of us. Those apples will come either into an export market we have great footing in, or they're going to really honestly hit the domestic market, which is going to lower price and it's going to lower that return even more back to the growers. So we advocate quite strongly for Washington to be able to ship as many of those apples out and keep the good ones for Michigan here for all of us. I'm going to flip around a little here to production research. We do have strong partnerships. Michigan Apples is one of the founding fathers of the Tree Fruit Commission, but we also have strong partnerships with AgBioResearch and MSU Extension. Project Green is incredibly important to us. Researchers utilize the dollars that Michigan Apple funds in research to kind of use as leverage for those funds that they can receive from Project Green. So we see that as a very important partnership for our industry as we continue to do the research at Michigan State. That's where the majority of our production research is happening. One of the biggest concerns I would say with that is as researchers retire, I'm sure you've all heard this, they're not replacing positions. And that is a concern as we continue to lose that knowledge base and not getting people back in those positions. That's incredibly detrimental to our industry. I mentioned that Michigan Apple does fund research as well. They assess themselves about $250,000 to $350,000 a year in research. So we do fund, like I said, majority production research. We do some marketing research, but that's pretty limited year to year depending on what we might have. And so we also have strong partnerships with the USDA's Specialty Crop Research Grants and our national organization, U.S. Apple, works really heavily with a lot of that as well. I mentioned the investments lost of researchers. The other thing when we see the federal cuts that happen to research, we were really concerned about those graduate and undergraduate assistants and people that are coming up in the industry and losing the ability to kind of cultivate that next generation. That's incredibly concerning for us as we see these positions not filled and not having that talent base that's coming up with it. So that's something that we continue to watch quite closely. And then the last thing I'm going to end with is agritourism. I mean, obviously we're coming off of apple season. Everybody is part of our heritage to go out to farm markets and cider mills. And, you know, those organizations, they're the face to our industry, quite frankly. They're the ones that are putting a face to where their food comes from to consumers, which is incredibly important to us. We want to make sure that we're connecting with consumers on all levels. And knowing where their food comes from is incredibly important for us. It's part of our tradition. October is National Apple Month, but it's also Michigan Apple Month. And so hopefully everybody got out and had some cider and donuts and some apples. We have a lot of award-winning ciders here in the state of Michigan, not only nationally but internationally. We have a really healthy hard cider, you know, organizations coming up. So we really appreciate them and our partnerships with those people. I think one thing that I would also mention is Michigan Apples was one of the, well, we were the first commodity group to do a partnership with Pure Michigan and definitely has the tourism aspect to our industry. It makes sense. It was a good connection for us. I would say if, you know, I know there's never money just floating around, but if there's ever extra money to be had, one thing that we I think would be really good for specialty crops, not just apples, but all specialty crops grown here in the state of Michigan, is marketing more to our consumers right here in our state. Having a little bit more of that buying local is so important, and I think that we could do a much better job of that on a state level. And Michigan Department of Agriculture did used to have a program, Select Michigan, in the past and other things where they could do that. Those programs have gone away, but also who's better at selling our state, Pure Michigan. So, you know, we see that as a potential in the future that we could find some funding to kind of have them advocate. They have the connections with resorts and hotels and visitors that are coming to our state. There's just so many opportunities, and I think that could be a really good win for us. So, and again, not just from an Apple standpoint. I mean, I am here for apples, but I think that would be good for all the fruits and vegetables that we grow here in the state. It's not just apples that are hurting. It's, you know, it's all of us. So, wanted to put that little plug in the back of your mind in case anything ever comes to light and you think that could be a good fit. So, that is my presentation. I kept it short and sweet, kind of hit the highlights, but if anybody has any questions, I'm happy to take them. Thank you. Rep. Leitner. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thanks, Diane, for being here. I know you obviously are part of the apple industry, but what I'm wondering about is you had mentioned H-2A, and, you know, there have been concerns this year in the budget, some language that was in there in regards to eVerify, and I'm just curious, one, how many of your members use H-2A right now, and also have used eVerify together, like for maybe the ongoing, not just the seasonal, because obviously they're for the seasonal, and what have you heard, like have there been issues with it? I'm just wondering if you can kind of let me know or let us know if there have been concerns and issues with the two together. Okay. So, eVerify has always been a thing with our industry that we've always been okay with it as long as it had comprehensive immigration reform. But H-2A, I would say the majority of our

growers that are growing large amounts of quantity of apples in the state are using H-2A workers year-round. Whether they have a higher influx coming in for harvest, but they have them year-round for pruning and other jobs that happen around the orchards. So they are being brought in from the Department of Labor. We do have some domestic workers. I don't know the stat on how many people are using eVerify in that respect. That's something I would have to look into, but I could look in to see if we can find some numbers or something that might be helpful. Yeah, I mean, if you have a member that has used both, I mean, I've reached out to one stakeholder before trying to get, I just want to ask them questions on the process because obviously H-2A is a money issue, but I have heard that there's issues with eVerify as well. They're like, well, we have a H-2A worker already, which is already processed through the federal government, and then we put them into the eVerify system and it flags it, and then there's a problem. So I would like to talk to an individual grower or operator, farm operator that has done both and ask them about the processes and procedures. Now, I get that those are federal issues, but those are things that I can talk to my congressman or Tim Wahlberg, Tom Barrett, whoever it may be, and try to get some consistency there. Because to me, if H-2A is already working, what's the purpose of doing another set with eVerify that doesn't follow the same system? Right. So if you could have that and provide that to the committee of someone willing to talk, that would be great. Thank you. Yeah, I will look into that for you. Representative Fox. Thank you, Diane. And I think I drive past about 10 million of those 17.6 million trees on my way here. You do. When I come down through Fruit Ridge and Sparta area. So long story short, two questions. One, I was a missionary in the Philippines for a few years, and their apples were treated very, very special because they don't raise them there. And they typically, what I was told in the Philippines was they imported them from China, and they wrapped them up in these special containers, and they were special Christmas presents given to people. Are we in the Philippine market and the Southeast Asia market? We are breaking into the Southeast Asia market. Actually, we have a trip with some of our sales organizations planned for January. Mainly, though, we're going to Thailand, Vietnam, and maybe Malaysia. The Philippines, we do not ship there. I would have to double check. New York State might be, but Washington is for sure. And they do. Asian countries, the apple is a gift for Christmas. It's a treasure. It is. It is. My second question is, as you think about your publicity, I grew up with the phrase, an apple a day keeps the doctor away. Now, is that something that you still build upon with your advertising and what have you? We do. We have actually, it seems extreme, we have three dietitians, the official dietitians of the Michigan apple industry, and that's just because one is retiring and we're bringing some new people up into the job. So we don't normally have that many. But health is definitely one of the top things that we talk about, the health aspects of apples. And we always will continue to do that because it is incredibly important for our industry. We probably can't use that phrase because the FDA would probably come down and say, prove that. So it would be incredibly difficult. But yeah, we would definitely, we do quite a bit with that, including television. We do a lot of news opportunities in Chicago and in the state of Michigan talking about health benefits. We also work with retail dietitians and the major retailers across the U.S. So we push that quite a bit. Okay, thank you very much. You're welcome. Representative Fox, or excuse me, Alexander. Thank you, Mr. Chair. And thank you, Diane. How long have you been at Michigan Apples? I have been there, I was hired at five because I've been there 30 years. I started actually as a student and I've held almost every job in the organization at this point. Very good. I know I reached out to you in 2014. I was working with you directly through some school tours and different things. You mentioned, was it PA 233 that changed your organization? Yes. What year was that? It was enacted in 1965. 65, okay. And just to answer your question, Honeycrisp is my favorite apple. Good. Which is also an extremely, it's a newer variety that's extremely hard to grow. The trunks aren't that great and they don't store well. So how many varieties does Michigan grow? We are actually known as a variety state. We grow more commercially than any other state. But I would say we really kind of tout 15 to 18 varieties. There are a lot of growers, actually, that do a lot of antique varieties. But we can't obviously market all of those. But the Honeycrisp is a bit, as I refer to it, I refer to it as a diva in every interview I do because she doesn't like to be grown. She doesn't like to be picked. She doesn't like to be packed, shipped, stored. She's a challenge and we've spent quite a bit of lot research dollars trying to fix all of that. Thank you. I appreciate your presentation. You're welcome. Representative Pies. Thank you, Mr. Chair. A little bit of just being a cheerleader here. About two weeks ago my husband and I went out to Yates. And for the next week I spent apple crisp, apple cider, apple lollipops, apple butter. I got appled out and it was terrible but really, really good. But I did want to mention that when my husband was 19 years and years ago he moved out to Oregon and picked apples there for a week. And the reason he stopped after a week was because it was really difficult work. And he really applauded the people who did it and did it year-round for a long time. So I just wanted to throw that out there about what tough work it is for the workers. It really is. And that a lot of Americans, like my husband, just couldn't deal with it. I'll tell you, I get out there and I'll have a picking bucket on and I'll be going at it and the workers laugh at me. I'm so slow. They're so fast. They know what they're doing. They're so skilled at it. It's a work of art. And so we're very, very fortunate to have such great workers that harvest our crop. Representative Rannigan. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you for being here. My question is about the H-2A visas also. So I was at a farmer roundtable in August ahead of when a lot of workers were regularly coming up from Mexico to do their regular annual temporary work here for harvesting in the fall. And there was a change in the process this year that everybody was really concerned about before it happened. And I was curious if, looking back now, was there anything that was disrupted? Things seemed to work okay? To work okay. Okay. Yeah, that's good to hear. Okay. Thank you. You're welcome. Representative Skaggs. Thank you, Chair. Just looking at the slide on cost production and the H-2As. So you say here that the new ruling will benefit growers in future seasons. And that there will be an adjustment. Is that because of the adjustment for housing costs? Yeah, we'll at least have that adjustment. So that will at least lower the hourly wage down. I will say to look at, if you look at the 56% cost per acre of labor, even if we have the most extreme cut, which we don't know what it will be yet, but if we did have the most extreme, it's only going to be a 2% difference. We're looking at 1% to 2% of that cost going down with these new, with the new AWAR stuff. Our hope, though, is really to get more of the methodology behind how they figure those rates out fixed on a national level, so that maybe in the future we can continue to keep these things from going up dramatically year after year. But yeah, we're not going to totally go down, but we're going to be maybe a little bit, maybe $2 less or so. So for the worker, they're going to continue to get the same housing they got in the past, but they're going to get a lower wage. They're going to get a lower wage, yes. So they're going to be worse off. Worse off, I would say, I think the allowance, the adjustment for Michigan was $1 something. So yeah, it's going to come down maybe, I think, was it $1.30 or something like that, I think. So that would come off the hourly wage, yes. And is there concerns that we're going to have a labor supply problem? As of right now, no, but we're also, I've heard from several growers that I don't know if it would be required. They can write their contracts for whatever hourly rate they're interested in paying, and a lot of these people have had the same workers year after year after year. So whether or not it will decrease forever

I don't know, some of those farmers might continue to pay at the same rate that they have been, just so that they can maintain that knowledge base of their orchards and their workers and keep them on hand, because that is important to them to have those same workers year after year. Thank you, Chair. Representative Worts. Thank you, Chair. So one question I had, I've worked in schools on and off, and you guys used to provide apples for lunches, and I think that they're sourced locally through Michigan. Do you know if that's still happening? Yeah, so that is the hardest place for supply that we've ever dealt with. It requires, you know, obviously for food service, so the Gordons and the Siscos of the world and being on the order form, and a lot of times that would just say red apple or green apple. And that was incredibly frustrating, especially if people were wanting to source local. So there are better opportunities, and I do have to say that the Gordons and the Siscos have done a better job, and they've said Michigan red or Michigan gold. They've done a much better job of that, but I think that continues to struggle. We do have quite a few farmers that do supply to their districts and take apples in. You know, the logistics of that isn't for everybody because it's taking a small load, you know, over to a local school. But they do try to do that. And I know Grand Rapids Public Schools does a great job of sourcing Michigan apples. I mean, they're kind of in the heart of apple country of our largest production area. But yeah, it's always a challenge to do that, and we do it wherever we can, but we're kind of at their mercy. I would just, yeah, I would say it would be really nice if we could work on that because the apples that get given out when you talk about consumption decreasing, I can tell you probably it's because of the apples kids are eating, which are red delicious apples, which are at the bottom of eating quality. And so, you know, then if that's a child's perspective of what an apple is, are they going to make that choice? And so how can we actually take the good quality production that we're growing in Michigan and feed it to our kids? We did do a program at Michigan Apple where we partnered with Blue Cross Blue Shield and Wayne State University of Michigan, and they would go in and do school tastings. So they would go into what we would do maybe 15 to 20 schools a year and go in with our printed pieces, and they would get to try three to four different varieties, and we would always make sure they were varieties that weren't red delicious. These were like varieties that, you know, people really want. So we'd go in with Fugees, we'd go in with Jonagold, Galas, you know, different varieties so they could have a taste of those. And then they would take something home with them at the end of the day saying, I tried these apples and this is my favorite. So they could take it home to mom and dad and say, hey, next time I go to the store, can we get some of these? So we do have that program that we do. But yeah, we need to definitely, if you ever have any ideas of how we can always make that better, we are always open to hearing them. Last question, Representative Pies. Thank you, Mr. Chair. So you were talking about research, and I just wanted to clarify something. So you had said that there were problems essentially because a lot of workers were either being fired or through attrition rate. And I wanted clarification that that's during this administration, this presidential administration. And also what you're doing to make amends for that, if you will. Sure. So yeah, earlier in the year, USDA had a lot of cuts that were made, and that really hurt the ability for researchers to keep postdocs and different things on projects, especially when they've lost if grants were discontinued because those fund those positions. So that was always a concern. Now here in the state of Michigan, one thing we do, we have a lot of partnerships between Michigan Apple Committee, the State Horticultural Society, the Michigan Tree Fruit Commission on doing startup packages and funding to help MSU make the case to hire more people. So anytime that we can have a partnership in that, we do. We've had an extension position that's been open on the ridge in the Sparta area for years, and we've had a really hard time filling it, and our growers need it. And honestly, the other extension people in the state need it because they need to not be spread so thin. So that is something that we have actively, and so I'm kind of a pest at MSU and constantly I'm bringing that to their attention. But we do try to, when we can, put funding of our research dollars and the assessments that are collected within the fruit industry towards startup packages to help with some of those hirings. All right. In the interest of time, we're going to end it. Thank you, Diane, for coming in and explaining the industry. Thank you for your team and taking the time. Looking forward to working with you more. With that, Representative Alexander moves to excuse all absent members. Being no objections, so moved. With no further activities, the committee's done. Thank you.

title: Government Operations — Thursday, November 13, 2025
transcript:
The Committee on Government Operations will come to order. Mr. Clerk, would you please call the roll? Chair McDowell? Here. Representatives Harris? Here. VanderWaal? Present. Fitzgerald? Here. McFaul? Ms. Jay, you have four members present, a quorum. Okay, thank you. Just a reminder to everybody, if you want to give testimony today on any of the bills that we have on the agenda, please fill out a card on the table here and turn it in to our clerk. Representative VanderWaal moves to excuse absent members without objection, so ordered. Representative VanderWaal moves to approve the minutes of the November 6 meeting without objection, so ordered. Okay, first on our agenda is Senate Bill 595. This is a bill that Senator Lindsey has sponsored. The bill will enable adjacent counties to survey the Michigan-Indiana state line and extends the deadline. Before we take testimony on that bill, we have a substitute H1 offered by Representative Harris, which would allow professional surveyors in adjacent counties to serve on the Michigan-Indiana State Commission. This would alleviate any quorum problems that they may have experienced in the past. Representative, would you like to speak on the amendment at all? Sure. Thank you, Mr. Chair. It's as simple as what the chair put. They're experiencing some quorum issues or have in the past, and this would allow surveyors that are residing in the county to solve quorum problems being able to serve on the commission. You're welcome, and I do move my bill. Okay, thank you. Representative Harris moves his amendment. Mr. Clerk, would you take the roll, please? On the motion to adopt the substitute, Chair Bergold? Yes. Representative Harris? Yes. VanderWaal? Yes. Fitzgerald? Pass. McFaul? Ms. Jay, you have three yeas, zero nays, one pass. The motion prevails. Okay, thank you. The motion passes. Okay, Senator, if you want to come on up, the floor is yours, sir. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thank you, members of the committee for the opportunity to testify on Senate Bill 595, and a special thank you for you taking quick consideration of this bill. We'll get into a little bit of the reasoning of that as I explain it. I serve the 17th Senate District, which you may or may not know encompasses the entirety of the Michigan-Indiana border. What a lot of people don't know is that the Michigan-Indiana border has not had a proper full survey and re-monumentation since the early 1800s. There are stories you can find, some I've talked with people about, that this has created some controversy sometimes. Examples like general stores not knowing if they're collecting sales tax in Michigan or Indiana. Sometimes on a residential level, people having post office boxes in one state while their driver's license is in another. But I would say the bigger reason that this creates a potential issue is that when you look at something like the way that our borders with other states have been determined, in the case of Ohio, it actually led to a conflict to ultimately solve the border. And then later on, the border with Michigan and Wisconsin was ultimately decided through a United States Supreme Court case. And part of what I'm trying to say is borders aren't usually an issue until they are, and when they are, it's a big problem. So there's been a longstanding effort to go back and make sure we have a good, accurate survey of the borderline of Michigan and Indiana. It's been a cooperative effort with Michigan and Indiana. And the recent, I mean, really it's gone on for decades, but most recently there was a state border commission that was reestablished in 2022, created an opportunity to undertake this re-monumentation and surveying process. So what's the problem? Well, a little bit of it is that it's a state-based commission that it did face some challenges getting quorum. You heard about that a little bit. Also just some procedural challenge. And then ultimately, and I'll let some of my friends at Laura who worked hard on this bill, and I really appreciate their help on it, explain some of what they saw. But ultimately, it wasn't the right solution to try to get this done. We already have re-monumentation programs at a county level. So what the bill is doing is two things. Number one, it's taking a sunset that's about to take place. January 1st, if we don't do anything on this bill, the entire commission will dissolve, the law that empowered it, and the resources that have been put into it, and we would go back to square one. That would mean that just in recent history, over 20 years of hard work that's been put into trying to solve this problem would just be reset. But that's not the only thing the bill does. It also makes a mechanical change so that we can get closer to success. And that's the change of allowing the commission to grant resources directly down to the county re-monumentation programs. These programs already exist. They do this exact type of work, and it really doesn't make sense to have a state-level commission that then has to go out and procure contracts with specific vendors just for one surveying project. So it's pretty straightforward, but again, I appreciate you bringing it forward expeditiously because, as I said, if we don't take action

Come January 1st, all the work that has been done will kind of be wiped away and will go back to zero. The last thing I'll add is that when the commission was re-established, there was actually money appropriated for this. It still exists. Those resources are there. We're not asking the state to invest any additional resources. I've worked a lot with some of the local surveyors, even talked with folks in Indiana who have done some of this work. There's a high level of confidence that the resources that are there will be sufficient to complete the work. So we're not asking the state to put any more resources in it, just to make a change and give a little bit more time so that we can make this process more efficient. I'll end my comments there and turn it over to our friends from Lara. Thank you. Sorry. Hello, Chairman Begola, members of the House Government Operations Committee. Thank you so much for allowing us to join today. I'm Paige Foltz. I'm the Director at Lara of the Office of Policy and Legislative Affairs. I just wanted to mention the Bureau of Construction Codes, or BVCC for short, is housed within our department. And you mainly know them for working to ensure that Michigan's built environment and the systems are sound, safe, and sanitary. One lesser known responsibility of the Bureau of Construction Codes is it houses the Office of Land Survey and Remonumentation. The office's day-to-day encompasses orderly and consistent review of subdivision plats. They administer statewide programs for monumentation and remonumentation. And they also review petitions that are set out by the State Border Commission. Today, Lara comes before you to discuss our support for Senator Lindsey's bill, SB 595, which would finalize the Michigan-Indiana State Border. Unlike other state borders, a clear line does not exist. As the senator alluded, the Michigan and Ohio border was settled with the Toledo War. The compromise from the U.S. Congress was granting Michigan statehood. Also, we gave up our rights to the Toledo Strip. Those went directly to Ohio in exchange for the Upper Peninsula. The Michigan-Wisconsin border was decided in court after a dispute arose with the original 1836 boundary line. Basically, a description was referenced. There was a situation that did not exist. It claimed the Montreal River originated from the Lake of the Desert, which was not true. And this actually has created a longstanding ambiguity of our state line with Indiana. The two states did sue each other, making it all the way to the Supreme Court. And in 1926, the Supreme Court did establish the Wisconsin-Michigan border. I have with me Andrew Briscoe. He is our Director of the Bureau of Construction Codes. We're happy to answer any questions you guys have regarding this bill and the work that the commission has done so far. Thank you so much. Thank you very much. You answered my funding question. Will this result in the erection of the big cement monuments that you have seen in other states right at the borders? Or will it be just something that's not visible to people? It won't necessarily. From my talk with some of the surveyors who have served on the commission, that's one of the decisions they could make is what does the remonumentation look like. But when you talk to a lot of surveyors now, they tend to focus on kind of lower footprint but permanent monumentation that may be even just metal rods in the ground. But I think so not necessarily. I think one thing that's going to help determine that is that they need to focus on doing the surveying of the sites first, and then the commission would have an option as that's done. And I think it may be pending resources too. You know, personally, I would think that if you get to county corners along the border at a minimum, it might make sense to have some, you know, more visible monuments depending right where those sit. But the focus will be more on the monumentation. And my understanding is that a lot of the modern surveying that goes on, they don't really default to these big concrete pillars anymore as much. Hopefully that answers your question. You did. Maybe this is a little too early to tell, but do we anticipate there's going to be any dispute on where that property line is, or we just don't know because it's been since 1800s? We don't anticipate a dispute. We've been working closely with Indiana. So this work has been happening. Part of the remonumentation process will be Michigan checking Indiana's work that their surveyors are doing and vice versa. So no, we don't anticipate an issue with our Hoosier friends to the south. Sounds good. Okay. Thank you very much. I don't see any further questions. So we do have a card to read in here. Not wanting to speak in support of the bill is Michelle Bottora of the Michigan Society of Professional Surveyors. Thank you for your testimony. We're going to go ahead and vote this out now just because of such important issue with a sunset that's already occurred. So Representative VanderWaal moves to report Senate Bill 595 H1 with recommendation. Mr. Clerk, will you please call the roll? On the motion to report. Chair McGold? Yes. Representative Harris? Yes. VanderWaal? Yes. Fitzgerald? Yes. McFaul? Mr. Chair, you have four yeas, zero nays, zero pass. The motion prevails. Thank you. The Senate Bill 595 H1 is reported with recommendation. Thank you. Okay, next we're going to take up House Bill 4669 sponsored by Representative Pohutski. Welcome, Representative. You may begin when you're ready. Good morning, Mr. Chair and members of the committee. Thank you all very much for the opportunity to testify on House Bill 4669, my bill to restore our ability as legislators to provide meaningful oversight to our corrections facilities. I'll be brief because this bill is pretty simple. It merely codifies the existing and pre-2022 practice of legislators being able to perform site visits without being required to provide a 72-hour notice to facilities beforehand. The issues with this are evident. We're prevented from providing meaningful oversight of MDOC facilities if we have to announce when we'll be attempting to do so. 72 hours notice can and has allowed the department to address, often superficially, issues with facilities or even to schedule appointments for inmates so that they cannot meet with their legislators. Earlier this year, we passed a budget that included boilerplate language requiring legislators be able to perform unannounced site visits. It's an important step, but we have to codify this practice rather than letting an executive department dictate how we perform our jobs. As it stands, MDOC is already promulgating rules to make sure that this happens smoothly and safely, as well as figuring out how they will communicate with legislative leadership to make sure that legislators are behaving appropriately during these site visits. It's important to know that these site visits do not give us unfettered or unsupervised access to every inch of a prison. But it's equally important to note that this has not been an issue before. The ability for us to visit facilities that we fund and where our constituents are being housed is a longstanding, fundamental, and crucial aspect of our job. I'm happy to take any questions, and I know we have other people testifying as well. Thank you, Representative. I'm just curious if there's exceptions to this bill. For instance, if there was an emergency going on or there was some conditions that would maybe make it unsafe for them to enter the facility. There isn't an exception in there. It's worth noting that previously, if there have been unsafe conditions or an issue where a legislator would not be safe or staff wouldn't be safe, inmates wouldn't be safe, that has been part of the department's or the corrections staff on site. Their decision about where legislators can go, whether or not they can get in. This just says that they can't be turned away at the gates. Do you know possibly how long this was in place before Ms. Washington? I don't. As far as I know, there was never a notice requirement. That might be wrong. I know that there's some previous legislators who predate me here, as well as some testifying. In the most respectful way, Representative. But no problems that you've been aware of in the past? There was an allegation of one that led to the change in 2022, and I've passed out an email. There seems to be some dispute as to what happened. There was a legislator who was making many site visits. Typically, her follow-up would include emails to every single member of the legislature, as well as the director, about issues that she had encountered or things that inmates had told her. Eventually, there was one particular visit that supposedly necessitated the need for this notice rule. The email I have sent out is from the warden of that facility, who contests those allegations that anything was unsafe. It's worth noting that legislator was also a former corrections officer. So there seems to be a dispute between the department and the people who were on the ground at the time of that visit as to whether anything untoward happened or if this was more an issue with that oversight element. Okay, thank you. And I do have the letter that you provided me.

Yes, I'll read that. So, okay, it looks like we have a couple questions. Representative VanderWaal. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you for being here and bringing this forward. I guess my question is, I understand the point of us being able to do a visit. I have a corrections facility in my area, but I also understand how we live on a schedule also. And my real question is, right now, how I read it is we could just pop into the front gate that day and say, here we are, and we want to take a visit without any notice. And knowing how facilities run and sometimes the urge of making sure the warden or whoever the proper people are, do you feel that there should be at least some time notification ahead of a visit than just popping in on the front gate? My understanding is that typically these visits were scheduled in advance anyway. As a matter of fact, the incident that apparently necessitated this policy change with the department, part of their reasoning was that she was late to the visit that she had scheduled. So I understand your point. And I think typically when people are trying to be there, they do call ahead, they do schedule. My concern with putting any particular scheduling requirements in law is that if there is an issue that necessitates, for lack of a better word, more of a surprise, lack of advanced notice because of the nature of the concern, I don't want us to be limiting our legislative authority for an issue that doesn't appear to have actually arisen. Follow up if I may. I guess I understand what we're getting at and what we're trying to do. We all want to be able to make sure we do what's right in our communities and in our districts. I also don't want us to be able to use ourselves as a weapon to kind of say, I got you. And what I'm looking at here is a reasonable amount of time notice I think is a fair request other than just a true surprise because of what it does to disrupt and safety of the people that are doing the inspection, et cetera. So I look forward to working with you and having more communication on this and hopefully some of those hot buttons will be discussed as we move on further. Thank you again for being here. No, thank you. And I understand what you're saying about specifically noting it, but it is worth noting that just because we show up doesn't mean we actually get to tour a prison. If there is something like a staff, we all know that there is a ton of staffing limitations in our corrections facilities right now. So it's not as though we show up and we immediately get a key either, but I understand what you're saying. Okay, Representative Fitzgerald. Thank you, Representative, for being here. I have not been around for a time where we had the ability to conduct these visits. One question I do have is if we're going to be reinstating this privilege or this opportunity to visit these sites, I actually have a concern about the ability to go as a group. Because I can see how there would be disruption if, say, 30 of us decided to show up and say, we're all here for our visit that we are duly entitled to, that there could be disruption if there is large groups. And then we say, well, we can only take 10 of you in at a time. We're going to have 20 of you sit outside for two hours. And then there's that gotcha moment that we might have inferred to. Is there a differentiation between group and individual or individuals? I think, I mean, let's be realistic. You can't get 30 of us to do something together most days of the week. So I have less of a concern about that. I will also just— Sometimes not even 56. I get it. Right, exactly. I do just want to say, like, you originally referred to this as a privilege. It's not. It is part of our job. So, again, if 30 of us decide that there is something pressing enough that we all need to be there, the department has the ability to say, we can only take 10 of you at a time. Like, the space does not allow for all 30 of you to come through. And that's a risk that 20 of us are going to take to have to sit outside in our cars for two hours. But, like, none of this dictates how the prison has to operate with these sites, just that we do not have to give—or with these visits, I'm sorry, just that we do not have to give them notice to possibly address anything that we are there to see, an untarnished picture of. Okay. Thank you. Thank you for your testimony, Representative. We do have some other people who would like to speak today in regards to the bill. First up is Eden Kinlock. Mr. Kinlock, maybe he's on Zoom? Hi. Good morning. Oh, I'm sorry. Mr. Chair and members of the House Committee on Government Operations, my name is Eden Kinlock. I am the State Legislative Affairs Associate for FAM. FAM submitted written testimony, and I appear today in support of House Bill 4669. FAM is a nonpartisan national sentencing and corrections reform organization. For more than three decades, we've advocated for sentencing and prison policies that are individualized and fair, protect public safety, and preserve families. And among these policies we advocate is the increase of transparency and accountability in our nation's prisons. House Bill 4669 doesn't just provide lawmakers with unannounced access to correctional facilities, but it's also a mechanism for creating a more accountable, transparent prison system that keeps us safe and has our trust. FAM believes that when it comes to prisons, you can't know if you don't go. That is, you should not create policy if you're not familiar with the people and conditions in our nation's prisons. Through a visit to prison campaign, FAM encouraged local, state, and federal lawmakers as well as judges and other elected officials to visit correctional facilities. We believe that policymakers who do take the time to visit prisons and witness the realities of incarceration will see that there are significant problems that need to be addressed. The first of which being that we lock up too many people for too long. Our prison population is getting older with more sick and elderly people serving extreme sentences. Many of these people have been rehabilitated and could be released safely back into the community. For this reason, FAM encourages lawmakers who visit prisons to sit down and speak with incarcerated people, ask them how they've changed and how the release would benefit their families and their communities. The second problem that is better understood from a prison visit is that many prisons are unsafe, both for the incarcerated people and for correctional officers and staff. Overcrowding, understaffing, lack of programming, and other factors can make prisons extremely dangerous. But there is very little and sometimes no oversight. Even the well-intentioned inspections are announced far in advance, allowing DOC to hide those problems during visits. For this reason, we encourage legislators who visit prisons to speak with correctional staff and incarcerated people and ask them how the facilities can be improved. Lastly, when lawmakers visit prisons, they can see more clearly how families face enormous challenges while trying to maintain bonds with their incarcerated loved ones. Visiting often requires traveling long distances and families are often left in the dark because prisons don't share basic information about the health and well-being of their loved ones that are in custody. So we ask that lawmakers spend some time in the visitation rooms when they go to a prison, and we encourage them to ask family members about the challenges in maintaining relationships with their incarcerated loved ones. The legislature is responsible for crafting the policies and passing the laws that allow MDOC correctional facilities to operate 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, with the lives and well-being of tens of thousands of staff and incarcerated people hanging in the balance. It's not possible for lawmakers to get a full picture of day-to-day operations from the director's annual reports alone. MDOC incarcerates nearly 33,000 people and employs over 10,000 Michiganders. So granting lawmakers access to MDOC facilities benefits every last one of these people, plus their families and their loved ones. House Bill 4669 empowers lawmakers to see firsthand how prisons are really operating and how their constituents' taxes are being used. Advancing this bill is an essential step towards promoting transparency, accountability, and public trust in Michigan Corrections. And in light of earlier testimony, I also want to mention that lawmakers visiting prisons and it being codified in statute is not unique. It is in the laws of Alaska, Florida, Minnesota, Missouri, and Nebraska. And in New York, judges are required to visit prisons every four years. Thank you for your time and your consideration of FAM's views, and I'm happy to answer questions if you guys have any. Not seeing any questions for you, so I appreciate your testimony today. Thank you. Thank you for your testimony, Representative. We do have some other people who would like to speak today in regards to the bill. First up is Eden Kinlock. Mr. Kinlock, maybe he's on Zoom? Hi. Good morning. Oh, I'm sorry. Mr. Chair and members of the House Committee on Government Operations, my name is Eden Kinlock. I am the State Legislative Affairs Associate for FAM. FAM submitted written testimony, and I appear today in support of House Bill 4669. FAM is a nonpartisan national sentencing and corrections reform organization. For more than three decades, we've advocated for sentencing and prison policies that are individualized and fair, protect public safety, and preserve families. And among these policies we advocate is the increase of transparency and accountability in our nation's prisons. House Bill 4669 doesn't just provide lawmakers with unannounced access to correctional facilities, but it's also a mechanism for creating a more accountable, transparent prison system that keeps us safe and has our trust. FAM believes that

Okay, next on Zoom, we have Jim Townsend, Director for the Carl Levin Center for Oversight and Democracy, who would like to speak in support of the bill. Mr. Townsend, are you on? Yes, I'm here. Can you hear me okay? Yes, sir, go ahead. Well, thank you, Mr. Chairman and ranking members and members of the committee for this opportunity to speak to you today in support of House Bill 4669. I'm Jim Townsend. I'm the director of the Carl Levin Center for Oversight and Democracy. We are an institute headquartered at Wayne State University Law School in Detroit. We also have an office in Washington, D.C. I am accompanied today by my colleague Ben Eikey, who's also on Zoom. And so I'd like to have, there's Ben. So what I'd like to do is to say a word about the Levin Center so you know who you're hearing from. Oh, that's perfect. So you know who you're hearing from. And then say a few words about why this legislation is so important. I'll turn things over to Ben and Ben will speak to his personal experience in visiting prisons and working on corrections matters. So first thing, the Levin Center is the nation's leading authority on legislative oversight. We were founded by Senator Carl Levin, who was Michigan's longest serving U.S. Senator. And our mission is to elevate and enhance the practice and theory of legislative oversight. And so we work in Congress with members of Congress and staff and with lawmakers all over the United States. In fact, Ben and I are speaking to you from Phoenix, Arizona, where we are later today going to be working with the Arizona legislature, helping them to improve their practice of legislative oversight. So I say all that because I want to emphasize that we are typically, we do not, we are first of all, our bipartisan organization. And we don't typically endorse legislation, except in rare cases when that legislation deals directly with your power to conduct effective oversight. And that is the legislation that we're here to talk about today. The other thing I want to mention in introducing ourselves here, I was a member of the Michigan House of Representatives. I was termed out in 2016. And Ben was a staff member in the Michigan House of Representatives, working for the Republican chair of the Appropriations Subcommittee on Corrections. And Ben will speak later about his extensive experience doing oversight in that capacity at a time when it was possible to visit prison facilities or correctional facilities unannounced. So anyway, it's a real pleasure to be here. I want to thank Representative Potetzky for inviting us. And it's a real honor to be before you. The thing that's most important here to remember is that what this legislation essentially does is empower all of you to conduct the kind of oversight that really the legends of congressional and legislative oversight have been able to do for decades, really for very many years in this country. And that is to show up. We call this oversight by showing up. And it is one of the most powerful tools you have in your arsenal or your toolbox to hold the government accountable for really delivering. And so I'm going to say a few words about some people who have done this very effectively in the past. And you have an opportunity to really follow in their footsteps. I can't think of any good reason, good reason, why lawmakers would not want this same power for themselves to appear announced and unannounced to make sure that they're gathering the unvarnished facts, unfiltered information about what's happening in these very important facilities where, as was previously mentioned, people's lives are hanging in the balance. I also can't think of an issue area where unannounced access is more important. Access to facilities that are spending taxpayer dollars. It is, with a few days' notice, it is just all too easy to hide or perfume the truth about what's going on in our state's correctional facilities. Now, we are not passing judgment on what's going on in these facilities. That is not something that currently we have done any investigations or oversight of. Ben will speak to his experience of having done that some years ago. So we aren't claiming expertise about what's happening right now, but what we know from experience is that it's very easy to make things look a lot better than they actually are. I also don't know of an issue area that has more bipartisan appeal than ensuring that this aspect of our criminal justice system meets high financial and operational standards. So many policies, and this comes from my years of experience as a lawmaker sitting in the very chairs you're sitting in, as well as my time as a congressional staff person and the six years I've spent directing this center. I don't know of an issue area that has more bipartisan appeal. I also don't know, really, how anybody can ignore the fact that what you're really faced with as lawmakers is the challenge of implementation. So many policies that we embrace fail in implementation. And criminal justice reform and corrections reform being a crucial aspect of criminal justice reform is one of those areas where we really owe it to the people of Michigan, whether those people are incarcerated or they're people who will never go near a state prison or any kind of prison, to deliver what they deserve. And that is a correction system that wisely spends tax dollars and upholds our values and our humanity. Lawmakers cannot achieve this objective by passing bills, passing budgets, and then passing the buck. No, you've got to follow up and make sure that implementation of those policies that you endorsed is actually occurring and it's occurring according to your intent. Now, Ben is going to mention some examples of what he witnessed conducting oversight by showing up when he was working on corrections issues. But I'd like to close my aspect of this, and we're happy to answer questions, by quoting the Supreme Court, the U.S. Supreme Court, in a seminal case where they were describing the power of the legislative branch to conduct oversight and why it's so important that lawmakers can obtain information that isn't necessarily being offered up to them. And I quote, information that is volunteered is not always accurate or complete. In other words, if you give people lots of notice about visiting their facility, you are not going to get accurate, likely not going to get accurate and complete information. And the best example of this is one I think many of you probably know about. One of the legends of legislative oversight was Harry Truman. Now, most of us obviously know Harry Truman as somebody who was a president in the United States. But before he was president, he was a senator from Missouri, from the Show Me State. Mr. Townsend, I hate to cut you off, but I'm going to have to ask you to give your final statement here and we'll move on to Ben just on the time frame here. Okay, well, I just want to say that Harry Truman made a great, performed a great service to our country by traveling across this country to visit defense contractors in the run-up to World War II. And he found incredible problems in those facilities. And a committee to oversee and do deep dives into our defense contracting system led to the savings of billions of dollars and the savings of countless lives in World War II. And it's that example that you have an opportunity to follow if you adopt a policy that allows you to visit and make full use of your oversight power. So I'd like to thank you all again and turn it over to Ben to talk about his personal experience with this. Thank you for your testimony. Mr. Eikey, if you want to go ahead and make a statement. Thank you, Mr. Chair. So again, my name is Ben Eikey. And back when I had hair, I was working in the Michigan legislature 2013 to 2017, three years of which my boss at that time, Representative Dave Pagel, was the chair of Corrections Appropriations Subcommittee. And I just wanted to also voice my own support of

you know, essentially reestablishing the authorities that my boss, that I used back in the 2010s, there's value, there's a lot of value to going and showing up to these prisons, both in announced visits and unannounced. I think about how some of the announced visits that we did were things that were of particular interest to the legislature. There was a great visit we did on vocational education. We learned about all the different types of skill sets they were trying to help to build with the prisoners. They have something to leverage into employment upon release. But then also the unannounced, because this is when you get a chance to kind of see more of the daily operations, kind of saw how things actually operated on a day by day basis, not even in a gotcha context, just trying to understand how things work. So that way I could help my boss in any way I could make informed decisions on the budget, on policy. So this was a tool that I would say it was rarely used, but it was so important to have that capacity, to have that ability to be able to show up unannounced was something that we knew we had and we had the ability and authority to do so. And I know that also improved department operations, knowing that we could should we wish to do so. I know that my boss used this for visiting prisoners with various people that he either knew from originally in his hometown or people that were dealing with some parole issues, trying to understand and develop better, just understanding the department and how it operates. It's a really important piece of a legislature to be able to do this, to show up unannounced. And then also there's a couple of other states across the country that are using this power and using it in a lot of positive ways. I know a few states were mentioned in previous testimony, but Missouri is a representative that's done over 200 unannounced visits and is now pushing for a stronger oversight commission. South Dakota is improving their ability to be able to do these types of unannounced visits. Ohio can do it. Florida can do it. So you're not alone here in wanting to be able to reestablish this authority. I'm happy to answer any questions and I really do encourage all of you to really think through how to be able to get this authority back into your own hands to be able to really use. Thank you, gentlemen. I don't see any questions. I appreciate your testimony today. Okay, next up we have Kyle Kaminsky wishing to speak in opposition of the bill. Good morning, Mr. Chairman, members of the committee. I appreciate the opportunity, Kyle Kaminsky from the Michigan Department of Corrections. I'd like to kind of cover the history of this, but I think it's important to kind of start at the end because a lot of the testimony that was just given, I think, sort of obscures where we're at. So to be clear, as part of that fiscal year 26 budget negotiations, we negotiated with our House and Senate chairs, our House chairs, Chairman Slaw, who both said they wanted to review this 72-hour notice rule. And we agreed to remove this 72-hour notice rule. And we are in the final steps of that process. So this primary question that's been raised in testimony today about unannounced versus announced visits, the department has agreed to return to the former policy of unannounced visits. That being said, we think it's very important that those visits continue to be governed by our policies. And those policies are much broader and more nuanced than what this legislation is. And so there were some questions earlier from the committee kind of saying, well, what if the department faced this or what if the department faced that? And the answer was sort of, well, the department would still have the authority to address that. No, we would not under this bill. What this bill says is that any legislator or any group of legislators can come in and we cannot enforce any of our other policies that exist for the operation and safety of very complex facilities. So going back a little bit on the history, as was mentioned, prior to 2022, the policy allowed for unannounced visits from legislators. That was very rarely exercised by legislators. Just for some background for folks on the committee who may not know me or may not know my history, I've been the department's legislative liaison for 12 years at this point. So I'm probably uniquely positioned to talk about legislative access to the MDOC's facilities because I'm the one who has to arrange this for everybody. We had allowed unannounced visits for decades and really did not see people take advantage of that, nor did we see significant problems. As we dealt with COVID, we had to implement a variety of different protocols during COVID, and that forced us to kind of look at what our processes were for when people could come in and how we set up those visits. In addition, we encountered some very real issues with past legislators conducting themselves in ways at our facilities that violated our policies or we felt endangered our staff or our operations. I think there was one example that was shared. I was there. I set up those visits. I also sat there for two and a half hours that morning waiting for a legislator who told me they would be there at a certain time to arrive. That legislator had requested visits at three facilities that day. So we had three facilities on call, ready with escorts, ready to show that person around to various things. That legislator arrived two and a half hours late to the first site and then declined to visit the other two sites that we had put on call for them. That's extremely disruptive to our operations, but that was not the only situation that we dealt with that influenced our decision on the policy. We also had a scenario where a legislator came to one of our facilities unannounced as part of a protest, entered our facility and tried to surreptitiously record staff in kind of a gotcha moment using their cell phone. So they were trying to provoke our staff who were just doing their job of keeping the facility safe and were trying to record that and essentially trying to get a reaction for the sake of social media. That's extremely inappropriate for our staff to be placed in a position like that. There was another scenario where a legislator called me and asked to schedule a tour and said that they wanted to involve a member of their staff in the tour, which we arranged that and many of your offices know that. So I asked for some basic information about that person so I could get their background check run. And when I ran their background check, it came back in kind of an interesting set of information. So I called the House Business Office just to confirm, is this person employed by the House? Because a legislator is asking for them to enter an MDOC facility as a legislative employee. The House Business Office informed me that they were not employed by the House. So that legislator was essentially trying to mislead and bring somebody into one of our facilities that did not have authority to do that. So those situations, COVID, other things, influenced our decision to institute the 72-hour rule. Getting back to kind of where I started, as part of this year's budget negotiation, Chairman Slaw, Chairman Schink said, those are past behavior by other people. We think it makes sense and we think the department should remove that 72-hour rule. To be clear, even with the 72-hour rule, the way the policy reads is 72 hours notice, but the warden can waive that. So if any of you showed up at a facility today, the warden would call me on the phone and say, hey, Representative so-and-so's at my facility and would like to visit. I would say, yep, go ahead and arrange that, let them in. We've agreed to update the policy. The policy will be updated in December. But we think this is still an issue that should remain in policy. And the reason it should remain in policy rather than statute is some of the things that were raised earlier today. We have scenarios like we have an emergency or we have something going on at a facility. We need to have the ability to determine who's in the facility at those times and who's not in those facilities. This bill does not allow us to do that. We need to have the ability to make sure that these visits, and we're fine with people going wherever they want to go in the facility, but we have to make sure that they're not disruptive or dangerous to our staff or the residents there. This bill, as it's currently crafted, takes that away from us. So again, I don't want to make it seem as if we're not supportive to the idea of oversight. I spend a lot of time actually asking legislators to come into our facilities. We love it when you come to our facilities. It's important to our staff. It's important to the folks that are incarcerated there. And many of you have visited our facilities. You know when I set those tours up, pretty much all I want to know is location, date, and time. And then when we get you there, we say, we'll take you wherever you want to go in the facility. We've got places we'd kind of like to showcase, schools, programs, but we're happy to take you anywhere else in the facility. Likewise, we're happy to arrange for you to talk to anybody you want in the facility, staff or incarcerated person. So I don't want to leave the committee with a sense that we're somehow objecting to legislative engagement with our facilities. We really like that. But we think the proper way to govern that and to manage that for the safety of our complex operations is within MDOC policy rather than within statute. And that's why we're not supportive of the bill that's before you today. Thank you very much. Okay, I don't see any questions for you. I appreciate you coming in today. Representative, do you have any other additional comments you'd like to make? Thank you,

The committee will take up House Bill 5234, which happens to be my bill, and we'll have Vice Chair Harris come up and take over while I switch positions. With me today is Chief Matt Bade from the Genesee County Metro Police. The committee will come to order, and as Chair Begol said, we'll be hearing testimony on House Bill 5234. Chair Begol, please continue whenever you're ready. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Current law provides that vehicles damaged in a collision are eligible for a salvage title if the cost, including parts and labor, is greater than 75%, but less than 91% of the vehicle's value prior to the collision. Prior to the Secretary of State issuing a registration for a salvage vehicle title, personnel from a police agency must first inspect the vehicle to make sure that the parts are not stolen and that the parts are in proper manner. Under current law, police agencies can charge up to a $100 fee for performing these vehicle inspections, but the revenue is currently restricted to purposes related to decreasing auto theft. My bill would provide more flexibility for law enforcement agencies to use these funds for not only recovering stolen vehicle parts, but also for equipment, training, and road patrol services that are necessary to protect public health and safety. Changing this law is just common sense because it creates flexibility to use what was once restricted funds to help with constantly changing needs in providing public safety and health. And I'll tell you a little bit more about that today is Chief Matt Bade. Good morning. Thank you for having me today. I appreciate you listening to what I have to say. I'm going to repeat probably some of the things that Representative Begole has already said. Currently, there are 86 police agencies, including 24 counties across the state, providing salvage vehicle inspections to their citizens and businesses. It is an optional service for agencies to perform, but a necessary one. Salvage vehicle inspectors must be a certified police officer or a previously certified officer appointed as a limited enforcement officer. Simply explained, vehicles that have had major component parts replaced due to damage which exceeds 75% of the pre-damaged value but do not qualify as scrap must be inspected in order to receive a salvage vehicle certificate. The Secretary of State requires an inspection in order to title and register such a vehicle. The fee charged for inspection creates a revenue stream to participating law enforcement agencies. Currently, this revenue is restricted. As Representative Begole said, law enforcement is restricted to law enforcement purposes related to stolen vehicles, including but not limited to equipment and road patrol services that increase the likelihood of recovering stolen vehicles or stolen vehicle parts and salvage inspections. While a large agency with a dedicated auto theft unit may be able to utilize this revenue within restrictions, the overwhelming majority of agencies are small to medium sized. Agencies are struggling with rising costs, which force difficult choices about training, equipment, and personnel. Unrestricting the revenue would allow agencies to utilize these monies for training equipment, vehicles, as well as personnel and purposes related to auto theft. Such an action by the legislature would be highly beneficial as it would allow more efficient use of this revenue. As chief of the Metro Police Authority of Genesee County, I respectfully ask that you vote House Bill 5234 out with recommendation. Thank you. Mr. Chair, I would like to comment that the chief and I did take this measure up last year, and we successfully did pass it through the House with a vote of 108 to 2. So I think it's well supported, but unfortunately it just got held up in the Senate, so we're hoping to advance it through again this term. Thank you both, committee members. Do we have any questions? Now, Chief, out of the communities that are offering this right now, have we seen a decline in the number of departments that are offering this? I don't know the decline in departments offering it. Of those 86 police agencies and counties that offer it, some of their salvage vehicle, we'll call them programs, are quite limited. They might have one or two officers that do this. Ours, for example, is fairly large. I know there's several in the metro Detroit area that have a fair number of salvage vehicle inspectors, which creates that revenue stream. Yeah, I know our prior department actually stopped the program because it was taking officers off the road from other duties, and it was restricted funds that we couldn't use to help replace some of that. So I think it's a great idea being able to open these funds up for other uses. For some perspective, we charge $100 for an inspection. The vehicle inspectors are compensated. They're not duty officers. They're officers working off duty, 80% of that. So they get $80. The agency keeps the $20 as a pass-through fee. Right now I have about $200,000 sitting there that I can't spend, along with all the things we've already spent on towards auto theft. There's still a lot of money, and other agencies experience the same thing. Sure. Okay. Well, thank you both for being here, and thank you for bringing this up. Thank you very much. Thank you. All right. I think we do have a couple of cards to read in here. All right. We'll defer to the incoming chair. We'll call the committee it is. All right. We'll defer to the incoming chair. Okay. As Representative Harris said, we do have a couple cards to read in here. The first one is Nick Anderary of the Michigan Department of State, not wanting to speak and is neutral on the bill. And then we have Matt Saxon of the Michigan Sheriff's Association, not wanting to speak in support of the bill. Seeing no further business before the committee, we will stand adjourned. Thank you.

transcript: The Committee on Labor is called to order. Mr. Clerk, will you please call the roll? Chairman Cherry? Here. Senator Camilleri? Here. Senator Kavanaugh? Here. Senator Albert? Here. Mr. Chair, you have four members present. There is a quorum. Thank you. I'll now entertain a motion to adopt the meeting minutes from October 30th. So moved by Senator Kavanaugh. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. Today, we'll be discussing Senate Bill 700, brought to us by Senator Camilleri on the topic that we last heard testimony on. Senator, would you like to discuss your bill? Yes. Thank you, Chair Cherry and my colleagues here on the Senate Labor Committee for taking action today on Senate Bill 700. This legislation provides a waiver for those who are overpaid on their unemployment benefits during the pandemic, protecting collection activity from taking place. As we are well aware from our last committee meeting, the UIA has begun clawing back funds that were distributed between February 2020 and September of 2021 to Michiganders who were in desperate need of financial assistance amidst the worst pandemic our country has ever seen. This was a time of panic, anxiety, and confusion for so many across Michigan. Our neighbors found themselves suddenly out of work and unable to make ends meet as we took steps to contain the spread of COVID-19. During this challenging time for so many, these UIA payments were what kept food on the table and paid rent for millions of Michiganders. I was proud that we fulfilled our responsibilities of state government and provided for the most vulnerable of our residents across the state by expanding payments and putting more money into the pockets of those left without a stable income. Now, as families are dealing with the on-again, off-again SNAP benefits and ACA premiums that are set to skyrocket due to Republicans in Congress refusing to act, these same residents are being told that they owe thousands of dollars back to the state to no fault of their own. I'm not talking about those who sought to commit fraud and take advantage of an overburdened system. We're talking about working families who were in dire need of government assistance during one of the darkest periods of our state's history. Grocery prices are up, utility bills keep climbing, and the holiday season is just around the corner. To add more financial stress to our neighbors is not what our state should be doing. The urgency of the pandemic necessitated that our government move quickly, which is what they did. And if mistakes were made and payments were sent to technically ineligible but otherwise well-meaning Michiganders, our government should own up and accept responsibility for those mistakes. Let's not forget that for-profit entities received nearly $800 billion in PPP loans from the federal government during this time, all of which was forgiven. Once again, we find corporate greed being rewarded while everyday Michiganders are being told that they need to foot the bill. This is unacceptable. So I'm asking today for your support of Senate Bill 700 to prevent Michigan families from facing further financial ruin. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you, Senator Camilleri. Any questions for the Senator? Senator Albert. Yeah, I appreciate that. I'm a little confused how PPP loans is evidence of corporate greed, but I guess that's not really part of the... Their loans were forgiven with no questions asked, and we're asking lots of questions of these individuals, so I think that there are some similarities to make. I said evidence of corporate greed. I don't think the PPP loans are evidence of corporate greed. So I don't know why this has to be an us-versus-them conversation. I agree there's a problem here, so I guess my question is there's obviously a lot of people in this group, of this cohort that this would apply to. Probably the overwhelming majority of them went through the system with a good conscience, didn't try to game the system at all. How do we separate in this bill those that did try to fraudulently game the system and those that use it in good faith? So we're talking about about 350,000 Michiganders that are being asked to repay. I believe that it is either something that we can just say, yes, we believe that most were not committing fraud, but let's investigate those that we know who did because I think that those are clearer examples versus the regular folks who were well-meaning, like you said. However, we are working on some substitute language that might give... We're still working on the full details of that, but it basically would go line by line, individual case by individual case through the department to make sure that we are catching those who are fraudulent. And Senator Kimballare, your bill currently, while we need to make some changes, does exclude those who were improperly paid because of fraud. Correct. Okay. Correct. All right. You have another question, Senator? Okay. I'm going to just, prior to recognizing you, note that we did receive some feedback from the department, and so we're working to make some, as Senator Kimballare noted, changes as we move through the process.
