First, let me start off by saying that I know that this current committee has not addressed transfer requests before, so I thought I would start with a brief explanation of legislative transfers and the transfer process in general. A transfer is an accounting adjustment that is made to increase or decrease expenditure authority for line items within department budgets. Transfers can be used to move spending authority from one line item to another to account for a deficit in a line item or to expand or reduce programs. Transfers cannot be used to create new line items, new programs, or new fund sources. Typically, what happens is the State Budget Office initiates and submits letters requesting the approval of transfers. These letters are submitted to the House and Senate Appropriation Committees. Though it is typical for the Budget Office to initiate transfers, you should know, too, that you members of the Appropriation Committees can initiate transfers as well as amend transfers that are submitted by the Budget Office. Under the Management and Budget Act, a majority of the members of the House and Senate Appropriations Committees must approve proposed legislative transfers. The transfers that are approved by the committees must be identical in terms of line item titles, funding sources, and dollar amounts in order to go into effect. If either Appropriations Committee withholds approval, transfers do not occur. There are two basic types of transfers that have different effects on levels of appropriations and overall state budget totals. The first type is a standard legislative transfer. This type of transfer shifts existing spending authorization between line items in a particular budget area with no net change in total appropriations. Standard transfers are proposed primarily when expenditures are higher than originally anticipated in one line item and then lower than anticipated in another line item. The second type is a contingency authorization transfer. This type of transfer results in an increase to total line item appropriations in a budget area when contingency spending authorization from boilerplate in the Budget Act is moved to a specific line item. Contingency authorization allows for the expenditure of additional revenue that becomes available during the budget year from a federal, local, private, or state restricted source. One example of this would be federal grant funding that is awarded to a state department after the budget is enacted. When the budget was developed, it was not known that this federal grant funding would be available to the state, so authorization is not included in that budget to receive it or expend it. An approved contingency transfer would allow receiving and expending the federal grant funding. Another example is private donations. When the budget is developed, there's no way anyone can anticipate the donation of funds to the state from a private source. Without this contingency authorization transfer mechanism, this type of budget adjustment would need to be made through a supplemental appropriations bill. Typically, several packages of transfers are reviewed and approved by the appropriations committees during a budget year. Kelly? Yes. Markkinen? Yes. Mueller? Yes. Slaw? Yes. Van Workum? Yes. Beeson? Yes. Horton? Yes. Roth? Yes. Cabot? Yes. DeSena? Yes. Kuhn? Steel? Yes. Robinson? Excuse me, yes. O'Neill? Pass. Rogers? Yes. Steikloff? Yes. Glenville? Sorry. Farhat? Pass. Martis? Pass. McKinney? Pass. Morgans? Price? Pass. Snyder? Pass. Longjohn? Pass. Madam Chair, you have 15 yeas, 0 nays, 9 pass. The motion prevails. Legislative transfer request 2025-8 as amended is as presented is approved. Without objection, absent members will be excused from today's meeting and seeing no... Oh, Rep Mueller moves to excuse absent members. Without objection, the absent members are excused from today's meeting. title: Oversight - Homeland Security and Foreign Influence — Wednesday, November 12, 2025
transcript:
The Committee on Homeland Security and Foreign Influence will come to order. Clerk, please take the roll. Chair Bruck. Present. Representatives Meerman. Here. Shriver. Present. Mensor. Present. Conlon. Mr. Chair, you have a quorum. All right. Thank you very much. We do have the minutes from the November 5th meeting. Representative Meerman moves to approve those minutes. Hearing no objection, they are approved. All righty. I'll put that there. Well, we were expecting a show-and-tell this morning of a baby. Congratulations, Representative. Thank you. To you and your wife. What did you have? I had a boy. Oh, congratulations. So if you don't mind sharing, I mean, you can share the name and the size. I mean, everybody wants to know the name and the size. The name is Otto Thomas Shriver, and he was born November 5th at 1229 a.m., and he was born 22 1⁄2 inches long and 10 pounds 6 ounces. So a big baby. Yeah. Well, congratulations. Thanks. Big baby. So congrats to you and Mrs. Shriver on that. That's awesome. That's awesome. You have a ways to catch up to me, but, you know, keep working at it. One at a time. One at a time is the best way. But, no, congratulations on that. We missed you last week. Representative Wise was here. He did a wonderful job. But that being said, we do have testimony today. We're going to be having the Vandenberg Coalition. We do have Thor Martinson here, and then we're going to be zooming in Mike Sobolek. He'll be zooming in for testimony, so we appreciate you being here. So just do an introduction when you come up, press the red button, and then we look forward to your testimony, and then we'll have probably certainly a lot of questions afterward. But we appreciate you guys making yourself available for this on the pertinent issues of homeland security here in Michigan and around the nation. So really excited about today. Thank you, sir. Well, thank you, Chairman Brock. I wasn't prepared to give testimony myself, but we are very happy to provide one of our advisory board members, Michael Sobolek, who is a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute where he focuses on competition with China. He previously was a legislative assistant in the office of Senator Ted Cruz in Washington, D.C., and has been a longtime leader on the threat China poses to the United States. Just a little bit of background about the Vandenberg Coalition. We are a 501c3 network of experts on all elements of foreign policy, national security, and defense policy. Our advisory board members, there's 120 of them, have served in the highest ranks of the United States military, presidential administrations, and other organizations that focus on all the important issues related to our military, our national security, and our standing on the global stage. And we are very proud to be named after Senator Arthur Vandenberg, a proud Michigander from Grand Rapids and longtime chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. So that's enough from me. Whenever you have Michael...

Don't know if he's on the other end. There he is. Hi. Yes, I am. Well, the floor is yours, Michael. Take it away, sir. Thank you very much. It's a pleasure to be here virtually with all of you on the Homeland Security and Foreign Influence Committee. Chairman Brook, Vice Chair Meerman, Vice Chair Menser, distinguished members of the committee. Glad to be here. As Thor just said, my name is Michael Sobolek, Senior Fellow at Hudson Institute and Advisory Board Member at the Vandenberg Coalition. Looking forward to our conversation today. Just one piece of housekeeping that I would like to say at the top. I am at my Hudson office today, and I just found out from our office administrator that there is a fire alarm planned for the building during the 1 o'clock to 3 p.m. time range this afternoon. So I have let them know that I'm testifying right now, and I hope that will assuage the powers that be to schedule us at a favorable time. If you hear sounds and sirens coming on my end and you see me needing to evacuate suddenly, I'm giving you fair warning right now. But I very much hope this does not become an issue, and this is the last we speak of it. But FYI. Getting to more pertinent matters. I shared a more fulsome, longer testimony with Thor, and I have some shorter prepared remarks right now. But to give you a preview of the written testimony that I have submitted, I'll share some of that now. The Chinese Communist Party is not a normal government. It's a one-party dictatorship determined to reshape the world to its advantage, to weaken the United States from within. Beijing's goal is clear, to displace America as the world's leading power, to export authoritarianism, and to erode our freedoms and institutions here at home in the United States. Xi Jinping is preparing his people for that conflict. He has told young Chinese graduates to quote-unquote eat betterness and endure hardship. His government is mobilizing reservists, tightening wartime laws, expanding recruitment, and building air raid shelters. As a few U.S. national security experts warned recently, Xi Jinping himself says that he is preparing China for war. But this nuance matters a lot for our conversation today. Xi Jinping also understands that he doesn't necessarily need to fire a shot to damage America. The Chinese Communist Party is already working to infiltrate, divide, and destabilize us in the United States through our supply chains, universities, and industries. In recent years, Washington has uncovered multiple avenues of CCP influence. Confucius Institutes in our universities, censorship pressure in Hollywood and in professional sports, and growing corporate dependence on Chinese markets. But the threat runs deeper than mere propaganda. Beijing has embedded itself within the physical and digital foundations of American society. Chinese-controlled entities have access points into critical infrastructure across the United States. Local law enforcement agencies, for instance, often rely on drones made by DJI, a Chinese company linked to the People's Liberation Army that can transmit sensitive imagery and mapping data back to China. Chinese firms like Huawei and SunGrow supply solar inverters that manage electricity flow to the grid, giving Beijing potential access to sabotage local energy systems. Moreover, ports across the United States use cranes from Chinese firm ZPMC, which are embedded with Chinese Communist Party-controlled software. And Chinese-linked companies are quietly buying land near sensitive U.S. military sites. There is a report just yesterday from the Daily Caller about Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri, which is home to B-2 bombers that were used in recent military operations against Iran this summer. And PRC nationals, interestingly, bought up the plot of land, an RV park, directly next door to that bomber base. Beijing wouldn't need to launch missiles from across the world or detonate an electromagnetic pulse from space to darken our cities. It could simply trigger the kill switches already hidden within our infrastructure. And at the same time, through TikTok, the CCP also holds a direct line to the minds of millions of Americans, which is capable of spreading disinformation and stoking division in a moment of crisis. Their strategy is straightforward. Sabotage America's systems, then convince Americans to turn on each other. These dynamics and these challenges are multitudinous. But today I want to identify four key issues where we see these challenges particularly pronounced. Critical minerals, robotics, biotechnology, and higher education. One of China's most powerful forms of leverage lies in critical minerals. In April, during trade negotiations with Washington, China imposed export controls on key minerals. By October, it expanded those restrictions globally. And this was a serious warning shot because China controls roughly 85% of global rare earth processing and nearly 80% of U.S. defense systems rely on these materials. Our weapons, vehicles, electronics, and clean energy technologies are all linked to supply chains that run through China. It wasn't always this way. For decades, the United States was the world's leading rare earth producer. The Mountain Pass Mine in California supplied global markets until environmental regulations and Chinese price manipulation forced it to close in 2002. Private investors tried to restart it, but the company went bankrupt. Today, the CCP's near monopoly leaves us dangerously exposed. Now, thankfully, the Trump administration has taken important steps by guaranteeing a price floor with Mountain Pass Mine, which has reopened, and signed long-term purchasing agreement with its operator, MP Materials. That deal can protect American producers from Chinese market manipulation. But that's not the full picture because mining alone isn't enough. We need domestic refining as well and manufacturing. Otherwise, we will extract the minerals here only to ship them to China for processing and return them as finished goods, which would further deepen our dependence on China. The United States needs a full ecosystem of miners, refiners, and manufacturers working together to break this stranglehold. It's not just an industrial challenge. It's a national security imperative. Robotics is a similar challenge. And by extension, we're talking about artificial intelligence as well. Robots are rapidly transforming manufacturing, agriculture, and dozens of other industries. As AI enables predictive maintenance, these systems will soon forecast repairs, cut costs, and expand machine lifespans. But every robot depends on software and hardware and components that China is eager to control. At the moment, the West, the United States, and our closest allies and partners still dominate two key technologies for humanoid robots in particular, ball screws and sensors. Companies in Japan, Europe, and the U.S. lead in these areas, but Chinese firms are racing to close the gap. Cunningly, a Chinese manufacturer with ties to Tesla's supply chain operates a marketing and production facility in Illinois, and interestingly for Michigan. Another Chinese firm, Sunrise Instruments, maintains a subsidiary in Canton, where it produces torque sensors for surgical robots and humanoid systems. Embedding PRC-made components into American robots presents real risks, data exfiltration, intellectual property theft, and even sabotage, particularly in the case of digital twins. These sensors can feed false information into AI systems, compromising maintenance schedules and disrupting supply chains. If done at scale, it could cripple industries essential to our economy and defense. By depending on PRC-sourced components, America hands Beijing leverage over one of the most critical technologies in the 21st century. And the CCP would have a backdoor into America's factories and even

living rooms. The stakes likewise could not be higher with biotechnology. In 2021, National Counterintelligence and Security Center warned, your DNA is the most valuable thing you own. The NCSC likened it to your health history, your future, it all is captured in your DNA, your unique code of who you are. And losing it isn't quite like losing a credit card because you can't replace it. Unfortunately, China has spent years of collecting global genetic data. Under its Made in China 2025 plan, the CCP identified biotechnology as one of 10 strategic industries that it intended to dominate. State-backed companies like BGI Group now lead the world in genetic sequencing and testing, thanks to government subsidies that allow them to undercut global competitors. The CCP's goal isn't to cure health maladies or primarily even medical innovation, it's control for national security purposes. In Xinjiang, China's westernmost region, Beijing has built a comprehensive DNA database to track and repress Uighurs, an ethno-religious minority in Xinjiang, as part of its ongoing genocide against them. Disturbingly, American companies have aided in this process. Thermo Fisher Scientific sold DNA sequencing equipment to Chinese authorities in Xinjiang, who described the machines as, quote, irreplaceable, unquote. Though Thermo Fisher later cut off the sales in response to public pressure, the episode reveals a broader truth. The CCP uses biotechnology as a tool of surveillance and coercion, not a tool for healing. China's National Gene Bank is now the largest in the world, collecting DNA samples from millions, including abroad. During the COVID-19 pandemic, BGI offered cheap testing kits worldwide, quietly gathering genetic data from unsuspecting populations. U.S. officials warn that it is nearly impossible to know exactly how Beijing is using this data, but possibilities include genetically tailored diseases, blackmail, or biological enhancement of its soldiers. And I recently published a report about weaponized biotechnology at Hudson and would be happy to chat about that further if it's of interest. Higher education, the fourth and final industry that I have prepared to discuss today. On June 3rd, the Department of Justice charged two PRC nationals for smuggling a dangerous fungus into the United States. The fungus was a potential episode of agroterrorism, and this particular fungus targets crops like wheat, maize, and rice. Both individuals used a laboratory access at the University of Michigan to advance this scheme, and it wasn't an isolated incident. In 2020, three PRC nationals, two of them students at the University of Michigan, were arrested for taking photos near a restricted naval base in Florida. In 2024, five more University of Michigan students were charged with spying on a U.S. military training facility. And last year, a PRC national, again at University of Michigan, illegally voted in the presidential election. These cases are bigger than just one university. This is unfortunately a nationwide problem, and it gets to a deeper challenge. American universities' financial dependence on tuitions from Chinese nationals. Roughly one in four international students in America come from China. Their tuition revenue has become essential to many colleges and universities, even though it opens doors to espionage and basic and applied research theft. The University of Michigan, again, is not alone, and Congress has requested information from multiple universities about their Chinese student enrollment policies, particularly in regards to sensitive STEM programs. To sum up, the CCP strategy is deliberate and comprehensive. There are many things that I would have loved to include in this testimony, and I'm certainly happy to chat about if it's of interest. Transnational repression inside of the United States, and that gets to a lot of human rights concerns. Confucius Institutes as well. I briefly mentioned TikTok. The problems are endless, and it is endemic of Beijing's broad designs. It seeks not only to surpass the United States globally, but to weaken us here. From our power grids and universities to our research labs and our communities. This is not a distant problem for Michigan or for any state. Michigan's auto industry, clean energy sector, and advanced manufacturing base all depend on supply chains that are vulnerable to Beijing's manipulation. Chinese companies already operate within Michigan's borders, producing technologies that could expose our industries to surveillance and possibly sabotage. State leaders have a critical role to play by vetting foreign investments, scrutinizing university partnerships, and protecting critical infrastructure. And I will note, Michigan has one of the biggest success stories nationally in pushing back against maligned CCP influence with the example of Goshen, an electric vehicle battery company that tried to set up shop inside of Michigan in partnership with Ford. And it was a stark and honestly optimistic example of how local and state officials and communities pushed back effectively against what would have been a very significant beachhead of CCP influence. The state can build on that success and many other successes to lead the nation, which we need desperately right now, against an adversary that seeks to win without fighting. And I'll pause there, and I'm looking forward to having a conversation and questions now. Well, thank you. Thank you, Mike. Thank you, Thor, for being here today. We do appreciate everything you have said. You gave us a 35,000-foot view in a lot of areas, but kind of hit a couple technicalities there as well. So we appreciate the think tank that you are coming from. A couple questions before we get actually into questions. I would like a little more background, like on the CCP and how that developed over the past, we'll say, maybe the past three decades or two decades. And with Xi Jinping in charge, you did bring up the 2025 model that they have promoted China first in 2025. Kind of just give us like 30 years ago, you know, we had some federal relationship building, you know, between different administrations when China got on the favored nation status. And maybe from that point forward, how much has it actually changed in the last 30 years in your opinion, especially with Xi Jinping in charge? Certainly. In the 1990s, there was a bipartisan gamble that was made. If we invited the People's Republic of China into the global economy, establishing, as you say, permanent normal trade relations, getting them into the World Trade Organization, that the following would happen. As China grew wealthier and wealthier and as its middle class began to take root and expand, there would be new political incentives that would begin to organically come from within China. And put, I guess, on a bumper sticker, if you can change China economically, maybe we can also change them politically and kill two birds with one stone. Make a ton of money for American companies who wanted access to China's market and then hope that that influx of wealth would liberalize the country. That clearly has not happened. If you look at the human rights abuses that were endemic in China, even in the late 80s and the 1990s, the most notable being the Tiananmen Square Massacre in 1989, U.S. officials were all aware of this. And yet they consciously made this gamble, which at the time was a defensible one, but there were many who dissented from it. And the Chinese Communist Party has turned out to be one of the most resilient political entities of the 20th and the 21st centuries. They've been through a lot to gain the status of power inside of China. If that history is

interest. I'm happy to rewind and talk about how the CCP got to the position it's in. But the reality is not only has it maintained a single party dictatorship inside of China since 1949, it has been incredibly flexible. Even though it is a Leninist political party, it doesn't quite have a socialist economy either. It is state run, but there is also state controlled competition within China. And the party has been able to absorb foreign capital and channel it in ways that advance the party's interests and keep the population in line politically. So by the time the financial crisis hit the United States in 2008, 2009, around that time, you saw this shift in diplomacy from China. There was a calculation made at the time Hu Jintao was the leader of China. And there was this calculation that the United States was not only tripping, but that it was stumbling, that American power had reached its zenith and that in the wake of Afghanistan and Iraq, we were beginning to fade as a global superpower and China's time was coming. And even before Xi Jinping came to power, you saw Chinese leaders and Chinese diplomats begin to have a greater air and a greater aura of self-confidence. And with Xi Jinping, it's not necessarily new under him that China was growing more and more confrontational against America, because even going back to Mao and Deng Xiaoping, Chinese political elites in the party for a long time viewed the United States as a natural enemy and adversary. But it happened around the time of Xi Jinping that they began to be a bit more honest and direct about that. And that's part of their calculation on some deep economic intractable problems that we seem to have at the national level with our debt. And even though China has an endemic debt crisis of its own, they can control their economy in ways that the US government cannot. So much has changed in terms of China's economy over the past three decades. What hasn't really changed is the party's intent. The Chinese Communist Party has always felt threatened by freedom, by anything it cannot control. And happy to get more into that ideological threat assessment if that's helpful. But the gamble that the United States made three decades ago has turned out to be a bad one. Okay. And I have one short question. I've heard this from other folks, but 23andMe, when you do that, that DNA, is that, you didn't necessarily mention that, but you mentioned those DNA tests, those are Chinese tests is what you're saying, or the data is being sent somewhere that they have access to? The COVID tests, many of them were Chinese-produced COVID tests. And interestingly, BGI tried to get their tests into the United States during the pandemic. Thankfully, US officials saw what the obvious ploy was, and they were able to block a lot of those. But I mean, the reality is the Chinese Communist Party is on a global mission to get the DNA of every single human on the planet, or as many as they can. And that is absolutely true for Americans. So the fact that you have a lot of American medical companies working with BGI, which does genetic sequencing and testing and has this huge database, you always have to ask the question of if there's any sort of partnership with a Chinese company that deals in genomics, I think you have to assume that the DNA of Americans are going into a database inside of China, which then introduces the question of what are they using this for? And this is where biotechnology gets quite scary quite quickly. I think it's really impressive whenever you see a precision-guided missile where we've seen a lot of war reporting in the Middle East about how these precise missiles can take out one apartment building through one window, which is impressive. Obviously, there's some collateral damage, but it's limited. But with DNA, you don't even have to fire a missile and you can calibrate it to either one specific person or a small group of people or maybe a large group of people, but exclude a lot of others as well. It's the ultimate precision-guided weapon. And the amount of ways that an adversarial entity like the Chinese Communist Party and the People's Liberation Army could leverage a capability like that is quite frightening. And that is a huge threat that I think folks in Washington at least are beginning to reckon with, but it also matters at the state level because you have companies for partnership reasons or for just need of services that it's often cheap to partner with Chinese biotech firms because they offer cheap services because it's subsidized. I think that's where the threat comes in at the state level. Okay. Thank you. Thank you. I have more, but we're going to move on to some other questions. We're going to go to Representative Shriver to begin. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Recently, President Trump talked about and defended that it's MAGA to have 600,000 Chinese students come to America. Would you say that there's any concern to having this occur with what you talked about with internal subversion by China and its government while we're already in a power, we're a power and decline already? I mean, this presentation, China being a threat within importing 600,000 Chinese students on top of this. Is that a concern to you guys? Profound concern. Yes. I think it's important to step back and acknowledge that when we talk about Chinese nationals here on student visas, two things are true at the same time. Number one, during the Cold War, it was, I think, a huge net benefit to allow Soviet nationals or USSR folks from the Soviet Union to come over here and experience America and to see what freedom looked like. And I think that is still true today with China. In many cases, no one is oppressed more by the Chinese Communist Party than the Chinese people. And there are many PRC nationals who are applying for these student visas, not because of some nefarious scheme that they are a part of willingly, but because they just want a good life. And for those people, I think it's in our interest, as far as we can, to open our doors to them and make sure that they are safe from their oppressive government. Thing number two, though, that is also correct and equally valid, is that the Chinese Communist Party weaponizes their own people. Whenever a Chinese national travels abroad by virtue of apps like WeChat and tech surveillance on the phones that they use, the CCP can coerce, silence, and intimidate anyone, no matter what country they're in. And you see when Chinese students come over here, they are monitored, surveilled, and organized either by consulates or by student organizations that operate on college campuses that report to consulates in the embassy. This has been a widely known concern for a long time. And the challenge here is that any Chinese national, even if they themselves are not nefarious, they can be operationalized or coerced into doing something for the CCP on American soil. And both of those things are true at the same time. We should want the Chinese people to see what freedom looks like, and we also need to protect our own people and our own stuff, just to put it bluntly. And that middle path is hard, but when I worked, as Thor mentioned, when I worked in the Senate for Senator Cruz, we tried to legislate what that middle path could look like. And what we did ended up looking like a proposal that empowered homeland investigations inside of Homeland Security to have expedited deportation authorities that they did not have to impose more penalties on universities that did not police their own partnerships as closely as they needed to. And also, too, from a civil liberties perspective, if there was ever any sort of official designation made against a U.S. entity like a university that turned out to be incorrect or unfair, that there was a legal path to challenge it. Because you're balancing so many different things all at the same time. I think it is a missed opportunity

entirely turn off the spigot and say no more Chinese students. China may eventually give us no choice but to do that. And I hope that day doesn't come, but I'm also open to the reality that that day could come because of how aggressive they are with their collections operations. But it's also a mistake, I think, to do what the president is doing, which is to open the doors wide to thousands and thousands, like I think hundreds of thousands of PRC students here. That's not in our interest because right now we don't have the capacity, the manpower to track everything as we need to. There needs to be a middle ground and getting there is hard. But if we're serious about upholding the best of ourselves and also protecting ourselves, then we need to invest in that middle ground. And I do have concerns about where the administration is on this issue at the moment. Thank you. Representative Meerman. Thank you, Chair. I guess I wanted to kind of get from your perspective how they're able to financially survive. It was my understanding that COVID and their lockdowns was pretty traumatic on their economy, as well as some of these trade wars with U.S. I know they do manipulation of their own currency to try to bring it up. But their pathway that they're trying to pave, I can't remember the terminology they use, but through Africa and through Asia, they're buying up ports and different things like that. It's incredibly expensive. I know the deals they make with these nations are China focused and they come out on the good end of the deal with what it costs the country to have this port there. But it just seems like there's almost no end to money for them and they don't really pay a consequence for overspending. And I'm not sure how that all works. China does have its own version of a debt problem in a huge way. It's hidden and off the books in a way that America's debt problem is not. For better or for worse, we are an open book. It's so easy to look up just today in this very moment and see what our national debt is. Or for states that are in debt to look up and see what's the financial situation. We are an open book. For better or for worse, I think on balance for the better. But China in so many ways, and this will come as no surprise, it's just the opposite. And the debt problem that China faces is primarily at the local level and at the provincial level. But there's a lot of papering over it. There's not really honest reporting. And that gets to a lot of the political, the bad political incentives inside of a single party dictatorship. Sometimes telling the truth can be dangerous for you. So they do have their own financial problems. But at least for the moment, it's like that old adage or cliche about going bankrupt. You go bankrupt very slowly and then suddenly all at once. And it often isn't obvious to others that you are in trouble until the actual crisis comes. For the moment, China is doing okay. And there are a couple of reasons for it. China is a production dominated economy. And that is by design and intention. Xi Jinping is unwilling to help the Chinese economy transition to a more consumer heavy economy because that would mean relinquishing control over production heavy industries and state-owned enterprises. The Chinese Communist Party is afraid of anything it cannot control. And it can control companies. It can control production. And that is how it primarily drives its GDP. And because it's not a true market economy, these companies will often produce way more than Chinese people can consume. There's this disconnect between supply and demand internally. So China will export that excess supply globally. And this is what so many presidential administrations have been upset with Beijing about this for dumping their overproductive capacity into the United States because it's bad for our businesses here. So that's one reason why China has been able to do this is because they can usually get that excess production somewhere and someone in the world will buy it for a cheap price. And that keeps them going. But there's also a financial component. American investment funds prop up a lot of the very Chinese companies that are the most threatening from a security perspective to Americans. It's this huge loophole that we have had in U.S. law for a long time. We're really good at sanctioning companies. We're kind of getting better at having export controls on our companies to make sure our good services and technologies don't go to problematic actors abroad. But we will allow investment funds to invest in companies that are sanctioned by the U.S. government, which doesn't make a whole lot of sense. And that shouldn't be that needs to change. It's this longstanding problem of, again, to the very first question when we brought China into the global economy. Foreign capital flooded China and boosted them in a way that jumpstarted their growth seismically. And even though China has strong domestic industry that they don't fully rely on foreign capital in the way that they used to in the 90s, still rely on it substantially. And one of the biggest reasons China is still strong, not just from an economic perspective, but even from a technological perspective, is because we invest in China. We are in many ways funding our own destruction. That's a point that former Representative Mike Gallagher from Wisconsin has made a number of times. And I think he's right. We are complicit. We Americans, the U.S. government, U.S. tech, banking, we are one of the reasons why China is as successful as it is economically and technologically. And I think that's a loophole that we need to address. The investment from the world in China is being done, though, because they see returns, and so they're going to do it. I guess I have – I agree. We are funding our own demise. I agree with that as well. Second question, is there a population cliff that might be driving China to feel like they have to act in the next 10 years as far as being globally dominant, where if they don't act in the next 10 years, because of their population cliff that they're facing, that they'll lose the opportunity? We'll see. And I know that might sound like an evasive answer. I think it's too early to tell. Let's talk about what we do know first. What we do know is that China's long-term demographic trajectory is bad. The one-child policy turned out to not just be morally atrocious. It was also actually bad for China because now they have more elderly people than they do young people that can support them. And that problem is going to get worse over the next couple of decades probably. The reason I say probably is because the big wild card in the stack that we don't know how to fully understand yet is robotics and biotechnology. The hope – I think probably the hope of the party is that automotive workers can prop up key industries from a labor perspective. So even if they have fewer workers graduating and entering the workforce, they can use robotics to ameliorate those problems. And with biotechnology, they're probably hoping they can also find ways to prolong lifespans. And this is actually super interesting. A couple of months ago, Vladimir Putin was in Beijing for a military parade that Xi Jinping was hosting. And a hot mic caught a conversation between Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, and they were talking about biotechnology from the perspective of creating new organs, that you could then get a new organ transplant for whatever organ you were on the verge of losing

And Xi Jinping made this interesting comment that 70 years old is now young because of the promise of biotechnology. So how robotics and biotech, whether it's an overstated promise or whether they actually are going to be that transformative from a labor pool perspective and from public health perspective, that will have an impact on China's demographic future. It is true that their outlook is bad just from a birth rate perspective. And the final part of your question that I haven't addressed yet is does this present a window for them in the next 10 years that if they don't move soon, they might lose their opportunity? I think it's hard to answer that without knowing how robotics and biotech will impact their situation. But I think it is important to ask about other windows that we do have. And one window we have is the lifespan of Xi Jinping. He has made it very clear that he wants to be remembered as the Chinese leader that restored greatness to China. And what he means by that is bringing Taiwan into China, subsuming it, either militarily or in non-kinetic ways. He wants that to be his legacy. And I do think that is concerning. And we obviously don't know how long this man is going to be alive. But that is a window that causes me significant trouble. Thank you. Thank you very much. Thanks for scaring the bejesus out of us too. But that's good. Representative Mensur. Thank you, Chair. Sir, are you aware that on the DGI drone website now they say that they can no longer sell to America? I am. And this is very interesting. And it happened, I think, correct me if I'm wrong, but I think this happened somewhat recently. That's very recently. I think it is a wonderful development that I celebrate. Agree. So, this is kind of an off weird question, but our president has made it very clear that he covets the rare minerals that China has. Does it bother you that we have made it clear how very much we want those minerals? Because that gives China leverage or a hammer. Even if President Trump were more circumspect in how he talked about those minerals, I actually don't think it would make a difference for the following reason. The big problem is we do not have an alternative supply chain to get those refined critical minerals. China has cornered the market to such a degree that it is a single point of failure for our access to refined critical minerals. And moreover, the Chinese Communist Party knows this, and they've known it for years. This is, I think, an unfortunate episode of policymakers in both parties for a long time knowing that one day China could play this card and actually exploit this leverage over America. But we did very little, next to nothing, for far too long to give ourselves a diversified supply chain. And now with this year, China played that card. And whether the president was public or not public about how we felt about it, the reality is Xi Jinping knows that he's got us in a tough spot. What would be very concerning to me is if the Trump administration were doing next to nothing to find a new supplier. Because the current, like the status quo is unacceptable. American consumers rely on these critical minerals for home appliances and for cars. And the U.S. military relies on these critical minerals for the most advanced fighting platforms that we rely on. What brings me encouragement is that in recent conversations with the Australians and the Japanese, the Trump administration is working quickly to lock down new supply chains that do not involve China. And as I briefly mentioned in the testimony, they are not only beefing up our own mines and industries here at home, like Mountain Pass Mine in California in particular, but they're insulating it from China's predatory dumping of supply, which is something that we need to do. I would prefer that we could live in a pure free market economy. And I think we can. I think we can have free trade with free countries. But the People's Republic of China is, I mean, yeah, it doesn't fit that category, unfortunately. So I think we will need some industrial policy to protect our companies from China's predatory practices. And I am encouraged that the Trump administration is doing it. That final thing I'll say, this is not the only thing that we rely on disproportionately for China. I am really concerned about pharmaceuticals. If China really wanted to mess with the United States and even escalate above the rare earth dependency, tomorrow they could restrict the export of active pharmaceutical ingredients to the United States. And just like that, the medicines that Americans rely on, even from things as like over-the-counter medications, supply would dry up very quickly. And they could throw our entire health care system into chaos. And this is, again, something that we know about. This is not a secret. People who are studying China and the medical industry are very aware of the supply chains. And I don't think the movement to resolve this is fast enough. And if there's any lesson we take from this critical mineral episode, we need to get ahead of the curve and find and establish new supply chains that don't rely on an adversary before they decide to exploit that dependency. Well, now that you scared the hell out of us, thank you so much. Thank you, Representative Mensah, for that. Representative Meerman, sir. Thank you again, Chair. What do you take from Canada Prime Minister seeming to make some announcements about getting things they need from China? It just sounds like because of the trade wars with us here in the United States, the Prime Minister is saying we'll make friends with the Chinese. Is that what you're hearing as well? The piece of news that I saw from Canada that was quite troubling was their consideration of lowering tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. And that might be one example of others. That's the only one I've seen recently. There may be more. But yeah, yes, that does concern me because electric vehicles made by China, again, this is a production-heavy economy that subsidizes its national champions, and they can sell things, cars included in this case, at below market prices. If a Chinese electric car, if like BYD or some other Chinese car company would be able to sell those cars inside of the United States, you could have cars that are comparable, competitive with things that Tesla is making for like $19,000. That would send Ford and GM and Tesla and foreign competitors like Hyundai into a tailspin. And you don't have to – that's not just me talking. These are the executives of Ford talking. This is a huge concern because not only would it be bad for our own companies, if you have a Chinese – essentially like an electric vehicle is a robot. It is a kind of robot that is connected, that sends data back to the cloud, which in this case would be in China. And the amount of kill switches inside of a Chinese electric vehicle, I don't know how many they are, but I can guarantee you that there are several. And having an American citizen in a dangerous situation like that would just be an unacceptable thing from a national security perspective. It's also bad for intelligence collection because the routes of Americans, where they drive, when they drive, how crowded a street is at a particular

moment, that is dangerous information to send to an adversary and that they can conglomerate and study and use big data systems to analyze. It would also be bad because we need Ford and GM and our own domestic car companies. We need them to be thriving because, like, remember back to World War II, we were building weapons on the manufacturing floors of our auto companies. They're a core critical backbone in our domestic industry. We need them to be strong. And if we were to do what it sounds like Canada is doing or at least considering doing of allowing, opening the front door to a Trojan horse like BYD or some Chinese car company to sell cheap electric cars here, that would be not just a potential extinction level event for our own auto companies. It would be welcoming in a severe national security threat. So I am troubled about what the Canadians are doing. I think it's a decision that they would live to regret. And I think it is something that policymakers in Washington should stay far away from. And I mean, from y'all's perspective in Michigan, this is clearly a real issue with the auto industry. So yeah, I think it would be an enormous mistake, and I am concerned about the Canadians on this. We heard from Congressman Molinar six months ago about 70% of routers having a backdoor to China controlling in municipal situations. Not all of them in municipal situations have critical infrastructure tied to them, but I don't know if you can elaborate on that a little bit more, if that's sort of a thing, and can they really open the sluice gate and let sewage flow out, for instance, using one of these routers? On the, I guess, soft end of the threat spectrum, and this would still be a problem, denying access, which, I mean, if you're in a home, if you're just a citizen and you have one of these routers and you can't access the internet, depending on how integrated and updated your appliances are, you actually don't have a functioning household anymore. So that would be bad. If it is a critical infrastructure situation, like the thing you're talking about, and there is a router, I guess you have two potential issues there. Either inability to access the internet or malicious code that can sabotage. And I share all of Representative Molinar's concerns, and I will also say, I believe this is something, one of the Chinese companies in question, I think it's called TP-Link. This is something that particular elements of the Trump administration are looking into, and I can't remember if they've acted against this already, but I expect, I would not be surprised if some forthcoming action on this exact problem of Chinese routers comes pretty soon. Thank you, Representative Bimmer. Switch topics just slightly. What do you think of the newest TikTok agreements that are potentially being made at the federal level? With the caveat that the agreement is between two companies and thus proprietary, and we may never actually see the terms on the pieces of paper itself. From what I have heard from the administration, and from everything I've read about this, I'm concerned. I do not believe that this deal complies with the law that Congress passed bipartisanly last year, and that the Supreme Court unanimously upheld. I guess we have a few problems. Number one, President Trump has not enforced the law. The law went into effect on January 19th, and at that time, TikTok disappeared from Apple App Store and the Google Play Store, and they disappeared because Apple and Google complied with the law and removed TikTok. But then the Trump administration convinced those companies to re-platform TikTok, and the president did not enforce the law for, I guess now we're in November, that he has not properly enforced the law, I would argue, for 11 months. And he did it for political reasons that are understandable. He wanted to negotiate a deal, but that was not, the way he went about this was not in compliance at all with the avenue that the legislation actually spelled out for how to go about separating TikTok US from ByteDance. So there's the process that led up to the deal itself that I am concerned by from a rule of law perspective. But then you actually have the deal itself, and to me, you have a few different concerns here. One is that there's a board member on this new joint venture that is this board member's from ByteDance, which I could potentially violate the law from allowing someone from ByteDance, which is controlled by a foreign adversary, into the inner workings of TikTok US. That could be a problem from a data perspective, from an algorithmic perspective. There's also the data issue where Oracle is going to be housing and supposedly securing the data of US officials, not US officials, of US users on TikTok. But again, if you have a board member from ByteDance, how secure is it really? And this also introduces the question of even when before this deal ever happened, Oracle was already controlling the user data and officials in China were still able to access it because TikTok employees work for ByteDance. And if you still have that relationship, how secure is US user data actually going to be? But to me, the most concerning part is with the algorithm. The law is incredibly clear that there shall be no cooperation on the operation of the algorithm between TikTok US and any foreign adversary. And ByteDance would be included in an entity controlled by a foreign adversary. Under this new deal, the algorithm is licensed from ByteDance to this new TikTok joint venture. We do not know what the terms of that licensing agreement are. It could be in a positive best case scenario. It could be that it's an in perpetuity license that gives this new joint venture complete control over how the algorithm is manipulated, how it is coded, and the ability to edit the algorithm and adjust it. But when the administration rolled out this deal and had calls on background with journalists in September, that is not how they described the deal. They described the deal of the licensing in particular that it would give this new TikTok joint venture the ability to monitor and to see what the algorithm is doing. That is not the same thing as being able to control the algorithm. I have not been convinced to this date that this deal actually places control of the algorithm in the hands of Americans. As far as I can tell, and I'm happy to be proven wrong about this, but as far as I can tell, ByteDance still retains control over the algorithm. So I have deep concerns over the deal. Okay, appreciate that in depth. I didn't know if you had an in-depth explanation on that. I truly appreciate that. You definitely know your stuff there. Representative Mensur. Thank you, Chair. So you have outlined for us multiple, very concerning safety failures here in the United States. If we were going to enact one thing, one thing to protect us as quickly as possible, what would it be? The top of the list, I'm thinking because there are so many and I want to make sure I get my prioritization correct here. If I were to focus on one thing, I'll answer this in two different ways. You can look at this from a downstream perspective or an upstream perspective. From a downstream perspective, I would focus on the incentives that companies in Michigan have to fix the big national problems that we share. The most immediate one right now being alternative supplies of refined critical minerals.

I know that there's overwhelming demand in Michigan for magnets in particular for car companies, but if there's any way to build on the pre-existing mines that are already operational inside of Michigan or to work with companies for exploration to identify new locations, that would be the biggest national security service that Michigan could provide to the country. We need more domestic mining and refining of these critical minerals. We can do some of this globally, but I think the biggest lesson that the United States is learning right now is we need to some degree some sort of domestic redundancy for the things that matter the most to our survival in the 21st century. These critical minerals are not rare in the sense that there aren't that many in the world. They're everywhere, but it's not terribly profitable to mine. And there are some environmental challenges with mining and refining. So this won't be easy, but this is what the country – again, I'm up here in D.C. I'm just answering this from a national perspective. This is what we need as Americans right now. We need alternative supply. And if there's any way for Michigan to play a role in that, that would be huge. It would be incredible. From an upstream perspective, I think state governments have an opportunity to get ahead of one area where D.C. is so woefully behind and lacks resolve to fix, which is the issue of foreign influence and lobbying. The Foreign Agents Registration Act was passed a long time ago and has been in need of updating for a long time because it's riddled with loopholes that allow foreign governments to evade reporting on how they influence public policy debates inside of Washington. And political interests for very unsurprising reasons are hesitant to update this law. So when I was working in the Senate in – I think if I remember correctly, it was around the time of 2018 when folks on the Hill really began to grapple with FARA is so outdated. But getting the political will requisite to change it is hard. But organizations like State Armour have been doing great work with state capitals around the country with saying, hey, even if Washington, D.C. can't get its act together and have proper disclosure of foreign lobbying, state governments can. And if this is something that you all have already done, you have my undying support and applause. If it's something that you have not done yet, I would urge you to seriously consider what disclosure of foreign influence could look like for lobbying inside of Lansing. I think that would be a great upstream investment to weed out or at least shine some sunlight on foreign malign influence. And sunlight is a great way to target political entities like the Chinese Communist Party, which prefer to operate in the dark. So President Trump has promised Selfridge Air National Guard Base here in Michigan, one of the most important defense bases here, especially in southeast Michigan, 21 F-15EX Eagle IIs. Those planes, those fighter jets are going to cost probably close to a billion dollars apiece. Do you have any concern that these kind of stealth, amazing fighter jets will be made with Chinese chips and parts? So interestingly, one of the upcoming tech concerns is displays, the displays we have on our laptops, our TVs, and the displays that pilots, that U.S. military pilots use inside of their helmets that help them with their decision making and with taking and processing data. I would be deeply concerned if the displays inside of whether it's the F-35 or the F-15, as you brought up, I do have concerns broadly speaking about CCP technology and components inside of our weapons platforms. I think that is something that we absolutely need to avoid. And I will also say with gratitude and thankfulness that the Pentagon is aware of this issue. And I do, if I remember correctly, they are taking steps, particularly on the issue of display technology, to make sure that we do not rely on Chinese displays or CCP components. But the problem there again is we can have these regulations all we want, but that doesn't necessarily impact the competitive space in the economy. And what Chinese companies are trying to do are undercut competitors that the U.S. military would like to partner with, like Samsung. So I think this is one of the challenges with China policy. The things that we can most easily control are saying to either the U.S. government or to American companies, thou shall not do X because it would harm national security. That's something we can do if we have the political will. But what's harder to do is to impact what the Chinese Communist Party's economic statecraft is and to protect foreign companies that we rely on from that exploitative statecraft. That is – I think that's something that we're still figuring out. And at least again in the display case, which has a direct connection to fighter jet technology, it's a live issue. I can tell you I've had three, two or three meetings about this exact issue over the past couple of months in D.C. And I think the most important thing is to make sure that Chinese competitors have no ability to access our market. And then if it happens to be the case that foreign companies that we rely on technologically are on the receiving end of predatory economics from China, that's a separate conversation, maybe with some harder solutions, but solutions that I don't think are impossible. But to answer your question broadly, I'm concerned. I think the Pentagon is tracking it. But for like the next-gen tech that's coming around, we have some problems we need to fix. Thank you very much. Well, I really appreciate it. I did have some more questions. I know we're getting near the end of time. But we have data centers being propped up all over the U.S., which I see as a very good thing. But I'm sure you probably have concerns with data centers as well. But storage of information outside of the U.S. is a big national security concern. Could you, in a minute, give us just kind of your viewpoint on data centers being built in the U.S.? One clarifying follow-up question. Are you talking about data centers from an AI perspective or something else? Yeah. Well, in Michigan, there's multiple proposals for data centers here. And I'm sure it's propping up the AI. It's propping up the cyber abilities here in the continental U.S. And I'm assuming that it's taking some of that data storage capability from countries like China. I mean we, as a national security concern, want data stored here and we want AI focused here. I don't happen to know exactly what they're using them for, but I'm sure AI has a lot to do with it, the need for that computing power. That's right. That's right. So briefly, data centers are a crucial part of winning the AI race with China. It is also one of the biggest advantages that we have over China because we can design and we can get access to far and away better chips than the Chinese can produce. So that is the biggest advantage that we have. And the data centers that are supporting the artificial intelligence market are less about data storage and more about supporting large language models that then support things like OpenAI's ChatGPT or Anthropic's Claude, different frontier models for AI.

As I understand it from the data center perspective, that is where a lot of these requests are coming from. So I don't have a lot of the concerns about China's ability to remotely access that. I think that's a separate one. For these data centers, the big thing is making sure that they can get built, that they can get permits and approved quickly, and that they can have enough energy to power them. And this is something we didn't even have a lot of time to talk about, but the energy needs for AI are enormous. And this is going to produce a big strain on our grid. And not just permitting to set up these data centers, but to get them the energy supply that they need, that will be another challenge. So I tend to be pretty favorable and somewhat optimistic about these data centers because I think we need them from an AI perspective to be competitive. Can we build them fast enough and can we get them the power that they need? I think those are the two challenges. Well, I certainly appreciate it. I know the fellow committee members appreciate your testimony. And I watched recently where it's a dark factory, Chinese car manufacturer, completely manufacturing vehicles, just pumping them out, not a single worker, not a single light. And at the end of the tunnel, end of the factory comes out brand new car that's and they're pumping out millions of these, which is a whole nother issue and topic, I'm sure. So but thank you for pointing out a lot of the things that we really need to be talking about here at the state. Appreciate some of the specifics geared toward Michigan. Certainly appreciate that. And thank you for your testimony, sir. It was an honor to be here. I wish I could have been in person, but honored to join you virtually. And thank you so much for the invitation. And Representative Menser moves to excuse absent members. No objection that prevails. And seeing there no further business before the committee, the committee stands adjourned.

title: Education and Workforce — Wednesday, November 12, 2025
transcript:
With the mic on, would the clerk please call the roll? Chair DeBoer? Here. Representatives Lansing? Here. McKen? Here. Fox? Yes, ma'am. Kuntz? Present. St. Germain? Pavlov? Here. Wilson? Here. Kulzhar? Here. Weiss? Here. Burns? Madam Chair, you have nine members present. You have a quorum. Thank you. Vice Chair Lansing moves to adopt the minutes of the November 5th meeting without objection. The minutes are adopted. Thank you, Madam Clerk. The committee will now take additional testimony on House Bill 5044, sponsored by Representative Wenzel. I do anticipate taking additional testimony on this bill at future committee meetings from the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services and other stakeholders. But today we have testimony from the Autism Alliance of Michigan. Welcome. If you could please introduce yourself and begin when you are ready. Good morning, Chair DeBoer and committee members. Thank you for inviting us back. I'm Heather Eckner. I serve as the statewide director of education for the Autism Alliance of Michigan. We are a statewide nonprofit. So we serve all lanes across our great state of Michigan. And my work focuses on helping to remove barriers to access for students with disabilities, those with autism, but it's also disability-wide and system-wide. So we are one of the primary supporters of House Bill 5044. And I just want to first say that I've either been physically present for the hearings that have happened so far or have watched the replay. And through all of it, it is very, very clear that all members of this committee are working really hard to understand the elements of this bill, the policy, the interplay of it. But what has also stood out to me is that it really is coming first and foremost from a place of being student-centered and trying to figure out what is going to be most helpful to students with disabilities. So for that, I thank you all and I really appreciate it. That really truly has been very clear. And so I come to this experience from a number of different roles. My teaching experience, I'm an educator by training. I've taught both in Ohio and Michigan. I've taught in private country day school settings, traditional public school settings, charter school settings, students with high English language learner populations. And with all of my experiences, I've been a general education teacher. I was not a special education teacher by training. But in every single classroom that I had, there were students with disabilities because fundamentally, disability is one of the kind of demographics of human population that crosses everything else, right? Wherever you're located, disability doesn't pay attention to income level or language or race. It's everywhere. It's in every school setting, as kids with disabilities should be. So fundamentally, all students are general education students. For some, because of their disability, they require additional services and supports and specialized instruction. And a lot of that comes about then because of our federal and state laws that provide those obligations and those protections. So what you've heard a lot in testimony so far is kind of this combination effect of we've got, you know, HB 5044. And then we heard a lot of testimony from school associations about, well, we've got this guidance document and we've already got these obligations under the law. And so really the clear distinction that I'm hoping to help make today is, yes, two things can exist simultaneously. The obligations that school systems have to serve students with disabilities appropriately through educational access, that's the federal law, IDEA. Our Michigan rules are called MARS for that. This guidance document, I hope it does get widely implemented. I hope it does get embraced and used with fidelity. We know currently in our system there are a lot of barriers for kids with additional needs. Our outcome measures as a state in Michigan are some of the lowest across every angle that you look at nationwide. So we collectively as people who care about kids, families, and education in the state have a lot of work to do together. Yes, yes to this. Yes to school districts building their capacity, hiring people with the appropriate certifications and background so that classroom teachers and students in classrooms can be supported. Yes to all of this. And these things can walk alongside each other. What HB 5044 does is it fundamentally talks about medical necessity, accommodation, and access under the Americans with Disabilities Act. Different law, different federal law. This is a reasonable accommodation for those that need it when it's connected to what is prescribed and recommended by clinical care providers. Where we have the common ground are mostly autistic kids in public school settings. That school setting is the common ground. Where those kids are now being educated is this confluence of, yes, we have to meet their educational needs that are required by law, which is the floor, not the ceiling. And we have outside community-based providers that are working with these kids outside of the school setting and want to be able to come into the school setting to provide those additional medically necessary accommodations. And we've heard a lot about least restrictive environment and just concerns about, like, how would this impact kids and school settings? And so I think those are all really valid concerns and questions that have come up. What I'm going to share with you today is, so I come at this as, you know, an educator first and foremost before I was a parent. But then I am the parent of two kids. Both are autistic. And my oldest, Marcus, is currently a junior in our local public high school. And his lifespan really kind of mirrors the trajectory and history of the Autism Alliance of Michigan in terms of its formation and the autism insurance benefit that passed. And so when my son was first born, he was born in 2008. And just after the first several months before he even turned a year old, our pediatrician had said to us multiple times,

I highly recommend you get evaluated through Early On, which Early On is our state's birth to three special education program. And because he wasn't meeting developmental milestones, like she just kind of saw this coming. So, you know, before he even turned one, we did the Early On evaluation and he was found eligible. We received an individualized family service plan, an IFSP at that time. And for those early years, they really focus on as much as possible the home-based setting, parent education, like how can you be the best parent to your child and nurture and support them now that they have some additional needs. But by the time children in that kind of early intervention window, before they turn three, you start talking with this combination now of the school team too, of transitioning to the IEP, the individualized education program, because that's when IDEA starts to pick up and kick in. So there's different parts of IDEA for that. So we started talking about that transition when my son was around two and a half. And the only placement that was presented to us by our local school district was a self-contained classroom with all kids with autism. So again, I go back to the concern of this committee that has been raised about least restrictive environment. Sometimes the first option that's given to families, or the only option that's given to families, doesn't start there, right? So that was our placement. It was four days a week, half days. And, you know, as a former, you know, as an educator, at that point I was a stay-at-home parent. But as somebody with a master's degree in education, I hear all of that and I'm like, well, shouldn't we at least try, you know, a regular classroom, like preschool setting? Shouldn't we try something out in the community? And the school team was kind of like, yeah, go ahead, you know, let's see how that goes. And so I did. I enrolled my son in a community-based preschool setting. And the difference between how he presented and behaved at home versus a classroom setting with lights and other kids, and I don't know if you've been in preschool settings, but sensory tables with lots of objects or sand. Boy, that kid could not come within three feet of a sensory table because everything in the table came out of it and was like airborne. He consistently eloped or left the classroom in search of large fans that were in the building. There were a couple of vacuums in the classroom that he really became fixated on. It's called perseveration and just would like only go to the vacuums. And it was just really chaotic. And the preschool staff were like, oh, we don't know what to do. So the school team came in. They observed him. They were like, this is lots of great data. And so then they said, OK, why don't we enroll him in our self-contained setting? And I said, OK, you know, we gave it a try. So at that point, though, I'm thinking like, but have we really thought through all the different angles of this? Right. Like, OK, we gave it a try, but like it wasn't successful. But now it goes from one end of the continuum to the other. Right. Like a pretty big gap. So I started what all parents do when they're down this journey is you talk to other parents. And there's a great kind of sense of shared community amongst the disability community where there's really a lot of generosity of parents who have come before you sharing what they know and have learned. That was true, too, of things like passing along contact information for BCBAs that were providing applied behavior analysis. So at this time in Michigan, the autism insurance benefit hadn't yet passed while my son was at this kind of two and a half, three year old stage. There were very few certified behavior analysts being kind of produced out of the training pipelines in the state and very, very few across the whole state. And, you know, like a good sitter, kind of like that contact information people want to hold on to it because it's like you want them to be available for you. A good BCBA is contacted that time really was like kind of held on to like gold. But a parent with autistic kids about 10 years older than my son, I was talking about like, I really want to try just regular preschool, but like he's tearing apart the sensory table and leaving to go look for fans. Like, what do I do? And she said, have you looked into finding a BCBA? Have you tried ABA? And I'm like, what's that? And she's like, well, we've been working with somebody for years. It's really helpful. They come in and they kind of look at the environment and they work with the individual to kind of get them to be like functionally able to like sustain different things. And I said, who's your BCBA? And with that generous spirit, she did share her name and I connected with her. And so my son started with ABA provision first in our home setting. And then, you know, he's going to his half day programs in the public school district self-contained classroom. But once we worked with him a little bit in our home setting of just things that are called like reciprocity, like kind of give and take, being able to kind of transition, some of those functional skills, we thought, you know what, let's give this a go again and see if we can enroll him in half day community-based preschool. So I went to a different preschool, change locations, give it a new lease on this. And in that community-based preschool, I said, you know, he had some past experience with some challenges. We've been working on some functional skills. And what I want to offer you is our behavior analyst, our BCBA is willing to come in and support him in the setting. The community-based private preschool never hesitated. They said, of course, absolutely. Come on in. Let's work together. So we talked about the environment. Our BCBA came in and, you know, kind of said, well, here's how I can help and here's where I'll step back and let you lead. And we integrated Marcus in a community-based preschool with BCBA support front-loaded. And guess what? There were no sensory tables unleashed. He didn't elope from the classroom. He was able to sustain and be in that setting. That was his LRE at that age. That was his least restrictive environment. So then while this is all happening in our personal lives, the Autism Alliance of Michigan was taking the lead on making sure that people had access to this through the Autism Insurance Law that was passed in 2012. So just kind of on our timeline, my son's now four when this passed. And I can pretty much guarantee you that Marcus, my son, was probably one of the first kids to receive that benefit because I was tracking what the Autism Alliance was doing. I was going to their information sessions. And when former Lieutenant Governor Brian Cowley signed the legislation, the next day I was on the phone with our insurance company saying, okay, we qualify. Like we need this. We're doing it. Like I need your help to like be able to make sure that I can cover this. And I called every single day. Who do I need to talk to? Take the notes. And so I guarantee my son was one of the first ones covered. And our BCBA was probably one of the first providers that were pulled into that system. So then that opened up a lot of greater access for us with that insurance coverage. And we kept working with our BCBA in the community-based setting. So then if I think about like at this point in time, he's in the self-contained public school district place like setting. Then I'm taking him to like the community-based setting. We're doing that for multiple years, right? And we're seeing lots of growth being around non-disabled peers. Again, his public school district classroom placement was 13 autistic kids, like all kids, you know, with similar needs, very structured environment, no integration. And so then we did that for two full years. Despite initial resistance and stereotypes from military authorities, Native American recruits were eventually sought out for their exceptional marksmanship and stealth. Company K played vital roles in the Battle of the Wilderness, Spotsville Courthouse, Siege of Petersburg, Ream Station, Peebles Farm, and Hatcher's Run. We've talked about the open carry of 18-year-olds, and while they're able to do it, this bill would clarify and help so many bad things from happening because the difficulty that it is to legally open carry at 18 years old is incredibly difficult. Other than taking a stroll down a public sidewalk, you're very limited. You can't enter a business that serves alcohol or sells alcohol. You can't go by the schools. There's so many things you can't do. So this would really clarify and solidify our young adults to be able to carry and do so responsibly and with the knowledge that they need to do that for themselves. So as a wife and a mother, I am absolutely here in support of 4586. Please let my babies protect themselves. Okay. Seeing no further questions, thank you, Representative. We are going to move on to the next bill. So I'll call up Rep. Outman. Oh, wait. Let me read these cards. Okay. In regards to 4586, not wishing to speak and opposes the bill, Kathy Tang, Everytown for Gun Safety. Oh, there is somebody that wanted to speak. I'm a resident of Charlotte, Michigan, for the past 25 years, and I've lived in Michigan my entire life. The gunman then took his own life, changing the lives of two families forever. I am testifying today in opposition to House Bill 4586, which is a bill to lower the age to obtain a concealed carry permit to carry concealed loaded guns in public from age 21 down to age 18. As you probably know, firearms are now the leading cause of death for American children and teens in America. House Bill 4586 would set a dangerously low minimum age for carrying concealed loaded handguns in public, despite research that shows that individuals aged 18 to 20 years old commit gun homicides at a rate of approximately three times greater than adults 21 and over. The area of the brain responsible for judgment and impulse control is not fully developed in 18-, 19-, and 20-year-olds, meaning that they can be more prone to aggressive behavior. Decades of scientific evidence demonstrate that adolescents and young adults make riskier decisions than adults. Unfortunately, our state and communities know all too well the devastating impacts of gun violence in the Oxford High School shooting. That includes the lives of almost 1,420 Michiganders, costing $16.8 billion in employer work loss, medical, police, criminal justice, and also loss of quality of life costs services. I urge members of this committee to please oppose House Bill 4586 and prioritize the safety of our communities by focusing on proven solutions to gun violence prevention. Thank you very much for your time. Thank you. I lost my card. I have lots of them up here. Next up, wishing to speak in support of the bill, Tom Lambert of Michigan Open Carry.
