One of those conceptions is that people who openly carry do not have a CPL. That is wrong. In fact, Michigan Open Carry strongly advocates that people who do openly carry a holstered pistol get their CPL. One of the main reasons we advocate for that is all of the legal pitfalls that simply having a CPL takes off the table. One of those pitfalls is that Michigan has a five-year felony for carrying a concealed pistol or a pistol otherwise carried in a vehicle. We are one of the most draconian states in the nation in terms of we have a very strict punishment, a five-year felony, not a lesser felony or a misdemeanor, and we cast that felony against a very, very wide net. It's not just something loaded on your person. It's unloaded. It's anywhere around you. It's anything in your vehicle. It's an incredibly wide net combined with a very, very strict punishment. Simply having your CPL takes ...

off the table. Now that the weather is getting colder, we also have an issue with what you wear. If your shirt slips over the holster of the firearm, if your coat slips over the holster of the firearm, even for a moment, you can be subject to prosecution under that felony. And I'm telling you affirmatively with strong conviction that this felony is absolutely enforced against inner city minorities far more than anyone else. Allowing 18 to 20 year olds not to carry, because that's not the issue on the table. They can already carry, as you've heard, allowing them to go through the training, go through the background check and simply get the licensing again to take those pitfalls off the table, whether it's carrying out in public or transportation. If you do not possess your pistol correctly in your vehicle while traveling to or from a gun range, again, you can be subject to that five year felony, even though you didn't have it loaded on your person, you weren't even trying to carry it. So is there a black market in guns that would be diminished by having a legal CPL? Is the question, is there any correlation that I know of between allowing 18 to 20 year olds to get a CPL and an increase or decrease in unlawful gun possession on the streets? Decrease. Decrease. I'm not aware of any correlation one way or the other. I know this is somewhat newer. The only thing I would point to in a micro context is that the individuals who might otherwise be said to be unlawfully carrying, even though they really weren't, they didn't tend to harm anybody, their coat just happened to be covering a pistol, that's technically treated as unlawful carry, even though it shouldn't be, that we could expect to see a decrease in that. Thank you. Thank you for your time. Thank you. I think that is the last one on that bill. Yes. Okay. Now, Representative Outman, thank you. 5113. Following her, you'll again hear from Steve Dolan, General Counsel for the Michigan Coalition of Responsible Gun Owners. Steve worked with Clerk Millard and me to craft this legislation and ensure we addressed the correct areas of law. But as you see, the main objective of House Bill 5113 is simple. It's to create a clear process for correcting errors on CPL applications to allow a short grace period while those issues are fixed. At the end of the day, this bill is about fairness and efficiency. It just ensures that law-abiding CPL owners aren't punished for simple errors or administrative mix-ups and that our clerks have that flexibility that they need to resolve these issues quickly and without unnecessary costs. So with that, I will turn it over to Clerk Millard to share her perspective from the county level. Good morning, Chair and the committee. Thank you for allowing me to testify. My name is actually Stephanie Bracey and I am Chris Millard's chief deputy clerk. She was unable to attend today, but I am here to testify on her behalf. So to kind of go to the point of Representative Outman, our concern came when the beginning of the year we started to have applicants that were actually renewing their CPLs and what was happening was they were coming back as disqualified. And what it was showing for disqualification were pending criminal charges that were from the early 1990s and these didn't show up on previous applications that they did. They had been CPL holders. We had a gentleman that was a CPL holder since 2005. He never had an issue with this. And then all of a sudden this year it was showing up and it was having him be disqualified. I had contacted the Michigan State Police on how we should handle this. And because it was a court's error that his disposition of the charge was not handled properly, it was not his fault. So what we went to Representative Outman was that we didn't feel that it should have been the individual's responsibility to have to pay that $115 renewal fee again for the second time. MSP did a workaround for them to be able to just reapply and not have to retake the class again that they still could reapply, but it still would cost them another $115. So what we went to the representative's office was try to get some legislation passed that would allow for these mistakes to be corrected possibly in a time frame where they wouldn't have to repay that $115. Now we don't have a ton that come through like this, but we are still seeing them. The most recent one we had was in August of 2025 that he was disqualified. He had been a CPL holder for many years and it was just now showing from the background check that they did. And that's all that I have for today. I just wanted to give a brief synopsis of what we were seeing. If you have any questions, I'd be happy to answer anything. Thank you. The timeline in the bill's business days, is it 21 business days to remedy the situation? Is that enough time to deal with the court system and the state police? I mean, as far as a smaller county, probably, but some of our larger counties, it could take a lot more time for people to get it resolved. How long did it take for you? I mean, were they expeditious in getting it done or just I'm just curious. Well, in our office, we're in charge of so how criminal history is used to be sent in the 90s was they had the judgment of sentence once they were sentenced was mailed into the Michigan State Police and they would manually update their criminal histories. Now when we do a judgment here in the clerk's office because we have we are the clerks of the circuit court, that judgment electronically gets sent. So it's very fast that MSP is able to get it updated on their criminal history. So the one individual that we had, we were able to go in and see what had happened that wasn't sent properly. We got it sent right over and they were able to fix it rather quickly. But that was in our court. So I can't speak for other courts, unfortunately, how quick it would be for them to do it. Like I said, some of the bigger counties, it probably would take a lot more time. Okay, thank you. And then next up, we have Steve Dolan. Go ahead, you have the floor. I think I'm sorry, I was unmuting. Yeah, hi, I'm Steve Dolan. I'm a member of the Board of Directors of Michigan Coalition for Responsible Gun Owners. I'm also an attorney in private practice. I mentioned I was honored to be included in the discussions leading up to this amendment that is in this bill. And that was because in my experience dealing with a lot of counties, we've got spotty reporting, frankly. It just kind of depends on the court whether or when a lot of things are reported from the courts to the relevant database here at MSP. And then there's another glitch that happens between the local database in Michigan and the federal database at FBI NICS. But that's not really the subject of this. But we've got a lot of time. I think the question was right on point. We've got a lot of time taken up trying to correct these errors in a lot of cases. So there's two different timeframes here in this language. 21 days is if the applicant makes a mistake. And if you've got a fat finger or you don't read the small print clearly enough, you can click the wrong box, essentially. And then under the current system, even if you say oops within minutes after, which was the case for one of my clients, under the current system, you've got to wait for the denial and reapply starting ab initio, right, from the beginning. And so this seems like common sense to me. This is just if I notice, if I get turned down on a renewal because I made a mistake or I checked the wrong box on the form at the clerk's office, either way, then I've got three weeks to come in and prove. How often does this happen or how often does this come to your attention? Well, it's come to my attention several times. I tend to get calls from all over the state with regard to these types of issues. So no one's gathering this data. Nobody knows how many people simply just kind of sucked it up and went through the process again and paid the fee and had to start all over. We literally nobody's got that data. Okay, because you did raise a great point about the three weeks if it's a situation by the applicant. But is there a timetable if it's by the courts or the clerk's office? No, the language that's in here says may submit a new application at any time. Okay, thank you. Rep. DeBoer. Thank you, Madam Chair. So I spent 12 years as a county clerk and this was a very common issue. And I appreciate you guys coming forward with this because things as simple as mistakenly checking the wrong box on a question would disqualify an individual even though their answer was not actually the accurate answer. And I'm going by memory. It's been a couple years now since I've been there, but it seemed as though there was actually a period of time they had to wait to reapply even when it was just a mistake that they had made. The other issue is that, you know, we may think that the courts all talk to each other, right? That they don't all talk to each other. So when a rejection comes back and the local clerk provides that letter of rejection, it's on the applicant to go out, go to the court of jurisdiction that the, you know, the denial came from and try to get that sorted out. And we had that happen many, many times, which resulted in them then having to get a new entry into the lien system that showed that that had been dissolved or had been adjudicated and they weren't subject to it. I mean, it was quite a process and it did end up costing applicants the additional $115 application fee or sometimes $115 already on prints, but it was an ongoing problem that we dealt with almost on a monthly basis to one degree or another. So, Rob, I really appreciate you coming forward with this bill. This really does make a difference. And thank you guys for what you do, by the way, up there. Can I add something to that? The prior comment, I've got a paralegal here in my office who averages about two days a month of billable time cleaning this kind of thing up for people. The just court's not reporting, et cetera. So they're not only paying the $115, they're paying law offices also. Thank you. I'm going to go ahead and call up Tom Lambert again on House Bill 513. You can just stay there, Rep. Owen. Supports the bill, wishes to speak from Michigan. I'll return the balance of my time unless anyone has a question. Oh, thank you, sir. All right, I'll read on the rest of these cards. Not wishing to speak, supports the bill, Casey Armitage. Not wishing to speak, supports the bill, Nick Bougie from NRA. Not wishing to speak and supports the bill, Brady from MCRGO. Brady asked. I'll write it out phonetically so I can say it right. All right, next up we are going to have Rep. Maddock up on House Bill 4980 in regards to CPLs also. And with him, he also has Representative Gary Eisen who supports the bill and wishes to speak with him. You know, one of the greatest things about this country is our ability and right to defend ourselves against bad people. And I think the last person that should get in the way of that sacred right that many of us enjoy in this room is a bureaucrat. And that's happening in Michigan. And this is actually a reintroduction of a bill that Representative Eisen got through the House a couple years ago. And it had a lot of support because this bill does make sense. It actually had 20 Democrats on the bill also who voted in favor of this bill. So I want to let Gary, who's had a lot of experience in this arena, he's been a CPL instructor for many, many years, and he's had feedback from a lot of people that he's trained when they hit these roadblocks and these horrible things that some of our counties are doing to people. All right. Thanks, Madam Chair and committee members. It's been a while to sit in this chair, but it kind of all comes back to you, you know. But yeah, I've been a CPL instructor for 20 years, and it came to my attention that I was doing most of my classes in Macomb and St. Clair County. All right. Pretty, I call them normal counties. But when I came to Lansing, I was starting to do classes for members and staff, and they came from different counties. And I was getting complaints from them that when I told them about getting their CPL, you go to the county clerk's office, you fill out your application, you pay your fee, and away you go. You get fingerprinted. It was like the same day, you know, maybe one day delay. But some of these guys were saying they had four months, five months, three months, and it just didn't make any sense to me why some counties can do it in a day and other counties take five, six months. And so being in the position I was, I thought, well, maybe I'll look into this and maybe we can pass some legislation to straighten this out. And at the time, I had my back desk, Nancy, sitting behind me, called several county clerk's office and asked them about the waiting time. And we had all kinds of times, from a day to, like I say, six months. And I'm going, why is this? And we found it not to be red and blue and all that kind of stuff, but we did find that more of the blue counties took a little bit longer than the red counties. That's just a fact, okay? Who was the longest? Wayne County was the worst with a four- to six-month waiting period. And it just didn't make sense to us. So I did pass a bill. We called it our Any County Bill. It was about three and a half years ago, and it did come out of committee, bipartisan, came off the floor, bipartisan, and it got stalled in the Senate. And one of the big reasons it got stalled was that the county clerk association came out

and it wasn't for any real reason except for the money. The county clerks wanted to keep the money. So if more people left Wayne County and went to St. Clair County, St. Clair County would get the fee. And my answer to them was, well, if you just got more efficient in doing this, people wouldn't feel the need to leave your county and go for it. So you got to remember, your driver's license is a state license. Your CPL is a state license. You can go anywhere in the state and renew your license. But you can't do that with your CPL. But you got to understand, all this information goes back to the state police. So it really doesn't matter where you file, the state police have the last call on it. They're the ones who, okay, the applications, they certify it. So if someone is in one of these counties with a waiting period and they decided to take a day off of work and drive up to Macomb or Sanilac or one of these counties that pretty much same day application, why is that such a crime? Why are we punishing law-abiding citizens because of a waiting period? It just didn't make any sense. And I got to remind everybody that this bill is not about buying guns or shooting guns or transferring guns. It's simply about filling out a piece of paper and giving it to the clerk and paying a fee. That's all it is. It's logistics. And whether you fill that out in St. Clair County or fill it out in Macomb County, who cares? That's my opinion. That was my opinion. Okay. And it just seems to me it's a very common sense bill. And now some people get their CPL for personal protection. Some just get it because it's easier to carry and some get it because it is easier to buy a firearm with a CPL. But to go through that whole process just to be told it's going to be another four or five months, it just didn't make sense to me. And that's why I put the legislation through before. And like I remind you, it was bipartisan. It came off the floor. And I thought it was a good bill and I still think it was a good bill. And if I got reelected this last term, I was going to run this bill again. Okay. That's just the way it is because it was a good bill. I don't see really anything wrong with it except for the opposition we had, and that was all about money. And it's too bad that money has to stand in the way of people getting that CPL. And more and more after COVID, it just seems more and more people are filing for their CPL, especially women. My last class two weeks ago was seven women, not a guy in the class. They all just wanted to be more responsible for their safety. They want to have more of an input on how they can protect themselves. And then I'm going to tell them that it's going to take an extra three, four, five months to do this. It just didn't make sense to me, and that's why I'm glad Matt had me come in to speak on behalf of the bill. And I'm willing to take questions or Matt's willing to take questions, I think. It's great having you here. I'm glad you asked me. All right. Thanks, fellas. It's good to see you again, Gary. For those that didn't know, Gary sat behind me for a couple of years on the House floor, so good to see you again. I used it. Did anyone else give you ammo? No. Oh, yes. Gary got me in present every so often. He'd bring a box of ammo, and that's always beneficial. But anyways, we do have some questions. Rep DeBoer. Gary, thanks, Madam Chair. Thank you. Gary, thanks for being here. I remember the conversation about this back in the day. I called you. Yes. And we did a really good job in St. Clair County getting these things out, but then when you went south, it was like months and months and months. You're right. It was all about the money. The opposition from the County Clerk's Association was all about the money. That's really all it was about. But additionally, was it about 2012 when it went to the SHALL issue, roughly? Is that right? About 2012. If you remember, though, we used to have a county gun board, right? And there was a little bit of discretion in that county gun board, right, which you could make an argument that maybe that's why we want you applying in the county that you live in, because if the prosecutor had a relationship with you, good, bad, or indifferent, there might be. But that's gone. That doesn't exist anymore. It's a SHALL issue. If you qualify, you qualify. So I think it's a great bill, Representative Maddox. Thank you for bringing it up again. It makes sense to service the citizens of the state of Michigan. So I'm completely in favor of this, but great job. Good to see you, Gary. Rep. Breen. Thank you, Madam Chair. I'm going to break my rule and ask a question I don't know the answer to. So I'm wondering about what discussions you've had with the clerks. They've had a lot of changes thrown at them lately, especially in regards to elections. I know they work hard. What I don't know is between the different counties, do the clerks use different systems? Is this going to be possible for them to implement? Is there a cost involved? And I know that you might feel like down south they're just delaying on purpose. I personally don't think that's the case. The bulk of our population is in southeast Michigan. So there's probably more applicants. I'm just wondering about the feasibility and whether or not there are going to be any glitches if they start in one county and then finish in another. Okay. Now you've got to remember I introduced this three and a half years ago, so all my data was from three and a half years ago. Now in the meantime, if the county clerks have improved their system, more power to them. Now I don't know how it's done. I don't know if it's politically motivated. I don't know. I really don't care. I just think that it should be more of a level playing field for everybody. Now is there a cost involved? Yes, they get a fee off that fee that I paid to get renewal. They get a fee off it. And if that's the case, they're worried about the fee, which they did tell me that. That was three and a half years ago. And that was the stumbling block at the time. Now whether or not that's today, I don't know. I just don't know if they have different systems that they work with as far as the technology. The way I look at it, every county has the mechanism in place and the procedure in place. And the counties that are doing a large volume are making a lot more money off these to cover their costs. So in my opinion, there's no excuse for Wayne County or Washtenaw County to have a long waiting period because they're getting that additional revenue. And, of course, they're always opposing anything we do because no one in government wants to change. But this is an improvement on what they do. My opinion to them, I'm sorry. Oh, I was going to just let Rep DeBoer intervene in this question. So there's a state system that CPL applications are processed through. And when you process them through, you enter all the pertinent information, including your counties that you're in. And then when the approvals come back, that comes back through that state system back to the county of issuing. So what that would mean is that if you came to St. Clair County and you filed your application, St. Clair County could process that application. But when the CPL is issued, it would be issued back through the county of your residence, which then they could distribute that as they do currently. They do that currently. It doesn't change. The additional thing is on an annual basis, you have to do a report to the state police on CPLs issued, both renewals and news, revenue that's been taken in on that, and your operational cost for you to execute that activity. So if you're executing that activity and you're taking the money in, it's helping to defray the cost. But if you're not executing that, you don't have the expense, right? So that entire system and structure exists. By the way, that data is readily available from every county, how many they've issued and what their operational costs were. And I've looked at that data, and it's pretty amazing to me to look at some of the counties that operate in the black versus the counties that operate in the red, that it costs them more to process a CPL application than it does that they take in, and it's rather telling. So this would, again, go to the premise of efficiency, who does it the best, who does it the quickest, and, frankly, that's where I would rather give my business is the place that does it the most efficiently and most quickly as a taxpayer. Thanks. Rep. Carter. Thank you, Madam Chair, and good to see you, Rep. Hate to spoil this, but everything's about the money, and you brought up a great point. Driver's licenses, Secretary of State, State Police, how about we move it to the state? I had mentioned that several times. The Secretary of State could probably do just as good as job since you have to go there anyway. You'll have one standard. Exactly. I mean, I'm not against that, and I actually brought that up years ago. And I actually believe the state police could do it all on their own too. Since everything you do goes to the state police for approval, and then they send out your CPLs, they mail them out, okay? I believe they mail them out. So could the system probably be better? Yes.

That was probably a musket gun, sir. And that was like the Spanish Inquisition, okay? I mean, they just railed you on why you felt you needed this and all that kind of stuff, but we come a long way since then. So, would you be open to that? I would be. Alright, thank you. I was for it before, so. Yeah, and through that, I actually renewed my CPL online this last year through the state police website. It was super easy. I just had to have a PIN number for my county clerk, which she actually had to send me twice because I lost it apparently. But, you know, it was super simple. They already have all the information anyway. But I will call up the next one. Tom Lambert, if you'd like to speak again, supporting the bill, you can come on up. Members of the committee, thank you again. How about some history? Rep DeBoer, you were talking about some history here. 1887, Michigan, one of the first states to criminalize the possession of concealed handguns. Fast forward to 1911, we actually created the county gun boards in 1911, but only required the license for counties with a certain population level. Very few counties at that time. Jump forward again to 1925, that's when we expanded those county gun boards to the extent that we used to know them. Jump again two years again to 1927, where they effectively redid the 1925 law, and ever since it's been this 1927 law that we've amended over and over and over again. That's why it's all referenced to Public Act 370 of 1927. Back in 1927, we did not have computers. Everything was local. In 2000, that's when we went shall issue, where we said you can't just decide to deny people if they meet the criteria, you have to issue a license to them. But everything was still through those county gun boards. I want to say sheriff, state police, and local prosecutor were the three members of the county gun boards. In 2015, that's when the law passed, it was Public Act 3, if I recall, effective in 2015, got rid of those county gun boards. We're not done yet. Two more years, 2017, they came back and had a cleanup bill shortly afterwards, where no longer did we not have those county gun boards, they added language into the law that specifically said that the county clerk had to issue the license based solely on the report issued by the state police. The county clerks asked for that, and I can understand why. They were not in the best position to make the determinations. They felt the state police, who were doing the background checks, was the best position to make those determinations. And so they wanted to say, we don't want responsibility here, hand it off to the state police, they're the best to handle it. That's what happened in 2017. So where we stand today, county clerks do not have discretion in this process. They are there to take the paperwork, collect their fees to repay their part, hand the paperwork off through a computer system to the state police, where the state police do most of the heavy lifting, and then report back to the county clerk who prints and issues the license. There's no reason why anyone couldn't go to any other county in the state and go through the exact same process that they would in any other county. Yes, there are absolutely counties that still do put hurdles in their system intentionally to slow the system down, specifically in Wayne County. We know this because Wayne County told us so. Back during the COVID era, Wayne County instituted an appointment process where you had to have an appointment to come in to simply apply for a license. State law doesn't say that. In fact, state law says that they can't do anything that's not in state law. Gun groups, we sued them. We said, you can't do this. It's not in the state law. State law even says you can't do anything not in state law. They then went ahead and issued licenses to all of our plaintiffs, and the court dismissed the cases, even though we had constitutional violations in there. They were absolutely not moot. Everyone else since then, with knowing that we were unable to get anywhere in the courts, and with applicants knowing that they're already paying $115, that they're probably struggling to meet, especially in Wayne County, they're not willing to litigate those. So they still have this COVID-era process in Wayne County where they're still throttling the number of applicants that they're taking. They've throttled it down since COVID era, since they do have fewer applicants then, but there's still a waiting period, this artificially generated waiting period. And one of the reasons Wayne County, in its own words, has told us that they do this, this throttling is that there's a 45-day period that if they don't make a determination within 45 days, the applicant automatically gets their license pending a decision on their application. And in the words of Wayne County's attorney, they have this throttling process so that 45 days is never invoked. That is against state law. They can't do that. That 45 days was put in on purpose. Now, we could go litigate again. We could spend money from an applicant. We can spend money from the county. Or we can simply let people go to any county that they want to and apply where there is no waiting period. And let that clerk that isn't artificially slowing down the process enjoy the profits that they receive here. Interesting that this comes up right after CPL fees, that we're hearing how much profit the state is making in the system. So, I hope that background was useful to you. You can understand how we got to where we are, how we started with county clerks, yes, being a big part of making the decision, but that's no longer the case today. I'm happy to answer any questions if you have any. I think we're all set. Thank you for your time. I am going to read in these cards here in regards to House Bill 4980. Does not wish to speak and opposes the bill, Kathy Tang, Every Town for Gun Safety. I don't know what, is it Town? I'm not sure. I'm sorry. Supports the bill, does not wish to speak. Nick Bougie from NRA does not wish to speak and supports the bill. Brady S. from MCRGO does not wish to speak and supports the bill. Casey Armitage. And then I need to go back to House Bill 4749 on Rep Roth and read in a card. Supports the bill, Trevor Van Dyke of the Michigan Supreme Court. All right. Seeing no further business before the committee today, the committee is adjourned. Thank you.

title: Health Policy — Wednesday, November 12, 2025
transcript:
The House Health Policy Committee will come to order. Would the clerk please take attendance? Chair VanderWaal. Present. Representatives Thompson. Present. Meerman. Here. Tisdale. Here. Bierlein. Here. DeBoer. Here. Preston. Schmaltz. Here. St. Germain. Here. Bonac. Frisbee. Here. Witzit. Carter. Witwer. Here. Neely. Hoskins. Here. Foreman. Here. Mr. Chair, you have 12 members present. You do have a quorum. Thank you, Madam Clerk. Representative Schmaltz moves to adopt the minutes of the November 5th meeting. There being no objection, the motion passes. Before we begin today, I know that we have three students, medical students from Wayne State University that are visiting committee today. They're in attendance in the front row. I just want to say welcome to Health Policy. Thank you for pursuing a future and a career in health care. And I hope you find the meeting today enjoyable, the committee meeting. But more or less, I just want to say thank you for spending a few moments with us and enjoy

day-to-day here at the Capitol. Thank you. Also today we have testimony on a number of bills as well as multiple votes. We're going to begin with testimony on House Bills 5201 through 5203 introduced by Representative Paquette, Wurtz, and Smith. Representatives, if you could make your way up to the testimony table. As most of you know, the red button at the base and whenever you're ready you may begin testimony. Thank you for taking some time and being here with us today. All right, thank you Mr. Chair. Thank you members of the committee for applying your minds to this legislation. It's pretty cut and dry. We hang here in the state. We have a lot of abortions that are occurring and this legislation is designed to give us data around these procedures to inform us to support women in these challenging times to try to come up with policy to decrease the amount of abortions that are happening in this state. And that partly has to be due to asking why. And so the legislation, this three bill package, delineates how we would do that, gather reporting requirements from the provider to then inform us here in the legislature to come up with policies to help support women in these most challenging times. But I'll pass it off to reports. Thank you Chair VanderWaal and committee members. I'm here to support House Bills 4201 through 4203. My Bill 4202 would reinstate reporting requirements for complications from an abortion. This law was repealed in 2023 and took effect last year. Since 1979, the actual year I was born, the CDC has collected and monitored data on the number of abortions and abortion related deaths nationwide. Nearly all states, 45 in fact, currently have reporting requirements for abortion deaths. 27 of those states require the reporting of complications including Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Minnesota, and Wisconsin. Virtually all of our neighbors. These bills would bring Michigan in line with most of the other states and with the data that is currently being collected federally. This is a no-nonsense step to protect women. No matter the circumstances of an abortion, like any medical procedure, there's always a risk. Requiring anonymous reports would preserve patient privacy while allowing the state to monitor the safety and care of patients that are receiving the abortion. This would work to protect women from dangerous and potential negative health outcomes that can occur. Thank you. I'm a little far from this. Good morning Chair VanderWaal and members of the committee. Today I am testifying in support of my Bill 5203, which would make disclosing confidential abortion information a felony offense under the criminal code with a maximum of three years in prison or a $5,000 fine or both. As you have heard in the previous testimonies from my colleagues, the other bills in this package would mandate standardized abortion reporting requirements. This bill, however, would provide the necessary punishment for anyone who discloses private patient information in these reports elsewhere. I am sure that many can agree that it would be a terrible thing for any patient to have their personal information publicly released. And anyone in our state who undergoes a medical procedure deserves to have their medical information protected. Nobody should fear other people, including the government, seeing that information. That's why this is a very critical piece to this package and I hope that the committee will join me in supporting both the mandated abortion reporting requirements and the medical privacy of the women here in our state. Thank you. Thank you. Committee, any questions? Rep Thompson. Thank you, Mr. Chair. So within your research on coming up with this legislation, is there any other procedure in the state of Michigan if failed or the patient is harmed that the physician isn't required to report it? I'll be glad to speak on that if I may. No. In fact, as I was preparing my research for this, I mean, we report data to the CDC on mortality and, you know, as a nurse and working in health care, I mean, we report, I'll give you an example, my grandmother died five years ago this month in a nursing home and we made very sure that her certificate of death said what she died of, which was Alzheimer's. She had just been tested the week before for COVID and so she did not have COVID and we wanted to ensure that that was not reported on her death certificate. So no, everything is tracked on death. So and just if I can elaborate a little bit, some of the common causes that would be reported is a hemorrhage, infection of sepsis, anesthesia complications, a prolapsed uterus or rupture, and then other complications. So we just want to know what those are and track those for the safety and protection of women. Thank you. That was kind of where I was going to this because you're tracking poor outcomes in any other procedure, an abortion is a medical procedure, those outcomes are tracked and reported. So it doesn't make sense to me as a health care provider why those wouldn't be tracked to ensure that women are receiving safe care. So thank you for this legislation. Thank you, Representative Tisdale. My question is similar to Rep Thompson's and I know we track mortality and complication rates on other procedures. Are there any other invasive or medical procedures where we track the kind of information that's being asked for in 5201? To my understanding, no. And then in 5203, what are the penalties in other procedures or medical places where I'm assuming we're talking about HIPAA rights here, where those are breached and how would this be different from other medical procedures where private information is breached? It wouldn't be any different. It would just be bringing this in line with those. So again, very important for the health and safety. And so in this particular medical procedure today, a person's HIPAA rights could be breached without penalty? Correct. Thank you very much. Thank you, Representative Bierlein. Any other questions? Representative DeBoer. So if there would be a not-so-great clinic where people are getting infections repeatedly and possibly dying because of those inept procedures, there would be no way for people to know to avoid that particular clinic. Is that the situation we have now? Yes. And are there inspections of the clinic for cleanliness and sanitary conditions like we do in all the other hospital facilities? There is not. And I believe this is the only medical procedure that I'm aware of where there is no inspections. That was all repealed and removed in 2022. This is why I believe this is very paramount and critical to support this legislation package. Yeah, I mean these women are going through so much. And then to have a complication and have nowhere to go, no way to follow up, no one to stand behind them, it's really hard. It's hard to make an informed decision too. As a woman, if that being an option to do, if you don't have any of these measures to look at either. No. Right. Thank you. Representative Meerman. Thank you, Chair. So along that line of questioning, would it be fair to say that today, without these bills passed, backyard alley abortions are allowed? Yeah, I can speak on that. So, I mean, anybody can provide the data. Actually, the CDC tracks that information or has tracked it, but we're not submitting that now in Michigan to the CDC. But when they look at what has caused a death by abortion, they look to determine the cause of death. They use two medical doctors to make that ruling, whether it was abortion related or not. Then the discrepancies are discussed.

And it comes to a consensus, and then each death is categorized by abortion type, whether it's legal-induced, illegal-induced, spontaneous, or unknown type. So, for example, I had a miscarriage almost 23 years ago now. So, by category, that would be a spontaneous abortion. I went septic. I nearly died. And the night my husband took me into the hospital, I had been sick that entire week. I actually passed out on the floor of the bathroom in the ER, which you get really fast service then. And they held me over. I was going to have a D&C the next morning. When my doctor came in, what was my baby, she was able to remove manually, and almost immediately my health improved. They kept me for observation through that day. I was put on antibiotics and sent home. But had something gone wrong, it would have been reported. I'm not even sure now, based on the current law we have, even our spontaneous abortions that happen naturally, are we reporting those under the law? And are we ensuring that even our hospitals, which are inspected and held in high regard, but sometimes there's situations out there, are we tracking that data as well? Yeah, we have two legislators and two experts on the issue. All right, very good. Just let me know, and we'll get your question answered if it's not. Next up, then, we have Patrick Neville, former Colorado legislator on Zoom. Patrick, welcome. The floor is yours. Well, thank you for having me. I'm Patrick Neville, as mentioned. I used to be the House Republican leader in Colorado, and to say I was a Republican leader, that also means I was a minority leader, and I think it's safe to say that even I did not have a strong reputation for being a bipartisan legislator in Colorado. I think that's probably an understatement, but even I was able to get this bill passed in 2022. It's almost the same exact identical bill. And so it's interesting. In Colorado, this bill went into effect in August of 2022. Some of the things you might be hearing is this might lead to a bunch of lawsuits. Well, in practical application in Colorado, this bill has only led to two lawsuits that I'm aware of. What this bill does is actually gives some power to the consumer, to the patient, to remedy some of these situations. An actual example that happened, patient went in, got an estimate, was told their out-of-pocket costs were going to be $1,500. Later on, she was billed $70,000 plus an additional $10,000 for anesthesia. She was able to use this and say, well, if you send me to collections, I will have recourse. The hospital came back and told her, you were correct, our mistake, billing error, $1,500, and she paid her bill. So that's what's actually happening is it's actually giving some consumers some recourse. And since we actually have almost full compliance because of this law in Colorado, it's created a bunch of people that have been out there developing some of these tools. I myself was able to use this. My daughter was in a severe car accident. She needed an MRI because she had a really bad concussion. The hospital I was referred to, and I'm on TRICARE, being medically retired from the military, so I knew it was going to be a $38 copay for me regardless, but I was able to, the MRI that she was referred to was going to be $3,800 plus a facility fee. Well, I was able to find an MRI that actually got her in two weeks earlier, five minutes from my house, and it was $400. And so just in that situation, I was able to save the taxpayer thousands of dollars. And what's even more important about this is businesses are starting to get smart since they're the largest payer, and they're starting to use these tools and encourage their employees to shop around, saving them thousands and thousands, sometimes cutting their health care costs for their employees up to 40% while getting better coverage. And so I would encourage you to really support this bill. I think, as was said earlier, it's not the silver bullet. And what I like to say is price transparency is not going to solve all the problems in health care, but nothing can be solved without it. And so with that, I'll sit back and I'll be available for questions. Any questions? Representative Tisdale. Yeah, with your experience, so there are, I mean, there are thousands and thousands of billing codes, and what the bill calls for is 300 shoppable services and 70 services specified by CMS. So the thousands, I mean, there's, I don't even know what the total number is, 15,000, 20,000 different billing codes. So that's compressed down to 370 shoppable?

No, so the bill, that's what's in the bill that codifies that portion of the federal regulation. There's two portions of the federal regulation. You actually have to do 300 shoppable services, but then you have to do a machine-readable file with all of your prices. If it's the service that's offered, you actually have to put a price for all of your codes. And so that's what the federal rule does. This gives recourse for patients on that. And so you can actually find any code that's billed and actually compare it to the machine-readable file. And what some of these tech companies are doing is they're starting to take all that information and actually develop like a Google Flights or an Expedia of healthcare. So companies can actually go out and give these tools to their employees, and they can go shop. And then there's other people doing direct-to-consumer, the same thing. And so that's the portion that I think is codifying just in the substitute is just the 300 portion. But then the federal rule also requires it for all services that are provided. Okay, I've looked at the pricing list online for one of the local hospitals here. The billing codes weren't in numerical order. The procedures weren't in alphabetical order. I mean, they were posted, but it was worthless because you could scroll through thousands of billing codes all day long and not have any idea of what you were looking at. But yeah, the information has to be accessible, not just posted. And so it's that search engine or that consumer-friendly ability to – and you're not going to shop if you're lying on the side of the road after being hit by a car. But if it is a total knee, you've got time to shop around for that. And I had a very similar experience with a CT scan. But that's all I wanted to ensure. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you very much for being here. Oh, and we have Representative Meerman. I'm sorry. Thanks again, Chair. Indulging me, Patrick. Appreciate your work on this. Could you just lay out some of the outcomes? Like what are other states seeing when this happens, when this transparency, when customers can see what the bill is going to be, what happens? Yeah, there's great outcomes. It's typically the employers that are getting smart and really taking advantage of this because once they can actually see the data, and a lot of them are self-insured, and so they're actually paying for these procedures themselves, and they can actually take the data and steer their employees to a less cost procedure. So, for an example, like there was an employer that was able to look at it, and a full knee replacement at one hospital is going to be $6,000. You went to another hospital is going to be $50,000. And so what they're doing is giving their employees incentives saying, well, hey, if you go to this hospital instead, we're going to cover your deductible, even give you more money into your HSA, just directly to it if you go to this hospital. And so win-win because the employee stays their deductible, they get more money in their HSA, and then you actually, the employer wins because they're saving. I mean, you talk about that much of a price spread, and that's not uncommon. A lot of these procedures, like I think it was mentioned before, over 90% of procedures are planned. And so only 10% are the actual emergency procedures. And so when these employers can do that, it's a win-win for the employee and the employer. Thank you. Thank you very much. Oh, Representative Bierman. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Excuse me. It works. Rolling them together. Is there any contingency room? So if the procedure says that it's going to cost, you know, it's some sort of surgery and it's going to be $20,000, and then there's complications and now it's $30,000, is there contingency to show that there was cause for more expense? Yes, and so the big thing with the machine-readable files is say there is a – I go in for a shoulder repair or something, and then something happens with my heart that's, oh, my gosh, that's a completely different procedure. So that could happen during surgery. Something happens, there's complication, there's heart, but then there's a different code for that. And that's why it's tough to get all these machine-readable files and actually parse them out. But in that situation, they would be able to bill that other code. So if something happens in mid-procedure or even during the procedure that makes it more complex, there's an additional billing code for that, and that would be allowed to be billed. Okay, thank you. Well, thank you very much for taking some time out of your schedule and being here today. We appreciate it. Thanks for having me. Next up on Zoom, we have Steve Fensberg, former Colorado legislator. Steve, welcome. Anytime you're ready. Well, thank you, Mr. Chair and members of the committee, and thanks for taking the time on this important issue. My name is Steve Fensberg, and I served in the Colorado legislature as well with Patrick. I can confirm all of the things he said about himself early on in his testimony. But this was a bright spot and something that was very rewarding for Democrats and Republicans to work together to do something that's really in the interests of Colorado consumers. So I served in the legislature for eight years. I recently turned out in January. In other words, I used to be somebody important, but now I'm working on issues that I'm passionate about, and health care price transparency is one of them because of the success that we've seen in our state. And the reason why I really love this issue is because, number one, it works. We've seen that the outcomes are very positive. And, number two, it's a bipartisan issue. More than 90 percent of the public supports this issue, and in this day and age, it's kind of hard to find something that everybody pretty much across the board agrees with in politics. Here's how I know it works. There's a federal rule, as we've discussed already in this committee. Its origins are actually in the ACA that requires every hospital in America to post their prices on their website. It's been supported by the Biden and the Trump administrations since it was implemented. However, the enforcement is pretty spotty at a federal level, and so compliance nationally is quite low. So they are required to do this. However, each hospital is probably doing it in a different way, and full compliance is quite low across the country. So Colorado passed a bill several years ago that gives patients – essentially what it does is it gives patients recourse for when they are charged for a service and the patient had no ability to know the price of that service on the front end. So recourse for when the hospital is not in compliance with those federal regulations. The result was that compliance actually shot up almost immediately, and the vast majority of hospitals in our state became compliant and therefore consumers had access to prices. This policy works, and like I said, it's bipartisan. In Colorado, the bill passed I think nearly unanimously. It was sponsored by Patrick, who was the minority leader, as well as the Democratic majority leader together at the same time. Ohio recently passed a similar bill, and it passed unanimously. Just a few months ago, the state of Nevada, as well as Oklahoma, both passed bills that are very similar, although probably a little bit stronger than the one that you're contemplating today. And those obviously passed in very different states. And then Senate Bill 95 doesn't put any – okay, just a moment. Sorry, my children are at home with me still, so they're interrupting me. But Senate Bill 95 doesn't put any additional requirements on hospitals than they're already obligated to be doing under federal rule. The difference is that the bill gives patients a recourse if the hospital isn't following those existing rules. So as Patrick said, the spread between – from one patient to another for a very similar procedure, depending on the hospital they're going to, can vary greatly. That can result in whether the patient is getting a bill that they absolutely can't afford versus one that they can manage. This policy has been implemented in red states and blue states and western states and eastern states. Michigan should follow their lead and pass the law to empower its consumers. Whether you're a Republican or a Democrat, rural or urban, this policy is the right thing to do for Michiganders and urge the committee to do so and happy to answer any questions. And I'm sure my daughters would be happy to answer questions if there's anything relevant for them as well. Well, Steve, I appreciate it because they're stealing the show right now, and that's the way our children should. But I'm sure that there's a few committee members that would love to ask some questions to them, but we'll probably leave them off the hook. But anybody on the committee have any questions today? We don't that I see right now, but I want to say thank you for your time. And you know what? You enjoy your day with your daughters, and that's the best job you could ever have right there. And congratulations on that. And thank you for your service, and we look forward to continuing to work with

undergoing Lindsay on this issue, so appreciate your time today. Next up, Hilaria Santiago, patient's right advocate on Zoom wanting to speak. You can help me and let me know how bad I did on that name, but thank you very much for being here. It's a different one. It's Hilaria Santiago, so you weren't far off. But good morning, Mr. Chair and members of the committee. My name is Hilaria Santiago and I'm the Director of Research at patientrightsadvocate.org, a non-profit, non-partisan organization seeking real prices, real choices, and a functional marketplace in healthcare. We strongly believe that the single most important way to achieve this is through system-wide healthcare price transparency. I'm here to speak in strong support of Senate Bill 95. This bill ensures that hospitals cannot pursue medical debt collection actions against patients if they were not in compliance with the federal price transparency regs at the time of service. It's a simple principle. If you don't show the price upfront, you shouldn't be able to collect afterwards. Healthcare is one of the only sectors of our economy where people are expected to buy without knowing the price upfront. We don't tolerate this elsewhere and we must stop accepting it in healthcare. As a nation, we have over 100 million Americans in medical debt. It's one of the leading causes of bankruptcy in our country. And over one-third of Americans are delaying care due to fear of unknown costs. We owe it to everyone and to Michiganders to do better and empower patients to shop for the best quality of care at prices they know they can afford. Transparent pricing allows Michiganders to compare prices and quality before getting care, budget responsibly for medical expenses, because 90% of care is shoppable and non-emergent, avoid crushing surprise medical bills, and most importantly, get the care that they need, ultimately allowing them to live longer, healthier, and wealthier lives. When prices are hidden, hospitals can charge whatever they want. Families are then stuck with crippling medical debt, competition suffers, and trust in our healthcare system erodes. This is not placing additional burdens on hospitals. Hospitals have been required under federal law since 2021 to post their prices. Unfortunately, compliance has been uneven, and many Michigan hospitals still fail to post clear, accessible, and transparent pricing. In our recent semiannual compliance report, only 2 out of 53, which is 4%, of Michigan hospitals were fully complying with the federal regulation. This bill gives the federal reg real meaning. It creates an incentive for compliance by linking transparency to a hospital's ability to collect medical debt, and it also ensures hospitals cannot build different amounts other than the ones recorded in the machine-readable files. And this is a problem we see across the board. That's fair, and it holds institutions accountable without imposing new burdens on hospitals or patients. It's not anti-hospital, it's pro-consumer and pro-accountability. It simply says, if you want to collect money from patients, you must first be transparent with them about what the costs are. We strongly support this bill. Every Michigan family deserves to know what the healthcare costs will be before they walk through hospital doors. This bill not only promotes price transparency, but it will also allow patients to take care of their physical health while protecting their financial wealth. Thank you. Thank you. Questions from the committee? I'm assuming you've helped several states with this legislation, is that correct? Yeah. Recent one, Ohio? Yes. Can you give us just some tidbits of what you saw in Ohio and what benefits they've accomplished through that legislation? Yeah, so what we were able to do in Ohio, which is really exciting, is create a shopping tool for all Ohioans instead of having to use these machine-readable files, which, you know, they are large. They're not totally consumer-friendly. And I don't think someone like my mom or dad would have that great of a time using them. So we created this database that pulls all of the information posted in the machine-readable pricing files. So instead of going into the file, you can go on our tool, type in whatever billing code you need, whether it's an MRI, you know, an X-ray, or something like a heart surgery, and we pull all of the prices posted by that hospital for that item and service. So we're able, once the pricing information is out there, we're able to create consumer-friendly tools that just makes, you know, this pricing data accessible to everyone. Very good. Thank you. Seeing no other questions, I want to say thank you for your time today. Appreciate it very much. Thank you. Next up on Zoom, Christian Deacon author Versan Consulting. Is he on? Should be. Maybe not. Yes, thank you. All right, the floor is yours. Thank you. Chair and members of the committee, thank you for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Chris Deacon, and I previously served as the Director of State Health Benefits for the state of New Jersey, where I oversaw the health benefits program for over 800,000 public sector lives. I've also recently testified before the U.S. Senate Health Committee as well as the House of Representatives Committee on Aging on healthcare affordability and price transparency. I'm also the author of the recent book, The Great American Healthcare Heist. The affordability of healthcare remains a dominant, obviously, fiscal concern at every level of government. And even as federal policymakers debate budgets and shutdowns, there is virtually no discussion of the underlying prices that drive spending. And that's largely because those prices have remained hidden. More than four years after passage of the federal hospital price transparency rule took effect, compliance remains inconsistent and enforcement not only uneven, but essentially non-existent. Without transparent pricing, as my colleague Patrick Neville mentioned, efforts to constrain or rationalize healthcare costs are structurally impossible. Michigan's data clearly demonstrates the urgency of this matter. The Department of Insurance and Financial Services, I read recently approved, or not recently, for last year, approved an average premium increase of 10 to 11 percent in the individual and small group market, with preliminary 2026 filings indicating potential growth up to 20 percent. And I've certainly confirmed that with several employers, large employers and unions that I have worked with in the state of Michigan. Hospital and facility prices are the dominant driver of these increases. According to RAND, Michigan hospitals are largely reimbursed at twice the federal benchmark, with very wide interstate variation that cannot be explained by case mix or quality metrics. Transparency is essential to identifying and addressing that variation. What this bill does is aligns compliance with consequence by prohibiting hospitals from initiating collection actions on debts incurred for periods of noncompliance with the law. It is narrow, it's targeted, and this enforcement mechanism supports, not supplants, federal rule and regulation. I have testified before state boards at the federal level, state legislatures on numerous occasions on this topic. And one of the, you know, there are four arguments that typically are raised in opposition, and I'd like to address those should they be raised. Hospitals often argue that compliance is complex, yet CMS has published very detailed technical specifications, and hundreds of institutions nationwide do meet them. Obviously, there's no other sector of the economy that would be permitted to obscure prices on the grounds that disclosure of those prices is administratively inconvenient or burdensome. There's also often the assertion that patients will not use the data or misunderstand its purpose. Price files are not solely consumer tools. They are essential for employers, unions, public purchasers, et cetera, who then aggregate and analyze that pricing information to inform their contracting and purchasing decisions. Some have asked, what happens if something unexpected occurs during a treatment? A valid question, but it doesn't undermine the principle of transparency. Every service, test, and intervention already has an established price. And so the purpose of transparency is not to demand advanced prediction of every known clinical contingency, but to ensure that when those contingencies occur, the prices are known, published, and accessible. Price transparency does not interfere with clinical judgment. It ensures financial accountability. And then finally, litigation risk. Hospitals and hospital associations often express concern about legal exposure. In reality, the current litigation imbalance

in the opposite direction. Thousands of Michigan patients face wage garnishments, liens, credit damage arising from medical debt. A report by the Pew Charitable Trusts found that in Michigan, about 10% of all debt collection lawsuits filed in the state from 2010 to 2021 were brought directly by medical providers. What this bill does is simply ensures that hospitals demonstrate compliance with existing law before invoking the courts against individual patients. We know that transparency is not a panacea, but no viable cost containment framework can succeed without it. This enforcement mechanism tethered to pre-existing federal obligations can enhance accountability and protect patients and purchasers from the consequences of opacity and no transparencies. So for these reasons, I would respectfully urge the committee to advance Senate Bill 95. Thank you, and I'm happy to take any questions. Well, thank you very much. We do have a question. Representative Meerman. Thank you again, Chair. Could you restate the percent Michigander receiving health care are overpaying compared to the rest of the nation? Yes, the RAND study found that Michigan payers are paying twice what the federal rate is, so that would be around 190 to 200% of CMS for their health care, inpatient and outpatient services facilities. There's a RAND price transparency study that is publicly available, and they've been putting this data together for several years. Thank you. Thank you. Any other questions from the committee? Seeing none, thank you very much for your time today. We appreciate it. We have one other card to read in on Senate Bill 95, not wishing to speak in support, Kaylee Hunt, Michigan Nurses Association. And then I inadvertently did not read one card in on 5162, not wishing to speak opposing the bill, Mike Jones from Lara. Representative Hoskins moves to excuse absent members. There being no objection, the motion prevails. There being no further business before the Committee of Health Policy, it'll stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Oversight - Weaponization of State Government — Wednesday, November 12, 2025
transcript:
The Oversight Subcommittee on Weaponization of State Government will come to order. Will the clerk please call the roll for today's attendance? Chair Regas? Here. Representative Shriver? Present. Wolford? Palatsky? Here. Legala? Here. Madam Chair, you do have a quorum. Representative Shriver moves to adopt the minutes from the October 22nd meeting. Hearing no objection, the minutes are adopted. Good morning and welcome to the hearing for the House Oversight Subcommittee on Weaponization of State Government. As chair, I am grateful to our witness, Matt Lyson, from the Michigan Duck Rescue and Sanctuary, and all Michiganders who have joined us today either in person, online, or through the growing chorus of voices demanding answers. Today we turn our scrutiny to yet another troubling chapter in the Michigan DNR's pattern of overreach, the shocking order issued to Matt Lyson to euthanize dozens of flightless wild ducks and geese at their nonprofit sanctuary in Salem Township. For nearly two decades, the Lysons had poured their hearts and their own five-acre property into a labor of love, rescuing domestic waterfowl dumped by impulsive buyers and providing humane care to injured or disabled wild birds that nature or human negligence has left behind. These aren't criminals running a black market operation. They're stewards of God's creatures, untangling fishing line from mallards, nursing roadside ducklings back to health, and offering sanctuary to Canadian geese stranded on frozen lakes. In October 2025, the DNR, without a signed letter, demanded these birds be put down within 30 days, citing deficiencies and facilities that the Lysons insist are fixable and that remarkably were swiftly corrected, leading to the order's reversal in just two days later amid public outcry. This is not an isolated incident. It's part of a disturbing trend under Governor Whitmer's administration where the DNR wields its authority like a blunt instrument against everyday heroes. Remember Peanut, the vision-impaired fawn nursed back to health by Detroit Animal Welfare Group, only for the DNR to order its death until House members, media pressure, and thousands of petition signers forced a reversal. Or the aggressive enforcement of invasive species orders against family pig farms and ranches, demanding records, footage, and lab tests in what feels less like conservation and more like a government shakedown. Even Ted Nugent, a lifelong conservationist, testified before this committee in June about the DNR's out-of-control regulatory assault on hunters, farmers, and animals alike. I would like to welcome Matt Lyson up to the computer and the microphone. And Matt, whenever you're ready, you can kind of start your presentation. But I would like you to start from the beginning and just run through kind of what has happened for the committee. Thank you.

Thank you. Thanks, John. So much to go over here, but just a few things up front. My wife and I, back in 2006, created an organization called Michigan Duck Rescue and Sanctuary, where our primary goal and purpose was to help neglected, injured, abused domestic animals that were purchased on impulse and at some point abandoned out in the wild where they would not survive. I'd like to preface by saying I am not a licensed rehabber, never professed to be one. I am a certified rehabber. The difference between the two is I have all these certifications, all the education to be able to be a licensed rehabber. I just don't have the license from the DNR. I have all the capabilities to do everything that I'm going to talk about in here. They just found some issues with the property that are easily remedied. So back in, with the DNR's case, back, well, first, also I want to say that not all, in fact, very few DNR agents are sort of, have gone astray. Most of the DNR agents we've dealt with, and there have been many, have been very polite, very courteous. They've been on our property. They've liked what they've seen with certain conditions, knowing that some of the animals we had maybe should have had, gotten there by other means, but they have been very, very respectful and responsive of what we've done. So I don't want to categorize, when I say certain agents, I'm talking about a very, very small handful of them. So I want to clarify that. So back in, in what started this actually is a couple of online trolls that have their way of getting through. Sorry. Sure. They have their way of getting into all these neighborhood groups and things, and they look for issues to stir trouble up. A couple of them are very well known. They have caused issues with DAWG. This is how some of this stuff began. And with themselves. They seem to have an ear into the DNR, where the DNR seems to respond to anything that they say immediately. But when someone calls for help for wildlife, and I'm talking dozens of people, probably weekly, monthly throughout the year, the DNR seems to be in a different sphere. And they have people that answer the phone basically saying, let nature take its course. We'll get into more of that later. So that's kind of the premise of what we've got going on here. Back in December of 2023, we had a situation where we had actually gotten a phone call. An individual said that he had a little mallard duckling, young juvenile, that needed a place to go. And I gladly accepted that because I have a rehabber at the time, Ginger Marley, who I know would have taken the duckling at that time of year. So the guy was sort of insistent on the phone, but he also said if I couldn't take it, he would find another place, to be fair on him. So I offered to take it. I was not home at the time. He ended up showing up at the property. My wife went out to the gate and lo and behold, three DNR agents, three vehicles came to the property for one duckling. That was the whole premise, one duckling. They had three vehicles. I can't emphasize this enough. Three vehicles, three individuals. This is about an organization that apparently doesn't have a budget. They have to raise prices, yet they had the nerve to bring three people. I'm no threat. They know I'm no threat. I invite them to my property all the time. I have no issues with them. When I get calls that say no caller ID, often I assume it's them. I answer the phone. We run from no one. We hide from no one. Our gates are always open. So once they got there, that picture they showed basically disappeared. They showed my wife another picture, and it was of a domestic ruined duck. I don't know if that's going to be, hopefully it's in here. I know they couldn't download some of the pictures. Unfortunately, they couldn't do it. A domestic ruined duck looks very similar to a mallard duck. The only difference is size. The mallard duck is much smaller, capable of flight. A ruined duck is not. It's a little bit bigger. Once you see the two, you'll understand completely the difference. So they showed my wife the picture of this ruined duck, which they thought was a mallard duck. My wife said, well, could you wait until my husband gets home? I ended up coming an hour later. We invited them in. It was kind of a nasty day outside just before Christmas. A lot of pretty bad weather out there. And if you know anything about ducks, when you have ducks, it gets muddy out there when you're on the property. So we invited them in, and it just so happened they came in the basement. We showed them everything. We had that particular duck in a small pen in the basement, and a picture that didn't come up. And there was a mallard, and it's unfortunate because you could see the two differences between them. So we happened to have a different mallard duck that was in the house that we took in from outside. We get all kinds of ducks flying in, geese, mallards, you name it. We get them coming because we're an open property. We have a couple-acre pond that we share with the neighbor. And we brought this one male duck in because he was getting beaten up by a bunch of other males. They do that throughout the years. We brought him in, put him in a little pen in the basement. We could look outside. He was warm. He was keeping from getting mauled down by some of the other ducks. Well, they came in, and they assumed that was the duck that they were talking about. And they came on the premise of a domestic duck. It just so happened we had a mallard in there. They took the mallard. They wanted to see the rest of the property. I had no problem with that. We showed them that. They found a couple other things that they had questions about. We had a couple of Canada geese that were waiting to find rehabbers, and we had them mixed in with some other ducks. It was other geese at the time because that's where our barn is set up. So they made some comments about they shouldn't be here and some other things. But the funny thing is even though they said some of these animals should not be here, that they might have been stressed, they took nothing with them. They had the capability to take whatever they thought was being put in a bad position. They only took the one duck. After a couple hours, they left. It was over and done. They said during that time, well, we're going to run this up the chain and see what happens. So almost a year goes by. We hear nothing. I happened to go get my mail out of the box, and there's some service papers for my wife and myself. We never got a formal complaint. We never got ticketed. We got nothing. We got letters in the mail that we were going to be prosecuted by the DNR on six misdemeanor criminal counts each. Now my wife, who by default of having her name on the house, was one of the persons that got drawn into this without respect to anything that she does on the property. So they brought her into this. So that's basically how. So we got the service. We knew there was court. We were fortunate to get attorneys. We got everything lined up, and we were going forward with the case. And we had great, great support from the public, and things worked out really well in the end. They ended up dropping the charges for the time being. But some of the things I'd like to go over along the process, this happened in December of 2023. In early 2022, I had begun to try to get my rehabilitation certification from the license from the DNR. I had nothing but pushback along the way. There's an individual that works in the permitting department. Her name is Casey Reese. I'm sure most of you may have heard of her. I don't know if they're shorthanded with help, what the situation is, if people just don't have the ability, the knowledge to know what they're capable or supposed to do. But we have a lot of emails back and forth. I tried to get information. They were very slow in getting it to me. I have some emails here that were not able to be put on there of where for three consecutive times over a month period I had implored with Casey, I will come into the office. Whatever I need to do, tell me what I need to do. They kept sending me the same package over and over again, saying, well, read the package. Well, there was something in the package that was not clear to me that I had asked specifically, Casey, can you call me? I want to go over it. I want to do this right. Because I've talked to other rehabbers. They say if you don't do it right, it's sort of a one and done. They kick you out, and you're done. So I've tried, and I've got the documentation to do this. And I've tried, and then at one point she totally ignored me until the case came into being. And then she hasn't even contacted me at that point even since then. So fortunately the case was dropped, but there are a lot of issues that I have with the DNR. One of the issues is because of what we do, I personally don't think licensing has anything to do with this. This is an example of one of the pieces of evidence that the DNR was going to use against us that I posted on this. at risk versus civil rights and accountability. And I think it's very clear which the ACLU is going to side with. If you have hardened criminals like this gentleman, this man who murdered the girl in Grand Rapids, had he fled into all kinds of safety zones before he murdered her, was that for public safety? There is a different set of rules for due process within 100 miles of an international border, which essentially means the entire state of Michigan to some extent is caught into that different rule. I just want to say that we have guards in front of our synagogue and we don't want to have to have our guards facing masked ICE agents. They're they're there to keep bad people out like you're talking about. But thank you so much. We appreciate both of you. Senator Irwin. Thank you. I just want to ask a related question. So what do you do now? individuals who are armed come to the door and demand entry but don't identify themselves and aren't wearing uniforms, what happens now? Sounds like a dangerous and chaotic situation.
