At a time when democracy is under threat across the country, it's more important than ever for states like Michigan with a democratic governor and Senate majority to fight to defend our democracy wherever possible. Our Constitution gives responsibility to the states to protect people's rights when there is federal overreach by protecting sensitive locations from immigration and law enforcement, requiring law enforcement to wear identifiable uniform and prohibit the use of masks, and require warrants for state and local governments to disclose information to federal immigration enforcement. We protect everyone's Fourth Amendment right to due process. Everyone here who drives likely has committed a civic infraction before due to a small traffic violation. For example, does that mean that we should all be labeled illegal? Does that mean that we should automatically lose our constitutional rights and can be swept up by an unidentified federal law enforcement agent, detained for an undetermined amount of time, and denied our due process? No, that is not the law. Being undocumented in this country is not a crime. It's a civic infraction, and that is not my personal opinion. That is the law. Despite the conflation of immigrants, Latinos, brown and black people with being dangerous criminal individuals, the Constitution guarantees all of us these basic rights. There are many reasons a person may be undocumented in this country, a key one being the desperate desire for them and their loved ones to be able to pursue a better life, a legacy that millions have fought for and lived out in this country, my family included. I came to this country when I was two years old with my parents and siblings fleeing generations of extreme poverty from both sides of my family. Thanks to my parents instilling the values of hard work, sacrifice, and education, I went on to graduate from public schools in the city of Detroit, got a bachelor's degree in public policy from a Michigan university, and a master's in urban education policy. And now I pursue a career fighting to improve the everyday lives of working class Michiganders across the state, a career that both my siblings also pursue. Our stories are not possible without the protection of the very fundamental liberties that motivated why this country was established in the first place. The protection of our constitutional rights is the foundation of our free society. History shows that when our governments start infringing on the rights of a few, those rights become fragile for all. SB 508 through 510 are about more than immigration and policy. They are about fighting authoritarianism and defending the fragile but important framework of our democracy. It's on all of us in Michigan, including our lawmakers, to use every tool at our disposal, elections, policy, the local press, the freedom of assembly, to establish and protect what real public safety can look like in our state. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you, Committee, for this opportunity. I'm in support of all three, but I'd like to focus on Senate Bill 508. My name is Kimberly Redigan, and I'm the Director of Campus Ministry at Detroit Cristo Rey High School in Southwest Detroit and a co-moderator of our school's Strangers No Longer Youth in Action for Immigration Circle of Support. Our small Catholic school is made up of hardworking families who make great sacrifices so that their children can receive a college prep high school education. My colleagues at our neighborhood public and charter schools would concur that the families we serve are the spiritual, economic, and cultural backbone of our vibrant community, a community that is currently being terrorized, traumatized by the presence of individuals often masked in unmarked cars who are stalking the neighborhood. Our students read the news and are deeply shaken by what they're seeing around the country. People being swept up with no due process, families separated when they show up for scheduled immigration appointments, ICE looming outside of churches and schools, masked men breaking car windows. The specter of immigration enforcement in the neighborhood coupled with the barrage of images that are inundating our young people is having a profound effect on them. School is a place where all students deserve to feel safe and protected. Like places of worship, schools are sacred spaces. Students should be concentrating on their classes. They should be playing sports, creating art, and going to dances. Instead, they're coming to school every day feeling unsafe and scared. They fear being racially profiled every time they get into their cars or walk down the street. How do you respond to a ninth grader who asks, why do people hate us so much? How do you keep your heart from breaking when you have to share hard and frightening information with young students at Know Your Rights trainings or sitting across from a family that's lost its breadwinner and has no idea what comes next? Our school is one of many schools and parishes that are part of Strangers No Longer, a statewide Catholic group called by faith to work for the common good by upholding the dignity of immigrants, advocating for just immigration policies, and accompanying families who are such a vital part of our community. I'm the president and CEO at the Michigan League for Public Policy. I will shorten my remarks today. We did provide a written copy. I do want to emphasize that we are pleased to support Senate Bills 508, 509, and 510. Immigrants are essential to our state and come here because our economy needs them. These opportunities exist among essential roles Michiganders will not or sometimes cannot fill. And yet right now, recent immigration enforcement actions threaten Michigan's economy

recovering by deporting our labor force and tax base while betraying trust in fundamental institutions. It ultimately harms our state's overall prosperity. And Senate Bill 509 prevents government entities from sharing personal information for immigration enforcement without a warrant, which is deeply, deeply concerning. These three bills recognize that Michigan's future depends on maintaining institutions that serve everyone. Children need to attend school safely. Families need access to health care without surveillance or risking data sharing. Enforcement must operate transparently under the law. So we strongly support and urge the committee to support all three bills. Thank you very much for your testimony. I appreciate it very much. I know there's a number of other cards, but I think that we are going to have Diana be the last speaker. And then we will read in cards probably at the next hearing. Me is the secretary of the organization, the state organization, Juan Marinas. We've worked with Mi Poder over the years, and we're just Juan's a great supporter of T-shirt wearing. But to Senators Kavanaugh, Chang, and Moss, thank you very much for your work in bringing boundaries to how Michigan law enforcement responds to our undocumented workers, many of which are from Latin American countries. My name is Diana Rivera, and I am the Vice President of LEAD Michigan, a 501c3 nonprofit organization with eight chapters in Michigan. With me, again, Juan Marinas, who was charged, actually, to oversee a refinement of the 2020 census, Michigan census, that showed that every county in Michigan has a Latino resident. I think there's only one that doesn't, right? No, there are two counties lost population, but there's still a population in those counties. Yes, and we claim that our increase in Latinos in Michigan, while there was outflight of other communities, actually saved a congressional district for the state of Michigan. Families who have helped Michigan through economic growth, especially in agriculture, is who we come from. Generations of our family members are also in countries where ICE has been present and threatening and enforcing fear. The LEAD Board of Directors, State Board of Directors, and the LEAD Detroit Southeast Michigan Chapter in particular, who has very specific concerns, are here to support bills 508, 509, and 510. We are in support of these bills because they help curb the behavior of what was the norm in 1929 and 1939 Michigan, the deportation also known as the Great Repatriation of Mexicans or Mexican heritage people. When thousands of Michigan residents, both documented and non-documented, and U.S.-born citizens were deported, our history shifted. Many times we were deported because of our language and skin color. However, though you have heard many of the concerns that we have in other testimonies, we hope in particular that two issues can be further studied and integrated into these bills where the detainees' locations and their families' pre-deportation status are unknown. That is a fear. People are talking about the fear of kids going to school, being deported, going to a doctor's office. The fear of not knowing where your loved one is has got to be the death of someone's soul. I'm going to ask you to just wrap up in the next 30 seconds. That's correct, yes. So today in Michigan, or in Detroit in particular, and cities like Grand Rapids and Western Michigan in particular, are families without their parents. And they are divided. They need assistance in reuniting. And this means finding legal help for them to be able to self-deport in a timely manner. This means settling their issue with property and cars through whatever means are available so they don't lose their homes that they've worked for. In many cases, the Detroit group is helping them find buyers or selling them. So primarily here, thank you for being on the right side of our current history to not have 1929 and 1939 repeated again. Thank you so much, and I appreciate you bringing up really important issues that we have absolutely seen happen in the community. Cards will be in the minutes, and then we'll read them in at the next hearing. There being no further business, the Senate Committee on Civil Rights, Judiciary, and Public Safety is now adjourned. Thank you. Thank you.

It frustrates our customers, but it's something that we believe that we need to do. So it is something we take very seriously, as I mentioned. We try to take every preventative measure that we can. Like I said, I have reviewed the bill, and I think the process for the licensing is fair. I think the fines are appropriate from what I've seen, and I think the senators who introduced it for addressing some of those from last year. Our primary concern with the bill is specifically with Section 1.3, and it's the three-year look-back period. And the issue with that for us is that our stores have a 105% average turnover rate every year. So on average, any one employee is employed by Wild Bill's Tobacco for less than a year. So there's a lot of turnovers, and it's actually a pretty good rate among retail stores in general across the board. But it's higher than other industries. So a three-year look-back period is difficult for us because sometimes you might have an employee that has a bad day or gets to ID. You might have an employee that simply just, you know, maybe they're on their way out and they know they're going to quit and they just don't care because, hey, we're one foot out the door. Or you might have a brand-new employee who maybe doesn't really quite grasp the seriousness of IDing despite the training that took place. So that three-year look-back period is important to us. There needs to be a little bit of room for error based on the turnover rate for employees just across the board on the retail level. And it tends to be onerous even for the most diligent of retailers. So upon review of the bill, one of the penalties, of course, is a suspension of the license. When you have a tobacco-only retail store, you're effectively closing the business. You know, there's not too many other products that can sustain that business in which they can overcome a prolonged suspension of their primary good.

So we'd like the committee to maybe perhaps take another look at that three-year look-back period and maybe address that so that it is more fair for tobacco-only retailers specifically on the retail level. And other than that, I'm happy to answer any other questions. Thank you. Are there any questions from committee members? Yes, Senator Lowers. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Do you have any ideas of how you would accommodate what you're seeking there? I mean, do you make some kind of a penalty that stays with the employee, or how would you go about addressing your concerns about your high turnover rate? So, you know, in our view, we think a 12-month look-back period would be fair. We have our own internal policies, and, you know, unfortunately, if someone fails to ID a minor or fails to ID anybody, really, that's grounds for termination with respect to our business. So we have our own internal policies, and, you know, despite that fact, you know, I hate to say it, but sometimes retail associates, you know, they don't take the threat seriously, although we do try to address that internally. So we think the 12-month look-back period would be fair based on our turnover rate. And I appreciate the fact that there is a portion there that does penalize the employee himself. We found that to be a greater deterrent across the board than our own internal policies. It's one thing when your employer says, hey, we're going to fire you if you fail to ID a customer. It's another thing if we say, hey, you're also going to get penalized and get ticketed by the state, and that's something that, you know, sort of sets off an alarm in a lot of retail employees. So we do appreciate that that is in there. We'd like to see that, you know, the employee fine maybe a little bit higher, but otherwise we do think a 12-month look-back period would be fair given the turnover rate in the retail market. All right. Anything else from committee members? All right. Thank you very much. And we'll resume our testimony, public testimony from Drew Beardsley representing the Michigan Retailers Association, neutral on the bills. Good afternoon, Mr. Chair, members of the committee. I'm Drew Beardsley with the Michigan Retailers Association, and on behalf of our nearly 5,000 members statewide, I want to thank you for the opportunity to speak to these bills. First, I want to thank the sponsors for their work in improving this legislation over the last couple of years. We really appreciate the moves that have been made to accommodate some of retailers' practical concerns. And so as it stands, the Michigan Retailers Association is neutral on the bills. You know, our position has long been that we are not inherently opposed to a license, as long as it is fair and reasonably mirrors the existing licensing processes that retailers hold today. So we appreciate the changes made to help reflect those concerns. You know, that said, we don't ultimately believe a retail license will solve the entire problem of youth access to tobacco. MDHHS's own survey data shows that most underage access comes from social sources, not store counters, friends and family who are of age and able to purchase these products on behalf of the youth. So yes, absolutely, retailers should face consequences for selling to minors. But if the youth who are using these products face zero consequences, then we're not addressing the whole problem. So still, we recognize that enforcement at the retail level can protect good actors. We believe our members are good actors in this space. And so we believe fair enforcement and accountability for all parties involved is the best solution. So thank you again for your time. I'm happy to answer any questions. Are there questions from committee members? Vice Chair Pohlhanke. Thank you, Mr. Chair. The Independent Retailers Association, that's not you, right? Correct. Bill Wild, does he run that? No, that's Jerry. Yeah. Is the president? Okay. Well, their group, because I have a- And they have a card in. They have a card in. Okay, because so just this is a tangent, but I have another bill that would outlaw intoxicating hemp products sold in gas stations. And what they did is they believe so much in that that they sent out a letter to all their retailers and said, pull them off the shelves. Get them off now. They did that before the bill's even been passed out of committee. Would you be willing to do that with your members? Yeah, I mean, absolutely. We don't want to see any products like, you know, to your point about the breeze earlier. That stuff that is not approved, we don't want to see that on shelves at all. So absolutely, that's- Is it on any of your shelves? Breeze? Of the people, yeah. Not to my knowledge. Okay. Because from my- From what I hear out there is everywhere. All right, thank you. Thank you. All right, any other questions? All right, thank you very much. I'm going to read in a whole stack of cards here. All of these groups are supporting the bills. Colin Ford representing the Michigan Chapter of American Academy of Pediatrics. Bob Kefkin, Michigan Association of Secondary School Principals. Noah Smith representing the Michigan Association of School Psychologists. Noah Smith representing the Michigan Association of School Social Workers. Taylor Alpert, Michigan Health and Hospital Association. Amanda Klein, American Heart Association. Danielle Ciriani, Michigan County Social Services Association. Parents Against Vaping. Genesee County Prevention Coalition. American Lung Association. The Cancer Network. Lisa Rutledge representing Western Wayne Family Health Centers. Kate Dorsey, Michigan State Medical Society. Paul Steiner, Tobacco Free Michigan. Rachel Richards, Michigan League for Public Policy. And a few other cards. Jerry Griffin representing the Michigan Independent Retailers Association. Not wishing to speak opposing the bills. And Mark Griffin, Michigan Petroleum Association, Michigan Association of Convenience Stores. Not wishing to speak opposing the bills. All right, great presentation again. And obviously we will be revisiting this at a future meeting. And that's all the business before our committee today. So we are calling the Committee on Regulatory Affairs adjourned. Thank you.

title: Natural Resources and Agriculture 25-11-06
transcript:
The Senate Committee on Natural Resources and Agriculture is called to order. Mr. Clerk, will you please call the roll? Chair Schenck. Senator Cherry. Here. Senator Singh. Present. Senator Polanki. Yes. Senator Daly. Here. Senator Victory. Senator Heinecke. Mr. Chair, we have four members present. There is a quorum. I'll entertain a motion to excuse absent members. So moved by Senator Singh. Without objection, absent members are excused. And just to note, Senator Schenck is stuck in traffic and she should be here in not too long, but she asked me to get started because there's a long list of folks who want to testify today. So on this morning's agenda, we have Senate Bill 685 through 690 and Senate Bill 699 introduced by Senator Singh, myself, Senator Daly, Lowers Victory, and Senator Schenck. And there's many people here today to testify. So if folks could please try to keep their testimony to three minutes, it would be appreciated. And I would like to invite Senator Singh to begin. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair. I appreciate the opportunity. First, I want to say this package of bills has been almost maybe four or five months in work. This issue was brought to my attention by Ingham County Farmland and Open Space Preservation Board. What we've begun to see throughout the state is sort of a reconsideration of how PA 116 has been used for preservation tax credits. And that change that has happened over the last couple of years has brought, I think, significant concern to a number of the local groups that have been doing preservation efforts throughout the state. And so that group, along with the Farm Bureau, have been, I think, great partners as we kind of work with the department, both at MDARD as well as Treasury, to see how we could resolve the situation. And so just to level set, and I know there will be others who will spend more time on this. Over the last few years, there's a different interpretation on farmland preservation property tax credits. We have been doing things a certain way for almost two decades. And that interpretation has changed more recently. That change was that MDARD or the state would have to be part of the permanent conservation easement. And that would, unfortunately, those that were already done in the past would not be eligible if they didn't make certain changes. And as many people know, when you do a permanent easement, you don't want to come in with amendments to make changes and so forth. And so I think as we talk to local groups, they were concerned that they would be out of sync with national standards. You know, we have currently right now, you know, 50-some families that have been receiving this tax credit that, unfortunately, Treasury has been holding off on giving them their credit based on wanting to resolve some of this legislatively. And so working with stakeholders, working with the departments over many months, we now have this package. So I'm pleased to be part of that. And I know we'll spend some more time with the department and others going through the details of this. But to me, this is an urgent matter. I'm hopeful that we can get this done over this week and next week, send it over to our partners in the House. I know speaking with Chair Nair over there, he's very anxious to receive this legislation because he wants to see it move. Hopefully the Speaker will move good legislation from this chamber, but we'll wait and see that issue. But I do feel like this is something that's imperative and that we need to do this in a very timely fashion. So, Mr. Chair, thank you for the opportunity to level set this conversation and be pleased to answer any questions if committee members have it. Thank you, Senator Singh. I believe Senator Daly was going to speak to his bill as well. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Members of the committee, I want to thank Senator Singh and MDARD and Farm Bureau and all the stakeholders that have worked really hard on putting this good package together. Where I played in in Senate Bill 686 is dealing with a situation where a farmer owns or purchases a piece of land, which might have an unusual parcel cut out of it or something. And it's been done in the past. MDARD under the previous director, Rich Harlow, for years has just automatically done these because they're common sense. But apparently in the law, it doesn't allow that to happen. But if a purchase, for instance, in this one, a constituent farmer of mine was enrolled in PA 116, purchased another piece, and desired just a small piece out. So if I can explain real quickly, it's an oddball one-acre piece for the farmhouse. And then you've got what we used to consider to be like a grandmother's house or something next door. And it was half acres. So it had an L-shaped piece cut out of the eight-acre piece that they had purchased. All they wanted to do was square that up and make it do a one-acre piece. The township supported it. The township wanted to see that happen because it made a better lay of the land and a better piece of property than a half-acre piece. And a person didn't even have room to have a septic field or a well on. So they weren't able to farm that little corner, so the person was using the property anyway. So it just made sense. But due to the size of modern farming, the equipment and regular shapes are hard to do. And under the current statute, there's no way farmers could do this from the PA 116 agreement. Therefore, they were forced to use these parts or actually eliminate parts of the land. So I don't think it was the intent of the law, and that was the reason why we're working on this. But this fits into this package really well. It does limit it to one acre of land is the most that can be split off. So it's pretty common sense, I think, and it would allow farmers to turn small, current, useless pieces of land toward another purpose while still maintaining the intent of the current law. I know that there have been some concerns raised about how often this relinquishment will happen and how much work it will create. But I want to assure you, this committee, that all the available evidence suggests that there are only a tiny handful of farms that want to do this in the entire state, and they've expressed an interest in such a program. This bill would not create a large regulatory burden on the department. In fact, it's something that's been being done occasionally over the years. It's just putting it in law so that they can feel comfortable in operating legally. So I'm happy to answer any questions as well. Members, any questions? All right, and I believe Chair Schenck was hoping that Anne-Marie Nicholson, legislative director for Michigan Farm Bureau, would testify. Oh, I'm sorry. I apologize. I had misheard. But actually, we'll take a diversion to that. You're saved by the day. She knows who she is. Testifying on your bill. Did you do it? No, I was about to. Okay. All right. I apologize, everybody. It took me two hours to get to work today. Thank you, colleagues. I am glad that so many of us have been able to work together on these bills to make changes to PA 116 Farmland Development Rights Agreement Program and how it interacts with people who have conservation easements on their land. Farmland conservation is very important to me. I've been working with farmers and landowners since the 1990s and on conservation easements specifically since the early 2000s. The willingness of a landowner to enter into a conservation easement is based on trust, and that trust has been broken by Treasury's change to longstanding policy. To paraphrase Director Boring at MDARD, and I'm not speaking for him, we need to understand the true value of our farmland. Both PA 116 and conservation easements are an essential part of this. This particular issue with PA 116 was brought to me by many people, both farmers and those working on farmland preservation in Washtenaw County. And then I heard it from others across the state. During a farmer listening session that I held in Ann Arbor Township earlier this year, almost 40 farmers showed up during a time that they would have preferred to have been out in the field. I heard concerns from my constituents that the state was modifying their PA

on 16 agreements and increasing their taxation due to a change in policy after a programmatic review by MDARD's Farmland Program and the Department of Treasury. My constituents were suddenly faced with years of back taxes that the government decided to impose now in spite of them believing that they were paying the right amount of taxes all along. This seems inherently unfair to me and with the profit margins on farming already so thin and other market pressures like tariffs hurting them, my constituents are rightly worried and upset. Farmland preservation, including PA-116 and private conservation easements, are important to people across the state of Michigan and I'm excited to see the collaboration and work that went into this package coming together to solve this issue for our constituents. I'm happy to sponsor two bills in this package. Senate Bill 685 ensures that farmers who had both conservation easements and farmland development rights agreements on their land prior to January 1, 2025 may continue to claim the tax credit. Senate Bill 699 increases the administrative cap for the PA-116 program to increase the department's ability to provide services and outreach. If my colleagues would like to share information about their bills, I welcome them to do so. And then the Department of Agriculture and Rural Development will come to give us a little more background on the PA-116 program and their approach to dealing with the situation. And I also want to thank Senator Singh for spearheading this package. Thank you. Any questions? Senator Balinky. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Someone who knows very little about farming here, so I want to see if I understand this. So up to 50 families in Michigan farmers were getting this tax credit where they used a little piece of their land for conservation purposes. And then because Treasury changed their policy, they're now being asked to pay back taxes? Pretty much. I guess I would say a lot of them have put a conservation easement on much of their land. A conservation easement reduces the value of the land. And so I don't want to get too much into the weeds, but simply answer your question. They put a conservation easement on their land, so they're restricting what they can do with their land. And they believed and were charged a certain amount of taxes based on that. Then Treasury was going back and charging them for years and expecting it to be paid. And what was the rationale for Treasury changing their policy? I can't speak to that. I think let's hear that from MDARD. Or I guess I could speak to that, but I don't want to speak for them. Understood. Are they here today? I don't think Treasury is here today. All right. I'll ask them. Thank you. Thanks. Anyone else? Thank you. I'll entertain a motion to adopt the committee minutes from October 28, 2025 meeting. So moved by Senator Cherry. Without objection, committee minutes are adopted. Okay. Next, we are going to have representatives from MDARD come and testify to the bills. When you're ready, you can go ahead. Thank you, Chair Schenck and members of the committee. Thank you for bringing up this package and for inviting us to speak. With me, I have Jamie Smetko-Summers. She is the director of MDARD's Agriculture Development Bureau, and I'm actually going to turn it over to her for a bit of background on the PA-116 program. Great. I think we can move to the next slide, please. Oh, right there's the mouse. Perfect. Well, good morning. Thank you for the opportunity to talk a little bit about the Farmland and Open Space Preservation Act and our program within the department, also known more commonly as PA-116, which is used to preserve farmland by protecting it from being developed for non-agricultural uses. So in front of you, you should also have a handout that outlines various programs and tools that we have within our Farmland and Open Space Preservation Program. The topic of our PA-116 program or the tax credit program is a voluntary program that landowners can voluntarily sign up for a temporary agreement creating an easement on their land. If the landowner submits all of the proper documentation and meets all of the qualifications outlined in the statute, they are then eligible to be enrolled in the program, which then would make them eligible to apply for a tax credit on their Michigan state taxes through the Department of Treasury, which will then exempt them from certain special assessments as well. In total, we have about 43,000 agreements in place covering over 3 million acres of Michigan farmland, and we continue to see slight increases in the number of acres enrolled each year in this program. Currently in 2025, we received 535 new applications for enrollment into this program, which we think is great to continue to see the interest in this program year over year with new applications being enrolled. So you've already heard a little bit about what spurred this bill package. A routine review of credit eligibility by the Department of Treasury led to tax returns being withheld for a few dozen landowners that were claiming tax credits under PA-116. So we're looking at about 43 out of 43,000. As Senator Schenck already stated, these landowners had entered into a permanent easement where the state of Michigan was not a co-owner. To support protection of farmland through these PDRs, the program utilized consent agreements, which were filed with registers of deeds and waived the state's interests in the name of sorting permanent protection. This allowed landowners to continue to receive those tax credits or to continue to be enrolled in the PA-116 program. However, those consent agreements resulted in the state providing tax credits for a leased right that we had no enforcement rights to. This was actually deemed then to be in violation of the statutory language. To simplify, the same parcel of land was enrolled in more than one option, which violated the statute and created confusion over ownership of development rights on the parcel. Once MDARD became aware of the extent of the problem for the impacted landowners, we worked together with Treasury to get a majority of the returns released. The routine review by Treasury actually spurred an MDARD review of the existing consent agreements. Impacted taxpayers were notified and kept updated as MDARD engaged in open dialogue in a search for solution. Our proposed solution was that landowners and conservancies would amend the easements to include MDARD as a co-holder. And that was based off of the statutory language that it had been determined that we were currently violating. Some of the conservancies we spoke to, some of the groups were concerned, though, that the solution would put at risk their nonprofit status and their accreditation. Given those concerns, MDARD was very happy to engage in discussions with the bill sponsors, with landowners, with conservancies to help develop the legislative fix that you have before you. We're not going to go into detail on what these bills do. We'll allow the sponsors have already done so, and I'm sure folks behind will also have additional comments to add. That said, MDARD does have a few concerns with the bill package. We appreciate the dialogue. We appreciate the intent. But as written, we believe the bills go beyond what is needed to rectify the solution. Or to rectify the situation and could actually substantially expand tax credit eligibility. The intent of PA-116 is to protect agricultural lands. As currently written, the bills could allow the inclusion of land under conservation easements that are not intended to protect agricultural land. We suggest changing eligibility language to be narrower in scope or adding specific expectations to exclude non-agricultural easements to protect the intent of statute. I do want to be very clear. We are not opposed to these changes. We just think that they need a bit more tweaking to ensure that we're adequately protecting farmland. Our larger concern is around the increased administrative burden.

In addition to expanding eligibility, which we are working with Treasury to calculate as written what impact these bills could have. They are still calculating that. I do apologize that we don't have that number ready for you today. These bills require MDARD staff to establish new procedures and process new types of requests. This will increase the strain on our already strained program. To continue providing the dedicated support that this key program requires with the expansion of the statute, we have to see an increase in the administrative cap. I appreciate Senator Schenk and Senator Singh for your communications on this, as well as to Senator Schenk for introducing Senate Bill 699. Currently, the statute caps administrative spending at $1.4 million. We are advocating for an increase to $2.1 million, and that is based on current and projected expenditures through fiscal year 2028. Right now, we are allocated $1.6 million and some change. We are unable to access the funds that have already been allocated to us because of the statutory cap. We've been advocating for an increase to this cap for the past legislative sessions. There have been some concerns raised about the bill proposals we put past in the past. We did hear those concerns. One of those was the inclusion of a consumer price index. We were happy to remove the CPI adjustment from this bill draft. The other common concern we hear is that raising the admin cap will actually reduce available funding for agricultural preservation grants. First, those concerns do not account for the staff time that are needed to administer grants and conduct outreach to eligible grantees. An increase in the administrative cap will provide the program with access to the funds needed to develop outreach and educational materials, as well as allow for an expansion of the program to cover more acreage. And while I have you guys here and your attention, we'd really like to advocate as well for an increase in the allocated funding for those grants. It's held steady at about $1.9 million for multiple years now. In front of you is a memo with additional details supporting the need for Senate Bill 699 to move along with Senate Bills 685 through 690. Happy to answer any questions. At the end of the day, we want to provide good customer service and protect Michigan farmland. We're asking for your help to ensure that we can. Thank you. Colleagues, any questions? Senator Paul Henke. Thank you, Madam Chair. So, I mean, my immediate concern is these 50 families who seem to be impacted because of a rule change in the middle of the game. So these bills would fix that and let them... Is Treasury holding on to their tax returns? No. So we worked with Treasury to make sure that those were released. Okay. So when Senator Singh, you said 50 families getting this credit that Treasury has been holding on to, is it... I think if we don't rectify the situation and go and provide the retroactivity that Senator Schenck's bill provides... Okay. So when Senator Singh, you said 50 families getting this credit that Treasury has been holding on to, is it... I think if we don't rectify the situation and go and provide the retroactivity that Senator Schenck's bill provides, they would then be on the hook of having to pay it back. Yeah. I don't think that's right. No, and we're supportive of the grandfathering clause that Senator Schenck has suggested. But the bill package as a whole, we remain neutral with funding just because we do have those concerns about the administrative cap and our ability to provide the good customer service that is necessary. Senator Daly. Yeah, I had a concern when you were talking about the program and preserving farmland, but this program is the farmland and open space preservation program. So it's not just farmers. It's not just farmland. It's open space as well. So I think those conservancies have a right to be in there and should be included. Absolutely. We agree. Thank you. I apologize for just referring to it as farmland. And I guess to expand a little bit on what you're saying, we also know that many farm plots have areas that might be considered open space. Woodlots, for example. And I want to keep things clean so that when someone's entering into an easement, they don't really have to worry quite so much about what's woodland, what's farmed, what's arable, what's not. Senator Daly again. I just wanted to mention that because part of my farm has been in this thing for what year did it start? The 80s? It must have been the early 80s, wasn't it? Yeah. And has been signed up and re-signed up and re-signed up over the years. But we've never taken advantage of it. So just to make everybody understand this, every farmer doesn't get this advantage. It's there for bad times. And it's there to protect us from problems when our property taxes are so darn high we can't afford to survive. So that's the intention behind it. Thank you. I just wanted to clarify that. Any other questions for MDARD? Thank you very much. Next, we have Rebecca Park from Farm Bureau. Ms. Park, thank you for your work on this. I look forward to your testimony. Good morning, Ms. Chair, members of the committee. Rebecca Park with Michigan Farm Bureau. I appreciate all the work of the bill sponsors, the stakeholders, the land conservancies, the landowners, as well as the departments in coming together to get the package before the committee today. I was just going to walk briefly through some of the bills, but first I want to hit on the timeliness of the package. So as we heard, there's some questions whether Treasury is still holding some of the returns or not. But it's my understanding that landowners have received notice from Treasury that if there aren't changes to their permanent easements, that they will not be eligible, very clearly will not be eligible for the 2025 tax year for those PA-116 tax credits. So making sure that we can move this package expeditiously is very important so that we can get this to the governor's desk for signature before the turn of the calendar year. The package before you really seeks to align statute with those previous programmatic practices that the departments used prior to the routine review that MDARD referred to. And so some of the really critical elements of PA-116, as well as permanent conservation easement programs, are maintained in this package, such as the definition of agriculture use. That definition is not changing in this package, so all of the property that is enrolled in PA-116, regardless of whether it has a permanent easement or not, would still have to meet the definition of agriculture use and farmland that has been in statute for a number of years, to your point, Senator Daly. So I'll just quickly walk through the bills. So Senate Bill 685 is the grandfather bill, essentially saying that all of those existing easements would not need to be opened and modified and instead would be considered to be in compliance with the law, and those taxpayers be eligible for the PA-116 tax credits moving forward. 686 creates the flexibility that Senator Daly talked about, giving the department the ability they would still need to approve less than an acre to come out for various purposes. 687 clarifies the state isn't required to be listed as a co-holder. There may be instances where it's appropriate and other instances where it's not in terms of whether state dollars are utilized or not in those easements. And it also includes NRCS language that is typically included when we utilize their dollars for those easement purposes in terms of third-party enforcement rights. 688 is a technical change due to some numbering in statute. And the final two bills, 689 and 690, again, are seeking just to align the statutory language with those programmatic practices. 690 also has a technical change. In a previous administration, changes were made to the Income Tax Act, and so we're just clarifying total household income versus household resources and the nuances there. So that's it in a nutshell, Ms. Chair. And I know there's been some questions from the committee. I'm happy to take those. I'm also happy at your discretion to defer to the many landowners and actual practitioners that joined us today to give you some real-life examples of why these two programs being allowed to continue to work in tandem is really critical for landowners across the state of Michigan. Thank you, Ms. Park. Colleagues, we could call Ms. Park back at the end if questions aren't answered or do you have questions now? All right, thank you. Next, we have Haley Stichman, Community Development Coordinator from Kent County, along with Danny Heffron. Thank you very much for coming to testify, and you may start as soon as you are ready. Yes, thank you. Good morning, Senators, and I thank you for the opportunity to speak on Senate Bills 685 through 690. As the chair stated, my name is Haley Stichman. I'm here along with Denny Heffron, a West Michigan farmer and chair of the Kent County Agricultural Preservation Board. I'll briefly share background on our farmland preservation efforts before turning it over

over to Mr. Heffron to speak to the on-the-ground impact. So farmland preservation has been a longstanding priority for Kent County. Development pressures and diminishing margins for agriculture production threatens the economic vitality of West Michigan and the rural character of our communities. We know from the USDA's 2022 Census of Agriculture, farming in the United States has experienced a gradual decline over the last past 25 years. Kent County has not been immune to this trend. Our county has experienced an 8% reduction in the number of farm operations and has seen the total number of acres under agricultural production reduced by 23%, outpacing the national trend. These trends underscore the importance of ensuring that farmland preservation tools are accessible to our landowners. Kent County's purchase of development rights, or PDR program, has been in place since 2002 when the Kent County Board of Commissioners adopted its first farmland development rights ordinance. Since then, the county has preserved approximately 3,000 acres through permanent preservation easements. It is not uncommon for properties to be enrolled in the Michigan Farmland and Open Space Program, commonly referred to as PA-116, when farmers apply to participate in the Kent County's PDR program. After decades of working seamlessly together, we've witnessed farmers who own land that has been preserved under Kent County's PDR program with easements that are not held by MDARD and enrolled in PA-116 being denied crucial tax benefits. Losing access to PA-116 tax credits jeopardizes the profitability of farms, particularly smaller family farms. This development also jeopardizes local programs as farmers may become skeptical of hidden impacts to permanently preserving their farms. To maintain the strength of both programs, it's critical that local PDR efforts and the PA-116 continue to work in tandem. Senate Bills 685 and 690 offer a path to restore that alignment and ensure farmers aren't penalized for participating in local preservation efforts. Thank you again for your time and consideration. I'll now turn it over to Mr. Heffron to share more about the impact on farmers directly. My name is Benny Heffron. I'm from Kent County. Our family farms in Kent County. This cannot be seen. It's a hard worker. Good morning. The House Committee on Government Operations will come to order. Mr. Clerk, would you please call the roll? Chair Bagul. Here. This morning, we're going to be hearing some testimony from Representative Brad Slaw. Representative? Oh, excuse me. Okay, we're going to have Representative McFaul approve the minutes from October 30th without objection. So ordered. Good morning, Representative. Representative's bill this morning is going to permit a wider variety of investment options for local governments. Is that correct? That is correct. Okay, we'll proceed when you're ready, sir. Thank you. So thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the subcommittee for giving me a few minutes to talk to you about this this morning. With me, I have John Glubinski from the Grand Rapids, who is the Grand Rapids City Treasurer, and he's going to provide more specifics and more details. I'm the top level stuff. He knows all the ins and outs. Under current Michigan law, local units of government are able to invest tax dollars in multiple kinds of investments. However, the investments that are allowed are mainly limited to U.S. bonds, investments backed by the state or local governments, bank savings accounts, bank CDs, that kind of thing, which all have typically a fairly low interest rate and therefore return. And so this legislation would allow us to have a little broader investment options, but those options would still require that they be very safe and wisely limited. When a local unit of government choose to invest public funds, they would continue to do so by resolution, ensuring that there's public transparency. It would also have provided approval policy to the Department of Treasury the way it's structured right now. And they would do that on an annual basis, ensuring there are sound investment decisions and additional transparency. John is going to help provide some additional details, and then we'd be happy to answer questions. And we believe there's probably some things that need to continue to be tweaked in this bill, but it needs to come before you to make sure that we're moving in the right direction. Okay, sounds good. Good morning, Chair Bogle and other committee members. And first of all, thank you, Representative Slaw, for being a fine member of Ottawa County for such a long time and helping us navigate. This bill is actually coming forward to you because we were looking at the fact that we ran through the COVID crisis where interest rates were held down to 0 to 0.25 percent for the longest period of time. A lot of times what we're finding is we were unable to find investments at the levels that we needed. And so we typically were structured as being in an area where we needed to focus on how can we get our reserve funds invested wisely to earn an appropriate rate of return and have the safety and security, which is our highest priority because we focus on safety, liquidity, and yield in that order. And what we're doing is looking at Public Act 20 as being more restrictive than what it should be. We actually went out and did a research study with finding 33 states that had different policies that would still have that safety and security for us, and we were looking to make those changes. So in this type of legislation, we're looking to spell out something that was very hard for us. It says agencies and instrumentalities of the United States. What is that? And so we actually were defining that. So through legal opinion over the years, we were able to define that. We would like to be able to go out and do deposits in other states. Right now we're restricted to just Michigan. As an example, Huntington Bank has to show me a rate in Michigan, but there might be a better rate in Ohio. That shouldn't exist. We should be able to go get certificates of deposits in other states that are also insured federally. We're also looking at corporate bonds. We already

investing commercial paper, which is unsecured corporate debt. Corporate bonds are higher on the chain that if there is a default, we would actually rank higher in collecting our funds first. Corporate bonds have a very, very low default rate. They are also limited, and we purposely put in guardrails that it can't be more than a five-year investment. You also have to work with specific qualified individuals, and you have to be a large institutional buyer called a quib. So organizations like Grand Rapids, where we have $700 million in reserves, we would qualify. You have to have over $100 million to do that, but you have to work with professionals in the industry. We also want to look at municipal bonds outside of Michigan. We prefer Michigan bonds when they're issued and if they're federally taxable. Right now, we go out and we see Macomb County bonds, and we want $10 million of those bonds, and we bid for those bonds. They're oversubscribed sometimes five to 10 times more than the quantity being offered, and so we're prorated. John, you were just awarded $2 million out of the $10 million you wanted to get. So then we're stuck in a position where we have to find another investment for those $8 million, but it comes back to us and sits in a bank account until we can find other investments. So we would actually like to have the ability to go out and get bonds in other municipals across the country. For example, I have Michigan State and University of Michigan bonds. Why can't I go get University of Indiana or Ohio State? No offense, Ohio State bonds, but those are our primary institutions that we want access to when we don't have the ability to find the investments in Michigan. Another one is that we really want to make sure that with all of these items, read into the bill is the safeguards, are the safeguards we put in place. They have to be the highest two levels ratings of investment structure because we do not want anyone going outside of this type of policy and investing in something that they shouldn't. To give you an idea of a financial impact, if I took $500 million of Grand Rapids reserve funds, if I only got an extra 25 basis points or 0.25%, that means we'd get another $1.25 million of interest earnings a year. Now, I also took this from my friends at Michigan Class and I look at their portfolio because they're the large local government investment pool in the state of Michigan. They have 950 municipal and authority participants with over almost $7 billion of assets under management. If they were to actually take advantage of this as well, that would be another $17.25 million of interest earnings that goes back to these 950 participants. We've had a very, very collaborative process. I never shied away from having a conversation over the past four and a half years and that's when it started was right around 2019, 2020. We've brought this to the Michigan Department of Treasury, Michigan Municipal Treasurers Association, Michigan Association of County Treasurers, Michigan Township Association, the Michigan Municipal League, Michigan Government Finance Officers, Michigan School Business Officials, and then the various financial institutions, brokers, dealers that we work with to ask for their input on this type of course. Does this make sense and is this secure enough to move forward? So this has been a very, very collaborative effort and I appreciate the time in front of the committee today to talk about this and I'm happy to be here to answer any questions that you may have. Thank you for that testimony. Maybe I missed it, but what body of people in a municipality would be reviewing those potential investments and what are their qualifications? So for the City of Grand Rapids structure, with our manager council form of government, I actually bring an investment policy to them every time we make a change. They have to read through my investment policy and see what those are. And so we talk to our commissioner about it. It has to be approved through the fiscal committee and then approved by the city commission for the guidelines of our investment policy. Every two weeks, I provide a treasurer's report to the city commission and it lists every one of our investments that we have. And so just the other day, November 1st, I went through the 132 coupon payments we had from all the Michigan municipalities for the bonds we hold. All of that is public knowledge for them to look through and review. And we also go through an audit every year that our auditors review our investment policy as well as that we're in compliance. Okay. It sounds like there's a lot of experience at Grand Rapids. What about a village? Is this something that obviously could potentially happen at a village level, but they're probably less likely to do these investments or they are? Or where would they find qualified individuals to coach them on what investments they should be making? A lot of those individuals are already part of Michigan Class. So they're already participating in a pool. What the local village or township would be doing would be having an investment policy also that they have to create under Public Act 20. They're supposed to all have an investment policy under Public Act 20. They can't go above those guidelines. So I would envision a smaller village or township is going to say, all we want to do is municipal bonds in the state of Michigan. Our bank accounts are certificates of deposits, and that's all we want to structure. So the local unit can structure how restrictive they wish to be. They just can't go above Public Act 20. And in all the education that we do, we talk to people about not going outside of what you know. And so we provide a lot of training through the Michigan Municipal Treasurers Association and through our other organizations to qualify people to get a certified public funds investment manager type training that's available to everyone. And definitely with the different people that are out there, your banks, your investment managers, parties like Michigan Class, and your professional network, we talk about this all the time. We don't want to see anyone get into a position where they should not be. You know, at a time like this, I would not advise any municipality to go into callable bonds 100%. That just isn't right. You're too stuck. And so it's having this network of professional development and also communication back and forth that we offer our assistance to have those communications. Thank you. Under this proposal, would Bitcoin be? Not at all. Not at all. Anything that's cryptocurrency is 100% prevented. No assets like gold, silver, things are commodities. That's all restricted by Public Act 20 already. Okay. All right. Representative VanderWaal. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank both of you for bringing this forward. And just to touch a little bit deeper with the question that was asked by the chair, when we get into some of our smaller communities, a lot of them have a part-time treasurer. And I understand some of the safety measures that you say are put in place, but a part-time treasurer, a lot of times they have a board or a council that is also part-time. I guess I'd worry about, in some cases, them being taken advantage on what they're talked into investing, et cetera. So that's kind of a little bit further of an answer on that. And then to finish up, there's several ratings. I believe there's AA and then there's higher. And I see in the bill it states a rating of A or better. And I guess my concern is if we lower it to A, I mean, if we went to the top couple tiers, I think in most cases they're pretty secure and there's little chance of failure. But when you start getting down in the lower, I guess I'd like your solution or your comments on that if you could help me out. Sure. And I'll start with your last point with the level A type of investment versus higher. The level A relates to corporate bonds and corporate debt. And so we're actually using qualified advisors. The level A has less, if I remember right, less than a 0.1% failure rate. So the default rate is very low. But in that portion of the process, you're also working with other professionals to make sure that you're placing your money in the right thing that's sound. We can always ask for default risk on a specific type of security. And then again, I'm also going to make a different choice too because I'm keeping my eyes to the market as to whether that company is one I really want to place my money in or do I want to place it in something like Caterpillar that's really strong for us in the past or Johnson & Johnson, other ones that are there. It also helps me navigate some of the political minefields if that company is somehow connected to the opioid crisis or something else. I can move my monies to different secure investment. When it comes

to your smaller part-time treasurers and part-time councils, we would never want them to go into something they shouldn't. Again, I think that with a part-time treasurer and council, they're more wanting to see their money in their local bank, their local credit union, the certificates deposit in their community, as opposed to going outright and looking to purchase a Michigan municipal bond. A lot of us are encouraging them that they want to go that route. They should be contacting Michigan Class and starting off in a local government investment pool to then gain the knowledge before they try to broaden their policy to such a level to do even further investing. And so that's why we're trying to get out to everybody. We want you to walk with us, talk to us, talk to the folks that are experienced. Start with your county. If I'm a local village or township, I should be having that conversation with my county treasurer as well. They're a great resource to help direct you in different areas and to get resources to you. We never want to see anyone take a leap out of faith that, oh, invest in this real estate investment company when your chance of losing money could be far greater than anything else we have. Representative Fall. Thank you, Chair. And thank you for bringing this forward. I have two questions. One, how many other states are doing something similar? My other question was do we know why in the original legislation that the restrictions were there? Was there a reason for that? Most definitely. There were misdeeds done in several levels, and so when that happens, we clamp on the security and say we don't want our public tax dollars to be at risk. They were making investments that were very speculative in nature. And so, again, when we start to see that and we start to see our population impacted by bad investments, we're going to slap on as tight as we possibly can to make it very restrictive. That worked very well. But, again, now we're talking about 1943 as opposed to 2025. And so different investments have changed. Our talents have changed. The availability of information has changed. We can go out and check broker licenses to see if people work are valid or not or they've had run-ins with FINRA or the SEC for the work that they do. We talk now. But we really want to go into this looking at we've done really well as a group of treasurers across the state of Michigan to not get into any trouble. We talk about it often. But really we want to continue our path to say, look, we also need to think of what's coming in the future. We'd like to build out our portfolios a little bit longer so that we don't get caught into a Fed pushing the rate down to 0 to 0.25%. But we also need to understand that we have a fiduciary responsibility to every one of our taxpayers in each one of our municipalities to do our best possible job. And this is what we're talking to do, trying to do, is do our best possible job to earn a little bit higher interest rate and secure investments and protecting all the taxpayer dollars. Okay, not seeing any further questions. May I offer one thing? Late yesterday we did get the legislative analysis of this bill. I do want to point out two things that is definitely put in here, and that is the protections, especially when we look at corporate debt. The second bullet point under new authorized investments, it specifically says that you have to be a qualified institutional buyer when it comes to the corporate debt. You have to have $100 million of assets under management in order to do that. So if I were to take a shot in the dark guess, 25 to 40 municipalities might qualify for that. But those are also the people that are already doing advanced investments like the Oakland County Investment Pool. Kent County Investment Pool could take part in that. And then your larger municipalities. I think that's very important to note. And the final one is at the very back. I went right to the very – what is the fiscal impact? The first statement is that there is no direct fiscal impact on state or local government. What this is is just us asking for more tools in our toolbox to do a better job in our communities. Okay. Thank you. Makes sense to me, especially on the low-risk investments and things like that. So I appreciate you coming in and giving testimony today. Thank you very much. Thank you so very much. Okay, we do have a card to read in, reference 4757. Not wanting to speak in support of the bill is Jeff Anderson of the Michigan Class Local Government Investment Pool. Okay, next we'll be hearing testimony on House Bills 4085 and 4087. I believe our majority floor leader, Representative Brian Posthumus, is here to speak in reference to those bills, which will allow cryptocurrency mining in areas that are zoned industrial and establish regulation for a strategic Bitcoin reserve. Representative, whenever you're ready. All right, Mr. Chair, committee members, thank you very much for having me. Actually, I feel like I've been here a lot lately. I think I was here last week. So, again, I appreciate it. I'm going to talk a little bit first from more of a 50,000-foot vantage point on this, and then I'll get into some of the specifics on these bills before I turn it over to some industry experts. So, first of all, 50,000-foot view. Why crypto? Why are we talking about this? So I will start by saying I believe, I fundamentally believe that sometime in the near future, whether that's five years from now, 10 years from now, or 20 years from now, digital assets and cryptocurrency will be the foundation of the financial world. And there's a lot of reasons for that. One reason is the speed of transactions, the overall security. Cryptocurrency and digital assets are far more secure than any other currency that we have in existence today. And so for those reasons, along with many others, it will be the foundation of our financial future. Unfortunately, the entire framework of policy in the state of Michigan is completely silent when it comes to the topic of cryptocurrency or digital assets. And too often in government, when there are advancements in technology or changes in technology, government's always playing catch-up. The legislative process falls way behind the technological advancement, and as a result, there's always, when you're trying to advance policies, there are vested interests that have created a fiefdom or an area of the market that they're always trying to protect and unduly influences the policies that are trying to be made and not necessarily for the best situation for the people. And so my hope is that we can put together at least the starting point for framework in a policy conversation surrounding cryptocurrency. Actually, I think there's maybe seven or eight bills up before different committees today surrounding cryptocurrency and digital assets, starting this process, starting to do this, making sure that our laws are no longer silent on something as important and critical to our future as cryptocurrency. On top of that, because this is a new and developing technology that we have, Michigan has the opportunity to be a leader in our country when it comes to cryptocurrency. We have that opportunity before us, but we have to lay the groundwork in order to do that. So the two bills that we're talking about today, we have the crypto strategic reserve. We'll start with that. Several states around the country are looking at enacting similar policies. I believe three states have already signed into law policies that will create a crypto strategic reserve. Essentially what this does is it allows the state

to have a fund that allows them to hold the best-performing asset over the last decade, and it gives the state the option to do that. It doesn't require the state to do that. It gives the option to do that. So that's the idea with the strategic reserve. And frankly, the authority to do that is already, because the law is silent, the argument could be made that the authority is already there to do it. So what this also does, while I think it is a good idea, I also think it's probably a good idea that we build some guardrails on it, because right now, there are none. And so the guardrails that we're talking about to ensure that we're protecting the taxpayers of Michigan, only a certain percentage of, only a certain amount of money can be held in the crypto reserve. So we're putting a cap on it. Also, only certain cryptocurrencies can be held in that. Right now, theoretically, I don't know if any of you all are familiar with the Haktoa coin or the Dogecoin or the Trump coin or any other random meme coin that's out there. Theoretically, right now, the state could invest its resources in any of those. I don't think that's a good idea. I believe that we need to have guardrails that ensure longevity of the cryptocurrency, that ensure its proven track record by setting a market cap floor, things of that nature. Also, only cryptocurrencies that are regulated by the federal government, the SEC, things of that nature. And so that's why we built those guardrails. For example, in order for the state to hold a cryptocurrency in the reserve, it has to be federally regulated, meaning, and it has to be an exchange-traded fund. So the SEC is regulating it. It has to have a certain track record of performance. By that, we say it has to have a minimum market cap of $250 billion. Right now, there are only two cryptocurrencies in existence out of the probably millions of coins that have been created that meet that threshold. Those are Bitcoin and Ethereum. And so we wanted to make sure that we're building the guardrails. So that's the pension fund. I'm sorry, that's the strategic fund. Now, on the other bill that we're talking about, and again, we're going to have other people testifying on this, but just real quick on it, we want to make sure that Michigan is a leader in the enterprise of cryptocurrency, in the industry, making it a hospitable environment for cryptocurrency miners and that sort of dynamic. So we wanted to make sure that industrially zoned areas in the state of Michigan cannot regulate cryptocurrency more heavily than they do any other industry. So we want to make sure it's an even playing field for cryptocurrency miners as it is for any other industry. So those are the main talking points from a 50,000-foot view. With that, I'll take any questions before we turn it over to some of the experts on this. Thank you, Representative. If I understand correctly, the state does not currently have any investment in cryptocurrency, correct? The state does not currently have any investment of tax dollars in it. The state is, however, one of the largest, the state pension fund, at the discretion of the state, is one of the largest holders of Ethereum in the world. That's right, and because there's no thing to prohibit that, they're able to do that. Correct. Has the Treasurer expressed any interest in possibly taking advantage of this?
