So it's very similar, there's very similar bills. We've been in communication back and forth with the department and with the Treasurer, working with them to figure out, all right, what is the best way to go forward? Our Treasury Department is very interested and involved in cryptocurrency and they understand that dynamic. So right now they are, my understanding is they're neutral on this bill specifically, but they're very interested in how that policy shapes up and we're working very closely with them. Okay, thank you. I don't see any questions for you. Okay, thank you. Looks like we have a couple other people here who'd like to provide some information in reference to these bills. Gentlemen, if you want to make your way up to the table together, first we have Tom McCarthy of Satoshi Action and we have Kevin Wysocki of Anchorage Digital. Did I pronounce your names correctly? Okay. Whoever'd like to go first, go ahead and proceed. Chairman and other members of the committee, thank you for holding this hearing today and for inviting me to testify. My name is Kevin Wysocki and I'm the head of policy at Anchorage Digital, institutional crypto platform that is home to Anchorage Digital Bank, America's first and only federally regulated digital asset bank. The bank is regulated by the United States Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. It provides secure digital asset custody related services such as settlement and staking and serves over 1,000 institutional clients. Today, the bank safeguards tens of billions of dollars in digital assets for investors, asset managers, and sovereign wealth funds. Our bank has spent tens of millions of dollars to comply with all applicable laws, including the Bank Secrecy Act. In addition to our bank custody services, Anchorage Digital also provides self-custody solutions, a self-custody solution called Porto. At Anchorage Digital, security is in our DNA. We were founded by two security engineers in 2017. We use military-grade encryption to protect and secure customers' digital assets. Our bank custody technology keeps clients' cryptographic keys offline using air-gapped hardware security modules. Clients retain secure access to move assets once users are authenticated and a quorum-based organizational approvals are met. Assets are held in segregated accounts and are never commingled or rehypothecated. Our self-custody solution, Porto, is powered by the same core hardware security module technology and gives clients the ability to secure and decrypt their private keys. I'm pleased to be here today to talk about House Bill 4087. If enacted, this legislation would effectively create two Michigan strategic crypto reserves composed of either spot cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin or Ether or exchange-traded products like a Bitcoin ETF. Specifically, this important legislation would authorize the state treasurer to invest up to 10% of available funds in the state's general fund and the counter-cyclical budget and economic stabilization fund. The bill provides two options for the custody of spot digital assets, something that is called a secure custody solution, which is a self-custody solution, or a qualified custodian, such as a bank. The custody provisions of this bill are of particular importance because cryptocurrencies are bearer assets. Functionally, this means that if the assets are stolen or misappropriated, they are very difficult to claw back, much like lost or stolen cash. The bill allows the treasurer to rely on regulated qualified custodians to provide custody, though additional due diligence will be necessary because not all qualified custodians have equivalent client protections. The bill also ensures that the secure custody solution provision is technology-neutral, allowing for advancements in self-custody over time. For additional context, Michigan is not alone in considering strategic crypto reserve legislation. New Hampshire, Arizona, and Texas have already enacted similar legislation into law, and at the federal level, the president has signed an executive order to establish both a strategic Bitcoin reserve and a U.S. digital asset stockpile. Thank you again for inviting me today, and I look forward to answering any of your questions. I don't see any questions for you. Go ahead and proceed. Thank you, Mr. Chair and the Government Operations Committee. I appreciate the opportunity to testify today in support of House Bill 4085 and 4087, which together advance Michigan's leadership in digital asset innovation by streamlining zoning for mining operations and integrating state finances with high-quality digital asset investments. My name is Thomas McCarthy, and I work at Satoshi Action Fund. We are a consumer and innovation-focused nonprofit organization dedicated to promoting education and advocacy for Bitcoin and digital assets at the state and federal level. Bitcoin and digital assets represent the next frontier of financial and technological innovation. Digital assets have grown from a niche experiment to a multi-trillion-dollar industry that offers new economic opportunities. Satoshi Action Fund strongly supports HB 4085 and 4087 because they protect users of Bitcoin and blockchain technology from discriminatory treatment, and this allows Michigan to attract investment and build a resilient economy powered by technological innovation. Focusing first on HB 4085, this bill, which has passed into law in multiple states, amends Michigan's Zoning Enabling Act by codifying digital asset mining as permitted use in industrial zones. Digital asset mining involves using electricity to power computers that secures the Bitcoin blockchain

verifying transactions and maintaining network integrity. Bitcoin mining can act as a flexible load by providing interruptible demand that enables rapid curtailment to reduce consumption during shortages. In simple terms, this enhances grid stability and strengthens resiliency by keeping an equilibrium between supply and demand. I encourage this committee to do its own research and find another large consumer of power that has this unique trait. The simple answer is that there currently is none, and Bitcoin mining is the most efficient tool to balance an electrical grid. Bitcoin mining also advances clean energy by using stranded and underutilized renewable energy while transmission lines remain stagnant. Bitcoin mining solves the chicken and egg problem found in renewables by acting as an energy buyer of last resort. This energy buyer can be turned on and off 24-7, 365. Once again, there is no greater tool that can act as a customer of energy than Bitcoin. And integrating Bitcoin mining with renewable energy can accelerate the transition to clean energy by making renewable infrastructure projects economically viable. Let me be absolutely clear. This bill does not ask for special treatment for digital asset businesses. Instead, all this bill does is ensure that all data centers in industrial zones are treated equally. HB 485 prohibits discriminatory restrictions on digital asset mining. Passing this bill will position Michigan to compete with other states where digital asset mining has driven billions in economic activity. Now I'm shifting my attention to HB 487, which has passed into law in three states. This legislation authorizes but does not direct the state treasurer to invest up to 10% of the General and Economic Stabilization Fund into high-quality digital assets such as Bitcoin. Since 2018 alone, the dollar has lost 25% of its purchasing power. With only a 3% allocation into Bitcoin, Michigan could have combated 100% of the loss of purchasing power in its state funds. Allocating into Bitcoin is a prudent method for protecting taxpayer funds. HB 487 emphasizes security by requiring digital assets to be held directly by the treasurer through qualified custodians or SEC-approved products that have multi-party governance and audits to mitigate risks. By integrating digital assets into Michigan state finances, HB 487 modernizes Michigan's economic competitiveness by updating its current outdated investment portfolio to the 21st century. In conclusion, HB 485 and 487 complement each other perfectly. One protects energy infrastructure, the other empowers Michigan to protect taxpayer funds. Passing both bills will drive growth, technological advancement, fiscal strength, and place Michigan on the map as a hub for Bitcoin and blockchain technology. I urge this committee to pass both bills. Thank you for your consideration and I'm happy to answer any of your questions. Okay, thanks. Obviously this is a new proposal and I'm assuming that both of your companies would stand to benefit somehow and I'm just curious how does yours find these sites for people? So I'll speak from the Satoshi Action Fund. Once again, we are a C4 nonprofit, so we actually advocate on behalf of Bitcoin users. We want to have users to be able to interact with this technology and I'll let Kevin. Yeah, Anchorage Digital Bank is a custodian, right? We're the only one regulated at the federal level. We hold tens of billions of dollars in digital assets for institutional clients like governments, large financial institutions. So yes, a number of states are looking at legislation like this and we would be a provider of custody services and related services like actually buying the digital assets. Okay, are you in a position to say what other occupations or opportunities might present other people if this was to occur in Michigan? I can touch on the Bitcoin mining aspect. So once again, I think the unique part about Bitcoin mining is often it's almost never found in cities. It's often in rural areas and it's not often where you can find in a rural area high paying tech jobs. I personally know from people who have been able to work at Bitcoin mining companies in Texas where in their community there's almost no jobs that pay as good as opportunities in the Bitcoin mining space. And so they've been thrilled to join. So for one, I'd say Bitcoin mining offers economic opportunities in rural areas where there's really no other high paying tech jobs in the area. Beyond that, I think one of the other things that's very interesting is that, you know, this industry is very remote. So developers and people will go to places where they feel that they're not going to be ostracized. I know many, many people in this industry were actually considering moving overseas because they felt fear that they were going to be put in prison simply for developing software code. Fortunately, now there's no fear to move overseas, but now it's a matter of states competing with each other to set up friendly jurisdictions to attract entrepreneurs to build businesses. I think like the majority leader, floor leader was saying prior to us coming up to the podium, digital assets and blockchains are fundamentally changing the current financial system. We're seeing right now the adoption of stable coins at a high level throughout the system. The federal government just passed the Genius Act, right? That'll go into effect in January of 2027, which enhances payments. So some of the advantages of blockchains are you have instant settlement right now on a lot of financial transactions. Maybe Venmo, maybe PayPal, maybe another payment provider fronts that money, but the money that you paid into it doesn't actually get to the person you're paying right away. It also affects small businesses, right? Retailers, they can be paying like something like 2% to 3% on transactions, blockchains, whether it's like using a token like a stable coin or some of the other cryptocurrencies that are out there. You can put those margins down to near zero. And again, you get that instantaneous settlement. The other thing is these markets have the ability to be open 365 and 24 hours a day, right? Which right now sometimes there are limits on some of these markets. So there are a number of advantages. Also, I'll bring this up. I know a lot of people are concerned about national security and blockchains and things like that. Well, one of the beautiful things about the blockchain is actually it's pseudo anonymous. You can actually watch illicit activity more easily and kind of build together afterwards like what had happened and track that. So it actually can enhance the ability to track illicit funds and stop it. So there are a lot of advantages with this. Again, I think you and the industry are in the early innings, but now is the moment to really consider these bills, especially these strategic crypto bills. Okay, thank you. Representative Fitzgerald. Thank you very much. Thank you gentlemen for being here today. I don't know if it's yourselves or the representative who might be best to consider this question. You know, recognizing that reading about cryptocurrencies of any type, I understand that Bitcoin and Ethereum have been around for much longer and have that market cap of, I think it goes $250 billion, with a B, $250 billion. Understanding that there is significant investment in those spaces. I think that there are still financial experts who would call these inherently volatile or financially hazardous. And so I'm concerned about the potential of 10% of the state's liquidity to be able to be put into such a, I don't want to say unregulated, but unexplored marketplace for state funds. So thank you so much for that question. And I appreciate your intriguing appetite to explore this further. So it hasn't started yet. Now I understand there's concerns in terms of volatility. People always bring up volatility as a point of concern. consistently makes lower highs. So every year consistently its lowest price point keeps going up and up and up throughout the year. So there's really only been one year that made a lower low compared to the previous year. So I would say instead of focusing on the short term, focus on the long term. Conversely, if you were to hold dollars, yes, you're going to in the short term, you're not going to be facing volatility, but you are guaranteed to lose value in the long term. And that's what we're trying to do is focus on the long term and protect Michigan's taxpayer funds to grow in the long term. I don't know if there's anything else you want to add. Yeah. Rep. Fitzgerald, I think you bring up an important point. All assets have risks associated with them, right? I think one of the panelists earlier that was up here was talking about interest rate risk, right? And planning for the long term. We saw in 2023, three banks fail and a number of other banks struggle in this country because they didn't anticipate interest rates going up. The Federal Reserve actually had to create a fund to unload those assets from these banks, right? So what's generally perceived as the most safe asset in the world, US treasuries, indeed was a very risky asset at that time. So I think it's beneficial for the treasurer to have options, whether they're traditional assets or whether these new crypto assets for the people of Michigan to potentially invest in. Yeah. And sorry, one last thing I forgot to add. To your concern about the 10% cap, you know, I personally would advocate, you know, at least in the beginning, you know, maybe do a 1% and then if 1% makes sense and the state treasurer and all stakeholders are happy, bumping up to 3%. But, you know, really all this bill does is it doesn't mandate it has to be purchased up to 10%. That's just the cap. But I can tell you just me personally, I think a 1% to 3% allocation would be prudent in the short term. And then as the years go on, that can change. But that's just my personal opinion. Okay. Thank you, gentlemen. Appreciate it. Thanks for your testimony. Okay, next we're going to hear from Judy Allen of the Michigan Township Association wishing to speak in opposition of the bill. Thank you, Mr. Chair and members of the committee. My name is Judy Allen. I'm Director of Government Relations for Michigan Townships Association. This is a preemption of local authority and it proposes to create a one-size-fits-all approach for one specific land use. Local units, when we create our zoning ordinances, we create standards that we have to apply those standards across the board. If an application comes in and it meets those standards, we have to grant that special land use permit. A local unit can create different standards within a specific industrial zone. For example, several zoning ordinances for industrial, you might have heavy and light. You might have light manufacturing, regular manufacturing, and heavy manufacturing. The simplest is the light industrial, heavy industrial, but you can have, we have some of our municipalities that have maybe four or five different types of industrial zones in their industrial zoning ordinances. Again, I can't stress enough that we cannot treat them differently than other properties located within that specific area. If they meet the standards, we have to approve. There are some also some additional concerns we have with bill as introduced in addition to this creates one size fits all is that in subsection one, there's use, term use, special land use or conditional use. We're uncertain what conditional use means. Old laws used to have that in, but now we don't refer to it as conditional use. So we're uncertain what that means. Subsection two specifically says a local unit cannot specify standards or excuse me, we're saying we cannot specify standards that are different. And again, I go back to that example because they specifically in subsection two refer to decibels. So if you have business A and business B and business C located in that specific industrial zone and there's decibel levels, that would be applicable to all of them. We can't pick and choose what that decibel level is going to be for that specific zoned area. We would have that in that zoning ordinance. Another concern with subsection two is it is not limited to industrial zones. For example, it simply states that, actually, I'm going to get the bill out to make sure I'm saying it correctly. It states the specific limit on decibels generated from digital mining other than any applicable limits set for sound pollution that apply to industrial zones. It doesn't say it's limited to industrial zones. Basically, it's saying whatever your decibels would be here, if you want it to locate one of these operations in a residential or agricultural, your decibel levels would have to be applicable from that industrial zone. So that creates a very, very big difference. I will say with subsection three, that's what we're required to do under the law. I mean, we are required to treat businesses the same. This just limits it to two specific types of industrial uses. So again, I'll just wrap up and say with a special land use, there's a process in place. You review that application and what they're doing. You look at, and again, these businesses are different, whether it's a data center or Bitcoin, and those are very similar. But even what they do within that building, do they cool with, you know, do they use air cooling, air cooling with fans? Do they use the water cooling system? And so I just say that, you know, we have to review that application. We have to review what they're doing at that location. And we also, when you have a special land use permit, we have a public hearing. Under this bill, you would eliminate that transparency. You would eliminate that public hearing process. This just says it's a permitted use. I go to that local unit and they have to do this. It does not give the public any input on what is coming into their community, and they don't know about it. So we're just asking. We don't think this bill is needed under the zoning law currently in terms of treating things differently. Under Section 207, you have to allow a specific land use within your jurisdiction unless you can indicate that it's deemed unnecessary. So we don't think this is needed. Again, if you have an industrial zone and you have the standards in place, it's going to apply to everybody who applies for a special land use permit within that zone. I'm happy to answer any questions. Okay. Thank you, Mrs. Allen. Thank you. Appreciate your testimony today. Okay. I do have a couple cards to read in. Committee will please come to order. The chair recognizes Representative Schuette. Thank you, Chairman Aragon. You wield the gavel very well there. House Bill 5127, and I appreciate the opportunity to testify in front of the Rules Committee today. House Bill 5127 is an effort to cut red tape to expand access to child care in Michigan while protecting adjoining businesses in operations in mixed-use facilities. So across the state of Michigan, from Bay City to Battle Creek, it is not uncommon that a child care facility is located within a multiple occupancy building. By being clear that the department cannot regulate areas within the building not part of or used by the center, we will ensure that other occupants' operations are not impacted. This will in turn expand access to child care in our state by allowing more centers to occupy spaces in a mixed-use facility without the current barrier of entry caused by departmental overreach. House Bill 5127 would limit the department's ability to regulate child care facilities to exclusively to apply to the child care facility. And joining me today to testify will be Jacob Manning from the Small Business Association of Michigan, who can speak more to how this bill will help provide more child care access throughout the state. Thank you to Chair Schutte and members of the committee for the opportunity to come speak today. My name is Jacob Manning and I am the Advocacy and Policy Manager for the Small Business Association of Michigan, also known as SBAM. With more than 33,000 members across all of Michigan's 83 counties, SBAM is the largest state-based organization of small businesses anywhere in the country. We are here today to express our support for House Bill 5127. This is a bill that would clarify Michigan's Department of Lifelong Education Advancement and Potential, or MyLEAP, and clarify that they can regulate the licensed child care space itself, but not unrelated tenants of multi-use buildings or unrelated areas of child care centers. Here at SBAM, we are engaged in the child care conversation in multiple ways. We hear consistently from our non-provider members that child care remains one of the leading obstacles in workforce shortages and employee retentions across the state. We also recognize that child care is a sector that is primarily dominated by small business providers, many of whom are our members. In fact, we work directly with providers through our Nurture Benefit Program, which is a partnership with MyLEAP to help providers offer competitive benefit packages for their employees. We know that there's no single silver bullet fix that will automatically solve our state's child care shortages overnight, but that being said, we hear from our providers that unnecessary or unclear regulations are one of the key inhibitors for their growth, success, and expansion opportunities. House Bill 5127 takes a meaningful and practical step towards improving our regulatory framework. The bill ensures that providers can focus their attention to the licensed child care space where children are actually present, rather than devoting time and resources to managing unrelated areas of a building, oftentimes outside of their own control. I want to emphasize that this

bill does not weaken health and safety protections, my leap plays an essential role in the process of inspections and regulations for child care facilities, and they are among some of our most valued partners at SBAM. The agency has dedicated a significant effort to alleviate the burdens on providers wherever practical, but every provider will tell you that the most important part of their work is ensuring the health and safety of their kids. This bill does not strip away any of the agency's ability to do their job, but helps ensure that the main thing stays the main thing. And it ensures that providers are not penalized for aspects of their center that are entirely unrelated to what should be regulated. So with that, I want to thank Representative Schutte for introducing this bill, along with the vast portfolio of bills that have been introduced this term as a part of the Red Tape Reduction Effort. We urge your support of House Bill 5127. Thank you for your time and consideration. I'd be happy to answer any questions you may have. Great. Thank you both. Real quick, how many members do you think of SBAM would this affect? I don't have an exact number of how many of our members are child care providers. That is probably something that I could get for you and follow up. Cool. Thank you. Any further questions from the committee? And I just know anecdotally from, in my region, both Greater Midland Community Center and the YMCA in Bay City are two mixed-use facilities that provide child care. This would help them a lot to make sure that they're able to provide the greatest number of parents to have access to child care. Thank you. Questions? Representative Martin. Thank you, Mr. Vice Chair. So more beholden on the child care center to make sure that the building is suitable to do child care, and Laura would still come in and do an inspection, was it annually? Yeah. Upon renewal of license? And upon the renewal of the license. So if there's social counseling for probationaries and so forth that have limits of how close they can be to children on some offender list or I don't know, anything else that has a limit like 1,000 feet, like dispensaries or anything like that, this would all be... Yeah, hazardous protections, like regarding sale of alcohol, sale of, you know, and also restrictions for people being within reach of minors, that's also, those provisions would remain. Hazardous protections. Thanks. Further questions from the committee? Being none, thank you both. Committee will go at ease, call the chair. The committee will come to order. I also want committee members to review written testimony in support from Terry Johnson and Andrea Seacrest from the Greater Midland Community Center. And do we have any other cards on that, Bill? Great. All right. And we'll next be hearing testimony on House Bill 4915. And Representative Maddox will be testifying. Representative, come forward and please begin when you're ready. And now you'll be joined by Dr. Rishi Mahabir from Do No Harm, also testifying in support. I'd like to make a correction to the record. He is not with Do No Harm. He is here independently on his own. Oh, great. Here independently on his own. Thank you very much for the correction. And I believe that this is my fourth time on the fourth floor. I don't get up here very often. Thank you, committee members, for having us here today. This is a great bill to end implicit bias. You know, doctors are some of the greatest people we have in our state, and we need to do everything we can to make it more comfortable for them to do business in our state. And this is something that makes many of them very uncomfortable. When I was doing my research in this bill, I realized that I am very biased. I really hate Marxism and the social division caused by awful policies like this. And so that's my bias, to be honest with you. And I hope you enjoy what the kind doctor has to say today. He's really passionate about this, as are many doctors in your profession. And we're just happy to have him here today so he can tell us about what's really going on with this horrible policy. Thank you. Thank you so much for letting me speak with you in front today. As he had mentioned, I'm representing myself and not an organization. My name is Rishi Mahabir. I'm an osteopathic physician. I've been practicing psychiatry here in Michigan for about the past 17 years. I'm writing this testimony to strongly oppose the continuation of mandatory implicit bias training for health care professionals under the Michigan Public Health Code. Implemented by LARA in 2022, this requirement mandates a one-hour training per year of licensure, totaling three hours over a typical three-year renewal cycle. The proposed intent of implicit bias training is to address the unconscious attitudes and stereotypes among health care professionals that can influence perceptions, actions, and decision-making that may contribute to unequal treatment of individuals based on characteristics such as race, ethnicity, gender, disability, and socioeconomic status. The training aims to educate professionals on recognizing and mitigating biases to promote more equitable treatment and reduce disparities in health care delivery. In June of 2023, I participated in and completed a three-hour live online mandatory implicit bias training for my state license renewal. It became quickly apparent that the intended purpose of the training had missed its mark by a wide margin. The first seconds of the meeting, I pretty much checked out. I was told that I was a racist and that I was biased towards all my patients. It's kind of hard to sit there and to learn something when the first couple seconds of the meeting you're being told that you're a racist and being biased towards all your patients. It's not conducive for learning, in my opinion. The training assumed that I, along with my health care colleagues, are inherently biased and or racist. The training felt more like indoctrination than education. It felt unnatural and forced. The content pushed a social agenda unrelated to medicine, ignoring evidence-based medicine and patient care. In my opinion, implicit bias training is forcibly injecting social agendas into the practice of medicine. Patient outcomes should be the priority, not political or ideological agendas. Instead of fostering understanding, the training reinforces divisions and encourages racial profiling in medicine. It inverts medical judgment and prioritizes ideology over evidence. I firmly believe that implicit bias training is an ineffective, ideologically driven component of the diversity, equity, and inclusion initiative, also known as DEI. It has no place in medicine. The practice of medicine must remain evidence-based. Implicit bias training diverts valuable time from core clinical education, fosters division among providers, and fails to improve patient outcomes. Even three hours is three hours too much, in my opinion. Like poison, even in a small dose, it could be lethal, undermining the scientific foundation and professional autonomy of medicine. Mandating courses and implicit bias training assumes all providers harbor biases that need correction. That, in turn, can breed resentment and undermine trust in the medical community. From a psychiatric perspective, forcing ideological training on individuals risks psychological harm. Participants may resist the top-down mandate that feels accusatory. DEI-driven mandates like implicit bias training erode professional autonomy, compelling physicians to endorse viewpoints that may conflict with their ethical or scientific beliefs, bordering on compelled speech. As a psychiatrist, I treat patients across diverse backgrounds and know that genuine equity comes from individualized care and not rote DEI exercises that treat providers as inherently flawed. Michigan's mandate affecting physicians and other health care professionals exemplifies government overreach into clinical practice, prioritizing political optics over patient welfare. Mandatory

Implicit bias training is a flawed DEI policy masquerading as medical reform. It lacks empirical support, risks harming provider morale, and distracts from true advancements in healthcare. I implore members of the House Rules Committee to advocate for its repeal. Let's return medicine to its foundation, which is science, compassion, and evidence, not ideology. I appreciate your time. More than welcome to take any questions you might have. I just have one quick question, Doctor. How many patients, when we met this morning for the first time, you said you had to reschedule all your patients to be in Lansing today, and you've been here approximately two hours, right? Correct. And you're going to be here another maybe an hour before you get back to your practice. How many patients did you have to, how many patients did you see an hour? I do medication management, so it's three patients per hour. So today, as I said, we scheduled one more patient. So I average about six to seven patients a week. Okay. So we have 22,000 doctors in Michigan, roughly. And if you, I mean, doctor's time is extremely valuable. If anyone's ever been in a hospital, everyone knows how busy they are. And for a doctor, it may not sound much, but when you add up the time spent doing this horrible training, it's roughly 66,000 hours. And that's a lot of patients doctors aren't seeing in 66,000 hours. I just want to point that out to the committee. And what I may add to that is one second of the training, in my opinion, is one second too much. If it was scientifically based, if it was evidence-based, that'd be a different thing. This is not scientifically based. It's not. There is no randomized controlled trial that I know of that shows that implicit bias training is effective. It's not. Randomized controlled trials is the gold standard of evidence-based medicine. And there's no randomized controlled trial that I know of that says implicit bias training is effective. And doctor, you know, this is a directive that was put in place in 2020 for, you know, the hundreds of years of the existence of the medical profession before this. Have we, in the years since it's been implementation, have we noticed any increases in broad quality of care, decreases in cost after implementing this implicit bias training? I have not noticed any positive. You don't see any evidence in the data in the field as somebody who's very familiar with it? I've seen more physicians, more healthcare professionals. Like I said, it starts off as an accusatory premise. It's pushing away physicians. It's pushing away healthcare professionals from the state of Michigan, in my opinion. It is. I think there is obviously a lack of healthcare providers in Michigan. This mandate is just going to make it worse, in my opinion. You know, it's one thing if it's a mandate, it should stand on its merit, in my opinion. If it's effective, it should stand on its merit. It should not be mandated. Thank you. Vice Chair Whitwer. Thanks for being here today. I appreciate it. It sounds like, you know, your first couple of minutes were pretty uncomfortable and offensive to you. And I can tell you that when I first got elected, I went through implicit bias training. I just wanted to experience it. And I can say I felt like I was extremely uncomfortable going through it. And I realized I had biases, much like what you mentioned. And I didn't realize that they were there, and it was pretty eye-opening. And I spent 22 years in healthcare, and I spent probably the first five on the floor in the burn unit. And I spent probably 10 in marketing, understanding the differences between how different ethnicities are treated and how they present, actually, with specific kinds of illnesses and diseases and some more than the other. And I really would like to know, outside of it making us uncomfortable and outside of it offending us, how, A, it is a bad thing for doctors, nurses, healthcare people that deal with people every day, not just the science of it. But when I go to my doctor, my doctor and I talk about my life, too. And they want to talk about how I feel in my life. And could I be depressed from this job? And different things. So I don't understand how, A, it is a bad thing to learn about implicit bias so that you can understand the different people that we deal with on a daily basis, especially in healthcare. It's your most personal relationship you have outside of your own family. And then what evidence do you have that supports that this is pushing doctors away? You're speaking about evidence. What evidence do you have that this is pushing doctors away from the field? The evidence I have is it's anecdotal. So it's not. I'm sure I could get you evidence. If you provide me with your contact information, I could provide you with evidence, data, research. Your first question. We all have, there is racial disparities in medicine. That's a known. That is a given. Yes. But we need to have a more effective treatment for addressing racial disparities. Implicit bias training, there is data after data after data that shows it is not effective. We need to go back to medicine. We need to go back to truth. We need to go back to the foundations of medicine. For example, standardized protocols. That takes out racial biases in treating patients. Standardized protocols, basically, for example, if you have a patient that comes into the ER with chest pain, okay, we're looking at step one, vitals. Step two, what do we, medication regimen, do we need to get them started on? We're now looking at their race. We're now looking at the color of their skin. It's a standardized protocol. There is several randomized controlled trials that show that evidence-based medicine is the only way we could address the racial disparities. There is also the advent of AI technology that's been very effective in removing racial biases in medicine. And, of course, there's also voluntary case reviews where you have a case presented to you in front of a group of other physicians, and you go over what did we do wrong, what did we do right. You're not being forced to sit there and listen to somebody tell you that you have inherent biases. You're looking at the medicine. You're looking at the facts, and that's the way medicine should be, in my opinion. Vice Chair, what were you? Just to follow up, I'm curious because I looked at who supports and who opposes, and I don't see like MSMS supporting it. I don't see any doctors' organizations supporting this. So if there were these evidence-based that this is pushing doctors out, are you planning on getting those big associations of docs if this is so offensive to doctors to do this? And I do see that the nurses are not for it. So just wondering, like, are we going to talk to the doctors about this? Yeah, I would believe so. I would believe so. As, you know, I'm a volunteer of Do No Harm. Now we have over 40,000 members in our organization, and we are all of the like mind that this training has no merit whatsoever. And you had mentioned, you know, other organizations like, for example, the American Medical Association and the Pediatric Association. We're trying to get them on board with us, but you have to remember these are the same organizations that feel that gender transition surgeries on children is okay. So we have a lot of work to do here to get back to medicine. Thank you, Doctor. Representative DeBoer, you have a question? And we have a couple other bills, too, so if we could keep it tight. Yeah, yeah. I appreciate your testimony. It's not easy. Nancy, can you hear Mike, please? Yep, of course. I appreciate you coming here. It's not easy to do. And I know you face a lot of things that go through your own mind after being condemned as you turned on the three-hour presentation. My husband came home from the beginning of the school year, and they had a presentation similar to that. And he was the most depressed I've ever seen him. After the opening for the school year, he loves to teach. He loves children. It doesn't matter what color they are. He loves to make them sing. He loves to bring out the very best in every child, in every concert. He gives his life to helping them understand how to be the best they can be.

And he's taught like 10,000 children. And everyone that comes up to him, admires or whatever, they'll stand and they adopt this posture of having been in his concert and wanting to produce the very best. And their parents would dress them accordingly and fill the auditorium. Thousands of people would come to hear the Christmas celebrations and everything. And it was not about bias. Never about bias. And he came home so hurt by all those accusations and all that pummeling of him psychologically. From a crude... Nancy, we've got 20 minutes. I'm sorry. Thank you. But I appreciate it. And thank you for your testimony, gentlemen. And Nancy, thank you for your support. All right. Next, we will be hearing... Oh, no, we have not wishing to speak, submitting written testimony in opposition, Kaylee Hunt from the Michigan Nurses Association. And submitting written testimony in opposition is the Michigan Dental Hygienist Association. And submitting written testimony in support is Dr. Miceli and Dr. Sarah Anuldo, volunteers with Do No Harm. All right. And now we will be hearing testimony on House Bill 4881 and 4882. Representative Nayer will be testifying. Representative, please begin when you're ready. Sorry. Thank you, Chair and Committee. This is also part of the red tape package of removing bills that are no longer effective here in our state. 4881 and 4882 is a bill package or it removes regulation that is placed upon potato wholesalers and requiring them to have bonds in case of nonpayment to the producers. This act has not been very relevant for several decades now and has little or no effect, especially now that there are federal guidelines in place that do protect the producers for payment. They're far more effective and basically duplicate of this. The potato industry in the state is a $2.5 billion plus business in the industry and a $100,000 bond which is required on wholesalers has very little effect or very little benefit for the producers. Currently, right now, it's managed underneath MDARD. There's less than 10 producers or wholesalers that are involved in the process. Very little relevance to that. And we feel and I feel that these MDARD's resources would be better spent. This has full support of the Michigan Potato Industry Council or Commission. And with that, I ask for your support on 4881 and 4882. I'm open to any questions. Well, thank you, Representative Nair. It is pretty incredible that we still require a license for this and you've mentioned broad stakeholder support including the department and the potatoes council. So this seems like something that is supported both by agency and by the industry. So I appreciate your due diligence. And with regards to the Agriculture Committee, this came out unanimously? Came out unanimously and also Kelly Turner from the potato industry gave a testimony there in full support of this. Gave some more details on basically the relevance of the program and it's just more of a burdensome burden to the industry and not very good use of MDARD's time. Great. Well, thank you. And any questions from members of the committee? Great. All right. Well, thank you very much, Representative. Representative, you're good to go. Thank you very much. All right. We are awaiting Representative Altman who will be testifying in support of 4914. I'm told he is on his way over, which is good. Committee will go to you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

The committee will come to order. And yeah, fresh out of economic competitiveness, we will now hear testimony on House Bill 4914, and Representative Outman will be testifying. Oh, there we go. Green button lights up. Let me get my notes real quick. Well, thank you, Chairman Schutte, members of the committee, here to talk to you about cryptocurrency. Just kidding. We just had a whole hearing on that where both Chairman Schutte and Brian testified. I'm here to talk about something else, here to talk about my bill, House Bill 4914. And what that would do is that would simply remove the requirement that two-thirds of a firm's principals be licensed to practice architecture, engineering, or surveying. Now, this bill comes from a February 2025 law report outlining ways in which the legislature could cut unnecessary red tape and promote businesses here in Michigan. Now, the removal of this requirement would not impact public safety or the quality of work being done. Any project being done would still have to be performed by an individual licensed by the state, regardless of the firm's ownership. Now, my hope in this bill is that it would also pave the way for an increase in the number of firms in the state. By removing that two-thirds ownership requirement, we open the door to more people taking a chance in opening a new business. So, again, Chairman Schutte and committee members, I thank you for the time and would welcome any questions at this time. Thank you, Representative Outman. So, first question, I know that, just as a point of clarification, states in our region, do they have this two-thirds requirement? So, not many. We are somewhat of an outlier here in this country, as a matter of fact. But specifically in the Great Lakes region, we are an outlier. For example, you look at the state of Wisconsin, they do not mandate a licensed professional be responsible in charge. You look at the state of Ohio, they still have a threshold, but it's a lower threshold. So, 50% of the owners have to be a licensed architect, engineer, or surveyor. Indiana does not mandate any sort of licensed professional ownership ratio. So, specifically in our region, it does seem like we are an outlier. But more broadly speaking, there's 27 states that use a more responsible, flexible charge model than what we're practicing here in the state of Michigan. Again, we are at two-thirds ownership ratio for those companies. Thank you. And so, work being completed by one of these firms, it would still have to be done by a licensed professional, correct? That's correct. Every project has to be signed, stamped, and sealed by a, again, a licensed architect, engineer, or surveyor in this case. And so, on the project, they'd still be subjected to those public safety standards that normal work is required. And it's important to keep a note that even here in the state of Michigan, where we have that two-thirds ownership ratio requirement, two-thirds of the owners do not have to sign off on a project. It is still up to one licensed professional that signs off, gives that architecture stamp on a project. So, really, just the ownership ratio doesn't make sense to me. It seems like a way to protect your turf, so to speak. And I think we would do Michigan a great deal of service by removing this unnecessary burden, in my opinion. Great. Thank you. Representative Martin? Thank you, Mr. Chair. So, Wisconsin and the other surrounding states, have we lost business to them, or do they have larger business in the architecture and engineering businesses than we do? Do we have statistics on that, that we're losing business to them because they have a different requirement? I don't have any statistics on that specifically, but I do know that, you know, in those states where they have a more flexible model, you know, there's no safety concerns by any means. And that's what the architecture groups and some of these stakeholder groups are going to come up here and say, that private equity is going to come over and take over all these companies, and that they're just going to be signing off on unsafe projects. That has not been the case in those other states. So, do, I mean, the other businesses, since an architect signs off on it, do they design buildings in the state of Michigan from out of state? I would assume so. Just for ownership in the state of Michigan, doesn't mean that an out-of-state one can't do business here. I mean, so, do we have more businesses going to the out-of-states because of that? It's possible. I mean, it certainly is. It's certainly an outdated and anti-competitive. But we have testimony from the professional organizations saying that, or is it just Lara's review? Well, I don't know. That hasn't been brought up to me specifically. Like I said, the stakeholders, the ones that I've talked to, their big fear is that these big private equity firms are going to be coming in, taking over, and these people are going to be, these architects, these licensed professionals, are going to be, you know, they're going to be signing off on these unsafe projects because of that influence. Right. But that just brings up the point. The way we do business in Michigan may not be the same as other states, but it doesn't appear to be broken in Michigan to be a repair for any kind of safety thing. So it's not broken in the state of Michigan. It's just not the same as other states. Yeah, I mean, I would say that's a pretty fair assessment. I mean, again, I think it's anti-competitive. You know, I think we do potentially. Allegorically, it's, I'm trying to say two words at once. Yeah. Both of those words. We created a new word in the roast room. We haven't had trade associations testimony on that. No, no. And it's not one of their priorities. Obviously, again, I feel like they want to protect their turf more than anything. But again, that's my humble opinion. Representative Woodward. Thanks, Rep. Outman. Just curiously, I have a family member that is an architect and many that are engineers. And if this requirement is eliminated, will there be an increase in problems with public safety? Because, I mean, I see what he does and it is such minutia that I would have never thought of. And it is there just to protect all of us, like what happens in this capital. And will it be a risk to the public safety? I don't think so. In the 40 other states that don't have this strict of requirement, that hasn't been the case. So I would argue that no, the evidence isn't there for that. Okay. And Representative Wenzel. So how many other states have a licensure requirement, either individually or firms? So there are 12 states in the union that have this two-thirds requirement. There are seven additional states that have a more strict requirement, oddly enough. Now, there are some states that had this requirement and then actually rescinded them. I use Iowa as an example. They had this two-thirds requirement. They repealed that back in 2014. And there's been no concerns from what I can see regarding that. So I guess, and who is wanting this? It seems like we're trying to, to Representative Martin's point, we're trying to fix something that doesn't seem to really be a problem. So obviously our whole mission here is to reduce red tape. I mean, so even if we're not seeing a huge issue with it, does that regulation make sense? I mean, is it anti-competitive? Is it preventing people from getting into the marketplace? So that's my counter to that. I mean, I haven't heard a lot of concerns. Again, it just seems like an unnecessary regulatory burden that we could at least pare down, if not outright eliminate. And the Department of Lara, they issued their red tape report. This is one of the ones that they highlighted that says it doesn't make sense. Get rid of it. And I agree with them. Do you know when this law was enacted, when the two-thirds came about? I think it's quite old. I don't know exactly the genesis of it, but I believe it's been in place for quite some time. Any other? Representative DeBoer. I know, like in the medical profession, depending on who's an administrator of the office, can change the dynamics of the care. And so my daughter-in-law worked at a clinic in Virginia, and they could do like a half-hour appointment. And then they got a more administrative person to run the office with more of a business focus, and it went down to like 15 minutes or 10 minutes. And it was very, very hard to do quality care and understand the patient's issues. And I've heard of other doctors that have left the regular GP world because of administrative overreach that makes their appointments so short that they feel they can't do the job they want to do for patients. And so when I heard of this, it gave me that same kind of catch in my heart that, yeah, you don't want to have only we understand what we do and no one else can be a part of it. But you're not saying that if you have a two-thirds administrative group, you can still have business-minded people, but you don't have, you know, and some of these equity groups really have no heart at all. And I can see why they would be concerned about that. And it is... So what is your overarching concern, I guess? That safety. Safety. So, again, even if we've removed this...

Strange ownership ratio. Every project has to be approved by a licensed professional. Do we not trust those licensed professionals? Do we not think that they're going to take due diligence or put their reputation on the line to sign off on something that's unsafe? Not initially, but they can be pressured. They can have administrators that say you're going to lose your job if you don't follow the, you know, we got a lot of people waiting in line for your position, too bad for you. I'm sorry, but it is a depraved world and people get pressured. Again, do you think a licensed architect and engineer is going to sign off on an unsafe project? You know, it wouldn't be horribly unsafe, but they could skirt things just for pressure. And members, I appreciate this discussion. I think we're journeying in a minute here. So and I appreciate that. We have a lot of cards of opposition. We're not going to be voting on anything today. We'll give you time to testify in the future next time we bring the bill up. So apologies for that. It's, you know, time got out of our hands. Representative, we have no absent members and we will stand adjourned. Thank you. Looks like we're going to have to take a look at this one. Yeah. Looks like we're going to have to take a look at this one.

title: Economic Competitiveness — Thursday, November 6, 2025
transcript:
The House Committee on Economic Competitiveness will come to order. Would the clerk please take roll? Chair Houghton. Here. Representatives Bonack. Here. Altman. Here. Harris. Here. Bagul. Here. DeBoer. Here. St. Germain. Here. Grant. Rixey. Here. Tate. Here. Kofia. Mr. Chair, you have nine members present. You do have a quorum. Thank you. Representative DeBoer makes a motion to approve our meeting minutes from October 30th. Seeing no objections, the minutes are approved by unanimous consent. Okay. Today, the House Committee on Economic Competitiveness will take testimony this morning on a bill package that would allow the state of Michigan to invest retirement funds into cryptocurrencies, establish a digital asset bill of rights, and allow orphan wells to be used for Bitcoin mining partnership programs. To follow, Representative Mueller has House Bill 4492, which will also take testimony on. We will begin with the cryptocurrency package. And since I have no idea where to begin with crypto, we're going to start off with Representative and Majority Floor Leader Postumus on House Bill 4511. Begin when you are ready, Representative. All right. Mr. Chair, thank you very much for having me. Committee members, I really appreciate it. So I'm going to talk a little bit about a 50,000-foot view first on why the overall package is. I think there's six or seven bills up before committees today regarding crypto.

currency. And Shudy has joined me in leading this effort, along with Representative McFaul. And so I want to give a 50,000-foot view on why in general for all of it, and then also get into a little bit on the crypto Bill of Rights. So first of all, the 50,000-foot. I believe I have a fundamental belief that in the near future, whether that's five years from now, 10 years from now, 20 years from now, cryptocurrency and digital assets will be the foundation of the financial world for a lot of reasons. Whether that is security, cryptocurrency is substantially more secure than cash, substantially more secure than credit cards, debit cards. Our current financial system is less secure outside cryptocurrency than it is inside cryptocurrency. That's one reason. Another reason, speed of transactions. If you've ever tried to wire money overseas, which I have, that is a mess. For me, it took 28 days, and the entirety of that time, none of the banks that I talked to knew where the money was. 28 days. And that was this century, right? With cryptocurrency, that transaction can happen in five seconds for a fraction of the cost. So for a whole lot of reasons, it makes sense that digital assets and cryptocurrency will become the foundation of our financial future. There's a lot more reasons outside of that, but those are the two that just are the easiest to make sense of. The pushback historically that I've gotten anytime I have conversations on cryptocurrency, number one is volatility, right? People are scared of cryptocurrency because of volatility. I would suggest two different things. Number one, actually three different things. Starting with the fact that it is the best performing asset over the last 10 years. No other asset comes close, none. If you're talking about real estate, any other stock markets, none of them come close. So if you're looking at a long-term 10-year horizon, nothing comes close. If you pick any point on a timescale during the existence of cryptocurrency, there is not a single four-year period where Bitcoin has lost money over a four-year period of time, not one. And so short-term volatility, sure, there is some of that, and there's that in all assets. So that's the pushback I get, but I want to make sure to be clear about that. It's also known. Also, a lot of that volatility is due to a lack of institutional acceptance and adoption. Over the last year, we've seen a lot of institutional adoption. We've seen the United States establish a crypto reserve. We've seen several states throughout the country establish a crypto reserve or start the process of establishing one. We've seen the Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund establish one and heavily invest. We've seen the three largest financial firms in the world go heavily into crypto. The worldwide institutional adoption of cryptocurrency will help stabilize any of the concerns with volatility. The second concern I get is, I just don't know anything about it, and so I don't want to talk about it. I don't want to legislate it because I know nothing about it. That's a challenge that we get into in government all the time. Anytime we have a change in technology, we have an advancement in technology, the technology takes off and government lags 10 years, 15 years, 20 years behind before it puts in place the parameters to help ensure public safety or other mechanisms. Right now, we are in a position where we can get ahead of the curve when it comes to crypto. Representative Schutte is going to talk about the pension funds. Right now, we can already invest in pension funds, but there's no guardrails. Representative Schutte is going to talk about why his bill is important to manage that. Right now, there are thousands of people, if not millions of people in the state of Michigan that hold cryptocurrency, but they have no provisions to protect the fact that they hold cryptocurrency. That's what the Bill of Rights does. House Bill 4511 establishes the right for individuals to hold cryptocurrency and not have the government step in and say, oh, wait, if you want to have that, you need to be licensed. Or if you want to pay for something with cryptocurrency, now you have to be licensed. It allows the open participation in the economy with cryptocurrency. Right now, that's already there, but at any minute, at any time, the government can step in, the executive branch can step in and say, nope, you can't. And a lot of individuals throughout the entire state will be in a world of hurt. So that's the general 50,000-foot view. That's the crypto Bill of Rights. I'm happy to take any questions on 50,000-foot or the Bill of Rights. Thank you, Representative. Oh, y'all are easy. Wait a minute, we do have Representative Altman. Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Brian, for your testimony. Just a quick question, kind of a 50,000-foot view question. And forgive my ignorance, but how does cryptocurrency work exactly? So do these investors, do they hold these digital assets in some sort of bank account or it's like a digital wallet? How does it work? It's a good question. So there's a lot of different ways. So we'll start with the old-fashioned way, which it's essentially an electronic wallet. Basically, you hold it on a flash drive or your hard drive, that type of thing. Also, as of now, over the last several years, something called crypto ETFs, exchange-traded funds, which we all commonly use in other financial aspects, they now have ETFs for cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin ETFs, Ethereum ETFs, that sort of thing. And so if you wanted to invest in cryptocurrency that way by holding a federally regulated exchange-traded fund, you can do it that way too. Thank you so much. Thank you. Before moving on, we do have a card to read in. All right, Representative. Fire at will. Thanks, Representative. Like I half understand this stuff, okay? What's the underlying asset of value that is represented by a Bitcoin value? If you're talking about Bitcoin, so there's a couple different ways to look at it. It could be any of them. Yeah, so we'll use Bitcoin as an example, and there's going to be other people testifying after me that can give a little bit better explanation of this, but I'll point out two things. One, unlike the U.S. dollar, which can be and is printed infinitely, right? There is a maximum number of Bitcoins that will ever be available in the history of the world, and that number will never change. It can't change. And there's 21 million Bitcoins available. There will never be any more than that in circulation. The fact that scarcity exists and finite ability to receive it exists in and of itself provides a store of value, whereas a U.S. dollar, as we all know, the U.S. dollar has lost 97% of its valuation over the past 150 years or 200 years due to the ever-expanding growth of the money supply. So that's one intrinsic value in it. Other cryptocurrencies would argue they have different things that provide value. Ethereum would argue that their overall technology and ability to use the transactions, that's what provides them value. So arguably it's a digital placeholder just as a $100 bill would be a digital placeholder, or I'm sorry, a tangible placeholder for value you've created, whether it be labor, whether it be product, whether it be... It's an exchangeable currency that is in a digital fashion that is not subject to things like inflation because we can't print more. For Bitcoin, that would be the case, yeah. Similar to gold, right? What gives gold its value? The fact that there's really a limited supply of gold and it can be utilized in a medium of exchange. Okay, thank you, Representative. One moment, Representative. We'll get you on the list. And I do want to remind members, you know, we're getting the 50,000 view right now. We're going to have more testimony that's going to bring that back down to ground level that may, in that testimony, answer some of the questions you do have. So if you've got things that are specific to the 50,000-foot view, now's the time. Otherwise, we do have a lot to get through. Right now, we do have a question from Representative Brixey. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Representative, do you have any... I don't see any kind of auditing requirements in the bill, and I have some concerns due to the newness of this. Are you referring to the pension fund bill? Which bill are you referring to? Your bill that creates a new act that says we can't ban... Oh, I see what you're saying. Okay, so there's no... One of the limitations of Bitcoin is that...

The auditing of it is challenging. And when you are talking about working on using investments for pensions, you mentioned there's never been a four-year span where they've lost money. But I think your front desker who's investing in their 401k really needs much more than a four-year view in terms of measuring what's the long-term stability of this investment type is. So I'll give you a couple things. Specifically on the pension fund, Representative Schuette will talk to that, and he'll be able to help address your concern when it comes to pensions. One thing I will say is on that front, the fiduciary in charge of the pension fund could invest in blockbuster stock today. She's not prevented from investing in that. So keep in mind there is a fiduciary responsibility still. That's the only thing I'll say on that. As far as the ability to audit, I'm not sure what your concern is. I don't know in the last time you're outside of taxes, which is still subject to the same auditability from a tax law perspective. I don't know when the last time your personal finances outside of tax preparation was audited, nor do I think it probably should be. I'm not supplying my personal finances as an asset that the government is investing in. I'm not following. So you're talking about the crypto bill of rights. The thing that that does is it provides the right for an individual to hold cryptocurrency without the government saying they cannot or have to be licensed to do so. So I'm not sure where auditing comes into play here. The auditing of the crypto, the people who are selling the crypto to evaluate its stability. I mean, the market evaluates the stability. I mean, you can look back at the price of Bitcoin or Ethereum from today all the way back to its creation and early existence. All right. Thank you, Representative. We'll move on. We have one more question for the 50,000-foot view from Majority Vice Chair Bonack. Thank you, Representative, for helping us try to understand this.
