If it was accurate, as we told our citizens, that the changes that we were doing at the pump were going to be revenue neutral to them, then every vehicle should have that type of treatment. And so that's what this bill does. There are a number of people who will be here to testify who can talk specifically about the language within the bill. But the intent of the language in the bill is to treat an electric vehicle same as we did with everyone else and make that revenue neutral. They'll still pay their surcharge. They'll still pay that registration fee. But what I'm trying to deal with is that extra $100 that we weren't able to address because of the complexity of the roads conversation. And, Madam Chair, that's what this bill does. And I'd be pleased to answer any questions, and more technical questions probably could be answered by people who will be coming up after me. Thank you, Senator. Members, are there any questions? Senator Bayer. I'm probably just screwing up this math, but maybe it's not math, it's a question. The $5 that is currently in the law, you want to reduce to $1.88? So that's still an increase. Yeah, well... For EVs, it's still got the $1.88. You're talking about an additional fee above what they already pay, right? An additional fee is more than they used to pay, so it's not revenue neutral. It's an increase. It's just a smaller increase. Right, I think what we're trying to do is create a level of fairness here with electric vehicles, and we think that the $5, the way it was written, was meant if everybody was paying a little bit extra, that that $5 should be there. The $1.88 has been put there to try to ensure that they're still paying their fair share, and I know others can specifically come to talk about why that was the number that was chosen. I think there's other ways of looking at it. Somebody asked, could we move the floor from $0.19 to $0.39? So I think there's multiple ways of looking at how to deal with it, but the intent was to still make EVs pay their fair share and probably a little bit more as you're acknowledging today, but this idea that they are supposed to be paying the $5 when the intent was this was to be revenue neutral to the customer, we're trying to address that issue. So it's revenue neutral for gasoline-powered, but EVs have to pay. I would ask that you ask that question for the next group that's coming up because they can explain how they got to the formula that was put into the bill. No, it's just the comparison of is it revenue neutral or not, and the answer is no, but it is for gasoline-powered vehicles. Okay, thank you. Thank you. Any additional questions? Oh, Senator Cherry. Thank you, Chair. Very quickly, so under the bill, what would be the additional fee that hybrid would pay? Or excuse me, electric vehicle would pay? I want to make sure that I'm answering the question accurately. And could you please introduce yourself? Thank you, Chair Anthony, and members of the Senate Appropriations Committee. My name is Chase Ottonasio. I'm a policy manager with Queenfields Michigan. We're a trade association that works with businesses working to accelerate the transition towards clean mobility in the state. I appreciate Senator Singh for bringing Senate Bill 593 up and working on it with us, and I know that there's others in the docket who can speak to the bill language as well. But I'll start with Senator Bayer. I'd like to address your question first. When we're talking about, I think we need to define what we're saying when we say revenue neutral. Really what Senator Singh was saying, in the same way that the road funding package that passed earlier this month, gasoline drivers will not see an net increase in the amount that they're paying at the pump. Their taxes stay the same. That same fairness or the equality was not afforded to drivers of electric or plug-in hybrid vehicles, and that's what this bill is intended to do. So that $1.88 increase, because the motor fuel tax base that was passed in the road funding package increases the motor fuel tax from $0.31 to $0.51, we need to decrease the amount that the EV registration fee increases per one cent of the gas tax. So instead of a $5 increase per one cent, a $1.88 increase makes sure that Michigan's, the surcharges that EV drivers are paying, and then Senator Cherry, this gets to your question, the surcharge that electric vehicle drivers will pay is $160.16, and for hybrid drivers, they'll also pay the same surcharge. Right now, EV drivers pay a $160 flat surcharge rate. So it's $0.16 more than what EV drivers are currently paying. But the goal of the bill, again, this bill achieves the outcome of electric vehicle drivers will pay the same EV registration fee that they're currently paying under the current tax system. There won't be new taxes at the turn of the new year. I think maybe my question, under current law, what's the additional amount that an electric vehicle pays, like total? Currently, before the new road funding package...

electric vehicle drivers pay a surcharge of $160. And under the new statute starting on January 1st, they would pay $160.16. Without Senate Bill 593, electric vehicle drivers would be paying $260 surcharge. Thank you. Thank you. Any additional questions? Senator McMarrow. Thank you, Madam Chair. And just for a point of clarification on the rationale behind the additional fee, it is to ensure that EV drivers are paying the same as the average gas tax for an internal combustion engine vehicle statewide, correct? That's correct, Senator. Thank you. Thank you. Additional questions? Okay. Thank you so much. I know we do have a representative from the Ecology Center, I believe, here with us in person. Thank you. Come on up. Thank you, Madam Chair, members of the committee. I'm Charles Griffith, the Climate and Energy Program Director at the Ecology Center. And thank you for the opportunity to testify today in support of Senate Bill 593, which we believe is necessary to prevent these new and highly punitive fees on EV drivers from taking effect next year. Without taking this action, Michigan would have the highest EV fees in the whole entire country, which is a distinction I think that we should at least pause before allowing to happen. And, of course, I would say that we shouldn't have that distinction. I just wanted to give a little bit of history, a little bit more history on this issue without taking too much time, which is that we started following this issue back when EV fees were first enacted in the last big road funding package about a decade ago when we raised the gas tax, I think, about 7 cents and then also raised registration fees. But these new fees on EVs were enacted at that point. And while the Ecology Center was supportive of EV drivers paying their fair share, we were also concerned that they were actually paying more than the drivers of similar or equivalent gasoline vehicles. I think, Senator McMorrow, you pointed out this is based on kind of an average vehicle on the road. But that was problematic for us from a variety of perspectives, and I wanted to share a little bit of the data and study that we did. We actually did a study back then and suggested some reform of the EV fees to make them a little more fair for EV drivers. But we conducted another analysis this year in the lead-up to this road funding discussion and found actually similar and even more compelling results. And the reason I say more compelling is because we now have the ability to compare EV models directly to gasoline versions of the same vehicle models. So, for example, the F-150 Lightning EV can be compared to the F-150 gasoline models, and we can do the comparison. It's more apples to apples. So in this new analysis, I don't know if anyone can see this graphic, but it's also in the written testimony that I've provided. You can see that for every vehicle of a popular EV model that has a gasoline counterpart, the owner of the EV would pay more in taxes and fees than the owner of a gas vehicle of that exact same vehicle. On average, we found about $47 more per year. But as you can see, for the F-150 and actually the Silverado EV, they're paying substantially more than that than their gasoline equivalents. And those vehicles, by the way, are made right here in Michigan. Now, as you're aware, as from the previous discussion, the new road funding package, if not addressed, would raise those disparities even greater. So, you know, we did that comparison for you, too. So you can see how much more the EV drivers will pay. And meanwhile, as we've heard, the gasoline vehicle drivers are paying essentially the same. So as the sponsors of the road funding package made clear that Michigan drivers were to be held harmless, we're just simply asking that EV drivers be held harmless, too. Now, that will mean that they'll continue to pay more based on kind of the current situation that we have, which is not, in my view, ideal. But it's better, way better than enacting the highest new EV fees in the country, which would be highly punitive to EV drivers. So, you know, I would prefer a better solution. But this is, I think, the easiest thing that we could do today. I know that there are discussions and there was support for a new road user charge study or pilot program to be developed, as I know Senator Kleinfeld is very interested in that, as well as many of you, I think. So we're going to be looking at new potential ways to revise how we do taxation going forward. And I think that provides a time to really take a bigger look at how we do this. But in the meantime, please help us to prevent from these highly punitive fees from going into effect and making Michigan, preventing Michigan from becoming known as the most punitive EV fee state in the country. Thank you. Thank you. Senator Cherry. Thank you, Chair, and thank you for your testimony. I heard in your testimony that you do think that there should be some parity between internal combustion engine drivers and EV drivers on what they're contributing to roads, right? That's what I thought I heard you. Yeah. Okay. So when I was looking up data on what an internal combustion engine driver, what they pay is dependent upon how much they drive and what the fuel efficiency of their vehicle is. So understanding how much they contribute to roads, you got to look at their usage and back out what their gas usage is. And so looking at the federal data, on average, a Michigan driver drives over 14,000 miles a year. And when you look at the average fuel efficiency of a vehicle bought over the past four years, it's 24.9 miles per gallon. You back that out, there's 574 gallons of gas bought by the typical Michigan driver. I think that's conservative because a lot of people are driving cars that are older than four years old. And in January, that means they'd be paying over $300 in gas tax. So I'm not sure that this bill would result in parity between what ICE drivers and electric vehicle drivers would be paying to contribute to roads. Well, honestly, I think what this bill would do would keep the current situation, which according to our analysis, based on that average mileage, this is the data that we have found to be true. And we do take into account the fact that EV drivers actually do pay higher registration fees than their equivalent gasoline models because those vehicles cost more and registration fees are based on the purchase price of the vehicle. So we do give some credit for that. But in addition to the $160 surcharge, we think that's only fair because actually today, until the new road funding package comes into full effect, there's actually more money raised by the registration fees than there is from the gas tax. That'll start to shift as this sales tax, gas tax swap goes into effect. But I think what I'm saying is that from our data, we clearly see that the EVs are paying more than their equivalent gasoline models based on average mileage. And keep in mind that the EV drivers don't get any break if they drive less than the average miles. They also don't pay more if they drive more than the average miles. My preferred approach would be a mileage-based solution for EV drivers so that it is more fair and there's more parity with what gasoline vehicle drivers are paying. Thank you. And I'm going to speed up a little bit because we are not voting on this bill today. And so it will give members an opportunity to ask additional questions before it comes before the committee again. Senator Kleinfeld. Just very quickly, first of all, I understand the importance of

of promoting EVs, and I also understand that we did sell it as being revenue neutral for everybody. My preference would be that it wasn't, because we have problems with our roads. But I've got to pick on you a little bit here. Fair enough. You're talking about apples to apples. Does a Ford Mustang that's an electric vehicle weigh the same amount as a Ford Mustang that's not an electric vehicle, and do they have the same wear and tear on the road? Because from a transportation chair perspective, I'm worried about that road. That's what I'm thinking about. And every group that we looked at possibly taxing came into my office and had the reason why they shouldn't be taxed. And I've got to tell you, I wanted to tax some more of them because we need to fix the roads. They need to be fixed. And our state seems to be afraid to deal with that, but all the states around us that are some Democrats, some Republicans, they're all putting mechanisms into place to fix it. I'm sorry. Do they have the same wear and tear, and are they the same weight? If you talk to most transportation engineers or road engineers, they'll tell you that in the lighter weight range, below 10,000 pounds, for example, it doesn't make that much difference. It's the big, heavy trucks that put really a lot of pound weight on each axle where that wear and tear is largely happening. I won't deny that EVs with those heavier batteries do weigh a little bit more. It's arguable that you could measure any additional wear and tear from that. Having said that, EV drivers are paying a little bit more based on our data, and I'm not... I know she wants us to stop talking, me particularly, but my point being it's hard to count apples against apples because we're just talking about two different things. I do support promoting EV vehicles, though. Thank you. Thank you, Senator. You can talk all day. No, I love you. Senator Huizinga. I'll yield my time as Senator Kleinfeld covered me. Thank you. Senator Albert, did you want to pass? Okay, thank you. Additional questions? Okay. Thank you so much. I do believe we have at least one person on Zoom. Let me see if we have them queued up. Okay, we can read cards as we're trying to queue up the Zoom. I believe it's Sophia Schuster from EIBC. Opposing Senate Bill 593, the groups are Michigan Infrastructure Transportation Association, the Michigan Laborers District Council, the County Road Association, and the Road Commission for Oakland County. Supporting Senate Bill 593 is the Sierra Club, the Michigan Environmental Council, the League of Women Voters, Evergreen Action, Michigan Auto, Tesla, General Motors, Michigan Clinicians for Climate Actions, Michigan Conservative Energy Forum, League of Women Voters, Michigan Climate Action Network, Transportation Riders United, and Michigan Interfaith Power and Light. Thank you. Okay. Do we have Sophia on? I'm here. Hi. Hi. Hi, can everybody hear me? We can. Thank you for joining us. Yeah, thank you for having me. Thank you, Chair Anthony and members of the committee for the opportunity to testify remotely today. And thank you, Senators, for introducing Senate Bill 593. My name is Sophia Schuster. I'm the Policy Principal for Michigan Energy Innovation Business Council, and I lead on our work related to mobility and transportation. Michigan EIBC is a trade association of about 160 advanced energy companies that invest and create jobs in Michigan. I'm here today to offer our support of Senate Bill 593, which will ensure that all Michigan drivers contribute fairly to Michigan road systems regardless of vehicle type. The momentous road funding package passed in October 2025 will improve the quality of road travel across the state, all without increasing overall taxes paid by drivers operating internal combustion engine or ICE vehicles. Despite these improvements, while ICE vehicle drivers will see no impact to the state taxes they pay, the same cannot be said for electric vehicle or EV drivers. Under the current tax structure, as my colleagues have stated, analysis based on Department of State data and a comparison of like EV and ICE models show that battery electric vehicle drivers already roughly pay at least $20 more in state taxes to support Michigan roads per year compared to their ICE counterparts. As noted by my colleagues, the gas tax increase resulting from the road funding package will trigger an additional $100 increase to these annual vehicle taxes. Depending on the vehicle model, this represents a 15 to 23 percent tax increase, with the heaviest burden falling on lower cost EV model drivers. Consequently, the tax structure adjustments set to go into effect January 1st, 2026 exacerbates an already existing disparity in road funding contribution between EV and ICE vehicle drivers and will effectively penalize cost-sensitive Michigan EV drivers. This disproportionate increase in annual EV taxes sends the wrong signal to manufacturers, investors, and consumers. As we are well aware, the Michigan state history and the rise of the automotive industry are inextricably linked. Home to nearly 19 percent of U.S. automotive manufacturing, the state's mobility sector contributes nearly $350 billion annually to the economy and supports more than 1.2 million jobs. Today, however, Michigan faces unprecedented competition from emerging domestic and foreign automotive manufacturing hubs. Most notably, having exported over 1.4 million EVs in 2023, China is rapidly advancing their EV leadership and market share. As EV adoption rates continue to rise, the state and the nation that lead the EV evolution will lead the future of the automotive industry. As such, Michigan is in a unique position to leverage this legacy as the global industry shifts to electric vehicle production. An increase to EV registration taxes raises the overall cost of vehicle ownership, thus impeding consumer choice and reducing EV demand. The impact of this reduced market demand would reverberate across the automotive industry and the industry sectors that support it, discouraging continued investment and weakening Michigan's competitive edge in the global market industry. Therefore, failure to correct this tax increase to EV drivers is a blatant signal to industry that Michigan is willing, if not eager, to penalize the very technologies our businesses are investing in and sacrifice its position as a leader in automotive manufacturing. Senate Bill 593 addresses this issue by lowering the tax on EVs that is tied to Michigan's gas tax. This will allow EV drivers to be rendered harmless by the new vehicle tax structure in the same manner as ICE vehicle drivers, ensuring an equitable contribution to Michigan's roads regardless of vehicle type. Michigan EIBC urges the legislature to act before the end of the year to pass Senate Bill 593, correcting Michigan's vehicle tax structure and reaffirming Michigan's commitment to being the best place in the country to design, build, and drive the vehicles of the future. Thank you for your time and I welcome any questions you may have. Thank you, Sophia. Are there any questions? Seeing none, thank you. I appreciate it. And thank you, Senator Singh and all those who came forward and presented cards. We'll move forward with Senate Bill 357 and 358 from Senator Bumstead and I regarding the SAF hold harmless bills. These bills establish a flat transfer from the general fund to the school aid fund to reflect the impact of recent tax exemptions passed by the legislature that would include a school aid fund hold harmless provision, mainly sales and use tax exemptions. This was an issue that was brought to us by the Department of Treasury. As you all know, when the legislature passes a sales and use tax exemption, legislators often raise concerns about the potential reduction of money going into the school aid fund. So as a result, we will often hear language that holds the school aid fund harmless, protecting school aid revenues.

clearly outlining the amount that was already held harmless will improve accuracy in our state budget and increase transparency in the budgeting process. We have two substitutes to reflect conflict caused by the recently passed budget bills and updated revenue estimates from the Department of Treasury. We also wanted to acknowledge input and worked from the Michigan Association of School Boards who has been instrumental in helping us work through these bills. Senator Bumstead, did you have any comments on these bills? No, you did a fine job. Oh, thank you so much. Thank you. All right, we do have a few folks here to testify. We'll like to bring up Peter Mormon, the Director of Legislative Affairs with the Department of Treasury, and Scott Dara. Yes, the Tax Analyst Division Administrator to come up and talk more about this issue. Welcome. Improved efficiency and transparency in tax administration and budgeting. You described some of the provisions that have been enacted recently. These include sales and use tax exemptions on data center equipment, feminine hygiene products, and on delivery and installation charges. Now, there might be an impression that... So the current language provides for Treasury to make an annual determination on the sales of these products to determine the loss, the would-be loss to the school aid fund, and to make the transfer of that amount from the general fund to the school aid fund. And there may be an impression that these determinations are easy to make because Treasury would have actual hard data on the sales of these products and on these transactions. But that's not the case. Sales and use tax returns do not specify sales by product. That would be extremely burdensome for businesses in making those returns. So while we can probably get pretty close for an estimate on something like feminine hygiene products, because external data is reasonably good, it's much more difficult for something like the separately itemized delivery and installation charges that are now being exempted based on legislation from the last couple of years. So as more of these provisions have come into play and have been added, the transfers are getting larger and more consequential, and we thought it made sense to start taking a different approach. So these bills would end the annual exemption by exemption determination and simply put the current collective estimate for all covered exemptions and put that number in statute. So $50 million in the sales tax exemptions and $16 million in the use tax exemptions. And then provide for an annual inflationary adjustment to capture the anticipated sales growth over time. So the bills are just maintaining the status quo. This is not increasing or decreasing the transfers. So again, we think it's a good approach for efficiency and transparency, and we encourage your support. Happy to answer any questions. Thank you. Senator Irwin. Thank you for the committee. It sounds like the taxes that are going to be sought to be backfilled by our current law and by this change are only for those three changes to sales and use tax. There are a whole number of other different ways that we offer positive tax treatment through industrial facilities exemptions. In fact, earlier today we were hearing about the recodified tax increment financing act. Are you aware of or is there in this bill any way for payments to be made back to the school aid fund for lost revenue to the school aid fund from things like the recodified tax increment financing act or industrial facility exemptions or any number of the other things that I hear constantly in Lansing are backfilled but aren't? As indicated, this bill just addresses the ones that the legislature has specifically provided for a backfill in statute. So in addition to the ones that you mentioned, that also includes the personal property tax exemptions going back 10 or 12 years from the personal property tax reform package, I guess it implemented 10, 12 years ago. So those are also included in this proposal. To get an idea of the value of the various tax exemptions and tax expenditures, our friend Scott here actually does a biannual report that we produce every two years that lists all of the tax expenditures through all the statutes if you want to get a flavor for what those are and how much they cost. We can send you that report. Thank you. Senator Cherry. I was going to say thank you for your report. I actually read it. Now I know who actually writes it. Thank you. Just so you know, there is somebody who actually reads it. Thank you. Nerd alert. Senator Albert. Thank you. Maybe if I read it, I wouldn't have this question. So is this new calculation, is it, so take the personal property tax, for example, there's a pretty definite way that you calculate that number. Is that going to go away and you're just going to use this number going forward and just use inflation? Yes, it would be annually adjusted for inflation, but it would take the current numbers, the most recent calculations from the 50 million in sales tax and the 16 million in use tax. Oh, okay. So I guess when I heard the term revenue neutral, I thought that meant going forward. So you can only really be sure it's revenue neutral for year one, correct? Because personal property tax could fluctuate 20 years from now. Is that not accurate? It could, yes. And is there any evidence to conclude that personal property tax is going to grow at the same rate as inflation going forward? The taxable value is capped at the rate of inflation. So to the extent that it's existing property, that would be true if the property is not depreciating faster than the inflation rate is going up. But that's not at all how it would happen in reality. And there are limits on the personal property that's covered here, so that that estimate is relatively modest compared to the totals we have here. The current estimate for the transfer for 2025, this is preliminary, but it's approximately $6 million for personal property. It's a relatively modest share of the two numbers that we have here. Okay, thank you. Thank you. Any additional questions? Thank you again for your testimony. I appreciate it. Okay, are there any cards? No cards? Okay. All right, I now need a motion to adopt the S-2 sub of Senate Bill 357, moved by Senator Bayer, supported by Senator Kleinfeld. Mr. Clerk, will you please call the question? Chair Anthony. Yes. Senator McCann. Senator Cherry. Yes. Senator Bayer. Senator Santana. Senator Schenck. Senator Irwin. Senator Hertel. Senator Kavanaugh. Senator Kleinfeld. Senator McMorrow. Senator Camilleri. Senator Bumstead. Yes. Senator Albert. Senator DeMoss. Senator Heisinga. Senator Altman. And Senator Tice. Madam Chair, you have 14 yeas and one nay. The substitute is adopted. Thank you. I need a motion to report Senate Bill 357 to the floor with recommendation it pass, moved by Senator Cherry, supported by Senator Hertel. Mr. Clerk, will you please call the question? Chair Anthony. Yes. Senator McCann. Senator Cherry. Yes. Senator Bayer. Senator Santana. Senator Schenck. Senator Irwin. Senator Hertel. Senator Kavanaugh. Senator Kleinfeld. Senator McMorrow. Senator Camilleri. Mr. Clerk, will you please call the question? Chair Anthony. Yes. Senator McCam. Senator Cherry. Yes. Senator Baer. Yes. Senator Santana. Yes. Senator Schink. Senator Irwin. Senator Hertel. title: Health Policy 25-11-05
transcript:
The Senate Committee on Health Policy is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairman Hartel? Here. Senator Santana? Here. Senator Voightno? Here. Senator Cherry? Here. Senator Kleinfeld? Here. Senator Geiss? Here. Senator Weber? Here. Senator Houck? Here. Senator Heisinga? Here. Senator Runstead? Mr. Chairman, you have seven members present. There is a quorum. Thank you, Madam Clerk. I will entertain a motion to adopt the October 29, 2025 committee meeting minutes, so moved by Vice Chair Santana. And without objection, the minutes are adopted. And I will accept a motion from Minority Vice Chair Weber to excuse absent members at this time. And seeing no objection, absent members are excused. We're going to begin with Senate Bills 449 through 451, which are sponsored by Senators Anthony and Lindsey. Senators, if you'd like to come forward and testify, please begin when you are ready. Thanks for being here. Thank you. Good afternoon, everyone. Chair Hertel and members of the committee, we just appreciate the opportunity to address this pretty significant bipartisan package to help tackle a growing issue in the state and across the country, which is that issue of medical debt. Medical debt is one of the leading causes of personal bankruptcy in the United States, affecting people from all income levels. Many individuals, even those with health insurance, face high deductibles and out-of-pocket expenses that leave them vulnerable after a single health emergency. For many, medical debt is not just a one-time expense. It can often lead to the beginning of a cycle of poverty. As a reminder, nearly 700,000 Michiganders are carrying medical debt, a particularly heavy burden on low- and moderate-income families. That's why it was important a few years ago in our state's budget that we started to tackle medical debt systemically. We invested $4.5 million to ease and erase medical debt, which approximately led to $450 million in medical debt being erased for roughly 180,000 Michiganders in communities across the state. We know this is just one part of the solution, however. So the bills that are before you would provide a proactive, practical approach to reduce long-term financial harm and help Michiganders combat the cycle of debt. Now, very importantly, we worked very closely with the Michigan Health and Hospitals Association throughout the drafting process to ensure that this legislation is written in a way that will work for a diverse array of hospitals throughout the state. Many Michigan hospitals are already providing these types of financial programs or what we often call charity care and financial assistance. So think hospitals like McLaren, Michigan Medicine, and Henry Ford. Our goal today is to build upon these existing efforts by standardizing these requirements and improving transparency so that every patient knows what help is available to them. Currently, under federal guidelines, nonprofit hospitals are required to provide some form of financial assistance. My bill, which is Senate Bill 449, along with Senator Lindsey's Senate Bill, which is 450, seek to do the following. First, they would codify and expand requirements into state law. Second, they would standardize charity care that is being provided. And then third, they would establish clear, consistent metrics for eligibility to ensure support is available for those who need it most. Specifically, hospitals would need to use income-based rules linked to the federal poverty level to decide who qualifies for these programs. They would help patients with unpaid hospital bills over 30% of their annual income. It would give up to 100% discounts to unpaid, I'm sorry, uninsured patients earning up to 350% of the federal poverty line level. And then consider insured patients' out-of-pocket costs and financial situations. Now, Senate Bill 451 would prevent medical debt from being included in consumer credit reports, protecting residents from long-term financial harm due to health-related costs. We'd like to give a shout-out to Representative Menser in the House for her partnership on this bill. We've been working with stakeholders on a substitute version of the bill that would update the definition of medical debt to align with federal guidelines, and this sub should be considered, if not today, in a future committee hearing. Lastly, I'd say that we are somewhat unique in the Midwest. States like Ohio and Illinois are enacting similar charity care laws, and several also limit how much medical debt is being reported to credit agencies. Michigan should keep pace to ensure our families have the same protections. No one should be condemned to a cycle of debt simply for seeking necessary medical care. So again, thank you for the opportunity to address the committee. I'd like to turn it over to my colleague, Senator Lindsey. Thank you, Chairperson Hertel, Vice Chairs, members of the committee, and thank you, Senator Anthony, for your leadership on this issue and for bringing me into the process. I hope we can all agree that health care is a top concern for our constituents. They have every right to be concerned. In the United States, we spend nearly 20% of our entire GDP annually on health care, and yet over the last 60 years, we've actually seen a decline in quality of many health care outcomes. I've made quality, affordable health care a top policy priority of mine, and I'm proud to have achieved some broad bipartisan support for steps we can take toward that end. So I'm happy to continue that bipartisan work today, but the legislation before you has a slightly different aim. Instead of talking about the common front end of access, affordability, quality, this is addressing what happens when someone uses our health care system and the result is a massive, unexpected financial burden, medical debt, all too common for too many of our constituents. My bill in particular, Senate Bill, I won't reiterate a lot of the comments. Senator Anthony did a great job of describing the package. My bill, Senate Bill 450, is largely technical in nature, making sure the existing law for boards of hospitals is updated to reflect the Hospital Financial Assistance Act. and that Michigan can achieve the same results. Medical debt erodes both financial and physical health. of the bill. Ashley Christian from Henry Ford Health not wishing to speak in support of the bill. Taylor Elpert, Michigan Health and Hospital Association, not wishing to speak in support of the bill.
