title: Oversight - Homeland Security and Foreign Influence — Wednesday, November 5, 2025
transcript:
The Committee on Homeland Security and Foreign Influence will come to order. Clerk, will you please take the roll? Chair Brock, present. Representatives Meerman, Shriver, Mensah, Conlon. Mr. Chair, you have a quorum. Alrighty. Seeing that Representative Shriver is absent, I am elevating alternate member Representative Wozniak. Thank you. You want to get Woods up too? She's probably not here, is she? No, I'm just kidding with you. If she was here, I would. It wouldn't help one of us, either one of us. We appreciate that. Representative Conlon is not here today. She had a wedding out of state to attend. Not her own, but a family member. So she is gone today. So we'll miss her. And I know she gave her regrets yesterday saying she really wanted to be here. But we are honored. Everyone has handouts. And we're honored to have General Rogers. He's an adjutant general for the Michigan National Guard, Air Guard. He's the highest ranking military member in the state, in the Guard. And so we appreciate you being here, General Paul Rogers. And please introduce yourself and your special guests as well, please. And then just press the red button and the floor is yours, sir. Excellent. Well, good afternoon, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. It's always a pleasure and honor to come and share our story and the things we're doing and answer questions and honor your oversight of our responsibilities within the department. I do have a guest here with me, Oliver. He was here in Lansing with his class doing a tour of the Capitol and learning about our great democracy. And fortunately, his mother is here with us. So she brought him, snuck him away and brought him over. And then he'll return to his class. But Oliver, would you like to say hello to the committee? Hello. There you go. Excellent. Excellent. That is awesome. This was not a preplanned strategy to keep you guys in control. So it was just an opportunity. We can't say a bad word when Oliver's sitting there. I know. So no, this is quite an opportunity, Oliver, for you to have you in committee. It's rare that we have, I think you're the first under 18 we've had in this room. So we appreciate you being here. And that's quite an honor to be sitting next to your grandfather, right? You said? No, no, just Heather's co-worker, brother's son here. Okay. Well, you're next to a military hero. I hope you know that. So look forward to your presentation, General. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. And good. So all questions, tough questions will go to Oliver, and I will handle the easy ones. So that was the deal here. But it's an honor to bring a young man up here and experience our democracy. And the military is always subordinate to civilian oversight and rule in our nation and in our democracy. And that's something I cherish and protect. So to be here and testify under your authority and oversight is something I take very seriously. I would like to, I did give you some handouts that I will reference throughout the brief. It's not something you have to dwell on, but they'll just be touch points that maybe help visualize what I'm describing at key moments in the presentation. I do want to just first describe the organization. And the Department of Military and Veterans Affairs, it's a position. I'm honored to be part of Governor Whitmer's cabinet and represent military and veteran issues within her cabinet. Also have a co-member on the cabinet, which is the director for the Michigan Veterans Affairs Agency, Director Love, Brian Love. So he's also an agency representative on the governor's cabinet and represents the veteran services part of our organization. But as characterized by the name Military and Veterans Affairs, of course, the military refers to the Army and Air National Guard presence in Michigan. And Michigan and present day, the largest military component or organization in Michigan is the National Guard. So I often refer to Michigan as a National Guard state because of that prominent role we play. In other states, large active duty bases tend to dwarf the presence of the National Guard. And they capture kind of that lead role in talking about the military and defense issues. But in Michigan, it is a National Guard and it's a responsibility I take as the senior military official in the state and an advisor to the governor. I take that role very, very seriously for defense and military veterans affairs issues. So I do work very closely in this capacity with the MEDC, Michigan Economic Development Corporation, as an advisor, as a contributor to some of the prioritization that they have for military aerospace and defense type initiatives. We do work closely with the state police within the Michigan ecosystem. And every state is a little different, but the way we're constructed, the emergency management lead for the state, all natural or man-made disasters, the lead for that is the colonel of the Michigan State Police. I am a supporting member of his collective team. So if there is an emergency, if there's a response necessary to a local community for whatever type of incident, they have the lead through the state emergency operations center. And then they call upon us to support that local community based on the needs of the local community. And our goal is to come in, augment, never take responsibility, but augment the lead on the ground. And then as soon as they are able to control the situation without our presence, we back away and return home. That's our National Guard role here in the state. But for emergency management, we do fall up under that whole of government response, which is led by the state police. So I often try to paint that picture just because it's unique. That's how Michigan does it. Other states do it somewhat differently, but it's, you know, 54 states and territories.

is in the District of Columbia in the United States that make up the National Guard were all constructed based on that local desire for the appropriate relationship. So as I start to talk about my department, again, I talked about the military and veterans affairs. So let me first talk about the military piece of it, just as an organizational construct, and then I'll get into the veterans affairs piece of it. So from military, we have both Army and Air National Guard that comprise the National Guard in Michigan. The total force structure is just under 10,500 members. About 2,500 of those are Air Guard. The other 8,000 are Army force structure. We're sitting based on strength just under 10,000 members. So we still have room, and we're actively recruiting across our communities and trying to find the best talent to bring in to our organizations with the skill sets that we're desiring. So we're actively engaging with our communities and community leaders to recruit additional members of that organization. So of those 10,000 folks, again, I gave you the breakdown, rough breakdown between the two services. That's our uniformed presence. They are here primarily for war fighting. We are resourced and trained by the federal government to the military standards. So we are part of that military response for our nation. And we are considered the operational reserve with the National Guard. So the first in, if there's a conflict overseas or if we go to war with somebody, the first in is that active duty unit that's leaning forward. But we are right on their heels. And you saw that play out in Global War on Terrorism as we then share the responsibility for that military response. And once you're activated, there is no lines between Guard, Reserve, or Active. We all are expected to do the same mission to the same standards. So that readiness and that training is our primary responsibility to the women and men who wear the uniform here in Michigan. And we take that very seriously. And I'll touch on that in a couple more opportunities as we go through. But in that response, being the primary, we also have a responsibility since my commander in chief and the commander in chief of the Michigan National Guard when we are not activated for federal service is the governor. So she is the commander in chief of the National Guard. And we work under her full authority and tasking. So that is very important, especially when there are emergencies like the ice storm this past spring up north. She has the ability to activate us and immediately put us into that response mode. The floods in Midland a few years ago, we were part of that response. The civil unrest in several of our cities during the George Floyd protests and riots, we were supporting the local law enforcement in that capacity. So the governor has the authority and oversight of the Michigan National Guard. She is the commander ultimately that I work for. Now, when a formation is activated, we then move over and we fall under a different federal statute and we now are under the authority of the President of the United States. And we have that obligation to support those mission sets under that federal responsibility. So the National Guard is very unique in that based on what status we're in, we fall under different chains of command. So it's something I always try to emphasize to folks. And I know many of the members of this committee understand some of this, but just for the totality and clarity of the organizational description, I wanted to share that. We do have a presence in 41 different communities across the state. We actually, I don't know exactly today, but at one point just a year or so ago, we had a member from every one of the 83 counties in the Michigan National Guard, which is something I cherish, right? We should represent our communities. We're really a community-based organization. We recruit our talent and our members from the local community. We invest in them as a person, but then they also serve their community by serving in the National Guard in their respective readiness center. So again, 41 communities have a fixed facility. And then of those 41 communities, three of them have, again, within the Air National Guard, Battle Creek has an air base, Selfridge Air National Guard Base, which I know is near and dear to the hearts of a couple of committee members because of the proximity to your district. That is the largest Air National Guard base in the country. It is considered a super base because it's wholly owned and operated by the military, and in this case, the Michigan National Guard operates that facility on behalf of the Air Force. So it's still Air Force owned, but in a lot of places, they have turned ownership over to a local municipality and it's become a non-military operating airfield, and they're just a tenant on it. In this case, we are the owner-operator and primary tenant on this air base, and we have 70 other tenants that have a presence on Selfridge Air National Guard Base to the tune of about 5,000 people on any given day can be working or training at that location. So it's a very large community. And then our third Air National Guard facility is up in Alpena, and that's a combat readiness training center, and there's only four of them in the country. We're blessed to have one of those, and that one is specifically designed to train and build readiness for the Air Force for air-to-ground or air-to-maritime type of military operations. If you go to Volk Field in Wisconsin, their specialty is air-to-air combat. So each one of the four has a different focus. Ours is air-to-ground, which makes our range complex critically important for that mission set. So again, that Air National Guard presence is Alpena, it's Selfridge, and then it's Battle Creek, and each one has a distinct and different mission set. Battle Creek, I love to talk about Battle Creek purely because as you drive by and you look through the fence, it's this quiet post, few people walking around, doesn't appear to be a whole lot going on, but most of their operations are highly classified, so they are in behind locked doors and windowless buildings, but they fly two combat lines of the MQ-9 Reaper in other parts of the world on any given day. So you have the pilot and the sensor operator sitting in a crew station, much like Oliver and I are sitting here today, where the pilot's flying an aircraft that might be in Africa, and the sensor operator is looking through that sensor and doing whatever mission responsibility they have for that day. So I always kind of paint the picture, and I've witnessed this myself, where the pilot, she's sitting there and she's flying her eight-hour mission, another pilot comes in and they hand controls over, and then she goes home and she picks her kids up from school, feeds them, takes them to soccer, and here she just ran a military combat mission in Africa as an example, right? And that's going on 24-7. It's a constant operation. And they also have cyber responsibilities. They also have an air operations group, which is partnered with the active duty air operations group in Germany. And at key moments, occasionally the Germany air operations group will hand off complete mission command to Battle Creek, and they'll shut down for a time period. So now you have an air operations group in Battle Creek, Michigan, controlling an air operation in the Middle East or in Africa or wherever in Europe. So we have the ability to be that backup and support augmentation to the air operations group in Germany. So for a quiet little post that's kind of inconspicuous, there's some incredible mission sets going on every single day there, and it's quite impressive. So that's the Air National Guard. On the Army National Guard side, again, we have readiness centers in 39 different locations. We do have our two large bases, Camp Grayling, which is up in Grayling, Michigan. That is the single largest reserve component training site in the country. With 148,000 acres for maneuver space. And then we have permitted access to 52,000 additional acres for low-impact training, particularly in jamming, spoofing, drone communications type stuff. So it's not the big maneuver formations. It's generally smaller units that are using high-tech equipment, such as electronic warfare jamming or cyber tools, to exercise one another, do combat in the electromagnetic spectrum sphere. So we do have that access. So sometimes we talk about 200,000 acres, but it's really 148,000 acres of maneuver space and then 52,000 acres for that.

low impact, low presence, training responsibility. So that's Camp Grayling. And then we have Fort Custer down in the Battle Creek area, which is a very well-developed facility with a lot of flat ranges. We do our formal educational things there. We have our officer candidate school and other things that happen at Fort Custer. And then the remaining communities are what's called readiness centers, or if you're of my age, I used to call them armories. And that's where units are based out of, and we have them all over the state. Again, about 39 other locations, we have Army Guard readiness centers. So very much community-based. And I apologize how long I painted that picture, but I think it's important for people to realize, number one, we're community-based. Number two, we are throughout the state of Michigan. We have members from every county most times. And then we do have some very large footprints that are critical parts of key communities across our state and big economic drivers for that location. So I wanted to spend a little bit of time on that. I now want to jump over and talk a little bit about operations and operational tempo. And if you're not familiar with that term, operational tempo, that's just the pace at which we're regularly doing training events or we're doing military operations. And I think unless you have a member in the National Guard, you probably don't appreciate as an individual how many things are going on at any given time. And throughout the year, this year in particular, right now as we speak, we have close to 1,100 members of the Michigan National Guard not serving in Michigan but serving elsewhere. 700 of those, roughly, it's 698 to be exact, but I'll round off. 700 are overseas, and they're conducting combat missions in Europe or the Middle East or in Africa. They're actually in 17 different countries as we speak right now. So we have 700 members of the Michigan National Guard doing military operations in 17 different countries across the globe. Simultaneously, we have over 400 that are doing operations in the United States somewhere. We have units on the southwest border, and we've had units there ever since the end of 2019, beginning of 2020. And periodically, they go in and come out, and that's part of that federal response. So we'll get a notification of sourcing through the Department of War that says this unit is needed for this mission, and here's their date to report, and that's where we start to prep and plan and train for their departure. And occasionally, you'll see departure ceremonies when units go overseas. If they go to the southwest border, they're typically there. Boots on ground is our reference. They're boots on ground for a full year, so their total mobilization could be 13 to 14 months, depending on how much time to get them ready and then take them off orders. If you go overseas, you're typically boots on ground for nine months, so it's about a year-long total deployment now. As we start to ramp up, put them on orders, ramp them, prepare them, and then ship them overseas, and then they're boots on ground nine months, and then they come home, and they have roughly a month to come off of orders and take care of any medical or any other issues that they need to. So there's an incredible operational tempo. It's very normal for us at any given day to have about 1,000 people on orders, federal orders, doing a federal mission somewhere in the world. That is very normal for us. We've been closer to 2,000 at times. We've been a little bit less, but if I had to pick an average number, it's right around that 1,000 number. So constant operations going on, constant units departing Michigan and then coming back to Michigan. So we have a very busy operational tempo for that. Given our priority for wartime training and wartime readiness, we do a lot of exercises throughout the year, a lot of training events throughout the year. One of our largest marquee events, training events, is Northern Strike. And many of you, maybe some of you have been up there. I know some of you have been up there, and you're always welcome. Every year we put out an invitation to our legislators to come up and see the training that's going on. It's quite impressive, and it's one of a kind in the country, and it's one of a kind for a couple reasons. First and foremost is our training environment here in Michigan is unmatched anywhere in the country. We have all five warfighting domains present in the same geographic location. And I'll just briefly describe them. So you have the standard land operations, air operations, and maritime operations. And then we can also do space operations, and we work with companies, many of them from Michigan, that do fly satellites or operate satellites, and we'll integrate those satellites into our training experience during our exercises. And then we also, because of the electromagnetic spectrum and the low density of residential or commercial enterprises in that area, we can do jamming, active jamming of our systems and compete in that electromagnetic spectrum. So if you really think what you see in the news in Iraq, I mean in Ukraine, I mean with Ukraine and Russia with the drone and the jamming and all of that kind of stuff, we can do that at scale in our training environment, which is very unique. But the fact that we can do maritime operations in Lake Huron, we have range complex in the middle of Lake Huron, it's all covered by 17,000 square miles of military use airspace. And then underneath that airspace bubble is not only Lake Huron training environment, but also Camp Grayling. So we can do land, air, maritime simultaneously with space assets, and we can do the active jamming that we have to. So we can replicate very high-end military environments that we would only witness or see in active combat. We can replicate that here in Michigan, which makes Michigan very prominent and recognized for that specialty and expertise. And because of that, we can hold these large exercises like Northern Strike. And this past year we had 7,800 people participate. They came from 35 different states in the Union. We had active duty, Guard, Reserve across all components, talking Marines, Navy, Air Force, Army, and even the Coast Guard. And then we had 10 nations with international soldiers serving here with us. So it's that ability to bring in a multinational force, train together in a live fire training exercise, and be able to do the full suite of military environments and training experiences necessary to prepare our women and men for combat. And I want to emphasize that again, because we have a professional obligation. I have a professional obligation to ensure every Michigander that puts that uniform on is ready for the worst day. So that realistic training, complex training, exposing them to all of the latest technologies, exposing them to the friction of combat at that scale is critical for their survival on the future battlefield. And that's something we take very personally. That's something we, again, we have a professional obligation not just to the members who have volunteered to be part of our military here in Michigan, but also to their families. So that's something we do not compromise, and it's something I never apologize for. And even when I have people of different opinions who may not really appreciate that or value that the way I do, or local communities who just don't like that disruption in their neighborhood, I just don't want to be tone deaf to it, and we go out of our way to appease and make sure we have empathy toward the local community. But at the end of the day, we can't explain why we didn't properly train our women and men for combat. There is no do-over when you fail to do that. So that has to be the primary purpose of everything we do. And these large-scale exercises are critical for that. And sometimes we very actively recruit industry to be part of our exercises because they bring the latest and greatest technology to our exercise. And, again, our men and women get to experience that firsthand. They get exposed to technologies in our training that they won't see until they're deployed and in combat in the future. So that relationship with industry is critically important. I'm not looking to make an industry profitable. I'm not looking to make them successful or satisfy their shareholders. I am so selfish about the men and women in uniform and making sure that they have the best of the best and that they get to experience the latest and greatest technologies available that they will only see when they're activated and deployed. So we work very aggressively to get after...

And that takes us to the first chart I had provided to you. It's the layers of the northern strike readiness exercise. And if you look at it just from the bottom, work from the bottom up, it's that collective training. It's building readiness at the individual and team level and making sure that they are proficient in their military specialty. And then as you move up, it gets into the joint fires. And now this is how you get all the different units integrating together across Army and Air. And you have that precision ability to control and coordinate the military operations across many different formations. Then you get up in the next level, which is the joint all-domain command and control. It's the ability of a commander to be able to see accurately all of those formations across many services, even across different nations, and be able to coordinate those actions to be successful against an armed opponent. And that's that joint all-domain command and control. And then we get up to the international. We never go to war alone. We always go as a coalition force. There's always one or two or three or 50 different countries on the battlefield with us. And it's so important that we work very closely with allies in peacetime, in training environments, so that we are prepared to effectively interoperate in a combat environment. So having that interagency and international participation is critical. And then you get up to the top block, which is that industry and technology piece. And I explained that briefly already about making sure we are seeing the latest and greatest technologies when we should be seeing them, which is in training. So that's kind of where I wanted to stop there and focus on that northern strike. Now, in addition to northern strike, we have four other national level exercises that are going to be playing out here in Michigan this coming year. One is Vigilant Guard. That's with NORAD Northcom. A lot of people only hear of NORAD Northcom when they're following Santa Claus on Christmas Eve type of thing on TV, right? But NORAD Northcom is responsible for tracking any threat to the homeland. So they are constantly watching for any type of missile launch, any type of activity that would be a potential threat. And 24-7, they have people on watch, watching radars, watching satellite feeds, making sure that we know exactly what any potential adversary is doing on any given moment of any given day so that we are not caught off guard or surprised. That's what NORAD Northcom does. We are partnered with them for Vigilant Guard, which is a homeland defense exercise that we layer in. This past year, we did it over our annual training exercise in June. This coming year, we're going to nest it more closely with northern strike. But that high level homeland defense of the nation, that exercise plays out right here in Michigan. There's Sage Eagle. There's Bold Quest. There's Evasive Warrior. These are all readiness building exercises for different services, Air Force in many cases. Bold Quest is actually a multinational, I'll call it a problems solving exercise, where many nations come together with a common challenge. It might be an interoperability of different systems, and they work collectively in that exercise to look at technical solutions or other things that would help mitigate the problems they have interoperating in a multinational event. Last year, it was held in Virginia. This year, it's coming to Michigan, and it's going to be conducted here in Michigan. So I share that not to get into the specifics of each one, but I share it to say Michigan has a differential advantage. We have one asset that no one else has, and that's a training environment that allows you to operate across all five of the domains I described earlier at a high level of warfighting competency and really helping the United States and its allies figure out how to be more effective and more efficient in the future. And hopefully deter any adversary actions. Ultimately, our goal is to avoid an armed conflict, not wish for one. That is the last thing we want. So that deterrence is a key part, and the more ready we are, the more difficult we are as an adversary, the less likely an opponent is going to start something with us. So it's really something Michiganders should be proud of. Most Michiganders are incredibly patriotic. They're very committed to the defense of our nation and the priority of our freedoms. And this is something that they should be proud of and value and cherish. So that's a little bit on the operations and the op tempo. I do want to be conscious of the time also because I could eat up the whole hour and not give you a chance to even say a word. But Oliver will try to keep me in check here. Right, Oliver? Okay, if you get tired of me talking, you're going to poke me? Okay, good job. All right, so let me talk briefly about some vulnerabilities. There are key vulnerabilities when we think about homeland defense. And first and foremost, we believe we're going to be contested in the next large-scale conflict. We will be attacked here at home as a precursor to an armed conflict elsewhere. It'll come in the form of a cyber attack. It'll come in the form of disruption of our daily lives. They will try to prevent us from getting from our homes, from a military perspective, to our ports of debarkation and into the theater in which we have to fight. We believe we will be contested throughout that entire chain. So what we try to do, again, is think through how could they disrupt our ability to form our units, move to a mobilization site, and then deploy. Vigilant Guard is one of those exercises that looks closely at that. But as we start to look at what could disrupt us, of course, cyber. People have been talking about the cyber risks, and we see that play out in our schools, in our hospitals, any given day, right? If you're really paying attention to what's going on just here in Michigan, there are communities and hospitals and schools that get cyber attacked on a pretty routine basis. And that response through the Michigan State Police with our DTMB cyber professionals, and if necessary, we have cyber professionals who can help organizations recover very quickly. But the diligence and being resilient is key on the front end, but then the quick recovery is key on the back end. There are a couple other risks that I want to just highlight. One is the timing. We are very, very dependent on GPS timing. Our communication devices work on GPS timing that are fed from satellites. And I think the ultimate authority comes from a Navy site that feeds the satellites and makes sure everybody is tracking very, very precise timing. It's key to our financial transactions. It's key to our critical infrastructure. It's key to our utilities. It's key to our communications, our self-driving cars, our aids, the MapQuest or whatever you use in your car to guide you on navigation. Just from the daily kind of things we've become used to, all the way down to critical financial services and hospital systems and everything that depends on that exact timing for a transaction, that can be disruptive by somebody jamming it or an attack on the satellite constellation in low Earth orbit that provides that service. It would be a massive disruption to our quality of life and our ability to function. And again, if we can no longer have dependable financing, just trying to do our financial transaction and ensure that order of business, that is a critical vulnerability, that GPS timing. There is a program that has been explored and is in a pilot state called NITRO, N-I-T-R-O, and I won't try to remember what the acronym stands for. But it's Project NITRO. The National Guard has rolled it out in 10 different states at a small demonstration level. And what this provides is timing, assured timing, as a backup to that satellite constellation that everybody's dependent upon. And then the critical infrastructure across those regions and those states then tie into that as a backup for resilience and recovery if anything were to happen with the primary signal. If you look at one of your charts, it's the third one, and it's Project NITRO. What we've done is we've mapped out what Project NITRO would look like in Michigan if we were to implement it. I'm here to tell you today that if we wait for the federal resources, we won't see it for years and years and years. It's moving very slowly. It's being rolled out in some priority areas with a lot of federal government infrastructure in those areas, and that's the priority. If we were to take this on for Michigan, we've estimated it's $8.5 million for the initial establishment, and then it's another $500,000

in a year to maintain it. And we just showed you the concept for the implementation leveraging the Michigan Public Safety Communication Systems 800 megahertz towers that provide the support to our first responders across the state. If we built on the back of that organization's infrastructure, you could see the green dots on your chart and then the red dots would be kind of the nodes off of that primary node that would exist within readiness centers across. And you could see we could pretty much cover all of the critical infrastructure across Michigan to ensure we had that timing. So, Mr. Chairman, I know that's something you had discussed with me a couple months ago. So I want to just very simply, top level, it could take a much deeper conversation to get into the specifics. But this is our initial estimate of kind of the geographic dispersion and then the cost, again, about $8.5 million initial cost and then about $500,000 a year to maintain if this became a priority for the state of Michigan. And again, for you to, I think, have greater context, I think we would have to dig into the details of how the threat would emerge and how it would disrupt the critical infrastructure. There's approximately 10,000 critical infrastructure locations across Michigan that are all in one form or fashion dependent upon precise timing. So anything from the Sioux Locks to our major utilities to hospital systems to financial banking, all the financial transactions that we depend on. So that is one area. The other one is what I'm going to term, and I'm going to transition to another topic, air domain awareness. A lot of people think of it as drones or counter drones or unmanned air systems and counter unmanned air systems. You hear about it in different ways. This is the drone field is very exciting. Michigan is leaning in very aggressively through our Office of Future Mobility and Electrification. Justine Johnson, if you've met her, she is leading it. We are partnered with her to look at air mobility and really encouraging the growth of drone companies here in Michigan, both manufacturing, but then the operational use of drones. On the other side of it, they can be used as we've seen in Ukraine and they've just seen in Rio de Janeiro with the Brazilian, with the police fighting gangs and the use of drones, armed drones against law enforcement in that city. In response, drones have a nefarious use too. There are thousands of incursions on our southwest border, almost all for ISR type things. They want to know where the border patrol is so they can avoid them. So they're using them for that eyes over the border. There are drone activities that have been reported over the years, people dropping contraband into prisons, over the walls of prisons. So these drones can be used in many, many different ways. But knowing where they're operating, how they're operating, detecting them, tracking them, identifying them, and then attributing them to somebody is key to being able to interdict a drone operation. And the only way to do that is to have an active ability to track drone usage. Now let me, that's the nefarious side. On the operational side, for good purposes, for FAA requirements, you either have to have a set of eyeballs watching the drone in flight, which means if you're going a long distance, you need a chase aircraft that follows the drone to meet FAA requirements. Or you have to instrument the airspace so that you are always tracking and you have redundancy of tracking those UAVs or drones in flight. So if we ever hope to get to a point where the drone capabilities for Michigan turn into an economic boom, we have to solve the beyond visual line of sight problem, which means we have to instrument with radar systems and other technologies, our airspace to be able to track all flying drones. So that's something we definitely have to take a look at. I think the first state to solve that air domain awareness will have an incredible economic bump as people flock there, because package delivery, FedEx, whatever, name the company, medical supplies, blood going to different places. If you're using a drone, you either have to have a chase aircraft right now, or you have to have some technical means of tracking those aircraft. And so the person who can solve that, and that's where we're working very closely with Justine Johnson in the Office of Future Mobility and Electrification and MEDC and the Michigan Department of Transportation Aeronautics Organization. So it's an all of government approach looking at what's possible. But that's something that I know she has laid out in her priorities for resourcing. But there's a vulnerability on the nefarious side and being able to track drone use, especially around airfields and airports, or around key infrastructure like sports stadiums, that kind of thing. So there's a purpose to know what's flying and where it's coming from and what it's up to. But then also for the positive economic use of drones, that the same technology, same capability would be of use. So I talked about two vulnerabilities there, the GPS timing and then the drone, the nefarious use of drone technologies, but then things we can possibly do as a state to counter it. So I do want to pause there. I've taken up a large amount of your time. I've tried to get after several of the topics you've brought up to me in the past, but I do want to afford you and the committee time to bring up special topics or dig deeper on any of these topics. So thank you for your patience. Thank you, sir. Very thorough. How'd he do, Oliver? He did all right. All right, he did all right. We'll see about getting an award for that one, right? We'll put him in for something. No, I appreciate you bringing up the nitro. That really is a very important thing that we're going to be focusing on moving forward. And certainly you talked readiness, you talked a lot of the response, and then there's reactivity. You didn't touch on that a whole lot on the reactivity portion, which there will probably be some questions, or I'll have some questions regarding that. As far as, you know, it's good to see, because I deployed in 2003, my first combat tour as a reservist, and vast disparity between reserve and active duty. I mean, it wasn't even close. The uniforms we wore to the radios we used to the equipment we had, the vehicles, the weapon systems we had to the night vision. You know, everything was two, three generations past, you know, in our arsenal versus active duty. And, you know, when I was up at Northern Strike this summer, you know, it's awesome to see that National Guard Reserve troops are getting the exact same thing that our troops being deployed have already on the active duty side. So, you know, that speaks volumes for what you and your folks are doing for your units at the state level. You know, but it also shows a difference what the war on terror has done, you know, on the federal side, looking at how are we providing for those troops we really, really, really do depend on. You didn't hit on the combat. So you have combat troops, and then you have logistical troops, and National Guard historically is combat arms, and reserve side are more your logistics, although there's certainly both in each of those. But just for the record, National Guard combat arms, primarily, reserve, generally logistics support, et cetera, when they're actually activated. And it's always good to know or to point out. We do have a number of questions, and I don't want to ask all mine because they might ask them as well. So I'm going to go to Representative Meerman to begin. Thank you, Chair. I guess what you're finishing, I mean, I got a whole list of questions, but I'll just ask a couple. Towards the end there, you were talking about the air domain awareness, and I guess I wasn't quite clear. I suppose part of it is we're still trying to figure out what it takes to have the air domain awareness, but from a legislative perspective, is there something you're suggesting to us? Yes, and thank you for that question. I didn't do it justice. I think it's a focused discussion around what the state of Michigan could do to really incentivize drone activation from an economic perspective, but then also protect critical infrastructure from, again, what I termed as nefarious drone use. You know, I think legislatively, I don't know of any hurdles that limits from a state level. I don't know of any hurdles that limit the activation of our airspace for drone operations. What

Truly is the limiting factor is to have a system of technology, radar-based technology, where we can track, accurately track unmanned or uncrewed system flight. And that's critically important. In fact, it's an imperative for FAA to approve the use of drones in any airspace. We have to be able to see them clearly, understand who it is, where they're going, and be able to communicate with manned aircraft so that there isn't a conflict in the same airspace. So being able to control airspace, know everything that's flying in that airspace so that you can deconflict with other aircraft systems, whether it's commercial or private pilots that are flying around. So again, today the only true accepted solution is that either you're on the ground and you can always see that drone that you're flying, or you are chasing it with a manned airplane. And that's the way we have to operate if we go long distances right now. We have the drone flying, and then we'll have the civil air patrol or we'll have somebody in a small aircraft following that drone. So you're always seeing the drone and you're making sure nothing else is in the same airspace. So there's a technical solution to get past that. There's a long process with the FAA to have that technical solution approved. We've worked with Justine Johnson and in the Office of Future Mobility and Electrification. We've worked with MEDC and the MDOT Aeronautics folks to lay out what we believe that solution could be. So now the biggest thing is that there is a financial ask to start to implement that. And I would encourage it to be implemented up north between Traverse City and Alpena in a corridor that we've already worked with partners to establish. But then as we gain approval for that system, expand it to cover the entire Michigan airspace. And by doing that, you'd be the first in the nation to get after it. But it does take resources. And the bottom line is it's money that gets us off the ground and really gets that built out into a meaningful way. So I hope I answered your question. Yeah, thank you. We had a situation we read about in the papers. I'm not asking for information that we don't want out there in public, but Chinese students were caught trying to leave the country. And it was my understanding, at least by news reports, Camp Grayling was the target. I'm sure that's something that's internally been worked on and trying to keep that from happening. But it sure seemed like it was a foreign country trying to gather data on us and one of our friendly nations. To me, that's pretty concerning, as I'm sure it is to you too. Yes, sir. And the People's Republic of China are very active in their information gathering, intelligence collection. Really, you see it through businesses. You see it through military sites, training. It's not uncommon. It's actually, I'd almost say it's pretty routine for Chinese nationals, PRC, People's Republic of China nationals to be tasked to go somewhere and actively try to get onto a base, a military base, try to gain entry into a restricted area. And if they get entry to collect certain pieces of information, whatever it may be of interest. But it's fairly routine and well established that this is an active, ongoing, I'll use the word operation on their part. We were very forward thinking here in Michigan where we've worked with federal agencies and state and local agencies. And we actually established a process for tracking activities. And that's how we were able to detect those five individuals in the course of trying to collect on training that was going on up at Grayling. And it was through those channels that ultimately fed back to an FBI investigation that identified them by name and then worked through the legal system to put warrants out for them. And they all fled the country. Two or three of the individuals were supposed to go to another university for an advanced degree. And of course that was stopped and they had to flee the country to avoid arrest. But that is one example. It's very prominent because it turned into a legal action by the Justice Department. But this is not unusual. It's happening everywhere. And I think folks would probably be a little shocked to see how frequent it's going on. I would assume that in some cases they're just trying to use volume to get information. And I suppose in other cases it's pretty targeted. And, you know, specialists, someone that's trained in it. You know, if you throw enough at the wall, maybe some of it sticks. Maybe they get some pictures back they want. Maybe all of the above. I mean, is that what you see them trying to do? I think that's probably a fair characterization. I would avoid any assertion that I'm seeing or hearing about everything that's going on. I'm privy to a few things. Definitely things that happen within Michigan that entail my or department presence here in Michigan. A year ago we had two individuals show up at the gate at Selfridge Air National Guard Base. They wanted to go and visit the museum. And they were both PRC nationals. And they got turned away by the guards there because they're not allowed to have access. That alone is like, okay, well, that could happen. You know, if somebody likes military aircraft and they want to show up somewhere. But the fact that those same two individuals showed up three days later at the same gate hoping to find a guard that would not be doing their due diligence and tried to gain access again using the exact same excuse. It's a constant probing. And it's a little cat and mouse. And they're not breaking any laws, right? So there's nothing that can be done about it. But you know it's not with good intent. So when you do find somebody who's been in the wrong place at the wrong time and has photos on a camera, and that's those five students, and they're able to show that they had collected some information they weren't supposed to and they were where they weren't supposed to be, that's what really was the underpinning of the legal investigation that played out there. Thank you. Yeah, I'd say those guards deserve an AAM, by the way, okay? Put that in retroactive. We do have a very – I'd say it's probably the most comprehensive drone package in any state right now that we are putting in. And we are identifying MDOT Aeronautics as that catalyst for aeronautical drone tracking, drone regulation. So that's one of the bills in the 14-bill set that we are actually having a press conference tomorrow morning about. But we're getting those in. I had one question before I'm going to go to Minority Vice Chair Menser. But the difference, you know, people – we've been talking drones a lot in this committee and cybersecurity, and I would certainly welcome and love to have your cybersecurity experts here at some point because we're going to be delving into cyber as well. But on drones, people look at drones or they say drones are this benign and, you know, China, for instance, we'll say the People's Republic of China, you know, they can get all the information they want from a satellite picture, et cetera, et cetera. Drones don't give them any more. But could you just give us maybe just a little of the threat or the concern with, you know, a drone physically flying over, you know, sensitive sites versus, you know, a satellite that can see whatever it wants whenever it wants from, you know, hundreds of thousands of feet up? So can you just kind of give us – like put that threat in perspective slightly, sir? I'll try. I think first for me, what jumps to mind first is the drone itself is not the issue. It's the intent of the operator of the drone, of course. It was inherent in the way you asked the question. So attributing drone operation to the individual who's controlling it and then understanding what they were really trying to do is critical. And that attribution is hard. And again, we have examples fairly routine of drones flying over our military locations, and you detect them and you start tracking them, but then they disappear and you never knew who was operating it. So you never get that closure. Was this just somebody out messing around and thought, hey, let's go look at this building over here not even thinking what they were doing? Or was somebody intentionally going to that location for the intent of collecting high-quality imagery of it?

So it's really hard to understand the intent of the operator unless you can capture the operator and have that interrogation, discussion, investigation with them. But the drone operations, we can see how they can be used in very unlawful ways and very malicious ways, and we see that around the world. I think it's the incident that I worry about is around airfields and the inadvertent collision of a drone with a manned aircraft or a commercial aircraft or something like that. And too often we're seeing drone operations around airfields for whatever reason. But again, without knowing the intent of the operator, it's hard to attribute what they're really up to. So I'm not answering your question, but I'm not sure there is a clean answer in my mind at this point. Well, we appreciate that. I'm going to go to Representative Menser. So this is a pretty exciting conversation. I think I love you. So I have a resolution coming out that will be hitting the floor today to prevent the early retirement of the A-10 Warthogs at Selfridge. Selfridge must, must remain a viable base here in southeast Michigan. It is very important. I think that it will be longer than we anticipate before we get those F-15EX Eagle 2s. So the early retirement of the Warthogs is not going to help us at all. And so hopefully all of my colleagues, and I'm just going to hand it to you right now and you can just sign the back. That's how you do it. Pass it to Meerman and Wozniak. But one of the things that I'm looking at is we've had some amazing presentations on drones. And more and more companies, because southeast Michigan is known as, Mark Hackle calls it the arsenal of democracy. We have more and more aerospace and defense industries coming into this area of Michigan. Vicki Rowinski from the McComb County Department of Planning and Economic Development and I met with a young man from a company called Westwood AI. He's over in the west part of the state. But we brought him over here to the Mount Clemens area to talk about what we could come up with for him to bring that drone company into the arsenal of democracy. He needed 90,000 square foot facility and 10 acres for his drones. So hopefully that will be something that's coming soon. But as we talk about drones and drones become more popular and other unmanned vehicles, when I was at Northern Strike, we saw so many incredible things. And it's not just drones in the air, but the equipment we saw on the ground. And I apologize, I don't know what to call it, but we watched a vehicle that was unmanned go out into the field to pick up supposed injured or wounded soldiers and bring them back, all completely unmanned. So the advances that are being made are just absolutely incredible. But just last week we had a presentation on EMP mitigation devices. So you see how we're transitioning from planes or fighter jets to drones and now we're talking EMPs. And so the whole manner of warfare is changing so drastically and so rapidly. And I am concerned that we're not keeping up, that we have gaps that we don't know about that either need funding or need legislation or need research and development for the research and development. So as you were talking, it's been in the news in the last couple of days of people flying drones over major airfields. There was one in London where they shut the whole airport down for several hours. That's happening here more and more. So what can we do as a defense for these drones, these hobbyists that get out there and they're having fun, to jam them, to protect us against them? And how do we advance the EMP mitigation devices? Because I think that's the next wave of warfare that's coming. Thank you for that question. And it's a great question. I can probably go in eight different directions with it. So I won't be satisfied with my answer no matter how I answer it at this point. But I think the drone operation over airfields, that goes back to that air domain awareness. We have to know it's there first or we have to see it coming so that we can deal with it. And then if you can track it back to the operator, then you can get after what was their intent. And what were they doing to deliberately disrupt airfield operations or something else or just reckless? What was their true intent? So that air domain awareness is key. Detecting a drone, tracking it, hopefully identifying it, but then ultimately knowing who the operator is. And that's where that investment into that airspace monitoring is key. And I'm happy to hear that there's going to be additional support and resources going through MDOT aeronautical. And again, hopefully with Justine Johnson, OFME and that organization and that all of government collaboration, I think we can get after some incredible solutions. I'm not a fan of these local drone parks that they call them where they just create this small piece of airspace for drone operations because it doesn't do anything to get after the challenge that you just described. But if we have the ability to see our airspace in three dimensions and be able to track it and build it out across major geographic areas, we will not only be first of a kind in the nation to do that, but we will have a unique ability to track drone operations or encourage drone development. And I think you'll see more and more companies flocking to Michigan because they would have that ability to operate in that space. So that's one aspect of what you brought up. The other, the electromagnetic pulse threat and the ability, anything with electronics, if it's not properly shielded, can be through an EMP, a pulse can be damaged, destroyed, and disrupt the function of whatever it is that's ongoing. Presuming it's a localized effect that somebody would implement, then that would have significant impacts to wherever it's being operated. There have been concepts in the past of like an EMP detonation in low Earth orbit that would take out all satellite systems. So it's been a concern, a threat, a capability that's been discussed for a number of years. But I think as technology matures and advances, the ability to implement it in smaller scale by non-state actors becomes greater. And it's something we have to track. And to a bigger context, it's these types of things, not EMP in particular, but why it's so important to bring industries in who are developing these latest technologies and make sure that the women and men who are training for combat are being exposed to what these things are, how they operate, their effectiveness, how to mitigate them, how to protect again, how to overcome, or how to use them for their own benefit and advantage over an armed opponent. So integrating technologies and making sure that we have them readily available is key. And I think germane to what you said, and I know I'm hitting like five different things here, but the next thread germane to what you said is technology is changing so fast that if you turn around and you invest a whole bunch of money into one solution, by the time you acquire that and field it, it might be outdated. So that's why the dynamic nature in which we're encouraging industry to come here and train with us and demonstrate their capabilities with us, we are seeing it real time, we're experiencing it, but we're not investing in something that may end up being outdated sooner rather than later. So again, probably didn't do your question justice, but I just wanted to touch on a couple of the threads that were buried in it. No, that was very helpful. And I'll tell you one of the things that has concerned me a little bit, we see drones everywhere now. Hobby people, police departments have them, fire departments now have them. Of course, you've got military uses of drones. When does there need to be a cutoff? Do we stop selling hobby drones? I mean, I'm thinking that we can become overwhelmed

As people are fascinated by these pieces of equipment and they buy more and more and we get them for legitimate uses like fire departments and police departments, I think our airspace will be full pretty soon. So how do we fix that? How do we stop that? Well, I look at the problem and avoid your question by saying something different, but I see it a little bit differently. Right now, China, PRC, produces 10 million drones a year. And they produce them at a price point, $300 to $500 that they sell that you can go to Walmart or wherever and buy it or online. The US in total, I think it was maybe 100,000, the number I heard, production that we produce per year. And the cheapest ones are about $1,500. I think that's the biggest concern to me. Because if we ever get into a conflict, who has the manufacturing base and the ability to produce at scale a weaponized drone? It's clearly not the US at this point. And it comes down to can we scale? So what I would rather approach is to encourage US drone manufacturers to scale up, to restrict the sale possibly of drones that we know have embedded capability to take all that imagery you're collecting around town and upload it to a server that ends up in an adversary's server farm. So as you're using, and the classic one is the DJI drone. The US military does not allow those things to operate anywhere near our facilities because that feed sends its data. It's possible that feed is being sent back to a server somewhere in the People's Republic of China. And now they have all that firsthand ground truth of what exists and what doesn't exist. So I would rather encourage a million drones being manufactured by US operator or drone companies and selling in the US. And that would bring the price point down and it would be something that we would have then some purview or oversight of how the information is being used. And if you look at DJI's website right now, it states that they are no longer able to sell to the United States of America. Yes, and we had DJI in here a few weeks back. Yeah, very interesting as well. I have a couple. Yeah, we have a little time. I know I was supposed to be out of here early, but it is what it is. We get the general here. So Representative Wise. Thank you, Mr. Chair. These are softball questions. What type of rifle is the rifle of choice in the Guard? So the M4 is the rifle that's issued now. They do have a new, that's a 5.56 millimeter firearm. They do have a new 6.8 millimeter firearm under development that's starting to get fielded. I think our first units will start to see them this coming year, I believe, but predominantly going active duty first. And as far as the membership of the Guard, are they all Michigan residents? No, they're not. We do attract some folks from neighboring states. And then based on specialty, like on the Army side, the explosive ordnance detachment, it's such a unique specialty. We've had people traveling as far as Virginia or California who wanted to be part of that unit with that explosive ordnance detachment expertise. On the Air Guard side, you have pilots, you have maintainers, you have folks who are in that aviation profession in their civilian career who it's not uncommon to have them traveling to Michigan for their weekend drill performance. So we'll take high quality talent from wherever it goes. But again, being a Michigan-based, community-based organization, we really strive to recruit from our local communities. Do you have any affiliation with the Space Force or do you anticipate that happening in the future? We do not have any. We did not have any Space Guard units. Ohio was the closest one, Alaska. There was seven different Colorado, seven different states that had Space National Guard units. They've all been dissolved and drawn into the Space Force. Right now, the position of the Department of War and the Space Force is that they will not have a National Guard component to that service. And that's something the National Guard is pressing to establish. I don't know if we'll be successful or not. There's legislative opposition to it at this point. Last question is whether or not, you probably can't answer this one, are you anticipating any action in Detroit? No, no. First and foremost, I think we have great law enforcement across Michigan, very professional. The city of Detroit has done a phenomenal job over recent years. And again, I'm not steeped in it. I'm not there engaging on every topic. And then the state police here is world class. I mean, they're recognized. You go to other states and Michigan State Police is recognized for their professionalism. So I really look to the law enforcement professionals to handle any challenges that Michigan may have. And we are always there to support if the need is there and if the governor directs us to. But I see no need for it in Michigan at all. Thank you for coming in today. Thank you, Representative. And yes, we did get that PA signed that we were all, I think, supportive of the Michigan Guard being able to utilize those fundings to help with your readiness and your soldiers that, you know, whether it's the health care issue or the child care on the weekends as well. The question of the regional drone centers, and there's been some conversation, there's going to be three areas, three locations in the U.S. and CONUS that are picked from the federal level that identify, you know, drone capable drone centers of expertise. And my understanding is that Michigan is in that running. Is that your understanding or can you expound on that at all? So, yeah, for context for others that may not be tracking it, you know, Secretary Hegseth announced that the Department of War will be identifying three key locations initially at least where they can do drone development testing to get after that quickly expanding capability that we need. So, of course, with our unique training asset up north and that immense airspace and our ability to conduct operations in many seasons across water or air, you know, ground, all of it, and be able to jam and do all the different types of testing, we are uniquely positioned for consideration. So my understanding is the National All-Domain Warfighting Center, in particular the Grayling, as the key location is being considered. That is in the running. Again, everything I get is kind of secondhand. It's hard. It's a little murky to see a decision-making process and understand exactly what's going on. But there's a half a dozen or so locations around the country, and I believe I've been led to believe that Michigan is one of those locations. That's awesome to hear, and we certainly look forward to, you know, it's not a matter of when or if low-orbiting satellites are taken out at some point. It's a matter of, you know, when. I truly do believe in the EMP that we had here last year, that discussion. You know, there's just so many things that hopefully, you know, position Michigan, and we can get on the right track, and manufacturing, we want it here in Michigan, but we definitely want to be the tip of the spear when it comes to drone and counter drone and just that whole enveloping, that air mobility space. My last question for you, you know, it's already been asked, you know, what can we do, and I know there will be some conversations afterwards, and we are working on a lot of things that hopefully help you and your folks, but what keeps you up at night? What wakes you up at night in your position that you wouldn't mind sharing with us? Yeah, you know, I got to admit I sleep pretty well. I got an amazing group of people in my organization, and they are just completely committed to their fellow men and women in uniform and veterans alike, too. I didn't spend a lot of time talking about the veteran stuff we do. I've got an amazing team of professionals, so I have the ability to sleep at night knowing that they've kind of got control over their area of responsibility, and they're doing great work with the team that they control. So I think from that vantage point, I'm probably a little spoiled. I think the things that do wake me up, I'm very competitive. I want Michigan to win. I want us to win day in and day out.

Again, just like getting fighters, it's Elfridge. I mean, that was an ongoing battle for years, and to finally get that accomplished, and not letting our guard down until they're flying in Michigan. But we need to be competitive, and we need to be at the forefront, and we need to be thought leaders, and we can't be responsive and waiting for opportunities to be offered up. What I've discovered in my career, that as soon as an opportunity becomes public, it has already been decided. And you might submit a competitive package, you might be led down this thing thinking that it's actually a decision to come. They're almost always preordained. So it's about being ahead of people, being at the table, being in conversations, doing our due diligence to make sure that we understand what's coming next and the opportunities that are inherent in what's coming next. And that's where I think it's about competitive advantage, differential advantage. What can we do today not to chase the opportunity that's here today, but to shape our opportunities of the future? And I think that's key, and that's why we work so closely with the Michigan Economic Development Corporation. I think this air domain awareness, you solve that problem, you have solved the problem nobody else has a solution to. And you just incentivize every drone manufacturer to come to Michigan because now they can operate in a safe, effective way without constraints. That's key. I think Project Nitro again, again human nature tells us that there will be a future war. We can hope for the best, but it always materializes in one form or fashion. And I believe these new technologies that we've been hinting to and discussing here today are going to be at the forefront of it. And it's all about disrupting the U.S.'s ability to take its military force overseas to fight the conflict. And they will cause chaos and confusion and friction here at home so that we can't respond in the way that we desire. And that's the assured timing. And if you just for a moment think about how disruptive it would be if all your financial institutions were brought to their knees, if all of the utilities stopped functioning as the way they're supposed to, if all the communications stopped working. I mean just think of, imagine that chaos and what that would mean for the average citizen. And then you have to solve that problem before you can even think about going overseas to fight. And so we've got to think about what are these things that we could face and then take some prudent actions ahead of time to set the opportunities in place. Well we really, really appreciate you being here, sir. Thank you for your leadership. Thank you for your foresight, especially when we're talking Grayling, whether it's Battle Creek, whether it's Selfridge or Alpena, and the things that you're doing, especially in this drone and cyber world. Appreciate your leadership and what you're doing for our state. And thank you, sir, for being here. Thank you, Oliver, for sitting through that whole ordeal as well. And thank you for your service. Maybe I didn't say that. Thank you for your service. Well, thank you all and thank you for your patience. I know I can drone on, to use that term. And Oliver, you'll never take an invitation to sit up at this table again, will you? You'll get stuck here. But hopefully one day you'll be wearing a uniform and you'll be the one testifying or sitting up there asking the hard questions, whatever you desire out of life. Made two bad choices in my life. But thank you all. I'm grateful for the time. Thank you. And we have minutes. Where's my paper here? We have to approve the minutes from last week. Representative Menser moves to approve the minutes of October 29th. Hearing no objection, they are approved. And Representative Menser moves to excuse absent members. And there being no further business before the committee, we stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Natural Resources and Tourism — Wednesday, November 5, 2025
transcript:
The House Committee on Natural Resources and Tourism will come to order. Will the clerk please take the attendance? Chair Martin? Here. Representative St. Germain? Here. VanderWaal? Present. Altman? I also want to thank Representative Fairbairn for sponsoring this important bill. In 2019, when Michigan passed Public Act 96, the legislation inadvertently changed the longstanding term limited licensed professional counselor, or LLPC, to limited licensed counselor, or LLC. While this may seem like a minor change, it has created significant and ongoing confusion in our field. For nearly three decades, from 1990 to 2019, Michigan used the LLPC designation. The change to LLC was not intentional. It was an oversight that has had unintended consequences. The abbreviation LLC, as Representative Fairbairn mentioned, is universally recognized as limited liability corporation in business and legal contexts. When our counselors use LLC after their names, it creates confusion among clients seeking mental health services, insurance companies processing claims, other health care providers making referrals, professional credentialing bodies, and the general public. Additionally, Michigan now stands alone in using the LLC terminology. Most of the country recognizes and uses LLPC for this level of professional counselor licensing. This inconsistency creates unnecessary barriers for counselors who are licensed in multiple states and adds confusion to interstate professional recognition. We respectfully ask this committee to support House Bill 4981, which would restore the limited licensed professional counselor, or LLPC, designation. I rise today in support of my bill, House Bill 4929. We live in an age where government at all levels continues to expand. While this expansion is caused by many factors, one such reason is that we have no shortage of unnecessary responsibilities in agencies and departments. My bill identifies an area of unnecessary burden that we can solve with a simple solution. Currently, there is no formal process for a medical professional to voluntarily surrender their medical license or registration with the State of Michigan. This means that even if the licensee knows that they no longer need their license or registration because of retirement, career change, or any number of reasons, there currently isn't a way to surrender it. If we simply create a process for these medical professionals to voluntarily relinquish their licenses, we could save the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs from having unnecessary work. We would clean the license and regulation records within the department, and the department would have fewer people to notify or monitor with issues like continuing education and renewal. So my bill creates an obvious solution. We have created a simple and effective process for the medical professionals to voluntarily surrender their license or registration. We have worked with the Department of Licensing and Regulation Affairs to put safeguards in place to prevent individuals from abusing this process to escape disciplinary action by the department. All in all, this is an obvious way to reduce unnecessary activities and workload, both for medical professionals and for state government. So I urge all my colleagues to vote in favor of House Bill 4929 to help our state government function a little more effectively. I like to call it the great little beautiful bill. I look back and I realize that most of my childhood was actually rooted in grief, losing all my grandparents by the time I was 18 and losing my father at the age of 14. It was actually my 28th year when I realized that I'd spent more time without him than I did with him that I think I really started to maybe actually fully unravel that grief that I grew up with. I think it's most important that we understand that there are people who carry those invisible or unaware scars. I myself still carry those scars. I actually had an interview today where I talked about what it meant to be a child with grief. And I will tell you that to all those kids out there today who don't have the opportunity to be here, to have their voices heard, or who may not be fully processing or aware of their own grief today, it was my grandfather who told me on December 9, 2004, about an hour and a half after my father had died, that it was going to be okay. The U.S. Department of Justice's demand to turn over Michigan voter data directly violates state and federal privacy laws. The federal government has absolutely no authority over voter registration. This resolution is a declaration. This resolution is a declaration. A declaration that the Michigan House of Representatives stands with the Federal Department of Justice. That we stand for election integrity and for clean and accurate voter rolls. And that we stand against lawfare and against the Michigan Secretary of State's refusal to comply with lawful requests from this legislative body and the nation's top law enforcement officer. House Resolution 196, that Michigan's chief election officer Jocelyn Benson execute her statutory duties by releasing an unredacted, I'll say it again, unredacted copy of Michigan's computerized statewide voter registration list, also known as the qualified voter file or the QVF. To do otherwise would be a violation of the Civil Rights Act of 1960. As I shared in my testimony before the Election Integrity Committee, it is inconceivable, even unconscionable, that we find ourselves here. Year after year under Secretary Benson, there have been reports of duplicate ballots and votes cast by deceased Michiganders. It's deeply troubling that Michigan is well behind in removing ineligible voters from our rolls compared to the national average. To ensure safe and secure elections in 2026 and beyond, we must verify that legal citizens of Michigan and only legal citizens of Michigan are eligible to vote. This is not a partisan issue. It's an issue of constitutional responsibility. The DOJ is not requesting this data to exploit it. After all, it's the federal government that gave us our Social Security numbers in the first place. They are simply asking to verify that Michigan's voter rolls are accurate, current, and compliant with federal standards. We must decide what is more dangerous, ensuring that our voter rolls are accurate or allowing who knows how many ineligible voters on our rolls under the quote-unquote guise of privacy. If we allow our chief election officer to defy lawful federal requests, we set a dangerous precedent. We risk eroding the very foundation of our election process. We risk telling the people of Michigan that transparency and accountability are optional. This resolution, again, is a declaration that the Michigan House of Representatives stands with the Department of Justice and its federal jurisdiction in upholding the rule of law, combating voter fraud, demanding transparency and accountability in Michigan's election processes. If, and I say if, there's nothing wrong with the qualified voter file, there should be nothing to hide. So I ask, what reason could there be to withhold this information from the people and from federal law enforcement? The people of Michigan deserve to know that their elections are secure, that their votes are protected, and that their leaders accept responsibility. So, colleagues, let us stand with the DOJ, the Federal Department of Justice, and stand for the integrity of our election processes. Thank you, Madam Speaker. is covered in that particular guidelines. It gives very specific guidance in terms of how do we add these services in the school setting.
