This is not my typical day job, but I appreciate you hearing my perspective. My name is Kelly Rogers. I am a school psychologist and a board-certified behavior analyst, and I am licensed in Michigan as a behavior analyst. For many years, I served as an autism education and intervention specialist for the Statewide Autism Resources and Training Project at Grand Valley State University, and I currently serve as a special education coordinator at Char-MISD up in the beautiful neck of Michigan in Charlevoix. My roles include IEP and IDEA monitoring and support, but I also coordinate the implementation of our trauma-presumed and neuroaffirming positive behavioral interventions and supports, often called PBIS, and our ABA, or Applied Behavioral Analysis in Schools, model. I also serve in numerous leadership roles and have over the years with statewide organizations such as MACE and have presented extensively on the implementation of evidence-based practices for students with disabilities in schools, including school-based ABA and IEP, ABA-informed IEPs. For nearly three decades, I've dedicated my career to helping schools build the internal capacity to educate and support our most vulnerable students, especially those with complex behavioral and developmental needs, so they can access school and make educational progress alongside their peers. So while I share the same goal as the sponsors of this bill, as a school professional, I also hold a responsibility to implement interventions and supports, including ABA, and address barriers to that implementation in a manner that aligns with the legal, ethical, and methodological obligations under IDEA. In the last several years, we've been responding to the growing needs of students with complex barriers to learning, specifically related to ABA, and Eric referred to this, the Michigan Department of Education and the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services released comprehensive guidelines for the provision of ABA in public schools last spring. I believe you have a copy in front of you in the packet. It looks like this. And so if you glance at that document in pages 1 and 2, you will see the list of topics that are covered, which Eric referred to, that address many of the issues that have been brought forth that perhaps the bill is bringing forth. And also if you look at page 3, you will see all the contributors that were part of the development of this guidelines, which includes educators, administrators, and ABA providers. In total, this guidance provides a roadmap to ensure access to needed interventions in school while balancing and aligning services with federal and state law, which Eric was referring to, that conflict with IDEA. However, since the distribution of this document occurred just last spring, schools really haven't had sufficient time to review the guidance, look at their own policies, and make adjustments as needed. I'd like to highlight two central themes that are also in the guidance. First, the critical role of the IEP or the Individualized Education Program process. Under IDEA, the IEP process is the tool by which IEP teams identify a student's needs that impact their access and progress in school and in general education and outline the supports and services that they need that are required for what we call FAPE or Free Appropriate Public Education in the least restrictive environment, which means in the least segregated environment is the intention of LRE. This includes the need for ABA. If a student requires ABA to receive a FAPE, then the IEP team already has both the authority and the legal obligation to provide it, whether through school-employed BCBAs or contracted specialists. And if there's disagreement between the family and the school about whether or not the student needs that ABA, parents have several options to challenge their district's decision with an expedited option if that is needed. The second central theme highlighted in that guidance is the critical importance of collaboration and really specifically coordination of services between the school and clinical providers. This ensures that students receive their full IEP and IDEA entitlements as well as those supplemental insurance-based ABA services. In addition to this joint guidance, there's numerous other ABA-rooted activities that have been initiated in recent years or are currently underway, including it's called Creating Safe Learning Environment Series, which is through the Michigan Association of Intermediate School Administrators or MAISA. You're probably familiar. The behavior action recommendations through Optimize, which is our Retaining Teachers Project, opening the pipeline of talent into Michigan special education. And Eric referred to this, the Hanley work, practical functional analysis and skills-based treatment in schools that is kind of supported through the statewide autism resources and training project. And the legislative appropriations for MACE's paraeducator training, which also includes training paraeducators to be registered behavior technicians. As a BCBA myself, in my own home area, we have 10 or 12 and continue to grow our paraeducators that are certified as registered behavior technicians. And we're providing that supervision to ensure that we can well implement ABA services in schools. Additionally, a group of school-based BCBAs initiated a professional learning committee. We call it a PLC, a couple years ago to provide space for collaboration on implementing school-based ABA. The PLC currently has over 80 members. These are school-based BCBAs hired by schools. We meet virtually monthly and we're actually planning an in-person event in the spring to really grow the collaboration of in-school ABA services. All of these coordinated efforts reflect a firm commitment to meeting the needs of all students through the IEP process, utilizing evidence-based practices, including ABA. As described in previous testimony, we recognize that some families have faced challenges in accessing quality services for their children. And as someone who spent my entire career advocating for kids and families, that's very disheartening. But this is precisely why these guidelines came into effect, to enhance consistency and coordination and access across systems, but still by adhering to our obligations under IDEA. As professionals charged with upholding the integrity of IDEA, we respectfully ask you to reconsider House Bill 5044, as it is not needed. The mechanism for the provision of ABA in schools is already established through the IEP process, and as such, the language of this bill creates conflicts, resulting in duplicate services and challenges to IDEA compliance. The better path forward is to continue the implementation process of our coordinated ABA in schools efforts and the joint guidance that was just released. Thank you for your thoughtful consideration. Thank you. And then I think we have some people on Zoom waiting. I think that they were here if you all had some questions that they could help field those questions. Okay, fine. Yeah. Would anyone have questions? Representative Weiss. Thank you so much for your testimony. There's a lot to unpack there, but I wanted to circle back to one of the comments that you made around potential conflicts for insurance purposes. So if, for example, you had a student who qualified for Medicaid, and they were receiving ABA services through Medicaid, and then also the school was billing Medicaid, how would that work? Would you be able to both bill Medicaid at the same time, or how would that function? Yeah, right now if you look at, because that's a private insurance, the medically necessary is a private insurance, and so Medicaid is the biller of last resort, whereas the exact same services provided by our ABA is the biller of first resort. So that's one of the tensions that are there, is, well, if you bring those services in, we're already providing them as part of the IEP, then we're getting the billing for that, so I don't know how we would pay for those services. For example, when we had things like speech or OT, we'd go out and we'd contract through a memorandum of understanding. We're very clear with that provider is the work that you're doing during school time, you're billing on our behalf through our system. We're paying you for those services, but anything that is recaptured in terms of revenue, you're billing on our time as part of the IEP process. This bill is unclear on how that will be resolved. So would that potentially increase costs then for school districts? Yeah, because if they're not going to get paid, then I would assume we'd have to have a relationship to pay for that. I would just add to that, that I think that's one of the big conflicts, because there's two parts of

One of them is school services program. It is Medicaid, and I think that's where it gets messy is people just hear Medicaid. But that's a specific allotted amount that's about school-based services that schools can bill for reimbursement, different than the insurance legislation from 2012 for ABA services, clinical ABA services. And part of the problem for me as a taxpayer and also as someone who works for the public, so has an obligation to be fiscally responsible, whether the clinical ABA is being covered by Medicaid, which, of course, is taxpayer dollars, but private insurance as well is all subsidized by taxpayer dollars. So here you take a funding source over here where we have it already in place to provide the services and receive the funds to do that, and now you're layering over another taxpayer service for the same hour of time. Sometimes I talk about double dipping, like that's a big thing, but I feel like we're quadruple dipping by having that be the case. Thank you. Representative Coons. Thank you, Madam Chair. Forgive me, is it Dr. Rogers? It is not. I'm an ABD. I wanted to be appropriate. So can you expand for me, how are the services referenced in the bill being delivered today? Help me with that. The services that would be in the bill are clinical ABA services. I think part of the challenge is that ABA has taken on this life. When a parent comes to me and says, I'd like ABA in school, my first question back always is, what do you mean by that? Because ABA is a science. It's rooted in learning theory. When we look at the chart on the right, we can see that retirement with the yellow bars and occupation transfers with the blue bars dominate in this chart. In other words, the majority of available job postings are driven by replacement needs rather than the net expansion of the occupations. And from the left chart, we can see that food preparation, office support and transportation occupations are projected to have the most annual job openings in Michigan from 2022 to 2032. Zooming in to detailed occupations, fast food workers, retail salespersons and home health aides are expected to have the highest number of job openings. Licensed and high skilled fields such as registered nurses and general managers also appear, showing the breadth of replacement needs across both entry level and professional jobs. The top 10 occupations with the greatest annual job openings are primarily entry level service and support roles such as food service, retail and largely driven by work turnover rather than the net growth. This growth typically require little formal education or experience and offer modest wages, highlighting the need for career development design and retention strategies in entry level service jobs. The only licensed occupation in this top 10 occupations is the home health aides, which also show the largest share of net growth. But still, it has 90% of the job openings are due to transfers and exits, which is echoing the need of retention strategies. Jobs like janitors, cooks, truck drivers and nursing assistants will also see strong annual demand, reflecting both replacement needs and modest job growth. Several licensed and skilled occupations such as registered nurse and heavy truck drivers offer higher wage and more stable career opportunities. In this slide, we adjust our measure of in-demand jobs slightly by applying two criteria. First, we include jobs in the top 10 percentile of annual job openings.

And then we ranked these jobs by the share of openings resulting from occupational transfers or job turnovers. Occupations such as sales representative, bartenders, and first-line supervisors show the highest share of job opening due to occupational transfers rather than new growth or retirement. These roles often require limited formal education and offer moderate wages, reflecting high worker mobility and turnover in the customer-facing and supervisory positions. Similarly, in this slide, we highlight 12 occupations with the highest annual job openings due to labor force access, especially retirement. Many of Michigan's top occupations with large exit-related openings are found in administrative support and service roles. In addition, three licensed occupations, including registered nurses, public school teachers, and home health aides, show high exit rates, reflecting workforce aging and replacement needs in essential sectors. To conclude, I want to revisit the different methods we used to identify jobs in demand, because each highlights a different dimension of workforce need. With projected employment change by percent, it can serve as an indicator of long-term structural shift in the economy. It can capture the fastest-changing demands in the product and service market and also the overarching trends such as the fast development of information technology, the increasing need of health service and social assistance, and also the use of new technologies and clean energy transition. And then the second indicator, the net employment change in numbers of new jobs, reflect the scale of expansion or contraction in workforce size. Occupations with large absolute changes have greater aggregate economic impact and could be useful for allocating resources or designing broad training or education programs. And finally, total annual occupation openings reflect both net changes and replacement needs. It reveals true hiring pressure to employers and offers a better picture of short-term or actual opportunity for workers, that is, how many positions will be available for me to enter, regardless whether the occupation is growing or shrinking. High opening may warrant more training programs, even if the occupation is not rapidly growing. And now I will hand it over to Ashley. Thank you. Thank you so much, Dr. Liu. It looks like we have a few minutes left. We are happy to try to answer any questions you all have today. Representative Weiss. Thank you for this presentation. I want to circle back to some of the charts you have around the professions that are seeing larger people leaving those professions to transfer to other occupations and increasing the need to be able to fill those. Obviously, there is a need there. And so my question is, do you see any in the data that you have here, do you see any trends or have you done any subsequent research to suggest why some of those positions may have higher turnover than other positions, particularly some of the ones that require a higher level of education? This is a very great question. Actually, our data is 100% able to answer this question. But right now, we didn't zoom in further to identify occupations with high turnovers in different education levels. But we can definitely do that in the future. So I don't have a clear answer for this question, like the turnover rate, what are the occupations with highest turnover rate, which require a bachelor degree or master degree. But I think this is a great perspective we can explore in the near future. Thank you. Any other questions? No? Thank you so much for your in-depth presentation and analysis. And we would like to probably pursue some more understanding beyond the data. But we appreciate your showing us what's on the horizon. And we definitely need this overview as we go into what other kinds of careers can we attach to a high school education and how can we help students find their way earlier in their career track that they can know of a career that would fit them and that the world needs at this time. So thank you so much for presenting. And thank you so much, committee. Thank you, Representative Paquette, for your return visit. Appreciate that. And there being no further business before the committee, the House Committee on Education and Workforce will stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Oversight - Corporate Subsidies and State Investments — Wednesday, November 5, 2025
transcript:
The House Oversight Subcommittee on Corporate Subsidies and State Investments will come to order. Will the clerk please take attendance? Chair Cara? Here. Representatives Green, Bierlein, Lagella? Here. Pahutski? Here. Mr. Chair, you have four members present. You do have a quorum. Minority Vice Chair Lagella moves to approve the minutes of the October 29th meeting. Without objection, so ordered. Originally, I had invited the MEDC to testify on the latest developments of the Gotion EV battery plant. They agreed but later reached out and requested not to testify today given the ongoing nature of the default and their efforts to claw back the $23.6 million in SSRP money that was disbursed. The MEDC has always been willing to testify and engage with the community on pressing topics regarding corporate subsidies, and I appreciate their participation. I understand the circumstance here and respect their desire not to testify at this time. Gotion's default is not surprising in the sense that corporate subsidy deals tend to fail. Time after time, this committee has seen recurring themes with massive corporate giveaways. Taxpayer dollars are wasted, jobs don't materialize, and the politically connected disrupt local communities in hopes of taxpayer-funded financial gain. A recent study conducted by the Mackinac Center revealed that only around 9% of announced jobs come to fruition from subsidy agreements. That's a poor return on investment for taxpayers and fiscally irresponsible from state government. The Mackinac Center study concentrated on data from 2000 to 2020. Since then, Michigan's track record with corporate handouts has only worsened. SOAR was created by the legislature in 2021, and it has produced a string of additional failures from the abandoned Gotion EV battery plant to the fledgling Blue Oval Project in Marshall to Sandisk backing out of the Mundy Megasite. As a state, we're batting .09, likely worse since 2020, and there's no reason to believe that will improve. Many see 25 years of failure and believe that our state government just hasn't found the right answer yet. The idea that we can continue the fundamentally flawed

The practice of corporate handouts in a way that is less bad is erroneous. There's no indication that the state is capable of facilitating economic development in a way that both respects market trends and provides significant return on taxpayer dollars. Besides, it's not the proper government to drive the economy. Putting up guardrails saying you can't poison your neighbor, lie to customers, or otherwise defraud people, and how many guardrails are needed and why are legitimate conversations. But what is not legitimate is to tell hardworking middle-class families and small businesses that they must pay higher taxes to subsidize government and big business centrally planned schemes that confiscate their money for the profit of the politically connected. Many also believe we can't give up on corporate welfare because states with better economies offer handouts to connected businesses. It's not our concern that other states have jumped off the bridge of corporate giveaways. Instead, Michigan has the opportunity to take the lead on protecting free and equal opportunity for all businesses by leading the charge with less rules, regulations, taxes, fines, and fees for everyone. Government doesn't know how to drive the economy, and it never will. The free market is the best economic driver, and market processes should not face artificial interference by government. While sore deals typically include performance metrics, the details are often generous and can easily be amended. I hope that clawback efforts will be successful because the people of Michigan are long overdue for some good news regarding Michigan's abysmal record with corporate giveaways. Goshen was particularly egregious. An EV battery plant was set to be located in a rural township who is still bogged down in litigation and should be reimbursed for legal fees battling this company tied to the CCP. As the committee previously explored, Chinese corporations are obligated to commit espionage on behalf of the Chinese Communist Party, a practice Michigan is already far too familiar with given recent incidents at Camp Grayling and the University of Michigan. The details of this deal were appalling. Years ago, I, along with two of my colleagues, talked to 36 residents of Green Charter Township. 30 of the 36 surveyed said explicitly they did not want the project. They deserve their money and their way of life back. Compelling Michiganders to pay for a project the local community was strongly against is a recurring theme. The state needs to make every effort to claw the money that was expended back. However, it's not just enough to claw the money back. The people deserve more than that. It's time to reconsider how we as a state approach economic development. The free market will yield better results for everyone rather than allowing state government to pick winners and losers. If a company wanted to talk to people and buy land for a factory in an honest and transparent way, more power to them. Let the market decide the details of production and protect free opportunity for all. Those are my opening remarks regarding the situation with Goshen. And I just want to now welcome up, we have one person testifying. That is the Honorable Joseph Sella. If you'll come up and give your testimony on the Goshen EV battery plant, looking forward to hearing from you as always. Well, good morning, Chairman Kara. Thank you. And good morning, Vice Chairman Wegela and fellow committee members. I appreciate the opportunity to be with you this morning. I come to you as a patriotic citizen compelled to shine a light on what is likely one of the worst examples of state-driven economic development in the history of the state of Michigan. The corrupted deal with Goshen Inc., a company deeply tied to the Chinese Communist Party, that wasted Michigan taxpayer dollars and jeopardized our national security. This was no mere business transaction gone awry. The Goshen deal was concocted and championed by Governor Whitmer, MEDC CEO Quentin Messer, the right place, and CCP-tied Goshen. Unconscionably, these government and business elites moved fast and in secret, rupturing the consent of the government. Zero transparency came from the Whitmer administration that had vowed to be the most transparent administration in Michigan history. This was made worse by the backers of the deal refusing to perform any strict scrutiny or due diligence, whether through a market analysis, technology assessment, studying consumer demand, the prospective ROI in taxpayer dollars, and certainly geopolitical dynamics. These backers also defied the directives of our national security and intelligence agencies to vet such a deal with a CCP-tied company that was involved in a textbook subnational incursion and influence operation designed to burrow deep into the heartland of Michigan. And I would note that's a short hop away from the secure U.S. military installation of Camp Grayling. Goshen was also lobbying without registering its lobbyists, only later registering after we at the Michigan China Economic and Security Review Group exposed them. And it is believed that Goshen still has an individual under their employ who appears to be operating as an unregistered foreign agent in violation of the Foreign Agents Registration Act. This deal entirely lacked best practices and wholly manifested the worst of practices. I'm going to do a bit of a rewind and tick through the timeline of this corrupted deal for you. September of 22, the Detroit News first reports the CCP-tied Goshen plant coming to Mecosta County. And days later, skids greased, three local township boards, Green Charter Township, among others, unanimously approved tax exemptions without public input, sparking a clamor of what local rank-and-file citizens considered as a surprise attack, if you will, and certainly lack of transparency. October 22nd, Governor Whitmer, MEDC, announces this, quote-unquote, the largest economic development project in northern Michigan history, $750 million in incentives, $175 million in grants, $540 million in tax breaks, and certainly the local opposition began to take shape then. It was much ballyhooed, with some saying once-in-a-generation deal, transformational deal, once-in-a-century project. February of 23, Detroit News reporter Beth LeBlanc revealed the Goshen deal and the Ford-Cattle deal were papered over with secret code names and binding punitive NDAs signed by lawmakers, staffers, and other government officials. April of 23, the monies were approved for Goshen by narrow votes, and protests began to scale with the locals. In June, concerns escalated into a very politically charged debate. Local residents and elected officials began to dig deep, and Goshen's CCP ties began to be revealed, though the company denied it and its representatives. August of 23, five University of Michigan engineering graduates who were Chinese nationals were found spying at Camp Greiling during Operation Northern Strike, a multilateral military exercise that featured Taiwanese troops. They were charged by the FBI and fled to China days later. November of 23, the governed in Greene Township mobilized a recall, recalling elected officials there, five of them, one actually in Big Rapids Township, who supported the Goshen project fully. February of 24, Goshen began cutting trees and preparing the land for the site of the proposed deal, purchased an old department store, and all of this being done without prior approvals being given. In March of 24, the township board voted to rescind the previously approved plan to extend the city's Big Rapids water supply to the site, prompting Goshen to file a breach of contract lawsuit. And I would note that that is textbook lawfare according to how the CCP rolls, and ironic in that a final contract was never approved by the Greene Charter Township Board. In May of 24, a federal judge issued an injunction requiring the township to abide by the original agreement, but the township appealed, and as you noted, Chairman, it now sits in the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals where Greene Township has appealed. At that point, Goshen paused its permitting process, and I think they knew at that point it was an uncertain future. It became a national political issue with unique focus after then-candidate Trump and then-candidate Vance campaigning highlighted the national security concerns and the corrupt nature of the deal. Later that year and earlier this year, Mecosta County revoked its support for the project after they won control of the county board based on the ties to those incumbents backing the Goshen deal. September of this year, the MSF sent a letter to Goshen declaring the company in default, voluntary abandonment due to no activity over 120 days. Goshen certainly responded a few days later with the shrill charge of being politically motivated opposition and immense challenges. And then the MEDC is now attempting to claw things back in the funding that was let from Goshen.

But this has been a total debacle and a colossal waste of time and taxpayer dollars. It's an example of how not to conduct business and do economic development, if that's even a role for state government to play. All of this, every bit of this, could have been avoided had the most basic of due diligence and strict scrutiny been performed. The weakness would have been on display for all Michigan taxpayers to see and you, their representatives. It took patriotic citizens weeks and months to pull back the curtain doing very hard work on the wizards secretly working the levers of this corrupted deal and expose them and all of its inner workings. While the dust is still settling and some unknown things lingering, I think it's good to, I guess, celebrate, take a breather from what appears to be Goshen's impending demise in Michigan, while remaining, as it is in Latin, semper vigilans, always vigilant. And I appreciate your good work here today to continue your deep dive on the way business has been done. Citizens in Green Charter Township exemplified how our founding fathers got it right. Sovereignty comes from the citizens. After government and business elites worked fast and in secret, they righteously rebelled, educating and mobilizing fellow citizens and exposing the head-to-tail corruption of this deal. The consent of the governed was violated. They rose up, exercised their constitutional rights against all odds through prayer and hard work and made history in the United States of America. It was the first time in our nation's history government officials faced a recall election and were thrown out of office because of their entanglement with their dealings with a CCP-tied company. These citizens are models of faith, courage, strength, tenacity, and patriotism. They wrote the playbook for other communities across the United States to follow who may face similar circumstances. And you here, representatives, I would suggest, are writing the next chapter of that playbook. It's very important and can't be overstated. It was a blessing, a joy, an honor, and a privilege to fight with these patriotic citizens who had the hardest jobs on the front lines of this battle in a community that was torn apart. Now my aim, and I hope shared by you, is to help make Green Charter Township whole through the paying in its entirety of their final attorney fees from the unconscionable lawfare being waged against them by CCP-tied Goshen. And I will remain vigilant with these citizens in the fight against other risky moves by government and business elites that may be afoot, particularly when it involves any entanglements whatsoever with the CCP and its agents and operatives. Chairman Kara and Vice Chairman Wiegela, ultimately, I hope you work together and say no more to these sort of economic development antics and perhaps even considering the elimination of the MEDC. I appreciate the opportunity to be here with you today and am happy to answer any questions you may have. Thank you, Ambassador Sala, and thank you for your testimony today. I just want to start off with the numbers. There was $125 million in CIP or Critical Infrastructure Project funding that never got appropriated to Goshen. But then of the $50 million in SSIP or Strategic Site Readiness Program funding, $23.6 million was appropriated to Goshen. And by this point, it seems like that is the main question in terms of money that has gone to them. Do you know where that money was spent? I want to get this right, and you may correct me later, but I believe that the $50 million line item went to the right place. And the monies expended, as I understand it, were for land acquisition, site prep, and engineering work. I've been told that the engineering work done is not much at all. I think there are sort of receipts circulating around out there for what was, I think, paid to the right place and others. But it is well known and really shocked the locals of the grossly inflated price that was paid for that land. And it's, again, just another element of the unconscionableness of this whole thing. So in terms of any type of infrastructure preparing for a massive building to be put there, it doesn't seem like that's been done. They've bulldozed a bunch of trees, and we just have this vacant area. And what do you think should happen with that property moving forward? That's a great question, Representative. I guess also of note is that apparently the tree cutting and the land clearing, I think there was some grading done. That was done ahead of Goshen or the right place before they received any approval from EGLE. So as far as the land is concerned, I guess if I were to have a wish list or I would say as a matter of justice, I would say through maybe plantings and transplantings, restore it to its once pristine state. I know that's some sensitive wetland there. I think that, again, wish listing here, an idea is to, God willing, Goshen plays nice and settles up with the state. And perhaps the state then does a quick claim deed and that is deeded to Green Charter Township for them to do with it as they wish. That seems to make sense. A question I'd have with that is we have the MEDC who had appropriated money to the right place and then the right place to Goshen. And then the MEDC wants to come in and say, well, hold on, you guys didn't do what you said you were going to do. And that's true. But who is the victim in this circumstance? Is the MEDC the victim or is it the taxpayers of Michigan and the township who are the victim? And what should happen with this property moving forward? Should the MEDC just be allowed to sell it to somebody else? Or do you think that it should probably go a different route? Yeah, I think that I leave it to your good offices to come to this. But I think that you use an interesting analogy. So I think back to the old cowboys and Indians days, the cowboys with the black hats and the cowboys with the white hats, sort of the good and evil representation. Symbolically, I would say that the actors, those involved, stakeholders wearing the white hats, I would definitely say are the Michigan taxpayers and the residents of Green Charter Township and Big Rapids Charter Township, I would say. Those wearing the black hats, I would just say would be Governor Whitmer and Quentin Messer and the right place and some other players out there that I just don't think had the interests of the governed at heart through this whole thing. So it's an open question. I think as a matter of justice, I mean, what they put Green Charter Township, the Michigan taxpayers through the meat grinder, and I think as a goodwill gesture, quit claim that deed to Green Charter Township. And it's a beautiful area and I trust the leadership there to do well with it. Very good. Next question from Vice Chair Green. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you for coming. It's always a pleasure to see you. And this may be out of your wheelhouse, but do you know what the annual budget of Green Charter Township is? I asked this last week and I know we need to ask the Green Charter Township folks this, but you may have this answer. Do you have this answer? I do not. Okay. And I guess just the reason I ask is both townships, I imagine their budgets are very similar to my township's budgets, very low, low maintenance. I mean, we're experiencing this right now in Greenwood, believe it or not, very similar situation. And I guess, do you know how much the total legal fees were? I don't. I think the meter is still on. I don't know if it's running anymore. I'm semi-confident that the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals is going to level an adversarial ruling for Goshen against Goshen. I think the meter will still run. We'll see what Goshen does at that point, but I would say that we're at this point looking at an off-ramp. So I don't know what it is. I would say it's probably south of a million dollars, but when you're talking about a rural township, not much tax base, very hardworking people who are in these tight inflationary times, work very hard for the basics. That takes a hit on their government. Now, they didn't seek this out. I think that there were some bad actors that got their township into this predicament. They did not have the rank-and-file citizens, the hardworking taxpayers' interests. They were not exercising their fiduciary responsibility in making these decisions. And it's just almost like a utopian hope and looked at this field of dreams would materialize, and it did quite the opposite, sadly. So

It has had an impact and that's why I would hope also as a matter of justice that you and your good office and colleagues will work to make Green Township whole with their final bill. I know there's a run at through a possible appropriation in the budget bill and that did not come to fruition. I know they did have some appropriated locally from the county through their marijuana proceed funds and that helped a bit, but there's more to go. Do you believe that Green Charter Township should be reimbursed for the legal fees that they have incurred in fighting against Goshen? One hundred percent. Yep. This is really an unconscionable effort by a $40 billion company tied to the Chinese Communist Party that requires its employees to take an oath of fealty to the Chinese Communist Party. There's a video of this. And to see our government on multiple levels in cahoots with such an enterprise, I think it's a real shame that they have put the exposed not only the taxpayers of Green Charter Township, Michigan, but also certainly exposing our national security. And justice ought to be served by making them whole. Thank you. Next question from Vice Chair Green. So it's very rare that we get a former ambassador. So I do have a nuanced question. So economic development is really important. And I know when you were in Southeast Asia, we have really strong ties with our friends, especially in Taiwan. And so there's levels to this because, one, we're using really good farmland and green spaces for these mega projects. So I think that's issue number one. But, I mean, issue number two is we do need to have some sort of economic development prosperity, and we want to partner with those actors who are good behaviors, I guess. Like, for example, like, and so do you have, like, recommendations from your experience on moving forward and how we can approach that in the future? Yeah, I would just I think to the end of transparency, which I think has been lacking heretofore with this corrupted deal, I would suggest you consider having hearings, field hearings, talk to experts, sit down with them, see what they have to say. But I would, you know, consider you study the model of what I think Governor DeSantis did. And I think he brought all things economic development into the governor's office. So you don't need a bureaucracy. You don't need a building, sell the building. And that could be done. And you hire the necessary staff within an executive office to do that. You don't need hundreds of people to do that. You work, find the deals, work the deals in a sound way, best practices, do all the stress tests that this did not get. And I think you'll get there. I think it might also be I think Representative Cara had represented, Chairman Cara represented or spoke to a study done in terms of the efficacy of the MEDC investments over the years. I'm not familiar with that, but I think as deep and a broad look at that to point to an alternative way where the burn rate and the ROI is negligible. So my modest suggestions in response to your question. Do you think it's likely that Guo Xuan, a high tech, bails out the American subsidiary, Goshen, for this project? Yeah, great question, Chairman Cara. I think that when you're talking with China, you may have a mothership in China, Guo Xuan, high tech. They sort of anglicize their name, Goshen, one part for PR purposes, but the money is all just fungible. I mean, you may be papered corporately, you may have a different bank account, but it's really one and the same. So candidly, they could have afforded all that Michigan taxpayers were put over the barrel for. And again, that just shows how influence operations and subnational incursions work. And unfortunately, we were duped. So I appreciate you and your colleagues here bringing light onto that to make sure that doesn't happen again. Very important. Next question from Minority Vice Chair Wagala. Yeah, I don't know if this is so much a question, but I just maybe we can get a response from it. But I was looking at the MEDC's website and, you know, on there they have reports and data. And I went to strategic site readiness programs. You click on there and it says no reports found. So I just was curious. Maybe you could talk a little bit about the importance of with any economic development deal, the importance of transparency and how some of that might be lacking here in the state. Yeah, I think that excellent point, Vice Chair Wagala. And I think that is almost symbolic of what has been lacking here with this deal. And I would also suggest the Ford Cattle deal in Marshall. But I applaud you for pointing that out and noticing it. And I think an opportunity, I think, to stay on this road, ask those hard questions. It's my understanding there may have been a CFO at MEDC and was sort of located within. And in recent weeks they were on the move to hire a new CFO. Why wasn't there a CFO? If they had a CFO in recent years, could all of this been maybe avoided? I don't know. But these, I think, I really appreciate your leadership and service and the oversight capacity. And I just keep after that and happy to reappear and offer any other answers or insights that you may need. Obviously, one way or another, something went wrong here with the process with Goshen. Who do you believe is at fault? Is it just Goshen alone or would it be the MEDC, the governor? Who's at fault in this process? Yeah, important question. A little bit of a lengthier response. I would say that I think you step back to maybe 35,000 feet and say, look, we're in the midst of the pandemic. I think a lot of government growth happened in this time. A lot of money moving. I don't think the best decisions were made. I think there was probably pressure on elected officials seeking to create jobs when jobs were lost. And certainly, I think riding this wave, this utopian green wave fueled by the Biden administration and Secretary of Energy Granholm throwing hundreds of billions in loans and grants and incentives for the Green New Deal. And I think it fueled and inspired governors like Governor Whitmer and those surrounding her to engage and advocate and advance this, I think, high risk, ill thought out and poorly executed deal that left us exposed, taxpayers, national security. So I think that in Michigan, you certainly say Governor Whitmer, Quentin Messer, the right place, Randy Thalen, Bill Pink, who's on the board of the MEDC, I think the strategic fund, if I'm not mistaken, also president of Ferris State University. So I appreciate the role of holding people to account that have had a seat at the table here and really didn't do the due diligence as they should have. And I would note also that you may remember there was a hearing, I think, in the Senate. And I think Senator McMorrow, who I think supported the deal, asked Quentin Messer about the due diligence done. And heretofore, when it came to the Goshen deals and the cattle deal, he had said that all had been done and super due diligence and thorough and squeaky clean. And then when she pressed him on that question, I'm glad she asked it, he had acknowledged that we really didn't do the due diligence that we ought to have. And really, sadly, too little, too late. And that should have been a thing on the front end done. As to the $23.6 million that has been disbursed to Goshen, do you think that we'll be successful in getting some of that money back, all of that money back? And are there any elements of this that might make it more likely that we'd get it back than in other circumstances? I don't know. I think whenever you're dealing with a company that's deeply tied to the Chinese Communist Party, all bets are off. So they have the money. They could walk away from it. In the midst of all of this fog of war or whatever you want to call it, as this deal unraveled, it seemed like the center of gravity of what they wanted to do shifted to Mantino, Illinois anyway, where they are in operation or soon to be in operation. I guess it remains to be seen. I can tell you that I'm picking up from the locals that there apparently is a company here in Michigan that I think they're trying to make lemonade

made of the lemon, so to speak, and have a company come in and pretend that all is well. But again, I think that this applies to both sides of the aisle. I'm very concerned that if that is indeed afoot, it is being done fast and in secret, the same problem that got us here in the first place. That's why we're here today. So I would just urge caution there and keep an eye on that, if you might, you and your colleagues. So I would just say we'll just have to see. I think a couple of things are being maneuvered here. I understand MEDC may sue Goshen. And if it comes to that, but parties often try to settle out of court, and they may. I mean, we'll just have to see. But I hope the better angels prevail in this instance, as they haven't in the past. Good. And I guess towards the concern, making sure that we're cautious, what should we do in terms of a process when we're considering deals with companies from foreign countries? Is there any special investigation or research that should be done, like perhaps a CFIUS review or something of that nature? And was it done? Superior question. I was reached out to in early February of 23. My first engagement with this out just after my former ambassadorial colleague and now Ambassador to Canada, Peter Hookster, wrote an op-ed in the Detroit News. And a local elected official in Green, pardon me, Big Rapids Township, reached out to me and they were looking for direction, help, advice, what to do. And the first thing I suggested was that they explore a CFIUS review. And they reached out to Goshen. They were not playing nice. It's a very turnkey thing. If there's nothing to hide, just open your books. There are states underway, discussions in states underway, and there may be practices in states in place where a state version of the CFIUS review is in place. So whether the MEDC stays or it goes, I would just implore you and your colleagues to do a deep dive on structuring a vetting process where strict scrutiny and due diligence is done, particularly when it comes to adversarial regimes like China, companies that are based there. And I would, in this, their corporate officers are named, their passports are seen, pardon me, and a lot could be found out from that. Good morning, Chair Leitner, Minority Vice Chair Carter, and fellow members of the Judiciary Committee. I have over 32 years of law enforcement experience and witnessed the rise of the meth problems beginning in the 1990s within our local communities. Representative McFaul and I have sponsored these two bills, a package to help continue the fight against the illegal production of meth by regulating the production, sale, and distribution of the substances contained in pseudoephedrine. My bill, 4947, would amend the Public Health Code and require all businesses selling the substance containing pseudoephedrine to require a participation in the National Precursor Log Exchange, also known as NPLEX. 20 years ago, in 2005, the federal government adopted the Combat Meth Academic Act. maximum sentence provisions but would change the description to failure to deliver or ship product containing ephedrine and pseudoephedrine directly to purchaser or comply with applicable federal law. Thank you to Representative Bagul and McFaul for bringing these bills forward. I know we're on limited time, so I'm going to try to be really brief here. They're effective, and they've been sold over the counter for nearly 50 years. The people that I represent, the makers of these products, pay for the system, and we think that's appropriate, and we want to continue to support that. We, the industry, think that's fair, and I do think it'll ensure that the long-term viability of the system for many years to come. As was stated earlier, Mississippi and Illinois passed similar legislation this year and a number of other states are going to be considered in 2026. I think this NPLEX system has become really critical for law enforcement and for the safety of residents, and we think it's really important to ensure the long-term financing of it. In terms of House Bill 4948, we also fully support. This modernizes Michigan's law to allow for online transactions. As was stated earlier, the Combat Meth Epidemic Act that passed Congress passed back in 2005. That was before the advent of the iPhone even. So obviously in the last 20 years, a lot has changed in terms of technology. Under current law, you're not allowed in Michigan to make a purchase outside the pharmacy. This bill would change that. I do want to emphasize, however, that any retailer that offers online sales capability must still satisfy all the requirements of current law. You'll still have to show ID. You're still limited in how much you can buy. But this will allow someone the convenience of buying online or to do curbside pickup or direct to home delivery. So we fully support convenient access to these medications. And I'll just stop there and try to answer any questions the committee may have. Thank you for your time and urge support for both of these bills. Thank you. Well, we do have another card in here in regards to House Bill 4947 and 4948. Does not wish to speak in support of this bill. Drew Beardsley of the Michigan Retailers Association. I don't have any questions right now. Thanks, fellas. I do understand the issue in updating the system and making the proper entities pay for it and also still having the verification. I mean, I'm sure there's a tedious process on what it looks like for the online verification at this point. And I would like to talk to you offline probably about that. So we're not mandating a house to house canvas or anything like that. Under election law, that's one thing that they can do as well. I would say in particular, there's not a specific definition that says, like, the clerk or their representative. It seems like this language would expressly prohibit the representative from being the determining factor in that. We've never interpreted election law or anything like that. That's even the same with election law. If it says the clerk, we interpret it as the clerk or the member of their staff. I'm sorry to interrupt. It seems like that might be a good thing to define because I see that as being challenged. So much of this seems to be parsing language specifically, and that language itself seems to be particularly problematic, again, given the difficulty of a clerk and how narrowly you're defining personal knowledge. If you're defining personal knowledge that narrowly and then you're defining clerk broadly, that's a conflict of visions right there. I think that's fair. I think that makes sense. I would say if for something like that, that might benefit from clarification in the law itself as well for the exact reasons that you've indicated. Or if we do the rulemaking route, that might need to be a separate rule that is like an overarching interpretation because that's the same even with election law. The same issue that you're raising is even with election law. So that might need to be something just totally independent is what I'm trying to say. I got it. You describe postal service information, and then you describe personal knowledge separately. We've had over the last many years national organizations taking a look to try to verify the truth of the voter rolls. And I want someone who's moved, who's got public information that they've moved, like the postal service lists, to be able to be challenged without the clerk knocking on their door, for example. So you specifically say that that postal information is not sufficient, and then personal knowledge requires that an individual live there and then also knock on the door and personally know that they moved. This seems to be creating a blockade where one doesn't need to be. So I'll back up for a second because the clerk doesn't have to knock on the door. That's not the only way. Well, you narrowed down the ability for an individual to know what's going on, or for a challenge to actually exist. And some of it is statutory, I'll give you that. But I have personal knowledge that the postal service list identified that they moved. That's personal knowledge. I'm okay to sign that affidavit saying I saw the list. The list says this. Here's the proof that the list says this, and that ought to be sufficient to initiate a challenge. So what we are saying with the rule is the only – and you even had just said it. All that you can say you have personal knowledge is that you looked at the list and that the list says this. Right, but the law requires that you identify where your knowledge comes from. Yes. So now I personally saw the list, that it's a government document. The postal service identified this person as having moved. That's a government document that I'm verifying. And then my attestation is that I have viewed that document. It's a governmental, trustworthy document. I'm attesting to having seen that, and then I can prove it to you. That seems to me that that ought to be sufficient for personal knowledge. What the rule – what I would point to is rule two in that instance because what the rules say is that that's not personal knowledge to the extent that you know for sure that that person doesn't live there. So, for example, we've had several instances in Michigan where individuals show up on an NCOA list because they are snowbirds and they live in Florida for a period of time. They end up on that list, but they're still eligible to be registered in Michigan. They still maintain it. That's the purpose of the challenge process is to send something out and let them go ahead and verify. That's what I was just going to say. So if you look at rule two, what the rules say, if you start with – sorry, I'm going to find it. I want to answer the question because I don't want to take too much time looking for it. But what the rules say with the 512 challenge, in that instance, if you don't have personal knowledge, the clerk can still process it, but they process it under 509AA process, which says in that exact instance, the individual comes in and says, this is the NCOA list. We specifically have identified the NCOA list as reliable information now under rule two. We've included that, and that triggers the cancellation notice then in that instance, which would give the four-year period instead of the 30-day period. That's how we've interpreted that exact situation that you're saying. What we're saying with the 512 challenge is that if you're going to cut that two cycle, excuse me, that four-year window, if you're going to cut that down to 30 days, you have to have personal knowledge about that very specific situation. Otherwise, we're going to follow the 509AA flow, which is the cancellation notice and the two cycle period versus the 30-day window. So personal knowledge in the sense of the 512 can be, I bought my house from Aaron Shore. I bought – or other way around. Sorry. I bought Aaron Shore's house. I know she doesn't live here anymore because I live here. That can be a challenge for me to say, I have personal knowledge. She does not live here. The clerk would look up, would investigate, for example, is Aaron Shore entitled to UACAVA status, for example. If yes, then the challenge is rejected. If no, we start the 30-day window. In the instance that you said, if I have this NCOA list and I have looked up on NCOA and I submit that to the clerk, the clerk can use that to start the four-year window because you're attesting to only have looked at the list. You have not created the list. You don't know how that list got generated. You don't have the specifics of each one of those voters. The requirement that the challenger have personal knowledge that the challenged voter is ineligible and not satisfied when the challenger's basis for their claim is reliable information. That a voter has moved or other third-hand information indicating that a voter is not eligible, including an online database, United States Postal Service information, you expressly prohibit that from being part of – which rule is this? Sorry. Rule 6. As a challenge process. But then we also in Rule 7 specifically say that if the challenge fails to properly assert personal knowledge, the clerk may attempt to independently verify that information. May. They may. That's the – so again with the conflict of visions, and I'm sorry for interrupting you. Thank you for your patience. There is a fundamental difference among some people believing that anybody and everybody who wants to vote should be allowed to unless you can definitively prove that they shouldn't. And from the votes – from the people who believe that you should be an American citizen and you should qualify as a resident of the state before you're registered to vote or if we allow those other folks to vote, they're taking away mine. And while I appreciate the may concept, if someone's definitively showing with reliable

and you and I disagree with what that looks like, that this individual shouldn't be on the voting roll. For example, a non-citizen who got registered just because they used their ID from their college, I want that to be able to be challenged. And I absolutely want it to be verified. And again, if there's a mistake made, we have same-day registration. We are not taking away somebody's vote. But this perspective that when proof is put in front of you, you get to ignore it just because, well, maybe you don't want to do the work, or maybe you have the beliefs. We actually had a clerk in my community that said, well, they own land here. I know they're a Canadian citizen, but I think they ought to be able to vote. That was an actual township clerk quote, paraphrasing, but that was the quote. I want Michigan citizens who reside here who are registered to vote to be protected from that mindset. I don't see that this rule set does that. And I understand that you're working within the HAVA Act and the federal law, but this seems to go way further than that by prohibiting reliable information from being used as reliable knowledge. I would again just cite to the distinctions. We're not prohibiting reliable information from being used. Allowing a clerk to completely ignore it, even when faced with it, should they choose to. If we got information that someone was not a citizen, how would we handle that? That could be an instance of a couple of things. We would investigate that, and we would potentially just immediately cancel the registration. It's a little bit complicated with that, like the steps and what the investigation looks like. But there's a distinction between reliable information and 512 challenge. Reliable information is that NVRA process. A 512 challenge is separate. A 512 is we're going to immediately cancel your registration after 30 days if you do not respond. There's a potential conflict with that. Like you've said, we're kind of in that confine between the NVRA and Michigan election law with what we can and can't do with that without violating federal law, without violating the NVRA. So I would say as far as Rule 7, that's why we've identified that. That's why we've said you still can, but you have to take that additional step. You have to independently verify. If it doesn't meet the law's floor, right? The law has set the floor on what that challenge has to have. And I certainly hear your concern about the may. I mean, we all want to have good roles, and I believe at least the vast majority of clerks want to have good voter roles as well. This rule is not the only place that speaks to the responsibilities of clerks to conduct voterless maintenance. Is that correct? Yes, that's correct. I mean, they're still under the obligation under election law and the NVRA under the specific requirements under both those statutes. And I know you're short on time, but we can pull some of those and share that information with the committee. I would be very interested in that because voter role maintenance is something that I would love to see happen regularly. To your point, how are you verifying the citizenship of the people currently on the roles? Is that an ongoing daily thing? What does that look like? Because I want that to be a 30-day-less cancellation. If you can't prove your citizenship, I want you off the role. There are instances in which it's an immediate cancellation. If we can prove that the individual is not a citizen, we know for sure. So let's say they go into a branch and they select, no, do not register me, and then they erroneously get registered. That's an immediate cancellation. We're not even sending a notice. We're not giving a 30-day. My understanding is that your office has been given access to citizenship lists at the federal level and they're not using them. Is that wrong? That is not correct. So first of all, there is no master citizenship list. This is referencing SAVE. And our office does use SAVE. We have used SAVE for a number of years. It is an individual voter-by-voter lookup. So it's a verification when challenged. It's not a review of the existing voter file. No, we look at it regularly. We don't wait for a challenge to utilize SAVE. SAVE is utilized as part of a regular ongoing process with that department. I'm curious how many voters, and you can get back to me, I'm assuming you wouldn't know this number off the top of your head, how many voters have been removed in the last year because they were found to be non-citizens? I don't know that answer off the top of my head. I would love to hear that. Thank you. I appreciate your grace and your grace with my many questions. Thank you. You're very welcome. So I understand you guys are on a time limit. Rep Johnson, you had one more question though. Real quick, and thanks for your extra time. Exempting overseas civilians from voter eligibility verification and treating them as a protected class. Can you comment on how that works and why are we doing that? Are you talking about a specific rule set? Rule set 13. 13 or 3? I think it's 13. No, there was a 13. I'm sorry, I meant like a specific rule that you're looking at, like language or something. I've got to look it up. I think it's rule 13, but it disappeared from the consolidation. I don't have a rule 13 in what we have submitted. I think we're going to do this again at a later date when you guys are available again, if you don't mind, because there seems to be still some confusion as to what's going on. And the example you used about buying Aaron's house, aren't you just hearsay and not reliable information? No, because I have personal knowledge because I bought her house. You do? Yeah, but you're not the clerk. I'm the clerk. What I hear from you is hearsay. Right. What we're saying, though, is that essentially think of it as double hearsay then, because if I'm relying on hearsay to present it to you as the clerk, then you're going to rely on hearsay, which is based on hearsay, essentially. So what we're saying with the personal knowledge is that it has to be correct. That's exactly why we're defining it this way. We'll do this again sometime when you're available. Let me know when your schedule is available. I'll let you know. And please consider putting the definition of clerk into the definition section of this set of rules. I think that would be important, and I think Senator Tice would agree with that, too. All right. Thank you for your time. I really appreciate it. Section 253 for next time. It is section 3? 253. 253. Okay. And thank you. Look, I know there was some question about next week, and I know Adam may or may not have to be in court next week. Whenever you're available. Thank you. Yeah, we're good. Wednesday morning sometime. Appreciate it. Is it? It's not a long time. So we're not changing anything? Not yet. Thank you. Okay. A couple cards to read. And thank you again for your explanation. Howard Green does not wish to speak. He opposes the bill. And Sherry Ritchie does not wish to speak and opposes the bill. Okay. There being no further business, this meeting is adjourned. Sorry, I'm all over the place. Thank you.

And just for the members, just to repeat what was said last week, many, many years ago we spent very few of these dollars on weatherization. During the last six or seven years, we've gotten up to 10%. And so this would codify our progress but also push it a little bit further. And that's what the substitute represents. It's just changing the number, which obviously makes it a little bit easier to deploy the funds probably. I was one of the people that asked questions about this, and I guess I'm still a little bit concerned. It makes sense to me that there's probably enough need out there to use this money. I'm not sure that there's always going to be enough capacity to get it where it needs to go. And what I will say is that for me personally, in a state like ours with the magnitude of need and with the age of our housing stock, we have some really old housing stock in the state of Michigan. So what I'm going to do is I am going to hand off the gavel here to my more than capable vice chair and join Senator Johnson. Thank you both, Senator Johnson and Senator Irwin. Today before us we have Senate Bill 585, probate guardians and conservators' requirement to have an appraisal for the sale of a real property, and also Senate Bill 586. This is a Johnson bill, probate guardians and conservators' requirement for the state on records, reason for moving the ward and for residence. And you all will go ahead and proceed to explain your bills. Thank you very much, and thank you members for your time and attention today. I'm very pleased and honored to be joined with Senator Johnson here today to work on a very important and difficult issue that has been bouncing around these chambers for a long time. You may remember some of the recent committee hearings we've had on the elder abuse task force that was led by Attorney General Nessel. And you may have heard, as I have, concerns in your community about the very difficult, very intimate, very challenging, nuanced area of what happens when someone gets to near the end of their life and they're incapacitated and they can't make decisions for themselves, and the state has to step in and name a guardian for that person. It's a very fraught process. I want to start by saying that I appreciate the folks who work in this space and who go the extra mile and dig deep to really try to help folks in our state who are in a really challenging position and help their families who are also put in a really challenging position by this process. The primary purpose of this bill is consumer protection to safeguard the assets of individuals who are unable to act on their own behalf. A conservator has a duty to make decisions in the best interest of that person and ensuring that property is sold for its true fair market value is a critical part of that responsibility. Without an independent appraisal, there's risk that property could be sold below market, permanently diminishing the estate or inheritance of the person the conservator is supposed to protect. Appraisers provide this independent, impartial, and objective opinion of value under the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice, USPAP. These standards require appraisers to act with ethics, independence, and objectivity, to be competent for the assignment, to clearly define their scope of work, and to maintain detailed records. Appraisers have no financial stake in whether a sale occurs or at what price. It's our job to provide an impartial evaluation. That's what sets us apart from a broker price opinion or a comparative market analysis, which are typically prepared for the goal of obtaining a listing and inherently involved a potential conflict of interest. Even the appearance of that conflict can be problematic when a vulnerable individual's property is at stake. I've seen firsthand this kind of, why the safeguard matters. title: Civil Rights, Judiciary, and Public Safety 103025
transcript:
I don't want to blindside anybody. The Senate Committee on Civil Rights, Judiciary, and Public Safety is called to order. Will the clerk please call and announce the roll. Chairwoman Chang? Here. Senator Schink? Here. Senator Voino? Here. Senator Irwin? Here. Senator Santana? Here. Senator Rundstedt? Here. Senator Johnson? Here. Madam Chair, there are six members present. There is a quorum. I'll entertain a motion to adopt the committee minutes from the October 23rd, 2025 meeting. Motion made by Senator Santana. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. First of all, thank you so much for everyone's patience. I'm very glad that our Senate took the action that we did today, but it did set us behind quite a bit, so we will try to be as efficient as we can. So today we're going to take up Senate Bills 611 and 612 by myself and Senator Johnson. And so we'll testify from our seats for efficiency. So again, just want to thank Senator Johnson for our partnership on this issue, and I want to recognize that October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month, which is a very important time for all of us to talk about domestic violence, find solutions, and support victims and survivors. A personal protection order is a court order to stop threats or violence against you. You must show the judge that someone is likely to assault, threat, harass, or stalk you. And there are three types of PPOs, domestic relationship PPO, a non-domestic stalking PPO, and a non-domestic sexual assault PPO. A domestic relationship PPO can prohibit the person from entering your home or another place, from assaulting you, interfering with you at your job, stalking you, and more as determined by the judge. This past August, Latricia Brown was stalked and murdered in her workplace by her estranged ex-husband, Mario Green, at Henry Ford Health's main hospital in Detroit. She had been stalked for a long time and was fearful of what might happen next. She had been granted a personal protection order, but that order had not yet been served. And I want to read from her July petition for a PPO. She said, I have tried being cordial because I feel that the system has now let me down each time that I have tried to make reports on this man. My father was murdered, and now with this situation, I am in mental distress and scared, not knowing what to do and where I have PTSD of this whole situation. I have to constantly look over my shoulder to make sure this man is not following me, to hurt me like he has done in the past with physical abuse. I am asking for help before this goes too far and things are too late. Latricia's PPO was never served on her ex-husband. And on August 22nd, he entered the basement of the hospital, pulled out a handgun, and shot Latricia several times. Michigan is a really unfortunate outlier in the United States, where 43 other states, the District of Columbia, and two territories require that PPO service take place free of charge. In Michigan, the cost to serve a PPO can include not just a service fee, but mileage traveled, which can easily amount to almost $100 or more. In fact, costs vary from county to county, so a PPO survivor in one county might have to pay twice as much as a survivor in another county to ensure their safety. The law currently also allows a victim to identify a friend or a family member to serve the PPO, but that can lead to a very dangerous situation. Our bills would require that a PPO be immediately served at no cost to the victim by a law enforcement agency as designated by a judge. The designated law enforcement agency would be reimbursed for the cost of service from the Personal Protection Order Service Fund, which we were very pleased to secure an initial $1 million for in the fiscal year 26 budget. The Violence Against Women Act ensures that a PPO granted in one state must be enforced equally in any state. But victims in Michigan are being left behind if they are unable to pay to serve their PPO. I want to recognize that it takes a lot of courage for someone who is experiencing domestic violence to ask for help, to share details of what one has gone through, put it on paper, file a petition for a PPO for a judge to consider is a truly brave and extraordinary step. And when someone is reaching out for help and trying to protect themselves, we should not be putting up a financial barrier to their safety. Quite simply, it is time that we remove this unnecessary and dangerous barrier for those experiencing domestic violence, stalking, harassment, or assault. The impact of this legislation will be felt not just by victims, but also their families and witnesses like Latricia's coworkers. I will now turn it over to Senator Johnson. Thank you very much, Senator Chang. I appreciate it. I want to start by thanking you for the work that you've done on this issue and for taking it up in committee today. I'm proud to work with you on these bipartisan bills during Domestic Violence Awareness Month. As you said, Michigan is an outlier, an unfortunate outlier. We must improve our efforts to protect Michigan residents who are facing often serious threats. Senator Chang, you mentioned the Violence Against Women Act, a federal law that passed in 1994. Among other provisions, it says that states cannot charge someone to serve a PPO. And the way Michigan, I would say, got around it is this provision historically is that our law says you can have a family member or friend serve a PPO for you, as opposed to a law enforcement or professional process server if you want the service to be free. But as you can imagine, that is often not necessarily the very safe alternative to put a family member or friend in the position to confront someone who has demonstrated threatening behavior. And it's much better to have a law enforcement properly and promptly serve that PPO. And again, this is how 43 other states are doing it now. For someone who's struggling to get out of an abusive relationship or marriage, for example, maybe that they're fleeing that type of situation in real time. Extra steps and extra costs can delay getting a PPO served, sometimes with painful outcomes. Unfortunately, we can't prevent every tragedy, but we must do better to help people like Latricia Brown. This is a very concrete step we can take to try to better protect victims of domestic violence and stalking in Michigan. I look forward to hearing additional testimony on these bills, and I encourage my colleagues on this committee to support this critical, common sense, and long overdue reform. Thank you. Thank you very much, Senator Johnson. I appreciate our partnership on this. Are there questions from committee members? All right. Thank you so much. Up next, we are going to hear from Bishanta Clark, who is the sister of Latricia Brown. There's a very small button at the base of the microphone to turn that on. My sister, Latricia Brown, was murdered. This tragedy exposes a profound failure in the legal system we depend on for protection. We demand accountability for the systemic negligence that precedes this loss. A law degree or professional designation does not inherently confer compassion or insight into a person's genuine fear for their life. Protection cannot be reduced to a five-second administrative decision. Dismissing a victim's terror over a technicality, whether it's being at the wrong precinct or a signature denying protection, is an administrative indifference that carries a lethal loss. When Mario Green tried to run my sister off the road, I was on the phone with her, and she was terrified. And she was in the Oak Park area where she had just moved, and she didn't want him to know that she lived in that area. She drove back to a police station that she knew, which was the third precinct right across from her job, and she was turned away. They would not let her file anything against him. They told her that she had to go back to the scene of the crime. I don't understand that kind of rejection in that moment that would send some person in fear for their life to go to another precinct. I don't understand that. I was told our sister received a police escort for her funeral. Due to my intense grief, it didn't even register we had a police escort during the processional. I must ask, where was the police protection when she was alive and desperately needed it? A funeral means she is dead. She no longer needs protection. The system must pivot from paperwork and financial burdens to human-centered care and reliable advocacy. We need a justice system that validates fear, provides true guidance, and ensures that

Bureaucracy never again stands between a person and their right to survive. Finally, we must acknowledge the impossible and agonizing position victims are placed in. For countless women, the fear is not just of the abuser, but of the system itself. They choose silence because the data and heartbreaking outcomes whisper a terrifying truth. Seeking formal protection too often escalates the danger without guaranteeing safety. They hesitate to involve trusted partners, family, or friends because the documented tragic pattern is often the victim's death or the death or incarceration of the loved one who tried to intervene. This devastating reality, this paralyzing choice between silence and escalating tragedy is the most damning evidence of a system that cannot currently safeguard those who need it most. A PPO is just a layer of protection, but more needs to be done. Her PPO was denied and she was offered a hearing if she filed within 21 days. I was told to get a hearing, it could take up to six weeks. My sister didn't have that long. Thank you very much for sharing and we're very sorry for your loss and I appreciate you also raising your voice to call for change. Thank you. Are there questions or comments? Senator Runstead. Okay. We are now going to go to Kim Worley, who is the Wayne County prosecutor. I want to thank you, Senator Chain, for asking me to come, and thank you, Senator Johnson, for this bipartisan effort. The preliminary examination is currently set for November the 6th, a week from today. You have laid out what the bills stand for, and the most preeminent part is not having victims anymore in Michigan, one of seven states that still has this law on the books, to have them responsible for service and for monetary fees that are connected with a PPO. That was just as outrageous as our state putting the onus, financial and otherwise, on victims and survivors who are granted lawful PPOs by judges and by courts. On top of being abused, disfranchised, disenfranchised, ignored, and marginalized, victims like Ms. Brown must literally run for their lives while looking over their shoulders, running looking back, as my grandmother used to say, and forced on top of that to do everything else for their own protection. We will never be able to definitively say that Ms. Brown would still be alive if her PPO had been served. The sad reality is that abusers often violate their PPOs frequently.
