The passage of these bills would certainly be good steps in the right direction to restore dignity, respect, and humanity to people within our state who have been abused, murdered, and victimized. They matter, and we must be accountable to them. We cannot just give lip service for victim and public safety. We must mean it. We must be better. These are the closing days, as has been mentioned by several people already, of Domestic Violence Awareness Month. And while I'm glad that we highlight annually every October Domestic Violence, we need to focus on the fact that this is a 365-day issue, a 12-month-a-year issue, and a 24-7 issue. Thank you. I'm happy to answer any questions from a prosecutor's perspective. Thank you very much, Prosecutor, and we appreciate your leadership on this. We do have a question from Senator Runstead. Thank you. Any other questions?

We launched it in Genesee County on Monday and since that day, as I sit here today, 12 PPOs have been served by my office. One of the first head entanglements, the individual had multiple warrants. Number two, it gives us an option to work with process servers who already have a great relationship with law enforcement that takes sometimes two to three days to serve these. But number two, the timing of these, as I read in the bill, is immediate. That can be subjective. The reason I say that is because our deputies that are serving these PPOs are doing this on top of their duties. Paramedics that are certified in Genesee County, local township agreements that have 911 calls, this is above and beyond. And when law enforcement knocks on the door, they may not be there. But immediate, even though the need is immediate, we have to make sure that the language allows us to have multiple attempts while we're doing everything else that is just as important for our community. Number three, this is a law enforcement algorithm, state police, county, and local. This is how we can roll it out. I'll be happy to help with any other logistic challenges that you may have to get this bill across the finish line. I will end with, I admire you for what you do every day. This is one in particular that I want to highlight. I appreciate Ross Jones doing the story and bringing attention to a family that's grieving because out of her death, lives can be saved. Any questions? Thank you. I appreciate your support for this as well as providing some concrete suggestions and also for taking action really quickly in your county on this really important issue. I'm hopeful that all of our sheriffs across the state will follow your lead in terms of figuring out ways to make this work. I appreciate that. Any questions? Senator Santana? It's more of a comment, Chair. I just wanted to uplift the fact that we have put dollars into the Public Safety Trust Fund to help support our local law enforcement as well as into PPOs this year. Hopefully, that will help to remedy some of the overall concerns that have been brought before us. Thank you. We also have a question from Senator Johnson. Thank you, Madam Chair. Sheriff Swanson, thank you so much for coming and waiting and everyone waiting for such an important bill that we're looking at these bills today. I was wondering as we're talking here and when people do get PPOs, is there anything else we can do to help them because they are still at risk? Yes. And again, I concur with the Senator's comments that it's not the one thing but it is a thing. And behind me, I know there's advocates who walk along domestic violence victims. Law enforcement has the resources and authority to locate and serve respondents efficiently, ensuring that protective orders take effect quickly, which can mean the difference between life and death. I am the chair of the Michigan Domestic and Sexual Violence Prevention and Treatment Board. Prior to my retirement, I worked as a legal services attorney in Washtenaw County, where I spent over 20 years, I'm not going to say how many, but it was over 20 years, representing many survivors of domestic violence, primarily in protection order and family law matters. As you know, the Michigan Domestic and Sexual Violence Prevention and Treatment Board, or the board, is a seven-member, governor-appointed board with legislative responsibilities, including providing policy recommendations on the issues of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, and intimate partner violence. PPOs would enhance the safety of victims by eliminating this financial barrier for those who have come to the court to ask for protection. Aaron Van Langenveld, Michigan Department of Attorney General, supports. There being no further business, the Senate Committee on Civil Rights, Judiciary, and Public Safety is now adjourned. The surgeons could not use his penis to create a neovagina, so they cut out a portion of his colon. This young person developed a massive infection and died. Despite a study having 70 participants, 68 of whom were homosexuals, and one dying, it was declared a success. But that success depended on a statistical illusion. I am devastated that my party, the Democratic Party, is still supporting gay conversion. I believed I was practicing compassion. I believed I was helping. Before I close, I want to say something directly to those who lived through this harm. To Johnny and Prisha, and to every young person who I led down this path. I am so deeply sorry. We called your distress and identity, and we medicalized your pain. All the while, we told you that you were part of a new civil rights movement. It was abandonment dressed up as compassion, and you deserved better from all of us, especially people like me who should have known better. I cannot undo these harms, but I can dedicate the rest of my life to telling the truth and to protecting others, and to try to stand beside you and walk with you as you try to rebuild your life. Around the world, countries that once led this movement are reversing course. In the UK, the Cass Review found that the evidence for pediatric gender transition was built completely on shaky foundations, and the Tavistock Clinic was shut down. Sweden and Finland, countries that as a liberal Democrat I once looked to as the pinnacle of what we wanted for our society, have now restricted puberty blockers. Even the global advocacy groups behind these interventions are starting to quietly admit that the evidence of benefit simply does not exist. Michigan has always stood for protecting children, not exploiting them. Yet in the name of progress, our institutions have repeated the mistakes others are now reckoning with. I am not here as a partisan. I am a lifelong Democrat who believes medicine should be grounded in evidence, ethics, and the duty to do no harm. And I am also a lesbian who believes that gender nonconformity should be embraced as a natural beauty, not pathologized. And I am also a whistleblower who believes that children should never have been sterilized for an adult ideology. Countries, liberal, democratic European countries are reversing course. The same will happen here. The only question is, how many children will continue to be harmed before we act? And how many of you will realize 20 years from now that you supported gay conversion and the castration of young gay men in the name of civil rights? Michigan can choose to lead to defend children's bodies, their minds, and their futures. Please help ensure what happened in my clinic, which has now been shut down, will stop happening here in Michigan. And this is ended as quickly as you possibly can do so. Thank you for your time and your service to the people of Michigan. Thank you, Jamie. Could you go into some detail about the support that is given to those that want to transition and those that want to detransition? Can you talk about the difference there? In our country currently, if you seek a medical transition as a minor or as an adult, I can immediately give you programs that will pay for every step of the way, that will physically pay to move you across state lines from states like mine where bans are currently in place to states like yours. If you seek a medical transition for your child, you will be not only supported fiscally with everything you have, but it will be declared by many people that this is a cheerleading effort for new civil rights. If you are a detransitioner, however, you will have zero pathway to seek medical care because there is not even an insurance code with which for your care to be billed.

Most of the detransitioners that I work with are gays and lesbians who have had their body parts removed, the parts of their bodies that we as gays and lesbians experience our pleasure from. They have been cut off their bodies and they will never be able to put those body parts back on. My former spouse is a detransitioner herself. Her hairline starts all the way back here because of the 13 years of testosterone use. There is no way, no one, no how who will assist her in paying for her hair reconstruction. She has had no one to assist her in paying for the laser removal to remove her facial hair. I don't believe any detransitioner has had any support to do that. They are simply not recognized because to even recognize their existence is to understand that the ideology itself has a crumbling, illogical fallacy. Representative Pickett. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you, Jamie. You mentioned the playbook and you being from Missouri and working there. I've been digging in here in Michigan and I've realized it's the exact same playbook that's being used. Meeting children who are now adults and trying to get information has been very difficult. Yet speaking with one gender doctor out of U of M, Jesse Krikorian, I realized very quickly that children are being told they need to freeze their egg or sperm because what they're going through at 12 years old will render them sterile with the medicalized path that they get put down. People don't realize what is happening specifically with young gay and lesbian children. With this and getting it made known, where have you seen difficulties? You mentioned and alluded to it a little bit where children aren't able to get care, people aren't able to get care after they're put down this path. There's no code for it. Why aren't, and you're all around the nation talking about this, why aren't people picking up this story and letting it be made known? Humans don't like to admit that they're wrong or that they've made a catastrophic mistake or that they were themselves tricked into believing something. We don't want to admit that. It's incredibly shameful to do. But I can tell you part of my job was to work with children on what you're referring to as fertility preservation. The sterilization of this protocol is primarily born onto the young boys who, if this protocol is done correctly and they're given a puberty blocker at Tanner Stage 2, their penis will never develop, their testicles will never develop, the pathways in which spermatogenesis, the way that the testicles would even produce sperm, doesn't develop. This is absolutely a sterilization and then later a castration protocol, especially on these young men. And I hope that people will pick up your story today and what you're talking about and realize that this playbook is being employed here in Michigan, and we've been leading the way in many very, very nefarious ways, and it's diabolical and it's wrong, and it needs to end sooner rather than later. So thank you so much, Jamie. Thank you. So the medical community and sort of society in general is supporting kids transitioning. Gets back to my other question. What are they left with when they want to go back, and what treatment can't they get when they want to try to go back? For a moment, though, I think I want to pivot and recognize that it's not just those who recognize that the harm has been done to them. It's not just those who say, I identify as a detransitioner. Even those who claim that this is something that has caused them happiness or that they do not regret, there is an 80% rate of serious surgical complications. There is the creation of a lifelong endocrine disorder that in many cases will shorten the lifespan and decrease the medical health of those who are undergoing it. I care very much for those who know that they've been harmed by this, but I also care very much for those who have been sold this concept that their body is wrong and that it somehow needs to change because most of the people that do transition, that were sold this concept, are homosexuals. And most of us do experience intense shame and pain as young people, feeling like we were born in the wrong body. Some of my earliest memories are not understanding why I wasn't born a boy. It takes a long time for gay people to come to realization of our alignment with our body and our sexual orientation. Even those that claim that this was perfectly causing them happiness are still left with myriads of medical problems. They're harmed. This is simply violence on the body. Is there a financial incentive for the medical community to continue down this path? Absolutely. So I worked in a pediatric endocrine division. In a pediatric endocrine division, you can ask any of your major hospitals, are they normally in the red or are they normally in the black? Do they normally lose money or do they bring money in? The endocrine division in pediatrics is a money losing division for the hospital because the primary group of who is being treated there are type 1 diabetic kids. Most of those kids are on Medicaid and most of those kids have significant medical needs. They need to be seen often. They need a lot of support care. As soon as the pediatric gender center opened in my hospital, within two years, the endocrine division suddenly was saying, we don't know what happened, but we're now in the black. We're actually making money now because the gender center initially thought that we were going to have 50 patients total and we ended up having close to 1,500 because there was also a social contagion that occurred at the same time. You get to charge same day surgical procedures, the endocrinologist, and oftentimes those implants are being swapped out multiple times across the lifetime. This is absolutely making money for the hospital. But the other question is how much money would the hospital lose when they openly recognize that they have been participating in one of the greatest medical scandals that has ever been seen in pediatrics in our country? They're going to go bankrupt if they openly acknowledge this. The American Academy of Pediatrics would go bankrupt if they openly acknowledged this. They're also being sued currently. They know they can't publicly say anything. Thank you. Thank you for your testimony. I'm grateful for today's testimony and everyone's willingness to come before this body. It is the intent of this committee to provide oversight of the care administered to minor children who are not yet equipped to make medical decisions that will follow them for the rest of their lives.

Life-altering care should not be offered to children. I have strong concerns that gender-affirming care was offered in a pediatric setting. The major hospital systems in Michigan that offered this care previously have now stopped. But as we learn today, we need to better understand the lifelong ramifications this care can have on our children. We must also learn how therapies and procedures were coded and billed through insurance. If efforts were taken to conceal care, there must be accountability. This is an issue in need of oversight that we will continue to investigate in the coming months. We have a duty to protect children who are not ready to make lifelong health decisions. There being no further business before the committee, the committee will stand adjourned.

title: Families and Veterans — Tuesday, November 4, 2025
transcript:
The House Families and Veterans Committee will come to order. Would the clerk please take attendance? Chair Small? Here. Representatives Wozniak? Here. Fox? Here. Johnson? Here. Thompson? Pablo? Our first order of business today is to hear testimony on House Bills 5035 through 5039 from Representatives Roth and Representative St. Germain. Welcome. Thank you, Madam Chair and members of the committee. Appreciate your time today to hear some interesting testimony in a situation that I certainly didn't come to Lansing about. This was something that brought to me by a constituent my very first year, four years plus ago. My constituent learned through the use of a DNA test that her dad she grew up with, thinking it was her biologic father, was not. It turned out that her whole world was going to be turned upside down when she found out the donor was actually the actual donor that her mom and dad brought to the IVF clinic. She thought she was 100% Scottish and you end up being half Jewish, where her biologic father was actually the mother's doctor. While preparing these bills, I learned of victims who chose their donor based on specific things that they wanted, going to a clinic, picking a specific donor also, and only to find out that that donor had lied about who they were. It would be a charge of a Class E felony with a five-year penalty. So long, long time ago when I was a little kid, there were three things I knew I wanted to be one day. I wanted to be rich. I wanted to be a wife, and I wanted to be a mom. And I just remember thinking to myself, like, you know, why is it my body doing what it was designed to do? You know, why the complications? What did I do wrong? And then when I came to terms of that thought process, what a silly thing to think about, like that it was so irrelevant. I was so lucky to be able to conceive and carry a baby and deliver a healthy baby. So I really can't imagine what women that want to conceive and have a baby, the feelings they go through. So with this legislation, you know, I can't thank Rep. Roth and everybody that worked on it enough. I think it's important, and it's the very least we could do. I hope this bill, this package of bills, makes it all the way through into the governor's desk. Thank you. And I will say Rep. Steckloff is also on the package. She wasn't able to testify today but supports it also. We've gone through a lot of process with this. So Representative Wolford. I don't have a question. Not yet. I usually do, but not right now. Okay. Sorry about that. Representative Shaw. Thank you, Madam Chair. Have you looked at what other states are doing because their class felonies are different? And is there a statute of limitation in this legislation? Because as we know, the process of finding out 40-some years later, I mean, will they still be able to prosecute and criminalize that? A lot of them are

too far down. And actually, Dr. Peven, who was the doctor out of Detroit area, has long since passed away. He passed away at 104 years old. The Fourth Amendment of the United States Constitution is clear in saying that the right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures shall not be violated, and no warrants shall issue but upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized. You would be hard-pressed to find even a single American that is in support of unreasonable or warrantless searches and seizures of property. Yet, as legislators, we must engage in debates based on facts and realities, not wishful thinking. The exact issue that House Bill 4073 seeks to address has been clearly settled by our nation's highest court. The Supreme Court of the United States has repeatedly stated that individuals cannot legitimately expect privacy for activities conducted out in the open except in the area immediately surrounding their home. Even if a property owner has gates and posted trespassing signs, the court has made it clear that searches for activities conducted out in the open for large properties, this means in the fields, wooded areas, or on open water, so long as the area is not immediately surrounding the home, need not comply with the requirements of warrants and probable cause. The actions of the DNR or any other state agency that is conducting open field searches are completely justified by previous SCOTUS rulings and are protected by federal law. These are not the actions of a rogue department, but rather the actions of a responsible department attempting to enforce our state's laws. I would also like to note that this bill would statutorily enact a departmental policy that is stricter than the federal government's search warrant policies. In doing so, this bill would curb the state's ability to manage wildlife, clean up toxic spills, and protect the public's health and the environment. I urge my colleagues to vote no on HB 4073. This is an important resolution. Evidence-based efforts to ensure young people have the information they need to make healthy choices is a public health imperative. And updates to Michigan's health education standards are long overdue. For over 20 years, our state's health education framework has remained stagnant while the world around our children and families has changed dramatically. These standards addressed with this resolution, which, by the way, are still in draft form, reflect just that. They are endorsed by the Michigan School Health Coordinators Association and Shape Michigan, trusted experts in school-based health education curricula. These are the professionals our school leaders rely on to support student wellness. Their recommendations didn't just fall out of their heads and land on a page. There are many experts in education and health who have contributed to these standards, following the available evidence to inform them. In today's digital age, our children are bombarded with misinformation. For example, 25 years ago, there was a push for abstinence-only education, and the result wasn't a reduction in teen pregnancy, but an increase in sexually transmitted infections and children seeking answers online to questions that should be answered by the trusted adults in their lives who know them best. When students don't see themselves or their lived experiences or the challenges they face on a day-to-day basis reflected in what they're being taught, or when their identity is treated as something to be hidden, they won't just tune out the education. They will more likely make uninformed and often unhealthy decisions. With regards to this resolution, the available evidence tells us that the absence of useful health literacy content can lead to higher rates of depression, anxiety, self-harm, and other serious mental health consequences. They are about informing and educating our students in a way that is inclusive about all the health risks they may face. They are informing our education to our students in a way that is inclusive, trauma-informed, and developmentally appropriate. The guiding principles of the framework emphasize safe and supportive environments. Our job here should not be to impose ideology on classrooms, but to ensure that every student in Michigan receives accurate, age-appropriate, and medically sound information. We can disagree about politics, but we should never legislate in a way that promotes ignorance. Let's empower parents and schools to apply the guidelines in a way that works best for them and keep politics out of the classroom and ensure that we are valuing science within it. For the health, safety, and dignity of all Michigan students, I urge my colleagues to vote no on HR 195 and keep focused on things that matter, like keeping children fed. The speaker recognizes Representative Thompson. Thank you, Madam Chair, for the opportunity to stand and speak in support of this resolution. By standing in support of this resolution, I am taking care of what matters, my children. I'm going to use a word that I actually never can pronounce accurately because I am so disgusted by this framework. I am vehemently opposed. That is a tough word for me to say. I had to practice it multiple times. This manipulative move is a clear circumvention of Michigan law. As a legislator, a mom, and a grandma who is raising three of her four grandchildren, my job is hard enough. We have the right to direct the education of our children. That is our fundamental right. That right does not come from the government or school boards. Michigan law protects this right specifically as outlined in Section 1507 of the Revised School Code. We are going to hear a lot of claims that are false, but I want to tell you things that are true about this proposed resolution. Parents no longer have confidence that SEL content will uphold their family's role to teach their child's moral, social, and emotional development. SEL blurs the lines. It begs to ask the questions. Do schools believe that it is their right to raise our children and not ours? I stand with parents, grandparents, and guardians to make sure that parental rights are upheld. This is not a Christian or a conservative issue. All parents of faith, including Jewish families, Muslim families, and very specifically Albanian Muslims in my district have asked me to stand opposed to this. These families want us to protect their right to direct their child's education when it comes to sexual activity. I am so proud to support this resolution, and I urge my colleagues to listen to Michigan parents and do the will of the people. For the love of God, do the will of the people and not the will of a rogue state sex education push. I do not co-parent with the government, nor would I force my constituents to do that. I urge a yes vote. Thank you. Speaker recognizes Representative Johnson. Thank you, Madam Speaker. Colleagues, today we take up a resolution that strikes at the very core of who we are as a legislature and what kind of state we want Michigan to be. This is not just

about curriculum. It is about the duty of government to uphold the law, respect parents, and protect the moral foundation of our schools. The resolution before us calls on the Michigan Department of Ed and the State Board of Ed to reject their proposed health education standards framework and return to the table with a version that honors the law, respects parents, and restores transparency in our classrooms or return to the current one that we already have. Section 1507 of the Revised School Code, which was passed and signed by Governor Granholm with a bipartisan legislature back in 2007, it requires that sex education be locally controlled, transparent, and optional. Parents must be notified in advance, given the opportunity to participate through local advisory boards, and allowed to excuse their children from instruction that conflicts with their family's values. These are not suggestions, they are statutory rights. Yet the department's proposed framework disregards that law. It embeds lessons on gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation into required health instruction, effectively removing parental choice and stripping away local authority. The department has crossed a line that this legislature drew to protect families from exactly this kind of government intrusion. During last week's oversight hearing, the interim state superintendent was invited to explain the board's rationale for this proposal. The speaker recognizes Representative Johnson. Everyone in attendance wanted their voices heard. That decision spoke volumes about the level of respect they have for legislative oversight and for the families they are supposed to serve. This is not modernization, it's indoctrination. It's a disregard for law, for parents, and for the constitutional role of this body. At a time when our students are struggling with the fundamentals of reading, writing, and math, the department has chosen to focus instead on social agendas that do nothing to improve academic outcomes. We conducted our audit of ORR in accordance with generally accepted government auditing standards, and those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain sufficient, appropriate evidence to provide a reasonable basis for our findings and conclusions based on our audit objective. Our audit objective was to assess the sufficiency of selected ORR efforts to protect and promote the rights of recipients of public mental health services. We concluded ORR's efforts were not sufficient. Our report has eight findings, four are classified as material conditions, and four as reportable conditions. Material conditions are deemed more severe than reportable conditions. For each material condition, we explain why we considered it a material condition within each finding in the area just before the recommendation. Findings one through four are the material conditions and relate to deficiencies noted in collecting and evaluating recipient complaints, timely initiating investigations, acknowledging receipt of complaints, providing investigation status reports, and completing investigations and interventions. We also noted deficiencies in ORR's monitoring of key activities

and an assessments of CMHSPs and LPHs recipient rights systems. The four reportable conditions are findings 5 through 8 and relate to needed improvements in communication of MHC guaranteed rights and contact information to recipients, timely provision and monitoring of ORR and SPH employee recipient rights training, appeals committee training and education practices, and user access controls for ORR's complaint system. MDHHS's response is indicated it agrees with 5 of our findings and disagrees with 3. Agency's disagreements are notable because government auditing standards require that when the audited entity's comments are inconsistent or in conflict with the findings, conclusions, or recommendations, the auditor must evaluate the validity of the comments and if they disagree, must explain in the report the reasons for disagreement. Heidi is going to begin by going through the material findings and then Ivy will walk through 5 through 8, which are the reportable conditions. Thanks, Yvonne, and good morning. Jumping right into finding 1 on page 14, we noted improvements are needed in collecting complaints at the state psychiatric hospitals, which we refer to as SPHs. Approximately 70% of complaints are submitted through drop boxes and ORR typically collects these complaints twice per week. The Mental Health Code, or MHC, requires ORR to immediately initiate an investigation for complaints involving alleged abuse, neglect, serious injury, or death, and to initiate an investigation in a timely and efficient manner for all other apparent or suspected rights violations. While the MHC doesn't prescribe time frames for immediately or timely, ORR's training materials define immediately as within 24 hours and timely within 10 business days from the receipt of the complaint. However, because the complaints weren't collected and evaluated on a daily basis, ORR couldn't ensure it immediately or within 24 hours initiated investigations for those alleging abuse, neglect, serious injury, or death. We completed a review comparing ORR's date stamp, which indicates the date the complaint was collected, to the complainant-provided date. For the complaints alleging abuse, neglect, serious injury, or death, we noted ORR's date stamp for over a quarter of complaints exceeded the complainant-provided date by more than 24 hours, averaging 6 days. We also noted ORR's date stamp for more than half of the complaints alleging other rights violations ranged between 2 and 53 days after the complainant-provided date, averaging 9 days. We consider this finding to be a material condition because of the significant exception rates, the potential risk to recipients if there are delays in imposing remedial actions, and the potential inability to ensure the protection of recipients' rights. And MDHHS agrees with this finding. Next is finding 2, beginning on page 16, where we noted improvements are needed in ORR's timeliness for many facets of complaint assessments and investigations, some of which were also reported within our 2014 performance audit. In part A, an ORR date stamp was missing on over 10% of sample complaints, and as such, we were unable to determine if any subsequent actions were performed timely. In part B, almost a third of our sample complaints alleging abuse, neglect, serious injury, or death were not initiated within 24 hours. These were initiated between 2 and 17 days after the date stamp. In part C, we noted ORR didn't always acknowledge receipt of complaints timely, which is particularly important for those complaints where it's determined neither an investigation nor intervention is warranted, because the acknowledgement is the only communication sent to the complainants. In part D, almost 40% of investigations reviewed had one or more required status reports overdue, or the investigation files lacked sufficient information to determine timeliness. In part E, ORR did not timely complete almost 30% of investigations, and on average took 175 days when they're required to be completed in 90. In addition, over 10% of interventions reviewed were untimely, ranging from 3 to 11 days late. We consider this finding to be a material condition because of the significant exception rates, and more than 30% of investigations reviewed had multiple instances of timeliness failures, the likelihood that deficiencies in meeting timeliness requirements are more pervasive, considering written complaints weren't collected daily, as noted in Finding 1, or consistently date stamped. MDHHS also agrees with this finding. Moving on to Finding 3 on page 21, we noted ORR needs to improve several aspects of its monitoring activities. In Part A, we noted improvements are needed in monitoring complaint responses to help ensure compliance with time frames, all of which were just discussed in Finding 2, and MDHHS agreed. In Part B, we noted ORR didn't monitor SPH's video surveillance and audio recording capability and availability. Based on investigation documentation, observations while on site, and interviews with ORR staff, we noted that all 5 SPHs had video surveillance systems, but were not always capturing video footage. 3 of them didn't have audio recording capabilities, and the 2 that did were unreliable throughout the facilities. We also noted video and audio evidence may have helped facilitate or further support ORR's investigation conclusions for over 40% we reviewed. MDHHS disagrees, indicating it doesn't believe monitoring video and audio is the responsibility of ORR, but rather the state hospital administration's responsibility. Our auditor's comment notes that state law established ORR to promote and protect the constitutional and statutory rights of recipients and empower recipients to fully exercise these rights. And ORR is responsible for monitoring the quality and effectiveness of rights protection systems, of which reliable and consistent surveillance systems are a key facet. In Part C, we noted ORR didn't have a process to monitor SPH incident reports to determine whether incidents were indicative of potential rights violations and reported to ORR. We reported a similar issue in our 2014 performance audit. MDHHS disagrees because ORR is not required to review all incident reports, and it does not believe it's an efficient use of resources. As noted in our auditor's comment for Part C, incident reports are a valuable resource that can be used to independently and proactively identify incidents impacting the health, safety, or welfare of patients. In addition, previous policy required an ORR review of all incident reports to ensure that recipient rights are protected. However, MDHHS rescinded that policy. In Part D, we noted improvements are needed in monitoring the documentation and timeliness of appeal committee activities, and MDHHS agreed. In Part E, we noted ORR should strengthen its monitoring of rights advisors' independence to help reduce the potential biases when handling complaints. Rights advisors are often solely responsible for all aspects of interventions and investigations, beginning with the collection of the complaints to concluding on whether a right was violated or not. And since they're stationed within the SPH, there is potential for familiarity with the parties and the complaints they address. MDHHS disagrees and indicated it doesn't believe rights advisors stationed on site and completing the essential functions of their jobs are inherent conflicts of interest. However, ORR also indicated they'll be adding to its policy for ORR staff to disclose potential conflicts of interest to their supervisors for any necessary assignment changes.

As stated in our auditor's comment, MDHHS contends it disagrees while simultaneously indicating it intends to revise its policy related to ORR staff disclosures. In part F, we noted ORR did not regularly monitor the categorization of complaints. We reviewed 201 complaints and noted 10 were not consistently and properly categorized, including 6 incorrectly determined to have no alleged rights violation and 4 containing allegations of abuse or neglect but not categorized as such. MDHHS disagrees for 6 of the 10 and indicated more than one category may be appropriate for an allegation. However, it will provide additional training to help ensure consistent categorization of complaints. As noted in our auditor's comment, we agree more than one category may be appropriate. However, ORR at a minimum should come to consistent conclusions on whether an allegation warrants investigation, intervention, or neither to appropriately address the allegation, and this was not always the case. We consider this finding to be a material condition because of the importance of timely and appropriately addressing complaints and appeals, ensuring availability and access to video and audio evidence, identifying significant incidents that are unreported to ORR, and ensuring complaints are handled by individuals independent of the complaint parties. The last material finding is number 4, which begins on page 29, where we noted improvements are needed for on-site and annual reviews of CMHSP and LPH recipient rights systems. In part A, we noted for all 16 on-site assessments reviewed, ORR's review documentation did not always clearly explain the procedures performed or contain other documentation fully supporting the final assessment results. In part B, ORR was unable to demonstrate how its review of statistical rights data fulfilled its responsibility to conduct an annual review to ensure CMHSP compliance with standards. We consider this finding to be a material condition because of the high percentage of assessment records that didn't fully support the final results, the potential exposure risk to the state if results are questioned or challenged, and CMHSP and LPH recipient rights systems address over 90% of complaints statewide. We reported a similar issue in our 2014 performance audit. MDHHS disagrees with the finding, indicating that documentation was maintained to support the completion of required on-site assessments, and all on-site assessments provide an exit interview to review the findings and allow for any further evidence to prove compliance with standards. MDHHS also intends to pursue legislative clarification to validate the interpretation of and compliance with the MHC's annual review requirement. As noted in our auditor's comment, we do not dispute that ORR's records indicated it conducted the on-site assessments. However, its review documentation lacked key information to support the assessment conclusions. In addition, while ORR's response indicates its practice was to conduct exit interviews for on-site assessments, none of the 16 we reviewed included evidence that these occurred. And that wraps up the material findings. I'll now pass it over to Ivy. Thank you, Heidi, and good morning. I'll be walking you through our remaining reportable findings. Finding 5 begins on page 32, where we noted ORR needs to improve its communication to help ensure recipients are aware of their guaranteed rights, the availability of ORR services to help ensure protection of those rights, and the appropriate contact information to seek ORR's rights protection services. The Mental Health Code requires ORR to notify recipients of these rights in an understandable manner, both at the time services are requested and periodically while services are being provided. During our facility walkthroughs, we noted that all four SPHs had standardized signage missing some or all of the necessary ORR contact information. We also noted ORR's recipient rights informational booklets provided at three of these hospitals were missing pertinent ORR contact information when the facility signage was also lacking this information. MDHHS agrees with the finding and indicates it plans to update the signage and informational booklet with pertinent ORR contact information. Finding 6 is located on page 34 and notes ORR needs improvements in its timely provision and monitoring of ORR and SPH employee training. The Mental Health Code requires ORR to ensure all MDHHS-employed individuals receive recipient rights protection training within 30 days of employment. But we found 40% of central ORR staff training was late, and ORR frequently was unable to demonstrate it monitored quarterly SPH staff training reports. We reported a similar condition in our 2014 performance audit. MDHHS agrees with the finding and indicated it has already enhanced its monitoring processes in relation to employee training. For Finding 7 on page 36, we noted ORR needs to strengthen its appeals committee training and education practices. The Mental Health Code requires MDHHS to appoint an appeals committee and provide due process for all recipients. While this committee is independent of ORR, ORR is required to provide training and education to the committee on the appeals process. We noted ORR was unable to support any of the committee members received the required training or education during our 34-month audit period. As Heidi mentioned earlier in our Finding 3 remarks, during our review of the committee's records, we observed instances of noncompliance with statutory and policy requirements related to timeliness, assessments of reinvestigations, and communications with appellants indicating the potential need for and benefit of strengthened committee training and education. MDHHS agrees that maintaining records clearly documenting training education material distribution will provide support as trainings were completed and improve the current process. However, the department disagrees that documentation of training had an impact on the appeals exceptions we identified within Finding 3 and further notes those exceptions occurred prior to 2024 when ORR made changes to its appeals coordinator position. As noted within our auditor's comment on page 37, while we agree the change to the ORR appeals coordinator position likely improved timeliness and documentation of appeals, we also believe ORR's inability to provide evidence committee members obtained training contributed to the exceptions we identified in Finding 3, Part D. Finding 8 is the last of our findings, beginning on page 38, and relates to improvements needed in user access controls over the CEVIL CRM system used by ORR to document and track complaint allegations against SPHs. MDHHS agrees with the finding and indicates it has already updated its processes to strengthen user access controls. This concludes our prepared remarks and we will now take any questions. related to the volume of complaints that were being received. And Chair, if I may. Sure. ignoring what is right in front of you. That all needs to be addressed. Listen, if you want change, it's got to be addressed by not only us, but all the healthcare professionals, this department.
