And I believe that it is equally important that we protect the administration of our elections against foreign funding and foreign influence. After all, we entrust election officials and their staffs to run elections in a fair, transparent, and ultimately in a fashion that is accountable to the voters and to the taxpayers of this state. That is why I strongly encourage passage of House Bill 5198. It is a straightforward measure that requires entities that offer funding, in-kind goods or services, or any

services to election officials for the administration of elections to certify that they are free of foreign donations and to regularly renew and update these certifications. The measure is in line with a provision of Proposition 2 from 2022, which passed on the ballot and which bars the use of foreign contributions or in-kind goods or services for election administration. That provision is common sense. After all, elections must be administered impartially, and the officials that we entrust to run them must always be accountable and exclusively accountable to the citizens of the state. But within the last few years, a cottage industry of nonprofits has sprung up targeting election officials with programs focused on training, support, services, and multi-million dollar privately funded grants. In some instances, election offices have been offered enormous grants that equal their annual taxpayer-funded budgets. The risk of undue influence from those programs is clear. One example of that problem is the Center for Tech and Civic Life, which was responsible for disbursing the majority of Mark Zuckerberg's controversial $400 million in private funding in 2020 and was accused of disbursing those funds disproportionately to swing state jurisdictions that ultimately voted for Joe Biden. After that first program prompted a majority of states to ban private election financing, many on a bipartisan basis, CTCL launched a new and ongoing venture, the $80 million U.S. Alliance for Election Excellence, a membership-based program bringing together various nonprofits to provide targeted election offices with everything from coaching and training to legal and policy advice. These groups cloak themselves in the banner of nonpartisanship, but they often appear to have hidden partisan agendas. That is highly concerning since these programs have a clear influence over the administration of elections. The potential for conflicts of interest are clear. In fact, right here in Michigan, Ottawa County Clerk Justin Roebuck walked away from the alliance and a corresponding grant in 2023, citing concerns over private financing casting doubt on the integrity of elections. And to quote from a letter that he released, particularly when the resources can be tied to individuals or groups who may also have contributed to political parties or candidates. That frankly is why a majority of states have passed laws to ban private election financing. Equally concerning is the prospect of foreign funding bankrolling these programs. Indeed, as we discussed with the prior bill, Swiss billionaire Hans-Joerg Weiss has funneled hundreds of millions of dollars into the 1630 Fund, which has put over $33 million into ballot measure campaigns in Michigan alone. Weiss has also given tens of millions of dollars to a 501c3 sister group to the 1630 Fund called the New Venture Fund. And New Venture Fund has provided at least $25 million to the Center for Tech and Civic Life, as well as supporting other election-focused nonprofits such as the Center for Secure and Modern Elections, the Institute for Responsive Government, and the Center for Civic Design. A recent report from Americans Republic Trust tracked an astounding $2 billion from foreign charities into various U.S. nonprofits, including a further $71 million from foreign sources into the bank account of New Venture Fund. In other words, the same pipeline that we've been discussing this morning of foreign money going into ballot measures exists in the realm of election administration. That is what HB 5198 aims to push back on with a simple certification filed with the Secretary of State certifying whether any non-governmental entity offering grants, in-kind goods, or services has received foreign donations. This is a necessary step that will aid in the enforcement of the existing law and bring greater transparency into this process. Thank you for the opportunity to testify. Thank you. We will take questions now. Representative Fox. Yeah, if I'm hearing you correctly, it sounds like we're battling with evil in this process, something that is trying to short-circuit a good process we've had in our country for years. And so I applaud what you're up to. I guess my question here, because as you started talking and then you said his name, Zuckerberg, I started thinking of Zuckerberg, do you think we are going far enough with these bills or do we need to, you know, draw the line, move the line a little bit further right with the types of monies we receive, you know, whether it be for petitions or for elections or what have you? Is there another bill needed? I'll ask it that way. Well, I think that a great first starting place is to make sure that foreign money is out of these processes. As it relates to private election financing, a majority of states have passed laws to ban that. Many of them have passed those laws on a bipartisan basis. The issue that you run into here in Michigan is that there is a constitutional provision that guarantees a right to private financing that was put into the Constitution as part of Proposition 2. And I note that because that was also a measure that passed with a substantial amount of money from the 1630 Fund. So there's some overlapping concerns here. But this will further the provision that was also included in that, you know, in all fairness, that no foreign money should be included in those processes. As we've already seen, though, the existing private financing systems that have been set up is drawing money and support from entities that are taking foreign money. And that's why I think this bill is so important. Just if I may make a final comment. I have learned to dislike the word nonpartisan since I've come and started working here because to me it always seems to be a cover up for something, you know. And so I applaud you for what you're up to and your encouragement. Thank you. Well, thank you. There being no further questions, thank you for your time today. Appreciate it. And I will read in the remainder of the cards. Not wishing to speak supports the bills. Sherry Ritchie from Pure Integrity Michigan Elections. Not wishing to speak opposes Bill 4720, Aaron Shore representing MDOS. Representative Fox moves to excuse absent members. And there being no objection, the motion prevails by unanimous consent. There also being no further business before the committee, the committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Appropriations — Monday, November 3, 2025
transcript:
You are listening to the Michigan State Capitol Commission. Thank you all for being here. Let's start out with the Secretary. Please call the roll. Chair Canler. Here. Vice Chair Bauer. Here. Commissioner Hobbs. Commissioner Land. Here. Commissioner Oberland. Here. Commissioner Starr. Here. Five members are present. We have a quorum. I'd like to entertain a motion to excuse Commissioner Hobbs, please. So moved. Moved and supported. Any objections? If not, Commissioner Hobbs is excused. Thank you. Item three is establishment of the future meeting date. Our scheduled meeting is December 1st. We're hopefully going to be in a situation in the beginning of December where we won't need to have a meeting. But just in case, we might have this blocked out. So if there's nothing to vote on or anything for us to do, we won't have a meeting in December. But so if any commissioners have something they want to bring up in December, let me know. But I think we're going to be in a position where we don't have to take anything up then. The next item is approval of the minutes. Has everybody looked at the minutes? Does anybody have any questions, concerns? First of all, a motion to Commissioner Starr. Support. Support by Commissioner Bauer. Any questions, comments, corrections? Now the secretary takes the roll, please. Chair Canler. Yes. Vice Chair Bauer. Yes. Commissioner Hobbs is excused. Commissioner Land. Yes. Commissioner Oberland. Yes. Commissioner Starr. Yes. Five yes votes. Minutes are approved. Thank you. Right now we're going to meet at a meeting. I have Executive Director Rob come forward and go through your agenda. Again, most meetings recently, we have quite a long list of projects going on. There's a lot to report. A lot of work being done around here. And you'll see it's pretty impressive that people can manage this building as historical site as it is, but at the same time a working Capitol building. It's really quite a trick to manage such a situation. So as you go through these projects, I hope you appreciate how much work goes into it and how complex the work is. Rob, go ahead. Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Commission. Appreciate your time today. The first thing on my agenda I'll give everyone an update on is the fourth floor ceiling project. The fourth floor east wing scaffolding has been removed and is substantially complete. I think there are some touch-ups that need to be done at the five-foot level and below. That will take place the next couple weeks. The fourth floor north wing where the stairwell is on the north wing, the ceiling is completed and they're in the touch-up phase and the scaffolding will start being removed next Monday, November 10th. The fourth floor west wing, that was where the bulk of the project was. The ceiling that was completely removed has been replaced and the plaster has cured to an acceptable rate to accept the paint and we anticipate that work finishing up and scaffolding being removed by Thanksgiving break. H424, which is one of the conference committee rooms, also in the west wing, is having the detailed decoration added to the ceiling to match H428, which is the opposite of it. This work will have the whole painting crew's attention in the final weeks. Our schedule currently shows them finishing this space by the end of the year. The good news is all the scaffolding will be removed by the Thanksgiving break, so when legislators and Representative Schuette comes back, he'll have a clear shot to his office with no scaffolding, ducking, slipping on tarps or anything else. The side room will be there to the end of the year. At this time, it's not on the agenda, but I will mention a couple months ago I introduced to the commission the fourth floor, the grand stair project that we wanted to open back up. It is going to be a beautiful project, but we're going to put a pause on this project due to the fact that Rep. Schuette is up in that area. We'll need to provide ADA access all the times that that office is up there. So we're going to push this down the road a year, maybe two. We're going to continue our design and detail and figure out what the logistics are going to be. But if we were to move forward next summer as planned, we would have a three-month period where you would have to go to the south grand stair, step all the way down and crawl all the way back up just to get access to the west side where that office is located. That doesn't work well unless we add a scaffolding system that would start on the east wing, loop around through the south stair like a plank, and then back over. It was quite an expensive addition, plus we think it's time to remove the scaffolding and let the dust figuratively and literally settle and give the people an opportunity to see some of the work that we have done. And then we'll pick this project up at a date that works for everyone in the future. So we're going to put that on pause, and as we work through the design, I will share more of that information with the commission, and then we'll plan a future date to execute that historical project. The glass floor update. We have finished phase one. It's taken an awful long time to finish phase one, but that was the most difficult due to detailing the level of tolerance that's allowable when you cut the glass. It's a cast iron frame, so therefore it wasn't 90 degrees. Sometimes it was bent in. We worked diligently with the glass company, Lansing Glass Installation, and Lucid Glass Restoration in Rhode Island. But we're now to a point. It's in our digital twin. We have it down to a science, and we already have removed all the pieces in phase two and have 60 percent of the glass. So as we move forward, the phases will start rolling over a little bit quicker. But if you go to the west, I've got to get my bearings here, the southwest side, you'll see the phase that's already completed. You will be able to tell a small difference because the grout color is mildly different right now. But once we have a winter season, it'll blend in. You won't be able to tell one from the other. So it was a very successful phase one, and hopefully we have just as much success in the phases coming forward. Also last time I talked about the east lawn tree removal and our planning update. That was approved by the commission. We did approve the 2025 and 26 plan, but we are going to start actually removing the trees this Thursday, November 6th, and the other targeted trees will be completely removed by Saturday, November 8th. The installation of the new plantings will start next week, probably the 10th through the 14th, and the whole landscape project should be complete and cleaned up prior to the Silver Bells in the City event, which is November 21st. And then once that's complete, again, we'll implement the 2026 plan at the same time next fall, remove and plant. But I wanted everyone to know those dates so when you start seeing activity out there, you'll know what's going on. Last meeting I discussed having our architects and consultants conducting a thorough investigation of House and Senate chamber ceilings. This is one of our biggest projects coming up. This work will take place during the week of January 5th through the 9th.

I've discussed these dates with the clerk of the House, Scott Starr, as well as Secretary of the Senate, Dan Oberlin. They confirmed that these dates will work for them and we will not interfere with any legislative business. Once we develop a final scope for this work, we'll develop our documents, share with the commission, and plan to schedule the work for the summer of 2027. We are still trying to figure out how this is going to work. There may be scaffold poles coming down from, let's say, gallery level to the chamber floor, but we should be able to, at any time during that summer, not interfere with legislative business. It may be a little bit clunky like it was during the restoration project, although during the restoration project, if you remember or not, there were actually times where the chamber floors were moved to the Roosevelt Building and alternate spaces to run legislation. We hope to never be in that situation again, but there will be, in order to get to that work, we will have to erect some scaffolding and it may be a little inconvenient at times. Again, as we develop this plan, I'll have many, many conversations with the commission so everyone knows what it looks like prior to us even executing. Last meeting, I spent a bulk of the time talking about our drone education and detection. Bill Candler and I with Michigan State Police had an opportunity to go down to the Michigan Central Station where Airspace Link is located. Airspace Link is a software program that is run by a Michigan-based business. When you plug in the sensors for this, it basically lights the sky up like air traffic control. You are able to see drone flights all over the area, whatever the radius is. Let's say they had a three-mile radius, so we are watching drones fly all over the city of Detroit. They are working with Oakland County. They are working with Amazon. We know that there's airspace rights available above the train tracks and there's even a donut shop who's bought into that and they can deliver donuts to certain areas within Detroit as a sample of how to start accessing space in the air for drones. This is moving so fast. Again, I mentioned this before. The technology is moving quicker than the policies that are being set and the laws that are out there. We are doing everything we can to stay ahead of it. As we move forward as this commission, I think the drone security strategy should be built in three phases. The first phase is a detection phase. The detection phase involves installing software and hardware to detect and monitor drone flights in and around Capitol Square. Matter of fact, we're going to be launching a proof of concept software system with Airspace Link in the next month. I'll have a lot more detail to share after a meeting this week. This software will display and detect all drone flights within a designated radius around Capitol Square. It will illustrate the drone and even show us where the pilot of the drone is located due to the updated technologies. This is very useful as we can compare this data with any registered flight plans from the FAA to see if they are in compliance. Once this proof of system is installed, I'll invite you all for a demonstration and show you how it works and how it will help our security team for this phase. I've also started communication with the Michigan Drone Association, Mr. Matt Reibart and Graham Filler. They are deeply involved with drones in Michigan and understand the existing technology, what kind of technology is coming in the future, and also working with the legislature as bills are being drafted for policy and future laws. I also had a conversation with Representative Bill Bruck last week. He is getting ready to introduce a package of bills with sponsors on both sides of the aisle that takes care of many issues that I haven't read the bills or understand it, but I know they'll address policies and procedures of laws, where they're manufactured, who has rights to the airspace. One of them is probably listing the Capitol as critical infrastructure, which all helps everyone. I'll continue that communication with them as we continue to move forward. The second phase will be a mitigation phase. This process will focus on reducing the severity or an impact of a negative event by taking specific actions to lessen the potential harm. Communication is the most important factor in this phase. This starts by making sure everyone understands what policies are in place, what's coming and going to be put into place, how to gain permission to fly within Capitol Square, and who to speak with prior to submitting a flight plan if you're going to be on Capitol Square. This is still way out for implementation, but the groundwork and understanding for this phase starts with communication and keeping ahead of it with communication with the Michigan Drone Association, Airspace Link, a lot of the manufacturers, and the legislator to see what policies and procedures are being put into place. The final phase would be an enforcement phase. This is the final stage of a legal or administrative process where a court judgment law or regulation is compelled to be followed. This is also where our enforcement team, the Michigan State Police, can now start taking action and enforce any future policies and laws. As you can see, there are many questions and issues that need to be addressed, and I will stay aggressive with my education and understanding of the drone world. I've already started to connect with these key and important associations that are deeply involved with this topic, and as I learn, I will continue to share and communicate with the commission of our plan and what we're going to do. But as we are right now, we are just going to do the first phase that I mentioned, which was the detection phase, and I will not move into any of the other phases until I have a better understanding of where we're going, and I won't do anything unless I have the permission of the commission prior to that as well. There was a lot there. Do I have any questions on that category before I move on? Okay, good. In your folders, you will see the brochure for the portrait conservation of Governor Fred Green. This is one that we removed from the caucus rooms, sent it to our conservator in Chicago, Julian Baumgartner. It was very successful. We are very pleased with the details of it. But this shows the highlights of the portrait and the artist itself as well. It highlights a brief history of the artist, the process that was taken before the painting, and finally some detail about the finished governor's portrait. It currently is being displayed on our conservation window in Heritage Hall. Feel free to stop by, and it's for everyone to enjoy and also share a lot of the work that is being done by our team that the general public doesn't necessarily get to see all the time. We're very pleased with the result, as I said, and we plan on sending another portrait out next year to Julian Baumgartner again for conservation. I do not know what painting that is as of yet, but I will share with the commission prior to sending it next time we do it. Capital education and tour numbers. In September, we gave 182 tours and served 4,800 people. This is 200 more people than we did in 2024. For October, we had 8,568 visitors on 286 tours. This is 18 more tours and 244 more people than October of 2024, which is great. In this past weekend, we were open on Saturday and we had 105 people show up and we served them for tours, which is we're happy. As you can see, we are continuing to grow this program, which is really our intent. Additionally, it's important to say that our marketing and our social media outreach has continually increased and we are reaching out to more users than we ever have. As we have monthly meetings with our marketing, they show us the direct impact of the social media postings, which isn't just tours. It's everything from what projects are we working on to what events are coming to highlighted events and highlighted special things in history that we collaborate with. We do know that we are reaching out to tens of thousands of people monthly and the new growth, it's over 10 or 15 percent a month of new viewers that we're outreaching as well. So that was the intent of the marketing and outreach for two reasons. Number one, making sure that we have a clear and balanced message instead of each of our groups sending out a different message. It's more collaborative, which is really better to control and also trying to reach the different groups that are out there, whether the museum groups, the reading groups, library groups, education groups, the portrait conservation groups. There's so many items that we touch with our programs here at the Capitol Commission that we want to make sure we share all that and share everyone who's interested in that. The next item is to talk about an annual cost of living adjustment. I proposed to the commission and Bill Candler a cost of living increase that took care of the COLA, but as well as a 3 percent lump sum. The challenge with working for the commission is trying to make sure that we keep up with all the competing agencies and all the other groups that are hiring people out there. We want to make sure to retain our best people, so we want to make sure that we're paying them a fair wage or a little bit more to keep them here. We all know that most folks that work here are very passionate and love to work here, but we don't just want to take that part for granted. We also need

show them that the wages that we give them are very competitive and fair in the surrounding community. Rob, you want to talk a little bit about what the jobs are that we're talking about as a group of people? Yeah, so if you think of our group, and our group, I've said this before, is very intellectually diverse. We have educators who have master's degrees and history degrees, and they're writers. We have decorative painters. We have a capital artist who commissions paintings, and other decorative painters who have perfected the craft that only can be done here at the building. Our grounds crews have come from golf courses around. As you can tell, our lawn looks better now than it did when I first came here 10 years ago. It really looks spectacular. We have hired master electricians, master plumbers, master mechanics, which have the building run even better. You don't see many lights out, but when you do, they're replaced right away. All of our systems are being monitored by computer experts. We have to consider the IT people that talk in here now. Even the porters that we hire to clean the building, you just can't come in with a mop and a bucket of water and start wiping the surfaces. If you have water on our wainscots out here, you're not cleaning dust off, you're wiping paint off. So it's specialty cleaning, and everything is to a higher level of detail than just a regular job out in the market. So those are the things that I have to deal with and want to share with you, but these are the type of people we want to retain who pay attention to detail at all times. Thanks, Rob. Commissioner Oberlin, you had a motion to make? Yes, Mr. Chair. I'd like to move to apply an annual cost of living adjustment of 3% to Michigan State Capital Commission staff pay retroactive as of October 1st, 2025, and a one-time lump sum grant of 3% for this fall. Second. Commissioner Starr seconds. Any conversation, any discussion, questions? Now, Secretary, take the roll, please. Chair Kamler? Yes. Vice Chair Bauer? Yes. Commissioner Land? Yes. Commissioner Oberlin? Yes. Commissioner Starr? Yes. We have five yes votes. Motion passes. Thank you. Thank you. A couple more things. Our Christmas ornament update. To date, we have sold almost 1,500 of our 2,500, and it's just November 3rd. We knew it would be a big sell this year, and we actually increased the price to cover our cost. But if you remember, it is a star with the actual piece of the glass floor in it, so it has an actual artifact. And the more people hear about it, the quicker they go. So I just wanted to share that with you. We're excited that we've already sold this many so quickly. Typically, we only order 2,000 ornaments. We ordered 2,500 this year, and we know we're going to sell out. So we're super happy about that. The last thing I'd like to share today, we did finish a battle flag video trailer that I want to share with the group here today. Just as a reminder, on December 6th, we have a couple premier showings of this video, which is going to be 35 minutes in length, I believe. But we'll have a little program before. We've invited anyone who's come back for the battle flag placement from last summer. I know the 4 o'clock, we're already, I think, 250 people out of 300 have sold or reserved. We know there's still more room at 7 o'clock, but we're now to the point we're going to market this video that you're getting ready to see to the media this week and open it to the public. So we know that the rest of these spots are going to fill up very quickly. So we'll have two premier showings on December 6th, about 300 to 350 each showing, and we know we're going to sell that out. So we're already starting to talk behind the scenes about what do we do to share for future because we know a lot more people are going to want to be able to view this video. So let me cue it up here. Civil War became a very deadly game of capture the flag. To lose your flag was a dishonor. To capture a flag was a great honor. And the men in the battlefields are remembering the promises that were made, and they're remembering those presentation ceremonies, and they're fighting the last man to defend these flags. In the chaos of battle, regimental flags were the heart and soul of the men fighting beneath them. Beacons of regimental cohesion, the colors were vital in maintaining order and combat and were carried front and center in the line of battle. Chosen for their precision, courage, and tenacity, the men who bore these colors were unarmed, high-value targets. Carrying far more than a banner, he carried the courage and honor of his regiment into battle. It was one of the most honorable yet deadly duties in the Civil War. This is the story of the battle flags of Michigan. I know we're all excited for it. I hope you have the opportunity to come. If you can't, that's okay. Again, we're going to have a few other showings in the future for this. But I just wanted to make sure that you guys had an opportunity to see that trailer before the general public. So I'm open for any questions. Anybody have any questions on anything? Commissioner Bauer? No. I just have a comment. With the number of tours last month, I was here with a third-grade class, my great-nephew. So I had done it a couple years ago with my great-niece from DeWitt. But I just have to say, you know, I'm amazed seeing it through the eyes of the chaperones and the teachers and the kids. It's so well organized. Our docent was excellent. Very good. I can't believe she could control those third-grade kids like she did. But, you know, just my hats are off. All of our staff are phenomenal. But that whole cadre of people who make that happen, it's just amazing. And I always can't help but think Heritage Hall. I mean, it's wonderful in many ways. But the fact, the impact it has on tours with groups of one after the other after the other of third graders who come in. It's hard to believe we used to do it differently and people were in the older part. So just, again, hats off and thank the staff for one small part of what goes on in this building. Thank you. Thank you. Any other business? Anybody? How about public? Any public comments? Anybody from the public wish to address the commission? If not, I move to adjourn. So moved. Commissioner Bauer. Supported by Commissioner Lamb. Any objections? If not, the meeting is adjourned. Thank you, everybody. Thank you.

title: Labor 25-10-30
transcript:
The committee on labor is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairman Cherry? Here. Senator Camilleri? Here. Senator Cavanaugh? Here. Senator Albert? Here. Mr. Chair, you have four members present. There is a quorum. Thank you. I will now entertain a motion to adopt the meeting minutes from October 23rd. So moved by Senator Camilleri. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. Today, we're going to be receiving testimony regarding collections on pandemic era overpayments from the unemployment insurance agency. We're going to have some folks who are going to discuss what they're seeing on the ground with clients and people that they represent. And then we're also going to have the director of the unemployment insurance agency come talk about what's being done and how those payments, collections are being handled. First, I would like to invite up to testify Jacob Fallman from the Sugar Law Center and Christine Wasserman from Wasserman Law. Thank you all for joining us today. There's a little button at the base of it that you can touch to turn it on. There you go. Thank you. Am I good to get started, Senator? Oh, thank you. So I really appreciate the opportunity. My name is Jacob Fallman. I'm the unemployment insurance policy coordinator with the Sugar Law Center for Economic and Social Justice in Detroit. In my role, I provide statewide advocacy support and training primarily to legal services providers that are directly supporting claimants as they deal with issues related to their unemployment benefit claims. So I'm really glad to be able to start us off today to sort of introduce where we are now and how we got here. So it's my understanding that about 85 or so percent of the collections that we're seeing right now that are the reason that we've called this hearing today is that they're related to the pandemic. And so I know we're all sort of eager to forget some of the things about the pandemic, but it's important to remember because that's the context that these claims arose in. So people were, you know, forced to stay at home. They were put onto unemployment insurance largely, you know, against their own choice. You know, they were told to apply and there was really no other option for them. And so it's important to remember also why these collections were paused in the first place. In 2022, the Saunders v. UIA class action settlement halted all collection activity because the UIA couldn't ensure that it was respecting claimants' due process rights against the workers that it was collecting against. And so the judge paused collections to give the UIA an opportunity to fix its collections processes and find a way to make things right for people that were facing improper collections and large bills. That injunction recently ended and when it ended, that put the UIA back in the driver's seat. So collections have started again against over 350,000 of our neighbors who have been asked to pay back thousands in benefits that they received years ago during the pandemic. The UIA is not sending new notices to people, only bills. So the people are not being told why they owe this debt, only that they the amount and that they owe it and that they need to start paying. People are expected to navigate a computer system that we all know is not very user friendly and has issues. And we know that because the state is currently investing tens of millions of dollars to replace that computer system and will have a new one next summer. So that's sort of why we are here. And, you know, who's facing these collections? The pandemic revealed the huge gaps in the coverage of our unemployment insurance system that we couldn't allow to stand when people were forced out of work and during the pandemic. Congress created new programs during the pandemic and states, including ours, did their best to implement them and pay people who were forced to stay home. But mistakes were made, understandably, because the rules and the guidance were changing sometimes by the day. And the government and everyone involved was doing their best to make sure that people that deserved payments could get them quickly and could pay their rent, pay their bills, and to prevent fraud to the extent possible. Individual workers should not have to bear the burden of the government's mistakes. And the government should be required to show its work if it wants to reach into Michiganders' pockets and bank accounts. It's not clear from what we're seeing now that the UI even knows for sure who it's collecting against or if it has a valid reason. Some of the same problems that made the Saunders pause necessary are still happening. Claimants are being collected against despite having made only timely appeals and have a hearing pending on their benefit entitlement, but they're still facing collection activities despite having no final determination. Claimants are being collected against even though they won their hearing or received a waiver and have a final order from a judge that said that they don't owe anything. Some of them are still owed benefits that the UIA refuses to pay. Some of these claimants, when we've had them set up meetings with the UIA, the UIA has told them in those meetings that those collections were a mistake and to ignore the notices. But we can't expect Michiganders to second-guess these bills when they receive them from the UIA. The UIA should know ahead of time, before it's trying to engage in these collections, whether that's a valid collection. So what steps need to be taken to prevent this from happening again?

The UIA is going to tell you that they have a legal obligation to collect. And they do. But they also have an equal, if not greater, obligation to respect the rights of workers who made good faith claims for benefits during a dark and frightening time in our history. Workers are entitled under our law right now to a waiver of overpayment that was caused by the agency's error. And there have been many agency errors. So we are busy. We do have the capacity right now. We've got a dedicated team. They're working long hours. They're working their overtime. The budget process did preserve our ability to bring on limited term staff when needed. That's very important for the UIA because when the economy goes one way, our demand goes the other way. It's a long hearing. No, no, that's okay. I appreciate it. Thank you very much. Thank you. transcript:
The committee on labor is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairman Cherry. Here. Senator Camilleri. Here. Senator Kavanaugh. Here. Senator Albert. Here. Mr. Chair, you have four members present. There is a quorum. All right. I'll entertain a motion to adopt the meeting minutes from June 12th and September 4th. So moved by Senator Kavanaugh. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. Today we will begin by considering Senate Bills 49 and 50, which I had introduced. So Michigan is one of 26 states authorized by federal OSHA to operate its own occupational safety and health enforcement program. Under the operating agreement, the state must be, quote, at least as effective as the federal program, including having consistent maximum penalties. In September 2021, the Department of Labor notified LEO that Michigan was out of compliance with the federal maximum penalties, that the state was obligated to adopt such penalties. So Senate Bills 49 and 50 make the changes necessary for MIOSHA to bring the program back into compliance with federal standards. The language also reflects some executive orders, which changed where MIOSHA program is housed. And to have additional information, I'd like to invite up MIOSHA Director Bart Pickleman and Brennan Smith to discuss. Thank you, Chairman. Thank you, Chair Cherry and members of the committee for allowing us to give some more background on this today. I just wanted to note that these are reintroductions of bills, and you may find yourselves seeing this presentation and recalling aspects of it from our previous testimony. So at this time, I'm going to turn it over to Director Pickleman. Good morning. Thank you for the opportunity to explain a little bit about this legislation or bill or need for it. I'll start with MIOSHA's mission, which is pretty simple, to help protect the safety and health of Michigan workers. And our motto, which has served us very well over the years, is to educate before we regulate, which means before we go out and enforce a new health or safety rule, we have our very robust consultation education and training division that goes out and prepares employers and employees for the changes that are coming before enforcement knocks on their door. A little bit about state plan basics. Michigan is one of 29 state plans that are authorized by federal OSHA. That bar that we must meet, as the chair said, is to be at least as effective as federal OSHA. The Michigan program covers 400,000 Michigan businesses and over 5 million Michigan workers. The benefits to having a state plan versus federal jurisdiction is the flexibility, accessibility, and accountability to stakeholders, a broader consultation strategy as a result of the additional state funds that are available. And most importantly, it covers additional 600,000 plus Michigan public sector workers that would not have coverage in the state of Michigan if it were not for a state program. Federal OSHA does not cover public sector workers. This just reiterates that fact. The public sector workers are your firefighters, your police, your paramedics, your road workers. And again, with federal OSHA jurisdiction, they have no protections, no OSHA protections. So federal OSHA increased the maximum penalty amounts for various types of citations in 2016. State plans are required to be at least as effective, as I said. When federal OSHA determines a state plan is not at least as effective, it takes measures to take over jurisdiction of that state plan. Federal OSHA has initiated steps to take over the jurisdiction in states of Arizona and Utah before they increase their maximum penalty amounts. And Michigan is currently one of only six states that have not adopted those federal OSHA maximum penalties. MIOSHA's current maximum penalty for a serious citation is $7,000. And for a willful or repeat citation, it is a maximum of $70,000. Versus the federal OSHA current maximum penalties for a serious citation is $16,550. And willful or repeats are $165,514. There is an annual adjustment according to the consumer price index at the federal level. MIOSHA's philosophy on penalties is that they are part of the deterrent effect, along with enforcement presence. I use the analogy of what keeps you driving the speed limit. Is it the price of the penalty or is it the number of police officers you pass on the way to where you're going? In my opinion, it's both. All penalty money collected goes to the state of Michigan general fund. MIOSHA does not receive any funding from the general fund. In other words, no quotas. MIOSHA penalties are not designed to be punitive. It's very difficult to put the price on someone's life or limb. When calculating penalties, MIOSHA evaluates, first of all, the severity of the injury or illness that could occur. High, medium, or mild. High being, of course, death or irreparable harm, loss of limb. Then we look at the probability of that injury or illness occurring in a lesser or greater context. That is also coupled with penalty reductions such as the size of the employer. In Michigan, we give up to 80% penalty reduction for small employers. And we also give up to 30%.

reduction for an employer's good faith, which means how well they interacted with the inspectors while they were there, and overall, how well is their safety and health program. And finally, we give up to a 10% reduction if the employer has not had any citations with MIOSHA for the last three years. Due to that severity probability and penalty reduction assessments, MIOSHA does not routinely issue that maximum penalty amount. MIOSHA's current serious penalty maximum, as I said, is $7,000. However, the average amount of penalty for serious citations for all employers averaged together is only $1,333. And for employers with 25 or less employees, the average is $637. MIOSHA will continue to calculate penalties using the same processes. If Federal OSHA were to take over jurisdiction in Michigan, the following advantage of the state plan program would be lost. First of all, and most important, those public sectors, those firefighters, police, paramedics, would not have OSHA coverage. The extensive consultative outreach and education for employers would be lost. Program administration located in Lansing with legislative control would be lost. Michigan stakeholders involved in policy development through advisory committees when we go to develop a new standard, or every five years we convene focus groups to help us with our five-year strategic plan. So we pull them together. That would all be lost. And affordable safety training through our MIOSHA training institute. I hit it too many. All right, key points. Again, penalties are a deterrent, but MIOSHA strives first and foremost to proactively educate employers through consultation and other services. Even when penalties are issued, MIOSHA reduces penalties based on numerous factors. The average penalty issued by MIOSHA for serious violations is only 20% of the maximum penalty allowed. OSHA is mandating that MIOSHA or Michigan update their penalties to match federal penalties, which were passed nine years ago. Since then, Michigan has received audit findings and a warning that failure to update our statute to match federal amounts may result in U.S. OSHA taking over jurisdiction in Michigan and the loss of the local oversight. If U.S. OSHA were to take over, more than 600,000 public sector workers, including those in some of the most hazardous occupations like firefighting, emergency response, and law enforcement, would lose the protections that are afforded them under the state-run plan. Michigan employers are not going to avoid the increase in the maximum penalties. It is a matter of who will enforce them, federal OSHA or MIOSHA. We do have customer survey cards that we send out to employers and employees during investigations and activities. And a result of those comment cards have said that comment cards used to rate MIOSHA services show more than a 98% useful rating for our services in the state of Michigan. So I think that answers the question who Michiganders would like to run the OSHA program. So with that, I'll take any questions. Thank you. Thank you, gentlemen. Members, are there any questions? Senator Albert. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you for your testimony today. Just looking at Senate Bill 49, could you kind of walk me through the investigation inspection process? When would a citation be issued? There's language in here that's talking about a conference. What does that timeline look like for all that to take place? Yeah, so the investigation initiates for a number of reasons. It could be a fatality. It could be an employee complaint. It could be just a programmed inspection because you're in a high hazard industry that we're targeting because you have high injury and illness rates. Once an inspection is initiated, an opening conference is held. We explain the purpose of our investigation, why we're there, and the process of the investigation. We then conduct employee interviews. We gather lots of information, documents. We do a walkthrough of the facility. These investigations can take days, months, or over a year to complete, depending on the factors involved in the investigation. Once we've collected all of the information we need, we hold a closing conference with the employer to go over our alleged findings and any alleged violations and explain the appeal rights that they have. The closing conference is the start of that 90-day clock for us to issue the citations. Once the citations are issued, then the employer has the right to appeal. If I may, Mr. Chair, help me understand, make sure that I understand this properly. So the federal law mandates a minimum of, or sets a benchmark, I should say, perhaps, of once the, at the start of the inspection and the start of the investigation, that the citation has to be given within 90 days. Is that what the federal benchmark is? No, the federal statute of limitations is the citation must be issued within six months of the occurrence of the violation. So if it's a fatality, it would have to be within six months of the fatality occurring. All right, thank you. And then to compare that to the state statute, as you said, the investigation is kind of indeterminate. It could be a year, it could be three months. It could be kind of however long it takes for the department to go through the process. Yeah, but there is also the factor that we are not made aware of fatalities and accidents in a timely fashion either. So in some cases, we're not made aware of a fatality in a year. So if we had that statute of limitations of six months, we wouldn't even be able to do our inspection and issue citations. Thank you. I just wanted to, I guess, flesh out what the federal standard was and to kind of compare to what is being proposed here in law. So thank you, Mr. Chair. Any further questions? Thank you very much. Thank you. And I think we have a few position cards. We do, Mr. Chair. Not wishing to speak in support of Senate Bill 49 and 50, Aaron Wyo, AFLW, representing the AFLW 876. Also not wishing to speak opposed to Senate Bill 49 as drafted, Amanda Fisher representing NFIB. And not wishing to speak in support of Senate Bills 49 and 50, Robert Jory representing Luna Michigan District Council. And the last card in support and not wishing to speak for Senate Bill 49 and 50, Ryan Siebel representing Michigan AFL-CIO. That is all of the cards, Mr. Chair. All right. Next, we will consider House Bill 4017 brought to us by Representative Nayor. Representative, please come forward. I believe you have Joshua Scramlin from Michigan Farm Bureau who's coming up with you. All right. Welcome. I think I got it. Thanks. Thank you, Chair Cherry and fellow senators for the opportunity to speak on this bill. It's ironic that we're here speaking on my OSHA issues again on the same day. When you have a family member that dies or is accidentally killed on a small family operation there, the last thing that's on your mind is to be contacting any department and filing the proper information. And unfortunately, that's what happened to the Eisman family here back in 2019. They did not file a report with my OSHA within eight hours of the death of Keith Eisman. And eventually they ended up being fined over $12,000 for failing to file or get that information to my OSHA in a timely manner. These are not, these small operations like Keith's Farm is not a large corporation, even though they are an LLC or considered a corporation. What this bill does is recognize that a small family farm does not have a large, or does not have an HR department, does not have staff that handles paperwork in these untimely events, and gives them a grace and does not get them out from the penalty, but also, but gives them a grace of reducing the fines by up to 80% and even more if they do not have any other compliance issues. This

Legislation had been introduced by former Representative Kali back in 2020. Made it all the way to the governor's desk. Unfortunately, we did not have, or at that time there wasn't a proper definition of a family operation, family farm operation. We have resolved that issue in this bill and it will definitely help out and make it much easier in these stressful situations when a family member is killed or injured on a farm and help that out. To add more detail, I'm going to turn it over to Josh and give some information and I thank you for your time. Okay, thank you Representative Nyer. Chairman Cherry, members of the committee, good morning. My name is Josh Scramlin. I am an associate legislative counsel with Michigan Farm Bureau. We are the state's largest general farm organization representing over 40,000 family farms in every corner of the state that produce everything from asparagus and apples to corn and dairy products. I'm here today to express our strong support for House Bill 4017 and we are grateful to Representative Nyer for reintroducing this important legislation and we commend the House of Representatives for its strong bipartisan passage of the bill on September 3rd. So like Rep Nyer said, in 2019, Keith Eisenman, a farmer from Lenawee County, tragically lost his life in an accident on his family's farm. And on March 6th of this year, members of the Eisenman family testified before the House Agriculture Committee in support of this bill. And I would certainly encourage everybody to watch that testimony because it underscores the human element of the legislation that we're talking about here today. So following Keith's death, MIOSHA imposed fines totaling $12,000 on his grieving family, primarily for not reporting the incident within eight hours. So what House Bill 4017 seeks to address is this issue by reducing the monetary penalties that MIOSHA can levy on a family farm after the loss of a close family member due to a farm-related accident. So to be clear, this legislation does not eliminate the reporting requirement. Furthermore, it applies only in cases where the accident occurs on a farm owned by the directly impacted family and involves the death of a direct family member. So we fully acknowledge the vital role that MIOSHA plays in protecting workers, and we do agree that timely reporting is important to ensure that unsafe conditions are not overlooked or concealed. Farming is, by nature, a hazardous profession. There's daily tasks such as working with livestock. Right now, a lot of our members are out in the fields for fall harvest, so they're moving machinery around, conducting building maintenance. These are all inherently tasks that carry risk no matter how many precautions are taken. So we firmly believe that imposing significant fines on grieving families does nothing to prevent future accidents. It only adds to the pain of an already traumatic situation. So our member-adopted policy book supports, quote, appropriate safety regulations, but it also opposes, quote, enforcement action against an owner-operator resulting from self-imposed accidental injury, and that is exactly what happened to the Eisenman family in 2019. So in the immediate aftermath of a tragedy, notifying MIOSHA may not be the priority. Families should not be penalized with steep fines for failing to make a phone call within eight hours of losing a loved one. So I do appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony, and I'd be pleased to attempt to answer any questions the committee may have. Thank you. Thank you very much for your testimony. So just to make sure it's clear, this reduction would only be in place if it is the owner and or their immediate family member. Yes, it would be brother, son, wife, husband, daughter, immediate family member, not second, third cousins, wife's cousin, or something like that. It's defined. It's in federal statute, the definition that we're using. So it will definitely close up that loop, which was the issue and the reason why it didn't become law the last time or when Representative Colley had it through. Okay. Members, are there questions? Senator Albert. Thank you for this. Unfortunately, this was vetoed. I've supported this in the past and happy to support it again. I just want to, I guess just to make sure, so this bill would require the fine to be reduced by 90%? No. By 80% and possibly more. I think with the previous presentation there, you see what the federal guidelines are. If there is no previous history with this farm having accidents or a fatality on the farm, that would probably be in consideration and give it even more flexibility to reduce it. We can't completely eliminate it because we're dealing with federal law. This is the best we can do. Sure. Thank you. I just want to make sure I understood it properly. I appreciate it. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Senator Kim Maleri. How many of these types of incidents happen every year? How many family members die on a family farm? I'm going to have to follow up with you on that because we did, so Michigan Farm News is a publication of Michigan Farm Bureau. We did just publish some data on that, but I do not know it off the top of my head, so I will follow up with your office on that. And then I think Senator Kavanaugh and I were sharing notes here, but why not just extend the period of time required for the report? So instead of the eight hours, make it the 24 hours for a family death. I think that entangles us with the federal regulations. And so this is the cleanest, simplest way to do it as best we could. We're making an attempt now that we're aware of this through Farm Bureau and other organizations to inform the farmers and also some of your first responders out there to help them make aware that when there is a situation like this that they need to sort of look at that, and hopefully through the education process we can keep people from having to deal with this situation. So what is the federal regulation that you're concerned with? It was just briefly touched on this morning there that when you do have a fatality on an operation, any and all operations there, that you should be notifying MIOSHA or OSHA of that fatality within a specified period. And I believe the previous presentation brought that up. Got it. Thank you. Any further questions? All right. Thank you very much for your testimony. And I believe we have a few testimony cards for 4017. Yes, Mr. Chair. Not wishing to speak opposed to House Bill 4017, Ryan Sebold representing the Michigan AFL-CIO. And one other card not wishing to speak opposed to House Bill 4017, Aaron Siku representing AFCW 876. And that is all the cards, Mr. Chair. All right. Thank you. There being no further business, without objection, the Senate Committee on Labor is now adjourned. Thank you.

Looks more like a chamber. Looks like, yeah. That's a big... That's not the Senate room, is it? I don't know. Good afternoon. The Senate Committee on Economic and Community Development is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chair McMorrow. Here. Senator Kavanaugh. Here. Senator Polanki. Here. Senator Moss. Senator Geis. Senator Victory. Present. Senator Lindsey. Here. Senator Weber. Here. Madam Chair, you have seven members present. There is a quorum. Thank you, Madam Clerk. I will now entertain a motion to adopt the committee minutes from the May 7th, 2025 meeting. So moved by Senator Kavanaugh. Without objection, committee minutes are adopted. We've got a couple of bills up on today's agenda. First on today's agenda for testimony only is Senate Bill 128, introduced by Senator McCann. Senator, please come on up and explain what your bill does. And we have some special guests joining us on the Zoom. Thank you very much, Chair McMorrow and colleagues on the committee. I appreciate the opportunity to discuss the bill today. I'll be brief. I know we're all running a bit behind on our schedules and have some great special guests joining by Zoom. So this bill would establish an Ireland-Michigan trade commission. The commission would seek to establish mutually beneficial trade relationships to help communities here in Michigan and abroad in Ireland through the creation of educational, economic, governmental, and people-to-people links. Importantly, Ireland is the only place you can access the European Union and the United Kingdom at the same time. And this commission can be a strong voice for Michigan in the EU this way. The legislation is modeled on laws that have been adopted in both New Jersey and West Virginia to establish Irish trade commissions within their states. Other states that have established similar commissions include Massachusetts, South Carolina, Connecticut, Maryland, Oklahoma, Maine, Montana, Ohio, South Dakota, Wisconsin, and Arizona. So we would not be alone here. Membership on the commission would include representatives of the Michigan Chamber of Commerce, a public institution of higher education in Michigan, people who represent Irish-American communities, and bipartisan appointments of the legislature. The commission would meet at least quarterly or more frequently at the call of the chairperson or at the request of five or more members. The work of this commission would be chronicled in an annual report to the governor, legislature, and the commission would be authorized to create and raise money for the Michigan-Ireland Trade Commission fund in order to minimize administrative costs and ensure no taxpayer burden. Thank you for your consideration. Here with me on Zoom from Ireland is the chairman of the Senate of Ireland, Mark Daly, with whom I'm pleased to have a great relationship with that's been built over the last few years, and former prime minister of Ireland, Bertie Ahern, to offer further testimony about how this bill will mutually benefit Michigan and Ireland. Thank you very much, Senator McCann. Before we invite our guests over Zoom to testify, do we have any member questions for the bill sponsor? Seeing none, thank you very much, Senator. Senator Daly, welcome to our committee over Zoom. We will begin with you, and you can begin your testimony whenever you're ready. Chair, thank you so much for allowing myself and Bertie Ahern, the former prime minister who negotiated the Good Friday Agreement, and I suppose in real terms, and Taoiseach Bertie Ahern will refer to this, but there are people alive in Ireland today because the U.S. got involved, but more importantly, stayed involved in the peace process, and Bertie Ahern was one of those two people who signed that peace agreement after nearly three decades of violence in Ireland, and the U.S. involvement was central to all that. I will speak more to the economic element, and Bertie Ahern will talk about the importance of this for the ongoing peace building in Ireland. One of those elements is that Ireland now is the largest English-speaking country in the European Union after the UK left the EU, so this is an all-Ireland commission, including Northern Ireland, so it would help with Michigan companies who are looking to access the UK and the EU market at the same time. But from a political point of view, it's about building bridges for the day you need it, and when Michigan has something of concern that is being proposed by the European Union, instead of contacting the State Department in Washington and then turning on to try and get somebody in the State Department in Brussels and maybe try and find someone in the bureaucracy in the European Union, through the network created by this commission and the commissioners appointed by the governor and Senate president and others and the speaker, it would build those relationships, and then if a call was required between the Senate or the House or the governor and the Secretary of Agriculture in Ireland or the Prime Minister, who's going to be at that table where the European Union is making that decision, that is one of the key elements of the political part of this, but also in terms of building those governmental relationships over time. The commissioners would be invited to Ireland every August where we have a summit, where we go to Northern Ireland, look at the peace walls, visit Northern Ireland and their Legislative Assembly, meet with members of our committees here, but also building relationships by having chairs of our committee go to Michigan on a regular basis and building relationships on trade and economics. And just on the, I suppose, on the peace building element, and then I'll hand over to Mr. Hearn, my good friend Bertie Hearn. Only last month, the UK and Irish governments appointed an envoy as a go-between between the paramilitaries in Northern Ireland and the British and Irish governments to try and see how we can bring the paramilitaries to an end in Northern Ireland. There are an estimated 10,000 paramilitaries in Northern Ireland. Most of them are not active, but the ones that are active are involved in criminality and drug dealing and racketeering. So that'll tell you that even though Bertie Hearn signed that agreement in 1998, we still face challenges in terms of implementing it, and that's why the support of Michigan and the members of the Senate and the House will be greatly appreciated as this is part of that peace building. And thank you for allowing me to be part of this testimony today. Thank you, Senator Daley, very much. Prime Minister Ahern, welcome to our committee here in Michigan. Thank you for your patience. As we extended our session today, you are welcome to begin your testimony. Thank you very much, and it's a privilege to speak with you and speak with your committee and to join the Speaker of the Irish Senate, Mark Daley. I know you've had a busy day in the Senate, so just to make a brief few words. I think for the last 30 plus years now, United States at all levels has been hugely helpful to us in helping to build a peace and create the circumstances that have continued on and allowed our economy to grow and allowed us to have a two-way relationship with the United States like we'd never been able to have before. Building educational, cultural, business ties. And that's been the back of, as Mark Daley has said, on the back of our peace process. One of the things that we've been trying to do in recent years started off, as you said at the outset, moving the bill of the New Jersey Assembly, setting up the trade commission legislation. And it's drawn, I think drawn in a very broad way so that there's mutual benefits for us all. My interest, of course, has been having to go

associated the piece, sustaining the piece. And I see many, many advantages for this. But hugely important also is the support of the Michigan Senate to be able to build up our relationships and continue to build that. And Northern Ireland, I think, has been peaceful today and remains peaceful mainly because of the interest shown by our good selves and by so many state legislators and so many people from Congress and successive presidents and administrations. And we appreciate that. And I very much appreciate. I think there are many, many benefits from this bill. It's not for me to enter today, but I think in time we work through very successfully. But thanks to you for giving us time to say these few words. And hopefully you'll see merit in supporting what we believe is a very good trade commission between both of us. Thank you. Thank you very much. Do we have any member questions for either the bill sponsor or our guests via Zoom? Senator Kavanaugh has a question. Thank you, Chair. I just wanted I think it's a little bit more to the bill sponsor. Is there and I don't think there is, but is there any other trade commission in MEDC? And how does the department feel about this creation of the Michigan Ireland Trade Commission? Yeah, thank you. I don't believe we have heard from the MEDC yet on this legislation. Appreciate the fact that we can have a hearing on it. And I look forward to getting their opinions on it. I know that recently the governor and the executive branch and MEDC established a relationship with United Arab Emirates or the KAR as it's referred to. So there are some examples of one country, you know, understandings, PACs, relationship building. And I think that, again, as you've seen a number of states have done this, I think it's to their collective and overall benefit. So my hope would be that, you know, I don't think that there's a downside to doing this. In my mind, I think it just builds us up and strengthens trade relationships and country relationships. Thank you very much. To Senator McCann or perhaps Senator Daly, could you expound a little bit on the funding mechanism for the commission? Senator, you noted that the members would be required to raise the funds to operate the commission. So this would be revenue neutral for the state of Michigan and not require any taxpayer dollars. I'm wondering if you could speak to that a bit more. And perhaps, Senator Daly, how has that worked in other states where this has been implemented? Yeah, if you want me to speak to that, Chair. Yeah, I mean, the key part of this, especially in Northern Ireland, taxpayer dollars and how it's spent is very important. So the key element is that the commission raises its own funds in terms of to do its work. And many of that comes from Irish companies that are established in those states, as well as US companies that use Ireland as a gateway to Europe. So we have about a thousand companies from around the world that use Ireland as their access to a market of 450 million people in 27 countries. And Ireland being the gateway for that. So that's one of the key elements. And as Senator McCann said, so far 25 US states have passed the Ireland Trade Commission legislation, seeing the value of Ireland as their voice in Europe, but also in terms of looking at Irish companies. And as the T-shirt pointed out, Ireland is the sixth largest investor in the United States of America. For a country that's about this size in terms of geography and with a population of just over 6 million people, it's a country which it's very easy to access the decision makers, no more than Michigan. But in terms of the funding model, I think it's the way forward in terms of saying, look, there's loads of support out there in each state for the commissions that have been established. Thank you very much. Do we have any remaining questions from committee members? All right. Seeing none. Thank you, Senator McCann. And thank you for joining us over Zoom. We greatly appreciate your time. Thank you so much. Thank you. All right. Next up on the agenda for testimony only is Senate Bill 200 introduced by Senator Singh. Senator, welcome to our committee. Please come on up and explain what your bill does. That's right. Thank you very much, Madam Chair and members of the committee for having testimony on Senate Bill 200. I'm pleased to be joined here by Mike Kruger. Mike is the owner of Crunchy's and Peanut Barrel, two establishments in the city of East Lansing. And he and his staff brought to my attention sort of a concern that they had. Currently right now, Michigan law prohibits dogs on patios. But if you go all across the state, depends on which community you're in, oftentimes you'll find patrons with their dogs on a patio. And it's been the local health department that oftentimes will come in in certain communities and say, no, you can't do this. And in other communities, health departments know what's happening but do nothing about it. And there's no implementation on it. And so the question was, could we make this very clear? And so I was pleased to work with Mike to help draft up this legislation. One, I want to say that this is nothing new. 23 other states already allow dogs on patios. So we use their implementation process that they have used. What this does is it doesn't require a restaurant to allow dogs on the patios. But if they elect to want to do that, this would provide them the opportunity. Obviously, there will be a set of rules that you'll see in the legislation that require how cleanup has to be done as well as ensuring that there's no dog hair. You can't bring your dog through the interior of a restaurant. It's only on the outside. And if a community really says this is not something we want, I want to also give that community the right to say, hey, there shouldn't be any dogs on patios. And they have the right under this legislation to say community-wide we don't want to have that. And so this way I thought there are probably hundreds of restaurants all across the state that are currently allowing dogs on patios. My staff, every time I see a dog on a patio, I take a picture and I send it to them. And we talked about having a slideshow for you all to see the dozens upon dozens of places that I've found dogs on patios. And oftentimes I think the owners don't even know that they're breaking the law. And so I think this is a common sense piece of legislation that sort of rectifies the situation, puts the onus on to the restaurant. If they want to do it, they can. And if a community decides this is not what's in their community, they can also decide to ban the practice. And so I just want to thank you for the opportunity, and I'll turn it over to Mike, and then we'll be able to answer any questions from the committee. Yeah, no, thank you guys for having me. Thank you, Chair McMorrow. Much appreciated. Sam kind of summed up pretty much a lot of the stuff, the points that I was going to make. Speaking about peanut barrel specifically, the reason I brought it to Sam in the first place was that under the previous peanut barrel administration, so to speak, dogs were more actively on our patio than they are now. And the reason that we had a health inspector in there one day who, while she was not on the clock, she mentioned to me, like, hey, you've got to not do that kind of a thing. And so I was like, yep, no, you're right. It shouldn't be happening. But then once we started implementing that policy of not allowing them on the patio, my staff got a lot of pushback. They got a lot of rude customers who had been previously allowed to do it and whatnot. And so that's kind of when I came to Sam to see if we could maybe do something about it and get it at least legalized in the state or at least have the option for all the businesses to do it. Because for us, it cost us quite a bit of business by having to turn people away who had dogs that wanted to sit on the peanut barrel patio specifically. And I've dealt with the same thing over at Crunchy's. And obviously service animals we allow, et cetera. But then now even in those situations, people are just saying that they're service animals. And there's only so many questions we can ask. And it puts my staff in a very awkward position to not have any actual rules that we can follow legally. So, yeah. Thank you both very much for being here. So I want to just emphasize a point that you made. There was some noticeable revenue loss or business loss when the dogs on patios allowance went away. I don't think they were ever allowed. It was just more that we started enforcing it, essentially. Excellent. Do we have any questions from members? Senator Lindsay has a question. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you for the testimony today. I actually think the idea is great. I do wonder as you're working

process and especially since we have a business owner here to speak to this, what strikes me though is that this whole section of law seems terribly overly burdensome and we're doing something to create an opportunity here, but even within that it's not exactly super simple. So you pull it up and we've got both a law about the food law, but a lot of what's happening in it is referencing regulations in the food code. You can pull those up. That's another 300 pages to go through and we're going to have a new line in there about when animals, you know, whether it can be crustaceans can be in and living tanks and then now we're going to have this special carve out for dogs. I just wonder, you know, I mean, is this not maybe also an opportunity to, you know, look for ways to make it even simpler? And maybe a question to you if you would, I mean, as a business owner, as a restaurant owner, I mean, is this burdensome? It looks to me like there's a lot you got to wade through and make sure you're crossing your T's and dotting your I's just to do business in Michigan. Yeah, I mean, reading through the bill, I mean, all of that stuff is pretty common sense from a restaurant perspective and a business owner perspective, you know, you know, dog's gonna have to be kept on leashes, you know, the owner's gonna be responsible for cleaning up their own messes if they were to make a mess and then ultimately be responsible for any kind of harm or, you know, damage that could come from, you know, one of these animals. But for me, it's just more about making sure that my staff have clear guidelines to follow and we can put those in place without any issue really at all. Senator, I think you're asking maybe even a larger point is that perhaps in the food law, there are other provisions similar to this one that probably don't make sense. And should we look at those types of regulations? You know, I'm always open to taking a look at other regulations as they come up. You know, obviously this is one where we had hoped that we could have done it for the last patio season. Obviously we're past patio season, but my hope is that we can move this piece of legislation through so for the next patio season, we'll be ready for it. But if there are things that we're seeing in the food code that feel burdensome, I'd be willing to have that conversation with you. And I'm sure our friends in regulatory affairs would be the ones that have to consider that if that ended up being the case. Thank you very much. I would also further like to clarify, always open for additional ideas to streamline regulations. And notably, this was an issue that I heard in my first campaign starting as early as 2017. So we are headed on 10 years later and still have not allowed for dogs on patios in a clear way. I know we have a question from Senator Polhenke. Thank you, Chair McMorrow. Senator Singh, where is the Michigan Restaurant Association on this? Do you know? I think there are some cards. I think the Restaurant Association is neutral. I think the Michigan Licensed Beverage Association is in support of it, but I do believe they both have cards that will be read in at a certain point. It just seems like if there's not enough personnel to enforce this and people are doing it, restaurants are doing it anyway, you shouldn't be penalized by losing customers because you're following the law. I think the law just needs to change. So thank you. Senator Geis. There we go. Okay. Is there anything in here that would allow a restaurant to have on its patio a dog-free section, kind of like we used to have some no-smoking sections in restaurants? Because there are going to be people who want to enjoy their favorite restaurant on the patio but might be allergic, might be scared, just don't want to... They left their dog home and don't want to be eating with someone else's dog. So is that something that could be included in this? I'll let Mike answer in a second, but I think that's up to the operational sense of each owner, right? I think there's nothing prohibiting having a dog-free section and having a dog section. I think just as Mike has heard people saying, hey, we're disappointed we can't have our dogs, if he heard a large volume of people saying, we don't want to come here anymore because of that, I'm sure he'll make operational changes. But it's really left up to the operator. There's nothing in here that restricts it, and obviously, like I said earlier, there's nothing that mandates it either. No, Senator Singh is absolutely correct. I mean, if we were to find that this isn't what people want, then at least having the ability to allow it in the first place and then figure that out ourselves, I think, is extremely important for us to be able to do. Thank you very much. Do we have any further member questions? Senator Lindsey, I see your light on. Okay. Just want to make sure. All right. Seeing no further questions, thank you, gentlemen, both, for joining us in committee today. We do have a couple of cards to read in. John McNamara with the Michigan Restaurant and Lodging Association not wishing to speak is neutral on the bill. Mason Doerr supporting the bill not wishing to speak from MLBA. All right. Great. We don't need to excuse any absent members. So seeing no further business, the Senate Committee on Economic and Community Development is now adjourned. Thank you.
