The committee will resume and will the clerk please call the roll? Chairman McCann. Present. Senator Singh. Present. Senator Baer. Present. Senator Schink. Present. Senator Hertel. Here. Senator Camilleri. Senator Chang. Here. Senator Polhenke. Here. Senator Lowers. Senator DeMoose. Senator Outman. Senator Houck. Here. Senator Bellino. Mr. Chairman, you have seven members present. There is a quorum. Thank you very much. I think we'll get another member or two as other committees wrap up on the day. I'll entertain a motion to adopt the September 18th, 2025 committee meetings moved by Vice Chair Singh. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. We'll make a motion to excuse any absent members. Being no objection, absent members are excused. All right. Well, thank you, Senator Chang, for making it. We've all been running by the seat of our pants today, but we have you up now to testify to your bill, Senate Bill 305. And I know there's a sub that we'll adopt momentarily. Why don't we have you do your testimony and then we'll adopt the sub and then we'll go to other testimony from there. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair. I'll just stay up here for efficiency and appreciate everyone's patience. Say I'm really grateful for the opportunity to talk about Senate Bill 305, a bill to create the Air Quality Enforcement and Mitigation Fund. This was Senate Bill 26 last term, and it did pass the Senate as well as the House Committee and unfortunately did die on the House floor. For more than a decade, ever since my first year as state representative, I've attended countless DEQ and now EGLE hearings related to air quality violations, both in and around my district. And at each of these hearings, residents would often advocate for certain changes and give their feedback on the proposed consent order developed as a result of conversations between the department and violating company. And at every single one of those hearings, residents would talk about how the fine being paid to the state for an air quality violation wouldn't be coming back to their neighborhood, even though they were the ones who experienced the air pollution as a result of the violation. Because the law does not say where the fines go, they go to the general fund. So I pulled together a few groups and community residents for a meeting at my office to try and figure out how we could change where the money goes. And so this bill is a result of those conversations. I will briefly remind folks that in Detroit, the asthma hospitalization rate for children is three times the statewide rate. And the burden is heavy for some of the neighborhoods that I have had the honor of serving in this legislature. And they want to see some of the money come from the fines back to their neighborhoods to help mitigate the impact of pollution. So what does Senate Bill 305 do? It creates the air quality enforcement and mitigation fund and outlines how the funds would be spent to mitigate air pollution in communities, especially those facing disproportionate environmental burden. Currently, when a company violates the air quality standards or their permit, the result is often a consent order that details the steps that the company must take to prevent that situation from happening again, along with a monetary fine. And the fines are calculated using EPA guidelines and then negotiated with the company. Right now, as stated earlier, our laws don't provide a mechanism to ensure that those fines go back to the community. So we would create a new air quality enforcement mitigation fund. And I do want to note that funding needed for supplemental environmental projects done at the facility for air pollution prevention, air pollution reduction, or air monitoring would still be allowed to occur under this new fund. And the money needed for those projects, such as improving air pollution control equipment or other changes, would not go into the air quality enforcement and mitigation fund. So 20 percent of the money in the fund would go towards EGLE functions that benefit environmental protection communities and are related to the mitigation of air pollution through a fund, would go towards EGLE functions that benefit environmental protection communities and are related to the mitigation of air pollution through increased air monitoring or improved compliance assistance. Last term, the number was actually 30

percent, but in the House committee we compromised with other industry stakeholders and House members and brought that down to 20 percent. And the rest of it, 80 percent, would go to nonprofits, local governments, colleges and universities or school districts through an air quality community impact grant program. And so that could be through air monitoring, health impact assessments, education, training, buffering, air filters, diesel engine retrofits and other mitigation projects in the community. EGLE would develop guidelines for implementation of this new grant program and would develop those in consultation with an advisory committee that includes a public health expert, representative from an environmental organization, DHHS, local health or environmental department, and two resident committee that includes a public health expert, representative from an environmental organization, DHHS, local health or environmental department, and two residents of environmental protection communities. And also at the request of the manufacturers and other industry stakeholders, we did add an industry representative with environmental mitigation experience to the advisory committee while the bill was in the House last term. The bill notes that the grants would prioritize environmental protection communities defined as geographic areas that EGLE defines using MIEJ screen, which is a really great tool that is online as communities facing disproportionate environmental burden using indicators such as sensitive populations, socioeconomic factors, exposures, and environmental effects. During the committee process in the Senate, we did work with EGLE to clarify how they would identify these communities, and we also narrowed down the tools. And actually in the S1 that we have, we narrowed further because one of the tools no longer exists because of the current federal administration. A report on grant allocations would be required annually and made public. I do want to note one last time that we made a lot of changes to this bill last term at the suggestion of both EGLE as well as industry, including both the manufacturers and the chamber. Some of those changes include clarifications that some of the funds can be used to support industry compliance efforts and prevention of future violations. We removed language that would permit EGLE to use this fund to hire staff. We also removed language that would allow the fund to take philanthropic funding money and also removed the possibility that the fund could be used for voluntary buyouts of homes. So again, lots of changes. The goal here is to mitigate damage done to communities. This legislation would divert money back straight into our neighborhoods that are impacted. And I do also want to point out the amount of money that we're talking about is actually quite small in terms of the impact on industry that would be pretty minimal, but a really large impact for individual neighborhoods and individual households. And so if this bill were to become law, we would be able to make a positive impact for communities affected by pollution in a meaningful way. Thank you so much for the opportunity. Thank you so much, Senator. Are there any questions of members for the bill sponsor at this time? I don't see any. So now we will move to adopt the S1. And do you have anything you want to say about the substitute, Senator? So I made a quick reference to this, but in the bill as we moved it last term, it made a reference to the EPA's EJ screen tool. In February, this current administration ended the use of the tool. It no longer exists. So we have taken that language out of the bill. And just for clarity, the Trump administration removed reference to environmental justice measures in the bill? Yes, I believe on day one, the current administration removed references to environmental justice. And also in February of this year, got rid of the EJ screen tool. So if you Google it, it goes to a link that has nothing on it. I'll entertain a motion to adopt the S1 moved by Senator Chang. Will the clerk please call the question? Chairman McCann. Senator Singh. Senator Bayer. Senator Schink. Senator Hertel. Senator Camilleri. Senator Chang. Senator Polhenke. Senator Lowers. Senator DeMuth. Senator Outman. Senator Houck. Senator Bellino. Mr. Chairman, there are eight yeas and zero nays. The substitute is adopted. Thank you very much. We'll now move on to testimony from others. And I believe we have from the Southwest Detroit Community Benefits Coalition, Simone Sagovac joining us. And if you are here on Zoom, please start speaking, and that should put you on our screens. Thank you. Good afternoon. Thank you for the opportunity to speak to a critical need for communities that host industry for Michigan. I'm speaking about the need for an air quality enforcement and mitigation fund. My name is Simone Sagovac. I have lived and worked in the city of Detroit for over 30 years in Southwest Detroit, which is our heavy industry engine for Michigan and beyond. I'm here to let you know about the type of community that needs air quality protection and some of the successful projects that are helping to improve health for thousands of people. Our community hosts industry that serves all of Michigan, yet we bear the life-threatening daily burdens. I don't know about each of your communities and how many air permits are required to emit pollution, but we have over 40 in the Detroit-Southeast Michigan area and many other sources of pollution. Within short distances of homes and schools and play areas, we have an energy plant and steel production that are coal-fired powered that generates soot, a lime plant, one of the largest sources of sulfur dioxide in Michigan, our wastewater treatment plant that serves one-third of Michigan with a dozen incinerators, multiple cement factories, an auto plant, our state's largest oil refinery, and our border crossings with Canada with 10,000 daily semi-trucks, just to name a few. Teachers in schools in our community have piles of inhalers on their desks for children in their classrooms to use during the school day for their asthma. Children have died in their sleep, walking home from school, and are even born with asthma. We need to do what we can to help. When air violations occur, it only makes sense that these fines received would somehow help those affected by the pollution that causes the violations. You may be aware that there is a certain health protective level set for each air pollutant, and we have many. When one level is exceeded, we are considered in non-attainment for air quality and health protection. In my community and for all of Wayne County, we have been in consistent non-attainment for over 15 years. Once in non-attainment, it takes years for agency plans to bring us back into the legal range of air pollution. We are now breathing illegal air at levels known to damage health in many ways and not only causing among the country's highest asthma rates, which means it has been known for years that our air is harmful to everyone who lives there, and especially to children who breathe faster with smaller lungs than adults. Now some good news. In recent years, we have been able to secure funds through supplemental environmental projects that result from different actions. These funds have been invested in helpful programs that are making a difference. But this has occurred only in special circumstances, not by using regularly collected fines for polluting. These regular pollution fines have gone to the state's general fund with no direct benefit to the people who have been harmed by the pollution. This doesn't make sense and should be a concern that the state is actually getting revenues from harm to its residents without using those funds to help. Some successful programs have included, we've gotten air filters placed in schools like Solon Elementary School in Dearborn that is surrounded by steelmaking and automaking emissions. We worked to put air filters in a number of various schools. Cleaner air in the classrooms means students can focus on learning. In other programs, we provided windows and HVAC systems for homes along the I-75 freeway where truck traffic is heavy. 175 families received this program and residents have been grateful. Residents say they can finally sleep through the night and feel rested for work the next day. Many homes in the area are not up to modern standards with old windows and doors that let polluted air into the home. Most homes don't have air conditioning. With our extreme high heat weather, that's a problem. Residents can't open windows to get air because of the air pollution that they let in that makes them sick. Programs can help solve these problems so that kids can focus on learning in school and families can be safe from pollution inside their homes. While small programs don't solve our big air pollution problem, community projects done with funds from pollution violations can make a difference and help many people. We have a responsibility to consider pollution impacts we put on others. This modest effort to create a fund is a common sense way to do what is right and reduce pollution impacts where possible. Thank you for supporting this fund to assure that some harm can be addressed. All right, thank you very much. I'm looking to see if there are any questions and I don't see any at this time so we greatly appreciate your testimony this afternoon. Thank you for being with us. And I think now based on the cards I have on the table here in terms of others wanting to speak, I just have now Nick Leonard from the Great Lakes Environmental Law Center.

And also, if you are coming to us via Zoom, I think if you start speaking, you should come up on our screens. Yes, sir. Thank you very much. My name is Nick Leonard. I'm the executive director of the Great Lakes Environmental Law Center, and I'm here to speak in support of Senate Bill 305. I've had the distinct honor of representing a lot of communities, a lot of individuals that live nearby a facility that has at one point or another violated an air quality law. And in general, all people have the same question when that kind of thing happens. And the questions are, what happened? What kind of health risks may I have to deal with now? And most importantly, how am I going to be sort of made right? How are the harms that I've suffered going to be addressed? And that's really what Senate Bill 305 seeks to, that's the problem Senate Bill 305 seeks to address. It basically calls on industrial facilities that have to comply with air quality laws to be good neighbors. I think everybody expects when somebody harms you, whether it's your neighbor next door or the industrial facility next door, you expect them to make it right. And in particular, when someone violates an air quality law that's meant to protect the health and air quality that all Michiganders rely on, residents expect something for the harm that they've had to endure. And unfortunately, how our current laws are set up, that's not the case. Oftentimes when somebody lives near a facility that has violated an air quality law, that has emitted too much pollution, that has put the public health at risk, the nearby residents are left with essentially nothing. I think it's important to note that residents aren't really looking for money. They're not really looking for compensation. They want something to help their community. And so when I've worked with communities in the past, the kind of projects that companies have been able to come together around with community members are community assets, like improving HVAC systems at local schools to improve indoor air quality to make sure that children have good air quality in the places that they're learning. Also means upgrading air filtration systems at community centers where seniors spend a lot of times. It could mean replacing diesel school buses with electric or low emission school buses so that there's not a significant source of air pollution traveling throughout many of these communities. It could also mean putting air purifiers in people's homes so that they can improve indoor air quality where people live. These projects often help to rebuild trust between industry and community members. Obviously, anytime there's an air quality violation, a lot of folks that live nearby those facilities are going to be hurt. And the trust that exists between the owners of the facility and the community members is frayed, sometimes very seriously so. And these kinds of projects can help to rebuild that trust. It helps rebuild sort of the community in a lot of ways. And I'll just close by this. When I've worked on these projects in the past, it's become clear that industry often wants them. Our Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy wants them. And the community wants them. This bill would more or less help remove the obstacles that exist to getting these projects moving. It would create a dedicated fund so that there's not so many procedural hurdles and logistical hurdles to getting these kinds of projects done in communities that desperately need them. And that's why I support this bill. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Leonard. I see a question from Senator Chang for you. Senator Chang? Thanks so much. And Nick, I really appreciate your testimony. And, you know, you and I have worked together on a lot of issues over the years. One thing I wanted to see if you could help clarify for the committee is, so you talked about some examples of supplemental environmental projects. And so I just really want to make clear for the committee that what we're talking about with this bill is it would be a different, supplemental environmental projects could still happen, but this bill would create a different process. And one of the things that I think is important to note is that a supplemental environmental project has to be mutually agreed upon, right, with the company. And so there have been times that I have seen where the community is asking for one thing, but then the thing that actually happens with the supplemental environmental project is not actually really the thing that the people wanted the most. And so that's why I think that this bill, you know, creating a different process where the community itself is determining what the money is used for, I think is really important. So I'm just wondering if you can share a little bit about how that process would be different. Yeah, absolutely. So the supplemental environmental project process has a lot of pitfalls. So for a bit of background, supplemental environmental projects are commonly kind of basically community benefits projects that are agreed to as a component of a settlement agreement stemming from an air quality violation. So the pitfalls are generally, mostly arise from the fact that these things happen in the context of an enforcement proceeding, which means there's a lot of sort of confidentiality concerns, which also means that basically these are agreements between the company that's violated an air quality law and the Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy. There's very little community involvement. That serves to basically kind of create a pretty significant chilling effect for the entry of supplemental environmental projects or the implementation of them. You know, if industry is going to agree to dedicate funds to those kinds of projects, they typically like to have a good degree of community buy-in. And that's just really difficult to do in the enforcement process, in the process of like negotiating a settlement agreement. So I think what this bill does, which is really important, is sort of take sort of this, the process for creating those projects out of the enforcement context where there's a lot of barriers to community engagement, barriers to community involvement, and puts it into sort of a separate forum that is more amenable to sort of basically industry, government, and community working together. Very good. I'm seeing no other questions. Thank you very much for joining us today. I don't have anyone else lined up for testimony on the bill, so I'll ask the clerk to read the cards into the record, please. The following are in support of Senate Bill 305. Samantha Pickering from the Michigan Environmental Council. Tim Minotis from the Sierra Club. Dylan Jabard from EGLE. Ben Polson from the Michigan League of Conservation Voters. Kathleen Sloninger from the Asthma Allergy Foundation of America Michigan Chapter. And the following are in opposition to Senate Bill 305. Michael Limo from the Michigan Chamber of Commerce. Joshua Antonini from the Mackinac Center for Public Policy. Chuck Lipstro from the Michigan Agriculture Business Association. Joshua Scramlin from the Michigan Farm Bureau. Mike Wachowski from the Michigan Manufacturers Association. Terry Quimby from the Michigan Chemistry Council. Adam Majestic from the Detroit Regional Chamber of Commerce. And John Boothroyd from the Michigan Sugar Company. All right, thank you very much. We'll come back to the bill at a later date. Appreciate all the testimony. We have a couple minutes left, and I'd like to accommodate a request for a speaker who's turned in a card to request to speak for no more than three minutes. John Schleicher from the Michigan Interfaith Power and Light. John? Yes. Yep, if you have a couple minutes, and then we'll have to wrap up. Please give us your name and your interest. You should get a red light. There we go. Name is John Schleicher. Try again at the base of the microphone. Thank you. John Schleicher, Bishop Emeritus of the Northwest Lower Michigan Synod of the Evangelical Lutheran Church, formerly chair of Michigan Interfaith Power and Light. I think this relates to 305, although I didn't know that coming in here. We are in opposition to the shutting down, not shutting down the Campbell coal plant. As you probably know then, and I'll just read this very quickly, Consumers Energy Campbell Coal Plant in West Michigan is one of the big

greenhouse gas emitters in the state. It was scheduled to close May 31st. The Trump administration extended it now twice. The last 90 day extension expires on the 20th of November. So I think I'm not planning to but I'm in support of what you have just adopted in terms of support for 305. And the reasons economically besides health, which was the big argument that I heard today, it was projected to save Michigan $600 million by 2040. They are saying consumers are saying that just to keep it open for five weeks costs $30 million. If it remains open for another 30 days, the price is expected to increase to $100 million. So what consumers is going to do and they've already said this is they're going to increase rates for all of us in order to meet the cost of keeping the coal thing in place. So I just am encouraged by what action you've taken today and ask on behalf of the health of our residents and the cost to all of us that this be passed and that in any way that you can can oppose further extension of the coal fired plant. Thank you. Thank you very much. Appreciate you being here today. Seeing no further business before the committee and without objection, we are adjourned. Thank you.

title: Government Operations — Thursday, October 30, 2025
transcript:
The House Committee on Government Operations will come to order. Mr. Clerk, would you please call attendance? Chair Bergold? Here. Representatives Harris? VanderWaal? Present. Fitzgerald? Here. McFall? Here. Mr. Chair, you have four members present, a quorum. Okay, thank you. Representative VanderWaal moves to approve the minutes from the August 21st meeting. Without objection, so ordered. Well, good morning, everybody. Today we're going to hear testimony on the Children Trust Michigan bills that our floor leader, Brian Posthumus, has up today. Representative, you want to come on up? You can go ahead and begin when you're ready. All right, good morning, Mr. Chair. Thank you very much. Committee members, thank you very much for hearing us out. I'm going to start with a little bit of background. Children Trust Michigan, as I'm sure a lot of you are familiar with the organization, has been around for a little bit. It just so happens that in the early 2000s, my mom was on the board of directors and chaired the organization. Interestingly, when I was growing up, and I'm not going to get too much into the personal side of this, but when I was growing up, I only ever saw my mom as just a stay-at-home mom. That's what I knew of her. That is the extent of it. She left the career field and her professional life before I was ever born and had to deal with my petulants and managing me as a kid and as a teenager. It wasn't until she took over and joined the board of directors for Children Trust Michigan that I actually saw that professional side of her, what she could do. She actually was the one that started the signature auction, which is now named the Pam Postumus Signature Auction. Many of you have probably been in attendance there. This organization is really near and dear to my heart. When Children Trust Michigan came to me earlier on this year and said, hey, we need to do some legislative changes in order to modernize as well as to update statute based on the name change because it was Children Trust Fund, Michigan Children Trust Fund. They wanted to modernize and also to follow through with the name change in order to better serve kids in the state of Michigan. That means making sure that the board of directors is more accessible throughout the state for highly qualified individuals, making sure the needs of children are met throughout the state, whether that's the Upper Peninsula or northern Michigan or anywhere in the state, by having members of the board be able to participate in meetings, whether or not they can make an eight-hour trip to Lansing to participate. A lot of the modernization of the organization. I'll actually turn it over to go through some of those details. Happy to take any questions. Thank you. Good morning. It's not funny. All right. Thank you for the opportunity to share the important bills before you today. My name is Amy Tatry-Lopp. I am the current chair of Children Trust Michigan. I'm in my sixth and final year of being the board chair. I've asked Suzanne Greenberg, who is our executive director, to be here with me to sit in case there are any questions that I'm unable to answer. She is not able to advocate as a state employee, and instead she will be here to educate if we need it. So before talking directly about the bills, I'll provide a bit of background to set some context. So what we shared with you is this map that shows that we have partners in every county across the state that we work with. It'll show you the different types, and it explains what the various forms of prevention are that we help provide. We also gave you this, which is simply a very—it's really a very simple document, but what it does is it tries to help educate new parents that it's normal that kids are going to cry, how to handle it, how to take care of yourself, how to calm a baby. So this is what we would call primary prevention material. That's just one example of what we try to do to ensure that child abuse does not occur. So CTM is a rather unique entity. I'll provide a bit of background to just provide some context, if I may. With our executive director and the team of our state employees, administratively housed within MDHHS, the board is an independent board that has gubernatorial appointment. And those people come from varying backgrounds as set in statute. Children Trust Michigan serves as a voice for children's families and children and promotes their health, safety, and welfare by funding effective local programs and services that prevent child abuse and neglect. So we are here for the partners that actually do the work. We are the only statewide entity that focuses solely on child abuse and neglect prevention. As I mentioned, we have partners in every county in Michigan who we work with to try to seek assistance before any abuse occurs. We serve as a hub providing to support financially and otherwise so the state has the boots on the ground that can expand their work they know needs to be done with their own community. While we seek to significantly impact our reach, just so you're aware, our 2025 budget is just over $4 million. The majority of our revenue comes from the state fund that was established in 2014 with bipartisan and bicameral support. We also receive federal community-based child abuse prevention funds from the federal government, and then we do our own fundraising. We are not in the state budget as it stands except for $200,000, and that has to do with retiree health benefits. So I just wanted to be clear. I think there's a misperception that we're getting money in the budget along the way.

We know, though, that there are much more resources that are needed. I recognize that the public officials hear this over and over around many topics. The difference is that we're here so that children and families never have to enter the child protective services system by providing early intervention and education. Our work is to help save taxpayer dollars down the road. We have one of our other board members, and I think maybe another couple here with us today. Angela Dudley is an amazing woman who has fostered over 224 kids. She's adopted 11. What Children Trust Michigan attempts to do is ensure that those kids don't have to go into the foster system. So that's our work. We were fortunate to receive ARPA funds that allowed us to expand our work. As you recognize, the funding's ended. We and our partners find ourselves having to make cuts and pull back on the critical work we've been doing. Our board and team are very passionate about what we do and what our partners do. A number of us, both the team and the board, have either experienced child abuse and neglect and or have other lived experiences and are very aware of the outcomes that often occur because of that. I do continue to be confused why so much funding occurs after harm has occurred. We've seen prevention work done for smoking, seatbelts. The medical profession is now focused more on prevention to promote healthy living and avoid complications later. However, the protection of our children has received only a fraction of this attention. That is why CTM and our partners are here, to educate and strengthen children and families so they never have to go through what some of us have. I provide this background to explain the importance of House Bills 4805 through 08, as well as to request that this committee consider the needs of children in the Michigan budget process as it proceeds and we work to keep them safe. Now, regarding the bills before you, you have 4807, which amends the Child Abuse and Neglect Prevention Act. The purpose of this bill is mostly updating out-of-date language, as the representative mentioned, such as our name change. It will also expressly give CTM the ability to partner with a 501c3 to expand our capabilities. So while CTM is a nonprofit under federal law, we are not labeled as a 501c3, and often what happens with foundations when we go to seek money and funds and help, most bylaws for these foundations require that the entity be a 501c3. So we were really looking for explicit authorities that we can do that. I also want to address an error that was made, our error, that was made in the original bills, and that was changed in the Senate in the S2 version. It was in regard to audit requirements. So that language has been stripped in the Senate bills. House Bill 4805 amends the act that establishes the Children's Trust Fund. Current law allows CTM to pull up to 5% out of the trust fund as long as the $23.5 million corpus stays in place. What we'd like to do is see if we can have that raised to 8%. The intent is not that we would take that 8% every year at all. It's only in times of economic downturn or some other major budget issues. We're working with Treasury right now to adopt a policy that in concert with them, and we've already talked with them. They came and presented to us at our board meeting last January about just being cautious and aware, and trust me, we are. We never want to get to a place where we don't have enough in there to take some of the funding. So that's the intent of that component. 4806 simply amends the vehicle code. It's simple cleanup language regarding our name change that allows CTM license plate. We originally were the only entity that did have the license plates that it was allowed for our designation, and now there are many, and so that also has impacted our revenue. Lastly, we seek to amend the Open Meetings Act. Our board is comprised of members across the state, Marquette, Kalamazoo, Southeast Michigan, Grand Rapids. This is very important to our mission that we do have the statewide organization. Having said that, because of the important roles that some of our board members do play in the state, such as being called into court or being called to rescue a child, that keeps them at times at the last minute from driving to Lansing for our board meetings. So, for instance, one of our board members is a prosecuting attorney in Marquette. If the judge says the trial is that day, it's that day, and there's nothing she can do to do anything other than take the two-day trip to Lansing, basically. We are requesting that we continue to follow the OMA in every way, except for the in-person requirement. We will always have in-person meetings. We're not trying to get away from that. We're not trying to just do Zoom. We're just trying to make sure we can get a quorum because we have had significant challenges with getting a quorum at times. Part of our board is made up of, in statute, it delegates how our board is comprised. So we need an attorney. We need a clergy, et cetera. So it's tricky. So we do respectfully request the committee's vote of support in these bills. We remain hopeful they will be enacted yet this calendar year with immediate effect to enable us to further and continue our work to keep Michigan's children safe from harm through early intervention. Thank you for your time. I appreciate it, and your commitment to the state. We're very happy to answer any questions you may have. I'll just wrap up. As she was going through the list of bills, as you can see, there's nothing that's big, monumental changes that are happening. It's literally everything is based on how can we best serve the kids of our state going forward in the most effective, efficient manner at all. So any questions, we're happy to take them. Okay, thank you for your testimony. I will say I'm awful impressed that we here in Michigan were second in the nation to have an organization that helps to prevent child abuse like this. So that's awesome. And to dedication, especially to somebody like Angela Dudley, who's fostered 224, that is absolutely amazing. So thanks for that dedication. I do have a couple questions. I think we're contemplating a new plate, or do we know the design, or that's already out there? That's out there. Okay. So the license plate. So basically, I don't know if you've seen the license plates. It's like all the different plates that you can get. Children Trust Michigan have one, and that was designed a few years ago. Okay. We did redesign it in the time. So the current one we have now is what we're going to keep? Yes. It's the pinwheel that you see there versus the hands that were there. I didn't understand what you meant by plate. Thank you. Sure. Do you know how much money that generates a year with the license plates? About $80,000. $80,000. And initially it was about $1 million when it started. Now it's $80,000. And again, that's because we were originally the only license plate, and then a number of other groups, as you know, have added on. Okay. And one other question is, was I correct in understanding when I read through this that there is a request to change the annual audit from the Auditor General to Michigan DHHS? No. Yes, that's how they were introduced. We misunderstood some information. So we then had an amendment in an S1 that said we could do a bid. That wasn't something that was supported, so we agreed to take that out because we didn't want to hold up the rest of the package. Okay. So that's been amended on the Senate side yet. The House bills haven't been amended. They will be. Okay. Very good. Representative Fitzgerald. Thank you so much for being here this morning. Appreciate you, Representative. I just wanted to quick clarify on 4808 regarding the Open Meetings Act. Current structure is that the in-person board meeting must take place and that a virtual option is not able to be held at this moment. I'm sure that during COVID there may have been some changes that were made to allow for that. We've moved away from that. Those orders were lifted. I guess I understand that we have a number of people from across the state. Tell me a little bit about, again, we have a 15-member board, correct? 15-member board all over the state. Tell me a little bit about how this is going to help to, I guess, promote the function of the board and the trust fund. Oh, sorry. So while some of our members may not be able to attend the meeting, the vast majority of time they at least are on screen. We offer that hybrid option, but their vote doesn't count for anything. So that's where we're having a problem with quorums at times. Our member of clergy who has been assigned to our board is in Detroit, but he travels nationwide for various conferences. And so, you know, it's just – and we went from six meetings to four in hopes that we would have – be able to get the quorums easier. It's just we're always at the last minute hanging on to see if people – you know, who's going to show and asking if they're going to be able to come. Well, I'm going to be 10 minutes late. I'm going to be 15 minutes late. I got stuck in traffic. And we can't do our business and have any votes unless we have that quorum. So it's just very challenging. And I assure you this is not any kind of attempt for circumvention of the OMA. We want to see each other. We want to be in person. So it's just that challenge we have sometimes. It's troubling.

Representative VanderWaal. Thank you Mr. Chair and thank all of you for being here today. As I read through when we have the two tiers of funding, I was just curious how many times have you been above the $23.5 million and how many times have you been below that in the lines of the funding model and how that would work? To my knowledge we've never been below that amount. We're at almost $29 million now so we could take 5% of the $29 million but we're very challenged this year. Staff has been let go and more are being let go at the end of the calendar year. So it's not a huge amount of money that changes from the $5 to the $8 but we just want to be able to do as much as we can. Very good, thank you. Okay, I got a couple cards to read in here, not seeing any further questions. Are you good with us? We're good. Alright, thank you. Thank you very much. Thank you for your testimony. Okay, not wanting to speak today in support of the bill is Megan Blue of Michigan Health and Hospital Association. Not wanting to speak in support of the bill is Gabe Basso of Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan. Not wanting to speak in support of the bill is Dr. David Michelson of the Michigan Education Association. And not wanting to speak in support of the bill is Matt Gillard of Michigan's Children. Stanley? Yes. Stevensdorf? Yes. Grant? Yes. Mr. Chair, you have 14 yeas, 0 nays, and 2 pass. The motion prevails. Thank you, Madam Clerk. We will go at ease. Call the chair. The committee will come to order. The chair recognizes Rep. Aragona to speak to his bill. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you, committee. Obviously, we've been having a number of presentations in this committee regarding marijuana, some of the laws surrounding that and some of the changes that we can make. Obviously, that industry is now facing a new tax as well. One of the fixes, I know we've heard a number of fixes last week that are potentials and things that we probably want to accomplish for this industry. This is another one of those. This is cash on demand. In the marijuana industry, you have growers, you have processors, and then you have dispensaries that actually sell to the public. What this bill will require is that when that marijuana moves from each of those licenses or within each of those licenses, that payment is then immediately required. This is kind of copying and basing off of a lot of our liquor laws, which is exactly what happens for beer, wine, and liquor. This is something that will add some fairness as well as some ease to this also highly regulated industry. That's about the crux of the matter. Mr. Chair, if there's any questions, I will take them now. Is there any questions from any committee members? Representative Tisdale? Thank you, Chair. Rep. Aragona, real quick question. The issue here is really federal banking. On the liquor side, I guess the question is when the distributor is receiving cash from the retail seller that's buying from the wholesaler, are those cash on demand sales being financed through lines of credit? And is that an avenue that simply is not available to the cannabis market? From my understanding, those payments, for instance, when a wholesaler delivers to a retail store, that's actually an EFT payment. It's coming out that day directly. What their finance side is on the back end to have that liquidity, I can't really tell you. I'm sure every company is a little bit different. But this is something that we're looking at in order to quell any of those issues, any of those disputes, and make the process cleaner. For the wholesaler, it's cash. They're done. The invoice is cleared out. But I guess the question becomes for the person making that purchase from the wholesaler, you get down to the second or third level, and they may have two or three different sources of credit that are helping to fund that transaction that might not be available to the cannabis industry. And I don't know what we can do at the state level to facilitate that. But I get it. It's a huge problem. Wholesalers can't be running around getting stiffed on a regular basis. And I don't know that it's a regular basis, but even a 5% or 10% hit could significantly damage their margins. So that's my overarching concern and question is does this really deal with that? But I appreciate you bringing it forward. And to that end, with the wholesaler, they also have cash on demand. So whenever they receive product, they also need to transfer cash in an EFT payment. As far as the actual marijuana companies, you're right. Banking is far more difficult. There is a couple of state charter banks, though, that do bank these companies. There's also, you know, if you don't have that financial market, many of them will find people who are liquid to offer some type of stock. So are there any other questions from the committee? The committee will stand at ease at the call of the chair. The committee will come to order. And we have a card of support with amendments from Clark Orthwin from Objective. He does wish to speak. Clark? Go ahead whenever you're ready. Thank you. Thanks. Chairman Aragona, members of the committee, thank you for having me here today. My name is Clark Orthwin. I'm a co-owner of Objective. We operate cultivation, processing, and retail in southeast Michigan. I've been actively managing operations for the past five years and have developed a deep understanding of the market. Up until today, I think you've largely heard from one side of the industry, and I'm here to share a more holistic perspective that serves all marijuana licensees, large and small. I think everyone can agree that Michigan has an oversupply problem, and proposals that limit demand by instituting a cap on retail licenses would only serve to exacerbate the issue and effectively legislate a monopoly for large retail groups. In reality, one of the largest issues plaguing this industry revolves around payment. There are currently no rules in place preventing a licensee from purchasing products on terms and then not honoring those terms or simply not paying. In fact, the status quo seems to benefit these bad actors because they can seemingly victimize one supplier after another with impunity. This simply is not a reasonable or responsible framework for a regulated industry. The solution to this problem is to enact legislation requiring for electronic funds transfer, commonly referred to as EFT, within one business day of delivery. EFT is the only viable solution for two reasons. The first is cash. Right now, a marijuana licensee can pay for product with a duffel bag full of cash with zero questions asked. This is a gaping hole for laundering illicit money into Michigan's banking system. Furthermore, when secure transport shows up to drop off the products and collect payment, the cash is typically inside an opaque, tamper-evident bag, and the contents aren't verified at all. They have no idea how much they're picking up. As you can imagine, this leads to he-said-she-said type arguments as to the actual amount of cash that was in the bag. Additionally, counterfeit bills are also another major problem, and unfortunately, this isn't caught until the bank verifies the deposit. The second issue is check. Marijuana licensees can intentionally or unknowingly issue checks in excess of the amount of the funds in their bank account, creating a not-sufficient funds or NSF issue. There are also frequently problems regarding post-dated checks, unsigned checks, or otherwise incorrectly populated checks that render them non-negotiable. The end result is lack of payment to the seller for extended periods of time, sometimes ever. Accordingly, the only practical, simple, and enforceable solution is to move to EFT within one business day of delivery. Building on this concept, EFT must be paired with a short and clearly defined return window in order for this to work. A defined return window is imperative to protect product integrity, consumer safety, and to provide finality to marijuana transactions. Otherwise, there would be no defined endpoint to a transaction, and licensees could simply use this as an end around to the EFT requirement. Let me give you a real-world example. After 15 days, a purchaser who at this point has sold half of the bulk, when I say bulk, I mean not individually packaged for sale, marijuana flower, and they claim they're planning on returning the remaining marijuana product to the seller as it's overstocked, they use this as an excuse for not remitting payment, effectively offering themselves terms and negating the EFT concept. This also creates major consumer safety issues as the product can be swapped, tampered with, adultered, or otherwise modified after testing

Of course, there'd be limited exceptions to this defined return window, including product safety recalls. Furthermore, if the purchaser elects to return the product within this window, the seller would remit the funds back to the purchaser within the same time frame. This framework holds everyone accountable to the same standards. A marijuana licensee's unwillingness or inability to pay for product or adequately staff its business to receive, verify, and intake product at the time of delivery is simply not a reasonable justification that outweighs the clear public policy benefits of moving to EFT with a defined return window. Namely, preventing theft, fraud, and nonpayment, preventing money laundering, protecting product integrity and consumer safety, and ensuring the timely remittance of tax revenue. Let me ask, how can one expect a cultivator or processor that's delivered product to a retailer and not been paid to then in turn remit the associated tax to the state? Obviously, they can't remit money that they don't have. We appreciate the sponsor of this legislation bringing this forward, taking this issue seriously, and taking steps to ensure marijuana retailers aren't effectively dictating terms to the state of Michigan. In short, these two concepts, EFT on delivery and a defined return window, combined with the addition of swift, meaningful penalties for unlawful, unlicensed, and or noncompliant behavior would very quickly create a level playing field that benefits all market participants, the state, and ultimately the end consumer here in Michigan. Back in 2020, we had remarkable high water levels at that time, and homeowners were literally having their houses fall into the lake. And they were having a dickens of a time trying to get permits from Deagle to put in structures and put in sandbags and things like that to prevent further erosion and sacrificing their homes. For those that were able to get it, eventually they put in various different structures, one of the main ones being sandbags, and that helped. And back in the summer of 2023, all of a sudden these homeowners received these letters

saying that you need to remove these structures. One, water was still high or threat of being high. And two, a lot of these structures have become part of the stabilization of the dune. So this legislation pretty much is saying that we want to keep these sandbags in place. There were some concerns about it, of making sure that we have walkability, that these structures are not preventing access to the lake. And we clarified that as part of this legislation. But the goal here is so when we have those threats, we don't take it to the brink where these houses are potentially falling into the lake. But people can talk to their locals, submit the plan to Deagle, submit what they're going to put in place, the location of what they're going to put in place, so that they can have an expedited review and get them set so that they can protect their homes. This bill, House Bill 4926, is a simple bill that aims to make life a little easier for our licensed health officials. Currently, we have a system in place where the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, otherwise known as LARA, tracks all continuing education requirements. As we know, maintaining the integrity and competence of our licensed health professionals is essential for public safety and trust. I think we can all agree on that. Under current law, LARA oversees the licensing of health professionals, including the management of their continuing education records. However, the existing system has its shortcomings, leading to unnecessary complications for both the health professional and their employers. If someone has a minor infraction on their record, such as a slip-up with their continuing ed requirements, it can hold them back from doing their job as well as the loss of income for both the employee and employer. So every two years, I have an insurance license, and every two years, I have to go through my continuing education requirements. I've been doing that for 28 years. And so some of you might think, you know, how hard is it to go online and complete these credits? Well, not long ago, I was faced with a family emergency where my husband had to undergo heart surgery. And even though I had two, three weeks to complete those continuing ed requirements, my life shut down, and I wasn't thinking of anything else. So lo and behold, I was late. I was reported to my employer, and I had to jump through a whole lot of hoops just to get back on track and get to, you know, doing my job and continuing on with my career. So I know what that's like. This legislation will enable individuals to submit an application for the removal of these minor continuing education violations, provided that they completed the CTE credits. So in short, House Bill 4926 removes burdensome red tape and supports our health professionals. Thank you, and I welcome any questions. Thank you, Representative. I know in our effort to cut red tape as a caucus, we're also trying to look at ways where we can reduce the burden of government, and this is one where in the face of a mix-up or a family emergency, we would provide that type of flexibility, and I think it will help government work better for Michiganders. So appreciate you bringing it forward, and I know your office has been engaging with the department on the rule promulgation, and they're supportive of it. Great. Well, thank you. This is an important legislation. Representative Whitmer. Thank you for being here. I, too, think it's really important to try and cut as much red tape as we can. However, I've been in health care my entire life, and it is really important that we can trust our health care providers to stay up to date with late-breaking whatever is going on, and I also think there are good reasons, like you just said about your husband, where you would miss these things, but how many – does this bill or do you – are you willing to change the bill at all so that it would identify how many set-asides someone could have should it be an indefinite amount of set-asides when it comes to someone's health care? Yeah, great question, and, of course, I'm willing to work with Lara and make the bill as best as possible, of course. I think we, in our communications, we're in active communication with the department right now on how many set-asides to have. So thank you. Great. Any other questions, members of the committee? All right. Representative, appreciate that testimony. And Representative Herzberg moves to excuse absent members, and there being no objection, the motion prevails by unanimous consent, and there being no further business, the committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.

I stand before you today as a proud breast cancer survivor. A testament to the strength and resilience that courses through the hearts of countless Michiganders who have battled this relentless disease. survivors like me, but for our entire community. Breast cancer is a disease that affects women, it affects men, and it affects their families across Michigan and this great nation. title: Oversight - State and Local Public Assistance Programs — Thursday, October 30, 2025
transcript:
Oversight Committee on State and Local Public Assistance Programs will come to order. Will the clerk please call the roll for today's attendance. Chair Wolford. Here. Representatives Brock. Yes. Kara. Here. Cerniglou. Here. Menser. Here. Mr. Chair, you have five members present. You do have a quorum. Thank you. The clerk will now read a letter from Oversight Chair DeBoer appointing alternate members to the subcommittee. Dated September 12, 2025. Dear Mr. Clerk, I appoint the following members of the 103rd Legislature to serve as alternate members of the following oversight subcommittees. State and Local Public Assistance Programs, Representatives Sarah Leitner, Karen Witzett. Sincerely, Jay DeBoer, State Representative, District 63. Thank you. Representative Kara moves to adopt the minutes from the September 18, 2025 meeting. Hearing no objection, the minutes are adopted. Director, you're welcome to come up to the front. I want to thank you for being here today. I want to start by first recognizing as a reminder that you weren't leading the agency during the height of the pandemic or the chaos that had followed that. We appreciate the cooperation. I appreciate the cooperation this committee appreciates, the cooperation that we've gotten from you and the UIA thus far. That said, the Michigan Unemployment Insurance Agency has had serious problems for years. Problems that we've seen that have hurt both taxpayers and the very workers that that system was meant to protect. From the massive overpayments and mismanagement during COVID to the Saunders v. UIA lawsuit that exposed just how unorganized that appeal process had become. It's clear that the agency has struggled to maintain both accuracy and accountability during that time. Those mistakes, just a reminder to those, were not just numbers on a page. They were and are real people who are receiving conflicting letters or got caught up in red tape. So our goal, obviously today here, isn't to rehash failures, but to make sure that those mistakes never happen again. Many citizens in Michigan are currently receiving UIA recovery letters and they're concerned, and rightfully so. I believe that most people are generally confused and wondering how, after nearly five years, they're now just receiving these letters. I'm sure that you'll cover that, but I'm assuming that this was due to the class action lawsuit and a stay order and the ability to collect. We're hopeful that we can work together to fix this broken situation and to ensure Michigan has a UIA that works efficiently and treats our claimants fairly and safeguards taxpayer dollars. We believe this committee and your leadership can truly work together to rebuild the trust and deliver that kind of accountability for the people of Michigan and the treatment that they deserve. And with that said, Mr. Director, the floor is yours. Thank you again for being here today. Thank you, Chairman Wilford and Vice Chairs, members of the committee. Thank you for inviting the UIA here on behalf of the entire UIA. We appreciate the chance to be here today to talk about the resumption of collections at the UIA and provide some clarity, context and transparency about how we are carrying out our legal responsibilities. So thank you. And I agree with your statements, sir, about working together. Thank you. Today, I will briefly discuss how we arrived at where we are today, explain what an overpayment is and who is currently receiving the notices that you referenced. I will outline the processes we are following as we resume collections. And, Chairman, at your request, at the committee's request, describe a little bit about the waivers and the waiver options that are available today. What I hope you see during my remarks is that the UIA is taking a considered approach in following our legal obligations as we return to overpayment collections. You know, it's important before we talk about what's going on today to talk about, like we do at this committee a lot, the unprecedented demand that was put on unemployment insurance across the country during the COVID-19 pandemic. We're all familiar with the economic charts where, you know, the jobless rate, you know, spikes and the initial claims spike. And we're all familiar with those charts that show just how the labor market reacted during COVID. But what people often don't see is pictures like I have up here on the board. This is a typical mail truck coming into our work distribution center during the pandemic. This represents some of the 9.2 million pieces of mail and faxes that the UIA was handling during COVID. We were, during that time, you know, handled 3.5 million claimants, 5 million claims, and paid out $41.3 billion in benefits. If you compare that to today's numbers, we're at about 300,000 initial claims so far this year, and we've paid out about $740 million in benefits. So just an illustration of the volume that was coming in to the UIA. The surge touched every part of the agency. It touched our processing, our adjudications, our determinations, appeals. And that scale is important for what is to follow. In 2022, the UIA was part of a class action lawsuit that centered on whether or not the agency collected overpayments before all protest and appeal rights were exhausted. It's important here to note that the UIA accepted appeals any way somebody wanted to submit an appeal. So that mail truck that I showed, people could have sent in handwritten notes that said, I appeal this decision. We allowed that. People could have written on a determination or redetermination that they appealed, and we accepted that. I believe that was in the name of providing good service to people and letting them appeal any way that they wanted to. But that was unsustainable during the pandemic. And with the volume of mail coming in, the reality was alleged that we were not getting to all those pieces

of mail before people would get those collections letters and some people are collected upon. So it was the class action lawsuit. As part of that class action lawsuit over UIA's objection, the court enjoined us from collections. So that happened in June of 2022, but it reached back on accounts and claims back as far as March 2020. So because of that preliminary injunction as part of the Saunders lawsuit, we could not send bills. We could not accept money. So collections had essentially stopped. What we could do and what's really important that this committee and that the public knows is that we continued the other business of the UIA. We continued to identify when somebody received benefits they should not have received. We continued to send the determinations and the re-determinations. We continued to preserve their protest and appeal rights so that people could, when they received those letters, continue to appeal. The part that stopped was the bills being sent, people being asked for money, and us accepting the payment. That's the part that stopped. On May 13th of 2025, so just recently, the Saunders lawsuit was settled and the UIA then had a legal responsibility to begin collections again. It is, again, just important to note that the collections that we are resuming are on balances owed before the collections pause, during the collections pause, and since the collections pause. So we are essentially doing five years of collections activity right now. The legal requirement to collect comes mainly from the Michigan Employment Security Act, but also from a patchwork of federal laws, rules, and requirements that we have with the Department of Labor. So it was important to this committee and important for me to share what is an overpayment and who are examples, what are some examples of people who might be getting these letters now. What I have on the screen here and what I'll talk about is some of the buckets of people who are affected. But before I get into that, I want to note that overpayments are part of the unemployment insurance system. They do not necessarily reflect a mistake. It's not always fraud. The system is designed to pay benefits quickly while information is still being verified. The system relies on claimants providing full and accurate information upfront and employers providing timely responses. And as additional information is received, sometimes an overpayment is established. Some common causes of an overpayment include when we asked the claimant to provide proof of employment or proof of their income and that was not received. Another example would be when a claimant was laid off, they claimed benefits, they may have returned to work or got a new job, but continued to certify for benefits as if unemployed. An example might be when a claimant files for unemployment, they indicate that they lost a job due to a layoff or were fired through no fault of their own. And then new information from an employer protest comes in that says that employee actually never showed up for work or had a voluntary quit. During that process, if the balance of the evidence cuts in favor of the employer, that would establish an overpayment on the weeks that person received while the information was happening. Another reason that overpayments occur is if a claimant did not provide proof of their work search, as this committee is aware right now in Michigan, claimants are required to do one work search activity each week. And I will note for the committee, as you are aware, that in July of 2026, that is bumping up to three activities a week. So those are all examples of people who might be getting these collections notes now. A common question that we get is why did the UIA pay me, only then to send me a letter telling me I owe that money back? The UIA must balance paying benefits on time with program integrity. The balance is a principle of unemployment insurance law and is monitored by the DOL through the performance metrics that I, as director, am responsible for achieving. So we have several metrics from the U.S. Department of Labor, but the two that I'm talking about right now are paying the first payment to a claimant on time and paying improperly. To balance those two things is part of my job. I kind of jokingly say to people that I can give you, I can pay everybody on time, but a lot of times will be wrong. I also can pay nobody on time, but will never be wrong. Where we need to be is balancing those two things. But to show that overpayments are a feature of the system, they're expected in the system, the USDL also requires states to collect any time we overpay. And I have a metric that I have to hit, which is 68% of the time when we overpay, we need to collect that money back, 68%. If you looked at the publicly available metrics today, you would see that Michigan is somewhere around 5%, 5%. We've been between 2% and 5%. That is very far below the 68% that we've got to hit, and that is reflecting the three-plus years of the pause in collections. It is very important that this committee know and that the public know that we understand at the UIA that not collecting since 2022 has confused claimants. Chairman, you recognized different letters coming. We recognize that has confused the claimants. It has delayed employer credits. It has undermined conformity of Michigan's, our program, with the federal rules and requirements and has reduced the UI trust fund. These are all reasons that the UIA objected to this collections pause in the first place. Nevertheless, the UIA is, you know, we're here now, and we are trying to take a considerate approach as we resume collecting. I am proud of what we've done so far as we've worked to resume collections. What I have up here is probably pretty hard to read, but let me talk through some of the things that we've done. So May 13th was when the court dissolved the preliminary injunction and sort of triggered our responsibility to begin collecting again. Since then, when the settlement was approved, we put out a press release. The top of the press release stated that the judge resolved that preliminary injunction and that collections would resume. We started doing stakeholder outreach. This included meeting with people who sit on the modernization work group. A couple of the members are here today, and I appreciate them being here. It included reaching out with your offices, your staff, the businesses, the advocate communities. That was the communication piece. But I think just as important was us looking internally at our processes, our procedures, looking at all of our settlement agreements, our legal responsibilities, and being sure that we were ready. On September 8th, that is when we started to communicate very publicly, you know, with the notices to claimants who may be affected. It's when we sent sort of more public messages. It is when we put out the press release, and that's when we started our live FAQ, which I want to talk about today because I'm really impressed with the FAQ that we have available to your constituents and the customers of the UIA. On the 13th, that is when notices went out with the final balances so people could see what they owe and when employer credits went out. On the 15th, the bills went out and employer credits went out, so, you know, there's that time between when it's available electronically and when it's mailed. On September 29th, the payments were, you know, the first were due. Ongoing, we continue to review and test

internal processes. We are providing claimant support in a number of different ways that I'll talk about in a second. And we're reviewing accounts. We're applying waivers when requested or at least accepting the waivers. And we are updating that FAQ. It is really important for this committee to know that in all cases, the people who are receiving the bills today previously received a determination letter. So it's what we call the 1301 or the 1302. So the people who are receiving bills today received that identification of an overpayment. And upon receiving that, they had their due process rights of their 30 days to appeal. We fully acknowledge and recognize that people may have forgotten about those letters. They may have forgotten about the debt. They may have assumed that we forgot or that it was resolved. Even if people tried to pay, we had to send that money back. Again, a reason that the UIA objected to this, but those realities are part of the pathways that we've built into trying to resolve these issues for the claimants now. How we are working with claimants today, we have developed an online coaching session that walks claimants through just on this topic. So we do online coaching sessions a lot that walk people through how to file a claim, how to read certain letters. But on this topic specifically, we developed an online coaching session that walks claimants through how to interpret their letters, find their letters, and work on this issue. We've maintained our in-person, actually expanded our in-person appointments, our phone appointments, and our virtual appointments. Chairman, I've been sitting across from claimants in our local offices hearing about this topic. That was important to me to hear what they're experiencing. So I've been sitting in on some of these appointments. Our contact center, we've extended the hours of our contact center so that we have representatives available until 7 p.m. just to respond to the surge in calls that we are getting. And then that FAQ continues to be updated. We are communicating with claimants that there are waiver options available. So if repaying this debt would pose an undue hardship, we're encouraging them to apply for a hardship waiver. We also are accepting waiver requests for an agency error or a wage reporting error. And at the committee's request, I'll talk a little bit about those in just a minute. It is also important to note that there are some protest and appeal rights still available. So if that determination is within the 30 days, they have their normal protest and appeal rights. They also, people can protest and if they can show good cause for a late protest, that issue may be heard by the appellate authority. UIA is very fact specific. So as we are hearing individual claimants reach out to us, as we are reviewing individual cases where we see issues, we are adjusting and we are taking that information and putting it into our FAQ. So if we find these one-off issues, we are trying to build that into our knowledge base to help future people as they're looking at the FAQs. We also are taking information we're receiving from your staffs on individual cases you're seeing in your offices and those also are making their way to our FAQ. Also things we're hearing from our appellate authorities. So our lower authority at more in the UIAC, our higher level authority, as they're seeing things, they're communicating with us and we are updating our FAQ to reflect that. This committee asked me to share a little bit about waivers. The question that we get is why doesn't the UIA just waive all of this money? We can't. Waivers are a limited exception to the duty to collect. And there are some provided by Michigan law, some narrow authority to waive. And federal law also has some limitations on waivers. There are, however, some blanket authority waivers through some of the federal programs, which I'll talk about in just a minute. Also a principle of unemployment insurance law is that it is a, it's an eligibility program that is available for people who lose a job through no fault of their own. So if people do not have a separation from an employer, they do not have, you know, if they're not the type of person who is unemployment insurance is intended to cover, we would not waive that. I have provided here the three examples or the three, you know, provisions in the Michigan Employment Security Act that allow for the exception to collections through a waiver, which is a claimant wage error, a financial hardship waiver, and an administrative or clerical error by the agency. A claimant wage error, that occurs when a claimant provided wage data without the intent to misrepresent and the employer provided no wage or upon request provided inaccurate wage. If that was the situation, yes. Excuse me, would you mind just backing up one slide and going over that again for those that may have missed that? Thank you. This slide here, sir? Yes, thank you. Okay, so the question that we receive is why not just waive all these balances? The Michigan Employment Security Act limits, so as I said before, we have a duty to collect. Anytime we overpay, we have a duty to collect. There's a limited exception to that through waivers. Waivers are defined by the Michigan Employment Security Act, and there's three buckets of waivers that I'll talk about in three different slides. Federal law also tells us, gives us guidance on what we can and cannot waive. Under the pandemic unemployment insurance and some of the COVID programs, we had waiver authority that we had to balance Michigan's Employment Security Act with federal waiver authority, and we used that authority, and I'll talk about that also. Then my statement was just that the Michigan Employment Security Act provides unemployment insurance as a program for people who, it is a temporary assistance program for people who lose a job through no fault of their own. Yes, sir. And then what I had stated is the three waiver exceptions, the claimant wage error, the financial hardship error, and the administrative or clerical. That's actually the slide I wanted. I just got messed up on your slides. Oh, okay. Well, yes, sir. So these are the three. So the Michigan Employment Security Act defines equity in good conscience in three ways, these three ways. And then I've given you the statutory citation here along with the text of the statute that tells us sort of what's in this waiver. This one is the wage reporting where the claimant without the intent to defraud or the employer did not provide, we can waive for that. The financial hardship waiver is mathematics. This one looks at the resources of a household and evaluates whether or not somebody can receive this waiver. And then the agency error waiver is a result of an overpayment, an improper payment, the result of an administrative or clerical error by the UIA. So, Chairman, you had asked me to sort of talk a little bit about waivers that we have granted. In these first three buckets, one, two, and three on my slide here, are examples of waivers that we granted with pandemic era concerns. And this is, I really want this to be clear that people who are receiving bills now, we get a lot of questions about, well, I remember during COVID, you know, Michigan had this rule and the feds had this rule and there was some confusion. That's what we're talking about here, where we had conformity issues or where Michigan was asking, we had more groups of people that we were allowing for benefits than the DOL, and we later assigned, established that we overpaid those people. Those have been waived. That was waived under our pandemic era, and this was pre-2023, you know, up during the pandemic, these waivers had run and processed. These were things, I'll give you one example. During the pandemic, Michigan asked people to provide their income, which we need to compute benefits. We didn't say gross or net. We later got, so as you might imagine, some people provided gross, some people provided net. If people provided gross, they would get higher benefits than if they provided net.

We later got clarification from the US DOL that we're supposed to collect net. So anybody who has paid benefits under gross, that's our error. We waived that. We always and continue to offer the financial hardship waiver. And we will, after the new system is in place, run some cleanup waivers on those pandemic era eligibility unemployment issues that I would be delighted to come back to this committee and talk about that process when we finish that. So these are the waivers that we have run up to this day. But the point I want to make is that waiver authority is a limited exception to our general duty to collect. I've given you here three ways that people can apply for waivers. So they can apply for a financial hardship waiver through their MIWAM account. They can mail their letters and they can fax their letters for the administrative error and the wage reporting error. They can mail those. And Mr. Chairman, that concludes my formal remarks. I hope that you and the committee can see that we are taking a considerate approach as we resume collections, understanding the confusion that the collections pause has caused for our claimants. Well, thank you for being here today. Thank you for being here today. I appreciate you. I think you're the only person that's come before this committee that said you'd be delighted to come back. So thank you for that. I appreciate that. With that said, we definitely have some questions that I see a few of our committee members have. So with that said, we'll start with Representative Brooke. Thank you, Mr. Chair. I appreciate that. Mr. Palmer, I truly appreciate you being here. You've been here twice now, or the agency's been here a number of times now, and I really appreciate you being here. And you obviously came into quite a mess, and it appears that you are doing your best to try to repair a lot of damaged relationships and the issues within the UIA agency. I do have a few questions here regarding the amount. So I think in earlier presentations, the $40 billion from UIA that was paid, I think we're the second most, if I remember correctly, state that paid out. I think California paid out more. A lot of that was federal benefits. When you're doing the collections, is there a distinction between whether those were federal UIA or state UIA benefits that are being recollected or collected, sorry? Yes, sir. There is not a distinction by what is being collected. We are collecting all debt that was established before the pause, during the pause, and since the pause. But we can look at the total pot of money that's being collected, and we know that between 15% and 20% of that is state UI, 80% or so is federal UI, representing the large amount of federal money that came in in 2020, 2021. Okay, because I know I've asked questions in previous committee meetings where there's approximately, I want to say it was between just ballpark $10 billion to $15 billion in overpayments or not fraudulent, but just missed payments. How much of that is UIA expecting? I know you mentioned number of waivers. Is there an expectation of what percentage of that will be reclaimed? So I've got the team tracking who's paying waivers, so we're getting all that data, right? We won't know for some time how collections is going, okay?
