But we expect to collect – our goal would be to collect it all, of course, but that 68% target that DOL gives us on overpayments that are established. Okay, and just to establish – I know it was mentioned taxpayer dollars and such, and nobody wants to get a bill saying they owe money. I mean, I hate getting those unexpected bills. I recently got a bill from 2021 from an insurance payout for service we provide with my business because it was some sort of double payment, and there were some missing numbers, and so I had to pay back stuff from four years ago, which didn't make me happy, but I had to do it to the insurance company. But as far as getting these dollars back, and you did mention that you are crediting the employers, then when there's a collection, the employer ends up getting that benefit back into their bank. Yes, sir. Okay, I just want to make that. It's an employer credit. They can choose how it's applied, future or past. Yeah, because I don't want to mix employer dollars with taxpayer dollars because I think this is an employer-funded system, so I appreciate what you're doing. And honest mistakes, obviously, there are some waivers. There are some things in place to apply hardship waivers, et cetera, but I appreciate the fact that these were employer dollars that were paid to individuals and that you were doing your best to collect these, as hard as it is. It wasn't, I suppose, your fault. I mean, there was that litigation, et cetera. And is every state doing this was my other question. Was Michigan the only state that couldn't recollect? You know, that's a good question, and I do not have the answer immediately. I know that all states have had, you know, the overpayments, the confusion, all these federal programs were rolled out very fast. But I don't know if other states have had these collections pauses. I certainly can find out. Okay. Thank you very much, but I'll wait. So I'm going to give you a scenario that happened to me and my business because I had a lot of employees and I had a lot that went on to unemployment. So we had one particular one where I called the UIA at the time. We had an employer that checked quit, and her payments went through. She was getting paid unemployment. I called the unemployment agency, and on that phone call, talking to multiple people, they said, well, it was flagged, but then it was overridden by a supervisor somewhere in the line, and it was passed through. In that case, is that something where that employee is going to be recouped or would that fall under that COVID, I don't want to say waiver process, but that COVID, you know, the dysfunction that was occurring then? Is that type of payments that are being recouped? So I appreciate the question. This is an example of how unemployment insurance is so fact-specific. You said a couple things. If the employee at claim filing indicated that you said they quit the job? Yeah, they actually checked the box that said quit. Okay. Director Palmer, just so you know, too, those are – I've had multiple people reach out to us as well with those same things with business owners saying that their employees literally just quit, and the same thing happened and they were paid out. So feel free to address that today or if you need time. Yeah, I would like to learn more about those cases. I don't – if you could give me some time to look into that, yeah. Okay. And I understand waivers for employees. I mean, there's hardships, and I would hate to put somebody in a very difficult situation to have to pay back money, but is there going to be a process, say it's a waived claim that was paid out. So technically the employer paid when he or she didn't have to, but that recollection is waived. Is there a process to give that employer a credit for that waived payment? And I guess that would be my last question. You don't necessarily have to answer it. I don't expect an answer, but that's just a request for an answer at some point. Thank you, sir, for being here. Yeah, of course. Thank you for the questions. Thank you, Representative. Representative Cernaglu. Thank you, and I do have a couple questions if that's okay. There was a lot we covered here. So let's see. These might not necessarily be in chronological order, but I'm just going to start with has there been any discussions or thoughts to temporarily expand

the advocacy program which provides legal assistance to claimants and employers for hearings to cover consultations and help claimants with these overpayment issues just because we have so many right now. Yeah, that's a great question. I appreciate the question. The UIA has committed to expanding the advocacy program. It's a contract-based program. It takes time to train the advocates. It takes time to do the contracts. But what we've done in anticipation of this collections pause and what we're continuing to do now is promoting the service. One thing that we've done is we've produced, this might not sound like a big deal, but we've produced posters that we can put, make available to like the Michigan Works offices. You know, posters that we can make available that tell people, you know, did you know that we have an advocacy program and that they can get a hold of an advocate to help with these types of things. Okay, thank you. And what would be the impact on our state and the UIA program if the legislature did pass legislation attempting to waive all of the overpayments? What would that look like? Or is it even possible with federal law? Yeah, I understand the instinct behind that question. And, you know, when you have, you know, people getting these bills, I understand the desire to help. The state, if the legislature was to expand waiver authority, we would, you know, do our duty and do the law. There would still be a conflict with federal law, so we would have to balance that. And there also would be a risk to, and as a result, there would be a risk to the federal unemployment insurance tax dollars that the state gets, because we would not be in conformity if we were waiving more than what we were allowed. And I suppose if we were waiving people for which unemployment insurance was not designed, it might create some incentives, you know, some behavioral incentives that we wouldn't want. Okay, thank you. So on the waivers that you're granting right now, how often would you say waivers are being granted or do you even have that information? That is a report that I'm getting each week. I can tell you that as of yesterday, we had received 18,000 waivers. I've approved my staff to work on overtime to begin processing these. We have handled 1,000 of them so far. It takes time, of course, to do this fact-intensive, you know, analysis of these cases, but we are working on it. Okay, so you do have options for waivers. You also have options for payment plans. Are there any other options out there besides that? Well, there are the, you know, there is the protest and appeal rights if the overpayment was established within the 30 days, and then there's always the option to show good cause for late, you know, for a late appeal. On the late appeals, so you had those examples of four different types of, oh gosh, where's that slide, examples of overpayments, like for example, when the claimant required to provide proof of employment or income and did not. So for those different types of examples, is it too late to do those things now? Or like the claimant did not provide proof of work search activities. So if those are issues, can people being sent bills, is it too late to provide that? Or does that fall under, you know, a potential late appeal? Yeah, so this is part of the confusion with the collections pause. So since somebody would be receiving a bill today, they may have forgotten about the overpayment letter that they got three years ago. They all got letters at that time. Yeah, they all got those letters, and that started their protest and appeal rights. There is a chance for people to submit a late or to show good cause for a late appeal. And that is handled by our appellate authority. Okay, so they can ask for a late appeal and provide reason. Do you know if those are, like any idea of how many of those are like granted? I don't know. Okay. So people did receive notices that they would have to pay it back. They just weren't being sent the bills. Is that? We were, yeah, we were enjoined from sending bills, sending the normal collections letters and attempts that we would do. And then I know you've said this before, but how much are we looking at here for the overpayments? What was that number? Yeah, so 2.7 billion. For overpayment, okay. Okay, I may have more questions later, but thank you for being here. And thank you, committee chair. This is a really important topic. I'm happy that you're covering it. Yeah, thank you. Representative Cara. Thank you, Mr. Chair. And thank you, Director Palmer, for being here again to answer our questions. My first one is the pandemic unemployment assistance application process. Did you say earlier that it was designed to make payments quickly while working through the process to verify the claim? Is that correct? I think that, yeah, I think that balancing paying claims on time with program integrity is a careful balance that is in our programs. Yeah, and for income, some people were reporting gross and some people were reporting net. And so there was some disparity there. But was there proof of income or was it just attested income? Yeah, so in the cases that I'm talking about where the agency made an error by asking for your income and you provided gross, but we later found out that DOL rules where we should have provided net, we should have asked for net, you would have provided that. We would have paid your claim based on gross. So it's provided by somebody just saying this is what my income was, or are they showing a W-2 or how? Yes, yes, sir. Are they showing a W-2? Yeah, so they're showing proof of employment, proof of income. And that's one of these buckets that we're collecting from now would be people who we reached out to saying, you know, in order to establish your claim, we need to verify income or employment. And if that was not received, those people would, and we paid some weeks on that claim, and then later did not receive the proof of income or employment, those people would have had an overpayment established and they would now be in, it would be a group of people that are getting these notices today. Yes, sir. I guess I still might be a little bit confused, but if you have not just provided income but proof of income, they're showing their W-2, how would the agency not be able to tell if it was gross or net by looking at the records they provided? Oh, I see what, yeah, okay. I would have to get the specific form. You know, I can't answer that question immediately, but it was probably just we were taking gross or net and we should have been using net according to the DOL rules. But you're certain that the application process wasn't simply asking people to attest what their income was, but they were showing proof of what their income was on the front end? So that's a good question. So when people apply for unemployment insurance and they're providing their income, we are supposed to be and our fraud investigations, our adjudicators are looking at that information and if it is suspicious, if it is, you know. Even if it's not suspicious, but they say this is my income because they're reporting their net income, but you guys want to know their gross income, if they're not just saying this is what my income is, but they're showing what their income is, I guess that's what I want to know is through that application process, are they required to show it or to provide it by saying this is what it is? They're required to provide proof of income or employment. You might be talking, respectfully, you might be talking about some particular periods with pandemic unemployment that I can't speak to the specific laws, but you might be speaking about some periods where self-attestation was allowed or that might be what you're talking about. Yeah, on the PUA claims. Yeah, I would have to get back with you on that, you know, how those people are treated in this collections pause. I'm happy to do that. I definitely would like to see that and who designed the PUA claim application process? So this was a

As we've talked about at this committee before, this was a federal program that was rolled out quickly to get money out during the days of COVID. Right, and so is that Christine Crabs? Was that Director Corbin? Was that Governor Whitmer? Whose plan was this? The pandemic unemployment? In terms of what information needed to be provided when somebody was seeking a claim for their unemployment? Yeah, I think this was a bipartisan push. You had, you know, I think you had a Republican in the White House and the Department of Labor, Democratic administration in Michigan. So I don't have an exact answer, but the pandemic unemployment insurance program was a federal program that states across the country had to administer. So you had a lot of people involved from the U.S. Department of Labor, state departments of labor. So are you saying that the federal government helped us design the state of Michigan's PUA application process? Sure, so as the program was rolled out, that's a lot of what we're talking about today with the waivers and the overpayments. There was a lot of confusion as this program was rolled out quickly, and states and the federal government needed and wanted to get money into the hands of people who needed it during COVID. So I think... One more quick question just to change gears for a second. What is the standard for a hardship waiver? Yes, sir. So the 150, so I've got it up here on the screen. We get this directly from law. So the application asks you to record your income, provide proof of your income, then this is evaluated. Okay. Thank you. Yes, sir. Thank you. Thank you. I have a few questions for you. They'll be in two different pods, one in the appeals area and then also payment plans. First, are you still allowing claimants to write handwritten appeals at this time? So that's a great question and one that I really appreciate. We are, but let me explain. So as you recall, one of the reasons behind Saunders was we were taking appeals any way somebody would do them. They could handwrite them and put them in the general correspondence line. They could appeal in a local office. So we would like to, and we are currently working with US DOL to require our appeals electronically. There are accessibility concerns, and we have to be aware of some of our residents who that might not be an option. So we want to provide an alternative path for that. To be sure we don't end up in a situation where we cannot handle an influx of appeals, we are strongly encouraging people to use the appeals form. However, they can still appeal on their, you know, however way they want to, but it has to go to a particular box. That mail truck, when that mail truck comes in, if we ever get those kinds of mail trucks again, this way we'll know what is general correspondence and what is appeals. I can then prioritize my team to work on appeals so that people have due process rights. So the answer to your question, Chairman, is kind of mixed. Yes, we are taking it by, you know, people can still handwrite an appeal, but in a targeted way. I hope to be able to come back to you soon and say that DOL is, that we've worked with DOL and here is our process. It's electronic and this is the one alternative. Great. Thank you. And then also under that same bucket, is this online or in-person appeals process? And then also would someone have to pay for an attorney to file an appeal? The appeals process is, we encourage people to do it online using their MyWAM account and the approved appeals form. People can appeal by printing out the form, filling it and sending that to the general line. People can also appeal in writing, but they have to send it to that particular line. People, we do have an advocacy program that the representative asked about. We are expanding that, but that is available to claimants who need legal advocates as they navigate the appeals process. So that is something that we make available and that we're planning to expand. Thank you. Also shifting gears to payment plans, let's say someone owes $10,000, we'll just use that as a number. Are you offering basically what type of payment plan will be set up for them and what type of payment plans are you offering? So when somebody receives a 1088, the bill, it would tell them what their minimum payment is. And I would have to validate this with my team, but the number that's at the top of my head is $150 would be the maximum that a payment would be. I can validate that for you, though, Chair. I had it in my head and now I'm not sure that's exactly what it is. It's okay. I appreciate that. Yeah, so one of the things that we have here, is it income-based in that process? On what would be accepted? No, I don't believe so. I believe that what the amount due is would be based on what's owed. The income-based piece comes in the hardship waiver where they could, if they meet certain income requirements, could have the payment waived. Okay, great. Thank you. And my last two, how would someone sign up for a payment plan and what happens if their circumstances change along the way? So the good news is you don't have to sign up for a payment plan. It's given to you on your form. You just would start paying the payment plan. They can always reach out to our benefit overpayment collections division, which is where they could talk about their options. But really what they have on that bill is how they would pay. If their circumstances change, like anytime they're on unemployment insurance, they can reach out to us and let us know about the change in their circumstances. How that impacts a waiver, I'm not exactly sure. Okay, great. Thank you. Representative Mensah? Thank you, Chair. Back on one of your very beginning slides, the background during COVID, you say here that you had 3.5 million claimants, and yet there were 5 million claims. So are you saying that multiple people had multiple claims? Oh, sure. Yeah. There was a mix of federal programs, state programs, and people had certainly applied for different programs through the federal first week or pandemic emergency. Yeah, so there were multiple programs taking place at the same time. Incidentally, that's some of the confusion. That also could explain why some people—I'm really glad you asked this question—that could explain why some people say, wait a minute, I have a letter saying that my claim was resolved, and that claim was. But this other claim might not have been. People have the multiple claims. That's a fairly standard practice where people have different claims. So they could be on the hook for repayment of multiple claims. Sure, sure. And what we—yes, they could be. But what they should be receiving bills for now would be the total. So they shouldn't be getting multiple 1088s, I don't believe. But I can validate that. You say here that there was $41.3 billion in payments and $2.7 billion in overpayments. Can you just go over a little bit on what you determined or what you use as determinants for the overpayments? So an overpayment is—they're not uncommon. We do them. It's a normal part of unemployment insurance as part of the balancing, paying a claim quickly with program integrity. So the examples that I provided would be people

Let's just use the separation one, because you owned a business, right? So if somebody says that they quit, or I'm sorry, someone says that they were laid off, we have to pay them quickly, right? So they're filling out the application themselves. We have to rely on that. But then you as the employer gets the notification that this employee said they were laid off, and you say, no, that employee, they quit showing up for work. So you have a chance to tell us that. That information goes in the file. And then we would go back to that employee. Our internal adjudicators would work on that claim. And if that employee never showed up for work, we would have to collect those benefits back that we paid out to that employee. That would be considered an overpayment. But that would be a standard process during any period of unemployment, not just during the COVID, correct? That would happen anytime, correct. That's happening today. How does this affect seasonal workers? One of my experiences with this was with a seasonal worker when I was in a local office. This can affect a seasonal worker just like it can affect any worker. Anybody who has paid benefits to which they were not entitled could get one of these notices. The narrow exception for a seasonal worker could be on the job search side. If they had a seasonal waiver for job search or these types of things, they may not have to do the job search, which would eliminate one of the paths to an overpayment. So let's say a landscaper and grater would be able to ask for a seasonal waiver because the nature of their job is seasonal? I don't know how that would work with that particular example. We work with the migrant and seasonal folks within the department on these waivers for the seasonal workers. The example you used, they might have a union exception to the hiring or something, but I'm not... Again, very fact-specific, very fact-intensive, so we would have to look at a particular case. Okay, thank you. Thank you, Chair. You're welcome. Representative Brooke. Thank you again, Mr. Chair. Thank you again, Director Palmer. Quick question on the amounts owed. I'm assuming, but is there... It isn't, but is there interest charged to the employees on debt payment? No, sir. Because of the collections pause, we did not toll the interest. Okay. And in a previous life... We did not charge the interest. I'm sorry. Okay. Previous lifetime, I happened to owe a lot of money to the Department of Defense and had to pay it back, and there was a process that they had where you could lower the amount paid back. So in the example earlier, there's $10,000 owed. Is it straight up you get a waiver, or is there a process where someone with a hardship, you know, instead of $10,000, maybe similar to the IRS when they settle, that because of a hardship, you would maybe not eliminate that complete payment that they owe, but reduce it by a certain percentage or cut it in half or something of that nature to fit their hardship? Is it all or nothing, that deal? Okay. Yes, sir. On the hardship waiver, yes, yes, sir. Okay. And then one last question, and I am done. On the workload, obviously, it sounds like your folks are inundated with a lot of waivers and a lot of workload going on. Is this any way affecting current claims and contesting claims from employers? Is it slowing down that process and going to exacerbate, you know, further overpayments? Or are you keeping up with the current and the backlog is just being done by people with spare time, I guess? On behalf of the UIA, I really appreciate you asking that. Thank you for asking that question. It is a lot of work. Our staff are very, you know, we are working hard. We've got the modernization that we're working on. We've got, yes, we've got the normal business of the UIA. So thank you for asking that. We are keeping up. We are working, as I stated, we've got some overtime that I've approved, allowing some staff to work on Saturdays to work some of this backlog. We've extended the hours in the call center. We've shifted some staff around. And so naturally, I believe, yeah, there are some tradeoffs, but our metrics on, you know, claims and processing are all in good shape. I will be sure to let you know if they're not. Thank you so much for being here, sir. Thank you. Thank you, Chair. Thank you. You're welcome. Representative Cerniglu. Thank you, Chair. Just a few more questions here. When people are first, you know, applying and being approved to get unemployment, is it explained or are they notified at any point that if they are overpaid, they'll be responsible for paying it back? Sure. But I think we, yes, but I think we can do better. So one of the things that we're doing at the UIA right now, we are working on producing some videos that, they're short, they're short videos, but that appear at different points in the application process explaining these types of things to people, telling them, you know, what you're doing now, what your requirements are. I'll use the registration and work search example. Just telling people, okay, you know, now that you've finished this part of your application, you must now go register for work at Michigan Works, and every week you're going to have to do three work search activities. Okay, so we need to do better. So that's one thing, these videos. But the other thing, and I'm so excited for this committee to see this, our new plain language forms. So UIA has been on a journey to redesign our forms, and I'm sure all of you would agree are confusing. They're long, they're legal. We have gone on a plain language journey where people can, they're going to get much more concise plain language correspondence from us that tell them why they're getting this letter, what they need to do, and what happens if they don't. And one of the things, can I add one thing to that, sir? What is really exciting about this is just this week, I had in our Lansing office, we had businesses, we had the advocate community, we had our higher and lower level appellate authorities in the room looking at these redesigned forms, giving us their feedback. So that somebody who owns a business can say, when I get this business form, it might be nice if it did this or said this. And the advocates are in the room saying when our claimants get this, this might help them. So not only are we redesigning the forms, but we're taking input from stakeholders into consideration. Okay. Yeah, that's great. I'm happy to hear that. So at the time, though, was it just in the form somewhere that they might have to? Sure, yeah. So I don't know where in a form it would be, but it was on there somewhere. Yes. Okay. Or on the websites, on the information at claim. But maybe not verbally explained to them, just kind of something they would have presumably read if they were applying. Yeah. Okay. So on the payment plans that you're currently doing, is there any interest on those? At this point, the interest, so this is a long process, so they'll get a notice, late notice, second late notice, a final late notice. So there's a long process before any of that would occur. But if they're doing a payment plan, like the $150 a month, they're not accruing interest while they're doing that. I'll find out the answer. Okay. And then do you know what the average amount is that's owed per individual? I don't, and that goes to Rep. Mensah's question. So because there's multiple, there could be like multiple claims on multiple, a person could have more than one claim, it's really hard just to do the simple math. So we have to go into the system and run queries. So I don't have that exact number. It's something that we're trying to get at, but I do not have that exact number. And just one last kind of area to ask about, I know Representative Brooke was asking about if people quit versus were laid off. Wasn't there like some different standards during the pandemic? Like I thought the searching for more work was waived and also just because, I mean, people weren't legally allowed to be doing certain, so a lot of that was waived at that time anyway, right? Either waived

If there was confusion between state law and federal or an overpayment was not established. Okay. Thank you. Thank you. And then last question and then we'll close. Representative Cara. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Is it true that there was a barrier before COVID to where you didn't get a payment released until identity was verified? I'm sorry, Rep. Was there a barrier in place before COVID to where if somebody applied for unemployment, they didn't receive it until they had proven their identity? I would have to get back with you on that specific question. I know that ID verification is part of our process. If that was a barrier or something during COVID. It's something you look into, but is it something you look into after payments have already started going out? So ID verifications are verified at the claims taking part. So if somebody did not provide their identity with a PUA claim, they would not receive any payments until they did prove their identity? That is my understanding. If there were particular times or if you're referencing something I'm not familiar with, I don't know. But yeah, that's part of our process. And then were there any circumstances where individuals received both UIA and disability simultaneously? I don't know. Okay, I think my last question is somebody calls the customer service line for the UIA, what type of experience is that like for them if they were to call today? Right now today, this week we're handling 70% of calls that come in and the calls that we're handling have, when they take the post-call survey, get really good responses. Okay, thank you. Thank you. I think in closing it's worth mentioning that this problem that we discussed today, this isn't a federal problem, it's not a COVID problem, it's not a Director Palmer problem. This was all due to a lack of leadership and unconstitutional shutdown in the state of Michigan that lasted too long. And then when held showing that this was unconstitutional, shifting powers to the fourth fictitious branch of our government, the administration state. This needs to be a reminder to those that are watching and listening, especially in the soon coming future, that appointments, those that are elected, there's consequences in those and our people are facing them today. This committee is facing them. You, Director Palmer, are facing them. And so thank you for being here today. I truly mean this from the bottom of my heart. Your ability to work with us and together means a lot to me. I look forward to meeting the needs of our constituents, those taxpayers, those business owners, and getting this resolved. So thank you. And there being no further business before the committee, this meeting stands adjourned. Thank you.

title: Health Policy 25-10-29
transcript:
The Senate Committee on Health Policy is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairman Hertel. Here. Senator Santana. Senator Boehner. Here. Senator Cherry. Here. Senator Kleinfeld. Senator Geis. Present. Senator Weber. Here. Senator Houck. Here. Senator Heisinger. Here. Senator Runstad. Here. Mr. Chairman, you have eight members present. There is a quorum. Thank you, Madam Clerk. I will entertain a motion to adopt the October 23, 2025 committee meeting minutes. So moved by Senator Cherry. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. And I will make a motion at this time to excuse absent members. And seeing no objection, absent members are excused. We are going to take testimony first on House Bills 4077 and 4078. We have Representatives Rogers and Mueller with us today, if you'd like to come forward and testify. And there are donuts here. And the tradition of Representative Rogers, she has brought donuts from Kalamazoo. So we will pass those around to committee members. Thank you. Even I couldn't eat this many donuts. No, I was looking at them. Well, he also owns an orchard, and I was very upset that he didn't also bring us some donuts, being it's that time of year. I brought apples. I'm health conscious. Thank you, Representatives. Begin when you're ready. Thank you, Chair Hertel and members of the committee. Representative Mueller and I are here to give testimony on our House Bills 4077 and 78. Together, the bills require timely certification of death certificates by physicians through the electronic death certificate registration system, or ERDS, a web-based system used by the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services and clarifies when the certification is to be conducted by a county medical examiner. These bills are reintroductions from last year. House Bill 5043 and 4 passed unanimously out of the House Health Policy Committee, passed with wide bipartisan support in the full House, and ran out of time in the Senate and lame duck. This term, House Bill 4077 and 8 again passed out of House Health Policy Committee unanimously and had a wide bipartisan support on the floor by passing to a margin of 106 to 2. The intent behind these bills is to modernize the medical certification of death certificates and to address a significant frustration facing many of our grieving families in Michigan, which is how long it can take to obtain medical certification on death certificates. Under current statute, both a licensed physician and a funeral director are required to complete a medical certification of the death. A physician is required to complete their portion within 48 hours of being presented, and failure to comply is a misdemeanor. However, many certificates of death are filled out physically and either faxed or snail mailed to a funeral director to be uploaded into the ERDS system. This can result in delays of families receiving death certificates, which are necessary to deal with insurance, proceed with a burial or a cremation, and settle legal affairs. These delays may sound minor, but to those suffering and grieving the loss of a loved one, it can put an added strain when they are already suffering emotional loss. My bill, House Bill 4077, requires physicians to enter the cause of death determination in the medical certification of death into the ERDS system. It also requires physicians to certify death records and replaces the misdemeanor penalty for failure to comply with medical license sanctions. Developed in consultation with MDHHS, the Michigan Funeral Directors Association, MSMS, and other stakeholders, there is wide support for these bills. During the onset of COVID-19, many of us saw a backlog of death certificates as we saw the tragedy of many deaths and delays in the system unfold because of the high volume in our state. Like other things, it exposed an issue in our system that needs to be addressed. Additionally, I have heard from county clerks who administer vital records that the slowness with signatures on death certificates can lead to delays in processing of other things for families. Now I'm going to turn it over to Representative Mueller to discuss his bill, 4078. Thank you for your time and consideration. And we also have a couple of experts with us. Thanks. Thank you, Representative. And thank you, Chair Hertel and the members of Health Policy for bringing this up. Even Senator Houck grabbed his attention. But my bill is pretty simple. It's the 4078. Currently, medical examiners, county medical examiners will come out to a scene if the cause of death doesn't seem natural, unexpected, an accident, they still come out. But it's 48 hours is what the medical, the doctors have. So if you've been seen by your attending physician within 48 hours, then the medical examiner doesn't have to come out. All this does is extend it up to a year. So then that way they can, the ME doesn't, the county medical examiners aren't burdened with going out to a lot of deaths if they've been seen by their physician within the last year for like a yearly physical. But it still doesn't rule out, like they said, if the police officer gets on scene and thinks there's something suspicious, they can call for the medical examiner to come out regardless of the statute. So it doesn't prevent them from coming out and doing an investigation because like I said, if an officer thinks that something is fishy, they can still come and do it. But it also frees up the medical examiners for the counties when the doctor is able to get notified. I was a police officer for 19 years and I still remember the first death investigation I went to. It was southwest of Manchester in Washtenaw County. And someone came up to visit or came up for their parents or their mom's funeral. And while they're up there, his wife passed away. Well, I had to sit out there. You sit out there for hours waiting for the ME to show up. And if you were able to get a hold of a doctor and they said, well, yeah, you can sign it. We could have called the funeral home and had the body removed a lot quicker. But instead, you know, you're out there sitting with the family of a deceased person. And it's kind of an uncomfortable situation. And like I think Representative Rogers said, there's also, you know, cultural things that involve, you know, with deaths. You know, some people get cremated, some religions don't like cremation, some have, you know, time frames where they have to be buried. And if they're waiting for paperwork to catch up to it, it can cause a lot of, you know, unwanted stress in an already stressful situation. Thank you, Representatives. Do we have any questions from committee members? Senator Cherry. Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Representatives, for your testimony. How often is it that death certificates get signed after that 48-hour period? Thanks for that question. I think the experts are going to address that. But in the House, that question came up as well. And my understanding is DHHS did a study on that. And in the last five years, 75% of death certificates were found to be not filled out within the 48 hours. So this is pretty widespread. Senator Heisinga. I just have one comment. When I was young, I worked at a doctor's office, and I was the guy that was typing out those death certificates. And the process of waiting for the diagnosis and waiting for the doctors is a real thing. And then just by virtue of moving to the modern times of saying you're creating electronically, clearly there's going to be a scope of efficiency there. And so I like this. I'm glad to see you bring it forth. So thank you both for doing it and your testimony today. Thank you. Any further questions? Thank you very much. We are now going to move to Zoom to Joe Bice, who is the funeral director with the Betzler Life Story Funeral Home. Joe, are you with us? Yes, I am. All right, please begin when you're ready. Thank you. Hello, my name is Joe Busey. I've been a mortuary science licensee since 1986. I just recently retired within the last two weeks after almost 40 years in this business. One of the first questions when I met with a family or when I meet with a family is, when can I get death certificates? It's frustrating.

families who have to wait several days for this document. Sometimes even a week or more. Many times services cannot be performed nor can they be scheduled without a death certificate such as in the case of cremation. Funeral directors need a signed death certificate by a doctor to obtain the cremation permit. Without a timeline on when someone is being cremated service plans are put on hold and it creates logistical problems for funeral homes having to shelter bodies for unnecessary amounts of time. These bills will help alleviate this problem by making doctors fill out and sign death certificates in a more timely fashion. Another positive outcome of this passage of these bills will be having the doctors fill these out and sign their portion of the death certificate electronically. Currently, as it was stated earlier, many of them are handwritten and filled out. Though this is, you know, currently you can do this electronically but so many doctors just refuse to do that. It's frustrating as a funeral professional as we sit there and we're trying to look at this illegible handwriting and many times the portions of that is not filled out properly. It'd never be accepted by the county clerk so we have to go back and follow up with that doctor several times. Frustrating at the technology is there for them to complete this but they refuse to. In my almost 40 years of helping families navigate through this funeral process, I've seen a difference in society in what they want from their funeral professionals. One thing they desire are death certificates in a timely manner so they can handle those business affairs. Passage of these two bills will create a positive outcome for funeral service and the families we serve. Thank you. Thank you. Do we have any questions for Joe? Seeing none, thank you very much for your testimony. Next, also on Zoom, Dr. Mary Pietrangelo, who is the medical examiner and serves as a member at large on the Michigan Association of Medical Examiners. Mary, are you with us? Yes, I am. Thank you. Please begin when you're ready. Okay. I'm Dr. Mary Pietrangelo. I'm a forensic pathologist and the chief medical examiner for Macomb County. And I'd like to take this opportunity to comment on two topics that are addressed by these bills. First is the responsibility for death certification and secondly is the expeditious death certification. Before I was a pathologist, I was a family physician for nine years. I was trained in a comprehensive family medicine residency program in a tertiary care center, yet I never heard one thing about death certificates during my residency or in medical school. During medical school, there was a pharmacology rotation where I learned how to write a prescription and I even was examined on how to write a prescription. But not one word about death certificates. The first time I encountered a death certificate was in the early weeks of my first family practice job when a funeral home employee appeared in the waiting room and presented me with one to sign. So because there's no training in how to do it, it's not surprising to me that completing a death certificate is not a comfort zone for many doctors and probably contributes to some of the reluctance and pushback that I've received as a medical examiner. From my perspective, the strong points of bills 4077 and 4088 are the clarification of responsibility for completing a death certificate for deaths occurring both inside and outside of an institution and for defining an attending physician as one who has seen a patient within the year preceding death. I also like that it does not exclude specialty physicians nor does it limit responsibility for this to solely primary care physicians. One phrase though that has been crossed out that I'd like you to consider keeping in is on page 7 of bill 4077 and that phrase reads, if the county medical examiner determines that the case does not fall within his or her jurisdiction, the county medical examiner shall refer the case back to the deceased physician. This statement validates the medical examiner's assessment of what is and what isn't jurisdictional. Physicians have refused to sign death certificates for a variety of reasons and I'm going to share a few of them with you. One is I don't feel comfortable. Another one is I'm a specialist. I never sign death certificates. Another is I wasn't there. Another is I don't know what they died from and some just flat out refuse. My sense is that they are uncomfortable and not being able to name the precise mechanism of death. Did they have a heart attack? Did they have an arrhythmia or a stroke? Did they have a diabetic complication? Rather than assigning the underlying condition that provoked the mechanism such as atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, hypertensive cardiovascular disease, and complications of diabetes mellitus. And I think likely this stems from not understanding the death certificate and not being trained to complete them, which really should have been addressed back in medical school or residency. I do expect arguments from community physicians with respect to the phrasing in bill 4078, pages 3 and 4, that a county medical examiner shall immediately be notified regarding an individual who died within the 48 hours immediately preceding the time of death unless the attending physician or a physician acting as the authorized representative of the attending physician, if any, is able to determine accurately the cause of death. I have encountered physicians who claim they can't accurately determine the cause of death. My next set of comments address the expeditious death certification process. Our office has used EDRS for electronic death certification for years, and it's not a problem to submit a death certificate to EDRS within 48 hours for cases that are brought into our office. If we aren't able to determine a cause and manner of death at the time of the exam, which happens in probably 70% of the cases, we then pend the death certificate. The death certificate can be pended, which allows it to be certified in EDRS and then amended when the final cause and manner of death are determined. Medical examiners are the only death certifiers that can use this term, pending. Our own delay in meeting the 48-hour deadline occurs when cases that require further investigation or involve medical record review. These are things like cremation permits, month-end death certificate review. Our office reviews every death certificate that was filed in the previous month to make sure that we don't miss any possible non-natural contributions to death. All hospital or hospice deaths that have a non-natural component, usually it's an injury, whether it's recent or remote. For these cases, we have to request medical records, sometimes going back weeks, months, or even years, and sometimes involving multiple institutions. Due to that inevitable delay, we have now begun automatically pending those death certificates so that they can be certified right away. Over the past years, I have noticed that it's taking longer and longer to get these medical records and medical conditions are more and more complex. So with the goal of getting a certified death through EDRS, just this week, we started automatically pending. We're not going to try and wait for medical records to be received. And that's it for my comments. I thank you very much. Thank you, doctor. Do we have any questions from the committee? Seeing no questions, thank you for your testimony. Next, I will call up Dr. Tom George, CEO of the Michigan State Medical Society. Thank you for being here with us, Dr. George. Please begin.

when you're ready. As a mass, we represent Michigan's physicians, medical students, and residents, and we are in support of this package of bills and are thankful that we were involved in its crafting. This issue of timeliness in signing death certificates was brought to our attention by the Funeral Directors Association, and we recognize that it is important that physicians take seriously their responsibility to complete medical records and death certificates accurately and promptly as possible. It's an important function for public health reasons, as you heard, for completing estate work and for giving families peace of mind and also for allowing cremation and burial to take place. In filling out the death certificate, sometimes it does involve a fair amount of work, you know, depending on the details of the case. The physician may need to review the patient's records, testing, their medical history, autopsy results in order to give their best estimate as to the cause of death. So it does sometimes involve a fair amount of work. Moving to an electronic format is a positive step. It should make it easier eventually to complete these records. It also, I think, will make for more accurate record keeping. You heard about allusions to doctor's handwriting, and by using an electronic format, it should be more legible. Also, electronic formats can use prompts to make sure that the records are filled out completely. It's estimated that as many as 30 percent of death certificates nationwide contain errors. So by using an electronic format with prompts and having it be legible, errors should be reduced. So we support the bills, and as we move forward on the issue, you know, we appreciate the communication with the funeral directors to make this process as facile as possible. I just also mentioned the comments about training that we heard. I think that's probably true, that it is not generally a component of medical school training. Of course, our medical schools are all independent. They'll have their own curricula. But I think it is probably true that they do not train students in filling out death certificates. However, it would frequently, hopefully, be something that they would learn during their residency program that follows medical school, you know, when they train to be a family medicine specialist or emergency medicine. They pick their specialty. I would think it would be part of that training normally, not so much in medical school but during residency. Thank you. Thank you, doctor. Do we have any questions for Dr. George from the committee? Seeing none. Thank you so much. Thank you. A few cards to read in for both House Bills 40, 77, and 47, 78. Sam Gibson from Michigan Association of Counties not wishing to speak in support of the bill. Charde Burton, Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, supports the bills, not wishing to speak. Bill Zagman, Michigan Association of County Clerks, not wishing to speak in support of the bills. And Jared Rozicki, Michigan Funeral Directors Association, not wishing to speak in support of the bills as well. We will look to take a vote on these bills hopefully next week, and I appreciate everybody being here to testify on them today. We are now going to move on to Senate Bills 475 and 476, which are sponsored by Senator Waino and Senator Santana. Senator Santana, would you like to begin testimony? Sure. Thank you, Chairman and committee members. Thank you for the opportunity to speak on Senate Bill 476, and thank you to Senator Waino for continuing to uplift this issue in his bill package for the past few years. This bill will respond to the deeply concerning practices of non-consensual invasive bodily exams performed on patients who are under anesthesia and unconscious. While this has generally occurred as a part of the educational practice, these exams can be extremely traumatic and violating, and the trust of patients placed in the health care system. My legislation, Senate Bill 476, is very simple. It amends the public health code to formally define invasive bodily examination, and it also clarifies such procedures must not be performed without informed consent. Taken together, these bills will ensure that Michigan law reflects the fundamental principles that every patient has the right to control what happens to their body. So I urge support for this legislation, and I will pass along to Senator Waino. Thank you, Senator. Mr. Chairman, committee members, thank you for considering these bills that are sponsored today by myself and Senator Santana. These bills are a reintroduction from last session, which passed the Senate Chamber unanimously, and also in 2020, a similar version passed the House by a vote of 108 to 0. My bill, Senate Bill 475, would prohibit an invasive body exam on an anesthetized or unconscious patient without their permission by a student who is in a health profession training program. In circumstances where the patient is unconscious and incapable of providing informed consent, and the invasive bodily exam is necessary for diagnostic or treatment, or a court has ordered the exam for collection of evidence, the exam may be completed. The reasoning for these bills is that Senator Santana and myself feel that it's an important issue for both medical students and patients. A survey of 101 medical students from seven major American medical schools found that 92% reported performing a pelvic exam on an anesthetized female patient. Of that group, 61% reported performing this procedure without explicit patient consent. In this survey, a total of 47 medical students that conducted exams under anesthesia without consent were uncomfortable with how their schools handled these exams. Two years ago, 16 states adopted legislation similar to this, and now today, 30 states have followed and adopted legislation that prohibits non-consensual pelvic exams. There's no firm data on exams under anesthesia being performed in medical schools here in our state. However, some schools have changed their standards, like the University of Michigan, which adopted a policy in 2019 requiring consent forms to be signed by a patient. If signed, it then requires medical students to meet patients before performing exams under anesthesia, and the doctors need to explain student involvement to the patient. Again, I want to thank the chairman and the committee for the consideration of these bills. I want to thank Senator Santana for her hard work. We do have several individuals here today who wish to testify, and also Bill Drake, my chief of staff, is also available to answer any questions committee members may have. Thank you. Thank you, Senators. Do we have any questions for the bill sponsors? Seeing none, thank you very much. We will now move on to Zoom. We have Dr. Kelly Beershey, who is the director of the forensic nursing program at Oakland University. Dr. Beershey, are you with us? Yes, I am. Thank you. Thank you. Please begin when you're ready. Yeah, good afternoon, Senator Hertel and other members of the Senate Health Policy Committee. I appreciate the opportunity to testify before you today regarding Senate Bills 475 and 476. I am currently an associate professor in the School of Nursing at Oakland University and the immediate past director of our forensic nursing program. I do remain as faculty there and provide education to nurses seeking a graduate degree in forensic nursing. I'm also a forensic nurse and have practiced as a sexual assault nurse examiner for close to 15 years. I want to thank the bill sponsors for their efforts in bringing forward this very important, insightful legislation aimed at protecting rights really of all patients, particularly those who are vulnerable as a result of being unconscious, related to anesthesia or otherwise, and it's protecting them from having medically unnecessary invasive body examinations. As a forensic nurse, I provide care to patients who have been sexually assaulted and conducting an invasive genital exam is often part of this treatment. These patients seek care after being victimized and at times we are also asked to consult on patients and provide exams for those who are unconscious. Part of my job and really the job of all health care professionals when we provide care, whether my patient is awake and alert or not, is to prevent them from experiencing further trauma or being re-traumatized. One way that we can accomplish this is to create opportunities where our patients have a voice and choice when making decisions about their health care. In order to do that, to make it happen, we have to obtain informed consent from that patient or in the case of them being unconscious, their authorized representative prior to conducting any kind of invasive body exam. As stated, there's legislation in over half of our states and currently Michigan does not have

into one of those states. And so what happens as a forensic nurse or healthcare provider in our state, we lack legal guidance on conducting these invasive exams. To date, our practice is then guided by policy that's developed and implemented within our place of employment. And as I'm sure you can imagine, there are thousands of places of employment in our state. And so what happens is there's high variability in how this care is being performed and carried out. And so there's differences in outcomes for our patients across the state. The lack of standardization that happens opens the door to ethical and legal ramifications, namely in the loss of our patient's autonomy, which is a key principle in our healthcare ethics. And what happens is ignoring those patient rights puts our licensure as healthcare providers at risk, as I could later be charged with assaulting my patient if informed consent has not been obtained prior to conducting these exams that could potentially harm our patients. Senate Bill 475 and 476 are critical pieces of legislation that can help to create standardized practice and offer much needed legal guidance, not only to me as a forensic nurse, but all healthcare providers who conduct invasive exams. The legislation puts patient self-determination to the forefront while also supporting our clinical practice. And we fully support this bill. So thank you so much for your time. Thank you very much. Do you have any questions from committee members? Seeing none, thank you for being with us. Next on Zoom, we have Zoe Scheinblum-Brewer, who is the Policy and Grassroots Coordinator for RAINN. Zoe, are you with us? I am. Can you hear me? Yes, please begin. Wonderful. Thank you, Mr. Chair and members of the committee. My name is Zoe Scheinblum-Brewer, and I am here on behalf of the Rape, Abuse, and Incest National Network, also known as RAINN. We are the largest anti-sexual violence organization in the country and the operator of the National Sexual Assault Hotline. The issue of involuntary pelvic exams came to our attention as survivors reported it to us. We're here in support of SB 475 and 476, which would ensure that patients give informed consent before healthcare providers or supervised medical students perform intimate exams while a patient is anesthetized or unconscious. This bill is essential to prevent re-traumatization, particularly for survivors of sexual violence. Research shows that 61% of medical students have performed pelvic exams on anesthetized patients without explicit consent, and over 80% of women were unaware that this could happen. 72% of women expect to be asked for permission before undergoing an exam under anesthesia, but 62% of these women say that they actually would consent if they were just asked. All patients deserve the right to informed consent. 30 states, including Wisconsin and Minnesota, have already enacted laws requiring informed consent for intimate exams of anesthetized or unconscious patients. Passing these bills would align Michigan with best practices all across the country, including best practices established by the University of Michigan Health System, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the American Medical Association's Code of Medical Ethics, all of which affirm the necessity of informed consent for patients. We urge Michigan to join them by passing SB 475 and 476 to uphold patient trust and dignity across the state. Thank you. Thank you. Any questions for Zoe? Seeing none, thank you so much for being here today. Not wishing to speak in support of the bill, Taylor Elpert, Michigan Health and Hospital Association. Also not wishing to speak in support of the bill, Dr. Matt Delaguila, Michigan Society of Anesthesiologists. Not wishing to speak in support of the bill, Paige Fultz from LARA. And not wishing to speak in support of the bill, Jeremy Murphy, Michigan Developmental Disabilities Council. Those are all the bills we have before us today. We will look at voting both these packages out next week. With no further business before us, we are adjourned. Thank you.

Those two members, Senator Peters and Senator Slocken, have repeatedly voted to keep the federal government shut down, including keeping SNAP benefits from the residents of the people of Michigan. I would like to hear the member that we have the honor of serving with here who wants to go and serve in that role stand up and tell the people of Michigan that she would be committed to reopening the government and making sure those programs are funded. But we didn't hear that. I'll be voting no on this resolution, and I hope everyone else will as well. Senator Bellino would also like Senator Lindsey's no vote explanation to be recorded as his own. The president recognizes Senator McCann. Madam President, I rise in support of this resolution. I, too, am disturbed by the USDA's alarming announcement to halt SNAP benefits starting in November, just days away, and the burden it will place on children, families, and communities across our state and nation. Already we've seen it on the news and in our communities, parents figuring out how they're going to make ends meet, like Bill and Mary, contemplating which bills they'll have to leave unpaid in order to put food on the table. We see food banks and community resources now scrambling to figure out how they're going to help provide for their neighbors to make up for the massive hole being blown in this critical safety net. But we must actually ask why. It's not just that it's immoral to deny food from the mouths of hungry children, adults, and communities in need, and it's not just an outright terrible political decision to play games with people's livelihoods while disrupting critical supports along with the economics of grocers, farmers, and small business owners, and it's not just that it doesn't make sense to hold people's food benefits captive in an attempt to undermine their access to health care, all while claiming to serve and support the very people whose lives you're wreaking havoc on. It's that this whole thing is completely and utterly avoidable. Congress created and invested in the SNAP contingency fund to prepare for this exact scenario, with millions of dollars in it and full legal authority by the administration to use it. These funds can and should be tapped to continue the flow of benefits during this shutdown. The Trump administration knew this to be true, and the current administration does as indicated by the USDA's recently posted lapse in funding plan, which has since been deleted from the USDA's website. Even in prior temporary federal shutdowns under both Democratic and Republican administrations, SNAP benefits have always continued to be distributed using available funding sources to prevent a disruption for families who depend on them. So to recap, the Trump administration's refusal to act and ensure the continuation of this critical lifeline runs contrary to the plain language of the law, deviates from the precedent that prior administrations have set, continues their own previously stated guidance, and flies in the face of the very mission we hold as elected officials, people who are entrusted to serve with care and compassion, people who were elected by the people for the people to make their lives easier and better. Colleagues, tell me how denying food from the plates and pantries of kids and seniors makes lives easier. Tell me how undermining people's ability to see the doctor makes lives better. Tell me how skewing our tax code to favor the top 1% and removing a critical food security program from those with the least accomplishes these goals. Madam President, it's my understanding that a state is only as strong and healthy as its people are. People who have access to nutritious food to nourish their bodies and health care systems that care for them when they are sick. And despite what Republicans in Washington would have us believe, we can and must help to provide both. I'm asking all of my colleagues here to join me in calling on the Trump administration and the United States Department of Agriculture to immediately release SNAP contingency funding so that our vulnerable families across the state and country keep food on their table in the weeks ahead. It's the right thing to do and I urge a yes vote on this resolution. Senator, would you like your remarks printed in the journal? Without objection, so ordered. The President recognizes Senator Irwin. Thank you, Madam President. I ask that my remarks be printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. Thank you. I don't know if any of you have been shopping anytime recently, but $180 a month doesn't go very far in this economy. $180 a month doesn't go very far in these grocery stores when people are being hit.

with inflation and food prices going up and up and up. Did you know that 42% of Michigan kids depend on SNAP benefits? They depend on SNAP benefits to eat. title: Oversight - Corporate Subsidies and State Investments — Wednesday, October 29, 2025
transcript:
The House Oversight Subcommittee on Corporate Subsidies and State Investments will come to order. Will the clerk please take attendance? Chair Kawa. Here. Representative Green. Present. Bierlein. Here. Wugela. Here. Pahutski. Here. Mr. Chair, you have five members present and a quorum. Vice Chair Green moves to approve the minutes of the October 22nd meeting. Without objection, so ordered. Today, we'll be hearing additional testimony on the Governor's overseas travel and also the Goshen EV battery plant. Welcome, John Mazina from the Center for Economic Accountability. If you'll please come up and begin when you're ready. Looking forward to hearing it. Thank you. Thank you, Chairman Kawa, Vice Chair Green, my fellow Vice Chair Wugela. Thank you for having me back in front of your committee for a third time. I'm very pleased that you've apparently found enough value in my perspective on economic development to bring me back again, and I look forward to getting the special jacket or whatever when I come back eventually for a fifth time, like Saturday Night Live host. I am John Mazina, President of the Center for Economic Accountability. We are a nonpartisan and independent 501c3 that is based here in Michigan and works around the country to bring transparency, accountability, and free market-based reforms to state and local economic development programs across America. While I'm here today testifying in that role I hold at the CEA, I will also note for full disclosure's sake that I'm also a senior fellow at the Reason Foundation specializing in economic development policy and hold similar fellowship roles at the nonprofit and nonpartisan think tanks Better Cities Project, ITR Foundation in Iowa, and Bluegrass Institute for Public Policy Solutions in Kentucky. My testimony today does not represent the position of any of those organizations. So, as I said, I work on economic development policy reform across the country, and as someone with that national perspective but a home and heart here in Michigan, it is heartening to see my beloved home state setting the standard for meaningful legislative oversight of economic development agencies and programs. I've pointed to this subcommittee as a model that other state legislatures should follow to impose desperately needed oversight on their own runaway economic development programs. That legislative oversight is incredibly important because we're sure as heck not getting meaningful oversight of the MEDC from anyone else. And that leads us to the topic of my testimony today, which is what the governor's overseas travel tells us about the way decisions are made, about how to transfer taxpayer dollars to private corporations, whose interests are prioritized in those deals, and who is making or influencing those decisions. As I have discussed with this committee before, the fundamental flaw in the way Michigan does economic development is that except for taxpayers, virtually everyone in a position of power or influence over the process benefits from the status quo. Nobody with a role in the corporate subsidy decision-making process has a meaningful structural incentive to push for transparency or accountability or to negotiate for the best deal possible for taxpayers or to try to kill a bad deal or publicize failures. Rather, everyone has a personal incentive to go along, to get along, and to keep the taxpayer dollars floating out the door. That applies to these international trips. The elected and appointed officials who get to go on them benefit from VIP working vacations to suspiciously pleasant destinations, and the companies that fund the travel get access and good feelings in return, along with potentially millions or billions of taxpayer dollars, thanks at least in part to the access they get along with their donations. According to its IRS filings, the Michigan Economic Development Foundation

mission is, quote, to lessen the burden of the government of the state of Michigan to promote the public welfare. That sounds laudable, but it's also worth considering the analogy that if you're lessening someone's burden, it means you're putting some of that on your own shoulders. And if you're the one now carrying that burden, it means you get a say in where it goes. This is where I will praise the Detroit News' excellent recent reporting on this topic, which found that companies with MEDF board seats have received $2.2 billion in subsidies from this administration. To that, I will add that it looks even worse if you go further back and further afield. All told, according to my research, of the 29 companies the foundation lists as supporters, 20 of them had some form of tax abatement, grant, or other subsidy for Michigan listed in the Subsidy Tracker database maintained by Good Jobs First. I'll note that number may actually be higher. I didn't go into all of the potential subsidiaries, DBAs, or other types of options, but this is the questions that Vice Chair Green and Minority Vice Chair Wigallo especially were asking at the last meeting about how many of the donors to the MEDF had received subsidies from the state. And the answer is, again, 20 of 29. To answer the question of how much this matters, we can simply look at what corporate site selectors themselves say about it. For the past 39 years, Area Development Magazine has surveyed corporate site selectors about what factors are currently most influential in their decisions about what to build and where.
