And that was the same thing that I've seen happen, we've seen that happen in this community, in Marshall, in Monteith, in any number of communities across the state where the issue isn't the nationality of the company involved or who the profits are going to, but rather the process through which these kinds of deals are negotiated, signed, and set supposedly in stone before the companies that are being, pardon me, the communities that are being transformed have any say in the issue if they ever do at any point in this process. In the last meeting, I know Minority Vice Chair Wiggela talked about the fact that he's opposed to subsidizing any company, whether from China or otherwise, and I think that is a perfectly legit, I share that, and we can avoid this entire topic just by saying that shouldn't be the purpose of the government of the state of Michigan. It should be to create an environment in which any business is welcome to come here and run a good business that creates good jobs and is a good member of the community. There were two different routes where money was being prepared by the state as these handouts to Goshen. You had $175 million total. $125 million of it was CIP funding, which was never appropriated to Goshen. Of the $50 million in the Strategic Site Readiness Program, the SSRP, $23.7 million had been given from the MEDC to the right place, and then from the right place, where all that went and what all it got spent on by Goshen. They bulldozed and tore down a bunch of trees, and there's not a building there, and there's not a whole lot of infrastructure to show for it. What they spent all that money on, I don't know. Do you have any knowledge on that or any feedback? No, not the details. I have not seen any indications, if I missed them I apologize, but I haven't seen any indications that that information has been publicly reported, which frankly, again, it should be. Companies are asking the people of Michigan, the taxpayers or just the people of Michigan, anyone who depends on the services of the government, anyone who's a resident of the state, to essentially become an investor in their company. That would imply to me that the people of the state of Michigan ought to have just as much access to information about the details of what's being done with the money they've invested as any bank loan officer or hedge fund operator or Wall Street trader or venture capital firm investor. If you're going to make the people of Michigan your business partners, then you have to treat us like your business partners and not just as a slot machine that you can put a nickel into and get a couple hundred billion dollars out of. What should happen with that $23.7 million that has gone to Goshen? My preference, and I think the sort of moral, ethical thing would be to get it back. As a practical matter, I would be surprised if it were possible to get it back. As you said, some of it's been spent on things like bulldozer fuel and the like. And I mean, hopefully as a practical matter, something else can happen, whether it's the one big project, or I know there's been some reporting about other opportunities for companies looking at smaller companies with more of an openness to engaging proactively and healthily with the community. I talked about taking some of that space maybe. In the grand scheme, the money shouldn't have been spent, as I said, without the deal being done. Everybody who needed to sign off, signing off. They signed off on poor management when you're putting money into something that still isn't done yet. And that's a question, again, that's one of those questions about what did we learn from this and what are you going to do in the future to get, whether it's the MEDC or MSF or the various local economic development agencies, to just be like, look, not a dime goes out the door before everything, all the paperwork is done. Preference would be to not do the deals at all, but if we're going to be doing the deals, that should be pretty basic. I mean, that's the way business would be working on it. Right. And there's a renaissance zone that is there in the community in Green Township. What should happen to that renaissance zone? And just for clarity, that's where they get their tax exemptions, local and to the state. Should we continue to allow that renaissance zone for another company to come in or get rid of it entirely? Renaissance zones, like sort of other situations where you're sort of drawing a border around a specific piece of geography, whether it's a renaissance zone, an opportunity zone, a TIF district, downtown development authority, all those sorts of things. They all have the fundamental flaw that overwhelmingly what you are doing is you are concentrating development in there because you're creating an incentive to be there. But the flip side of that is it's sort of the seen and the unseen in the French economist Bastiat's famous formulation that you see all the growth. What you don't see is the growth that doesn't happen elsewhere. So it's the analogy I've used is sort of like you spread a bunch of poker chips on the table and you reach out and you sort of scoop them all in one place. And that zone is looking great. There's a lot of chips there, but now there's not as much for everybody else at the table. So these zones are a sort of rob Peter to pay Paul or at least subsidize Peter to impoverish Paul mechanism. And in virtually every case of which I'm aware, I'm not saying 100% of the time, but I could imagine situations where there might be some value here and there, disaster relief and things along those lines. But in virtually every sort of general use, they are more of an exercise in political favoritism and the kinds of picking winners and losers at the sort of municipal rather than corporate level that leads to bad public policy. Next question from Minority Vice Chair Wiggela. Yeah, this one for me, I don't really I think it's necessary for like the opposition to this project just because it's from China. Like and I'm not saying China is not shouldn't have any criticisms, right? It should. But like as all countries do. I mean, our country is actively sending our tax dollars to fund a genocide right now as well. So what I will say, though, is I think that any I'm not going to sit here and listen to your crap anymore about. Representative, let's let him share his perspective. What I'm saying is I don't believe I think the argument is stronger when we say no corporations should receive taxpayer money. Right. I think that makes a lot of sense. Most people in this country, I think, would agree they don't want their tax dollars going to fund private business. And I think that that's a strong argument. I'm curious if you think the argument on its face is stronger to have a united front to say, you know, me and Rep Carr here don't agree on everything, but we agree that corporations should not receive taxpayer funded money and have certain advantages over others. Insofar as I agree with you to the concept of we just should not

be subsidizing businesses of whatever nationality or background. That is not a useful function of the state. It's not good economics. It's not a good idea, and we shouldn't be doing it. As to the other assertions, I think that I agree with you that if we simply did that, it would mean that we didn't have to have those kinds of disagreements as we just heard about. So to the economic policy of just simply not doing subsidies, yes, absolutely. That is one of the founding principles of our organization is that at the long run, there is no evidence that we should be doing this. It's morally wrong. It's economically wrong. And the real-world evidence just is that it doesn't work. So let's stop doing things that don't work, and then we can disagree on the other policy areas in the way that the political process works. I'll just briefly say, Minority Vice Chair Magella, I'm going to give myself some latitude here to just say that the conversations and the perspectives that you have, we do not always agree. But like I say with Bernie Sanders, he opens the book up to the correct page. I just believe he has the book upside down. And I love the conversations that you and I get to have, and we get to tackle these types of questions and look into this type of corruption. And I just want to let you know I appreciate where you're coming from as much as we disagree at times. And keep doing what you do to ask the right questions, and we'll do the best that we can to get to the bottom of what's going on, whether we agree or disagree. So I just wanted to say that. I will just ask one last question, I think, because I don't see any other questions. My last question I'll ask you, Mr. Mazina, is with Randy Thalen, my thoughts on it, he's testified here before. And I thought when he testified and when I spoke with him briefly other than that one other time, he seemed to be a very pleasant guy, a very likable, great demeanor. And he's just operated as the type of businessman who has involved himself very closely with that working relationship with government, finding those ways to get those special tax breaks, seeing where you might be able to find an edge here or there. And when he has this explicit position that is meant for somebody of the private sector, yet his entire work environment has been around these what seems like taxpayer-funded public purposes, then we have Article 4, Section 30 that says that you need two-thirds support in order to appropriate funds for private purposes. Is it private purposes or is it public purposes? It seems like they want to have their cake and eat it too in terms of is this following the Michigan Constitution when we give these handouts without two-thirds support? Is it a private purpose or is it a public purpose when we give these big tax-free handouts? What are your thoughts? I agree with you that I believe it should be a public purpose. I believe that both here in Michigan and around the country, most state constitutions have gift clauses or other mechanisms that would seem just sort of from a straightforward textual reading to oppose these kinds of handouts. And yet over time, we've gotten these sort of giant money fountains that have built up sort of despite that in various courts and various opinions and the like have made it so that these constitutions don't get applied in a way that would seem fairly straightforward. Again, personally, I haven't spoken a great deal with Mr. Thalen. I believe that he's a well-intentioned, experienced professional. I've said in the past I have had very pleasant, thoughtful discussions with Mr. Messer at the MEDC. I think that overwhelmingly the people in these roles are good folks who are trying to do right as they see it within the environment that they are given, within the environment that they see it, that they believe that sort of like maybe that it's the game that they have to play because that's what the game is. So let's do the best that they can, at which point I would say that it is this legislature's job and duty and responsibility to change that game. To Vice Chair McGillis' point of shouldn't we just not be subsidizing anything, to create an environment in which these professional, experienced, well-intentioned, good-hearted people could do more useful and important things that would actually improve the business climate for everyone in Michigan, every business, small, big, intermediate. I say that whether it's the governor's trips or projects like Goshen or whatever, we have this bias towards sort of big game hunting. But one of the single most dependable factors that you could look at in terms of predicting what a place's economy is going to look like in the future is the small business formation rate. Growth comes from small businesses growing into big businesses. Big businesses are big. They've gotten their growth done already. So an environment, if this legislature could move us to an environment where it is conducive to everyone, to entrepreneurs and big businesses alike, we'd be much better off. Okay, thank you. One last question from Minority Vice Chair Baghela. And I'll be brief. I think 40 percent of Michigan families are struggling to pay their bills and meet their needs right now. I don't think any of us up here would argue that things fundamentally in our economy need to improve for working class folks. Would you argue, can I get you to concede that if we can make life better for the working class, I think we might have different theories on how to get there, but it is kind of an absurd gesture right now to have this level of inequality in this country with big business having such access to the political establishment, if you will, and then so many people struggling that actually if we could raise the bar for people, whether that's through free market policies or through things that I would argue for, that actually would be better for business in general because people would have more money to spend and have a better standard of living. Yeah, there's some stuff in there to pick apart, but broadly, yes, absolutely. I mean, the making life better for everyone in Michigan is both sort of the fundamental job. Let's go on protecting people's rights, life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, as well as a practical economic matter. As I referenced the site selection survey from Area Development Magazine, when you've got sort of workforce availability, workforce costs, and quality of life are among the top things. And what does that mean? Well, that means is this a place where there are sort of those working folks you talk about. Do they have a good quality of life? Is this the kind of place where you want to be? If you're somebody like an electrician or a mechanic or a CNC machinist or any number of these other jobs that are hard to find, truck driver, do you want to live in Michigan? You could go pretty much anywhere in the country and get a job. I have a young cousin who's an auto mechanic and sort of looking at where he wants to go live because he knows wherever he can, wherever he moves, he'll be able to get a job. Does he want to stay here in Michigan? Well, frankly, the thing that's keeping him here is family and not the environment or the potential future. So I think to that point, yes, absolutely. If we can focus on broad-based policies that improve things like education, health care, all those sorts of stuff, whatever that might be, that is, in fact, the fundamental answer for how you grow an economy. Well, thank you for your testimony as always, Mr. Mazina. Thank you as always for having me. And next up we will have Representative Tom Koontz. He represents the area where Green Township is. Looking forward to hearing what you have to share with the committee today. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee that are present, thank you for having me here today. I appreciate that. My goal is to be a little bit more pragmatic and practical. I don't want to talk macroeconomics. We understand corporate subsidies are not working. What I want to do is unwrap this issue. This is my district. These are my people. And the pointy end of the spear has been a little township called Green Charter Township, north of Big Rapids, and they have led the fight on this. I put in a legislative spending request to help them with their legal fees, and that didn't make it through the budget process. That remains a priority of mine, so I'm still going to push for funding to help them in this fight that I think we all agree now was misdirected. But I do have some specific questions, and I'm going to apologize in advance. I'm asking questions that may unfairly – I don't expect you to have them, but I wanted to get these out. This is what I'd like to know. So I don't expect you to have the inner workings of the MEDC or the right place or the Michigan Strategic Fund or the state readiness plan, almost a corporate shell game there. But I think it's important that we realize here's what I'm trying to do. So specifically we talked about the Renaissance Zone, and Mr. Chairman, would you like me to go through my questions or what is best? It's your time, however you'd like to do it. Very good. Well, I'm trying to be respectful. I know Representative Fox is back here anxious to testify also. So this project, there's a lot of unanswered questions. And I think you said something, Mr. Chairman, that really stuck with me. The buck stops here. Well, it's literal and figurative, but this committee should find out where was the money

spent and how do we get that back? And that's what I'm trying to do with these questions here. So there is a lien on the property. As a matter of fact, the state of Michigan is in second place on the lien. So West, forgive me, I always say this wrong, East-West Bank has a UCC filing on this property. So here's where my legal knowledge stops. But yes, there is a lien on the mortgage, $24.6 million on a $6 million piece of property. And we're in second place. So I don't know, Mr. Chair, if this is the committee's intent to get these questions answered and to move forward, but that is my goal. I'd like to find out the answers. And then, of course, there is ongoing legislation right now, litigation, excuse me, there is ongoing litigation against my township. So I'd like to get that resolved. Any resolution of this project has to include a cessation of litigation against Green Charter Township. And I'd like to talk about recouping some of their legal fees. So in the essence of time, I'm not going to go through and read my questions. They have them. I've detailed them. I do have a couple copies left. I'll share with the audience. But does the board have any questions for me? I think just one quick one from me. Please, I don't believe you that it's a quick one. But how much is the request for the legal fees that you had in your LDSI request? I requested $275,000. And that is not— $275,000, and they got $175 million was the proposal for them. It seems like compared to that number, that's a small dollar to assist the community after everything they've gone through. Correct. I agree. I was disappointed it didn't make it through the budget process. I understand. But that does remain a priority of mine, Mr. Chair. And then a quick question from Vice Chair Greene. Do you know how much the annual budget of that township is? Representative, I apologize for that. That's fine. Usually townships that size, that is their annual budget is about $200,000. Correct. And I was going to say we're right in that $250,000 to $300,000. So they have run a deficit the last few years. They're working on this. But their Green Charter Township is the pointy end of the spear. They're leading the fight against this. And it is the definition of David versus Goliath. And we know how that story ends, and it did again. There certainly is a sticker shock to a lot of the dollar amounts that we hear in this committee. But I guess this sticker shock for that number was on the other end of how small it is. Very good. Well, thank you, Representative Koontz, for... And I'm not entirely sure that is their total legal fees. I think total... The issue is I don't know there's total legal fees. There's outstanding legal fees. Some have been paid, even if we could recoup some of those. Yes. Thank you, Representative. Thank you very much for your time. Thank you. Appreciate you. All right. And last but not least, we have Representative Joe Fox. If you'll come up and testify when you're ready, looking forward to hearing from you. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you to the committee. And I think I have just been asked to come and tell a story. So I will tell my story. Right now, you know, I represent the county that runs right next door to Greene Township. And the great fear of people in my county was what happens if? Because the Muskegon River ran nearby, and it runs all the way through Newago County. So that's how I got my nose into this. Besides that, being a person who encouraged the Greene Township people attending many meetings, attending a rally. And I plan on attending a gathering this Saturday where they're going to be rejoicing. You know, the song that's being sung in Greene Township is Ding Dong, the Witch is Dead. Which old witch? The wicked old witch, okay? In relation to the ending of Greene Township. So this story, just very quickly, to give you a microcosm of what I experienced. I went in the spring of 2023, along with Rep Cara and along with another rep, to visit Greene Township. We were going there for a rally that was going to happen later that afternoon. And at that rally were people like presidential candidate Perry Johnson, who was standing against it. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra. I think Rep John Molinar was there. A lot of people wandering up and down the street near Ferris. But beforehand, Rep Cara, myself, and the other legislator decided to stop by Greene Township and see what could happen. So we planned to meet with Jim Chapman, the supervisor of Greene Township at that time. And I felt like I was walking into an old West saloon in some ways, okay? Because Mr. Chapman came in with his sidearm strapped on his side against these three big mean legislators who were sitting there. I'm being a little bit sarcastic. There were no cookies and milk offered to us. Just a seat at the table with a gun strapped to his side. I don't know what he thought he was doing, but definitely based upon meetings I had attended, it was a crazy situation because I had watched in previous meetings where, again, a former township trustee had snickered when asked, you know, they'd kind of giggled when asked, well, how much are you profiting from this, okay? And stuff like that had gone on. It was just totally clear. So long story short, Mr. Cara got into the whole questioning, which he is good at all these type of questions. You know, is this a free market situation or is this a central planning thing? What's driving this, you know? And I will say there was nothing racist rattling around in the room, okay? And he was just met with belligerence, you know, in the responses. Finally, I had had enough, and this is getting to the end of my story, and I just basically looked at Mr. Chapman and I said, Mr. Chapman, what will your legacy be? What will your legacy be? What are you going to leave behind after all is said and done? And my personal opinion is he's already experiencing his legacy right now as people sing, ding dong, the witch is dead. Mr. Chapman got up and walked out of the room in a huff, and, you know, we as three legislators decided to do a house-to-house survey in the nearby houses, and we ended up finding out real quickly before we went to the rally that we interviewed 36 people at their doors. 30 people were against Goshen moving in. Six people were for it, okay? That was our simple, quick, hour-long, house-to-house survey. Then we went to the rally, and it just became clearly evident that, generally speaking, the people in that neck of the woods were not in favor of Goshen. Story concluded. Thank you. Absolutely, Representative Fox. They would try to make claims like there was a silent majority who was in support, and that simply was not the case. And we saw the hundreds of millions of people who showed up for that rally. No, it was millions. It was hundreds. I'm used to those big numbers. My apologies. No, there were hundreds. I wouldn't say there were even thousands, but, yes, there were hundreds of people who showed up for the rally. Thanks for the correction. I didn't even know I had missaid that. Anyway, it was quite the experience with Mr. Chapman, and it was just entertaining because he went back and forth with me for 15 minutes on the economics of it all and just took from a gentle giant like yourself a good man just asking him what his legacy was going to be in the most calm way possible, and he stormed out of the room. So that was surprising to see, but I appreciate what you do, Representative Fox. And I would say we're done there, but did you have a question, Representative Green? Vice Chair Green has one quick question. So it would be because your townships are not alone in these battles with these either mega sites or data centers or solar projects across the state of Michigan. So if you had encouragement to give to other municipalities, what would that encouragement be? My encouragement again and again in relation to this and a whole lot of things is let's start from the local and work our way to the state and not vice versa. You know, we've got to talk to local people. We have to make sure that our local ordinances are in line. We as a state are not God, and I know the local people aren't God either, but there's a whole lot of them, and they really care. Farmers really care about their agricultural land, you know. These green township people really care about the streams and the rivers and the creeks that run there nearby. And we've got to start from, and I don't like to call it the bottom, we've got to start from local and go to state and not vice versa. We have a question from Minority Vice Chair Wagala. Yeah, so kind of like building off what I was talking about earlier, and this is kind of to pinpoint, as we heard people come in and testify about this, it was very clear to me that this was about more than just being the company Goshen, right? It was about environmental concerns. It was about land.

snatched up and what that might do. And you're on the ground in the district here, so my question is, if this factory was going to be built by, say, Ford rather than Goshen, would the pushback still been the same? Because the understanding I have is that it would have been, that people did not want this project for a variety of reasons and they did not believe it should be taxpayer funded. I would agree that I think there's a variety of reasons and very honestly, you know, the China piece of the puzzle was one of the puzzle pieces on the table. It wasn't the puzzle piece. And again, I would stress that the local people need to be involved, you know, and I'm not a fan of the solar projects, not a fan of the wind projects. And again, because of our mentality of top down, you know, telling the locals what to do. So. Thank you for your testimony, Representative Fox. Thank you very much. And I'm sorry I have to excuse myself to another meeting. Seeing no further business, we're done here as well. The committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Natural Resources and Tourism — Wednesday, October 29, 2025
transcript:
House Committee on Natural Resources and Tourism will come to order. Would the clerk please take the attendance? Chair Martin? Here. Representative St. Germain? Here. VanderWaal? Present. Altman? Here. Hoadley? Here. Johnson? Here. Preston? Here. Bonaf? Here. Fairbairn? Here. Wurtz? Here. McFaul? Here. Scott? Present. Weiss? Arbit? Foreman? Myers-Phillips? Wooden? Here. Mr. Chair, you do have a quorum. Thank you. Vice Chair McFaul, I'll make some motion to approve the minutes of our previous meeting. The minutes are approved by unanimous consent. We're going to now take up House Bill 4855, sponsored by Representative Preston, which allows for the possession of a pistol by a bowhunter. Representative Preston. Welcome, sir. Thank you. Thank you, Chair. Members of the committee, thank you. This legislation is straightforward. It permits bowhunters to carry a sidearm for personal protection while hunting. Michigan law generally allows legal gun owners to openly carry firearms. However, many are unaware that the Natural Resources and Environmental Protection Act prohibits carrying weapons in areas frequented by wild animals, unless the weapon is used for hunting under a valid license or the individual holds a concealed pistol license, a CPL, which is required for both concealed and open carry in these areas. This creates two significant issues. One, a lack of public awareness, as many hunters and even the general public are unaware of this restriction, and two, the unnecessary burden the law places due to obstacles on law-abiding gun owners seeking to enjoy their time in Michigan woods. The issue is particularly acute for bowhunters. Unlike firearm hunters, who can use their hunting weapon for self-defense against predators like bears, wolves, and the cougars, bowhunters face significant challenges defending themselves. This bill addresses that disparity by allowing bowhunters to open carry a sidearm for personal protection without requiring a CPL. Hunters take their time in the woods seriously, often using their limited PTO for hunting season. Requiring a CPL to carry a sidearm imposes financial and time burdens. Obtaining a CPL costs at least $200, including class fees and paperwork, and requires taking at least one full day off of work for the course. I'd like to note here that typically CPL training lacks wildlife-specific components, adding no relevant value for hunters that are already trained and are legally required hunter safety courses. The additional requirement of a CPL forces hunters to choose between entering the woods without adequate protection or navigating a costly and time-consuming process. For context, Michigan allows open carry in public spaces like streets, sidewalks, retail stores, restaurants, yet it is restricted in the one place where everyone would expect to encounter open carry of a firearm, which is the woods during hunting season. This bill seeks to align state law by allowing law-abiding gun-owning hunters to carry sidearms for personal protection in the wilderness. The rising predator populations in Michigan, and especially in the Upper Peninsula, have led to increased human-wildlife interactions. While not every encounter results in an attack, many are unsettling even for the most seasoned outdoorsman. You've received written testimony, which I urge you to read, from hunters in the Upper Peninsula detailing their personal experiences with wildlife encounters in the woods. These stories in our networks on Facebook and throughout exchanges, the amount of interactions that go on up there is troubling, to say the least. Entered into the committee record is written testimony from two UP hunters, Adam Sherman of Delta County, that's just north of where I live, and Joe Hansen of Marquette County. Both of these men are experienced hunters, and their interactions with predator species have left them cautious about their time in the woods. They have come across wolves, bears, and even cougar. While hunters across the state are familiar with bears, Michigan's bears can still be intimidating. In 2010, a bow hunter was attacked by a black bear with her three cubs. He escaped with his life, but it was a close call, and he required 40 stitches. In his written testimony, Joe Hansen describes how on opening day of our

season, he also came across a sow with her cubs before daybreak. She acted aggressively towards him. Fortunately, he was a licensed CPL holder, and he was able to get his pistol out if it became necessary. The bear charged him in the dark, only veering off and running away at the last second. Fortunately, he did not have to discharge his firearm, but it was important for him to have had that option. Joe got his CPL strictly for the defense in the woods. He's not a CPL holder. He has that license only for protection in the woods. These accounts highlight the need for this legislation to ensure hunter safety. CPLs are a great tool for people who want to conceal their firearms in day-to-day lives, but they are an unnecessary burden for someone who is looking to open carry for self-defense in the woods. You will hear directly from a couple more UP hunters today whose experiences further underscore the importance of this bill. I look forward to their testimony. I think you'll find it compelling, and I'm happy to answer any questions that you might have right now. Thank you, Representative. Kind of a personal story, secondhand. A friend of mine I was stationed with in Fort Carson, Colorado, bow hunted for a grizzly up in Alaska, of course. It dovetails into what our next presentation is, and the guide was required. They're required to have a guide, and of course, the guide had a rifle. Grizzlies are nothing to mess with, obviously, but he had probably eight knives tucked all around his body because he was unable to carry, and he said he wasn't going down without a fight, so I get it. It bears are the ones that have always concerned me the most, especially for the bow hunters, because, you know, that time of the year, the cubs, they're getting they're very active. It's the end of season. They're well fed. They're climbing trees. They're getting in trouble, and you know, there's the number of times that a bow hunter has found himself between the cubs over his head and the sow at the bottom of the tree, and that's the worst place you want to be as a bow hunter is between a sow and its cubs. Plenty of hunters have gotten ripped out of their tree stands or had to jump out of their tree stands just to save their life. Representative Weiss. Thank you, and thank you for this. Just a clarifying question. Do you know the reasoning why right now? Because if you're able to conceal carry in the woods, do you know why you're not currently allowed to do this under law? Just because of the way the law stands right now. I can tell you that the vast majority of hunters up in the UP that are bow hunting are probably not even aware that they're breaking the law. But you have to, my understanding, and I might be reading this wrong, you have to have a concealed carry license to be able to open carry? No, open carry is legal. If you're a law-abiding gun owner, you can open carry in this state. But not while you're bow hunting. But not while you're bow hunting. Yes, that's the rub. Okay. Are there any other types of, I mean, I don't know, there are other types of hunting other than bow hunting and gun hunting? I don't know. I know a couple of guys that hunt black bear with spears, but they're a different breed. All right. Those are the ones that cover themselves with knives, probably. Thank you. Anybody else? You described your experience, but, you know, when you're talking about vulnerable populations, the elderly, the handicapped that are out taking part in this, that's kind of what encompasses the need for more people in the hunting group than you would traditionally see. And on the targeting and dispatching of the animal, when you're talking about a bow especially and a large bone animal like a bear, rib deflection, I mean, you can be the best shot in the world, and you're still not going to get around a second, third, fourth rib deflection. That's going to go right or left into the gut, and that animal is going to continue on. And you're going to have to continue to try to dispatch that animal. It's not as clear cut, even if you are the best shot. High power rifle adds a different dimension to that. But at the end of the day, yeah, you can have the best shot, and you can still have an incredibly dangerous animal at the bottom of the tree or at your bait pile. I even know a good friend of mine that shot one in the head, thought it was dead. He only knocked it out and woke up when he got down there to skin it or to gut it out. So, I mean, accidents do happen, and I think having a legal path for someone to have a secondary shooting position, because you can't just buy a bear tag unless you were issued a permit for it. So this just would allow somebody to have a secondary tag as a safety backup, and with an apex predator like this, I guess I don't understand the point of disagreement when it's just a safety-oriented issue, because this is regarding a bear that's already had a tag pulled for it and a hunter that's trying to take it. That's all. Well, I would just agree to disagree, and I would say, though, you mentioned about those handicapped or disabled elderly. Myself, along with some other MBH members, we're involved with an organization, Wheeling Team 457. It's out of Lapeer where we take some disabled hunters and stuff out into the woods. And I could certainly see some allowances for those that have disabilities that can't get back if the bear isn't disposed of. I certainly don't think that it should be against the law for a handler or a guide at that point in time to dispatch a bear that they can't get the hunter to. I think there's a big difference between that, though, and at the site of, in most cases, I would say that that's the truth. Okay, and we're calling on Representative Fairbairn next. I just want to make caution to everybody. We have Fairbairn and another speaker wishing to ask questions, and we have another bill to take up and a presentation. So if you can keep your comments short. Yeah, I think that, and I appreciate your testimony, the gist of this bill and why we're doing it, it gives them the option to take this measure. It's not forcing a bow hunter to buy this. If you're alone in a tree stand or on the ground hunting over bait, we're not forcing you to buy this. If you want to hunt, and frankly, those are unsafe conditions. I wouldn't go out bear hunting on my own. I don't think that would be pretty dangerous, but I get where you're coming from. But even if you have a clean shot, and not 100% of your shots are going to be clean, I think this just creates a layer of safety that isn't there right now that our bear hunters are asking for. Representative Wooden. Thank you, Chair, just very quickly. You've mentioned, thank you for your testimony, you've mentioned repeatedly you just don't think this legislation is necessary. Is there an underlying concern that allowing this assistance will inconvenience or reduce bear population for people like yourself who hunt alone, or that it might increase the number of individuals who will use rifles for hunting bear with a second shooter at the expense of bow hunters hunting bear without one? No, it's certainly not going to change the harvest of the bear population. It's one tag, it's one tag, so it's certainly not going to change or have fewer bears on the landscape because they have a second shooter that's harvesting a bear that's been wounded. I just don't think that it's necessary. I wouldn't want somebody to finish a bear that I shot, and by Michigan law, as you guys know, that's why we're discussing this today, you're not allowed to shoot an animal that you don't have a harvest tag for, and that's what you guys are changing here, or talking about changing. But bears aren't the big, mean animal that you think they are. They are when they're cornered, but they're more afraid of you than you are of them in most cases, and the instances are very few where bears are a danger. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Jones. Continuing on the Representative Fairbairn show, we now have testimony on House Bill 4822. This would mandate life

Natural Resource Commission. Representative Fairbairn, take the floor. Thank you, Mr. Chair. All right, this is a pretty common sense bill. I'll keep it short. It's going to be sweet. I appreciate the opportunity to come before you for a second time today, this time in support of House Bill 4822, which would require the Natural Resource Commission's meetings to be live streamed to the public. And before I get started, I do want to mention that I have a request of a substitute to correct an error in the language of the bill, which currently indicates live video conference, but this will change it to live video stream. And I'll provide that to the chair before the next meeting on this. So with your permission, I'll speak to the proposed substitute in there. I have introduced this bill in the interest of governmental transparency and access to the public, requiring the Michigan Natural Resource Commission to live stream commission meetings and to make recordings of those meetings available in a searchable archive on its website. The NRC has exclusive authority to regulate hunting, trapping and sports fishing in Michigan, and the discussions they hold and the votes that they take have a direct impact on some of Michigan's most cherished traditions, not to mention an $11 billion sector of the state's annual economy and some 170,000 jobs it supports. A public body with this much power and influence needs to be accessible to the residents of our great state. In addition to providing for a live stream broadcast of meetings and a searchable database, notice of the meeting's agenda and link would need to be available by the department not less than 24 hours in advance. Just as legislative committee meetings such as this one and hundreds of local government meetings throughout the state are announced and live streamed in public. I could go on about the common sense nature of this legislation and the importance of such access and transparency, but I don't think it's necessary as this type of openness has been a topic of discussion for all levels of government for years. And I believe it's time to bring it to the Natural Resource Commission. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and I'm happy to answer any questions. So changing it to live streaming is in line with other committee type like this committee being live streamed. Exactly. I want to interrupt for one second just so I don't forget this. On the last bill, 4937, Chris Emmerich with the DNR not wishing to speak neutral. To continue on now, do we have any? Representative Fall. Thank you, Chair, and thank you for your second testimony. Is this just live streaming? They're not expected to take any public comment or anything else. It's just live streaming, correct? Exactly. Just the ability to watch these because you look at the Natural Resource Commission, they go all over the state of Michigan and have their meetings. And if they're up in Houghton County and you want to get there and you're down here in Lansing, that'd be a long drive to get to that meeting. And there's no other way to watch it unless, of course, MUCC does a live stream on Facebook, but it's very poor quality and you can't hear it very well. So this would make it a lot more accessible to a lot of people. Thank you. I would mention I had a constituent at my office hours did travel to Houghton because she wanted to speak. So it was worthwhile for her to do that. But yes, just to monitor and see what's going on. It's a long way just to sit there and listen. Representative Weiss. Thank you. I know there are other commissions in the state. Are there similar requirements for other commissions or is it just every commission is kind of doing its own thing? Yeah, from my understanding, every commission's doing their own thing on this. This is an important one, I believe, just because of the amount of money and the power that the NRC has to regulate Michigan hunting and fishing. So I think it's important we have this access. We've got a lot of people who hunt and fish and they deal with a lot of other issues, too, that a lot of people want to listen to. So this is an important one. Are there any concerns from that were when you were talking to the commission about this in terms of just implementation? Like, are they getting any kind of resources technology wise to be able to do this that they don't already have access to? I hope they have a computer and I hope they have a video camera. So I think they've got the resources to do it. We'll work with DNR on this, but I believe this should be very cut and dry. Thank you. Thank you very much for keeping it short. I want to read in a few cards. Not wishing to speak neutral on the bill. Again, Chris Simmernick with the DNR. Not wishing to speak supporting the bill. Keith Schaefer from Michigan Bear Hunters. Not wishing to speak supporting the bill. Mike Thorman from Michigan Hunting Dog Federation. And not wishing to speak supporting the bill. Justin Tomey from the MUCC. Now the moment we've all been waiting for. So it's my pleasure to bring back to the committee Amy McMillan from Metro Parks, Chief Executive Officer. When I was a Genesee County Commissioner, my first term, Amy was the Parks Director for 11,000 acres in Genesee County. And really enjoyed that and glad to have her here to expand even a larger project and how much it covers southeast Michigan. Thank you. Thank you so much for the opportunity to be here today. I wanted to introduce Michaela Vasquez from my department who is going to run the laptop because otherwise I would most certainly mess that up for you today. If you're from southeastern Michigan, I hope you're familiar with the Metro Parks. The Metro Parks serve the five counties of southeastern Michigan, Wayne, Washtenaw, Livingston, Macomb, and Oakland counties. Until Saturday, we had 13 parks and 25,000 acres in those five counties. As of Saturday, we have a 14th Metro Park, which is in the city of Detroit. It is part of the Ralph Wilson Jr. Centennial Park, and it was opened to great fanfare on Saturday in the city. It is the Huron Clinton Metro Parks Water Garden that has recently joined our system, and we are so excited by it. As I said before, the Metro Parks are a regional park system. We have 14 parks, 25,000 acres throughout the southeastern Michigan area. We have 400 miles of trails in the Metro Parks. Those are nature trails, those are biking trails, those are walking trails that connect people to nature through our parks. In the average year, we have about 7.3 million visitors that come through our parks. We feel very strongly that it's our job to connect people to nature, every person who lives in our region for their entire lives. And we work really hard every day to do that throughout the work that we do in our parks. Regional parks are kind of a different thing. Everybody here certainly is familiar with the state parks, you're familiar with your city parks, your county parks. But regional parks were created to serve a bigger area. And the Metro Parks probably serves the biggest area of any regional park system. But in the chair's own backyard, the Genesee County Parks, for example, have a regional component that serves both Genesee County and Lapeer County. So all of our systems look differently throughout the entire state. This is an issue that is near and dear to my heart, and I'm sure that it is true of every single person who sits on this committee and of all of your constituents. The fact that public parks are such an important part of the experience of living in Michigan, regardless of where you live, whether it is a community park, whether it is a big natural area. Public parks are part of the experience of being a Michigander, right? It is part of our memories. Public parks are our third space. We get up in the morning and we go to work or we go to school and we come home. But one of the places that we look forward to when we're done with work, when we're at the weekends and we're with our families, is to be in our parks together, whether it's to be with our friends and our families or to find a spot that is just ours. And our family memories are connected to public parks. They're the places where we've learned to throw a ball or to fish or to stay on a beach to camp overnight. Parks are also part of the economy of the communities in which they are located. And at the Metro Parks, we are no exception. The people who come to the Metro Parks every year, there's 7.3 million people who visit our parks, are buying gas. They're staying at local hotels sometimes and campgrounds. They are

They're buying their bikes and their cameras and the things that they use to experience the parks. And the more time that people spend in public parks, including the Metroparks, the healthier they are. And that contributes to all of our bottom lines, particularly in these days when it is so expensive to access health care. The mental and physical health benefits of parks are well known. And I think even if you haven't read a study on the subject, you just know by your own experience how much better you feel the moment that you step out into nature or that you are sitting beside a river or sitting on the beach. Most public park systems are big employers in their communities as well. And the Metroparks are no exception to that. At the height of our season, we have a little over a thousand employees that work for the Metroparks. One of my first jobs was working in my home community. I ran a playground program in Midland, Michigan. That's where I'm from and my family still lives there. And my first job with the Metroparks about a hundred years ago was as a college intern. And we employ everyone from police to lifeguards. And because we are an authority, we are our own system. So we have accountants and we have park maintenance people. In many ways, the Metroparks operate as cities in and of themselves. Because we have 25,000 acres and 14 parks, we contribute a lot not just to our own infrastructure, but to the infrastructure of the communities that are around us. In particular, stormwater management is a critical function at the Metroparks. We also operate roads and trails and dams that have an influence beyond our own borders. At the Metroparks, we take fiscal responsibility and fiscal management and funding as a key component of the work that we do. Yep, it's great to be outdoors. It's wonderful to have all of the fun that you have in a park. But really taking the business of parks seriously is a critical element of making certain that there are parks every single day, every single year for generations to come. And we are really proud of the fact that we've been a great partner with the state. Thank you for, as you work on issues with things like the Michigan Natural Resources Trust Fund, the Land and Water Conservation Fund. Last year, two years ago, we received an enhancement grant from the state that is allowing us to restore the North Marina at Lake St. Clair Metropark, or some of you might know better as Metro Beach. And so we use these partnerships, we use these grants to enhance and to elevate the money that the public invests in the Metroparks through the millage that funds about half of our operations. To give you some sense of how this works, we wanted to share with you the revenue that we generate from many of our core activities, particularly golf. We have seven regulation courses throughout the Metroparks, and particularly since the pandemic, that is our third highest source of funding. The only way we could put more people on our golf courses at the Metroparks is if the days were longer, because golf has made such an incredible resurgence throughout the entire country, including in southeastern Michigan. And then you can look at some of the other things that we do throughout the year, including renting our pavilions and renting boats and paddleboards and all of the things that some people have of their own and some people need to have access to when they come to our parks. So this weekend, we were able to highlight one of our biggest partnerships, and that was with the Detroit Riverfront Conservancy. But we have partnerships of all shapes and sizes at the Metroparks. No system, no community can do all of the work that needs to be done on their own. So we have partners in small groups like the people of Palmer Park. We have, we are partners with the Y and our Everyone in the Pool program, with local schools, with county park systems and city park systems to make certain that we are providing service to absolutely everyone who lives throughout our region. Outdoor education is a key component of the work that we do at the Metroparks. We have a department called our Interpretive Department that is staffed by outdoor educators. They are teachers, and they go into schools throughout our regions. They host field trips from schools throughout the entire region. They impact tens of thousands of kids every single year. They get them excited about being outdoors. They get them to understand how they connect to the outdoors. They get them ready to be part of careers in science and resource management. And they train those kids to teach their friends and their families and their parents. Kids are one of the most powerful constituent groups we have in connecting adults to the outdoors. Because when they come home from school and they are excited about something they've learned, they share it with their parents and with their family members. At the Metroparks, a big part of the work that we do is hosting events from throughout the region. We do a ton of fundraiser events. We host cross-country meets from throughout the region. But we also have some of our own programs that require people to register. Just last year, there were 641 of those programs, and over 12,000 people attended just that small group of programs. One of the things I don't think we talk about often or we visualize, we talk about golf and we talk about being outdoors. But one of the sports that is becoming more and more a big part of our business and has such an impact on local economies is disc golf. And it is a really great way of engaging people of all ages and abilities. And it brings people from quite literally around the world to the Metroparks, either in person or watching some of the tournaments that we host on ESPN. I had no idea until a few years ago that disc golf was worthy of an ESPN time slot. But let me tell you, if you're a disc golfer, you know that is the case. And one of the things we're super excited to have announced this year is the Metroparks at Kensington Metropark are going to host the World Disc Golf Championship. We are working with the sports commissions in the same way. Well, OK, it's a smaller way than the NFL draft was, but still an incredible amount of time and attention goes into this because it brings people into our communities who are going to eat in our restaurants, shop in our sporting goods stores, stay overnight in our hotels. And this would not be possible without these public courses that are available through the Metroparks and other systems. This year, we were also really excited with our partners in Oakland County and Wayne County parks to co-host the Special Parks District Forum, where we brought people from all over the United States. We stayed in the city of Detroit at the Courtyard Marriott. We bought out the place for the district conference and people came from all over the United States to see what we are doing here in the state of Michigan. And every single one of those people that I talked to was excited about what's happening in Michigan and took something back from us to initiate in their home parks and their systems. And so we're really proud to be leading at a national level here in the state of Michigan. We are getting ready to enter the fourth year of our Everyone in the Pool program, which is also a program through which we partner with public and private partners throughout our five counties, school systems, the Ys, cities and counties to teach kids in our communities to swim. In southeastern Michigan, we have a dismal rate of kids who know how to swim. About 70 percent of our kids don't know how to swim, which makes it impossible for them to enjoy the water. And if there is one thing that is important to be able to do as a resident of the state of Michigan, it is to be able to enjoy the water safely. And so this is a program that in our last year we had over 3,000 individual kids learn how to swim for free in that program. Because one of the things that is the biggest obstacle to learning how to swim is the cost of learning how to swim. Years ago,

The parks director in the city of Ypsilanti, I think we charged about five bucks a kid for a week-long session of swim lessons. It costs over $100 a child for the average swim lesson program right now. And so this is really critical work for us and just part of connecting kids to the outdoors. And then selfishly, I got to tell you, we're also hoping to grow our own lifeguards throughout this program, throughout the state of Michigan and nationally, we have a lifeguard shortage. And so when we start by engaging kids early, we are perpetuating our ability to keep our pools and our lakefronts safe. And these are just some of the statistics that are part of our program. Once a child is part of a swim lesson program, they learn really quickly. And the way that it changes families is incredible. There is never a single session of swim lessons where we do not hear from one of those families who has lost a family member or a neighbor or somebody in their community that they know to drowning. Each year in the metro parks, we have experienced drowning and our goal is every summer to make certain that that never happens to another family again. We are really proud of the work that we do in the metro parks and managing our natural resources. We are really intentional about this work. We have our own natural resources department and we focus in on the things that are important to keep our natural environments safe and healthy for the flora and the fauna throughout our entire state. And we have a really dedicated team that does that. And we take our knowledge on the road and work with other communities to help them. One of the things that we did a couple of years ago that we were super proud of and continues today is we partnered with the city of Detroit in doing a controlled burn program at Rouge Park, which is the biggest park in the city. And now that group is able to do those programs on their own year after year after year. At the metro parks, we are working very hard to put our words where our action is. And we do things like expanding our no-mo zones. We work really hard to educate people throughout the region who are interested in learning how to be great stewards of the environment by managing stormwater in their own backyard, by teaching their kids, and also even by doing things like managing our own fleets throughout the metro parks. At the metro parks, when we talk about setting a goal, we always have a plan that goes with that goal so that we can measure our progress season after season, year after year. It is one of the ways that we hold ourselves accountable to both our board, ourselves, and to our community. And as you can see by this slide, just in our first year in some of our goals in this area, we've accomplished over 70% of those goals within one year as a demonstration of our commitment. If you want to stay connected to the metro parks and our work, there are all kinds of ways to do that. We have a great website that's really interactive. And just a plug for our pop-up shop, if you want some metro parks swag, you have until Friday to do that. You can follow us on Facebook, Instagram, and all of our other channels. And before I thank you today for the time to share with you a little bit about the metro parks, I hope I've inspired you to spend some time in your own community parks and also think about the ways that in the work that you do on this committee and the work that you do in your hometowns, how you can advocate for public parks. To have a great public park system requires a tremendous amount of attention and intention and investment. And this group is in a great position to think about that really strategically and work with local professionals and look at how we can address these issues on a statewide basis so that every community has a healthy and thriving park system and that these resources that attract so many residents to our state, that are the reason why people who live here, live here generation after generation. I am a fourth generation Michigander and my nieces are fifth generation Michiganders. They're the reasons kids in college who are making decisions on where they want to stay, want to be near a park system with a great disc golf course. When we ask our communities what's important to them, it is why they answer time after time they want more trail systems. And so in all of the great and important work that you do, I hope that you consider how you can address public parks, public park funding and strategy throughout the entire state. And we would be happy to be part of that discussion. So thank you. Thank you for refreshing my memory that Genesee County Parks was regional into Lapeer with some property on Holloway Reservoir and the Columbiaville softball complex, I think it is. Yes. So in Genesee County has, I was the county parks director for just shy of 18 years. Two regional parks within the county. One is the Holloway Regional Park System, which includes Wolverine Campground and the Hogbacks and that entire system that reaches into Lapeer County. And then the Mott Lake is part of that too, right? Yeah. It's a critical piece of the economy in Genesee County. And on your metro parks, it's just funny to me. I'm sure Representative Weiss and McFaul living down in the area, Representative Scott, when you mentioned Palmer Park, it's not actually, it's a city or is it a park also? It's a city. Palmer Park is a neighborhood in the city and we bring programs to the park. Yeah. Oh, I'm sorry. I mean, I've golfed at Palmer Park and I was just curious how that was part of the metro parks. It's not a metro park, but it is part of the partnerships that we do. So our interpretive program shows up at neighborhood picnics and all kinds of other programs in different parks. And a lot of the way that in Genesee County, they partner with the city of Flint and other local park systems. I mean, parks people are parks people, right? We're there for everybody. Yeah. Okay. Thank you very much. We have to run this session. Thank you for your patience. I want to excuse absent members. So Representative Bonick moves to excuse absent members. Seeing no further business come before the committee, we're adjourned. Thank you.
