transcript:
A committee on Homeland Security and Foreign Influence will come to order. Will the clerk please take the roll? Chair Brock, present. Representatives Meerman. Here. Shriver. Present. Menser. Here. Conlon. Here. Mr. Chair, you have a quorum? All right. Representative Conlon moves to approve the minutes of October 22nd meeting. If there's no objections, they are approved. All right. Well, welcome back. Two weeks in a row. It's been so long since we've had two weeks in a row, so it's nice to have you. We had a very good discussion last week on Zero Eyes, and I think, you know, getting us back in the Homeland Security mentality and thinking about things that maybe we don't even know to think about. And so today we happen to have a very, very good guest, Keith Masrin. He is the president of MidAmerica Group. He does – he's going to tell – you're going to give an introduction about yourself when you do come up, too, but you're welcome to come to the – to the speaker. Just push the red button there. But he travels the world. He rubs shoulders with people I've never thought of rubbing shoulders with before and does a lot of work in the defense arena around the world for the U.S. military on various bases, and he is the president of MidAmerica Group, and he has even brought a show-and-tell item today, too. So I'm sure he's going to talk about that, but hopefully he'll give a little background on MidAmerica Group and such and then go right into your presentation, sir. So thank you for being here, Keith. Appreciate it. Thank you. Wow, what an honor to be here today. Thank you, everybody, for taking the time and come talk to us today. I'm seventh generation in the big town of Monroe County. Pretty proud of that. My family came here and settled. We're still farmers. We still farm. So my life goes back to the old roots. Currently I'm president of MidAmerican Group. I do construction and engineering services for the power generation worldwide. We do infrastructure for the steel industry, petroleum, and also the DOD military, NATO. I'm here today to talk a little bit about EMP and what we discovered and what we designed. We came across this. I met this firm in Spain. I bought the company and brought it back to Michigan in 2012, and it was about lightning protection. While we're doing lightning protection, we were testing constantly to know what we actually owned and what we actually produced. For the lightning side of things, we have about 35,000 units worldwide. The Panama Canal alone has 400 of our units protecting it just for lightning. What it does is it's passive. It collects the ions of the air. Nikolai Tesla invented this and built this program. So it's a Nikolai Tesla

program. Collects all of the ions. It balances the air so the lightning does not have conduit to come to ground, cloud to ground. So that's the whole science behind these units. It takes no power. You just got to run a ground cable to these units to the ground. While doing testing, we were trying to create lightning and we were starting to create a very mild EMP. Didn't realize what we were creating, but every time we had to replace our computer, we realized we're doing something. So after seven years of testing, we finally figured out what an EMP is and how we're controlling an EMP. When I mentioned earlier about collecting those ions and balancing the air, an EMP pulse cannot travel through. We stop that pulse from traveling. It's like taking a boat out of water. So now we have a situation where we know an EMP can't travel. How do we contain it and how do we dissipate? So our whole science behind this unit here in front of me today in the presentation is about absorption and dissipation. And we figured that out. After seven years of testing, and I just about gave up. I was on my last wit. Last week, I didn't think I'd ever be able to figure it out. And if we didn't find it by accident because the unit was not level. It was on a five degree angle. And that day we found out a pulse has to be bisected, the whole pulse, not a piece of the pulse. So it's something else we could talk about later on. But finding that by accident led us to this unit here. This is called the V8. This unit's been tested by several laboratories here in the United States to take up to a 300,000 volt pulse. And we'll talk a little bit about that in our presentation today. It's the first time ever in the world that something out there is presentable. What this does is protects infrastructure. So how do I get this? Do I do it on a computer here? The screen or does somebody else do the screen? Okay. I'm not very computer savvy. So give me one second. Let me play with it. Okay. All right. I figured that out. Thank you. I'll go back up. So first presentation is threat. When seconds decide the future. And what we're finding out is an EMP pulse, by the time we figured out we've had a pulse, it's already too late. And it's not a matter if it'll happen. It's a matter of when it'll happen. We first discovered an EMP pulse during the blast days of testing our nuclear warheads. And we know that the blast at 30 miles, it put radiation coverage at a 25 mile radius. But we figured out an EMP pulse at a 12 mile radius. An EMP pulse, electrical magnetic pulse, overwhelms everything that we own electronically. Everything we own electronically gets destroyed. Cables, your computers, your refrigerators, your freezers, your dishwashers, your computers, your cell phones, everything's destroyed. Automotive. An EMP pulse overwhelms and destroys every bit of electronics. EMP pulse comes in a couple variations. A nuclear blast is how we discovered what an EMP pulse is. But we also get it naturally from the sun, solar flares, and we also know that today several countries are making man-made EMP guns. And those guns are here to destroy our infrastructure, our grid. And that's where I got into business. I want to protect our grid. How do I protect our grid? To protect my family and my neighborhood. And that's how we first started in this business. All right, so real world examples. We have a couple examples on here that I pulled off that we've always used as our background. 1962, a high altitude blast actually took out 900 miles away in Hawaii, took out the grid, took out the power infrastructure. And then also 1989, a Quebec solar storm as a natural EMP collapsed the Quebec hydro grid for 90 seconds. Potential results. As such, if the US was targeted, what we came up with on a timeline, this is actually from the government site, 0 to 10 seconds, the power grids will fail. The SCADA systems, which is the computer systems, will be offline. Within one minute, communication GPS is blocked out. 0 to 60 minutes, hospitals, air traffic, and emergency response fail. There's no communication and there's no engines to run anybody. And hours later, the banking, logistics, and fuel supply collapse. Once again, this is the VMAX. This blocks an EMP. It absorbs it and dissipates it. For this unit here, to protect, let's just say this building. This building will probably take about eight units to protect it. Put these in a series and a series around the top of the building and on the roof could absorb an EMP pulse and dissipate it to the ground before we even know we had an EMP attack. It takes no power. It's naturally charged. And once it's there, it's there for life. This is some data from our testing that we did through Elite Electronics Laboratories in Chicago. This is the first time that a unit actually passed and survived an EMP. At a 5 kV, it eliminates all electronic cables. All data cables collapse. They burn and a connection fails. At a 20 kW, that's when your laptops, your cell phones start to decay. And then at 35 to 50 is a massive kV pulse that takes out all the rest of the electronics. So what we have here today is we have a product that actually can protect our infrastructure. And that's what I came here today to talk about. What we discovered, what we designed, what we've engineered, and what's available as of today. We're a Michigan-based company out of Monroe, Michigan. And we're the first time ever in the world something like this is available and this much of a robust system. And that's me. Well, thank you. Thank you, Mr. Mazur, for that. Before we go into questions, which we have, could you go a little more into the threat? Because obviously you're installing thousands of these around the world. You're installing with DOD and various places. I assume airports and such as well, possibly. But can you describe, like, obviously you touched on the threat itself, but is there more to that that you can talk about or the potential of that threat? Yeah, so the threat comes in three levels. There's E1, E2, and E3. So what we had to design was to take all three aspects. And E1 is a massive amount of energy and it's really fast. It's overwhelmingly higher number. It's actually in the millions of volts. So if that were to actually come from a nuclear blast, if that would come over, let's say, Lansing, it would destroy every bit of our infrastructure that we have. Like I say, all of your home computers, your office computers, our infrastructure, our grid, there would be nothing left. Every bit of a magnet explodes upon that blast. It's unreparable. There's nothing out there that can repair a cell phone or your computer or even your vehicles once that blast hits. It would take out everything we own. From there, you have an E2 and an E3. They're a lot less. We know that they're man-made. We know that they're out there. And so we actually wanted to actually make sure that we can actually support that too, which is a lesser amount of energy and it's a slower amount of energy, but we actually hit all three levels. Working with the military on infrastructure, talking about protecting the troops, as you know, sir, out in the field, what would happen if the carriers were to go out? So how do we protect carriers? How do we protect our men and women and harm's way? So that's another reason why we came to the next level is how could we protect moving targets too? The actual threat of that, they have not examples that have occurred, but obviously there is that threat, which is why the DOD or DOW is doing hiring and installing these, correct? So the DOD right now is installing Faraday cages everywhere. And the Faraday cage is to help absorb and then eliminate a pulse. They're very, very large. They're very bulky and they cannot be for mobile. So currently this year is the first year we're actually presenting this product, and we just started installing these at certain facilities. So this is the first time this is actually being introduced.

Faraday cages, can you describe that a little bit as well? Yeah, so a Faraday cage is a massive amount of iron. It could be plate, it could be pipe. You put a Faraday cage over top of your infrastructure, this building, a campus, to absorb and dissipate the pulse. The price for a Faraday cage is in the millions to do a very small area. To do a building that's maybe 24 by 24 square foot, or 24 foot by 24 foot, would probably cost in a measure of about $4 million to actually cover that with a Faraday cage. Where this product, the good thing about this product, it can be installed immediately, and it can be done just for a couple hundred thousand. So look at the savings we're going to have, and look at the opportunities we're going to have. Well, thank you. I have more questions, but I'm going to allow Minority Vice Chair Mensah to ask the first series of questions. Thank you. Thank you, Chair. Is that the actual size of the VMAX? Yes, it is. Would it make any difference? You said you deployed several of them in one location. Would it make any difference if they were bigger? You could. You could. But this is the size that we found was the most capable for any installation, which would be an airport, a school, a bank, the grid. This was the size that we actually came up with. But we could actually expand. And what I was kind of wondering is, can this system actually detect EMP pulses, like maybe before they start or as they're starting? Because it sounds like this system comes into place once the EMP has occurred. I'm just wondering about, you know, like prevention. Yeah, good point. So an EMP pulse itself, there's really no way of detecting it until after it happens because it comes so fast and so vast. In both man-made and natural? Yes. But on our units, we actually have metering. So we know what the pulse was and the volume of the pulse because we're actually looking at even a natural from solar flares. We want to know how that affects us and how we're absorbing that too as it comes in because we don't know that happens. Sometimes we might know by activity, but typically we find out later on. And do you feel that we've been having more natural solar flares than, say, 20 years ago? We have, yes. And are you finding too that, let's just call them antagonists, some of our antagonists, they have developed these as a weapon system for EMPs? Yes, they're out there. And are those being tested over the United States right now? Currently we're working with the military about doing additional testing. We've met all the mill specs, the military requirement specs, and now to go to the next level, we're hoping the military will actually come in and support us by taking this unit to go to the next level. That's amazing. I tried to get the government involved at the beginning, and nobody wanted to talk to me until I got to a certain point. Now I got to that point. Now there's more interest to talk to us and support us. And just out of curiosity, I mean, we've had a lot of conversations about drones and drone capabilities. Would there be, and this is probably fantasy, but would there be a drone that could carry a VMAX and maybe alert you quicker when it's a natural or enemy? That's a good idea. Something we can work on. We don't have that currently, but that's actually a pretty neat idea. We'd have to learn how to dissipate the energy if we did absorb it, but it's something we can work on. I'm available for hire. There you go. You're the best. Thank you. Thank you. No, thank you. Good, very good questions. And just for the record, you do a lot of defense contracting on U.S. bases and NATO facilities. What type of contracting do you do? I know you do skiffs and such, but also the protection. You do counter-UAS or UAS tracking or anything as well? We work on guidance systems. That's about all I can talk about. But besides that, yeah, skiffs and control rooms. There's a huge need for that today. And so we were able to be fortunate to be part of that program to actually install skiffs, mobile, temporary, and permanent installations. So this definitely fits in with protecting that. I guess it would be like data centers, too. I mean, very high electronic, heavy, smaller areas. Yeah, good point. I appreciate you bringing that up. So the data centers, we're in a data center boom, right? 25, 26, we're going to start seeing data centers come over the country. This is going to be ideal to help protect their assets, too. Representative Shriver, sir. Thank you, Mr. Chair. What size of a room or building would a device like that be able to defend against an EMP? Yeah, good question. Good point. So this unit alone, we know as of right now, we're good for about 125-foot diameter per unit. Okay. As far as known EMP devices, you mentioned EMP guns. Yes. So what would the target range look like for some of these known EMP launchers, so to speak? For the devices that we're aware of, we know that they're mobile, we know that they're small, and we know that they can actually shoot a pulse a couple miles from their target. So the max range is a couple miles that you know of. Okay. And that's changing every day. Oh, yeah. And that's, like you said, what we know of. As far as the impact of what we know in terms of EMP devices, what type of radius of destruction are we talking about with some of the greatest sizable EMPs that we know of? Well, earlier we had the – I'll go back to the beginning there. We do know that a blast covers about 12 miles, 12-mile diameter. And that's from a nuclear blast. And the man-made units, I don't really know where we're going to stand. It's not that vast. It's not that robust. But it'll be more centralized. So it's going to take a wide range. The farther it goes, it expands out, like a cone. But there's a certain point it's not going to be as strong and as robust from the very beginning. So we don't really know what that is yet, that delta. Have there ever been any known uses of man-made EMPs across the world? Yes, sir, there has. Can you give any detail on that? No, sir, I don't have the detail with me. Okay. As far as counter-EMP technology, obviously this is available for government use and commercial use. Is that right? That's correct. Are there any alternatives? I know you mentioned the Faraday cage being, what, 10 times, 15 times as expensive. Are there any other alternatives aside from those two options in terms of defending against an EMP residentially for our government, for our state? What would that look like? There are other products out there. They're smaller. There's bags. They're like a lead-based bag. You can put your products in your cell phone and certain things. And it's all good. But if the cell phone survives but the infrastructure around it doesn't survive, I don't know what good that is. Some of the other products that are out there, I haven't tested everything yet, but we've been playing with a little bit of opportunity. There's filters out there for your electronics. There's filters out there for your wiring to your computers so it doesn't come through the landline into the computer that way. Some of those do work probably 50% of the time. So would you say, and this is my final question, Mr. Chair, would you say that the technology is not yet there in order to protect an entire town, like an ecosystem involving fuel lines, Internet service providers, just to create kind of an isolated defense against an EMP? Because let's say I had one of those in my home and it protected me.

my car from being affected by the MP, but the fuel station down the road isn't, you know, what good is my car? And that's just kind of a hypothetical example. So my question is, what would it take technologically in order to create, you know, a bubble to contain an entire ecosystem of technology against an EMP blast? Well, that would be something. That would be something. And I will say that by protecting your assets, that's what I'm after. I'm after protecting assets. You're protecting your assets, your investment from being totally destroyed. Because someday things will come back, someday things will be rebuilt, and you'll be farther ahead than anybody else. Well, here's the thing, and I'm sorry to interrupt you, but what's on my mind is every single Michigan resident, all 10 million. And so, you know, what good is, you know, me saving my stuff in my home or whatever, you know, especially in this position? You know, I'm looking out for everybody. And so my mind goes to 10 million people, and, you know, covering 125 feet at a time would be a pretty big lift to cover the whole state of Michigan. And so that's kind of where my mind goes in terms of protecting the entire state. Yeah, very good point. We'll have to just start with the infrastructure we need. We need the banking. We need the hospitals. We need certain things to protect it. So that's actually a way of getting started. Very good. Thank you so much for what you do. And thank you again for bringing that company from Spain into Michigan. That's amazing. Thank you so much for that. Thank you, sir. Jewel. Jewel. Yeah, definitely. And I think the key infrastructure was highlighted, I guess. It'd be impossible to put one of those on every home. I mean, it's just not probably financially stable or necessary maybe, but key infrastructure is really what you focus on. Yes, sir, at this point. And obviously, so just for instance, I have, before I go to Representative Colin, like on a base, bases are large, depending. I mean, they're all large. Some are much larger than others. When you're doing the EMP protections for a base, is it, again, just the key components on that base that you're being hired to do? Yes, at this time, it's building by building, the most important infrastructure at a time. Okay. All right. Representative Conlon. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thanks for being here. And yes, when cool companies come to Michigan, I like to say please stay in Michigan as you grow. My question is, if there were, obviously, I had the question about the solar flares that Representative Mentzer asked, but if there are these nuclear explosions, like to some extent, if it's a ground explosion, things are going to be taken out sort of all over. But it would appear there's also like this sort of atmospheric one that would this detect that? I guess it's kind of her question, does it detect it? Would we know if it happens or would we only know because this would respond? And then I'm just wondering, because I've just always been curious about when you hear about Israel and the dome that it has, that air defense system, does that have anything built in around something like this too? Not that I'm aware of for the dome. And that's what we're talking about, how to do the whole Michigan. I guess it'd be the golden dome that Trump's talking about maybe someday. But nothing at this point actually protects from an EMP. And when you had another question, I'm sorry. Just when it's that high blast up in the atmosphere. Yeah, you'll find out after the blast. You're going to know. But unfortunately, there's no way of detecting that prior to it. I thought you were thinking. I'm thinking because it's very cool. No, it is. I mean, so again, my mind keeps going back to the threat level. You know, nuclear bomb, that's bad, bad juju. And everyone would know. Dirty bomb would create a smaller but similar scenario. But really, your focus or probably the largest threat is more of a targeted EMP weapon system. Is that correct? Yeah, that's what we're basing our model off of. That's what we started with, knowing that might be our biggest threat we'll have at this time. And that's how we actually got started in the business. Okay. Representative Mensur. Thank you. Thanks, Chair. I just had one more question about. So as we see our military equipment growing and advancing, unmanned vehicles on the ground and in the air, and we look at how things are changing, you've got drones with amazing capabilities now, and now you also have anti-drone systems, guns, radios, things like that. Are you and the military members that you have worked with, are you anticipating that EMP strikes will become more prevalent and happen more frequently in matters of war and dispute? It's our understanding that EMP is one of the biggest threats we're facing today, and that's something we're going to have to learn how to deal with here in the near future. So I do believe that there's more we could do with this, and there's more we can actually learn from this, and we can only grow on this to protect us. And the idea of the drones, I like that. I'll stay up the next five or six nights thinking about this one because that's a really good point. I love that. We're looking at satellites, how to protect satellites from EMP. So there's opportunity. There's ideas out there, and we can work it out together. It's absolutely just amazing what people dream up, I guess in defense of their own nation. The war weaponry we see now is just mind-blowing. And like the others, thank you. Thank you for coming to Michigan, and thank you for looking at this, and thank you for considering our future and our future needs when it comes to our antagonists. Thank you. My mind goes back to, I mean, your start, MidAmerica, was building the concrete tripods, right? That's what we do. The claim to fame or, you know, doing things with concrete and just maybe for the record or if you can, but you have a number of patents yourself, correct? Yes, sir. I have 27 patents. He might be a farmer. Some are not listed. I was told not to list them just yet, but yeah, yes, sir. So working with somebody that truly – I've known Keith for many years, and Keith truly is a red-hearted, red-blooded American that wants to help protect our troops, and he's working around the world doing that, and it's really cool to have you here, Keith. Representative Shriver. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Without getting into anything classified, just going back to my point about doing what is best for all Michigan residents, critical infrastructure being the greatest starting point for that, can you tell us, as far as Michigan's critical infrastructure, how hardened is it against an EMP attack? Is there a percent measurement in terms of readiness as far as our infrastructure goes? I do believe that there's filters out there for, like, the grid, but I don't believe we're ready. I don't believe we have anything really set to take a threat. This will be the first time we'll actually have something to help support it. And then final question, is there any changes to law that you would recommend to address this potential challenge? Not that I'm aware of, no. Good point. I appreciate that. That's actually huge. I think just awareness is the biggest thing we need to work on. We'd love to talk to you more about this at another time. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Representative Shriver. You said that EMPs, you know, I am fascinated with it. I know I hope I'm not asking too many questions on it, but an EMP weapon system, how hard would that be to get to the states or to create in the states? Is it something that's difficult to do? I don't believe it is, sir. I don't believe it's difficult to make. I don't think it's difficult to create. And you said the range, possible range of two miles. I mean, that's farther, as Casey said, that's farther than a sniper can reach. I think Kyle from Texas, Kyle, Chris Kyle, sorry, Chris Kyle, you know, he hit it at like a mile and a quarter, a mile and close to half. But say Fermi, because Fermi's right in your backyard. You can see it from your house, from where you live. Could you describe if someone had an EMP and

a specific facility, what would be the ramifications of that? So once again, all electronics and all communications would be destroyed. And most of it would not be repairable. So once you take away the communication, once you take away their power source, it would take them a long time to rebuild, to get the material in, to figure out how to actually sustain the facility after all the damage. I can't imagine how many miles of wire are inside for me to a nuclear power plant. I'm just using it as an example, we talked about it. And how do you chase that all down to actually figure that all out? What's operable, what's not operable, it would take a long time. So it would be down for probably months, if not years. Yeah, it'd be for a while. And so with your, and I know there's things you can't talk about or discuss, but you know the threat level, you've been in a lot of meetings that none of us have been in, but the threat level is more of a targeted threat level, not necessarily dirty bombs that we've seen in movies and such. Yes, I do believe, yes, that's exactly right. But recently when we had those balloons flying over our country, that's when it dawned on me. I bet that was a test to see what we could do, and I bet that would be a test of an opportunity for them to use a dirty bomb at that point. I do believe that. I don't have no actual one, I'm just saying out of my heart. When I seen that happen, that's what I believe. So the higher up a dirty bomb, the further the EMP force would go as well then potentially, and in the wrong location, much more destruction. And then drones, EMPs would take out a drone. I know we discussed having that on a drone, but a drone would be null and void. Unless you could protect it. And probably, you mentioned the three, the E1, E2, E3. E3 is the lowest level? Yes, sir. And is that more of the mobile systems you're talking, or is that something even less? That would be the man-made systems and some solar flares too. Hmm. Oh, maybe we got some counter-UAS capability with EMP guns as well. But, oh, very interesting, very interesting, the impact that it could have. And obviously the government or the Department of War feels it's very necessary. It's a real threat and a threat here in the U.S. So we appreciate, and Shriver asked a question about legislation, but if there's anything that comes to mind, please reach out to me as far as legislatively, how can we help protect our state, which is really what this committee focuses on, and each of the members have backgrounds and very, I think, Representative Collin worked for the State Department, right? Or journalism, sorry. But she was all over the world. Well, we've covered many embassies. So she is, and Representative Mensers, right up there near Selfridge and has a lot of ties to, we won't talk all those ties that she has to military folks, but she's very concerned as well. So we appreciate you being here again and what you and your family have done around the world and here in the States. There's probably not many bases around the world that you haven't touched personally. You know, as a wrap-up, I want to say thank you. When I called you and I said, you know, we're on a program, I would like to present it, you went into action right away. So how impressive that is to, Michigan has my heart. I'm seventh generation on my farm. I'm not going anywhere. Michigan, I'll always be here. My kids will always be here. And this will always be here in Michigan. And I do believe that things come up. At least I know who to turn to now. And as I'm trying to grow this, I know that you'll always be there too. So I appreciate it. Thank you. And I'd be remiss to say that, you know, I know St. Charles had their festival and stuff and your company installed barriers around that. You know, just Keith truly, as I said before, he loves Michigan and Michiganders. And I know you did that, I think, free of charge. You know, but you provided safety just to ensure that people attending a festival can do so in safety and such. So we appreciate your ingenuity in this and your forward thinking and bringing a company from Spain here and looking at how can you personally have a big impact here in the U.S. and around the world. So thank you, Keith, for being here. We appreciate it, sir. Thank you very much. And barring any questions, yeah. We appreciate it, sir. Oh, that's awesome. Thank you, everybody. Yes, sir. All righty. And there being no absent members and no further business before the committee, we stand adjourned. Thank you.

My court staff is very much in favor of working with the crossover, and we understand that there's going to be a transition period here. We're happy to take whatever assistance from SCALE and Grand Traverse County we can get, and we're standing by to get started. Thank you. Rep. Boyer. Thank you, Madam Chair. I'm familiar with what you're trying to accomplish. St. Clair County has a single circuit court, a single district court, but they do have a district court that is separated also, so we have it in two locations because of the length. It is about an hour and 15 minutes from the south end of the county to the county seat, so similar circumstance. My question is I do see that there's a fiscal analysis that hasn't come out yet. Is there going to be an additional state cost to this, or is it really going to be more the district? I believe it's local in the county. Right, for the staffing and those kinds of things, no additional state expense, no additional judge, obviously, right? A judge is moving. We can get that for you. Yeah, okay. Thank you. I do know that county is going to take on some more cost also, but they are willing. The county commissioner is willing to do that. Thank you. Thank you. Okay, with that, we're going to move on to cards in regards to House Bill 4749. Does not wish to speak, supports the bill, Samantha Gibson of Michigan Association of Counties. I'm guessing, Trevor, you don't wish to speak on the bill? Okay. Does not wish to speak and supports the bill with some changes, Trevor Van Dyke from SCALE. And that's it for that bill. Thank you. Next up, we're going to take up House Bill 4833, Representative Steele for a district court judge in Oakland County. Thank you very much, Madam Chair and committee. And I have with me today, Honorable Diane DiAgostino from the 48th District Court. And I'm going to speak first, but if I can make sure that she's there. So I'm not sure how to pull her up. Diane, yeah. Judge Diane, are you on Zoom? Yes, I am here. Okay. We're going to have Rep. Steele speak real quick. I'm going to turn on my camera, too. I'm sorry. It's fine. You have a few minutes. We're going to have Rep. Steele introduce the bill real quick, and then we'll have you speak immediately following. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. So I'm speaking on House Bill 4833. And it preserves the third judgeship in the 48th District Court. So in the 2011 legislation, bills were passed regarding the reduction of the judiciary. So the analysis at that time concluded that the 48th District Court had a judicial excess of 0.7 district judge. So as a result, the legislation decided that they would reduce one judge through attrition. So either they, sorry, I didn't mean to say she, but they would age out or if they retired. So then they would be down to two judges. So while I am a limited government legislator and generally support efforts to reduce the size of government, I am also a Milton Friedman fanatic. So one of the three things of government should be that we provide military support, enforce our internal contracts, and protect the citizens from crime. And having a strong judicial functioning service within our communities will provide civil society and make sure our communities are safe. The basic levels of what government is intended to do, we need our judicial liaison to be able to protect our personal freedoms. So since 2011, there were sweeping reforms that have been enacted, including criminal justice reform, landlord-tenant law changes, clean slate legislation, auto insurance reforms, and more. And each of these have significantly expanded the responsibility and the caseload of our district courts, requiring additional judicial time and resources. So the 48th District Court serves seven municipalities, Bloomfield Township, West Bloomfield, Birmingham, Bloomfield Hills, Kegel Harbor, Orchard Lake, Sylvan Lake, and reducing the court would jeopardize the court's ability to keep pace with the caseload. And so by saying yes on House Bill 4833 would preserve the three-judge bench system that is currently prevailing right now. So with that, I would like to pass it over to Judge DiAgostino, and hopefully we can see her face as well. Oh, lovely. Thank you. Now we can't hear you. You're on mute. There you go. Can you hear me now? Oh, yes. Thank you. Thank you all very much. Good morning. Thank you, Representative Steele and Chairperson Leitner and distinguished members of the Judiciary Committee. My name is Diane DiAgostino, and I am the chief judge of the 48th District Court. To tell you a little bit about myself, I've been a judge for 25 years and was elected to the 48th District Court in 2000. Prior to that, I was an assistant prosecutor in Oakland County for nine years. My election in 2000 was profound for my Chaldean community as I am the first judge of Chaldean descent in Michigan. Like many, my parents came to Michigan from Iraq to seek the American dream in the late 50s. And I can say without hesitation to all of you that my election as a judge was reaching the American dream. I have been reelected four times since my initial election. In each of my three contested elections, I have won every precinct in my seven communities. I tell you this so that you hopefully conclude that I come here credible in the understanding of my community and the dedication that I have in serving them. Representative Steele went through the jurisdiction of the court, so I will not do that. But while the seven communities are the voting communities, anyone may have a case in the 48th District Court facing either a misdemeanor, felony, civil case, landlord, tenant, small claims, or traffic case. As you probably know, the district court is the most widely used court by the public. Again, Representative talked about the 2011 legislation. I'd like to just state that due to the significant legislative changes over the past 14 years, many stakeholders are

start with the consequences should the reduction become effective. Stakeholders include my colleagues, Judge Small, Judge Barron, court staff, police agencies, attorneys, and local municipalities. Since 2011, the legislature has implemented a myriad of changes from criminal justice reform, landlord-tenant modifications, clean slate legislation, auto insurance reform, and more, all of which have significantly increased the court's caseload and the complexity of case adjudication. Additionally, please take note, the court's civil docket has burgeoned with an increase of 84% since 2021, and it continues to rise. If the reduction occurs, the plan would then require additional staffing at the court and would shift more costs to the court's local funding units of Bloomfield Township, West Bloomfield Township, and Birmingham. Thus, I implore your committee to evaluate the serious ramifications that will occur into the future if the court eliminates the judgeship. I have also made contact with most of the legislators in the court's district on this issue, and I have received enthusiastic bipartisan support from both your colleagues and the senators. I would like to now testify on HB 4833, and I hope my remarks will be useful to this committee. Please stop me. I know that you have all had a long morning. I just want to go through some of the numbers to help you understand how our caseload has increased on the relevant cases, not civil infractions, but relevant cases. I'll start off with auto insurance reform, civil cases. In 2019, no-fault insurance amendments caused our caseload to significantly increase. These cases involve parties filing increased summary disposition motions, which require laborious hours of research, analysis, and oral argument. In 2024 alone, the civil docket had a 58% increase compared to 2023. These reforms did not exist in 2011 when the judicial reduction plan was enacted. Clean slate legislation. As you know, in 2021, legislation went into effect which automatically set aside convictions and also greatly expanded the type of convictions that were eligible to be set aside. Under the new legislation, the number of hearings has increased, mostly because operating while intoxicated, known as drunk driving, is now eligible for a set aside. So in 2019, 38 set aside hearings were filed. In 2024, the court surpassed 150 set aside hearings, which require the judge to now review all of the closed files, hold a hearing with the defendant, and make specific findings on whether that conviction should be set aside. In 2011, these mandates did not exist. Criminal justice reform, effective in 2021. This legislature enacted new sentencing guidelines and violation of probation mandates. These changes require more time at violation of probation hearings and at sentencings. Defendants also are now allowed to ask to terminate probation after completing half of their probation. This requires, again, many additional hearings for each judge. These mandates, again, did not exist in 2011 when the reduction plan was enacted. Landlord-tenant changes. In 2023, the Supreme Court issued an order that continued and expanded provisions of the Landlord-Tenant Act that were used during COVID. This order currently mandates an additional day of landlord-tenant hearings for each judge, which is often over 60 cases. Again, this second hearing mandate did not exist in 2011 when the reduction plan was enacted. Police agencies. Unlike most courts, our court provides service to eight different police agencies. The reduction plan would impact the police agencies and would cause delays for their needs. Police regularly seek a judge or a magistrate for many matters, including search warrants, swear-to complaints, or arraignments. The court must be available 24 hours a day for search warrants. There has been a major increase in search warrants, and I believe it's correlated to the rise in digital crimes and evidence. At present, search warrants are handled by the judges and magistrates, both during the day and after hours. In 2011, the police sought out 241 search warrants. In 2017, 394 search warrants. And last year, 24,725 search warrants. Our DWI drug treatment court. In 2021, the court's new hybrid treatment court was instituted for the treatment of substance-using offenders and to protect the community. It did become certified by SCALE in 2023. This specialty treatment court requires additional hearings with defendants, evaluations, probation meetings, graduations, and SCALE mandates. The treatment court did not exist in 2011 when the reduction plan was enacted. Michigan Indigent Defense Commission, created in 2013 to foster improvements to the legal system. The MIDC works to ensure the state's public defense system is fair, cost-effective, and constitutional. The commission changed the fee structure for appointed attorneys, reflecting the time and effort expended on each case. Attorneys are now holding more preliminary exams, motions to dismiss, and jury trials than ever before. Again, these modifications did not exist in 2011 when the reduction plan was enacted. Continuing Judicial Education, effective in January of 2024. The Michigan Supreme Court mandates 24 hours of continuing legal education every two years for each judge. This also did not exist in 2011 when the judicial reduction plan was enacted. If I'm going too long, please stop me. I really appreciate your time, and I'm sorry I'm talking so fast because I just want to get all of this in. The due process impact of judicial elimination. First off, case backlog. Undoubtedly, a reduction to two judges would create delays in scheduling criminal and civil matters, most notably delaying trials and sentencing. It would create increased wait times for police, attorneys, witnesses, crime victims, defendants, and family members. Criminal trials have increased at our court by 58% since last year and 6% on the civil trials. Due process for crime victims and defendants. With the sweeping changes that your Michigan legislature and the Michigan Supreme Court have enacted with criminal justice reform, the reduction plan is entirely inconsistent with those goals. Defendants and victims should not experience delays in our court system. This legislature is keenly aware of the seriousness of domestic violence. These cases require immediate attention when addressing arraignments, bond, and no contact orders. There is great concern that there could be delays in addressing these issues immediately. Also, in my sobriety court, when a defendant violates, those violations are recommended to be treated immediately so that the defendant and the court can address what is happening with the person in treatment court as soon as possible. Negative economic impact. The slower judicial process would negatively impact businesses and those who rely on timely court decisions for property disputes, landlord-tenant cases, contract cases, and land contract forfeiture cases. Cases may also be delayed regarding scale guidelines for case completion. They give us guidelines to complete civil cases within 273 misdemeanor cases. Judge, I'm sorry. I'm going to interrupt you for just a moment. If you can get it wrapped up so we can ask a couple of questions in the next minute, that would be great. Absolutely. Chief judge duties. Unlike the circuit court, the district court chief judge does not have a reduced docket. The chief judge handles budgets, administrative issues, court staff working with municipalities. Lastly, it's the community outreach programs. Myself and my colleagues are very involved with the local schools. We all have field trips to the court. We are routinely going to the local middle schools and high schools to talk about substance use, making good decisions with the kids. I don't want that to be impacted. So, yes, absolutely, I am here to take your questions, but on behalf of my colleagues, we are very grateful. We are seeking your assistance in passing 4833 to preserve a three-judge bench, not create an additional judgeship. This is not creating an additional judgeship. Thank you. Thank you. Rep. McGold. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thanks for coming in, Representative. You mentioned there were seven communities. Would you happen to know the population, total community population, that those judges are serving currently? West Bloomfield and Bloomfield Township would be the biggest, followed by Birmingham, and then the city of Bloomfield Hills, Kego Harbor, Sylvan Lake, and Orchard Lake are the smaller communities. I don't want to say specifically it's about 140,000. Combined total? Combined total. It could be 120, my apologies for not knowing that right now, but the district has experienced some increase in population. Okay, thank you. Rep. Breen. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you, Judge. I actually used to practice with your husband many moons ago. Oh, wow. Yes. I'm wondering, the scale report for the judicial resources does not come to the same conclusion that you have, and I'm wondering about the difference and if you can explain why you think you arrived at the conclusion that you need some additional help on the bench personally. I'm inclined to listen to the boots on the ground, sorry, scale, but I'm wondering if you can explain why we've got different conclusions here. Absolutely. I received the opinion from Deputy General Counsel Trevor Van Dyke last night. I can tell you presently we are actually under secondary review by scale. I confirmed that this morning with our representative

that Jim McGrail, that we are under secondary review, so I was a little bit confused by the, I guess, the position that Mr. Van Dyke took. But let me comment on that. In this opinion, he does state that our case filings surpassed 54,000 in 2007. We were at 28,000 in 2024. We are increasing this year. Our caseload, we are expected to close at 32,800 in 2025. What must be noted here is the type of case. So when you see 54,000, candidly, more traffic tickets were being written in 2007. After COVID, statewide, and you probably know this, traffic tickets really came down and they're starting to go back up. But during COVID and post-COVID, they were coming down. So when you look at 54,000 and these high numbers, a good amount of those numbers are traffic tickets. What I'm asking you to look at are the substantive cases. When our civil caseload goes up 54% in one year, SCALE is actually taking note. In fact, the reason they're giving us a secondary review is because of our civil caseload. With the no-fault changes, for some reason, they are filing more cases in our court than the other courts in Oakland County. It could be for a lot of reasons. I won't speculate based on where attorneys live, where their offices are. But to have a 53% increase in one year, since 2021, we increased by 84%. When you look at those numbers on these third-party provider no-fault lawsuits, SCALE is really watching that. And again, that's why they're giving us a secondary review, because those cases take a lot of time. There are a lot of motions for summary disposition on really novel issues, especially with the changes in the law. So that is one of the reasons SCALE is taking another look at our court. There are other things that can't be quantified. We service eight different police agencies. If you take a look at most of the district courts, especially in Oakland County, that's a lot. That's a lot of different police agencies to be available for all of them. But setting even that issue aside, if you want to look strictly at our caseload, we are up this year. We are going up to, like I said, over 32,000 cases. And in large part, it is because of our civil docket, which is really exploding. On any given week, we will have dozens of motions for summary disposition, and they take a lot of time. I also want to comment on one conclusion that Mr. Van Dyke made at the end about— I'm sorry, but we really, really need to wrap it up. And we still have two more questions. I'm going to allow Rep. Breen to do a follow-up, but we really need to wrap this committee hearing up in the next, like, four minutes. Okay, I'm sorry. This just requires a yes or no answer. Just one, you're saying that the changes in the no-fault law did not result in decreased litigation. And two, you mentioned the rep was Jim McGrail. Is that Wayne Law Class of 01? Just want to know if we're talking about the same person. I'm not sure when he graduated, but he is our SCALE representative, and he confirmed this morning that we are under secondary review on the judicial needs report. Thank you. Rep. Wozniak. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you for your testimony, Judge. With regard to the total cases, and obviously you disagree with SCALE on their findings, could you clarify the docket for—and I agree with you on substantive cases that come before you now. They do take a lot more time. But what is the docket load annually for each judge, and what is your total now? Is it 32,000? Right. We're expected to close out this year. We're preparing the budget right now at about 32,500 cases divided by three judges. That would be roughly 11,000 per judge. But I want to be really clear with you. I don't want to count the civil infractions. These are the tickets that people can come into the courthouse and pay at the counter or handle by Zoom. Those are not taking up time. I want to talk about the 5,000 and something civil cases, the criminal cases, treatment courts, search warrants, availability for the police, domestic violence cases. This is what is taking up the court's time. And when you look at some of the analysis from SCALE, they mention this in yesterday's summary, but what they don't mention is that because of our burgeoning civil docket that we are under a secondary review right now. Thank you. Thank you. Last question, Rep. DeBoyer. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you, Representative, for being here. Judge, thank you for taking the time to be here on this issue. My question is, so it's under a secondary review with SCALE. That secondary review could result in them changing their position, correct, on that? Correct. So I think first it would be prudent that we wait until that secondary review come back. And then additionally, if you do believe indeed that they come back and don't change their position, that's a broader issue because my question to you is how many jurisdictions have requested this type of modification? How many of those modifications have been granted? And are we going to set a precedent with the legislature just changing what SCALE's perspective is based on the facts that they use? Because I would argue that SCALE is the expert in the room, whether I agree or disagree with them all the time is a different conversation. But they have a standard that they have to hold us up to. So are we ahead of that a little bit too much right now until we make that decision, I guess, is the question. I think that's a really good question. First off, SCALE is saying this is a new judgeship. It is not a new judgeship. Please let me clarify that. That is maintaining the three-judge bench. There is a huge difference there because we are not seeking to build new courtrooms and hire additional staff. SCALE makes their determination based on case analysis. They did change after 2011. Other courts were modified that were slated for either the courts combining services or having reductions. This is not entirely new. But I would say to you, if a court is seeking to change a recommendation from 2011, let them prove it. Let them prove it. And that's why I'm here to you to talk to you about all of these things. Your very legislature added on so many categories that never existed in 2011. And if SCALE's position is they don't take extra time, well, I can tell you right now I've got a courtroom of people waiting to expunge cases. And it takes a lot of time. And we all put great time and effort into our cases. And I would welcome any of you to come here. I have invited SCALE and their analysts to come here and watch what we do. Please don't look at this as a numbers game. Because when you start to look strictly at numbers, you have to look at what type of cases we are all talking about and whether we're on the same page. Thank you, Judge. Thank you, Rep. Steele. Rep. DeBoer, to answer your question, too, on a committee level, you know, this is obviously we did Ralph today. It's a topic of conversation. As bills got dropped, information has come to light, but it's being reviewed. So we're not moving these right now. We're just doing testimony. But in regards to that, House Bill 4833 does not wish to speak, opposes the bill, and has submitted written testimony already is Trevor Van Dyke of SCALE. Thank you. With that, seeing no further business before the committee, committee is adjourned. Thank you.

title: Appropriations - State and Local Transportation — Wednesday, October 29, 2025
transcript:
Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for being here today. The Appropriations Subcommittee on State and Local Transportation will come to order. And will the clerk please call the roll for today's attendance. Thank you, Madam Chair. Representative Steele. Here. Representative Slaw. Present. Representative Borton. Here. Representative Casina. Representative Robinson. Representative Morgan. Here. Representative Edwards. Here. Madam Chair, you have five of seven members. You have a quorum. Thank you, Clerk. Representative Borton moves to adopt the minutes of the October 22nd meeting. There being no objection, the motion prevails by unanimous consent. So a recent Bridge Magazine article brought to light a new rail study that MDOT will be conducting. Today we will hear from Peter Annister and the Administrator of the Office of Rails at MDOT. So, Peter, if you want to step up here and proceed with the testimony. And I appreciate you coming into our office the other day and giving us an overview. And I just thought I would like to bring it before the committee so everybody has the same information that you shared with us the other day. So I'll ask my questions after you present. So thank you. Yeah, absolutely. And thank you for inviting us in to speak to the committee. We did want to give you a little bit of an update on our passenger rail and some of the things that are going on in the Office of Rail. There's a lot of opportunity there and it's an important mode of transportation. So something that we want to continue to look at, the ways that we can make improvements. As the chairwoman said, I'm Peter Annister. I'm the director of the Office of Rail at MDOT. I was going to start a little bit by talking about our existing passenger rail services in Michigan. We have three Amtrak routes that are in operation today. Those are combined five round trip trains, you know, seven days a week. So 10 trains essentially going eastbound, westbound, mostly to Chicago and then points in Michigan. There's a map up here. You can see those routes serve 22 station communities throughout Michigan. So both a mix of rural and urban. We do hit a lot of our university, you know, and medical population centers. So that's something that is really of interest to us and how we can support those communities with rail. Michigan does own some of track, which is a little bit unusual. Most of the passenger rail service throughout the country and even some in Michigan operate on the host railroads. So we operate on the freight railroads essentially. But in Michigan, Amtrak actually owns some track, which is fairly unique outside of the northeast corridor up in New England. And then MDOT owns about 139 miles of track between Dearborn and Kalamazoo. And the purchasing of that track essentially allowed us to make investments to operate at speeds up to 110 miles per hour on that section of

corridor and then Amtrak section is also we're able to run at speeds of up to 110 miles per hour. Again, that's fairly unique outside the Northeast Corridor. I think there's only one other line in the United States, the Chicago to St. Louis line that runs at speeds up to 110 miles per hour. So something to be proud of here for us. We serve about 700,000 passengers per year on our existing Amtrak services. You can see from this chart we had a dip during COVID like a lot of transportation operators, but we've been building that service back up. We just in fiscal year 25, which just ended on September 30th, we had about 713,000 riders on all three of our Amtrak services. You also see our revenue as the blue line. We're essentially have record revenues for our Amtrak services, which is great. In FY24, we switched to more of a revenue model that's similar to the airlines, where when there's more demand, the tickets are more expensive, less demand, less expensive tickets. And that has had a nice positive impact on the revenues that we're bringing in for our services. One of the other things that we find really important is our on-time performance. So are we getting passengers to where they want to be on the schedule that we've proposed for those routes? You can see for each one of our three lines, we have seen improvement in that area since FY19, which is great. The FRA, the Federal Rail Administration, has a threshold of about 80%. And as you can see, only one of our lines, the Pierre Marquette, which runs between Grand Rapids and Chicago, currently is at that threshold. But we're continuing to work with Amtrak and our host railroads to make improvements on on-time performance. So that's something that we'll continue to work towards. So when we look to the future, the FRA created a new program called the Corridor Identification and Development Program. We call it Corridor ID. So that was a program that we put in applications for all three of our existing routes. And really to look at ways of how we can improve reliability and service on those routes. And then also looking to make improvements all the way up to adding frequencies. So we were accepted into that program for all three of our routes, which is fantastic. It does bring some federal money. There were 69 corridors throughout the United States that were selected for this program. That includes some existing routes. It includes some routes that are expanding. And then it includes some totally new routes between areas throughout the country. So for each one of those, for each one of our three existing routes, we did get an initial federal funding of about $500,000 to do the initial stage of that Corridor ID program. And it was important for us to apply for that really to make, again, to continue to make improvements on our routes. So we're really looking at providing reliable on-time performance. So are there things or investments that we can do to really improve and enhance that service at our stations or the timelines on our routes? Or maybe there's a choke point with the infrastructure that we need to address. And the idea of this Corridor ID program is to really develop that plan that looks at all of those areas and comes up with a list of recommendations or projects that will need to take place to kind of move forward to meet those goals. We also talked about increasing frequencies. So we have the five round-trip services today. We want to basically double those services. So our Pierre Marquette route, which is the one between Grand Rapids and Chicago, we have one round-trip service right now. We'd like to double that to two round-trip services. Our Blue Water route, which runs from Port Huron through East Lansing to Chicago, we have one round-trip route currently. We'd like to double that to at least two round-trips. And then the Wolverine route, which runs from Oakland County, Pontiac, Royal Oak, Troy through Detroit to Chicago, there's three round-trips that operate every day now. We'd like to double that up to six round-trips. And then for that service, the other unique thing we put in our application was reestablishing international service between Detroit and Windsor. Via Rail, there's an existing CPKC tunnel that handles freight railroad, and that is available to be used for passenger rail service. So that's kind of considered an extension of our Wolverine, our existing Wolverine route, but that was something we included as well. So as the chairwoman mentioned, there's also been some talk about a new service for what we call the coast to coast, which is a service that doesn't exist today. It's something that we're looking at to look at service between Grand Rapids, Lansing, and Detroit. So more of an interstate service for Michigan, really connecting our two major population centers. That study is not part of the federal corridor ID program that FRA sponsors that our other three routes have been accepted into, but it was something that was recommended by the governor's Growing Michigan Together Council. That was occurring about the same time that we were going through the corridor ID process with FRA. So when that recommendation came forward to really look at enhancing passenger rail service, particularly between that Grand Rapids, Lansing, Detroit corridor, there was an opportunity to kind of build on what we were already doing through this FRA corridor ID program. And that coast to coast was really the genesis was a Michigan Environmental Council study that was completed back in 2016 that had identified three potential routes for that coast to coast service. So what we did is basically as we were looking for our three existing services, we ended up hiring a consultant that's going to help us take us through that corridor ID process. And as part of that consultant RFP, essentially we added this coast to coast project to that. So while we have that support from that consultant, again, it's not necessarily part of that federal corridor ID program. So here's a map of some of the alternative routes on that coast to coast corridor. I think the vision is, you know, it would connect all the way over from Holland and Grand Rapids through Lansing and then on to southeast Michigan. I think there's a couple alternative routes of how you would get to the southeast Michigan portion once you arrive through Lansing. There are tracks that freight tracks between Lansing and Jackson. So you could kind of take a southerly route and then connect to our existing Wolverine corridor. Or there's tracks that CSX owns between Lansing and southeast Michigan through Howell, Ann Arbor as another option. So this study that we're embarking on will try to build on some of these alternative recommendations and really take a look at what some of those options might be. You know, overall, when we're talking about the future of passenger rail service, it's really looking at that connectivity and travel experience. We're really looking at how do we make improvements to really make rail a more attractive and sustainable option for residents and visitors. And then I'm going to talk a little bit about the vision and a little bit about what's included in the study as well as the FRA study. This is kind of a snapshot of all the different things going on in Michigan around passenger rail. You'll see the kind of the purple, the blue, and the red. Those are our three existing Amtrak services. They're numbered one, two, three here on this slide. The coast to coast is kind of the green dotted line numbered four on this map. So again, that's a potential service. It doesn't exist today. We're really just embarking on the study to say, you know, is this feasible? What's the market for something like this? What kind of investment would be needed if we were going to operate that service through Michigan? And then you'll see there's a couple other gray dotted lines. There's a couple other initiatives going on right now as well. There's a north-south service that's under study right now.

by a group called Groundworks, which is a Traverse City-based nonprofit. They're looking at a feasibility study of rail service between Traverse City and Ann Arbor and southeast Michigan. They did get some federal funding for that and some state funding for that, so that's an ongoing study. And then you'll notice that if you look in southeast, there's a dotted line between Detroit and Toledo that goes on easterly to Cleveland. That is another FRA corridor ID route that was actually submitted by the Ohio Rail Development Commission in partnership with us that would connect basically Detroit with Cleveland and Toledo. So they are the lead on that study, but that's something, again, that doesn't exist today and is a potential route at some point in the future. So to talk a little bit about the funding for these service development plans, the step one of the plan is basically putting together the study. That's 100% federally funded, so that's money we got through that FRA's corridor ID program. Step two of that process is really to complete the service development plan, and that part is 90% federally funded, and we have 10% state match. And then step three is once you identify the projects, the infrastructure projects that need to occur under that plan, step three has funding available from the feds to complete the preliminary engineering and the NEPA environmental activities. So that is 80% federally funded, and we would have to come up with 20% match for any project that we wanted to put through that. The coast-to-coast study is, again, since it's not part of that FRA program, we do not get federal dollars for that. That's being funded through state appropriations. There was a one-time appropriation in FY24 for intermodal capital investment grants, and that's the funding source that we are using to basically fund that coast-to-coast study. So no new money is needed or will be used. That's money that was appropriated back in FY24. And then at the end of that process, when you get to actual projects that are needed, maybe you need to invest in some additional rail or something like that, then being in the corridor ID program gives us preference for other federal grant programs that are already existing out there. So once we get to final design and construction, we'll have to compete for competitive grant funding at the federal level, but being in this program gives us a leg up compared to routes that aren't in the corridor ID program. So again, this is just a visual, that three-step process for the corridor ID. Step one is really the scoping and program initiation. Step two is that service development plan creation. And then step three is kind of the first step in project development around that PE, preliminary engineering, and environmental NEPA clearance. And then you can see the future phases. That's when you do final design construction. Timelines, we're kind of really in the orange box in the early engagement on all of these studies. And basically in step two, we're going to look to begin that in early next year. We are close to being completed with step one for the three corridor IDs and the coast to coast. So those are basically the ones that need to be reviewed by FRA are being reviewed by them. They're having some resource changes at the federal level, so that could take a little longer than maybe previously anticipated. But we think by early next year, we'll be well underway and moving towards the actual work in our service development plans. Again, step one, we're nearing completion of this now. It's really developing the scope and schedule of that service development plan. Step two is looking at that service development plan planning. We expect to start that in spring of next year and really have most of the heavy lifting done in the next 18 to 24 months, although all elements of that are probably going to drag on a couple of years past that. The coast to coast plan is expected to be completed in 2028 as well. That will involve engaging with stakeholders, really looking at the infrastructure that exists. When you take an existing freight line and you want to upgrade it to passenger rail, there is quite a bit of new investment that's going to be required on that route. The biggest being positive train control, which is FRA requirement for any passenger rail served route in the United States. Freights aren't required to have that positive train control. So anytime we're trying to engage new service on a freight route, that'll be part of that investment equation on the front end. And then we have started some initial stakeholder coordination really with talking with some of the communities that would be served. We've had a lot of meetings with the freight railroads. Obviously, both freight and passenger railroads are a big priority for us in Michigan. So we want to make sure that all of our freight partners, be it a class one or a short line railroad here in Michigan, are understanding what's going on and how they may be involved in this. And we want to make sure that they have opportunities to offer their input as well. We're also meeting with some of our stakeholder groups like Michigan Association of Rail Passengers and other stakeholder groups that have an interest in rail. And those conversations will just get more robust as we move further into this process. We do have a website. If you go to michigan.gov slash michiganpassengerrailfuture, that's where we plan to keep providing updates for all four of these potential plans and routes and information that's going on. There's also, I think, a way to sign up for a newsletter. So if you want to have information pushed to you, you can put in your email and we'll share any updates that are going on. Also, if people have comments, they can go to this site that's live now. People can provide their input and comments on some of the plans and what's going on with passenger rail service in the U.S. So that's a snapshot. I know that was a lot. It was probably a little bit confusing because it did get into the details a little bit. I think the biggest takeaways is that we're looking for ways to continue to improve rail in Michigan. We're looking at this coast to coast is really at the initial phases of trying to understand what it would mean and what it would take to actually bring that service into reality. What the market is for that sort of service, what type of investment and equipment would we need to support that service. So I'm happy to answer any questions and clarify any of the comments I made from the committee. Of course I have five questions first. Thank you. I appreciate your coming here today and just enlightening us on this. So just to clarify, you received a grant to do a study on the three existing routes and while you had the consultant available, you're doing the study on the coast to coast as a feasibility study to see if we can add a fourth line. Yes. So that we did not apply for that coast to coast when we applied for the three existing routes. But since there's a lot of similarities in those activities, we wanted to take that opportunity to move that forward too. And then you had mentioned that there was a study done on basically how to move Michigan forward and it was the results of that study that made us do this study. Wasn't there another study that was done a handful of years ago saying that we might need a fourth line? So I guess my question is how many studies did we have to say that this is something that we should study more? For the coast to coast, the biggest study was really this Michigan Environmental Council from 2016. And that's the baseline that we're going to build from when we're looking at that coast to coast study. There's been other studies in Michigan that have looked at routes in southeast Michigan. There's been commuter rail studies. There's also existing service development plans for our three existing Amtrak routes, at least on the Wolverine service. And then Michigan's also part of some studies that have happened that have looked at Midwest Rail

So there's also two or three studies out there that have looked at Midwest. But when you're looking at that coast to coast, really the baseline is that Michigan Environmental Council study that was done in 2016. So we don't have an actual study of how much it costs to do that, just studies saying that we should study it. I don't mean to be facetious, but I'm actually wondering, we don't have anything, because I was looking for reports to actually review prior to this meeting to see if there was some information of previous studies to say, okay, we really do need a fourth line or we don't have a fourth line. Typically how these things work is that initial study will be very visionary and tip your toe in the water, kind of put the vision out there and see what kind of reaction you get. The studies that we're doing here are going to be, I'll say, a little more quantitative in that they're going to say, the vision is great, but what is it actually going to take to make some of these things happen so that those decisions can be made? So these will look more at truly like what kind of investment is going to be needed to make these expansions or to create a new coast to coast service. And the service development plan, it's a very prescriptive FRA requirement. So there's really specific things you have to do around market studies and investments and things like that. So it's going to be much more of, I'll say, a hard scale study than anything that's kind of been done previously. And then if I could get a copy of the 2016, if you have it, I mean, if you could send us that. Yeah, we could email it over. We do. Okay. We just did. Apparently we have it, so I just need to review it. So sorry about that. And then I have a couple of questions, but I'm going to pass it to the other representatives and then come back. So first, Rep. Slaw. Thank you, Madam Chair. And I've got a couple of questions. I don't know if you want, Madam Chair. I've got a couple of questions. Would you like me to do multiple? Okay, perfect. So thanks for being here. I appreciate that. I'm in your materials that you had gave to us on page three. It's the ridership and revenue graph that you have. And interestingly, your revenue has consistently since 16 tracked below your ridership from a growth perspective, right? And all of a sudden you're over top of that. How is that that that seems, that revenue seems to be going up faster than your ridership? Yeah, so that was that we made a change in FY24 around how we managed revenue and ticket sales. So previously in the past, we had more of a static fare to ride our services. And in FY24, we made that much more dynamic based on ridership demand. So that allowed us when we had heavy ridership that we could increase those ticket prices. And then when we had less ridership, we could lower those ticket prices in order to enhance, you know, entice more riders to get on the train. So that difference really allowed us to grow revenues faster than just the number of tickets we were selling. Thank you. On page four of the materials that you handed out, it shows the on time performance. And just can you give me some reasons why you don't think we're able to meet that 80% threshold? Yeah, there's a myriad of reasons. So a couple of things that have been happening recently. One is literally construction. So much like the same on the highways, we have a rail construction season in Michigan that happens. And if we're doing track work or something adjacent to the track, then those trains can't operate at their normal speeds. They have to slow down. Instead of operating at maybe 79 or that 110, they may have to go through those construction areas at 25 miles per hour or something like that. So we've had quite a bit of major construction projects on our Amtrak services. So that's been a piece of it. We're also we have new equipment in Michigan, both our locomotives and our passenger cars. And Amtrak is our servicer of that equipment. And we haven't had the availability as much as we need. And the equipment has had a few kind of mechanical issues that they've been working through. So that sometimes delays trains as well. If they're trying to work on an issue with equipment. So those are two of the bigger ones. And then there could also be freight train interference. So we share tracks with the freight industry. If we get behind a freight train, you know, that could slow us down on our schedule. We could even have passenger train interference. So, you know, as we go in and out of Chicago, there's other routes as well, not just Michigan's routes that are using those tracks. We might have to wait for other passenger rail service. And then the other biggest one typically is related to that positive train control. So that's the signaling between the train and the infrastructure. And with all technology, sometimes there's a hiccup in that technology. So we have to operate at a little bit slower speeds when those incidents occur. So those are probably the biggest reasons of some of that delay. And you just, one of my questions was positive train control because I really didn't know what that was. So what you're telling me is that's the technology that allows you to maximize when trains can be on the track, where they're going to be at, how are we going to stop and start a freight train versus the Amtrak coming through. Yeah. So the PTC basically overrides the locomotive engineer. So if there's a curve that's supposed to be taken at 65 miles per hour, if that train is traveling faster than that, then that positive train control will kick in and take control of that train, essentially, or provide alerts and that sort of thing. So it's a FRA requirement on all our passenger rail routes in the U.S. And then my last question is just can you go back over the number of miles of track owned? Yeah. So for the passenger rail, we own 139 miles of track. We also own freight track. So in total, we own 665 miles of track in Michigan. But a vast majority of that's on our freight railroads. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Chair. And that's out of a, I'll just, there's about 3,300 miles of track throughout all of Michigan. So the even larger majority is owned by the private railroads. Thank you, Madam Chair. Peter, thank you very much for your presentation today. My question is who owns the Holland to Detroit line? So CSX Railroad owns that infrastructure. Are they supportive of adding passenger service on that line? We haven't had in-depth conversations, but in our preliminary conversations, they understand our goals and I think are willing to work with us. Okay. That partially answers my last question was are they going to be involved in this study? Yes. Okay. Absolutely. They're going to involve all of our freight rails because we don't want to do anything.
