It's not a zero-sum game for us. So we don't want to gain passenger service by losing freight service. We need to make sure whatever investments we're doing can support freight and passenger rail. Okay. Thank you. Rep. Morgan. Thank you, Chair. I'm very excited to hear more about passenger rail here. I think this is really exciting. I think there are a lot of great opportunities ahead of us in this area. A couple of questions. One, really looking at particularly page six of your presentation around enhancing existing services. What are the barriers to – I mean I think as the Chair was kind of asking, we've done a lot of studies on rail in Michigan. I've been on several of those committees. I've read as many of those as I can. But what does it take to actually make these things happen, start making them happen, and which ones are most viable? It seems like increasing frequencies on our existing routes is probably the most viable, but I'm curious how do we move beyond studies to implementation and seeing increased frequencies and more routes being built up, and what do we need to do on our end? Yes, and I would agree that expanding existing routes where investment has already been made and passenger service is already operating is a much easier path than creating new service. I think there's two things that really are going to have the biggest impact on how and when we can expand that service. One is equipment. So if you're going to have more trains and more riders, you're going to need more equipment. And there's not enough

overabundance of equipment right now in the national rail network. In fact, there's probably a lack to meet the needs that are out there right now. So any new expansion is going to need new equipment. Equipment is expensive and there's a long lead time to buy locomotives and rail cars. I think it's probably about five years right now from when you could place an order to when you actually may get that equipment being delivered. So that's one of the biggest hurdles is making all that kind of come together at the right time. The second piece is just rail capacity, so the infrastructure. You know, and our biggest in Michigan, it's interesting because the biggest capacity constraint we have on our rail infrastructure is when we have to go through Indiana and Illinois around Lake Michigan and into Chicago Union Station. So when we operate on that portion of our route, we operate on Norfolk Southern owned rail. And that is literally their super highway of rail. I think there's 110 trains a day that pass through that rail. And it's double tracked and there's a few bridges in that that due to the age of those bridges, even though they're double tracked, there can only be one train at a time that passes through those bridges. So really to further enhance that capacity, there's going to need to be some investment made, particularly looking at that south of the lake segment. So we are working with the Federal Rail Administration and Amtrak and other state partners through really this corridor ID process to determine, again, what types of investments are going to be needed. But that's probably the other big piece is how do we ensure that we have that infrastructure in place that is going to allow us to have all those trains moving. But if we wanted to, you know, one of your things listed is double the frequencies on Wolverine or to two for Blue Water or Paramarcat. Could we just do those tomorrow if we had the financial resources for it? Or, you know, what do we how do we make those happen? Yeah, you I think if you could, I mean, anything you do where you use a freight route there, you need to get their approval to do that. So it's not like we could just tell us, hey, we're going to start running more trains on your tracks. There has to be an agreement put in place. But if you looked at Interstate, so let's say we're not going to we're just going to run between Kalamazoo and Ann Arbor on tracks we own. Really, that biggest hurdle is equipment. You know, having the equipment essentially to do that. OK, can I just ask one more? OK, the other one last question here then is, would we be able to are there some of these route options that would allow us to pull in more federal funds or federal resources, whether it's connecting through Toledo through that corridor ID or connecting internationally? Are there routes that we could secure more federal support for rail in Michigan? And what does that cost look like either way? Thank you. Yeah, I think there's federal opportunities for all of these routes. We've been fairly successful in getting federal grants for our infrastructure and investments we want to make in Michigan. There's an opportunity right now of the feds having NOFO out that we're looking at and considering, I think, three to four projects for that funding. So we always want to take advantage of that federal funding. And I don't know that it's determinate by route. It's just kind of more it's more project determinate. You know, what's infrastructure is needed? What are you applying for? One thing to note about federal grants is that rail, unlike other modes of transportation, does not get any formula funding from the feds. Like any rail funding we get is through strictly competitive grant rounds, which obviously makes things a little difficult because you're not sure if you're going to get funded or not and when those dollars are going to show up. So we definitely I think there's going to be opportunities for more federal funding to help us with some of these visions and goals. And we're certainly going to take advantage of as many of those opportunities as we can. Thank you. And just to piggyback on Rep. Morgan is that enhancing existing services is a vision, but you're actually doing this study to see how to implement that vision, like increasing the round trips to Wolverine and how much it would cost to do that and how many more rails that we need and how many more cars we need, very specific answers to how to increase if we choose to increase. That's what this study will be accomplishing. Yes. Okay. There'll be a specific list of projects that says if you want to go from three to six, these are the things that are going to have to be completed. And ideally, we'll have some price tags with some of that stuff too. Okay. And you don't have a piggy bank there for all this stuff as of right. No. And again, that's where I think we would say, hey, let's apply this one for a federal grant, right, and see if we can tick that off. Some may be small investments that may not be infrastructure driven. Maybe there are things we can do at the stations that make things more efficient. And maybe we can use just some of our existing resources to do those things. Low hanging fruit. And then start picking off the big ones if it's feasible. Okay. So I appreciate that. So I have two quick questions. And is on page 11, there's three other lines in the gray that are being studied again. And they're not a part of this study. Are they with the same consultant that's doing our study to say, okay, we're doing this as a group project or are we doing individual projects in silos? Yeah. So the north south is a different consultant. But what, you know, with our involvement in these, there's going to be a recognition that what happens there is going to impact, you know, what we're trying to do and vice versa. So there'll be a lot of, you know, coordination there. And the consultant that's doing that north south study is very familiar with Michigan. They work with us on other projects, just not specifically on that north south. The gray line between Detroit and Ohio, that one, Ohio has not selected a consultant for that yet. But the reality is it's a pretty small world in the rail consulting business. And the consultants that operate here in the Midwest, it's likely that whoever they hire is going to have some familiarity with the Midwest and Michigan and what's going on. And then the service development plan process will really help to ensure that some of that coordination is happening. So I think, you know, while there's different pieces going on, that holistic view is something that we can accomplish and make sure we're not tripping over each other working in conflict with each other. Yeah. Go ahead. Thank you. And then you had mentioned something when you came into our office the other day that we always think passenger train, we always think Amtrak. And that, you know, we do have our service provider with the cars. But you had mentioned that there's other providers that might be able to have the boxcars or not, what are they, the train that they could provide for us. So can you elaborate on that a little bit? Yeah. So, you know, Amtrak is definitely the dominant passenger rail operator throughout the United States. But that's changing a little bit. There's some new services down in Florida by a company called Brightline. So that's a, you know, private company that essentially is operating passenger rail service in Florida. They're also looking at now service in California and Nevada. So, you know, that's a separate operator. And then even here in the Midwest, Illinois is looking at a new route where they have selected Metro, which is the commuter rail operator in Chicago, to really look at some of their inner city passenger rail service. It could be that those providers do have equipment, but it's probably more likely that, well, they would be happy to be your operator. You would still have to invest in new equipment within that partnership to get them. I don't think Brightline is sitting on a whole lot of extra equipment and Metro maybe, but it may be more commuter rail type of seating and equipment than, you know, inner city passenger.

I have to buy New York's leftovers. I don't have any other questions. Any other questions? Okay. I'll allow you one more, Morgan. One more I had here was looking at how much do we spend on passenger rail operations currently in Michigan? I know there's some metric of we pay the difference, I think, between what we bring in in revenue and what it actually costs us. I'm curious, what do we spend currently and is there kind of an estimate of a dollar amount per route? So thinking through like if we wanted one more route on Pier Marquette, how much does that ballpark look like? Yeah, so in total we spend about $25 million per year to support our Amtrak services. So again, that's the nexus between all the expenses and then the ticket revenues that we receive or Amtrak receives. The routes, obviously there's a little bit of economies of scale that the more frequencies you have, the operational cost per seat, if you want to call it that, is less because there's some fixed costs that are built in. So if we double service on the Blue Water Pier Marquette, it doesn't necessarily mean we're going to be doubling our costs per se. So each route is individual. It's hard to just say, hey, if we spend another million bucks, we're going to get X result. You kind of have to build it in these stair steps, right? So I don't have a good number in that kind of context. But with the investments we already made and with some of the operations we have existing, there should be some things that we can build on to really help hold some of those additional costs down as we add future operations. Okay, with no further business at hand, I would like to adjourn the meeting. I don't want to. Okay.

title: Health Policy — Wednesday, October 29, 2025
transcript:
All right, everybody. We're going to get rolling. The House Health Policy Committee will come to order. Would the clerk please take attendance? Chair VanderWaal. Present. Representatives Thompson. Here. Meerman. Here. Tisdell. Here. Bierlein. Here. DeBoer. Preston. Here. Schmaltz. Here. Saint Germain. Here. Bona. Here. Frisbee. Here. Whitsitt. Carter. Here. Whitwer. Here. Neely. Here. Hoskins. Here. Foreman. Mr. Chair, you have 12 members present. You do have a quorum. Thank you, Madam Clerk. Representative Preston moves to adopt the minutes of the October 23 meeting. There being no objection, the motion passes. Today we're going to be taking testimony on a few bills that will affect dentists in the state of Michigan. First, we're going to take testimony on House Bill 4935, introduced by Representative Fairbairn. And is he here? He is not here. Yeah, we'll move on from there. I know he's been suffering some back issues, so we'll move on and hopefully he gets here soon. Next up, we'll be taking testimony on 4910, introduced by Representative Borton. Representative, you could make your way to the testimony table. You know the drill. Press the red light, and the testimony table is yours. And thank you for being here. Thank you, Chair VanderWaal and members of the committee. I appreciate the opportunity to testify today on my bill 4910, which would expand continuing education options for dentistry professionals. Michigan aims to offer rewarding careers and affordable living, but government regulations and licensing requirement can often present burdensome obstacles. Obtaining professional licenses requires paperwork, training, and fees, which consumes time and money and may discourage people from those fields. This legislation simply will allow dental professionals who belong to a recognized organization, like the Michigan Dental Association, count approved activities such as meetings, committee service, or legislative work towards continuing education credits for license renewal. The goal of the legislation is to help cut red tape by simplifying licensure and continuing education, offering dental therapists greater flexibility in meeting continuing education requirements. To receive credit, dental therapists must be dues-paying members in good standing, provide proof of participation, and the association must be approved by the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs in consultation with the board. This bill does not change continuing education requirement hours. However, it allows dental therapists more flexibility in how they earn part of their continuing education hours and acknowledges that professional engagement can be just as valuable for professional development as traditional coursework. I appreciate you allowing me to speak today, and I welcome any questions you may have. Well, thank you, Representative. I know that we have somebody else that wants to testify. Is there any questions from the committee at this time? If not, thank you. We'll move on to the next person, and we'll direct our questions to them. But thank you again, Representative, for being here. Thank you. Wishing to speak in support of the bill is Sandy Sutton. Well, that's 4935. We do not have anybody. I apologize for that. I thought that we had somebody else to testify. Was there any other questions for anybody on that bill? If you could step back up real quick, Representative Beerline. I'm sorry, Representative. Sorry, Representative Borton. Is there a cap to the number of hours that can be received through these alternative methods, like attending a board meeting or going to a legislative forum or things like that? Yeah, my legislation doesn't have a cap to it. We're leaving that up to the professional organizations to determine what that cap should be. Thank you. Sorry about that. Thank you. Seeing no other questions, thank you for being here. Appreciate it. Next, we'll move back. Representative Fairbairn is here to give testimony on his House Bill 4935. You take your seat, and then your guest is Sandy Sutton, correct? When you're ready, the two of you, if the red button's on, the testimony table is yours. Thank you both for being here. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Good morning, members of the committee. I appreciate the opportunity to come before you this morning and speak about the merits of House Bill 4935. This is the Dentist and Dental Hygienist Compact. To start, I'd like to tell you about the origins of the compact in support of which the Council of State Governments has partnered with the Department of Defense, the American Dental Association, and the American Dental Hygienist Association to significantly increase the mobility of licensed dentists and dental hygienists. In so doing, they are seeking to create reciprocity among

participating states and reduce barriers to licensed portability. There are approximately 200,000 licensed dentists and 215,000 licensed dental hygienists across the United States, but licensees are generally restricted to the state in which they received their license. The Dentist and Dental Hygienist Compact seeks to provide licensees with opportunities for multi-state practice, which would increase mobility for individuals who are looking to relocate. It also improves public safety and promotes workforce development by reducing unnecessary licensure burdens. By joining the compact, Michigan would enhance workforce development and strengthen labor markets, expand consumer access to highly qualified practitioners, and enhance public safety through a shared interstate data system of licensure and disciplinary information, thereby allowing for rapid verification of licensure status and cooperation among states, all while preserving state sovereignty. To provide you a little more details and professional perspective, I'd like to introduce Michigan Dental Hygienist President Sandy Sutton. Thank you. Thank you, Chair VanderWaal and the rest of the Committee on Health Policy. My name is Sandy Sutton, and I'm happy to speak to you today. I'm a registered dental hygienist and the current president for the Michigan Dental Hygiene Association. I'm here to speak in favor of House Bill 4935, the Dentist and Dental Hygienist Compact. This bill is already enacted in 12 states, including neighboring states of Ohio and Wisconsin, and legislation has been introduced in six additional states already. It would help to permit licensure portability for dentists and dental hygienists. Dental hygienists are licensed healthcare professionals and providers integral to the dental team and often the first provider a patient sees. The Dentist and Dental Hygienist Compact, also known as the DDH Compact, originated through the Department of War alongside the Council of State Association of Governments. The Dental Hygienist Association, the American Dental Association, as an interstate occupational licensure compact. This would directly access workforce shortages and access to care concerns. This compact enables licensed dentists and dental hygienists to practice in all states participating in the compact, as opposed to getting a separate license, taking additional board exams in each state, and maintaining additional continued education requirements. Similar to other professional interstate compacts, such as the Physical Therapist Licensure Compact or the Nursing Compact, the DDH Compact facilitates multi-state practice, expands employment opportunities, supports the relocating of military spouses, and reduces the burden of maintaining multiple licenses. The DDH Compact is a solution to workforce shortages and access to care issues while maintaining high state standards. Currently, dental professionals seek significant barriers in attempting to practice in different states relating to receiving licensure due to individual state costs for licenses, the scheduling of additional board exams, and additional education to maintain each of those in each state that they're licensed in. The DDH Compact helps to streamline this process by giving the hygienist or dentist compact privileges to be able to practice in each of the participating compact states. The DDH Compact language establishes a commission with shared information system allowing participating states to share licensing information on practitioners with compact privileges. Furthermore, participating states retain sovereignty over all their laws. Relevant to our state, this compact bill is supported by the Michigan Dental Association, the Ohio Dental Hygienist Association, the Indiana Dental Hygienist Associations, the Michigan Primary Care Association, and other professional dental organizations. I urge you to support this compact. We do not wish to monopolize our profession as the American Association of Dental Boards is asking us to do. We ask that you please support the DDH Compact House Bill 4935. Thank you. Thank you for your testimony. We have several questions. Start with Representative Preston. Thank you, Chair. Thank you for bringing this bill forward. Capacity building has been a central aspect of this committee's work so far as well as my own. Can you speak to, and I think I already know the answer, in fact I know I do, can you speak to the effect that this compact will have on oral health care and dental deserts such as the UP with its participating state being Wisconsin and how that could leverage available health care professionals into the UP which are desperately needed. We've got ratios of 1,000 to 2,000 to every dentist up there. We've got dentists that will not accept insurance because there's not a high enough amount of private sector. The Upper Peninsula is in an incredibly tough spot when it comes to dental care and really all oral health care. Well, I mean this bill would address that and you look at Wisconsin, we're trying to make the state of Michigan more competitive. This would do that. Being representing the Eastern UP, I've heard from a few dentists across the area and they have a hard time finding someone to replace them as they're looking to phase out of the workforce and retire. And that's happening all over Michigan but the UP in particular. So this would help address that. Thank you, Representative. Representative Carter. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you for your testimony. My question is pretty much in the line of Representative Preston. Could this legislation unintentionally increase dental care costs for low-income and rural communities? I would say it would do the opposite. If we're introducing more competition into the area, the hope is, I mean, we've got Ohio as a neighboring state. This would help the southeast area of Michigan out big time, creating more competition and the hopes of driving down price. Okay, follow-up, Mr. Chair. Absolutely. Thank you. What is the fiscal impact of the state joining the compact? Will it require additional resources to implement? Yeah, I don't know the answer to that, Representative, but I'd be happy to look into that for you. Thank you very much. Any other questions from the committee? The only question that I have, Representative and Sandy, is do we have an estimate of how many people potentially this could bring into the workforce that are in our neighboring states right now? I do not have that estimate at this time. Okay. Yeah, we can look into that. That would be great. As we work very hard, we know that there's a lot of people that are on the borders of several areas, Wisconsin being one, and, of course, our southern border and the more opportunity to come to a great state of Michigan and work is what we want to do. So thank you. I see no other questions from the committee. Appreciate you both being here. I have one card to read in, not wishing to speak in support of the bill. Bill Sullivan, Michigan Dental Association. Next up, we will be taking testimony on House Bills 4593 and 4594, introduced by Representative Beerline and Martis, about an issue that pertains to dental specialists. Representatives, if you could make your way to the testimony table. I also believe that we have one on Zoom, but Dr. Doug Ledoux, correct, is here to speak in person. We'll let you three take off first, and then we'll finish with the gentleman that's online. So the testimony table is yours. Remember to punch the red button before you speak, and the floor is yours. Thank you. Well, thank you, Chair VanderWaal and members of the committee for the opportunity to speak today on House Bills 4593 and 4594, which I'm proud to sponsor with Representative Martis. These bills address a simple but important issue, ensuring Michigan patients are not misled by false claims of dental specialization. Under Michigan's public health code, only licensed professionals can use certain titles. Just as only licensed dentists may call themselves dentists, only those who have completed advanced training and earned recognition in a specialty field, such as orthodontics or oral surgery, may call themselves specialists. However, a 2020 lawsuit against LARA led to rule changes allowing general dentists to market themselves as specialists in unrecognized areas like implantology or cosmetic dentistry. Patients often don't realize the difference and trust these claims when seeking complex care. As you'll hear from others, this has led to serious complications

costly corrective procedures, and loss of trust. This situation undermines patient safety and fairness for those who have legitimately earned specialty credentials. House Bill 4593 closes this loophole by clarifying that only dentists licensed in a recognized specialty may represent themselves as specialists. House Bill 4594 reinforces this code by protecting the term dental specialist under the Public Health Code. Together, these bills restore honesty in advertising, protect patients, and uphold integrity in Michigan's dental profession. I want to thank Representative Martis for his partnership and respectfully ask for the committee's support in advancing these bills. With that, I'll turn it over to Representative Martis. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, committee members, and Representative Beerline. When Representative Beerline brought this package to my attention, I thought it would be a great opportunity to work with a good friend and colleague. And then as I started to look into the issue, I started to see how widespread this problem is. If you'd like to impress your friends, you can reference something called the Bader-Meinhof phenomenon, which is one of the three things that I remember from AP Psych in high school. It's when you learn a new word and all of a sudden you see that word in everything that you're reading. When I learned about this problem of folks listing themselves as specialists when that isn't necessarily the case, I actually started to see that in my own district and in other parts of Michigan. And so this started as a good opportunity to work with a good friend and colleague, and then I started to see how some of my own constituents could potentially be misled, not getting the proper care, and I became even more passionate about this opportunity to work on this legislation. Thank you, doctor. The floor is yours. So I'd like to thank you for the opportunity to discuss this. I have a couple of examples with my patients. My first one is a six-year-old boy that I saw on September 12th, and he had recently moved back to Michigan. We don't take his insurance, but his brother, I do take his insurance, had an appointment with me, and mom asked if she could bring him along to determine whether he had an abscessed tooth or not. And I said, sure. Just bring him along and I'll take a look and just let you know whether there's an abscess there or not. The child was not swollen, but he did have a draining fistula at tooth S, down on the lower right. Draining fistula is a hole in your gums where the infection and the pus is leaking out from a tooth that is necrotic. So as I usually do, I had mom come over and I showed her how I could take my explorer, the little pokey thing that you touch your teeth with, and I could stick it into the side of his jaw, five or six millimeters, and the child was unaware I was doing that because the fistula and that's how it leaks. It's not sensitive as long as you're careful right there. And told her that that tooth needed to be extracted and if she could change her insurance to one I accepted, I'd be happy to do it and gave her the paperwork to do that. Five days later, I was in the OR at the Children's Hospital, got a call from our receptionist. I can't talk, but my assistant can talk back and forth. And this mom was very angry. She reported she took this little boy to another dentist who said he does not have a necrotic tooth and does not have an abscess. I said, you need to take your child to a pediatric dentist. They will be able to correctly diagnose this. And she insisted that she had and she even explained to that dentist how I'd taken my explorer, poked it in the side of his jaw, and that's how you know there's an abscess there. The dentist insisted she would not take out a perfectly healthy tooth. Mom was confused, doesn't know who to believe, and was calling us. I reiterated, you need to take him to a pediatric dentist. She insisted that she had and told us where she took him. And at that point, I realized that is an office. It was a general dentist office, but they had hired pediatric dentists in the past. So I just said, I will check this all out, do some homework, call you in the evening, and asked my receptionist to retrieve the records. X-rays, op notes, figure out who it was and what they had included. So we got the X-rays, and they had not even taken the correct X-ray to do the diagnosis, but they took several others. And you could see plainly there was an abscess at tooth S, bone loss, et cetera. Even my hygienist saw the pan and said, oh, that tooth's abscessed, without knowing any of this. The mom insisted it was a pediatric dentist, but when you went to look on the website, it was in the same, she's in the same wing. It's all the kids' dentists, but there's actually just a general dentist. She doesn't refer to herself as a general dentist or pediatric dentist, but a family dentist. I explained all this to mom that indeed that tooth is necrotic and needs to be extracted, and this dentist is not a pediatric dentist, and she needs to take her to a pediatric dentist. That's one example. Another example is an assistant that now works for me. And she was an intern for me while she was in assisting school. And somewhere along the way, she asked these series of questions over a span of about two months. And I didn't know where she was headed with all of this, but you'll see where we got. So she first asked me when dental sealants were invented. And I told her, I don't know when they were invented, but they were being placed in the 1970s. A couple weeks later, she asked me, do all pediatric dentists place dental sealants? And I said, I am not aware of a single pediatric dentist that doesn't recommend and place sealants. A few weeks later, why doesn't my dentist, my pediatric dentist, believe in dental sealants? He did not do them for me, and he won't do them for my little sister. And I said, well, he's probably not a pediatric dentist. And she said, no, he is. And I said, who is this? And she told me, and I said, no, no, he is not. Check his website. And so a week later, she said, I checked his website. He is a pediatric dentist. And I said, no, look for the tiniest print. He is not a pediatric dentist. And she came back and said, I checked it again. He is a pediatric dentist. I literally had to go to this website, find the webpage with the little disclaimer, find the tiniest script to show her that he is not. It says he's not licensed in pediatric dentistry. He is just a general dentist. She's livid that she had been seeing that guy for 12 years, and he's not a pediatric dentist. And her little sister still was seeing him. Her next question was, do you think the reason I needed four crowns and a root canal on my molars is because I didn't get sealants when I was a little kid? That part I don't know, but that is a legitimate question to ask. So how that happened with this particular patient who's now an assistant. Her mom had specifically moved her to this dentist looking for a pediatric dentist that would be better with children. And that was in about 2007 when she was six. She was dismissed from the practice when she was turned 18 because he's a pediatric dentist. Her sister, who's about 10 years younger, was still going to that dentist. And when he wouldn't do sealants on her teeth, that's what prompted all these questions to me. So he was able to mislead this family for 16 years. Not until she was in the dental community was she able to figure out that indeed they were being lied to all this time. And this is something that I deal with once or twice a month from parents. And they are always very upset and ask me, is this legal? And it is. There's no law saying they can't say these things. Very good. I've got a few questions. We'll start with Representative Meerman. Thank you, Chair. In the first scenario that you walked through, I guess I think he was advertising, he or she was advertising themselves as a family dentist. What went wrong there? She's advertised as a kid's dentist. So this practice previously had pediatric dentists that worked there. They would hire them and then they would move on, purchase their own practice. So

Because you described a building that had mostly kids dentists in it, but she was just a family, I thought you said she said she was a family dentist. In her website, she says it's family dentist. It doesn't say she's a pediatric dentist. It doesn't say she's a general dentist. It just says she's a family dentist. Is there anything wrong with saying that? No, but it's very misleading because it's all in the kids portion of their website and in the she works in the kids wing, which is where pediatric dentists used to work. So the website needs, under these bills, the website would be what, designate her as a general dentist? I'm not sure how the bills would affect that. That's kind of what we're looking to address. So in a case like this, this dental, this practice had multiple tabs. You click on the tab for pediatric dental care and it shows all these dentists that some of them are specialized. This person is not, but because they primarily provide pediatric care, they're listed under those pediatric dentists. It's not a pediatrician, not a specializing in pediatric care. There were some other examples that were presented to us. People on their website specifically said specializing in pediatric dentistry and then in real small print, not a pediatric specialist. I specialize in health policy. I'm not a medical professional. You know, it's that kind of thing. Okay, thanks. Representative Tisdale. Thank you, Chair VanderWaal. So the triggering event for this is a license. You have to be licensed in the specialty that you're claiming. That is correct. Okay, so there isn't a, my brother, for example, is an orthopedic surgeon, took a fellowship in foot and ankle, and he advertises as a foot and ankle specialist, but he's not licensed as a foot and, he's licensed as a physician. So there aren't fellowships or residencies that provide specialty training. If you get one of those, you're specifically licensed in that specialty training? I believe there are four dental specialties that you can be separately licensed in. I think there's six. It kind of depends on the state. And there is a residency that's associated with that. Okay, so if you don't have one of those six specialty licenses, that's the criteria. Then you are a general dentist. Yes. Got it. Thank you. So for me specifically, my training, I was trained as a general dentist at the University of Michigan, and then I spent two years at the University of Minnesota in a pediatric dental residency. And then I was able to get a specialty license in pediatric dentistry. It's not just specialty training. It's a license. And board certified as a pediatric dentist. Very good. Thank you. Thank you, Representative. Representative Carter. Thank you, Mr. Chair. And I was going back and forth in my mind when you were talking about how this could protect young people. And I was thinking in my mind, would this legislation also protect our seniors from this type of exploitation? Certainly. I mean, it's clarity. People can still make the decision to go. I tell my current dentist now all the time that my dentist as a child growing up who did everything, he was a general dentist, did all of it, did my braces, did all of that, was also a lawyer. And when you walked into his office, you could pick the door. Right? I mean, this is small town stuff. People get to make choices. We just want to make sure you have the accurate information to make the proper choice that's best for your family. Thank you. I'd say as well, particularly on the cosmetic dentistry, that's the issue that I started to see in my district where you're seeing this proliferation of veneers and other sorts of medical decisions people are making to have their teeth look better. And that's kind of what I started to think about for my constituents is making sure that's a pretty big adjustment you might be making that's going to impact a lot of different aspects of your health. And we just want to make sure folks are going to the right professionals to do that. Absolutely. Thank you for that. Representative Preston. Thank you, Chair. Up in the UP, we're lucky to have general dentists just in of it by itself. I'm assuming that this is strictly an advertising aspect and that general dentists could still treat if the person chooses, their child or a senior, correct? Yeah, absolutely. It is an advertising issue, and it was never really an issue until this lawsuit in 2020 with Lara. And then they changed, they re-promulgated the rules. Representative Thompson. Thank you, Mr. Chair. So could a general dentist perform an extraction on a child if they chose to? Yeah, they certainly can. So what I've seen with my grandchildren, and we went through a ridiculous circle of this for a very long time, was the family dentist you go to, you get the x-rays and the checkup, and then if it came about that one of the kids had, they needed an extraction or a root canal, then they would say you need to go see a pediatric dentist. We don't do that here. The only thing we do at family dentistry is clean and do x-rays. So then you go to another place that's labeled as family dentistry, we treat kids, we keep kids healthy, happy, whatever. You go there, and then they say, no, we don't do that either because we don't have a pediatric dentist. And I went through this with two of the grandkids for probably about six months. And then the frustrating part was, and I'm hoping that this would help solve this problem, because it is a specialty field, until you get your first appointment with that pediatric dentist, you could wait six months for the appointment. So I had been waiting for a six-month appointment with the assumption that this was a pediatric dentist that could handle the situation, come to find out they couldn't do it either. So then I'm, like, in the office screaming and yelling that now I have to go find somebody else. And this went on for quite a while until I found an actual true pediatric dentist in Taylor that now I only take the kids to. So I hope that this would help with that as well. And then on the side of the cosmetic dentistry, we're seeing a lot of stuff on Instagram and TikTok and Facebook and Reels telling people that have had dentures or implants that they can get these things done in an hour, a day, and it seems a little far-fetched, but I think people are buying into that. So I'm hoping that there's some way that this, too, could address that. Thank you. Thank you for this. Any other questions from the committee? And then just to kind of piggyback a little bit on that, I think we, you know, exactly what you do. I don't have a newspaper really in my area that has advertisements, but we see advertisements pop up on the media that says specializing in. But then if you read further down, you go, you know, and most people are very quick in perception. They only hear or they read the main point. And what we're really working here and clarify to the committee is we really want to put these rules in place so that we're protecting the consumer, that when they make a choice, they know truly that they are receiving the proper care and the specialty service that they need for their children or adult, correct? Very good. All right. Seeing no other questions, I think the three of you, did you have? Yep, I'm going to read on to that person right now. And we have Dr. Betty, Michigan Association of Orthodontists on Zoom. Hopefully we can pull you up. Can you guys hear me? There we are. Thank you. We can hear you loud and clear. The floor is yours. Good morning, everybody. Thank you so much for taking the time. Thank you, Chair VanderWaal, for your interest and support in holding this hearing on this issue. My name is Dr. Josleen Betty. I am a board-certified orthodontist here in Michigan. I've been serving the southeast Michigan area for the past 15 years, ever since I graduated from the University of Michigan in 2010. I'm going to talk to you about orthodontics specifically here in a moment. I just wanted to go back and just clarify a couple things that I heard from questions from the committee. In no way are we saying general dentists can't do all of these things. They can, just like a family doctor can read an EKG and do all of these things. But there are many times and many instances you need to see a specialist, and it goes to patient consent. A patient has to understand who they're seeing in order to consent to getting treatment from that person. So when you're seeing an orthopedic surgeon, it could be true that you could see a general surgeon, but when you're seeing a specialist, you understand that they've done a little extra training in an area that allows them to be an expert in the treatment you're going to receive. And being able to say you're anything like a dental implantologist, a dental anesthesiologist, or a dental

thing that doesn't actually exist is extremely problematic. But I'll go to a couple of examples I have here in orthodontics. I mean, I would say in the past five to eight years with the invent of all of these companies that make orthodontics seem like such an easy thing to deliver treatment in, that we see a lot of practitioners who are not specialists deliver the treatment of orthodontics, especially with adults. What I've seen often is that patients often think orthodontists see children and general dentists advertise themselves as specialists in adult orthodontics, and they don't actually understand that orthodontists are the specialists for any age of orthodontics and the importance of seeing somebody who is board certified. In the past two years, I've had four patients transfer and start re-treatment with me. I would like to talk about one patient who came for a consult recently, and it was very jarring to see what was happening with this young adult patient. She was 19. She came in for a consult because she had been seeing what she thought was an adult orthodontic specialist, but this person was a general dentist in town, and her lower teeth were extremely loose. And so when anyone comes into an orthodontist's office, we do a set of records. It's the golden standard. We are, by license, supposed to take, as a specialist, a certain number of records, x-rays, et cetera. When I took her initial records just to take a look at what's happening, this patient had a large cyst in her lower jaw, and the teeth were being moved into the cyst. She had no idea she had a cyst. Her general dentist did not take any records before starting orthodontic treatment, any x-rays. He did take a scan. That's how you send the model over to the company. And because no due diligence was done on the front end, there was no knowledge that there was a cyst in the mandible, and now this person is going to lose her lower front teeth. I had to send her to an oral surgeon. I said, I have to stop right here. You have pathology in your jaw. We don't know if it's benign. We don't know what it is, but you need to go be seen. And she is 19 years old, and she has lost her lower front four incisors because she had a cyst in the bone that needed to be removed before orthodontic treatment was delivered. So that is just, she just could not understand why the website said specializes in adult orthodontics, even though everywhere else it said family dentist, dentist, dentist. It still had a tab that said orthodontics, and it said specializes in Invisalign, diamond provider in this company. So she just assumed that a residency or some type of specialty training had been done by this provider. So that's one example. Of the four that I am now retreating in town, all four of them thought they were being seen by a specialist. I had to explain that they were not being seen by a orthodontic specialist nor a board-certified orthodontist. And because one in particular was a very complicated case that appeared not complicated. If you're not trained enough to know what a complicated case can be when you look at certain x-rays to understand what the skeletal component is here. And she ended up having large open bites. And what that means is her back teeth no longer touched at all. They were actually so far apart, she could no longer chew her food. And so they ended up in my office, and it took me two years to undo everything that was done and re-get her into an occlusion where her teeth were now touching the way they should be in a proper bite. And so she could chew again. And again, a young adult, 19 years old, was in college. You know, they're young. A lot of young people look at social media, assume that the advertisement coming to them is real. And they often also ask, like Dr. Ledoux said, is this legal? And unfortunately, currently in Michigan, it is legal. And it's very hard to understand when I graduated 15 years ago in the state of Michigan, I had to take an additional orthodontic specialty license to be able to call myself an orthodontist in the state of Michigan. I mean, Michigan didn't care if I had taken the American Board of Orthodontics. I still had to take an additional test, go and take the test at the Capitol, and prove that I knew what I was doing after I had graduated residency, just like any doctor in any specialty has to go and do board certification to be able to say that they're licensed and boarded in the specialty. So, you know, these are just a few of many, many examples I could come up with today. I could talk to you about patients I see that I've sent to an oral surgeon, went to somebody else who wasn't an oral surgeon, and their implants were placed very poorly. I mean, there's many examples of how patients assume what they read is what they read, and that's correct information. So specialty laws are very important. And again, they go to patient consent. You can go anywhere you want. And certainly there are general dentists who do everything under the sun beautifully, but the patient should know who they're going to see. Thank you, doctor. I do know that we have a question from Representative Meerman. Sure. Thank you, Chair. So that general dentist, if they had said, I'm a general dentist that does orthodontic work, would that fit? No, their website said specializes in adult orthodontics and have treated 500 cases. And so because they say they specialize in adult orthodontics or they do adult orthodontics, when you say that, the patient or the consumer assumes they're seeing somebody who has done additional training. My understanding is that you can say I'm a general dentist who does XYZ, but when you don't have the laws there to say you cannot say I specialize in orthodontics, that renders the assumption that you are a specialist. So just say I'm a general dentist who also does orthodontic work? Right. You could say I do braces or I do clear aligner therapy. Most general dentists are not doing braces, but many do clear aligner therapy such as clarity, Invisalign, those kinds of things. Thank you. Are there any other questions? Any other questions? Excuse me. All of a sudden I have a little coughing spat here. Any other questions? Seeing no other questions, I want to say thank you very much for being here. Very good information, and I think the general consensus that I can read right now is this is an issue and we'll continue to work to make the right decisions here on the committee. So thank you for your time. Thank you again for your time to the House Committee and the Chair. Thank you. We have a few cards to read in. Not wishing to speak in support, Mandy Lentini, Council of Michigan Dental. Not wishing to speak in support, Bill Sullivan, Michigan Dental Association. And not wishing to speak in support, Kevin McKinney, Michigan Association of Orthodontists. Representative Beerline moves to excuse absent members. There being no objection, the motion prevails. There being no further business before the Committee of Health Policy, we will stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Joint Committee on Administrative Rules — Wednesday, October 29, 2025
