The joint committee on administrative rules will come to order. If you would like to testify on a rule set on the agenda today, please fill out a testimony card and you can turn it into any sergeant that's here or to our clerk. Will the clerk please take the roll for today's attendance? Chair Wozniak. Here. Representative Strongson. Here. Worts. Farhat. Brenda Carter. Senators Wino. Mayer. McMorrow. Tice. Here. Ronstadt. Mr. Chair, you have three members present. Thank you. No quorum. No quorum. Okay. As a reminder to the committee members, any action by the JCAR committee shall be by concurring majorities of the members from each house. This means that three representatives and three senators must vote in the affirmative on any motion for that motion to prevail. Today we'll be hearing testimony on JCAR rule set 25-61 from the Department of State Bureau of Elections. We had requested the Bureau to be here today, but they had a conflict in their schedule. But we're going to have another hearing next week, and they will attend that. So if you want to come back next week, you can. But I wanted to make sure everyone had an opportunity to testify, not get cut off by time limits, and make their issues known to the public. That's the main thing we want to do in JCAR is to make sure the public understands what's happening in government. Many times people say they don't know what's going on. This is supposed to be informative and not actually a debate, but a conversation of what's going to happen in government with new rule sets. So who would like to go first? Okay, Patrice. I'm sorry. I should have called you Ms. Johnson. Oh, that's fine. Johnson's such a good name. Even if it's got an E in it, right? Right. Yeah, thank you. Good morning, Chairman Wozniak, Senator Tice, and Representative Johnson. Thank you. I'm Patrice Johnson, Chair of Peer Integrity Michigan Elections, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to accurate and transparent elections. And I'm here because Rule Set 13 is unlawful, it's unworkable, and it's harmful to Michigan voters. First, these rules invent law out of thin air. Some other states do, but not Michigan. Yet Rule 13 demands direct observation and proof a voter is not a resident, unquote, while excluding every document, USPS, death certificates, obituaries, and online sources. And by extension, it would be excluding federal databases. Law MCL 168.512, which is the law, requires only a sworn affidavit. No state law says otherwise. Also, this violates the Administrative Procedures Act, MCL 24.233, proving a negative, because proving a negative is impossible. The rule isn't unclear, it's unworkable. The Secretary of State's office didn't interpret statute, it rewrote it. Second, Rule Set 13 makes voter list maintenance optional. Three times in Rule 2524, it includes language saying the clerk is not obligated. Rule 2525 uses the language chooses. Rule 168.2571 says not required. It encourages clerks to ignore cleanup and consider citizens' sources as unreliable. But HAVA mandates, HAVA, the Help America Vote Act, mandates accurate lists. 52 U.S.C. 21083A and Michigan Compiled Law 168.509R require the qualified voter file to be accurate. Michigan cannot make optional what federal and state law make mandatory. That's not discretion, that's defiance. Third, they impose a civil rights barrier by imposing unreasonable costs. R168.2562 and R168.2593 require separate notarization, which could cost around $15, and certified mail, around $8, per voter. So if you were to submit 100 challenges, that would be $2,300. Pricing citizens out of their MCL 168.512 right. This violates the Voter Rights Act, which is 52 U.S.C. 10301, and the 14th Amendment. Fourth, they violate federal law. R168.2522 allows 20-year retention, five times the National Voter Rights NVRA maximum of four years, which is U.S.C. 20507A4. Committee members, you have a clear authority under MCL 24.245A to reject rules that exceed statutory scope and violate law. These do both. If you cannot oversee the Secretary of State's rules, then who can? The final version is worse than the draft version was. It's more discretionary. It has more exclusions. It imposes higher costs. That's not good faith rulemaking. Michigan voters deserve mandatory maintenance, not if we feel like it. They deserve challenge processes that work, not $2,300 barriers per 100 challenges. And they deserve rules that follow the law and do not rewrite statutes. So I urge you to please reject Rule Set 13 in its entirety. Send it back. Tell the Secretary of State to comply with federal and state law, to respect statutory limits, and serve voters, not obstruct them. The law is clear. The violations are documented. Your authority is explicit. Please exercise it. Thank you for your time and service to Michigan. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Johnson. Are there any questions from the committee? Senator Tice. Thank you for your testimony. I appreciate it very much. So I was shocked when I got to the part that references the 20 years. Are you aware of any place else that's looking at 20-year lack of voting before you can consider removing somebody? No, that's against federal law. Federal law is not... Two federal terms. Two federal terms, that's right. So it's in...

blatant violation of federal law. I'm not aware of it being, I'm not aware of other states' laws, but that's so peculiar that I can't imagine it would be in any state law without federal challenges. I found it shocking, but I also think that that opens all of this up to legal question. It does. It makes you ask, you have to wonder why. Why would they want to keep voters on the rolls for 20 years? My perception of this rule set is that they defer to keeping someone on the voting roll almost no matter what. Well, you know, I think that's true, and the claim is voter suppression, but we should keep in mind that Michigan has same-day registration. So if somebody is inadvertently removed from the rolls, all they need to do is go vote because we have same-day registration. We don't have obstacles to registering in Michigan. Thank you. Any other questions? Me. Great. Okay. I've actually got two questions for you. Improper reasons for making a challenge. One of the reasons is the voter's inability to read, write, or speak English. Now, is there an assistance level at the voting place that can help a person that can't read, write, or speak English? I think there was some talk about mandating that. I don't believe that law passed due to the expense. But generally, the election inspectors and the clerks are all available to help people, whether they're disabled or have language impairment. Yeah, disabled is a different issue, I think. Right. Now, we've got, in this new rule set, a 30-day response from the challenged voter to respond to any notice that they get from the election people. But a couple weeks ago, we had testimony here that said that the voter information at the clerk level is to be destroyed, except for a thumb drive, which is to be returned to the state. To me, that seems in conflict, one with each other. Seven days to destroy everything at the local level, but then the challenger has 30 days to respond. Does that make sense to you? Yes. The 30 days, I believe, comes when a registration is challenged. The clerk sends out a letter to the challenged registrant saying, you need to come in and show your ID or whatever the issue is. And so they're allowing 30 days for that to be resolved. The other issue on the poll books, though, that's rule set 14, and that is a real serious issue because that isn't even asking, that is requiring seven days after certification to erase the poll books and making it very difficult for the public then to access the information through their local clerk. They'd have to get it through the state. And that eliminates redundancy. It eliminates the ability for citizens or anyone to oversee local elections and see how they compare to the state's database and to identify if there's manipulation going on at the state level, which is really important. It's very important to be able to verify that the local poll books matched what the QVF is showing. Speaking of the QVF, it's meant to be accurate. Do you think these proposed rules promulgate that to make it accurate? I think what they do is they encourage the clerks to see it as just discretionary rather than as mandatory. And I think it places a very heavy hand on citizen involvement, saying that citizens are not to be taken seriously and not to be considered reliable sources. So it cuts out citizen participation in cleaning the voter rolls. And right now folks in our organization, for example, partner very closely with the clerks. We bring in information and help them see that there's someone, here's a picture, here's the death certificate, here's a picture of the grave site, this person is deceased. Otherwise the clerk has to do all that research herself or himself. Did you have any opinion on reliable sources as far as the definitions? Well, yeah, reliable here is a real problem. It's considering any documentation basically as unreliable. In the draft version it named certain online sources as unreliable. Now it's basically saying unless you have firsthand knowledge, personal knowledge, it's unreliable basically. So it's putting a real burden on the clerk to show that she's not discriminating or violating any laws when she issues a challenge and checks into the whereabouts or whether a person's alive or dead. So I think it imposes a real high bar, an impossible bar, because you have to prove that a person is not in the state firsthand. How do you do that? You go stand in front of their empty house? I mean, you can't do it. So I think it violates federal law in that respect of the Administrative Procedures Act, which doesn't, it forbids you from having to prove an impossible. Ms. Johnson, do you have any questions? Could you speak a little bit to what your organization does and how can people contact your organization? The booklet you handed me, I haven't had a chance to look at it yet, but if you could speak to that. Sure. Well, Peer Integrity Michigan Elections was founded in 2021. Six of my husbands and my friends, we were sitting around a kitchen table and we decided we better get involved with elections. So it started very small. Now we're up to about 3,500 people around the state. And we're a 501c4, which is a nonprofit organization. We're nonpartisan. Our concern is that we want to be sure the elections are fair and transparent. So anytime we see something that obstructs citizen involvement or transparency, we're opposed to it regardless of party affiliation. And we could be reached at peerintegritymichiganelections.org, also at mifairelections.org. Great. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Johnson. Thank you. All right. Next we have Jeff Schaefer from Southeast Oakland Patriots. That's right. On my way here from Troy, Michigan, I left my prepared statement on the desk, but I have rapidly recreated it. Okay. I'm Jeff Schaefer. Thank you all for being here today. We oppose rule set number 13 as written. The personal knowledge criteria is just way too restrictive, and I would echo many of the points that Ms. Johnson just made. Public sources do tend to be reliable, like death records, national change of address. And we use that and other means, like the QVF output file, to do determinations if a person is still residing at the address that they live at. The past few years, citizens like Pure Integrity Michigan, Southeast Open Patriots, and Michigan Fair Elections have developed processes and systems that work, that have proven to be reliable and accurate over time. I would say that government entities also use these same resources to determine voter eligibility. For example, national change of address, the clerk can send something out, they get something back, so this person's moved, they do some maintenance. Ohio is another example of when a state does use outside sources to verify. Just recently, Secretary of State LaRose sent over 1,500 criminal referrals to their attorney, basically saying that these people are not eligible voters, yet somehow they did cast a ballot. Please look at it. Now, we had a case where the Secretary of State, Benson, sent to Nestle 16. Now, if Benson had used the same criteria used by, I would say, Secretary of State LaRose, I wonder how much more we would find. And again, accurate voter rolls is critical. There's two types of voter suppression. One is when you prevent a legitimate citizen from voting. The second one, and the one that civil rights also worked on tirelessly, is that when an ineligible ballot is cast that cancels the vote of a U.S. citizen, that is also voter suppression, and that is the fear that we have with the bloated voter rolls. And our efforts to clean these voter rolls is critical to the effort to make sure that our elections are free, fair, and accepted by the public. So I urge this committee to reject this rule set as overly restrictive.

Secretary of State and require her to follow Michigan and federal law. Thank you. Any questions? I do. But I wanted to follow up on your question, Senator Tice, regarding the 20-year requirement before you can take somebody off the rolls in this rule set. Yes. That is very off-putting. So somebody that is deceased or moved out of state, you know, I ran for Troy School Board back in 2021, or 23, excuse me, and I was walking with my walk list, knocking doors, and I would walk up to a house that had a Smith, a Thomas, and a Jones listed as being residents. I'd knock on the door, and a person named Sumit Patel would answer it, and she wasn't a U.S. citizen. And those three other entities' names were registered to vote at that address. So keeping excess names or registrations, I don't call them voters. I call them registrations. All right? Keeping excess registrations on the QVF just causes confusion and causes potential for harm. That would be my statement. Again, that just shows that you're maintaining sloppy records. Now, I came out of the internal control world in corporate America, and one of the things that, you know, you want to have is accurate records. And if you find sloppy record-keeping, you almost find problems in, and it's not criminal intent. It's just problems. So clean records equals clean elections equals confidence in the results of our election. Thank you very much for your testimony, Mr. Schaefer. So, yeah, oh, okay, Senator Tice. Thank you. To your point, in this rule set, the scenario that you just gave would be insufficient for this rule set to, well, you could tell the clerk, but then what the clerk would have to do as follow-up, according to this rule set, is the clerk would have to go to the house, and the clerk would have to have the conversation with the individuals at the house to verify that. The deputy clerk is not even authorized under this. During a house-to-house canvas, the clerk speaks to an individual who lives at the voter's registration address, and the individual informs the clerk that the voter has permanently moved. Nobody else from the clerk's office is allowed to do this, only the clerk himself or herself. I just find that. I think Janet Winfrey would take great exception to that rule if you would put it in front of her. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Schaefer. Thank you very much. I had personally thought that we would have a large crowd for these issues, as we did for the previous issues we've discussed. So the Bureau of Elections could not make it today, but we're planning a second hearing next week, and they should be here, at least we're planning on them being here. And if you wish to have an opportunity to speak, you will. Is there anybody else in the audience that wishes to speak? Yes, ma'am. Just hit the red button and go ahead. Good morning. I'm Amanda Love, a community organizer and candidate for Michigan Secretary of State. I'm opposing the new voter registration rules, specifically R-168-251 and 168-256, the personal knowledge requirement for voter challenges, not mandated by MCL 168.512, restricts community members from using reliable data to flag ineligible registrations, stifling civic engagement. By barring sources like USPS records or online databases from qualifying as personal knowledge, the Secretary of State creates a barrier to public participation in election oversight, a right enshrined in Michigan's law. The rules' vague language also risks inconsistent enforcement, potentially disenfranchising communities who rely on collective vigilance to ensure fair elections. Additionally, the removal of specific unreliable sources like checkmyvote.org in R-168-252 reduces transparency, leaving our clerks and voters guessing. I urge the SOS to eliminate the personal knowledge standard and restore clear, statute-based guidelines to empower communities. Our Secretary of State, who is currently running for governor, should be focused on restoring confidence in our elections, not pushing more bureaucracy that undermines it. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Love. You've appeared before us. Any question? No. All right. Well, thank you. Thank you. Okay. If we didn't read any cards in, they'll be included in the minutes of today's meeting anyway. Senator Tice moves to excuse absent members. There being no objection, the motion prevails. Well, we can't really vote on that. We don't have a quorum. Some of the rules we have with this committee are very complicated. So hopefully in the future, we'll be able to do something with affecting the rules. So for the better, I hope. With that being said, this meeting is adjourned. Thank you.

title: Natural Resources and Agriculture 25-10-28
transcript:
Good afternoon and welcome to the Senate Committee on Natural Resources and Agriculture. Chair, will you please call the roll? I'm sorry, I'm calling it to order and will you please call the roll? Chair Schink? Here. Senator Cherry? Senator Singh? Senator Bolyankee? Senator Daly? Here. Senator Victory? Present. Senator Hoidinga? Here. Madam Chair, you have five members present. There is a quorum. Thank you. I'll entertain a motion to adopt the committee minutes from September 9, 2025. So moved by Senator Bolhanke. Without objection, committee minutes are adopted. Today we're taking testimony only on Senate Bill 140 and Senate Bill 141 introduced by Senator Irwin. Welcome to the committee, Senator Irwin. Will you please come up and explain what your bills do? Sorry. It's okay. Sorry. Absolutely. Thank you, Chair Schink and other members of the committee for your time today. If it is okay, I will just run through both bills very briefly and thank you for the time and attention today. So there are two bills in front of the committee today that I've introduced. Senate Bill 140 represents a concept that I've been working on for almost 10 years now. Back when I was a House member and I was looking at the state budget, I recognized that the state general fund, the taxpayers of Michigan, were subsidizing the oil and gas industry to the tune of about $4 million a year. And the reason why this happens is because way back when this system was set up, the legislature created something called the surveillance fee. And the surveillance fee was meant to cover the costs of the program at DNR, now EGLE, that manages the permits and the well closures and all of that for the oil and gas industry. Now this fee was originally set with a cap of 1%, and then the department was supposed to align the fee on an annual basis to make sure that the costs of the program were covered, but increase the fee during years where costs were going up and decrease the fee during years when there's enough money. Well, unfortunately, what's happened due to changes in the oil and gas industry and due to the march of time, it's been decades since these policies were initially set forth, that 1% doesn't raise nearly enough to support the program anymore. Our program has been, our surveillance fee has been at the 1% cap for many, many years. It's never been reduced because there's, once again, not enough money coming in from the 1% fee to cover the costs that the legislature initially intended these fees to cover. So what my bill does is my bill just simply says, let's increase the cap on that surveillance fee from 1% to 2%. Let that fee float just as it always has at a level necessary to raise the revenue needed to cover the cost of the program so that at the end, Michigan taxpayers are no longer subsidizing the fossil fuel industry here in our state and that they're just simply paying the costs of the system that permits their use and permits their access to often public lands here in the state of Michigan. So that's the goal there is to just realign that fee with its original intent. The second bill that's before you is Senate Bill 141. This bill is meant to codify best practices in oil and gas drilling by reducing waste and pollution. We know that methane has much more powerful climate changing effects than CO2, and that's why I think there's been a little bit more attention to trying to control methane releases. Also, here in Michigan, we've made a policy decision to lean more towards natural gas or methane for electricity generation. And so the impetus and the reason, the rationale to get more serious about reducing waste in this system is even greater now that we're relying on it so much more. So once again, what this legislation does is it simply codifies best practices in oil and gas. It limits when and how firms can do flaring. It just generally makes an effort to reduce the amount of methane that is leaking at the wellhead or in the system. And the reason we're doing that, once again, is to reduce waste, to reduce pollution, and to reduce the impact that we're having on the climate. Now, the best drillers, the best operators in our state are already doing all this stuff. And in fact, in 2024, there was a federal rule that was finalized that implemented all the sort of standards that I'm proposing in this bill. But I think that if anybody's watching the federal government, we're probably expecting anything that puts controls on fossil fuel companies to be eliminated. And I think that this new rule implementing best practices for oil and gas drillers is probably one of those things that's on the chopping block. So I thought this was a good idea last year to codify what was already going forward at the EPA level. It's an even better idea now that the federal government is turning its back on clean air. Thank you, Senator. Thank you, Senator. We were talking about, you were talking about the subsidies. And so the oil and gas industry does a lot for Michigan, the amount of people they employ, the trust fund. I believe they do pay their fair share. Let's compare that to the subsidies of wind and solar. So if we're discussing subsidies, you brought up the $4 million, which I would kind of dispute for other reasons. But do you know how many subsidies we give to wind turbines and solar panels? I suspect that there are probably some that I don't know of. Like, for instance, when I talk to residents, oftentimes they don't know that they're paying about $2,900 a year federally to support the fossil fuel industry through their federal taxes. A lot of people don't know that.

People don't understand just how subsidized the fossil fuel industry is. And so while we have hydrocarbons here in the state of Michigan that probably should and are definitely going to be liberated to heat homes and run industry and whatnot, and while I'm appreciative that those oil and gas companies are willing to give the state 12% of the value that they pull from public lands and are willing to contribute to the Michigan Natural Resources Trust Fund and all the great things that happen from those revenues, I think that's good. I'm not proposing that we stop that. What I'm proposing is that while these companies are coming into Michigan, pulling up often public resources and selling them for profit, that at a minimum we shouldn't be subsidizing them through the permit program. The legislature decades ago said let's set this fee so that it just supports the costs of facilitating this industry in the state of Michigan. And I'm simply proposing that we realign this fee so that it continues to support the costs. Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Senator, for your presentation. Two small questions on Senate Bill 141. So first, what I thought I heard you say is essentially these regulations are already in place, and so this would just be codifying them into Michigan law. Is that correct? I think that that is substantially correct. I've had some conversations with folks at the department and in the oil and gas industry who are saying like, oh, this one here we think is a little different. We certainly designed it in an effort to codify the federal rules, but I think you might hear from some other folks that there are some very small variances. That was the intent. Okay. And then the other question is I'm just reading through the analysis, and I'm just confused. One piece it says it bans flaring, but then another piece it says flaring or other method approved by the department is an option. So can you explain that to me? I haven't read the analysis that you're looking at, so I'm not sure I can explain that, but I can tell you what's in the bill. The bill allows the department to put additional regulations on flaring, but it doesn't ban it. It says that flaring should be used in responsible ways, and sometimes that is the best way to deal with fugitive gas on a wellhead is my understanding, right? And so this would just really say let's codify those best practices so that the flaring happens when it should happen and it doesn't happen when it shouldn't. And so you did make a statement that I do agree with. You made a statement that we've come a long way. So oil and gas has come a very long way with technology with addressing emissions. But to the point, the federal government is very clearly going to try to set out new guidelines. I have checked their website to see have you updated yet, and they're working on this. So why would we want to jump the gun on this if some federal standards could trump everything? A very chaotic treatment towards industry across the board, and particularly with respect to oil and gas, over the coming decades. We've already seen the last administration say we want to move forward on some of these pollution prevention moves. Now we're seeing this administration saying we want to walk away from these pollution prevention moves. What I'm saying is that here in Michigan, it will be a service to our citizens, and I frankly think it will be a service to industry as well if we have reasonable but strong standards for protection of the environment, if we have reasonable but strong standards to reduce energy waste. I think that will mean that the best operators in Michigan who are already complying with these rules and better will continue to thrive. And so we're meeting, to be clear to the public, you're meeting a 95% quota here, so it's a lot for the emission standard. And so I don't know if there's a penal code for this, but it does say an operator failing to meet the 95% emission standard is subject to a $100,000 fine and can revoke the operator's permit. Is there any fear of if we're revoking permits? Do we have any fear? I can tell you now that the grid is run with oil and gas, a reliable and affordable energy source. And so is there any fear if some of these permits are pulled and we have a deficit, are the wind turbines and solar panels going to operate our grid fully? Do you understand what I'm asking? I did until the very end of it. I did until the very end of it. So, look, there is an element in this proposal that would give the department the authority to issue fines for people who can't meet these reasonable standards. But these reasonable standards were set at a level not to completely eliminate pollution, not to put the oil and gas industry in a position where they were asked to meet standards that they can't make, but rather we're asking them to meet standards that are very attainable. And in fact, just last week we were talking with the department about how, okay, let's make sure that we define this very, very carefully because we don't want folks to think that they have to keep reducing and that they're going for this very vanishing parabolic tiny amount of emissions. No, we're saying that let's meet these broad, attainable standards that were set at the federal level already. And even if the federal government is going to cast asunder these clean air protections, we can still require drillers in Michigan to observe best practices to minimize their waste of energy and to minimize their damage to our environment. So I have a question, and one of the things that I'm wondering is I have heard that Michigan's regulations around oil and gas drilling and also the fees that we charge are much lower than Texas, which we think of as an oil state. And I'm wondering if you have, because I couldn't find it online, any comparisons to Texas. I mean, I couldn't find it online because I don't have internet right now. Chair Shank, I have heard this as well, but much like I think some of the more technical questions that others could ask me, you know, when you get sort of past the high level here, I don't really know. So I've heard that same rumor, and, you know, it may be a situation like it is with many of our environmental and conservation policies here in Michigan, where there was a time back in the 50s where we had this real bipartisan meeting of the minds around protecting the Great Lakes, protecting clean water, protecting clean air. And Michigan was doing really great things with conservation and with wetlands, and we were leading the nation during those years. And then, you know, during the 90s we started stepping away from being a leader on environmental protection. I'd like to see us get back into that leadership position. That's why you see me working on things like bluter pay and things like microplastics and things like trying to implement best practices for oil and gas drilling in Michigan. There's no reason we should let these oil and gas drillers waste energy and unnecessarily pollute our environment when there are attainable standards that we know they can meet and that we're already in federal rules. Thank you. I think it seems clear that if other states do charge more or they do have stricter regulations, that it's not shutting down their oil and gas industries and our oil and gas industry should be just fine. Senator Daly. Thank you, Senator. Wouldn't it be, I mean, you probably can't answer this question. I don't know, but I'm going to ask you anyway, but probably the oil companies, when they come up here, it must be a reason why they're not capturing that product now. Is it cost prohibitive? Is it too expensive to capture it and going to drive the price up so much that it doesn't make sense? I mean, I think you're right that that's a better question for the oil and gas drillers, right? I suspect, just my intuition, is that when you're thinking about that wellhead, you know, it's probably more expensive to design it and to equip it in such a way where it is more sealed. And it's probably less expensive to do less. Like, for instance, I know, you know, Michigan has rules for how deep the concrete casing has to go that are different than other states. Well, if you're required to go deep in, it's going to be more expensive. So I suspect it's an issue like that, but I don't really know. Thank you. Anyone else? All right. Thank you, Senator Irwin. I would now like to invite the following people to testify. We'll go one at a time. Dylan Gephardt, sorry, Legislative Liaison, and Adam Weigand, Director of the Geologic Resources Management Division of EGLE. Thank you for coming to talk to us today. Thank you, Chair Schenck and members of the committee for the opportunity to testify on Senate Bills 140 and 141. I wanted to introduce myself first as EGLE's new Legislative Liaison. My name is Dylan Gephardt. Looking forward to working with you all on this committee in different capacities. To my right is Geologic Resource Management Division Director Adam Weigand, who's going to provide some testimony on the bills. We are no position at the time and hope to eliminate some concerns as well as efforts that we're currently making to reduce methane emissions. An important topic, and we look forward to getting into it more with you today. Thank you, Chair Schenck and committee members all for the opportunity to discuss our surveillance fee. I'd like to give a little history and some realities about funding mechanisms for regulatory programs.

For over three decades, Michigan's surveillance fee covered the revenue necessary to administer Michigan's oil and gas regulatory program. But around 2015, due to declining production and extremely low oil prices, the point came at which the 1% no longer paid for the program. The new normal is that the current fee pays for about half of the revenue necessary for the regulatory program. All funding mechanisms really have strong and weak points, and Michigan's surveillance fee weakness really comes towards the end of the program, where you still have many wells on production, but with declining production rates and especially commodity prices. When you couple that with commodity prices, insufficient revenue situation is created and it potentially gets worse. The department was, as noted, before the legislature multiple times explaining this shortfall and weakness of the funding mechanism, and the program was supported by a few one-time general fund appropriations, and ultimately an ongoing appropriation was secured for the program. When I say that all funding programs have their weaknesses, a contrast is programs that have high fees up front. I have counterparts in other states where hydraulic fracturing came on, and they were very proud of really, really high permitting fees and a la carte, you know, whatever you needed, you would pay for each of those things. The problem is that they are experiencing now is they got really high fees up front, but as noted, these wells go on decline, and then they tend to produce for really long times. So some of those other funding mechanisms all have some weak spots. So the next consideration related to this is a matter of equity. Senate Bill 140 certainly seeks to fund our program, and for that I'm appreciative. The nature of commodity prices can cause fluctuations. We're even seeing oil prices drop right now, and 2026 prices are anticipated to be lower. Even a full doubling of this fee may not be fully enough to fund our program. In the past, their oil and gas fund, when there was sufficient revenue from the 1%, we had an overstatement of a probe, and it allowed us to keep that $7 million fund balance and at times build it a little bit, use it to address severe compliance issues, and maintain our IT systems as an important part of transparency. I'll note that just department IT costs have nearly doubled. Our ability to keep tools out there and put data out that are important for industry, environmental organizations, and folks. So when I talk about equity of the solution, the current bill, I would note that the fees on gas storage wells, for instance, are $20 apiece per year. Right now, out of our 15,000 wells we regulate, about 2,000 of these wells are gas storage wells, and they pay a $20 well per year fee, which generates about $45,000, $50,000. When you contrast that with that's 10% of our wells, and they likely should be in the neighborhood of producing about $600,000 to $700,000 worth of revenue, it calls into the question of that equity. And in fact, in our mineral well program, where there is annual regulatory fees, those fees are closer to $200 to $300 per well. Further to the equity standpoint, there's wells that are shut in or temporarily abandoned. They still require permitting, or I mean oversight, inspection. They still may leak, and they contribute no revenue towards the surveillance fee. I would note that in the 2026 appropriations bill, appropriation boilerplate was put in that charged the department with initiating stakeholder engagement to address this matter, talk about it, find solutions for the funding of the oil and gas program, and presumably that would come out with a more multi-pronged approach than the simple doubling of this fee. I would like the committee to know that having run the program with the general fund, we've been appreciative of that. It allows us to do other things as well, flexibility to deal with those fluctuating commodity prices, low periods of production, such as that we saw in the COVID years and we may be seeing now with some lower oil prices. It's allowed us to support the upper peninsula geologic repository in Gwynn and support this division that provides a lot of unique geologic experience. Our geologic hazards, our group is very unique, and we often get calls about odors. If it's got a rotten egg odor or a petroleum odor, we have to go. Whether it ends up being oil and gas industry or not, because petroleum odors can be explosive, H2S orders can be concerning as well. So we go. Mystery pipes sticking out of the ground, we go. They might be just a hand-driven point, but we look into those things. I would also note that our team carried out over 24,000 inspections last year. Finally, some states such as New York, they do fund their programs with general fund, and we've heard the sentiment in the past when we were fully funded by the surveillance fee that it's like the fox watching the hen house because they pay our full salary. So I've personally enjoyed being a recipient of partial general funding for the reasons noted. I don't think it's a problem either way. Like when we were accused of being the fox watching the hen house in the past, I mean, our program staff have a lot of integrity, so I don't think it's an issue either way, but that is out there. So those are kind of the considerations that I would like the committee to just consider in their deliberations, and certainly we're talking with the sponsor about with respect to this bill. Thank you. Any questions? Okay, thank you. Next, we have Dr. Barry Ray, professor emeritus of environmental policy, U of M Ford School. Did you want us to come back to talk about 141? Oh, I'm sorry. I thought you – no, no, just stay there. I know I'm long-winded, but – No, no, no, no. I thought that you were standing up and walking away and that you were done. No, I just didn't know if you wanted to talk about 141. Okay, you were just waiting for me to say go ahead and talk about 141. All right, thank you for the opportunity to talk about 141. Thank you for reminding me that you were here. So I'd just like to note that the division, the department, we're supportive of measures to reduce fugitive emissions from oil and gas sites. We do a lot to press industry through our active well management and cooperative efforts to reduce leaks, reduce emissions, find solutions, all of those things. The industry was charged with taking big steps on new and modified sources in around 2012 with the passage of Quad OA. But our division has pushed folks towards beneficial use of associated gas solutions for other than flaring and the use of high-efficiency combustion devices. Michigan's oil and gas history is kind of interesting. It's over 100 years old. We've been regulating it very closely for 100 years. We know even prior to that quite a lot about where the wells were before we started permitting them. And I guess just to educate a little bit in the oil and gas industry, so you have some of these old, old wells. They're scattered around Michigan. We call them marginal production, if you will. They're not newer wells. When you have a big oil play like you had in the Albion Scipio in the 50s or you had in the 70s and 80s the Niagara Reef play or in the 90s and early 2000s the Antrim play, there was aggressive upstream and midstream gathering of any associated gas from those oil wells to go to sites. But we still have a lot of oil and gas sites that are not associated with those big plays, and they're spread out, and it's very costly to run pipelines and gather that gas. And with the EPA assumptions, I think they overly assumed in states like Michigan that you could bring that gas to sale from all these other sources, that it was economically and technically feasible. So I think it's just important to note that what we're dealing with is a lot of these sources and how it organically started. Some of these wells have some casing head gas that does vent. It's nowhere near sufficient to run a flare, probably run a low-pressure gas lantern in all seriousness. You have wells that have flares that there's not sufficient gas there to do beneficial things like run lease equipment, run compressors or generators to generate air to replace pneumatic devices, all those things, right? So sometimes, as the senator noted, there is instances where you do need to flare. So it's important to note that just Michigan in many of these wells, the volume's not there. And in fact, you'd be setting up a propane tank in some instances to run 24-hour to destroy a small amount of gas in some of these. We don't see that our

Emission factors in Michigan are consistent with some of the other numbers given to other states and may not represent our geology or our low gas oil well ratio or account for the low density of wells that we have. So in other states, we have high densities of wells in high density population areas, not exactly what we see here in Michigan. As part of our orphan well program, we've tested all of our orphan wells and found the emissions from those wells to be very low. But through the methane emission program, we are going to do a study. We have $500,000 of IIJA money to look at the actual emission factors from marginal wells. And I think that's going to help us a great deal understand the extent of this issue. Having laid that background, as noted, the Biden administration passed a methane rule that would have captured these existing sources. It would have required states to do a state plan. We started working on that. The Trump administration now has put those up for reconsideration. We don't know exactly where those plans and those requirements will ultimately land, but we do think that there will be something there. In the previous comments that I made to the US EPA on the Biden rule, I acknowledged the need for this fugitive methane emission reduction. I cautioned them on some of the short compliance timeframes they have here. I appreciate in the senator's bill, the newer introduced version is that it charges the department with creating administrative rules and extending us the trust to create performance schedules and compliance schedules such that might meet actual conditions here in Michigan and operators' ability to comply. Because we have a concern that policy could result in a lot of uneconomic wells all at once. Our office continues to push the industry to plug uneconomic wells and to bring them into regular production. I can't state how much working with companies on an annual basis towards compliance schedules and towards reducing emissions is making a difference. I had frustration with the EPA regulations that they did not adequately appreciate, I guess, the technical and economic implications of having to retrofit these sites, assess the sites, and comply with the methane rules. Again, I appreciate that the senator has extended trust in this to allow the department to do that piece, to review the actual technical data associated with wells and what's technically and economically feasible. So I guess I'll skip ahead here. I feel like I'm saying a lot of words today. The state policy may still be somewhat premature, as I said, related to the federal. I do think that there's some simple changes to the bill that would address and provide clarity around the reductions. It should be better clarified as to what is meant by volatile organic compounds and how they'll be reduced because the term VOC can mean a lot of things. In the supervisor of wells orders, which I've issued of late, I've used the federal language that talks about requiring flaring be done with combustion devices that are 95 percent efficient for destruction of methane and VOCs. There's an opportunity to slightly change the bill language instead of requiring a 95 percent reduction in methane and VOCs, which does not recognize the efforts and gains of industries already made since those QUAD-O-A regulations came into effect. So in other words, the bill would technically require getting 95 percent of the 5 percent that may be left, which may not be technically feasible. So instead, the regulation could require the reduction of methane and VOCs by any number of means that are specified in the bill that any capturing of the gas or destruction of the gas would operate on a 95 percent efficiency. And perhaps the threshold of just 40 tons per year of methane because adding the VOC without clarification really clouds the ability to comply. So whatever the solutions are, ultimately we look forward to continuing to work with the sponsor. Just at this time, not able to take a position on the bill. I think it needs some benefit from some work. Thank you. Colleagues, questions? Senator Hoitinga. I do appreciate you put me at ease a little bit because you're acknowledging the volatility of the industry and how vague some of this language is. And it does give you a lot of room to, I don't know, do good or bad things there. And so some of this I feel like should be pulled in, but I cannot stress enough that we should wait until the federal government has made some decisions and handed them down to help guide you in things for compliance. So I appreciate the acknowledgement that there is some vagueness and some work needed and the volatility because I do feel like this could potentially hurt some of our oil and gas industry. And we need them. So thank you. Thank you. I am wondering, as we're talking about this, and it sounds like you have some communication with your counterparts in other states, if you know, if you have a hand, any knowledge of what some of the other states are charging as a percentage of value. So, like, if Michigan's fee is 1% of value, I believe that Texas's is, because now I have some numbers, that Texas might be 4.6% of the value of the oil and gas that comes out of a well. And are there any other states that you can highlight? Yeah, I'd have to look into that to see. I can look at the IOGCC. They have a summary of state regs, and they may have the summary piece on how state regulatory programs are funded, but I'm not able to speak offhand how that relates, how the Texas Railroad Commission funds their program in entirety. I suspect it's a combination. Thank you. Any other questions? All right. Thanks so much. Thank you. Next, we have Dr. Barry Rabe, Professor Emeritus of Environmental Policy at the U of M Ford School, who is going to be on Zoom. Good afternoon, everyone. I appreciate the opportunity to have a conversation about these matters with you today. I'm sorry I cannot be in person. I'm actually in Canada. I'm a visiting scholar at the University of Waterloo at this point in time. For background, I have worked in the area of methane mitigation policy in the U.S. and globally for about 15 years, including a lot of direct involvement with state governments, both executive and legislative branch leaders in states like Oklahoma and North Dakota, very large producers, as well as smaller ones, and then others around the world and even into Canada. So I'll try to sort of draw from some of that and just in my time make a few very broad generalizations. First and foremost, this is, has been, and is all likelihood will remain a state governance issue. This issue has a long history, longer than we might realize. The Texas legislature, which has been discussed a few times already, first began to turn to the issue of methane loss from oil and gas production in 1877. And I'm not sure that there has ever been a legislative session in Texas, including the one recently concluded in Austin, where this has not emerged as some issue. Among the questions and issues that emerged over time is waste and loss of revenue. That state does have a very high extraction tax or sequence of extraction taxes and royalties as well as fees. Some of those have gone long into trust funds established at the point that Texas came into the union and fund higher ed and K through 12 education in the state. But the point being that historically this has been state based, and while I very much appreciate the points that were raised in this conversation about the federal level, while I do think if we were talking in 2023 or 2024 about a possible expansion of the federal role, all the indications in the months of 2025 suggest that that probably is not going to materialize. The new federal fee or charge on methane statutorily approved in 2022 has been frozen, will not begin until 2034 at the earliest. Not only is the Environmental Protection Agency freezing all of the new Biden era regulations that have been noted, but all the comments that I have seen from EPA Administrator Zeldin or leaders in the different subunits suggest that they are going to look to dramatically reduce the federal structure and scope of these regulations and delegate much more of this into state hands. As you also may know, there are some real possibilities that methane reporting on a national level will be changed quite significantly. And if we look at the staffing arrangements within the EPA, the area of broadly defined methane is one where staffing losses and cuts is just really quite large. It is a very different entity than it was one year ago. So while it is hard to know with any degree of certainty,

I know a number of your counterparts in other oil and gas producing states have been dealing with the likely reality that this will be a state-driven initiative for some time. And so then we do need to think about what the state of Michigan should be doing in a situation where it will continue to be the predominant source of governance and leadership. The concerns that have been raised historically in this area, of course, and these have already been discussed, the permanent loss of a non-renewable natural resource and waste issues and loss issues in terms of severance tax revenue, in some cases other forms of fees and the like, but also air quality and public health concerns. And then the fact that methane is a global warming super pollutant. About one third of the global warming we have experienced to date comes not from carbon dioxide but from methane. And globally, oil and gas and coal production is a dominant source, certainly here in North America as well. With that in remaining time, I just want to comment briefly on the two bills, 141 and 140. In many respects, these square a lot with what we have seen in terms of individual best practice emerging in a great number of states over the last, I would say, 10 or 15 years. If we look at Wyoming, if we look at Colorado, if we look at Pennsylvania, other states that produce a lot of oil and gas, but particularly in this case, gas or associated gas through oil production, some of the basic frameworks here in terms of discouraging the flaring activity, the 95% rate actively encouraged. There's quite a bit of statutory text about encouraging gas capture. These are things that we have begun to see increasingly over the last decade or so as a great many states have gone back to look at this. And to be clear, I don't think the 95% standard is particularly ambitious. Generally, industry best practice measure around the world is 98% is the minimum for excellence. And if we really look around the world at other jurisdictions, in Canada, for example, in Norway, in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, they have flaring rates that are very, very low in comparison to the United States. And when we look especially at atmospheric release data, methane emissions intensity scores, the US actually has a hard time to keep up with. The US performance has been uneven. Generally, some huge steps using relatively simple technology for gas capture, disclosure kinds of provisions, subsidies and incentives to move in this direction, but it is highly uneven. The World Bank reports that American flaring has been roughly stable. But in the Bakken region, which includes North Dakota, flaring increased 27% last year. And so these issues really do not go away. And so I see the bill, although I don't have time to go into all the nuance and detail of it, as in general consistent with what we are seeing in a number of states that kind of cut across the large and small production, as well as partisan control of the state kinds of issues. On the issue of fees, and this is always a really interesting issue in question, how you set these fees or for that matter, revenues that might come from severance or production taxes or other sorts of things. I would say generally Michigan is sort of in the middle of the pack, but on the low end, I've actually looked at these numbers quite a lot in terms of where these fees have and are being set. And here I would just note that some of the things that in other production states that the expectation was going into this year, that a lot of federal funds would be transferred to states to cover administrative costs, technical costs, working in collaboration with the industry, even on things like reporting or some of the kinds of episodes that can often emerge. States are actively looking at their equivalent fees and in some cases talking about expanding them. There have actually been two major initiatives in Texas just within the relatively short legislative session to begin to do that. And so I don't want to suggest that there's a magic formula to this or a magic level, but the idea of substantial federal support declining, states have chronically, production states have had a hard time attracting and keeping good employees, routinely in production states, staff who come initially into an agency can be hired away by business and the whole question, the industry and the question of maintaining excellence in the state regulatory capacity and support capacity is a really significant one. And so to me, some changes in the formula here or the fee structure are certainly what we're seeing in this legislative session and other states. And in some cases, the things that have been done over the last four to 10 years in the majority of other states. I'm mindful of time and so I will close there, but I do thank you for the opportunity to say a few words with you this afternoon. Thank you. Colleagues, any questions? Dr. Rabe, we don't seem to have any questions, but I do want you to know that you have several of your former students here in this room and they all say hi. Thank you. Next, we have Dr. Kelsey Billsback, principal scientist of PSE Healthy Energy, who will be talking to us from Zoom. Good afternoon, Chairman and committee members, and thank you for the opportunity to testify. My testimony is most relevant for Senate Bill 141. My name is Dr. Kelsey Billsback. I'm a principal scientist at PSE Healthy Energy, an independent scientific research institute. Our mission is to generate science-based energy and climate solutions that protect public health and the environment. And today I will summarize three key insights drawn from over 10 years of research conducted at PSE examining the air quality impacts and health risks of gas systems. The first insight is that hazardous air pollutants are nearly always present in natural gas throughout the supply chain. Hazardous air pollutants are chemicals identified by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency because they are known or suspected to cause cancer, neurological harm, or other serious health effects. A well-known example is benzene, a confirmed human carcinogen with no safe level of exposure according to the World Health Organization. To understand how often these pollutants occur in natural gas, PSE has compiled the most extensive speciated gas composition database in the U.S., and it includes over 8,000 upstream samples reported to state regulators, hundreds of samples from interstate pipelines and transmission infrastructure, and direct samples collected by our team in 14 U.S. cities. We have found that hazardous air pollutants persist across the natural gas supply chain, with the most prevalent being hexane, benzene, ethylbenzene, toluene, and xylene. In May, we published our upstream gas composition data in Environmental Research Communications. Because SB 141 focuses on wells, this is the most relevant data set. Across 11 states and 19 oil and gas basins, more than 99% of samples contained at least one hazardous air pollutant, and over 97% contained benzene. A second key insight is that methane emissions events from oil and gas infrastructure can release hazardous air pollutants at concentrations that can pose health risks to nearby communities. In August, our team released the Methane Risk Map, a nationwide web tool that uses methane emissions data, gas composition information, and regulatory-grade air quality models to estimate the air quality impacts and human health risks of large methane emissions events, or super emitter events. And these are defined as events releasing more than 100 kilograms per hour of methane. To date, we have modeled 1,394 upstream methane emissions events. And of these, our models indicate that 99.7% of events resulted in benzene air concentrations exceeding California's short-term health benchmark of 8 parts per billion for benzene. And these are levels associated with elevated health risks. On average, the exceedance extended up to 2 miles from the methane emission source. The third insight is that policies that successfully reduce methane emissions will likely lower hazardous air pollutant concentrations, protecting the public health of workers in nearby communities. If Senate Bill 141 successfully reduces methane emissions, our research suggests that this policy would reduce hazardous air pollutant emissions, lowering health risks, particularly for residents living near oil and gas infrastructure. This is important given that Michigan has an estimated 297,000 people living within one mile of an active oil or gas well. In closing, the scientific evidence is clear. Natural gas emissions nearly always contain hazardous air pollutants. Methane emissions events can impact air quality and pose health risks to nearby communities. And policies that successfully reduce methane emissions can likely protect public health. I'd be happy to answer any questions. Thank you, colleagues. Any questions? Thank you for your testimony. I found

on the fact that the methane emissions can impact areas up to two kilometers. Shocking. I didn't realize that. So thank you very much, among the other things that you said. Next, we're going to move to Carly Knott, Energy and Climate Policy Manager of MEC, who is testifying in person. Thank you. We're glad you're here. You can start whenever you're ready. The red light, yes. Okay, now it's on. Hello. Hi, Chair Schink and other members of the committee. My name is Carly Knott, and I'm the Energy and Climate Policy Manager for Michigan Environmental Council. I'm here today to testify in favor of SB 140 and 141 because these bills outline common sense solutions that should be implemented here in Michigan. I just want to start by saying I'm proud of our state for setting robust and achievable climate goals, both to achieve economy-wide carbon neutrality by 2050 and to have our utilities powering our state with 100% clean energy by 2040. Reducing our statewide emissions is crucial to combating climate change and for reducing pollution in the air, especially in overburdened communities. And so far, we've made great progress in transitioning away from high-emitting coal plants in Michigan, partially due to the rise of natural gas. And while natural gas emits half the CO2 levels of coal, methane emissions from oil and gas wells are still significantly contributing to Michigan's overall greenhouse gas emissions. This is important because methane has 80 times the warming power of CO2 over the initial 20-year time span. So that means that the best way to reduce the impact on the climate in the short term is to better control these methane emissions. In addition to the harms to the climate, oil and gas wells, as we just heard, are also contributing to air pollution from the release of volatile organic compounds, or VOCs, which are co-released with methane during venting, flaring, and general leaks. VOCs can also interact in the atmosphere to form ozone, which has a number of documented health detriments, including the exacerbation of respiratory conditions such as asthma, increased hospital visits, and premature death, particularly among children, the elderly, and individuals with pre-existing health conditions. So for communities living near oil and gas wells, including many rural and lower-income Michiganders, reducing these emissions will mean cleaner air, fewer hospital visits, and a better quality of life. Frontline communities have long borne the burden of industrial pollution without reaping many of the benefits, so we believe that these bills would take a step toward correcting that imbalance by holding all operators accountable for maintaining equipment that prevents pollution at the source. I also wanted to point out that there is an economic argument to be made by capturing the methane that gets released. During the extraction phase, the process would become more efficient and more of that gas would be able to be used as energy. With natural gas prices becoming higher this year and reasonable costs for capture, operators could stand to profit from improving these practices. Similar common-sense standards are already being developed and implemented in other leading states, such as Colorado, New Mexico, and Pennsylvania. These states have shown that methane regulations are feasible and cost-effective, with operators bringing more gas to market rather than wasting it through leaks or flaring. But since we know resale may not always be the best solution for capturing that methane, the bill also provides flexibility for operators to either route gas to a sales line, use it on-site, reinject it, or otherwise capture it and flare under limited circumstances. So these readily available and cost-effective solutions exist to cut methane now, and it's an opportunity that we can't afford to miss. As the committee reviews these bills and EGLE develops implementing rules, we would encourage strong provisions for leak detection and repair of equipment and want to ensure that there's sufficient staffing and funding for EGLE that will be critical to verify compliance and support operators through a fair, transparent process. We believe that collaboration between regulators, industry, and community stakeholders will be the key to lasting success here. In closing, Senate Bills 140 and 141 recognize a practical opportunity to protect public health, reduce natural gas waste, and keep Michigan on track towards its climate and clean energy goals. The technology exists today to significantly reduce oil and gas methane emissions, and the benefits for our health, air, economy, and future are undeniable. I urge this committee to advance Senate Bills 140 and 141 and make Michigan a leader in responsible methane mitigation. Thank you very much for your time and consideration, and I'm happy to answer any questions. Thank you. Any questions? Senator Hoitenga? We continue to compare us to other states, and I think as somebody testified previously, in Michigan, our industry has contracted quite a bit. And so to compare Michigan to Texas, who is a powerhouse, or New Mexico, this is where they drilled, this is what they do. I mean, this is their economies. This is not Michigan's main economy like it is there. So to compare, we could talk all day about how it's inappropriate to even try to compare that. So in the bigger states where they are a powerhouse, you have large corporations and stuff. Here in Michigan, you have, in a lot of instances, smaller operators. And so if we're going to double their fees in any way, some of them are barely surviving. I talked to some of them, and they're like, we are just feed to death, fee, fee, fee, fee. And they do contribute, especially to the trust fund, their taxes, the people they employ. They are barely hanging on. This is a smaller, for Michigan, smaller operators. Do you not worry, I ask this of the bill sponsor, that if we continue to keep dinging them in a way that puts them out of business because they just can't withstand anymore, do you worry at all about the grid, having some reliability on the grid? We need this oil and gas production to have a reliable grid. Does that concern you at all? Yeah, thank you for that question and for that perspective. I would just say that I think changing the cap from 1% to 2% is reasonable to cover the surveillance fees and the costs of monitoring. So rather than having taxpayers pay for that, it makes sense the operators would pay for that. And yeah. Thank you. Any other questions? All right, thank you so much. Will the clerk please read in the testimony cards? Madam Chair, Tim Minatos with Sierra Club of Michigan does not wish to speak but supports the bill. Joshua Antonini, Mackinac Center for Public Policy does not wish to speak, is opposed to the bill. Jason Greer, Michigan Oil and Gas Association are opposed to the bills. Nate Love, American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers are opposed to the bills. Adam Majestic, Detroit Regional Chamber, opposed to the bills. Mike Witkowski, Michigan Manufacturers Association, opposed to the bill. And Tim Lenholt, MFIB, opposed to both bills. Thank you so much. Now we are going to change topics and going to hear testimony on House Bill 4013, which was introduced by Representative Slaw. And Eric Dean from his office is going to be coming up and explaining what the bill does. Thank you so much. Representative Slaw apologizes for not being here in person. They're still in session. So thank you, Madam Chair. I am Eric Dean. I'm Representative Slaw's legislative director. Appreciate the members of the committee as well for your interest in this common sense bill or what we think is a common sense bill. Just some background on how we came up with the bill. In the fall of 2022, a constituent of Representative Slaw's reached out because he was having issues with unauthorized people trespassing on his hunting land. He had a significant number, and by significant I mean 40 to 50 signs at a half mile by quarter mile piece of property. He reached out to law enforcement, and when they came out, they wouldn't prosecute because they didn't have enough signs along his property boundaries. Under the current law, a property owner is required to either construct a fence around the entire perimeter of their property, and that can obviously get very expensive, or they can post signage in the form of no trespassing signs. If they do

signage option. It has to be spaced to enable a person to observe not less than one sign at any point of entry upon the property. And when we were doing some research on that particular language, the DNR mentioned that they interpret a point of entry as any opening in a tree line. So it could literally mean a sign is required to be nailed to every tree along the boundary of the property. So Representative Slaw's bill would change this to require signs to be posted at intervals of not more than 250 feet along the property boundary. It will provide a clear and attainable and a reasonable standard for both property owners and law enforcement so that our recreational trespassing law can be enforced as intended. And we've reviewed the proposal with MUCC, with the Michigan Farm Bureau, the Michigan Realtors, and also the DNR, and they all support the bill or have no opposition to it. So we would ask for your support, and I'm happy to answer any questions you might have. Thank you. Colleagues, do you have any questions? I'm trying to think of 250 feet, and I guess what I'm wondering is if we're walking up to a tree line, how far back do you think you need to be to be able to see those signs every 250 feet? Well, first I would say that if you are on a piece of property that you know is not yours and you know that you don't have permission, you know you're trespassing anyways. But we did some kind of a little bit of just on-the-ground research and said, okay, if you're literally in the middle of that 250 feet, so you've got 125 feet on one side, 125 feet on the other, we could see 125 feet over onto the left and onto the right. So somebody that is not supposed to be on the property, it would be fairly unreasonable to have them take the position that they didn't see the signage. Okay, thanks so much. Senator Daly? So this is basically to deal with hunting, period, right? Yeah, this is recreational trespassing. So if anybody's on my property and they do something illegal, they're still breaking the law. We have been told law enforcement is going to have a hard time prosecuting if you don't have signs on every single opening in the tree line. So I wish it was, I wish I had a different answer. So if there's an existing tree line, you don't have to have those signs? So any opening in the tree line or any entry point, and again, the DNR interprets an entry point as any opening in a tree line or any opening along your boundary, you're supposed to have a sign. So if you have a high-tensile wire fence around your property? If you fence it, then no, you don't have to have the sign. You don't have any signs? That would be probably a good question for the DNR to answer, but I don't believe so. I think it's either or. Okay, thank you. Any other questions? Senator Hoedinka? So if my hunting property is surrounded by state land, and I'm kind of in the middle, so I would have to, and people just remove the no trespassing signs. We're taking them down. So I'm just kind of thinking out loud, how would this work? So this would reduce the number of signs that you have to worry about because you would only have to post them every 250 feet. So right now, technically, you should be posting every single tree along the boundary of your property. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Dean. Thank you. Next, we have Chris Semernack, the liaison from the Department of Natural Resources. Thank you for coming to talk to us today about this. Thank you, Senator Schenk and members of the committee. My name is Chris Semernack, Legislative Liaison for the Department of Natural Resources. I won't belabor the point. Eric did a great job of laying out the bill. It's fairly straightforward, but happy to testify in support on behalf of the department. As Eric alluded to, right, I think this bill is just a common-sense bill that helps, obviously, private property owners, but from our perspective, helps our law enforcement division and our conservation officers have a much clearer guideline for enforcing recreational trespass laws. You know, I think a lot of our officers, and I wish our chief of law enforcement could be here today, see this quite often, right, especially during hunting season, and oftentimes, right, and similar to Senator Hoedinka's point, with signage being taken down, you know, not being quite visible, sometimes it creates awkward situations for a lot of our officers in being able to prosecute those cases. I will say, Senator Hoedinka, that same question came up from Representative VanderWaal in the House committee, and I will say our chief of law enforcement laid out our officers see that quite a bit, right, signage being taken down, removed, how do we navigate that? I will say most of our officers follow the guidance of a pretty reasonably prudent way of going about it, where they work with private landowners where there might be a suspected trespass, and if that individual is no longer trespassing on that property, you know, it's sort of an after-the-fact case, and they say, you know, I had the sign up and now it's gone. We work with that landowner oftentimes to get that signage back up, and we 99% of the time will just say, hey, can you take a photo of it, right, or, you know, show some kind of proof that the signage is there. Next time that happens, we'll come out, and if we see the signage being taken down, we can work to investigate that and address it again. So I will say our officers are very reasonable when it comes to this sort of issue, and they deal with it quite often. But happy to answer any other questions. Again, a very common-sense bill that we're supportive of. So thank you. Any other questions, colleagues? Thank you. Yeah. Clerk, will you please read in the testimony cards? Madam Chair, Siobhan Cecil with Michigan Realtors does not wish to speak and supports the bill. Thank you. We don't need to excuse absent members because we don't have any. So with that, there being no further business, the Senate Committee on Natural Resources and Agriculture is now adjourned. Thank you, Clerk. Thank you, Clerk.

title: Transportation and Infrastructure 25-10-28
transcript:
Good afternoon. The Senate Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairwoman Geis. Present. Senator Kleinfeld. Here. Senator Voino. Senator Hertel. Senator Chang. Senator McCann. Present. Senator Bolino. Here. Senator McBroom. Senator Victory. Here. Senator Bumstead. Madam Chairwoman, you have seven members present. There are many Michigan families who do not qualify for the Gold Star Family license plate, but have loved ones die while serving our country. Senate Bill 507 creates a next of kin special registration plate, allowing eligible family members of armed service members who lost their lives while serving on active duty or while assigned in an Army Reserve or Army National Guard unit in a drill status to apply to the Secretary of State to obtain this plate. The plate would be inscribed with special identification numbers preceded by the next of kin insignia, a gold star within a circle surrounded by sprigs of oak, and would have words next of kin inscribed beneath the registration numbers. It would look something like this. Senate Bill 507 is a reintroduction of Senator Lawers' SB 352 of 2023, which passed the Senate unanimously at the end of last session. At the request of the department, there is an amendment to the enacting section. The department asked for it to be changed from 90 days to 180 days. Senator Lawers has asked Senator Hertel to offer up the amendment. This issue was brought to us in 2022 by a now former constituent, Karen Straffen. Karen is here via Zoom to testify in support of the bill, and she is currently Senator Hertel's constituent. Thank you so much. Do we have any questions from members? I see no questions from members. Thanks so much. We do have on Zoom to testify Karen Straffen. And if we can get Ms. Straffen up. I'm here. Okay, fantastic. Thank you so much. Thank you. My husband spent 30 years in the Army, and he retired as an infantry brigade commander. I worked for the Army for 35 years, and we both retired about 17 years ago. And since then, we have spent our time volunteering for military retirees, Gold Star families, next of kin families, Medal of Honor recipients, disabled vets, and everything in this state. In 2020, we raised during COVID $100,000 to build one of Woody Williams, the last living Medal of Honor recipient from Iwo Jima, a Gold Star family monument in Clinton Township in seven months during COVID. And when we were building it, we noticed that the next of kin families are treated differently by some Gold Star families because Gold Star families sometimes don't think that being that their loved one did not die in combat.
