Each one of them, whether they died in combat or non-combat, they all signed a blank check payable to the United States of America for an amount up to and including life. Some Gold Stars were actually so traumatized over in Iraq and Afghanistan, they committed suicide over there. They are Gold Star families because that was a combat zone. But if they came home here and struggled and struggled with survivor's guilt and everything else, they don't get the same recognition. The importance of the next of kin plate is extremely, extremely great because these families deserve the same recognition that other ones get. And people don't even know about them. And it's also extremely important because we are not engaged in any armed conflicts. So there won't be any, hopefully, combat and Gold Star families. There will be next of kin and we must honor them the same. The Gold Star family lost their loved one in a combat zone. The next of kin did not. They came home. But training accidents, the cancer deaths, they're all stemmed and their suicide rates are all stemmed from the combat experience. So I am humbly, humbly begging you to please sign this into effect so that all people

can be honored. It shows that they had a loved one that gave their all for our country. Are there any questions? Thank you so much, Mrs. Straffin. Do we have any questions from members? Senator Hertel. I just want to thank you, Karen, for your persistence. I know we've talked a few times about this legislation over the years, and I think it's incredibly important not only to honor your loved ones and get this legislation across the finish line, but it wouldn't have happened without you continually pushing for it as well. So thank you for all you've put into this. Thank you. Thank you again for your testimony and for your persistence and hard work on this legislation. Thank you very much. It's my humble honor. Do we have any other questions from members? Seeing none, thank you so much. There is a card that was turned in. Madam Clerk, if you will read. Not wishing to speak, supporting the bill, Aaron Shore from MDOS. Thank you so much. Because we don't have a full number, the entire committee here, I would like to wait until we have all of the members here to be able to adopt the amendment and vote out the bill. So, which would happen in hopefully next week, if we have everyone here. Thank you again. And thank you. Thank you very much. Okay, next we are taking up Senate Bill 532, which is sponsored by Senator Cherry, who is here. Will you please come up and explain your bill for the committee? Thank you, Chair and members of the committee for taking up this legislation. The bill before you would allow active duty military members to request a special registration plate for their vehicle in the same manner that our military veterans can currently request a plate with their respective vignette. According to the Department of Defense, Michigan is home to more than 4,500 active duty service members. And then given the recent announcements regarding new investments in bases such as Selfridge Air Force Base, thank you to Senator Hertel, the active duty population could continue to increase. Under current law, only National Guard members, Air Force Reserve members, and former members of any branch of the armed forces are eligible to apply to the Secretary of State for a special registration plate. My legislation would permit active duty members to also apply for those same plates. In Michigan, we take pride in our constituents who have devoted their lives to service, especially those willing to make the ultimate sacrifice in defense of our nation. By permitting those active duty military members to request special plates, we enable our constituents to share in the pride of their service. Again, I thank the committee for taking testimony on this legislation and would be happy to answer any questions you may have. Thank you so much. Do we have any questions from members? I see no questions from members, so thanks. We do not have anyone else testifying in person or via Zoom. Do we have any cards to read in? Not wishing to speak in support of the bill, Aaron Shore from MDOS. Thank you so much. Okay, we will also, again, because I'd prefer to have us vote when we have all of our members present, we will hopefully do that next week. title: Education 25-10-28
transcript:

I think it was you, Madam Chair, but I'm not 100% sure, but somebody's talked about how these products are constantly changing, and that is a huge issue. So the flexibility that's written into this bill is excellent. And I don't want to take up too much time because basically almost all those questions you guys have asked, Abby is a great person to have answer. I just wanted to take one moment to sort of address a question from Senator Johnson earlier about effective use of money for prevention. The state, I can only talk about the tobacco. I can't talk about cannabis because I don't know it. But our tobacco control program in the state of Michigan is excellent, but it is extremely underfunded. So even they do know how to get these messages out. They have a lot of great programs. They just can't get the word out about them. So, again, talking to separate bills I don't want to get into, but when we do get around to appropriations, I urge you to give them more money as well. But I'll pass it over to Abby. Hi, I'm Abby Green. Thank you for the invitation from Paul to speak today. I apologize if I talk really fast. I'm a little bit nervous. This is a little out of my wheelhouse. I am a certified prevention specialist through McBAP, and I am a part of a very small team of people. There are three of us who are the funded prevention providers for Barry County, Michigan. Barry County is very rural. We have no highways. We have four grocery stores. We have five school districts in total. It is my job to provide evidence-based prevention services in schools. We provide evidence-based media messaging across all kinds of platforms, and we also have shifted a little bit of our focus into early intervention services. When we're talking about prevention services, we only provide evidence-based, and those begin in the third grade. And we are seeing these students almost every single year talking about the dangers of tobacco. We started out with, you know, we were still very much in the don't smoke, it's really bad for you. But that market has completely changed, and it's turned into something that hit us with a force that we weren't necessarily prepared for because we thought we had tobacco under control. But I get calls every single day about students who have been vaping since elementary school, fourth grade, fifth grade, who are showing signs of dependence to nicotine, and they are in sixth grade at this point. They are years into a tobacco dependency. And we as adults recognize that a person quitting smoking is one of the hardest things they will ever do in their lives. And students and youth are left in the lurch. They're expected to figure it out, or they are expected to be suspended for a little while and then come back, and that problem hasn't been dealt with. So one of the things that my coalition did was we started doing early intervention and restorative programs. So our school systems, they have a suspension procedure, of course. But as part of that restorative, they will remove a couple days of that out-of-classroom time if those students come and sit with me, and they learn about nicotine, about messaging, about what that does to their brains and their bodies. And I always talk to them about I'm not here to make that decision for you or tell you what is wrong. I'm here to make sure that you have all the information because I know you didn't get it from whoever gave this to you or whatever you learned on TikTok or YouTube. We are consistently hearing about a very low perception of harm when it comes to not only Zen pouches or synthetic nicotine products or nicotine salts that are coming in these vapes, but also cannabis products. When we do a, we call it a student quick screen, a screening or brief intervention referral to treatment program for students who are caught using a substance other than nicotine at school, these students and their parent have to come in, and we do a screening for them to see what that level of dependency is at, and then we refer them to treatment if that's necessary. But every time we have those, almost 100% of the time in the past five years, it has been a THC-related offense. Not only that, but the students don't think it's dangerous and the parents don't think it's dangerous, and almost all of the time these products are coming from home. So there is a large need to get information into homes because these students, by the time they get to me, may be in the high school and they recognize that they've been addicted to a product for five years and they're ready to be done because it's controlling their life. They're scared. They're scared because they don't have control over that anymore. So I think that the sooner we can get that information into parents' hands and to be able to recognize that just because it doesn't smell like a cigarette and just because it doesn't look like a cigarette or taste like a cigarette, it has probably more nicotine than that cigarette. It is potentially, I don't want to use the term more addictive because I'm not a doctor, but it's taken away all of those negative immediate impacts of a cigarette that we think about, and it has made it easy to hide. These things look like pens or they look like other things.

That's not developed for an adult who's been smoking forever and who is legally allowed to do that. Those are made to get a whole new population of people addicted. Thank you for your time. If I could just add one quick thing based off that. The students in Hastings are extremely lucky to have somebody like Abby. There was a recent survey done by the State Health and Human Services of schools that only about a third of students that have been caught vaping are provided with information about how to quit or access to somebody like Abby. And also only about a third of parents are provided with that information. So this really would address a big need. And hopefully next year we won't see 700 kids from Detroit Public Schools be sent to the hospital because of THC or vaping. Senator DeMoss. Thank you Madam Chair. I just wanted to thank you for your testimony because it just reminded me, I just highlight the importance of this. My closest friend from college, we were talking a few years ago and his son was a 17-year-old and he kept catching him vaping. And finally he caught him for the third or fourth time and he said, what is going on? And the kid, big tough 17-year-old guy broke down crying. He said, dad, I'm trying to stop but I can't. And he had no idea what starts as fun is, oh, I'll try, I'll try. And then they're hooked and it's a real problem. The other thing I hope just as a dad that we include in this is this keeps me up at night to no end. My kids are good kids. I don't think they're out there smoking things, but kids do dumb things. And especially with fentanyl, with all the drugs being laced with things, I think we need to include that information because it scares me to death. What if in a weak moment my son says, all right, I'll try it. And it's laced with fentanyl and he dies. And this is a new thing that we didn't used to have to face when we were kids. So I appreciate your efforts and I especially appreciate the way you brought that up because you're right. Really, your heart does go out to these kids who thought they were just having fun. It does, yeah. And if I could just add, part of those evidence-based programmings that we have, we adjust them every year to be able to change with the times, like Madam Chairperson said. They're changing so fast and they're changing faster than we can research them. But one thing that we know is that teaching kids to say no isn't effective. Teaching them how to interact with their peers and get out of a situation they're uncomfortable in because it is that moment of weakness. And just being like, well, just say no. That isn't easy. It's not easy for adults, let alone for children. And being able to teach them to recognize that in themselves and figure out how they can say no. Because we know that 25% of children who are casually maybe trying these products are showing signs of addiction within 30 days. Thank you. Thank you for your testimony. Madam Clerk, can you please read the cards for the record? Certainly. Regarding Senate Bill 433, not wishing to speak in support, Noah Smith representing the Michigan Association of School Psychologists. Also not wishing to speak in support, Noah Smith representing the Michigan Association of School Social Workers. Not wishing to speak in support, Stephanie Glidden representing the Michigan School Counselor Association. Not wishing to speak in support, Danielle Sarayani representing the Michigan County Social Services Association. Not wishing to speak in support, Taylor Alpert representing Michigan Health and Hospital Association. Not wishing to speak in support, Jennifer Smith representing Michigan Association of School Boards. Not wishing to speak in support, Annie Kuhn representing the Michigan League for Public Policy. Not wishing to speak in support, Amanda Klein representing the American Heart Association. Not wishing to speak in support, the American Lung Association of Michigan. Not wishing to speak in support, Shardé Burton representing MDHHS and they provided written testimony for the members. Not wishing to speak in support, Robin Schneider representing Michigan Cannabis Industry Association. Not wishing to speak in support, Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids. And the last card, not wishing to speak, also in support, Christina Holmes representing Michigan School Health Coordinators Association. That's all the cards, Madam Chair. Thank you. Maybe we'll vote on this as soon as next week. We'll see. Being no further business, the Senate Committee on Education is now adjourned. Do we have next week? Oh, we might.

For example, if Jim Beam expands from bourbon and starts making ready-to-go cocktails and uses the Jim Beam name, that would be considered a brand extension and the distributor would have the right to distribute that new product. We had some concerns that small brewers were getting inadvertently caught up in this and that it could be negative. But we're glad to be able to work with other interested parties, the beer and wine wholesalers, and get to a place where we're supporting and don't feel as concerned. And Senate Bill 512 addresses many issues. Senator Singh, you did a great job summarizing those. I'd be happy to add clarification, but don't really feel like I need to go through it again. So happy to answer any questions. Are there any questions? All right. Thank you very much. Thank you. I'll read in some additional cards. Sean Hammond from the University of Michigan submitted testimony in support of the bill, not wishing to speak here today. And Scott Ellis, MLBA, not wishing to speak in support of 512. And this is at the same time that inflation is affecting, as all of you know, food, shelter, and other things. This water affordability is a large struggle for seniors. As of 2023, about 55% of senior-led households in Chiawassee County fell below the ALICE threshold, meaning they didn't bring enough income to afford a bare-bones budget. Many of these seniors are on fixed incomes that do not rise with the cost of inflation. The rising costs of water forced them to make impossible choices between medicine and the water they need to stay healthy. I, again, come here. I have experienced firsthand the dual challenges of water quality and water affordability. I know what it's like to have my son, who at the time was age 7 and he's now 17, wake up every morning, brush his teeth with bottled water, and quite frankly, just be afraid of the water, right? Can I bathe with it? My house was a test site during the water crisis. I volunteered to have it tested. It's a very difficult situation. Well, the legislature has advanced meaningful bipartisan efforts around water quality. This package will begin to address the equally important issue of water affordability. These issues are intrinsically linked. One cannot be properly addressed without addressing the other. I want to share my encouragement and support for this legislation as a common-sense step in addressing this issue. This is a nonpartisan issue. We have an opportunity to work together on common-sense legislation to improve the lives of Michiganders. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Gaskin, for your thoughtful testimony and for uplifting some of the impacts that people feel that are even outside of the economic impacts when they have their water shut off. It's very real, so I appreciate you bringing that today. I'm not seeing any questions from any members, so I'll thank you again. And I will ask, next we have Sylvia Orduño, who is the organizer for the People's Water Board. Thank you very much for coming back to offer your thoughts to the committee on this important issue and for your work on it over the years. Thank you, Senator. Thank you, Senator Irwin. Thank you, committee members. It's a pleasure, again, to be here, and again, I very much appreciate the work that you've continued to do across the Senate for this issue. I just want to start off with mentioning Senator Demuth in particular. I've really appreciated and I've been moved by the passion that you put into this and the things that you've said about that there's more to just the bean counting around this. There are some bigger issues here that I'm hoping that you all are really taking into consideration. I can tell you, as I've mentioned before, I've been working on water affordability for more than 27 years at the local level. We're exhausted. This is a grassroots effort that many of us are involved with. We come to Lansing, oftentimes out of our pocket. We're not lobbyists. We're mostly unpaid people, and we're trying to, again, talk to residents across the state to also talk to you about this urgent need. You've done many things over the years to help provide the energy sector with the needs that they have. They come and they make their case for how important it is to make sure that energy is affordable, but we don't always have that same sort of lobbying arm with our local water providers. And so we're very much hoping that you're going to maybe be able to, this session, pass this important package of bills. We've seen too many residents continue to suffer. This is not theoretical. It's not anything about charity or free water or blaming and shaming. It's a very real Michigan issue, and it's something that's happening statewide. The data is here. We've heard for many years that there's no data, there's no evidence, it's a statewide problem. It is a problem, and you can see it in every county, even if it's a small number of residents. Oftentimes people are unseen. It is a problem. We're hoping that, again, this will make a difference this time around with the changes in the bill package. We've been talking extensively to members of the majority in the House. It seems as if they're pleased with the changes that have been made. We've been continuing to have conversations in their districts. I can tell you that about a week and a half ago we were in Bay City. We met with residents there that are talking about their unaffordable water bills. We followed up with a meeting with the city commission, who recently completed a survey over the summer, and 51% of the residents said that they were experiencing very high water bills and they're highly dissatisfied with the costs that they're paying there. Tonight we're going to be in Jackson. We're meeting with the city council. We're talking with residents tomorrow night about their water bills. And, again, these are residents that are asking for help, asking for ways to figure out how to get the message across to their lawmakers that they've got problems that they cannot manage. This is very much both a household issue and a local water provider problem. It's oftentimes been just talked about in terms of these are just people that don't want to pay their bills. It's very much not that case. Everyone wants to pay their bills. It's just that we've got to find a way to make it so that households and water providers, local governments, can manage in this day and age. We are going to continue to have meetings across the state. We're very much interested in having you engage in these conversations, but please know that residents are not just fed up. They're frustrated and feeling that this is something that, while it's fixable, government is still not hearing them. And I appreciate that, as a Senate, you have been addressing this. Please help us be able to move our colleagues or your colleagues in the House. I believe we're finally there with this bill package, but we need a more concerted effort to really finally make this pass. Thank you. Thank you again for your testimony and for the passion and persistence that you've continued to bring to this. I do have a question from Senator DeMoose for you. Yeah, I mean, thank you for your kind words. I really appreciate that. But this isn't about that. You're the first one I've really heard bring this up. We do these things for power, electricity, and these type of things. And I wondered if you could talk a little bit about how important water actually is, because I could tell you we were without power based on the ice storm I referenced for 13 days. We were fine without the power and without the heat because we had a wood-burning stove. The problem is the well didn't work. And you really find out two weeks without water is a big, big deal. It's a lot worse than just a power outage for a couple days. I mean, tell me about some of the hardships you've heard about. I think that I'm going to actually just bring a moment up about a meeting I had maybe a year or two ago with you, Senator Lindsey, and you very much talked about how you'll hear from constituents about their energy problems, right? But very much energy and water are interlinked, right, in terms of how you use them. I live in a house with a boiler. I have no heat without water, right? This is the case of many people who are in older homes. Again, you need pumps and electricity to be able to move water. And so we're finding that while we've solved one part of the equation for one sector, we haven't also done that for our municipal water providers. And we know that this is, again, a solvable issue. It's not as if it's something that we can't figure out the solutions, but we haven't really sort of bridged the conversation about how we need both to be able to have safe housing and communities. I mean, I just want people to understand that without power it's a terrible thing, but people survive for thousands of years without power. The problem is when you don't have water, you can't flush toilets, you can't drink. It's

for having me, Chairperson Irwin and all members of the committee. So we appreciate the opportunity to testify today. My name is Molly Maciejewski and I serve as the chair of the Michigan section of the American Water Works Association. We represent over 2,300 water professionals across the state. Our members include utilities, engineers, operators, scientists, and public servants dedicated to just one goal, protecting public health through safe and reliable drinking water. Michigan has more than 1,300 public water utilities, from large regional systems to small rural providers, some of which you've heard from today already, where people live. Because each system is unique, there is no one-size-fits-all solution to water affordability. But through collaboration, our members have found common ground in a shared commitment to policies that keep water systems strong and water accessible for all Michiganders. Michigan AWWA is grateful to Senator Chang for inviting our members to participate in the Water Affordability Work Group that has been going on. This gave utilities a voice in shaping policies that they'll ultimately implement. Our members brought practical insight about rate structures, billing, payment plans, and technology to ensure this legislation is workable for water systems of every shape and size. The result is a common-sense, fiscally responsible framework that balances household affordability with long-term water system sustainability. Although every water system is unique, water utilities across the state face the same challenge. The cost of delivering safe water continues to rise, while many households struggle to keep up. Local water systems depend entirely on customer rates, so when families can't pay, utilities must make hard choices. Do we raise rates? Do we cut service? Or do we delay critical infrastructure investments that we're already behind on? A statewide water affordability program won't solve every challenge. We know this, but it will give communities a vital tool to maintain financial stability while protecting public health. For that reason, Michigan AWWA respectfully urges your support for the 2025 Water Affordability Bill Package, Senate Bills 248 to 252, to establish the Water Rate Affordability Fund, Task Force, Program, Transparency Act, and the Shutoff Protection Act. Our water professionals are committed to delivering safe, affordable water to every customer, and we ask the state to be a partner in our mission. Thank you so much today. Thank you again for your testimony and bringing the subject matter expertise from the association to the discussions that led to this bill. I'm not seeing any hands, so I'm going to thank you again. I'm going to move on to Steve Merritt. Steve Merritt is also on Zoom, a colonel with the Salvation Army. Are you with us, Mr. Merritt? Yes, I am. Good afternoon. Thanks for being here. Please offer your testimony. Thank you. And thank you, Chair Senator Irwin and the committee members for the opportunity to speak today. My name is Lieutenant Colonel Steve Merritt. I'm the divisional commander of this Great Lakes Division of the Salvation Army. My wife and I oversee all of the work of the Salvation Army across our wonderful state of Michigan. The Salvation Army's mission is to preach the gospel of Jesus Christ and to meet human needs in his name without discrimination. Salvation Army supports water affordability and was honored to be invited into this conversation over a year ago with Senator Chang. Every day, our staff and officers work in 61 locations throughout the state, helping Michigan families and seniors who are struggling because they must choose between, as we've heard repeatedly today, paying utilities, food, or rent. Through the MEEP program, the Salvation Army administers $11.3 million, serving nearly 12,000 Michigan residents. The water affordability bill builds on this. It's a statewide step in the right direction that addresses a problem that cannot be fixed with emergency assistance alone. It offers a path forward with a compassionate, practical solution that would help families stay in their homes, avoid eviction, and maintain stability during times of financial strain. We, the Salvation Army, are ready to implement this solution. We have long partnered with local utilities, the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, United Way to deliver emergency energy assistance, establishing one-time bill payments, enrollment in affordable payment plans, self-sufficiency. We would, throughout those 61 centers across the state, we would be able to roll up this water affordability into that same program with the same caseworkers and be able to reach many people in need across Michigan. A water affordability bill is about people, people that should not lose their home over a bill they simply cannot pay. On behalf of the Salvation Army, I urge you to support this legislation. Let's work together to make Michigan a place where every family has the dignity of clean, affordable water and the sustainability of a home they can count on. Thank you today for your time and for your leadership, everything you are accomplishing. God bless you. Thank you again, sir, for your testimony. I'm not seeing any hands for questions, so I'll thank you again and we will move on to Gary Brown, who is here with us today and is the director of the Board of Water Commissioners for the City of Detroit. Thank you for being with us today. Thank you. I am the director of the Detroit Water and Sewer Department. I also sit on the board of directors of the Great Lakes Water Authority, which services about 120 communities with water, sewer, or both services in the state of Michigan. State appropriations provided to date have been greatly appreciated and have protected 30,000 households in Detroit from service interruption because they cannot afford to pay their bill. Water providers will require continued appropriation to support water affordability programs until we can pass legislation with a dedicated funding source. This issue is about stabilizing finances to meet infrastructure needs. There's aging infrastructure around the state. Some of the infrastructure is 100 years old. You have seen headlines about large water main breaks disrupting service to thousands of households and businesses and causing property damage as well as economic decline in communities where you have long-term water losses. Raising rates high enough to cover actual costs is often politically unpopular. So local officials may intentionally keep rates low to avoid public outcry. Over time, insufficient rates can lead to underinvestment in critical infrastructure, deferred maintenance, and financial instability. Utilities are not mismanaging funds. They are trying to balance the true cost of service without overburdening vulnerable customers. Water providers use options allowed by law to collect from delinquent customers, such as liens or shutoffs, but these methods are not effective for low-income households that can't afford to pay their entire bill. Under this legislation, enrolled customers are billed based on average household income. Detroit learned firsthand with its lifeline plan that when you give a low-income household bill they can afford, they will pay. They are contributing to system costs, and that's good for business and good for everyone. The legislation ensures monthly fees stay within the region and also includes opt-out provisions for local water providers. Finally, this bill package is compassionate, comprehensive, fair to all customers, and administratively feasible. It is patterned closely after MEAP, which continues to enjoy bipartisan support. I urge the committee to support this legislation. We believe ensuring water service for low-income customers is equally important to gas and electrical services. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Gary Brown, for your service to the great city of Detroit. I'm not seeing any questions for you today, but thank you again for coming to Lansing and offering your testimony. I will move on next to ask the clerk to read in the considerable number of testimony cards that we've gotten on this important legislation. All right. Before we do that, I'll recognize Senator Lindsey. You want us to ask a question of someone? Of Senator Chang, if that's okay. Just going back to the beginning of this, it was great to hear all the testimony about this today. One thing I'm trying to wrap my head around with this package, or any of the sponsors that are involved, frankly, is I've heard it said time and time again that no matter how we do this, people are going to pay for the people who are unable to pay their bills. Whether that comes in the form of them not paying and rates go up on everybody, is that a fair characterization of one of the problems that's trying to be solved with this, is instead be proactive and create a mechanism that handles that on the front end?

What we're trying to do is solve the problem in a sustainable way, right? So the legislature, we've appropriated money here and then there and then again and again, but it's never actually been totally enough. And I think that you've heard from water providers, both the Statewide Water Association as well as Detroit, about how they have to make hard choices when they're just literally not collecting, right, from folks who just can't pay their water bills. And so they have to make some really tough decisions. If we are able to pass this, we will set up a sustainable funding mechanism that is very reasonable and basically mirrors what we already do on the energy side. And I think will eventually, in the long run, really help even things out. Because if you think about it, with all of the plumbing repairs that are going to be made, as well as getting people water bills that they can actually afford, we're going to be bringing in more money into our water systems, which will help to invest in a number of the infrastructure upgrades, as well as just bring about long-term sustainability. And so we have been as intentional as possible to give providers as many options as we can give them to provide solutions for our residents. I would just add to what Senator Chang said, that as we heard today, when people's water is shut off, it can immiserate these families, which is something that I certainly care about. But in the context of your question, Senator, I would point out that not only is that a hardship for the families that get shut off, it's also very expensive. And one of the things we learned from energy shutoffs is that sending crews out there to turn it off and turn it back on is very expensive. That's something the ratepayers will have to pay for as well. And so just having a more efficient system that helps people when they need help can actually be very cost effective as well. So that's another reason why I'm a part of this package and why I'm specifically a part of the package that seeks to stop wasting money in the criminal justice system trying to go after folks who are poor. One follow up? Sure. This is the Senate Housing and Human Services Committee. Why not? Let's do one more. So I do wonder, you know, on that point, Mr. Chairman, you know, has anybody considered just starting with the protection side of it and saying because the assumption is that we the system adjusts itself already. You can't provide water for free. So these systems have to, you know, figure out how they're going to set rates, et cetera. And some of the cost is already shared inside the system. So if some steps were taken to prevent, you know, wasted resources on shutting off and bringing it back and also mitigate some of the challenges of shutting people's water off who have no access. And wouldn't the system already sort of self-correct and bring in more revenue through rates naturally to cover those costs without having to set up a new we have to fund this and take a rate from people on the front end? I think the answer is no. And the reason why. And so so let me tell you about sort of like how my own thinking has evolved on this. Right. So I came into the legislature in 2015. We started with this like really ambitious, you know, water affordability package that, you know, banned all shutoffs and, you know, set affordability, you know, created affordability programs that had to be income based and all of these things that, you know, I think, you know, were great in theory. But then once we actually started talking to water providers and really learning, you know, how the systems work and also the fact that we have, you know, I can't remember the total number, but over a thousand. We heard it earlier, but over a thousand water providers in the state. Some of them are so small. Right. And so they don't have the capacity to be able to do the things that a larger provider does. And some of the larger providers might have just so much extreme need that, you know, to completely ban shutoffs or build in certain protections is just literally not feasible. So that's why we have spent, you know, many years refining this legislation to be something that not only protects people, but also is doable for the providers. And that is why, you know, where in years past we might have actually seen water providers in opposition to a concept like this, we've actually created something where we know this is implementable because they have directly shaped what the program is. Thank you, Senator Chang. Next, I'll recognize Senator Bayer. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair. I wanted to also comment and sort of make sure we note how important it is the fix part of this. Right. When we fix water problems, we actually bring the whole total cost down. It's a big part of the system. Right. Understanding what goes on out there and all of these different providers, all of them have people that cannot afford to repair their plumbing. And that is such a fundamental thing when you can't pay your bill because of a leak and you can't afford to fix the leak. You're just forever doomed at that point. The only way to do it is to get help to fix. So it's a critical component that we don't make a big enough deal about, but it really can change the system forever just doing that one part. The rest of it, when we have providers that are just when you know, you know, we think of these providers as businesses, you know, you collect the money that you need to run your business. It doesn't work that way. They're public. Right. GLEWA is a nonprofit that we created at the state and then sort of abandoned. Like, good luck, everyone. And raising the rates enough to be able to actually pay the bills to maintain that ancient infrastructure. I wouldn't be able to afford it. You wouldn't be able to afford it. Nobody would be able to afford their bills. It's just not possible. We have to do it differently. Eventually it will get better as we fix the system, but we have to invest to do that. And this is an amazing way to do it. Thanks to all those people. Thank you, Senator Bayer, for sharing your perspective. I just want to let members know that this is an important issue, but it's also an issue that there's a lot of moving parts. So I encourage you to consult with other members or with your local utilities and your local community action agencies to figure out what you think about this because it's my hope that we will be voting on this next week. Due to time so we can get out of here and make more room for the next committee, we'll have the cards read in next time before we vote on the bills, but the cards will be included in the official record of this meeting, but we'll hear about them next time. And so there being no further business before the committee without objection, the Senate Committee on Housing and Human Services is adjourned. Thank you, Senator.

title: Families and Veterans — Tuesday, October 28, 2025
transcript:
The House Families and Veterans Committee will come to order. Would the clerk please take attendance? Chair Smalls? Here. Representatives Wozniak? Here. Fox? Present. Johnson? Here. Thompson? Here. Saslow? Here. Wolford? Present. Young? Here. Burns? Here. Reingans? Here. Song? Present.

I have 11 members present, a quorum. Thank you, Mr. Clerk. Representative Wozniak moves to adopt the minutes of the October 21st meeting without objection, so ordered. Our first order of business today is to hear testimony on House Bill 4530 and 4531 from Representative Bihutsky and Representative Riggis. You can start anytime, and thanks for being here. Good afternoon, Madam Chair and members of the committee. Thank you for allowing us to testify on House Bill 4530 and 31, bills that aim to address hurdles that arise during some CPS investigations. The legislation originated as part of a series of recommendations from the Office of the Child Advocate in 2021. I believe you all have a version of the report. Following an investigation into a tragic murder-suicide. The mother had been reporting suicidal and homicidal ideations to a number of people, including mental health professionals, and although there was one CPS investigation that had already been closed and another that was in process at the time of the incident, intervention didn't occur in time to prevent her from taking her own life and that of her child. My bill, House Bill 4530, would amend the amount of time that a mental health professional has to respond to a records request from a caseworker from 14 to 7 days. Given the extremely short time frame that caseworkers have to complete the reports and the time-sensitive nature of some of these investigations, time is crucial. Representative Riggis is going to discuss her bill, but suffice to say it's a straightforward addition to existing training for mandatory reporters to ensure it also covers the warning signs of abuse and neglect. I do just want to highlight that there's a substitute under discussion that would just change what section of law these trainings fall under. The reason for that being that the statute in the substitute that we're discussing is more appropriate, but it didn't exist when these bills were first introduced in 2022. I do want to be transparent in the fact that neither of these bills is going to prevent every tragic event in this state. But both of these policies are practical, actionable, and common-sense steps that we can take to get information to caseworkers faster. I'm going to hand things over to Representative Riggis, and I'm happy to take questions. Thank you, Representative Pahutski. Thank you for the opportunity to speak on House Bill 4531. House Bill 4531 requires that all mandated reporters, such as teachers, doctors, and social workers, to complete a training every three years. The training developed by the Department of Health and Human Services will help ensure these mandated reporters can recognize signs of child abuse or neglect and to better understand their legal responsibilities when reporting it. The goal is to keep children safer by making sure those on the front lines are consistently informed and prepared. Regular training helps prevent warning signs from being missed and ensures that mandated reporters are acting with those current knowledge and standards. Requiring the department to develop curriculum also ensures that they learn from mistakes and build better mechanisms for better protecting our most vulnerable, our children. Thank you again for allowing us to speak on this bill. I'm happy to also answer questions. What is the requirement for training now? I believe that the Office of the Child Advocate can speak better to that, but there's continuing education for all of these mandatory reporters. The suggestion from the OCA was just to ensure that some of that training that they periodically go through includes the signs of neglect and abuse. So they go through, I believe it's yearly training, but I don't want to misspeak. I think the Office of the Child Advocate can speak better to that. Do we have any other questions? No. Okay, thank you, Representatives, for your testimony. Next, we'll have Ryan Spidel, the Michigan Child Advocate from the Office of the Child Advocate, to offer testimony. Good afternoon, Madam Chair and distinguished members of the committee. I appreciate being before you again. It's good to see you. I'm here to testify on House Bills 4530 and 4531. Simply put, they will keep Michigan's children safer. House Bill, I'm going to repeat some of the things that were said, but House Bill 4530 provides a change to a requirement in the mental health code. Currently, when mental health records are requested as part of a child protective services investigation, the health care provider has 14 days to provide those records to CPS. CPS needs these records to properly evaluate cases. It is vital to an investigation with concerns about a parent's mental health affecting the safety of children. House Bill 4530 would shorten the 14-day time frame to a seven-day period. Switching to House Bill 4531, this adds a provision to Michigan's child protection law that would require mandated reporters of child abuse to attend mandated reporter training developed by the department once every three years. Currently, there is no requirement to repeat this training. In my tenure at the OCA, I have read several thousand CPS cases. To date, we have closed over 5,000 OCA investigations. I can speak to you from my experience reviewing these cases. These recommendations did come out of a specific child death investigation we conducted in 2020, and the story is twofold and has a direct correlation to both of these House Bills. In response to our recommendation, MDHHS did agree with these updates to statute. This particular case involved a mother who, over a period of several months, expressed suicidal and homicidal ideations with her 11-year-old son being the voice target of her intent. On June 28, 2020, this mother shot her 11-year-old son in the forehead and then turned the gun on herself. The OCA found during the course of our investigation that there was one prior CPS complaint and an ongoing CPS investigation at the time of the murder-suicide. During this CPS investigation, as the investigator should, they attempted to collect multiple times, they attempted to collect mental health records from mental health providers, only to be met with resistance from the provider who is also a mandated reporter. The mental health provider slash mandated reporter was required to provide CPS with the requested records under Michigan's Mental Health Code. They were unaware of that. The provider refused to give these records without a signed release from the mother. So in a sense, the provider wanted the abuser to give the department permission to get the abuser's records from the provider. I would simply say that the provider was not educated in his or her requirements under the law. Additionally, as part of the OCA investigation, the OCA requested the mother's mental health records. After some talking and explaining about the statute to the mental health provider, we did get those records. They were over 500 pages long. CPS has 30 days to complete an investigation. Imagine being on day 20 and you find out that the alleged perpetrator of your investigation has experienced mental health episodes and is meeting with a therapist regularly. There are over 500 pages that you have to go over, and that would be if you get the records within those 10 days. Remember, currently it's a 14-day time period. Your case is due in 10 days, but the provider has 14 days to provide those 500 pages of records. Mandated reporters are required by law to report suspected child abuse or neglect. We have found that mandated reporters do not possess the knowledge of when to report nor what constitutes potential signs of abuse and neglect that should be reported. Mind you, I'm speaking from worst-case scenarios. We review child death and very bad child protective services and foster care cases. But I want to provide some examples. In a past investigation, the OCA interviewed two veteran detectives at a very large sheriff's office. Both are mandated reporters. Neither of these mandated reporters knew of the requirement in law to investigate child abuse as a multidisciplinary team. We were informing them of that. They were also unaware that the county possessed a protocol on how to investigate child abuse and how to conduct those investigations. The protocol itself and adhering to that protocol are both required by statute. Recently, we reviewed a case where another law enforcement agency took a report of serious child abuse. That law enforcement officer did nothing with that report. They did not forward it to the Department of Health and Human Services, and that child was later beat to death by the mother's boyfriend. In speaking with teachers, psychologists, school administrators, and various other mandated reporters, it is clear a regular training is needed. These mandated reporters consistently remind me that they want and need more training around the recognition of child abuse injuries. I do believe that if both these bills were signed into law, it will make Michigan that much safer for children. Educating our mandated reporters on a regular basis is badly needed. With that, I would open it up to any questions you may have for me. Thank you for your testimony. Obviously, anything we can do to better protect our children is very important, so thank you for being here. We do have a question, Rep. Thompson. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you for your testimony and for seeking out some of these answers for us. When you talk about the protocol for mandated reporters, when it comes to law enforcement, is there any protocol for the connection between the CPS worker and law enforcement? Or if law enforcement were to reach out to CPS about something they're concerned about, even vice versa, can you tell us a little bit about what that law should look like?

Likewise, currently statute requires the department to report child abuse to the police and vice versa. It also requires the police to report child abuse to the department. And there's a purpose behind that. These agencies are supposed to work together in their investigations to conduct a joint investigation into the child abuse. What we see is that not happening in our worst case scenarios. We see them operating in silos and not communicating with each other, not reporting these things to each other. I believe that the mandated reporter training would help with that. Thank you. We recently had an incident in my district where it was the law enforcement had reached out several times to CPS and CPS had not followed through for three years. There was multiple encounters. So I agree with you. I think that this would help make a little bit of a difference. So thank you for bringing this before us. Thank you. Rep. Burns. Thank you, Chair Schmaltz. Thank you for your testimony today and for the work that you do. So I just have a question based on, you know, some of the real life scenarios that you've just shared, which are heartbreaking. It sounds like folks who are required to release these mental health records currently under a 14 day time period were not aware of that. Yes, correct. We find that quite often that providers, mental health providers specifically, are requesting the department to provide a signed release for those documents and that's not required under statute. Right. And so thank you for that. My question would be, I understand that Rep. Hudson's bill, HB 4530, would require, you know, the time frame to move from 14 days to seven, which I think is a good idea. My question is, how can we ensure that folks who are required to release these records would be aware of that time frame? I also understand the other bill in the package requires the mandated reporter training every three years, which I also appreciate, and I think that's a good idea. I'm just trying to figure out how can we ensure that folks are aware of the seven day period? Because again, I appreciate that it's a tighter time frame, but is there a mechanism for that? Can you speak to that? So my understanding is that the Department of Health and Human Services is in the middle of creating this training. Right now it's out to community stakeholders, mental health providers, providers of medical practitioners around the state. I think what needs to happen is that training, that part of the statute needs to make it into training, specifically for medical practitioners. Right. Okay. Thank you. That's helpful. Rep. Johnson. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you. Good to see you again. I completely agree we need to keep our children safer, and these stories are horrible. Mandated reporters, what is the fullest of a mandated reporter? They mentioned teacher, mental health professional. Yeah, it's spelled out in child protection law. It's pretty extensive. I wouldn't be able to read all of them because it includes like law enforcement officer, physical therapist, speech pathology. So there's a lot of different specialties that are included in there. I don't know the list off the top of my head, but it is particularly spelled out in the child protection law. So if this gets passed, you're probably going to have a way to, like Representative Burns was saying, a way to let this whole extensive list know there is a new guideline, and I would hope. That's a good question. I mean, this office is charged with educating the public. I don't see why we couldn't use our GovServe, GovDelivery address to do something just to that extent, just to let them know there's a change in statute. Especially if they're licensed for some reason through the state. Correct. Yeah, and the enforcement of this, what if they don't do it? What if someone consistently doesn't do this? Are you going to know and have a way to re-educate, redirect, enforce it? Yeah, currently that's not in any provisions of the bill. I think at this point it's important to get this into statute, so there is that requirement. There are plenty of statutes out there that don't have an enforcement side to it. Two come to mind, one being the requirement for the state of Michigan to have a balanced budget before July 1st. We didn't get to that this year, but there's nothing to enforce that, but we did get to it. We as professionals worked together to get to that point. Another one is a part of my act that says that you cannot hinder an investigation of the OCA, but there's no enforcement, there's no punishment for that. It just says that you can't hinder in statute. So I think, and to make it palatable for most of the groups that this is being pressed upon, we want it to be viewed in a positive light and not something that's negative. Thank you. Why wouldn't the Department of Health and Human Services be responsible for making sure that everybody knows what the requirements are? Why is that on your shoulders? I think that would be a question for MDHHS. I'm sure that they have plans. Their tentacles reach far when it comes to both the health and human services side of their work. Okay. Rep. Wozniak. Thank you, Madam Chair. When does the seven-day clock start? That would be at the time of the request. From you? Well, from the CPS investigator that submits the request. Okay. And on the list of, it's a very extensive list of mandated reporters. I think there's at least 14 categories, if not more. Does CPS then contact every mandated reporter? No. What they would do is they'd reach out to a specific provider that they need to get the records from, and that's who they would submit the record to. I mean, there's, so we sent out a training video several months ago to most of Michigan's mandated reporters, and we sent out about 600,000 emails to reach these mandated reporters. And it was a training on how to recognize child abuse injuries. So we have the ability and the capability to do that. And you feel the seven-day requirement is a lot better than 14 days, obviously. Absolutely. Are there any reporters that give up their information voluntarily without waiting the seven days? Yes. Yes, absolutely. I mean, my office, our office is granted the same authority that Child Protective Services is in requesting records. So very often we request these records. We do get them within a certain time frame, usually before that two-week mark. Thank you very much. Another question from Rep. Thompson. Yeah, just for clarification, thank you, Madam Chair. This legislation only deals with mental health workers. So although the Regus bill is going to make sure that all mandatory reporters are receiving training once every three years, the actual legislation is only dealing with mental health professionals who may have access in their files during therapy sessions that a family member is at risk of harming their child or some similar situation. So when the CPS or law enforcement are reaching out for those records, they're not giving to them in a timely manner and children are losing their lives because they didn't know that they had to give them without the consent of the parent. Correct. Okay, thank you. Rep. Reingans. So there is a reason that mental health providers are so protective of their mental health records of their patients, and that's in part to protect their own patients. My husband is a trauma therapist and has worked with people in crisis and suicidal thoughts before, and it's just based on those conversations it is hard to figure out the balance of certain topics in therapeutic setting where you're trying to counsel a patient to overcome and regulate those thoughts or urges. At the first sight of a thought or urge like that, reporting them voluntarily also may completely destroy the therapeutic relationship. So what is the consideration in this balance here, making sure that we're definitely protecting children from actions that arise from those thoughts or urges and also protecting the therapeutic relationship for people to continue their mental health? I'm the child advocate, so I'm going to land on the side of the children here, and that's paramount in this picture, protecting those children, and they're required to report suspected child abuse, suspected child neglect if they believe that's what they have before them. So there is already currently that requirement in statute to do that. Right, and so what you're saying is that this needs to happen, like your rep, Husky, I saw you came back, are reducing the timeline only under an investigation. Correct. So to be clear, this changes nothing about when records are requested, when they are required to be handed over, and although these two bills work hand in hand in terms of making sure that all mandatory reporters, including mental health professionals, have adequate information about their responsibilities, signs they should look out for. This doesn't change anything about the responsibilities of mental health professionals other than the timeline for turning over records they're already required to turn over.

I guess my concern is more on the training end. Like I just want to make sure that the mental health providers have a really clear decision point. This is when you first report to make sure that we're protecting kids from those thoughts or urges that may arise in a therapeutic session. Sure. No, that makes sense. And I think that's the idea with creating this new training. I mean, MDHHS has taken this upon themselves before any of this came to fruition because of the need, because of the constant ask of mandated reporters out there in the ether. It's become apparent that this is needed on a regular basis. Thank you very much for your testimony. I think the bottom line is making sure that we protect our children at all costs. So thank you for being here, both of you. We do have some cards to read in, all in support. Ashardei Burton, Department of Health and Human Services, in support of the bill. Heath B. Lowry, Michigan Coalition to End Domestic and Sexual Violence. Amy Zagman, Michigan Council for Maternal and Child Health. Rachel Richards, Michigan League for Public Policy, all in support of the bill. Our next order of business is to vote on House Concurrent Resolution 1. We do have a substitute from Rep. Song. Would you like to speak on your substitute? Thank you, Madam Chair. I'd like to motion to vote to adopt H1 sub, which would also include sudden and unexpected loss of family food assistance. As we all know, with the federal shutdown, many families are going to lose access to food come November 1st, and I think that this would be an adverse effect for many children. Okay. We have a substitute on the floor. Would the clerk please take the roll? On the motion to adopt the substitute. Chair Schmaltz? Yes. Representative Wozniak? Yes. Fox? Yes. Johnson? Yes. Thompson? Yes. Pablo? Yes. Wolford? Yes. Young? Yes. Burns? Yes. Ringen? Yes. Song? Yes. Madam Chair, you have four yeas, zero nays, seven pass. The motion does not prevail. Thank you, Mr. Clerk. Rep. Burns moves to report House Concurrent Resolution 1. Will the clerk please... It can be anybody. Rep. Johnson moves to report House Concurrent Resolution 1. Will the clerk please call the roll? On the motion to report. Chair Schmaltz? Yes. Representative Wozniak? Yes. Fox? Yes. Johnson? Yes. Thompson? Yes. Pablo? Yes. Wolford? Yes. Young? Yes. Burns? Yes. Ringen? Yes. Song? Yes. Madam Chair, you have seven yeas, zero nays, four pass. The motion prevails. Thank you, Mr. Clerk. The vote has passed in House Concurrent Resolution 1. It is reported to the floor with recommendations. Rep. Thompson moves to report House Bill 4959 as H1 substitute. Will the clerk call the vote? On the motion to report. Chair Schmaltz? Yes. Representative Wozniak? Yes. Fox? Yes. Johnson? Yes. Thompson? Yes. Pablo? Yes. Wolford? Yes. Young? Yes. Burns? Yes. Ringen? Yes. Song? Yes. Madam Chair, you have seven yeas, zero nays, four pass. The motion prevails. Thank you, Mr. Clerk. House Bill 4959 is reported to the floor with recommendation as an H1 substitute. Rep. Wolford moves to excuse absent members. There are no absent members without objection. So ordered. Thank you. There being no further business before the committee, the committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.

For years, Michigan has required CPA candidates to complete 150 credit hours of higher education before licensure. While this was well-intentioned, this requirement has proven costly and rigid. It often delays entry into the workforce, disproportionately affects candidates from economically disadvantaged or underrepresented backgrounds, and limits opportunities for those who might otherwise excel through professional experience and examination. Employers across the state tell us that these barriers are contributing to the talent shortage, leaving businesses without the skilled professionals that they need. House Bill 4893 provides a modernized solution. It focuses on the core components of licensure, a bachelor's degree, two years of qualifying professional experience, and passage of the CPA exam, while adding the flexibility of creating an alternative to the 150 hours. This ensures that candidates will still have the option to pursue additional education but are no longer required to do so, that they can demonstrate proficiency through their experience. This approach also reflects the updates that were recently made to the Uniform Accountancy Act, referred to as UAA. This would align Michigan with the growing national movement among other states to modernize the CPA licensure. As both a CPA and an educator, I see firsthand how the current 150-hour mandate impacts aspiring professionals. Many of my students are highly capable and eager to enter the workforce, yet they face financial and logistic hurdles in completing that additional coursework. House Bill 4893 offers a balanced solution. It preserves rigorous standards through examination and experience while introducing flexibility that reflects real-world competencies. By adopting these changes, Michigan will not only help our students succeed, but will also strengthen our economy by ensuring businesses have access to the skilled professionals they need. The CPA profession has a national model, the UAA, that can be adopted

as a whole or in part to meet the needs of the individual jurisdictions. The UAA has undergone significant modernization to reflect the realities of today's profession. The UAA now offers three pathways to licensure. The post-baccalaureate and the 150-hour education model with one-year qualifying experience and the addition of a baccalaureate degree with two years qualifying experience. The new additional pathway incorporates a broader role for professional experience to be determined at the jurisdiction level. This change was not made lightly. It followed years of research, stakeholder engagement, and analysis of workforce trends. The UAA's goal was clear, maintain the integrity and rigor of the CPA credential while removing unnecessary barriers that limit those entering the profession. Importantly, Michigan is not acting alone. As of today, 24 states and jurisdictions have already adopted legislation creating this additional pathway, including our neighboring states, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, and Wisconsin is soon to follow. This regional momentum underscores the urgency of Michigan to modernize the requirement to remain competitive and consistent. This change also aligns with the Michigan Department of Licensure and Regulatory Affairs Cutting the Red Tape report, which recommends reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens and creating flexible pathways to licensure. By aligning Michigan's requirements with the national standards and the state-level strategies, we ensure consistency across jurisdictions, support mobility for our professionals for interstate commerce, protect the public interest, and strengthen our ability to attract and retain talent in this competitive marketplace. By adopting this legislation, we will achieve four goals. We'll cut the red tape, reducing a one-size-fits-all educational mandate with a competency-based model rooted in education, experience, and exam. We'll expand the CPA pipeline, opening doors for more qualified candidates, ensuring businesses have access to the financial expertise they urgently need. Strengthen our economy by supporting small businesses, corporations, and nonprofits across Michigan by addressing the talent gap and stay nationally consistent, keeping Michigan aligned with the other states already modernizing the license requirements. To be clear, this is not about lowering standards. The CPA exam remains rigorous and the CPA-verified experience ensures real-world readiness.
