And I think you can look at that additional year can provide a competitive advantage over students who are getting their bachelor's degree. It could make a more well-rounded business professional. And ultimately, depending on what that CPA wants to do, you may need a master's degree. So if they want to go into, like, a C-suite executive, they may require a master's degree, or if they want to go into education, it may require a master's degree. So when we think about how we're talking to students, we really do have to sit down and understand what are their future expectations in order to guide them appropriately. That helps. Thank you so much. You're welcome. Representative VanderWaal. Thank you all for being here. I appreciate it, Mr. Chair. Where do we line up as a state compared to our surrounding neighbors and lines of continuing ed credit? Sorry. I know, right? I thought I had a booming voice enough for that, but where do we sit in continuing ed credits versus our neighboring states? So in order to maintain mobility, all 55 jurisdictions that license CPAs, all 50 states and a few others, they all have what's called under reciprocity and substantial equivalency. All states currently have the 40 hours of continuing education per year. A little different nuance, like the change we're making to make it 38 of just anything and then 2 of ethics. But I will say on a national level, there is discussion on looking at those continuing education requirements and looking at different competency-based models and things of that nature to potentially either look at reducing the number or looking at how do you kind of measure competency with all this continuing education for the CPA license. So it's something that's being looked at nationally. One more follow-up, if I may. You may. Do we have a minimum of how many credits you have to take per year? So you can do 0, 0, and then 120. So it's a two-year licensing cycle, and it's 40 hours for the first year, and then anything over 40 hours can be carried over into the second year of the two-year licensing cycle. So, frankly, a CPA could get 80 hours in the first year and not require anything in the second year in order to utilize the concept of carryover, which is a great benefit. Many states do not offer a carryover model. They have to get that 40 hours per year, and so it's nice to have that for our CPAs to be able to take advantage of here in Michigan. Thank you. And if I may, just to clarify, what's relatively unique about Michigan, which we're hoping to change with this, is the auditing requirement, which a relatively small fraction of Michigan CPAs are actually involved in. Yeah, one of the – I'll admit we get a lot of complaints from

Does that feel like they're wasting that eight hours if they don't do audits? Of course, many CPAs that do, particularly large firms, they're getting that education anyway throughout their normal training that they attend, so this will just kind of relieve that burden for those individuals that feel like they're wasting a day if they have to go to a conference or do some online training or something like that to meet that requirement. Thanks for your testimony. Any other questions today? Michelle, I just need you to state your last name again. Randall. R-A-N-D-A-L-L. Thank you. Thank you. And we will go at ease. Thank you very much. I'm going to call the meeting back to order. We do have one card to read in on House Bill 4892 and 93. Not wishing to speak in support, Paige Foltz, Licensing and Regulatory Affairs. Thank you. I think that's it for the day. Yeah. Motion to excuse absent members. Representative Aragona, thank you. Being no other business in front of this committee, the meeting is adjourned.

title: Oversight - Public Health and Food Security — Tuesday, October 28, 2025
transcript:
The House Oversight Subcommittee on Public Health and Food Security will come to order. Would the clerk please take the attendance? Chair Bierlein. Here. Representatives Paquette. Here. Green. McDonald. Here. Cerniglue. Here. Mr. Chair, you have a quorum. Will the clerk please read in the letter from Oversight Committee Chair Jay DeBoer? In a letter dated September 12, 2025, Dear Mr. Clerk, I appoint the following members of the 103rd Legislature to serve as alternate members of the following oversight subcommittees, Public Health and Food Security, Representatives Alicia St. Germain, Karen Witzette, Sincerely, Jay DeBoer, State Representative, District 63. Representative Paquette moves to approve the minutes from the August 19th meeting. Hearing no objection, they are approved. Representative Cerniglue moves to approve the minutes from the August 26th meeting. Hearing no objection, they are approved. Today we'll be taking a closer look at the implementation of Michigan's Filter First law, which requires schools and child care centers to install certified filters at drinking water outlets to help protect children from lead exposure. We'll be hearing from a variety of perspectives, including representatives from schools, a child care center, and a licensed plumber who are directly involved in meeting these requirements. I appreciate each of our speakers for taking the time to share their experiences, challenges, and suggestions with the committee today. My office did reach out to both EGLE and MyLeap to invite them to testify today. Unfortunately, neither department was able to send a representative. However, we do hope to hear from them in the future, whether that is in this committee room or through their responses to the information that we hear today. Our goal is to gain a clear picture of how implementation is going on the ground, what's working well, where challenges exist, and what adjustments might help ensure this program achieves its intended purpose. As always, our focus is on accountability, transparency, and improving outcomes for Michigan families. With that, again, I thank everyone for being here, and we'll begin by inviting our first testifier to the table. Please welcome Steve Clark, the superintendent of Vassar Public Schools. Steve, whenever you're ready, have a seat, push the red button, and the microphone will be yours. Good morning, Chairman Bierlein and members of the subcommittee. My name is Steve Clark, and I am proud to serve as the superintendent of Vassar Public Schools, a district of about 750 students in Tuscola County. Thank you for the opportunity to share our experience with the implementation of the Filter First Law. Let me start by saying that I fully support the intent of this legislation. Every child deserves access to safe drinking water. As a superintendent and as a taxpayer, I value the health and safety of our students and community above all else. The intent behind this law to protect Michigan's children from lead exposure is unquestionably the right one. That said, as with many well-intentioned laws, the reality of implementation has revealed some unintended challenges that I believe are important for you to understand if the goal is to strengthen the policy moving forward. One, a disconnect between intent and impact. While the law's purpose is admirable, its focus is too narrow. Children consume most of their daily water at home and in the community, not only in schools or child care centers. By targeting only educational settings, the law gives the appearance of comprehensive protection but doesn't meaningfully reduce children's total exposure risk. If we truly want to protect public health, we have to address the broader water infrastructure, treatment, distribution, and aging service lines, not just the last few feet of plumbing inside our schools. Filter First doesn't get us there. Two, implementation barriers. Our district received a $46,000 grant through the Healthy Schools Grant 12A to help comply with the law. We are using that funding to retrofit hallway drinking fountains and food preparation sinks. However, the grant did not cover classroom sinks or other locations where students might fill water bottles or cups. More frustratingly, the Filter First grant prohibited the use of inline or entry point filtration systems, options that would have been far more practical and cost effective. We were forced into a piecemeal approach when a single building-wide filtration system could have protected every fixture at a fraction of the cost. Three, financial and staffing...

Once installed, the financial responsibility shifts entirely to districts. The cost of replacement filters is significant and the maintenance workload adds up quickly. For a small district like ours, this means spending both time and money that could otherwise go toward teaching and learning. This is not a matter of unwillingness. It's simply unsustainable for local schools to absorb these recurring costs year after year without dedicated funding. Four, testing results and ongoing compliance. Recently, our district did a full-scale test through DHHS on all of our faucets in three buildings, 110 faucets in total. The collection and processing of this testing was very time-consuming, taking well over three hours to collect the samples. The ongoing cycle of testing, documentation, replacement, and reporting has created a new layer of operational complexity. Unfortunately, the communication and guidance from EGLE have not always been clear or consistent, which only adds to the frustration and uncertainty at the local level. Five, recommendations for improvement. I offer a few recommendations that I believe would make this law both more effective and more manageable for districts. Allow inline and entry point filtration systems as eligible uses of grant funds. Provide sustainable funding for long-term filter replacement and maintenance. Adopt a broader public health strategy that includes investment in water infrastructure beyond school properties. In closing, I want to thank the committee again for the opportunity to testify. I genuinely appreciate the legislature's focus on children's health and safety. Filter First was created with good intentions, but to fulfill that promise, it must be practical, flexible, and sustainable. With clear guidance, adequate funding, and a broader public health lens, Michigan can lead the nation in protecting children from lead exposure, not just in schools, but in every place they live, learn, and grow. Thank you for your time and your commitment to Michigan's children. Thank you, Steve. What kind of communication have you had during this process, prior to or after receiving a grant from EGLE? Primarily, it's been through newsletters, emails, that kind of thing. I've had no personal contact. Has that created any barriers in your installation process? Have you had questions come up? Have they been responsive? It leads to a lot of us trying to decipher intent or meaning for particular requirements. I think I did try to get on a webinar at one point, and it was inaccessible. So yeah, it's just a lot of us guesswork, essentially. How much of your installation have your grant funds covered? We're just beginning that process. We have reached out to all five manufacturers that were approved through EGLE, and we only received responses from two of those. Multiple providers, but two producers, so LK and the Morris Group. Morris Group was interesting because they did not offer faucet filters, only water bottle fillers. Are there any other questions from the committee? Thank you, sir, for your time. I appreciate you coming down. Next, through Zoom, we will have Eric Hopstock. Eric is the superintendent of the Berrien County RISA. He covers Cass, Van Buren, and Berrien counties. Whenever you're ready, sir. Thank you for having us. Thank you for also being flexible, Chair and Representatives, to allow us to meet with you via Zoom. It is greatly appreciated. Yeah, we agree that the intent of safe drinking water is an admirable one, but it has resulted in some implementation barriers, funding barriers, and then communication. Particularly in the communication, it is the ever-changing nature of the communication. Guidance that we get maybe months ago, it changes, and then that requires a rethink. I have brought with me today Troy Boone. He's our director of facilities and security here at Berrien RISA to talk about the implementation. His voice really represents monthly meetings he has with facility directors throughout our county, Van Buren, and Cass counties. So when you hear his comments, they're really reflective of 30 school districts within this southwest area. So, Troy. Thank you for having me. I'm Troy Boone with Berrien RISA. You're going to hear a lot of redundancy from me based on the superintendent from Vassar Schools. Implementation-wise, the initial grant covers startup costs only. No funding exists for ongoing labor and materials moving forward. The process outlined by EGLE is very labor-intensive. Each building requires us, and we're relatively small, about 15 to 25 staff hours per sampling cycle. Each school must certify compliance by the end of 2025-26 school year, which EGLE has not yet determined what that compliance looks like. They're telling us that we have to justify that we're following all of the filter-first guidelines, but there's no guidance on how to actually get that information to them. For our district, this workload could exceed the available manpower quickly, and we're going to exhaust all efforts relatively fast just trying to comply and do our sampling cycles. The frequency of the filter replacement is still unknown for us, making planning for future replacements very difficult. When it comes to the funding side, filter-first, they're going to reimburse us for filtered bottle filling stations, faucet mounting filters, filtered pitchers for daycares, and also replacement cartridges. Inline filtered costs are excluded for reimbursement, which we have to have those just based on how our plumbing layouts are in our facilities. And it also talks about retrofitting bottle fill stations, but anything that's prior to 2014, EGLE doesn't give us any guidance on if we can install new bottle filters on those existing water coolers or not. But at Berrien RISA, what we're doing is to protect our general fund. We are holding off doing any kind of implementation or any kind of installation until the beginning of next year. We're hoping that more funding will become available for inline bottle fill stations, which that's going to be the bulk of what we install in our facilities. The EGLE guidance is highly detailed and continues to cause confusion around fixture classifications, approved filters, notification requirements, like schools are supposed to notify families and staff of testing results, yet no standard process or templates have been provided. Clear and simplified communication guides would help to ensure consistent messaging statewide before the July 1st, 2026 deadline. EGLE's signage guidance has changed repeatedly. Initially allowed one sign per group of non-potable filters. Later, EGLE came out and said individual signs for every fixture for non-potable fixtures, and now we're back to group signage again. So just some clarification from EGLE on how we need to identify potable versus non-potable water would be helpful. So thank you for the opportunity to give our experiences. Like I said, these are reflective of many of the districts within our areas. So if you have any questions, we'd entertain those now. Representative Green. Did your water test positive for lead? No, our water does not test positive for lead. Okay. But you have to put a lead filter according to the law on your stuff. Yes, that's correct. I have a migraine, so I'm trying to navigate through this. Okay, that's, there's a reason, I guess. Okay. So you're going through this with 30 different school buildings or 30 different districts? 30 different districts, so we're talking 150 buildings. And each building will have to meet these requirements despite whether or not they have lead in their water, as Rep Green mentioned. Correct. So are you aware yet of what the funding gap is between what is being provided by the state in grant funds?

and what the school districts will have to make up to finish installation? Well, the funding gap really is circled around that 2014 fixture date. So anything prior to 2014, you can't install a filter on it per EGLE's guidelines. You have to upgrade all of your fixtures downstream in order to use that inline filter. So anything after 2014, you can install that inline filter, which they have accepted that as an approved filter, but they will not provide funding for an inline filter. Some of the difficulties in answering your question is because of the inconsistencies we're getting from EGLE. And because of that, the number is going to fluctuate because we don't know what is acceptable and what is not. Representative McDonnell. Thank you, Chair. Actually, I just wanted to ask for some clarification. My staffer told me, heard from someone that what we're talking about is there used to be a test and chase program, but that costs more. Is that correct than what we're doing now? And that this is supposed to be a way to make it more efficient, but it's just not working? Or what is the basic issue? We're talking about a legislation that was passed last term that said every school district, any potable water has to be filtered specifically for lead, whether there was ever lead in the system or not. And it's not just school districts, it's also daycare centers, both private and I guess they're all private. Okay. So I don't know about the previous test and chase method. Okay. But this is obviously I can hear that this is not going very well. Thank you. What information specifically do you feel like you're currently missing from EGLE moving forward so that you can meet the requirements? Because these are things that we can request and try to get answers to. We would actually hope that they would clarify filter compliance and if it's an acceptable filter. I don't know if that's through a submittal process, but that's something that would help us decide if these apparatuses are what we could use to comply with EGLE. The other thing is just straight communication. I mean, it's just been back and forth on, you know, like just how do you label your fixtures? You know, if we have to do every single fixture in every single building, that's going to take an ungodly amount of manpower. Granted, that's only one time that you have to do that at the beginning, but then all the bottle sampling and everything that you have to do and get it third party tested if you don't, I don't understand why we have to do third party testing if we could do that internally. That's another thing that's going to cost every district moving forward a lot of money outside of the initial. And then, you know, we have to be certified by we got to show certification by July 1st of 2026, but there's no guidance on what does that look like? What do you need from us? What do we need to show you that we're following the filter first guidelines, which we're really not 100% sure on what we're doing. Any other questions? Thank you, gentlemen. Appreciate it. Thank you. Next on Zoom, we have Jim Ply. Jim is a former principal and the current facilities special projects coordinator for Montrose Community Schools. He's been helping his district manage initiatives like Filter First and we appreciate his time this morning. Thank you. And thank you for the invitation. I'm just going to throw numbers at you. It's pretty much what we're going to do. We have not been fortunate enough to get a grant yet. We're in the current cycle with the Healthy Hydration Grant and hopefully we will get that. Otherwise, the cost of all of this is going to fall directly on us. We're fortunate enough. Montrose is a small school district in northern Genesee County serving about 1,400 students. I will agree with everyone else when I say that the idea of clean, safe drinking water is extremely important. Again, not just at school but everywhere. In order for us to comply with the minimum requirements of the law, we're going to have to install six new fountains throughout our three buildings. That's going to cost us approximately $24,000 in the cost of the units and in hiring a plumber to come in and do this for us. The other issue that we're going to have is we really need about 18 inline filtration systems because we need to filter the water in our several areas within our kitchens in each of our buildings. Also, our teacher's lounges because they pull water out of the sinks to make coffee with and those, by law, now have to be filtered as well. And then the real problem we're dealing with is all of our early elementary pre-K programs have drinking fountains within their classrooms because it's extremely disruptive to pick 15, 20 kids and we're going to march out and we're all going to get in line at the drinking fountain and we're all going to get a drink, whether you need one or not, and then we're all going to march back in. So, in the design of those rooms, drinking fountains were put in those rooms to make it more convenient for those kids and those teachers. We're going to have to see if we can put inline filters in there if they qualify. If not, then we'll have to come up with another solution for those early elementary classrooms. Altogether, we're looking at, just to meet the compliance, about $32,000 that we're going to have to come up with out of our general budget. And again, if we are lucky enough to get the grant, I believe the grant's only going to cover about $18,000 of it. And that does not include, as has been brought up, the manpower and cost of testing that's going to have to happen in our buildings throughout the course of the year. Also, the cost of replacement filters, which are not cheap. We're looking at, for our drinking fountains, it's probably estimated at about $4,200 we're going to have to spend yearly on filter cartridges. And if we are able to put in inline filters, that's another $1,000 for inline filters. So, the cost is a bit prohibitive, especially if we do not get the grant. But beyond that, it's also the burden it's going to put on our maintenance folks. Well, we only have two. So the burden it's going to put on those two guys to do the sampling, to do the flushing of the lines, to meet the requirements of the law. It's, again, a great idea because safe, healthy drinking water is important. We already had that because our testing results have not come back with any issues with lead or other particulates in our water. But we're still going to have to meet the law, even though we haven't had a problem. Jim, when you guys have done that testing in the past, do you test it when it comes into the building? Do you test it at individual drinking fountain sources? How does that work? So in the past, what we've done is we've tested at source. So we'll go to drinking fountains and pull tests randomly from different buildings, from different fountains. We've never tested them all at one time, which is what will have to happen here. We'll see. Have you currently, just to recap, you've currently applied for a grant and you're waiting to see if it's being awarded? Yeah, so the second version of the healthy hydration grant came out this fall. We have applied for that. From what I understand, we should know by December if we have qualified or not. And then do you guys meet as like an ISD and kind of talk as superintendents and principals? Is this a reoccurring theme in the schools in Genesee County? Yeah, so our maintenance directors get together every other month, and this is a large topic that consumes a lot of time from everyone. And everyone is very confused on what it's going to take to fulfill this. And again, I think it has been brought up by the Berrien County superintendent. How do we report it? I think my favorite issue with this is when I contacted EGLE back a year ago to say that we have completed our

We've put together our plan as directed by the law. And where would you like me to submit this to? And their response was, well, you don't submit it. You just make sure it's available in case anybody wants it. So ours is available. And to clarify, you've never had any sort of negative test in your water system for lead? We have in the past, yeah. You have? And how did you address those when you have them? In the past, we would bring in an independent third party and just ask them to, we did some testing both of water and of air quality in the buildings. And that's how we would do it. We just contract a third party. Thank you very much for your time. No further questions? Oh, Representative Green. Okay, so do you have your own well? No. Okay, so Montrose has municipal water that is pumped to your building? Correct. Does Montrose conduct, I know they do, so you don't have to answer this. Montrose does conduct regular testing. Have they ever tested from coming into the buildings? All of our testing has been at the actual water source, so drinking fountains. So when you did test positive for lead, was the rest of the municipality testing positive for lead too? We have not tested positive for lead. Oh, I thought, I'm sorry, maybe I misunderstood. Oh, you've tested for it previously and it was always negative? Correct. Okay, and same with the municipal drinking source as well? Yeah, Montrose's drinking water is tested fine every time I've seen reports. Okay, I'm just, I remember this bill being passed, but I'm just trying to wrap my brain around. Because then, I guess, and this is not necessarily directed to you, but do we have any water experts coming? Because at some point, they're pulling everything good out of the water too. We do not today. We were hoping to have both Eagle and Miley. We weren't able today. We're hoping to get them either in the committee in the future or just to have them respond to the committee. I just want to verify. So you believe that your filter replacement is going to be about $4,200 a year, which, I mean, in the scheme of things, it doesn't seem like a lot of money to make sure that kids are getting safe drinking water, except they're already getting safe drinking water. So it's just additional cost to the school district that I'm sure you're not sitting on piles of cash. Yeah, so we're anticipating $4,200 a year just for the drinking fountains in the hallways. If we put in the inline units, then it will go up from there. Okay. Thank you very much, Jim. We appreciate your time today. Thank you. Next, I would like to welcome Steve Schreiner with Schreiner Mechanical out of Frankenmuth, Michigan. Steve and his team have been an important part of helping schools and child care centers in our district meet the filter first requirements. His company has worked hands-on with local facilities to install and maintain their filtration systems. So, Steve, we appreciate you taking the time today to share your perspective as a licensed plumber and contractor who's been directly involved in this process. Thank you. I believe it takes a lot of energy to make this happen today, and I really want to commend you for doing this. I think persistence by us, you're listening, and maybe not agreeing, but listening brings this together. And, yes, safe drinking water is something that I've worked with for over 40 years. I'm a master plumber, mechanical contractor, and a boiler contractor. I've done a lot of work in schools, churches, houses. We have to follow laws. We're under the guidance of the state of Michigan with the Bureau of Plumbing, mechanical, boiler codes, cross-connection. I'm a cross-connection licensed contractor for many years. I gave that up two years ago when the lawsuits all became very in front of me with the Genesee County program, and cross-connection is a big program, but I was a licensed cross-connection contractor for many years and still follow and still work in that profession helping. Safe water, 2014, it was very clear all water faucets had to be lead-free by a certain content. No lead was allowed in these faucets, and if there was, it was a very minute amount. We used to, as plumbers back years ago, we used to use something called solder, 50-50 solder, which had lead content in it. We are no longer allowed to use that. Since then, PEX pipe, different types of copper, silver solder, different ways of putting things together to create safe water. Water heaters from manufacturers, whether it's A.O. Smith or whatever manufacturer is out there, even Bradford White out of Michigan, they all use what they call glass lining. Why is that? To keep your water safe, NSF approved. So I follow these laws, and I have followed these laws for many, many years, along with every other plumber. When the plumbing inspector comes in, most times if you're in a school, you're asked to flush the water and test. So I've been through this for many years. My dad, my grandfather, this is not anything new to our family. I was sick. I had West Nile. For 14 years I suffered with water, suffered with my own water at home, and I had it tested. So, yes, I do understand water very well when it comes to contaminants. When it comes to arsenics, and when it comes to all the other stuff that's in the water, in your aquifers, that's coming up and you're drinking it, it's amazing what's in that water that you're allowing your children and or family to drink or use. Now we're talking about schools. Talking about daycares. In Frankenmuth, Michigan, our water is the lowest lead level that it's been in the history of our water. City of Frankenmuth normally had to test every year for lead content in their water. They've now been told by EGLE they do not have to test every year. It's every three years. Wow, that's pretty neat. But I've been involved with this program since the crisis down in Genesee County, and I've been watching, been listening, and then here comes this program. And I thought right away, told my guys, this isn't good. It's going to be unsafe. It's not going to be under control. It's going to be out of control. The money is going to be filtering out, going to places where it doesn't belong, and we're not protecting the schools that need to be protected. As in Frankenmuth, we've done a lot of work with them schools. I know the people that have done work in those schools, if it wasn't myself or our company, and I know the state inspectors that did the inspecting. I know that it was safe. I know that they did their job. So my question is always, why can't I do a ground study before I do anything to find out do I have or do I not have lead in my system? We know coming from the city of Frankenmuth or from any municipality what is the content of that. What's in the content of that water? So with that being said, there is no reason why I should not be able to, as a plumber and or as a facility operator, have water testing done in my own facility, whether it's my house, whether it's my church, or whether it's my school, whether it's my daycare, and I can send that water to a facility that is approved for lead testing. There are several in the state. I approached to have this happen last week. I did my due diligence, got a hold of the lab. I drove down to the lab, which was an hour from the shop, told the gentleman what I was doing. I picked up multiple sample bottles. He gave me directions. The next morning, after eight hours of non-movement of water, we did our sampling. I'm sorry. We picked them up on Friday, and Monday morning I took them. No, I'm sorry. It was Friday. Took them back down. I had one of my guys drive down with the samples with a check. He came back to the shop and told me that I was going to get a phone call with a phone call being from the testing lab that they will not test the water. They feel uncomfortable. They didn't like the paperwork. They don't want to be in the middle of a mess were the exact words that were spoken by the testing lab that I took the water samples to. I thought, wow, I'm being slapped in the face. All I want to do is check St. Lawrence Lutheran School for lead. And I had talked to the administration of the school, and I was granted that permission to do so. Actually, the testing, the samples were taken by the administration and by the facility manager for the water. But again, they refused to do the testing because on grounds they didn't want to be in the middle of a mess. So I took it upon myself to get another testing lab from another area, Western Michigan, told them exactly what I was doing, and again, this lady said, well, not again, but this lady said, we will absolutely do this.

problem. What I find interesting is the differences in the way that the testing is to be performed. The first one, I just get bottles, I fill them up, I take them back down, and in 24 to 48 hours I have results. The second one, they sent me a cooler, a glue cooler with the bottles in it and said the water is to be collected and how I'm supposed to do it, how I'm supposed to label the bottles, and it would be between 5 to 7 days for results. That's how long it takes for them to get results from the water. I thought that was odd. Why would one be 24 to 48 hours and why be the next one be 5 to 7 days? So with that being said, I find that aggravating as a plumber. And as a contractor, a business person, a taxpayer, as a person that's just trying to do his due diligence of finding out the absolute truth about our school and whether or not it has any lead content at all. And if it did have lead content in it, then correct it. Find out where it's coming from and correct the problem. I've been asked by several school districts for filters. How much are they? Where do I put them? I had three walkthroughs in schools with manufacturers. The manufacturer first round would tell us what we had to do. We had to put a filter on the hot. We had to put a filter on the cold. We looked at the early development center and underneath those sinks it would be very difficult to apply these filters. Then it changed to only the cold. Then it changed again to you can't run that through that faucet. You've got to put a separate faucet in. Then you have to put signage up. Each and every time that we did this, all I found was a complete different story from the previous trip that we had through the school. There was an absolute direct phone call that came from EGLE to the gentleman that was taking us through the manufacturer as we were in the kitchen at St. Lawrence Lutheran School. I said, what about the ice maker? They were putting in a new large ice maker. It was an exact program of how do I filter that? You don't need to filter the ice maker. That's not in the program. That threw my flag up. I as a plumber, I'm looking at this saying, how can you not have to put a filter on an ice maker but you're putting it on everything else? Then also a refrigerator in a classroom that has ice and water through the door does not need to be filtered. That's not in the program. It's not part of the program. How is that exempt? Who made this list? I have to follow laws as a plumber in the state of Michigan. There is no such thing as exempt from this and exempt from that. I am not allowed to put in a faucet that has lead content. I don't know of any faucets that have lead content. If you want to know the truth, I have gone to Kohler. I've talked to the owners. I've talked to their platform engineers. I've gone to Delta. I've gone to American Standard and I've gone to Moen. All faucet manufacturers have had the exact same comment. Who said we have lead in our product? It wasn't me. I didn't say it. But I know since 2014 what we've done as plumbers. And even before that, safe plumbing practices always continued. So my feeling is that water needs to be tested prior to. And if there is lead present in a program, we need to address that in a proper way. We don't put a filter in that went from $20 to $100 in a matter of one year. We don't put a filter in that's going to be changed by somebody that may not be qualified. Or we may not change it at all because of the cost of the filter. We just completely disembark. We straight line it. Who's going to look at that? Nobody. One other item that was brought to me very clearly at the beginning of this program is that all these devices that are going to be installed in these schools and or applications are going to have to be done under permit by a state licensed plumbing outfit program. And there's not enough plumbers in the state of Michigan. I don't think that could do this. Number one. Number two, I do know that most facilities are doing this on their own. Which I have no problem with. But there are no permits being pulled for these apparatuses that are being installed. Which the plumbing department clearly stated that they are going to require a permit for each and every device that's being installed. Thank you. I don't know if I'm helping, hurting, or what I'm doing for this. But as a plumber, my heart's in this. I have grandkids. I've got kids. And yes, I want safe drinking water. Thank you, Steve. I'm going to start with the first question that I know Rep. Green has at least one. So you've been a contractor for a while. Not to say how old you are, but you've been doing this a while. Are change orders something that you like to get as a contractor? Change orders are normal. That's part of our business. Do they drive up costs typically if you have to go back and change what you've already done? Or at least change what you've planned for? So is the lack of communication from EGLE and the lack of clear guidance been a problem? Schreiner Mechanical has no... There's no communication between EGLE and plumbing houses. I'm also on the Plumbing Inspectors Association. I'm involved with that. I'm a member. And that is one thing that has been brought up at our association meeting that there is no communication between EGLE and the plumbers or the inspectors. This is... From my understanding, this has been between the schools, building owners, and those folks. It's not something that's coming to us. We can look it up, yes. But that's what we have to do. We have to go after it. It's not coming to us. Representative Green. Thank you, Chair. Okay, I want to go back to the ice machine because I'm still trying to wrap my brain around that. So the ice machine, which goes... Ice goes into our beverages. That does not have to have a filter. Ice machines are not in the program as I was told. So no, you do not have to filter an ice machine. So there could potentially be lead coming from the water to the ice machine and then they have lead in the ice? Is that... That would be a correct statement. Okay. I'm just... I'm trying to wrap my brain around all of this and it's really hard. You can't. Okay. So another question. You were talking about the source. And I just want to put this out there because a little fun fact. The headwaters of the Flint River as a Superfund site pouring and leaching chemicals in it. But nobody seems to care about that. But then they keep wanting to put filters on every single faucet possible. So they're not even... Because you talked about the source. Like where water comes from in the ground, where water comes from in the plant. And usually that's clean. And obviously we've had the whole Flint crisis and that's because of the switching of the pipes and the sources of it. But just fun fact that the Metamora Superfund site is leaching into the Flint water system. Which nobody seems to care about. And I'm glad we're caring finally about water for children. But I think if we're really going to care about water, we need to start paying attention to what's going on in the state. Because I know Metamora is not alone in that. So that's just a little fun fact. Thank you. Thank you. Do you anticipate that once installation is complete, will school maintenance staff be able to maintain these systems? Is it going to take a plumbing contractor? Is it going to take some specialized training? Just in your years of experience. Manufacturers that build these, they put their filters on there. And these filters have to be put in in a specific way. They're just not something that you throw in. So the person that is doing this, yes, has to be somewhat qualified, gone through training so they understand how the filter is going to be taken out, properly disposed of, and then also a new filter being put in. Yes, absolutely. Facility management most likely will be putting these in. But I do not believe that the training to the facility management is going to be there enough because the changes that I've seen in the way that manufacturers build and how they do things, they change every year. So this is going to be a yearly program that these folks are going to have to go through, which is going to have to be paid for, put on. And I'm sorry, but I'm not one that's going to sit in front of a computer for two hours listening to some guy tell me how to change a filter. It needs to be done in person to show people it has to be a hands-on. That's the only way this can be done and done correctly. Again, these filters, when they're taken off,

put back on or filters are being changed. Nobody's talking about what's going to happen to those filters that they're taking off and or the cartridges that they are taking off to put the new filter in. Cross-contamination between the old filter and the cartridge are putting the filter back in. There's going to be some issues that are going to come on down the road with that. And I think I just have one more question for you, Steve. So over the course of your career, I'm sure this isn't the first time that you've installed a filter on a water system anywhere. Have those changed much over the years, the filter systems? Have they advanced? Has new technology come out and somebody deems that what was previously the proper filter system is no longer adequate to do the job that we hoped it would do? Absolutely. I at my own residence, I put in a full reverse osmosis program for my house because my water was so tainted coming from the aquifer that it was deemed as unusable water. Even though I have neighbors living right next to me and I took the results of those tests to the county health department where I live and they just shrugged their shoulders. There isn't nothing we can do. But what you're saying as far as our changes, yes. Every year these changes are being made to create more difficulty for people to understand how these things work. It becomes, for me as a plumber, it gets really difficult for me. So I can only imagine, I've been doing this for a long time, how can a guy or a person that, you know, he just got hired in as a facilities manager or hired in as doing this type of work, you know, in the facility, how can he comprehend how this stuff goes together and then the following year the changes have been made. Oh, now instead of doing that, you've got to do this. And it's just going to, it's going to get muddied. So yes, that's true. Representative Green. Well, just for clarification, so you are, what you just stated was that the process of doing, putting and installing the filters are changing the regulations from the government. But I guess for clarification, a reverse osmosis system hasn't changed in technology though, has it? No, the filtration of the water before it gets to the RO system has. So the way you're taking iron out, how you're taking and running the water through maybe softeners or products before it gets to the RO, so the RO will last longer. So you do pre-filtering before you get to the RO, yes. But that, I mean, technology-wise, how much has that changed in the last 20 years? Quite a bit. Oh, really? Yes, quite a bit. The type of beads that are being used for the iron filters, things of that nature. And also companies, manufacturers are also recognizing all the chemical and all the stuff that's in the water. So they're trying to advance what they're doing to help take that out. I wanted to mention one more thing. I have a school district that's close by. They put new water filtration program in, and this is in the Millington district. He said I can mention this, so I'm going to mention it. They put their own water bottle filling stations in. These filters are supposed to last approximately a year. They are not into their first quarter of the year, and the filters are already blinking, and they've got to change them. Millington's on well water. Their water's not as clean. The TDS is higher. So guess what happens to the filters? And he was asking me for pricing on filters, and I've made that accommodation. My cost on that filter is $86 apiece, and I would believe that I would say within a year, you're going to see those filters probably at $114 to $115 once this gets rolling. So a district like Millington then would benefit from a pre-filter or a whole system well water filtration system then to get to those end ones. But then you used another example, or is it Frankenmuth or Montrose? Sorry, I'm starting to lose track of the school districts. But their water is already clean, so their filters will last long. So there is then a disparity between then districts depending on their source of water. As a plumbing contractor, I feel that every school before it opens, the water should be tested, period. It should be tested at the beginning, and it should be tested at different locations within the school. No filter is going to stop the lead. We need to stop the lead if the lead is there. But if there's no lead, why are we spending all this money on projects that don't make no sense? $85 million high school was built in Saginaw, Michigan. It's brand new. It opened up in 2025. They have to follow under the same program as what we are following. That was under state guidance through the whole program. Why would that school have to follow through the same program if there's no lead coming in and everything that was put into that school is up to code by the state of Michigan approved for occupancy? And I guess the comment would be is then so like a district like Millington that's already a smaller district is going to need more funds than a school like the brand new Saginaw school, but there aren't going to be enough funds to then comply according to our grant system. And that's what it seems like. Again, would you want to know first with Millington, do I have lead in the water? If I have no lead in the water, why am I putting these filters in? That would be first. Let's do our groundwork. Let's make sure we're clean before we go to the next step. Steve, thank you very much for your time and your experience. Next, we have Kimberly Zender. Kimberly is the owner and operator of Eduplay Discovery Center. Kimberly has been a strong advocate for early childhood education and has taken an active role in navigating the filter first requirement at her center. As both an administrator and educator, she brings valuable insight into how these new regulations are impacting child care providers from the application process for grants to the installation and maintenance of filtered water systems. Kimberly, we appreciate your time and expertise, and if you go ahead and get started whenever you're ready. Thank you. Good afternoon, Chair Bierlein and members of the subcommittee. I appreciate you allowing me to sit here and share this information with you. My name is Kimberly Zender. I am the owner and operator of Eduplay Discovery Centers in Frankenmuth and also Saginaw. Child care and preschool programs that serve about 130 wonderful children every day, from tiny little infants just learning to crawl to excited little preschoolers who are asking 100 questions during lunchtime. I'm also a lifelong Michigander, a mom, a small business owner who has spent the last 13 years making sure that we're in a place that parents can trust, a place that's safe, clean, and also joyful. Let me begin by saying that I completely support the goal of ensuring safe, lead-free drinking water, especially for our most vulnerable population in Michigan schools, child care, and preschools. No one disputes that clean water is an essential to children's health and development. The intent of the filter first requirements, wanting to protect kids from harmful exposure, is very admirable. But the reality of this bill, as written, would create serious unintended consequences for child care providers like mine, for local schools, and for the very families that this bill aims to protect. Although from a child care standpoint, as of October 24th, child cares were already underneath the umbrella of having to have their water tested and also having the water management plan in place. The first issue is the cost of funding gap. At EduPlay, we operate on a very razor-thin margin, as do the majority of child care centers and preschools. Every dollar is carefully budgeted between staff pay, food, curriculum materials, and also facility maintenance. The high costs and ongoing expenses and inadequate budgeting. So the cost does not end with the installation. Districts and schools must also pay for the recurring testing and ongoing filter replacement, creating a perpetual financial strain on budgets that are already stretched thin. And again, this is in the child care arena. However, as you've heard from the people that have come previous to me, it's as well in the schools with the budgets. We've already looked at what that might mean. So several thousand dollars up front, hundreds more each year to maintain compliance. There's no stable state funding to be able to support that requirement. The grants available today are limited. They're inconsistent. They don't cover all centers. In a small community like Frankenmuth, that means tuition increases, program cuts, neither of which families can afford in any community. They're working parents, teachers, nurses, small business owners already stretched thin by

inflation and child care costs. So the next issue is pretty redundant and unnecessary for many centers. EduPlace water comes from Saginaw County, which it cedes its testing requirements. Our building is new. We opened in 2018 and everything was built from the ground up. Our plumbing is modern. Our testing is already part of our licensing and environmental health requirements. Yet under this law, we'd be treated exactly as the same of an older school building with century-old pipes. This one-size-fits-all approach doesn't make any distinction between facilities that are already compliant and those that genuinely need remediation. The funding and money is best used in areas that need it. The funding and money is best used in areas that need it. Need remediation rather than funding being used for areas that are meeting and exceeding standards already. I believe our focus should be targeted, investing resources where testing shows contamination. Otherwise, we're just asking responsible centers to divert funds from teacher salaries and child safety improvements to pay for filters that we don't need. The money is best spent in areas that really, truly need it. My final concern is the false sense of security that this bill creates. A filter is not a magic fix. It's temporary. It only works if it's properly maintained and replaced exactly on schedule. In a busy child care center and a school of any size, it's a real risk. You have staff turnover. You have human error. You have simple oversight that can compromise a filter's effectiveness. The public sees a filter first sticker and assumes that the water is safe, but that filter could be past its lifespan. Meanwhile, the root cause, the aging lead service lines and outdated infrastructure completely remains untouched. If we truly want safe water, we have to fix the pipes, not just the faucets for those areas and those centers and schools that need it. There's a smarter, more sustainable path forward. First, target the funds where they're needed the most, the schools and the child care facilities that actually test positive for the lead. Second, prioritize replacing lead pipes and service lines, not layering new mandates on top of already functioning ones. Third, allow for flexible compliance. Centers with clean, verifiable water should be able to opt out for periodic professional testing instead of permanent filter installations. And finally, let's integrate oversight into the system that already exists, like county health departments, which already monitor child care every two years. We have great county health department in Saginaw County and it keeps us accountable. Even all the way back from being an in-home child care provider, we had to have our water tested in a well. They came in, they would test your water, they gave you the results, and you couldn't move forward until it was compliant. I don't understand why having that in place under this system wouldn't be something that would make sense. I believe that we can do better. I believe that we can protect children's health without punishing responsible providers and the schools and actually giving the funding and the help to the schools and the areas that they need it. I'd like to have you take time to consider this regulation. Maybe there's ideas that we can do to help tighten it up, to give the money and the funds, to give the focus to those that truly need it. One that restores public trust, supports small businesses, and also provides every Michigan child with genuinely safe water in all areas, including those with disparity. Thank you so much for your time and for your commitment to the children and the families of Michigan. Thank you, Kimberly. Were you able to apply for one of the first filter grants? I was not. From a child care standpoint, there were several different areas that you had to log into to be a part of, going on to my login, my login business, from gems to EEM. Although we are a part of a lot of those, the application wasn't allowing us to get in because I was consistently denied by EGLE to be able to connect to their system. I had made multiple calls. That was one of the last systems that I was required to on the list to connect to. Now we have ISD preschools. So we have GSRP. So I already am connected to a lot of those different funding sources on my login and my login for business. So why I was unable to connect for hours and hours, I made multiple calls. It just didn't happen. So how have you gone forward with implementation? Because you said you had to be compliant four days ago. How has that gone without the grant funding? So without the grant funding, from a child care perspective, putting it in place is easy. The area that I find interesting is that in a child care setting, it is not required for the pitchers, like the water filter pitchers, to have to be tested. So we could have pitchers everywhere and regularly changed like we do our filters, but those don't need to be tested. However, I did go ahead and submit my information to have my water tested because I'd like to see like where we at, you know, how does it come out. Although it was not necessarily required in our setting with the choices that we've been able to use, you know, we'll see where it comes. I still have not gotten those results back, but I was also told 24 to 48 hours. Have you heard from any of your colleagues in the area? Have they had similar experiences? Is this a common theme in early childhood? Yes, a lot of other providers are very frustrated, the majority of which are also using pitchers within their rooms. For my center specifically though, I do believe in water being able to be readily available to the kids at all times. So when I built in 2018, I have water fountains in every single one of my classrooms. So it was just an added thing that I put into effect automatically. And now they have a sticker over them that says not safe to drink. And if you know kids, they're very, very literal. So when they're coming home from school or coming in after school and they're looking at all of these signs and they're just beginning to read, so like they're in kindergarten or, you know, they see this not safe. What does that tell our kids? That's what does that tell our kids? Oh, goodness. I'm sorry. That's just it's frustrating and it's a waste. It's a waste of resources. I can just kind of anticipate this, you know, future when we get the school supplies list that it includes a Brita filter for every kid to put in a can. What things do you think could have been better on the early childhood side? I mean, I think everyone's kind of expressed the same. Our facilities are all operating with water that we've been testing. We have it tested and we know it's safe. And there are some folks that do need filters. But I'm looking back. I can remember a few years ago. It's probably more than a few now. You know, schools try to get bonds and sometimes while they're trying to get those bonds, maintenance can be deferred because they don't have a choice. And I remember local school district trying to get a bond and there was a picture of the little kid bathtub sitting in the hallway collecting water from the roof. So do you think they're going to, if money is tight, do you think they're going to replace filters or are they going to try to fix the roof? They're going to try and fix the room. They're on razor thin budgets as it is. And so it's kind of interesting even to send in the water. There's no checks and balances system whatsoever. Somebody could, you know, make the choice to do things in a way that is, you know, wrong. And I don't think that it offers the right options for us. I believe that it needs to be facilitated through a state system similar to when you're an in-home child care provider. In the schools

from this. Being able to have the oversight say from environmental health like we did, where they come in, they test the water, you know, and it's done every couple of years. If for some reason something's wrong, then at that point there's steps for change. But ultimately if something is not wrong, why are we throwing money at something when that money needs to go into Metamora? You know, there was an example there. You know, I mean that is money well spent when it can be able to clean up an area that really needs it. You know, with the Flint water crisis. This money can go to how about, you know, the homes, the families, the children at home when they're there the majority of the time versus schools. Are there any other questions? Thank you, Kimberly, for your time today. Really appreciate everyone taking the time to drive down to Lansing to participate through Zoom. I think, you know, from our perspective it will be really good to hear from the departments and kind of some feedback from them. There being no further business before the committee, the committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.

repelled the invasion and launched their own counter-offensive that marked the first victory of Allied forces in World War II. Their courage inspired the free world. Greece's resistance forced Hitler to divert his forces south into Greece, delaying the invasion of the Soviet Union, a delay that ultimately contributed to the eventual downfall of Nazi Germany and European fascism. Since 1940, Greeks in their homeland and throughout the world, as well as here in America, have celebrated Ohi Day as a day of national pride, a time of recommitting themselves to the principles of self-determination, freedom, and democracy. title: Oversight — Tuesday, October 28, 2025
transcript:
The House Committee on Oversight will come to order. Would the clerk please take attendance? Chair DeBoer. Here. Representatives Bierlein. Here. Meerman. Here. Paquette. Here. Cara. Here. Brock. Here. Green. Here. Regas. Here. Shriver. Present. Wolford. Present. Miller. Here. Pahutski. Here. Conlin. Here. McDonald. Here. Mencer. Here. Cerniglou. Here. Wigella. Here. Mr. Chair, you have a quorum. Thank you, Mr. Clerk. Representative Mencer moves to approve the minutes of the September 30th meeting. Hear no objections. They are approved. Today's meeting, we will be having testimony and comment on the recent updated health education standard framework that has been proposed by the State Board of Education. After all testimony and questions have been exhausted, we will hold a vote on House Resolution 195. First up to testify today will be Dr. Sue Carnell, Interim State Superintendent, to testify to the proposed health education standards. Dr. Carnell, begin whenever you are ready. Good morning. Thank you for the opportunity to be here. I just want to introduce a couple of people that are with me today. We have Dr. Pamela Pugh, who is the State Board of Education President, and I also want to introduce Dr. Diane Golzinski. She's the Deputy Superintendent in charge of school health and among other things. Also with me today are other department staff. So thank you again for this opportunity. My name is Sue Carnell. I'm the Interim State Superintendent. You requested my attendance today to address your concerns about the proposed 2025 Comprehensive Health Education Standards under development for consideration by the State Board of Education. I'd like to start today with three areas that I believe we have common ground. First one. The first common area or first common ground area that I think that we have in common is that we must follow

There are three laws that I will reference for this committee that the department follows related to health standards. First one, MCL section 380-1278 delegates to the department the responsibility of developing standards for both health education and sex education. This section also requires health education as a part of graduation requirements. Second law, 380-1169, which requires instruction of dangerous communicable diseases, including but not limited to HIV, AIDS, and best methods for restricting and prevention. This instruction stresses the abstinence from sex and as a responsible and effective manner for prevention. And the third law is section 1507, requires decisions about sex education be made at the local level. Local school boards decide what to teach and parents can opt their children out of any and all sex education lessons. That's been the case in the past and nothing is changing with the proposed new standards. The second area of common ground is parents' rights. We believe in the natural fundamental right of parents and legal guardians to determine the direct care, teaching, and education of their children. We believe parents have the right to a voice in the process and outcomes for their own children. And the third common ground I want to mention is academics. We believe that as a state we need to focus on academics. English and language arts and other core areas are extremely important. So how do we address what we believe are common ground issues? Well, let's take a deeper look at the three laws. Developing standards. This process of bringing new or updated education standards to the Board of Education for consideration is as follows. And this is as they relate to health education. The National Health Education Standards were drafted, reviewed, and passed in March of 2024 by the Society for Health and Physical Education. The national standards provide a comprehensive framework for educators to deliver high-quality instruction and make a positive difference in the health and well-being of every student. There was a National Health Education Standard Task Force comprised of diverse group of stakeholders from grades K through 12, higher education, and national health education organizations. MDE then reviewed the national standards and compared them to our 2007 standards. We reviewed the standards from other states and developed the Michigan version of the updated health education standards. First round of interviews included a small group of content experts, those that are in nutrition and mental health and safety, to review any missing skills or determine accuracy of terminology. The MDE team made edits and sent the first draft out for a second review. The second round was sent to statewide organizations and individuals who are health educators, teachers, and administrators. The final draft was then presented to MDE leadership team for review and revision. We presented the draft health education standards to the board at a public meeting on September 9th. The draft standards were posted on our website, then opened up for public comment for a period of 30 days. We also put out social media posts and a press release encouraging public comment. On October 14th, we sent additional press releases and social media posts sharing that parent opt-out remained unchanged. We are currently editing the draft standards based on public comments within the parameters of the law. Based on what we are reading and hearing, we know that revisions are necessary to add clarity to the opt-out provision. At a future board meeting, we will bring new draft standards to the board for consideration. Let's talk about sex education requirements. According to 380-1169, dangerous and communicable diseases, HIV and AIDS, awareness on prevention, teaching of abstinence from sex must be taught in every public school in the state. This requirement is for sex education and usually is embedded in health education at the local level. It must be taught by a trained professional and it must be medically accurate. We agree that the goal of health education is to develop an individual who is health literate and engages in practices that lead to an overall healthy lifestyle throughout their life. Before adopting any revisions to a curriculum implemented under this section, included but not limited to the revisions to provide for the teaching of abstinence from sex as a responsible method for restriction and prevention of a disease, a school board shall hold at least two public hearings on the proposed revisions. The hearings shall be held at least one week apart and public notice of the hearings shall be given in a manner required in section 1201 for board meetings. A public hearing held pursuant to this section may be held in conjunction with a public hearing pursuant to section 1507. Now let's look at 1507. The board of a school district may engage qualified instructors to provide facilities and equipment for instruction in sex education, including family planning, human sexuality, and emotional, physical, psychological, hygienic, economic, and social aspects of the family. Instructions may also include the subject of reproductive health and the recognition of prevention, the treatment of sexually transmitted disease. The class shall be an elective. It is not a requirement for graduation. A school district shall not offer this instruction unless sex education advisory board is established by the board of the school district. Since October 1999, the choice of a curriculum to teach topics must be approved by the local school board. The board must hold at least, again, two public hearings and they must be one week apart. Sex education standards were also embedded in the health and education standards in our 2007 version. Let's talk about parents' rights. Parents' rights under section 380-1170 still exist for the required HIV-AIDS instruction. And parents' rights still exist under section 380-1506 regarding opt-out, of which states upon written notice request of the pupil's parent or guardian, the pupil shall be excused without penalty or loss of academic credit. Let's talk about academics. While the focus is on ELA and math, that is very important, but it doesn't mean that other subjects or content should not be taught. There is a connection. The research is clear that for all students, feeling seen, heard, and valued at a school is the foundation for successful academic engagement and achievement. According to PubMed Central out of the National Library of Medicine, which did a longitudinal study on feeling of safety at school, found that students who feel unsafe in school show statistically significant reduction in education attainment. We believe it is our duty to protect all students from harassment in school. This includes teaching the basics of tolerance, respect, acceptance as early as possible. Section 385-15-07B, subsection 2H, the law states that we must teach that the pupil has the power to control personal behaviors. Pupils shall be taught to base their actions on reasoning, self-discipline, a sense of responsibility, self-control, and ethical considerations such as respect for self and others. It is our legal and ethical obligation to protect students

from harassment. Laws passed by this legislature require schools to maintain a safe and inclusive learning environment free from discrimination and harassment. In 2023, this very legislature amended the Elliot Larson Civil Rights Act, Public Act 6 of 1923, to include provisions that ensure equal opportunity for quality education and promote inclusiveness, which includes sexual orientation and gender identity. This act added sexual orientation and gender identity or expression as a protected category. We cannot possibly meet the standards of our own civil rights without health standards that meet the needs of all students. So let's talk about all students. The research is also clear that when such things as gender identity are presented in a way that is medically accurate and developmentally appropriate, children experience lower rates of bullying, harassment, and suicide. If we want children to excel in the basics of reading, writing, and math, we must provide atmosphere where all students feel safe. Gender diverse students often report feeling unsafe at school and experience greater rates of harassment. They indicate that they rarely report discriminatory incidents because when they do report them, they feel unprotected. Gender diverse students experience greater gender-related stress at school and are more likely to be absent, have a lower GPA, and report higher levels of depression, engage in more substance use and risky behaviors, and are at an elevated risk for suicide. Michigan's gender diverse students are 1.8 times more likely to have been threatened or injured with a weapon at school, 2.1 times more likely to skip school because they feel unsafe, 1.6 times more likely to have been bullied at school or online. It is important to note that gender diverse students are not inherently prone to mental or physical health risks because of their sexual orientation or gender identity. They are at a higher rate due to experiences of discrimination, stigmatizations, victimizations in society. So the question has been asked, why Massachusetts? If we take a moment to look at Massachusetts, it ranks number one nationally in reading and math based on national assessments of educational progress for 2024. It rates of high school students reporting being bullied on school property or electronically are lower than ours. The rates of students feeling sad or hopeless or attempting suicide are also lower than ours. And Massachusetts' health education standards are based on national health education standards, just like the ones we drafted and posted on our website. Let's talk about the process of standards versus curriculum and the local board, local boards of education approval process. Just to be clear, these are educational standards. They're not a curriculum. A curriculum is a program created by local districts that outline the content and method of instruction, including activities, lessons, and assessment. Standards are educational goals and benchmarks that define what students should know and be able to do at each grade span. Standards are typically developed at the state level. Michigan is a local control state when it comes to education, so the state does not determine curriculum for health education. Standards are typically, the standards typically do not provide all the details, particular skills, or fundamental information that may be part of the curriculum. School districts have discretion to determine how standards will be implemented at the local level within the parameters of Michigan law with an input from parents specific to sex education. Educator qualifications for teaching health education. A teacher with an elementary certificate in grades K through 5 is qualified to teach health education for grades designated all subject on a certificate. Although the law allows elementary teachers to teach health education without a specific endorsement, it is highly recommended by the Michigan Department of Education that teachers receive professional development from an approved program in health and sex education that includes training in the curriculum implementation, best practices, and current state law related to health education. The regional school health coordinators can assist with this training. A teacher with a certificate in a secondary setting, grades 6 through 12, is authorized to teach health education with any one of the following endorsements. MA in health, MC, which is K through 12 health and physical education, MX, which is health and physical education, recreation and dance, or a KH, family and consumer science. Let's talk about local education and parent choice in sex education and HIV AIDS instructions. LEAs determine what content within sexual health instruction they will include in their health education program. LEAs are encouraged to use student and community data, parent input, and community values to determine which content will best support the health and well-being of students in their district. Michigan is one of the top states that require parent input on sex health instruction. Sex education advisory boards must consist of at least 50% parent membership to review student data, review curricula, and make recommendations to the local school board of education for review and approval. Parents have the right to review sex education curriculum prior to instruction and can opt out their child from any or some of the sex education and HIV AIDS instruction. I'm going to talk a little bit more about parent input and choice. As we presented to the state board in September, local control and parent choice remain unchanged with these proposed standards, no matter where sex education is mentioned within the standards. The standards change, but the local control and parents' ability to review curriculum and opt their child out does not change. The word parent or family can be found almost 60 times in our Michigan health education standards framework. As stated in 1507, if a district choose to offer sex education, there are safeguards in place that prioritize parents' input and choice.
