The last thing here on the first part about these concerns and just general is how are local school boards supposed to navigate all of this? The conflicts between state law and the health standards. What about the opt-out issue? Is a local school board just supposed to say, well, we think they opt out, now you can opt out of health class. Well, I can see a lawsuit saying, no, you can't do that. It's a required course under state law. You see the conflict and, again, the risk of federal funds. Let me just briefly go to the second liability exposure because this is huge. And I'm telling you, I've litigated these cases, and frankly, a plaintiff comes to us, I'll be bringing a case like this. And the most important one is First Amendment civil rights violations. I think it's crystal clear here. In three ways. Students don't lose their civil rights. They don't lose their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse door, the Tinker case. You're all familiar with that. So what if a child refuses to go to a class where something is being taught in the social studies or the history and they're talking about gender identity and the student says, gets up, no, I'm leaving. I don't have to listen to this. Are they going to be disciplined? Are they going to lose grades? Are they going to be kicked out of the class? Are they going to face truancy charges? You see the problems. Parents, as we've already discussed above, the various statutes and their constitutional rights, I think it's very clear. And all of this is 1983 actions in federal court. We wouldn't be going to state court. We'd be going to federal court on these things. But finally, and one I haven't heard anything about really this morning, teachers. Okay, teachers don't lose their constitutional rights in these areas either. These standards would require teachers to teach areas that directly violate their First Amendment rights and beliefs. It's going to violate their rights, free speech and everything else. The government cannot compel teachers to speak in a manner that violates their conscience. West Virginia versus Barnett, and we can go on and on. I'm just bringing this to your attention that there are many legal issues and problems with what I read in these standards. I had a teacher talk to me just yesterday at my church, a public school teacher, and he came to me and said, do you know about this? If they tell me I have to teach this stuff, I'm not teaching it. I'm going to get fired. You know? What do you do about those teachers? Secondly, the failure to follow federal law. Again, I won't belabor the point in federal funding that comes from that. Third, schools failing to notify parents of these gender issues. Look at the Rockford lawsuit that's going on right now. What about opting out provisions, all these things? Parents have the right to notice, to review, and to opt out. It's not just opt out. How are they going to get this notice or review of anything under the health standards? It's not there. Finally, health standards require teaching on topics that can trigger psychological harm, as Senator Tice was talking about. There's no counselor there. There's no psychologist there in the classroom. Look at MCL 380.1506, which includes psychological functions and how that plays into this. Again, parents have to have the right to opt their children out of these types of classes. The bottom line here, from my perspective, is this. These health standards undermine the rights of parents, teachers, and students in teaching values in the areas of sex and reproductive health to their kids as permitted under state law. Secondly, I see this as a clear attempt to circumvent and sidestep the notice, review, and opt-out requirements for sex education by throwing it into health education and then across the board who knows what other classes they're going to do it. It's a clear attempt to circumvent that law. Finally, it veers away from schools teaching academics and teaching as opposed to teaching their social justice issues, and I just think this is something that we as a state should not be doing. These health standards should not be adopted as drafted, and I urge you to support HR 195. Thank you for the time. I'm happy to answer a question if I've raised anything that anybody has a question on. Good morning, Chairman and members of the committee. My name is Catherine Bussard. It's an honor to speak with you this morning. I do serve as the executive director of Salt and Light Global. I also sit on my local public school board, and I've worked in K-12 education for the vast majority of my career as an instructor and administrator, and I bring that lens of experience today as I speak in my personal testimony. I just want to start talking at the very beginning about the statutes and what they require. As a member of my local school board on the policy committee, we look at the law. We look at the recommendations from the department or the standards, whatever they are, and we try to follow those and adopt our policies and curriculum based on that. It's important to understand what the statutes actually say, and I really believe that Dr. Carnell did a disservice to this body when she spoke earlier because she misrepresented the facts. MCL 380.78, which she said authorizes the department to create standards for sex ed, does no such thing. The word sex, reproductive health, or HIV, to Rep. Meerman's question when he pressed her on that, none of those words even appear in the statute. How can it authorize them to teach something that isn't even a part of the statute? Quite frankly, that was misinformation. Similarly, with MCL 380.1169, she spoke about how that statute also authorized the department to teach these standards, but it really focuses the department's authority very narrowly to train the trainers of teachers for HIV information, and second, to give medically accurate information to schools so that teachers can use it. But that same law also says that any training on HIV has to follow the process set out in our sex ed law that has the sex ed advisory board working with the local school board to develop the curriculum. It is not a centralized state standard of what is taught on those subjects. That was not accurate information. And finally, with MCL 380.1507, our sex ed law, she made it very emphatic that nothing is changing here. Well, it's really hard to say that nothing is changing when sex ed and health education are two separate classes, two separate courses, and they may be taught together at the same time, but that's really at the scheduling convenience of the local district as to whether or not they even teach sex ed and where they place it in the school's calendar. To say that nothing changes here is simply not true. What they've done with these health standards is really unprecedented. If you look back at old health standards, there was teaching about what the law requires, about nutrition and hygiene and first aid and things like that, disease prevention and drugs. Don't do drugs. That was health education. Then we had sex education tacked on at the 2007 standards, which, by the way, were a bipartisan effort that was signed under the Granholm administration. This was not some radical, polarized issue at all. It was a very bipartisan effort. Those standards set aside sex ed as Strand 7. It made it very optional whether or not schools were even required to teach it. It reminded local districts of the law very clearly that if you should teach this, the first thing you have to do is notify parents. You have to allow for curriculum review. You have to allow them the right to opt out without penalizing students or grades or anything like that. It said these are just truly some suggestions, but the health standards were the health standards. And it's important to understand that brings me to my second point. Well, I guess I would just say it brings me to my second point that there's a big difference between standards and guidelines. And today we were almost gaslit into this idea that somehow these standards being proposed are really just a suggestion from the State Department of Education on how to teach health education. A local board like mine really doesn't need to take them seriously. We can teach whatever we want. We can pick and choose what's in the standards. That was the suggestion and impression that was very clearly, emphatically, and repeatedly painted by Dr. Carnell. However, that is not consistent with the law. And when I look at the law, again, just a school board member doing my best to follow this, this would be what I would read in MCL 380.1278. The very first line says, In addition to the requirements for accreditation under Section 1280 specified in this section, if a board of a school district wants all the schools of their district to be accredited under Section 1280, the board shall provide all pupils attending public school in the district a core academic curriculum in compliance with Subsection 3 in each of the curricular areas specified in the State Board recommended model core academic curriculum standards developed under Subsection 2. Health class comes up, as you continue reading the statute. By the way, again, sex ed does not. Health class comes up. In other words, if my district wants to be accredited, we must teach, at a minimum, the standards promulgated by the Michigan Department of Education. If we fail to do so, we can lose our accreditation. So personally, I don't view that as a suggestion. I think that every student in my district is entitled to actually do the work

graduate and have the state of Michigan recognize their diploma. I don't think we should be cheating children out of that. It is not a mere suggestion. This is not a flexible thing. And that also brings me then to think about the content here. What's embedded in these standards is really unprecedented. We've never seen climate and environmental activism or this emphasis on not trusting parents or this emphasis on sex and social issues put into health curriculum. Health curriculum needs to follow the law. And I also want to mention with parental rights here that, you know, the department has suggested that nothing's changing. Again, going back to that 1507 statute. Yes, the law is still in place. But how is a local district like mine supposed to actually enforce that? When sex and gender, just those two words, not to mention reproductive health and other things, when just those two words are listed 111 times in these health standards, if we teach health class in accordance with these standards, with this all mixed in, not just in sex standards, but in, you know, decision making and relationships, all these other areas of the standards, if we have to notify parents 111 times, every parent in the district, every time this comes up in a health class, I don't know what your districts look like where you live, but my district is very small. We don't have that big of a staff. I'm really concerned about that notice being effective. And if you notify parents, you know, I've asked the department, what does that look like? If you notify parents just once at the beginning of the year, hey, we're going to teach this, parents don't know when it's appropriate to opt their child out. If you notify parents every single time, those notices start to kind of become something parents are desensitized to, and it's really hard to keep track of. And actually in the Mahmood case, the Supreme Court actually spoke to that and said that it can be a civil rights violation if we don't make it clear that these are the times when there should be notice and these are the times when it's not really relevant. If we don't clearly notify parents and if we embed this offensive material throughout the entire curriculum, making it harder for parents to know when to opt out, that in and of itself can actually become a civil rights problem. And then more parents will be visiting Mr. Coleman. And as what Dr. Carnell said, you know, when Representative Green pressed, what are parents to do when these standards are violated? It's a problem right now. There are parents sitting behind me who have been denied the right to review the sex ed curriculum in their district, Grand Ledge Public Schools. There are parents in this room who have had their children taught things that they have expressly opted them out. The damage is done. Their child has been exposed to something against their values. The remedy for a parent becomes an attorney. That's very expensive. And it's not just expensive for the parent. It's expensive for districts like mine that are already cash strapped, trying to teach kids how to read and write. All of these things that we're talking about today, when the department clearly goes beyond the scope of the law, it takes the focus away from academics. It takes the focus away from children learning to read and write and do math and all the things that we want our children to learn so they can be successful in life. It's important that we follow the laws. It's important that parents have the right to opt out. And as I conclude, I want to share the story of a female student in my district. You may know that the Michigan Dashboard on Adolescent Sexual Health reports that we do have a problem in this state. While our good sex ed laws are doing many wonderful things, one problem that we haven't fixed yet is that 10% of Michigan students report being raped. Among female students, that number is closer to 20%. And I will never forget the day as a school board member when I received a call from a mandatory reporter, and on the line with that mandatory reporter was a mother of a student who, through sobs and tears, told me that her daughter had been raped by a boy at her school. And although the daughter was receiving counseling and all the help that her parents could possibly offer to her until certain legal procedures happened, she still had to attend class every day with that boy, see him every day in a very small district. Imagine having to sit through a health class under these standards where topics like sex and dating violence and all these other things are embedded, where your parent hasn't necessarily received notice because there is no notice for health class, and all of a sudden you walk in blind to health class, you're hit with this thing that triggers the most traumatic nightmare that you've ever lived through, and you're stuck, numb, remembering that. And then you're supposed to walk out when the bell rings, and somehow you're supposed to learn algebra, or somehow you're supposed to focus on English lit. That emotional trauma is re-triggered, and as Attorney Coleman said, there's really not psychological help available. And by denying notice, by denying transparency, we're shutting parents out of that critical conversation who would love to be there to help children, who would love to be there to look out for their child's best interest, and we're denying them that opportunity. Sex education and health education are separate in our laws for a reason. Parental involvement exists for a reason. Opt-outs, safeguards, local control, all of these things exist for a reason, and the laws that we have on the books exist for a reason. They deserve to be followed with the utmost care, and that's why I encourage you to support Representative Johnson's resolution and do everything that you can to encourage the Michigan Department of Education and State Board of Education to reject these standards and to redraft them so that they clearly, carefully follow the laws and respect the rights of Michigan families. Thank you. Thank you. Appreciate everyone's testimony. I know Senator Tice does have to get going, sessions beginning. I do have a question for you specifically. I don't know if any members have a specific question for Senator Tice, but, you know, just talk about it. It got touched on briefly by David, but tell us about the impact on teachers that you've recognized or you've understood on how this proposed standards has impacted some teachers. Thank you for asking that because it's extremely important. I've got some family members who have recently retired as soon as they could get there out of the education system because of the conflict nature that's going on between the parents and the teachers and their administration. And I'll just remind you that in this country there are three major faith traditions that are oppositional to what this teaches. So it goes well beyond my personal faith. It's pretty much around the country. But when you have a teacher who's required to teach the curriculum in front of them, and it's violative of their deeply held religious beliefs, they have a right to sue if they're forced to do that. The parents, understandably, have a right to push back against the curriculum, and it's the teacher that that lands on. And so we have a lot of good teachers who are walking away because there are parents who are very angry about what is indoctrinating their children. They're trying to stop it, and they're just aiming at anybody that's imparting this on their kids, understandably. We've got a whole group of people that started out because education was teaching their kids things they shouldn't be teaching them. And I absolutely relate to everything they're doing. And if what we want is to have more teachers in our schools, we need to quit putting them in a position where they're in conflict with the parents. They should be partnered with them. And you can't help them when you create guidelines like this. Help the teachers. Help the parents. Support this resolution, and MDE reject these guidelines and start again. If you don't mind, I think we do have one question for you, Senator, additional. Representative Miller? Yes. Thank you, Senator. When this issue was first brought to you, did you make a recommendation that this should be a bill? Since this resolution carries no legal capacity, has no legal force, what was the intended outcome here beyond opinions and statements? And why not introduce a bill that actually addresses the concerns raised here? And if the resolution doesn't change policy, what is the purpose and how does passing a resolution today help improve student health, education, plain and simple? And to the point that was made on suicides, how often or more likely is an LGBTQ student more likely to attempt suicide than their peers when they feel supported and affirmed at school? Does that risk drop? Have you completed your questioning? Okay. So first off, we're not asking to create new law. We're asking the Department of Education to actually abide by the law that's in front of them, and they're not. They've gone way out of their lane. So what the resolution does is speak to legislative intent and remind them of what the law already says. They don't have the authority to do this. It's not within the existing law that they do this. Not only is it oppositional to existing law, parents can take them to court because it's violating federally First Amendment rights. It's violating teachers' First Amendment rights. Now, with respect to the suicide, if you look at the actual data, what's happening is kids who have comorbidities

borderline personality disorder. If you measure all of the comorbidities and you put that up against the general population, they are aligned. Most of the kids they're identifying in the LGBTQ area have comorbidities associated with them, over 30% autistic, actually. So if you align them with the general public, what you find is those comorbidities correlate. And then what happens, and this is my experience with my detransitioning friends, is they end up with all kinds of guilt and discomfort and depression over having permanently changed their bodies in ways that they cannot correct, and they become more, not less suicidal. So I thank you for asking that question. So to that point, do you have data in any peer-reviewed studies done either with national associations that show those conclusions that you can share with us? The CAS review. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Representative. Thank you, Senator, for taking the time to be here. I'd like to move quickly as we are coming up against a hard stop here soon. Representative Green. It's fine. Sure? Yeah. Okay. Representative Wigella. I'm not going to pretend to forget. I just need to set up the question because it's important. So there's been a lot of conversation about how this can, you know, talk, conversation about gender identity and sexual orientation can make their way into other classrooms. And, like, I was a U.S. history teacher, and I guess, like, what I'm really curious about, like, are we arguing that, like, the mere acknowledgement of gender identity or sexual orientation and those individuals' contributions to history, such as in World War II, thousands of gay individuals served in the Army, like, is that, like, are you saying that that shouldn't happen in those cases? Because I would argue that that is an appropriate part of discussion. I'm happy to respond to that. Of course not. I mean, we're all Americans. We've all participated. We've all played a part in getting here today. That's not what we're talking about here. And that's part of the problem is how do you differentiate legitimate historical, social, other things that are totally appropriate to be taught and talked about versus sex education or telling students issues on gender and things like that, that the parents in sex ed, that should be more for sex education. That's the problem is how do you split those out? It's a real problem. And these standards muddy it all together. That's the problem. These standards even go to the point of teaching attraction and teaching how to engage in various behaviors. That's different than just teaching about Americans living their lives. Of course. Thank you. Representative Merriman. Thank you, Chair DeBoer. Catherine, could you, I don't see in the law passed in 2007 sort of the overlap that I'm seeing here being tried. And the doctor, say superintendent, was suggesting that it was taught in the 2007 law signed by Governor Granholm. Is that your understanding? That's a great question, and no. This is really totally different. We've never seen this emphasis on sex in health education ever. And we've also never seen it interwoven and intermingled throughout the entire curriculum. In the past, they've always had age standards for health education. And if anything, that most recent 2007 standard, it kind of had like an appendix called Strand 7, where sex ed, it was very clear this is totally a local control issue. If you teach it, here's the law. Here's the parental protections, student protections. And it was set aside kind of like as a bonus section, an appendix. It was not interwoven into the core health standards so that it was very clear to districts this is what you need to teach, totally optional. And these standards completely lack that clarity. We do have time for one more question. Representative Pahutski. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Going back a little bit to the point about not hearing from the families of queer or trans kids about possible bullying, why would you expect a parent of a queer or trans kid to reach out to someone who is actively scapegoating them to distract from the fact that 1.4 million Michiganders are about to lose their food assistance? It would be you that would ask such a stupid question at this hearing. Do you have an intelligent answer? Hey, we're going to stay on topic here, please, both. Thank you. I'd be happy to respond to that just briefly. It wasn't for you. Please, please, please, please. As we are well past our time here. First, I'm going to apologize. There's a number of individuals that put in cards to speak. Sheila Kuhn supports the bill, put in a card wishing to speak. I apologize to you that we will not be able to get you up. David, obviously you're here. Eileen McNeil supports the bill, wish to speak. I apologize to you. Catherine Bouchard supports the bill. I apologize to you. Kristen Lee supports the bill. I apologize to you. Lisa West supports the bill. I apologize to you. Sandra Tannehill opposes the standards. I apologize to you. Brittany Houseman opposes the bill, wish to speak. I apologize to you. Additionally, we had 170 either electronically or personally submitted. Excuse me. The resolution. Standards, I guess you could imply, but the resolution, they support the resolution or oppose the resolution. 170 turned in that support the resolution that did not wish to speak. We're going to notice them for the record. Is that the end of it, clerk? That is the end of the wishing to speak. I'm sorry, and also wishing to just make their position known. Representative Green moves to report House Resolution 195 with recommendation. Will the clerk call the roll? On the motion to report, Chair DeBoer? Yes. Representatives Beerline? Yes. Meerman? Yes. Paquette? Yes. Cara? Yes. Brooke? Yay. Green? Yes. Regas? Yes. Shriver? Yay. Wolford? Yay. Miller? No. Pahutski? No. Conlon? No. McDonald? No. Menser? No. Cerniglou? No. Wugela? No. Mr. Chair, you have 10 yay, 7 nay, 0 pass. HR 195 is reported with recommendation. Thank you, Mr. Clerk. Seeing no absent, there being no further business before the committee, the oversight committee will stand adjourned. Thank you.

title: Appropriations - School Aid and Department of Education — Tuesday, October 28, 2025
transcript:
House Appropriations Subcommittee on School Aid and Department of Education will come to order. Clerk, please call the roll. Representative Kelly. Here. Representative Jenkins-Arnold. Here. Representative Markin. Here. Representative Beeson. Here. Representative Borton. Here. Representative Glamby. Representative Steckloff. Present. You have a quorum. Thank you. Representative Beeson moves to approve the minutes of October 21st, 2025 meeting. Being no objections, the minutes are approved. Good morning. Welcome, everyone. Today we have some presentations by, I don't know quite how to title this, but missed opportunities, something in that order. I think a second chance to take a look at some of the products, services, processes that some of these presenters are going to have and perhaps, again, weigh the value of these efforts. And with that, we're going to start with a presentation by the Future of Learning Council. Dr. Lori Haven, Superintendent Perry Public Schools, as well as Dr. John Van Wagoner, Superintendent Traverse City Area Public Schools. You both come up, press the red button, and we'll get the show going. Good morning, and thank you all, representatives, for allowing us to testify today. We are made up of a group of superintendents and districts, originally started about eight years ago with 12 superintendents that organically wanted to get together to talk about what would different look like, what in our system is not working that needs to change for schools, and really wanted to say, you know, if not us, then who to make that change. And so we've been meeting with different groups across the nation, school visits, other states, looking at what are models that can be different to improve student achievement and allow students to be able to learn outside the four walls. Really the time when Governor Snyder started the anytime, anywhere, any pace, any place learning, we wanted to look at what would that mean for Michigan schools. And one of the groups that we met with to give you an idea is the Carnegie Foundation. They are really the initial, you take Andrew Carnegie, you take the way school was designed based on an hourly, six hours of a high school day, 50 to 55 minute courses. And if you talk to the people now that are the evolution of that organization, they are actually advocating for the abolishment of that structure. And so we are a group of superintendents and districts. Right now we are about 80 school districts, superintendents with our staff, as well as we have quite a few intermediate school districts and charters that are a part of our group. We meet monthly and we bring in presenters and facilitators from all over the country. And one of the things we've talked about is we no longer want to be a flyover state. So when these national experts that are making differences in student achievement fly over our state and go to other places, we want them to land here and be a part of what we're trying to do here in the state of Michigan. We're a 501c3 network that is, you know, we don't have a profit, none of us are paid. We're in it to really change education. We have superintendents and educators from every region of our state and we're united to transform our K-12 system away from the time-based student-centered structure we have now. All of our pupil accounting structure, everything in the state of X based upon how long a kid sits in a seat and that they're there, not necessarily the learning that happens while they're there. And we are really trying to look and be champions for that innovation, instructional practice and policy that supports personalized learning and competency-based mastery learning. Knowing that a kid knows what they're supposed to before they move on. But we can't have that based on a time. Some kids it's maybe six months for a course, maybe it's 14 months. Like how do we build structures that do that versus the only way that our system structures it for pupil accounting now. This work will create that student-centered learning for students to learn 21st century skills. We know with AI, all of these things that are coming, our system has to change and adapt. Or we will struggle and continue to fall further down in education in the state of Michigan. And as educators, we want to lead that charge to not let that happen. We have to improve and we need to have a grassroots effort to be able to do that. So what we do is, again, we meet monthly for professional development, bringing in national experts to come in and work with cohorts of districts from where they are to be able to move towards this system. And be able to look at what can we begin to challenge our system of education, whether that be through legislative act, our Department of Education, our individual local school boards, what does it take to do that? We have tailored coaching that's helping to build capacity with people that have done this work from other states and even other parts of the world to come in and talk about the student achievement they've been able to raise and how they've been able to create much more effective learning for those students. And so we're really trying to make sure that we have this on-demand learning, AI-supported professional development, micro-credentials. We have three cohorts of learning, a discover, a design, and thrive group. And we have the goal of providing strategic grants to empower that innovation and sustainability. We want to be able to find a way to have small pockets of funding that can allow our districts to move forward and have the resources to be able to do that. Not a lot. We're not needing a lot, but we need a little bit for them to understand and learn what different can be. And so why now? We know the urgency. We have an outdated, time-based learning model that's not preparing students for 21st century careers. We know what this is going to look like. AI is changing the face of our state right now as we sit here. We know that industries are changing rapidly, and we need to be able to prepare students to be able to enter that workforce and compete on a global system. We know there are workforce shortages in certain areas, especially in skilled trades and technical fields. We want to see what does it look like to redo a junior and senior year to have students be able to do more than a 50% work-based internship, actually get clinical learning while they're in high school in a job field. As we know, there are many fields that do not require a four-year degree. It may be a two-year degree

maybe a technical certificate. How can we make it seamless for kids while they're in high school to be able to transition to that system without having to retake courses in a college? How can we make that true system of learning and again, not have it based on six hours in a day where a kid has to sit in a seat in a specific four walls? And understand our system and our pupil accounting system under the state aid act is exactly set up only to do that. We need to transition and change that. And so we are really trying to say our economic mobility is stalling and particularly in our underserved communities, we need to be able to change that. And it's only going to happen by the people that are in schools, in classrooms today from that ground up mentality. So our opportunity is again, Michigan, we can begin to lead as a state in our nation that is not where any of us want it to be. We have to stand up and we have to change and it is immediate that that needs to happen. And we believe personalized learning and a competency based system that aligns that real world learning, whether that's through project based opportunities that show a student masters it with different type of assessment system, performance based assessment. We need to be able to change our system with that like other states are starting to do and be able to have students have the transferable skills that prepares them for that lifelong 21st century employment, but continue lifelong learning. And we have districts again, we have many districts already that are a part of this movement. We do not recruit, we do not advertise, we do not tell people, hey, you have to do this. These are districts that have stepped up and said, we want to be a part of this. We see what's happening with the Future of Learning Council and we want to learn from other people that are being successful. How can we be a part of this? And so they're willing. We just need to be able to have some help to be able to help change the structure, provide the supports for people to be able to learn in that and those minimal resources that we do need to help districts to be able to make that shift. So I will go ahead and pass it off to Dr. Hadden to talk about Perry Public Schools and what they're doing as a member of the Future of Learning Council. Thank you very much. First off, thank you so much for allowing us to be here today and listening to a little bit about FLC, the Future of Learning Council. I'm Lori Haven. I'm the proud superintendent of Perry Public Schools where I've been the last seven years. Perry is a small rural district and we have a higher than average poverty rate. We're small but mighty and we have been looking for change. And so we joined the FLC, gosh, right close to its inception. And the reason for us, our why, was our sense of urgency. We know that our kids deserve better. We know that what we are providing, the opportunities we provide are not equipping them for life as it's ever-changing once they leave our school walls. And so we started with our building principals and I, again, we're a smaller district so we have a smaller admin team. So we brought our principals and we went through the first year of professional learning series with FLC and just the consistent, cohesive learning experience, it is like nothing that we have been offered. This is my 28th year in education and I have yet to find a system like FLC or an organization that provides that year after year consistent, action-based, action-oriented, research-based opportunity for us as leaders to grow and learn and then bring that to our adults who can then take it to our kids. So that's something that is very unique about the Future of Learning Council. They are results-focused and they have a broad system of support. So not only are they bringing in amazing, research-based presenters and facilitators of learning from across the country, but they're also coaching. So when I look at the other states that have higher grades and, like, why do they have higher grades and what can we do, a lot of it is being more victim-centered and making sure that our service providers have financial means to provide the services for victims. Michigan just really doesn't have a lot of financial support for these groups that are providing the beds for individuals who are just coming out of a trafficking situation, providing the drug treatment for individuals who may need it, job training, long-term assistance, helping people really get back on their feet. We just don't really have a ton of funding that goes to those specific organizations. So that is something that other states do contribute more information to. Also public awareness. Michigan just lacks having a grander public awareness aspect to human trafficking, and it does seem like some of the states that do better, they do more public awareness campaigns. There's more exposure. I will say that some states are trying to get, like, stuff into the schools where it's part of the curriculum, more on, like, social media issues. You know, we know that our kids are inundated with things on their phone and social media apps and all these different apps that they use and traffickers are using to get to them. So awareness about what those apps are, there are some states that have been implementing more criteria for being taught about those specific things so that our students can have a stronger grasp on it and can protect themselves as well. So that is something that provides them with higher scores as well. Okay. I just want to iterate that this does not just impact kids. It's also impacting adults. I remember in Detroit when we were seeing put on telephone poles signage for, you know, need extra money, here's a job, and, you know, tabs, you know, you pull off the phone number, and these were people who were being human trafficked. So I definitely think that there needs to be more public outcry about this issue and making sure that we're investing and getting that message out there. Thank you. Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Senator. Thank you very much. Any other questions? All right. Thank you. Thanks, ma'am. Up next, we are going to hear from Katie Papke, who is the chair of the Human Trafficking Commission. All right. We'll try to figure that out. Let me try to figure that out. But in the meantime, we will move on to Greg Toutant, who is the CEO of the Great Lakes Recovery Center, who is on Zoom. Yes, thank you, Madam Chair. Hopefully everyone can see me and hear me okay. I appreciate the opportunity to zoom in from the Upper Peninsula of Michigan. As indicated, I have the fortune of being the CEO for Great Lakes Recovery Centers. We're the largest behavioral health provider in the Upper Peninsula, and we want to lend our support to this package of bills, this very important package of bills, because it provides added restrictions and accountabilities around such a critical issue. We can attest certainly to the damage created by trafficking in all its various forms, and we want to be able to say it's not just an urban issue, it's an everywhere issue. We see it rurally. As a treatment provider, a longstanding one, we have one of the very few remaining

adolescent residential treatment programs left in the state as well as services for adults. So we have some vulnerable populations. We've seen the rise in reported trafficking cases and what our clients tell us as they have been victimized through the process of trafficking. We see in children that we serve, our 12 to 17 year olds, the increase around trauma. Cognitive, emotional, psychological, developmental, the delays associated with early exposure is critical. We spend a significant amount of time trying to deconstruct the damage created through trafficking. We see the issues around parental rights and what happens around issues of quasi-abandonment or abandonment related challenges. And so we know that prolonged exposure and involvement to parents that ought to have earlier intervention in relation to their rights is significant around the ongoing trauma provided to our children. The element of shame and embarrassment, anger, depression, all the troubling feelings and behaviors that are associated with exposure to victimization is something that is very real. And so the added aspect again of what these bills can do to further publicize and advocate and prioritize the restrictions and accountabilities for perpetrators is significant. What we see relative to women and addiction. And so often both our children and our adults tell us they were forced into a lifestyle of addiction, being enslaved into addiction through the exposure of substances and chemicals as a pathway to and through a trafficking scenario. And it is extremely interrelated and correlated between long-term addiction and psychological challenges as it relates from trafficking. So we spend a great deal of our limited resources helping children and women and those that have been exposed to try to cope with everything they've been through traumatically without substances going forward in their lives. And so that exposure, as you all know all too well, is real, it's significant, and it has definitely risen in terms of how widespread trafficking is. So I know I want to keep my comments brief for others to talk, but we want to be able to help advocate for the victims that are out there. So thank you. Thank you very much. Appreciate your testimony. Any questions? Okay. Up next, we're going to hear from Sarah Gonzalez, who is the Director of State and Local Government Affairs for Delta Airlines. Chairperson Chang, members of the committee, thank you so much for the opportunity to join you here today. I will be brief. For those of you who I don't know, my name is Sarah Gonzalez, and I'm the Director of State and Local Government Affairs for Delta Airlines. Delta Airlines is the largest commercial air carrier in Michigan with more than 6,000 employees serving 12 airports and carrying more than 23 million passengers annually from the state of Michigan to over 380 destinations across the globe. A recent study of Polaris shows that 71% of survivors flew on an airplane at some point when they were being recruited, and almost 40% of victims have flown on an airplane when they're being exploited. So for Delta, with 100,000 employees across the globe, 205 million customers we serve a year, we know that as a company we not only need to engage against human trafficking, but we need to lead in any way that we can. We began our efforts to fight human trafficking in 2011, becoming the first airline to sign the EPCAP Code of Conduct. This includes a network of organizations working together to eliminate the commercialized sexual exploitation of children. Delta was also one of 12 founding companies of the Global Business Coalition Against Human Trafficking in 2012. Since then, Delta has developed training for employees to identify and report human trafficking, and more than 60,000 employees have completed the training to date. We've committed $3 million to anti-human trafficking experts Polaris to help support the U.S. National Human Trafficking Hotline, and Delta SkyMiles members can join the fight by donating miles to Polaris through our SkyWish program to help cover airfare survivors need to return home, receive critical services, or reunite with their families. To date, more than 5 million donated miles have helped 326 survivors reach safe haven locations. In collaboration with Wellspring Living, we've launched an apprenticeship program to provide survivors with career skills, mentorship, critical work experiences, and help them chart courses to new opportunities, including those at Delta. And I'm proud to serve as a member of Delta's Anti-Human Trafficking Steering Committee, which is dedicated across divisional group focused on human trafficking. So that said, we've found very early in our work at Delta on combating trafficking that it's not just a business issue, it's a moral imperative. We're proud to use the power of our brand and the power of our people to work to fight something so morally reprehensible. Working alongside government partners, particularly at the state level here, alongside local, federal level, it's a crucial part of the work that we do at Delta as a part of our anti-human trafficking efforts. So we're proud to see Michigan take such big steps in eliminating trafficking by introducing these bills. We know that a lot has been done and there's more work to be done. That's why we felt it was so important to be here today, because one victim of human trafficking is one too many, and we are here with you in this fight until there are no more. So thank you so much for the opportunity to be here today, and we stand in support of this legislation. Thank you. Thanks so much. I appreciate you sharing information about what you all have been doing. So are there any questions? Senator Schink. Thank you. I guess, you know, in the airports we see the signs and things like that. I wonder if you have any statistics about how many people have been recognized as being potential victims of human trafficking and have been, I guess, whatever statistics you have around that, I would be interested in. Absolutely. I will follow up with that information. Are you looking specifically for DTW or overall? Yeah, I think we'll Michigan. Okay. I'd be happy to follow up with that. Thank you so much. Yeah, I appreciate that. Is Katie Popka here? Okay. I guess not. All right. We will move on. Up next, we are going to hear from Gonzalo Peralta, who is on Zoom and is with the Michigan Immigrant Rights Center. Thank you, Madam Chair. Good afternoon. As stated, my name is Gonzalo Peralta, and I'm a senior staff attorney at the Michigan Immigrant Rights Center. MERC is a statewide legal resource center that works to ensure the rights of immigrants are respected and upheld across Michigan. We strongly oppose passage of Senate Bills 522 and 523 in their current form. Although on their face these bills aim to protect children, the result most likely will be the separation of parents from their children and potential weaponization by traffickers. These bills attempt to hold traffickers accountable, but as this so often happens with sweeping efforts written too broadly, these bills could bring harm to the very trafficking victims they intend to help, especially farmworker families. Simply put, the proposed language could be used against victims of trafficking. Farmworkers often travel and work with their families, and children are legally permitted to work in the fields. If a family unit were trafficked by an employer or a labor contractor, this law may be used to threaten to sever the rights of parents who were trafficked alongside their children as a way to silence potential complainants. We already see this occur within the immigration law context, wherein victims of trafficking are threatened with referrals to ICE to deport them if they report their traffickers. An additional concern is instances of parents allowing their minor children to work in permissible and legal forms of labor, but who may be incorrectly deemed traffickers. Children may then be removed from their parents' care, causing incalculable harm to families. But the bill language could still be changed to prevent this, and we are hopeful that we can work with you all to make the needed changes before the next hearing. The analysis necessary to determine whether someone is a victim of labor trafficking is complex. These bills make the analysis even more confusing by requiring staff to look for signs of trafficking by a parent without requiring finding the parent trafficked their own child. MDHHS staff and family court judges are not equipped to make an accurate assessment of whether a child is the victim of labor trafficking or whether a parent is a trafficker. For example, will parents be accused of contributing to labor trafficking if they sign a consent form for their child to work? Would that be an example of providing or obtaining as required by current Michigan state criminal law? Or if they drop their child off at an after-school job, would that be considered transporting? Is the very nature of a parent and child relationship coercive such that coercion can be presumed, thus meeting a necessary prompt to determine whether trafficking has occurred?

Even with extensive training, staff and judges in the family court system may not be able to accurately determine whether a minor child has been defrauded or coerced into forced labor by their parent. It is also concerning how such discretion could be misused in the current anti-immigrant climate. In the case of parents who work in agriculture, the Fair Labor Standards Act permits children as young as 12 to work on farms in non-hazardous conditions, as long as parental consent is provided. If a child's parent or guardian owns or operates a farm, those children can work in hazardous conditions regardless of their age. Even though this is permitted under Michigan law, the department considers such working conditions to be exploitative and amount to labor trafficking by the parent. All these questions undergird the potential harm families, especially low-income families, would face if they lawfully decided to permit a child to work. In short, MERCA opposes the current language and we urge Senate lawmakers to revise the language before proceeding. We hope that lawmakers make the changes necessary to ensure farmworker families, who are often victims of labor trafficking themselves, are not doubly penalized and immigrants are not considered acceptable collateral damage in the process of passing these bills. We all want to keep children safe. In America, we especially want labor traffickers to be held accountable. But legislation must be written with the precision needed to not inflict further harm on vulnerable populations. We look forward to working with you on these bills so we can protect all children, including children in farmworker families. Thank you. Thank you so much, Gonzalo. We appreciate your testimony and we know that we had what I would describe as a productive conversation yesterday with a number of stakeholders in the Attorney General's Office, so I'm hopeful that we can find some way to resolve the concerns. Are there questions from the committee? Okay. Next, we are going to hear from Elizabeth Campbell, who is with the Human Trafficking and Immigration Clinic at the University of Michigan Law School, and she is joining us on Zoom. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you for the opportunity to speak. My name is Elizabeth Campbell. I'm the director of the Human Trafficking and Immigration Clinic at the University of Michigan Law School. In this capacity, I directly represent survivors of trafficking all over the state of Michigan in a variety of legal matters. I have been working at the clinic for about 15 years, and I have represented hundreds of survivors in the state of Michigan. I'm testifying today in regards to Senate Bill 522. I'm specifically referencing the portion of the bill that adds, quote, the court may terminate a parent's parental rights to a child if the court finds that the parent is convicted of a violation of MCL 450-62A through 462H. This refers to the criminal human trafficking chapter. This addition means that any person convicted of human trafficking, regardless of whether that trafficking involved a child, is subject to termination proceedings. I believe this provision will be harmful to survivors as they are all too frequently arrested and prosecuted. So in addition to being criminalized, they now risk losing their children. It is also overly broad. I'll speak to both of these points. Research shows survivors are far more likely to be arrested or prosecuted than treated as victims. A National Polaris study found 62% of survivors were arrested, cited, or detained at least once, and 80% of those arrests happened while they were still being trafficked. A National Survivor Network survey reported over 90% of survivors have been arrested, almost always for crimes tied directly to their trafficking. In short, the system routinely mislabels victims as offenders. These statistics highlight how the bill would compound harm to survivors. I recognize that the intent of this bill is to be passed in tandem with the affirmative defense to human trafficking in a House bill. However, such an affirmative defense is an insufficient protection for survivors. First, there have been victims over the last decades that have not been afforded this affirmative defense and who may have been convicted of human trafficking, having nothing to do with a child. Excuse me. And now they could be subject to the termination of their parental rights. Two, the affirmative defense will require time and a culture shift in order to become widely known and used. Thus, I'm confident that victims will unfortunately continue to be criminalized. And third, affirmative defenses will be unavailable to some victims who continue to be controlled by their traffickers. Many victims are represented by attorneys that are funded by traffickers and therefore are not in control of their own defense. So what we will see is we will unfortunately be criminalizing victims and then putting them into the termination proceedings. Again, for a situation that may not involve a child at all. Furthermore, this bill would unnecessarily hurt children. It collapses the legal requirement to prove a child's specific harm. A farmer convicted of labor trafficking for exploiting migrant workers on his land may have children in his home. These bills would treat his conviction as automatic evidence that he is an unfit parent, even if his children were never harmed or exposed to the trafficking. It makes little sense to assume that human trafficking adults, while very serious, directly proves a parent is incapable of caring for their own children. The result would be unnecessary family separation and the loss of children by both victim parents and others where there is no demonstrated link between trafficking and parenting capacity. I'm concerned that we will put more kids in the system that then makes them vulnerable to trafficking, as being in the system is one factor that is very common for individuals who are victims of human trafficking. For these reasons, I urge you to eliminate this addition in Bill 522. And as Senator Chang indicated, we had a very productive conversation about this just yesterday, and I'm hopeful that we can attend to this matter. Thank you. Thank you very much, Elizabeth, and appreciate the work that you do every day to support victims and survivors and appreciate your testimony. Are there questions or comments? Okay. Up next, we will hear from Megan Reynolds, who is a family law attorney with the Michigan Poverty Law Program, who is also on Zoom. Good afternoon. Thank you for the time to address you today. Thank you to Chair Chang and to the other sponsors who, as has been noted, have been working with stakeholders in recent days to address some of the concerns that have been raised today. I want to add a concern as it relates to Senate Bill 523. And that is the not only adds so both 522 and 523 add human trafficking to the list of grounds for which a parent can have their parental rights to their child or children terminated. 523 does so in a manner of defining human trafficking, adding it to the list of what have been defined as aggravated circumstances. With aggravated circumstances, not only can parental rights be terminated, but they can be terminated in an accelerated fashion where the state can seek the immediate termination of parental rights and the state is not held to the usual responsibility of providing services to the parent. So, for example, if there's an allegation that the child has not been sufficiently well cared for by a parent and there may exist grounds for termination, after making that finding, there's a period where the state has a responsibility to make reasonable efforts to reunify the child and the parent. When the offense that is alleged against the parent is on the list of aggravated circumstance, the state does not have that responsibility and the parent cannot have visitation with the child or other services that are meant to address any deficiency and it can go automatically and directly into the dispositional phase of termination. So, while the objective or the aim of both 522 and 523 is to protect children from a parent who might have met all the elements of having human trafficked their own child, that is actually not the result because the juvenile code has an expanded definition of how a parent can be found culpable for not adequately protecting their child from harm and it could result also in termination in that accelerated fashion under 523. I want to draw your attention to the provision that does that. In 523 at MCL 722-638-2, it reads as follows. This is not an amendment. This is not a change. This is already there. At sub 2, in a petition submitted as required by subsection 1, if a parent is a suspected perpetrator, meaning they have not been adjudicated as a perpetrator, they have not been found in a criminal context by a reasonable doubt standard that they are a human trafficker, but they're suspected of being, so that would be one, or is suspected of placing their child at an unreasonable risk of harm due to the parent's failure to take reasonable steps to intervene to eliminate that risk. So that means exactly as Gonzalo mentioned earlier, that if you have a parent who themselves was labor trafficked, they are a farm worker, maybe they're a hair braider,

They work in a situation where they are being trafficked by someone and they have children in their home or they have children in the migrating group that is coming to Michigan to pick our blueberries. If the CPS worker were to say, yes, mom and dad, you were trafficked, but you did not under Sub 2 eliminate the risk to your child. So in a powerless position where you're being trafficked, you didn't do enough to protect your child from the real trafficker. That would create grounds for that parent to not only have a petition to terminate their rights filed, but then to have that accelerated in the definition of aggravated circumstances. So it's been represented that there are a lot of judicial safeguards here, that there can be a finding of termination only if the parent meets all the definitions in the criminal statute of human trafficking with their child being the victim. And that's not true. This would allow exactly the scenario of a trafficked parent being found not to sufficiently have protected their child from the harm that befell the whole family when the whole family was labor trafficked. And that's the concern. And we have had productive conversations. I again appreciate the time that's been set aside for the stakeholders to contribute our insights on this. And we are looking forward to continuing to work on that and to narrow the language so that parents are not doubly victimized. Thank you for your time. Thanks so much. Appreciate your testimony. And we will continue the conversations with both of the Attorney General's Office and with the stakeholders who have spoken so that we can try to find some resolution. Are there any comments or questions? Okay. Madam Clerk, could you read in the testimony cards? Not wishing to speak in support of Senate Bills 520 through 524, Heath Lowry representing the Michigan Coalition to End Domestic and Sexual Violence. Not wishing to speak in support of Senate Bills 520 through 524, Austin Lowe, Chairman of the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians. Not wishing to speak supporting in concept Senate Bills 522 and 523, Nicole Rodriguez, Children's Law Section of the State Bar of Michigan. Not wishing to speak in support of Senate Bills 523 through 524, Dawn Connors representing the Michigan Anti-Trafficking Project. Not wishing to speak in support of Senate Bills 523 through 524, Michelle Isbister representing Hope Against Trafficking. Not wishing to speak opposed as written, Senate Bills 522, 523, Duane B. Jack representing the National Association of Social Workers Michigan. That's a duplicate card. Oh, the other bills. Thank you. It's a duplicate card. Very good. Okay. And the last card, not wishing to speak opposed to Senate Bill 522 and 523, Gabriel Dressner representing the ACLU Michigan. That is all the cards, Madam Chair. Thank you so much. I will move to excuse the absent member. Without objection, the motion carries. Being no further business, the Senate Committee on Civil Rights, Judiciary and Public Safety is now adjourned. I did. I checked that later. I do agree.

to the journal. Without objection, so ordered. Thank you. Colleagues, actions have consequences and perhaps even more significantly, inaction has consequences. During the Vietnam War, many Hmong people were recruited by the CIA to fight in a secret war in Laos. They saved the lives of countless American troops. And in the aftermath of the fall of Saigon, they fled, knowing they would otherwise be persecuted by the Lao government. Lu Yang was one of the many Hmong children who was born in a refugee camp in Thailand. He's now in his 40s. He's father of six children. He's a caretaker for a 99-year-old grandmother and is a hard worker in our automotive industry. He is the president of the Hmong Family Association here in the Lansing area. When he was very young, he was involved in a low-level, nonviolent offense that was expunged in 2018. Thank you to every organization, advocate, elected official, community member who has written, called, or spoken out in favor of Lu Yang's pardon. For months now, Representative Song, Senator Singh, Representative Dievendorf, Representative Cerniglou, and other elected officials on both sides of the aisle have been communicating with Ann Vu, the wife of Lu Yang. Ann is a tenacious fighter for her husband, for her family, and for her community. She has been helping not only her own family in the aftermath of his arrest, but also the families and children of other Hmong families. It's been around 100 days since Lu was arrested, and he has spent more time in ICE facilities than he's spent in Michigan facilities for his conviction that was expunged in 2018. Over the summer, Ann stated, deporting him not only turns a respected community leader into a political casualty, it would be a grave and irreversible injustice. Lu Yang was previously held for months at the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin, Michigan, but recently he was moved back and forth between various ICE staging facilities in Louisiana. Late last night, Lu Yang and other Hmong and Lao refugees were boarded in shackles on a large plane to Baltimore, and its final destinations are likely several Asian countries. The last flight that we know of that went to Laos, people were shackled for more than 50 hours on multiple flights. This morning, we believe Lu is still in the United States. We still have a chance. The plane is still in our country's airspace, so we are urging ICE to bring Lu home, to return him to his family here in Michigan where he belongs. Cone Singmani is a Lao man who recently turned 49 years old this summer. He was born in Laos and then lived in a refugee camp in Thailand for five years. He and his family live on the west side of the state. When he was a young man, he committed a low-level offense that was in 1996. He has turned his life around. He's married. He started a family. He works at an automotive shop called Bendler. He was also held at the North Lake Processing Center along with Lu Yang up in Baldwin before also being moved to Louisiana. We understand that he is on the same plane that went from Louisiana to Baltimore and is still in our country. Cone, like Lu, deserves to return home to Michigan. The last person I want to talk about is another Lao man named Kongsei. And I've spoken with her sister who lives in Detroit. Earlier this year, she said, in speaking with my brother, he wants everyone to know how desperately he longs to be reunited with his family, especially his son. He asked for the chance to come home to continue providing love, care, and support. And he thanks everyone for their kindness, prayers, and advocacy. She went on to say, I have no other living family besides my brother, and he has no one else but me. Growing up without a large family and now facing the possibility of losing the only family I have is one of the most painful experiences I can imagine. I am pleading with ICE to release my brother so he can return home to his family. On behalf of Cone Son, Kongsei's sister, Lu Yang's wife, Ann, and their families, we are all urging ICE to bring these men home. They are members of our community. They are fathers, and their families deserve to have them by their sides. What kind of America do we want to live in? I know the choice of the America that I will keep fighting for. And so we urge ICE to return Lu Yang and the others to Michigan where they belong. Thank you. The President recognizes Senator McBroom for the purpose of making a statement. Thank you, Madam President. I'd like my remarks printed in the journal. Without objection, so ordered. Thank you. You know, I want to make it

I don't necessarily oppose a fee increase per se. There could be significant justification for doing it. My point has been that we cannot just simply accept the department's recommendation and begging for a fee increase when we don't know how real the need is and where the funds are going to go. And the lack of accountability in this department has been shown again and again. Whether it's on multiple law enforcement issues, public-facing issues and controversies that have recently come up like the fawns and the coyote. The unlegislated programming that they're doing now with carbon capture. We've never established a program allowing them to do it and yet they're out there doing that. And the pursuit of more public lands in areas that are already overrun with it. And a failure to follow sound scientific management principles as the law requires. Instead, they chase money. Proposal G, passed by the citizens of this state with 69% in 1996, stipulates, it requires that the commission be given the power to regulate the taking of game and that they do it with the principles of sound scientific management. Sound scientific management. We did this to eliminate politics as much as possible from decisions that it comes from hunting and fishing. And yet, the department has made it very clear in the passage of 276 and 277 that the need for money trumps science. It trumps the principles of sound scientific management. How does it do that? It does it by getting rid of the feeding and baiting ban. Something that we were told had to be done because science justified it. But now it's just going to evaporate away. And I'm not against it going away. I don't think science dictated it. I don't think science has improved that it's necessary. But because they're getting the money, they've agreed to let it go away. This is just like what happened, and I'm going to say it again, with the pigs when they put the invasive species order out there and they said, by the way, we'll repeal that if you pass a program that gives us thousands of dollars a year.
