transcript:
The committee on labor is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairman Cherry. Here. Senator Camilleri. Here. Senator Kavanaugh. Here. Senator Albert. Here. Mr. Chair, you have four members present. There is a quorum. All right. I'll entertain a motion to adopt the meeting minutes from June 12th and September 4th. So moved by Senator Kavanaugh. Without objection, the minutes are adopted. Today we will begin by considering Senate Bill 49 and 50, which I had introduced. So Michigan is one of 26 states authorized by federal OSHA to operate its own occupational safety and health enforcement program. Under the operating agreement, the state must be, quote, at least as effective as the federal program, including having consistent maximum penalties. In September 2021, the Department of Labor notified LEO that Michigan was out of compliance with the federal maximum penalties, that the state was obligated to adopt such penalties. So Senate Bills 49 and 50 make the changes necessary for my OSHA to bring the program back into compliance with federal standards. The language also reflects some executive orders, which change where my OSHA program is housed. And to have additional information, I'd like to invite up my OSHA director Bart Pickelman and Brennan Smith to discuss. Thank you, Chairman. Thank you, Chair Cherry and members of the committee for allowing us to give some more background on this today. I just wanted to note that these are reintroductions of bills, and you may find yourselves seeing this presentation and recalling aspects of it from our previous testimony. So at this time, I'm going to turn it over to Director Pickelman. Good morning. Thank you for the opportunity to explain a little bit about this legislation or bill or need for it. I'll start with my OSHA's mission, which is pretty simple to help protect the safety and health of Michigan workers. And our motto, which has served us very well over the years, is to educate before we regulate, which means before we go out and enforce a new health or safety rule, we have our very robust consultation, education and training division that goes out and prepares employers and employees for the changes that are coming before enforcement, knocks on their door. A little bit about state plan basics. Michigan is one of 29 state plans that are authorized by federal OSHA. That bar that we must meet, as the chair said, is to be at least as effective as federal OSHA. The Michigan program covers 400,000 Michigan businesses and over 5 million Michigan workers. The benefits to having a state plan versus federal jurisdiction is the flexibility, accessibility and accountability to stakeholders. A broader consultation strategy as a result of the additional state funds that are available. And most importantly, it covers additional 600,000 plus Michigan public sector workers that would not have coverage in the state of Michigan if it were not for a state program. Federal OSHA does not cover public sector workers. This just reiterates that fact. The public sector workers are your firefighters, your police, your paramedics, your road workers. And again, with federal OSHA jurisdiction, they have no protections, no OSHA protections. So federal OSHA increased the maximum penalty amounts for various types of citations in 2016. State plans are required to be at least as effective, as I said. When federal OSHA determines a state plan is not at least as effective, it takes measures to take over jurisdiction of that state plan. Federal OSHA has initiated steps to take over the jurisdiction in states of Arizona and Utah before they increase their maximum penalty amounts. And Michigan is currently one of only six states that have not adopted those federal OSHA maximum penalties. My OSHA's current maximum penalty for a serious citation is $7,000. And for a willful or repeat citation, it is a maximum of $70,000 versus the federal OSHA current maximum penalties for a serious citation is $16,550. And willful or repeats are $165,514. There is an annual adjustment according to the consumer price index at the federal level. My OSHA's philosophy on penalties is that they are part of the deterrent effect, along with enforcement presence. I use the analogy of what keeps you driving the speed limit. Is it the price of the penalty or is it the number of police officers you pass on the way to where you're going? In my opinion, it's both. All penalty money collected goes to the state of Michigan general fund. My OSHA does not receive any funding from the general fund. In other words, no quotas. My OSHA penalties are not designed to be punitive. It's very difficult to put the price on someone's life or limb. When calculating penalties, My OSHA evaluates, first of all, the severity of the injury or illness that could occur. High, medium, or mild. High being, of course, death or irreparable harm, loss of limb. Then we look at the probability of that injury or illness occurring in a lesser or greater context. That is also coupled with penalty reductions, such as the size of the employer. In Michigan, we give up to 80% penalty reduction for small employers. And we also give up to 30% reduction for an employer's good faith, which means how well they interacted with the inspectors while they were there, and overall, how well is their safety and health program. And finally, we give up to a 10% reduction if the employer has not had any citations with My OSHA for the last three years. Due to that severity, probability, and penalty reduction assessments, My OSHA does not routinely issue that maximum penalty amount. My OSHA's current serious penalty maximum, as I said, is $7,000. However, the average amount of penalty for serious citations for all employers averaged together is only $1,333. And for employers with 25 or less employees, the average is $637. My OSHA will continue to calculate penalties using the same processes. If federal OSHA were to take over jurisdiction in Michigan, the following advantage of the state plan program would be lost. First of all, and most important, those public sectors, those firefighters, police, paramedics, would not have OSHA coverage. The extensive consultative outreach and education for employers would be lost. Program administration located in Lansing with legislative control would be lost. Michigan stakeholders involved in policy development through advisory committees when we go to develop a new standard, or every five years we convene focus groups to help us with our five-year strategic plan, so we pull them together, that would all be lost. And affordable safety training through our My OSHA Training Institute. I hit it too many. All right, key points. Again, penalties are a deterrent, but My OSHA strives first and foremost to proactively educate employers through consultation and other services. Even when penalties are issued, My OSHA reduces penalties based on numerous factors. The average penalty issued by My OSHA for serious violations is only 20% of the maximum penalty allowed. OSHA is mandating that My OSHA or Michigan update their penalties to match federal penalties, which were passed nine years ago. Since then, Michigan has received audit findings and a warning that failure to update our statute to match federal amounts may result in U.S. OSHA taking over jurisdiction in Michigan and the loss of the local oversight. If U.S. OSHA were to take over, more than 600,000 public sector workers, including those in some of the most hazardous occupations like firefighting, emergency response, and law enforcement, would lose the protections that are afforded them under the state-run plan. Michigan employers are not going to avoid the increase in the maximum penalties. It is a matter of who will enforce them, federal OSHA or My OSHA. We do have customer survey cards that we send out to employers and employees during our investigations and activities, and a result of those comment cards have said that comment cards used to rate My OSHA services show more than a 98% useful rating for our services in the state of Michigan. So I think that answers the question who Michiganders would like to run the OSHA program. Thank you.

I'll take any questions. Thank you. Thank you, gentlemen. Members, are there any questions? Senator Albert. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you for your testimony today. Just looking at Senate Bill 49, could you kind of walk me through the investigation inspection process? When would a citation be issued? There's language in here that's talking about a conference. What does that timeline look like for all that to take place? Yeah, so the investigation initiates for a number of reasons. It could be a fatality. It could be an employee complaint. It could be just a programmed inspection because you're in a high-hazard industry that we're targeting because you have high injury and illness rates. Once an inspection is initiated, an opening conference is held. We explain the purpose of our investigation, why we're there, and the process of the investigation. We then conduct employee interviews. We gather lots of information, documents. We do a walkthrough of the facility. These investigations can take days, months, or over a year to complete, depending on the factors involved in the investigation. Once we've collected all of the information we need, we hold a closing conference with the employer to go over our alleged findings and any alleged violations and explain the appeal rights that they have. The closing conference is the start of that 90-day clock for us to issue the citations. Once the citations are issued, then the employer has the right to appeal. If I may, Mr. Chair, help me understand, make sure that I understand this properly. So the federal law mandates a minimum of, or sets a benchmark, I should say, perhaps of once the, at the start of the inspection, in the start of the investigation, that the citation has to be given within 90 days. Is that what the federal benchmark is? No, the federal statute of limitations is the citation must be issued within six months of the occurrence. Six months of the occurrence. Of the violation. So if it's a fatality, it'd have to be within six months of the fatality occurring. All right, thank you. And then to compare that to the state statute, as you said, the investigation is kind of indeterminate. It could be a year. It could be three months. It could be kind of however long it takes for the department to go through the process. Yeah, but there is also the factor that we are not made aware of fatalities and accidents in a timely fashion either. So in some cases, we're not made aware of a fatality after in a year. So if we had that statute of limitations of six months, we wouldn't even be able to do our inspection and issue citations. Thank you. I just wanted to, I guess, flush out what the federal standard was and to kind of compare to what is being proposed here in law. So thank you, Mr. Chair. Any further questions? Thank you very much. Thank you. And I think we have a few position cards. We do, Mr. Chair. Not wishing to speak in support of Senate Bill 49 and 50, Aaron Swio, AFLW, representing the AFLW 876. Also not wishing to speak opposed to Senate Bill 49 as drafted, Amanda Fisher, representing NFIB. And not wishing to speak in support of Senate Bills 49 and 50, Robert Jory, representing Luna Michigan District Council. And the last card in support and not wishing to speak for Senate Bill 49 and 50, Ryan Seabolt, representing Michigan AFL-CIO. That is all of the cards, Mr. Chair. All right. Next, we will consider House Bill 4717 brought to us by Representative Nair. Representative, please come forward. I believe you have Joshua Scramlin from Michigan Farm Bureau who's coming up with you. All right. Welcome. Got it. Thanks. Thank you, Chair Cherry and fellow senators for the opportunity to speak on this bill. It's ironic that we're here speaking on my OSHA issues again on the same day. When you have a family member that dies or is accidentally killed on a small family operation there, the last thing that's on your mind is to be contacting any department and filing the proper information. And unfortunately, that's what happened to the Eisman family here back in 2019. They did not file a report with my OSHA within eight hours of the death of Keith Eisman. And eventually, they ended up being fined over $12,000 for failing to file or get that information to my OSHA in a timely manner. These are not these small operations like Keith's farm is not a large corporation, even though they are an LLC or considered a corporation. What this bill does is recognize that a small family farm does not have an HR department, does not have staff that handles paperwork in these untimely events, and it gives them a grace and does not get them out from the penalty, but also it gives them a grace of reducing the fines by up to 80% and even more if they do not have any other compliance issues. This legislation had been introduced by former Representative Colley back in 2020, made it all the way to the governor's desk. Unfortunately, we did not have at that time there wasn't a proper definition of a family operation, family farm operation. We have resolved that issue in this bill, and it will definitely help out and make it much easier in these stressful situations when a family member is killed or injured on a farm and help that out. To add more detail, I'm going to turn it over to Josh and give some information, and I thank you for your time. Okay. Thank you, Representative Nyer. Chairman Cherry, members of the committee, good morning. My name is Josh Scramlin. I am an associate legislative counsel with Michigan Farm Bureau. We are the state's largest general farm organization representing over 40,000 family farms in every corner of the state that produce everything from asparagus and apples to corn and dairy products. I'm here today to express our strong support for House Bill 4717, and we are grateful to Representative Nyer for reintroducing this important legislation, and we commend the House of Representatives for its strong bipartisan passage of the bill on September 3rd. So like Rep Nyer said, in 2019, Keith Eisenman, a farmer from Lenawee County, tragically lost his life in an accident on his family's farm. And on March 6th of this year, members of the Eisenman family testified before the House Agriculture Committee in support of this bill, and I would certainly encourage everybody to watch that testimony because it underscores the human element of the legislation that we're talking about here today. So following Keith's death, MIOSHA imposed fines totaling $12,000 on his grieving family, primarily for not reporting the incident within eight hours. So what House Bill 4717 seeks to address is this issue by reducing the monetary penalties that MIOSHA can levy on a family farm after the loss of a close family member due to a farm-related accident. So to be clear, this legislation does not eliminate the reporting requirement. Furthermore, it applies only in cases where the accident occurs on a farm owned by the directly impacted family and involves the death of a direct family member. So we fully acknowledge the vital role that MIOSHA plays in protecting workers, and we do agree that timely reporting is important to ensure that unsafe conditions are not overlooked or concealed. Farming is, by nature, a hazardous profession. There's daily tasks such as working with livestock. Right now, a lot of our members are out in the fields for fall harvest, so they're moving machinery around, conducting building maintenance. These are all inherently tasks that carry risk no matter how many precautions are taken. So we firmly believe that imposing significant fines on grieving families does nothing to prevent future accidents. It only adds to the pain of an already traumatic situation. So our member-adopted policy book supports, quote, appropriate safety regulations, but it also imposes, quote, enforcement action against an owner-operator resulting from self-imposed accidental injury, and that is exactly what happened to the Eisenman family in 2019. So in the immediate aftermath of a tragedy, notifying MIOSHA may not be the priority. Families should not be penalized with steep fines for failing to make a phone call within eight hours of losing a loved one. So I do appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony, and I'd be pleased to attempt to answer any questions the committee may have. Thank you. Thank you very much for your testimony. So just to make sure it's clear, this reduction would only

be in place if it is the owner and or their immediate family member? Yes, it would be brother, son, wife, husband, daughter, immediate family member, not second, third cousins, wife's cousin, or something like that. It's defined, it's in federal statute, the definition that we're using. So it will definitely close up that loop, which was the issue and the reason why it didn't become law the last time or when Representative Colley had it through. Okay. Members, are there questions? Senator Albert. Thank you for this. Unfortunately, this was vetoed. I've supported this in the past and happy to support it again. I just want to, I guess, just to make sure, so this bill would require the fine to be reduced by 90%? No. By 80% and possibly more. I think with the previous presentation there, you see what the federal guidelines are. If there is no previous history with this farm having accidents or a fatality on the farm, that would probably be in consideration and give it even more flexibility, reduce it. We can't completely eliminate it because we're dealing with federal law. This is the best we can do. Sure. Yeah. Thank you. I just want to make sure I understood it properly. Appreciate it. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Senator Kim Lurie. How many of these types of incidents happen every year? How many family members die on a family farm? I'm going to have to follow up with you on that because we did, so Michigan Farm News is a publication of Michigan Farm Bureau. We did just publish some data on that, but I do not know it off the top of my head, so I will follow up with your office on that. And then I think Senator Kavanaugh and I were sharing notes here, but why not just extend the period of time required for the report? So instead of the eight hours, make it the 24 hours for a family death. Yeah, I think that entangles us with the federal regulations, and so this is the cleanest, simple way to do it as best we could. We're making an attempt now that we're aware of this through Farm Bureau and other organizations to sort of inform the farmers and also some of your first responders out there to help them make aware that when there is a situation like this that they need to sort of look at that and hopefully through the education process we can keep people from having to deal with this situation. So what is the federal regulation that you're concerned with? It was just briefly touched on this morning there that when you do have a fatality on an operation, any and all operations there, that you should be notifying my OSHA of that fatality within a specified period. And I believe the previous presentation brought that up. Got it. Thank you. Any further questions? All right. Thank you very much for your testimony. And I believe we have a few testimony cards for 4017. Yes, Mr. Chair. Not wishing to speak opposed to House Bill 4017, Ryan Siebold representing the Michigan AFL-CIO. And one other card not wishing to speak opposed to House Bill 4017, Aaron Sekou representing AFCW 876. And that is all the cards, Mr. Chair. All right. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker. Today I rise in support of my resolution recognizing World Spina Bifida and Hydrocephalus Day here in Michigan. Joining the national observance each October, I rise especially to offer this resolution in support of a friend who lives with this and his brother, Nate, who passed from it as a young man. This resolution is about education, compassion, and hope, making sure families affected by spina bifida and hydrocephalus know that their state sees them and honors them. Spina bifida is a birth defect that occurs when a baby's neural tube fails to develop or close properly in early pregnancy. It is the most common permanently disabling birth defect that is related with life. In the United States, about one in every 2,800 babies is born with spina bifida. That's over 1,300 infants each year and nearly 166,000 Americans are living with it today. Thanks to medical advances, people with spina bifida are now living longer

fuller lives than ever before, with 75% of those affected now adults. Similar, Madam Speaker, I want this chamber to be aware of people affected by hydrocephalus. Hydrocephalus is a neurological condition caused by abnormal accumulation of cerebral spinal fluid within the brain's cavities. More than one million Americans are living with this condition. For many of these Americans, this condition can mean a lifetime of multiple brain surgeries. Dozens and even hundreds of brain surgeries are common. Awareness matters. Behind every statistic are real people, children who want to play, students who want to learn, adults who want to live independently. Awareness leads to early interventions, better outcomes, and stronger inclusion in schools, workplaces, and communities. By passing this resolution, we send a clear message. Michigan values every resident of every ability. Colleagues, I urge your support. Let us recognize the dignity of those living with spina bifida and hydrocephalus, honor the families and caregivers who care for them, and commit ourselves to building a future where every Michigander has the chance to thrive. Speaker recognizes Representative Tate. Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in strong support of my resolution commemorating the 95th anniversary of the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel, a remarkable engineering achievement and an enduring symbol of partnership between Michigan and our neighbors in Ontario, Canada. On November 3rd, 1930, the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel officially opened to traffic following a historic telegraphic signal from President Herbert Hoover. The tunnel was born from a shared vision of cross-border cooperation that began in 1919, championed by Detroit Mayor James Cousins and Windsor Mayor Edward Blake Winter. Completed ahead of schedule and under budget, it stands as a testament to what our region can accomplish when we work together across borders, communities, and governments. For nearly 95 years, this tunnel has connected downtown Detroit and downtown Windsor, enabling the flow of people, goods, and ideas that strengthen both of our economies. In 2023 alone, over 3.7 million vehicles passed through this tunnel, more than 11,000 each day, including commuters, tourists, and commercial carriers supporting industries from auto parts and steel to agriculture and health care. The tunnel supports over 325 jobs in Detroit and contributes more than $595 million annually to the city's economy. It continues to foster tourism, workforce mobility, and cross-border trade that sustains thousands of families on both sides of the river. But beyond the numbers, the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel represents something deeper. It symbolizes the spirit of cooperation and friendship between Michigan and Ontario, one that has endured for nearly a century. It reminds us that borders need not divide us, they can connect us. As we celebrate this 95th anniversary, we also look forward to the future of continued innovation, collaboration, and shared prosperity across the Detroit River. The tunnel's legacy continues to inspire us to build links and connections, both literal and figurative, that unite people and strengthen communities. I urge my colleagues to join me in supporting this resolution. Thank you, Madam Speaker. The question before the House is on the adoption of House Resolution 197. you all do. I appreciate the question. We are an organization of over 40,000 members. Anyone is able to join. So it's concerned citizens as well as health care professionals, lawmakers, anyone. Thank you. I do appreciate the robust conversation, but we do have to have to move on. So we do have a couple individuals that know just card. We're just reading. I thought I wish to speak. Well, great. That'll make it a lot easier. A couple. Thank you both for your for your testimony. And we'll look forward to continued conversations. Thank you for all you're doing. Thank you. So we do have a couple cards to read in on this bill in opposition of the bill. We have Danielle Atkinson from Mothering Justice. Also opposing the bill is Paige Faults from from Lara. Great. So moving on, we're going to take testimony from Representative Fairbairn on House Bill 4927. Representative, would you please come up and begin when you're ready? And yes, bring your bring your guests up at the same time as much as we can do to expedite moving this along would be great. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Mr. Chair. Yes, Representative. Thank you. While we're getting ready for the next bill, I'd like to formally request that you give us another meeting of testimony on the previous bills. I didn't get a chance to ask my questions. Thank you. Noted. Go ahead, Representative. Thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. I'm here this morning to speak. It's almost afternoon now, actually, but still a morning to speak in support of House Bill 4927. It's a bill I sponsored as a part of a really great package, the 2025 Red Tape Reduction Package. Though this bill is intended to reduce the statutory requirements for obtaining a barber's license in the state of Michigan. In order to provide a bit of perspective by telling you what it takes to become a commercial pilot and fly people and cargo, let's say Lansing to Mackinac Island, an aspiring commercial pilot needs to complete 100 hours of pilot in command time, 50 hours of cross country time, 20 hours training with an instructor, 10 hours of complex aircraft time, 10 hours of instrument training, 300 nautical mile cross country flight, 100 hours of ground school, 10 hours of solo training, 5 hours of night flying, 20 hours of instrument flight, which totals about 250 hours. Now this sounds fairly thorough and extensive preparation, and I don't know about you, but it gives me some level of confidence in the ability of a young pilot to handle an aircraft, a single engine aircraft. But that 250 hours really pales in comparison to the 1,800 hours that the state of Michigan requires an aspiring barber to complete before being issued a license to cut your hair. If we were talking worst case scenario in the case of the pilot, it's a pretty bad circumstance. Worst case scenario in the case of a barber, you get a nick or a shorter haircut than you had hoped for. I'm not in any way diminishing the barbering profession nor those who practice it. On the contrary, I'm saying that these professionals should have a lower barrier to entry into their chosen field and would appreciate your support in really passing this legislation and changing the licensure hours from 1,800 to 1,500. To give you a professional perspective, I have with me today Lauren Moser, branch director, and then Roderick Samuels, education director of Hair Lab Detroit Barber School. With your permission, I'd like them to testify. Hello, everyone. I'm honored to be here to speak on behalf of the barber industry. My name is Lauren Moser. I have been a licensed cosmetologist for over 25 years, and I have run a barber school for the last six. It's in those six years that I have become really involved in reform of the barber industry. Hearing those numbers about pilots is a little scary, to be honest with you. And there are a lot more than bad haircuts coming out of deregulating the barber industry. There's disease prevention and things like that. So while they're learning haircuts, that's this much of the education. More of it is disease prevention and keeping the public safe. So we want to maintain some of the hours, but we just want to modernize it. So I sit here today to speak in strong support of Bill 4927, which would reduce the required hours for barber licensure from 1,800 to 1,500. This is a smart, necessary, and long overdue step towards modernizing a system that no longer serves today's students, schools, or workforce. We have come a long way in our technology, right? Everyone knows that information comes fast and hard. So we're able to grow a little faster, learn a little faster, get through programs a little faster. So this would bring us into 2025. Barbering is one of our country's oldest and most respected trades, but in Michigan, it's a trade trapped in a system that is both over-regulated and under-enforced. We have layers of outdated requirements that make it harder to enter or teach in the field, yet at the same time, we lack consistent enforcement and oversight to protect the public and support legitimate schools. What we need is reform, not deregulation. Modern, common-sense updates that align our laws with today's realities. Right now, our framework burdens those trying to do things the right way, while unlicensed activity continues to grow unchecked because there simply aren't enough licensed barbers or inspectors or schools to keep up with the demand. The 1,800 requirement is one of those outdated barriers. Reducing to 1,500 brings us in line with the majority of the country. There are only four states in our entire country that require barbers to go to school over 1,500 hours, and we're one of them. Our license in the state of Michigan is a little bit different because our barbers can do chemical services and things like that. Some of the other states that have the lower requirements, like 1,000 hours, typically do not. They aren't licensed to do chemical services. So keeping it at 1,500 continues to protect the public and make sure that these people understand how to use the chemicals that they're licensed to use. Chemicals used the wrong way can cause permanent alopecia. I don't know if anyone's aware of that. So it's beyond a bad haircut. We want to make sure that they're getting the full education so that they can continue to protect the public while bringing us into modern day. Reducing the hours to 1,500 brings us in line with the majority of the country. States that have training thresholds of 1,500 hours have seen higher completion rates, faster entry into the workplace, stronger pipeline for skilled professionals. This bill keeps every safeguard intact, the same testing, sanitation, and safety standards, but recognizes that modern curriculum can produce the same level of excellence in less time. Our reform is only part of what's broken. Michigan's barber industry is facing a critical instructor shortage, and current laws are a major reason why. A licensed barber must wait two full years and then complete an additional 1,000-hour and one-year instruction program before they can even begin teaching on their own. Yet there are only a handful of instructor programs left in the entire state, and most barbers can't afford to take a year off to attend them. I hear from barbers all the time who are ready to teach passionate, skilled professionals who want to give back, but they simply can't step away from their livelihood to do it. It's a system that is unintentionally discouraging the very people we need most. The result, schools are closing because they can't hire instructors. Whole regions of Michigan no longer have barber schools at all, meaning fewer licensed barbers, more unlicensed activity, and growing risk to public health and consumer safety. If we paired instructor reform with this bill, an additional bill that could be added later, Michigan could become a destination for qualified barbers and educators, a state known for opportunity, not red tape. We could attract instructors from around the country, open new schools, create legitimate licensed training programs that feed directly into our workforce and small business communities. HB 4927 is a meaningful start, but it should mark the beginning of a broader reform. Let's fix the barriers that are holding back our industry, our workforce. Let's make Michigan a model for how smart, responsible reform can strengthen education, create jobs, protect the public all at once. We have a real opportunity here to make Michigan a place where barbers, educators, and entrepreneurs want to build their future. HB 4927 is the first step towards that, and I urge you to keep going. Every time a student can't finish or a school can't open, we lose a taxpayer, a small business, and a community anchor. This reform isn't cosmetic. It's economic. Thank you for your time.

and for your commitment to modernizing our state's workforce laws, and I'm happy to answer any questions, as well as my Director of Education. Great. If you'd like to continue on, but if we could keep it really short, I mean like 30 seconds, we do have questions and we do have other bills to get through in the next 20 minutes, so please. You can't be nasty and needy, so I wanted to say thank you so much for allowing me this time. Good afternoon, Chair and Chair and members. My name is Roderick Samuels. What this bill is going to do is it's going to help so many young professionals, people in our industry, people in our communities, to give them an opportunity to work in trades, right? Not everybody's built for university. Not everybody's built for four-year college, but I do know for myself, being a college kickout, not a dropout, my mom and dad came to pick me up because my grades made it home before I did. Now, if I give him an opportunity to maybe not do 1,800 but 1,500, I seem to be the sweet spot, not just across the country but here in Michigan where our things are very, very antiquated. And in closing, as someone who still works in the classroom every day, still mentoring, still shifting heads, shaping heads and shaping lives, I do want to ask you guys for some grace on this and please give us the opportunity to push this forward. Thank you. Great, and thank you for keeping that brief. I am the son of a preacher, so I don't want to make you happy twice. Got it, and I'm not going to air any grievances of bad haircuts of the past. Well, but yours looks really good. Thank you. Minority Vice Chair Grant has a question. Thank you. No, actually, the cosmetology license is also 1,500 in Michigan, and if you look at the curriculums next to each other, they're essentially identical. That's a great question, and being no further questions, I thank you both, all three of you, for your testimony, and hopefully we can get more people in there, Mr. Sams. Thank you. We do have a couple cards to read in in support of the bill is Paige Fultz from Lara. Also in support of the bill is Janet Skorp from the Mackinac Center for Public Policy. All right, moving on, and Representative Steele, with obviously nerves and patience of steel, is going to come up and testify on House Bill 4933. So begin when you're ready, Representative. Thank you, Chair and committee members for the opportunity to speak. House Bill 4933 addresses licenses regarding renewal and relicensures. So this bill increases accountability by requiring Lara to issue or deny a license not more than 90 days or 30 days if it's a real estate broker. If that deadline isn't met, the applicant receives a refund and a 15% discount on the next renewal, ensuring the government meets the same service expectations we expect of the private sector. So these changes will put the onus on the department to reissue a license if the license lapses in a quick time manner, and so these licensed professionals can go back to work quickly and easily. So additionally, the bill supports our military service members by exempting them from the fees and continuing education while they are deployed protecting their professional standing while they serve the country. In short, this bill is about fairness, efficiency, and respect for the professionals and for our taxpayers, of course. So Laura did reach out to our office, and they did have a couple implementation amendments that seemed worthy if you guys had the opportunity to look at them, and that's it. Thank you. Great, and thank you for your testimony, Representative. I see no questions, so you were thorough. Thank you. Thank you. And members, too, I know today seemed kind of rushed, and so I'd urge further questions on any of these bills. Get with your minority vice chair or myself or the bill sponsors themselves. Get some of them questions cleared up. So that's it for testimony today. So no questions, no cards, so that concludes our agenda for this morning. Our plan will be to vote these out. So seeing no further questions, Representative Bagul moves to excuse all absent members. There being no objection, absent members are excused. title: Regulatory Affairs 25-10-22
transcript:
Good afternoon. I'm calling the Senate Committee on Regulatory Affairs to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chair Moss. Here. Senator Polanky. Here. Senator McCann. Present. Senator Bueno. Here. Senator Santana. Senator Hurtel. Here. Senator Singh. Present. Senator Houck. Here. Senator Weber. Here. Senator Lowers. Senator Bellino. Mr. Chair, there are nine members present. There is a quorum. Thank you. I'll take a motion from Vice Chair Polanky to adopt our committee minutes from our October 15, 2025 meeting without objection. The committee minutes are adopted. We have three bills on the agenda today. We will start with Senator Lindsey's 595, which we will take a vote on because there's a timing urgency behind it. So I'll call up Senator Lindsey along with Paige Foltz from Lara and Andrew Brizbo, Director of Bureau of Construction Codes. And you can pull up a third chair. It might be tight up there, but I know all of you want to testify all together. Like a three-headed monster. It's perfect. Chair Moss, Vice Chairs Polanky and Houck, members of the committee, thank you for the opportunity to testify on Senate Bill 595. As you may know, my district includes the entirety of the Michigan-Indiana border. The border between our states was initially set by Congress in 1816 and later surveyed in 1827. Surprisingly to many, that 1827 survey was the last official complete survey of the Michigan-Indiana border. And unfortunately, rigorous permanent monumentation was not included, leaving ambiguity to this day. In recent years, the governments of both Michigan and Indiana have worked towards resolving this issue. Most recently on our side, Public Acts 81 and 82 of 2022 reestablished and funded a commission to undertake the remonumentation of the Michigan-Indiana border. All of you on this committee, save Senators Singh and Weber, who were not serving in the legislature at that time, voted in favor of that legislation for which I thank you. While the commission was able to complete some of the preparatory work, including a cost study, multiple attempts to secure contracts with surveyors willing to undertake the entire project were unsuccessful. As a result, the work has not yet been completed, and the authority and funding established by those laws are set to expire about 10 weeks from now. The Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, whose representatives are here today, is involved in the duties of the commission and have worked hard towards a solution for which they have my gratitude. Senate Bill 595 does two important things to solve the problem before us. First, it moves the sunset date from January 1st of 2026 to January 1st of 2030. This will prevent decades of work on this subject being reset to zero. Second, it creates a mechanism for the existing funding to be granted to county remonumentation programs. This is critical because we cannot simply extend the timeline and hope for better results. We need to adjust our approach. County remonumentation programs already do this exact type of work, and they have the local expertise necessary. Importantly, this legislation does not ask for additional resources to complete this work. It simply asks for more time and a new approach to deploy the existing resources. By making these two changes, I'm confident we will be able to work expeditiously with each border county to achieve the goal of surveying and remonumenting the Michigan-Indiana border. Thank you for considering this legislation, and I welcome any questions. Our officials want to chime in. Great, thank you. Chairman Moss, members of the committee, thank you so much for having us speak today. I'm Paige Foltz. I'm the Director of the Office of Policy and Legislative Affairs at LARA. The Bureau of Construction Codes, or BCC for short, is housed within LARA. They mainly work to ensure Michigan's built environment and the systems within it are sound, safe, and sanitary. But one of their lesser known responsibilities is they house the Office of Land Survey and Remonumentation. This office's day-to-day consists of orderly and consistent review of subdivision plats and reviewing those subdivision plats, administering statewide programs, and remonumentation of the original U.S. government public land survey corners. And they also review petitions for the State Boundary Commission. And today we come before you to discuss LARA's support for Senate Bill 595. This will finalize the Michigan-Indiana state line. Unlike other state borders, a clear line does not exist. The Michigan-Ohio border was settled by the Toledo War. The compromise from that, the U.S. Congress granted Michigan statehood, and also Michigan had to give up their claim to the Toledo Strip in exchange for the UP. The Michigan-Wisconsin border was decided in court. It was a dispute that arose between the original 1836 boundary description that was referenced did not actually exist. It claimed the Montreal River originated from the Lake of the Desert, which is not true. That actually caused the longstanding ambiguity that exists today. Ultimately, the two states sued each other, and in 1926 it went all the way to the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court's final decision issued the bounty line at that time. To dive deeper and answer questions into Senate Bill 595, on today's agenda I have with me Andrew Brisbo, the Director of the Bureau of Construction Codes. Thanks, Paige. Thank you to the committee for the opportunity. I won't belabor the points. I believe they've been made, but we're confident in BCC that with the changes in this proposed bill sponsored by Senator Lindsey, that the work can be completed and this can be wrapped up. It's been in the process for 15-plus years now, and we think the flexibility that's afforded in the language that's been proposed will allow us to complete this work in a timely fashion. Thank you. Thank you. We'll do questions from committee members, but I'll lead off. So I remember passing this bill. The whole presentation makes sense to me. How much more time do you think is needed past the next sunset of this or the next expiration of this? How much more work do you think is needed on completing this? Well, now that we've completed the preliminary study, we have a good sense. So a surveying firm completed that study, did an analysis of the work to be done, and we're in coordination with the state of Indiana as well that has a similar commission. So really it's just about executing those contracts, distributing the funds, and getting the surveying work done. That should be able to be done within a couple of years, and then the reconciliation between the two states will take a little bit of time as well. But the extension of the sunset should provide adequate time to get all of that done. Yeah, so we're expiring it now in 2030. You actually think it could go the length, or at least, you know, that's the appropriate amount of time? Correct. Okay. Vice Chair Polanky. Oh, sorry, did I? I was just going to say, as he was discussing distributing of the funding, I just want to make sure to make it clear, the funding is there. It was allotted in a Kim Lasada bill in 2022. So this is granting LARA to be the authority to execute those funds. They are available and sitting there for our use. This is just a matter of allowing the state of Michigan to continue to participate in this. Yes, please. Got it. All right. Vice Chair Polanky. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Senator Lindsey said you couldn't find a surveyor. What was that about? So the completion of the cost estimate was done, and then we put out an RFP a couple of times in order to grant the funds to a surveying firm to complete the work, and we didn't receive any qualifying bids. So we went back and discussed with the commission whether it might be a better approach to provide the funding to the county surveying programs on the border in order to just add it to their existing programs, which we also provide grant funds to through another program. So they have the capacity to do the work, and they can just build it into those programs in order to get the work done. That's what you mean by changing the approach? Correct. The statute as it was written requires us to engage in an RFP to a single firm in order to complete the work. So adding that allowance to work through those existing programs at the county level we think is a better alternative. Senator Bellino. Thank you, Mr. Chair. I just want to make a couple comments. The trade for Toledo for the UP was an excellent trade because if I had Toledo in my district, I wouldn't be here today. And second of all, I'm glad it was a Lasada bill a couple years ago because if it was your bill, we wouldn't have voted for it. Seriously, we like Kim Lasada. Thank you. Noted. Thank you. All right. I'm not going to get in the middle of that. Vice Chair Houck. Yeah, I just have a short comment. If someone would have told me that Senator Lindsey would be sitting at a table with two representatives from LARA agreeing on something when he first came in, you've grown so much. No further questions? I'll take more questions if anybody else wants to chime in. No, that's it? All right. We have no further questions. As has been mentioned, we've got to get this passed because this expires at the end of this year. I will read in cards of folks who wanted to weigh in on this but did not wish to speak. Brett Hollinsworth, professional surveyor supporting the bill. John Kerr from JFK Land Surveying Consultant, Inc. supporting the bill. Arthur Brintwall, professional surveyor supporting the bill. And Michelle Bottora, Michigan Society of Professional Surveyors supporting the bill. So seeing no further questions, we can

Senate Bill 595 to the floor with the recommendation that the bill pass. So moved by Senator Weber. Will the clerk please call the question? Chair Moss. Yes. Senator Balinky. Yes. Senator McCann. Yes. Senator Bueno. Yes. Senator Santana. Senator Hurtel. Yes. Senator Hurtel. Yes. Senator Singh. Yes. Senator Houck. Yes. Senator Weber. Yes. Senator Lauer. Senator Bolino. Yes. Mr. Chair, there are nine yeas, zero nays. The bill is reported. All right. We will move on to our agenda now. It's just testimony only. We will go on to Senate Bill 443 from Senator McCann. I know he's going to be joined by Ben Frederick, brand manager of Smoke Evacuation, Ellie Kircher, BSN, RN, CNOR, and Michelle Schafer, RN, CNOR. This testimony requires a presentation. And I know that folks know that this floor has been under rehab. If anything is damaged, it is Senator McCann's fault. Fully. I want that to be put in the record. Mr. Chair, I ask for forgiveness, not permission most of the time. Well, thank you. Thank you, Chair Moss and my colleagues on the committee for the opportunity to discuss Senate Bill 443. This bill seeks to address the very real concerns that medical professionals and patients also encounter in the operating room with what is referred to as surgical smoke. Surgical smoke is the dangerous byproduct of heat-generating surgical tools like lasers and electrosurgical pencils that are used in an estimated 90% of all procedures, including cesarean sections, knee replacements, and mastectomies. This smoke can contain over 150 hazardous chemicals, including carcinogens, immunogens, and can potentially transmit live viruses. Thus, operating room staff in Michigan are exposed to this smoke daily, which can have health consequences. A study published by the British Association of Plastic Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons estimated that the impact of surgical smoke exposure is equivalent to being exposed to the smoke of 27 to 30 unfiltered cigarettes per day. Another study published in the Association of Perioperative Registered Nurses Journal found that perioperative nurses report twice as many respiratory problems as the general population. Senate Bill 443 seeks to address this harmful exposure by having hospitals and surgical centers establish measures for the clearing of surgical smoke in operating rooms. Smoke evacuation systems are proven, cost-effective solutions that remove airborne contaminants at the source without requiring facility construction or HVAC changes. Currently, without a legal requirement, many hospitals do not use evacuation consistently, and it can often depend on a single team member's preference. Colleagues, I believe that Michigan should join the 20 other states, including Ohio, Minnesota, and Illinois, in enacting a surgical smoke evacuation law to protect operating room teams and patients. Everyone deserves a safe and smoke-free environment, including our essential health care workers. Now to speak further to the necessity of this legislation, I'd like to introduce two Michigan operating room nurses, Ellie Kircher from the University of Michigan and Michelle Schaefer from Corwell Health Farmington Hills, along with Ben Frederick, brand manager with Stryker, who will perform a demonstration for the committee about how surgical smoke evacuation systems can work. Then we'd be happy to take any questions you have. And I think we're going to have Mr. Frederick do a very quick demonstration, and then we'll have Ellie and Michelle speak as well. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Great. I think you needed this center area. Yeah, go ahead. Yeah, perfect. It's not often we get kind of a show and tell, so I think we're all very excited about this. Let me put that on top of it. Oh, it's wireless. Okay, all right. It's high tech. Yeah, we did bring lunch for everybody. No, we won't be eating this steak. The brief demo I have for you today shows a normal setup that would take place in hundreds of operating rooms across Michigan. What you're looking at is an electrocautery device. I'm going to show you that here. The electrocautery device is used in over 80% of surgeries that happen in operating rooms in Michigan and across the country. This device, which I'm about to show you, generates a smoke plume. Inside of this smoke, there have been over 150 chemicals identified, 18 of which are EPA priority pollutants. The amount of smoke generated in an operating room in a standard day is the equivalent of 27 to 30 cigarettes burning. And nurses who work in the operating room have two times the rate of respiratory illnesses as nurses who work outside of the operating room. So this is the device that generates a plume today. What I'm showing you now is a type of device. There are many devices on the market, but this is one device that evacuates smoke while you're using the electrocautery device. So you can hear the filter turning on, and you can see there's no longer any plume arising from the point of cauterization. And so what's happening is that smoke is funneling down this tubing through a vacuum, and it's being filtered out through a special filter called an Ulpa filter that has activated charcoal that breaks down the smoke, so it can no longer be inhaled by nurses in the room. Thank you. All right, now, Bolino, you wanted that? All right. Thank you, Ben. I really appreciate the demonstration. And now we'll go to our nurse friends here. Thank you very much. Hello, and thank you, Chairman and Committee members, for allowing me to speak today. My name is Ellie Kircher, and I'm a certified operating room nurse, State of Michigan, and I've been a registered nurse for seven years. I've been in the operating room for the last four. My main job is to be a patient advocate for patients in their most vulnerable state, anesthetized and undergoing surgery. But today I speak to you as an advocate for my fellow nurses and the OR personnel in the operating rooms. Thank you for allowing me to speak about this issue I and thousands of nurses encounter every day that we go to work. When I started working in the OR, there was many differences from when I was a nurse in the emergency department. One of the most abrupt changes was the smell. There is a smell that comes with that plume from the surgeons using electrocautery devices. I call this the ultimate if you know, you know, because to be blunt, it is the smell of burning tissue and flesh as surgeons cauterize blood vessels to perform operations. Eliminating the electrocautery device is not an option as it has revolutionized how surgery is performed. However, the solution does come in the way of a smoke evacuation and filtration away from the staff and the patient in the room. Now I was planning to come in here and pull out a cigarette and light it up, but I'm quite sure that the security here would escort me to leave quickly. So please be at ease. I did not bring a lighter and cigarettes into the Capitol today because your workplace has prioritized your health and declared that you cannot smoke in public buildings with Michigan's Smoke-Free Indoor Air Law enacted over 15 years ago. However, according to studies done about the smoke in an operating room, the staff is exposed to the equivalents of 27 to 30 cigarettes worth of smoke in an eight-hour shift. So you'll understand that me smuggling in 27 cigarettes would have been even more difficult. So the point I'd like to make is that it took a bill being passed to make it so that smoke was removed from public spaces. And I am here to ask you to expand that to an area not generally seen or known by the public, my workplace, the OR. The hospital I work at already has the equipment needed to evacuate the smoke, but without policy or law, I, as the staff nurse in the room, have very little to no say of whether or not the smoke evacuation device is used. Sometimes it is utilized. Most times it isn't. We need legislation to protect all staff and the patient in the room. I think one of the frustrating aspects for the—sorry. One of the frustrating delays in getting this passed in adherence to the best practice is the vagueness of symptoms that come with the prolonged exposure to smoke. I'm quite sure everyone here has probably experienced a headache or two from their job, but when you realize that it's most likely caused by the toxic chemicals you are exposed to out of your own control at your job, it's a different type of injustice. There is almost nothing I can do as one single person to protect myself in the OR. The masks that we wear during a case are not rated for filtration of the size of particle that is in the plume, and we have no control over the equipment selected by the surgeon or whether or not they choose to use smoke evacuation on a case. So, in Ann Arbor, where I'm from, you may understand that there is a lot of competition with certain neighboring states regarding certain football teams. However, disappointingly, when it comes to smoke evacuation, Ohio has

far surpassed us by making smoke evacuation mandatory in all operating rooms in 2023. Operating rooms across the country are in need of quality nurses, and being able to show that we as a state prioritize the health of nurses and the OR personnel is essential for attracting and retaining staff. There are currently 20 other states I could go to and know I would be breathing cleaner air in the OR than in our state right now. So I believe it is past time that we get on board with this movement, and I would like to be the 21st and not the 50th state to pass this legislation. So we have the research, we have the solution, and we have the opportunity to stop exposing perioperative staff to the over 150 toxic chemicals found in surgical smoke. But we do need a bill to consistently and uniformly mandate this safety standard so that it is no longer an option or preference and Michigan nurses can breathe cleaner air. I want to go back to focusing on my main role as a patient advocate and not have to be concerned about my own health while doing the job that I love. So please be with me, the AORN, OR personnel, and nurses across the state in supporting Senate Bill 443. We have been breathing in this problem for too long, and now it is time to clear the air, protect nurses, eliminate surgical smoke, and please support Bill 443. Thank you. And now I'm going to pass it to my colleague, Michelle. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Michelle Schaefer and I am here to express my support for Senate Bill 443, a bill to require a surgical smoke evacuation policy for hospitals and ambulatory surgery centers in Michigan. I was born and raised here in Michigan, and I have been an operating room nurse for 15 years, with the last four years being a nurse educator in the OR at Corwell Health Farmington Hills. The occupational hazards of surgical smoke are more than just statistics or data points in a study. This was a daily part of my life. It is estimated that the amount of surgical smoke produced in an OR during an eight-hour day is equal to 27 cigarettes. This means that my time in the OR caring for patients exposed me to the equivalent of 77,220 cigarettes. And I have never smoked a cigarette a day in my life. When I first started in the OR, I experienced headaches nearly every day at work. I attributed it to being a new nurse in a new learning environment because no one talked about the hazards of surgical smoke. And I didn't even know that that was the likely cause. Surgical smoke is the result of human tissue contact with lasers and cautery pencils commonly used during surgery. In other words, it's the smoke of burning flesh. According to the CDC, research studies have confirmed that surgical smoke plume can contain toxic gases and vapors such as benzene, hydrogen cyanide, formaldehyde, bioaerosols, blood fragments, and viruses like HPV. Surgical smoke causes eye and respiratory irritation and creates visibility problems for the surgeon. The smoke has a horrible odor and has the potential to cause genetic mutations, potentially leading to cancer. Repeated exposure to surgical smoke, like any toxin, increases the possibility of developing adverse health effects. While I have been the educator in the OR, I have seen firsthand the harmful effects that surgical smoke can have on our new OR personnel. Cynthia, a nurse that had just graduated from nursing school, started in the OR. It was her dream job and she was so excited. During her first few weeks, she would come to me with complaints of headaches, nausea, and dizziness. She was emotional and scared that she wouldn't be able to continue in the OR with how she felt every day. Around that time, I listened to an AORN webinar that examined the hazards of surgical smoke. It really wasn't until then that I truly realized the significant and horrible effects that surgical smoke has on everyone in the OR. And I realized that this is what Cynthia was experiencing. We decided that we needed to make a change for the health and well-being of our OR personnel. We started the conversation to convert our ORs to being smoke-free. It took significant planning, education, and leadership support. Our smoke-free implementation date came, and I instantly felt safer knowing that we were evacuating toxic chemicals, HPV, and cancer cells from the air we were breathing every day at work. I was so proud of our team for their commitment to our health and safety. Another nurse, Ali, started about a year after we had been smoke-free. He was doing great, and he loved being an OR nurse. One day, he called me for assistance in the OR because the smoke evacuator wasn't working. I went in, and immediately, I was hit with that all-too-familiar smell of surgical smoke. Ali told me that he was so nauseous, and his throat was so irritated that he had to step out of the room for fresh air. When he returned, he told me that he was so thankful that we were a smoke-free OR because there would be no way that he would be able to work in an environment like that every day. In the operating room, we are required to wear x-ray lead during radiation and N95 masks during TB and COVID cases and eye protection during all cases because those keep us safe. There was never a requirement to evacuate surgical smoke, even though there's an article from the AORN Journal in 1997 stating that patients and perioperative personnel should be protected from inhaling the smoke generated during surgery. This was in 1997, and we have still not put policy in place to protect our OR personnel. Most surgical facilities in Michigan already have surgical smoke evacuation equipment available. And while many of these facilities may evacuate surgical smoke during some procedures, few facilities evacuate consistently during all smoke-generating procedures. Senate Bill 443 proposes a solution to a hazardous workplace issue faced by thousands of healthcare workers for decades. At a time when healthcare workers are experiencing burnout and leaving the profession, Michigan can take an important step to the health and safety of OR staff and support the workforce that Michigan residents rely on for their healthcare. We all deserve a safe work environment. The time to regulate is now. Help us join the 20 other states that have already protected their nurses and surgical staff. Please vote yes on Senate Bill 443, which enacts a simple, accessible solution to a surgical smoke problem faced by OR personnel. Thank you for this opportunity to share with you my experiences of the occupational hazards of surgical smoke in Michigan's operating rooms. All right, thank you very much. Thank you for your perspective on this. I am obviously a recent recipient of a surgery, and it's just something I would never even thought of. I was under, so I wouldn't have even known about the surgical smoke in the room, but your perspective as operating room nurses has been very enlightening. And the presentation obviously demonstrates that right away. We will start with questions from Vice Chair Polhenke. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Who makes the decision if a smoke evacuator tool is used? Generally, it's surgeon preference. We as a hospital decided to go smoke-free, so our hospital only provides smoke evacuating cautery devices for our surgeons, so they have no choice. But that was what we worked on. Are the doctor's groups for this, or do we not know yet? Senator Polhenke, we don't have the benefit of a conversation or input at this point. I'm just thinking what doctor wouldn't want this, because they're the ones like literally every day. You know, I don't understand why. I mean, I read it might get in the way of the procedure. I don't know. But are there different, is there just this one brand of little tool, or are there multiple brands that can be purchased? There are multiple. And how much would one of those cost? That's a great question. So what you looked at originally was what's been used on the market for probably 70 years. That was the one that was generating smoke. It costs about $5. And then the one that I showed you afterwards that evacuated the smoke, Stryker makes one, but so do about five other companies. Those costs in between $15 and $30. And our research has found that the average Medicare reimbursement for a surgery like a knee replacement is about $13,000. So the cost increase we're talking about is less than 1% of what a hospital would be reimbursed for surgery. Oh, yeah, that's nothing. And then you said the masks don't work. Yep. It's a certain kind of filter that the smoke has to go through in order to break down the carcinogens. Got it. The masks that the nurses are wearing in the room aren't approved for that type of filtration. Okay, thank you. Maybe just a follow-up question. How many of these devices, I know there are different sizes of hospitals, different bed sizes all throughout the state, but how many of these would be needed on average in a hospital? That's a great question. So if you look at the handout we have in front of you, the left-hand side shows the type of equipment that's needed per operating room. So like the white machine you're seeing down here is the filter. It's breaking down the smoke. Something like that, some kind of filter, will need to be in every operating room. Michelle, you may say hospitals vary in their OR sizes. Some have five, some have as many as 50. But when we polled members of a nursing association in Michigan, 97% of them said their hospital already has this type of equipment on site. Great. Senator Bellino. Yes, that was so

When I had my kidney surgery last year, thank you Mr. Chair for letting me talk. Well, when you had his surgery last week, he's okay because he has got a mask on and getting oxygen and they're taking care of him, right, the anesthesiologist. So he's not being affected. It's the workers, correct? Technically the patient could be at risk as well. Really? C-sections, yep. C-section mothers are awake, right? They're breathing in the air just next to everybody. Smoke travels 35 miles an hour, so it gets to the patient very quickly and everyone in the room. As well as if I could just add laparoscopic surgery, that smoke, you might have just those small little incisions, that smoke is inside your belly. And there are studies that show that it can create metastasis at the port site where those little incisions are. And also that smoke is absorbed into your bloodstream when you have a minimally invasive surgery. I think we have grounds for a lawsuit, sir. No, absolutely. We'll go to Vice Chair Houck first and then Vice Chair Polhanke. But I want to really kind of pinpoint what we're talking about here today. There are hospitals that accommodate for us. There are hospitals in Michigan that do not want this surgical smoke infiltrating the nursing staff, infiltrating the patient. And they have internal policies and equipment like this. What this bill is requiring that every hospital in Michigan come up with a plan, correct? So many of the hospitals that maybe we've gone to have already accommodated, including your workplaces. We're just trying to require that every hospital has a plan to mitigate this surgical smoke. Vice Chair Houck and then Vice Chair Polhanke. So my wife worked in, she's an RN and she was a surgical nurse for like five years. And she's talked about a lot of, I don't have to tell you about what goes on. She's never talked about smoke. So I took a picture of the non-smoke evacuating. And this is what she said. This tool creates a lot of smoke. And in Midland, I think the scrub techs would hold the suction close to the site to suck up the smoke. An evacuation system would be very good though because they are thinking that a lot of surgeons are getting cancer from smoke. And then I showed her that thing and she said, oh, that's cool. Vice Chair Polhanke. Thank you. Super quick. So the little tool itself is $35. How much is all this? Yep. Great question. So the note at the top says 97% of survey respondents said that already is at their hospital. The cost for something like this ranges between $3,000 to $15,000 depending on the model. And again, not one specific company benefits from this. There's all types of industry partners that make things that evacuate smoke. The hospital would be able to shop around to find a price that worked for them. Any other questions from committee members? All right. Thank you very much. I'll read in some cards from some folks who did not wish to testify. Jennifer Pennock, the Association of Perioperative Registered Nurses, supporting the bill. And Stephen Rapundalo from the Michigan Biosciences Industry Association, not wishing to speak in support of the bill. All right. We will revisit this at a future meeting. I really appreciate the presentation. All right. Last on today's agenda for testimony only, again, is Senate Bill 604, introduced by Senator Polhanke. Thank you, Chair Moss. Do you want me to sit here? Wherever you want to sit. All right. I'll sit here. Whoever there's the least amount of smoke. Thank you, Chair Moss, members of the committee, for the opportunity to testify in support of my bill, Senate Bill 604. This bill makes necessary updates to Michigan's spirits distribution system to ensure long-term stability for the state, our distributors, and distillers that rely on a dependable system to reach their customers. As many of you know, the Michigan Liquor Control Commission serves as the state's wholesaler for all distilled spirits. The commission works with ADAs, or Authorized Distribution Agents, who deliver every bottle on behalf of the state. Our state's largest ADA, Republic National Distributing Company, is located in my district and employs 680 hardworking Michiganders. And I've toured it. It's very cool. It's a partnership that's worked well for years, but like any system, it needs to evolve with the times. Rising costs and overall inflation have made it increasingly difficult for distributors to absorb costs and plan ahead. Under current law, there is no structured or transparent way to account for these changes. Instead, we have adopted a piecemeal approach where the fee is increased on an ad hoc basis, sometimes with years between adjustments. And I have a little chart here, and it has every year listed, and there's one period from 06 to 2013 of six years, and then with no adjustment, and then there was a period of three years after that and two years. So it's very random and unpredictable. Senate Bill 604 brings a common-sense fix to that. It sets up a fair, predictable way to handle adjustments to distribution fees by tying them to the consumer price index or 5%, whichever is lower. The bill also gives the Liquor Control Commission the ability to respond quickly when the emergencies rise. If there's a sudden disruption, whether from economic conditions, supply chain issues, or something else, the commission can use one-time funding to keep operations running smoothly. My bill is a steady, thoughtful solution that keeps Michigan's spirits industry strong and sustainable for years to come. I know the gentleman from Republic are here today and can also ask questions, but I'll take any questions if there are any. Any questions from committee members? We have some folks that are wishing to testify, some folks that put in cards that are not wishing to testify, but any questions for the bill sponsor? All right, we'll call up Tony Mitchell, Executive Director, Michigan Spirits Association. Steve Rochow from Vice President of RNDC Michigan. Thank you, Chairman Moss. Thank you, members of the committee, and thank you, Senator Polhanke, for introducing the bill. The Michigan Spirits Association represents the majority of the suppliers, brokers, and ADAs in the state of Michigan and is a partner to the state in growing the spirits industry responsibly. Partner to the state is an important phrase because the state of Michigan doesn't just tax the sale of spirits. The state is in the spirits business. Across the country, the spirits industry works under a three-tier system where you have a supplier, a middleman or distributor, and then the retailer or restaurant. In the state of Michigan, the state is the middleman. Michigan was the first state to ratify the repeal of Prohibition in 1933 and made the choice at that time to be in the spirits business, as did 17 other states, all of which are called control states. Michigan is one of the top 10 states for spirits sales in the country, also one of the top 10 of the highest tax states for spirits in the country. The spirits business brings the state of Michigan over $600 million a year in revenues from taxes and profits. The authorized distributor agents are the agents of the state and the heart of the spirits industry in the state of Michigan. They deliver every bottle to over 11,000 accounts in the state of Michigan between restaurants, bars, and stores. And they have to do this if any of those accounts orders one case or more a week wherever they're at in the state of Michigan. So there's extreme costs in doing this. And in a moment, Steve will speak a little bit more in detail about some of those costs. But it's important that we keep the ADA system healthy to keep those revenues coming into the state of Michigan. And because of the lapses in years where the ADAs did not get increases, as pointed out by Senator Paul Hanke, it's not always been healthy and they've struggled when they haven't been able to recuperate the costs that they're putting out for delivering these spirits. Increasing fees as costs go up has been discretionary, as Senator Paul Hanke pointed out, also. And we believe it needs to be codified so that future increases are tied to CPI and paid from the state's markup, which is currently 65%. The fees are also currently capped by law. So actually until something's done, the fees couldn't go up, which could create a major problem. In summary, again, we just want to keep the system protected, keep it healthy, and I'll turn it over to Steve, who will get into more details, and then we can answer any questions. Thank you, Senators, for your time today. My name is Steve Roshow with RNDC. I've been there 33 years with the company and four decades in this industry. The ADA system is the backbone of the state's spirit wholesale business. This business makes them over $600 million a year, and we do everything for the state. We do the storage, the picking, the delivery, the EFT collection. We also have a group of customer service seven strong to handle all the complaints and calls, and we come to a solution to all of our customers. Since there's no bottle picking fee, we pick roughly about 130,000 bottles per night. What does that mean to you? We're a national company in 38 states throughout the country. We pick more bottles in the state of Michigan

twice as many as the rest of the states combined. So the challenges we have are extreme. We employ almost 700 people, and 65% of our splits are bottle pigs. To put in perspective geography, we would be delivering on the same groundwork to Nashville, Tennessee, every single day with nine trucks. That's the distance we have to go to service our customers. Look, we're very, very grateful for the fee increases we've received recently, but we're capped. We just went through negotiations with our drivers, 180 union drivers, which is never easy, and we end up negotiating with them. We did fine, but it's very cost significant. I'm just going to throw you a few other expenses out there, and then any questions, I'd be happy to answer. Just for example, cardboard boxes. We have to take all of our spirit cases that come in from our suppliers and repack them into what we call them splits, cardboard boxes. We spend almost $5 million a year just on cardboard. Our labor between just the drivers and warehouse, in essence, are over $40 million a year. It's very cost prohibitive to do this business, and what we're asking for today is your support. The system produces a lot of money, and we just need your support so we can continue the ADA system for many years to come. I appreciate your time and look forward to any questions. Are there any questions from committee members? No, you said it all. We appreciate it. We have some cards to read in from some folks in the industry who do not wish to speak, wanted to signal their support for Senate Bill 604. We have Joe Sicola and Larry Sicola from Imperial Beverage supporting the bill, Kevin Koch from Edrington Spirits supporting the bill, Brian Pizzutti, R&Dc Distributing supporting the bill, Jim Moran, Luxco Spirits Brands supporting the bill, Sam Audish, President Michigan Spirits Association and VP West Brands supporting the bill, Andy Deloney, Distilled Spirit Council of the U.S. supporting the bill, Jerry Griffin, Midwest Independent Retailers Association supporting the bill, John McNamara, Michigan Restaurant Lodging Association supporting the bill, and Lou Grecumbo, Great Lakes Wine and Spirits supporting the bill. So a lot of support for the bill. Seeing nothing further, we will revisit this at a future meeting, but we appreciate your testimony here today. No other committee can you get Indiana border, spirits distribution and surgical smoke. That's why I love this committee so much. Wanted to also put a flag in here. We had Senator Lauer's virtually joining us who wanted to signal his support for Senator Lindsey's bill as it passed through committee earlier. And with his absence and Senator Santana's absence, I'll take a motion from Senator Hertel to excuse absent members from our committee without objection. Those members are excused. And with no further business, our Senate Committee on Regulatory Affairs is now adjourned. Thank you. Thank you.

title: Finance, Insurance, and Consumer Protection 25-10-22

The Committee on Finance, Insurance, and Consumer Protection is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairwoman Kavanaugh. Here. Senator Irwin. Here. Senator McCann. Present.
