I will welcome Senator Victory to join me in the testimony and turn the gavel over to Vice Chair Irwin. Well, thank you, everyone. As you know, our agendas always say any other business properly before the committee. So at this time, we're going to hear from our colleagues, Chair Kavanaugh and Senator Victory. Please take it away. Thank you, Chair and committee members for making this decision to hear my bills and our bills today and for testimony. Scam and nuanced robocalls are one of the most persistent customer frustrations facing Michiganders across the entire state today as we constantly hear from our constituents. Interrupting our lives, exploiting trust, targeting vulnerable residents, and in worst cases, stealing millions of dollars from hardworking Michigan residents. From fake IRS and social security scam targeting seniors to constant calls about your car's extended warranty. These calls are persistent and evasive. In 2024 alone, Michigan residents received over 1 billion robocalls, costing Michiganders time and money. That's why I've partnered with my colleagues, Senator Victory, Senator Anthony, Moss, and McBroom on a bipartisan bill package, Senate Bill 351 to 355, to tackle these malicious practices and strengthen our consumer protection here in the state. Senate Bill 351 establishes the Telephone Solicitation Act regarding both voice calls and text messages. This bill does have an S1 that we will hope to adopt to clarify the act does not apply to religious, political, public policy, or educational purposes or to bonafide surveys or opinion research to ensure that your First Amendment rights are protected while not stifling civic activity in our state. This package of bills prohibit caller ID spoofing, misleading or abusive call patterns, and unconsented recording messages while requiring telephone solicitors to clearly identify themselves and the organization they represent, limits calls to the following hours of 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., and mandating that any contract made through telephone solicitation be provided in writing and signed by the consumer before payment is accepted. This legislation also gives the Attorney General the authority to bring civil actions against violators with fines up to $25,000 and all the way up to $100,000 for persistent and knowing violations that are targeting our vulnerable residents. It is at its core, the bipartisan package is about protecting Michigan residents, especially seniors and people with disabilities from exploitation and ongoing harassment. It is about ensuring that when someone receives a call from a number they don't recognize, they don't have the fear of being scammed out of their savings. I want to thank you for hearing my testimony. I'm happy to answer any questions, but will also note that the Attorney General's team and other consumer protection experts can speak on a little bit more expert on the language and also the legislation, but want to turn it over to my colleague, Senator Victory, for any testimony. Thank you, Madam Chair and Mr. Chair and members of the community. Thank you for the opportunity for me to testify on Senate Bill 352. Senate Bill 352 is part of the package of bills implementing the Telephone Solicitation Act. This package of bills will help protect Michigan consumers from telephone solicitation. Senate Bill 352 specifically would allow individuals to file a civil action suit against a telephone solicitor who do not follow the following newly implemented guidelines. Many of my constituents have reached out about the robocalls affecting their day-to-day lives. Some seniors have reported receiving up to 40 calls a day. Let me repeat that, 40 calls a day. And probably some members of the community probably experience close to that number. These solicitors disrupt the individual days, often predatory in nature, and distract people from calls that they actually do matter. My hope is that these bills will dissuade telephone solicitors from using deceptive and misleading tactics by implementing stricter guidelines and adding accountability. And thank you, Madam Chair and members of the community for taking up this legislation. And if you have any questions, please, but I also look at the opportunity in front of us because many times we see, you know, the general public see a divided government and sometimes we're always looking for those 80-20 issues. I think this is an 80-20 issue, but let me even build on it. I think it's a 98-2 issue, 98% support and those 2% who are in the industry probably would advocate on behalf, you know, the robocalls. So with that there, thank you very much. Thank you, Senators. First, I'll recognize Senator Bayer. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you for this. I'm really actually excited about it. I've been a victim, but I do have a question. So would political donation solicitations or solicitations I'm thinking from police or firefighters or fundraising like that, would that be legal under this law? So we have an exemption for the S1 substitute is clear for religious, political, and public policy and educational communication surveys and opinion research. So it all depends on how that lands under, but definitely that would... Purposes that do not involve sales or marketing. Yep. So soliciting donations is not... So if that is required any sort of donation or anything, then they would just need to let them know who they are, where they're coming from, and kind of background from that, but it won't exempt them from reaching out if they are under the qualified of that act of making sure that it's coming from a person, coming from something locally, and they know who it's from. Okay. Thank you. Thank you. Next, I'll recognize Senator Tice. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. My question involves your bill, Madam Chairwoman. On page two, you give a definition for charitable organization, and within that, the language explicitly excludes religious organizations. Now, since the dawn of our country, religious organizations have been the primary charitable giving throughout the country. Like charities originated in our faith places to begin with. Why are we excluding them from the definition of charitable organization? Yep. So we are working across with stakeholders as well as bipartisan to make sure that the S1 substitute doesn't want to exclude religious, political, and public policy, as well as educational communication, but we do see that there is an exemption

for them soliciting and asking for money if they don't have any background with a customer. So we are working to make sure with the Attorney General and other stakeholders that it's going to be consistent and making sure it's not infringing on the First Amendment. So as of right now, they do need to fill out making sure who they are, where they got that contact if they want to ask for money. But we are working to figure out a little bit of consistency and making sure that we're not addressing anything that might hinder the First Amendment right. So if I might follow up, I see the language that was added in the S1, but we're treating a religious charitable organization differently than a non-religious charitable organization. And I don't know how that supports your First Amendment rights in any way, shape or form. I'd love to have continued ongoing conversation because we did exempt all non-charitable organizations as long as they do a criteria of letting them know who they are, what they're asking for, and making sure that they actually have a relationship. But I am having ongoing conversation about the issue of making sure that they can just reach out and solicit. So we're having ongoing conversations about that. But as of right now, it is that they just need to acknowledge where they're coming from and have to have an ongoing relationship with the person that they're reaching out to. That's true for all of the solicitation, but you expressly exempt religious from being a charitable organization. I think the correction to that would just be crossing that exemption out of that paragraph. So that's what I would advocate for. No, I agree. I see the inconsistency. So we're working with stakeholders to make sure that all issues are addressed as we move this legislation forward. Appreciate your comments. Thank you for the questions and the answers. In today's environment, phones are more than just a telephone. And I hear from folks and I continue to also be bashed by constant texts. Any parts of these policies include texts and unsolicited requests for, I think, especially purchase of property, the house that you have and on and on. So are texts included in this package at all, too? Yes, text messages are. And then how would we see this actually operationally moving forward, especially considering probably a lot of these things come from, I would guess, foreign countries and or other states? Is that, do we possibly run into conflicts with interstate commerce and other issues related from state to state if they originate from other locations? No, we actually worked hand in hand with the Attorney General's Office. And we actually, this legislation builds on the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as well as allowing our attorney and almost like what you asked in practice, this actually allows private citizens to pursue recourse for malicious situations occurring in Michigan. And that's never before is something that incurs to the person that they can just make sure that they have the agency to see recourse. And so that also allows for that. And so we can actually see it play out a little bit faster than what we're seeing at the federal level. Great. Thank you so much. Thank you, Senator Heisenga. It looks like that's the end of our questions for our sponsors. So thank you very much. And as the chair comes back to this seat, I will continue to prattle on and try to hold the floor for all of those who are waiting for our chair to make it back to the center of the room. Thank you again. So before we move and welcome additional speakers, we'll be considering the S1 I described in my testimony. I will entertain a motion to adopt the S1 version of Senate Bill 351. So moved by Senator Bayer. Will the clerk please call the question? On adopting the S1 to Senate Bill 351. Chairwoman Kavanaugh. Yes. Senator Irwin. Yes. Senator McCann. Senator Bayer. Yes. Senator Camilleri. Yes. Senator Heisinga. Yes. Senator Tice. Yes. Senator Daly. Madam Chair, there are six yeas and zero nays. The substitute is adopted. Thank you. And next we will hear from the Attorney General's Office. Ashley Steffen, Director, Office of Legislative Affairs, Assistant Attorney General Kathy Fitzgerald and Michael Hill. Welcome to committee. Thank you, Chairwoman Kavanaugh, for having us. Like she mentioned, I'm Ashley Steffen. I'm Director of Policy and Legislative Affairs. With me is Kathy Fitzgerald and Michael Hill from our Corporate Oversight Division. And I'm here because I've been unable to reach you about your car's extended warranty. I'm just kidding. And in particular, we're looking at VoIP providers that are often the first phone carrier that takes the call from offshore and then transits across the United States and into Michigan. And if we're able to hold the VoIP provider liable, which we would be, then we can stop the calls from reaching us. This would really help the enforcement of these important rules that currently is very vastly under-enforced and expand the extent to which individual harmed consumers are able to sue when they become victims. This would help ensure compliance with federal standards that have gone long unenforced or under-enforced and critically empower the victims to sue when they're harmed. Respectfully, when people are harmed, they should be able to sue. The claim of frivolous lawsuits are overbroad and the devastating or nonsensical decision to prevent people from bringing lawsuits when they're directly harmed outweighs the risk. We need more levers of consumer protection, not less. What's left out when we hear the concerns about having to defend lawsuits are the consumers that are left up the creek without a paddle, having to just hope and pray the AG has the time to take a case that may or may not provide them recourse when they are harmed. This bill would not stop schools from sending emergency texts or utilities from sharing when there's a last-minute shutoff. It would set up methods of transparency, control, and consent for text messages and other messages as well. It should not outlaw text messages. And as Senator Ir

many CSPs have seen positive results. A few of them are Florida, Oklahoma, Maryland, and New Jersey, that increase potential enforcement opportunities against bad actors and set clear protections to improve transparency and reduce the scammiest of calls. And again, those jurisdictions have seen improvements in their numbers. The bills also prohibit caller ID manipulation, regulate auto dialers, and require transparency again. These measures are not only reasonable, they're essential. I urge the committee to advance these bills and don't bring down Michigan to the standards set out by the 2021 Supreme Court standard, but rather up to the other states and sort of bring consumer protection to Michiganders, as you have rightfully mentioned. We don't need another task force. We don't need another study. We need action and actionable laws in consumer protection. This represents a straightforward response to a crisis that affects every Michigander, especially seniors, low-income families, and other vulnerable communities. Thanks for your time and leadership on this issue, and thanks for the opportunity to testify today. Happy to answer any questions. Thank you for being here, and thank you for your testimony. Any questions from committee members? No? Appreciate your testimony. Last, I'd like to welcome up Elizabeth Benton, Director, Consumer Law Attorney, Michigan Poverty Law Program on Zoom. Thank you, Madam Chair and members of the committee. Thank you for this opportunity to provide testimony regarding Senate Bills 351 through 355. The Michigan Poverty Law Program is a statewide support organization for the state's legal aid programs. These programs provide representation to low-income consumers and very low-income families and seniors across the state. MPLP advocates on behalf of the state's low-income residents on issues related to low-income housing, elder issues, public benefits, family law, foreclosures, and consumer issues. MPLP is pleased to support Senate Bills 351 through 355, which would provide important new protections from unwanted, abusive, or deceptive telephone and text solicitations. As others have said, this legislation comes at a critical time. Regulators and law enforcement across the state, and just us average consumers, are seeing a dramatic increase in scams and frauds. Last year, the Federal Trade Commission reported a 25% increase in consumer losses due to fraud. It received over 53,000 fraud complaints from Michigan consumers who reported losses of $204 million to fraud. Consumers reported losing the most money to investment and imposter scams, the types of scams that often start with unsolicited phone calls. Moreover, the FTC has warned that the emerging use of AI voice cloning technology to impersonate the voices of loved ones and family members will only turbocharge this fraud going forward. Senate Bills 351 to 355 will help prevent scammers from getting through to vulnerable consumers. When they do, the legislation will allow individuals and the Attorney General to bring actions to stop this solicitation going forward and to recover damages and impose civil fines for violations. Strengthening these state-level consumer protections is especially important given recent federal developments. The federal administration's proposed budget cuts would reduce staffing at the FTC, one of the federal agencies charged with enforcing the federal rules governing telephone solicitation. Recent federal court decisions have also limited the FTC's ability to protect consumers, particularly its ability to obtain monetary relief on behalf of consumers. Across the country, states are stepping up to fill this void with new state-level protections and increased enforcement. We must ensure that Michiganders are not left behind. Senate Bills 351 through 355 provide much-needed state-level consumer protections. The Michigan Poverty Law Program, on behalf of Michigan's low-income residents and seniors, supports these bills and encourages you to vote for them. Thank you. Thank you for your testimony and thank you for being available for committee. Any questions from committee members? Not seeing any. Thank you for being here. Mr. Clerk, can you please read the cards in for the record? Brad Ward, Michigan Realtors, opposes 351 through 355. Tim Langholz, NFIB, opposes the package. Ronald Taylor, Detroit Area Agency on Aging, supports the package. Michael Ima, Michigan Chamber of Commerce, opposes the package. And Jake Listock with CTIA opposes the package. Thank you. And there being no further business, the Senate Committee on Finance, Insurance, and Consumer Protection is now adjourned. Thank you.

title: Health Policy 25-10-22
transcript:
The Senate Committee on Health Policy is called to order. Will the clerk please call the roll? Chairman Hertel? Yes. Senator Santana? Senator Voino? Senator Cherry? Senator Kleinfeld? Senator Geiss? Senator Weber? Senator Houck? Senator Heisinga? Senator Runstead? Mr. Chairman, you have eight members present. There is a quorum. Thank you, Madam Clerk. I will entertain a motion to adopt the September 10, 2025 committee meeting minutes. So moved by Senator Voino without objection. The minutes are adopted, and I will make a motion to excuse absent members. And seeing no objection, absent members are excused. Today we're going to take testimony and some presentations regarding Senate Resolution 81 that is focused on calling on Congress to renew the tax credits for plans purchased on the health care exchange for the Affordable Care Act. I think we are all seeing this discussion play out at a national level and how it will directly impact families all across the country. People will see their premiums or out-of-pocket costs double, triple in some instances, and those letters are going out now. We're seeing families that are understanding the impact of this who are already struggling with increased costs from things like groceries, prescription medicines, and everything they need to pay for on a day-to-day basis. This will just compound those issues and make it harder for them to get by. We've seen in recent years that we have seen an increase in enrollment on the exchange, which is a good thing. More people are finding out that they can have affordable access to health insurance here in the state of Michigan. It has promoted more access to care for individuals, specifically preventative care, so that they can get the medical treatments that they need. But this, without the renewal of these tax credits at a federal level, will cause thousands to lose access to affordable health insurance, therefore losing access to that care that they need. It will also change our insurance pools because younger, healthier people who buy plans on the exchange today will be less likely to purchase those plans going into the future because they will not be able to afford them. And when that happens, costs will go up for everybody, as we will see insurers here in the state forced to cover some of the sickest lives in the state without having some of those healthier lives to balance out that cost. And so we want to understand today the exact impact that these decisions at the federal level will have directly here in Michigan for patients and for folks that buy their insurance on the exchange as well. So we will begin with a presentation from DIFs. I'll call up Joe Sullivan, the Director of Innovation and Research, and Jenny Gee, Legislative Liaison Manager, Office of Innovation and Research as well. Thank you for being here today. Good afternoon. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today about the impact of recent federal changes to the Michigan Health Insurance Marketplace. Chair Hertel asked us to give an overview of the health insurance marketplace, DIFS' role, and related consumer protections. We will detail efforts to ensure a stable health care marketplace while maintaining the most affordable and quality health care possible for Michigan residents. A little bit about DIFS' authority. DIFS works to ensure the safety and soundness of the state's insurance industry. In addition to the Michigan Insurance Code, 19 other primary state statutes govern the insurance work we do. There are also several dozen federal statutes that govern our operations, such as the ACA, HIPAA, COBRA. However, Medicaid, Medicare, and self-insured employer plans are primarily regulated by the federal government. At the program level, as you are all aware, Medicaid is also overseen by DHHS. How the health insurance marketplace was established by the ACA and is a federal-operated insurance marketplace where individuals and families can purchase and compare health plans. These plans cover 10 essential health benefits, including doctor services, inpatient-outpatient hospital care, prescription drug coverage, pregnancy and childbirth, mental health services, and more. And some plans cover more services. The plans also provide consumer protections, like requiring coverage for those pre-existing conditions, requiring coverage for dependents up to 26, and prohibiting annual lifetime limits. DIFS is responsible for recommending the certification of qualified health plans that provide essential health benefits, follow established limits on cost-sharing, and meet other requirements under the ACA. The marketplace only includes individual plans, and for Plan Year 2025, Michigan had over 530,000 Michiganders enrolled in the individual market, which is primarily what we'll be discussing today. I'll kick it over now to Joseph. Thanks again for the opportunity. So I'm going to start with the DIFS rate-making process. So the DIFS Office of Rates and Forms is responsible for reviewing insurance policy rates and forms for compliance with state and federal statutory requirements.

not set the rates. Rather, companies are responsible for setting the rates for their policies, but these rates must comply with Michigan law and must not be unreasonable and must be actuarially justified and not unfairly discriminatory or excessive. This year, due to uncertainty in evolving guidance at the federal level, states had to find a way to be nimble in their rate and filing review procedures while still meeting the CMS deadlines, all without compromising our duty to thoroughly evaluate each proposed rate increase. The timeline and process for filing insurance rates are typically a busy time for our office. This year's timeline has been unprecedented. Due to uncertainty about possible congressional action related to cost-sharing reductions, DIFs initially required insurers to file two sets of rates. We worked closely with health insurers through the rate review process to navigate various changes and deadlines. As always, we use outside actuaries in our review of rate filings to ensure that any increase is justified and that consumers are protected. Due to the requirements on insurers to submit two sets of rates and other necessary changes that were atypical for a filing year, DIFs had a significantly increased workload and expenses for actuarial reviews with its review of filings this year. DIFs will publish the Plan Year 2026 final rate report on the November 1st start of open enrollment. This report will be posted on our website and will provide a detailed summary of those rates. Next, I want to talk a little bit about the impact to health insurers in our state. Because of the volatility this year, CMS announced a deadline of September 25th for issuers to withdraw plans. There are usually changes to plan offerings, but as seen in many other states, the volatility caused by the inaction on enhanced premium tax credits and marketplace reforms have led to a variety of types of withdrawals, including issuers declining to offer certain plan types or remain in certain areas of the state. Some withdrawals from just the marketplace or withdrawals from the individual market as a whole. If an issuer exits the individual or group market entirely, there's a five-year market reentry ban. Issuers generally try to avoid this, which is a good thing for market competition. Historically, Michigan has had a robust insurance marketplace with more plans offered than in most states, allowing for more competition and consumer choice. Next, I want to give a little bit of a background on the advanced premium tax credits, which have played a critical role in making health care on the individual marketplace affordable for consumers. From the outset of the ACA, the federal subsidy was designed to help eligible individuals and families with low to moderate incomes pay for health insurance purchased through the marketplace. Eligibility and the amount of the tax credit are based on an individual's estimated annual household income, household size, and geographic location. Based on an individual's income estimate, the marketplace will send the APTC directly to the individual's insurance company each month. The insurance company then bills the consumer for the remaining premium amount. The credits are a mechanism to reduce health insurance costs for those who don't qualify for Medicaid or Medicare, don't have employer-based insurance, and many are consumers who may not have purchased health insurance otherwise. Next, I'll talk about the enhanced advanced premium tax credits, which were established by the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 and extended through 2025 by the Inflation Reduction Act. These enhanced credits expanded eligibility and increased the amount of financial assistance available. For Plan Year 25, a record of over 530,000 Michigan residents were enrolled in a marketplace health insurance plan, and the majority of those consumers were able to purchase this coverage due to the availability of enhanced credits. For 2024, nearly 90% of enrollees qualified for a subsidy, saving an average of more than $380 per month. This figure includes APTCs as well as enhanced APTCs. Next, I want to talk about the impact of those subsidies. Failing to extend the enhanced tax credits beyond the end of 2025 will impact marketplace consumers' out-of-pocket costs and will have the biggest impact on those who use these tax credits to obtain affordable coverage, but also the entire market as a whole. If Congress sunsets the enhanced tax credits, beginning in 2026, premiums will increase by over 75% on average, according to an analysis from KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group, but some consumers could see much higher increases based on their location, age, income, and other variables. In Michigan, an estimated 40,000 Michigan families currently enrolled in coverage through healthcare.gov will no longer receive any premium tax credits. Next, I can provide an example which may be helpful. According to the Center for Budget and Priorities, a 60-year-old couple in Michigan making $82,000 a year will see their monthly premium go from $580 a month to $1,710 a month. So that's over a $1,000 increase a month. As a result, many residents may risk going without health insurance entirely. These individuals may still get injured or sick and will need to seek care somewhere, even if they're not insured. The expiration of the enhanced subsidies will also increase costs when a pool of relatively young and healthy individuals decide not to purchase coverage on the marketplace. This would worsen the risk pool and increase premiums for both subsidized and unsubsidized consumers and potentially lead to more consumers and insurance carriers considering leaving the marketplace as a result. Next, I'm going to turn it over to Jenny to close us out and provide some action steps that you all can take. So what should your constituents know and what can they do? This year, due to new CMS guidance, information about increased monthly premiums for 2026 may not be included in notices insurers send to their current customers. Consumers may not notice it, like any changes, until their first bill. On November 1st, constituents can log into their marketplace accounts and review their new premium amount. Residents should gather important information and income verification documents, take time to shop around and compare health insurance plans, and keep track of the shortened deadlines and new requirements. Residents who utilize healthcare.gov for their health insurance should be aware of the following changes. Health insurance marketplace policyholders may need to be prepared to update their income and other information quickly, as the amount of time allowed to resolve data discrepancies was shortened from 150 days to 90 days. If consumers automatically re-enroll, they should log into healthcare.gov long before the December 15th, 2025, and review their information during open enrollment, especially since information about monthly premiums for 2026 may not be included in this year's notices that is sent to them. For new enrollees, including those who enroll outside the open enrollment due to a life event or income change, may need to prove eligibility before they can receive subsidies. Looking ahead to next year, open enrollment will be shortened by a month, ending December 15th, 2026, rather than January 15th, 2027. So what is DIFS doing to get the word out? Every year, DIFS works diligently to get the word out about open enrollment and what actions consumers need to take. The department has updated its health insurance website at michigan.gov forward slash health insurance with resources to get covered during open enrollment. We're updating the department's on-hold messaging system with open enrollment information. We've been implementing earned media strategies that emphasize the importance of open enrollment and contacting DIFS for more resources. We will also share a legislator and stakeholder media toolkit to help you communicate with your constituents, including sample social media graphics. Furthermore, we'll be offering online open enrollment webinars, and we would be happy to partner with you on any outreach events. In addition, DIFS Office of Consumer Services provides consumer information and assists consumers with questions and complaints. This includes connecting consumers with all available resources, including answering questions through our live call center and connecting people to health insurance navigators who will help them assess their options, sign up, and stay enrolled in the marketplace plan. The office also receives the DIFS call center, which serves as the initial point of contact for all incoming calls and visitors, which many of you, I believe, have already used. Our call center has representatives who take live calls Monday through Friday, 8 to 5 p.m., and can call 877-999-6442 or online. Per Governor Whitmer's Executive Directive 2025-6, DIFS is proactively communicating updated information to consumers so that they are prepared to make informed insurance decisions during the open enrollment period. Our approach has been to protect consumers to the greatest extent by balancing a competitive health insurance market while ensuring any rate increases are actuarially justified. We appreciate the opportunity to come before you today to share this information, and we look forward to continued collaboration in protecting Michigan consumers. Happy to take any questions. Thank you both for being here and for all the work you've done to at least help folks understand and deal with problems as they arise, as these changes occur. I think, unfortunately, and listen to your testimony,

The reality is, though, that from the decision that is being made at the federal level to not renew these to this point, it's created a lot of uncertainty here in the state. But the ultimate effect is it will increase costs to families who currently purchase plans on the exchange and have these tax credits. I think we've seen this in other states and nationally. We've seen some large national insurers simply say that they will not even sell plans on the exchange going forward because of this tax credit going away. Do we have plans here in the state of Michigan that you were able to speak about today that will be leaving the exchange? Yeah, on that, I can note that our comprehensive rate report, which is a federal requirement and also a boilerplate requirement in Michigan budget, will be out next week. It'll detail all of the plan changes in the state that you're experiencing. But yeah, in short, that's correct. I think companies have had to face difficult decisions and reevaluate their position in the market and determine whether or not it would be beneficial for them to stay in the state, which means that almost 200,000 people are potentially going to be losing their insurer and they need to be crosswalked onto different insurance plans. And it's been a volatile and interesting process, to say the least. But yes, you're correct. And I would argue that as that happens, we see less competition occur, which changes the dynamics on the exchange as well. We had some folks that would qualify, depending on where they are within that sliding scale for the tax credits, for $5 or $10 plans. They could no longer qualify for some of those plans. And it changes the ability for insurers to be able to offer different products. And as less are insuring folks here in the state, that lack of competition only moves us in the wrong direction. And I would venture to guess that we're seeing the beginning of it this year with the uncertainty and this being the first year in a long time these credits will not be available. But as we go forward and those risk pools change, this only gets worse over time as it's more unaffordable for people here in the state and across the country to afford some of those plans. Senator Chaird. Thank you, Chair, and thank you for the presentation. When I was listening to you, you talked about how the enhanced premium tax credit increased eligibility for the tax credit. Can you clarify? I might have missed it. It got enhanced. What was previous eligibility and then who became eligible for tax credits with the enhanced provisions? So the enhanced tax credits, there's a calculation that goes in. It's income-based. It's based on a variety of variables that determine whether household size, a number of things. And then a consumer would be eligible for an enhanced credit, which would be a higher dollar amount, which would provide that individual more cost savings. The intent is to try to get those individuals on the market. You're typically looking at people that don't qualify for Medicaid. They make too much money to qualify for Medicaid. So you're trying to incentivize those folks. So it's in addition to the APTCs, you have the enhanced APTCs, which is essentially a greater subsidy that only certain folks qualify for. So what I thought I heard you say in your testimony is that eligibility is based on a percentage of federal poverty level, but that enhanced eligibility, like it increased eligibility. What did it increase from into? It was an enhancement in the dollar amount that the consumer was receiving based on federal poverty level and other variables, which is what we said in our testimony. Okay, so there's no expanded eligibility. It was just increased subsidy for those who are already eligible. Yes, that's my understanding. Thank you. Seeing no further questions, appreciate the information today. Thank you for all you're doing. Next, I will call up Dominic Pallone and Christine Shear from the Michigan Association of Health Plans. Thank you for being with us today. Thank you for having us. Good afternoon, Chairman Hertel and members of the committee. My name is Christine Shear. I'm Deputy Director of Legislation and Advocacy for the Michigan Association of Health Plans. MAHP represents 10 health plans covering nearly 4.1 million Michigan residents through the Medicaid, Medicare, and commercial products, as well as 45 business affiliates. Joining me today is Dominic Pallone, MAHP's Executive Director. On behalf of our 10 member health plans, I want to thank you for inviting our input on this important discussion regarding enhanced premium tax credits. MAHP members continue to lead the nation in expanding access to effective, affordable, and equitable health care. Policy discussions like today are essential in ensuring consumers remain informed about health care access and affordability. We especially appreciate Chairman Hertel's leadership and his measured, thoughtful approach to this critical issue. He, his office, and caucus policy staff have consistently sought input, shared ideas, and engaged in constructive dialogue with our member plans. MAHP represents a diverse group of health insurance providers serving individuals and families across the state and nationally. Our association is uniquely positioned to share insights and experiences regarding the implications of expiring EPTCs. In 2024, more than 24 million Americans selected health care coverage through the Affordable Care Act marketplace, the largest number ever to choose coverage through an open marketplace of competing health plans. We are proud to stand with national and state partners, including the American Hospital Association, the American Medical Association, the Federation of American Hospitals, America's Health Insurance Plan, American Academy of Family Physicians, the Michigan State Medical Society, the Michigan Health and Hospital Association, and the Michigan Primary Care Association, in urging Congress to make enhanced premium tax credits permanent. EPTCs directly reduce the cost of coverage for consumers and lower average premiums across the marketplace. In Michigan alone, more than 500,000 residents enrolled in the marketplace plans last year, with approximately 90 percent, about 450,000 people, receiving federal tax credits that lowered their monthly premiums, making quality, comprehensive coverage attainable. If these tax credits are allowed to expire, the impact will be immediate and severe. According to the Kaiser Family Foundation, premiums in the individual marketplace could increase by as much as 114 percent. Nearly 100,000 Michiganders will likely lose coverage altogether, driving up the state's uninsured rate and straining health care providers. As open enrollment begins in just a few weeks, nearly half a million Michigan residents face greater uncertainty rather than ever before. The potential loss of federal tax credits combined with rising medical inflation and escalating prescription drug costs could result in some of the steepest premium increases seen in nearly two decades. I will now turn it over to Dominic Pallone, our Executive Director, to discuss possible policy solutions. Thank you, Christine, and thank you, Chairman Hertel and members of the committee. Again, appreciate the opportunity to be invited here to talk about this important issue, and such an important issue as health care affordability is for our citizens. Affordable health insurance is at the forefront of everyone's mind, not only here in Michigan, but nationally. Rising health care premiums attributed to higher prescription drug costs, elevated acuity of claims, or the cost of those claims, and then coupled with the potential loss of these enhanced consumer tax credits, will leave employers and customers with sticker shock as we head into next year. It's more important than ever that the state and federal policymakers consider policy solutions to help make health care more affordable. These trends underscore the need for proactive policy solutions. Our association prides itself in being a resource to policymakers on this topic, and our unique membership of state and national health plans have identified various policy ideas and best practices from other states that can help health insurance become more affordable in Michigan. I've attached some background information to the written testimony that we've submitted here today on how to make health care more affordable in Michigan. And this document contains about a dozen different policy solutions that policymakers could consider and that we would encourage a conversation around. I want to share just a couple of ideas with this committee here and would employ everyone to think big and explore ways in which we can stabilize the individual market together. One of these topics to bring your attention to is that some states have allowed individual

with incomes just above the Medicaid eligibility threshold to purchase Medicaid-like insurance policies. Policymakers could explore legislation here in Michigan or similar to legislation passed in other states to create a basic health program. Some of those other states that have gone down this path include Oregon, New York, and Minnesota. This would help those who might be left and unable to afford the individual marketplace insurance today. And then the other thing I'll note here is that nearly a decade ago, the federal government expanded access to association health plans, allowing small businesses, self-employed individuals, and independent contractors to purchase health plans in the large group and at lower costs. Michigan could codify an upcoming federal rule once issued to preserve the expanded scope of accessibility of association health plans in Michigan. Doing so would give small businesses more flexibility to provide lower-cost insurance options for their employees. And as Christine mentioned, and just to close here, I again want to thank the chairman, staff for the committee, and all of the committee members themselves for their willingness to take on this difficult issue here today. Certainly, we, as Christine noted in her testimony, we very much agree with the importance that Congress should act. There is still time for Congress to act on extending permanently the enhanced premium tax credits that are available to many on the individual market today. Thank you. Thank you very much. One of the things we've heard at the federal level is that if Congress doesn't act in pretty short order, an open enrollment begins on November 1st, goes through January 15th for this year. What were to happen if Congress were to, by the end of the year, say in December, while open enrollment is already open, expand the tax credits? Have you had discussions with any of your members on how that might work? We have not had detailed discussions over that exact timeline, Senator, but I can share, as of right now, the change occurring this late in the process, as was noted by the folks that testified from DIFs earlier, final publication of rates are due on November 1st, right? So any change between now and then is still very difficult, but could occur, and certainly our members, all the plans that have decided to stay on the market, would do what they can to educate potential enrollees, either existing or future, as to what those premium costs will be. There is still time. I worry as we get later into the year, though, that that window will close. As I've watched the federal conversation occur, I think we've seen a lot of people that have said, well, we can kick this can down the road and we can deal with it later on. As you noted, we're already at a difficult point to have that conversation, but it only gets worse the longer this goes. Any other questions from committee members? Seeing none. Oh, Senator Chair. My light's not going on. There we go. Thank you, Chair. Appreciate the testimony and had a chance to read through some of the materials that you sent out before committee. One of the options that I guess you guys put forward as a recommendation, the basic health program, can you talk a little bit about how that works in other states that have done it and what that might look like in Michigan? Yeah, there's a few ways in which it could be done that other states have explored. I mentioned Oregon, Massachusetts, and New York as some states that have gone down this path in their own unique ways. But at a high level, if I can try to summarize their activities here and what that might look like in Michigan, it's creating new products that are very similar to the coverage for Medicaid itself. Some states are doing Medicaid buy-ins where you are actually buying into managed care Medicaid products. So the product design itself would be similar to or could even be identical to the Medicaid core benefit structure. And then from a cost perspective, this creates an affordability level usually in states. They're limiting people based on federal poverty limits. I think New York goes up to 250% of federal poverty. So those above the expansion population but still under 250% in the New York example could qualify for this benefit. It's usually not done as an open-ended, anyone can buy in type of a benefit. So there's a few variances there on what Michigan could consider. And again, a lot of discussion would need to be had, a lot of work with the good folks at DIFs and MDHHS around the Medicaid program itself if it were to be a buy-in option versus a individual market that is designed like a Medicaid benefit. All right, thank you very much. Appreciate the information. Next, I will call up Rachel Richards, Jill Murphy, and Diane Holland from the Michigan League for Public Policy. Thank you for being here. Please begin when you're ready. Good afternoon, Chair Houtal, members of the Senate Health Policy Committee. I am Rachel Richards. I'm the Fiscal Policy and Government Relations Director for the Michigan League for Public Policy. And I really want to thank you for having us here to testify on this really important issue. We echo a lot of the concerns that have been voiced by the folks at DIFs and the health plans. But I also want to provide a little bit of the more human context to this conversation. You know, in Michigan, more than 480,000, sorry, more than 480,000, 84,000 benefit from a health care tax credit in order to afford their health care on the marketplace. The lack of extension of these enhanced premium tax credits are going to have an impact on not only the quality of care that folks can purchase on the exchange, but also the number of families who will purchase coverage to the exchange. As we've heard, a 60-year-old Michigan couple that's making roughly $82,000 a year would see their annual premiums increase from just shy of $7,000 a year to more than $20,000 a year. So their health care will now take up about a quarter of their annual income. And we've also, in a single person mid-40s making $31,000 a year, their health insurance premium will go up by about $1,300 a year. So this will have a significant impact on the costs that families are expected to pay. And this is especially important at a time when we're also seeing the rates of health insurance just increase generally. So families that are losing the enhanced premium tax credits will really see a double whammy in terms of the hit that they'll receive come November 1st. I also want to say that it's important to note that though HR 1 also eliminated automatic reenrollment for marketplace enrollees, and this is a practice that 54% of marketplace users leveraged in 2025. So in addition to the impact that the EPTCs will have, we're likely to see about 700,000 Americans lose coverage by 2034 because of that provision alone. So going back to the EPTCs, the Urban Institute recently did an analysis where they determined that about over 100,000 Michigan residents would lose their subsidized coverage, and about 64,000 would ultimately end up going uninsured because they could no longer afford their health care. And then to a point that was, I think, Senator Chair was trying to make, you know, with November, or maybe it was you, Chair Hertel, but with the November 1st deadline coming up when the marketplace opens, this is when folks will really kind of start window shopping in terms of their coverage. And our big concern is that if Congress doesn't act and extend the enhanced premium tax credits, people are going to look once and they're not going to come back. And so even if Congress does something, say in December, when they say we have more time to do this, I think there will be a lot of families that ultimately get caught up in that, that, you know, like I said, we'll check once, we'll see what their rate is, we'll see what their tax credit is, and then we'll ultimately not go back and we'll just increase that number of folks who are going without insurance and then therefore will have this huge impact on our health care system in total. So I'm happy to answer questions. I'm also happy to answer questions once our guests also testify.

Hi. Hello and good afternoon. Thank you for the opportunity to speak to the committee today. My name is Jill Murphy, she, hers, and I live in Macomb County. I recently transitioned off Medicaid because I now have a job that offers a small health care stipend. I'm grateful for that.
